docs.title: NGED ML research
docs.text:
This site holds the machine-learning experiments and studies for the NGED substation forecast. The production service, its architecture, and its roadmap are documented in the nged-substation-forecast docs.

The two kinds of research page live in two sections. The Studies section holds open-ended studies, each with a page of its own. The ML experiments section holds the small, focused experiments that test one change to the research default, together with the research defaults themselves.

docs.title: ML experiments
docs.text: Each folder here is one small experiment that tests one hypothesis about improving the production forecast, and the experiments are grouped into themes. A theme has three pages: a Summary (where one has been written) that states the answer so far, an Experiments page that lists every experiment tried, and a Research plan that lists what is planned next. The folders are named <id>-<slug>, where the id is a five-digit integer that orders the experiments by the order in which they were started. A folder holds result.md and its figures.

docs.title: Themes
docs.text:
• Calibration and uncertainty: Whether the forecast's quantiles and ensemble members are well calibrated, and how to widen or sharpen them.
  • Curtailment cost: Scoring a forecast by the curtailment cost of its errors, and by how well its tails are calibrated.
  • Demand inputs: Which extra inputs lower the error of the substation demand forecast.
  • Differentiable physics: long history and drift: Whether a differentiable-physics model of Primary substation demand can use old years of history and cope with drift in the demand level.
  • Generator forecasting: Forecasting the output of solar and wind farms.
  • Gross-demand simulation: Whether a simulator of the assets behind a substation, fitted to its metered power, would be useful to NGED.
  • Hierarchy and pooling: Forecasts that share information across substations or across levels of the electricity network hierarchy.
  • Lagged power and error correction: Where recent measured power should enter the forecast, and how to correct the forecast's recent errors.
  • Production reference and best guess: How the production forecast compares with the best-guess recipes and with a perfect weather input.
  • Retraining and training history: How often to refit the XGBoost models, and how much training history to give them.
  • Solar disaggregation: Separating embedded solar from substation demand.
  • Switching detectors: Detecting load transfers between substations, called switching events, from power data alone.
  • Switching labels in the forecast: Using switching labels to forecast the demand under the normal running arrangement.
  • Weather products and blending: Which weather data improves the forecast, and whether blending several weather products helps.

docs.title: How an experiment is recorded
docs.text:
The front matter of result.md is the only place that records an experiment's theme, verdict, and status, and the theme pages build their tables from it. The Experiments table of each theme, the planned-experiments table of each Research plan, and the candidates table below are generated from the front matter when the documentation is built, so adding a finished experiment means writing its result.md and editing nothing else. The ml-experiment skill (.claude/skills/ml-experiment/SKILL.md) lists the front matter fields and their allowed values, including the optional kind and promoted_to fields of the research default rule.

uv run python scripts/mkdocs_hooks/experiment_tables.py --check validates every front matter block, and the documentation build runs the same check. uv run python scripts/mkdocs_hooks/experiment_tables.py --theme <theme> prints a theme's Experiments table as markdown.

docs.title: The research default
docs.text: The research default rule fixes one forecast per target family and one test for adding a change to it. The log of versions lists each family's versions, for example "Primary demand research default 1". An experiment with kind: change in its front matter is measured against the current version, and the rule says when a win is adopted.

docs.title: Data processing
docs.text: The data-processing page lists the processing that the experiments showed the data needs. Each entry says whether it applies to experiments, to production, or to both.

docs.title: Background
docs.text: The background pages state what earlier experiments established about the data sets and the scoring rules, and a planner reads them before planning an experiment.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: The glossary defines the terms that the experiment pages and the theme Summary pages use without redefining. Each definition links the experiment or code that fixes its meaning.

docs.title: Planned experiments and their order
docs.text:
Each theme's Research plan page holds its own priority table and the detailed proposals for that theme. A planned experiment has a result.md with status planned, committed before any code runs. An idea that has no folder yet is marked "proposed" in the priority table and carries a tentative id, P1, P2, and so on, which the proposal sections use as headings. A proposal receives its numeric id when its plan is committed, and the tentative id then disappears. The design under test is the staged probabilistic forecast, in which stage 1 turns weather into power, stage 2 calibrates the result, uses lagged power, and blends weather products, and a coupling step restores coherent ensemble members.

The sample resolves gains of roughly 0.3 points of capacity or more, and no smaller gains. A point of capacity is 1% of a series' capacity. The sample is 16 Primary substations, 9 generator series, and one validation year with 12 months. The Research plan pages flag the experiments whose planned contrasts the sample cannot resolve.

docs.title: Candidates for the next release
docs.text:
These experiments are flagged candidate and are not yet adopted. The flags are proposals for the maintainer to confirm. The maintainer decides which candidates to port into a new model release. The release log records which experiments each release adopted.

Experiment Theme Verdict Take-home message 00684 backtest-positive-demand-output-distributions-and-physical-solar-night-zero production-reference-and-best-guess partly supported A Gaussian mixture conditioned on power at or above zero fixes the negative lower quantiles at the four demand series. CRPS improves clearly at two series, is indistinguishable at one, and worsens by 0.03 points of capacity at one, so the model is a candidate to replace the post hoc clamp. A gamma mixture inside the same shared network made two series much worse and is dropped. A hard zero at night at each half-hour's own sun position removes every non-zero solar night quantile, changes no daylight score, and lowers night CRPS, while the share of night observations above q99 rises because the gate sets those quantiles to zero. 00683 walk-forward-calibration-of-the-quantile-bands-in-the-one-year-backtest-files calibration-and-uncertainty partly supported Widening the stored bands by a factor fitted only on earlier months brings the bulk supply points, grid supply points, solar, and the prevailing Primaries output to within 2 points of the nominal 90% coverage, with a CRPS rise of at most 0.047 points of capacity. Widening does not rescue the normal-running Primaries: coverage stays at 87% on average and at 80% in two winter months, which is consistent with bands that are wrong by more than their width. A learned width head or a winter correction to the median are candidates for the next experiment, and a median-level shift fitted per series made every file worse. 00681 extra-lagged-power-inputs-for-the-prevailing-forecast lagged-power-and-error-correction small gain Giving the prevailing forecast 8 to 14 extra lagged power inputs makes it follow a new load level about 20 hours sooner on 1152 simulated load shifts, and 120 hours sooner at D5 in one verified real transfer (D16 did not change), without making the normal-running (NRA) output or the event-free forecast worse. The gain is under the 24 hours set in advance as worth the extra inputs. On injected events 8 inputs give 19.1 of the 20.4 hours, but at D5 only 72 of the 120 hours, and the 8-input set scores worst inside the real events, so which set to port is open. 00667 one-year-backtest-of-the-two-output-demand-network-at-primaries production-reference-and-best-guess inconclusive The Candidate with a 14-day survival head forecasts a year of daily origins at 16 Primaries with a CRPS between 3.5 and 4.4 points of capacity, rising 28% (prevailing) or 18% (NRA) from days 0 to 1 to days 7 to 14. Both outputs are too narrow: the q05 to q95 band covers 0.81 (NRA) and 0.85 (prevailing) of half-hours, and as little as 0.72 for the NRA output in August. The prevailing output has the lower CRPS on average and in 9 of 12 months (a comparison that is not like for like, because the NRA output deliberately excludes load shifts that the metered power contains), but the November and December folds use a fallback survival curve with no trained head, and the prevailing output loses to the NRA output at two Primaries. The year overlaps the development months and the final test, so none of this is a ranking. advice: - >- Do not read the q05 to q95 columns as a 90% interval. Widen or recalibrate them before use; the width is a follow-up, not something this backtest tuned (coverage by lead band table). - >- Treat the prevailing rows of 2025-11 and 2025-12 as the fallback method: they equal the NRA rows on 74% and 65% of origins (Method). - >- Read the survival output beyond day 10 as the bank generator's duration prior, not as an estimate from observed events (Caveats). 00659 simple-shared-network-with-fixed-physics-lite-power-wind-and-solar generator-forecasting partly supported A small shared neural network that sees only the average and spread of the ensemble weather forecasts is no worse than the current, more elaborate defaults for the 3 wind farms and the 6 solar farms over the 5 development months. Its wind lead over wind default 2 is mostly the default scoring badly on idle readings set to zero, so read it as "no worse", not "better". A hand-written power curve as an extra input made no difference for wind and a small one for solar. The upper tail on very sunny days is still too low in every arm. 00640 demand-fit-age-refit-k1-k3 retraining-and-training-history refuted A demand network fitted 4 weeks before the forecast month scores about 3% worse (K1) than one fitted at the month's start. The loss reaches about 10% at 16 weeks and falls back to about 6% at 26 weeks, with wide intervals. K3 loses less in the first 4 weeks. The loss at D15 and D18 is several times larger, but this experiment cannot say whether fit age, their short training history, or level shifts in their power cause it. A refit every 4 to 8 weeks is worth running for K1, and weekly refits are not shown to be worth more. 00620 bakeoff-final-test-demand-networks-at-primaries production-reference-and-best-guess partly supported A network trained once on data before July 2026 and never refitted scored no better than the manual heuristic over the next four months, and no worse for K1 and the candidate. K1 and the candidate beat the heuristic at 12 of 16 Primaries on CRPS. They lose at four Primaries, D14, D15, D16, and D18, and the losses at these four are what the wins at the other 12 offset. All three bands are too narrow, so the neural networks are over-confident. The pooled result rests on one unlabelled load transfer between D14 and D18: on event-free rows K1 and the candidate beat the heuristic by 0.26 and 0.25 points, and without D15 and D18 by 0.24 and 0.20 points. Both are descriptive second readings, not used to rank. Refitting during the window, which weekly production retraining would do, is untested. 00613 nra-roster-contrasts-with-intervals-five-seeds lagged-power-and-error-correction partly supported The class 2 candidate matches the gate on injected load-shifts: its coverage and safe-side share are within 0.01 of K1's. It still fails the rule fixed in advance, because its event-free CRPS is not shown equivalent in 3 of 4 cells. The candidate follows less of an injected shift than K1 does (lower is better), and it covers more event-free rows only because its band is wider. Five seeds did not tighten the event-free comparisons enough to prove that O2 equals D5, so that swap rests on the point estimates and on explainability. 00612 nra-combined-networks-three-class-roster-completion lagged-power-and-error-correction partly supported With tail constants fitted on each neural network's own forecasts, the steadier offset O2 does not measurably change coverage in K1, K2, or K3. The test is too coarse to prove O2 equal to D5, and three small differences go against O2. The class 2 candidate, with a band 12 to 18% wider than its unscaled band, covers like K1 on injected load-shifts. The candidate follows and absorbs far less than K1 does. The claim that the candidate replaces the gate rests on point estimates inside the tolerance, not on intervals inside it. Removing the offset raises the follow of an injected shift by 0.036. 00608 nra-combined-networks-per-class-and-leave-one-out lagged-power-and-error-correction partly supported On injected load-shifts, the lag-and-gate network (K1) keeps the normal running arrangement inside its band on 0.927 of rows from day 4 of a shift to its end, and the gated band is the largest single part of that (0.041). In the tested arm, the steadier offset narrows the band, so the lag neural network keeps the current offset D5 in this test. The event-free band is too narrow (0.88 against 0.90), and the two-constant widening repairs it only at the eight MVA Primaries. 00606 nra-lag-encoder-signal-permutations-gap-averages-and-neighbours lagged-power-and-error-correction partly supported Giving the demand network's lag encoder a weighted history of how far each recent lag sits from the lag-free forecast, and the same history at its electrical neighbours, cut the share of an injected load-shift that the forecast follows from 0.119 to 0.035. Stretched to the hand-built gate's width, the network then covers the normal running arrangement as often as the gate does (0.932 against 0.928, within noise). Two fold months, injected events that mirror each shift at one neighbour, and a cost in event-free CRPS (up to 0.068 points of capacity at the six MW Primaries) mean this is a candidate to test further, not a replacement for the gate yet. 00601 nra-curtailment-cost-and-tail-calibration-of-assembled-candidates curtailment-cost partly supported On injected load-shifts the G4 band brings the q95 exceedance close to the nominal 0.05 in the 7 days after the end (0.048 to 0.049) and lowers the curtailment cost of both forecasts at limits 0.75 and 0.5 of the past maximum. At the headline limit of 0.9 the reduction is small and rests on one Primary. On the real December 2025 pair the band does not help D16, the Primary whose load rose, so the cost of that event is almost unchanged. 00600 nra-long-lead-scoring-of-assembled-candidates-at-24-120-and-120-240-h lagged-power-and-error-correction partly supported At 5 to 10 days ahead, the neural network A1 with the G4 band covers the normal running arrangement inside its 5th-to-95th-percentile band on 0.905 of rows during injected load-shifts, but the interval includes values below the 0.90 target, so reaching it is not shown. C1 with the G4 band covers 0.891. The G4 band adds less coverage than at 1 to 5 days ahead, so a band that is already wide when the forecast is issued, before the gate fires, is the next test. Event-free rows at 5 to 10 days ahead are also under-covered (0.855 to 0.877), which a fix aimed at load-shifts would not be expected to repair. 00597 nra-assemble-c1-and-a1-with-g4-gate-as-single-forecasts lagged-power-and-error-correction supported We built two single forecasts from stored parts, C1 with the G4 band and A1 with the G4 band, and scored them on injected load-shifts and on the two real December 2025 load-shifts. On the injected load-shifts both hold the normal running arrangement inside the q05-q95 band on at least 0.91 of rows from day 4 to the end, and A1 + G4 on 0.925, at no measurable cost on event-free rows. The median still follows about 0.11 of an injected shift, and the two real events show gaps that the injected shifts do not, so the next test worth running is a shift in the power itself. 00592 nra-snap-back-gate-faster-onset-and-snap-back-trigger lagged-power-and-error-correction partly supported A gate that watches the freshest power turns the wider forecast band on about 5 days sooner than a gate that watches day-old power. On injected load-shifts it lifts the share of rows with the normal running arrangement inside the band, from day 4 of a load-shift to its end, from 0.889 to 0.913. It turns on falsely 2.6 times per Primary-year, unless it also requires an opposite-sign gap at a neighbouring Primary, which brings that to 0.2 per year. The gain is not seen on the two real December events, so the next step is to test it on real load-shifts. 00584 nra-candidate-pack-x6 lagged-power-and-error-correction partly supported The best of the five arms puts the normal running arrangement inside its 90% band on 0.93 of rows after an injected load-shift ends, up from 0.76, and about 0.04 of that comes from a band that is wider only while the gate is on, not from width alone. On the verified December pair of real load-shifts the band still falls short of 0.90 (0.84 and 0.58), so the real-event answer is open. 00581 robust-multiweek-lag-encoder-x3 lagged-power-and-error-correction partly supported A median over five weeks of power lags does not stop the forecast following a load-shift event, probably because the day-old lag carries the event too (not tested directly). Fine-tuning on lag-only synthetic events roughly halves the following and moves the safe-side coverage of q95 and q05 from 0.77 to 0.89, at a small loss of CRPS. On the one verified 15-day transfer the coverage in the week after it ends is still only 0.45 to 0.59, so the tails stay below the 0.90 target there. 00574 part-d-primaries-only-modular-recipe-lag-encoder-offset-and-add-one-arms lagged-power-and-error-correction partly supported The best demand recipe we have fitted (P5) combines experiment 572's lag-encoder neural network and offset with a fresh mixer fitted on the whole ensemble history up to the cutoff, a 3-day embargo, and the thermal-lag and solar-gain columns. At the six MW Primaries it improves on P0, the best earlier recipe, by 0.22 points of capacity at 1 to 5 days (interval excludes zero), and at the eight MVA Primaries by a smaller 0.09 (interval includes zero). P5 beats the daily-refit references at every lead band, and follows an injected 7-day shift of the history less than half as much (2.9 against 7.3 points). The multi-variable ensemble spread columns do not help the network and should stay out. 00572 two-offset-part-1-lags-versus-the-slow-output-offset lagged-power-and-error-correction partly supported A slow output offset does not make lags unnecessary: at the eight MVA Primaries the best forecast uses both, and the lag network with the offset beat the offset alone by 0.224 points of capacity at 1 to 5 days. At the six MW Primaries the offset alone and the lag network are not distinguishable. The stop rule of the brief (the gain at both groups) is not met, so continuing on the lag network with the offset rests on the eight MVA Primaries alone. 00565 drift-embedding-variants-six-designs retraining-and-training-history partly supported A slow, per-Primary offset added to the demand forecast improves it at the eight MVA Primaries, and in the injected-shift fits we ran it leaked no more of a recent load shift than the plain network. The other four ways of carrying slow change showed no gain, so the next step is the offset alone, on more random seeds and at the six MW Primaries, where the direction holds but the interval still includes zero. 00555 issue-time-lags-at-06-12-18-utc-lag-light-demand-network lagged-power-and-error-correction supported Reissuing the demand forecast at 12, 18, 00, and 06 UTC with the lag-light network keeps its whole advantage over the lag-free network: its probabilistic error (CRPS) is about 0.28 points of capacity lower at 0 to 12 h at the eight MVA-only primary substations, the same as at 09:00 UTC. The gain comes from the day-ago and week-ago readings, which were already available; a fresher newest reading adds nothing. A network fine-tuned on issue-time rows, or a fresher weather run, may improve on this. 00553 lag-light-release-candidate-lag-dropout-with-trailing-temperature-windows lagged-power-and-error-correction partly supported One demand neural network can use the day-ago and week-ago power readings, the trailing temperature windows, and lag dropout together. With 15% dropout it forecasts as well as the network without dropout when the readings are present, and as well as the lag-free network when they are absent, and its response to an injected load shift stays under the agreed limit. It misses the 85% target by three points (82% of the gap closed), so it is a candidate for the first release and the final bake-off should compare it with the lag-free recipe on more seeds. 00551 lag-light-release-safety-lag-timestamp-audit-holidays-and-lag-removal lagged-power-and-error-correction partly supported No lag input looks ahead of the forecast origin, so the lag-light networks' gains are genuine. R-DW is 0.17 points of capacity worse than the lag-free network in Christmas week at the eight, past the 0.10 limit, and it loses 0.2 when its readings are removed. R-DROP does not have either weakness but keeps under half of the gain. The next step is to decide whether R-DW with a Christmas-week fallback or R-DROP goes into the release candidate. 00550 lag-light-network-trailing-temperature-windows-with-placebo lagged-power-and-error-correction supported The three trailing temperature windows still help the lag-light demand network on cold winter nights by about 0.10 points of capacity, the same size as without the lags, so the day-ago and week-ago lags do not already carry that information. Over all rows the windows do nothing we can show. The next step is to judge the windows on cold nights, with more winter folds. 00548 lag-free-release-candidate-assembly-with-trailing-temperature-windows lagged-power-and-error-correction partly supported A demand forecast that sees no recent power but does see the recent temperature scored slightly better than the same forecast without the temperature, although no interval excluded zero. At 5 to 10 days ahead its gap to the forecast that does see recent power was inside what the seeds can resolve. At 0 to 5 days ahead, for the eight Primary substations metered in MVA only, it stayed 0.13 to 0.34 points of capacity worse. The temperature columns did not close that gap. Of the approaches tested in experiments 539 and 541, only adding the power from a day and a week ago closed most of it, and that approach also made the forecast follow an injected load shift more closely (5.68 against 4.49 points of capacity). 00526 lagless-demand-network-trailing-weather-window-placebo-repeat demand-inputs partly supported Trailing temperature windows lowered cold-night error at the eight MVA-only Primaries by 0.093 points of capacity more than a shuffled-day placebo of the same three columns did (11 seeds, 9 of 10 folds), which is a small gain only just above what the seeds can resolve. Nothing resolved at the six signed-MW Primaries or in summer, and the check that persistence-filled windows match the default build failed, so this is a candidate and not a settled result. 00524 two-stage-lagless-forecaster-stage-1-and-ensemble-calibrator retraining-and-training-history partly supported The lag-free demand network does not need lead time or ensemble spread as inputs to its main weather-to-power network: removing both and adding a small calibrator that sees them scored the same as the current network (within noise, if anything 0.03 to 0.10 CRPS points better at the eight MVA-only substations), as long as the main network keeps being fine-tuned on recent ensemble forecasts. Freezing that network and letting only the calibrator adapt made the forecast 0.06 to 0.15 points worse, so the recent-data refit cannot be dropped. 00517 lagless-demand-network-lockdown-flag-removal demand-inputs inconclusive No arm is a clear replacement for the lockdown flag, and the experiment cannot rank the arms. Removing the flag while keeping the lockdown rows scored 0.029 points worse at the six signed-MW Primaries, and dropping the lockdown rows as well scored 0.033 points better than keeping the flag at the eight MVA-only Primaries, but leaving out one Primary at a time removes the first difference and weakens the second. Every difference is below the minimum detectable effect of 0.12 to 0.13 points. 00512 lagless-weekly-finetune-december-2024-sensitivity retraining-and-training-history partly supported A second Christmas confirms the direction of experiment 510's weekly-refit gain at the six signed-MW Primaries (0.70 points in 2024, 0.28 in 2025) but not at the eight MVA-only Primaries (0.02 and 0.31), and the 2024 result came with only 7 months of ensemble history. In the first week of the month the weekly and monthly fits are the same, so the weekly gain is zero there. Two Christmases are still two events, so this is more support, not a test. 00511 lagless-network-refit-cadence-half-life-and-mixed-pretraining retraining-and-training-history partly supported Refitting the lag-free network every day instead of every week improves its forecast by about 0.065 points of CRPS (about 1.3%), enough to pass the point-estimate, interval, q99, and cold-night bars of the porting rule but small, with the injected-shift leak 1.1 points above the weekly network's on the day after a bad block, and it leaves the network 0.07 to 0.09 points behind the lagged network K2-S1. A shorter recency window and the mixed ERA5, CAMS, and ENS pretraining do not help. A daily refit needs one fine-tune of about 3 seconds a day. 00510 lagless-demand-network-weekly-finetune-and-recency-weights retraining-and-training-history partly supported A lag-free demand network that is refitted every week forecasts clearly better than one refitted every month (0.17 to 0.19 points of CRPS, far more than the 0.02 to 0.08 we predicted), and a 90-day recency weight adds a further 0.07 to 0.08. That narrows the gap to the lagged network K2-S1 from 0.39 to 0.41 points down to 0.13 to 0.16, but does not close it, and the 90-day weight makes the forecast follow a recent load shift more closely. Dropping labelled events, or adding a latent outlier component, did not cut that leak. In the Christmas week of 2025 (both groups) and the last week of January 2026 (the six only) the weekly lag-free network scored better than K2-S1, so a weekly fine-tuned lag-free network is worth testing as a first-release candidate, with the weekly refit counted as part of its serving cost (about 5 fits per month instead of 1). 00499 two-constant-tail-widening-in-place-of-table-p-for-wind-and-solar calibration-and-uncertainty inconclusive Two numbers per farm tune the wind and solar tails about as well as table P's 16 factors per farm did on the stored forecasts: pooled coverage differs by under 0.005 and tail pinball loss by under 1% (intervals reach 2%). The stored year is too short to certify that formally, so table P stays for now. For solar, table P leaves 1.98% of actuals above q99 against the 1.5% limit; one pair for all six solar sites meets that limit (1.50%) but misses table P's q05 coverage by 0.0145. 00496 simplify-demand-network-input-and-output-pruning production-reference-and-best-guess partly supported The demand neural network can drop its 7 ensemble-spread inputs (46 inputs down to 39) with no loss on the scored whole sample: the CRPS change was +0.012 points at the 8 MVA-only Primaries and -0.043 at the 6 signed-MW Primaries, both inside the limit, although it scored 0.187 points worse at the six on cold winter nights (3 folds, almost all from December) and 0.408 worse at the six on rows with a labelled event. The other three simplifications were not shown equivalent: merging the holiday columns (at both groups), dropping the weekly lag (at the eight), and using one Gaussian instead of three (at the eight). 00494 simplify-demand-network-refit-cadence-and-pretrain-once retraining-and-training-history partly supported In five scored months, the demand neural network pretrained once and fine-tuned each month scored within 0.03 points of the same network pretrained at every refit, and would drop about 42 of the 80 GPU seconds that refitting one network takes. A network refitted 3 months earlier scored about 0.07 points worse at the eight MVA-only Primaries than a freshly refitted one, with an interval across months too wide to say how much worse. Whether to refit less often than monthly is therefore open until a larger test. 00493 solar-annual-against-quarterly-refits metered-solar-farms supported The solar neural network can be refitted once a year instead of every quarter: for both networks we tested, the quantile score changes by less than 0.6%, inside the 1% limit, with little margin for the encoder and from one refit date and one scored year. One further comparison fails: at Solar E the one-pass network with annual refits is 1.3% worse than the 51-member encoder with quarterly refits, and most of that gap comes from the network design and not from the schedule. 00492 two-constant-tail-widening-in-place-of-table-p-for-demand calibration-and-uncertainty partly supported At the eight MVA-only Primaries, one lower constant and one upper constant per metering group, fitted on earlier months, recalibrate the demand forecast as well as table P (20 factors per metering group) does, so table P can be dropped there. At the six signed-MW Primaries, the constants leave q95 coverage 0.011 to 0.013 below table P's, so table P stays. Wind and solar were not tested. 00483 uncertainty-rerun-on-the-first-release-demand-candidates calibration-and-uncertainty partly supported The first-release demand candidates are too wide on the lower tail and too narrow on the upper tail, so a widening of both tails makes the lower tail worse while it repairs the upper one. Widening only the upper tail, or applying one factor per tail, fixes the eight MVA-only Primaries for A-pool and A-gam-in alike. At the signed-MW six, one factor per tail narrowly misses its pass rules, and cold winter nights stay under-covered there. 00481 seed-averaging-diminishing-returns-for-demand-and-wind production-reference-and-best-guess partly supported A second seed gives the largest gain and later seeds add little: for Primary demand, two seeds score 0.035 points better than one (the 99.55% interval is +0.025 to +0.053, across the 0.03 bar for porting), and each later step gains at most 0.011. For wind, one seed scores within the minimum detectable effect of ten, though a second seed gains 0.041 points. Averaging seeds of the lagged neural network S1 is weaker than adding the lagless head: at two networks, S1 with the lagless head scores 3.441 against 3.628 for two averaged S1 seeds. Each added seed costs another fit per monthly refit. 00480 xgboost-cams-columns-at-mva-only-primaries-lab-conditions demand-inputs supported Giving the XGBoost demand model the satellite-measured sunshine of each half-hour lowered its error at all 16 primary substations in the point estimates, by 0.36 points of capacity over the eight that report apparent power and by 0.48 over the six that report real power. A live service cannot have this input for the first day ahead, because the satellite data arrives about a day late, so the gain is an upper bound. The next step is to measure how much of the gain remains when the columns come from the ensemble weather forecast. 00472 anchor-plus-correction-with-a-strong-penalty-and-a-seed-averaged-anchor lagged-power-and-error-correction partly supported A stronger penalty does not make the lag correction safe. A penalty of 100 shrinks the correction to almost nothing and keeps only 18% of its gain, so the penalties tried (1e-3 to 1 never bound, and 100 binds) do not both limit the correction and keep the gain. Averaging the lagless forecast over three seeds and correcting that average with the recent readings scored better in this experiment. The five other Primaries tested show no clear gain, so the cap should be treated as specific to D5 for now. 00211 dp-boosted-tree-calibrator-and-input-ablations differentiable-physics-forecast-engine supported A gradient-boosted tree model given the same inputs as the neural network, and no recent errors, lowers the error score of our best day-ahead forecast by about as much as the network does (0.098 against 0.100 points). The interval is wide, so a loss of up to 0.03 points against the network is not ruled out. The gain comes mostly from two inputs, the forecast level and the weather-data era. 00205 dp-gamk-gap-robustness-coast-or-frozen-gam differentiable-physics-forecast-engine inconclusive When readings stop for 3, 6, 24, or 72 hours, keep running the Kalman filter, which corrects the convex demand model using its recent forecast errors, without feeding it new readings, and widen the quantile bands. At each of those four gap lengths that forecast scored 0.25 to 0.44 points of quantile score better than the convex demand model with no correction (a quantile score is an error measure in percent of the substation's effective capacity, and lower is better; the gain is 8% to 14% of the uncorrected model's score). At 72 hours the 99.4% bootstrap interval for the gain runs from 0.04 to 0.48 points, so the gain may be small. The data cannot show whether dropping only the filter beats coasting after a gap of about 72 hours: at every gap length the difference between the two forecasts is smaller than the variation between months. The forecast with the filter, winter night offset, and recipe R was still 0.025 points worse than its no-gap score 48 hours after a 24-hour gap ended. The filter alone was within 0.02 points of its no-gap score 24 hours after the gap ended. 00202 dp-ens-two-number-rolling-replay differentiable-physics-forecast-engine supported A weather layer that stores two numbers per half-hour (the mean and spread of the 51 ensemble members' solar-generation estimates) and refits its two scaling factors every month, using only runs that had finished before the month began, lowers the daylight quantile score (the score for the forecast's uncertainty bands) by 2.3% at five substations over one year, which is as much as running all 51 members. This confirms experiment 193's result under production-style timing, so the next step is to build the two columns into the weather layer. 00195 switching-neural-plus-detector-features lsc-detectors partly supported A learned score on the features that RO-NC and the pair alarm already compute finds 22 to 24 of the 35 real transfers over 1 day, against 18 or 19 for RO-NC, at the same number of unexplained alarms. A plain logistic regression finds 22 even without any look-ahead feature, so most of the gain is in the features, and the extra transfers are small ones (under 1 MW each). The next step is to test whether the extra alarms help the gated mask, which this experiment did not run. 00193 dp-ens-two-number-solar-summary differentiable-physics-forecast-engine supported Summarising the 51 ensemble weather members' solar estimates by their mean and standard deviation lowers the daylight quantile score by about 2% (98% of the gain from running all 51 members, 93% in the replicate months), at the five substations scored over one year. The weather layer could store two columns per half-hour instead of 51, and the 10th and 90th percentiles add nothing measurable. A follow-up experiment could test the two numbers in the live weather layer. 00187 dp-ens-members-in-stack differentiable-physics-forecast-engine supported Running each of the 51 ensemble weather members through the solar part of the demand model still improves the daylight forecast bands by about 2% on top of the full best-guess stack, and night is untouched. About two thirds of the gain needs that day's own members, and two numbers per half-hour (the mean and spread of the members' solar responses) carry nearly all of it, so a cheaper two-number version is the next thing to test. 00180 dp-sunny-daylight-fix-d5-solar-shape differentiable-physics-embedded-generation supported D5's net power flattens like an export limit: capping the solar output the forecast subtracts from demand at 60% of the capacity held for D5 cuts the best GAM's sunny-daylight loss to BG2 from 0.20 MW to 0.07 MW, and moves the two placebo substations, D10 and D16, by under 0.01 MW on sunny half-hours. A different panel tilt or azimuth does nothing measurable. D5 is the only one of the six substations whose site table marks an export clip, so the next question is whether the 60% ceiling is stable from year to year. 00167 dp-full-history-gam-24-months-or-all-years-with-drift differentiable-physics-long-history-and-drift supported Adding a drift term (a slow adjustment to the demand level) improved the forecast at 11 of 12 quarterly refits. The quantile score, where lower is better, fell by 0.40 points when training on the last 24 months and by 0.55 points when training on all years back to late 2019. Training on all years instead of 24 months adds only 0.10 points on top of a drift term, and gives no gain without one, so extra years of history help little. 00160 calibration-band-width-fix-on-stage-2-winner calibration-and-uncertainty supported The 90% prediction interval (from the 5% to the 95% quantile) of experiment 155's best forecast was equally wide on lead days 2 to 5, because its stored spread table has only four lead bands. Interpolating the table between the band centres removes the equal days and raises the quantile score by 0.002 points, below the pre-registered ceiling of 0.01, but it narrows the interval at 24 to 72 hours and widens it from 72 hours on, so one substation loses 0.009. It does not fix the cold-night upper tail: the forecast exceeds the 95% quantile on about 15% of cold-night rows, against 5% for a calibrated forecast. 00158 dp-partly-pooled-gam-shapes-heating-and-calendar-curves differentiable-physics-pooling-across-substations partly supported In this test on six Primary substations, fitting the demand model's shared curves (heating, lighting, daily profile, holidays) across all six let a substation with only 3 months of history score 3.01 points instead of 3.64 (lower is better), within 0.17 points of the same substation with 24 months of its own history. The gain was largest in winter and on Christmas rows. For a substation with 24 months of history, pooling changed the score by less than 0.02 points, which is too small to justify making each forecast depend on five other substations' data. The test cannot say whether pooling the heating curve alone would help a 3-month substation. 00155 dp-bg-stage2-assembly-night-offset-and-error-correction differentiable-physics-forecast-engine inconclusive Adding recipe R, which subtracts 0.75 times the mean error of the last 14 days by half-hour, lowers the stage 1 assembly's score by about 0.04 points (1.3%), and the winter night offset adds nothing once R is in. The assembly with R scores 2.754 against BG2's 2.780, which is better by 0.026 points with an interval too wide to rank the two. The pre-registered placebo control failed, so the formal verdict is inconclusive, but the choice of winning arm (R alone) does not depend on it. 00148 switching-end-rule-lookahead-ro-nc lsc-detectors supported On injected transfers, a live service needs only 6 hours of data after the candidate end to fix the end of a switching interval, with no loss of recall against the offline rule. The call then comes a median 30 hours after the true end, and 24 of those hours are the step statistic's own window, so a longer lookahead of 24 or 48 hours only delays the call to 48 or 72 hours without finding more. The 35 real transfers give the same 18 found at every lookahead from 1 hour up. A lookahead of 0 hours is wrong in six transfers in ten, because the end is called about 8 hours early. 00147 causal-live-end-rule-for-ro-nc lsc-detectors supported The end of a switching interval can be called from data available at the time, with no loss of recall against the offline rule, by waiting until the step statistic falls to 0.8 of its running peak. The call comes a median 29 hours after the true end. Ending the interval at the first sign of a return step is wrong in about six transfers in ten, because it fires about 8 hours early. Merging overlapping alarms on one Primary substation cuts the share of transfers reported as 2 or more intervals from 0.57 to 0.03. 00145 differentiable-physics-analog-day-error-correction-on-gam-k differentiable-physics-forecast-engine small gain Averaging the errors of the 20 most similar past days (same day type, within 13 weeks of the same date, last year's days included) beat recipe R (the 0.75-weighted mean error of the last 14 days) by 0.041 points at day D+1, the calendar day after the forecast origin (about 1.7% of R's score of 2.436). That gain is larger than the 0.011 points that the weekday term of experiment 134 gained. Matching on forecast temperature helped by only 0.005 points, and copying the error of the same holiday last year made holidays worse, so the next step is a day-type profile with a season window and no correction copied from an earlier holiday. 00121 differentiable-physics-mh-multi-hinge-heating-curve-and-night-step differentiable-physics-demand-calendar-and-weather inconclusive Adding night-time levels indexed on the UTC clock lowers the day-ahead error on winter nights by about 0.23 points after the recent-error filter, at all 5 substations in both winters, and the forecast then shows the 01:00 jump in demand that the current forecast misses on cold winter nights. Five heating bends instead of one gain only 0.016 points, within noise. The synthetic tests could not show that a step this small can be detected, so the night result needs a test on weather forecasts and an audit before it enters the model. 00111 differentiable-physics-6-ens-forecast-engine-against-bg2 differentiable-physics-forecast-engine partly supported Driven by real ensemble weather forecasts, the physics-based demand model with a filter on its recent errors (GAM-K) scored 2.80 points against 2.78 for the production recipe (BG2) at five Primary substations. The 0.02 difference cannot be told from zero (-0.109 to +0.157), and the comparison is not like for like. GAM-K scored 0.13 points better than lagless XGBoost with the same filter (-0.305 to +0.014, 4 of 5 substations better), so the verdict is partly supported. The filter's gain is the firmly supported part: 0.15 points, 0.39 in the first day, with the sign held in the replicate months. Giving lagged XGBoost the physics model's forecast as a starting point changed nothing measurable. The known-answer gate passed 22 of 22 readings on its second run, after a sign error in the gate's own test data (both runs are kept). The departures were that the XGBoost compute estimate was 20 times too low, so the margin arms refitted monthly; lagless XGBoost for the scored year reused SIMP1's refits and had no spread factor; and the confirmation comparison was not run. GAM-K is a candidate for Flexpectation v2's roughly 1,300 substations on the measured filter gain, with four caveats: five substations over one year, a short XGBoost history, the undecided XGBoost comparison, and a margin that gave no gain. 00102 simp1-simplifying-the-bg2-best-guess-before-production production-reference-and-best-guess partly supported Removing the three recent-power inputs from the best-guess XGBoost forecast makes it worse at Primary substations (by 0.36 points of capacity once one substation's commissioning months are cut, and most of that comes from one substation whose demand level fell in March 2026) and at supply points (by 0.28). The wind farm forecasts lost nothing measurable and the solar farm forecasts little. The blend of 5 models can shrink to 3, and the solar offset lowers the score by 0.18 points at midday in summer at the 5 substations that use it. 00094 explicit-heating-offset-primary-demand demand-inputs small gain The heating term lowered the quantile score by 0.143 points of capacity in cold hours at leads up to 48 hours (98.75% interval -0.203 to -0.034), under the 0.3 threshold, and by 0.022 over all rows (-0.042 to +0.000). 00087 bg2-best-guess-assembled-with-drop-one-ablations production-reference-and-best-guess partly supported BG2 beat the previous best forecast at the 16 Primary substations by 0.283 points (98.75% interval -0.425 to -0.146) and at the 4 bulk and grid supply points by 0.634 (-1.111 to -0.279). 00082 sw2-18-19-combined-refit-offset-and-same-sign-count lsc-detectors supported Using the refit offset and the same-sign neighbour count together found 0.770 of the moved power on injected transfers, against 0.656 for the benchmark detector. The gain of 0.114 is about the sum of the gains of 0.056 and 0.050 from each change alone. On the 35 labelled real transfers of more than 1 day the combined detector found 12 and the benchmark 8, which is a weak signal on a small sample, and transfers lasting 15.6 to 60 days gain nothing. 00081 r11-control-member-second-validation-year-demand retraining-and-training-history supported C1, weekly minus the stack: -0.240 points (99.17% interval -0.360 to -0.145). 00078 pvdis-5-current-capacity-vintages solar-disaggregation small gain Re-estimating the solar capacity before each forecast run lowered the error of experiment 64's best forecast by only 0.018 points of capacity (98.75% interval -0.036 to -0.004), under the 0.05 threshold, and by 0.033 (-0.086 to +0.012, an interval that includes zero) at leads under 48 hours. 00071 sw2-18-refit-offset-and-gap-bridging lsc-detectors supported The detector ignored every alarm within 24 hours of the monthly refit of its forecasting model, which lowered recall by about 5% of the moved power. Lifting that rule recovers the loss, and the second residual model added to replace the ignored alarms adds nothing on injected transfers. 00070 sw2-19-same-sign-neighbour-count lsc-detectors supported Counting the neighbours that step the same way as the alarming substation found 0.048 more of the moved power on injected transfers than the single-series detector, at the same number of unexplained alarms. The 35 labelled real transfers are too few to confirm the gain (7 found, against 8 for the benchmark), and the gain does not extend to transfers lasting 15.6 to 60 days. 00064 pvdis-5-net-demand-as-demand-minus-forecast-solar solar-disaggregation supported Giving the XGBoost model the forecast solar output as a starting offset, with a weight fitted on the training window, beat the best guess d0 by 0.152 points of capacity (98.75% interval -0.199 to -0.111; leads under 48 hours -0.272, -0.420 to -0.145), and each of the four arms beat its own placebo twin. 00049 vp1-screening-reference-under-p-roll-demand retraining-and-training-history supported B1, the blend minus its best member: -0.076 points (99.17% interval -0.135 to -0.023). 00048 weekly-retraining-confirmation-and-extension-demand-generators retraining-and-training-history supported C1, weekly retraining minus the stack: -0.20 points (99.44% interval -0.40 to -0.035). 00035 lead-weighted-quantile-blend-of-stored-models calibration-and-uncertainty supported Averaging the quantiles of three stored demand models lowered the Primary demand error by 0.10 points of capacity against the best single model (98.33% interval -0.19 to -0.03), so the estimate clears the 0.05 threshold for moving it into production. For solar and wind the gains were too small to resolve on 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms. 00034 retraining-cadence-and-cheap-proxies-demand retraining-and-training-history inconclusive C1, monthly retraining minus the stack: -0.20 points (99.375% interval -0.44 to +0.08, 95% interval -0.38 to -0.01). 00033 best-guess-architecture-vs-production production-reference-and-best-guess supported The best guess lowered the quantile score below production's by 4.89 points of capacity for Primary demand (98.33% interval -5.66 to -4.06), 3.81 for solar (-5.07 to -2.64), and 6.27 for wind (-7.65 to -5.28), each wholly below its threshold. 00030 lagged-power-feature-sets-primary-demand demand-inputs inconclusive C3, all 13 lags minus N1 (seed 0 only): -0.01 points of capacity on the quantile score (99.375% interval -0.45 to +0.43). 00024 pooling-groupings-demand-xgboost hierarchy-and-pooling supported Pooling the 16 Primary substations into 3 or 4 XGBoost models (with the series identifier) scored 0.15 points of capacity worse than 20 per-series models (99.44% interval +0.03 to +0.26), inside the 0.30 margin; one model for all 20 series was 0.29 worse, and dropping the identifier cost 0.8 to 1.0. 00020 solar-wind-stack-cams-stage0-spread-margin calibration-and-uncertainty partly supported For wind, a starting guess from the turbine power curve lowered the error by 0.055 points of capacity (99.58% interval -0.110 to -0.007), and adding a spread factor made the total 0.071 (-0.133 to -0.014); the spread factor's extra -0.016 (-0.036 to +0.004) is not detectable. For solar, no change helped detectably, and the full stack was 0.035 points higher with an interval that includes zero (-0.075 to +0.116). 00019 primary-demand-stack-vs-manual-heuristic production-reference-and-best-guess supported C1, the full stack minus manual_heuristic, quantile score over all leads: -0.56 points of capacity (99.44% interval -0.93 to -0.26). 00017 training-window-and-retraining-rule-drift-demand retraining-and-training-history supported C9, the 14-day correction against A: -1.52 points (99.44% interval -1.95 to -1.13). 00016 pooled-mixture-calibration-solar-wind calibration-and-uncertainty partly supported For solar, one spread factor brought the 5% to 95% band from covering 94.3% to 95.3% of cases down to 89.5% to 91.8%, with no detectable change in accuracy. For wind, no planned correction fixed the first two days, and a spread factor on two lead groups, added after seeing the results, brought every lead band to 90.7% to 92.5% coverage and has not been tested on another year. 00014 cams-trained-stage1-with-stage0-ens-correction-demand weather-products-and-blending inconclusive C2, stage 0 minus raw ENS for the CAMS-trained arm, Primary quantile score over all leads: -0.067 points of capacity (97.5% interval -0.094 to -0.039), better than the planned -0.03. 00006 stage1a-demand-input-feature-sweep demand-inputs partly supported P1, hour and weekday against the weather block alone, Primary substations: -0.55 (99.4% interval -0.71 to -0.41) on the selection year and -0.46 (-0.61 to -0.30) on the confirmation year, the largest single input but about a third of the predicted size. 00002 stage2-calibrator-and-mixture-vs-ens-quantile calibration-and-uncertainty partly supported Pooling the ERA5-trained solar and wind quantiles over the 51 weather-forecast members beat a model trained on archived weather forecasts: wind by 0.62 points of capacity (95% interval -0.99 to -0.26) and solar by 0.24 (-0.36 to -0.06), with the gain in the first six days. A second calibration model on top did not improve on the pooling and made solar worse by 0.40 points (+0.26 to +0.61). The result rests on 6 solar farms, 3 wind farms, and one validation year. 00001 era5-trained-stage1a-vs-ens-trained weather-products-and-blending supported P1 (revised), s1_memberavg minus ens_trained, all leads: wind -1.70 (-2.33 to -1.08), solar -0.57 (-0.83 to -0.32); material up to day 6, not beyond.

docs.title: What the experiments taught us so far
docs.text:
• Retrain the Primary demand model weekly, and do not add a 14-day error correction. Weekly retraining without the correction scored 0.20 points of capacity below the best-guess stack, whose frozen model has the correction (99.44% interval -0.40 to -0.035), and a 7-day correction on the weekly model raised the score by 0.16 (-0.06 to +0.36), unresolved (00048). Experiment 34 found the 14-day correction stops helping once the model is retrained, and hurts at weekly and daily cadence. The 14-day correction (00019, 00021) was measured on a frozen model, and the retraining results supersede it for Primary demand.
  • The 14-day correction on a frozen model is a historical result. It lowered the quantile score of N1, a model frozen at its training end, by 0.99 points (00019). At 4 bulk and grid supply point series it did not lower the score (00021), and at the supply points in experiment 87 adding it raised the score by 0.305 points.
  • A weather product as accurate as ERA5 would lower the Primary demand score by 1.9%. ERA5 weather in place of ENS weather lowered the quantile score by 0.10 points, nearly all from shortwave radiation and none up to 2 days ahead (00022).
  • Check for calendar memorisation. When the same valid time repeats across many ENS runs, a model with calendar columns can memorise it. Give each experiment a climatology row, and group folds by valid time.
  • Choose a row set that covers every weekday. The 53 Tuesday runs of 00001 and 00002 put every case of the first day on a Tuesday or Wednesday, which does not suit demand.
  • Training on ERA5 weather helps solar and wind, but a longer history does not add to it, and for demand a long history hurt. The solar and wind gain appeared even when the ERA5-trained model saw only the ENS-era months, so the gain comes from the weather it was trained on and not from the years. For demand, training from 2019 was worse than training from 2023, probably because the customer mix and embedded generation drifted.
  • Put recent power in the stage 2 calibrator, and calibrate before judging it. For Primary substations, the calibrator with recent-origin inputs beat a stage 1b correction, and a lag-free calibrator is worth about 1 point of capacity at short leads (00005).
  • The term and return-to-work columns showed no detectable gain on top of the Christmas column for Primary demand. Over the three validation years, the return and term columns moved the Primary error by +0.06 points from 2 to 20 January (99.2% interval -0.17 to +0.30), +0.20 at Easter (-0.19 to +0.59), and -0.29 over the half terms (-0.68 to +0.07), and Both was not 0.2 points better than a calendar shifted by 17 days (00011). The arm with the full history and the COVID indicator scored 0.26 points higher on the whole year than the base arm.
  • A change that helps the point forecast of solar or wind need not help the pooled mixture's CRPS. CAMS-trained solar lowered the member-average error by 0.14 points (00012) and the mixture's CRPS by 0.009 (00020), and a stage 0 mapping widened the member spread by a quarter. A power-curve base margin lowered the wind CRPS by 0.055 (00020).
  • Attach the forecast solar term to the XGBoost model as a base margin, with a weight fitted on the training window and zero beyond 10 days. The base-margin arm lowered the Primary demand quantile score by 0.152 points (98.75% interval -0.199 to -0.111) against the best guess d0 and 0.256 against d1l, where the fixed-coefficient shift of 00046 lowered d1l by 0.056, and subtracting the forecast solar from a model trained on gross demand was not shown to match the best guess (00064).
  • Do not expect a zero start to help the production XGBoost models. Experiment 78 found that a zero base margin lowered its reference model d0 by 0.071 points, but on the production recipe the zero start changed the Primary score by -0.017 (-0.072 to +0.054) and the solar score by -0.010 (-0.036 to +0.028), and worsened wind models without a power-curve margin by 0.049 (00080).
  • Refresh the capacity table that feeds the base margin once per season-year. A table refreshed that often captured almost all of the gain from a current capacity (00078).

docs.title: Data processing to apply in future experiments and production
docs.text: The experiments so far show that the power readings, the switching log, and the embedded-solar capacity estimates all need processing before an XGBoost model trains or scores on them. This page lists each step as an instruction. Every entry says where the step applies (experiments, production, or both), links the experiments that are the evidence, and states the scope the evidence covers. An entry whose evidence is a first look at the data gives its confidence in words. A plan for an experiment begins by reading this page.

docs.title: Terms used on this page
docs.text:
• D code: an anonymised series label, such as D4, used in the experiment write-ups (see experiment 51). The page also names a few substations (Stickney, Kirton, Wrangle T1, Wrangle T2, and Mount Bridge Boston) as the experiment write-ups name them. A D code and a substation name are different labels, and the page does not say which D code matches which name.
  • Primary: a Primary substation, which steps 33 kV down to 11 kV. Sixteen of the 32 trial series are Primaries.
  • Point of capacity: 1% of a series' capacity. Scores in points of capacity are smaller when the forecast is better.
  • Season-year: a 12-month period running from September to August.
  • Best guess: the project's current forecasting recipe, assembled in experiment 33.
  • Skill: the percentage by which the best guess's quantile score is lower than the score of the rule-based forecast manual_heuristic.
  • Dark row: a half-hour in which the irradiance from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) is below 1 W/m².
  • Closure: a period in NGED's switching log in which an operator closed a switch that is normally open.
  • Transfer: a switching operation that moves part of one Primary's demand onto neighbouring substations for hours or days. The Primary that loses the load is the donor substation, and the receiving load is the usual load of the substations that gain it.
  • Labeller: a language model that reads the power readings and judges whether a transfer is visible, as in experiment 41.
  • Residual panel: the stored table of residuals, each the measured power minus the power an XGBoost model predicted.
  • Error correction: the 14-day correction that adds the forecast's recent errors to the next forecast.
  • Abnormal running arrangement (ARA) and normal running arrangement (NRA): an ARA is a period in which an operator has closed a normally open switch, so that one Primary carries load that belongs to a neighbour. The NRA is the usual layout.
  • Tail coverage at q95: the share of observed values that fall below the forecast's 95th percentile, which is 0.95 for a forecast with correct tails.
  • Curtailment cost: the avoidable cost, in pounds, of a forecast's errors when a node is held to a limit (experiment 84).

docs.title: Series and units
docs.text:
Count 32 time series in version 1 of the trial area. They are 16 Primary substations, 6 solar farms, 3 wind farms, 2 grid supply points, 2 bulk supply points, and 3 other generators or storage units, as the home page lists. Applies to experiments and production.

Read each series' unit from the units column of the metadata table, and treat the Primaries metered in MVA as a different kind of series. A series is metered in MW (signed active power) or in MVA (apparent power, which is never negative). Eight of the 16 trial Primaries are metered only in MVA. Applies to experiments and production. Evidence: experiment 79 found no reverse flow at 7 of the 8 MVA-only Primaries from April to September, and experiment 56 could not tell the best guess's skill at the 8 MVA-only Primaries from its skill at the 8 MW Primaries (inconclusive). Experiment 110 fitted a power factor to only 2 of the 8 MVA-only Primaries (and recovered one of them, D12), because the other 6 have almost no reverse flow in their training rows. It held the power factor at 0.97 at those 6, and modelling the meter as apparent power scored 0.13 points of capacity better than reading it as real power. Experiment 204 summed the apparent-power children of two bulk supply points into the bulk supply point's reading: reading the magnitude as signed power or converting it with a fitted sign scored within 0.03 points at one bulk supply point and 0.02 to 0.03 points better with the sign at the other, where Stickney (D12) has reverse flow. Provisional.

Read power through the cleaned table, and read the raw table only when the question is about availability. The cleaned table holds only unflagged rows (nged_data.storage.scan_cleaned_power). Applies to experiments and production. Evidence: the data-cleaning roadmap page and experiment 6, which scores on cleaned power.

Count a series' history from its first unflagged row, which is later than its first row of any kind (high confidence). D9 starts in 2023-04 and its first unflagged row is in 2023-08. Only five Primaries hold long histories: D5, D10, and D11 start in 2019-09, D14 in 2019-10, and D16 in 2020-12. The late starters begin between 2023 and 2025. Applies to experiments. Evidence: experiment 103.

Drop a candidate that recurs in many injected worlds before scoring a detector on injected truth (experiments; medium confidence). The injected worlds are built on the real record, which holds transfers that no log lists, so a decoded candidate with the same Primaries and day in 10 or more of the 40 worlds of experiment 680 is a real-record event, not a false one. In experiment 692, 5 such events made up 111 of 460 false candidates. The evidence covers 15 Primaries from 2024-01-01 to 2026-06-30.

Do not treat a missing half-hour at a solar or wind farm as a fault (medium confidence, provisional). None of the 6 solar and 3 wind series has a half-hour that reads exactly 0 after 2026-03-26, although each read 0 in 47% to 68% (solar) and 0.3% to 4.8% (wind) of half-hours a month in the six full months before. The cause is not determined. Applies to experiments, and to production if the cause lies in the source. Evidence: experiment 605, which covers 2025-09 to 2026-10. Until the cause is known, do not compare a score over the rows present before and after late March 2026: score the generators on the rows present, and also on a version that fills solar night half-hours with 0.

Do not clip a solar farm's forecast or reading at 100% of capacity (medium confidence, provisional). In the stored solar forecasts of experiment 430, 11.3% of the daylight rows (those whose stored median is above zero) have a stored q95 above 100% of capacity, and 2.3% of the readings exceed 100%. Clipping the quantiles at 100 raised the q95 exceedance from 6.1% to 7.4% across the 6 solar farms. Applies to experiments and to any client that rebuilds scenarios. Evidence: experiment 628, 44 forecast runs of 2025-09 to 2026-06, from e00628_clip_check.py. Clip solar at 0 only.

Extend each cached input to the end of the window before scoring on it (high confidence for the dates). A cached input is a file built from the stored tables, which a candidate trains and scores on. The cached inputs stop at different dates, for example the ensemble summaries at the run of 2026-06-30, the ERA5 stage-1 tables at 2026-07-31, the ERA5 site tables at 2026-09-10, the CAMS site tables at 2026-09-11, and the observed-power cache at 2026-10-14, while the production power and ensemble tables reach 2026-11-06. Applies to experiments. Evidence: experiment 605.

docs.title: Trim the start of each series
docs.text:
Cut the first months of most demand series (high confidence for D4, D14, D9, D16, and D18, medium to low for the rest). The first 1 to 19 months of a series often sit far from the same months in later years. A new meter can read near zero for days to weeks and then step up, and a new site can commission in stages. Cut until the level, the daily shape, and the share of rows present match the same months in later years. Cut more when the match is uncertain, and let a later look move a cut later and never earlier. Applies to experiments, and to production for a series that has just started reporting. The cuts found so far cover 16 of the 20 series examined (experiment 103, figure 4):

Series Cut Confidence Reason D4 19.4 months High Level 1.5 to 2 times too high, a stuck plateau, then too low, until a step on 2021-04-12 D14 8.3 months High Level about half of later years until a step of 2.2 MW on 2020-06-15 D17 5.6 months Medium Reads about 0, then 4 months of ramp and erratic swings D5 4.5 months Medium Night level 15% to 30% low until a step on 2020-01-09 D3 3.5 months High Night level 30% to 50% low and 15% to 60% of half-hours missing D18 2.6 months High Zeros, then a level near 0 to 1.5 MW with negative rows, then erratic D1, D10, D21 2.5 months Medium D1 unusually smooth then volatile; D10 and D21 have 30% to 70% of half-hours missing D22 1.5 months Low Gaps in most days and a night step D9, D16 1.3 months High Near zero, then a staged switch-on D13, D19 0.9 months Low Level steps in the first weeks D15 0.8 months Medium Erratic for 2 weeks while the meter was commissioned D12 7.4 months Low Night level 1.5 to 2 times later years; the start-of-series review recommends no cut, and the 15-point rule cuts it

Figure 1 shows the dropped months sitting far from the kept months at D4, D14, D9, D16, and D18. The figure draws 7 Primaries, and the cut dates come from the start-of-series review that experiment 103 confirmed. The grey dropped months are read from the raw power table, because the cleaned table removes flagged rows and the early months are often flagged. The blue kept months are read from the cleaned table. At D10 and D5 the dropped months look less different from the kept months, which fits their medium confidence.

An uncut start hurts a model without recent power far more than a model with it (high confidence for D18). In experiment 102, D18's training rows began with a late start at zero output. A weekly-refitted XGBoost model without the three recent-power inputs forecast 20% of capacity in December 2025 against an actual of 75%, and its score at D18 was 5.7 points of capacity worse than the same model with the inputs. With the start cut (training from a later date), the difference at D18 fell to -0.03 points. The cost of removing the inputs across the 16 Primaries fell from 0.710 to 0.361 points. Applies to experiments, and to any comparison of a model with and without recent power. A comparison that cuts the start for one arm must cut it for every arm.

Train D15 and D18 only on rows from 2025-03-01 on (medium confidence, provisional). On the monthly XGBoost demand model, this cut lowered the days 1 to 10 CRPS by 1.3% at D15 and 1.2% at D18 against training on every row, and was lower in all 4 scored months at D15 and 3 of 6 at D18 (experiment 399, 2026-01 to 2026-06). A longer cut is not safe: dropping 6 months raised D18's CRPS by 7.2%. Removing readings within 0.009 MW of zero does not help, because at D15 most of them are real crossings of zero. Applies to experiments and to production. A cut does not fix D15's level error (median forecast 16 to 21 points of capacity too low).

docs.title: Decide which rows are demand
docs.text:
Use a Primary metered in MVA for demand only on dark rows (high confidence). An MVA reading cannot show reverse flow, so the solar output behind the Primary reads as demand in daylight. A filter that keeps rows with irradiance below 100 W/m² still keeps rows with solar output, because the filter admits irradiance above 1 W/m². After the start cuts, the dark rows leave 2.4 to 3.3 site-years per MVA Primary with the 2020 lockdown kept, 2.3 to 2.7 with the fixed lockdown window removed, and 0.9 to 1.0 in 2023-07 to 2025-06. Applies to experiments. Evidence: experiment 103.

Figure 2 shows that the daylight half-hours at an MVA-only Primary carry a solar dip that the dark half-hours lack. The grey daylight half-hours sit in the middle of each day, where embedded solar output reduces the net flow and the apparent power cannot show its sign. The blue dark half-hours form the smooth evening and night curve that holds demand alone. The figure draws one Primary (D2) for two weeks of July 2025.

Do not let a loss on the absolute value of a latent power set the sign of the latent power (medium confidence, provisional). A folded loss cannot tell a latent power from its negative, so the sign follows the start of the fit. At six signed-MW Primaries with no injected solar, a folded XGBoost model still reported negative power at sunny midday on 41% to 97% of half-hours. Applies to experiments. Evidence: experiment 387. The readings at D12, the Primary with known reverse flow, do not reach zero: the 0.1% quantile of its training readings is 4.3 points of effective capacity.

Do not treat grid supply points or bulk supply points as clean demand (high confidence). The grid supply points are dominated by generation: D1 is below 5 points of capacity on 75% of nights. The bulk supply points sum the trial Primaries: D17 reverses flow on 51% of May to August days at midday. Applies to experiments. Evidence: experiment 103.

Screen for embedded generation with the share of negative dark half-hours (high confidence). Series with 26% to 82% of their dark half-hours negative carry embedded generation or an exporting grid connection. The screen cannot work on an MVA Primary. Applies to experiments. Evidence: experiment 103, figure 9.

Count the half-hours that substation_zero flags before scoring a detector on a transfer. (Provisional.) The rule flags a reading of exactly 0 at a Primary substation, and a transformer that was switched out read exactly 0 in the 5 transfers we checked. At the series P12 and P13, the two transformers of one Primary substation, the rule flagged 426 half-hours inside 5 of the 6 labelled real transfers lasting more than 1 day, and the panel of residuals used to score detectors held no readings there. The cleaned power table keeps flagged rows with their original readings, and restoring those half-hours let the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC) find 4 of the 6 transfers. This applies to experiments on switching. For production, the maintainer has to decide whether the rule should keep a zero reading when the other transformer of the same Primary substation carries the load of the switched-out transformer. Evidence: experiment 132. Confidence: medium, from 5 transfers at one Primary substation.

Treat an isolated zero reading between readings of 43 to 59% of effective capacity as missing (provisional; low confidence). The cached power readings hold 6 half-hours of exactly 0.0 MW at two Primary substations, D9 (5 half-hours) and D16 (1 half-hour). The zeros look like telemetry dropping out. A scorer that keeps them adds about 42 points of capacity to the error of each affected forecast row. Experiment 87 stored these actuals as missing, and experiment 379 scored them. The signed-MW six's CRPS then moved by about 0.002 points. Applies to experiments. For production, the maintainer has to decide whether the rule applies. Evidence: experiment 379. Confidence: low, from 6 half-hours at two Primary substations.

docs.title: Unlabelled jumps
docs.text:
Before reading flow on two substations with no interconnection (a placebo pair) as a fault of a method, check whether either substation has unlabelled jumps (low confidence). In experiment 131's replicate year (2024-25), the edge-flow fit with a drift term put 4.27 MW-days a year on D16 and D10. Of those, 1.58 lie inside the two D10 windows described under "Expect D10 to carry unlabelled jumps" below. Applies to experiments. Evidence: experiment 131.

Do not train a learned load-shift score with every real candidate as a negative and then score it on the months it trained on (medium confidence). Real load shifts that start in the training months are then taught as negatives: the score trained that way found 0 of the 15 logged load shifts that start in training months, against 7 for the same score with logged and labelled spans removed from its negatives. In the 20 load shifts that start in other months both found 13 (post hoc, experiment 302). Applies to experiments; provisional.

At D8 only, no gain was found from removing the gas engine's output from the training target and adding a calendar average of the engine back at forecast time (low confidence, provisional). In experiment 695, the CRPS (continuous ranked probability score, smaller is better) of the cleaned arm minus the raw arm's was +0.117 points of capacity, with a 98.3% interval from -0.070 to +0.412 that includes zero. A post hoc interval that averages the seeds first is +0.036 to +0.245. That reading is over all rows, and is suggestive because it bootstraps only 8 months. The pair is not worth porting for D8. A point of capacity is one percentage point of D8's effective capacity of 10.379 MVA. Applies to experiments on D8's forecast. Evidence: experiment 695, D8 only, 8 monthly refits from 2025-11 to 2026-06.

docs.title: Fixed windows
docs.text:
Use the fixed lockdown window, 2020-03-23 to 2021-07-19, and do not detect the window from the data. Experiment 6 defines its indicator with these dates, and the indicator lowered the error by 0.26 points of capacity on the selection fold. A window found from the data picks up drift and solar growth as well (experiment 103, figure 12; medium confidence): a drift-removed fit finds April 2020 more than 5 points low only at D11 (-26 points) and D10 (-7 points), and August 2020 to September 2021 sits 5 to 17 points above the fit at D5, D10, D11, and D14. Applies to experiments and production.

A dataset of dated events that ends before 2021-07-20 cannot be compared with the demand-model fit's training rows, because the lockdown window removes every earlier row from training. The feed-in tariff register, a list of small solar installations, ends on 2021-03-24, so none of its dates falls in a month on which the fit trains (experiment 215). Applies to experiments.

Check how many days of training rows a demand-model fit kept after the lockdown window is removed, and flag a fit with fewer than 180 days (provisional; medium confidence). Leaving the lockdown window out of training left Christmas 2020-21 fits with 51 to 143 days of rows. Every substation's Christmas 2021-22 fit had the same 104 summer days and no winter, and D9's 2023-24 fit had 31 days. The fits with under 180 days scored 1.38 to 1.91 times their ordinary-weekday error pooled over substations at Christmas, and D9 alone scored 5.6 times, where fits with at least 180 days scored 0.97 to 1.22 times (experiment 173; the 180-day threshold was chosen after the scores were read, and thresholds of 90 and 270 days gave the same picture for 2022-23 onwards). The Kalman filter and recipe R in that experiment do not repair a fit that saw little or no winter. Applies to experiments and production.

Give the series that changed regime an individual start date or a flag (medium confidence). D8 weekday daytime demand falls from about 9 MW to about 3 MW between 2023-10 and 2025. D12 switches between a high-night and a low-night regime. D18 steps up about 1.1 MW at night around 2026-07-03 (a date after the experiment's window, not rechecked there), and D5 shows a flat midday floor since 2022. Month-mean steps of over three monthly standard deviations occur at D6 (a drop of 218 MW in 2023-07) and D11 (2020-04). Applies to experiments. Evidence: experiment 103 for the step list and D8.

Treat D8's reading as including one gas engine's output until 2023-08-15, and as excluding it afterwards (provisional, medium confidence). The engine connected on 2023-06-13 and its own readings carry output from 2023-07-03. While those readings arrived, D8's residual rose by 0.02 MW per MW of engine output, where a reading without the output would fall by 1 MW per MW.

D8's share of half-hours with a residual below -2.5 MW then stepped from 0.010 to 0.257 in the week of 2023-08-14 and stayed between 0.10 and 0.46 in every month to January 2026. The share fell from 0.292 in January 2026 to 0.070 in March and 0.008 in April, with no matching change in the engine's own readings, so whether the engine is visible in D8 from 2026 is unknown. Applies to experiments; whether it applies to production awaits NGED's answer. Evidence: experiment 194.

Give a forecast the engine state it will have at forecast time, and train the engine term on that same lagged state (provisional, medium confidence). Applies to: experiments. D8's engine detector gives a state for each half-hour that is built from that half-hour's own reading. A coefficient fitted on that contemporaneous state is 3.6 MW per half-hour with one or more units running, but the state of the last settled day is worth 0.15 MW (interval -0.06 to 0.32) out of sample, so applying the contemporaneous coefficient to the lagged state makes the quantile score 10% worse. Trained on the lagged state, the coefficient is 0.9 to 1.0 MW and the score is 3% better than a model without the term (experiment 294).

Treat D8's reading as apparent power that folds, and do not read its steps as signed (provisional, medium confidence). Applies to: experiments. Where demand is below about 3 MVA, an engine start appears as a rise in the reading, and where demand is above about 8 MVA it appears as a fall. A tracker that assumes every start is a fall misses the low-demand starts. On real D8 data, a filter that models the fold predicts held-out months better than the same filter without it in 9 of 9 months, by 51.6 log-likelihood units in total, and the two filters flag nearly the same share of half-hours (0.268 and 0.267). The fold has no demonstrated benefit in known-answer scores (experiment 694; D8, 2023-09 to 2025-02).

Do not fit calendar and seasonal terms exactly (by variable projection, which solves the linear coefficients exactly at each step) to a window of three months or shorter. An exact least-squares fit of a per-substation model with holiday, tent, harmonic, and profile terms to 4 weeks or 3 months of data extrapolates those terms badly: the per-site fits scored 70.6 and 48.4 points at the five decision substations, against 15.1 and 5.5 for the gradient fits that stop before convergence. No window between 3 months and 2 years was tested. The pooled model with its interaction network failed the same way on four days of the scored year, where an exact fit with weak penalties forecast up to 280 points too high (experiment 112; medium confidence; provisional). Applies to experiments.

Treat a heating threshold above a substation's highest temperature, and any per-site threshold of a pooled model, as unidentified. Above the highest temperature the heating hinge is always on, and the deviation absorbs a shift, so only the prior sets the threshold; at real noise (standard deviation 5 points) a synthetic fleet with a 14 degree threshold was recovered to 2.7 to 5.7 degrees with the interaction network off or on (experiment 112; medium confidence; provisional). Applies to experiments.
