Production code for the same job. The production repository's documented extension point for a new model is a BaseForecaster subclass with its own FeatureEngineer. Whether the neural networks use it is not decided.

  • Exists. Series of type BSP and GSP exist in TimeSeriesMetadata.substation_type, and the same generic XGBoost forecaster could be run on them. No forecaster is specific to them.
  • Differs. The research neural network reads 3.5-hour power lags, 51-member ENS summaries, and thermal-lag columns, is pooled per group, and outputs 11 quantiles. The production lag rule nulls any lag that is not older than the lead time and has no 6-hour power-delay constant. The production BaseForecaster.train and predict take AllFeatures rows keyed by ensemble_member, and the research network reads one row of 51-member summaries per half-hour, pooled over two series, after pre-training on ERA5 and CAMS rows. The flag file of experiment 398 is a snapshot of the production cleaning, so a port reads the live cleaned table instead.
  • Missing. The same pieces as for the Primaries, apart from the neighbour list and the prevailing head, and the group-pooled fitting.
  • Untrained origins and stale runs. The neural network was trained and scored only at the 09:00 native origin of the same day's 00Z run, relabelled to 12:00. The production live_forecasts asset runs at 00:00, 06:00, 12:00, and 18:00 UTC. The ecmwf_ens schedule starts at 10:30 UTC and retries every 30 minutes up to 8 times, so the run can arrive as late as about 14:30 UTC. live_forecasts uses the freshest run present, so a late day forecasts from the previous day's run. With that run every lead is 24 hours longer, which exceeds the 351 hours seen in training, and every lag is older. The page gives no degradation rule for these cases. Rule 1 of the production repository's inherent-stability page requires the service to degrade, widen the bands, and record the degradation on the row. The training masks both lags on 30% of days, so an absent lag is a state the neural network has seen.

docs.title: Port notes
docs.text:
• Reproduce exactly. The 3.5-hour lag cap, the one-neural-network-per-group pooling, the offset of design 5 of experiment 565, the thermal-lag columns of experiment 437, and the schedule of experiment 574.
  • Unvalidated. Experiment 669 reports no curtailment cost against the manual heuristic for the BSPs and GSPs. Load shifts are not modelled, and NGED's event labels are incomplete.
  • Open questions. Whether the 3.5-hour cap or a longer one gives the better score with the same refit schedule, which experiment 669 did not test on matched schedules. The D1 median is on average 18 MW below the observed median, and its monthly mean error swings between -39.8 MW and +25 MW. Which forecast slots (00:00, 06:00, 12:00, and 18:00 UTC) this neural network must serve, and what it does with a stale run, is not decided.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The three wind farms are forecast by the simple shared neural network S of experiment 659, a two-layer network with a Gaussian mixture output. The backtest is experiment 666. The only inputs are ensemble weather and the lead.

  • Inputs, 16 in all. The mean and standard deviation over the 51 members of 10 m wind speed, 100 m wind speed, the sine and cosine of the 100 m wind direction, and 2 m air temperature (10 columns). The lead as three columns: the sine and cosine of the lead in hours modulo 24, and the lead in hundreds of hours. A one-hot wind-farm column for each of the 3 farms, in the order of the farms' anonymous labels. One wind farm is a MW series and two are MVA series. There is no power lag, no calendar column, and no physics-lite input. The per-case summaries do hold the mean and standard deviation of a physics-lite power curve (pl_mean, pl_sd), but the fit does not read them.
  • Lead definition. The wind lead is the time from the run's 09:00 UTC availability stamp to the valid time, so the first forecast half-hour (12:00 UTC) has a lead of 3 hours and the last has a lead of 338.5 hours. The solar network measures its lead from the 00Z run instead (see the solar section).
  • Standardisation. Each input column is standardised with the mean and standard deviation of the fit rows, and the standard deviation has a floor of 1e-6.
  • Layers and output. Two hidden layers of 64 units with GELU activations, feeding 9 outputs: the log weights (a log-softmax), the means, and the standard deviations of 3 Gaussian components. These describe the residual of power as a fraction of capacity from the mixture's centre, which is the mean of the training target. The last layer starts with zero weights, a bias of 0 for the weights, of -0.1, 0, and 0.1 for the means, and of log 0.08 for the log standard deviations. Each standard deviation is exp(clamp(raw, -6, 1)). The 11 quantiles are read from the mixture by 40 bisection steps on the mixture's cumulative distribution function, over a residual range of -2 to +2 (in fractions of capacity) around the centre. They are clamped to the range 0 to 1 of the neural network's own capacity scale, and then sorted within each row.
  • Weather. The 00Z ENS run of the origin day, treated as available at 09:00 UTC, with leads of 12 to 347.5 hours from the 00Z run. Where ensemble steps are 3 or 6 hours, the half-hourly value is interpolated as in experiment 310 and experiment 430. No ERA5 or CAMS pre-training, and no ERA5 or CAMS input at inference time.
  • Cases kept. Every case must hold all 51 members, numbered 0 to 50. The feature script raises an error when a case does not, and when a run from 2025-11-01 lacks any of its 672 half-hours.

docs.title: Input tables
docs.text:
The wind fit reads tables that earlier scripts build, and it does not build them. The page appendix follows import statements only, so it lists the modules a fit imports and misses these scripts, which write data and are never imported. All the data paths below sit under the data folder (DATA_PATH_INTERNAL). The source data of every table is the production repository's own stores: the ECMWF ENS Nwp Delta table (NWP, from 2024-04-01), the cleaned power Delta table (NGED/cleaned_power_time_series.delta), the metadata table (NGED/metadata.parquet), and the effective_capacity Delta table.

  • Member rows are built by the production feature engineer. Each member-row script calls the production TabularFeatureEngineer().engineer in bulk mode on one run's Nwp rows at the farms' H3 resolution-5 cells (h3_res_5 of the metadata table) and on the cleaned power.   • Files from experiment 615 and experiment 666 overlap. Experiment 615 cut its runs at valid times before 2026-07-01, which truncated the runs from 2026-06-16. The 666 script rebuilds those runs to a full 15 days, and member_paths in e00666_wind_features.py takes the rebuilt file wherever both exist.
  • Run order. The scripts below run from the repository root, with DATA_PATH_INTERNAL set. The second, third, and fourth read e00259_common, e00615_common, and e00303_common and need the experiment folders on PYTHONPATH, as the docstrings of the scripts say.

    2. e00259_hindcast.py.
    3. e00615_wind_members.py.
    4. e00659_wind_features.py.

The wind-speed detector in e00210_analysis.py writes the mask from that table. We found no script in either repository that builds the handover file, so it is an open question (below). The mask ends on 2026-09-13 at 17:30 UTC.
  • Where "need only that folder" is wrong. The appendix says wind and solar copy their code into the 666 folder and need only that folder. That holds for the import statements of the fit scripts. It does not hold for the inputs: the wind fit reads tables written by scripts in the experiment 210, 259, 615, and 659 folders.

docs.title: Training regime
docs.text:
• Refits. Wind refits on day 0 of each month (12 refits), on ensemble runs and valid times before the 62 days that precede the refit, and uses those last 62 days for early stopping (experiment 666). Experiment 659 refitted twice a month. One pooled network is fitted over the 3 farms for each refit and seed. A fit row needs a run stamp and a valid time that are both before the 62-day boundary, and a stopping row needs a run stamp from the boundary on and a valid time before the refit. The script asserts that no training row has a valid time at or after the refit, and the farm's capacity uses power from before the refit only. The last 62 days therefore never enter a gradient.
  • Optimiser. AdamW, learning rate 0.002, batch 2,048, weight decay 0.0001, and 40 epochs. Every epoch runs, with no patience rule, and the epoch with the lowest negative log-likelihood on the last 62 days is kept. Training leads run to 351 hours from the 09:00 stamp.
  • Seeds. Three seeds (0, 1, and 2), averaged quantile by quantile and then sorted.
  • Idle readings. Readings flagged by the idle mask of experiment 210 are set to zero in training and scoring until the mask ends. The mask is a research rule and not part of the production cleaning code, and from its end date idle readings count as observed, in scoring and in the training target of the last refit. That makes the last weeks of the backtest year a different scoring target.
  • Capacity. The 99.9th percentile of the farm's cleaned power over the 730 days before each refit, which is 1.02 to 1.12 times the production effective capacity. The neural network trains with this scale and the scores divide by the production effective capacity.
  • Target and output scale. The target is the observed power divided by the farm's production effective capacity (the last value in the effective_capacity table), with idle-mask rows set to zero, and then divided by the ratio of the new capacity to that effective capacity. The fit writes each quantile as the fitted fraction times the new capacity, in MW (or MVA for the two MVA farms).
  • Hardware and run time. About 20 minutes of GPU time in 3 parallel processes for the 36 wind fits and 12 solar fits together (experiment 666).

docs.title: Post-processing
docs.text: The wind file has no post-processing and no calibrated copy. Its stored coverage (0.913) already exceeds 0.90, and a scale did not improve it (experiment 683).

docs.title: Scores
docs.text:
The neural network beats climatology to day 10 and is 1.8% worse than climatology at days 10 to 14. The CRPS gain over climatology at days 10 to 14 is -1.8% (95% interval -3.3 to -0.4). The table gives CRPS in points of capacity from experiment 668, over 709,776 scored half-hours.

Lead band CRPS Climatology CRPS Days 0 to 1 4.58 9.72 Days 1 to 3 5.47 9.73 Days 3 to 7 7.68 9.67 Days 7 to 10 9.36 9.69 Days 10 to 14 9.86 9.68
  • Scale of the CRPS on the experiment 666 page. Experiment 666 reports CRPS values half as large as these (for example 2.29 at days 0 to 1), because it defines CRPS as the mean pinball loss and experiment 668 as twice that. Compare numbers only within one page's convention, and use the experiment 668 convention, which experiment 667, experiment 669, and experiment 683 share.
  • Coverage. 0.913 over all rows (experiment 668). Wide bands at long leads may explain why the coverage stays near 0.90 (experiment 666).
  • Matched check. On rows that experiment 659 also covers, the backtest scores 4.174 where experiment 659 scores 4.179, with both using the capacity of experiment 659. Both figures use the convention of the experiment 666 page.

docs.text:
Last change is the merged nged-ml-research pull request that last touched the file on origin/main, with its commit. Production code for the same job. The production repository's documented extension point for a new model is a BaseForecaster subclass with its own FeatureEngineer. Whether the neural networks use it is not decided.

  • Exists. NWP wind components at 10 m and 100 m, derived wind speed and direction (_derive_wind_features in tabular_feature_engineer.py, packages/weather_utils/src/weather_utils/wind.py), and time_series_type with a wind value. The research member-row scripts call the production TabularFeatureEngineer in bulk mode, so the production code already yields the per-member wind inputs.
  • Differs. Production has no wind-specific model. The research network S reads the mean and standard deviation over the 51 members and a one-hot farm column, and outputs a mixture's 11 quantiles. Production trains on the control member.
  • Differs in the interface. BaseForecaster.train and BaseForecaster.predict take AllFeatures, one row per time series, origin, valid time, and ensemble member, and predict returns a PowerForecast with an ensemble_member index and no column for a quantile level. The research network S needs one row per case that holds the 10 summaries over the 51 members, and one pooled fit over 3 farms for each refit. Its output is 11 quantiles at fixed levels.
  • Differs in the origin. The research network trains and forecasts only from the 00Z run relabelled to a 12:00 UTC origin. Production starts ingesting the 00Z run at 10:30 UTC, retries every 30 minutes up to 8 times, and forecasts at 00:00, 06:00, 12:00, and 18:00 UTC. On a day when the 00Z run arrives after 12:00 UTC, the 12:00 slot would use the previous day's run, 24 hours older. The wind lead feature would then exceed the 351 hours of training, and the last day of a 14-day forecast would lie beyond the 15 days of that run. The service must degrade in that case (the production rule is to widen the bands and record the degradation on the row), and no degradation rule for the neural networks is decided.
  • Missing. Network S, the mixture head, ENS summary features, a capacity scale of the 99.9th percentile of the last 730 days, the idle mask (a research rule, not production cleaning), monthly refits, and quantile output.

docs.title: Port notes
docs.text:
• Reproduce exactly. The 64-by-64 layers with GELU, the zero-weight initial last layer and its biases, the 3-component mixture centred on the training mean, the standard-deviation clamp of exp(clamp(raw, -6, 1)), the input list, the lead measured from the 09:00 stamp, the 730-day 99.9th-percentile capacity, and the monthly refit with a 62-day early-stopping window.
  • Unvalidated. Wind has no power lag, so the neural network cannot react to a recent change of level. The idle mask is not production code. The behaviour on a stale or missing ensemble run, or on a case with fewer than 51 members, is untested: the research scripts raise an error there.
  • Gotchas.
    • The quantiles are clamped at the network's own capacity, which is 1.02 to 1.12 times the production effective capacity. The README of the backtest folder lists runs of up to 9 identical non-zero q50 values at Wind A for that reason.
    • Two capacities are in play: the 730-day 99.9th percentile that the network trains on and the production effective capacity that the scores divide by.
    • The last 62 days before each refit serve for early stopping only.
  • Open questions.
    • Whether to drop or damp the forecast beyond day 10, where the neural network scores worse than climatology.
    • Which script builds data/handover/era5_wind_at_nged_wind_farms_anonymised.parquet, which the idle mask needs. We found none.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The six solar farms are forecast by the simple shared neural network PLP of experiment 659, which adds a fixed physics-lite power to the ensemble weather. The backtest is experiment 666.

  • Inputs, 18 in all. The mean and standard deviation over the 51 members of shortwave radiation, air temperature, and 10 m wind speed. The ensemble means of relative humidity, longwave radiation, precipitation, and surface pressure. The mean and standard deviation of the physics-lite power and of the Faiman cell temperature. The sun's elevation and the sine and cosine of its azimuth. The lead. There is no farm column and no calendar column. One pooled network is fitted over the 6 farms for each refit and seed.
  • Lead definition. The solar lead is the time from the 00Z run to the half-hour's valid time, so it runs from 12 to 347.5 hours. The wind network measures its lead from the 09:00 stamp instead.
  • Physics-lite power. The physics-lite power is clip((G / 1000) * (1 - 0.004 * (T_cell - 25)), 0, 1), where G is shortwave radiation in W per square metre and T_cell is the Faiman cell temperature T_air + G / (25 + 6.84 * wind speed). The formula runs on each of the 51 members separately, and the neural network reads the mean and standard deviation. The mixture is centred on the mean physics-lite power. It has no fitted parameters.
  • Layers and output. As for wind: two hidden layers of 64 units with GELU activations and a 3-component Gaussian mixture over power as a fraction of capacity, with the same last-layer initialisation, the same standard-deviation clamp, the same 40-step bisection over a residual range of -2 to +2 around the centre, and quantiles clamped to the range 0 to 1 of the neural network's capacity scale and then sorted. The input standard deviation has a floor of 1e-6.
  • Night gate inside the neural network. The neural network forecasts only the half-hours where the mean cosine of the solar zenith angle over the ensemble step is above zero, and sets the quantiles of the other half-hours to 0.

docs.title: Input tables
docs.text:
The solar fit reads one table per farm that e00666_solar_inputs.py builds from the production stores, and it needs no earlier experiment's table, ERA5, or CAMS. The table is data/ml-experiments/00666-*/solar_inputs/<site>.parquet, with one file for each of the 6 farms. It holds every half-hour of every 00Z run from 2024-04-01 to 2026-10-31, in the 14 day bands described below, with daylight, the 18 inputs, and actual. The 18 inputs and actual are null where the half-hour is not a daylight half-hour or a stamp is missing, and actual is also null where power is unobserved. The script reads the ECMWF ENS Nwp Delta table (NWP), the cleaned power Delta table, the effective_capacity table, and the metadata table, all under DATA_PATH_INTERNAL.

  • Run order. e00666_solar_inputs.py, then e00666_solar_fit.py, then e00666_export.py (which writes wind.parquet and solar.parquet together). e00666_solar_gate.py is an optional check that compares the inputs with experiments 430 and 659. It imports modules from experiments 310, 430, 461, and 659 and is not part of the pipeline.
  • The farm's weather comes from the nearest H3 cell by its centre. nearest_cell picks the store's H3 cell whose centre is nearest the farm. The wind member rows instead use the cell that holds the farm (h3_res_5).
  • Complete stamps only. The script keeps a stamp only when all 51 members are present, and it raises an error when a run from 2025-11-01 to 2026-10-31 lacks a complete stamp up to a lead of 348 hours.
  • Stamps and day bands. The ensemble stamps are 3-hourly up to a lead of 144 hours and 6-hourly after. Day d (1 to 14) holds the half-hours whose lead from the 00Z run is in [12 + 24(d - 1), 36 + 24(d - 1)) hours, so each half-hour of a run appears once and a run's 14 days cover 672 half-hours.
  • Shortwave is a period mean spread by the zenith. The ensemble value is a mean over the period that ends at the stamp. The script spreads it over the period's half-hours in proportion to the cosine of the solar zenith at the half-hour's midpoint, so that the period mean is unchanged.
  • Temperature and wind speed are interpolated. Each is interpolated linearly between the previous stamp and the period's stamp, to the half-hour's midpoint, and falls back to the stamp when the previous stamp is missing. Relative humidity, longwave radiation, precipitation, and surface pressure are the ensemble means at the period's stamp, without interpolation.
  • Relative humidity is derived, not stored. The production Nwp table has no relative-humidity column. The script computes it from the ensemble-mean 2 m temperature and 2 m dew point with the Magnus formula (constants 17.625 and 243.04): 100 times the ratio of the saturation vapour pressure at the dew point to the one at the air temperature, clipped to 0 to 100.
  • Sun position. pvlib gives the apparent zenith and the azimuth at the half-hour's midpoint. The elevation input is 90 degrees minus the apparent zenith. A half-hour is a daylight half-hour when the mean cosine of the zenith over its 3-hour or 6-hour period is positive.
  • Constants. Temperature coefficient -0.004, U0 25, U1 6.84, all in e00666_common.py.
  • Imports versus inputs. The solar inputs come from the production stores through one script in the 666 folder, so the appendix statement that wind and solar need only that folder is right for solar's code and its data sources. It is wrong for wind (see the wind section).

docs.title: Training regime
docs.text:
• Refits. The solar neural network is refitted quarterly, on the first day of the first month of the backtest year and of each third month after it (2025-11-01, 2026-02-01, 2026-05-01, and 2026-08-01). Each fit scores the next three months, uses three seeds (0, 1, and 2), and has no pre-training. Training uses valid times before one day earlier, with the last 61 days for early stopping, 20 epochs, daylight rows only, and leads below 348 hours from the 00Z run, as experiment 666 states (experiment 430 and experiment 659 stopped at 251.5 hours, so the lead range is extended). Solar trains on all daylight half-hours, including more low-sun half-hours than experiment 659 kept. The script asserts that no training row has a valid time at or after the refit.
  • Optimiser and seeds. As for wind (AdamW, learning rate 0.002, batch 2,048, weight decay 0.0001), keeping the epoch with the lowest negative log-likelihood on the last 61 days, with no patience rule. The target is the observed power over the farm's production effective capacity, divided by the ratio of the new capacity to that effective capacity. The network sees raw power, because solar has no idle mask.
  • Capacity. As for wind: the 99.9th percentile of cleaned power over the 730 days before each refit. The fit writes each quantile as the fitted fraction times the new capacity, in MW.
  • Hardware and run time. See the wind section.

docs.title: Post-processing
docs.text:
The solar file carries a hard zero at night, set at each half-hour's own sun position, and a calibrated copy adds a band scale.

  • Night clamp. Every quantile is zero on half-hours where the sun is not above the horizon at the middle of the half-hour. The clamp changes 271,808 of 1,471,680 rows (18.5%), the largest change is 6.1% of capacity, and the daylight rows are bit-identical to the unclamped file. It is needed because the gate inside the neural network uses the mean cosine over the 3-hour or 6-hour ensemble step, so a step that contains a sunrise or sunset leaves small non-zero quantiles at night.
  • The same rule as a gate. Experiment 684 applied the rule as a gate on the stored neural networks of experiment 666 and found no non-zero night quantile left and no change to any daylight or dawn-and-dusk score, with a lower night CRPS. The share of night observations above q99 rises, because the gate sets those quantiles to zero. Dawn and dusk (sun elevation under 5 degrees) stay badly calibrated: the q05-to-q95 coverage is 0.69 and 0.75 at the two farms tested, and 0.30 and 0.24 of observations fall below q01. The gate was tested at two farms over three months of origins.
  • Walk-forward band scale (calibrated copy only). See "Walk-forward band calibration" below, applied to daylight rows from 2025-12 with night quantiles kept at zero.

docs.title: Scores
docs.text:
The neural network beats climatology at every lead band, and the gain shrinks from 37.1% at days 0 to 1 to 7.6% at days 10 to 14. The table gives CRPS in points of capacity on daylight half-hours (685,472 scored) from experiment 668.

Lead band CRPS Climatology CRPS Days 0 to 1 4.83 7.68 Days 1 to 3 5.33 7.69 Days 3 to 7 6.35 7.71 Days 7 to 10 6.89 7.73 Days 10 to 14 7.18 7.76
  • Coverage. 0.893 on daylight half-hours. About 11% of observations exceed q99 on the sunniest days of experiment 659, so the upper band fails on very sunny days.
  • Scale and row set. Experiment 666 reports CRPS values about half as large, for the reason given in the wind section, on a daylight flag defined by the mean cosine over the ensemble step. Its solar numbers are therefore not comparable with the table above.
  • Seasonal bias. The solar median is high in spring and low in autumn, and the neural network has no calendar input. One year with quarterly refits cannot separate a seasonal effect from refit age (experiment 666).
  • At days 10 to 14, the neural network scores worse than climatology from November to March and better from April to September (experiment 666).

docs.title: Port notes
docs.text:
• Reproduce exactly. The physics-lite formula with the Faiman cell temperature, the 18 inputs, the mixture centred on the mean physics-lite power, the GELU layers and the last-layer initialisation, the daylight-only training rows, the lead measured from the 00Z run, and the post hoc night rule at each half-hour's own zenith.
  • Unvalidated. The night gate was tested at two farms and one refit. Dawn and dusk coverage is poor. Arm b of experiment 684, which would feed the physics-lite power at each half-hour's own zenith to the neural network, was not run. The behaviour on a missing stamp or a stale run is untested: the research script raises an error on a gap in the archive.
  • Gotchas.
    • The quantiles are clamped at the network's own capacity, which differs from the production effective capacity that the scores divide by.
    • The last 61 days before each refit serve for early stopping only.
    • The solar daylight flag of the networks uses the mean cosine over the ensemble step, and the night clamp uses the half-hour's own zenith. The two differ at sunrise and sunset.
  • Open question. Whether a calendar input or monthly refits remove the seasonal bias in the median.

docs.title: Walk-forward band calibration
docs.text:
The backtest files hold one calibration, a scale on the width of the quantile bands fitted only on earlier months, which brings the four calibrated outputs close to 0.90 coverage. Experiment 683 tested it on the origin months 2025-12 to 2026-06, and the README of the backtest folder describes the four calibrated copies. The scale is post-processing on stored quantiles and is not part of any neural network above.

  • Method. Each quantile's distance from q50 is multiplied by one factor per series, output, origin month, and lead band (days 0 to 1, 1 to 3, 3 to 7, and 7 to 14). The factor is the 90th percentile of the ratio of the actual power's distance from q50 to the stored half-width of the band on that side (q95 - q50 above, q50 - q05 below), which makes the scaled band cover 90% of the fitting rows. The fitting rows are the half-hours whose valid time lies in the 90 days that end 6 hours before the month starts, because power is available only up to 6 hours before an origin. The factor is bounded to 0.5 to 3. In the code, a cell with fewer than 20 fitting days keeps a scale of 1, and rows whose stored half-width is under 0.05 of capacity are left out of the fit. There is no level shift, so q50 is unchanged. After scaling, the quantiles of MVA series, wind, and solar are clipped at zero.
  • Where it applies. The prevailing Primaries rows, the BSPs, the GSPs, and solar. It does not apply to wind, whose coverage already exceeds 0.90, and it does not apply to the NRA Primaries rows. Two arms of experiment 683 tried the NRA rows. Arm 2, the walk-forward scale, brought their coverage to only 87.1% and raised their CRPS by 0.081 points. Arm 1, the fixed factor 1.0934 about the median that experiment 613 fixed, lowered their CRPS by 0.027 points (interval -0.031 to -0.023) and raised their coverage to 86.0% to 87.6%. The backtest files apply neither arm to the NRA rows. The first month, 2025-11, has no earlier forecast to fit on and is left as stored.
  • Effect on coverage. On 2025-12 to 2026-06, the q05-to-q95 coverage and CRPS change are as in the table, each coverage a range over the four lead bands (experiment 683).
Output Stored coverage Calibrated coverage CRPS change Prevailing Primaries 84.0% to 87.9% 88.0% to 88.4% +0.047 BSPs 87.5% to 89.3% 89.8% to 90.9% +0.005 GSPs 86.4% to 90.3% 89.1% to 89.8% +0.003 Solar 87.8% to 89.5% 89.4% to 91.0% -0.002
  • Adding a level shift made the files tested worse. A per-series level shift fitted on earlier months raised the NRA Primaries CRPS by 0.306 points and the GSPs' by 0.842, and experiment 683 reports that every file got worse. The median bias changes from month to month.
  • A scale fitted through an unexplained stretch overshoots afterwards. A scale fitted through the July and August 2026 load transfers overshoots after they end: D18 (identifier 13) reaches 97.5% coverage in 2026-09 under the scale. The calibrated copies hold D18 and D14 (identifiers 13 and 16) at their 2026-06 factor from 2026-07, a rule chosen after seeing the final-test months, so it is post hoc. D18 stays at 63% to 77% coverage in 2026-07, 2026-08, and 2026-10 even so.
  • The winter NRA shortfall is mostly error in the median. Experiment 688 dropped the half-hours inside labelled and verified load transfers and shifted each band by its month's observed median error, and the coverage of the NRA Primaries rose from 80.1% to 90.1% in 2025-12 and from 80.3% to 88.6% in 2026-01. The shift used the month's own errors, so it is a diagnostic and not a method. The 80.1% and 80.3% baselines are the NRA bands after the walk-forward scale (arm 2 of experiment 683). The stored files give 81.7% and 77.7%. Experiment 688 supersedes the suggestion of experiment 683 to try a learned width head, because the stop rule that would have justified it did not fire.
  • A width scale fitted on a fixed lookback does not remove the steps in band width at a refit. Experiment 689 took the 151 series-and-lead-band cells (of 384, 16 series by 6 refit boundaries by 4 lead bands) whose stored band width changes by more than 10% across a refit boundary from 2026-01 to 2026-06. Under the 90-day scale of experiment 683, 15.2% of those cells end with a before-to-after width ratio of 0.90 to 1.10, against a predicted 90%. A 45-day lookback gives 9.9% and a 180-day lookback gives 7.3%. The 90-day scale moves the ratio farther from 1 in 67% of the cells. Fitting the scale on each seed's quantiles and averaging gives nearly the same ratios: they lie within 0.05 of the seed-mean scale's in 89.4% of cells, just under the pre-registered 90%, so the steps are not an artefact of averaging the quantiles of two seeds.
  • Caveats of experiment 689. The 151 cells share 6 refit boundaries, so they are not 151 independent trials. The mechanism is untested: the scale for a month is fitted on forecasts of the neural network that the refit replaces, and the experiment fitted no scale on any forecast of the new network. The September step of D18 (identifier 13) lies after the last scored origin month and was not tested. Only the NRA output has per-seed files, so the prevailing output was not tested.
  • Calibrated copies on disk. primaries_calibrated.parquet (prevailing rows), bsps_calibrated.parquet, gsps_calibrated.parquet, and solar_calibrated.parquet. The NRA rows of the first are copied unchanged. The prevailing rows of primaries_calibrated.parquet were built from the version of primaries.parquet from before the extra lagged inputs, so they do not yet carry them. The README of the backtest folder lists their SHA-256 prefixes.
  • Open questions. Whether to refit the scale at every refit of a forecasting neural network (not decided, because the diagnostic was not run). The band width steps at some month-start refits, and the scale then overshoots for more than one month: the days 10 to 14 width of six Primaries (D11, D22, D5, D16, D21, and D2, identifiers 8, 15, 17, 18, 24, and 25) widens by 1.21 to 1.48 times at the February refit, and their calibrated coverage goes from 76.3% in January to 93.1% in February. D18 widens by 1.48 times at the September refit, and D4 (identifier 11) narrows by 0.76 times (experiments 683 and 689 list this as the April refit, and experiment 668 as the refit that starts May 2026).
  • Research code. ml-experiments/00683-walk-forward-calibration-of-the-quantile-bands-in-the-one-year-backtest-files/e00683_calibrate.py holds fit_month (the scale), apply_arm, and the scoring, and e00683_refit.py measures band width across refits. The clamps are in ml-experiments/00668-documentation-of-the-one-year-backtest-files-models-training-and-performance/e00668_clamp_fixes.py. The scripts that wrote the four calibrated copies are in ml-experiments/00689-fixed-lookback-width-scale-versus-seed-averaging-at-refit-boundaries/calibrated_copies/ (see its README.md). e00689_make_calibrated_supply_and_solar.py writes the BSP, GSP, and solar copies from the arm 2 output of experiment 683, and e00689_make_calibrated_primaries.py writes the prevailing Primaries copy and its table of scales, including the hold of D18 and D14 at their 2026-06 factor. That README states that the four copies reproduce the stored files byte for byte.
  • Production code for the same job. None. The production repository has no clamp, calibration, or band-widening step.

docs.title: Production-port notes across forecast types
docs.text:
• Series and units. Carry the unit with the series, because the 8 MVA Primaries and 2 of the 3 wind farms are apparent-power series and the rest are MW.
  • Origin and lags. Every neural network reads the ENS 00Z run of the origin day as available at 09:00 UTC and is relabelled to a 12:00 UTC origin. The Candidate's own lags are at least 24 hours old at its 09:00 origin, the BSP and GSP lags at least 3.5 hours old, and the prevailing head's extra lags at least 6 hours old. Wind and solar read no power lag. Experiment 572 tested a 3.5-hour lag cap at the Primaries, and none of the pages read for this one tests it together with the Candidate's neighbour signals and the prevailing head.
  • What a production forecasting service has to store. For each demand and generator neural network, the fitted weights of each monthly (or quarterly, for solar) refit. For the prevailing head, a bank of injected-shift rows per earlier month. For calibration, a scale per series and lead band refreshed each month. For the Primaries, the lag-free forecast table: the median of the lags-masked neural network at the freshest earlier origin with a lead of at most 24 hours, for the Primary and for every neighbour, produced every day. The calibration also needs the neural network's own stored forecasts from the previous 90 days beside the observed power.
  • Serving path. The chain for a Primaries forecast is longer than loading a model and calling predict. The lags-masked neural network writes the lag-free forecast table; the table feeds the neighbour and gap signals and the 14 extra lags; the Candidate runs for each seed (2 seeds) and the seeds are averaged; the survival head acts on the Candidate's quantiles to give the prevailing output; the MVA clamp acts on the quantiles of both outputs; and a calibration step reads 90 days of stored forecasts and observed power and rescales the bands. The clamps and the band scale are therefore not the only steps that act on predicted quantiles. Sources: ml-experiments/00667-*/e00667_cand.py (ensure_tables), ml-experiments/00598-*/e00598_signals.py (build_lag_free_table), ml-experiments/00683-*/e00683_calibrate.py (LOOKBACK_DAYS = 90), and experiment 668 (seeds and head). The production CLAUDE.md states two design principles that this chain trades away: keep the serving path close to "load a model, call predict", and put a capability in the training loop when it could live in either place. The band scale could be fitted at refit time, which is the second principle's case. The page records the trade and does not decide it.
  • Unmetered solar. None of the neural networks above has an explicit term for unmetered solar behind a Primary. Experiment 673 reads the capacity of unmetered solar from a neural-network probe of the response of net demand to sunshine, and calls its figures provisional. The probe gives 2.4 to 3.9 MW at six of the eight MW Primaries (D5, D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16) and 1.25 to 6.62 MW at five MVA Primaries (D2, D3, D4, D19, and D21). Experiment 679 measures the loss in recovery of an added solar farm when MW readings are converted to MVA, as 0.5 percentage points (80% interval -1.0 to 7.7) if the meters read power factor 1 with a small reactive floor. These results are context and are not inputs to any neural network above.

docs.title: Gotchas across forecast types
docs.text:
Each item below caused a wrong number or a wrong assumption in the backtest, or would in a port. The per-type sections give the detail where it belongs.

  • Forecast every half-hour. The stored test matrices of the earlier experiments drop half-hours without an observed reading, because they are training matrices. Experiment 669 rebuilt them for the BSPs and GSPs in ml-experiments/00669-*/e00669_testrows.py, and experiment 667 rebuilt the Primaries' rows from 2025-07-01 onward (REPLACE_FROM in e00667_extend.py). A port must forecast every half-hour of the horizon.
  • The last 62 days of a wind refit window only stop training early. Wind cases whose origin is at or after the cut-off (62 days before the refit date) and whose valid time is before the refit date are used to choose the best epoch and never enter a gradient (STOP_WINDOW_DAYS in e00666_wind_fit.py).
  • ERA5 arrives about 5 days late. At a real cut-off, the last roughly 5 days of ERA5 and CAMS pre-training rows could not be read. The BSP and GSP section states this. The same lateness applies to any Candidate or wind input built from ERA5.
  • Injected lags use later power for proportional shifts. In the Primaries' injected-shift bank, the lag inputs of a proportional shift use the month's later power. Experiment 667 lists this as a caveat.
  • The unclamped prevailing q01 is more negative than the NRA q01 at some MVA Primaries. The lowest prevailing q01 is -2.26 MVA at one MVA Primary against -1.21 for NRA, before the clamp (experiment 667, Caveats).
  • Wind A has flat q50 runs. Runs of up to 9 identical non-zero q50 values occur at Wind A, because the quantiles are clamped at the neural network's own capacity (backtest README).
  • At least two capacities are in play. The wind and solar networks train with the 99.9th percentile of the 730 days before each refit. Every score divides by the production effective capacity, one value per series. The neighbour power ratios of the demand neural networks divide the capacity_mw column of site_map.csv (set in world() of e00647_data.py), a third capacity that is not the effective-capacity table.
  • Hide all power after the cutoff in every refit. Experiment 667 sets the power after the cutoff to NaN in its train phase (TRAIN_ONLY in e00667_fold.py). Experiment 669 has the same switch (E00669_HIDE=1), and its docstring says that only the pre-flight gate used it, so the year's fits relied on row selection alone. A port should hide the power by construction and test the rule (test 2 in "Tests to write").
  • Regime changes in the training history. D8's reading includes one gas engine's output until 2023-08-15, and the data-processing page recommends an individual start date or a flag for such a series. The Candidate's pre-training spans 2019-09 onward. Whether the Candidate's rows handle this change is an open question below.

docs.title: Open issues for the porter: where production conflicts with the research fits
docs.text:
Each item states a fact about production and the matching fact about the research code, with sources. None is an agreed design.

  • The neural networks were trained on one origin, and production runs at four origins with a stale-run fallback. Every research network was trained only on a 09:00 native origin from the same day's 00Z run, relabelled to 12:00. Production live_forecasts runs at 00:00, 06:00, 12:00, and 18:00 UTC (defs/live_forecast_assets.py). The ecmwf_ens asset ingests at 10:30 UTC and retries every 30 minutes, up to 8 times, so the 12:00 slot can use the previous day's run (defs/schedules.py). With the previous day's run, every lead grows by 24 hours, past the training lead range (experiment 666 gives a cap of 348 hours for solar, and the Candidate's range was not checked), and the lag ages change. The research page set has no rule for this regime. Rule 1 of docs/design-philosophy/inherent-stability.md in the production repository requires production to degrade, widen the bands, and record the degradation.
  • Some research inputs do not exist in production at inference time. The previous day's CAMS irradiance enters two columns of the Candidate and of the BSP and GSP networks at inference, and production stores no CAMS (weather_schemas.py defines Nwp for ECMWF ENS only). The monthly pre-training reads ERA5 and CAMS from 2019-09 to the cutoff, and ERA5 arrives about 5 days late. The solar network's relative humidity is not a column of Nwp, which has temperature and dew point, so the research code derives it with the Magnus formula (constants 17.625 and 243.04 in e00666_solar_inputs.py) from the ensemble-mean values. The demand neighbour lists are read from two NGED files, Monitor Direction.csv and Primary Substation Interconnections.csv, in e00400_blend.py, and the production repository mentions the second file only in docs/roadmap/data-sources.md.
  • The analysis proxies differ. The production proxy is the control member of the freshest run, filled column by column from older runs. The research proxy is the ensemble mean of the freshest run published by the origin, which is the previous run's first day (ml-experiments/00437-*/e00437_features.py). A port needs the research definition for every column that weather lags read.
  • The serving chain is longer than load and predict. See "Serving path" in "Production-port notes across forecast types" for the chain and the two production principles it trades away.
  • The research models do not take AllFeatures. The production BaseForecaster.train and predict take a pt.LazyFrame[AllFeatures], keyed by ensemble_member. The Candidate needs pooled rows of 51-member ensemble summaries, inputs from neighbouring series, and multi-stage pre-training on ERA5 and CAMS. A different FeatureEngineer can supply a different data view, according to the production CLAUDE.md, but the page read no code that does so for these networks. The forecast-type sections list the mismatch under "Differs".
  • The output contract differs. See "Output contract": production has no quantile columns and no output-kind column, and its valid_time constraint excludes the lead-0 row of the backtest files.

docs.title: Where the pages disagree
docs.text:
• CRPS scale. Experiment 666 defines CRPS as the mean pinball loss, and experiment 667, experiment 668, experiment 669, experiment 683, and this page define it as twice that. The wind and solar numbers of experiment 666 are about half the numbers here. The current convention is the experiment 668 one.
  • Prevailing Primaries scores. Experiment 667 reports a prevailing CRPS of 4.14, for the head without the extra lagged inputs. Experiment 668 reports 4.09 for the file after nged-ml-research PR 353. The current page is experiment 668.
  • Clamp counts. The body of PR 342 counts 202,598 rows changed in the Primaries file, and experiment 668 counts 206,487. The current page is experiment 668.
  • The D4 and D18 width steps. Experiment 683 places the days 10 to 14 narrowing of D4 (identifier 11) at an April month start, with a factor of 0.76, and experiment 689 agrees. Experiment 668 places it at the refit that starts May 2026 and calls it about a third, and the README says about 37%. For D18, experiment 683 gives a widening of 1.48 times, experiment 668 about half, and the README 55%.
  • The first month on the survival head. The README says the refit that starts 2026-02 is the first month on the survival head that replaces the fallback head, and experiment 668 and the README's own "Known limitations" list say the fallback head serves 2025-11 and 2025-12 and R-haz serves 2026-01 onward. The current page is experiment 668.
  • Calibrated-copy scores. The README gives CRPS changes of +0.044 (prevailing Primaries), +0.001 (BSPs), +0.026 (GSPs), and +0.006 (solar), against +0.047, +0.005, +0.003, and -0.002 in experiment 683. The README's prevailing figures come from the file from before the extra lagged inputs. The current page for the experiment's own numbers is experiment 683.
  • "As stored" NRA coverage. Experiment 688 calls 80.1% and 80.3% the bands as stored. They are the scaled bands of experiment 683, whose stored values are 81.7% and 77.7%.
  • BSP and GSP coverage. Experiment 669 gives pooled q05-to-q95 coverage of 0.883 to 0.870 across its four lead bands for the four series together, and experiment 668 gives 86.7% for the BSPs and 87.7% for the GSPs, each as one figure per group. The two pages pool different rows. The pages do not state whether the row sets also differ, and this page did not check.
  • Solar lead cap. Experiment 666 gives training leads below 348 hours and experiment 668 says the range was extended to 336 hours. The current page is experiment 666.
  • Width factor of the Candidate. Experiment 612 mentions a band scaled by 1.12 to 1.18, and experiment 613 and experiment 620 use 1.0934. This page uses 1.0934 because the final test used it.
  • Extra-lag reaction gains. Experiment 681 reports 19.1 and 20.4 hours sooner for 8 and 14 inputs, and experiment 687 reports 1.25 days sooner for extra lags, on different banks and folds.
  • Calibrated copy of the prevailing Primaries rows. primaries_calibrated.parquet was built before the extra lagged inputs, so its prevailing rows differ from those of primaries.parquet that this page scores.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
These are listed for the maintainer. None is decided here.

  • Whether the Primaries Candidate should read 3.5-hour lags, as the BSP and GSP neural network does, and what the answer does to the prevailing head.
  • Which extra-lag set the prevailing head should use: the 8-input set or the 14-input set (experiment 681).
  • Whether the truncated Gaussian output should replace the post hoc clamp at all eight MVA Primaries, and what it does to the prevailing output (experiment 684).
  • Whether to refit the band scale at every neural network refit, and how to treat the band-width steps at month-start refits (experiment 683 and experiment 689). Experiment 689 shows that a fixed-lookback scale does not remove the steps, and it did not test a scale fitted on the new network's own forecasts.
  • Whether the band scale belongs in the training loop or in the serving path (see "Serving path" above).
  • Which forecast slots (00:00, 06:00, 12:00, and 18:00 UTC) each neural network must serve, and what a stale ENS run does to each (see "Open issues for the porter").
  • Whether a port rebuilds the cached input tables from source or ports the lineage of experiments 607, 437, and 564 (see the "Input tables" subsections).
  • Whether the Candidate's pre-training rows handle D8's gas-engine regime change on 2023-08-15. The code was not read for this.
  • Why the NRA bands of D18 and D14 (identifiers 13 and 16) cover only about 22% to 28% of observations in July and August 2026. Experiment 668 suggests a load shift that normal running ignores. Experiment 685, an event table on the final-test window, finds no transfer between the two Primaries in those months, and names a level offset in the lag-free forecast as an untested candidate. Experiment 690 fitted a smooth slow level in hindsight, with the candidate windows masked, on a different forecast's residual. The level tracks the change (weekly correlation 0.66 at D18 and 0.87 at D14), and adding it to q50 halves the median absolute error at both Primaries, in hindsight and not as a forecast. The level ramps over months and does not follow the step on 1 July. It moved the median absolute error of two control Primaries by 5.5% and 7.5%, against a limit of 5%, so the verdict is partly supported, and the experiment proposes no new method. The miss is still not explained by a load transfer (experiment 685), and the current pages are experiments 685 and 690.
  • Whether wind needs a power lag or a different long-lead rule, given its score against climatology at days 10 to 14.
  • Whether a calendar input or more frequent refits remove the solar median's seasonal bias.
  • How to model load shifts at the BSPs and GSPs, where the largest observed miss looks like one.
  • Whether the BSP and GSP fine-tune carries synthetic lag-only shifts. The code path suggests that it does not (e00669_fit.py calls the fine-tune of experiment 574 directly, where the Candidate's chain uses synthetic shifts), and no run checked this.

docs.title: Tests to write
docs.text:
A port should pass the checks below before any score is compared, and each check states the property it protects and the source that supports it. The thresholds come from the pages named. A threshold that no page states is marked as a choice for the porter.

  1. No lookahead, by perturbation. Property: no input depends on power or weather that was not available at the origin. Perturb all power after the cutoff and after the native origin minus each lag cap, which is 24 hours for the Candidate, 3.5 hours for the BSPs and GSPs, and 6 hours for the extra lags, and check that no input, no lag-free table entry, no signal, and no output moves. Repeat with the NWP of later runs. Sources: experiment 668 (a test perturbs every later half-hour for the extra lags), experiment 669 (a perturbation test found no leak; no lag index is newer than 05:30 on the origin day).
  2. Hidden-future training. Property: a refit at month M reads no row at or after M. Fit one fold with all power after the cutoff set to NaN and require identical weights. Sources: e00667_fold.py (TRAIN_ONLY), e00669_fold.py (E00669_HIDE=1), and experiment 667 (reviews found no leak into any fold's training data).
  3. Golden output. Property: the port reproduces the stored forecasts. Re-run one stored fold, for example 2026-03, and compare with the backtest file within a tolerance. The GPU re-run of the 2026-03 GSP fold matched the stored forecasts to 5e-6 of capacity (experiment 669). For the Primaries, the 12:00 NRA rows equal the native 09:00 seed-mean quantiles times capacity exactly, with a maximum difference of 0.0 (experiment 667, "Checks").
  4. Contract. Property: the output has the layout in "Output contract". Check 672 rows per origin and series, no duplicate key, no null or non-finite quantile, no crossing in any adjacent pair, UTC, Int8 identifiers, valid_time as the end of the half-hour, and one NRA row and one prevailing row per Primary key. Sources: experiments 667, 668, and 669, "Checks". Validation against the production PowerForecast needs a quantile column set that production does not have.
  5. Clamps and gates. Property: the post-processing rules hold. MVA Primaries have no quantile below zero. MW Primaries are not clamped. Solar quantiles are zero where the zenith at mid-half-hour is 90 degrees or more, and daylight rows are bit-identical before and after the clamp. Sources: the backtest README ("Post-processing and checksums") and experiment 668.
  6. Calibration. Property: the scale follows the rule in "Walk-forward band calibration". The q50 is unchanged. Each factor lies in 0.5 to 3. Each factor uses only valid times at least 6 hours before the month starts. A cell with fewer than 20 fitting days keeps a scale of 1. Coverage on the fitting rows is 90% when no bound binds. Sources: e00683_calibrate.py and the backtest README.
  7. Scores and coverage by lead band. Property: the port reproduces the published scores. Recompute the tables of experiment 668. The Opus review of experiment 667 reproduced every score to 3 decimals, and the Sonnet audit of experiment 669 reproduced its scores within 0.03 points. A tolerance for a port is a choice for the porter.
  8. Monthly refit. Property: the refit loop is walk-forward. A refit at month M trains only on data before M (check 2), and the band-width step at each refit is reported as experiments 683 and 689 measured it.
  9. Degradation. Property: the service degrades and never raises when an input is missing, as rule 1 of the production inherent-stability page requires. Check a missing lag (the Candidate trains with 30% lag masking), a missing neighbour, a stale or missing ENS run, missing CAMS, and fewer than 2 banks for the survival head. The service must always output a forecast, widen the bands, and record the degradation on the row. No page defines the widening for these cases.
  10. Architecture and parameter count. Property: the port builds the architecture that was fitted. Assert the layer widths of each network and the parameter count against the stored .pt files in data/ml-experiments/. The widths are stated in each forecast-type section, and the count is not stated on any merged page.

docs.title: Appendix: modules each fit imports
docs.text:
This appendix follows import statements only, so it lists the modules that a fit imports and does not list the scripts that write the cached tables a fit reads. The cached tables, and the scripts that build them, are in the "Input tables" subsection of each forecast-type section. Wind and solar copy their code into the 666 folder, and the fit imports of wind and solar need only that folder, but their inputs are built elsewhere (see "Input tables"). The lists below come from following every import e00NNN_... and import p667_... statement from the entry files, so they name files that a porter must read or copy. The Candidate fit and the prevailing head share most of their modules.

The research code also imports modules of the studies package. The package is at src/studies/ in the research repository, and the files that import it include the entry files above. The modules found by a search of the fit, export, and calibration scripts are studies.sources (data folder paths), studies.power (scan_power), studies.pv_dataset (pv_sites and wind_sites), studies.solar (zenith), and, in the scoring and figure scripts of the experiment folders listed, studies.eval_protocol (metrics and slices). e00666_solar_gate.py imports no studies module and belongs to the wind and solar folder; the page read no evidence that the backtest export imports it, and the closure of its own imports was not walked here.

docs.title: Glossary of terms used in the experiment pages
docs.text: This page defines each term that the experiment pages and the theme Summary pages use without redefining. Every definition gives its source: the experiment that introduced the term, or the code or contract that fixes its meaning. Terms appear in alphabetical order. The data-processing page has its own short list of terms for the processing steps it describes.

docs.title: 14-day correction
docs.text: The 14-day correction adds the mean error of the last 14 days to every forecast quantile. The error is the observed power minus the forecast median, taken over the half-hours whose power was already observed when the forecast was issued, and the correction is zero when fewer than 3 days of errors exist (experiment 19 and its scoring script).

docs.title: Abnormal running arrangement (ARA) and normal running arrangement (NRA)
docs.text: The normal running arrangement (NRA) is the electricity network as it is when no load transfer is on, and an abnormal running arrangement (ARA) is the period while an operator has closed a normally open switch, so that one Primary substation carries load that belongs to a neighbour. An "NRA forecast" predicts the demand that the substation would have drawn under the NRA (experiment 88, experiment 89).

docs.title: Base margin
docs.text: A base margin is a starting prediction that an XGBoost model receives for each row, in place of the single base score that XGBoost otherwise estimates from the training labels. The wind models use the power that the turbine power curve gives at the forecast wind speed. The solar offset of the Primary models uses the forecast output of the unmetered solar panels behind the substation (experiment 80, experiment 87).

docs.title: Best guess
docs.text: The best guess is the forecasting recipe assembled in experiment 33. For Primary substation demand it is N1 with the 14-day correction and a spread factor of 1.15, which is the stack without its half-life (experiment 19's stack_minus_h arm, rebuilt in experiment 33 as n1_cs). For bulk and grid supply points it is N1 alone. For solar and wind farms it is a mixture, over the 51 ENS members, of XGBoost models trained on ERA5 weather, with a spread factor and, for wind, a power-curve base margin.

docs.title: BG2
docs.text: BG2 is the second best-guess recipe, assembled in experiment 87 from the best earlier ideas. For Primary substations it is a quantile blend of five members, with a solar offset at the five Primaries that have a clean solar capacity estimate. The members are a weekly-refitted XGBoost model, a monthly-refitted XGBoost model, an analogue model (the experiment's summary does not state its type), a model pooled by substation type, and the stack. For bulk and grid supply points it is the weekly-refitted XGBoost model with no correction. Experiment 97 recalibrates only the stored weekly-refitted forecast and calls it BG2. Production does not run BG2: it serves xgboost_baseline, which scored 10.536 points on the Primary quantile score in experiment 87, against 5.260 for BG2.

docs.title: Bulk supply point and grid supply point
docs.text: A grid supply point (GSP) is a substation where the transmission network feeds NGED's distribution network, and a bulk supply point (BSP) is a substation one step further down. NGED's GSPs step voltage from 400 kV or 275 kV to 132 kV, and its BSPs step from 132 kV to 33 kV or 66 kV (NGED's network and its data). A Primary substation sits below a BSP. The trial area holds two GSPs and two BSPs, and the experiments report them together as "supply points" or "BSP and GSP". The data-processing page says not to treat them as clean demand.

docs.title: Capacity and points of capacity
docs.text: Capacity in the experiment scores is the effective capacity of a series: the 99th percentile of the absolute power over the series' whole observed history, in the series' own unit (MW or MVA). The EffectiveCapacity contract fixes this definition for version 0.1 (packages/contracts/src/contracts/power_schemas.py), and the experiment scripts divide power and forecast by effective_capacity_mw. A point of capacity is 1% of that value, so a score of 5.26 points on a series of 20 MW capacity is an error of about 1.05 MW. A lower score is better.

docs.title: Climatology
docs.text: climatology is a baseline forecaster that predicts each half-hour from past power in the same calendar cell. A cell is a series, a local month, a local half-hour of the day, and a weekday-or-weekend flag, smoothed over the neighbouring months and half-hours. The forecaster stores 51 equiprobable quantiles per cell and consumes no weather (packages/baseline_forecasters/src/baseline_forecasters/climatology.py).

docs.title: Control member
docs.text: The control member is the one ENS run that starts from ECMWF's unperturbed analysis of the current weather. The other 50 of the 51 ENS members start from perturbed analyses (ENS horizons). N1 is trained on the control member and then applied to all 51 members, and the 51 sets of quantiles are pooled (experiment 13).

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text: The coverage of a forecast quantile is the share of observed values at or below it. A correct q05 covers 0.05 and a correct q95 covers 0.95. The coverage of the 5% to 95% range is the share of observed values between q05 and q95, which is 90% for a correct forecast (experiment 19 reports it as "5% to 95% coverage").

docs.title: CRPS
docs.text: The continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) scores a whole forecast distribution against the observed value, and the experiments approximate it from the forecast quantiles. The approximation is twice the probability-mass-weighted sum of the pinball losses, which is the quantile score (studies.cross_validation.crps). Experiments 2, 16, and 20 report it under the name CRPS, and experiments 13 and 33 say that the quantile score is its estimate.

docs.title: D codes
docs.text: A D code (D1 to D22) is the anonymised label of one of the 22 demand-side series in fold A: 16 Primary substations, 4 bulk or grid supply points, and a battery and a biofuel generator. The labels are defined in experiment 3 and are used with the same meaning in the pages checked (experiments 5, 27, 46, 51, 53, 64, and 74 and the data-processing page), for example D1 is a grid supply point and D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16 are the five Primaries with a clean solar capacity estimate. A D code and a substation name are different labels. D codes are not the same as the detector names D0, D0M, D1, and D2 (see Detectors D0, D0M, D1, and D2), nor the labels P12 and P13 of experiment 101. Generators carry separate anonymous labels such as "Solar farm A", assigned by studies.anonymise.

docs.title: Detectors D0, D0M, D1, and D2
docs.text: In the switching experiments, D0, D0M, D1, and D2 are names of detectors, not series. D0 is the single-series detector. D0 raises an alarm when the average residual over a window steps by more than a threshold. D0M is D0 with its threshold chosen by the same search that sets D2's threshold and with no veto; at the 24-hour window it uses 4.0 noise units and ends each alarm interval with a level tracker that stops after 60 days. D0 at the thresholds of experiment 43 (6.0 noise units at the 4-hour window and 4.0 at the 24-hour window) is a separate arm, although the search returned those same thresholds. D1 is the neighbour-balance detector of experiment 37, which also requires a neighbouring substation to step the opposite way (thresholds 3.75 at the 4-hour window and 2.5 at the 24-hour window). D2 is D0M plus a neighbour veto (experiment 37, experiment 43, experiment 55, experiment 58, experiment 66). Experiment 49 also uses D0 as the label of a spread-factor contrast, and experiment 87 uses D1 and D4 as labels of decisions.

docs.title: ENS, ERA5, and CAMS
docs.text: ENS is the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) ensemble forecast with 51 members, and ERA5 and the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) irradiance are estimates of past weather. ENS is a forecast issued before the weather happens, and the live forecast is given ENS. ERA5, the fifth-generation ECMWF reanalysis, arrives about 5 days late (experiment 10), so a result that uses ERA5 as a forecast input is a ceiling and not a usable product. CAMS is a satellite-based estimate of sunlight (experiment 7). An XGBoost model trained on ERA5 or CAMS learns from weather that was not forecast.

docs.title: Frozen XGBoost model
docs.text: A frozen XGBoost model is trained once, on data up to the start of the validation year, and is not refitted during that year. In experiment 87, the frozen forecast without the 14-day correction scores 6.927 for Primary substations (S1), and the frozen forecast with the correction is the stack (S2, 5.543).

docs.title: Half-life
docs.text: A half-life of 0.5 years gives a training row a weight of 0.5 raised to the power of the row's age in years divided by 0.5. The weight therefore halves for every 0.5 years of age (ml-experiments/00017-training-window-and-retraining-rule-drift-demand/e00017_fit.py, experiment 17).

docs.title: Injected and real load transfers
docs.text: A load transfer is a switching operation that moves part of one Primary substation's demand (the donor) onto neighbouring substations for hours or days. An injected transfer is a synthetic transfer that the experiment adds to the real power readings, so its start, end, and size are known. A real transfer is one of the 66 hand-labelled operations of experiment 41, of which 35 last over 1 day. A transfer is "large" when it moves at least 25% of the receiving substations' load.

docs.title: Interval-level convention
docs.text: Each interval states its level, and the level depends on how many contrasts the experiment planned. An experiment that plans one contrast reports a 95% interval. An experiment that plans N contrasts divides the 5% error rate across them with a Bonferroni correction, so nine contrasts give a 99.44% interval (1 minus 0.05 divided by 9). Intervals resample whole calendar months (.claude/skills/ml-experiment/SKILL.md, experiment 19).

docs.title: manual_heuristic
docs.text: manual_heuristic is a baseline forecaster that predicts each half-hour as an ensemble of the power observed at the same weekday and time of day in earlier weeks and years. Under its configuration the 13 ensemble members are the same time in each of the last 6 weeks and the same time 49 to 55 weeks earlier; a lag that would not yet have been observed at the forecast origin is absent. The forecaster consumes no weather (packages/baseline_forecasters/src/baseline_forecasters/manual_heuristic.py).

docs.title: MW and MVA
docs.text: A series is metered in MW (signed active power, which can be negative when the substation exports) or in MVA (apparent power, which is never negative). The unit is the units column of the metadata table. Eight of the 16 trial Primaries are metered only in MVA, so solar output behind such a Primary appears as demand in daylight. See the data-processing page and experiments 56 and 79.

docs.title: N1
docs.text: N1 is the single-stage XGBoost quantile model, one per series, that is trained on the ENS control member with recent power as inputs. It receives power lags measured from the forecast origin and weather columns from the ENS member, and its output quantiles are pooled across the 51 ENS members (experiment 13).

docs.title: Noise unit
docs.text: One noise unit is 1.4826 times the median absolute deviation of a substation's 24-hour residual step on odd-numbered months. A step of 4.0 noise units is therefore four times the usual size (experiment 66).

docs.title: NWP
docs.text: NWP is numerical weather prediction: a physical weather model run forward from the current state of the atmosphere. ENS is the NWP product that the live forecast consumes. Other NWP products in the experiments include the Met Office UKV and NOAA's GEFS.

docs.title: PF14
docs.text: PF14 is the benchmark end rule of the switching experiments, written after seeing results. It ends each alarm interval at the first opposite step that is at least half the onset step (and at least 1.5 noise units) within 14 days, takes the largest step back within one window after that, and keeps the tracked end when no step qualifies (experiment 66, experiment 69).

docs.title: Pooled mixture
docs.text: A pooled mixture applies the XGBoost quantile model to each of the 51 ENS members and pools the resulting quantiles as equal-weight points. The forecast quantiles are the weighted quantiles of the pooled values (experiment 13, experiment 2).

docs.title: Pre-registration, decision rule, and verdict words
docs.text: An experiment pre-registers its hypothesis, prediction, and decision rule in a result.md that is committed with status planned before any code runs. The decision rule states which interval and threshold make each verdict, so the verdict follows from the numbers and not from the author's reading. The verdicts are supported, partly supported, small gain (the interval excludes zero in the predicted direction but misses the threshold), not supported, refuted, inconclusive, invalid, and failed. See How an experiment is recorded and .claude/skills/ml-experiment/SKILL.md. A write-up marks a verdict that its decision rule does not cover as not pre-registered, as experiment 13 does.

docs.title: Primary substation
docs.text: A Primary substation steps voltage down from 33 kV or 66 kV to 11 kV. NGED operates 1,161 Primary substations (NGED's network and its data), and 16 of the 32 trial series are Primaries. A Primary is fed from a bulk supply point, which is a higher-voltage substation (see Bulk supply point and grid supply point).

docs.title: Quantile score and pinball loss
docs.text: The quantile score is twice the probability-mass-weighted mean of the pinball losses over the forecast quantile levels, in points of capacity. The pinball loss of a quantile at level τ is τ times the shortfall of the forecast below the observation, or (1 − τ) times the excess of the forecast above it. Each level's weight is the probability mass between the mid-points to its neighbouring levels, so the score is not a plain mean over the levels. Experiments 33, 34, and 48 use nine levels (0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.40, 0.50, 0.60, 0.75, 0.90, and 0.95), and experiment 87 and later use 11 levels (those nine plus 0.01 and 0.99) (pinball_quantile_score in ml-experiments/00087-bg2-best-guess-assembled-with-drop-one-ablations/e00087_common.py). Scores from experiments with different levels, row sets, or series cannot be compared.

docs.title: Recall (MW-weighted)
docs.text: MW-weighted recall is the share of the moved megawatts that sit in found transfers. A detector finds a transfer when it raises an alarm starting within 2 hours of the transfer's start and places the end within the larger of 6 hours and 10% of the transfer's duration (experiment 66, experiment 101).

docs.title: Refit and rolling refit
docs.text: A refit retrains the XGBoost model on newer data at a scheduled interval, such as weekly or monthly. A rolling refit (P-roll) retrains monthly on a rolling 12-month window with 150 boosting rounds (experiment 34). Weekly refits are the cadence of BG2.

docs.title: Research default
docs.text: A research default is the fixed forecast of one target family, against which every change experiment is measured. Each version has a name made of the family, the words "research default", and a number, such as "Primary demand research default 1" (the GAM stack A+H+S). An adopted change makes the next version. A research default is not what production serves: production serves xgboost_baseline, and "champion" and "promote" are production words (rule, log).

docs.title: Residual
docs.text: In the switching experiments, the residual is the measured power minus the forecast of an XGBoost demand model trained on ERA5 weather that uses no past power. The detectors look for steps in the residual (experiment 66).

docs.title: RO-NC
docs.text: RO-NC is the refit-offset neighbour-count detector. RO-NC is PF14 with two changes. The step is taken from whichever of two residual models, refitted half a month apart, did not refit within 24 hours. The candidates are scored by a logistic regression that includes the count of neighbours stepping the same way as the alarming substation (experiment 82, experiment 101). X is the refit-offset detector alone. The experiment scripts under ml-experiments/ still name RO-NC XL in code, for example in the arm names lagmw_xl and mask_xl of experiment 86, so a search of the code for XL finds the RO-NC detector.

docs.title: Season-year
docs.text: A season-year is a 12-month period, and its start month depends on the series of work. In the solar-disaggregation experiments it runs from September to August, such as 2019/20 (experiment 39). In the differentiable-physics series it runs from July to June (FIRST_SEASON_MONTH in src/studies/dp_calendar.py).

docs.title: Skill
docs.text: Skill is 100 times (1 minus the best guess's quantile score divided by manual_heuristic's quantile score), pooled over the series being compared. A positive skill means the best guess beats manual_heuristic (experiment 56).

docs.title: Spread factor
docs.text: The spread factor scales each forecast quantile's distance from the median. A quantile q becomes the median plus the factor times (q minus the median), so a factor of 1.15 widens the band by 15% and a factor below 1 narrows it (experiment 19). For solar and wind farms the factor is fitted on earlier cases to bring the 5% to 95% coverage near its target (experiment 33).

docs.title: Stack
docs.text: The stack is N1 with the 14-day correction and a spread factor of 1.15, and the experiments differ on the half-life. The stack of experiment 19 weights older training rows with a half-life of 0.5 years. The stacks of experiments 33, 34, and 48 use a half-life of 2 years, and are trained once. The experiment 87 scripts use the same 2-year weighting for its stack, which its write-up does not state, and there the stack is the frozen forecast plus the 14-day correction.

docs.title: Stages 0, 1a, and 2
docs.text: Stage 1a is an XGBoost quantile model per series, trained on analysis weather (ERA5 and CAMS), with no power lags and no lead time. Stage 0 maps ENS weather toward the weather that stage 1a trained on (a quantile mapping in experiments 16 and 20). Stage 2 is a calibrator, a second XGBoost model that corrects the stage 1a quantiles and can use lagged power (staged probabilistic forecast).

docs.title: Tail coverage
docs.text: Tail coverage is the coverage of a quantile in the tails: the share of observed values below the 0.01 and 0.05 quantiles or above the 0.95 and 0.99 quantiles. A correct forecast has a tail coverage equal to the quantile's level on the lower tail, and equal to one minus the level on the upper tail. Experiment 87 reports it at those four levels beside the pinball loss there (experiment 87).

docs.title: xgboost_baseline
docs.text: xgboost_baseline is the production-style forecast: the stored forecast of the XGBoost model that the project's production recipe produced. The experiments read it from the power_forecasts Delta table for the fold mid_2025_to_mid_2026. Experiment 87 did not confirm whether the local Dagster cross-validation assets or S3 wrote that table, so none of the experiments we read confirms that the stored forecast matches the deployed one (experiment 13, experiment 87).

docs.title: How the Kalman filter corrects the demand forecast
docs.text:
This page hosts an animated explainer of how a Kalman filter corrects the forecast that a generalised additive model (GAM) makes of Primary substation demand. The explainer uses real data from one Primary substation (anonymised as D11) for one winter week, 4 to 10 February 2026. It shows no series from a metered generator. Press Play, drag the slider, or use the arrow keys to change scene. Open the explainer full-screen on a phone, where the frame below is small.

The explainer has six scenes.

  • Scene 1, "GAM alone": the forecast of the additive model without any correction.
  • Scene 2, "The error": observed demand minus the additive model's forecast.
  • Scene 3, "Filter state": how each new reading moves the filter's two-part state.
  • Scene 4, "Forecast": the corrected forecast at one issue time.
  • Scene 5, "Bands": the uncertainty band around the corrected forecast.
  • Scene 6, "Not fixed": the error pattern by time of day that the filter leaves behind, and the time-of-day terms of stage 2 that shrink the pattern. The pattern shrinks, but the mean absolute error barely changes (4.17, 4.12, and 4.16 points).

The explainer departs in three ways from a single-state Kalman filter whose variance sets the forecast band.

  • The state has two parts, and four filters run side by side. Each filter holds a slow level and a fast part that fades with a half-life of 19.1 hours. One filter exists per hour band: night (00:00 to 05:59), morning (06:00 to 10:59), midday (11:00 to 15:59), and evening (16:00 to 23:59), in local time. Each reading updates both parts of its band's filter, with a gain (the share of the surprise that the filter takes on) averaging about 8% for the level and about 42% for the fast part over the week. The correction holds the level flat across the lead time and fades only the fast part. The filter code is dp_assimilation.py, with the noise parameters that experiment 133 learned.
  • The band comes from a table of past forecast errors, not from the filter's variance. The table holds quantiles of past forecast errors for each lead-time band, hour band, and calendar quarter (LeadHourSpread in dp_ens.py). Neither the filter's variance nor the spread of the weather ensemble enters the band. Experiment 169 found that adding the ensemble spread improved nothing. The week shown uses the forecasts stored by experiment 136. The current Primary demand forecast uses the smoothed table of experiment 160, widened on forecast-cold days by experiment 164.
  • The explainer leaves out the neural-network head and the solar summary. The scenes draw the additive model plus the filter, and the time-of-day terms of stage 2 from experiment 155. Primary demand research default 3 also holds a small neural-network head and a solar summary, as the log of research default versions lists.

The week was chosen to show the filter working. The additive model under-forecast on 99% of the half-hours of the week, and the filter lowered the mean absolute error from 6.6 to 3.0 points of capacity at the last of the six issue times. A week where the additive model had no persistent error would show less.

The rule page defines the families and the eight items in each row, and each family's evaluation protocol defines the adoption conditions. The pull request of the adopting experiment adds the row, and a row is never edited afterwards except to change its status.
