docs.title: Bulk and grid supply points
docs.text: No version exists. The family accepts no adoption until its first default is named.

docs.title: The research default and the rule for adopting a change
docs.text:
Each target family has one fixed research default forecast, one fixed rule for adding a change to it, and a log of versions. An experiment of kind change asks whether the research default plus change x beats the research default. A win produces the next version of the research default. The rule exists so that the experiments build one forecast in order, and so that a gain is always measured against the current forecast and never against a stale or partial one. How a change is scored, and when it is adopted, is fixed by the family's evaluation protocol: Primary demand, metered solar farms, or wind farms.

Adopting a change into the research default does not put the change into production. The release-model skill governs production changes. This page says "research default" and "adopt" because production deployment already uses "champion" and "promote" for the deployed XGBoost model. Every version has a name made of the family, the words "research default", and a number N that counts up within the family from 1, for example "Primary demand research default 1" for the GAM stack A+H+S. "C1" and "C2" already name the planned contrasts on every result page, so a bare "default 3" or "v3" is never used. Every result.md and pull-request body cites the version by name, for example "default plus x versus Primary demand research default 1". The two arms of a change experiment are called "default" and "default plus x".

The research default is not what runs in production. Production serves a much weaker XGBoost model, stored as xgboost_baseline. The demand protocol gives its score beside the score of the frozen reference BG2.

docs.title: Families
docs.text:
Each family has its own research default, series, retraining cadence, and version line. The family definition below fixes these values once, and an experiment's plan never sets or changes them. The row set, lead range, headline metric, protected groups, and benchmarks of each family are in its evaluation protocol.

No adoption until then Weekly

docs.title: Reusing the research default's code and forecasts
docs.text:
A change experiment starts from the stored forecasts of the research default and, when the change acts inside a fitted stage, from the default's code. The change is one of two kinds, and the experiment's page says which.

  • Tier 1 changes act on stored forecasts. A clip, a band-widening rule, a blend, a recalibration, or a quantile interpolation needs only the research default's stored forecasts. The D8 as-of widening, the lead-band interpolation, the D5 clip, and the blend of experiment 287 are all of this kind.
  • Tier 2 changes act inside a fitted stage. A change to the convex model, the head, the solar summary, or the features needs the research default's code. The experiment imports that code directly from the folder of the experiment that holds it, with that folder on PYTHONPATH, as the ml-experiment skill describes. The code moves into src/studies in a reviewed pull request only when several experiment folders need it or when production might one day need it.

The research default's definition holds four items. These are the code (a script in an experiment folder and its commit, a module and commit in src/studies, or "stored forecasts only"), a configuration file naming every setting and the seed policy, the stored forecasts for every scored, replicate, and holdout period, and the scores. The seed policy matters: averaging three seeds of the correction network scored 0.123 points below arm D, against 0.104 for the mean single seed (experiments 201 and 220), so "more seeds" would otherwise adopt as a change.

Each version's stored forecasts are written once and never overwritten. Several worktrees share one data/ folder, and a re-run by one session would replace the evidence of another. Experiments in flight read Primary demand research default N while Primary demand research default N+1 is being built. Each version is written once with experiment_store.write_predictions under the adopting experiment's id and a fixed name. Where a refit is needed to reproduce the default, the reproduction uses the default's cadence exactly, because refit cadence is itself a contrast (experiment 278).

docs.title: What an experiment must contain to be eligible
docs.text:
An experiment is eligible for adoption only when its front matter says kind: change and its plan, committed before any score is read, states five items. Diagnostics, audits, data checks, and detection or decision studies are kind: other and never adopt. The five items are the following.

  • The family and the research default version the experiment starts from.
  • The arms: the default, and the default plus x. The default's arm reads the stored forecasts of that version, with a reproduction gate when the experiment refits the default, as experiment 278 did.
  • The tier of the change (tier 1 or tier 2) and its complexity tier, as the evaluation protocol of the family defines them.
  • The pre-registered default-plus-x arm or arms.
  • The controls that apply: a known-answer test, a placebo, a leakage check.

docs.title: When a change is adopted
docs.text: A change is adopted only when the conditions of the family's evaluation protocol hold. The conditions, the candidate status for a change that fails one of them, the rules for several arms and for blends, the holdout, and the interval conventions are all in the protocol. The reference text is the section "When a change is adopted" of the demand protocol.

docs.title: Experiments planned before the rule
docs.text: Experiments planned before the rule are grandfathered, and their winners reach the research default only through a rebase run. Their front matter has no kind, and experiment_tables.py --check accepts its absence for an experiment whose id is below the cut-off id of 320. A proposal with no plan commit yet is re-planned as kind: change where it tests a change.

docs.title: The rebase rule for stale results
docs.text:
A result measured against an older version stays valid as an estimate of x on that version, but it answers a stale question. The estimate (Primary demand research default 3 plus x, minus Primary demand research default 3) is still correct for Primary demand research default 3. The estimate does not apply to x on Primary demand research default 4. Adoption one change at a time is path-dependent: a change that failed against one version may pass against a later one, and two changes that act on the same error can both win alone while only the first to merge adopts. The two gains of experiment 220 added to a stacking ratio of 0.99, while the drift term improved the bare GAM-K by 0.40 points and worsened arm D by 0.03.

  1. A result that passes against a version that is no longer current becomes a candidate with the status "candidate (stale)".
  2. A short rebase run scores (current default plus x, minus current default) against the stored forecasts of the current version, under the same adoption conditions and with no new plan.
  3. A rebase is needed unless every adoption since the experiment's version belongs to a different family.
  4. Where two candidates change the same component (two widening rules, for example), the rebase scores them head to head.
  5. Adoptions go in merge order. The second of two overlapping changes gets a rebase run against the new version.
  6. Changes rejected against the last few versions stay on a retest list that the periodic ablation revisits.

After every fifth adoption in a family, an ablation experiment removes each adopted component in turn. The ablation is an experiment with its own id and a planned result.md. The demand protocol states when a component is dropped.

docs.title: Who adopts, and what the log holds
docs.text:
The experiment's own pull request carries the adoption. Its front matter holds promoted_to (the name of the new version, for example "Primary demand research default 2") and the scores against the three benchmarks, and the same pull request adds a row to the log. The reviewing session checks the adoption conditions before merging and assigns the version number. Versions are serial within a family.

Each log row holds eight items. These are the change, the adopting experiment, the scored-year and replicate gains with intervals, the absolute headline score, the three benchmarks' scores on the family's rows, the stored-forecast name, the commit of the code, and the status "scored-year gain is an upper bound". A result against an old version keeps its verdict with the status "candidate (stale)" until a rebase runs. A component that a later ablation removes sets production_status: superseded on its experiment.

Adoption needs the maintainer's approval in four cases. These are a new data source, a cost above £30 or a recurring cost in production, a change that would need a serving-path change to port, and a change whose code must enter src/studies. Other adoptions run autonomously under the merge rules in the ml-experiment skill.

A model release is a separate step. The Primary-demand research default is a GAM stack, and a model release is a numbered, trained XGBoost model, so most demand adoptions are not release candidates until the GAM stack has a production design. The release-model skill starts from the log of versions since the last release.

docs.title: Retraining cadence
docs.text:
The cadence is part of the research default, so each family's definition states one, and a change of cadence is a change experiment. The evidence differs by family.

Family Evidence on cadence Cadence Primary demand, XGBoost benchmark BG2 Weekly beats monthly by 0.123 (experiment 87) to 0.13 (experiment 48) points Weekly, with a 12-month-window monthly refit as a research proxy (experiment 85) Primary demand, GAM stack Weekly minus monthly +0.001, quarterly minus monthly +0.010 (experiment 278) Monthly Bulk and grid supply points Weekly beats monthly by 0.160 points (0.066 to 0.247, experiment 87) Weekly Metered solar and wind farms Monthly minus frozen -0.044 for solar and +0.007 for wind (experiment 48), inside a ±0.05 band A single fit, or monthly, as the family's first version states

Quarterly refits are not used for the XGBoost-based families. Experiment 85 found that quarterly refits scored 0.38 points above weekly refits on the same 12-month window, and advised against using them to compare arms that differ in cadence or in how fast they adapt. For the GAM stack, quarterly refits save about 19 seconds per arm-year and add a loss of 0.010 points (99% interval -0.014 to +0.032), concentrated in winter, so they are not shown adequate. Their effect on the power of a default-plus-x contrast has not been measured.

docs.title: Scoreboard for Primary demand
docs.text:
On the current rows, Primary demand research default 3 scores 2.90 against BG2's 3.02 at the six Primaries that report signed megawatts, and 4.42 against 3.78 at the eight that report apparent power only. Both scores are the mean continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) for forecasts 1 to 10 days ahead, in points of effective capacity, and smaller is better. The difference from BG2 is -0.12 (-0.31 to +0.06) at the signed-MW six and +0.63 (+0.35 to +0.94) at the MVA-only eight (D8 included, with donor spread; 99% intervals). Without D8, the MVA-only gap is +0.16 (-0.02 to +0.35). This page is descriptive: it adopts nothing, and an adoption is decided by the evaluation protocol in an experiment.

BG2's score here differs from experiment 379's by up to 0.006 points (3.78 against 3.788 at the MVA- only eight), because the shared half-hours differ slightly.

The page scores every stored forecast on one shared set of half-hours, so progress is read from one table and never from a chain of contrasts on different rows. The script scripts/scoreboard_demand_rows.py scores the stored forecasts and scripts/scoreboard_demand_page.py rebuilds this page from them. Run both again whenever the protocol version changes. No forecast is refitted.

docs.title: CRPS at every Primary, days 1 to 10
Does an ERA5-trained weather-to-power model beat the same model trained on ENS?
docs.text:
We asked whether a model that turns weather into solar or wind farm output works better when it is trained on estimates of past weather than when it is trained on archived weather forecasts. We trained one model each way for 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms, gave both the same 51 weather forecasts for the days ahead, and compared their errors over 53 weekly forecast runs in one held-out year. Training on estimates of past weather gave the smaller error for forecasts up to 6 days ahead, and the benefit was not shown beyond that.

Verdict: supported up to day 6, not supported beyond. Stage 1a (one XGBoost model per series, trained on ERA5 (a reanalysis, an estimate of past weather) and CAMS (the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service's satellite estimate of sunlight), no calendar and no power-history columns) applied to the 51 members of ENS (the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts' ensemble forecast) and averaged has a smaller error than the same columns trained on ENS weather, for lead bands up to 6 days, for 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms, in one held-out year (fold A, 53 weekly runs). The planned contrasts were revised after two scientific reviews, so they are not pre-registered. The full write-up is the study README in studies/stage1_pilot/README.md.

docs.title: Input columns
docs.text:
Every arm except c0 gets the same columns, and none is a calendar column or a power lag. Solar zenith and azimuth carry the time of day and the time of year.

  • Solar farms (9 columns): shortwave, longwave, temperature_2m, dew_point_temperature_2m, pressure_surface, precipitation, wind_speed_10m, solar_zenith, solar_azimuth.
  • Wind farms (6 columns): wind_speed_10m, wind_speed_100m, wind_dir_sin_10m, wind_dir_cos_10m, wind_dir_sin_100m, wind_dir_cos_100m. The wind farms' ERA5 cells have no temperature or pressure on disk.
  • ens_trained_plus_s1 adds one column, stage1a_prediction.
  • The *_calendar arms (the first run) add hour_sin, hour_cos, doy_sin, and doy_cos (solar 13 columns, wind 10).
  • c0, the production control, has 24 columns: categorical_precipitation_type_surface, dew_point_temperature_2m, downward_short_wave_radiation_flux_surface, geopotential_height_500hpa, local_day_of_week, local_day_of_week_cos, local_day_of_week_sin, local_time_of_day_cos, local_time_of_day_sin, local_time_of_year_cos, local_time_of_year_sin, local_utc_offset_minutes, power_lag_24h, power_lag_48h, power_lag_168h, power_lag_336h, pressure_reduced_to_mean_sea_level, pressure_surface, temperature_2m, windchill, wind_direction_10m, wind_direction_100m, wind_speed_10m, wind_speed_100m.

docs.title: Planned contrasts (revised)
docs.text:
• P1 (s1_memberavg minus ens_trained) is material up to day 6 for both technologies. Wind -3.18, -4.04, and -2.37 points at 0 to 24 h, 1 to 2 days, and 3 to 6 days; solar -1.23, -1.41, and -0.73. At 7 to 10 and 11 to 15 days neither passes.
  • P2 (adding stage 1a's prediction as a column to ens_trained) is not material anywhere. Solar -0.06 (-0.12 to -0.01), wind +0.02 (+0.01 to +0.03) over all leads.
  • Beyond day 6 stage 1a is within about 1 point of climatology.

docs.title: What else the study found
docs.text:
• Averaging the 51 members is associated with a much larger drop in error for the ERA5-trained model (-0.70 solar, -2.23 wind) than for the ENS-trained model (-0.15, -0.22). With the control member alone, ERA5 training is associated with lower error at 0 to 2 days and higher error at 7 to 15 days.
  • Removing hour and day-of-year columns lowered the ENS-trained error by 1.13 (solar) and 3.40 (wind) points and the ERA5-trained error by 0.23 (solar) and 0 (wind). The first run's control, with 24 production columns, looked like it memorised calendar position.

docs.title: Effect of the feature lists (post hoc)
docs.text:
Removing the hour and day-of-year columns helped the ENS-trained model a lot and the ERA5-trained model little. The first run gave every arm those four calendar columns, and the production control also had 24 production columns including power lags. The table gives each change in mean absolute error over all leads, in points of capacity, with 95% month-resampled intervals. Every row is post hoc. The first run's arms are the *_calendar arms, scored on the same cases.

change solar wind ERA5-trained, calendar columns removed (F1) -0.23 (-0.47 to -0.08) +0.03 (-0.08 to +0.15) ENS-trained, calendar columns removed (F2) -1.13 (-1.71 to -0.65) -3.40 (-4.81 to -1.97) ENS-trained, 24 production columns replaced by the common columns (E13) -0.49 (-0.70 to -0.29) -1.99 (-2.73 to -1.31)
  • The ENS-trained model with calendar columns is the one that does worse. The ENS training frame repeats each valid time about 15 times, once per lead, so a model given the calendar position can learn the weather of that day rather than a weather-to-power relation.
  • The first run's headline against the production control was largely this effect. The common feature list, with no calendar column, is used in every arm of the revised contrasts.

docs.title: Gains in the tails (exploratory)
docs.text:
For wind, the gain from ERA5 training is much larger on the largest outputs; for solar it is larger in points at short leads but uncertain. The tail is the cases where observed power exceeds the series' 90th percentile of cleaned power in stage 1a's training window (20,020 solar and 9,747 wind cases per seed). The table gives s1_memberavg minus ens_trained in points of capacity, with 95% month-resampled intervals, against the same contrast on all cases.

  • Relative to each arm's own error, the wind gain is about 12% in the tail and 10% overall. The top-decile error of ens_trained is 53.22 points and of s1_memberavg 47.08, against 17.09 and 15.39 over all cases. At 0 to 24 h the tail gain is 42% of the error against 27% overall.
  • For solar the relative gain is smaller in the tail (4% against 7% over all leads), and every solar tail interval over all leads and at 0 to 24 h and 3 to 6 days spans zero.
  • Tail errors are large for every forecast, and the weather input is associated with most of them. era5_ceiling has a top-decile error of 13.16 (wind) and 18.43 (solar) points. Without a second model, both ERA5-trained and ENS-trained forecasts miss most of the largest wind outputs.
  • The control member alone gives the same tail result for wind (-6.95, -8.39 to -5.23), so averaging the members is not needed for the tail gain, unlike the all-cases gain.
  • Selecting on the observed value truncates the outcome, so slopes on this subset are not comparable across studies; only paired differences are reported. Tail pinball loss, exceedance Brier scores, and reliability for the probabilistic forecasts are in the stage 2 experiment.

docs.title: Failures and limits
docs.text:
• The first run compared against a control that memorised calendar position, and the headline was revised after two Opus reviews. The revised contrasts were chosen after seeing the first run.
  • One held-out year, nine generators in two weather regions, fold A only, 24 decisions without a multiple-comparison correction.
  • ENS is biased against ERA5 (10 m wind 13% to 15% slower, shortwave 7% brighter). Mapping ENS onto ERA5 before stage 1a is untested.

docs.title: Lessons for later experiments
docs.text:
• Give every arm the same feature columns, and add a control without calendar columns whenever the training rows repeat a valid time.
  • Report the benchmark's absolute score and a climatology row beside every contrast.
  • Predictions: the per-member predictions of every arm are under data/studies/per_study/stage1_pilot/ (stage1a/, ens_trained/, scores/). They have not been written into data/ml-experiments/00001-era5-trained-stage1a-vs-ens-trained/predictions/ with a manifest, because the experiment_store module of PR #1187 does not exist yet.

docs.title: Does a stage 2 calibrator beat the pooled stage 1a mixture?
docs.text:
We asked whether a second model, which corrects the spread of the forecast (its 5% to 95% band) produced by a first weather-to-power model, makes solar and wind farm forecasts better than simply pooling the first model's output over the 51 weather forecasts. We compared both with a model trained directly on archived weather forecasts, for 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms over 53 weekly forecast runs in one held-out year. Pooling the first model's output beat the model trained on archived forecasts. The second model gave no improvement over pooling, and made the solar forecasts worse.

Verdict: the pooled ERA5-trained mixture beats the ENS-trained quantile model, and the stage 2 calibrator and learned blend did not improve on it, and were worse for solar. Study 2b ran in one held-out year (fold A, 53 weekly runs) for 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms. The full write-up is the Results section of studies/stage1_pilot/README_stage2.md. ERA5 is a reanalysis, an estimate of past weather. ENS is the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts' ensemble forecast, which has 51 members. The stage 2 calibrator is a second model that corrects the forecast quantiles that stage 1a produces.

docs.title: Input columns
docs.text:
The columns are those of experiment 00001, with no calendar column and no power lag.

  • Solar farms (9 columns): shortwave, longwave, temperature_2m, dew_point_temperature_2m, pressure_surface, precipitation, wind_speed_10m, solar_zenith, solar_azimuth.
  • Wind farms (6 columns): wind_speed_10m, wind_speed_100m, wind_dir_sin_10m, wind_dir_cos_10m, wind_dir_sin_100m, wind_dir_cos_100m.
  • The calibrator takes the stage 1a quantiles for one ensemble member plus the same columns.

docs.text:
• Q1 (stage 2 minus the mixture) is not material. Solar +0.40 (+0.26 to +0.61), wind +0.26 (-0.17 to +0.64).
  • Q2 (stage 2 minus the ENS-trained quantile arm) is material for wind only. Wind -0.36 (-0.59 to -0.12), solar +0.17 (-0.03 to +0.50).

docs.title: What else the study found
docs.text:
• For the mixture and stage 2 arms, the long ERA5 history changes the CRPS by 0.01 to 0.09 points against stage 1a trained on the ENS months only.
  • In the tail the ERA5-trained gain for wind is not larger than at the centre of the distribution. The exceedance Brier scores of the 90th and 95th percentiles improve by 0.50 and 0.27 over the ENS-trained arm.
  • The ENS-trained arm under-forecasts wind exceedances, and stage 2's bins above 0.30 are also under-forecast.
  • The learned blend does not help reliably. It changes the CRPS by +0.00 to +0.08 for stage 2.

docs.title: Failures and limits
docs.text:
• One fold, one weather product, single-member training rows, no power lags, no per-series calibrators, and 12 validation months.
  • Quantile-mapping ENS onto ERA5 before stage 1a is untested.
  • Long feature lists were not run in this experiment; experiment 00001 reports that comparison.

docs.title: Lessons for later experiments
docs.text:
• Report the pooled mixture beside any stage 2 arm, because the mixture is the reference stage 2 has to beat.
  • Predictions are under data/studies/per_study/stage2_pilot/ and are not yet in data/ml-experiments/ with a manifest.

docs.title: Does an ERA5-trained weather-to-power model beat the same model trained on ENS, for demand?
docs.text:
We asked whether a model that turns weather into electricity demand is more accurate when it is trained on estimates of past weather than when it is trained on archived weather forecasts. This repeats for demand the test that experiment 00001 ran for solar and wind farms. We trained the model both ways on 22 series that are not wind or solar farms (16 Primary substation demand series, 4 flows at bulk supply points and grid supply points, a battery, and a biofuel generator), scored both on the same 51 weather forecasts, and repeated the comparison after adding the calendar and recent power to both. Training on estimates of past weather gave the larger error.

Verdict: not supported. The ERA5-trained model has a larger error than the ENS-trained model for these 22 series, both with weather only and with the calendar added. The plan below was written before the first scored fit. The experiment repeats experiment 00001 for the 22 series of the fold A frames that are not wind or solar farms. The write-up below the plan is filled in after the run. ERA5 is a reanalysis, an estimate of past weather. ENS is the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts' ensemble forecast, which has 51 members.

docs.title: Plan
docs.text:
Question. Does stage 1a (one XGBoost model per series, trained on ERA5, applied to each of the 51 ENS members' weather and averaged) forecast demand better than the same model trained on ENS weather, and does the answer change when the calendar and lagged power are added to both?

Series. The 22 series of fold A that are not wind or solar farms, labelled D1 to D22: 16 disaggregated primary-substation demand series, 4 bulk-supply and grid-supply point flows, and 2 others (a battery and a biofuel generator). The results report the three groups separately. Each series takes ERA5 weather from the nearest cell of the 121-cell stage 1 box.

Row set and folds. Validation 2025-07-01 to 2026-06-30, on the 73 runs of the row set fold_a_every5d_v1: every fifth day at 00:00 UTC from 2025-07-01. The fold A frames of the quick-wins study hold Tuesday runs only (row set fold_a_tuesdays_v1), which puts every case of the 0 to 24 h band on a Tuesday or Wednesday. The five-day step cycles the run's weekday, so every lead band has about 14% of its cases on each weekday of the valid time. The ENS-trained arms train on the control member of every daily run from 2024-04-01 to 2025-06-30, keeping valid times up to 2025-06-30. Both sets of rows come from demand_build_ens.py, which reads the ENS archive and uses production's half-hourly resampling; for the 2025-07-01 run it reproduces the fold A frame's weather columns and 24 h and 48 h lags exactly. Stage 1a trains on valid times from 2019-09 to 14 days before the first run. Seeds 0, 1, and 2. A first fit on the Tuesday runs was run before this row set was chosen and has not been scored; it is kept as a labelled reference.

Weather columns, the same in every arm (ENS serves each; ERA5 gives the same quantity): temperature_2m, dew_point_temperature_2m, shortwave, longwave, pressure_surface, pressure_msl, precipitation, wind_speed_10m, wind_speed_100m, and the precipitation-type code (an integer 0 to 8). ERA5 shortwave is clipped at zero before use. No 500 hPa geopotential height is used, because it is not on disk for ERA5.

Variants. Each variant gives every arm the same extra columns.

  • V0 (main): the weather columns only. No calendar column and no power lag.
  • V1: V0 plus the local hour of day and the local day of week.
  • V2: V1 plus the power lags at 24, 48, 168, and 336 hours, null where the lag is no longer than the lead. The ENS-trained arm reads the lags from the fold A frames. For the ERA5-trained arm each training row draws one lead uniformly from 0.5 to 351 hours and nulls the lags that lead rules out.

Arms.

  • ens_trained: the columns trained on the ENS control member, applied to each of the 51 members and averaged (the benchmark).
  • s1_memberavg: the columns trained on ERA5, applied to each member and averaged.
  • s1_short: as s1_memberavg, trained on ERA5 from 2024-04 only (isolates the training weather from the training length).
  • ens_trained_dedup (V1 and V2 only): the ENS-trained arm on one row per valid time (the shortest lead). The ENS training frame repeats each valid time about 15 times, once per lead, which lets a model with calendar columns memorise the calendar position, as in 00001. The dedup arm is the guard.
  • s1_recency, s1_nocovid (V0 and V1; exploratory): stage 1a with weights that halve every 2 years of age, and stage 1a without 2020-03 to 2021-07.
  • climatology (mean by local month and half-hour of the day) and climatology_dow (the same, separately for weekdays, Saturdays, and Sundays), 2019-09 to 2025-06-16.

Planned contrasts (mean absolute error, points of capacity; ensemble-mean forecast):

  • D1: s1_memberavg minus ens_trained, V0.
  • D2: s1_memberavg minus ens_trained_dedup, V1.
  • D3: s1_memberavg minus ens_trained_dedup, V2.

Every other number is exploratory: the contrasts against ens_trained in V1 and V2, the short-training and regime arms, the contrasts by series group, the top-decile contrasts, and the climatology rows. The top decile is the cases where observed power exceeds the series' 90th percentile of cleaned power in stage 1a's training window. Intervals resample whole validation months and the three fitting seeds, as in 00001. Absolute scores are reported for every arm.

Check before any fit. The diurnal profile of ERA5's ssrd against the solar zenith is compared with ERA5's hour-ending convention, and the result is reported in the write-up, in case the label is shifted. The weather columns of ENS member 0 at short lead are compared with ERA5 at the same valid time, as in 00001.

To be added. A CAMS arm: stage 1a with CAMS shortwave irradiance in place of ERA5's in training only, as in 00001, at the 22 locations. The CAMS download is running; the arm is reported when it finishes.

Not tested here. Where lagged power should enter a two-stage forecast, several weather models, quantile forecasts, and a second fold.

docs.title: Input columns
docs.text:
Every arm gets the same columns within a variant. The columns are not production's.

  • Weather, 10 columns (V0): temperature_2m (°C), dew_point_temperature_2m (°C), shortwave (W/m², mean over the half-hour), longwave (W/m²), pressure_surface (Pa), pressure_msl (Pa), precipitation (kg m⁻² s⁻¹), wind_speed_10m (m/s), wind_speed_100m (m/s), and precipitation_type (an integer code). ERA5 gives each from its nearest cell of the stage 1 box, with ssrd and strd divided by 3600, tp converted to a rate, and the wind speed taken from the components. ENS gives each directly, or from its wind components.
  • Calendar, 2 columns added in V1: hour_local (fractional local hour of day) and day_of_week_local (Monday is 1).
  • Power lags, 4 columns added in V2: power_lag_24h, power_lag_48h, power_lag_168h, and power_lag_336h in MW, null where the lag is no longer than the lead.
  • Not used: the 500 hPa geopotential height, windchill, rolling weather means, sine and cosine time columns, the UTC offset, wind direction, the lead, and spread across the ensemble members.

docs.title: Checks before the fits
docs.text:
• ERA5 ssrd label: its correlation with the top-of-atmosphere cosine of the zenith is 0.899 for the unshifted hour-ending label and 0.860 and 0.869 for labels one hour earlier and later. The label is not shifted.
  • ENS against ERA5 at the same valid time (member 0, lead under 36 h): the continuous weather columns correlate 0.93 to 0.999. Precipitation correlates 0.67 and the precipitation-type code 0.35. ENS also carries a code 12 that ERA5 never shows. Mean 10 m wind speed is 4.81 m/s in ENS and 5.46 m/s in ERA5, so the two sets of inputs differ in more than noise; this shift is a candidate explanation for the ERA5-trained loss that the study does not isolate.
  • Row set fold_a_every5d_v1: every lead band has 14% of its cases on each weekday of the valid time. In the Tuesday-only set of the fold A frames, 0 to 24 h has 60% Tuesday and 40% Wednesday. The new extraction reproduces the fold A frame's weather and lag columns exactly for the run of 2025-07-01.

docs.text:
Mean absolute error in points of capacity, over the 22 series, with 95% intervals that resample whole validation months.

arm weather only (V0) with calendar (V1) with calendar and lags (V2) ens_trained 13.67 (12.36 to 14.80) 11.62 (10.70 to 12.43) 11.19 (10.38 to 11.89) ens_trained_dedup 11.33 (10.34 to 12.20) 15.44 (14.83 to 16.02) s1_memberavg 15.04 (13.91 to 15.95) 13.00 (12.09 to 13.80) 11.29 (10.36 to 12.06) s1_short 13.96 (12.56 to 15.15) 11.71 (10.64 to 12.59) 10.91 (9.94 to 11.66) climatology 13.92 (13.05 to 14.70) climatology_dow 13.76 (12.91 to 14.52)

docs.title: Planned contrasts
docs.text:
• D1 (ERA5-trained minus ENS-trained, weather only) is not material, and the sign is against the hypothesis. All leads +1.37 (+0.68 to +2.17), 1 of 12 months better. Every lead band is positive.
  • D2 (ERA5-trained minus the one-row-per-valid-time ENS-trained arm, with calendar) is not material, and also positive: +1.67 (+1.11 to +2.29).
  • D3 reads as material, and the reading is wrong. The reference arm is the one-row-per-valid-time ENS-trained arm with lags, which scores 15.44 against 11.19 for the ENS-trained arm on all rows (+4.25, +3.58 to +4.99). Keeping only the shortest lead of each valid time leaves the lags present in nearly every training row, which is consistent with the model failing at leads where the lags are null (the arm scores 8.25 at 0 to 24 h and 18.01 at 11 to 15 days). The fairer comparison, against the all-rows ENS-trained arm, is +0.10 (-0.26 to +0.50): no difference. The decision rule was written before the run, so D3 stays as planned, and the planned contrast is not evidence for ERA5 training.

docs.title: What else the study found
docs.text:
All rows below are exploratory.

  • The long ERA5 history is associated with the larger error. Training on ERA5 from 2024-04 only is associated with an error lower by 1.07 (V0), 1.30 (V1), and 0.38 (V2) points against 2019 onward. Weights that halve every 2 years are associated with an error lower by 0.50 and 0.53 (V0, V1), and dropping 2020-03 to 2021-07 with 0.18 and 0.23. The short-history model is within 0.3 points of the ENS-trained model in V0 and V1, and 0.28 points better with lags (differences of level means; no paired interval was computed).
  • Weather alone has little skill for demand. Weather-only models score 13.7 to 15.0, the climatology by weekday type 13.8. Adding the calendar is associated with an ERA5-trained error lower by 2.04 points, and adding lags with a further 1.71. The ERA5-trained weather-only model is worse than the climatology (+1.12, 0 of 12 months), and the ENS-trained one beats it by only 0.25.
  • The ENS-trained arm with calendar columns is slightly better with one row per valid time (-0.29, -0.46 to -0.12), so the repeated valid times were associated with a slightly larger error here. The difference is -0.08 (-0.19 to +0.04) for the 16 primary-substation series and -1.42 for the 4 grid flows, so the grid flows carry it.
  • The ERA5-trained model gains on the largest values of primary demand. In the cases where observed primary-substation demand exceeds the series' 90th percentile, the weather-only ERA5-trained error is 2.74 points lower (-3.56 to -2.22; 12 of 12 months), and the contrasts with calendar (-1.61) and with calendar and lags (-2.44) are also below zero. The decile is chosen after seeing the observed power, a post hoc subset to which the decision rule does not apply, and selecting on high observed power favours any model that predicts higher values. Across all 22 series the top-decile contrast is not distinguishable from zero (-0.33, -0.93 to +0.22).
  • The loss is larger for the grid flows and for the battery and biofuel series. D1 is +0.82 for the 16 primary-substation series and +2.56 for the 4 bulk and grid supply flows, and +3.35 for the battery and biofuel series. The grid-flow interval (+0.19 to +5.28) rests on 4 series.

docs.title: Is the long history's loss bad early data or drift? (post hoc)
docs.text:
Bad early data explains almost none of the loss; the error falls steadily as the training start moves later. The ERA5-trained model was refitted with different training windows, in the weather only and weather plus calendar variants (demand_history_check.py). The table gives each window's error against the 2019-onward model, with 95% month-resampled intervals.

training window weather only with calendar 2019 onward (reference) 15.04 13.00 first 6 months of each long series dropped -0.09 (-0.12 to -0.05) -0.11 (-0.18 to -0.05) from 2020-09 -0.07 (-0.12 to -0.01) -0.15 (-0.21 to -0.08) from 2021-09 -0.37 (-0.49 to -0.25) -0.42 (-0.53 to -0.31) from 2022-09 -0.90 (-1.28 to -0.57) -0.91 (-1.24 to -0.62) from 2023-09 -1.32 (-1.81 to -0.90) -1.49 (-1.88 to -1.11) from 2024-04 -1.07 (-1.76 to -0.48) -1.29 (-1.81 to -0.83)
  • The early months look normal. Monthly levels and spreads of the three series with the largest gap show no flat runs and no implausible values. The first-6-months cut changes the error by about 0.1 points.
  • Three series carry most of the gap. Weather-only error for D6 and D1 (grid flows) and D8 (primary demand) falls by 9.2, 3.9, and 8.6 points between the 2019 and the 2024-04 start. For 13 of the 22 series the windows differ by less than 0.5 points.
  • The levels of those series shifted over the years. D8's median power over capacity falls from about 0.75 to about 0.3, and D6's changes sign. This is consistent with changes in the electricity network or in embedded generation, which the study does not isolate.

docs.title: Failures and limits
docs.text:
• One held-out year, one fold, 73 runs. The 22 series include 6 that are not demand (4 flows, a battery, and a biofuel generator), which the groups report separately.
  • D3's reference arm fails by construction. The three-variant design should have given the one-row-per-valid-time guard only to V1.
  • The climatology falls back to the series' mean by half-hour of the day (and by day type, for climatology_dow), then to its overall mean, for a month a short series has no training data in.
  • The ERA5 history includes 2020-03 to 2021-07, and the study does not separate the effects of the pandemic, growth in embedded generation, and changes of electricity network topology on the long history.
  • No hyperparameter is tuned per arm: every model uses 500 boosting rounds with the same settings.
  • A first fit on the Tuesday runs of the fold A frames was run before the row set was chosen and has not been scored.

docs.title: Lessons for later experiments
docs.text:
• Give a guard arm the variant it guards, and check that the guard arm's own error is sensible.
  • A later experiment could test ERA5 training on recent years, or recency weights, with the short-history effect separated from demand drift.
  • Report the weekday-by-lead balance of any row set whose runs share a weekday.

docs.title: Where should lagged power enter a two-stage demand forecast?
docs.text:
We asked where recent measured power should enter a demand forecast built in stages. Stage 1a turns weather into a demand forecast. Stage 1b is a second model that corrects stage 1a using recent power. Stage 2 is a calibrator that sets the spread of the forecast (its 5% to 95% band). Recent power can go into stage 1b, into stage 2, or into both. We fitted each placement on the same inputs for 16 Primary substations (substations that step power down to the local distribution network), and compared the forecast error up to 48 hours ahead. Giving recent power to stage 2 lowered the error more than giving it to stage 1b, so the idea that stage 1b is the better place was refuted.

Verdict: refuted. For the 16 Primary substations, lagged power improved the forecast more when it entered the stage 2 calibrator (arm L3) than when it entered stage 1b (arm L2c, which pairs stage 1b with a calibrator that has no lagged power). The planned primary contrast, L2c minus L3 for leads up to 48 hours, was +0.84 points of capacity (99% interval +0.28 to +1.50), and 9 of the 12 validation months favoured L3. We had set the bar for refutation at a difference of at least +0.15 points with the interval wholly above zero (every value in the interval above zero), and both conditions hold. The plan below was committed before any fit, and the results above it were written after the run. A point of capacity is 1% of the series' effective capacity.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Lagged power in the calibrator scored as low as any arm at every lead for the Primary substations. Up to 48 hours ahead, the quantile score (twice the mass-weighted pinball loss, an estimate of the continuous ranked probability score, in points of capacity; smaller is better) was 5.31 for L3 and 5.25 for L2+L3, against 6.14 for L2c, 7.11 for the lag-free calibrated arm R0c, and 8.12 for stage 1a alone (R0). Over all leads the scores were 6.36, 6.34, 6.95, 7.47, and 7.88. The advantage of L3 over R0c shrinks from 2.0 points in the first 24 hours to 0.8 points at 11 to 15 days, and stays below zero.

All five planned contrasts were computed for the Primary substations. Negative means the first arm is better, and the intervals are at 99%.

  • C1 (primary), L2c minus L3: +0.84 up to 48 h (+0.28 to +1.50), and +0.59 over all leads (+0.22 to +1.06). The interval for C1 is above zero in every lead band, but L2c is better in 8 of the 16 series up to 48 h, so the advantage of L3 is an average over mixed series.
  • C2, L3 minus R0c: -1.80 up to 48 h (-2.72 to -1.00), negative in 12 of 12 months and 16 of 16 series.
  • C3, L2c minus R0c: -0.97 up to 48 h (-1.25 to -0.66), negative in 12 of 12 months and 16 of 16 series.
  • C4, L2+L3 minus L2c: -0.90 up to 48 h (-1.55 to -0.32).
  • C5, L2+L3 minus L3: -0.06 up to 48 h (-0.15 to +0.03), so using both placements adds nothing detectable to L3 up to 48 h. In the first 24 hours the difference is -0.12 (-0.22 to -0.02), below the 0.15 bar.

The plan's second prediction also failed. The plan predicted that C1 would lie within plus and minus 0.15 from the 3 to 6 d band onward. C1 was +0.73 (+0.28 to +1.25) at 3 to 6 days, +0.52 (+0.18 to +0.91) at 7 to 10 days, and +0.44 (+0.11 to +0.84) at 11 to 15 days, so stage 1b's persistence does not fade into equality with the calibrator.

The BSP and GSP results are descriptive, from two series each, and do not decide anything. Up to 48 h, L3 scored 6.48 for the two bulk supply points and 15.21 for the two grid supply points, against 6.32 and 15.50 for L2c. C1 was -0.17 (-0.54 to +0.20) for the bulk supply points and +0.29 (-0.42 to +0.82) for the grid supply points, so no difference between the placements was detected there. The grid supply points' error is dominated by drift: stage 1a alone scored 21.1 over all leads from the 2023-09 window and 26.4 from the 2019-09 window.

A lag-free calibrator lowered the quantile score at short leads, and the calendar columns made no detectable difference to stage 1a or stage 1b. In the exploratory contrasts (95% intervals, Primary), the lag-free calibrator lowered stage 1a's score by 1.02 up to 48 h (E4) and stage 1b's by 0.52 (E3). Those two arms are the only ones with an uncalibrated twin, and the intervals of both gains include zero at some leads, for example E4 at 7 to 10 days. The calibrator raised the median's mean absolute error up to 48 h, from 9.07 to 9.41 for stage 1a and from 7.57 to 8.17 for stage 1b. Stage 1a alone scored 8.12 up to 48 h and day-type climatology 8.14, so stage 1a without a calibrator is no better than climatology on this score. Dropping the calendar columns changed stage 1a's score by +0.07 (-0.23 to +0.34) up to 48 h (E12) and stage 1b's by -0.02 (-0.34 to +0.25) (E13), and C1 was not repeated without the calendar columns. The 2023-09 training window beat the 2019-09 window for stage 1a by 0.95 (E10), and C1 keeps its sign from the 2019-09 window (+1.11, E7). The ENS-trained reference R1 scored 7.69 up to 48 h, and L3 beat it by 2.38 (E14).

In typical runs, the three arms follow the daily shape and differ mainly in the first day's level. The examples are seed 0 and the three lowest-labelled Primary substations, with each run picked by L3's quantile score over 72 hours. In the worst runs, all three arms miss the level by about the same amount, so recent power does not repair a persistent offset between the weather-driven forecast and the substation. That rule for the worst run is unfavourable to L3.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The lagged arms are a ceiling. The residuals at lag times use ERA5 weather at the lag time, which production does not have in time. L2, L2c, L3, and L2+L3 are an upper bound on what production can do.
  • Stage 1a's input columns come from experiment 00006. The input-feature sweep chose them on its selection fold before it scored any 2025-07 data, so this experiment's validation year did not influence them. This experiment used days_to_christmas as experiment 00006 listed it when the fits started. Experiment 00006 later weakened the evidence for that column: its confirmed set is the weather block, the clock columns, and covid_indicator, and the holiday flags were the most consistently supported calendar columns.
  • The 2023-09 start of the primary window was chosen after seeing results. The start comes from experiment 00003 and from the confirmation year of experiment 00006, not from a selection year. The 2019-09 window gives the same sign for C1.
  • One column list was used for all 20 series. Experiment 00006 suggests different lists for the BSP and GSP series, so their results may understate what a tuned list gives.
  • The reviews used Sonnet, not Opus, for the code. The ml-experiment skill calls for Opus on the code of a complex experiment, and the maintainer asked for Opus only where vital.

docs.title: Lessons learned
docs.text:
• Put recent power in the calibrator first. For Primary substations, the calibrator with recent-origin inputs beat the calibrator plus stage 1b up to 48 h by 0.84 points, and using both placements lowered the quantile score by at most 0.12 points.
  • Calibrate stage 1a before judging lags. At short leads the lag-free calibrator is worth about 1 point of capacity on the quantile score, so a comparison against uncalibrated stage 1a overstates what lags add. It does not improve the median.
  • Check drift before comparing series groups. The grid supply points' error falls by a fifth between the full history and the 2023-09 window, so a mean over series types would mostly measure drift.
  • Report the number of series that agree with each mean. C1 favours L3 on average, and L2c is better in half of the series.

docs.title: Plan
docs.text:
Question. A two-stage forecast has two places to put recent observed power. Stage 1b adds a learned correction to the weather-only forecast of stage 1a. Stage 2 calibrates the ensemble's distribution and can take the recent power as inputs. Which placement gives the better probabilistic forecast, and does using both placements together add anything?

Series. The 20 demand series of experiment 00003 whose substation_type in the TimeSeriesMetadata table is Primary, BSP (bulk supply point), or GSP (grid supply point): 16 primary substations, 2 bulk supply points, and 2 grid supply points, labelled D1 to D22 as in 00003. The battery and the biofuel generator of 00003 (D7 and D20, both of substation type EHV Customer) are dropped, because the maintainer asked for substation series only. The inference is to these 20 series, which the bootstrap treats as fixed. NGED cares most about Primary substations, so the 16 Primary substations are the headline of every score and contrast. The 2 BSP and 2 GSP series are reported separately, as descriptive results from two series each, and no mean over all three types is a headline. The write-up reports the number of series on which each contrast has the sign of its mean.

Row set and folds. The validation year is the 73 runs of fold_a_every5d_v1: European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) ensemble (ENS) runs at 00:00 UTC every fifth day from 2025-07-01 to 2026-06-30, as in 00003. Nothing is scored on or after 2026-07-01. The fitting seeds are 0, 1, and 2. The XGBoost hyperparameters are those of 00003 (eta 0.05, depth 6, subsample 0.8, 500 rounds, no early stopping), with colsample_bytree and colsample_bynode both 1.0.

Information available at forecast time. A forecast initialised at T may use observed power up to and including T - 0.5 h, the newest half-hour observation before T. This origin is T0. Both placements use it. The write-up states this assumes no telemetry delay.

Recent-origin inputs, identical for stage 1b and for the stage 2 calibrator. For a target time t and a lead t - T, the inputs are the stage 1a residual (observed power over effective capacity minus the stage 1a forecast at the observed ERA5 weather) at T0, at T0 - 1 h, at T0 - 3 h, at the latest time of day equal to t's that is at or before T0, and at the latest time of the week equal to t's that is at or before T0. They also include the four power lags (24, 48, 168, and 336 hours before t) and the four lag anomalies (observed power at the lag time minus the stage 1a forecast at that time), each null where the lag is no longer than the lead. Stage 1b and the calibrator also receive the lead. Neither receives a calendar column. This gives the two placements the same information, so a difference between them comes from where the information enters.

Stage 1a input columns (from experiment 00006). The 13 columns are: the nine weather columns shortwave, longwave, temperature_2m, dew_point_temperature_2m, pressure_surface, precipitation, wind_speed_10m, solar_zenith, and solar_azimuth (the sun position at the midpoint of the half-hour); the local hour_local and day_of_week_local; covid_indicator (1 from 2020-03-23 to 2021-07-19, otherwise 0, so 0 throughout validation); and days_to_christmas (signed days to 25 December, clipped to plus and minus 14 days). Experiment 00006 chose this list for Primary substations on its selection year (2024-07 to 2025-06) and confirmed it once on 2025-07 to 2026-06. It suggests different lists for BSP and GSP; this experiment uses one list for all 20 series, and reports BSP and GSP separately as descriptive. ERA5 supplies the weather columns at the series' nearest cell in training, and the ENS member supplies them in forecasting. Experiment 00006 also found that weighting recent years more improves its selection-fold error. This experiment keeps equal weights, and treats a recency-weighted run as an exploratory extra, to be added only if the primary results leave a question it could answer.

Caveats on the column list and the window, added while the fits ran. This experiment used days_to_christmas as experiment 00006 listed it when the fits started. Experiment 00006 later weakened the evidence for that column: its confirmed set is the weather block, the clock columns, and covid_indicator, because days_to_christmas changes sign every late June and its gain is small and uncertain. The 2023-09 start of the primary window comes from experiment 00003 and from the confirmation year of experiment 00006 only, so it was chosen after seeing results and is not a selection-year result. The fits do not change.

Training windows. Each ERA5-trained arm uses the training window starting at 2023-09 (primary) or at 2019-09 (exploratory). The 2023-09 start was chosen after seeing 00003, which found that error falls as the start moves later, and the write-up says so wherever it is used. R0 is also run from 2024-04. Stage 1a's final fit uses ERA5 valid times before 2025-06-17, 14 days before the first validation run. Stage 1b's final fit uses targets up to 2025-06-30 23:30. Residuals after 2025-06-16 come from the final stage 1a, which has not seen them.

Out-of-fold residuals. Stage 1b and the calibrator are trained on residuals of stage 1a, which must not be in-sample. Within each arm's training window, the ERA5 history before 2025-07-01 is split into six time blocks. The residuals of a block come from a stage 1a fitted on the other blocks, leaving a 15-day purge on each side of the held-out block. Those residuals are out of sample for their own block but come from a model that has seen later blocks. The page states this. Residuals at valid times from 2025-07-01 come from the final stage 1a.

Arms. All quantiles are 9 levels (0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.75, 0.9, and 0.95).

  • R0: stage 1a alone, lag-free, with the 9 empirical quantiles of the 51 member forecasts. Windows 2019-09, 2023-09, and 2024-04.
  • R0c: stage 1a, then the lag-free stage 2 calibrator.
  • R1 (reference): one XGBoost model on ENS weather, trained on the control member of every daily run from 2024-04-01 to 2025-06-30, with stage 1a's 13 columns and the four power lags nulled by lead. Training uses every lead of every run. Quantiles are the 9 empirical quantiles of the 51 member forecasts. R1 repeats valid times across leads and has calendar columns, so it can memorise the calendar position (00001), and it is a reference only.
  • R2 (reference): climatology by local month, half-hour of the day, and weekday or weekend, with the 9 quantiles of the training power pooled over the neighbouring months and half-hours, as the ClimatologyForecaster of the baseline_forecasters package defines its cells. It is trained on the window 2019-09 to 2025-06-16, and repeated once per seed.
  • L2: stage 1a plus the stage 1b correction, uncalibrated. Stage 1b is one XGBoost model per series trained on ERA5 history with simulated origins: each target time draws four leads uniformly from 0.5 to 351 hours, which gives the training rows the full lead range. The target is the residual at the target time, and the inputs are the recent-origin inputs. The forecast is stage 1a for each member plus one correction computed once from observed power, then pooled over the members. Fading with lead is learned.
  • L2c: L2's member forecasts, then the lag-free stage 2 calibrator. This is stage 1b with a calibrator that sees no lags.
  • L3: lag-free stage 1a, then the stage 2 calibrator with the recent-origin inputs.
  • L2+L3: L2's member forecasts, then the stage 2 calibrator with the recent-origin inputs.
  • No-calendar control: R0 and L2 are repeated without hour_local, day_of_week_local, and days_to_christmas (window from 2023-09), to show how much of any gain is the calendar position. The sun position and the lockdown indicator stay.

Stage 2 calibrator. One multi-quantile XGBoost model per series (reg:quantileerror at the 9 levels; depth 4, eta 0.05, 300 rounds, no early stopping, power over effective capacity). Its inputs are the stage 1 statistics over the 51 members (mean, standard deviation, and the 10th, 50th, and 90th percentiles), the lead, and, for L3 and L2+L3, the recent-origin inputs. It trains on every third daily ENS run from 2024-04-01 to 2025-06-30, with valid times up to 2025-06-30 23:30 and all 51 members. The stage 1 inputs on these rows come from a quarterly forward chain: for each quarter from 2024-04, stage 1a and stage 1b are fitted on ERA5 targets that end 15 days before the quarter starts. No calendar column enters the calibrator. Output quantiles are sorted to remove crossings.

Planned contrasts (quantile score over all leads and by lead band, points of capacity; training window from 2023-09; each read at 99% because five are planned). The five are defined on the 16 Primary substations. The same five are also computed for the BSP series and for the GSP series and reported separately, with no decision attached and the multiplicity unchanged:

  • C1 (primary): L2c minus L3. This is placement: both are calibrated and both receive the same inputs. The decision rule applies to cases of leads up to 48 hours.
  • C2: L3 minus R0c (do the recent-origin inputs help at stage 2 at all).
  • C3: L2c minus R0c (do they help through stage 1b at all).
  • C4: L2+L3 minus L2c.
  • C5: L2+L3 minus L3.

Exploratory, and labelled so: the contrasts against uncalibrated arms (L3 minus R0, L2 minus L3, L2+L3 minus the better of L2 and L3, which take their reference from the validation data), the same contrasts from the 2019-09 window, the contrasts by series group and by lead band, the equivalence statement for leads from 3 days, and the mean absolute error of the median. Absolute scores of every arm are reported by lead band with intervals.

Verdict mapping. Supported, refuted, or inconclusive by the decision rule above. A material difference in the opposite direction (L3 better) is a refutation and is reported as such.

Calendar guard. Stage 1a trains on ERA5, which has one row per valid time. Stage 1b and the calibrator have no calendar columns. The no-calendar control above covers stage 1a. No arm uses early stopping, so no inner validation split is needed.

Ceiling label. Residuals at lag times use ERA5 weather at the lag time, which production does not have in time. The write-up labels the L2, L2c, L3, and L2+L3 arms a ceiling.

Reviews. The plan, the code, and the write-up each get a fresh Sonnet reviewer, because the maintainer asked for Opus only where vital. The ml-experiment skill calls for Opus on the code of a complex experiment, so this is a deviation, and the pull request says so.

Size. Complex. The experiment stores predictions and a published page. It does not touch the production serving path or any degradation rule. More than one design defensibly tests the hypothesis. Its new code lives in ml-experiments/, which no other package imports.

docs.title: Not tested here
docs.text: Generator series, a second fold, and several weather models.

docs.title: Which inputs work best for the ERA5-trained demand model (stage 1a)?
docs.text:
We asked which extra inputs most improve a model that turns weather into electricity demand, beyond the weather itself. We tried the hour of day and day of week, a flag for the COVID period, weighting recent years more heavily, and windchill, and compared each with a model given only weather, on 16 Primary substations (substations that step power down to the local distribution network) over a selection year (July 2024 to June 2025, used to choose the inputs) and a confirmation year (July 2025 to June 2026, used to check the choice). Hour of day and day of week helped most, by about a third of the gain we had predicted, and windchill made almost no difference.

Verdict: partly supported. For the Primary substations, the clock (hour of day and day of week) is the largest single input against the weather block alone (W) (-0.55 points of capacity on the selection year and -0.46 on the confirmation year), a third of the 1.5 points the hypothesis predicted. Restricting the verdict to Primary was decided after the plan, at the planning session's request and before the confirmation year was scored; the plan's contrasts were not split by type. Across all series the clock leads on point estimates only (-0.51 against -0.45 for recency weights and -0.40 for the COVID indicator, each against W on the selection year), with no paired interval between them. For the two grid supply points (GSP) the hypothesis fails: the COVID indicator beats the clock, and the clock is not material. Windchill changes the error by less than 0.05 points, as predicted. The hypothesis lists columns, so this page counts recency weights as a training choice and not as an input.

Primary substations are the headline, because NGED cares most about them. Every score below is split by substation type, and no mean over all types is quoted as a result, because the two grid supply points (GSP) have errors about four times those of the Primary substations and would dominate it. A point is 1% of the series' effective capacity, and every score is the mean absolute error of the median. The substations are labelled P1 to P16, B1 and B2, and G1 and G2; no identifier, name, or coordinate appears on this page.

docs.title: What to use for each substation type
docs.text:
The Primary set is the weather block, the clock, a COVID indicator, and the days to Christmas. Greedy forward selection on the selection year (2024-07 to 2025-06) was run for each substation type, starting from the weather block W plus the clock, and stopped when the next addition gained less than 0.1 points. The sets differ by type, and BSP (bulk supply points) and GSP have only two series each:

Substation type Columns added to W plus the clock, in the order selected Series Primary COVID indicator, then days to 25 December (-0.25, then -0.14 points) 13 BSP holiday flags: the day, the day before, and the day after (-0.16 points) 2 GSP COVID indicator, days to the nearest holiday, heating degree-hours (-1.67, -0.24, -0.14 points) 2 One set for all three types (recommended if a single set is required) COVID indicator, days to Christmas inside a 14-day window 18

If one set must serve all three types, use the weather block, the clock, the COVID indicator, and the days to Christmas inside a 14-day window, and weight Primary substations' evidence above that of BSP and GSP. The clock is the largest gain for Primary substations and helps BSP, and its small effect on GSP has an interval that includes zero. The COVID indicator gains -0.26 points for Primary (99.4% interval -0.40 to -0.10) and -1.74 for GSP (-2.76 to -0.69) on the selection year, and is neutral for BSP (-0.02). The days to Christmas gains little over a year (-0.10 for Primary on the confirmation year) and a lot at Christmas: inside 15 December to 7 January it lowers the Primary error by 1.78 points, in each of three years (see the special-day windows below). The column is windowed, meaning it takes the days to 25 December inside 14 days of it and is missing otherwise, because the unwindowed column also marks the half-year, and in the summer school holidays it raises the BSP error by 0.43 points and the GSP error by 2.22. The holiday flags are left out because only BSP selected them, and they raise the BSP and GSP error at Easter. On the confirmation year this set scores 7.61 for Primary, 9.34 for BSP, and 26.65 for GSP, against 7.57, 9.41, and 26.47 for the Primary set with the unwindowed days to Christmas. The BSP set scores 9.53 and the GSP set 27.71, so for those two types the single set beats the set chosen for the type. Recency weights are a training choice, not a column, and are unaffected by this recommendation.

The clock helps Primary substations and BSP but not GSP. On the confirmation year the clock changes the error by -0.46 for Primary (99.4% interval -0.61 to -0.30), -0.30 for BSP (-0.41 to -0.17), and -0.08 for GSP (-0.43 to +0.27, against W).

Only the Primary set was written into this page before anything was scored on 2025-07 to 2026-06. The BSP and GSP sets were selected before the confirmation fits but were not written into the page until after scoring, so their confirmation rows are not pre-committed. The first selection, over all series, chose the days to the nearest holiday where the Primary-only selection chose the days to Christmas, and the Primary-only set replaced it before the confirmation year was scored. The discarded set scores slightly lower on the confirmation year (7.53 against 7.57 for Primary, and 7.04 against 7.11 with recency weights), a difference inside the noise. The Primary set's columns are hour_local, day_of_week_local, covid_indicator (1 from 2020-03-23 to 2021-07-19, and 0 in all later data, so it reads 0 at forecast time), and days_to_christmas (days to 25 December, negative after it, clipped to 14 days either way). Only days_to_christmas is outside the set of derived columns the stage 1 pilot already had. Each column is computable at forecast time from the calendar alone.

Dropping one group at a time from the Primary set shows the clock and the COVID indicator matter most. On the selection year, removing the clock raised the Primary error by 0.59 points (95% interval +0.49 to +0.69), removing the COVID indicator by 0.30 (+0.20 to +0.40), and removing the days to Christmas by 0.14 (-0.06 to +0.35), so the Christmas column is the least certain member of the set (see the Christmas control below).

docs.title: Absolute scores on the confirmation year (2025-07 to 2026-06)
docs.text:
Every Primary arm that adds columns to the weather block scores lower than the weather block alone. The table gives the mean absolute error of the median in points of capacity, with 95% intervals that resample whole months, averaged over three fitting seeds, one XGBoost model per series. The confirmation year scores 14 Primary, two BSP, and two GSP series. The selection year scores 13, two, and two, and a series with under a year of history before a fold is left out of that fold.

Arm Primary (14) BSP (2) GSP (2) Climatology (month, half-hour, weekend) 8.93 (8.61 to 9.28) 13.11 (12.02 to 14.27) 36.62 (33.86 to 39.24) Weather block W 8.31 (8.00 to 8.61) 9.90 (9.01 to 10.85) 30.05 (27.83 to 32.22) W plus clock 7.85 (7.48 to 8.23) 9.60 (8.71 to 10.58) 29.97 (27.83 to 32.02) Primary set (W, clock, COVID, Christmas) 7.57 (7.29 to 7.85) 9.41 (8.57 to 10.26) 26.47 (25.07 to 27.84) Primary set, recent years weighted more 7.11 (6.84 to 7.39) 9.04 (8.36 to 9.74) 23.98 (22.56 to 25.16) Primary set, trained from 2023-09 6.71 (6.37 to 7.10) 8.99 (8.44 to 9.52) 21.73 (19.35 to 23.87) Primary set, weighted, from 2023-09 6.68 (6.36 to 7.05) 8.98 (8.44 to 9.50) 21.51 (19.12 to 23.68) BSP set (W, clock, holiday flags) 9.53 (8.57 to 10.59) GSP set (W, clock, COVID, nearest holiday, heating) 27.71 (25.75 to 29.56)

The weather block, the weather block plus clock, and the Primary set each beat the climatology for every substation type. The paired 95% intervals exclude zero in every case. For Primary the differences are -0.62 (-0.94 to -0.31) for W, -1.07 (-1.42 to -0.73) for W plus clock, and -1.36 (-1.67 to -1.08) for the Primary set. The other arms score below the climatology too, but without a paired interval.

docs.title: Planned contrasts
docs.text:
The contrasts P1 to P9 were fixed in the plan below before any fit. The intervals for the nine planned contrasts are Bonferroni-widened to 99.4%, and the table labels each interval's level. All numbers are changes in the mean absolute error for Primary substations, so negative is better, with three fitting seeds.

Contrast Year Change Interval Material? P1: clock against W selection -0.55 -0.71 to -0.41 (99.4%) yes P1: clock against W confirmation -0.46 -0.61 to -0.30 (99.4%) yes P2: one harmonic of time of year, against W plus clock selection +0.04 -0.40 to +0.37 (99.4%) no P3: holiday flags, against W plus clock selection -0.11 -0.21 to -0.02 (99.4%) marginal (0.106 against the 0.1 floor), and not material on the second selection year P4: previous-24-hour mean temperature selection +0.04 -0.01 to +0.08 (99.4%) no (slightly worse) P5: guarded windchill, against W selection +0.003 -0.011 to +0.016 (99.4%) no effect P6: COVID indicator selection -0.26 -0.40 to -0.10 (99.4%) yes P7: recency weights selection -0.32 -0.49 to -0.13 (99.4%) yes P8: Primary set against W plus clock selection -0.40 -0.73 to -0.10 (99.4%) yes, but the set was chosen on this year P8: Primary set against W plus clock confirmation -0.29 -0.58 to +0.02 (99.4%); -0.50 to -0.07 (95%) not at the planned level P9: trained from 2023-09, against the full history selection -0.05 -0.60 to +0.59 (99.4%) no P9: trained from 2023-09, against the full history confirmation -0.86 -1.19 to -0.48 (99.4%) yes

The selection and confirmation years score different series. The confirmation year scores 14 Primary series and each selection year 13, and two of the 16 Primary series in the metadata are never scored, so a comparison of the 0.55 and 0.46 figures mixes a change of series with a change of year.

P8, the step from the clock to the Primary set, is supported at 95% but not at the planned 99.4% level on the confirmation year. The COVID and Christmas columns together lower the confirmation-year error by 0.29 points, and the planned-level interval touches zero.

The 2023-09 start helps on the confirmation year and not on the selection year, for Primary substations, and the two years differ in season coverage as well as length. On the selection year the start trains on only ten months (2023-09 to 2024-06), which contain no July or August, so two validation months lie outside the season it saw. Adding it to the recency-weighted set changes the error by +0.17 (95% interval -0.18 to +0.57). On the confirmation year it has 22 months, including one summer, and lowers the error by 0.86. The 2023-09 start also makes covid_indicator constant at zero in training, so "Primary set from 2023-09" is in effect the weather block, the clock, and the days to Christmas, and the contrast measures "drop the lockdown handling and keep only recent data". For BSP the contrast is -1.48 (-2.75 to -0.30, 99.4%) on the selection year and -0.42 (-1.09 to +0.15) on the confirmation year. For GSP it is -5.37 (-11.63 to -0.19) and -4.74 (-9.36 to -1.58). The explanation that the long history carries drift is plausible and was not tested. The confirmation year influenced no choice of the selected set, and the 2023-09 start needs a fresh year before anyone adopts it.

P2, P4, and P5 show no detectable gain from these columns, within the intervals. P5 stays within 0.01 points of zero. P2 is +0.04 with a 99.4% interval of -0.40 to +0.37, which allows a gain nearly as large as the clock's, and P4 is +0.04 (-0.01 to +0.08), which is not material. A second selection year (2023-07 to 2024-06, 13 Primary series) repeats P1 -0.50 (-0.66 to -0.34), P2 +0.07 (-0.44 to +0.47), and P7 -0.42 (-0.61 to -0.24) at 99.4%. P4 and P5 change sign (-0.04, -0.12 to +0.03, and -0.005, -0.021 to +0.013), and P3 (-0.07, -0.26 to +0.03) and P6 (-0.11, -0.27 to +0.06) are no longer material. P3, marginal at 0.106 against the 0.1 floor on the selection year, is therefore treated as not material.

The BSP and GSP selection-year contrasts mostly share the Primary signs, with wider intervals from two series each. P1 is -0.37 (-0.59 to -0.16) for BSP and -0.35 (-0.68 to +0.03) for GSP. P3 is +0.01 for GSP against -0.11 for Primary, and P6 is -0.02 for BSP against -0.26 for Primary, so the holiday flags and the COVID indicator do not carry across every type. P6 is -1.74 (-2.76 to -0.69) for GSP.

docs.title: Which columns help and which do not
docs.text:
No single input beats the clock against the weather block alone. The add-one-in contrasts against W on the selection year, for Primary substations, are -0.56 for the clock, -0.29 for recency weights, -0.22 for the COVID indicator, -0.19 for dropping the lockdown months, and every other column lowers it by 0.11 or less (some raise it).

The training-history choices are as large as the best added column. For Primary substations on the selection year, against W plus clock, weighting recent years more (half-life 2 years) lowers the error by 0.32 points, the COVID indicator by 0.25, and dropping the lockdown months from training by 0.21. The graded lockdown indicator (1 for the national lockdowns, 0.5 for the restrictions between them, from approximate dates) scores 7.130 against 7.142 for the 0/1 indicator, so grading adds nothing. On the confirmation year, weighting recent years lowers the Primary error by 0.46 points (95% interval -0.53 to -0.38) more than the unweighted chosen set, and training from 2023-09 lowers it by 0.86 more than the full history (see the table above for the selection year). Adding recency weights to a 2023-09 start gains only 0.03 points (6.71 to 6.68), and adding a 2023-09 start to recency weights gains 0.43 (95% interval -0.61 to -0.24).

Two holiday columns help a little. For Primary substations on the selection year, holiday flags lower the error by 0.10 points (95% interval -0.17 to -0.04) and the holiday name by 0.07 (-0.13 to -0.02). The days to Christmas (-0.10, -0.33 to +0.12) and the days to the nearest holiday (-0.07, -0.24 to +0.09) have intervals that include zero, so only the holiday flags and the holiday name are supported. These intervals use one fitting seed and 12 months. The bridge-day flag changes the error by -0.004 points.

No weather-derived column helps Primary substations. The 24-hour, 72-hour, and 7-day trailing mean temperatures add +0.04, +0.03, and +0.07 points (the 24-hour mean is worse, with 95% interval +0.01 to +0.07), the weighted temperatures (12 hours, 72 hours, 7 days) +0.21 (0.00 to +0.43), heating degree-hours +0.03, the day length and hours since sunrise +0.01, the UTC offset +0.02, and wind-driven heat loss +0.01. The mean of the 3 by 3 block of cells around the nearest cell, in place of the nearest cell, changes the error by -0.01 points. Sun azimuth as sine and cosine lowers it by 0.04 points (-0.08 to -0.02), too small to matter.

Time of year shows no detectable gain in the full weather block. One harmonic of the day of the year adds +0.04 points (-0.28 to +0.29), two harmonics +0.10, and the month as a categorical +0.09 against the weather block plus clock. The intervals allow a gain of up to about 0.3 points.

The masking ablation removes the columns that could carry the season, and time of year then helps. Time of year lowers the Primary error only when the weather block loses sun position and temperature together: -0.56 points (95% interval -0.94 to -0.20) with one harmonic, -0.49 with two, and -0.54 (-0.81 to -0.27) with the month as a categorical. Removing only the sun position gives -0.28 (-0.67 to +0.04), and removing only the temperature and dew point gives +0.09 (-0.16 to +0.32). This supports the explanation that the sun and temperature columns carry the season, for the Primary substations only. A coarser encoding (one harmonic, or month) does no better than a finer one, so the data give no sign that a fine day-of-year encoding lets the trees memorise individual weeks of the training years. In the full weather block, the permutation importance of the sun position and the temperature is large (see below).

Without a time-of-year column the error is highest in November, December, and January, and the one-harmonic column removes December from the worst months. Without the column, the Primary error on the selection year is lowest in July to September (about 6.1 to 6.7) and highest in November (8.97), December (9.17), and January (8.29). The one-harmonic column lowers December by 1.3 points (9.17 to 7.89) and raises July by 0.5 and October by 0.5, without removing the seasonal shape.

docs.title: The unwindowed Christmas column also acts as a half-year flag
docs.text:
days_to_christmas as built also flips sign every late June, so it separates January to June from July to December. The signed distance to the nearest 25 December is clipped at 14 days, and outside the window the clipped value takes the sign of the nearest Christmas. A code reviewer found this after the confirmation year had been scored, and the control was run on all three folds. The column keeps its place in the frozen set, and the control is post hoc. Each row is the change in Primary error against the weather block plus clock plus COVID indicator, with 95% intervals and three fitting seeds:

Encoding added Selection year 2024-07 to 2025-06 Second selection year 2023-07 to 2024-06 Confirmation year days_to_christmas as built -0.14 (-0.36 to +0.06) -0.18 (-0.44 to +0.09) -0.13 (-0.36 to +0.11) Days to Christmas inside a 14-day window, otherwise missing -0.11 (-0.26 to -0.01) -0.14 (-0.39 to +0.03) -0.10 (-0.25 to +0.02) Half-year flag only -0.04 (-0.19 to +0.12) -0.10 (-0.35 to +0.14) -0.03 (-0.21 to +0.15) One harmonic of time of year -0.06 (-0.33 to +0.18) +0.01 (-0.36 to +0.36) -0.15 (-0.42 to +0.14) Holiday flags -0.10 (-0.17 to -0.04) -0.06 (-0.17 to +0.02) -0.07 (-0.14 to -0.02)

Averaged over the year, the data cannot separate a Christmas effect from the half-year step. The windowed column keeps three quarters of the point-estimate gain of the column as built, and the half-year flag alone gains under 0.1 on every fold, but no paired test between these point estimates was run, and every interval of the Christmas column includes zero except the windowed column on the selection year. Only the holiday flags have intervals that exclude zero on two of the three folds. The days to the nearest holiday (clipped at 7 days) has a milder version of the same half-year step, because England has no bank holiday between late May and late August. The next section scores the columns inside the Christmas weeks themselves, where the half-year flag does not reproduce the gain, so the gain there is a Christmas effect.

docs.title: The Christmas columns cut the error at Christmas, and the Easter and summer windows show little
docs.text:
Over 15 December to 7 January the days to Christmas lowers the Primary error by 1.62 points, in each of three years, against 0.13 over the whole year. A column can help on a few hard days and hardly move a yearly average, and the NGED forecasts are most needed on such days. This check was run after the experiment and none of it was pre-registered. It reads the Christmas-control predictions (three folds, three fitting seeds, every substation type) and cuts the valid times into calendar windows by local date. Each window has three occurrences, one per fold, and neighbouring days are correlated, so the 95% intervals, which resample whole days, describe these three years only. Primary substations are harder to forecast at Christmas: the base error (the weather block, clock, and COVID indicator) is 9.66 points over 15 December to 7 January and 11.23 over 24 December to 1 January, against 7.52 on the other days.

Primary, change in error against the base 24 Dec to 1 Jan (27 days) 15 Dec to 7 Jan (72 days) Other days (859 days) Days to Christmas as built -3.35 (-4.21 to -2.51) -1.62 (-2.12 to -1.17) -0.06 (-0.10 to -0.02) Days to Christmas, 14-day window -3.64 (-4.55 to -2.73) -1.78 (-2.30 to -1.26) 0.00 (-0.01 to +0.02) Holiday flags -2.04 (-3.07 to -1.10) -0.73 (-1.20 to -0.30) -0.02 (-0.03 to 0.00) One harmonic of time of year -3.43 (-4.33 to -2.50) -1.74 (-2.25 to -1.25) +0.04 (-0.02 to +0.10) Half-year flag -0.37 (-0.60 to -0.15) -0.08 (-0.24 to +0.06) -0.06 (-0.10 to -0.02)

Over Christmas 2025 the windowed Christmas column follows a substation whose power drops there, and the base set does not. The figure shows 20 December 2025 to 3 January 2026 in the confirmation fold, for P12 (the median-error series), for P10 (the series the windowed column helps most, chosen after the fact from the outcome), and for the mean over the 14 Primary series. It draws the observed power, the base (weather block, clock, COVID indicator), and the base plus the windowed column; the errors of the other configurations are given here and not drawn. Over the window, the mean absolute error of the base is 3.96 points of capacity for P12 and 22.23 for P10, and adding the days to Christmas gives 3.92 and 4.43, the windowed column 3.95 and 4.13, the holiday flags 3.87 and 18.40, and the half-year flag 4.01 and 21.13. P12 is almost unaffected, so the Christmas gain comes from a subset of series. The error of the 14-series mean is 5.15 for the base, 2.84 with the days to Christmas, 2.62 with the windowed column, 3.70 with the holiday flags, and 5.01 with the half-year flag. The holiday flags capture only the bank-holiday days, so they miss the days either side of them, which the days to Christmas covers.

The gain is a Christmas effect, because the half-year flag does not reproduce it. The half-year flag lowers the error by 0.08 over 15 December to 7 January, and the days to Christmas by 1.62.
