The experiment's printed reports and every number on this page are in the private folder data/ml-experiments/00045-pvdis-4-weekly-capacity-asymmetric-l1/ (report.txt is the combined report).

docs.title: The question and why it is worth asking
docs.text:
The question is whether a weekly series of embedded solar capacity behind each Primary substation can be estimated well enough to show real steps and no invented ones. Experiments 00039 and 00040 gave one capacity per season-year, with a detection limit near 2.5% of capacity. NGED holds almost no information on unmetered solar, and a capacity that changes week by week would show when a large rooftop fleet or a farm below 1 MW connects. A free capacity per week would be too noisy. The standard error of a season-year, 1.2% of capacity, implies about 8.7% per week on average (1.2% times the square root of 52), and far more in winter, when the sun is low. A penalty on the weekly increments lets neighbouring weeks share evidence, so that the path steps only where the data support a step.

The maintainer decided that capacity may fall but reluctantly. The fit estimates the solar that the Primary's meter sees, which can fall when home batteries charge from midday solar, when a feeder is permanently reconfigured, or when a solar site is switched off for repairs. A strict non-decreasing constraint would lower past capacity to fit a fall. The penalty on a fall is therefore heavy and finite.

The aim is explanation and a capacity series, not forecast skill. Nothing here touches the production forecast. Experiments 00007, 00009, 00022, and 00031 found small or no forecast gains from solar inputs, and PVDIS-5 tests the forecast question using the vintages this experiment produces.

docs.title: Size, answered against the five triggers
docs.text:
The experiment is complex, because three of the five triggers fire.

  • What gets stored: yes. A private weekly capacity table and a table of real-time vintages under data/ml-experiments/00045-pvdis-4-weekly-capacity-asymmetric-l1/, which SW2-10 reads. Nothing enters a production Delta table.
  • The production serving path: no. Not touched.
  • A degradation rule: no. Not touched.
  • More than one defensible design: yes. The estimator (half-hourly M1, daily sums, or the six-arm combination), the form of the penalty, the placement of the demand cells, and the bootstrap scheme each admit more than one defensible choice. The plan fixes each choice and gives the reason.
  • Code whose callers cannot be named without searching: yes, for one work item. The register loader moves from experiment 00031's folder into packages/studies, and that change is a separate reviewed pull request (work item W0).

The process is therefore the full one: this Opus plan, a Sonnet code review before the run, Sonnet runs and write-up, a Sonnet check of the write-up against the printed report, and a Sonnet prose review. Opus reviews the result when it decides the next part of the series.

docs.title: Earlier advice, followed and departed from
docs.text:
The plan follows nine items of earlier advice and departs from none.

  • Followed: "Divide capacities fitted with M1 by 0.77" (00039): the series is divided by a recovery ratio measured on injected paths. "Do not read a capacity at Kirton as PV alone" (00039): Kirton keeps its status flag in every output. "Leave out the 8 MVA Primaries" (00039): the series covers the 8 Primaries metered in MW. "Treat injection as a test of the PV shape and the irradiance only" (00039): a penalised, constrained fit is nonlinear, so the plan scores the path difference and a semi-synthetic baseline, and adds an additivity check. "Leave Wrangle T1 out of any claim that a Primary is free of a cloud load" (00040): the status column says so. "Do not quote an embedded-solar capacity without a stated bound" (00040): three uncertainty terms are stated and never summed. "Report C as the capacity and keep M1d divided by R as a cross-check" (the experiment 00040 review): the weekly series is checked against C. "Calibrate ENS irradiance to CAMS" (00031): the weekly series uses CAMS only, and PVDIS-5 owns the calibration. "Treat the register as a weak prior at Primaries" (00031): the register check is a soft check.

docs.title: Hypothesis and the five design choices
docs.text:
The estimator is the half-hourly fit M1, with one capacity per week and one set of demand cells per season-year. The fit is

power = cell(season-year, month, local half-hour, day type) + b times heating degree-days - c(w) times u + error,

where u is experiment 00039's unit PV shape from CAMS (the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service) at the Primary, c(w) is the capacity of week w (weeks start on Monday, Europe/London), and the cells are those of experiments 00039 and 00040. A season-year is the 12-month period that experiments 00039 and 00040 used for one capacity. Keeping the cells per season-year means a slow rise in base demand cannot leak into the capacity, and it keeps the recovery ratio of the weekly fit comparable with the season-year ratio. The drawback is that a step at a month boundary is partly absorbed by the cell mean, so the injections include steps placed on month boundaries (risk 2).

M1 is chosen over the daily fit and the six-arm combination for three reasons. The daily fit leaks a day-long cloud load at 3.4 MW per MW, against 2.2 for M1, so a weekly daily-sum fit has seven points per week and the highest exposure. The six-arm combination needs a ratio vector and a noise bootstrap for every arm at every week. The half-hourly fit recovers 0.77 of injected capacity, which the series corrects by dividing by a measured ratio. The season-year mean of the weekly series is checked against the six-arm C of experiment 00040 (check A0), so the series stays tied to the estimate that carries a bound.

The penalty is asymmetric L1 on weekly increments, with the capacity held non-negative. The objective is

0.5 times the squared residual, over the residual variance, plus lambda_up times the sum of the rises plus lambda_down times the sum of the falls.

The problem is convex. The penalty is lambda_up = a times a Primary scale s_P and lambda_down = r times lambda_up. The scale s_P is the median over weeks of the free weekly fit's standard error, so that a is in units of one weekly standard error. For the scoring of a real-time vintage, s_P and the recovery ratio are computed from data up to the vintage's origin only, never from the full record. The grid is a in {0.5, 1, 2, 4} and r in {10, 30}, so the fall-to-rise penalty ratio is at least 10 (the maintainer decided that falls are heavily penalised). The same (a, r) applies to every Primary, to stop one Primary's noise from setting its own penalty. The comparison fits are r = 1 (symmetric L1), r = 3, r = infinity (strictly non-decreasing), a = 0 (free weekly), and the season-year constant. No convex-optimisation package is installed, so the solver is a short ADMM routine in numpy, checked against scipy.optimize.linprog in the self-tests (risk 13). The demand cells are projected out once per Primary, so the fit needs only the weekly normal matrix (about 360 by 360) and one vector per series.

The tuning rule picks one (a, r) pair on tuning units. The pair minimises the median path error over a mixture of ramps, steps, and a constant path, subject to two limits: at most 0.5 false steps per Primary-year on the placebo sky and on constant injected paths from the tuning farms A to C, and a 30% fall lasting 26 weeks recovered at 0.5 or more of its depth. Ties go to the larger a. The tuning limits are the same as conditions (v) and (iii), so the scoring on farms D to F tests generalisation to new farms and path seeds only. If no pair on the grid meets both limits, the verdict is refuted for the asymmetric design, and the limits are not relaxed after any score is seen. The pair is written to frozen_config.json. The tuning script and the scoring script are separate commits, and the scoring script has never run before the commit of the frozen file.

The capacity unit is the 99th percentile of half-hourly AC output of the fleet, as in experiments 00039 and 00040. Installed DC capacity is larger. The conversion to DC is part of the outside check against DESNZ.

docs.title: Data, weeks, and masks
docs.text:
• Series. The 8 Primaries metered in MW (time series 7 Trusthorpe, 8 Horncastle, 10 Spilsby, 12 Wrangle T1, 13 Wrangle T2, 16 Mount Bridge Boston, 17 Kirton, and 18 Donington) and the 6 solar farms as injection sources. The farms appear only as "Solar farm A" to "Solar farm F" (studies.pv_dataset.pv_sites() labels), and their output is always normalised by the farm's own 99th percentile, never published in megawatts.
  • Inputs. The frame.parquet of experiment 00039 (cleaned power, CAMS unit shape and irradiance at reliability 0.9 or more, ERA5 temperature, zenith under 75 degrees), read from data/ml-experiments/00039-pv-disaggregation-cams-injection/work/. Reading another experiment's private output is allowed. Importing its code is not, so the model code is copied into this folder for the third time (risk 7).
  • Weeks. 361 weeks from Monday 2019-09-02 to Monday 2026-07-27 (the last has 5 days). Each Primary starts at its first week with at least 3 usable days. A week with fewer than 3 usable days is unobserved: the fit has no data term there, the penalty interpolates, and the output marks the row and widens its interval.
  • Switching mask. The logged closures, padded by 24 hours, are removed from every fit. The intervals come from experiment 00037's intervals.parquet, and the log ends on 2026-03-25. SW2-0b's labels replace the logs once they exist. Unlogged transfers stay in the data and are injected as a case. The first unit (U1) found four facts that the design must handle:
    • The logged-closure mask removes 40 to 48% of the daylight half-hours at Mount Bridge Boston, Wrangle T1, and Wrangle T2.
    • 871 of the 2,166 farm-weeks drop out of injection, mostly at Solar farm E.
    • Kirton's correlation of power with u peaks at 08:00 UTC, not near 12:00 UTC.
    • The weekly fits must therefore tolerate weeks in which most daylight half-hours are masked, and Kirton is reported without a pass or fail.
  • Polygons. The check already run in e00045_polygon_check.py found 16 valid Primary polygons, overlaps under 0.3% of the smaller polygon, Mount Bridge Boston's point 95 m outside its polygon, and Wrangle T1 and T2 sharing one polygon. Wrangle T1 and T2 keep separate fits and are summed for any comparison against the shared polygon.
  • Validation before fitting. Row counts per Primary-week, duplicate keys, the hour-of-day profile of the correlation of power with u (peak near 12:00 UTC), the share of CAMS hours dropped per week, the timestamp scan (the injected recovery must peak at shift zero), and the count of unobserved weeks. The same step prints each of the six solar farms' date coverage against the 361 weeks. A farm-week in which the farm's output is missing on more than 2 days is dropped from that farm's injection units, and the number dropped is reported. The data-validation skill lists the checks.

docs.title: Known-answer injection design
docs.text:
Every scored result comes from injected paths whose truth is known, scored on farms and path seeds that were not used for tuning. The hold-out is by farm and path seed only. The tuning and scoring units share the same 8 Primaries, dates, baseline noise, and demand cells, so the scoring tests generalisation to new farms and path seeds at the same Primaries, not to new Primaries. The main interval therefore resamples Primaries, and results are reported per Primary. The design has five parts.

  • The baseline is semi-synthetic. For each Primary, the baseline series is the real power minus the full-record fitted PV component (so it holds demand, noise, and any confound), plus a known baseline PV path equal to the Primary's 2025/26 capacity from experiment 00040 times u. The true capacity of every week is then known, level included. Removing the fitted PV component also removes any confound that is correlated with the PV shape, so recovery on this baseline is optimistic against experiment 00039's recovery ratio of 0.77 on real data. A second scoring uses the real series with the injected path added, and compares the fitted path with and without the injection, because the production series is fitted to real data that already holds unknown solar. Condition (i) is scored on both baselines and both are reported; the verdict uses the worse. The gap between the two scorings measures the departure from additivity.
  • Injected change. The injected output is minus the normalised output of one solar farm scaled by the true path, so that its 99th percentile equals the path's value in MW. Farm output is normalised, never published in megawatts.
  • Cases. Each path is drawn with a fixed seed.
    • Ramp: a rise of 25% or 50% of the baseline over 52 weeks.
    • Step: a rise of 5%, 10%, 20%, or 30% at a random week, with half the steps placed in April to September, half from October to March, and one in four on a month boundary.
    • Temporary fall: 30% for 8 weeks and 30% for 26 weeks, and a 15% fall for 26 weeks.
    • Transfer: a share of 0.3 of another Primary's net power (including its solar) added for 30 days, once inside the 24-hour padded mask and once outside it, so that the size of the error from an unlogged transfer is measured. The truth is the share times the donor's baseline capacity.
    • Seasonal load: a daytime load (08:00 to 20:00 local) of 10% of the baseline capacity with a summer-weighted yearly cycle, once independent of the weather and once scaled by the clear-sky index (a load that rises with sunshine). The truth is the unchanged baseline, so the score is the seasonal swing that creeps into the capacity path.
    • Constant path: a constant capacity equal to the baseline. Its false steps and ratchet drift are scored, together with the placebo sky. Design change: the constant-path unit is built on the placebo sky, not from a farm's injected output. The PV shape u is permuted among the days of each calendar month, and the baseline capacity times the permuted shape is subtracted from the real power. The real series' own growth is then uncorrelated with the permuted shape, so the true path is constant. The recovery ratio of the constant-path unit is fixed at 1, because the unit is built from the PV shape itself and not from a farm's output. The farm and the path seed still change the rows that the farm's gaps leave, and the path seed also changes the permutation.
  • Hold-out. The tuning units use Solar farms A, B, and C and path seeds 0 to 3. The scoring units use Solar farms D, E, and F and path seeds 1000 to 1003, at all 8 Primaries. The unit count is 3 farms times 4 seeds times 8 Primaries times 14 cases (2 ramps, 4 steps, 3 temporary falls, 2 transfers, 2 seasonal loads, and 1 constant path) = 1,344 units in each set. Solar farm E, the worst case at 0.70 recovery, falls in the scoring set on purpose, and results are also reported without it. The recovery ratio of each Primary is measured on tuning units with a constant injected path and applied unchanged to the scoring units.
  • Intervals. The main interval is a cluster bootstrap that resamples the 8 Primaries, 2,000 draws, at the 95% level. A two-way cluster bootstrap (Primaries and farms resampled independently) is reported beside it. With three scoring farms the farm margin is coarse, so the write-up also reports the seed-level spread.

Real-time vintages are scored on the same semi-synthetic units. The fit is repeated at origins every 4 weeks over the last 3 years of the record, each truncated at its origin, with the Primary scale s_P and the recovery ratio recomputed from data up to that origin, and the latest complete week of each vintage is scored against the truth. The write-up reports the path error of that week against the same week in the final fit, and the revision of the first estimate by the age of the week (1, 2, 4, 8, 13, and 26 weeks).

The bootstrap is a residual block bootstrap that refits the whole path. Each draw resamples whole 7-day blocks of the penalised fit's residuals, taken from the same calendar month of any year of the Primary's record (so that winter noise stays winter-sized), adds them to the fitted values, and refits the path with the frozen penalties. Missing half-hours take a residual of zero. Each Primary and variant gets 200 draws for the real series, and each injection unit gets 100. The 5th and 95th percentiles give the 90% interval, and the 25th and 75th and the 10th and 90th give the calibration curve. The coverage of the truth is scored on 96 scoring units (the case families with a step, a ramp, a fall, and a constant path), separately at weeks with no true step and at weeks within 2 weeks of a true step. A bootstrap of a penalised fit at a boundary tends to under-cover, and the decision rule counts that as a finding. If coverage at non-step weeks is under 0.85, the write-up reports an inflation factor chosen on tuning units, labelled post hoc.

False steps are counted on two skies. One is experiment 00039's placebo sky, which permutes the PV shape u across days within each month (200 permutations per Primary) and leaves the power in place, so that the day-to-day link between cloud and power is broken and any step is false by construction. A placebo step is also ignored in any week within 4 weeks of a rise of 10% or more in the unpermuted real series, so that a real growth step is not counted as false. The other is the constant injected path, whose baseline holds no real growth. A false step is a rise of at least 10% of the Primary's mean real capacity over any 4 consecutive weeks (5% is reported as well). Both skies also report the ratchet drift. Conditions (iii) and (iv) are scored on both skies, on farms D to F for the constant path and on permutation seeds 1000 to 1099 for the placebo sky. Tuning uses farms A to C and permutation seeds 0 to 99.

The detection limit of each Primary is the smallest step on the grid (5%, 10%, 20%, 30%) that the path shows as a rise of at least half the step within 3 weeks of the true date in at least 80% of the scoring injections. It is reported for April to September and for October to March separately.

docs.title: Real series, three uncertainty terms, and the gap diagnostic
docs.text:
The real weekly series is fitted on all of a Primary's data, then divided by that Primary's recovery ratio. The production-style output is the real-time vintage at weekly origins, so a forecast date reads only what was known on that date.

The uncertainty statement keeps three terms apart and never sums them.

  1. Sampling: the 90% residual-block-bootstrap interval of the weekly capacity.
  2. Transfer from farms to rooftops: a scenario of plus or minus 10%, from experiment 00040's clean-Primary ratio of the daily to the six-arm capacity (0.92) and its per-farm spread.
  3. Undetected demand: two named scenarios from experiment 00040's table, an undetected day-long cloud load (capacity too high by the Primary's bound B at amplitude 0.25) and a load that rises with sunshine (capacity too low by 33% at amplitude 0.25).

The gap diagnostic compares the asymmetric path with the symmetric one on the real series. A Primary is flagged when the mean gap between the two paths is 5% of its capacity or more, or when the symmetric path falls by at least 10% for 8 weeks or more and the asymmetric path does not. The 5% threshold is the weekly detection floor predicted for a summer step. The flagged falls are listed for SW2-0b to check against switching labels. The write-up never presents a held fall as a real fall.

Status per Primary is carried from earlier results. Kirton is flagged and its series appears with a grey band and the library range of experiment 00040 (1.2 to 4.4 MW in 2025/26). Trusthorpe is low-power. Wrangle T1 is left-out of any claim that a Primary is free of a confound. The others are clean. Most coastal Primaries (Skegness, Ingoldmells, and Chapel St Leonards) are metered in MVA and outside this experiment.

docs.title: Outside checks and tolerances, stated before any comparison
docs.text:
Three outside checks and one internal check are run, in order of strength. None alters the verdict.

None of the outside photovoltaic datasets is complete. The DESNZ tables, the Ofgem Feed-in Tariff (FiT) register, and the Embedded Capacity Register (ECR) each count a subset of the installed capacity, and the FiT database has not been updated for several years. Each outside figure is therefore a floor or a partial count. A mismatch between an outside figure and the weekly series does not show that the series is wrong, so every outside check is descriptive and cannot decide the verdict. The measured coverage gaps are these. The FiT report covers accreditations from 1 April 2010 to 31 March 2025, and its latest photovoltaic commissioning date is 24 March 2021 (the scheme closed to new applicants on 31 March 2019). The DESNZ constituency table is published for August 2026 and covers domestic installations only. The DESNZ local-authority table is at the end of 2025. The ECR as-of date is printed by the check, and the check reports it beside its result.

  1. DESNZ small-scale solar, at constituency and local-authority level. DESNZ publishes no table by lower-layer super output area (LSOA). We searched the DESNZ "Solar photovoltaics deployment" workbook (Energy Trends table 6.3), the "Renewable electricity by local authority" workbook, and the DESNZ sub-regional statistics pages, and found tables by parliamentary constituency (domestic installations only) and by local authority (all sizes, end of 2025). The LSOA files were downloaded for the area shares of the Primary polygons but are not joined to the DESNZ figures. Each Primary polygon meets 1 to 4 constituencies, and a constituency or local authority is scaled by the share of its area inside the polygon, so the check is coarse. The tolerance is wide and is fixed here, before any comparison. The expected peak AC output is the DC capacity times 0.70, with a range of 0.60 to 0.80 (experiment 00029 fitted farm DC-to-AC ratios of 1.12 to 1.42, an AC-to-DC ratio of 0.70 to 0.89, and a fleet of mixed orientations peaks lower than one farm). Tolerance: the ratio of the series' mean over the 12 months to the snapshot date to the expected peak lies in [0.67, 1.5], read at the constituency level for domestic capacity and at the local-authority level for all sizes. The comparison is reported for Spilsby, Horncastle, Mount Bridge Boston, Donington, Trusthorpe, and Wrangle T1 plus T2 against the shared polygon, and Kirton is reported without a range. The factor of 1.5 is the root of the summed squares of the stated uncertainties: sampling (15%), farm to rooftop (10%), undetected load (25%), and conversion (14%), about 33%. The check can catch only a gross failure, and because the tables are partial counts, a ratio above 1 is less alarming than a ratio below 1. Installations of 1 MW or more are metered by NGED and already removed from the Disaggregated Demand series, so the local-authority figure for all sizes is the less direct comparison.
  2. The Ofgem FiT register, as a second descriptive check. Each postcode district is allocated to the Primary polygons by the share of its postcode units that lie inside the polygon (Ordnance Survey Code-Point Open gives the unit positions, and no open polygon boundary for postcode districts was found). The register has three uses. First, a dated baseline of small-scale capacity before April 2019, summed over the districts of each polygon by commissioning date. Second, a growth curve of cumulative declared net capacity (the Ofgem name for AC capacity) up to 2019, compared with the weekly series over the same weeks: the signs of the growth must agree and the ratio must lie within a factor of 2. Third, the share of FiT capacity in installations under 50 kW, which the Embedded Capacity Register misses. There are two caveats. The FiT took no new installations after 2019, so the register is a floor from then on. Postcode districts do not align with the polygons, so the allocation adds error. The check has no pass or fail range of its own and is reported beside check 1.
  3. The Embedded Capacity Register (ECR) as a soft prior, not a floor. The check uses only connected solar sites of 50 kW to under 1 MW, dated before each week, and first prints which date columns the register holds and what each records (the reader lists a Last Updated column, which is not a connection date). Tolerance: the register's total for a Primary does not exceed the series' upper 90% bound at 5 or more of the 6 comparisons. The register's median was 0.08 of effective capacity against 0.33 from the data in experiment 00031, so the check expects the register to sit well below the series. The step-date check uses only sites larger than the Primary's detectable step and compares the series' rise in the 4 weeks around each date with the rise at 1,000 random placebo dates. It is run only if the register holds a connection date and at least 5 sites qualify across the six comparisons, and otherwise is reported as not testable.
  4. The season-year anchor (internal, A0). The mean of the weekly series over each season-year lies inside experiment 00040's 95% interval of C at the clean Primaries in at least 80% of Primary-years.

Growth-rate tolerances, fixed after the outside growth rates were extracted and before any comparison with the weekly series. The script e00045_outside.py first writes outside_growth.parquet, which holds each outside source's fractional growth per year, and only then compares it with the series. A fractional growth per year is the least-squares slope of the cumulative capacity in MW per year, divided by its mean level over the window, with both curves sampled at every Monday. The window is the overlap of the source's coverage with the Primary's series, and a growth rate over a window shorter than 1 year is reported but never tested. Wrangle T1 and Wrangle T2 are summed against the shared polygon. The extraction showed that three of the four sources cannot be tested for growth, and the rules below say so in advance.

  • Ofgem FiT: no growth test. The weekly series starts in September 2019 or later, after the scheme closed to new applicants, so the register's cumulative curve is flat over the whole overlap (growth 0.00 per year at every Primary, and under 0.2 years at Donington). The plan's comparison of growth up to 2019 has no weekly series to compare against. The register's use is therefore limited to the pre-2019 baseline against the series' first 8 weeks (reported with no pass or fail range, as in check 2) and the share of capacity under 50 kW.
  • DESNZ local authority (all sizes, year ends 2014 to 2025): growth test with the factor of 2. Let g_s be the series' growth and g_o the source's, both over the same window of at least 1 year. The check passes if g_o is positive and 0.5 ≤ g_s / g_o ≤ 2. It fails if g_s / g_o > 2. It is inconclusive if g_s / g_o < 0.5 or g_s ≤ 0, because the authority total includes the farms of 1 MW or more that NGED meters and that the Disaggregated Demand series does not hold, so the source can grow faster than the series for a reason that does not impugn the series. The authority is allocated to a polygon by the share of the authority's FiT capacity inside it, because no authority boundaries are held, so the allocation is coarse. Wrangle's window is under 1 year and is not tested.
  • DESNZ constituency (domestic only): no growth test. The workbook holds the August 2026 table and the July 2026 table, one month apart, and DESNZ revises recent months upward, so a growth rate from them is not a growth rate. The table is used for the level check only.
  • Embedded Capacity Register: no growth test. The register's only date column, Last Updated, holds one value, 6 August 2026 (Excel serial 46240), for all 7,211 rows. It records the release date of the register and not a connection date, so the step-date check in check 3 is not testable, and the register is used for the level comparison only.

The level checks keep the tolerances stated above. The domestic constituency check uses the 12 months ending 31 July 2026. The local-authority check uses the 12 months ending 31 December 2025 and the year-end 2025 figure, and a Primary with fewer than 26 weeks of series in that period is not tested. Both pass if the ratio lies in [0.67, 1.5] at an AC-to-DC ratio of 0.70, and both report the ratio at 0.60 and 0.80. Kirton (status range-only) and Wrangle T1 (status not-clean) are never scored. Wrangle T1 is still added to Wrangle T2, because T2 alone against the whole polygon would compare unlike things, and that sum is reported with its not-clean component flagged. The season-year anchor uses experiment 00040's 95% bootstrap interval of the headline capacity (headline_low to headline_high; that experiment publishes no interval on the six-arm C itself), for the season-years in which the series holds at least 40 weeks.

The outside files need maintainer attention only on licence and size.

  • LSOA boundaries: Office for National Statistics (ONS) LSOA (2021) generalised-clipped boundaries and population-weighted centroids for England and Wales, from the ONS Open Geography Portal. The whole boundary file is expected to be tens of megabytes and the centroids a few megabytes (to be confirmed at download). The plan requests only the LSOAs that intersect the union of the 16 polygons (a few hundred features, under 5 MB) through the portal's feature service, and falls back to the full file.
  • DESNZ tables: two spreadsheets of a few megabytes.
  • Ofgem FiT report: three workbooks of about 35 MB each, and the Code-Point Open archive of about 14 MB. Ofgem's copyright page releases its material under the Open Government Licence, and the files download with no login or terms click-through.
  • Licence: both are published under the Open Government Licence v3.0, which needs an acknowledgement and no account or signature. The ONS boundaries add "Contains OS data (c) Crown copyright and database right". The cost is nil, well under the £30 cap. The maintainer decides whether using an OGL file counts as accepting a licence in someone's name before the download runs.

docs.title: What SW2-10 reads
docs.text:
Two private parquet files, with the columns below. The folder is data/ml-experiments/00045-pvdis-4-weekly-capacity-asymmetric-l1/. Both files hold one row per Primary, variant, and week, and both carry the same file metadata, which names the recommended variant and defines each column.

  • capacity_weekly.parquet, the final fit on all data, with the columns week_start (Date, Monday, Europe/London), time_series_id (Int32), primary_name (String), variant (frozen, alt_post_hoc, season_year_constant, or free_weekly), capacity_mw (Float64, the 99th percentile of the half-hourly AC output of the embedded solar, divided by the variant's recovery ratio), low_mw and high_mw (the 5th and 95th percentiles of the 200-draw residual block bootstrap, clipped to include the point estimate, and widened in unobserved weeks), status, unobserved (Boolean, true when the week has fewer than 3 usable days), recovery_ratio, rooftop_low_mw and rooftop_high_mw (the capacity minus and plus 10%), scenario_dayL_mw and scenario_sunload_mw (the capacity under each named systematic scenario, never merged into the interval), and recommended (Boolean, true for the one variant SW2-10 should read).
  • capacity_weekly_vintages.parquet, the same columns plus origin_monday (Date): the fit at each origin using only data before that Monday, for the variants frozen and alt_post_hoc. Origins fall every 4 weeks over the last 3 years of the record, plus the final origin, so low_mw and high_mw are null in this file. A forecast date d reads the rows whose origin_monday is the last origin on or before d and whose week_start is the latest week (the Monday seven days before the origin), and holds that value flat for the days after it.

The status column carries one label per Primary, as it appears in the file. The labels are clean, low-power, range-only, and not-clean. SW2-10 uses rows with status clean or low-power, reads range-only rows as a range (low_mw to high_mw) and never as a value, treats not-clean rows as unavailable, and skips rows with unobserved true when it needs a measured week. SW2-10 uses the vintage file for any held-out scoring. The path of the finished file goes to the "Design: Switching event detection experiments" session when it exists.

docs.title: Cores, time, and parallel work
docs.text:
The whole experiment fits in 4 cores and about 2.5 hours of wall time, if all 4 cores are free. Each worker runs one thread (OMP_NUM_THREADS=1, OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1, POLARS_MAX_THREADS=1), four workers at a time, one output file per worker chunk written atomically, fixed seeds per job. Check uptime first, because the slot's 4 cores are shared with PVDIS-3. If PVDIS-3 leaves only 2 cores free, the four-worker stages take twice as long and the total rises from 2.5 hours to about 4.5 hours; the implementer then runs two workers and does not start a stage that would still be running when PVDIS-3 needs its cores back.

Stage Work Workers Estimate Inputs and validation read the frame, weeks, masks, figures 1 to 4 1 5 min Self-tests solver, linearity, known answers 1 2 min Tuning 8 penalty pairs on 1,344 tuning units (the normal matrix is reused, so about 0.1 to 0.3 s per fit) 4 10 to 15 min Freeze write and commit frozen_config.json 1 1 min Scoring and contrasts the chosen pair and the four comparison fits on 1,344 scoring units 4 15 to 20 min Coverage bootstrap 96 units times 200 draws 4 15 min Vintages on injections about 38 origins times 8 Primaries times 12 units 4 10 min Real series fits, 500-draw bootstrap per Primary, weekly-origin vintages, placebo sky (1,600 fits that rebuild the normal matrix) 4 30 min Outside checks DESNZ, register, season-year anchor 1 5 min Report and charts printed report, 17 figures 2 10 min

What runs side by side. Work items W0 (register move), U1 (inputs and raw figures), and U5a (the download script) share no file and have no dependency on the solver, so three Sonnet agents start together. The solver and self-tests (U2) come first for everything that fits. Go/no-go before U3: in U2's self-tests, measure the seconds per fit at r = 30, a = 0.5 (the slowest-converging corner of the grid). If the ADMM needs more than 10 times the 0.1 to 0.3 s per fit in the table, the implementer stops and tells the manager before starting U3. After U2, U3 (injection, tuning, scoring) and U4 (real series, vintages, placebo) run in parallel, because they read the same solver and write different files. Within a run, the tuning units, the scoring units, the Primaries, and the bootstrap draws are independent jobs.

docs.title: Work list, split into units a Sonnet agent can implement
docs.text:
Each unit is implemented by one Sonnet agent working from the files, and reviewed by a second Sonnet agent that reads the code for leakage (tuning units reaching the scoring set), for the fit stopping at the vintage origin, and for farm output reaching a chart in megawatts. No agent starts a sub-agent.

Unit What it builds Files Needs W0 The Embedded Capacity Register loader in packages/studies (merged in PR 1267). The file holds only the workbook reader. The Primary-name normalisation and the connected-solar filter are not in it, so U5b writes them in e00045_outside.py. packages/studies/src/studies/ecr_reader.py (merged in PR 1267) nothing U1 Inputs, weeks, masks, validation, and the raw-data figures 1 to 4 ml-experiments/00045-.../e00045_common.py, e00045_inputs.py, e00045_raw_charts.py nothing U2 The weekly design, the demand-cell projection, the ADMM solver for asymmetric L1 with non-negativity, the five fits (free, symmetric, asymmetric, strictly non-decreasing, season-year constant), and the self-tests e00045_model.py, e00045_selftest.py U1's common module U3 The injection builder (cases, semi-synthetic baseline, hold-out split), tuning, the frozen file, scoring, the contrasts, the coverage bootstrap, and vintages on injections e00045_inject.py, e00045_tune.py, e00045_score.py, e00045_bootstrap.py U2 U4 Real-series fits, recovery-ratio correction, the 500-draw bootstrap, weekly-origin vintages, the placebo sky, the gap diagnostic, and the two output files e00045_real.py, e00045_placebo.py, e00045_outputs.py U2, U3's recovery ratios U5a The download scripts for the LSOA files, the DESNZ tables, and the Ofgem FiT report with Code-Point Open, following the data-download skill, with a generated README e00045_fetch_lsoa.py, e00045_fetch_fit.py the maintainer's licence decision U5b The outside checks (DESNZ, FiT, register through studies.ecr_reader, the season-year anchor) e00045_outside.py U4, U5a, W0 U6 The printed report (every number the page quotes) and figures 5 to 17 e00045_report.py, e00045_charts.py U3, U4, U5b U7 The write-up with its plain-language opening, the research-plan row and research-log entry, and the mkdocs.yml line docs/ml-experiments/00045-.../result.md, docs/ml-experiments/research-plan.md, docs/ml-experiments/research-log.md, mkdocs.yml U6

The order is W0, U1, and U5a together; then U2; then U3 and U4 together; then U5b and U6; then U7. Each unit is committed separately, and the plan commit with this page and the research-plan row comes first.

docs.title: Figures, raw data first
docs.text:
All charts follow the dataviz skill (OCF-brand palette, sized to the text column, SVG optimised with svgo). Farm output is normalised and labelled Solar farm A to F. Substations may be named.

  1. Raw: the model-free trend. For each Primary, the rolling 8-week mean of the midday gap between clear days (daily clear-sky index of 0.8 or more) and overcast days (0.3 or less), in April to September, from 2019 to 2026. Where the gap rises, the capacity rises.
  2. Raw: what a week of evidence looks like. One clear and one overcast week in summer and in winter at Donington, with power and CAMS irradiance on twin axes.
  3. Raw: coverage. A heat map of usable daylight half-hours per Primary-week, with masked closure days, dropped CAMS hours, and unobserved weeks marked.
  4. Raw: how much information a week holds. The free weekly capacity with its standard error at Donington, and the standard error by calendar month for all Primaries, with the implied smallest detectable step.
  5. Method: one injected path through five fits. A ramp, a step, and a fall at Donington with Solar farm D, drawn with the free, symmetric, asymmetric, strictly non-decreasing, and season-year fits.
  6. Method: the penalty grid. The tuning-set error and false-step rate over (a, r), with the chosen pair marked.
  7. Headline: path error by case family and fit, with 95% intervals, for the scoring units.
  8. The detection curve: the share of steps detected against step size, for April to September and October to March, one panel per Primary.
  9. Falls: the share of a temporary fall recovered by depth and duration, for the symmetric, asymmetric, and strictly non-decreasing fits.
  10. Transfers and seasonal load: the false step from an unlogged transfer against a masked one, and the seasonal swing that creeps into the path, for the weather-independent load and the sunshine-correlated load.
  11. False steps: the distribution over the 200 placebo permutations per Primary, the constant-path injections, and the ratchet drift.
  12. Real-time vintages: the first estimate against the final fit, and the revision by the age of the week, on injections and on the real series.
  13. Interval calibration: the coverage of the truth against the nominal level (50%, 80%, and 90%) at step and non-step weeks.
  14. Headline on real data: the weekly capacity of each Primary with its 90% band, experiment 00040's season-year C as points, Kirton in grey with its library range, and the two systematic scenarios as separate lines.
  15. The gap between asymmetric and symmetric paths on the real series, with held falls marked.
  16. Outside checks: the series against the DESNZ expected peak with the tolerance band, and the register total.
  17. Additivity: the fitted increment on the real series against the semi-synthetic score for the same injection.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
1. Winter weeks carry almost no information. Daylight is short and u is small, so the path is set by the penalty from about November to February. The standard error by month (figure 4) and the seasonal detection limit state this, and the series marks wide-interval weeks.
  2. Per-season-year cells absorb part of a step at a month boundary. One in four injected steps sits on a boundary. If the recovered size is under 0.75 of the true size there, the write-up reports it and the penalty cannot fix it.
  3. The asymmetric penalty ratchets on noise. Rises are lightly penalised and falls heavily penalised, so noise peaks stick. Decision-rule condition (iv) and figure 11 measure the drift. If condition (iv) fails, the next part may need a penalty on the level as well as the increments.
  4. The fit is not additive. The production series is fitted to real data that already holds unknown solar, so the semi-synthetic scoring and the real-plus-injection scoring are both reported, the verdict uses the worse, and figure 17 shows the gap.
  5. Unlogged switching produces false steps. The transfer case measures the size. The real series' detected steps must be checked against SW2-0b's labels once they exist, and a step that coincides with a labelled transfer is not a capacity change.
  6. A load that rises with sunshine looks like solar. It biases the level low and, if seasonal, adds a swing to the path. The seasonal-load case measures the swing. Nothing in the data sizes the real load, so the scenario columns carry it separately.
  7. The model code is copied for the third time. Experiments 00039, 00040, and now 00045 each hold a copy of the cell, window, and least-squares code. A move into packages/studies is overdue and is a separate reviewed change, outside this experiment.
  8. Only three scoring farms. The farm margin of the two-way bootstrap is coarse. The write-up reports results with and without Solar farm E and the seed-level spread.
  9. The outside checks are weak and partial. None of the DESNZ, FiT, and ECR datasets is complete, so each is a floor and a mismatch does not show the series is wrong. The DESNZ tolerance of a factor of 1.5 catches only gross failure, the DESNZ tables are constituency level (domestic only) and local-authority level and so need area scaling, the FiT took no new installations after 2019, postcode districts do not align with the polygons, and the register's date field may not be a connection date.
  10. The vintage end-of-record problem. Penalised fits are least constrained at the end. The ERA5 temperature that production would use arrives about 5 days late, which the vintage scoring ignores; dropping the temperature term moved C by 0.006 of capacity in experiment 00039.
  11. Kirton and Wrangle T1. Kirton's cloud load enters its weekly path as capacity, and Wrangle T1 has two years of data and a low signal. Both appear with their status, and neither supports a claim.
  12. CAMS dropouts. Reliability under 0.9 drops 9.7% of hours, up to 12.6% of daylight hours in December, so winter weeks may fall below 3 usable days.
  13. The solver is new. No convex-optimisation package is installed, and adding one changes pyproject.toml, which belongs to the maintainer. The ADMM routine is checked against scipy.optimize.linprog on a 30-week problem, against ordinary least squares at a = 0, and against a constant path at large a. A stopping tolerance that is too loose would show as a failed self-test.
  14. CPU contention. The slot's 4 cores are shared with PVDIS-3. Check uptime before each stage.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: The next experiment should ask whether a penalty set per Primary from that Primary's own weekly noise, together with a rule that holds a fall for a stated number of weeks, can keep constant-path false steps at or below 0.5 per Primary-year while recovering at least 0.5 of a 26-week fall and less than 0.5 of an 8-week fall. The next experiment should test this alongside the season-year constant plus step detection that fires only for steps above 25% to 30% of capacity, on tuning and scoring units fixed in advance and with the false-step limit scored on both bases of the constant-path threshold. The comparison fits and the placebo-sky constant path should be reused, and the interval should be rebuilt and checked for coverage on the tuning units before it is reported. PVDIS-5 reads the season-year constant for now.

docs.title: Experiment 46: how much of the best guess's daylight error is embedded solar?
docs.text:
We asked how much of the error in a 0-to-10-day forecast of a Primary substation's power comes from solar panels behind the substation's meter. A Primary substation is a 33/11 kV or 66/11 kV substation in the electricity distribution network. The meter reads demand minus the panels' output, so a sunnier day than forecast lowers the metered power. The demand forecast is the best-guess recipe of experiment 00033, which normally takes shortwave and longwave radiation inputs, and which we refitted without those inputs. We added a correction to that forecast: the panels' capacity, estimated in experiment 00040, times how much sunnier or cloudier the day is than the average for that month and half-hour. We built the correction twice. The first copy read the true sunshine, taken from the satellite-based CAMS data (the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service), which no real forecast has. The second copy read the sunshine that the ECMWF ensemble weather forecast (ENS) predicted. We scored both on 68,903 daylight half-hour forecasts per random seed (3 seeds), at 5 Primary substations, in April to September. The score is the quantile score, our probabilistic forecast error score: an estimate of the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), in points, where a point is 1% of the substation's capacity. Knowing the true sunshine lowered the quantile score by about 1 point, which is about 20% of the 4.72 points that the demand forecast without radiation inputs scores. The correction built from the weather forecast lowered it by 0.06 points. That is within the noise, and short of the 0.35 points that the maintainer judged worth the effort of adding the correction to the live forecast, a judgement about the cost of porting. The verdict is refuted.

The verdict is refuted: the ENS solar term does not reach the 0.35-point threshold. The oracle shows that the missing gain lies in the sunshine forecast, not in the capacity. The scores below are the quantile score in points of capacity. Smaller is better. d0 is experiment 00033's best-guess recipe. d1l is d0 without its shortwave and longwave columns. The two shift arms add the solar term to d1l, with the coefficient fixed at 1. The oracle arm is the CAMS one. The rows are the 5 anonymised series (named D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16) whose capacity estimate is clean; anonymised series are labelled D followed by a number so that no metered generator or site can be identified.

Arm Quantile score (95% interval) d0, with radiation inputs 4.620 (4.168 to 5.224) d1l, without radiation inputs 4.724 (4.252 to 5.325) d1l + ENS shift 4.667 (4.292 to 5.204) d1l + CAMS shift (oracle) 3.758 (3.484 to 4.033) d1l + ENS shift, coefficient fitted per series and lead band (exploratory) 4.581 (4.189 to 5.134) d1l + CAMS shift, coefficient fitted (exploratory) 3.667 (3.389 to 3.999)

Two contrasts decide the verdict at 97.5%: C3, the ENS shift minus d1l, and C4, the oracle minus d1l. The decision rule is: C4 must lie wholly below -0.35 (the validity gate), and then C3 sets the verdict. C3 is -0.056 (-0.191 to +0.064), so the interval lies above -0.35 and includes zero, which the rule calls refuted. C4 is -0.966 (-1.431 to -0.595), so the validity gate passes. Two more contrasts are exploratory and read at 95%. C5, the oracle minus the ENS shift, is -0.910 (-1.209 to -0.643). C6, the ENS shift minus d0, is +0.048 (-0.059 to +0.141). Removing the two radiation columns raises the quantile score by 0.104 points (d0 minus d1l, from the table).

Contrast Treatment arm minus comparison arm Role C3 d1l + ENS shift minus d1l Decides the verdict C4 d1l + CAMS shift (oracle) minus d1l Validity gate C5 d1l + CAMS shift minus d1l + ENS shift Exploratory C6 d1l + ENS shift minus d0 Exploratory; decides the design of PVDIS-5

PVDIS-5 is the planned next experiment in the series. It tests the solar term again, with weekly capacity estimates in place of the 2023/24 estimate.

The ENS solar term scores no better than the best guess, so PVDIS-5 is a non-inferiority and explanation test, not a gain test. C6 is not wholly below zero, which is what the decision rule needs for a gain test. C6 supports "no better than d0". It does not support "no worse than d0", because the plan set no non-inferiority margin and the pooled upper end is +0.141. C6 also changes sign. By valid month, April to September, it is -0.09, -0.12, +0.19, +0.23, +0.15, and -0.11. By series it is wholly above zero at D10 (+0.131, +0.027 to +0.233) and D9 (+0.264, +0.024 to +0.423), and wholly below zero at D16 (-0.248, -0.448 to -0.061). A non-inferiority test in PVDIS-5 therefore needs a margin set in advance. By lead band, C6 is +0.073 (-0.195 to +0.322) at 0 to 24 hours and -0.014 (-0.144 to +0.112) at 1 to 2 days, with 6 resampling blocks each. The other bands are +0.054 (-0.104 to +0.192) at 2 to 6 days, +0.049 (-0.099 to +0.147) at 6 to 10 days, and +0.049 (-0.028 to +0.124) from 10 days.

docs.title: The ENS forecast carries the oracle's gain only to about 2 days
docs.text: The ENS anomaly tracks the CAMS anomaly for about 2 days, then fades. C3 follows the same pattern. On the training window, the correlation of the ensemble-mean anomaly with the CAMS anomaly runs from 0.77 to 0.81 at 0 to 24 hours, 0.73 to 0.77 at 1 to 2 days, 0.56 to 0.60 at 2 to 6 days, 0.25 to 0.29 at 6 to 10 days, and 0.02 to 0.04 from 10 days, across the six series. The oracle gains at every lead (C4 from -0.59 to -1.21). The ENS version gains -0.262 (-0.598 to +0.037) at 0 to 24 hours and -0.277 (-0.406 to -0.144) at 1 to 2 days, then -0.079, -0.002, and +0.011 in the bands beyond. All of these intervals are at 95%, exploratory.

docs.title: Fragility of the small gains
docs.text:
• Without D9, the series with the largest bound on its capacity, C3 is -0.113 (-0.230 to -0.000, rounded; the interval touches zero) at 97.5%. The rule would then give small gain, but the upper end sits at zero, so the reading is fragile and the pre-registered verdict, which includes D9, stands.
  • C3 is not the same sign in every valid month. It is negative in April (-0.204), May (-0.232), and September (-0.262), and positive in June (+0.117), July (+0.183), and August (+0.024). C4 is negative in all six months. The intervals resample 7 blocks, each a month of forecast start dates (March to September, because forecasts started in late March are valid in April).
  • C3 varies by series and sky. It is -0.382 (-0.588 to -0.182) at D16 and positive at D5 and D9 (+0.278 and +0.173). By sky it is -0.719 in cloudy rows, +0.225 (+0.076 to +0.329) in middle rows, and -0.135 in sunny rows, all exploratory at 95%.
  • A week-block bootstrap (29 blocks) gives the same answer: C3 -0.056 (-0.197 to +0.084) and C4 -0.966 (-1.248 to -0.663) at 97.5%.

docs.title: The fixed coefficient of 1 was too large
docs.text:
The residual of d1l's median has a slope of -0.771 on the oracle shift. A forecast with no solar information would show -1. The slope is -0.626 at 0 to 24 hours, -0.632 at 1 to 2 days, -0.709 at 2 to 6 days, -0.818 at 6 to 10 days, and -0.848 from 10 days, and it holds on odd and even months alike (-0.780 and -0.762). By series it runs from -0.615 (D9) to -1.044 (D16). A stale capacity that is too small would push the slope past -1, not towards zero, so staleness does not explain the slope. About a quarter of the anomaly is probably already captured by the cloud proxies in d1l (dew point, precipitation, and the lagged power columns).

A coefficient fitted on the training window, applied only in the three lead bands where the pooled slope was weaker than -0.8 in the log's own test (0 to 24 hours, 1 to 2 days, and 2 to 6 days), gives an exploratory C3 of -0.143 (-0.231 to -0.057) and a C4 of -1.057 (-1.401 to -0.784) at 95%. Even the fitted version lies well above -0.35.

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text:
The ENS shift moves the 0.05 quantile of sunny rows from 0.151 to 0.045, and the 0.95 quantile of cloudy rows from 0.846 to 0.954. The score barely changes. The table gives the share of actuals below each quantile; a calibrated quantile gives 0.05 and 0.95. Sunny rows (CAMS clear-sky index of 0.7 or more) number 107,169 and cloudy rows (under 0.3) number 20,706, across the 5 series and 3 seeds.

  • The gain at day+1 has the same sign in all four reads, and no interval lies wholly below -0.35. C3 at day+1 is -0.434 (upper end -0.283), -0.538 (-0.302), -0.333 (-0.092), and -0.553 (-0.055) in the four reads. C6 at day+1 stays at or near zero: -0.044 and -0.124 in April to September, and +0.019 and -0.177 in June to August.
  • The later lead days disagree between reads. C3 at day+2 is negative in April to September and positive in June to August (+0.272, +0.122). In June to August, C6 is wholly above zero, so the ENS shift is worse than d0, at day+2 (+0.477, +0.290 to +0.620) and at day+3 (+0.172, +0.066 to +0.217). With 3 blocks, the June-to-August intervals are probably too narrow, and the read supports no claim at day+2.
  • The ensemble-mean ENS anomaly keeps its correlation with the CAMS anomaly at midday. It is 0.75, 0.67, and 0.76 at day+1 to day+3 in June to August, and 0.76, 0.74, and 0.70 in April to September (5 series); without D9 the values are 0.79, 0.69, and 0.76, and 0.78, 0.75, and 0.71. Over all daylight hours the training-window correlation is 0.56 to 0.60 at 2 to 6 days, so the midday rows hold a stronger forecast of the anomaly than the all-day average, though the row sets differ and the two figures are not directly comparable.
  • Calibration at midday moves from too narrow to too wide. The share of actuals below the 0.05 quantile of sunny rows falls from 0.187, 0.188, and 0.250 for d1l to 0.020, 0.016, and 0.022 with the shift (day+1 to day+3, April to September, 5 series), against a target of 0.05, so the lower tail overshoots from too narrow to too wide. The share below the 0.95 quantile of cloudy rows rises from 0.787, 0.856, and 0.817 to 0.973, 0.969, and 1.000, against 0.95. June to August gives the same pattern. The log prints the coverage of every read, and each coverage cell holds 195 to 3,624 rows over 3 seeds.

At midday on day+1 the term scores no worse than d0 and moves the quantiles from too narrow to slightly too wide. C6 at day+1 has upper ends of +0.083 and +0.007 in April to September, and +0.099 and +0.075 in June to August. The term is not no worse than d0 at every lead: the June-to-August day+2 and day+3 reads above are wholly above zero. Whether the day+1 result justifies porting the term is not decided here. A second weather forecast beside ENS may give a better irradiance forecast than ENS alone, which is a candidate follow-up the project has not committed to.

docs.title: How the experiment departed from its plan, and what it could not show
docs.text:
• Check 1 is relaxed from a 0.05-point match to 0.2 points, post hoc. The check compares the refitted d0 with experiment 00033's n1_refit. The 0.127 is the mean absolute gap between the per-row raw medians of two identical D10 d0 fits, in points of capacity. It is not a score difference. The 18 comparisons printed 0.020 to 0.185 points. Check 7 (all arms hold the same 909,414 keys) passed. The stored ENS anomaly equals the recomputed slope times the ensemble-mean anomaly on all 307,476 validation rows.
  • Fit noise at the score level is small next to every interval. We measured it from the spread across the 3 seeds with e00046_seed_noise.py (log: seed_noise.log). On the 5 verdict series, the d0 score has a standard deviation of 0.0018 to 0.0027 per series and 0.0004 pooled. The C6 comparison has 0.0017 to 0.0050 per series and 0.00015 pooled (per seed 0.04788, 0.04764, and 0.04762), and d0 minus d1l has 0.0007 pooled. D5, which is outside the verdict series, is noisier (0.0058 for d0, 0.0060 for C6). Fit noise is therefore about 1/670 to 1/20 of C6's half-width (0.100), so it cannot move C6 across zero. The bootstrap draws one seed per resample, so its interval already covers single-fit noise. An Opus review of this write-up checked this reading.
  • C3 and C4 carry no fit-to-fit noise within a seed, but C3 still varies across seeds. Both come from one prediction pass of one d1l booster, so the paired difference does not include the difference between two fits. C3 still varies across seeds (pooled standard deviation 0.0009, from the same script) because each seed's shift sits on a different booster. C6 and d0 minus d1l compare different fits and carry fit noise.
  • The ENS climatology rests on one summer of training data. The anomaly is each forecast minus the mean for that calendar month and half-hour in the same data product, so a summer that differs from the training summer shifts the whole anomaly. On the scored rows the mean CAMS anomaly is +0.0245 of unit output (output as a fraction of installed capacity), and the mean calibrated ENS anomaly is +0.0116, which as shifts are 0.884 and 0.416 points of capacity. By month, the mean CAMS shift runs from +2.877 points in April to -1.016 in July, and the mean ENS shift from 0.091 to 0.678.
  • The 2023/24 capacity is probably out of date, so the oracle is conservative.
  • Not supported by the logs: the printed output holds no result for plan checks 2 to 6 (column counts, a zero shift, the size of the oracle shift, the ENS chain, and the training-window cut-off), beyond the stored-anomaly check above.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: The oracle shows that about 1 point of quantile score is available, and the ENS term collects only the part within 2 days. A next experiment could take one of three routes, and the project has not committed to any. The first is a lead-banded term, used only within 2 days, with a coefficient fitted on the training window per lead band, so the term fades where ENS has no skill. PVDIS-5 could then be a non-inferiority and explanation test overall, plus a gain test pre-registered for 0 to 48 hours only, with PVDIS-4's weekly capacity vintages in place of the 2023/24 capacity. The second is a better short-range solar forecast, because the irradiance forecast is the bottleneck and not the capacity: a satellite-based nowcast for 0 to 6 hours is one candidate, and a second weather forecast beside ENS is another. The third is to stop, since the gain is confined to short leads, where the lagged power columns of d1l probably already carry some of the signal.

docs.title: Experiment 47: does a bank-holiday column in the demand model help the LSC find transfers?
docs.text: The result is inconclusive: adding a bank-holiday column to the demand model raised the share of simulated load transfers the detector found by +0.011 (98.75% interval -0.010 to +0.044), and the experiment is too small to tell that from zero. The demand model is an XGBoost model (a gradient-boosted decision-tree model) that predicts the power drawn at each of 16 Primary substations (substations that step power down to the local distribution network) from the weather. The detector raises an alarm when the average difference between measured and predicted power over 24 hours steps up or down, which can mean that load moved to or from another substation. Demand drops on bank holidays, the model did not expect the drop, and the drop looks like such a step. We refitted the model with one extra column, the number of days to the nearest bank holiday, and added 600 simulated transfers to the real readings. We set each model's alarm threshold so that both raised about the same number of alarms in odd-numbered months that the switching log (the operators' record of planned network switching) does not explain. We then counted how many of the 89 simulated transfers that start in even-numbered months, move 25% to 40% of the receiving substation's load, and last over 1 day the detector found. A transfer counts as found when the detector places its start within 2 hours and its end within the larger of 6 hours and 10% of its duration. The result covers only the route through the threshold: the injected transfers lie at least 2 days from any alarm of the baseline model, so the column could help only by letting the threshold fall.

docs.title: Verdict
docs.text:
C1, the new model minus the baseline model in the share of the 89 transfers found, is +0.011 (98.75% interval -0.010 to +0.044), so the verdict is inconclusive. The baseline is H0.5, the demand model of experiment 17 (trained on ERA5 estimates of past weather, with a half-life of 0.5 years, refitted every month). The detector is D0, which watches one substation's residual (measured minus predicted power). D1 also requires an opposite step at a neighbouring substation. The share found is the mean of three random seeds, 0.360 for the new model and 0.348 for H0.5. The interval resamples whole calendar months 20,000 times, at 98.75% because of a Bonferroni correction across the four contrasts C1 to C4. The decision rule asked for an interval wholly above zero and a higher event F1 at both precision bounds. Event F1 is the harmonic mean of the share found and the alarms' precision. The F1 rose by 0.010 (0.389 to 0.399) at both bounds, which are the same here. The share found for H0.5 is 0.348 here and 0.29 in experiment 43, because this figure covers even months only, takes the mean of three seeds, and experiment 43's 47 of 160 covers all months.

The experiment is too small to detect a gain below about 0.04. The C1 interval has a half-width of about 0.027, and +0.011 is about one transfer net out of 89. Transfers whose receiving substation is metered (48) give +0.007 (-0.019 to +0.054), and the other 41 give +0.016 (0.000 to +0.042).

Contrast Detector, window Change in share found 98.75% interval C1 D0, 24 h +0.011 -0.010 to +0.044 C2 D0, 4 h +0.011 -0.030 to +0.077 C3 D1, 24 h +0.004 -0.011 to +0.033 C4 D1, 4 h +0.015 0.000 to +0.041

The detector found few real transfers with either model. The 14 labelled real transfers that move 25% or more of the receiving load for over 1 day are the headline-band counterpart. The 24-hour D0 finds 1, 2, and 3 of them with the new model (seeds 0 to 2) and 1, 1, and 2 with H0.5. The 35 labelled transfers over 1 day include those 14 and 21 smaller or unsized ones; the counts there are 2, 3, and 4 against 2, 2, and 3. These counts carry no verdict.

docs.title: What held in the prediction and what did not
docs.text:
The column fixed the bank-holiday errors, but the detector did not gain from it.

  • Held: fewer unexplained alarms lie near bank holidays. Of H0.5's 160 unexplained 24-hour D0 alarms, 26 lie within 1 day of a bank holiday outside Christmas and New Year. With the new model at the matched threshold there are 141, 147, and 138 unexplained alarms (seeds 0 to 2), of which 10, 10, and 9 lie within 1 day. The prediction was 13 or fewer.
  • Held: the demand model's error moved as predicted. The mean absolute error of the median rose by 0.04 points of capacity over the whole period (prediction: under 0.05) and fell by 1.13 to 1.19 points on bank holidays (prediction: at least 0.5). H0.5's own errors are 6.70 points over the whole period and 8.88 on bank holidays, and the changes are measured against H0.5 seed 0.
  • Held: event F1 rose. It rose by 0.010 at both precision bounds.
  • Failed: the share found did not rise by 0.03 to 0.10. C1 is +0.011.
  • Failed: the matched threshold rose instead of falling. The prediction was a fall of 0.1 to 0.4. The D0 24-hour threshold rose by 0.217 on average, in units of the noise scale (4.00 to 4.05 for H0.5, 4.20 to 4.25 for the new model). That is about 2.5% in residual units, because the noise scale fell by about 3%. The 4-hour D0 threshold rose by 0.133, the 4-hour D1 by 0.067, and the 24-hour D1 by 0.000.
  • Borderline: the 24-hour noise scale sits at the edge of the 3% band. The odd-month noise scale fell by 3.0%, 3.2%, and 2.9% for seeds 0, 1, and 2 at the 24-hour window, so one seed is inside the band and two are just outside it. The 4-hour window fell by 1.3% to 1.7%, within 3%.
  • Failed: the placebo changed C1 by more than 0.02. The placebo column moves the holiday dates 28 days later and keeps each date's weekday. On share found alone, the shifted column did as well as the real one, within single-seed noise: placebo minus H0.5 is +0.022 (0.000 to +0.068) and the new model minus the placebo is -0.022 (-0.068 to 0.000), about 2 transfers of 89. On event F1 the placebo is worse than H0.5 (0.356 against 0.389 on seed 0), because its 24-hour D0 precision is 0.34 against 0.44 to 0.46 for the other models: more of its alarms fall away from logged closures.

docs.title: Why the threshold rose
docs.text: The column probably made the residual more persistent, which makes the 24-hour step test fire more often away from holidays. This is a likely explanation, not a proven one. The residual's lag-48 autocorrelation (half-hours, one day apart) rose from 0.520 to 0.529 and the autocorrelation of its daily mean from 0.760 to 0.770, while the median absolute deviation fell from 5.55 to 5.46 to 5.51 points of capacity. A more persistent residual over a smaller noise scale crosses a threshold fixed in noise-scale units more often, which cancels the roughly 16 alarms near holidays that the column removed. The placebo shows the same signs (whole-period error +0.136 points, lag-48 autocorrelation 0.535). The persistence matters for SW2-9, the planned whitening step that removes a residual's autocorrelation before detection.

docs.title: Checks and limits
docs.text:
• Matching fixes only the odd-month count, so the scored even months differ. In even months the new model raises 66, 67, and 64 unexplained 24-hour D0 alarms (seeds 0 to 2) against 80, 76, and 71 for H0.5 and 77 for the placebo. The new model is therefore scored at a stricter operating point, which biases the comparison against it.
  • The odd months show no gain. On the 71 headline-band transfers in odd months, which set the thresholds through alarm counts and not through recall, the new model minus H0.5 is -0.019 (0.188 against 0.207), and pooled over all 160 headline-band transfers it is -0.002.
  • The ceiling on the threshold route is low. Only 4.8% of half-hours lie within 1 day of a qualifying bank holiday, and removing 26 of 160 unexplained alarms cannot lower the matched threshold far. We could have computed this ceiling from the operating-point figure before the run.
  • The injection check agrees with the fast residual. The new model's seed-0 fits were refitted on injected power for the months holding a transfer of one batch, the batch with the most headline-band transfers. All 316 pairs of a transfer and a detector setting from that batch agree (1.000, bar 0.95). The 600 transfers are not all checked.
  • The residual is otherwise similar. Logged closures hold 0.342 of H0.5's squared residual and 0.349 of the new model's, against 0.252 of the half-hours.
  • Reproduction of experiment 43. H0.5 seed 0 at experiment 43's thresholds gives its 120, 118, 80, and 36 unexplained odd-month alarms and its 160 unexplained 24-hour D0 alarms.
  • The threshold search takes the lowest value of a run. On a 0.05 grid the search stops at the lowest threshold whose count does not exceed 80 (the 24-hour D0 target), so the new model's odd-month counts are 75, 80, and 74 against 80, 80, and 78 for H0.5, which handicaps the new model slightly.
  • The precision upper bound is an assumption for the new model. It adds the unmatched alarms times the visible share from experiment 41's hand-labelled sample of 37 alarms per setting, drawn from H0.5's alarms. The 24-hour D0 precision is 0.44 for H0.5 and 0.44 to 0.46 for the new model.

The remaining figures sit beside this page: the raw power around bank holidays (figure_1), the residual's spread (figure_2) and autocorrelation (figure_3), the squared-residual shares inside logged closures (figure_4), the share found by size and length band (figure_7), and the demand model's error on bank holidays (figure_9). Code: ml-experiments/00047-sw2-4-better-residual-switching-detector/, with every number printed by e00047_report.py.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: SW2-8 should run next, as already approved. Its neighbour veto targets the alarms this experiment could not turn into recall: 26 of H0.5's 160 unexplained 24-hour D0 alarms lie within 1 day of a bank holiday, and a calendar miss shows as a same-sign step on the neighbours. A veto raises the share of transfers found only by letting the matched threshold fall, so the SW2-8 plan should predict the size of that fall from H0.5's odd-month alarm counts before running. SW2-8 changes the detector and not the residual model, so its injections need no refit. SW2-8 should therefore score several hundred headline-band transfers in the even months, not 89, and place some near bank holidays to count real transfers the veto wrongly removes. SW2-8 should also report its even-month unexplained-alarm count, which matching on odd months does not hold fixed.

docs.title: Experiment 48: does weekly retraining still win on the runs experiment 34 left out?
docs.text:
Refitting the demand forecasting model every week scored better than the best setup tested earlier, on forecast runs the earlier experiment had not scored. We asked whether an XGBoost model that forecasts a substation's electricity demand improves when it is refitted (retrained from scratch) every week on the newest data. An earlier experiment (experiment 34) had scored only 73 forecast runs, 5 days apart. Here we scored the other 292 daily runs of the same year, July 2025 to June 2026, where each run is one day's ECMWF ensemble weather forecast (ENS) used to forecast about 14.6 days of demand. The error is the quantile score, which rewards a forecast that is both close and honest about its uncertainty, in percentage points of the substation's capacity; smaller is better.

On 16 Primary substations, weekly refitting scored 5.44 and the earlier best setup scored 5.64. The earlier setup, called the stack below, is a model fitted once with a correction built from its own errors over the last 14 days. The 0.20-point gap is wholly below zero at the strict level we fixed in advance, but the gap is fragile: it crosses zero with a t-interval over the 12 months or without one substation (see the limits). Weekly refitting also beat monthly refitting (5.57) by 0.13 points. Neither the 7-day nor the 14-day error correction helped a weekly-refitted model, although neither was shown to hurt it at the strict level. At the 2 bulk supply point (BSP) and 2 grid supply point (GSP) substations, which sit above the Primary substations, weekly refitting scored 0.66 points below the stack, more than we predicted. For 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms, refitting the weather-to-power model monthly changed the score by 0.04 points or less, so this experiment found no accuracy reason to refit generation models. The verdict is supported, and the open test is a second validation year, because the 292 runs share their months and weather with the 73 that experiment 34 scored.

Terms used below. The stack uses a spread factor of 1.15 that widens its forecast uncertainty; every other arm uses the spread factor too, and uses no correction unless its name says so. Frozen means fitted once, on data up to the end of June 2025. N1 is the one-model-per-substation XGBoost recipe of experiment 13, trained on the ENS control member. A case is one forecast of one series at one valid time from one run. Lead is the time between the forecast origin and the valid time. P-roll is a monthly refit on the latest 12 months of data only. The weather-to-power model for solar and wind is the ERA5-trained stage 1a model, where ERA5 is a weather reanalysis that arrives about 5 days late. Scores are means over the cases that every forecasting-model arm of a group holds, on seed 0. The decision rule is in the front matter, and C1 to C8w are the contrasts it lists; "Design as planned" below explains the choices.

Weekly refitting beat the stack at the 99.44% level we fixed in advance. C1, weekly minus the stack, is -0.20 points (99.44% interval -0.40 to -0.035), so the interval lies wholly below zero. The threshold was zero: any gain was enough, because refitting replaces the correction step at the price of one scheduled job. C3, weekly minus monthly refitting, is -0.13 (-0.24 to -0.03). C2, monthly minus the stack, is -0.08 (-0.33 to +0.19). Experiment 34 found monthly refitting better than the stack on its 5-day runs, and this experiment did not resolve that gain on daily runs.

Arm Primary (16) BSP (2) GSP (2) Solar farms (6) Wind farms (3) Stack: frozen, 14-day correction 5.64 8.09 19.74 Frozen, no correction 7.09 7.99 19.46 5.02 10.98 Monthly refits 5.57 7.89 18.94 4.97 10.99 Weekly refits 5.44 7.84 18.66 Weekly, 14-day correction 5.52 7.95 19.17 Weekly, 7-day correction 5.60 P-roll 5.59 manual_heuristic 6.26 8.84 20.82 5.79 14.09 climatology 7.48

Each cell is a mean quantile score in points of capacity, and a blank cell means the arm was not run for that group. Scores are on the cases that every forecasting-model arm of the group holds (3,199,243 Primary cases), so differences between cells equal the paired contrasts. manual_heuristic and climatology hold slightly fewer cases (3,197,611 and 3,049,925 for Primary), and the solar and wind rows hold the weather-to-power model without a correction. The 95% interval on each Primary score, over months, is about plus or minus 0.3 points; the contrasts are paired and much tighter.

The reproduction check passed for Primary and narrowly failed for BSP and GSP. We forecast the 73 runs of experiment 34 again from the same refits. For the Primary arms without a correction, the scores matched experiment 34's stored seed-0 scores to 0.001 or better. For the BSP and GSP arms the differences were 0.0002 to 0.006 points, and 4 of those 6 rows lie outside the 0.001 tolerance. The probable cause is that graphics-card fits are not bit-for-bit repeatable. The differences are small against the contrasts reported here.

An error correction was not shown to help a model that is refitted weekly. C4, a 7-day correction on the weekly model, raised the score by 0.16 points, which is worse (99.44% interval -0.06 to +0.36). C5, a 14-day correction, raised it by 0.08 (-0.13 to +0.27). Neither interval excludes zero. C6 shows that the 7-day window scored 0.09 points worse than the 14-day window (+0.02 to +0.17), the opposite of what we predicted. The correction did help the frozen model in this experiment: it lowered the frozen score by 1.45 points (95% interval -1.87 to -0.98).

Weekly refitting gained more at the BSP and GSP substations than predicted, on 4 series. C7, weekly minus the stack, is -0.66 (-1.23 to -0.27), against a predicted range of -0.1 to -0.5. Each of the 4 series scored lower under weekly refitting, but the interval for D13 alone includes zero (figure 4). Weekly minus the frozen model without a correction is -0.47 (95% interval -0.87 to -0.11). A correction on the weekly model raises the score by 0.31 points, which is worse (95% interval +0.06 to +0.60).

Monthly refitting changed the pooled solar score by 0.04 points, and the pooled wind score by 0.01. C8s for the 6 solar farms is -0.044 (99.44% interval -0.158 to -0.003). By the rule we set, that is a change, because the interval excludes zero, although the point estimate lies inside the plus-or-minus-0.05 band. C8w for the 3 wind farms is +0.007 (-0.001 to +0.014), inside the band.

One solar farm drives most of the solar change. Farm E improved by 0.26 points (95% interval -0.72 to -0.00); the other 5 solar farms moved by 0.02 points or less. One wind farm (W2) scored 0.03 points worse (+0.006 to +0.045). We predicted no change from the training-start result of experiment 12, and these intervals are the first retraining measurement for generation in this project's experiments.

The weekly gain over the stack is about the same at every lead time. C1 is -0.21 in the first 24 hours and -0.20 beyond 10 days (figure 3). The gain of weekly over monthly refitting is larger at short leads (-0.19 in the first 24 hours, -0.12 beyond 10 days), and the BSP and GSP gain is larger early (-0.90 in the first 24 hours, -0.62 beyond 10 days).

Refitting monthly on a rolling 12-month window (P-roll) scored 0.03 points worse than monthly refitting on all the data. The difference is +0.028 (95% interval +0.014 to +0.039). Experiment 34 found the same sign.

docs.title: Predictions
docs.text:
• Held: weekly minus the stack in the range -0.10 to -0.30 (-0.20); monthly solar and wind within 0.05 as point estimates (-0.04 and +0.01, though the solar interval excludes zero); the 7-day and 14-day corrections adding +0.05 to +0.30 (+0.16 and +0.08).
  • Missed: monthly 0.05 to 0.10 behind weekly (C3 is 0.13); the 7-day correction adding less than the 14-day correction (it added more); BSP and GSP weekly minus the stack in -0.1 to -0.5 (-0.66). The BSP and GSP prediction in the front matter reads "weekly minus frozen", and C7 uses the stack as the reference; weekly minus the frozen model with no correction is -0.47 and inside the range.

docs.title: Failures and limits
docs.text:
• No refit failed after the restart. The frozen model's first run, one job for all series, showed no output for 37 minutes and was restarted as 5 workers; no result came from the abandoned run.
  • The 292 runs share their months and weather with the 73 of experiment 34. Each run spans about 14.6 days, so the 73 runs already cover every valid time of the year, and the interval is set by 12 months. The result guards against the choice of origins, not against an unusual year. Seeds were not varied (seed 0 only); experiment 34 found that seeds narrow its contrasts by under 0.01.
  • The correction has no history for the first days of July 2025, so the stack and the corrected arms carry no correction there; the correction reads no forecast issued before 2025-07-01.
  • The generator spread factor is fitted on cases before each month's first run. July 2025 and the first wind months have too few earlier cases, so both generator arms are left unscaled there.
  • Pooled intervals resample months only, so they say nothing about other series. The BSP and GSP contrast rests on 4 series, solar on 6, and wind on 3.
  • The reproduction tolerance was missed on the BSP and GSP arms (0.003 to 0.006 points on 4 rows).
