docs.title: Do the two residual models disagree?
docs.text: The two residual models' step statistics differ by far less than the alarm threshold, and their forecasts show no jump at either refit. Where neither model refits within 24 hours, the median absolute difference between the two statistics is 0.136 noise units, taking each series' median and then the median over the 16 series (0.211 for the series with the largest difference). The 99th percentile of the difference is 0.889 noise units, again the median over the 16 series. Both are below the 4.0 noise units that raise an alarm. The forecasts themselves differ by about 2% of a substation's median power at every hour from the refit. The printed report does not count return steps near the splice stamps; it counts alarms only.

docs.title: What held in the prediction and what did not
docs.text:
• Held: the zone split (+0.431 where a gain of at least +0.3 was predicted, and -0.005 where about 0 was predicted); C2 within +-0.003 (it is +0.000); at least 2 of the 3 real refit transfers found (3 are); the threshold rising above 4.0 (it is 4.1); PF14 finding about 0.67 of the moved MW (it finds 0.665).
  • Not held: C1 of +0.01 to +0.04 (it is +0.050, above the range), an interval about 0.05 wide (it is 0.095 wide), and inconclusive as the likely verdict (the verdict is supported).

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The detector uses up to 14 days of hindsight, so it serves training-time masks and the event table, not live inputs.
  • Injected transfers do not distinguish X from L. Injection adds the same power to both models' residuals on top of the real refit jumps, and the control L, which keeps the first model's jumps, loses no recall to them. Only the 3 real refit transfers separate the two arms.
  • The real transfers number 35 and the refit class 3, so "3 against 2" is not a result with an interval.
  • The residual that fixes an interval's end when no return step is found switches to the second model inside a zone. That switch can change the level by the difference between the two residual models.
  • The scaled onset tolerance is scored on injected transfers only, so the real transfers table uses the 2-hour tolerance.
  • A fresh draw is new in the placement of transfers and in the injection noise only. It reuses the same residual table, series, months, and set of 25 long operations as experiments 66 and 69.

docs.title: A correction to the plan's wording
docs.text: The pre-registered prediction says that series 12 and 13 have "no power telemetry at all" before December 2025 and February 2026. The raw power table holds rows for both series from 2024, and the residual panel is what starts later (March 2026 for series 12 and February 2026 for series 13). The conclusion is unchanged, because bridging needs residuals on both sides of a gap.

docs.title: Reviews
docs.text:
• Plan review (Sonnet agent): accepted reordering the verdict rule so that small gain is tested before refuted, rewording the hypothesis to concern arm X only, a zone split of C1, a draw with onsets forced into the zones, the splice-agreement and alarm counts near the splice stamps, a control arm with the suppression lifted, a statement of the second model's training cut-off and a refit of the first model that must return the stored forecasts (it does, to the last digit), the tuning rule for the alarm count, and the refit guard on gap bridging. Rejected calibrating the noise scale on pseudo-gaps, because arm G is descriptive and almost nothing is bridged, and an example time series of the spliced statistic, because the splice-agreement figure covers the question the example would answer.
  • Code review (Sonnet agent): found no leakage and no splice error. Accepted an off-by-one in the refit guard of gap bridging, a tolerance on the check that the first model's refit reproduces the stored forecasts, a finite check on the power comparison, a warning in place of a stop when an arm exceeds 80 alarms, and the two missing planned counts (alarms near the splice stamps and transfers whose outcome the gap bridging changes). The count of return steps near the splice stamps was not added.
  • Fact check against the printed report (Sonnet agent): every number matched. Accepted rewording the claim about series 12 and 13 (their residual panel has no earlier rows, but the raw power table does), "at most 80" for arms with fewer than 80 odd-month alarms, a note on the rows left out of the donor-step table, an account of how 8 found transfers become 10, and two further items of the held and not-held lists. Rejected nothing.
  • Prose review (Sonnet agent): accepted rewriting the title and the opening so that D0M, PF14, noise units, found, injected, unexplained alarms, and the 98.33% interval are defined before use, defining the injected shapes and bands, splitting several leads, using "alarm threshold" and "second residual model", replacing the money metaphors, and several count clarifications. Rejected rewriting the pre-registered front matter.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
Two remaining groups of misses are not mechanical: 8 real transfers with a sharp step of 2 to 4 noise units, and 3 with an alarm 2 to 12 hours from the labelled start. Neither group changed under any arm here. A threshold lowered to reach the sharp small steps raises the unexplained-alarm count, and experiment 69's weak-alarm rule, which accepts a weak alarm that a matching step back confirms, did not reach them without losing recall elsewhere. The scaled onset tolerance did not separate the arms on injected transfers, so the 3 timing cases need a score on real transfers with a duration-scaled tolerance to say whether they are a scoring artefact.

Code: ml-experiments/00071-sw2-18-refit-offset-and-gap-bridging/, with every number printed by e00071_report.py.

docs.title: Experiment 72 (P35): can a step-loss monitor find a lost inverter at the solar farms?
docs.text:
Take-home message: a solar farm's daily power readings show that the farm has lost 25% of its output only if the loss lasts 90 days or more, and they show a smaller or shorter loss rarely or never, so they cannot give early warning of one lost inverter.

We added artificial losses to the real power of 5 solar farms (a loss multiplies the farm's power by a fixed share for a set number of days) and ran three monitors over the result. A monitor is a rule that reads each farm's daily power, relative to the other farms' power, and raises an alarm when the level drops. The best of the three found 0.84 of the 25% losses that lasted 90 days, 0.26 of the 10% losses that lasted 90 days, and 3% losses barely above chance (0.02 to 0.07, against 0.00 to 0.02 when no loss was added). Over a 30-day loss it did worse: the change-point monitor found 0.45 of the 25% losses, and the hysteresis monitor found 0.86 of them but 0.13 or less of the 10% losses. In these 3 monitors on 5 farms, the limit came from the data and not from the method. A farm gives only about 3 usable days a week (days with clear sky, no inverter clipping, and no stuck meter), and the daily reading wanders by 6% to 11% of its normal level. A second source of evidence, such as outage notices from National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED), could test the losses that the readings cannot show.

We asked whether the power a solar farm delivers shows that the farm has lost part of its generating capacity, for example because an inverter failed. We also counted how often each monitor raised an alarm when no loss had been added (a false alarm), and whether each monitor found the three months in which farm A really did run low. The plan set a stop rule: the experiment is refuted if the change-point monitor finds fewer than 0.80 of the 25% losses that last 30 days. It found 0.45, so the verdict is refuted. The page says "5 solar farms" because the sixth farm, farm E, has only 2.7 years of record and is monitored but not injected.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
The verdict is refuted by the first stop rule. The change-point monitor found 0.45 of 25% losses lasting 30 days (April to September starts; 100 losses). Each monitor was tuned on a week-shuffled placebo to about 0.35 false alarms per farm-year. The monitor found all three of farm A's low months. Its false-alarm rate was 0.29 per farm-year on the scored placebo, which meets the limit of 0.5. On the unmodified record it was 0.54, which meets the limit of 1. The change-point monitor beat neither baseline by an interval that excludes 0 (the two contrasts below), and the other three stop rules did not fire.

Loss, April to September onset Change-point fit Rolling median Hysteresis rule (HYST) Change-point, 7-day segment (post hoc) 25%, 30 days 0.45 0.30 0.86 0.64 25%, 90 days 0.84 0.72 0.82 0.84 25%, to the end of the record 0.80 0.70 0.78 0.82 10%, 30 days 0.04 0.05 0.13 0.05 10%, 90 days 0.26 0.16 0.07 0.25 10%, to the end of the record 0.38 0.12 0.13 0.37 3%, 90 days 0.03 0.04 0.07 - 0% (no loss; chance of an alarm in the window) 0.01 to 0.02 0.01 to 0.02 0.00 to 0.01 0.01 to 0.02

Each cell pools 100 losses (5 farms, 20 draws). Among the 25% losses that were found, the median delay from the first day of the loss to the alarm was 1 day for the change-point fit, 3 days for the rolling median, and 14.5 days for the hysteresis rule. The rolling median's size estimate was 9.8 points too low. A loss that starts from October to March is found less often: 25% losses lasting 30 days at 0.27, 0.14, and 0.57 for the change-point fit, the rolling median, and the hysteresis rule. Losses from that half-year decide nothing.

The two planned contrasts are positive but their intervals include 0. On 10% losses lasting 30 and 90 days, C1 (the change-point fit minus the rolling median) is +0.045 (97.5% interval -0.015 to +0.090), and C2 (the change-point fit minus the hysteresis rule) is +0.050 (-0.010 to +0.105). Farm A sits below 0 against the rolling median (-0.05), and farm D below 0 against the hysteresis rule (-0.03). The interval resamples 5 farms that share one 25 km square of satellite irradiance, so it is a rough guide.

False alarms were 0.29 per farm-year on the placebo and 0.36 to 0.54 on the real record. The unmodified record has more alarms than the placebo because it holds real steps, year-level drift, and the winter dip at farm D.

Six of the 18 unmodified-record alarms are farm D's winter dip. Farm D raised one alarm in November or December of each year from 2020 to 2025. Farm A's low months raised 2 further alarms. The count of 18 excludes those 2.

docs.title: Why the monitors fall short
docs.text:
A 30-day loss holds about 13 valid days, and the change-point fit requires segments of at least 14 valid days. A farm has 3.1 valid days a week from April to September and 2.0 from October to March. The daily signal has a robust standard deviation (the standard deviation estimated from the median absolute deviation) of 0.061 to 0.114 (6.1% to 11.4%) at farms A to D and F. The hysteresis rule needs only 7 valid days below the threshold, which is why it finds 25% losses lasting 30 days better than the change-point fit does.

A shorter segment helps by 19 points at 25% and 30 days, but stays under 0.80. The post hoc arm with a segment of 7 valid days found 0.64 of 25% losses lasting 30 days (against 0.45), kept 0.31 false alarms per farm-year on the placebo, and left the 10% rows unchanged. The change-point fit with 7-valid-day segments still fell short of the 0.80 required.

A temporary loss needs two change points, so the fit finds temporary losses less often. An L0 fit (a fit that charges a fixed penalty for each change point) whose penalty is tuned to 0.35 false alarms per farm-year must pay that penalty twice for a loss that starts and ends. A permanent 10% loss (one change point) was found 0.38 of the time and a 10% loss lasting 90 days (two) 0.26 of the time.

docs.title: Post hoc checks
docs.text: Neither check changes the pre-registered verdict. A window that opens 14 days before the loss raises the rate of 25% losses lasting 30 days by 19 points for the change-point fit, 13 points for the rolling median, and 1 point for the hysteresis rule: 25% losses lasting 30 days at 0.64, 0.43, and 0.87 for the change-point fit, the rolling median, and the hysteresis rule. A change-point fit with a minimum segment of 7 valid days is the post hoc arm in the table above.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
Signal. Each farm's daily ratio of power to the power a physics model expects on clear, unclipped hours, divided again by the median of the other pool farms' ratios of the same day (four for a pool farm, five for farm E), and centred on the farm's median over the unmodified record, with farm A's three low months set aside. Farm E is monitored but is never one of the other farms, because E has 2.7 years of record and an export cap. A day with fewer than two other farms is dropped.

Monitors. The change-point fit is an optimal partitioning of the valid days (a search for the split into level segments that has the least squared error plus a fixed penalty per change point, called an L0 penalty), with a minimum segment of 14 valid days. Each value is first clipped to 3 robust standard deviations around the median of the 15 valid days centred on it, the penalty is the multiplier (6.0 once tuned) times the robust variance times the logarithm of the number of valid days, and every alarm is floored at a 5% step. The rolling median is the centred 28-valid-day median, and the hysteresis rule is hysteresis_level of the capacity studies. Each has one parameter, tuned on 20 week-shuffled placebo copies of the 5 farms (20 random shuffles) to 0.35 false alarms per farm-year and then frozen (e00072_frozen_config.json). The scored placebo uses 20 other shuffles.

Injection. A loss multiplies one farm's real power by 1 - f from an onset to the end of the loss. Each farm, draw, and half-year gets four runs: one run of four losses lasting 30 days (sizes 0%, 3%, 10%, and 25%, where 0% is a control that measures how often a window holds an alarm by chance), one run of the same four sizes lasting 90 days, and two runs of one permanent loss each (10% and 25%). Five farms, 20 draws, 2 half-years, and 4 runs make 800 runs, and all 800 placed their losses. A loss starts at least 60 days after the farm's first valid day and 120 days before the end of the record, losses in one run are at least 150 days apart, and farm A's losses start at least 90 days from its low months. The injected farm's neighbours keep their unmodified power, and only the injected farm is scored. The injection scales a whole farm's power, so it emulates an inverter loss and cannot emulate a string loss on a farm that clips.

Known limits. The monitors remove no snow days and no negative-price hours, fit no trend for panel degradation, and ignore the day's maximum power, which a lost inverter would also lower. NGED has not given us a record of any real loss apart from farm A's three low months, so the injected losses are the only known-answer test.

docs.title: Order of the work
docs.text: A first scoring run happened before the code review, and its detection table was read. The review then found four faults. The rolling-median baseline subtracted a median that included the injected loss. The week shuffle moved missing days into the record. Farm-years were counted on the shuffled signal. The alarm sizes of two monitors were not floored at 5%. All four were fixed, the first run's tables and frozen parameters were moved to a superseded folder of the private data store (not committed), and every table on this page comes from the second run. The second tuning chose the same parameters as the first (6.0, 0.12, and 0.10), so the first run's reading did not steer any choice.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: Which real events at the 6 solar farms can be labelled, so that the monitor is tested on more than farm A's three low months? NGED's outage notices, protection-trip logs, and curtailment records for the 6 farms would give real losses. With them, the next experiment can ask whether a loss that the telemetry cannot show (10% or less) can be found from another source, and whether the hysteresis rule at 25% gives a useful early alert.

docs.title: Experiment 73: can the mix of solar panel orientations and the DC to AC ratio be recovered?
docs.text:
We asked whether two properties of the solar panels behind a substation can be read from the substation's power alone. The first is the share of panels facing east, south, and west. The second is the ratio of DC capacity to AC (inverter) capacity, which sets the level at which output flattens at midday. We tested each fit first on answers we know. We added made-up east-south-west output, and the real output of 6 metered solar farms, to the real power of 8 Primary substations (the substations in Lincolnshire that step power down to the local electricity network and are metered in MW), and checked what the fit recovered. The orientation fit has three non-negative capacities, one per orientation. We scored it by total-variation error, the share of capacity assigned to the wrong orientation (0 is exact and 1 is the worst possible).

With no noise added, the median error over the injected cases was 0.09, against 0.30 for always guessing the usual fleet mix (0.2 east, 0.6 south, 0.2 west). With the real series' noise added the median error rose to 0.20. On the real power, the fitted shares changed by a median 0.24 between consecutive September-to-August years. Even so, a blend of the three shapes predicted 28-day blocks of power that the fit had not seen 1.3% better than assuming every panel faces south.

The DC:AC search tries ratios from 1.00 to 1.60 and keeps the one whose clipped shape fits best. The search found each farm's ratio from the farm's own output, but not once the farm's output was added to a Primary's power, so we dropped the search before touching the real series.

Take-home message: the fitted solar shape, a blend of three shapes, is a better solar shape than all-south panels at every one of the 8 Primaries, but it is a more flexible shape and not a measurement of panel orientation. The shares that make up the blend swap from year to year and miss by about 0.2 on a noisy known answer, so none of them should be published as a finding about a Primary's panels. The DC:AC search did not recover a farm's ratio once the farm was added to a Primary's power, so the solar term keeps the fixed ratio of 1.15. The next test is whether the three-shape blend lowers the error of the forecasts of experiment 64 (PVDIS-5), and not only the error of the fit.

Verdict partly supported, read by the rule written before the run. Orientation passes its pre-registered known answers (median share error 0.088, at most 0.15; upper limit of C1, the fit's error minus the guess's, -0.122, below -0.10) and gains on held-out blocks (upper limit of C3, the change in held-out error against all-south panels, -0.54%, below -0.5%). DC:AC is not identified. Exactly one part is identified with its held-out gain, which is the rule's partly supported. After the code review we added a known-answer test that carries noise, because the pre-registered one cannot fail (see below). The chosen arm fails the added test (median error 0.200, C1 upper limit -0.075), so the shares are not identified, and the verdict describes the blend and not the shares.

docs.title: Known answers
docs.text:
Without noise, injected east-south-west mixes are recovered far better than a guess. The arm chosen on the tuning units (solar-farm locations A to C) was the pooled fit with no prior. On the scoring units (locations D to F) its median share error is 0.088, against 0.300 for guessing the fleet mix. C1, the arm's error minus the guess's, is -0.181 (98.75% interval -0.228 to -0.122), pooled over the five true mixes. With Primaries as the clusters the interval is -0.248 to -0.084. Per true mix, the guess is exact at the fleet mix itself and the fit is not, and the fit wins at the other four. Of the noise-free scoring units at the fitted tilt, 0.192 hit one of the two bounds (a negative increment set to zero, or a total increment under 0.3 MW).

A known-answer test that adds no noise cannot fail. A least-squares fit is linear, so the fitted capacities with and without an injection differ by the fit of the injection alone, whatever the series' own noise. The first test therefore measures only the sky mismatch between the farm location and the Primary, plus the cases where the non-negative constraint binds. The code review found this. We added a second test (post hoc, after the code review and before its result was seen). It builds a series with no solar of its own: the Primary's fitted solar is added back, the part left after removing the calendar cells and the weather terms is shuffled between days of the same month, and the known output is subtracted. The fit then has to find the injection in the real series' noise, and is scored on its fitted capacities directly.

True mix (east/south/west) Pooled fit, no noise Pooled fit, with noise Guess: fleet mix Guess: all south all south (0/1/0) 0.102 0.315 0.400 0.000 fleet mix (0.2/0.6/0.2) 0.097 0.226 0.000 0.400 east-heavy (0.5/0.4/0.1) 0.097 0.198 0.300 0.600 west-heavy (0.1/0.4/0.5) 0.100 0.190 0.300 0.600 east and west (0.5/0/0.5) 0.045 0.084 0.600 1.000

With noise, the pooled fit's median error on the scoring units is 0.200 against 0.300 for the guess. The noisy C1 is -0.107 (98.75% interval -0.139 to -0.075), so the upper limit of the noisy C1 does not reach -0.10, and the noisy median error is above 0.15. The free fit on each season-year scores 0.169, the clear-day fit 0.296, and the pooled fit with the smallest prior 0.177. All arms miss by more than 0.15 at the tilt of the fit, so the shares are not identified.

The robustness arm shows the fragility. Injected shapes at 15° and 40° tilt, with the fit at 25°, gave noisy median errors for the pooled fit of 0.277 and 0.163 over all farm locations.

The DC:AC ratio is found from a farm's own output and lost once the farm is added to a Primary. The knee gate was applied to each farm's median across its farm-years, not to each farm-year as the rule states. That median number of clear-day half-hours at or above the knee at ratio 1.15 is 165 to 188 for five farms and 110.5 for farm D, against the threshold of 100, so the gate passed. Three of the 37 farm-years fall below 100 (the lowest has 84). The search on each farm's output alone has a median absolute error of 0.055 over the 6 farms and beats the constant guess (the median ratio of the other five farms) on 5 of 6. With 10 MW of the farm's output added to a Primary's power, the median error is 0.195 and the search beats the guess on 0 of 6, so DC:AC is not identified. The searched ratio sits at 1.00 to 1.10 for every farm in that case. The Primary's own solar is still in the series, so this case measures a farm plus a fleet, and not only the farm.

Farm True ratio Error, farm alone Error, added to a Primary Error of the guess A 1.15 0.050 0.150 0.070 B 1.17 0.020 0.170 0.050 C 1.22 0.070 0.220 0.050 D 1.42 0.220 0.320 0.250 E 1.12 0.030 0.120 0.100 F 1.26 0.060 0.260 0.090

The ratios of experiment 29 come from the same CAMS irradiance and the same clipping form as the search, so the farm-alone case is the easiest test of the search. With 6 farms the intervals are descriptive, and the decision rests on the number of farms, out of 6, where the fit beats the constant guess.

docs.title: The real series
docs.text:
The shares of the real series are not stable. The free fit to each Primary-year changes its shares by a median total-variation distance of 0.237 between consecutive September-to-August years (33 pairs), and the clear-day fit by 0.326. The pooled fit holds one mix per Primary across its years, so the year-to-year test does not apply to the pooled fit. The pooled fit's 95% intervals (200 resamples of 7-day blocks of clear days) are on average 0.49 wide, on a share that runs from 0 to 1.

Primary Capacity (MW) East South West Kirton (experiment 40 flagged a daylight load there) 1.58 0.00 (0.00 to 0.10) 0.95 (0.68 to 1.00) 0.05 (0.00 to 0.29) Trusthorpe 7.58 0.33 (0.01 to 0.49) 0.08 (0.00 to 0.40) 0.58 (0.41 to 0.65) Spilsby 2.57 0.27 (0.07 to 0.44) 0.24 (0.00 to 0.66) 0.49 (0.21 to 0.65) Horncastle 3.03 0.31 (0.00 to 0.49) 0.19 (0.00 to 0.66) 0.50 (0.30 to 0.59) Mount Bridge Boston 3.65 0.06 (0.00 to 0.30) 0.51 (0.19 to 0.75) 0.43 (0.23 to 0.57) Wrangle T1 (little power) 3.71 0.27 (0.00 to 0.64) 0.23 (0.00 to 1.00) 0.50 (0.00 to 0.92) Donington 3.27 0.30 (0.00 to 0.48) 0.23 (0.00 to 0.58) 0.46 (0.32 to 0.59) Wrangle T2 2.69 0.49 (0.18 to 0.89) 0.29 (0.00 to 0.71) 0.22 (0.00 to 0.53)

The capacity column is the mean of the years' south-only capacities times the sum of the shares. It differs from experiment 40's capacities (for example 7.58 MW against 2.48 MW at Trusthorpe). The orientation fit trades capacity against shape, so these totals are not capacity estimates.

The fitted mix predicts held-out blocks better than all-south panels at all 8 Primaries. Each fit uses alternate 28-day blocks of a season-year, and the other blocks are scored, in both directions. The south-only comparator has the same total capacity as the mix, so the two differ only in shape. C3, the relative change in held-out root mean square error of daylight power, is -1.3% (98.75% interval -2.4% to -0.5%, 80 held-out year-folds). The threshold for a gain is an upper limit below -0.5%, and the upper limit is -0.54%, so C3 is a gain by a narrow margin. The change ranges from -0.1% at Kirton to -3.8% at Trusthorpe. C4, the same comparison for the DC:AC ratio, was not computed, because the DC:AC fit failed its known answers.

The blend improves the fit although its shares are not identified. The three shapes let the fit place solar output earlier or later in the day. Evening demand that resembles west-facing output would give the same gain, and this experiment cannot separate the two.

Five of the 8 Primaries have a pooled west share of 0.46 to 0.58, against 0.2 in the fleet mix. The interval of Wrangle T1 runs from 0.00 to 0.92, so 4 Primaries support a lean: the intervals of Spilsby (0.21 to 0.65), Horncastle (0.30 to 0.59), Donington (0.32 to 0.59), and Trusthorpe (0.41 to 0.65) all exclude 0.2.

docs.title: Changes from the plan
docs.text:
• The held-out cell minimum is 5 rows, not 20. With alternate 28-day blocks, no cell reached 20 fitted rows, so every held-out row was dropped in the first run. The change was made before any held-out result existed.
  • The null arm became a bootstrap. The plan injected nothing and reported the fitted shares, but with no injection the fitted capacities do not change, so the increment is exactly zero by construction. The page reports the pooled shares' 95% intervals from resampled blocks.
  • The noisy known-answer test was added after the code review and is reported beside the pre-registered test. The verdict follows the pre-registered rule.
  • The held-out comparison rescales the shares to a common total. The first version, before the code review, compared the unnormalised pooled capacities with the south-only capacity, which mixed shape and total capacity, and gave +0.8% (-0.9% to +2.8%). The corrected comparison gives the figures above.
  • The pooled arm with ridge 0 won the tuning, so the ridge prior toward the fleet mix never entered the chosen arm.
  • The knee gate uses each farm's median across its farm-years, and not each farm-year.
  • The 5 MW injection was dropped, as the plan review advised, and the 10 MW injection decides.
  • DC:AC has no fitted parameter beyond its grid, so all 6 farms are scored, and no tuning split applies. The 8 Primaries' own series were searched without injection as a reference only (41 Primary-years, quartiles 1.00, 1.00, and 1.30, range 1.00 to 1.60). The plan stops real-series fits for DC:AC, and this reference is not a claim about the Primaries.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The known answers use one physics. Passing the known answers is necessary and not sufficient, as the 15° robustness arm shows.
  • Farms A to C and D to F share the same 8 Primaries, so the tuning and scoring split gives little independence. The Primary-cluster interval is reported beside the farm-cluster interval.
  • Only 6 farms score DC:AC, so the count of farms where the fit beats the guess is a coarse test.
  • The plan had one Sonnet review and no Opus review.
  • The pooled fit takes each year's total from a south-only fit, floored at 0.1 MW. East-heavy or west-heavy fleets then have shares that sum to more than 1, which is why the pooled capacity differs from experiment 40's capacity. The held-out comparison rescales the shares to a common total.
  • The 6-farm inner join drops Primary rows where any farm location's CAMS reliability is under 0.9, a small loss correlated in time.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
The next experiment should ask whether the fitted solar shape lowers the error of the forecasts of experiment 64 (PVDIS-5), and not only the error of the fit. The held-out gain of 1.3% is for the daylight power of a fit with the weather inputs known, and a forecast has only forecast weather. The test is whether the per-Primary shape, used as the solar term of experiment 64's arm am, lowers that arm's score by more than the 0.5% threshold. The shares that make up the shape should stay fixed across all training years, or drift only under a strong year-to-year penalty. Refitting the shares freely each year would carry into the forecast the median change of 0.24 between consecutive years that the free fit shows, which is noise.

A second test should compare the west capacity fitted on daylight rows with the response of demand after dark. If the two match, the west share is probably evening demand and not panels. The test fits the same three shapes to rows after sunset, where no solar exists.

docs.title: Size: medium
docs.text:
• What gets stored: only private work tables under data/ml-experiments/; no Delta table.
  • Serving path: untouched.
  • Degradation rule: untouched.
  • More than one defensible design: yes, so the plan fixes three orientation fits and one clipping search before any result.
  • Callers: the machinery is experiment 39's and 40's code, copied into this folder; no caller outside ml-experiments/.

The process was the full one, with Sonnet throughout: a plan, one plan review, an implementation, a code review, and a write-up with a prose review.

docs.title: Earlier advice followed
docs.text:
• From experiment 40: do not quote a capacity without a bound, and leave Wrangle T1 out of any claim that a Primary is free of a load. Every real-series table here flags Kirton and Wrangle T1.
  • From experiment 45: the capacity is held constant within each season-year, not weekly.
  • Departure: none.

docs.title: Data and fits
docs.text:
Inputs are experiment 39's frame, read and never rebuilt: half-hourly power of the 8 directional Primaries and 6 solar farms, CAMS irradiance, and ERA5 temperature, on daylight half-hours (zenith under 75°). The fit window is April to September of each season-year. The demand term is the calendar-cell term of experiment 40's arm M2h (fixed effect per month, half-hour, and day type, heating degree-days, and cloud terms in three hour bands). The solar shapes come from studies.pv_separation.solar_basis at 25° tilt, which gives the AC output of 1 MW of east-, south-, and west-facing panels, clipped at min(r × irradiance / 1000, 1).

Orientation arms. Each fits non-negative east, south, and west capacities to a Primary's season-year.

  • O1, free: three free capacities.
  • O2, free on clear days: O1 on days whose mean cloud response is below 0.15. The cloud response is 1 - min(ghi_u / ghi_u_clear, 1) at the Primary's CAMS point, averaged over the day's daylight half-hours (experiment 39's frame columns). A Primary-year needs at least 20 clear days or it is dropped from O2 and O3 and the count is reported.
  • O3, pooled with a prior: one mix per Primary shared by all its season-years, clear days only, with a ridge penalty pulling the shares towards the fleet mix. The penalty is chosen on tuning units from the grid 0, 0.1, 1, 10 (relative to the mean squared column norm).
  • References: G guesses the fleet mix; S assumes all south.

DC:AC arm. For each ratio r on the grid 1.00, 1.05, ..., 1.60, fit one capacity to the clear-day rows with the shape min(r × irradiance / 1000, 1) (south, 25° tilt) and keep the r with the lowest residual sum of squares. A ratio of 1.00 never clips in GB. The interval is the 2.5th to 97.5th percentile of the best r over 200 resamples of 7-day blocks.

docs.title: Known answers, run before any real fit
docs.text:
• Orientation: inject 3 MW of synthetic output, 3 × (wE uE + wS uS + wW uW) with the shapes built from CAMS at each solar farm's location, so the injected sky differs from the sky the fit uses at the Primary. A robustness arm, reported and not decisive, injects shapes at 15° and 40° tilt while the fit stays at 25°, and passing the known answers is necessary but not sufficient. The five true mixes (wE, wS, wW) are (0, 1, 0), (0.2, 0.6, 0.2), (0.5, 0.4, 0.1), (0.1, 0.4, 0.5), and (0.5, 0, 0.5). Units are Primary × season-year × farm location × mix. The estimated shares come from the increment of the fitted capacities, with negative increments set to zero. A total increment under 0.3 MW counts as an error of 0.5. Each arm reports the share of units that hit either rule.
  • DC:AC: the DC:AC ratios of the six farms are experiment 29's PyTorch fits: 1.15, 1.17, 1.22, 1.42, 1.12, and 1.26. Run the search on each farm's output alone against its own location's shape, and on each farm's output scaled to 10 MW and added to a Primary's real series. The farms are tuned and scored in the same split as orientation (A to C, D to F).
  • Noisy known answer (added after the code review): rebuild each series with no solar of its own and day-shuffled residuals, inject the known output, and score the fitted capacities directly, because the increment test above is blind to noise.
  • Self-tests that stop the run: a made-up all-south mix reproduces the south-only fit; noise-free injection into zero demand returns the true mix to 1e-6; noise-free clipped output returns the true ratio; linearity of the increment.

docs.title: Real series
docs.text: The real-series fits use the same designs. The free and clear-day fits are per season-year. The pooled fit has a 200-draw block bootstrap. Contrast C3 fits on alternate 28-day blocks, scores the others, and reverses, with the capacities fixed from the training blocks and the calendar cells and nuisance terms refitted on them.

docs.title: Experiment 74: do same-time analogues add anything once the solar forecast is explicit? (AN1)
docs.text:
Take-home message: telling the XGBoost model of a Primary substation's power about sunshine, in either of two ways, lowered its daylight error by 0.09 to 0.15 points, and the two ways help in different conditions. One point is 1% of the substation's capacity. The explicit forecast of the solar panels' output wins at leads under 2 days (a lead is the time from the forecast start to the half-hour being forecast) and on cloudy rows (rows with a clear-sky index under 0.3, which is the ratio of the measured sunshine to the cloud-free sunshine). The analogues, which are recent days at the same time of day with similar sunshine, match the explicit forecast on sunny rows and in August and September. Using both scored best, at 4.518 points against 4.584 for the explicit forecast alone, but one validation year (the 12 months from July 2025 to June 2026) cannot resolve a gain that small. The next test needs more forecast weeks and one new variant, analogues matched on the day type alone. The verdict is inconclusive.

We asked how to tell a forecast of a Primary substation's power about the sunshine. A Primary substation steps 33 kV or 66 kV down to 11 kV in the electricity distribution network. Solar panels behind the substation's meter cut the metered power on a sunny day, so the forecast needs the sunshine. We tried two ways on five substations over daylight half-hours of April to September. A row is one half-hour forecast of one substation from one forecast run. In the explicit way, the panels' output is forecast as their capacity times the forecast sunshine, with a fitted weight, and the XGBoost model receives that output as a starting offset: a value added to the model's prediction for each row before its trees. The forecast sunshine comes from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts ensemble (ENS). In the analogue way, we search the recent days for the 3 whose measured sunshine was closest to the sunshine forecast for the target, among days at the same half-hour and of the same day type (working day, weekend, or bank holiday). The measured sunshine is a satellite-based estimate, CAMS, from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service. The XGBoost model then receives the metered power on those 3 days as input columns. We refitted the XGBoost model every month on the latest year of data for both ways. Experiment 34 found that a model that is never refitted overstates the value of an input that follows the recent level of power. Both ways beat the same monthly refit without either input. The explicit way beat it by 0.15 points, and the analogue way by 0.095 points. The experiment could not tell which way is better, and could not tell whether the analogues add anything once the offset is in the model.

Legend of the arms. R0 is the monthly refit without either input, the reference. E is the refit with the explicit offset. E_twin is E given the sunshine forecast of another date, a placebo that keeps the capacity and the spread of the sunshine and removes its timing. A1, A3, and A5 are the refits with 1, 3, and 5 analogues. A3E has the 3 analogues and the offset. A3S has 3 days drawn at random from the same recent days, ignoring sunshine and day type, a placebo for the matching. R0_rad is R0 plus the radiation inputs, a context arm. The analogue columns are the mean and the standard deviation of the 3 days' power, the mean gap in sunshine, and the number of days found.

docs.title: The planned contrasts
docs.text:
The decision rule was committed before any code ran. The rule has six contrasts on the quantile score, an error measure where lower is better. Every contrast is a paired difference of two arms' scores, with whole weeks of forecast start resampled, and every interval is 99.17% (a 5% error split across six). Seed 0 decides the verdict. C3 is the head-to-head contrast. C4 asks whether the analogues add anything once the offset is in, and needs its upper end below -0.05 to be worth porting, which means building the analogue columns in the live service. The rule has four verdicts. refuted needs C3's upper end below zero or C4's upper end below -0.05. supported needs C1's upper end below zero, C3's lower end above zero, and C4's lower end at or above -0.05. small gain is the same as supported except that C4's upper end is below zero. Neither of the first two is met, so the verdict is inconclusive: C3 runs from -0.053 to +0.161, and C4 from -0.149 to +0.015.

Contrast Arm minus arm Difference 99.17% interval C1 E (offset) minus R0 (reference) -0.149 -0.201 to -0.104 C2 A3 (3 analogues) minus R0 -0.095 -0.185 to -0.007 C3 A3 minus E +0.054 -0.053 to +0.161 C4 A3E (both) minus E -0.066 -0.149 to +0.015 C5 E minus E_twin (offset from another date) -0.246 -0.322 to -0.173 C6 A3 minus A3S (3 random days) -0.081 -0.165 to +0.001

The values are differences in quantile score, in points of capacity. A negative value favours the first arm. The rows are 68,903 rows from 29 weeks of forecast start, at five Primary substations anonymised as D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16, one forecast run every 5 days in July to September 2025 and April to June 2026. Every interval except C1's has a half-width above the 0.05 porting threshold, so C4 could not rule out a gain of that size. The half-width is half the interval's width: 0.05 (C1), 0.09 (C2), 0.11 (C3), 0.08 (C4), 0.07 (C5), and 0.08 (C6).

The arms' absolute scores sit close together, and the pairing is what separates them. Scores are in points of capacity, with 95% intervals from resampling whole weeks:

Arm Quantile score R0, reference 4.734 (4.441 to 5.057) E, explicit offset 4.584 (4.302 to 4.909) E_twin, offset from another date 4.830 (4.531 to 5.159) A1, 1 analogue 4.631 (4.338 to 4.952) A3, 3 analogues 4.639 (4.343 to 4.960) A5, 5 analogues 4.673 (4.367 to 5.006) A3E, 3 analogues and the offset 4.518 (4.229 to 4.832) A3S, 3 random days 4.720 (4.431 to 5.040) R0_rad, reference plus radiation inputs (context) 4.614 (4.338 to 4.933)

For context, three frozen models of experiment 64 score 4.620 (d0, its best guess), 4.723 (d1l, the best guess without radiation inputs), and 4.466 (am, the offset model) on the same rows. They carry the 14-day correction, an average of the recent forecast errors added to the forecast, so no contrast uses them.

docs.title: The offset wins at short leads and on cloudy rows; the analogues catch up on sunny rows
docs.text:
Both gains are largest within 2 days of the forecast start and are gone from 10 days, and the offset gains more at the shortest leads. At leads under 48 hours, C1 is -0.439 (95% interval -0.578 to -0.306) and C2 is -0.237 (-0.316 to -0.172), so C3 is +0.203 (+0.060 to +0.346). The analogues add to the offset in that range: C4 is -0.153 (-0.227 to -0.086). From 10 days, no contrast differs from zero. All reads on this page other than C1 to C6 are exploratory, at 95%.

The split by sunshine shows why the two ways differ. On cloudy rows (a clear-sky index under 0.3), the analogues trail the offset by 0.429 points (0.224 to 0.657). On sunny rows (an index of 0.7 or more), C3 is -0.050 (-0.199 to +0.098) and C4 is -0.138 (-0.251 to -0.023). On these 5 substations' rows, the forecast sunshine helped most on cloudy days, and a similar past day helped most on sunny days. By substation, C3 favours the offset at D9 (+0.166, +0.066 to +0.269) and D11 (+0.101, +0.051 to +0.153), and is under 0.04 in size, in either direction, at D14 and D16.

By month, the analogues match the offset only in August and September. C3 is +0.110, +0.139, +0.067, and +0.043 in April to July, +0.006 in August, and -0.062 in September, so the analogues trail the offset in the first four months. C4 is -0.163 in August and -0.175 in September. The monthly figures are means of each month's differences, each from 5 to 7 weeks of forecast start. The 95% intervals are in the printed report, and most of C3's include zero.

docs.title: Other reads
docs.text:
Every read in this list is exploratory, at 95%, except C5 and C6, which are planned and use 99.17%.

  • Matching probably helps on sunny rows. A3 against A3S, the 3 random days, is -0.081 (-0.165 to +0.001) over all rows (C6, planned), so the upper end is a hair above zero. The gain from matching is -0.197 (-0.275 to -0.130) at leads under 48 hours and -0.188 (-0.307 to -0.060) on sunny rows. On cloudy rows the contrast is +0.137 (+0.002 to +0.293), which means that matched analogues are worse than random days there.
  • One analogue scored as well as three. A1 minus A3 is -0.008 (-0.037 to +0.019), and A5 minus A3 is +0.034 (+0.014 to +0.060).
  • The offset adds to the analogues. A3E minus A3, the offset's gain on top of the analogues, is -0.121 (-0.157 to -0.086).
  • The offset carries solar information. C5 (planned) shows the offset beats its twin by 0.246 (0.173 to 0.322), and experiment 64 found the same direction (0.300).
  • At night the analogues are close to random days. At night rows of April to September, A3 minus A3S is -0.020 (-0.042 to +0.002), A3 minus R0 is -0.006 (-0.030 to +0.017), and E minus R0 is +0.004 (-0.001 to +0.009).
  • Radiation inputs help the reference too. R0_rad minus R0 is -0.120 (-0.151 to -0.090), a context read that no contrast uses.
  • Coverage. The 0.05 quantile lies above the actual power on 13.5% to 15.0% of sunny rows in every arm, and the 0.95 quantile lies above it on 80.6% to 82.9% of cloudy rows.
  • No analogue exists for 8.7% of rows (a bank holiday, or no day of the same type with observed power and CAMS data in the window), and 89.4% of rows have all 3.

Seeds 1 and 2 changed no planned contrast by more than 0.003 points. The widths of the intervals come from the weeks of forecast start, not from fit noise. The verdict from seeds 0 to 2 together is also inconclusive (C3 lower end -0.048, C4 upper end +0.016). The seed check is post hoc.

docs.title: Which predictions held
docs.text: Prediction made in the plan Result C1 at -0.10 to -0.25 Held: -0.149 C2 at -0.02 to -0.10 Held, at the end of the range: -0.095 E beats A3 by 0.03 to 0.20 Held in the point estimate (+0.054); the interval includes zero C4 within -0.03 to +0.02 Not met: -0.066, with an interval from -0.149 to +0.015 E_twin worse than E by 0.15 to 0.35 Held: 0.246 A3S worse than A3 by 0.01 to 0.06 Not met: 0.081, slightly beyond the range A3 and A3S within 0.02 at night Not met, at the edge: -0.020 (-0.042 to +0.002)

docs.title: Departures from the plan
docs.text:
The experiment departed from its plan in four ways, none of which changes the hypothesis, the prediction, or the decision rule.

  1. A ninth arm, R0_rad, was fitted as context. It enters no contrast.
  2. Seeds 1 and 2 were fitted after the verdict, as a post hoc check.
  3. The prediction sets are stored under lower-case names, r0, e, a3, and so on, for seed 0, and with the suffix -s012 for seeds 0 to 2, because a stored set cannot be overwritten.
  4. The common starting level is the median of the training labels, not zero. Experiments 76 and 78 found that starting from XGBoost's estimated base score raises the score by 0.07 to 0.10 points against a start at zero in the same pipeline. The plan gave every arm one common level so that the contrasts do not carry that effect. Whether a start at zero would change R0, or the ranking of the arms, is not tested.

Limits that the plan stated hold. The capacity table is experiment 64's and is 5% to 19% below experiment 45's 2025/26 values, which experiment 78 found worsens am by about 0.02 points. The weights and the sunshine calibration are fixed on data to 2025-06-30. The analogues are matched in training to the ensemble-mean sunshine and at inference to each member's own, which widens the pooled spread of the analogue arms. The candidates share a half-hour of the day in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), so a window that straddles a clock change shifts a local-time profile by an hour. The placebo twin of E is a cyclic shift over the whole window's rows. A donor for a row from the early window may therefore be a forecast issued after that refit. Only a sunshine anomaly crosses that boundary. No power or label does.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: The next experiment should test the analogue columns on top of the offset with more forecast weeks, one analogue, and a variant matched on the day type alone. A second validation year with as many weeks (experiment R11, which needs the ENS backfill) would cut the half-width of C4 from 0.08 to about 0.06, because the half-width falls with the square root of the number of weeks. That is still above 0.05, so the plan should either set the threshold near 0.06 or ask for a third year. The plan should also read sunny and cloudy rows separately and add the day-type-only variant, because C6 does not separate the sunshine from the day type. The decision whether to port either way belongs to the maintainer and the roadmap. The offset costs a table of capacities and weights. The analogue columns cost the last 3 to 16 days of telemetry, a CAMS-like sunshine record, and a bank-holiday calendar at every forecast.

docs.title: Reviews
docs.text:
Plan review (Sonnet), triaged. Accepted: give every arm one starting level, state the rule that separates small gain from supported, rebuild the training inputs for the whole P-roll window, state how E_twin is trained, note the column-count difference between arms, one definition of day type, and the prose faults. Rejected: none.

Code review (Sonnet), triaged. No leakage and no wrong join. Accepted: add the ninth arm to the plan, make the guard in known_rows check the origin as well as the valid time, and state the mismatch between the training and inference sunshine shape. Rejected: a check of an A3 variant matched to the ensemble-mean shape at inference, because the arm of experiment 64 shares the same design and the experiment answers the plan's question without it.

Number check (Sonnet), triaged. Accepted: the September value, the context scores copied from experiment 74's own printout, the night prediction row, the half-width range, the exploratory labels, the claim that the monthly figures have no interval, and the unsupported statement that a second year would resolve a 0.05-point gain. Rejected: none.

Prose review (Sonnet), triaged. Accepted: an opening that defines every term before use, a legend of the arms, the four verdicts, the pronoun and bare-noun fixes, the money-metaphor fixes, and the research-log rewrites. Rejected: moving all the legend ahead of the take-home paragraph, which would bury the conclusion.

docs.title: Experiment 75: can a Primary demand forecast learn the normal running arrangement from labelled load shifts?
docs.text:
Take-home message: outside switching, the Primary substation demand forecast was already close to the normal running arrangement, so neither removing the labelled switching from training nor telling the model how much load switching moved changed the quantile score by more than 0.06 points of capacity. The experiment cannot show that removing the switching is harmless within its 0.02-point margin. It also cannot show a gain from either extra input. The plain weekly-refitted XGBoost demand model stays the v1 candidate. Subtracting the moved MW from each lag lowered the score by 0.42 points on the few half-hours whose lag sits inside a labelled event, but the interval (-1.51 to +0.02, not adjusted for several comparisons) does not show it, so SW2-12 (the same test with a detector's labels) should try it first. The verdict is inconclusive.

An electricity network operator sometimes closes a normally open switch, so that one Primary substation (a substation that steps down to the local distribution network) carries load that belongs to a neighbour. The metered power then differs from the power in the normal running arrangement (NRA). We asked whether an XGBoost demand model forecasts the NRA as well when its training targets leave out the half-hours of labelled switching events, and whether the signed MW that switching moved at each lagged power input, or each lag minus that MW, lowers the error.

We refitted the model every week for 16 Primary substations on four arms. We scored the arms on the 292 daily forecast runs of experiment 48, on half-hours outside labelled switching and logged closures. The score is the quantile score, in points of capacity, where smaller is better. The 82 labelled events come from experiment 41. Their onsets, ends, and moved MW are hindsight values, so the result is an upper bound on what a detector could achieve.

  • Arms (all weekly, seed 0, N1 recipe of experiment 48). plain: trained on all rows. nra: training rows inside a labelled event are dropped. nra_mw: nra plus the signed MW at each of the three lags. nra_lag: nra with each lag replaced by the lag minus that MW.
  • Rows. 3,199,243 cases, of which 2,928,842 are NRA rows. Every arm holds the same cases.
  • Score on the NRA rows (points of capacity). plain 5.257, nra 5.261, nra_mw 5.274, nra_lag 5.264. Benchmarks from experiment 48: weekly with the 14-day correction 5.334, the stack (frozen model, 14-day correction) 5.448, manual_heuristic 6.121, climatology 7.479. The two baselines hold slightly fewer NRA cases (2,927,210 and 2,783,317).
  • C1, nra minus plain: +0.004 (98.33% interval -0.026 to +0.025). The upper end exceeds the +0.02 margin, which is the most that experiment 44 says a perfect detector could gain. The training-target mask is therefore not shown to be harmless. It is not shown to be harmful either, and the plain arm is the v1 NRA candidate.
  • C2, nra_mw minus nra: +0.013 (-0.013 to +0.052). C3, nra_lag minus nra: +0.004 (-0.019 to +0.019). Neither interval lies below zero, so neither arm is supported.
  • Half-hours with a lag inside an event: 37,394 (1.3%), in 8 months. There the mask lowered the score by 0.50 (95% interval -2.08 to +0.35), the corrected lags lowered it by a further 0.42 (-1.51 to +0.02), and the MW columns raised it by 1.07 (-0.19 to +3.31). These intervals are not corrected for several comparisons.
  • Reproduction check. The plain arm's mean score on all cases, 5.4403, matches experiment 48's stored weekly score, 5.4402. Only 9% of per-case scores match to 0.001. The largest gap is 4.39 points, because repeated graphics-card fits are not bit-for-bit identical. The 0.004 in C1 is therefore at the level of fit-to-fit noise.
  • Caveats. Only 22 of the 82 labelled events fall in the scored year. Events before January 2022 are not masked in training. The result rests on one validation year and one seed.
  • Next. SW2-12 repeats the arms with the detector's labels. It adds first the corrected lags together with the MW columns, which this experiment did not run.

docs.title: Experiment 76: does experiment 64's gain beyond 10 days come from a leak?
docs.text:
Take-home message: we found no route for a leak, and a refit with no solar term at all reproduces the gain of experiment 64's best arm at 10 days and beyond. The gain therefore matches the XGBoost model starting its fit at zero, which happens whenever a base margin is supplied, and not the solar offset. A caveat limits that reading: the reference model d1l was fitted in experiment 46's pipeline, so a refit of d1l in this pipeline would show whether the start-at-zero effect is real.

We asked whether the lower error of experiment 64's arm am at forecast leads of 10 days and beyond could come from information that was not available at forecast time. In am, the XGBoost model starts from a base margin: a starting prediction, added to each row, equal to the substation's solar capacity times a forecast of how sunny the day will be, times a weight fitted on the training years. The weight, and so the margin, is zero from 10 days. Yet am still scored 0.082 points below the best guess d0 there. The score is the quantile score, an error measure in which lower is better, and 1 point is 1% of a Primary substation's capacity. A Primary substation feeds 11 kV circuits from the 33 kV network. d0 is experiment 33's best-guess recipe, and d1l is the same recipe without the radiation inputs, from experiment 46.

We read the code and checked the margin at every training row and at the validation rows at 10 days and beyond in the first 8 forecast runs of each series. We also made two new sets of forecasts. am0 is am refitted with a margin of zero in every row, so that it starts from zero like am and carries no solar term. am_train_only is the stored am model predicted with the margin set to zero at every lead.

The verdict is supported. The prediction of no leak held. The prediction that am0 scores 0.03 to 0.08 points above am at 10 days and beyond held after the 14-day correction in size (0.035) but its interval reaches zero, and without the correction the difference is +0.004.

docs.title: The audit found no route for a leak
docs.text:
All 20 checks of e00076_audit.py pass, 4 for each of the 5 Primary substations.

  • The margin is zero from 10 days. Of the training rows, 98,965 to 98,973 per series have a lead of 10 days or more, and the largest margin among them is exactly 0. In the first 8 forecast runs, 1,784 validation rows per series have a lead of 10 days or more, and zeroing the margin changes none of their predictions. The weight is set to zero for those leads by construction, so this confirms that the lead bands agree and that the margin reaches the model as zero. At shorter leads, zeroing the margin changes the quantiles by up to 0.086 points.
  • Every training row is at or before 2025-06-30 23:30 UTC. The weights are cross-fitted on those rows, the capacity fit leaves out the week of 2025-06-30, and the calibration of the ensemble forecast of sunshine stops with an error if a row is outside the training window. The audit checks the training rows themselves. The weights, capacity, and calibration were checked by reading the code of experiments 46 and 64.
  • Prediction applies the margin once. Rebuilding am's predictions from its stored models with the margin that the validation code supplies reproduces experiment 64's stored quantiles exactly for seed 0 (largest difference 0).

Across all 5 series and 3 seeds, the 244,185 prediction rows at 10 days and beyond have raw quantiles that are identical between am_train_only and am (largest difference 0). At shorter leads they differ by up to 0.17 points of capacity.

docs.title: The gain matches a start-at-zero effect
docs.text:
Mean quantile score at 10 days and beyond, in points of capacity, after the 14-day correction and the 1.15 spread factor: am 4.904, am0 4.939, am_train_only 4.941, d0 4.986, and d1l 5.025. Without the correction (the spread factor kept), am scores 4.739, am0 4.735, and d1l 4.837.

Contrast at 10 days and beyond Difference Interval am minus am0, corrected (offset in training) -0.035 -0.074 to +0.003 (98.33%) am0 minus d1l, corrected (start at zero) -0.086 -0.135 to -0.040 (98.33%) am minus d1l, corrected (whole effect) -0.121 -0.176 to -0.064 (98.33%) am minus am0, uncorrected +0.004 -0.012 to +0.021 (95%, exploratory) am0 minus d1l, uncorrected -0.102 -0.158 to -0.047 (95%, exploratory) am minus d1l, uncorrected -0.098 -0.150 to -0.048 (95%, exploratory) am minus d0, corrected (experiment 64) -0.082 -0.126 to -0.038 (95%, exploratory) d1l minus d0, corrected +0.039 +0.006 to +0.074 (95%, exploratory) am_train_only minus am, corrected +0.037 +0.001 to +0.072 (95%, exploratory)

A negative difference means that the first arm has the lower error. The three corrected decision contrasts are read at 98.33%, which is a 95% interval split across three contrasts (a Bonferroni correction). Every other row is exploratory, meaning that it is not in the decision rule, and is read at 95%. All intervals come from 50,000 resamples that draw whole ISO weeks of forecast start (26 weeks at 10 days and beyond) and the 3 seeds, on 21,658 scored rows per seed.

The decision rule, as written before any code ran, names the effect a start-point effect. The rule applies when am0 minus d1l has an upper end below zero and am minus am0 does not, and the corrected rows meet both conditions. The uncorrected rows agree: the offset in training adds +0.004 (-0.012 to +0.021), and the refit with no solar term accounts for all of the gap to d1l.

The 14-day correction moves the corrected contrasts by about 0.03 points, because it uses each arm's own recent errors. am_train_only scores 0.037 points worse than am at 10 days and beyond although its raw quantiles are identical. We infer that the correction, which adds the mean of an arm's own recent median errors, carries the margin's effect from shorter leads into the longer ones. The uncorrected rows remove that route, and the corrected am minus am0 of -0.035 shrinks to +0.004.

The XGBoost model am0 scores worse than d0 at leads under 10 days (+0.051, interval +0.002 to +0.099, exploratory). Starting at zero therefore does not help at every lead. The mean scores at those leads are 4.267 for am and 4.502 for am0, so the solar offset lowers the error there by about 0.24 points, which agrees with experiment 64 (no interval computed here).

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The start-at-zero reading is not isolated. d1l is experiment 46's stored model, and am0 is fitted in experiment 64's pipeline, so any difference between the two pipelines is in the contrast. The mechanism, that an XGBoost model given a base margin starts from zero instead of from its estimated base score, is the documented behaviour of XGBoost and is not tested here.
  • The validation rows are experiment 64's. They are daylight half-hours at five Primary substations from July to September 2025 and from April to June 2026, and the result is measured on 26 weeks of forecast start at 10 days and beyond.

docs.title: What a next experiment could answer
docs.text: A refit of d1l in this pipeline, with the same seeds, compared with am0, would show whether the start-at-zero gain is real. If the two matched, the gain beyond 10 days would be an artefact of the pipelines. If am0 stayed lower, the base score of the production XGBoost model would merit a test of its own.

docs.title: Experiment 77: does the fitted solar shape lower the error of arm am? (PVDIS-6b)
docs.text:
Take-home message: the shape of the solar panels in the solar term does not limit experiment 64's best forecast. Experiment 64 forecast a substation's power with an XGBoost model (a gradient- boosted tree model) that starts from an explicit solar term: the substation's solar capacity times a forecast of how sunny the day will be. We call that forecast arm am. Replacing its south-facing panel shape with a blend of east-, south-, and west-facing shapes, fitted to each substation's own power, left the error unchanged, and so did using another substation's blend. What did matter was the forecast of the sunshine itself: giving the same arm the sunshine of another date worsened the score by 0.32 points (the quantile score, an error measure in which lower is better). The next work on the solar term should go into the sunshine forecast and the capacity table, not into the panel shape. The verdict is refuted, which here means that the fitted shape does not lower the error by 0.5% or more.

We asked whether a forecast of the power drawn at a Primary substation improves when its solar term is built from a blend of east-, south-, and west-facing panel output instead of south-facing panels only. A Primary substation is a 33/11 kV or 66/11 kV substation in the electricity distribution network. Experiment 73 (PVDIS-6) found that the blend fits the half-hourly power of Primary substations 1.3% better than south-facing panels do, although the shares of the blend (the fraction of capacity assigned to each orientation) are not identified. We fitted one set of shares per substation on rows up to 30 June 2025, rebuilt the solar term of arm am with the blend, and scored the forecasts on the same rows as experiment 64: 5 Primaries, 68,903 daylight half-hours per seed in April to September, and 3 seeds (repeated fits with different random numbers). One point of the score is 1% of a substation's capacity. The blend scored 4.466 points and am 4.467.

The verdict is refuted, read by the rule written before any arm was scored. The rule uses three contrasts, each an arm's score minus another arm's, at a 98.33% interval from 50,000 resamples of whole weeks of forecast start. C1 is the fitted shape minus am. C2 is the fitted shape minus all-south panels at the fitted shape's tilt of 25 degrees, which separates mixing from the tilt change. C3 is the fitted shape minus its placebo twin, the same arm given the forecast sunshine of another date. The threshold is 0.5% of am's score, which is 0.022 points. The rule says refuted when the lower end of C1 is above -0.022 and the upper end is at most +0.022, so that a gain of 0.5% is excluded and a loss of 0.5% is not shown.

Contrast Difference 98.33% interval C1: fitted shape minus am -0.001 -0.018 to +0.014 C2: fitted shape minus all-south at tilt 25 -0.001 -0.014 to +0.011 C3: fitted shape minus its placebo twin -0.323 -0.441 to -0.212

The differences are in points of capacity, and negative favours the fitted shape. The interval of C1 has a half-width of 0.016 points, below the 0.022-point threshold, so the design could have seen a gain of 0.5% and did not.

docs.title: Every arm scores the same, except the placebo twin
docs.text:
The fitted shape, the all-south shape at either tilt, and another Primary's shape are not distinguishable. Absolute scores, in points of capacity, with 95% intervals from the same resampling:

Arm Quantile score d0, the best guess (experiment 33) 4.620 (4.294 to 4.946) am0, am without the solar term (experiment 76) 4.640 (4.295 to 4.977) am, all-south shape at tilt 35 (experiment 64) 4.467 (4.143 to 4.785) am_s25, all-south shape at tilt 25 4.467 (4.142 to 4.783) am_blend, the fitted shape 4.466 (4.144 to 4.781) am_shuffled, another Primary's fitted shape 4.465 (4.143 to 4.781) am_blend_twin, fitted shape with the sunshine of another date 4.789 (4.430 to 5.157)

The fitted shape minus the shuffled shape is +0.001 points (95% interval -0.006 to +0.007, exploratory). If the shares carried information about a Primary's panels, the shape fitted to the Primary's own power would score below the shape fitted to another Primary's. This agrees with experiment 73's finding that the shares are not identified, and the same holds for the forecast.

The forecast sunshine carries the gain. The fitted shape scores 0.173 points (95% interval -0.227 to -0.121) below am0, the same arm without a solar term, and 0.323 points below the same arm given the sunshine of another date. The fitted shape scores 0.153 points (-0.193 to -0.116) below d0, as am does in experiment 64. A season-year capacity vintage does more than the fitted shape: the fitted shape scores 0.017 points (+0.002 to +0.033) above experiment 78's am_sy.

docs.title: Lead time, series, and month show no gain either
docs.text: The fitted shape minus am has an interval that includes zero in every lead band, at each of the five series, and over leads under 48 hours (+0.006, -0.031 to +0.044). Beyond 10 days, where the weight of the solar term is zero, the difference is -0.010 points (-0.023 to +0.002), and experiment 76 found no route for a leak there. By local valid month the difference runs from -0.022 points in April to +0.019 in August with no pattern, on 29,715 to 39,663 rows per month over the three seeds.

docs.title: The fitted shapes, and the evening-west check
docs.text:
The five fitted shapes differ little from all-south panels at a tilt of 25 degrees. As Figure 2 shows, the five fitted shapes have a lower midday peak and a larger afternoon and evening share, by amounts small beside the error of the sunshine forecast. The shares behind them are a flexible shape and not a measurement of panel orientation: the south share is 0.06 to 0.15 at three of the five Primaries and 0.34 to 0.57 at the other two.

The evening-west check does not settle whether the west share is evening demand. For each Primary we removed the mean of each calendar cell (month, half-hour, and weekday or holiday) and the heating degree-days from the after-dark half-hours of April to September (18:00 to 23:30 local time) and regressed the remainder on that day's mean daytime cloud. The change from a clear to a fully cloudy day is +0.29 MW at D9 (95% interval +0.04 to +0.59), which has the largest fitted west capacity (3.04 MW), and between +0.01 and +0.10 MW at the other four, with intervals that include zero. Five Primaries give too few points to show a relation, and D9 is a low-power Primary with two training years. The check is descriptive and no verdict reads it.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text: • Weights differ by arm only through the shape. Each arm refits the weight w on its own cross-fit of the same XGBoost model without a solar term. GPU fits are not exactly repeatable, so w carries a small amount of noise that differs between arms. The mean weights are -0.32 to -0.48 (blend) and -0.38 to -0.52 (all-south at tilt 25). - The capacity of the Primary D14 is scaled, not fitted. D14 has no 2024/25 weeks, so its capacity is experiment 64's capacity times the median ratio of the shape's capacity to experiment 64's at the other four series. - The capacity keeps the recovery ratio of the all-south shape. Each shape's capacity is divided by experiment 45's recovery ratio, which was measured with the all-south fleet shape and not with the blend. The weight w is refitted per arm and absorbs a constant scale error, so the effect is expected to be small, but it was not tested. - The shares of the Primary D9 rest on two training years. The other four Primaries have five or six. - The result is for ensemble-forecast sunshine at five Primaries in one trial area. A different weather forecast with less error could make the panel shape matter more.

docs.title: Candidate next experiments
docs.text:
The solar term of arm am is limited by its inputs, not its panel shape. The candidates that the evidence supports are a better sunshine forecast (experiment 50 and experiment 53 compared other weather forecasts) and a capacity table that is current (experiment 78 found a gain of 0.018 points from a season-year vintage).

The sections from here to the end are the plan as committed before any code ran. The last section lists the changes made after the plan and before any arm was scored.

docs.title: What is held fixed and what changes
docs.text:
One set of shares per Primary, fitted on the training window only, replaces the all-south shape. Experiment 73's pooled fit (one set of east, south, and west shares per Primary, shared by every season-year) is refitted on summer half-hours up to 2025-06-30 only, on experiment 73's plane-of-array shapes at a tilt of 25 degrees and a DC to AC ratio of 1.15. Experiment 73's own shares used rows up to 2026 and are not reused. The shares are held fixed across training years, which removes the median swing of 0.24 in the shares between consecutive season-years that experiment 73 found.

The blend replaces the all-south shape everywhere that the solar term is built. The CAMS shape, the CAMS and ENS climatologies, the ENS anomaly and its calibration slope per lead band, the capacity, and the weight w fitted on the training window are all rebuilt for the blend, by the code of experiments 46 and 64 with the plant output replaced by the blend of the three orientations' output. The per-member ENS anomaly is computed from the shortwave radiation of each of the 51 members, as in experiment 46. The weight w absorbs a scale error in the capacity, so the capacity keeps experiment 45's recovery ratio of the fleet shape; the Caveats section says what that choice does to the comparison.

docs.title: Arms
docs.text:
• am_blend: arm am with the fitted shape.
  • am_s25: arm am with all-south panels at a tilt of 25 degrees, the control for the tilt change. The script prints the AC capacity of am_s25 and of am_blend for each series, and the weights w, so that a difference in level between the arms is visible.
  • am_blend_twin: am_blend with the forecast sunshine taken from another date, by experiment 64's permutation of runs within series, month, half-hour, and lead band. The donor run is the same for the east, south, and west anomalies, so the twin keeps their mutual timing.
  • am_shuffled: am with the shares of another Primary (a fixed cyclic permutation of the 5 series), refitted capacity and weight. This is exploratory.
  • Reference rows, read from experiment 64's stored predictions: am, am_twin, d0, d1l, climatology, and manual_heuristic.

Each XGBoost arm has 5 series and 3 seeds, 15 fits, with experiment 64's settings and column list. Each XGBoost model is trained on its own history.

docs.title: No fitted quantity sees the validation period
docs.text: Every fitted quantity is read with a valid time up to 2025-06-30 23:30 UTC, and the scripts assert it. The quantities are the shares, the AC capacity, the CAMS and ENS climatologies, the calibration slope per lead band, the weight w, and the 14-day correction and spread factor, which are refitted per arm on training rows only. Each script prints the latest timestamp of every table it fits. The shares are fitted on rows of shapes.parquet and the frame up to that time. The ENS members' half-hour irradiance is read from the archive and passed through the plane-of-array calculation for the east, south, and west orientations at 25 degrees, since the stored ENS tables hold only the fleet shape. The reliable-hour mask of the CAMS shapes must give the same scored rows as experiment 64's; where it does not, all arms are restricted to the intersection, and am is rescored on it.

docs.title: The evening-west check
docs.text: A west-leaning share at some Primaries may be evening demand and not solar. Experiment 73's advice recommends a check before the west share is read as solar. For each Primary, using training rows only, we remove the calendar cell and heating degree-days from the half-hours after dark (solar zenith above 90 degrees, 18:00 to 23:30 local time), and regress the remainder on that evening's mean cloud cover and on its mean temperature. If evening demand were the source of a west share, the after-dark residual would rise in dull weather, so a positive cloud slope is the expected sign. We tabulate, for each of the 5 Primaries, the slope as a share of the Primary's capacity beside its west share. With 5 Primaries, no rank correlation has power, so the table is descriptive, and no verdict uses it.

docs.title: Size
docs.text:
• What gets stored: prediction sets under data/ml-experiments/ (private, uncommitted); nothing in production.
  • Production serving path: not touched.
  • Degradation rule: not touched.
  • More than one defensible design: yes, in how the shares are fitted (fixed, or under a year-to-year penalty) and at which tilt. The plan fixes the shares across years because that choice removes the instability experiment 73 found, and uses am_s25 to separate tilt from mix.
  • Callers not nameable without searching: the code is copied from experiments 46 and 64, so the callers are known.
  • Size: medium. One Sonnet plan review, one Sonnet code review, one Sonnet write-up review, and one Sonnet prose review.

docs.title: Changes made after the plan was committed and before any arm was scored
docs.text: • The flat-timing control am_blend_flat is dropped. A reviewer of the code showed that a single scale on the south shape cancels: the calibration slope, the capacity, and the weight w absorb it, so the arm would equal am_s25. A per-cell version was not built. - The evening-west check regresses on the day's mean daytime cloud and heating degree-days. The frame holds no cloud measure after dark, because irradiance is zero then, so the cloud variable of the plan's "that evening" is the same day's daylight cloud. - The fallback capacity of the series with no 2024/25 constant (D14) is scaled by the shape. It is experiment 64's capacity times the median ratio of the shape's capacity to experiment 64's at the other four series. - Exploratory contrasts against am0 and am_sy are added, at the request of the experiment-manager session, because experiment 78 found that a zero base margin alone lowers d0's score. am0 is experiment 76's am without the solar term, and am_sy is experiment 78's am with a season-year capacity vintage.

docs.title: Earlier advice followed and departed from
docs.text:
• Followed: use am (a starting offset) and not an input column or a shift after the fit (experiment 64); describe the blend as a fitted solar shape and not as a measurement of orientation, and do not publish shares (experiment 73); hold the shares fixed across training years (experiment 73); check the west lean against after-dark demand (experiment 73).
  • Departed from: none.

docs.title: Experiment 78: does a re-estimated solar capacity lower the error? (PVDIS-5, check 2)
docs.text:
Take-home message: re-estimating the solar capacity before each forecast run lowers the quantile score of am, the best-scoring forecast of experiment 64, by only 0.018 points, so a capacity table refreshed about once a season-year is enough. The quantile score is an error measure in which lower is better, and 1 point is 1% of a substation's capacity. A larger finding sits beside this one. XGBoost starts each model from an estimated starting prediction (its base score). Starting from zero instead lowered the score of the reference model d0 by 0.07 points, and by about 0.10 points for the model that carries no solar term, so part of the gain that experiment 64 reported over d0 was a start-at-zero effect. The solar term still lowers the score by 0.100 points against a d0 that starts from zero. The next experiment should test the starting point, which needs no extra production work to change.

We asked whether a better estimate of how much solar capacity sits behind each Primary substation improves a forecast of the substation's power. A Primary substation steps electricity down from 33 kV or 66 kV to 11 kV. Experiment 64 forecast power with an XGBoost model that starts from a solar term: the substation's solar capacity times a forecast of how sunny the day will be, added as a base margin (a fixed starting prediction supplied for each row). That experiment fixed the capacity at the value estimated from data before July 2025. Here we re-estimated the capacity before every forecast run from only the data available then, and predicted again with the same fitted XGBoost models. The score fell by 0.018 points. We also refitted two reference models, d1l and d0, to find out whether the start-at-zero effect that experiment 76 suspected is real. The start-at-zero effect is real.

The verdict is small gain. The pre-registered rule is in the front matter and was committed before any code ran. The headline contrast C1 is the quantile score of am_sy (am with the season-year vintage of the capacity) minus that of am (experiment 64's held capacity), over all leads. The upper end of C1 is -0.004, below zero but not below the threshold of -0.05. The threshold is a third of experiment 64's gain over d0, because a weekly refit of the capacity table is a production step that a fixed table does not need. C3 and C4 in the table confirm that the solar term carries solar information.

Contrast Difference in quantile score 98.75% interval C1: am_sy minus am, all leads -0.018 -0.036 to -0.004 C2: am_sy minus am, leads under 48 hours -0.033 -0.086 to +0.012 C3: am_sy minus am0, all leads (the solar term) -0.190 -0.267 to -0.118 C4: am_sy minus am_sy_twin, all leads (a wrong-date sunshine forecast) -0.357 -0.496 to -0.227

The values are in points of capacity and come from 50,000 resamples of whole ISO weeks of forecast start (29 weeks) and of 3 seeds, on experiment 64's 68,903 scored rows per seed: daylight half-hours of April to September at the five Primary substations D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16, in July to September 2025 and April to June 2026. am0 is the XGBoost model with a base margin of zero and no solar term (experiment 76). C2 does not meet the rule for a gain at short leads, because its interval includes zero.

docs.title: The arms
docs.text:
• am, am_twin, d0, d1l: experiment 64's stored forecasts. am has a base margin of the weight times the held capacity times the forecast sunshine anomaly. d0 is the best-guess recipe, and d1l is d0 without the two radiation inputs.
  • am0: experiment 76's stored forecasts: am's recipe with a margin of zero in every row.
