  • C1 RB minus R (decides the verdict, 99%). Scored year -0.0112 (-0.0234 to +0.0030), 3 of 5 substations; replicate months -0.0134 (-0.0221 to -0.0015), 3 of 5. Excluding holiday-like days the scored year is -0.0135 (-0.0243 to -0.0034). Over all leads the C1 estimate is +0.0062 (+0.0016 to +0.0138), 0 of 5 substations: the score is worse beyond day D+1 (48 to 144 hours: +0.0108).
  • C2 RW minus R. +0.0165 (-0.0073 to +0.0432) scored; +0.0126 (-0.0110 to +0.0371) replicate: a pure same-weekday profile is noisier than the all-days one, as predicted.
  • C3 RB minus K0. -0.0998 (-0.1423 to -0.0654), 5 of 5; replicate -0.1049. C4 RB minus L1. -0.1111 (-0.1328 to -0.0883), 5 of 5; one week of same-weekday errors alone is no better than K0 (L1 minus K0 +0.011).
  • C5 RB-day-types minus RB. -0.0108 (-0.0186 to -0.0010), 4 of 5; replicate -0.0145 (-0.0275 to -0.0084), 5 of 5. Against R (exploratory, 95%): -0.0220 (-0.0364 to -0.0065) scored and -0.0279 (-0.0414 to -0.0161) replicate.
  • C6 RB minus Rh (diagnostic, 95%). -0.0153 (-0.0225 to -0.0086), 5 of 5 substations: with the holiday rule held fixed, RB scores 0.015 points better than Rh. Rh minus R is +0.0041 (-0.0001 to +0.0116): the holiday rule alone raises the score by 0.004 points, with an interval that includes zero. C1 in the Christmas window is +0.0726 (+0.0285 to +0.0842, 0 of 4 substations), and C1 on Easter is -0.0835 (one set of 720 rows); C1 mixes the weekday term and the holiday rule, and the holiday rule's own effect in those windows was not printed.
  • Weekdays (scored year, C1). Monday -0.0375 (-0.0575 to -0.0165), 4 of 5; Friday -0.0525 (-0.0819 to -0.0218), 5 of 5; Tuesday +0.0044, Wednesday +0.0069, Thursday -0.0043, Saturday -0.0113, Sunday -0.0014, all with intervals that include zero. The replicate months show the same pattern, with Tuesday also negative (-0.0150).
  • Winter (scored year, C1). November to March -0.0115 (-0.0364 to +0.0271), 3 of 5; winter evening 16:00 to 20:00 -0.0488 (-0.0654 to -0.0333), 5 of 5; non-winter -0.0110 (-0.0185 to -0.0013). Cold-snap days (daily mean under 3 degrees C): +0.0036 (-0.1191 to +0.1565) with 2400 rows, too few to read. Easter has one set of 720 rows.
  • COPY7. On the 7-days-ago subset, scored year, COPY7 scored 7.067 at D+1 against 2.521 for K0 and 2.421 for RB; copying last week is much worse, as predicted.
  • Tails (scored year, D+1; coverage gap in points, pinball). RB: q01 +1.41 (0.1883), q05 +1.81 (0.6087), q95 -1.02 (0.6554), q99 -1.12 (0.2115); R: +1.39, +1.76, -1.01, -1.16 with pinball 0.1875, 0.6138, 0.6573, 0.2124. The tails barely move.
  • Predictions. Held: C1 within -0.01 to -0.04 (at its upper edge); RW minus R within 0.00 to +0.05; COPY7 worse than K0; best lambda 0.25 (inside 0.25 to 0.75). Failed: RB-day-types was expected within 0.01 of RB and was 0.011 better.

docs.title: Gate
docs.text: The known-answer gate passed, and it was run on the tuning months before any replicate or scored forecast was read. A +3-point shift on Saturdays 17:00 to 21:00 for 8 weeks (2 November to 21 December 2024) was recovered at the third to eighth Saturday as follows (median of five substations, share of the shift): R 0.089, Rh 0.089, RB at the reference setting 0.318 (at least 0.15 and more than twice R), RB tuned 0.215, RW 0.394, and the placebo (weekday labels shifted by 3 days) 0.045 at the reference and 0.067 tuned. The placebo condition on recovery (at most R plus 0.05) is nearly arithmetic, because a profile from the wrong weekday carries only the shrunk share of any shift, so the second check is the informative one. The share cannot reach 1: removing each day's mean, as the profile does, lowers the largest recoverable share to about 0.83. On the tuning rows, the placebo's mean absolute error at D+1 (4.217) is above Rh's (4.130) and RB's at the reference (4.098), so the placebo's error does not improve: the benefit needs the correct weekday.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median forecast minus mean forecast per site (scored year, D+1, points). K0: D10 +0.003, D11 -0.022, D14 +0.014, D16 -0.014, D5 -0.097. R: +0.009, -0.019, +0.002, -0.015, -0.037. RB: -0.003, -0.010, -0.012, -0.002, -0.039. No shift over 0.04 except D5 for K0.
  • Mean absolute error of the median and of the mean forecast beside each contrast (scored year, D+1). C1: median -0.0183, mean -0.0183; C2 +0.0436 and +0.0439; C3 -0.1955 and -0.1977; C4 -0.2133 and -0.2112; C5 -0.0172 and -0.0183. The quantile score and both errors point the same way.
  • Triggers. None fired. The gate passed; the results agree with the predictions except C5's size; the quantile score and the errors agree; leaving out one substation never flips C1's sign (-0.0053 to -0.0161 scored; the scored-year interval includes zero in four of five leave-one-outs, as in the full set, and D11's upper end is +0.0000); no nested arm beats the arm containing it (RB contains Rh and RW as special cases and beats both, which is the expected order); the closest sister interval, experiment 115's KW minus R, is a different contrast; no later experiment depends on this result. No audit was run.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Five substations and one independent winter. Settings were chosen on the tuning months with the mean absolute error of the median, not the quantile score, and R's kappa was not re-tuned.
  • The shift applies at every lead as recipe R does, so the weekday of the target is only right at day D+1 (leads 15.5 to 39 hours); this is the likeliest reason for the loss beyond 48 hours.
  • Weekday labels use UTC days of the valid time while the profile uses local half-hours. The gate's Saturday is the UTC day. The 3.5-hour telemetry delay is assumed, as in experiment 115.
  • RB-day-types was not pre-registered as the best arm; its advantage over R is exploratory.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Test day-type profiles at day D+1 only, with lead-aware weights, tuned on the quantile score, and replicated on the even months.
  • Test a Monday and Friday weekend-edge term on its own, since all of the gain sits there.

Every number above is printed by ml-experiments/00134-*/e00134_report.py; its output is report.txt.

docs.title: Plan, committed before any fit
docs.text: This experiment asks whether the forecast's recent-error correction should look at the same weekday as the day being forecast, rather than at the last 14 days alike. It reuses experiment 111's stored GAM-K forecasts and experiment 115's K0 and recipe R, and refits no demand model. It follows experiment 115, whose recipe R is a plain average of the last 14 days' errors by half-hour. None of experiments 111 to 115 tested a weekday-specific version. Shrinking a weekday profile towards an all-days profile is a partial-pooling step of the kind described by Gelman and Hill (2006). The naive baseline of repeating the value from seven days ago is a seasonal-naive forecast, as defined by Hyndman and Athanasopoulos (2021).

docs.title: Arms
docs.text:
• K0. GAM-K as stored (control).
  • R. Recipe R reproduced exactly as experiment 115 stored it: K0 minus kappa times the mean of the last 14 UTC days' D+1 errors by local half-hour, each day's mean removed, kappa 0.75, no holiday rule.
  • Rh. R with the holiday rule below, kappa re-chosen on the tuning months. It separates the effect of the holiday rule from the effect of the weekday.
  • COPY7. The actual power at the same half-hour 7 days earlier as a point forecast (all 11 quantiles equal), reported beside the arms and never corrected, on its own subset: the rows where that reading exists, with K0 and RB rescored on the same subset.
  • L1. K0 minus kappa times last week's same-weekday D+1 error profile (one sample).
  • RW. K0 minus kappa times the mean same-weekday error over the last n weeks; n from 2, 3, 4.
  • RB (lead arm). Profile = A + lambda (W - A), where A is Rh's 14-day all-days profile, W is the n-week same-weekday profile, and lambda lies in 0 to 1. Where W has no usable day, W is A.
  • RB-day-types. As RB, with W built from days of the same day type: Monday, Tuesday to Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday.

No lookahead. At the 09:00 UTC origin on day D the target is D+1. Each source day is a UTC day fully observed by D 00:00 UTC, so the same weekday of the target last counts on day D-6. A day enters a profile when at least 40 of its 48 half-hours have a reading, as in experiment 115.

Holiday rule (Rh, RW, L1, RB, RB-day-types). A holiday-like day is an English bank holiday, Easter Saturday or Sunday, or 24 or 27 to 31 December. Holiday-like days are left out of every profile as source days, and a holiday-like target gets no correction. Holiday-like targets are scored separately.

docs.title: Settings and how they are chosen
docs.text:
• Grids. kappa from 0.5, 0.75, 1.0; lambda from 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1; n from 2, 3, 4.
  • Rule. Fleet-wide settings (one set for all five decision substations), because each substation has about 3,000 tuning-month D+1 rows and the weekday profiles use 2 to 4 samples; a per-substation choice would mostly fit noise. The setting with the lowest mean absolute error of the corrected median at D+1 on the tuning rows, in points of effective capacity, pooled with equal weight per row over the five decision substations, wins. Holiday-like targets stay in the tuning rows (they carry zero correction in every arm). Weeks n is chosen separately for RW and RB, and the tuning-row scores of the kappa 0.75 slice of the RB grid are printed. Lambda takes 0.25, 0.5, and 0.75 in RB, because lambda 0 is Rh and lambda 1 is RW, which are tuned separately. Each arm's spread is then refitted on the tuning rows and its factors chosen per lead band, as for every arm of experiment 115.
  • Sensible limits. If lambda = 0 wins, RB equals Rh and the verdict says so.

docs.title: Known-answer gate (reported before any score)
docs.text:
On real tuning-month residuals, add +3 points to the readings of Saturdays 17:00 to 21:00 local for 8 consecutive Saturdays (2 November to 21 December 2024), run every arm's full profile code on the changed readings, and measure the share of the shift each correction recovers at the third to eighth Saturday. The Saturday is the UTC day of the valid time, and the half-hours are local. The injection goes through the same 40-of-48 reading filter, holiday rule, and fallback as the real scoring, so the gate can fail for a real reason. The share is linear in the weights: with kappa 0.75, R recovers about 0.75 x 2/14 = 0.11, and RB at lambda 0.5 and n 4 recovers about 0.19.

  • Settings. The gate runs at the tuned settings and at a fixed reference (kappa 0.75, lambda 0.5, n 4), so the result does not depend on where tuning lands.
  • Pass conditions, at the reference. RB recovers at least 0.15 of the shift and at least twice what R recovers; the placebo (the profile reads the weekday that falls 3 days after the target's; same settings, not re-tuned, because the placebo only has to show the gain needs the right weekday) recovers at most what R recovers plus 0.05; and on the tuning months the placebo's mean absolute error at D+1 lies less than halfway from Rh's to RB's.
  • Tuned settings. Reported beside the reference. If lambda 0 scores best in tuning, RB equals Rh and the verdict says so.
  • A failed condition caps the verdict at inconclusive. The gate runs before any replicate or scored forecast is read.

docs.title: Predictions
docs.text: • C1 (RB minus R) is -0.01 to -0.04 points at D+1; C2 (RW minus R) is 0.00 to +0.05, because 2 to 4 samples per weekday are noisy; COPY7 is worse than K0 overall; the best lambda lies between 0.25 and 0.75; RB-day-types is within 0.01 of RB (C5).

docs.title: Contrasts and decision rule
docs.text:
• C1 RB minus R (decides the verdict), C2 RW minus R, C3 RB minus K0, C4 RB minus L1, C5 RB-day-types minus RB. C6 (diagnostic) RB minus Rh.
  • Supported if C1's scored-year interval has its upper end at most -0.02 points; the replicate year has the same sign and an estimate at least half the scored estimate; at least 3 of 5 substations improve in both periods; the winter C1 estimate is at most 0 with its upper end under +0.02; and the gate passes. Small gain if the scored interval lies wholly below zero but its upper end is above -0.02. Not supported if the interval includes zero. Refuted if the interval lies wholly above zero. A gate failure caps every verdict at inconclusive.
  • C1 and the holiday rule. C1 is RB minus R as the brief states, so it includes the holiday rule. The write-up reports C1 on non-holiday rows and C6 (RB minus Rh) beside it, and says so when the weekday effect and the holiday rule point in different directions.
  • Threshold, with the reason. 0.02 points (about 1% of the score), because the change adds one profile of the same size as recipe R to the serving path.
  • Intervals. 99% intervals, month blocks resampled, paired across arms (studies.bootstrap.bootstrap_difference_at_level).

docs.title: Breakdowns and checks
docs.text:
The winter evening peak is 16:00 to 20:00 local from November to March. "Last n weeks" counts the last n same-weekday dates, and a date left out by the holiday rule or by the reading filter is not replaced. Charts and tables use D-labels only. result.md opens with the take-home message, then one headline chart with intervals, then the weekday-by-weekday chart.

Each weekday separately; winter (November to March) and the winter evening peak; cold nights (daily mean under about 3 C, as in experiment 122) with q95 coverage; holidays, Christmas windows, and Easter; non-winter; per substation (5 of 5 counts); tails (coverage and pinball loss at q01, q05, q95, q99); and the "Checks" list the ml-experiment skill requires.

docs.title: Compute and schedule
docs.text: CPU only, at most 4 cores and 8 GB under systemd-run --user --scope -p MemoryMax=8G -p OOMPolicy=continue. Each arm is a correction on stored member forecasts, so a fit takes seconds. No retraining happens: experiment 111's monthly refits are reused.

docs.title: Experiment 135: does fitting the demand model through the Kalman filter beat fitting it first and filtering after?
docs.text:
Fitting the demand model so that it is judged after the Kalman filter's correction made the day-ahead forecast much worse, and tying it to the ordinary fit removed the damage and added no gain. The quantile score at leads 12 to 36 hours (our error score for a forecast with uncertainty bands, in points of capacity; smaller is better) rose by 5.4 points without the tie (arm J1; 97.5% interval +3.3 to +8.5). With a ridge penalty that ties the fit to the two-stage coefficients (arm J2), the score changed by -0.0045 points (-0.013 to +0.003), which cannot be told from zero. The verdict is not supported. The two-stage design stays: fit the demand model, then filter its residuals.

We asked whether the convex demand model forecasts the next day better when its coefficients are chosen to minimise the error that remains after the Kalman filter has corrected the forecast. The demand model is GAM-K, the convex additive model with a Kalman filter on its residuals from experiment 111. The filter tracks a slowly moving level and a quickly decaying transient of the demand model's error in each of the 4 hour bands of the day, with the noise settings that experiment 133 chose. In the two-stage design, the demand model is fitted first and the filter then runs on its residuals. For fixed noise settings the filter is linear in the residuals, so the joint fit is an exact bounded quadratic problem. We solved it on a graphics processing unit (GPU) with no gradient descent. The idea follows de Vilmarest and Goude (2022), who run a state-space correction on the residuals of a generalised additive model for electricity load. They correct the residuals after fitting, and this experiment fits through the correction.

The experiment compared three arms on fold_a_daily_gap_v1 at the five decision substations (D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16, with D9 beside them):

  • TS: the two-stage fit, as in experiment 111, with experiment 133's filter settings (its GRID arm, which chose the settings per substation by next-day score).
  • J1: the joint fit with no tie to TS.
  • J2: the joint fit plus a penalty (a ridge) that pulls the coefficients towards TS's coefficients, with a weight chosen per substation from {0.1, 0.3, 1, 3} by the score on the tuning months (odd months of 2024-07 to 2025-06). The choice was 3 at five substations (D5, D9, D10, D11, and D14) and 0.3 at D16.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• J1 scores worse at every lead and at every substation. C1 (J1 minus TS) at 12 to 36 hours is +5.419 points (97.5% interval +3.330 to +8.465) in the scored year (2025-07 to 2026-06), and none of the five substations improve. In the replicate months (even months of 2024-07 to 2025-06) it is +4.323 (+2.988 to +6.281). The gap grows with lead, from +3.96 at 0 to 24 hours to +7.56 at days 4 to 7 (figure 1). The absolute quantile score at 12 to 36 hours is 7.907 for J1 against 2.488 for TS. Over all leads (0.5 to 168 hours), J1 scores 9.563 and TS scores 2.783. D9, scored beside the decision substations, shows the same pattern (J1 6.009 against 2.151 at 12 to 36 hours).
  • J2 is indistinguishable from TS. C2 (J2 minus TS) at 12 to 36 hours is -0.0045 points (-0.0132 to +0.0025) in the scored year, with three of five substations improving, and -0.0002 (-0.0027 to +0.0018) in the replicate months, with three of five. The interval rules out a worsening of the score by more than 0.003 points and an improvement by more than 0.013 points. Over all leads, C2 is -0.0015 (-0.0106 to +0.0048), within the non-inferiority bound of +0.02. D10 contributes most of the scored-year difference (-0.0144, figure 2), and leaving D10 out leaves a mean of about -0.002.
  • The tuning months prefer the strongest tie on the grid. The mean tuning-month score is 2.7136 for ridge weight 0.1, 2.7067 for 0.3, 2.7028 for 1, and 2.7020 for 3, against 2.7028 for TS (J1 is 8.200). The score falls as the tie tightens and reaches TS's, so the tuning months prefer the two-stage fit. The best weight lies at the edge of the grid at five of six substations.
  • J1's fitted curves move far from the two-stage curves, and J2's barely move. For each term, we took the root-mean-square difference between a joint fit's curve and TS's curve, as a share of the spread of TS's curve, and then the median over the 27 monthly refits and five substations. For J1 the shares are 444% for the weekly profile, 46% for the tent (a term for the temperature response), 56% for the harmonics (the yearly cycle), 27% for heating, 41% for the holiday term, and 33% for lighting. For J2 at weight 3 they are 2%, 7%, 3%, 4%, 9%, and 3% (figure 3). Most of J1's weekly-profile difference is a constant offset: a median of 51 points of capacity as it stands, against 10 points once the offset is removed. The filter's level absorbs that offset.
  • Breakouts, at 12 to 36 hours in the scored year (descriptive). C1 and C2 are:
    • Winter (November to March): +6.53 (+2.17 to +12.93) and -0.007 (-0.023 to +0.004).
    • Winter nights: +1.85 (+0.05 to +4.26) and -0.004 (-0.025 to +0.007).
    • Cold nights: +2.44 (+0.64 to +5.80) and -0.017 (-0.048 to +0.013).
    • Christmas and bank holidays: +4.32 (+3.88 to +5.15) and -0.061 (-0.209 to +0.023).
  • Tails. J2's coverage matches TS's to within 0.001 at every quantile shown, so the cold-night shortfall of the 0.95 quantile that experiment 125 and experiment 133 found is unchanged. The values for TS, J1, and J2 are:
    • 0.95 quantile: 0.942, 0.886, and 0.941 over all hours, and 0.864, 0.945, and 0.864 on cold nights.
    • 0.01 quantile: 0.020, 0.046, and 0.020.
    • 0.05 quantile: 0.064, 0.078, and 0.064.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• P1, reproduction (blocking): passed. TS's scored-year mean forecasts equal experiment 111's stored GAM-K rows, and its mean and median forecasts equal experiment 133's GRID rows, with a maximum absolute difference of 0 at all five decision substations.
  • P2, the linear filter equals the filter: passed. Unit tests in packages/studies/tests/test_dp_joint_fit.py match the corrected loss to run_kalman and correction_at to a relative 1e-9 in float64, with gaps in the readings and a binding variance floor. They also match fit_gam to 1e-6 when the filter is switched off.
  • P3, the solved loss is the true loss: passed. At all five substations, the loss of the filter run on the joint solution's residuals (the summed squared error after correction) is lower than the loss at a perturbed set of coefficients and lower than the loss at TS's coefficients. At D10 the three values are 1,120,985, 1,121,407, and 1,150,502. The fit does minimise the loss it was given, so J1's poor score comes from that loss and not from the solver.
  • P4, known answer: failed for J1, passed for J2. The target was simulated from TS's own curves plus a slow level, a decaying day anomaly, and white noise. The summed centred root-mean-square error of the recovered curves over the five substations was 36.6 points of capacity for J1, 11.2 for TS, and 10.4 for J2. J1 loses even when the assumptions of the joint design hold. The weekly profile accounts for 27.3 of J1's 36.6.
  • Absorption control: J1 failed in 4 of 15 substation-cut pairs, and J2 in none. A term fails the control only if it moves by more than twice its noise floor, which is how far it moves when the training cut-off moves back by 7 days. J1's noise floors are large, so J1 can move a long way without failing. J1's weekly-profile noise floor has a median of 19 points of capacity and a maximum of 95, against 1 point for J2 and TS. The J1 failures are D10 at the 2025-01, 2025-07, and 2026-01 cuts and D5 at the 2026-01 cut. A term had a noise floor above 1 point (unidentified) in 14 of 15 pairs for J1 and 10 of 15 for J2. The holiday term has a noise floor above 1 point in 11 of 15 pairs for J1 and 10 of 15 for J2 and TS, because few holidays fall in a training window.
  • Predictions against results. C1 was predicted at -0.05 to +0.02 points, and the result of +5.4 is more than 100 times the top of that range. C2 was predicted at -0.03 to +0.01 and came out at -0.0045, inside the range. J1's curves were predicted to differ from TS's by 5% to 15% of each term's spread, and they differ by 27% to 444%. J2's were predicted to differ by under 5%, and that held for four terms but failed for the tent (7%) and the holiday term (9%). The absorption prediction (J1 fails, J2 does not) held.
  • Error of the mean forecast beside each contrast (12 to 36 hours, scored year). The mean absolute error is 4.374 for TS, 11.027 for J1, and 4.367 for J2, in points of capacity. The C2 contrast on the mean forecast's error is -0.0073 (-0.0207 to +0.0032), the same sign as the quantile-score contrast, so the audit trigger for a disagreement did not fire. The median forecast minus the mean forecast is -0.156 for TS at D5 and -0.154 for J2, against -0.319 for J1, and is within 0.05 for TS and J2 at the other four substations.
  • Audit triggers. Trigger 1 (a control fails) fired, because P4 failed for J1. Trigger 2 (a result against its own prediction) fired for C1. The shape distance, the noise floors, and P4 support the explanation that the filter absorbs a shift of the slow terms, so the loss leaves them to the penalty alone. No variant of the loss was run to test that explanation. Trigger 4 (one substation drives the contrast) did not change a verdict: C1 is positive at every substation, and C2's full interval spans zero while the mean of the four substations other than D10 is -0.0019 (an interval for those four was not computed). No Opus audit was run, by agreement with the experiment manager, so triggers 1 and 2 are unresolved caveats.
  • Biases stated in advance. At the joint fit, the filter reads in-sample residuals from the training weather (the fifth-generation European Centre reanalysis, ERA5, and the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service, CAMS). At forecast time it reads out-of-sample residuals from the analysis proxy, the stand-in for past weather. The noise settings were chosen on TS's own residual stream, which favours TS. J2 is a family of fits, with the tie weight chosen on the tuning months. These biases favour TS, or tie J2 to TS, so they cannot explain J1's poor score. They do limit what a null for J2 says about a joint fit with retuned noise settings.
  • Retraining schedule and cost. All arms refit the convex model monthly, as in experiment 111. The joint fits of all five weights (J1 and four J2) took 0.33 GPU hours in total, about 3.3 minutes per substation for 27 refits. The fits, tuning, forecasts, scoring, and controls together took about an hour and a half of wall-clock time.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
• Whether learning the filter's noise settings together with the coefficients helps. This experiment held the settings fixed at experiment 133's values, so a null for J2 does not rule out that joint learning helps. That experiment would need a loss in which the slow terms stay identified, and J1's failure suggests tying them to a reference fit.
  • Whether a ridge weight above 3 changes J2. The tuning months preferred the strongest tie at five of six substations, so a wider grid would show whether a tie stronger than weight 3 gives any improvement.

docs.title: Experiment 136: does GAM-K with everything that has helped, on the ensemble mean, match BG2?
docs.text:
Putting every earlier gain into the convex demand model and driving it from the ensemble mean gave a forecast that scores the same as BG2 and as experiment 111's GAM-K, and the experiment cannot rank the three. The assembled arm scored 2.791 points against 2.780 for BG2 and 2.800 for experiment 111's GAM-K, and the 99% intervals are 0.11 to 0.34 points wide. Using the ensemble mean instead of the 51 members made the quantile score 0.039 points worse (higher is worse). The heating split (T-all) and one shared filter noise setting together lowered it by 0.048 points, which is not distinguishable from the loss. The verdict is inconclusive. The experiment narrows the next step to the spread: a single table of residual quantiles around the mean forecast is too narrow in the lower tail, and a spread that restores the mixture's lower tail could turn the assembly into a gain.

We asked whether the convex demand model with the Kalman filter on recent errors (GAM-K, experiment 111), given the heating split by day type (T-all, experiment 114) and one filter noise setting shared by every substation (POOL, experiment 133), forecasts demand at the five decision Primary substations 0.5 to 168 hours ahead as well as the production recipe (BG2, experiment 87). The convex model was driven by the ensemble mean of the ensemble of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF ENS) instead of its 51 members. We added three changes one at a time (the ensemble mean as input, T-all, and POOL) and scored each arm on the same half-hourly rows. All three were already built and tested in earlier experiments.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Arms and schedule. A0 is experiment 111's GAM-K on the ensemble mean. A1 is A0 plus T-all. A2 is A1 plus POOL. A3 is A2 refitted weekly instead of monthly. A0 to A2 refit monthly on a 24-month window, as experiment 111's fits do. A3 tests weekly refits, because a monthly-refit arm would equal A2. The quantiles are the corrected mean plus a residual table fitted on the tuning months, with every spread factor at 1.
  • Rows. fold_a_daily_gap_v1, 561,172 half-hourly rows in the scored year (464,228 at the five decision substations and 96,944 at D9), outside the hand-filtered switching events; BG2 exists only for the scored year. D9 is in the table of arms and in no contrast.
  • Absolute skill, scored year, leads 0.5 to 168 hours (points of effective capacity). A0 2.839, A1 2.818, A2 2.791, A3 2.795, experiment 111's GAM-K 2.800, BG2 2.780, manual heuristic 3.497, climatology 3.804. A2 is 20% below the manual heuristic and 27% below climatology.
  • By lead band (A2, BG2, experiment 111's GAM-K). Under 24 hours: 2.363, 2.434, 2.373. From 24 to 72 hours: 2.630, 2.646, 2.653. From 72 to 168 hours: 2.980, 2.936, 2.983. A2 scores better than BG2 below 72 hours and worse from 72 to 168 hours; experiment 111's GAM-K trails BG2 at 24 to 72 hours as well.
  • C1, A0 minus experiment 111's GAM-K. +0.039 (99% interval +0.018 to +0.060), 0 of 5 substations better, 2 of 12 months negative; replicate +0.029 (+0.011 to +0.052). The prediction was within 0.03, so the ensemble mean worsens the score by more than predicted.
  • C2, A1 minus A0 (T-all). -0.021 (-0.039 to -0.004), 5 of 5 substations better, 10 of 12 months negative; replicate -0.037 (-0.082 to -0.008). The prediction of -0.02 to -0.04 held.
  • C3, A2 minus A1 (POOL). -0.027 (-0.069 to +0.017), 4 of 5 substations better; replicate -0.017 (-0.082 to +0.032). The prediction of -0.01 to -0.03 held in size, and the interval includes zero.
  • C4, A3 minus A2 (weekly refits). +0.004 (-0.012 to +0.021); replicate 0.000 (-0.018 to +0.019). The prediction of within 0.02 held.
  • C5, A2 minus BG2. +0.010 (-0.164 to +0.174), 3 of 5 substations better. The prediction of -0.03 to -0.12 missed, and the interval cannot exclude BG2 being better by 0.17.
  • C6, A2 minus experiment 111's GAM-K. -0.009 (-0.058 to +0.054), 4 of 5 substations better; replicate -0.025 (-0.099 to +0.065). The prediction of -0.06 to -0.15 missed.
  • Verdict by the pre-registered rule. C6's interval includes zero and C5's upper bound (+0.174) is above +0.05, so the hypothesis is inconclusive.
  • Breakouts, A2 minus experiment 111's GAM-K (scored year, all leads). Winter -0.028, winter nights -0.055, cold nights -0.070, and holidays and Christmas +0.063 (18,913 rows, interval -0.058 to +0.094). The point estimates are lower in winter and on cold nights, which are the hours NGED cares about, and higher on holidays; every one of these intervals includes zero.
  • Why the ensemble mean worsens the score by 0.039 (C1, tested after the result, post hoc). A0's pinball loss is worse than experiment 111's GAM-K at the 0.01, 0.05, 0.10, and 0.25 quantiles (0.2252 against 0.2082, 0.7471 against 0.7084, 1.1992 against 1.1487, 2.0333 against 1.9842) and also worse, by smaller amounts, at the 0.40 to 0.99 quantiles (for example 0.7433 against 0.7300 at the 0.95 quantile). A0's coverage at the 0.05 quantile is 6.3% against 5.8%, and at the 0.10 quantile 11.4% against 10.1%. The mean forecast's error rose by only 0.007, so the loss is in the spread. The mixture of 51 members putting more mass in the lower tail than one residual table around the mean does is consistent with these figures, and was not tested further (e00136_levels.py).

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, per site (A2, scored year, 12 to 36 hours): 0.000 at every site, because the residual quantile table is built so that its median is zero. Experiment 111's GAM-K: -0.005, -0.021, +0.018, -0.009, -0.097 and -0.052 at D10, D11, D14, D16, D5, and D9.

  • Audit triggers that fired, none triaged by an audit. Trigger 2 (a result contradicts its prediction): C1 (+0.039) contradicts its prediction of within 0.03; the explanation above was tested and recorded. Trigger 3: C5's quantile score contrast is +0.010 while its mean-error contrast is -0.061; A2's mean forecast is better than BG2's median (BG2 has no separate mean) and its spread is worse. Trigger 4: leaving D10 out turns C6 from -0.009 to +0.002, and leaving D16 out turns C5 from +0.010 to -0.033. Neither flip changes the verdict, because both C5 and C6 are inconclusive already, so we did not run the Opus audit; the manager can ask for one.
  • P1 control passed in experiment 133 (its FIX arm reproduces experiment 111's GAM-K within 1e-4 points).
  • P2 control passed. T-all with a huge penalty matches experiment 111's stored fits to within 2.6e-6 points, looser than the plan's 1e-6 because the ridge is divided between the pieces.
  • Prediction miss on cold-night coverage. Predicted 73% to 85%, observed 88% to 90%.

docs.title: Width of the bands by lead day (arm A2, scored year, descriptive)
docs.text:
The median 5% to 95% band width is a staircase in lead, not a smooth widening. The spread table has four lead bands (up to 24, 48, 144, and 168 hours), each fitted separately by hour band and calendar quarter, so the width is constant across lead days 3 to 6 and steps at days 1, 2, and 7. Over a whole year the medians never fall, but in a single week the width can fall between bands, because each band's table for a given hour band and quarter is estimated on its own.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Caveat on POOL. POOL was chosen on experiment 111's fits, not on T-all's.
  • Caveat on the interval. C5 and C6 have 99% intervals 0.11 to 0.34 points wide, so effects smaller than that cannot be resolved against BG2 or experiment 111's GAM-K. C1 to C4 have intervals 0.04 to 0.09 wide.
  • The filter uses no future weather. Its residuals use an analysis proxy built from earlier ENS runs, and the proxy is available at forecast time.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Fit the spread around the ensemble mean to match the mixture's lower tail, for example by tail-specific factors or a skewed residual table, then re-run A2 on the same rows.
  • Run the same assembly with the 51 members, to see whether T-all and POOL add -0.05 on the mixture, which would put the assembly about 0.04 below experiment 111's GAM-K.
  • Check POOL's cold-night tails before adopting it.

docs.title: Plan
docs.text:
Question. Does the convex model with the Kalman filter (GAM-K, experiment 111), given the pieces that helped in later experiments and driven by the ensemble mean, forecast Primary demand at least as well as BG2 (experiment 87), and better than experiment 111's GAM-K? No new modelling: every piece exists.

Arms. All arms share the rows, the weather calibration and solar shrink of experiment 111, and the pinned capacity.

Arm Fits Filter noise Weather input Spread BG2 as stored (experiment 87) K111 as stored (experiment 111's GAM-K) experiment 111's values 51 members, mixture as stored A0 experiment 111's monthly fits, 24-month window experiment 111's values (FIX) ensemble mean refitted on the tuning months A1 A0 with T-all FIX ensemble mean refitted A2 A1 POOL (experiment 133) ensemble mean refitted A3 A2 refitted weekly POOL ensemble mean refitted

Departure from the brief, and why. The brief's A3 is "A2 with monthly refits", but experiment 111's fits are already monthly with a 24-month window, so A0 to A2 already refit monthly and the brief's A3 would equal A2. A3 is therefore A2 with weekly refits, the production cadence, which tests whether the monthly cadence the arms use changes the result.

Ensemble mean as the input. The forecast is one pass of the model through the calibrated ensemble-mean temperature and irradiance, which replaces the 51 member passes of experiment 111. The quantiles are the corrected mean plus the residual table fitted on the tuning months from the same arm's own forecast (e00133_ens.fit_spread_from_frame), as K0-w does in experiment 125. The mean of a model with a hinge on temperature differs from the model at the mean temperature, so C1 is not zero by construction.

T-all. Experiment 114 fitted T-all at yearly cuts with its own design code. This experiment copies that design code and fits it at every monthly (and weekly) cut, and predicts on the ensemble-mean-driven cache.

Filter. The filter runs on the proxy-driven residual stream of each arm's own fits, with FIX for A0 and A1 and POOL (the single shared cell of experiment 133) for A2 and A3. POOL was chosen on experiment 111's fits, not on T-all fits; this is a caveat.

Rows. fold_a_daily_gap_v1, 09:00 UTC power_fcst_init_time, leads 0.5 to 168 hours, rows outside hand-filtered switching events. The scored year is 2025-07 to 2026-06; the tuning months are the odd months and the replicate months the even months of 2024-07 to 2025-06, as in experiment 133. D-labels only.

Breakouts. Lead bands (under 24, 24 to 72, 72 to 168 hours), winter, cold nights, holidays and Christmas, and tail calibration at the 0.01, 0.05, 0.95, and 0.99 quantiles, with the q95 coverage on cold nights. Absolute skill is reported for BG2, climatology, and manual_heuristic beside the contrasts. The curtailment cost saving against the manual heuristic follows once a node metric exists for these substations; if not run, the write-up says so.

Spread factors. Every spread factor is fixed at 1, because experiment 125 found that factors tuned on alternate months scored worse out of period.

Controls. P1: the FIX arm of experiment 133 reproduced experiment 111's GAM-K within 1e-4 (passed in experiment 133). P2: the T-all code, run with a difference penalty so large that the arm becomes B0, must reproduce experiment 111's stored gamk forecasts at the same cut to within 1e-6 points; this checks the copy of experiment 114's design code. P3: A0's forecast frames, scored on the rows of experiment 111's stored GAM-K, differ from it only through the weather input, so C1 is read against a within-method difference of 0 +/- 0.03.

Five triggers. Stored: private files only. Serving path: not touched. Degradation rule: not touched. More than one design defensible: yes (mean input, spread refit), pre-registered above. Callers not nameable without searching: no, the scripts copy experiments 111, 114, and 133.

Resources. Central processing unit (CPU) only, at most 8 cores with one thread per worker, each job under systemd-run --user --scope -p MemoryMax=16G -p OOMPolicy=continue.

Advice followed. From experiment 125, do not rely on member spread for tail skill. From experiment 133, test one shared noise setting before any per-substation fit.

docs.title: Differentiable physics, E7 forecast: does an Economy 7 night-step term lower the day-ahead error on winter nights?
docs.text:
Take-home message: the day-ahead forecast runs low on cold winter nights from 01:00 UTC, and a correction learned from its own past errors removes that bias. The experiment cannot say that the bias grows with cold. On cold winter nights from 01:00 UTC the base forecast ran 2.5 points too low on average (a point is 1% of a substation's 99th percentile of demand; "cold" means a forecast daily mean below 3 °C). With the night correction (an additive term fitted on the forecast's own past errors) it runs 0.2 points too low, and 93% of actual values fall below the 0.95 quantile, against 80% for the base forecast. The correction lowers the day-ahead quantile score (twice the mean pinball loss) by 0.484 points on those rows (99% interval from resampling calendar months, -0.777 to -0.169) and by 0.032 points over every row of the year (-0.054 to -0.012). A second analysis by a fresh reviewer (the audit, below) showed that a plain winter night offset with no temperature does as well, so the data show a winter night bias and not a cold-driven step. The verdict is inconclusive: the shuffled-night placebo control failed, and the 365 headline rows are too few for the rule committed in the plan (at least 3 months and 50 rows per substation).

We asked whether the step in Primary substation demand at the start of cheap night-rate electricity (Economy 7), which experiment 123 found, can be added to the day-ahead forecast. The base is the convex-optimisation demand model with a Kalman filter, driven by the mean of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) ensemble (ENS) weather forecast (experiment 133's shared-noise arm). We fitted a ridge regression of the base's own past errors on the half-hour (UTC), the forecast temperature, and the day of the week, refitted monthly on data before each month, and added the fitted correction to every forecast quantile. We scored it on the six decision substations over the year from July 2025, with winter 2025-26 as the only winter.

Results (every number is printed in report.json, produced by e00137_report.py):

  • Arms. Base (no term); t_site (one fit per substation, ridge penalty 100, chosen on the odd tuning months); t_pool (one fit shared by the six substations); oracle (the term fitted on the scored year itself); fixed123 and fixed123b (experiment 123's step inserted); t_const (post hoc: the per-half-hour constants only); placebo (temperature shuffled across nights).
  • Rows. The scored year of fold_a_daily_gap_v1, forecasts issued at 09:00 UTC, leads 12 to 36 hours, six substations, outside the hand-filtered switching events. Headline rows: the half-hours ending 01:00 to 03:00 UTC on winter nights whose forecast 24-hour mean temperature is below 3 °C (365 rows in 3 months by valid time; 35 rows at each of D5 and D16, 60 to 85 at the others).
  • C1 (term per substation minus base), headline rows: -0.484 (-0.777 to -0.169); 5 of 6 substations improve (D9 does not: +0.100); leaving each substation out gives -0.400 to -0.599. The pre-registered readability rule (3 months, 50 rows per substation) is not met, so by the rule the contrast is not assessable.
  • Wider row sets: all winter nights in the 01:00 to 03:00 window (3,353 rows): -0.352 (-0.482 to -0.245), 6 of 6 substations. All winter-night half-hours at leads 12 to 36 hours (16,089 rows): -0.115 (-0.178 to -0.056). Cold winter nights, every night half-hour (1,752 rows, post hoc): -0.194 (-0.249 to -0.134).
  • C2 (term shared by substations minus base): -0.454 (-0.731 to -0.190). C5 (per-substation minus shared): -0.030 (-0.094 to +0.089). Sharing one fit across substations loses nothing measurable.
  • C4 (non-inferiority, every row, every lead): -0.032 (-0.054 to -0.012), 6 of 6 substations; the upper bound is below the +0.01 limit.
  • Oracle minus base: -0.540 (-0.840 to -0.226). The term achieves 90% of the oracle's improvement.
  • C3 (experiment 123's step inserted, minus base), invalid arm: +2.643 (+1.541 to +3.551); the summer-adjusted fixed123b (post hoc): +1.979 (+1.247 to +2.615). The audit found both arms specified wrongly (finding 4 below), so these numbers say nothing about experiment 123's step.
  • Placebo minus base: -0.170 (-0.271 to -0.091). The constants-only arm t_const gives -0.156 (-0.268 to -0.112): about a third of the term's gain needs no temperature at all.
  • Absolute scores (points), headline rows: base 2.190, t_site 1.706, t_pool 1.736, oracle 1.650, placebo 2.020, t_const 2.034. Every row of the year: base 2.706, t_site 2.675.
  • Tail calibration, headline rows (coverage / pinball): q95 coverage 0.800 (base), 0.932 (t_site), pinball 0.613 against 0.444; q99 coverage 0.959 against 0.995, pinball 0.132 against 0.113; q05 coverage 0.041 against 0.047; q01 coverage 0.033 against 0.038, pinball 0.217 against 0.270. The term lifts the whole distribution, so the upper tail improves and the 0.01 quantile gets slightly worse. Every row of the year: q95 coverage 0.948 against 0.951.
  • Mean forecast error, headline rows (actual minus mean forecast): 2.519 (base), 0.230 (t_site). The mean absolute error falls from 3.748 to 2.864 (-24%).
  • Curtailment-cost metric: not run. The metric needs a forecast for a connection point and its generators, which this experiment does not forecast; the shift matters most for the upper tail, where q95 and q99 coverage improve.

Predictions against outcome. C1 was predicted at -0.5 to -2.0 points and came out at -0.484, just short of the range. The term recovered 90% of the oracle's gain (predicted at least 50%; the oracle's interval lies wholly below zero). The mean forecast's signed error shrank by 91% (predicted at least a third); the mean absolute error shrank by 24%, short of a third. The all-row score (C4) changed by -0.032 (predicted -0.03 to +0.01).

Controls.

  • Leakage: passed. Adding 100 points to actual from the monthly fit dates of 2025-11-01, 2026-01-01, and 2026-02-01 on, and rerunning the whole monthly fit, changed no corrected quantile of that cut's month (maximum change 0.0).
  • Injected step (an 8-point step plus 0.5 points per degree below 15.5 °C, which is 14.25 points at 3 °C): passed. The fitted step minus the clean fit's was within 3.7% of the truth at every substation at every winter cut from November 2025 to March 2026 (t_pool: within 0.6%).
  • Reproduction: passed. The base's score over five substations (the five that experiment 133 scored) at 12 to 36 hours is 2.4622 against experiment 133's 2.462.
  • Shuffled-night placebo: failed. It gained 0.170 points where the band was +/-0.1. The placebo keeps each half-hour's constant, which carries a third of the gain (t_const). The verdict is capped at inconclusive by the plan.

Checks.

  • Median minus mean forecast, per substation (base and term alike, since the term shifts both): D5 -0.125, D9 -0.019, D10 -0.045, D11 -0.035, D14 +0.013, D16 +0.000 points.
  • Mean-forecast error beside each contrast: the mean absolute error changes in the same direction as the quantile score (C1 headline -0.884, C4 -0.059), so the audit trigger for a mean-forecast error that moves against the quantile score did not fire.
  • Leave-one-substation-out: no flip of sign (-0.400 to -0.599 on the headline rows), so trigger 4 did not fire.
  • Triggers fired: the failed-control trigger (the placebo) and the trigger for a control that moves the score by more than its paired interval's half-width. The audit is in the next section.

Audit. A fresh Opus agent re-derived the contrasts from the stored predictions with its own code (report in the private briefs folder, e137_audit_report.md). Findings and triage:

  • Finding 1, accepted: a post hoc arm that swaps cold for a November-to-March indicator scores -0.432 on the headline rows; the temperature term minus that arm is -0.052 (-0.123 to +0.022), and -0.000 (-0.018 to +0.015) on cold winter nights, all night half-hours. On all winter window rows the temperature term is worse than the offset by +0.094 (+0.016 to +0.143). The take-home message, headline, and advice say this. A shuffle of cold within each calendar month keeps most of the gain (-0.25 to -0.39 over 12 seeds).
  • Finding 2, accepted: the planned placebo shuffles across the whole history, so it carries no season and falls back to the per-half-hour constants (t_const -0.156). Its failure is the constants working, not leakage. The plan's cap at inconclusive still applies.
  • Finding 3, accepted: the headline rows fall in 3 months by valid time (2025-11, 2026-01, 2026-02; report.json counts 4 by origin month), and D5 and D16 hold 35 rows against the 50 required, so C1 is not assessable under the rule. The readable cold-night subset (1,752 rows) gives -0.194; the same seasonal explanation applies.
  • Finding 4, accepted: fixed123 and fixed123b omit experiment 123's actual summer rise, correct the forecast's rise and not its level, use each substation's own fit where the plan says the pooled step, and insert the step in summer. Both arms shifted the forecast by 4.4 to 17.6 points where 2.4 to 4.4 were needed. Both arms are marked invalid above and were not rerun.
  • Finding 5, accepted: the leakage control compared fits on filtered rows, which cannot fail. It now corrupts actual from three cuts on, reruns the whole monthly fit, and compares the corrected quantiles of each cut's month. The audit's own end-to-end test passed as well.
  • Findings 6, 7, and 9, no fault found: the temperature window, the ridge and noise choices, the quantile shift (no crossings), and the 2.4622 reproduction check out. Tail coverage on cold nights, every half-hour: q95 0.913 (base) and 0.937 (term); q01 0.031 and 0.022.
  • Finding 8, accepted: the code's window is the half-hours ending 01:00 to 03:00 (five rows); the plan's text said 01:30 to 03:00, and the plan section below now says 01:00 to 03:00.

Caveats and what to try next.

  • The scored year holds one winter, and the term trained on one earlier winter (2024-25) at the start of it. A second winter would settle the verdict.
  • The term moves the whole night, including the 22:00 to 23:00 half-hours, where the mean error on cold nights goes from about zero to about +2 points (figure 3). A term confined to the half-hours after 00:30 would test whether that raises the score.
  • The temperature feature is a 24-hour ENS-mean temperature from 09:00 UTC on the evening date, so a "cold night" here is not experiment 123's daily mean below 3 °C.
  • Next: test a seasonal night offset, or a fix to the base forecast's winter night level, and retest when winter 2026-27 exists, with a within-month placebo for any temperature term.

docs.title: Plan, as committed before any code ran
docs.text: The text below is the plan as committed in the first commit of this branch, with the amendments of the plan review applied before any code ran.

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Experiment 123 found that demand at 13 of 14 Primary substations steps up around 01:00 UTC on winter nights, by about 10 points at a daily mean of 3 C, and that the day-ahead forecast of experiment 114 runs below actual demand from about 01:00 on cold nights. An operator sees that step and the forecast's miss. This experiment asks whether an explicit night term, learned from the base forecast's own past errors, closes the miss.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
• Base. Experiment 133's pool arm: the convex GAM with a Kalman filter (GAM-K) on the ENS ensemble mean, with one shared noise setting. Its prediction frames are read from experiment 133's private folder (tuning months 2024-07 to 2025-06, odd and even, and the scored year). No file of the best-guess assembly is edited.
  • The term. For a half-hour at UTC clock time h in the night set (21:00 to 08:30 UTC, 24 half-hours) on the night of evening date D, the correction to every quantile is a[h] + b[h] * cold + c[h] * weekend, where cold = max(0, 15.5 - T), T is the ENS-mean temperature averaged over the 24 hours from 09:00 UTC on D to 09:00 UTC on the next day, which a 09:00 UTC run always covers in full for the night it forecasts, and weekend flags Saturday and Sunday evenings. Coefficients are a ridge regression of the base forecast's error (actual minus the mean forecast) on those 72 columns, fitted per substation (T_SITE) or shared across the six substations (T_POOL), on all rows whose run origin and valid time are both before the first of the month being forecast (an expanding window, refitted monthly, starting from 2024-07). The ridge penalty is chosen on the odd tuning months from a fixed grid. The spread around the shifted median is unchanged.
  • The clock is UTC. Experiment 123 found the step follows UTC on British Summer Time nights (a post hoc finding at 13 of 14 substations). The term therefore uses UTC and does not test that choice.
  • Two reference arms. FIXED123 inserts experiment 123's estimated step (the pooled fit_headline step at the forecast temperature, with its estimated ramp) minus the step the base already forecasts on the same night. ORACLE is T_SITE fitted on the scored year's own rows, so it bounds what any term of this form could gain.
  • Weather at forecast time. T is the ENS-mean forecast available at the origin. No ERA5 value enters any score. Experiment 123's winters are used only by FIXED123, and end before the scored year.
  • Resampling. Month resampling for C1 draws only the calendar months that hold C1 rows; the contrast is readable only if at least 3 months and 50 rows per substation hold them, and is otherwise reported as not assessable. With one winter the expected verdict is inconclusive, and the write-up says so rather than relaxing the rule.
  • Limits stated now. The expanding window holds one training winter (2024-25) for the first scored winter months and grows through winter 2025-26. The scored year holds one winter, so the cold-night rows are few and the month-resampled interval will be wide.

docs.title: Rows and subsets
docs.text:
• Rows: fold_a_daily_gap_v1, 09:00 UTC init, six decision series, scored year (the runs stored by experiment 133).
  • E7 window rows: valid time 01:00 to 03:00 UTC (the half-hours ending 01:00 to 03:00, five rows).
  • Cold nights: T below 3 °C (the same T as the term's regressor; a 24-hour mean shifted 9 hours from the calendar day, so it is not experiment 123's daily mean).
  • Winter: November to March.
  • Headline subset: E7 window rows, cold winter nights, leads 12 to 36 hours. Beside it: all winter nights, all E7 window rows, all rows, and a figure of the step against the forecast on the coldest nights.

docs.title: Controls (run before any scoring)
docs.text:
• Injected step. Add a synthetic step of known size to the actual of every night in the stored frames (a ramp from 0 at 00:30 to 8 points at 01:30 UTC, held to 08:30, plus 0.5 points per degree of cold), refit T_SITE and T_POOL with the same code, and read the fitted correction at 3 °C. Pass: the fitted step at 01:30 to 03:00 UTC is within 25% of the truth (8 + 0.5 * 12.5 = 14.25 points) at 5 of 6 substations, from the first scored winter month on.
  • Shuffled-night placebo. Permute cold across the nights of each substation and refit. Pass: the C1 contrast on the permuted term is within +/-0.1 points of zero.
  • Leakage. Corrupt actual (add 100 points) at every valid time on or after each monthly cut in a copy of the frames and refit. Pass: the coefficients of every monthly fit are identical to the uncorrupted fit, and the corrections applied to the month are unchanged.
  • Reproduction. The stored base rows reproduce experiment 133's pool score at 12 to 36 hours to within 1e-4 points.
  • Stop rule. If the injected-step control fails at 3 or more substations, stop, record the verdict failed, and write what was found. No scored contrast is read after a failed control.

docs.title: Compute
docs.text: CPU only. The ridge fits are small: a run is expected to take minutes on 4 cores, well inside the 16 GB memory cap. Predictions are written under data/ml-experiments/00137-*/predictions/ with q01 to q99, actual, lead_hours, and time_series_id, so studies.tail_calibration can score them.

docs.title: Prior work followed
docs.text:
• Experiment 123's estimated step, timing, and cold slope (read first, not re-estimated).
  • Experiment 133's stored frames, scoring and month-resampled intervals, copied by pattern.
  • advice from experiment 123: judge on cold winter nights from 01:00; try the UTC clock. Departure: the term is fitted on the forecast's errors, not on the observed night mean, so that the part of the step the base already models is not added twice.

docs.title: Experiment 138: does a detector for weaker, slower onsets find more of the moved load?
docs.text: Making the load-transfer detector fire on weaker and slower starts did not find more of the moved power on injected transfers. A load transfer is a switching operation that moves part of one Primary substation's demand onto neighbouring substations for hours or days. We added synthetic transfers to real power history, and counted the share of the moved megawatts (MW) on which a detector raised an alarm. The detector, the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC), flags a step in one Primary substation's forecast errors, helped by an opposite step at its neighbours. A noise unit is the usual size of that step in odd-numbered months. The forecast is the convex demand model of experiment 130, with its coefficients held fixed. Three changes aimed at weak first steps (2 to 4 noise units) were a lower threshold for what counts as a candidate, a persistence feature, and a 72-hour window. Each found 0.79 of the moved MW, the same share as the unchanged detector (arm B), at the same budget of 80 false alarms, counted on odd-numbered months. The verdict is refuted, because no change had an interval reaching +0.02. Most of the weak first steps that stay missed are at a donor substation whose load moves to a receiving substation with no power meter, and none of the three changes separates them from noise. On the 35 real transfers lasting over 1 day, the three changes find 21 to 23 and arm B finds 18. The injected transfers show no such gain.

docs.title: Arms and rows
docs.text:
• B (control): RO-NC on the frozen convex residual, candidates at 2.5 noise units or more on the 24-hour step, logistic score on the step, the largest opposite-sign neighbour step, and topology counts. It reproduces experiment 130 exactly: 7,745 rows of detector outcomes per transfer and shape, none differ, and recall is 0.794.
  • W1: candidates from 1.5 noise units, same score features.
  • W2: candidates from 1.5 noise units, plus the step still present 1 to 2 days after the candidate (a 24-hour mean after a one-day gap, minus the day before).
  • W3: B's candidates plus peaks of a 72-hour step at 3.0 noise units or more, and the 72-hour step as a score feature.
  • Rows: experiment 82's fresh headline-band draw, 602 transfers per shape in even months, shapes S2 to S4 pooled, 15 series. Each arm fits its own logistic score on odd-month injections and sets its threshold at 80 unexplained odd-month alarms. Interval: whole calendar months resampled 20,000 times.
  • Lab shortcuts: the residual uses ERA5 weather that arrives about 5 days late, the end of each alarm is chosen with hindsight, and the moved MW is the injected amount.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Recall (95% interval): B 0.794 (0.719 to 0.856), W1 0.789 (0.711 to 0.852), W2 0.796 (0.725 to 0.855), W3 0.787 (0.707 to 0.848).
  • Planned contrasts (98.33% interval): W1 minus B -0.005 (-0.017 to +0.006), W2 minus B +0.001 (-0.009 to +0.018), W3 minus B -0.008 (-0.028 to +0.002). The best lower end is under zero, and every upper end is under +0.02.
  • Alarm counts: every arm has exactly 80 unexplained odd-month alarms by construction, and 65 to 68 on even months, so weak candidates show up as lost recall, not extra alarms. In the unmetered 4 to 6 noise-unit band W1 finds 225 of 380, W2 226, W3 213, against 233 for B.
  • Weak steps stay missed: for transfers with no metered receiver and a donor step of 2 to 4 noise units, B finds 59 of 365, W1 44, W2 50, and W3 59.
  • Long transfers (15.6 to 60 days): each weaker-onset arm minus B is +0.005 (+0.000 to +0.026, 95% interval).
  • Real transfers over 1 day (descriptive): B 18 of 35, W1 21, W2 23, W3 22. The scores were fitted on injected transfers only, and the real set is too small to rank the three arms.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Control: arm B reproduces experiment 130 row for row.
  • Forecast checks: no forecast is scored here, so the median-minus-mean and mean-forecast checks do not apply.
  • Audit triggers: none of the seven conditions in the ml-experiment skill fires. The result contradicts the prediction (+0.02 to +0.06), and the by-step table is the tested explanation: added weak candidates replace stronger ones at the fixed 80-alarm budget. The nested arm W2 does not beat W1 by more than its interval. The real-transfer lead is descriptive, and no later design depends on it.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Injected transfers are rectangular steps, so a persistence or slow-window feature has little to add there. Real transfers are less regular, which may explain why the real count rises while the injected recall does not. This is a guess that the experiment did not test.
  • The real-transfer count is 35 transfers at one threshold, and arms W1 to W3 were never tuned on them.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Check the real-transfer lead on a larger labelled set before porting W2.
  • Look for a signal other than the residual step for weak transfers with no metered receiver.

Code: ml-experiments/00138-weaker-onset-detector-on-the-ro-nc-convex-residual/; every number above is printed by e00138_contrasts.py.

docs.title: Experiment 139: does an as-of solar capacity in GAM-K lower the forecast error on sunny half-hours?
docs.text:
Take-home message: replacing the pinned solar capacity with a capacity read from each substation's own power did not help, and made sunny half-hours worse by 0.11 points of capacity. The as-of arm was better on the darkest third (-0.042 points), but the sunniest-third loss decides the verdict. A more accurate capacity (the hindsight arm, which sees the future) only matched the pin. The accuracy of the solar capacity is therefore not what limits the solar part of the forecast. This experiment does not locate the remaining sunny-day error. The verdict is refuted under the pre-registered rule: the interval of the as-of arm minus the pin on the sunniest third lies wholly above zero. The replicate months agree in sign but their interval includes zero, so the scored year carries the verdict.

In this page, the pin is experiment 45's capacity held fixed, the as-of capacity is read from data before each 1 July, the hindsight capacity is fitted on all data (a ceiling), and the sunniest third is the third of daylight half-hours with the highest unit solar shape at each Primary. The quantile score is twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles, in points of effective capacity. GAM is a generalised additive model, CAMS is the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (the irradiance source for the solar shape), and ENS is the ensemble forecast of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF).

We asked whether the solar capacity subtracted by the convex demand model with a Kalman filter (GAM-K, experiment 111) should come from experiment 129's capacity read from the substation's own power, fitted only on data before each 1 July, instead of experiment 45's pinned capacity. The pin and the as-of capacity both feed the same convex demand model, driven by the mean of the European Centre's weather ensemble as in experiment 136. Only the capacity changed. The known-answer test passed and the forecast got worse. Experiment 111's design also fixed the injection: the test adds a synthetic plant to the scored half-hours only, so no fit or filter sees it.

docs.title: Arms and rows
docs.text:
• Pin (control): experiment 45's frozen vintage, passed through the adaptor. It reproduces experiment 111's fits (largest coefficient difference 0.0 at all six Primaries) and experiment 136's a0 forecasts at D5 exactly.
  • As-of (scored arm): experiment 129's arm 2, fitted on rows before the latest 1 July origin (2023, 2024, or 2025) and held for the following season-year, divided by a recovery divisor rebuilt from known-answer fits cut at the same origin. The rebuilt estimates for 2025-07-01 agree with experiment 129's published ones within 0.05 MW (leakage check). The origin is 1 July and not the 1 September of the design note, because the convex demand model's season-years run July to June.
  • Hindsight (ceiling, never a result): experiment 129's published estimates, fitted on data to 2026-07-31. No PV (floor): capacity zero.
  • Post hoc, not pre-registered: as-of x 1.15 (one over the known-answer recovery of 0.87) and as-of in the convex demand model's own units (the raw capacity, before the divisor).
  • Rows: fold_a_daily_gap_v1, 09:00 UTC power_fcst_init_time, leads 0.5 to 168 hours, outside the hand-filtered switching events. D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16 are pooled. D9 has no experiment 129 table, so it has the pin and no-PV arms only. Monthly refits on a 24-month window, filter noise as experiment 111, 4 to 8 seconds per Primary for a whole year of fits and forecasts.
  • Slices: the thirds are per Primary, over daylight half-hours (CAMS-driven unit solar shape above 0.01), by that shape. Night half-hours are in no third.

docs.title: Headline numbers
docs.text:
Quantile score in points of effective capacity, five Primaries, scored year (2025-07 to 2026-06). Intervals are 98.75% intervals from the month-block bootstrap with 20,000 resamples.

Arm All Sunniest third Darkest daylight third Pin 2.840 4.452 3.000 As-of 2.852 4.562 2.959 Hindsight 2.840 4.481 2.963 No PV 3.389 5.502 3.983 As-of x 1.15 (post hoc) 2.860 4.615 2.910 As-of, model units (post hoc) 2.874 4.569 3.050
  • C1, as-of minus pin: all half-hours +0.013 (-0.003 to 0.028); sunniest third +0.110 (0.038 to 0.181); darkest third -0.042 (-0.076 to -0.003). The error of the mean forecast agrees: sunniest third +0.221 (0.114 to 0.359).
  • C2, hindsight minus pin: sunniest third +0.029 (-0.020 to 0.085); all half-hours +0.001 (-0.011 to 0.013). The ceiling gives no gain over the pin.
  • C3, hindsight minus as-of: sunniest third -0.081 (-0.125 to -0.043). The hindsight arm also holds one value per season-year, so the gap comes from the information date: the hindsight arm sees the following year's power, and the as-of arm does not. The comparison is therefore not a pure test of staleness.
  • No PV minus pin: all half-hours +0.549 (0.407 to 0.727); sunniest third +1.051 (0.467 to 1.650). At D9, +0.275 (0.062 to 0.460). An explicit solar term is worth about 0.55 points over all half-hours (1.05 on the sunniest third). The choice of capacity moves the sunniest-third score by 0.03 to 0.16 points in the arms above.
  • Post hoc arms: as-of x 1.15 minus pin on the sunniest third +0.163 (0.100 to 0.218); as-of in model units minus pin +0.117 (-0.024 to 0.255). Scaling worsens the as-of arm on sunny half-hours; the model-units arm is level with it. The post hoc scale of 1.15 came from the scored-year known-answer recovery, so its scored-year contrast is not out of sample.
  • Replicate months (even months of 2024-07 to 2025-06, origin 2024-07-01): the sign is the same. As-of minus pin on the sunniest third +0.072 (-0.030 to 0.115) and on the darkest third -0.028 (-0.070 to 0.014). Absolute scores: pin 2.765, as-of 2.774, hindsight 2.768, no PV 3.265. The stop rule (as-of worse than the pin on the sunniest third after the replicate, interval wholly above zero) did not fire, because the interval includes zero.
  • By Primary: leaving out any one Primary leaves the sunniest-third sign positive (+0.060 without D16 to +0.153 without D14); the interval includes zero when D10 or D16 is left out.

docs.title: Known-answer test
docs.text:
• Passed at five of five Primaries for all three plant classes (real farm, east-west, south-west): raising the capacity by half the as-of capacity removed 0.86 to 0.88 (real farm), 0.84 to 0.87 (east-west), and 0.78 to 0.80 (south-west) of the injected output on the sunniest third. The real-farm figures are medians over five real farms. The pre-registered band was 0.75 to 1.25.
  • The injection enters the scored rows only, so no fit or filter sees it. The test checks the shape match between the ensemble-driven forecast and each plant, not whether a fit absorbs a change.
  • The calibrated-fake-ensemble gate of experiment 111 was not rerun. This experiment uses the stored calibration and ensemble of experiment 111 and 136.

docs.title: Tail calibration and checks
docs.text:
Nominal levels are 0.01, 0.05, 0.95, and 0.99. Both arms leave too many actuals in the tails: 0.021 of actuals fall below the 0.01 quantile, and 0.054 rise above the 0.95 quantile. Pinball columns are in points of effective capacity.

Arm Below q01 Below q05 Below q95 Below q99 Pinball q01 q05 q95 q99 Pin 0.0216 0.0632 0.9465 0.9828 0.225 0.747 0.743 0.231 As-of 0.0208 0.0629 0.9463 0.9824 0.226 0.757 0.741 0.233
  • Audit triggers: two of the experiment-audit triggers fired. The result contradicts the pre-registered prediction of a 0.03 to 0.10 gain, and the session tested two explanations: the information date (the hindsight arm, which closes 0.081 of the 0.110 gap) and units or damping (the two post hoc arms, which do not). Downstream work (the full-history arm, the calibration experiments, the partly pooled GAM, and the card rebuild) waits for this headline. No Opus audit was run; Sonnet reviews of the code and the write-up were.
  • Predictions missed: three pre-registered predictions failed. The as-of gain had the wrong sign. The hindsight arm beat the as-of arm by 0.081 and not under 0.03 points. The no-PV loss on the sunniest third was 1.05 and not 0.2 to 0.6 points.
  • Benchmarks: climatology and manual_heuristic were not rescored here. Their absolute skill at these Primaries is in experiment 111's results, on the same rows.
  • Median minus mean forecast: 0.0 at every Primary and arm, because the spread table is centred by construction, so it checks nothing here.
  • Curtailment cost saving against the manual heuristic: not computed. No node-plus-generators metric exists for these five Primaries.
  • Weather and availability: the ensemble mean is available at forecast time. The as-of capacity uses data before each 1 July origin only, and e00139_asof_table.py rebuilds the divisor per origin.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The scored arm holds one capacity for a year, so C1 includes the staleness of the as-of capacity. A live service could refit monthly. The hindsight arm (also one value per season-year) bounds what accuracy alone gives, and it equals the pin.
  • The loss is concentrated at D16 and D10. As-of minus pin on the sunniest third, per Primary: D16 +0.313 (0.138 to 0.490), D10 +0.222 (0.163 to 0.303), D11 +0.034 (-0.001 to 0.071), D5 +0.040 (-0.183 to 0.344), and D14 -0.060 (-0.131 to 0.008). Staleness fits D16, where the pin (3.9 to 4.7 MW) sits above the as-of capacity (2.98 MW). At D5 and D14 the as-of arm is level with or better than the pin, so the pooled loss leans on two Primaries. The post hoc arms rule out a simple unit or damping fix but do not identify the cause.
  • Tertile edges come from the pin frame over the scored period, including D9.
  • The origin is 1 July, so the 2025 estimate used for the scored year covers the 2025 season-year from the 2025-07-01 cut.
  • Replicate months cover six months only, so the replicate intervals are wide.
  • The adaptor lives in this folder (e00139_adaptor.py). Moving it into packages/studies would be a module change that needs the maintainer's review.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Keep the pin. The capacity is not the limiting input; the next solar experiment should target the sunny-day forecast of the ensemble mean (per-member solar, or the cloud damping of the irradiance calibration) or the fixed solar shape.
  • If a capacity source is still wanted, test one refitted monthly and compared with the pin weekly path, since a flat annual value loses to the hindsight value.

docs.title: LSC fed into the GAM-K forecast
docs.text:
Take-home message. Telling GAM-K's filter when a load transfer started and ended helped inside the transfer and hurt in the 72 hours after it. GAM-K is the weather-driven demand forecast of earlier experiments, and its Kalman filter corrects each forecast with the most recent errors. A load transfer moves a block of demand from one substation to another, for example when a switch is thrown, and it shows as a step in the forecast error. We simulated transfers and gave the filter either the switching detector's alarm or the true start and end. Scores are quantile scores in points of effective capacity, and a positive difference from the filter alone (K0) is worse.

The answer in numbers. The arm given the true interval (S-ORACLE) scored 0.126 points better than K0 inside a transfer (95% interval 0.075 to 0.219), and 0.310 points worse in the 72 hours after the transfer ended (0.195 to 0.695), because the filter holds the step flat over the whole 7-day forecast. The detector's alarm arrives 48 hours after the step, and the arm that used it scored the same as a placebo that used random times. On the pre-registered measure, C1 (the 48 hours after an alarm), the deployable arm scored +0.059 points (-0.004 to +0.378).

docs.title: What we asked
docs.text:
We asked whether the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC, the detector of experiment 130) lowers the forecast's error when its output is fed into GAM-K's Kalman filter. RO-NC looks for steps in the forecast error that appear at one substation and are matched by opposite steps at neighbouring substations. We added transfers of 25% or more of the receiving load that last over a day to the real forecast errors, in 44 simulated versions of the data that touch six Primary substations. The transfers are the headline-band draw of experiment 147. We ran the detector with the causal end rule of experiment 147. We then gave the filter a second "switched" regime whose level variance is a multiple of the fitted one. The method follows experiment 111's Kalman filter, combined with a two-regime mixture in the style of the interacting multiple model filter used in target tracking.

Every setting scored worse than the filter alone on the tuning months. The stop rule (stop before the real year if the tuning months show no gain) therefore ended the experiment before the real year was scored.

docs.title: Arms, rows, and numbers
docs.text:
• Arms. K0 (GAM-K's filter, no detector). S-KF (the two-regime filter; prior 0.5 of the switched regime while a causal alarm is active, level variance 4 times the fitted one, chosen on the tuning months from prior {0.5, 0.9} and multiplier {4, 16, 64, 256}). S-HE (the same filter with the hindsight end, not deployable). S-ORACLE (prior 0.5 inside the true transfer interval, not deployable). Placebo (the causal prior shifted by a random whole number of weeks). Variance inflation (the placebo prior with no likelihood update). Two post hoc arms keep the prior on longer: S-KF 48 hours after the end is called, and S-ORACLE 72 hours after the true end. All arms use K0's uncertainty bands, so each contrast is a difference in the forecast's location only.
  • Rows. fold_a_daily_gap_v1 runs at the five decision substations and D9 (labels as in experiment 134), replicate months (even months 2024-07 to 2025-06) and the scored year (2025-07 to 2026-06), leads 0.5 to 168 h, rows outside the hand-filtered switching events. Three row sets, by target time: inside a simulated transfer (279,332 rows, 11 months), the 48 hours after a causal alarm on a simulated transfer (127,468 rows, 10 months; this is C1), and the 72 hours after a simulated transfer ends (281,864 rows, 12 months). Alarms from the real forecast-error series alone are not scored. Intervals resample calendar months of target time.
  • C1, S-KF minus K0, 48 hours after a causal alarm: +0.059 points (-0.004 to +0.378); K0's own score on these rows is 5.46 points (4.24 to 6.94). Mean-forecast absolute error: +0.064 (-0.008 to +0.397). The interval includes zero, so C1 does not show a gain.
  • Inside a simulated transfer (K0's own score 8.84, 7.24 to 15.03): S-KF -0.027 (-0.224 to +0.002), placebo -0.028 (-0.218 to -0.009), variance inflation -0.027 (-0.211 to -0.009), S-HE -0.111 (-0.250 to -0.068), S-ORACLE -0.126 (-0.219 to -0.075).
  • 72 hours after the transfer ends: S-KF +0.071 (-0.008 to +0.446), placebo +0.074 (+0.023 to +0.390), S-HE +0.264 (+0.169 to +0.602), S-ORACLE +0.310 (+0.195 to +0.695).
  • 48 hours after a causal alarm, other arms: S-HE +0.084 (+0.017 to +0.402), S-ORACLE +0.124 (+0.065 to +0.484), placebo +0.047 (-0.006 to +0.399), variance inflation +0.046 (-0.005 to +0.390). The controls were run on the simulated data only.
  • The post hoc longer-prior arms (labelled post hoc): S-KF kept on 48 hours longer is +0.061 (+0.000 to +0.377) after an alarm, -0.024 (-0.235 to +0.007) inside a transfer, +0.074 (-0.007 to +0.450) after the end. S-ORACLE kept on 72 hours longer is -0.121 (-0.213 to -0.074) inside, +0.264 (+0.166 to +0.549) after the end. Keeping the switched regime on after the end did not remove the loss.
  • What the pattern says. The filter's correction is a level held flat at every lead. The true interval lets the filter correct fast inside the transfer. For a forecast made inside the transfer, the same correction is wrong at the targets after the transfer ends. The causal alarm is known only 48 hours after the step, by which time K0 has adapted too. The inside-transfer gains of S-KF, the placebo, and variance inflation are the same (about -0.027), so the detector's timing adds nothing to them.
  • K0 adapts slowly at the one substation tested. On D9's real residuals with an 8-point step lasting 4 days, the Opus audit found that K0 still misses 5.4 of 8 points after 24 to 36 hours and 3.3 after 3 days. e00141_synthetic.py uses illustrative settings and a single hour band, so it does not represent the fitted filter.
  • Tail calibration (48 hours after a causal alarm; K0 and S-KF alike): q95 coverage 88.2% against a nominal 95%, and q05 coverage (the share of actuals above q05) 85.0% against 95%. On winter nights (a proxy for cold nights: UTC 00:00 to 06:00, November to March, 6,696 rows) q95 coverage is 85.7% for K0, 85.6% for S-KF, and 83.3% for S-ORACLE. No q01 or q99 results were computed.
  • By site, S-KF minus K0 after an alarm: D10 +0.257, D14 +0.040, D16 +0.027, D9 +0.026, D11 +0.008, D5 -0.001. By period: replicate months +0.002, scored year +0.031. Dropping D10 leaves +0.020, and dropping any other site leaves +0.063 to +0.071.

docs.title: Checks and audit
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast per site (rows after an alarm; K0 and S-KF share the same value): D10 -0.12, D14 +0.02, D11 -0.05, D16 +0.00, D9 -0.07, D5 -0.48 points of effective capacity. D5's median sits half a point under its mean on these rows; the correction is common to all arms, so contrasts are unaffected.
  • The mean-forecast error beside each quantile-score contrast points the same way as the quantile score for every arm (printed in report.json).

  • Triggers fired: a failed known-answer control, and an arm with more information scoring worse. S-ORACLE scored worse than K0 on the pre-registered rows (triggers 1 and 5 of the ml-experiment skill). The Opus audit (one review, approved by the manager) found no bug in the filter, the prior, the injection, or the scoring, and traced the loss to the 72 hours after the transfer ends. Its findings and their triage:

    • Accepted: the rows labelled "inside a transfer" included the 72 hours after it. The page now scores the two separately.
    • Accepted: 88% of the alarm intervals in the first scoring were alarms from the real forecast-error series repeated in every simulated version. Only alarms on a simulated transfer are scored now.
    • Accepted: "the filter adapts within about a day" was false for the fitted settings, and S-ORACLE is not an upper bound because its prior is off at the reverse step. Both claims are removed.
    • Accepted: the first tuning used the mixed rows and favoured the smallest multiplier. It is re-run on the corrected row sets and still picks prior 0.5 and multiplier 4 (mean gain +0.003, so the stop rule still fires).
    • Not applied: the audit's suggestion to re-tune on rows inside the transfer only, which would tune the deployable arm on rows that it can only see 48 hours late.
    • Noted, no change: the detector's timestamps sit one half-hour later than the site's grid timestamps. The forecast-error series and the scored actual shift together, so no number moves.

  • Leakage review (one Sonnet reviewer, code only). It found no way for a deployable arm to see data later than its forecast time. The filter runs forward, the 96-half-hour onset lag matches the alarm statistic's window, known_from is the stamp at which the end statistic is computable, and tuning reads only the tuning months. Its other findings and their triage:

    • Accepted, as a limit on the controls (not re-run): the placebo prior is shifted by whole weeks, so it seldom falls on the scored rows, which sit around events.
