Of the 586,232 rows, 27,095 lie within a logged transfer or the 72 hours after it, and 559,137 are outside. Scores that involve BG2, and the absolute scores below, use the rows shared with BG2. The alarm is active at the forecast origin on 14.7% of rows for the pair alarm (D5 32.2%, D9 0%), 10.2% for RO-NC, and 22.2% for the union (D5 35.7%, D10 28.6%).
  • Absolute scores, outside logged transfers (shared rows). K0 2.725, MASK_NEW 2.758, MASK_UNION 2.826, MASK_RONC 2.986, GAM_ONLY 3.029, BG2 2.693, arm C 2.664, manual heuristic 3.390, climatology 3.652.
  • C1, outside logged transfers (95%, resampling calendar months). MASK_UNION minus K0 +0.102 (-0.013 to +0.205); MASK_NEW minus K0 +0.033 (-0.042 to +0.105). Winter (223,434 rows): MASK_UNION +0.012 (-0.217 to +0.208), MASK_NEW +0.010 (-0.180 to +0.195). Other months (335,703 rows): MASK_UNION +0.161 (+0.064 to +0.273), MASK_NEW +0.049 (+0.018 to +0.090). MASK_UNION minus BG2 +0.134 (-0.076 to +0.343); K0 minus BG2 +0.032 (-0.113 to +0.185). Leaving out one substation, the upper end stays at or above +0.17 for MASK_UNION. By substation, MASK_UNION minus K0 is +0.265 at D9, +0.255 at D10, +0.052 at D16, +0.044 at D11, +0.021 at D14, and -0.052 at D5.
  • Where the mask adds error. On rows outside logged transfers where no pair alarm is active or in its 72 hours after, MASK_NEW minus K0 is +0.002 (-0.000 to +0.003) on 489,420 rows; for the union it is +0.004 (+0.001 to +0.010) on 446,365 rows. While the union alarm is active at the forecast origin outside logged transfers (111,159 rows; the means use the rows shared with BG2), MASK_UNION scores 3.475 against 2.979 for K0, +0.496 (-0.070 to +1.081). While the pair alarm is active (68,539 rows) the difference is +0.258 (-0.335 to +0.905). In the 72 hours after the union alarm's end is known (1,613 rows), MASK_UNION minus K0 is -0.171 (-0.400 to +0.008).
  • C2, during a logged transfer (INSIDE, 5 transfers, 12,540 rows, observed power contains the transfer). K0 5.838, MASK_NEW 10.494, MASK_UNION 11.156, GAM_ONLY 12.151, ORACLE 10.238. MASK_UNION minus K0 +5.318 (+2.977 to +6.750); MASK_NEW minus K0 +4.655 (+1.013 to +5.622). The rows before the first alarm (BEFORE, 2 transfers, 2,440 rows) score the same for every stack arm, because no alarm is known yet.
  • C3, the 72 hours after a logged transfer ends (AFTER). Shared with BG2 (7 transfers, 3,675 rows): K0 13.686, GAM_ONLY 6.936, MASK_NEW 6.321, MASK_UNION 6.307, MASK_RONC 7.406, ORACLE 6.354, BG2 10.091, manual heuristic 7.649, climatology 7.494. All stack rows (11 transfers, 13 transfer-substation pairs, 5,993 rows): K0 10.129, MASK_NEW 6.083, MASK_UNION 5.177, GAM_ONLY 5.218, ORACLE 4.790. MASK_UNION minus K0 is -7.379 (-9.839 to -0.042) on the shared rows and -4.952 (-8.341 to -0.031) on all stack rows; MASK_NEW minus K0 is -7.365 (-9.832 to -0.025) and -4.047 (-7.933 to +1.122). MASK_UNION minus BG2 is -3.785 (-6.005 to +0.001); MASK_NEW minus BG2 is -3.771 (-6.004 to +0.011), with no threshold. Leaving out D5 or D16 widens the interval of MASK_UNION minus K0 to include zero (-3.307, -7.699 to +0.290, and -3.648, -7.327 to +0.307).
  • Tail calibration (share of readings at or below the quantile; pinball loss in points). Outside logged transfers, MASK_UNION: q01 0.0201 (0.210), q05 0.0612 (0.728), q95 0.9563 (0.714), q99 0.9884 (0.202); K0: 0.0146 (0.195), 0.0493 (0.687), 0.9578 (0.710), 0.9882 (0.208); BG2: 0.0097 (0.208), 0.0404 (0.617), 0.9445 (0.738), 0.9831 (0.249). After a transfer ends, MASK_UNION covers 0.172, 0.218, 0.832, and 0.896; K0 covers 0.409, 0.453, 0.757, and 0.832; BG2 covers 0.0035, 0.323, 0.745, and 0.842, so every forecast is too confident in the days after a transfer, because coverage should be 0.01, 0.05, 0.95, and 0.99. The node-plus-generators curtailment metric is not scored, because the experiment forecasts six Primaries alone.
  • D8's 29 multi-day drops of experiment 159 (descriptive; D8 has no frozen GAM here). An alarm onset lies within 24 hours of the drop's start for 3 drops with the pair alarm, 5 with RO-NC, and 7 with either, out of 79 alarms on D8 in the union table (46 from the pair alarm, 37 from RO-NC). An onset up to 24 hours after the start counts, so a later onset would not have been known at the start.
  • Predictions against outcome. The union mask outside logged transfers was predicted 0.04 to 0.15 worse: +0.102. After a transfer, MASK_UNION was predicted at 5 to 8 points (6.31), K0 at 12 to 15 (13.69), and BG2 at 9 to 11 (10.09). The mask was predicted to score worse than K0 during a logged transfer (+5.32). While an alarm is active the mask was predicted within 1 point of K0: +0.50 outside logged transfers, +0.72 on all rows.
  • Post hoc, labelled. The row split by the alarm active at the forecast origin and the leave-one-substation-out checks were not part of the pre-registered verdict.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, identical for every stack arm: D10 -0.064, D11 -0.027, D14 +0.033, D16 +0.014, D5 -0.135, D9 -0.021 points of capacity.
  • Error of the median forecast beside the quantile contrast. Outside logged transfers (shared rows): K0 4.773, MASK_NEW 4.853, MASK_UNION 4.961, GAM_ONLY 5.334, BG2 4.734. After a transfer: K0 18.232, GAM_ONLY 10.726, MASK_NEW 9.639, MASK_UNION 9.616, BG2 15.467. Both agree with the quantile score in direction.
  • Triggers. Trigger 4 fired in part: leaving D5 or D16 out makes the interval of MASK_UNION minus K0 after a transfer include zero (C3), but the sign holds and the not supported verdict rests on C1, whose upper end stays at or above +0.17 whichever substation is left out, so no verdict could change and no audit was run. Trigger 5 holds as in experiment 163: the mask scores level with the logged-interval mask (ORACLE) after a transfer (-0.05 points, 95% -0.14 to +0.25), so the logged interval is not a ceiling. Triggers 1, 2, 3, 6, and 7 did not fire: the no-alarm rows score within +0.004 of K0, every result lies in its predicted range, the two error measures agree, the interval widths match experiment 163's, and no later design depends on this result.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• 11 transfers, 7 shared with BG2. The 72-hour test rests on 11 logged transfers. The per-transfer figure shows most of the gain at two transfers, as in experiment 163.
  • Active alarms are common. The union alarm is active at the forecast origin on 22.2% of rows, and 111,159 of those rows lie outside logged transfers. Some of those rows are real switching that the log lacks, so the extra error from the mask on those rows may be overstated.
  • Lab conditions. The filter's residual uses the analysis proxy, and the alarm tables are experiment 156's, tuned on odd months of the same stream (experiment 156).
  • Masked history persists. After an alarm ends, the readings inside it stay missing in the filter's history, That missing history explains the +0.004 on rows with no alarm active.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: The next question is whether a mask from the pair alarm alone, or a mask used only in winter, keeps the gain after a transfer and keeps the extra error outside logged transfers under +0.01. A gate on the alarm's step size, or a partial mask that down-weights recent power instead of removing it, are the two variants the pattern of extra error suggests.

docs.title: A mask on recent power that trusts only balanced pair alarms, and a soft mask that inflates the filter's observation noise
docs.text:
When a detector flags that load may have been switched between substations, a forecast that ignores recent power only for trustworthy flags keeps 99.6% of the gain after a transfer and removes almost all the extra error elsewhere, but one year of data cannot show that the extra error is below the limit we set. Our forecast corrects itself using recent power. After a load transfer between substations has been recorded in NGED's switching log (a "logged transfer"), recent power misleads the correction, so experiment 165 ignored recent power (a "mask") whenever a switching alarm was active. That helped after a transfer but added error on other days. Here the "gated" mask ignores recent power only for alarms whose opposite steps at a neighbouring substation roughly cancel (a balance score of 0.7 or more). In the 72 hours after a logged transfer ends, the forecast error score is 6.34 points of a substation's effective capacity with the gated mask, against 13.69 with no mask and 10.09 for best guess 2 (BG2, the production-style XGBoost forecast of experiment 87). On the 559,137 real rows outside logged transfers the gated mask scores 0.009 points worse than no mask (95% interval from resampling calendar months, -0.068 to +0.081), where the mask from either alarm of experiment 165 scored 0.102 worse. The limit set before scoring was an interval within +/-0.03, so the verdict is not supported. A soft mask, which keeps the readings but treats them as noisier, changes almost nothing (at the three pre-registered factors) or gains and harms about as much as a hard mask (at factors we added afterwards). The next step is to re-test the gated mask on a longer period.

We asked whether recent power can be ignored less bluntly while a switching alarm is active. The forecast, called the stack here, is a frozen generalised additive model (GAM) with a Kalman filter (Kalman, 1960) that corrects each forecast using its recent errors, as in experiment 163. Experiment 165 set the filter's readings missing from the moment an alarm was known until the end rule (the rule that decides an alarm has ended) of experiment 147 and experiment 148 fired. That mask helped after a transfer and added error elsewhere. Here the gated mask applies only to the pair alarms of experiment 156 (two metered substations step in opposite directions within hours) whose balance score is at least 0.7. The balance score is the smaller of the ratio of the two steps and its inverse, so 1 means the steps cancel exactly. The soft mask keeps every reading and multiplies the filter's observation-noise variance, from the moment the alarm is known until the end rule fires, by a factor that rises with the balance score. Scores are twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles (a standard loss for quantile forecasts), in points of effective capacity; lower is better.

By the pre-registered rule the verdict is not supported, for different reasons in the two parts. Part 1 (the gated mask) passes the gain test, G2: it keeps 99.6% of the hard mask's gain, against a required 70%. It fails the no-harm test, G1, because the interval is wider than the required +/-0.03, although the point estimate of +0.009 lies inside it. Six of the 13 transfer-substation pairs (one logged transfer seen at one substation) have a gated alarm known before the transfer ends, so the part is scored. Part 2 (the soft mask) fails the gain test, S2, at every pre-registered factor: at best the soft mask recovers 0.53 of the 7.38 points. The other two soft-mask tests pass trivially, because a soft mask that does nothing also does no harm.

  • Arms. K0 (the stack with no mask), GAM_ONLY (the GAM alone), MASK_NEW (hard mask, every pair alarm), MASK_RONC and MASK_UNION (hard masks of experiment 165), MASK_GATED (hard mask, pair alarms with a balance score of 0.7 or more), SOFT_F10, SOFT_F100, SOFT_F1000 (soft mask on every pair alarm, observation-noise variance multiplied by up to 10, 100, and 1000 at a perfect balance and by less at lower scores), ORACLE (the logged interval, event rows only), BG2 (experiment 87), experiment 155's arm C, the manual heuristic, and climatology. Post hoc, labelled: SOFT_F10000, SOFT_F100000, and SOFT_F1000000, added after the three pre-registered factors changed almost nothing. The stack arms share the K0 spread of experiment 115, so they differ in location only. The GAM and the filter are frozen, so no refit schedule applies.
  • Rows. The same 586,232 rows with a reading as experiment 165, at D5, D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16 (anonymised substation labels), July 2025 to June 2026; 581,078 are shared with BG2. The scores of K0, MASK_NEW, and MASK_UNION match experiment 165's to the last stored digit. The gated alarm is active at the forecast origin on 10.3% of rows (D5 23.1%, D9 0%), the pair alarm on 14.7%, and the union on 22.2%. Of the 282 real pair alarms, 113 pass the gate (figure 5).
  • Absolute scores, outside logged transfers (shared rows). K0 2.725, MASK_GATED 2.733, MASK_NEW 2.758, MASK_UNION 2.826, SOFT_F1000 2.727, SOFT_F1000000 2.757, GAM_ONLY 3.029, BG2 2.693, manual heuristic 3.390, climatology 3.652.
  • Absolute scores, 72 hours after a transfer ends (7 transfers shared with BG2). K0 13.686, MASK_GATED 6.336, MASK_NEW 6.321, MASK_UNION 6.307, SOFT_F10 13.684, SOFT_F100 13.640, SOFT_F1000 13.155, SOFT_F1000000 6.406, GAM_ONLY 6.936, ORACLE 6.354, BG2 10.091, manual heuristic 7.649, climatology 7.494.
  • G1, outside logged transfers (95%, resampling calendar months). MASK_GATED minus K0 +0.009 (-0.068 to +0.081); winter (223,434 rows) +0.003 (-0.191 to +0.188); other months (335,703 rows) +0.013 (0.000 to +0.032). MASK_GATED minus MASK_UNION -0.093 (-0.176 to -0.023). MASK_GATED minus BG2 +0.041 (-0.123 to +0.206). Leaving out one substation, the estimate ranges from -0.024 (D10 left out) to +0.025 (D16 left out), with every interval wider than +/-0.03. On the 514,228 rows with no gated alarm active, MASK_GATED minus K0 is -0.000 (-0.001 to +0.001). On the 44,216 rows outside logged transfers while a gated alarm is active it is +0.116 (-0.816 to +1.005), against +0.258 (-0.339 to +0.896) for the pair alarm and +0.496 (-0.066 to +1.090) for the union.
  • G2, 72 hours after a transfer (shared rows, 7 transfers, resampling transfers). MASK_GATED minus K0 -7.349 (-9.822 to +0.007), against -7.379 (-9.832 to -0.042) for MASK_UNION, so the gated mask keeps 99.6% of the gain (required 70%, 5.17 points). On all 13 transfer-substation pairs (11 transfers): MASK_GATED -4.377 (-8.104 to +0.298), MASK_UNION -4.952 (-8.405 to +0.027). Leaving out D5 or D16 gives -2.478 (-7.229 to +0.382) and -3.736 (-7.373 to +0.146). The gain sits in 3 transfer-substation pairs: two at D5 and one at D16 (figure 4).
  • Gate coverage. Six of 13 transfer-substation pairs have a gated alarm known before the transfer ends (required for a verdict: 5). Six gated alarms in all on D8, none within 24 hours of a start of the 29 multi-day drops at D8 of experiment 159, against 3 for the ungated pair alarm and 7 for either alarm (descriptive; D8 has no frozen GAM here).
  • During a logged transfer (INSIDE, observed power contains the transfer; 5 transfers, 12,540 rows). K0 5.838, MASK_UNION 11.156, MASK_GATED 10.463; MASK_GATED minus K0 +4.625 (+0.282 to +5.620). On the 3 transfers shared with BG2, the soft mask scores worse than no mask by +0.008, +0.083, and +0.631 at factors 10, 100, and 1000, against +5.378 for MASK_UNION.
  • S1 to S3, soft mask at the pre-registered factors. Outside logged transfers, SOFT_F10, SOFT_F100, and SOFT_F1000 minus K0 are -0.000, -0.000, and +0.003, so minus MASK_UNION they are -0.102, -0.102, and -0.099 (S1 passes). After a transfer they change K0 by -0.002, -0.045, and -0.531 points (S2 needs at least 5.90; fails). During a transfer the harm is +0.008, +0.083, and +0.631 points (S3 allows up to 6.45; passes). No factor passes all three.
  • Post hoc soft-mask sweep. SOFT_F10000: outside +0.020 (+0.007 to +0.036), after a transfer -2.824 (-4.213 to -0.039). SOFT_F100000: +0.034 (+0.003 to +0.076), -6.280 (-8.257 to -0.027). SOFT_F1000000: +0.033 (-0.036 to +0.099), -7.280 (-9.698 to -0.025). The factor that recovers the gain adds the extra error of the hard mask from every pair alarm (+0.033).
  • Tail calibration (share of readings at or below the quantile; pinball loss in points). Outside logged transfers, MASK_GATED: q01 0.0136 (0.186), q05 0.0485 (0.678), q95 0.9554 (0.709), q99 0.9879 (0.203); K0: 0.0146 (0.195), 0.0493 (0.687), 0.9578 (0.710), 0.9882 (0.208); BG2: 0.0097 (0.208), 0.0404 (0.617), 0.9445 (0.738), 0.9831 (0.249). After a transfer, MASK_GATED covers 0.176, 0.233, 0.835, and 0.898; K0 covers 0.409, 0.453, 0.757, and 0.832; BG2 covers 0.0035, 0.323, 0.745, and 0.842. Coverage should be 0.01, 0.05, 0.95, and 0.99, so every forecast except BG2 at q01 is too confident in the days after a transfer, and BG2 is too confident at q05, q95, and q99. The node-plus-generators curtailment metric is not scored, because the experiment forecasts six Primary substations alone.
  • Predictions against outcome. The gated mask was predicted within +/-0.03 (interval): the estimate is inside and the interval is not. The gated gain was predicted at least 70% of the hard gain: 99.6%. The soft mask was predicted to beat the hard mask outside logged transfers by at least 0.051 at the best factor: the soft mask does, because the soft mask does almost nothing. It was predicted to keep 80% of the gain after a transfer: it keeps 7% at best (factor 1000).
  • Post hoc, labelled. The three added soft-mask factors, the leave-one-substation-out checks, the winter and other-month split, and the split of rows by whether a gated alarm is active.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, identical for every stack arm: D10 -0.064, D11 -0.027, D14 +0.033, D16 +0.014, D5 -0.135, D9 -0.021 points of capacity.
  • Error of the median forecast beside the quantile contrast. Outside logged transfers (shared rows): K0 4.773, MASK_GATED 4.809, MASK_UNION 4.961, SOFT_F1000 4.778. After a transfer: K0 18.232, MASK_GATED 9.666, MASK_UNION 9.616, SOFT_F1000 17.653. Both measures agree with the quantile score in direction.
  • Triggers. Trigger 2 fired in part: the interval for G1 is wider than the +/-0.03 the plan required. The explanation was tested and holds: the arm scores -0.000 (-0.001 to +0.001) on the 514,228 rows with no gated alarm, so the width comes from the 44,909 rows outside logged transfers while a gated alarm is active or has just ended, and the extra error is confined to them. That width is 0.149 here and 0.147 for the pair alarm in experiment 165, so trigger 6 did not fire. Trigger 4 fired in part: leaving out D5 or D16 makes the interval for the gated gain after a transfer include zero, but the sign holds, and the not supported verdict rests on interval width, which no leave-one-out check changes. Triggers 1, 3, 5, and 7 did not fire: there is no control, the two error measures agree, the gated mask (a subset of the pair-alarm mask) scores within 0.015 points of it after a transfer, and no later design depends on this result yet. No audit was run.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Six of 13 pairs. The gain after a transfer rests on 3 transfer-substation pairs, at D5 and D16. One year of data is the limit, not the gate.
  • The gate threshold of 0.7 was fixed after counting how many alarms pass. It was not tuned on any forecast score; gates of 0.6 and 0.8, planned as post hoc checks, were not run.
  • Lab conditions. The filter's residual uses the analysis proxy, the alarm tables are experiment 156's, tuned on odd months of the same stream, and the end of each alarm is known by the 6-hour rule of experiment 148.
  • The soft mask applies to the pair alarm only. Its comparison with MASK_UNION in S1 mixes the change of alarm set with the change of mechanism, so the comparison with MASK_NEW and MASK_GATED in the post hoc sweep is the cleaner one.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: The next question is whether the gated mask keeps its no-harm point estimate on a longer history. The interval half-width is about 0.075 points, so reaching +/-0.03 needs roughly six times as many months of rows, if the residual stream can be rebuilt for a longer history. A second question is why only 6 of 13 transfer-substation pairs have a pair alarm that passes the gate.

docs.title: Does the GAM with explicit PV gain from training on every year of history back to late 2019, with or without a drift term, compared with the last 24 months?
docs.text:
Adding a drift term lowered the forecast error much more than training on extra years of history did. A drift term is a slow, smooth adjustment to the level of demand, fitted to the history and held at its last value over the months being forecast. "Score" below means the quantile score, where lower is better, measured in points of each substation's effective capacity. The demand model trained on all years of history (back to late 2019) with a drift term scored 0.50 points better than the same model trained on the last 24 months without one. A drift term on the last 24 months alone gives 0.40 of that 0.50. The extra years add the remaining 0.10, and without a drift term the extra years give no gain. By the rule written before the fits, the verdict is supported. The verdict needs a qualifier: the rule compared "all years with drift" against "24 months without drift", and most of the gain belongs to the drift term.

We asked whether the demand model, with an explicit solar term, can train on every year of history instead of the last 24 months. The model is a generalised additive model (GAM) of demand minus solar output, the convex model of experiment 107. Its heating terms are split by day type, as in experiment 136 (the split is called T-all), and the photovoltaic (PV) capacity is pinned to the as-of table, which holds each Primary substation's capacity as estimated at the time of each refit. We refitted the model every quarter from July 2023 to April 2026, which gives 12 refits. Each refit was scored on the following 3 months at five Primary substations (D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16, the decision substations; the codes are anonymised labels). All arms used past weather only: ERA5 and CAMS estimates of the weather that occurred. The refit schedule and the baseline spread (each arm's own recent residuals, by hour band and calendar quarter) follow experiment 107. The quantile score is twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles, in points of each substation's effective capacity (its rated maximum output).

Figure 1 shows the drift gain at most refits and the extra-years gain mixed in sign. The figure shows C1, C3, and E2, which the Results section defines. C1 is below zero at 10 of 12 refits, with one clear exception (the July 2025 refit, +0.563 points). C3 (drift on all years) is below zero at 11 of 12. E2, which compares all years with 24 months with drift in both arms, is below zero at 8 of 12 and ranges from -0.45 to +0.13 points.

Figure 2 shows both drift arms ahead of both no-drift arms at D5, D10, D11, and D16, and behind at D14.

Figure 3 shows that the drift gain is largest at D10 and has the opposite sign at D14. With D10 left out, C1 is still -0.311 points (interval -0.531 to -0.104), with 9 of 12 refits below zero.

Figure 4 shows that every arm is too narrow in the tails. The drift arms are closer to nominal at q01, q95, and q99, and no closer than 24 months without drift at q05. At q95 the all-years drift arm has 91.6% of measured values below its forecast.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Arms and rows. Every arm is the T-all GAM with the PV capacity pinned to the as-of table, experiment 104's penalty settings, and past weather. The four arms are m24 (24 months, no drift), all (all years, no drift), all_d1 (all years, drift D1), and the exploratory m24_d1 (24 months, drift). The decision substations are scored at 12 refits for D5, D10, and D11 and 11 for D14 and D16 (243,741 scored half-hours per arm, outside the hand-filtered switching events), identical across arms. D10's two windows of level jumps with no recorded cause are removed from training and scoring.
  • Absolute scores (points; m24, all, all_d1, m24_d1). 3.177, 3.220, 2.673, and 2.774. D9 is described beside the five and scored at 3 refits only: 2.232, 2.249, 2.376, and 2.360.
  • C1, all_d1 minus m24 (headline): -0.503 points (98.33% interval from resampling calendar months -0.770 to -0.234); 10 of 12 refits below zero. Winter-quarter refits -0.772 (-1.123 to -0.403), 5 of 6 below zero; summer-quarter refits -0.233 (-0.571 to +0.092), 5 of 6. Leaving one site out gives -0.311 to -0.671, and the verdict stays supported.
  • C2, all minus m24: +0.043 (-0.092 to +0.167); 5 of 12 below zero.
  • C3, all_d1 minus all: -0.547 (-0.756 to -0.341); 11 of 12 below zero.
  • E1, m24_d1 minus m24 (exploratory): -0.402 (-0.639 to -0.154); 11 of 12 below zero.
  • E2, all_d1 minus m24_d1 (post hoc, not pre-registered): -0.101 (-0.188 to -0.019); 8 of 12 below zero; winter-quarter -0.133 (-0.269 to +0.001), summer-quarter -0.069 (-0.168 to +0.012). The drift penalty scales with the number of training rows. All years therefore smooths the drift about three times more than 24 months does, so E2 mixes the effect of history length with the effect of smoothing.
  • Tails, decision substations (coverage at q01, q05, q95, q99; nominal 1, 5, 95, and 99%). m24 5.2, 9.9, 84.9, and 93.8%; all 7.1, 13.5, 86.7, and 94.4%; all_d1 3.9, 9.9, 91.6, and 97.4%; m24_d1 4.2, 10.5, 91.0, and 96.9%. Pinball loss at q99 (m24, all, all_d1, m24_d1): 0.302, 0.288, 0.205, and 0.224.
  • Without the D10 mask, C1 is -0.455 (-0.723 to -0.191) and C3 is -0.484 (-0.703 to -0.277). The mask moves each by about 0.05, and the verdict is unchanged.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast. The median forecast minus the mean forecast is zero at every site and arm, because the baseline spread is centred on the median residual.
  • Mean-forecast error beside the quantile score. The mean absolute error contrast has the same sign as the quantile score on every contrast (points): C1 -0.780, C2 +0.026, C3 -0.806, E1 -0.618, and E2 -0.162.
  • Audit triggers. The ml-experiment skill lists seven conditions that call for an audit. Trigger 2 (a result contradicts its own prediction) fired: the prediction was C1 of -0.10 to +0.05 and C3 of -0.15 to -0.40, and the measured C1 is -0.503 and C3 -0.547. The explanation was tested and is recorded here. Experiment 107 also found a drift gain (-0.451), and masking D10's jump windows moves C3 by only 0.06, so the prediction was wrong to assume that the jumps carried the drift gain. Trigger 5 (a nested arm beats the arm that contains it) did not fire, because all years without drift against 24 months is a tie (+0.043, interval spanning zero). Triggers 1, 3, 4, and 6 did not fire, because leaving one site out keeps the verdict. Trigger 7 stays open until a later experiment depends on this result. No Opus audit was run.
  • Code review. A Sonnet code review found no lookahead. It found that the history rule counted meter readings instead of trainable rows, and the final code counts trainable rows.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The pinned capacity is hindsight at the earliest refits. The first as-of capacity table dates from 2023-08-07. The 2023-07-01 refit therefore uses a table built partly from readings after the refit date, and the four earlier cuts, which only build the baseline spread, use a growth prior. All arms share this, but the all-years arms lean on the old capacity path more.
  • Drift is a recent-level term here. Its last value is held over the scored 3 months. Part of its gain may therefore come from tracking the recent demand level, an effect that experiment 111 did not separate from the rest.
  • Past weather, not forecasts. Every arm uses ERA5 and CAMS estimates of the weather that occurred, which are not available when a live forecast is issued. The contrasts therefore rank training windows, not forecasts.
  • Not scored. The curtailment-cost saving against the manual heuristic is not scored, because the experiment ranks training windows on past weather.
  • Schedule. Quarterly refits on the whole history, frozen between refits, as in experiment 107.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Port the drift term to the GAM with ensemble weather and check D14 first.
  • Test whether all-years training still adds 0.10 points under the same drift smoothing in both windows.

docs.title: Experiment 168: issued every 6 hours, the forecast is about as good as once a day
docs.text:
Issued every 6 hours with power readings 3.5 hours old, the stage 2 forecast scores about the same over the next 24 hours as the once-a-day forecast (-0.007 points; 99% interval -0.076 to +0.037), and its largest loss, 0.073 points, falls between 09:00 and 12:00 UTC. The pre-registered test of this was confounded, so the verdict is inconclusive. Scores are twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles, in points of a substation's effective capacity. Lower is better, and every contrast is the first schedule minus the second, so a positive contrast means the first schedule scores worse.

The stage 2 forecast is arm D of experiment 155. It is the convex demand model (a generalised additive model) with a Kalman filter on recent errors (GAM-K), driven by the ensemble-mean weather forecast, with two corrections added: a winter night offset and recipe R, which subtracts 0.75 times the mean error of the last 14 days by half-hour of the day. "Daily D" below means this forecast issued once a day, and "6-hourly D" means the same forecast issued four times a day.

Production would issue a forecast every 6 hours from the newest ECMWF weather run. ECMWF (the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts) publishes one run a day, at about 09:00 UTC for the 00:00 UTC run, so the weather forecast is 12 to 30 hours old when a forecast is issued. Experiments 136 and 155 issued one forecast a day at 09:00 UTC. We re-issued each stored run at 12:00, 18:00, 00:00, and 06:00 UTC. The origin of a forecast is the time it is issued. The filter reads only power readings that ended at least 3.5 hours before the origin, because production receives telemetry about that late. The page scores one row per forecast of one substation's power for one half-hour, at the five Primary substations D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16 (anonymised labels) in the scored year, which runs from July 2025. The replicate months are the even months of the year before, used to check signs.

The pre-registered contrast, C1, is confounded, so the verdict is inconclusive. C1 is 6-hourly D minus daily D at the same run and lead, pooled over leads 0.5 to 24 hours. C1 reads +0.076 (99% interval from resampling calendar months +0.009 to +0.129). The plan fixed a threshold of +0.05 before any score was read, and by that rule +0.076 is refuted. The once-a-day origin is always 09:00 UTC, so each lead falls on one hour of the day. An independent audit (see Checks) found that, within lead bands, C1 runs from -2.09 to +1.24 points, so +0.076 is a small remainder of large effects that cancel.

H is a post hoc contrast that holds the hour of the day equal. At every half-hour request time in the scored year, H compares the newest forecast that each schedule holds: the once-a-day schedule holds the 09:00 UTC forecast, and the 6-hourly schedule holds the newest of its four. Both forecasts are scored at the same valid times (the half-hours being forecast), 0.5 to 24 hours after the request time. H is -0.007 (-0.076 to +0.037). The plan's +0.05 threshold applied to H would read supported, but H was chosen after the audit.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Method. Each stored run of experiments 136 and 155 is re-issued at origins 3, 9, 15, and 21 hours after its original 09:00 UTC origin. The weather input is the same run's ensemble mean and the GAM fit is the same, so only the filter's state and the lead change. The GAM's raw mean is experiment 136's stored mean minus its stored filter correction. Arm D's shift (offset and recipe R) is experiment 155's stored shift for the same run and valid time, and each arm's spread is refitted on its own tuning-month forecasts. Experiment 136's T-all fits, filter, and pooled filter noise are copied unchanged. No new modelling.
  • Reproduction control (passes). An origin shift of zero hours reproduces the stored means to within 1.3e-6 points and the stored quantiles to within 1.5e-5 points at every substation.
  • Rows. fold_a_daily_gap_v1, scored year, five decision substations (D9 beside them in the tables), outside the hand-filtered switching events. Leads run to 147 hours at all four origins and to 165 hours at fewer, because the stored window ends 168 hours after the original origin. The once-a-day arms have 464,363 rows and each 6-hourly arm 1,723,837. H holds 3,107,085 pairs of (request time, valid time, substation).
  • Absolute scores over leads 0.5 to 24 hours. Once-a-day arm D 2.306, once-a-day arm D with no delay 2.277, 6-hourly arm D 2.386, 6-hourly arm D with no delay 2.339, once-a-day arm A 2.364, 6-hourly arm A 2.441, BG2 2.433, manual heuristic 3.506, climatology 3.801. Over leads 0.5 to 147 hours: once-a-day arm A 2.774, arm D 2.738; 6-hourly arm A 2.797, arm D 2.763; BG2 2.771; manual heuristic 3.532; climatology 3.832. BG2, the manual heuristic, and climatology are once-a-day forecasts. These scores by lead differ in the hour of the day each arm sees, so contrasts are read from H, C3, C4, C5, and C7.
  • H (post hoc), the newest forecast held, 6-hourly D minus once-a-day D. All horizons -0.007 (-0.076 to +0.037); replicate months -0.014 (-0.096 to +0.050). By horizon: 0.5 to 3.5 hours +0.036 (-0.000 to +0.067), 3.5 to 9.5 hours +0.023 (-0.039 to +0.071), 9.5 to 24 hours -0.030 (-0.112 to +0.019). By request time: 09:00 to 12:00 UTC +0.073 (+0.049 to +0.096; replicate months +0.078), all other request times -0.016 (-0.092 to +0.033). By substation: D5 +0.039, D14 +0.019, D10 -0.026, D11 -0.033, D16 -0.029. The mean absolute error contrast is +0.003. Winter nights -0.045 (-0.141 to +0.010); cold nights (daily mean temperature below 2 degrees Celsius, 37,146 pairs) -0.099 (-0.115 to -0.034) in the scored year and +0.110 in the replicate months, which is too unstable to read. The same contrast for arm A alone is -0.009 (-0.077 to +0.035), and for the no-delay forecasts (6-hourly D with no delay minus once-a-day D with no delay) -0.027 (-0.085 to +0.023).
  • C1, 6-hourly D minus once-a-day D at the same lead. Under 24 hours +0.076 (+0.009 to +0.129; 5 of 5 substations, 10 of 12 months worse); all leads to 147 hours +0.017 (-0.021 to +0.042). Assigning rows to the month of the original run instead of the new origin moves the lower bound under 24 hours to +0.0005. Replicate months: +0.041 (-0.020 to +0.095) under 24 hours. By origin under 24 hours: 12:00 +0.028, 18:00 +0.101, 00:00 +0.091, 06:00 +0.085. The hour-band subsets of C1 (winter nights, cold nights, and holidays) are not reported. The paired row of the daily arm sits 3 to 21 hours earlier in the day than the 6-hourly row, so the subsets compare night with day.
  • C3, the 3.5-hour delay at the 6-hourly origins (no-delay forecasts subtracted). Under 24 hours +0.047 (+0.020 to +0.074); leads 0.5 to 3.5 hours +0.299 (+0.184 to +0.420); 3.5 to 9.5 hours -0.011; 9.5 to 24 hours +0.009; all leads +0.014 (+0.004 to +0.026). By origin under 24 hours: 06:00 +0.067 (+0.038 to +0.095), the others +0.034 to +0.045 with intervals that include zero. Replicate months +0.044 (+0.025 to +0.060) under 24 hours.
  • C7, the same delay at the once-a-day 09:00 origin. Under 24 hours +0.029 (-0.018 to +0.081); leads 0.5 to 3.5 hours +0.260 (+0.114 to +0.413), close to the 6-hourly origins' +0.299.
  • C4 (post hoc), 6-hourly D minus once-a-day D at the same run and valid time. Under 24 hours -0.024 (-0.110 to +0.029); all leads -0.019 (-0.058 to +0.004). C4 holds the weather run fixed, so it measures only the refresh of the filter, with a shorter lead for the same valid time. C4 is not a bound on the effect of the 6-hourly schedule. At the 18:00 origin C4 is +0.032 (-0.029 to +0.075), so a filter state 9 hours fresher scored slightly worse there. No explanation was found.
  • C5, arm D minus arm A at the 6-hourly origins. Under 24 hours -0.056 (-0.091 to -0.025); all leads -0.034 (-0.061 to -0.012); all 5 substations lower. Replicate months under 24 hours -0.042 (-0.097 to +0.014).
  • The mean absolute error gives the same signs as the quantile score. The C1 contrast on the mean forecast is +0.136 (+0.024 to +0.225) under 24 hours and +0.032 (-0.022 to +0.073) over all leads.
  • Lead check of experiment 155. The 6-hourly arm D scores +0.021 points higher at 3.5 to 9.5 hours than at 0.5 to 3.5 hours. The once-a-day arm D scores -0.522 points lower, because its first 3.5 hours of lead are 09:00 to 12:30 UTC, among the hardest hours of the day (figure 2). The difference in growth is +0.543 (+0.232 to +0.906) and fails the pre-registered limit of +0.02, but the once-a-day growth is set by the hour of the day, so the check cannot tell us about growth with lead.
  • Predictions against outcome. C1 +0.076 against +0.00 to +0.03 (a miss, high, and the contrast is confounded). C3 +0.047 against +0.01 to +0.04 under 24 hours (just outside) and +0.299 against more than +0.04 in the first 3.5 hours (inside). C4 -0.024 against -0.02 to -0.06 (inside). The 06:00 origin has the largest C3 (+0.067) but not the largest C1 (18:00, +0.101), so that prediction missed. The cold-night prediction (C1 at most +0.10) cannot be scored, because the cold-night C1 is not reported.

docs.title: Tail calibration (scored year, five decision substations)
docs.text:
Subset Arm q01 cov q05 cov q95 cov q99 cov Pinball q95 Pinball q99 12-36 h Daily D 0.024 0.069 0.945 0.982 0.648 0.201 12-36 h 6-hourly D 0.025 0.072 0.948 0.983 0.666 0.206 12-36 h BG2 0.009 0.036 0.948 0.985 0.699 0.242 Cold nights Daily D 0.041 0.089 0.838 0.946 0.933 0.316 Cold nights 6-hourly D 0.045 0.094 0.841 0.946 0.929 0.303 Cold nights BG2 0.019 0.033 0.761 0.866 1.347 0.788
  • The tails match the daily forecast's. The 6-hourly q95 and q99 coverage at 12 to 36 hours is within 0.3 percentage points of the daily forecast's, and the cold-night q95 coverage stays near 84%, as in experiment 155. The 12 to 36 hour rows hold 66,838 daily and 267,126 6-hourly forecasts.
  • Curtailment cost. The node-level curtailment metric and the saving against the manual heuristic need node forecasts, which this experiment does not produce, so neither is reported.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, per substation. 0.00 points at every substation for both arms at 12 to 36 hours, because the spread is centred on the mean.
  • Audit triggers. The ml-experiment skill lists seven conditions that call for an audit. Two held. First, a result contradicts its own prediction: C1 (+0.076) against the predicted +0.00 to +0.03. The hour of the day explains it, as C4, the no-delay contrast, and C7 show, and the audit confirmed it. Second, a later design depends on the headline: the GAM-K serving design does. The other five did not hold: the reproduction control passed, the mean-error and quantile-score contrasts agree in sign, every substation's C1 is positive so leaving one out keeps the sign, no nested arm beat the arm containing it except at one origin (C4 at 18:00, +0.032, a later origin scoring worse than an earlier one, for which no explanation was found), and we found no sister experiment on these rows to compare interval widths with (searched ml-experiments/).
  • Audit. A fresh Opus agent re-derived every printed number from the stored predictions and found no leakage. It found that C1 is confounded with the hour of the day, so the verdict is inconclusive, and it proposed H. Its report is in the private data/ml-experiments/briefs/ folder. It also found that the hour-band subsets of C1 compare night with day, so they are not reported, and that C1's lower bound moves to +0.0005 when rows take the month of the original run.
  • Order of work. The planning commit precedes the scoring script. The build script had run once, and its reproduction control had been read, before the planning commit. No score had been read.

docs.title: Caveats and what to try next
docs.text:
• The pre-registered contrast cannot be repaired from this folder's files. Holding the hour of the day equal at the same lead needs ensemble runs at 06:00, 12:00, and 18:00 UTC, so H is the nearest estimate that this folder's files allow, and the plan did not name it.
  • Leads beyond 147 hours have fewer origins. The stored window ends 168 hours after the original origin, so leads from 147 to 165 hours are not in the all-lead figures.
  • The monthly GAM refit is not re-timed. A 00:00 or 06:00 origin on the first of a month uses the previous month's weights, where production would have used the new ones.
  • Arm D's shift is the stored shift. The offset and recipe R are those fitted on the once-a-day forecasts' errors, not on the 6-hourly forecasts' errors.
  • Next. Measure how soon after a half-hour ends production can read its power telemetry, and score one extra issue between 09:00 and 12:00 UTC. These arms hold only delays of 0 and 3.5 hours, so the effect of a delay between them is not measured.

docs.title: Experiment 169: the combined calibration fixes, and whether the ensemble spread sets the width
docs.text:
The ensemble spread does not predict how wide the forecast's errors are once the cold-day widening is in place; widening the q95 and q99 offsets by 4% and 10% gives the same cold-night coverage. A quantile is a level of the forecast's error distribution: the q95 is the forecast value that the demand reading should fall at or under on 95% of rows. Its offset is the q95 minus the mean forecast. Coverage is the share of rows on which the reading falls at or under the quantile. A cold night is a winter night (November to March, evening or night hours) whose ERA5 day-mean temperature (the ECMWF reanalysis, an estimate of past weather) is below 2 °C. We asked two questions about the demand forecast that experiment 155 selected as its best. First, do the two calibration fixes found since then work together? They are the smooth spread table of experiment 160 (a table of quantile offsets, read by interpolation along the lead) and the one-sided widening of the upper offsets on forecast-cold days of experiment 164 (fix O). Second, does the spread of the 51-member ensemble weather forecast (how much the members disagree about temperature and about downward shortwave radiation) predict how large the forecast's errors are? We fitted a quantile regression model on the tuning months (the months used to fit every multiplier). We scored it on the scored year (2025-07-02 to 2026-06-29) and on the replicate months (other months of the earlier year), as experiment 164 did. The mean forecast is unchanged. The two fixes combine without loss: the combined forecast reproduces experiment 164's cold-night q95 coverage of 0.896. The spread model lifts that coverage to 0.907, which meets the pre-registered rule in the scored year. In the replicate months the coverage is 0.918. The upper end of the 95% interval of the all-row score change there is +0.0145, which exceeds the allowed +0.0100, so the rule is not met in the replicate months. A control with the spread terms switched off reaches 0.906, so the lift comes from a widening that does not use the spread. Scores are in points of effective capacity (percentage points of each substation's rated demand), and lower is better.

  • Arms. I: experiment 160's interpolated spread table. A: I plus experiment 164's fix O (multipliers 1.65, 1.36, 1.26, and 1.16 on q75, q90, q95, and q99 on forecast-cold days). AT: A plus the q01, q05, and q10 multipliers of experiment 164's fix T. SP: A with each offset from the mean multiplied by c + sum a_k max(z1 - k1_k, 0) + sum b_k max(z2 - k2_k, 0) for the levels 0.01, 0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.75, 0.90, 0.95, and 0.99. Here z1 is the standard deviation across members of the 24-hour mean temperature, z2 the same for shortwave radiation (each divided by its 90th tuning-month percentile), the knots are their 25th, 50th, 75th, and 90th tuning-month percentiles, and a and b are non-negative. SP0 (post hoc control): SP with a and b set to zero, so only the fitted intercept c remains. The pinball loss is linear in the coefficients, so each level is a linear programme (HiGHS) on 150,000 tuning rows.
  • Row set and schedule. fold_a_daily_gap_v1, the five decision substations D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16 (D9 beside), leads 0.5 to 168 hours, rows outside the hand-filtered switching events. The mean forecasts are experiment 155's stored monthly refits, so no contrast depends on the retraining schedule. Scored year: 2025-07-02 to 2026-06-29, 464,228 rows at the five substations. The ensemble spreads come from experiment 111's stored 51-member forecasts, which exist at forecast time. The store holds temperature and shortwave radiation, not wind, so the wind spread and the spread of the GAM-K forecast (the additive-model forecast of experiment 111) across members were not tested.
  • Fitted coefficients. Every fitted intercept c lies between 0.84 and 1.10: 0.99 at q01, 0.94 at q05, 0.91 at q10, 0.84 at q25, 0.92 at q75, 1.00 at q90, 1.04 at q95, and 1.10 at q99. The temperature-spread terms are zero except above the 90th percentile of the spread, where the coefficient is 0.49 (q75), 0.18 (q90), and 0.10 (q95). The shortwave terms are non-zero at every level, at most 0.18 per knot for the lower levels and 0.02 to 0.88 for the upper ones (figure 4).
  • Contrasts. C1: A minus I (the assembly). C2: SP minus A (the pre-registered test of the spread). C3: SP minus I (descriptive). C4: AT minus A. C5: SP minus SP0 (the spread terms alone). C6: SP0 minus A (the intercept alone). Each is a paired difference in quantile score.
  • Assembly (C1, A minus I), scored year. All rows -0.0010 (95% interval -0.0032 to +0.0008); cold nights -0.095 (-0.143 to -0.048); cold-night q95 coverage +0.050 (+0.031 to +0.070). Replicate months: all rows +0.0002 (-0.0029 to +0.0036), cold-night q95 coverage 0.913.
  • Spread model (C2, SP minus A), scored year. All rows +0.0014 (-0.0056 to +0.0077); cold nights -0.006 (-0.040 to +0.021); cold-night q95 coverage +0.010. By lead: under 24 hours -0.0011, 24 to 72 hours +0.0006, 72 to 168 hours +0.0024 (-0.0062 to +0.0103). Replicate months: all rows +0.0062 (-0.0025 to +0.0145), cold-night q95 coverage 0.918.
  • Control (C5, SP minus SP0, and C6, SP0 minus A). C5, scored year: all rows +0.0007 (-0.0013 to +0.0026); cold nights -0.001 (-0.002 to 0.000); cold-night q95 coverage +0.000. C6: all rows +0.0006 (-0.0067 to +0.0070); cold-night q95 coverage +0.010. Replicate months: C5 all rows +0.0037 (+0.0005 to +0.0075), C6 +0.0026 (-0.0056 to +0.0081).
  • Lower tail (C4, AT minus A). All rows +0.0003 (-0.0038 to +0.0045); cold nights +0.018 (-0.001 to +0.054). Fix T's lower multipliers raise the cold-night q05 coverage from 0.090 to 0.107, away from 0.05.
  • Absolute scores, scored year, all rows. I 2.7529, A 2.7519, AT 2.7522, SP 2.7533, SP0 2.7526, BG2 (the best-guess forecast of experiment 87) 2.7804, manual heuristic 3.4968, climatology 3.8038. Replicate months: I 2.6819, A 2.6821, AT 2.6807, SP 2.6883, SP0 2.6846.
  • Tail calibration, scored year, cold nights (coverage / pinball loss). I: q01 0.045 / 0.391, q05 0.090 / 0.950, q95 0.846 / 0.934, q99 0.933 / 0.328. A: 0.045 / 0.391, 0.090 / 0.950, 0.896 / 0.819, 0.959 / 0.282. SP: 0.046 / 0.394, 0.098 / 0.965, 0.907 / 0.798, 0.970 / 0.247. BG2's q95 coverage is 0.756.
  • Tail calibration, scored year, all rows (coverage / pinball loss). A: q01 0.022 / 0.216, q05 0.065 / 0.713, q95 0.948 / 0.745, q99 0.982 / 0.232. SP: 0.022 / 0.216, 0.068 / 0.714, 0.954 / 0.748, 0.987 / 0.228. SP0: q05 0.075, q95 0.952. On all rows, C2's q99 loss changes by -0.0042 (-0.0105 to +0.0016) and its q95 loss by +0.0031 (-0.0011 to +0.0073).
  • By lead day (q95 coverage, all rows). A: 0.946, 0.948, 0.951, 0.951, 0.952, 0.946, 0.943 for lead days 0 to 6. SP: 0.951, 0.953, 0.955, 0.956, 0.957, 0.952, 0.951. SP changes the median q05 to q95 width by -0.15 to +0.38 points depending on the lead day (wider on 5 of 7 days).
  • By hour band (q95 coverage, all rows). A: 0.954, 0.951, 0.934, 0.951 for the four bands in order (night, morning, midday, evening as studies.dp_calendar orders them); SP: 0.959, 0.956, 0.941, 0.956.
  • Bank holidays and Christmas, scored year. Bank holidays (9,812 rows): q95 coverage 0.934 (A) and 0.943 (SP); C2 -0.0044 (-0.0246 to +0.0137). Christmas, 24 December to 1 January (8,641 rows): 0.934 and 0.940; C2 +0.0052 (-0.0172 to +0.0055). The q05 coverage on Christmas rises from 0.075 to 0.089 under SP, so the lower tail is thinner there.
  • Curtailment-cost proxy (the node-only rule of studies.node_curtailment on each substation's own demand, scaled limit 0.9 times the maximum before the scored year, GBP 2,000 per MWh, leads 12 to 36 hours). Avoidable cost against the perfect forecast, summed over the five substations: I GBP 1.321 million, A 1.272 million, SP 1.310 million, SP0 1.309 million, BG2 1.881 million, manual heuristic 3.332 million. The 95% month-resampled intervals overlap (A 0.11 to 3.14 million), so the proxy cannot rank the arms. A Primary substation has no published export limit here and a demand series is treated as the flow that can breach, so the figures show the arithmetic and are not a curtailment forecast.
  • What remains miscalibrated. (1) Cold nights: SP's q95 coverage is 0.907 against 0.95 nominal, and its lower tail is thin (q05 coverage 0.098 against 0.05, q01 0.046 against 0.01). (2) The lower tail overall: q05 coverage is 0.065 to 0.075 on all rows in every arm. (3) The coldest forecasts are biased low (experiment 164 found a mean residual of +3.1 points at 0 °C or below), which no scaling of the offsets removes. (4) Economy 7 steps and switching rows were not scored separately here. (5) Christmas lower-tail coverage (0.075 to 0.089).
  • Caveats. The scored year's cold-night figure rests on 10 cold days; the day-block 95% interval of SP's coverage is 0.858 to 0.956 and contains 0.90 (the probability of at least 0.90 is 0.61, against 0.45 for A). Leaving out one substation moves SP's cold-night q95 coverage to 0.901 (D5), 0.922 (D10), 0.924 (D11), 0.886 (D14), or 0.903 (D16), so the pass in the scored year depends on D14. In the replicate months SP's all-row upper bound (+0.0145) is over the +0.010 limit, and leaving D10 out gives 0.896. The tuning and replicate months share cold days with each other. The spread model has no quarter or hour-band term, so the prediction that the shortwave coefficients are larger in summer was not tested. SP0 is a post hoc arm, so its pass on both periods is a suggestion, not a pre-registered result. The spread terms do change some quantile scores: C5 is -0.0028 (-0.0043 to -0.0014) at leads under 24 hours in the scored year, and +0.0037 (+0.0005 to +0.0075) over all rows in the replicate months, so they help slightly at short leads and hurt at long leads out of sample.
  • What to try next. (1) A bias correction of the mean forecast on days the ensemble forecasts at 0 °C or below. (2) Fit and score the widening over at least two winters. (3) A spread model with hour-band and quarter terms if a wind spread becomes available.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, per site, at 12 to 36 hours. Exactly 0.000 for every arm at every substation: the spread table has median zero, and no arm scales the q50 offset.
  • Mean-forecast error beside each quantile-score contrast. The mean absolute error of the mean forecast is identical across all arms (contrast 0.0000), because the mean is unchanged.
  • Reproduction control. Arm I rescored from experiment 164's stored forecasts scores 2.75291, a gap of 7e-6 from experiment 160's printed 2.7529. Arm A scores 2.75191, a gap of 1e-5 from experiment 164's printed 2.7519. Both are inside the 0.001 cap.
  • Prediction check. Cold-night coverage rose by 0.010 (predicted 0.00 to 0.03) and the all-row score by +0.0014 (predicted -0.01 to +0.005): both inside the ranges. The prediction about shortwave against temperature coefficients by quarter could not be tested.
  • Audit. A fresh Opus audit re-derived the headline coverages (A 0.8962, SP 0.9066, SP0 0.9064) and the contrasts from the stored forecasts with its own code, and agreed. Its findings and triage: (F1) the pass is two rows deep: SP beats A by 56 cold-night rows and the refuted line is 54, and refitting on a different 150,000-row sample gave +0.0085 (refuted), while a fit on all 361,676 tuning rows gave +0.0108 (partly supported); the verdict stays partly supported, as pre-registered with the 150,000-row cap, and the margin is recorded here. (F2) SP0's intercepts were fitted together with the spread terms, so a true intercept-only refit is wider (1.03 at q75, 1.06 at q90 and q95, 1.11 at q99), reaches 0.910 (scored year) and 0.921 (replicate months) cold- night q95 coverage, and raises the all-row score by +0.0021 and +0.0066 against A (worse); the conclusion that the widening, not the spread, produces the lift stands, and the advice quotes the refit values. (F3) the month-resampled intervals on cold-night coverage rested on three months and are removed. No leakage, no effect of sorting the quantiles (7 of 484,113 rows), and the leave- one-out figures were confirmed. The audit report is private (data/ml- experiments/briefs/e169_audit_report.md). The audit trigger that fired is the one for a verdict that flips when one site is left out; the other six triggers of the ml-experiment skill did not fire.

docs.title: Does a drift term still lower the score of the stage 2 assembly (night offset and recipe R), and how do Christmas, Easter, and bank holidays score?
docs.text:
The Kalman filter on recent errors already removes the slow demand-level error that a drift term fixes, so the drift term does not improve the stage 2 assembly. In experiment 167 the drift term improved the quantile score by 0.40 points. Here it worsened the score by 0.03 points. Lower scores are better throughout. The quantile score is twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles, in points of a substation's effective capacity (its rated maximum output), over forecasts 0.5 to 168 hours ahead at five Primary substations (D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16, anonymised labels) in the year from July 2025 to June 2026 (the scored year).

The drift term is a slowly varying demand level added to the demand model, and the Kalman filter updates a demand level from each recent forecast error. Arm D of experiment 155 is the demand model with the filter, a winter night offset, and recipe R (the mean error of the last 14 days by half-hour, subtracted at 0.75 times its size). It scored 2.756. Arm D with a drift term, trained on the last 24 months, scored 2.787 (C1, +0.031; 99% interval from resampling calendar months +0.008 to +0.059). Arm D with a drift term trained on all years back to late 2019 scored 2.767 (C3, +0.011; -0.027 to +0.039). The plan asked for a gain of at least 0.20 points, so the verdict is refuted. Training on all years scored 0.020 lower than 24 months (C2; -0.066 to +0.014). That gain is under the plan's 0.05 threshold, and its interval includes zero.

Without the Kalman filter, the drift term improves the score by 0.19 points (not significant), so the filter appears to remove the level error that the drift term would fix. The stage 1 forecast (before the offset and recipe R) improved by 0.19 points with a drift term on 24 months and no filter (-0.482 to +0.069), the same sign as in experiment 167. Adding the filter improved the no-drift forecast by 0.41 points (-0.662 to -0.178). With the filter, the drift term worsened the forecast by 0.03 points (figure 3). A review by a second Claude model (Opus) proposed a mechanism, and its diagnostics fit it: at each monthly refit, the new drift fit's held level absorbs the same recent error that the filter's carried-over level already holds, so the first weeks after the refit would correct the same error twice. The refit's jump in demand level is 2.39 points root mean square with drift and 1.16 without. The jump correlates +0.73 with the filter's level. The loss sits in days 1 to 20 after each refit. Re-basing the filter at each refit, without lookahead, cuts the loss from +0.028 to +0.011 (-0.002 to +0.026), and the drift term still does not win. The code that makes the drift fits is checked by a reproduction control: the same code with no drift reproduces experiment 136's stage 1 forecast exactly.

Christmas is only 1.13 times as hard to forecast as an ordinary weekday, and recipe R improves the score on those days by 0.04 points. The experiment also scored 24 December to 2 January, Easter, and the bank holidays. The quantile score on 24 December to 2 January was 1.13 times the score on ordinary weekdays at the same half-hours of the day (arm D; 1.10 in 2024-25 and 1.19 in 2025-26). The plan predicted at least 1.5 times, and predicted that recipe R would worsen the score on those days. Both predictions failed.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Arms and schedule. A row below is one forecast of one substation for one half-hour at one lead time, and D+1 means forecasts for the next calendar day. Every stage 1 arm is experiment 136's T-all demand model (heating split by day type and half of the hour band, lighting split by day type) with the pinned solar capacity, driven by the ensemble-mean weather, with the filter noise POOL (experiment 133's single shared filter setting) and monthly refits. The fit sets are no drift on 24 months (a2_repro), drift D1 on 24 months (m24_d1), and drift D1 on all years (all_d1), with experiment 104's tuned penalties. Each stage 1 arm gets experiment 155's four stage 2 variants: none (_a), offset (_b), recipe R (_c), and offset then R (_d). Prefixes are r (no drift), s24 (drift, 24 months), and sall (drift, all years); a155, c155, and d155 are experiment 155's stored arms.
  • Rows. fold_a_daily_gap_v1, scored year 2025-07-02 to 2026-06-29, five decision substations, outside the hand-filtered switching events; 561,172 rows shared by every arm and BG2 in the scored year (464,363 at leads up to 168 hours for the stage 1 diagnostic, which has no BG2). The replicate year (even months of 2024-25) gives the sign check.
  • Absolute scores, all leads (points). A 2.791, C 2.754, D 2.756, BG2 2.780. Drift on 24 months: A 2.819, offset 2.802, R 2.786, both 2.787. Drift on all years: A 2.818, offset 2.791, R 2.767, both 2.767. Day D+1: D 2.432, drift on 24 months 2.445, drift on all years 2.435.
  • C1, D plus drift (24 months) minus D (headline): +0.031 (+0.008 to +0.059); 1 of 5 substations and 2 of 12 months lower. Replicate year +0.063 (-0.017 to +0.201). Mean-forecast absolute error +0.066.
  • C2, drift on all years minus 24 months: -0.020 (-0.066 to +0.014); 4 of 5 substations and 6 of 12 months lower. Replicate year +0.002 (-0.027 to +0.035).
  • C3, drift on all years minus D: +0.011 (-0.027 to +0.039).
  • Drop-one table. Dropping the drift term improves the score by 0.031 (C1). Dropping the offset improves it by 0.001 on 24 months (C4, +0.001; -0.005 to +0.007) and changes it by 0.000 on all years (C6). Dropping recipe R worsens it by 0.016 on 24 months (C5, -0.016 for the full assembly minus the assembly without R; -0.031 to -0.003) and by 0.025 on all years (C7, -0.025; -0.040 to -0.012). Without drift, R lowered the score by 0.037 in experiment 155.
  • Cold nights (day mean below 2 C, 5,395 rows). D 3.342, drift on 24 months 3.153, drift on all years 3.080. The contrast C1 on those rows is -0.189 (-0.378 to +0.150). On winter nights as a whole C1 is +0.048 (+0.013 to +0.100), and D+1 over all rows +0.013 (-0.005 to +0.035). The q95 coverage on cold nights is 83.7% for D, 86.2% for drift on 24 months, and 85.2% for drift on all years.
  • Christmas rows of the calendar (Christmas Day, Boxing Day, and the Christmas run; 7,775 rows, one Christmas). D 3.176, drift on 24 months 3.215, drift on all years 2.900, BG2 2.309. BG2 beat arm D by 0.87 points on those rows, from one Christmas and 12 runs, as in experiment 155; it is not a ranking.
  • Tails, all leads (coverage at q01, q05, q95, q99; nominal 1, 5, 95, and 99%). D 2.4, 7.0, 94.7, and 98.3%; drift on 24 months 2.5, 7.2, 94.8, and 98.2%; drift on all years 2.4, 7.3, 94.8, and 98.2%. Pinball loss at q99: 0.232, 0.234, and 0.232.
  • Stage 1 with and without the filter (all leads). No drift 3.202 without and 2.791 with the filter; drift on 24 months 3.012 and 2.819; drift on all years 2.995 and 2.818. Drift minus no drift without the filter: -0.190 (-0.482 to +0.069) on 24 months and -0.207 (-0.498 to +0.075) on all years; with the filter: +0.028 (+0.008 to +0.053) and +0.027 (-0.009 to +0.056).

docs.title: Christmas, Easter, and bank holidays score 1.04 to 1.13 times an ordinary weekday
docs.text:
The score on each event is divided by the score on ordinary days at the same local half-hours of the day. Christmas is 24 December to 2 January; Easter is Good Friday to Easter Monday; the bank holidays are May Day, the Spring and Late Summer Bank Holidays, and one-off holidays. The tuning months fit the spread, so only the replicate year and the scored year are scored. The ratios are for leads 0.5 to 168 hours; printed_report.txt has the D+1 and Sunday-reference rows.

Event (dates, rows) Ratio to weekdays, arm D Ratio, drift on 24 months with offset and R Ratio to Sundays, arm D 24 December to 2 January (20 dates, 25,673 rows) 1.128 1.115 1.214 Easter (8 dates, 12,140 rows) 1.045 1.044 1.125 Other bank holidays (5 dates, 6,340 rows) 1.057 1.037 1.138
  • Christmas by year. Arm D scored 1.099 times a weekday in 2024-25 and 1.194 in 2025-26; arm A (no corrections, no drift) scored 1.089 and 1.194. The 2024-25 rows hold December origins only, so 1 January and 2 January are forecast at long leads there.
  • Recipe R on Christmas. R lowered the quantile score by 0.041 points without drift (5 of 20 dates worse, 1 of 5 substations worse) and by 0.040 with drift (3 of 20 dates, 2 of 5 substations). The mean-forecast absolute error moved by -0.093 and -0.083 (an improvement).
  • Recipe R on Easter and the other bank holidays. R raised the score by 0.016 and 0.023 points without drift and by 0.026 and 0.033 with drift. The 14-day profile that R subtracts averages ordinary days, which are further from a holiday than from Christmas.
  • The drift term on Christmas. Drift changed the Christmas score by +0.023 (24 months, no R); the sign differs by Christmas (+0.081 in 2024-25, -0.078 in 2025-26).
  • Holiday-aware filter update. Experiment 143 found that leaving holiday readings out of the filter's update was not supported, so this experiment did not add it as an arm.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast. Zero at every substation and arm by construction, because each spread table is centred on the median residual.
  • Mean-forecast error beside the quantile score. The mean-forecast absolute error contrast has the same sign as the quantile-score contrast for C1 (+0.066), C2 (-0.037), C4 (0.000), and C5 (-0.047).
  • Controls. The reproduction control passed: a2_repro reproduces experiment 136's stored A2 mean and quantiles exactly (largest difference 0), and the stage 2 code run on it gives arm D's 2.756 (R1 and R2 are 0.000).
  • Audit triggers. Trigger 2 (a result contradicts its prediction and an earlier experiment) fired: C1 was predicted at -0.20 or lower and is +0.031, against experiment 167's -0.40. The filter diagnostic above is the tested explanation. Trigger 5 (a nested arm beats the arm that contains it) fired, because the arm with a drift term scores worse than the arm without. A fresh audit by Opus ran (private report data/ml-experiments/briefs/e170_audit_report.md) and found no leakage and no defect in the drift fit, the filter's residual stream, or the scoring, and did not change the verdict's decision. Triage: (1) the audit found that a t-interval over the 12 months gives C1 as -0.002 to +0.063, so the label refuted could read as inconclusive; the pre-registered month bootstrap stands, and the decision to drop the drift term holds either way, because supported needed -0.20 or lower. (2) The refit double-count is in the opening section. (3) Shrinking the last knot (+0.016), holding the second-to-last (+0.021), or holding the mean of the last three (+0.021) leaves C1 positive. (4) The no-filter gain rests on D5 (-0.65) and D16 (-0.38), and D10 goes the other way (+0.16), so it does not replicate experiment 167's size. (5) The filter's POOL settings were tuned without a drift term (a limitation, not re-run). Triggers 1, 3, 4, and 6 did not fire: leaving one site out keeps C1 positive (+0.021 to +0.038), and the contrasts on the mean-forecast error agree in sign.
  • Lead check. The growth in score from 0.5 to 3.5 hours to 3.5 to 9.5 hours, minus arm A's, has a 99% upper bound of +0.041 for drift on 24 months and +0.033 for arm D; neither passes the 0.02 bound, as in experiment 155.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Past drift fits are monthly, and the last drift knot is held. Experiment 167 refitted every 3 months and held the last knot for 3 months. This experiment refits every month and holds it for 1 month, so the held level is more recent but also noisier.
  • D10's unlabelled jumps stay in training. Experiment 167 removed two windows of unlabelled level jumps at D10 (November to December 2024 and 2025). Experiment 136's fits, which arm D copies, left them in, so this experiment does too. The scored rows leave out the hand-filtered switching events.
  • Two Christmases. The Christmas ratios rest on 20 dates, of which the 2024-25 Christmas holds only December origins. They describe these two years and carry no interval.
  • Not scored. The curtailment-cost saving against the manual heuristic is not scored, because no drift arm beat arm D.
  • The filter's noise settings (POOL) were tuned without a drift term. The drift arms' refit jumps are twice as large, so the settings are not neutral between the arms; the audit's re-basing removes most of the effect a retune could target.
  • Schedule. Monthly refits on a 24-month window or on all years, as in experiments 136 and 155; the contrast could differ under weekly refits, which the filter might not absorb as fully.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Keep the stage 2 assembly of experiment 155 (arm C or D) as the best guess. Recipe R is the part that improves the score.
  • If a drift term is tried again on a filtered forecast, re-base the filter's level at each refit first; the audit found no gain over no drift even then (+0.011).
  • If a drift term is wanted for cold nights, test it as a winter-night-only term. Its gain on nights with a day mean below 2 C (-0.19 points) is not significant, rests on 3 months, and did not appear in the replicate year on 24 months (D 2.182, drift 2.190), so it is a lead and not a result.

docs.title: Does the gated mask on recent power do no harm on ordinary days, once 27 months of rows are pooled?
docs.text:
The gated mask scores 0.030 points of effective capacity worse than no mask on 27 months of rows outside logged transfers (95% interval -0.011 to +0.074). The interval includes zero and is wider than the limit of +/-0.03 that we set in advance. The verdict is therefore inconclusive: harm below 0.03 is neither shown nor excluded. Most of the difference comes from one substation, D10.

Background: what the mask is. Our forecast corrects itself using recent power. A "mask" sets recent power aside while a switching alarm is active. A logged transfer is a movement of load between two substations recorded in NGED's switching log. Experiment 166 masked recent power only while a "gated alarm" was active. A gated alarm is a pair alarm (a step at one substation matched by an opposite step at a neighbouring metered substation, from experiment 156) with a balance score of 0.7 or more. The balance score measures how nearly the two steps cancel, and 1 means exactly. Experiment 166 found a gain of 7.35 points in the 72 hours after a logged transfer ends. It could not show that the mask does no harm on other rows, because 12 months of rows gave an interval of -0.068 to +0.081. A score in points of effective capacity is the score in megawatts divided by the substation's effective capacity (as in experiment 166), times 100. Primary substations are the substations that step power down onto the local distribution network.

The first year's near-zero harm (+0.009) is reproduced here (+0.011), but the earlier 15 months give +0.045. We scored every cached forecast run of the same six Primary substations, 27 months instead of 12, on rows outside logged transfers. A row is one forecast for one half-hour from one forecast origin. The forecast, called the stack here, is a frozen generalised additive model with a Kalman filter (Kalman, 1960). The filter corrects each forecast using its recent errors, as in experiment 163. Nothing is refitted; only the rows change. Scores are twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles, in points of effective capacity; lower is better. The gain of 7.35 points is taken from experiment 166 (7 logged transfers, 72 hours after each ends). It is not pooled with the rows outside logged transfers.

docs.title: Design and results
docs.text:
• Decision rule. G1: the pooled contrast has a 95% interval inside -0.03 to +0.03. G2: the November to March contrast has an interval inside -0.05 to +0.05. The verdict is supported when both hold, partly supported when only G1 holds, refuted when the pooled point estimate is above +0.03, and inconclusive otherwise. The limit of 0.03 is there because the mask adds alarm tables to the serving path, which is worth doing only if ordinary rows do not get worse.
  • Arms. K0 (no mask), MASK_GATED (readings set missing from the moment a gated alarm is known until the end rule of experiment 148 fires), and for reference MASK_NEW (every pair alarm) and MASK_UNION (pair alarm or refit-offset neighbour-count alarm, as in experiment 165). The stack is frozen. The K0 forecast spread of experiment 115 is shared, so arms differ only in where the forecast distribution sits.
  • Rows. 1,579,711 rows with a reading, from 811 cached forecast runs (one per day) at D5, D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16 (anonymised substation labels), forecast origins 2024-04-10 to 2026-06-29. Each row's valid time lies outside every logged transfer from onset to 72 hours after its end. Each substation has more than 12 months of past forecast errors before its first run, because the power panel starts in 2022-01. The cached forecasts start in 2024-04, so none earlier were available to score.
  • Absolute scores, pooled. K0 2.718, MASK_GATED 2.748, MASK_NEW 2.773, MASK_UNION 2.915.
  • G1 and G2. Pooled (27 months): MASK_GATED minus K0 +0.030 (-0.011 to +0.074), half-width 0.042 against the limit 0.03. November to March (10 months, 579,096 rows): +0.036 (-0.060 to +0.135), half-width 0.098 against the limit 0.05. April to October (17 months): +0.026 (+0.002 to +0.060).
  • Reference arms, pooled. MASK_NEW minus K0 +0.055 (+0.009 to +0.105). MASK_UNION minus K0 +0.197 (+0.078 to +0.342). Masking on more alarms, including the ones with no balanced opposite step, raises the error further.
  • Post hoc, labelled: the two periods. Valid times from July 2025, the 12 months of experiment 166's scored year (here on every row of those valid times, where experiment 166 used the forecasts shared with best guess 2): +0.011 (-0.066 to +0.085). Valid times before July 2025: +0.045 (-0.000 to +0.102). The two intervals overlap almost completely.
  • Post hoc, labelled: by substation. Alone: D5 -0.027 (-0.099 to +0.009), D9 0.000 (no gated alarm from 2024-04-10 onwards), D10 +0.170 (+0.011 to +0.383), D11 +0.010 (+0.001 to +0.024), D14 +0.001 (-0.004 to +0.007), D16 +0.023 (-0.105 to +0.167). Leaving out D10: +0.002 (-0.036 to +0.035). Leaving out any other substation leaves the estimate between +0.031 and +0.040.
  • Post hoc, labelled: rows with a gated alarm active at the forecast origin. 122,598 rows (7.8%): +0.386 (-0.164 to +0.893). The other 1,457,113 rows: 0.000 (-0.001 to +0.001), rounded from a value below 0.0005 in size. A mask changes the forecast only while a gated alarm is active or its filter state is recovering, so the 7.8% carry the whole difference.
  • Gated alarms and masked half-hours. The table counts gated alarms known from 2024-04-10 (2024 is April to December and 2026 is January to June) and the half-hours between each alarm being known and its end being known.
Substation 2024 gated alarms / masked half-hours 2025 gated alarms / masked half-hours 2026 gated alarms / masked half-hours D5 1 / 186 7 / 3,639 3 / 979 D9 0 / 0 0 / 0 0 / 0 D10 4 / 3,528 7 / 1,982 4 / 819 D11 4 / 928 5 / 1,711 6 / 1,133 D14 4 / 711 10 / 2,093 3 / 598 D16 0 / 0 4 / 1,765 3 / 979
  • Share of masked half-hours outside every logged transfer. Gated alarms: 65 alarms, 21,051 masked half-hours, 17,028 outside (80.9%). Every pair alarm: 146 alarms, 39,789 half-hours, 86.2% outside. Either alarm: 178 alarms, 54,660 half-hours, 89.2% outside. Most masked half-hours therefore fall outside logged transfers, though the rows scored here are defined by valid time and the half-hours by the alarm's span, so the two sets overlap without matching.
  • Prediction against outcome. The interval was expected to be about +/-0.05 wide, not inside +/-0.03, so the prediction that it would fall inside +/-0.03 failed on its own terms. The observed half-width is 0.042. The winter half-width is 0.098 against a limit of 0.05; the winter subset has 10 months against 27 pooled. The point estimate stayed below +0.03 (0.0297).

docs.title: Checks that did not change the verdict
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, per substation (identical for every arm). D5 -0.146, D9 -0.019, D10 -0.058, D11 -0.030, D14 +0.037, D16 +0.017 points.
  • Error of the mean forecast beside the quantile contrast. Mean absolute error of the mean forecast, MASK_GATED minus K0: +0.064 (-0.003 to +0.140), in the same direction as the quantile score.
  • Audit triggers (the seven conditions in the experiment procedure that call for an independent audit). None fired. The wide interval was predicted. Leaving out D10 moves the estimate from +0.030 to +0.002, but the estimate stays positive and the verdict stays inconclusive. The half-width of 0.042 is 0.57 of experiment 166's 0.075, not under half. No audit was run.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The 27-month limit comes from the data, not the method. A half-width of 0.03 would need about 54 months at this variance, if the true harm is well below 0.03.
  • With 27 months, 10 of them in winter, the resampled interval is itself uncertain.
  • Pair alarms appear at both ends of one transfer. D5 and D16 share identical 2026 gated alarms, so the rows of neighbouring substations are not independent.
  • Three conditions favour the mask in this test. The residual uses the analysis proxy (a weather estimate for the recent past), the alarm tables of experiment 156 were tuned on odd months of the same stream, and each alarm's end is known by the end rule of experiments 147 and 148, which uses a 6-hour wait. The filter and spread settings were tuned on the odd months of 2024-07 to 2025-06, which are inside the rows scored here.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: The next question is why D10's 15 gated alarms raise the error: whether they follow real switching that no log records, or false alarms. Leaving D10 out gives +0.002. More than 7 logged transfers are needed to measure the gain before the mask can be added to production.

docs.title: Is the forecast's error spread over ordinary days, or does a small share of labelled days carry most of it?
docs.text:
A small number of bad days carries a large share of the forecast's error. We asked whether the forecast's error is spread over ordinary days or sits on a few days that the project already knows how to label. We took the forecasts of experiment 155's arm D (a convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors, plus a winter night offset and a 14-day mean-error correction) for five substations, D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16, over 2025-07-03 to 2026-06-30. D9 is scored beside them and sits in no headline number. For each substation we scored every day, subtracted the substation's median day, and ranked the days by this excess loss. The worst 5% of substation-days (72 of 1,392) carry 41.7% of the total excess loss. Of those 72 days, 48.6% overlap a switching event, a holiday, a cold snap, a flagged reading, or an Economy 7 step (the night-time step in demand from off-peak storage heating), against 14.5% of all days. The main answer is that the error is concentrated enough to target, and that about half of the worst days have no label yet.

The pre-registered verdict is inconclusive. The share clears its 30% threshold and the labelled fraction misses its 50% threshold by 1.4 percentage points, which would give partly supported. The decision rule caps the verdict at inconclusive when the injected known-answer control recovers fewer than 90% of injected days, and it recovered 89.2%. The control's failure sits at D16 alone (see Results). The labelled fraction is 35 of 72 days, so one more labelled day would reach 50%.

Excess loss is a day's mean quantile score minus the substation's median day. The quantile score is twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles, in points of effective capacity (1% of a series' own 99th percentile of cleaned demand), over forecasts made 15 to 39 hours ahead. Days are local calendar days. The rows exclude the hand-filtered switching events, as in experiment 155.

docs.title: Worst days
docs.text:
The 20 worst days of the 72 are below. The full list is in worst_days.csv.

Substation Local date Day's score Excess over median day Labels D5 2026-01-15 21.0 +18.3 switching D16 2026-05-12 15.6 +13.8 switching D5 2026-01-16 13.2 +10.5 switching D16 2026-01-15 11.4 +9.5 switching D16 2026-01-16 11.3 +9.4 switching D10 2026-06-11 11.1 +8.7 switching D16 2026-05-11 9.9 +8.0 switching D10 2025-11-20 9.0 +6.7 cold snap D16 2026-01-17 8.5 +6.6 none D16 2026-05-14 8.1 +6.3 switching D16 2026-05-16 8.1 +6.3 switching D16 2026-04-20 7.9 +6.0 switching D11 2026-01-04 7.8 +5.8 switching, cold snap D10 2026-05-26 8.2 +5.8 none D16 2026-05-15 7.6 +5.8 switching D10 2025-12-01 7.6 +5.3 switching D16 2026-01-19 6.5 +4.6 none D5 2026-01-17 7.4 +4.6 switching D16 2025-12-27 6.2 +4.4 switching, holiday D5 2026-01-24 7.0 +4.3 switching

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Share of the excess in the worst 5% of days: 41.7% (95% interval 33.5% to 46.9%, resampling the 12 months of the scored year). By substation: D5 42.2%, D10 37.6%, D11 34.4%, D14 37.3%, D16 52.9%, and D9 35.7%. Leaving one substation out gives 38.1% to 43.3%. The worst 10% carry 59.2%, the worst 25% carry 86.7%. The excess of a site is summed over its days with positive excess.
  • Labels on the worst 72 days (against all 1,392 days): switching event 29 (9.5% of all days), holiday 8 (4.2%), cold snap 7 (2.0%), flagged reading 0 (0.0%), Economy 7 step 0 (0.9%), any label 35 (14.5%). A day can carry several labels. The labelled fraction by substation is 27% (D14) to 71% (D16).
  • Share of the total excess on labelled days: any label 35.8%, switching 29.2%, holiday 7.2%, cold snap 5.3%.
  • Unlabelled worst days: 37 of 72, spread across 11 of the 12 months (every month but February). We did not look for a further label in them. January 2026 holds 19 of the 72 worst days.
