  • Test the same clip at D9, the second substation where the GAM trails BG2 by +0.079 MW (it has no clip flag in the site table, and no pinned-capacity vintage before 2025-04).
  • A learned response from irradiance to solar output is still untested. The learned response's target is now D9 and any residual at D5 after the clip.

docs.title: Pre-registered plan
docs.text:
Reading the earlier advice. The plan follows experiments 139 and 157 (the pinned capacity stays untouched in every arm), experiment 111 (month-block bootstrap on paired differences), and experiment 178 (state the row definition and the lead range with every gap). It departs from experiment 73, which dropped the search over the DC:AC ratio as unidentified: arm P searches tilt and azimuth only and holds the ratio at 1.15. Experiment 77's null result for a fitted shape is the main reason the prediction above expects failure.

Row set. Experiment 178's rows: the 291 daily runs of fold_a_daily_gap_v1 in the scored year (2025-07-02 to 2026-06-29), leads 0.5 to 168 hours, outside the hand-filtered switching events. A half-hour is sunny when it is in the top third of its substation's daylight half-hours ranked by the fixed fleet unit shape on CAMS irradiance. The ranking uses the fixed fleet shape in every arm, so every arm is scored on identical rows. Forecast rows stay before 2026-07-01.

Control. Experiment 155's arm D re-run through the same code path as the arms, with the fixed fleet shape (tilt 35, south, DC:AC 1.15, 0.4%/K de-rating, cell temperature = air + 25 K x shape). The control's median forecast must reproduce the stored arm D's to 0.005 MW mean absolute difference at all six substations, or the comparison does not proceed. The chain is experiment 136's A2 (T-all monthly fits, pooled noise setting, calibrated ensemble mean), then experiment 155's winter night offset and recipe R. Each arm reruns the whole chain, including its spread table, so the pinball contrasts include that refit. The pinball scores are arm D's, not the calibrated quantiles of experiments 160 and 164, which change quantile offsets only; the median forecast of 178's GAM equals arm D's, so the headline mean absolute error is comparable.

Where the solar shape enters, and how an arm swaps it. The shape enters the training rows (unit_pv_shape from CAMS), the analysis proxy (proxy_cache), and each ensemble member (SunGeometry.pv_shape_and_ghi). Each of the three takes an optional plant. The pinned capacity, in points of effective capacity, multiplies the shape in all three places, and stays as it is. Three more couplings are fixed here. First, the temperature de-rating and the finite-row and last-trained masks (derated_unit_shape, LAST_TRAINED_MIN_SHAPE, the filters in dp_gam, dp_ens, and experiment 136's scripts) read the swapped shape, as the control reads the fleet shape. Second, any rescaling of an arm's shape is applied after the inverter clip. Third, the sunny-row ranking reads a separate frozen copy of the fleet shape, never the swapped array, and the scripts assert that every arm's scored row keys equal experiment 178's. The code review checks each of these readers.

Arms L and N apply their nonlinear response to the calibrated ensemble-mean irradiance, because the chain forecasts from the mean as one member. A response fitted on CAMS rows therefore meets a smoother input at forecast time. The write-up reports this as a limit.

docs.title: Stage 0: inspect D5's solar properties (CPU, no fit, before any arm)
docs.text:
Each item is reported as a finding, not only the one that explains the gap.

  • Orientation: the hour-of-day profile of D5's net power on clear days, against the fixed shape's profile at the same hours, at D5 and at the placebo; the time of the net-power minimum against the shape's peak (an east or west bias moves it); the same for the nearest metered solar farm, if one lies within 30 km.
  • Solar share: the share of D5's demand that is solar (night mean minus sunny-daylight mean over the night mean, as experiment 178), beside the other five substations.
  • Shading and clipping: whether the clear-day output flattens at midday (a clip, which experiments 103 and 110 flagged at D5, whose clip flag in the site table is true and is false at the five others) or drops sharply at one end of the day (shading).
  • Capacity: D5's pinned capacity per season-year against experiment 129's inferred 80% range for D5, and the pin's year-on-year step.
  • Neighbouring generators and meter: any metered generator in the NGED table within 30 km of D5, and D5's meter type (the site table gives units MW, signed, role mw_long).

docs.title: Known-answer gates (before arms L, N, and F)
docs.text:
• Gate 1, held-out farm: fit each learned response on five of the six metered solar farms (A to F, as experiments 129 and 157 use) and score it on the sixth farm's metered output, against the fixed fleet shape's best single scale. Arms L and N each have their own gate. The response and the fleet shape each get one scale fitted on the held-out farm's first calendar year and are scored on its later years, so both see the same amount of the held-out farm. The response must lower the held-out MAE by 10% or more at 4 of 6 farms. The farms' output comes from experiment 179's cleaned_solar_farms.parquet (rows with a null drop_reason), which is provisional until experiment 179 merges. The metered-PV session adds the same test; its code is reused if merged. Farms appear on any page only under their anonymised letters.
  • Gate 2, injection: inject a metered farm's output at 50% of the substation's pinned capacity into its net power for the forecast year, with the shape held at the response learned without the injection. The recovery is (mean absolute error on the injected half-hours with the injection and the old capacity, minus the same with the raised capacity) divided by the injection's mean. It must lie in 0.75 to 1.25 (experiments 129 and 157). The injection enters the training rows of the monthly refits, and the forecast year's refits are the ones scored. The gate runs at D5 and at the placebo only.
  • Stop rules: if gate 1 fails, arms L, N, and F do not run, the shape ceiling (experiment 157 found one scale of the fleet shape fits a median 0.92 to 0.94 of a farm's output) is written up as real, and the verdict is capped at inconclusive. Arms P and K change only the shape's fixed parameters, have their own selection rule, and still run. If gate 2 fails at D5 or at the placebo, the confounding is reported and only arm F runs.

docs.title: Arms
docs.text:
Every arm changes only the solar term of the control. Arms run at D5 and at the placebo; arm P also runs at the four other substations (D9, D10, D11, D14) as the no-harm check.

  • C, control: the fixed fleet shape.
  • P, per-substation tilt and azimuth (the lead arm): the shape comes from plant_power_mw for the substation's chosen tilt (15, 25, 35, 45, 55 degrees) and azimuth (135, 157.5, 180, 202.5, 225 degrees), DC:AC 1.15. Each candidate shape gets one scale per substation, fixed so that its sum over all daylight half-hours from 2023-04-01 to 2024-03-31 on CAMS irradiance equals the fleet shape's. The scale is then frozen for every later cut. This keeps the pinned capacity's annual meaning. The selection rule is fixed here: for each of the 25 cells, fit T-all at the quarterly cuts 2023-04-01, 2023-07-01, 2023-10-01, and 2024-01-01, score each fit on the following quarter's sunny daylight half-hours (the fleet-shape ranking, with the CAMS-driven shape), and take the cell with the lowest mean absolute error over the four quarters. The scores of all 25 cells are reported per substation. D9 has no pinned-capacity vintage before 2025-04, so it keeps the fleet shape. At the other substations the early cuts use the later vintage's level (hindsight, as the dp_pinned_capacity docstring says); the capacity is the same for all 25 cells at a cut, so it cannot favour one cell. The chosen cell replaces the fleet shape only if its error is at least 1% lower than the fleet's (35, 180), a guard against selection noise that the reported surface lets a reader judge; otherwise the substation keeps the fleet shape, and arm P equals the control there. The write-up lists the substations that changed, and arm P is left out of the best-arm choice at D5 if D5 keeps the fleet shape. All selection data end before 2024-04-01, the first scored-chain run. If the selection fits take more than 4 hours at the slot's cores, the grid shrinks to tilt 25, 35, 45 and azimuth 157.5, 180, 202.5 before any score is read.
  • K, export clip: the control with ClipSpec (multiplier 1, p_max_share 1, the default sharpness) of studies.dp_gam, at D5 and the placebo. Experiment 110 found the clip helps at D5 and fails its gate; this arm tests it on 178's rows.
  • L, convex learned response: the solar output as a tensor-product spline in the ensemble-calibrated irradiance (non-decreasing, through cumulative basis functions) and sun elevation, per substation, in MW per unit of pinned capacity. The coefficients are non-negative, so the fit stays a bounded quadratic. A quadratic penalty pulls the response towards the coefficients that reproduce the fleet shape, so where the data cannot tell solar from demand the response falls back to the physics. The temperature de-rating is applied as in the control.
  • N, small neural network: a monotone multilayer perceptron from irradiance, direct and diffuse irradiance, sun elevation, sun azimuth, and air temperature to unit solar output, backfitted with the GAM by alternating least squares and gradient steps. It runs only when the best of C, P, K, and L leaves D5's gap above +0.10 MW. Its GPU share is at most 4 GB.
  • F, farm-learned response, frozen: the response of L or N learned on the farms A to F pooled, then frozen and used at D5 and the placebo. It runs only if gate 1 passes and gate 2 fails.

Placebo: D16 is the placebo, and D10 (-0.009 MW) is a second placebo for every arm because both are cheap and neither is the target; D16 is chosen before any fit because it has the most negative sunny-daylight gap in experiment 178's rows (-0.025 MW; D10 -0.009, D11 +0.013, D14 +0.048, D9 +0.079, D5 +0.202). Every arm that changes the solar term at D5 also runs at D16, which must move by under 0.02 MW. A larger move means the change is not specific to D5's shape.

docs.title: What is recorded
docs.text:
• The learned response drawn per substation against the fixed shape (output against irradiance at four sun elevations), and the chosen tilt and azimuth per substation.
  • Whether gate 2's recovery of capacity falls at substations where capacity is growing (D10, D16).
  • The sunny-daylight error by clear-sky-index band for each arm, since 178 found the gap depends on the definition of sunny.
  • Absolute scores per arm: MAE and pinball loss at D5, at the placebo, and for arm P at all six substations, on the maintainer's by-condition slices (all days, sunny daylight, winter, winter nights, cold nights, Economy 7 step hours, Christmas, bank holidays).
  • Per-substation fitted solar properties, for the substation cards.

docs.title: Stop rules
docs.text:
• After the replicate period (the even months of 2024-07 to 2025-06), stop if the best arm minus control at D5 has an interval wholly above zero on sunny daylight half-hours. The best arm is chosen on the replicate period, and the scored year then tests it once.
  • If D5's gap stays above +0.15 MW with every arm and no interval lies wholly below zero, say the cause is not the solar shape and stop. Arm K's earlier failure at D5 (experiment 110) counts as prior evidence for this outcome.
  • Arm F is descriptive and outside the four-contrast correction.

docs.title: Compute and reviews
docs.text:
• At most 8 cores (OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 per worker), systemd-run --user --scope -p MemoryMax=16G -p OOMPolicy=continue per job, and a GPU share of at most 4 GB for arm N only. One monthly T-all fit is timed at D5 before any grid is launched. The fit count is about 27 monthly fits per arm per substation (arms C and P at six substations, K, L, N, F at D5, D16, and D10), plus 25 cells x 4 cuts x 5 substations = 500 selection fits. The 4-hour shrink rule counts the selection fits only, at the timed cost per fit and 8 cores.
  • Reviews: one Sonnet plan review (done; the manager's brief asks for Sonnet reviewers, so the Opus plan and code reviews of the full tier are skipped), one Sonnet code review for leakage (no response sees data after its fit's cut) and for the control reproducing arm D, and one Sonnet prose review. An Opus audit runs only if one of the seven triggers in the ml-experiment skill's "Audit before merge" fires. The experiment adds no production code.
  • Departures from the design brief, for the manager to overrule: arm K is added; the DC:AC search is dropped from arm P; arms P and K run when gate 1 fails; and arm P's selection keeps the fleet shape unless a candidate is at least 1% better.

docs.title: Experiment 181: why were 17 block days missed, and can a block detector find them?
docs.text: A detector built for blocks finds none of the 17 unlabelled worst days. The days are short blocks of 1 to 4 noise units, where one noise unit is the usual spread of the forecast residual (observed minus forecast power) of that series. A block is a switching-like change in the power a Primary substation draws: it steps up, stays level, and steps back. Experiment 175 found 17 sharp-edged block days among the 37 worst days that no label explains. Neither RO-NC (the refit-offset neighbour-count detector of experiment 82) nor the opposite-step pair alarm of experiment 156 fired on any of them. We asked why, wrote a rectangular-block detector, and counted how many of the 17 days it finds when it is allowed the same 80 unexplained alarms in odd-numbered months as RO-NC. It finds 0 (prediction: at least 12), so the verdict is refuted. RO-NC finds more real transfers on the convex-model residual than on the XGBoost residual, but most of the difference comes from Primaries that the XGBoost panel does not cover. A transfer is a labelled period in which switching moved load from one Primary substation to others. On the 35 labelled transfers lasting over 1 day, RO-NC finds 18 on the residual of the convex demand model and 12 on the residual of the XGBoost model. Four of the 6 extra transfers sit at Primaries where the XGBoost panel (its table of readings and forecasts) has no readings. NGED is National Grid Electricity Distribution; a Primary substation steps transmission voltage down to distribution voltage. The 35 transfers are those of the 66 labelled real transfers that last over 1 day.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Part 3, like-for-like table. RO-NC's threshold gives 80 unexplained odd-month alarms on each residual. A transfer counts as found when an alarm falls within 2 hours of the labelled start and the alarm's end within the larger of 6 hours and 10% of the duration. The same code scored both residuals. The MW-weighted figure is the share of the moved megawatts that the found transfers carry, and the interval resamples transfers 20,000 times.
Transfers XGBoost residual found (MW-weighted) Convex-model residual found (MW-weighted) Paired MW-weighted gap (95% interval) All 35 (42.7 MW) 12 (0.357) 18 (0.657) +0.300 (+0.089 to +0.505) 29 with readings in both panels (31.2 MW) 12 (0.489) 14 (0.604) +0.115 (-0.046 to +0.300) 6 with no readings in the XGBoost panel (11.5 MW) 0 (0.000) 4 (0.800) +0.800 (+0.402 to +1.000)
  • Injected transfers (experiment 130, quoted): 0.794 convex against 0.772 XGBoost, a gap of +0.023 (-0.001 to +0.046).
  • What differed between experiments 101 and 130: nothing in the matching rule or the 35 transfers, because experiment 130 copied experiment 101's scoring code. The two differ in the residual, in the 15 series (against 16, with the same 12 found by the XGBoost arm on either), and in the 6 transfers at two Primaries that the XGBoost panel lacks. The convex model also trained with these real transfers masked, which flatters it on them.
  • Part 1, step 1: why the 17 days were missed. On the convex-model residual, the best-fitting block of each day has a median score of 2.3 noise units (largest 4.4) and a median length of 12 hours; 13 of the 17 best-fitting blocks last 12 hours or less. RO-NC's 24-hour step statistic has a median of 2.2 noise units against its threshold of 4.35, and exceeds it on 2 days (5.2 and 7.2), where RO-NC still raises no alarm; why is not tested. All 17 days have at least two metered interconnected Primaries, so a missing partner does not explain the misses. No RO-NC or pair alarm falls inside any of the 17 local days.
  • Part 1, step 2: block detector. Threshold at 80 unexplained odd-month alarms: 4.37 noise units (78 unexplained alarms in even months). S0 finds 0 of 17 days (0 of the 5 in even months). Neighbour support (S1, threshold 5.37) finds 1. The post hoc S2, which divides by the previous 7 days' spread, finds 5 of 17 (4 of 5 in even months; 84 unexplained even-month alarms). S0 finds 7 of 17 only at about 1,300 unexplained odd-month alarms.
  • Injected-block control. Blocks of height 5 noise units are found 57% to 65% of the time at lengths of 6 to 48 hours, and 6 noise units 89% to 92%, so the detector works on blocks of the size it is tuned for. At 3 to 4 noise units it finds 5% to 29%.
  • Part 2, candidate label table: 133 rows in data/ml-experiments/briefs/sw_block_detector_label_table.csv (private, not committed): 17 block days (3 of medium confidence), 21 balanced-opposite alarms (all low), 29 drops of D8 (23 of medium confidence, with a logged closure within 24 hours), and 66 labelled real transfers (50 of medium or high confidence). Columns: onset, end, depth in MW, duration, pair, source, confidence.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, and the mean-forecast error: not applicable, because no forecast is scored.
  • Trigger 2 (a result contradicts its prediction) fired: 0 days found against a prediction of at least 12. The explanation that the blocks are too small is tested by the threshold curve and the injected-block control. The audit that trigger 2 calls for was not run here.
  • Trigger 4 (leaving a site out) was not run. Triggers 1, 3, 5, 6, and 7 did not fire: the injected-block control passes.

docs.title: Deviations and caveats
docs.text:
• Residual. The block detector reads the convex-model residual of experiment 130 (ERA5 weather, frozen), not the forecast residual of arm D (ensemble weather and Kalman filter) on which experiment 175 found the days. The blocks are visible in both, but the noise unit differs, and the Kalman filter in arm D absorbs a multi-day block. This is the main caveat on "0 of 17".
  • Found rule. The plan said an alarm within 3 hours of the block's onset. The median block length of 8 hours in the plan came from an earlier look at the detector's edges, and 12 hours is the best-fitting block's median here. The strongest edge of experiment 175 can be the block's return edge, so the headline counts an alarm inside the local day or within 3 hours of it. The edge rule finds 0 (S0) and 2 (S2).
  • Peak rule. Alarms are local peaks within 48 half-hours, as in RO-NC, so a day whose best score (D5, 4.38) exceeds the threshold can lose to a larger peak nearby (4.56, outside the day). The count would then be 1 of 17.
  • Looser than the plan. An alarm of either sign, or one that the masks call explained, counts as found; the injected-block recall includes chance exceedances. Both favour the detector. The noise-unit floor of S2 uses all months. The like-for-like intervals resample transfers, not Primaries, and "has readings" means at least half of the transfer's half-hours are present.
  • The 5-of-17 result is exploratory. S2 was added after the 17 days were seen, so its count is a hint for a later pre-registered test and not evidence that block detection works. No Opus audit was run, by the manager's decision.
  • Post hoc. S2 was added after S0 found nothing. Its threshold is set on odd months, but the choice of S2 followed the 17 days.
  • Unexplained alarms may include true unlogged switching, so the budget is conservative for any detector that finds real blocks.
  • Two choices that live use would not allow. The residual uses past weather that arrives about 5 days late, and block extents use hindsight.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
Send the candidate label table to NGED to learn which of the 17 blocks are switching. A block detector on the arm D residual, which has a smaller noise unit on these days, is the untested alternative, and needs a longer history than the one year experiment 175 covers.

Code: ml-experiments/00181-switching-block-detector-and-like-for-like-table/; the numbers above are printed by e00181_like_for_like.py, e00181_why_missed.py, e00181_block.py, and e00181_block_control.py, and kept as printed_*.txt in that folder.

docs.title: Experiment 182: do D8's multi-day drops coincide with failed analogues of its two disaggregated farms?
docs.text:
The two farms' own readings cannot answer the question, because they are absent from the power table for the whole period of the drops. D8 (Marsh Lane) is a disaggregated Primary substation: the metadata table says the output of two solar farms was added back to its reading, and that the analogue (the stand-in measurement that supplies each farm's output) of both farms is "not working". Experiment 159 found 29 multi-day drops at D8 that no neighbour step or detector explains. The hypothesis was that, when an analogue fails, D8's reading loses that farm's output, so a drop equals the lost output. Farm 1 has one reading in the power table, and farm 2 has 4,643 readings, of which 441 are above zero and none come after 2026-01-26. The farm reading is therefore "missing" inside all 29 drops and inside every random window (Figure 2), so the pre-registered count (at least 15 of 29 against at most 5 for random windows) cannot be met on the random side. The verdict is inconclusive.

D8's shortfall does lean towards daylight. In 24 of the 29 drops the shortfall (expected minus metered power) is deeper from 10:00 to 15:00 local time than from 22:00 to 04:00, by a median of 1.5 MW (bootstrap 95% interval 0.5 to 3.7). The hourly extra shortfall inside drops correlates with clear-sky irradiance at Spearman +0.44 (p = 0.033) across the 24 hours, against -0.12 outside drops. The extra shortfall is also large at 20:00 to 22:00 (2.4 to 3.3 MW), which a solar farm cannot explain, so the daylight pattern is a hint and not a signature.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Farm readings: farm 1 has 1 reading on the grid (a zero on 2024-09-26) and farm 2 has 4,643 (2023-04-11 to 2026-01-26), 441 of them above zero and the last on 2026-01-23. Farm 2 is typed "Other (Generation)" in the metadata table, so it need not be solar.
  • Per-drop status in daylight (Figure 2): farm 1 is missing in 29 of 29 drops, and farm 2 is missing in 28 and all-zero in 1. In the 7 days before a drop, farm 2 is missing in 28 and normal in 1. A farm anomaly that was not present in the previous 7 days appears in 1 of 29 drops, against a mean of 0.5 in 1,000 random draws (share of draws at or above 1: 0.37).
  • Farm output against drop depth: the farms' combined daylight median over the 7 days before is 0.0 MW in the 10 drops that have any reading there, against a median depth of 2.71 MW. The other 19 drops have no reading to compare.
  • Random windows: 1,000 draws of 29 windows of the same lengths and times of day, from 2023-07-01 onwards, show a farm anomaly in 29.0 of 29 on average (5th to 95th percentile 29 to 29).
  • Depth by hour (Figure 3): the extra shortfall inside drops is about 1.5 MW from 00:00 to 06:00, 2.4 to 3.2 MW from 07:00 to 15:00, 0.7 MW at 17:00 to 18:00, and 2.4 to 3.3 MW from 20:00 to 22:00. Per drop, the Spearman correlation of hourly depth with clear-sky irradiance has a median of +0.49 and is positive in 23 of 29 drops.
  • Metadata information field: 5 of the 33 series have a value. They are D8's own note about the two disaggregated farms, "Analogues not working" for the two farms, "Analogues suspect" for one of the six metered solar farms of experiment 179, and "Customer has not exported since June 2026" for a biofuel generator. The last two are not connected to D8, so no other note explains a D8 anomaly.
  • Raw JSON: in the files read for D8 and the two farms (15.8 MB: the whole-history file and the first and last six-hour file of each series), every reading holds only startTime, endTime, and value, and the top-level fields are the ones the metadata table stores. The Information field is null in the whole-history file (to 2026-03-26) and set in the July and October 2026 files, so the notes are a snapshot and the files carry no history of when an analogue failed.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Drop table and panel: the drops are the 29 of experiment 159, unchanged. D8's expected power is the frozen convex demand model of experiment 130, so "shortfall" is relative to that model.
  • Daylight rule: daylight is clear-sky irradiance above 50 W/m² at D8's location, and one rule (under half present, all zero, or 6 or more identical positive readings) is applied to both farms.
  • Triggers for audit: none fired, because no forecast is scored.

docs.title: Caveats and next steps
docs.text:
• The test cannot discriminate because absence is the baseline for both farms, not because the hypothesis failed.
  • The hourly pattern comes from 29 drops chosen by their depth in the residual, and the evening peak has no solar explanation.
  • Next, either obtain the farms' output and capacity from NGED, or model them from capacity and weather estimates and compare with the drop depth by hour. A neural component is not suggested, because the limit is missing data.

docs.title: Is the flat top of metered solar farms C, D, E, and F a fixed export cap or a panel-plane effect?
docs.text:
Four metered solar farms (anonymised as farms C, D, E, and F) show a flat top, meaning output that stops rising at a roughly constant level around midday on clear days. That level is lower in summer than in spring, so the flat top does not behave like a fixed export cap, a limit on grid export. We asked whether each farm's flat level, measured as power divided by capacity, stays constant across the months (as an export cap would) or changes with the season (as heat derating or the panels' tilt and azimuth could make it). We took the half-hours in which the modelled clear-sky irradiance on a horizontal plane exceeds 650 W/m², from the cleaned power series of the metered-solar-farm exploration (experiment 179). For each farm and month from April to August we then took the 90th percentile, across those half-hours, of power divided by capacity, which the page calls the flat level. No forecasting model was fitted.

The pre-registered prediction fails and the stop rule fires. The prediction was that at least 3 of the 4 farms keep a flat level that varies by under 3% across months, where the variation is the range of the monthly levels divided by their mean. The variation is 5.9% to 8.9%, so no farm is seasonally constant. The stop rule then says that the per-farm plant fit (follow-up 2, a fit of each farm's panel tilt, panel azimuth, direct-current (DC) capacity, and alternating-current (AC) capacity) must fit tilt and azimuth, not only a clip level. September has under 30 qualifying half-hours at every farm and is left out. The 650 W/m² threshold is the irradiance above which experiment 179's figure showed the flat top.

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text:
• Flat level, 90th percentile, range over mean, April to August, farms C to F: 7.2%, 8.9%, 5.9%, and 8.6%. Each farm's level is highest in April (1.04 to 1.05 times capacity) and lowest in July (0.96 to 0.98 times capacity).
  • Replication by years: even years alone give 5.0%, 8.7%, 6.4%, and 8.1%. Odd years alone give 9.8%, 13.2%, 5.4%, and 11.9%, and farm E's odd-year figure covers April to July only. Every farm varies by more than 3% in both halves, so the result of 0 of 4 constant farms is replicated.
  • 99th percentile (post hoc), range over mean: 1.4%, 5.8%, 2.7%, and 3.4%. Farms C and E would pass the 3% rule at this percentile. Farm F narrowly fails at 3.4%, and farm D fails at 5.8%. All four 99th-percentile levels still fall from April to August (for example farm F, 1.06 to 1.03 times capacity).
  • Morning against afternoon (90th percentile, same half-hours): the ratio is 0.99, 1.02, 0.99, and 1.00 for farms C to F, so the level does not depend on whether the sun is east or west of south. A south-facing array and a fixed cap would both give this ratio, so the ratio does not separate them.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• More cloud in summer could lower the 90th percentile. The clear-sky filter uses the clear-sky model, not observed irradiance, so cloudy half-hours enter the 90th percentile. The 99th percentile is less exposed to cloud, and its range across months is smaller. Part of the 90th-percentile range may therefore be cloud, but the seasonal fall at the 99th percentile remains at all four farms, and at farm D its range (5.8%) is close to the 90th percentile's (8.9%).
  • Heat derating, panel tilt and azimuth, and a seasonal export cap are not separated, because no temperature, no panel tilt or azimuth, and no export-cap record was used.
  • Absolute levels are not meaningful, only their change across months. Power is divided by the effective capacity from studies.pv_dataset, which may itself be estimated from the output, so a level near 1.0 is partly by construction.
  • A monthly difference could come from sun elevation. The qualifying half-hours in April and August are near midday only, so month and sun elevation are confounded.
  • Audit: the audit rule for a result that contradicts its own prediction applies in form. The explanation that cloud lowers the 90th percentile was tested with the 99th percentile above, and the seasonal fall remains. No audit was run.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
• Does a per-farm physical plant fit (panel tilt, azimuth, DC capacity, AC capacity, and a heat-derating loss) reproduce the fall from April to August better than a clip level alone? The prediction is that it does; it fails if the clip-only fit does as well.
  • Does each farm's flat top coincide with the hours in which the network operator limited grid export (studies.export_cap identifies these hours)?

docs.title: Experiment 184: does the ensemble help calibrate the bands in daylight?
docs.text:
Running each of the 51 ensemble members through the solar part of the demand model improves the daylight bands by about 2%, and two placebos show the gain is information about cloud. The demand forecast's bands are quantiles of its error: the q05 is the value that the reading should fall under on 5% of half-hours. We asked whether the disagreement between the 51 members of the ECMWF ensemble about cloud helps those bands in daylight, where cloud changes demand through embedded solar generation. Experiment 169 had found no gain from the ensemble spread over all half-hours. We scored daylight (the sun 5 degrees or more above the horizon) and night separately, on the forecast that experiment 169 called arm A. One arm passed each member's irradiance through the solar term and left every other input at the ensemble mean. It lowered the daylight quantile score from 3.632 to 3.551 points in the scored year (-2.2%). Night is unchanged because the arms only change daylight rows. Scores are in points of effective capacity (percentage points of each substation's rated demand), lower is better.

  • Method of the member arms. The fitted model is linear in its coefficients, so member m's forecast is arm A's mean plus the response of experiment 136's T-all fit to the member's unit PV shape minus its response to the ensemble mean's unit PV shape. Arm A's 11 quantile offsets from its mean, times one factor per calibration lead band (fitted on the tuning months), go around each member, and the 51 members are pooled as in experiment 111. The fitted factors are 0.95, 0.90, 0.90, and 0.85 for leads of 0 to 24, 24 to 48, 48 to 144, and 144 to 168 hours: the member spread supplies part of the width that arm A's offsets supplied.
  • Arms. A: reference. M: members through the solar term. Mc: M with the responses centred on zero. F: members through every weather input. S: arm A's daylight offsets times a scale fitted by linear programmes on three spread statistics of the members' clear-sky index (standard deviation, range, and 4 p (1 - p) for the share p of members at 0.8 or more). MR (placebo): arm A's offsets times a factor per lead band, no members. MP (placebo): M with each row's 51 responses taken from a random row of the same substation, calendar month, and hour band. SP (placebo): S's coefficients on statistics from such a row. K (the filter's observation variance) was not run, because it needs a refit of the filter's residual stream, outside the stored data.
  • Row set. fold_a_daily_gap_v1, D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16 (D9 beside them, in no contrast), leads 0.5 to 168 hours, outside the hand-filtered switching events. Scored year 2025-07-02 to 2026-06-29: 464,363 rows, 211,576 in daylight, 225,774 at night, 27,013 in twilight (0 to 5 degrees, scored and unchanged). Mean forecasts are experiment 155's monthly refits, so no contrast depends on the retraining schedule. Ensemble weather is the stored 51-member forecast of experiment 111, available at forecast time; the weather source at lag times is the filter's, as in arm A.
  • Headline, C1 and C2 (daylight, change from arm A). M: -2.23% (97.5% interval -3.07% to -1.38%) in the scored year, -1.76% (-2.68% to -0.93%) in the replicate months. S: -0.34% (-0.72% to +0.04%) and -0.11% (-0.51% to +0.39%). Arm M meets every part of the pre-registered rule in both periods. Arm S does not.
  • Controls. MR -0.23% (-0.49% to +0.03%), MP -0.08% (-0.55% to +0.37%), SP -0.13% (-0.38% to +0.11%) in the scored year; replicate months +0.04%, +0.24%, +0.15%. Mc -1.99% (-2.76% to -1.30%). F -2.22% (-2.98% to -1.45%), the same as M, so temperature spread adds nothing in daylight.
  • Absolute scores, scored year (quantile score). Daylight: A 3.632, M 3.551, F 3.552, S 3.620, MR 3.624, MP 3.630. Night, all arms 1.981. All rows: A 2.752, M 2.715, S 2.746. Replicate months, daylight: A 3.453, M 3.393, S 3.449.
  • Calibration, daylight, scored year. The q05-to-q95 coverage (nominal 0.90) is 0.854 for A, 0.894 for M, 0.877 for S, 0.881 for MR, and 0.889 for MP. Coverage alone cannot separate M from the placebos, which is why the scores matter. The mean q05-to-q95 width is 24.6 points for A and 26.8 for M.
  • Tails, daylight, scored year (coverage / pinball loss). A: q01 0.027 / 0.265, q05 0.078 / 0.907, q95 0.933 / 0.924, q99 0.979 / 0.262. M: 0.013 / 0.230, 0.053 / 0.837, 0.947 / 0.880, 0.986 / 0.243. S: 0.021 / 0.251, 0.069 / 0.889, 0.946 / 0.920, 0.987 / 0.253. Most of the gain is in the lower tail, where high irradiance from some members lowers demand.
  • By clear-sky index band of the ensemble-mean irradiance (M, scored year). Overcast (under 0.4, 18,210 rows) -1.04% (-1.69% to -0.46%); partly cloudy (0.4 to 0.7, 100,922 rows) -2.71% (-3.66% to -1.68%); clear (0.7 and over, 92,444 rows) -1.87% (-3.26% to -0.87%).
  • By lead band (M, scored year). Under 24 hours -1.55% (-2.01% to -1.13%); 24 to 72 hours -1.96% (-2.53% to -1.34%); 72 to 168 hours -2.48% (-3.68% to -1.34%); 12 to 36 hours -1.82% (-2.35% to -1.19%). The prediction that the gain sits under 72 hours was wrong.
  • By substation (M, scored year). D5 -3.15% (-4.41% to -1.83%); without D5 -1.89% (-2.66% to -1.13%); D10 -1.30%, D11 -1.09%, D14 -1.73%, D16 -3.42%. The five-substation result holds without D5 and without any one substation. In the replicate months D11's interval includes zero (-0.65%, -1.92% to +0.91%).
  • Sunniest third (experiment 178's rule). M -4.85% (-7.67% to -2.92%) in the scored year; MP -1.77% (-3.74% to -0.47%). The gap to BG2 in the absolute error of the median, over 74,728 sunny half-hours at the five substations: arm A +0.044 MW, reproducing experiment 178's +0.044 MW (the interval 0.007 to 0.072); M +0.026 MW (interval includes zero, -0.020 to +0.059); MP +0.034 MW. Without D5: A +0.007, M -0.0075 MW. At D5: A +0.202, M +0.170 MW. D5 holds most of what remains.
  • Checks. Median minus mean forecast per substation at 12 to 36 hours: exactly 0.000 for A and S, and -0.14 (D5), -0.05, -0.05, -0.05, and -0.05 points (D10, D11, D14, D16) for M, because the members' skewed responses pull the mixture median below the mean. The mean forecast's own daylight error changes by -0.13% (-0.45% to +0.27%) for M, the same direction as the score. The reproduction control G1 rebuilds experiment 136's mean to 5e-6 points on every row of all three periods. Experiment 178's gap for arm A is reproduced. Gates. G2 passes: the unit PV shape built from CAMS irradiance equals the cached shape (slope 1.000, largest gap 0) at all six substations. G3 fails its monotonicity criterion: member responses fall with the multiplier on 1,036 of 1,058 daylight rows (22 rows, 2.1%, fail) of the fake ensemble (a post hoc subset: 868 of 884 where the fake clear-sky index stays at or under 1.1). The failing rows examined (five of them) are at elevations of 14 to 16 degrees, where the unit PV shape from SunGeometry.pv_shape_and_ghi itself falls as irradiance rises (0.099, 0.124, then 0.090 as irradiance rises from 97 to 227 W/m2 at one half-hour), so the cause lies in the existing shape function. The wiring checks of G3 pass exactly: the response of the multiplier-1 member is zero, responses at night are zero, and the fake ensemble's spread statistic equals the known multiplier spread. The pre-registered rule caps the verdict at inconclusive on a failed gate, so the verdict is inconclusive, and every other part of the rule is met by arm M in both periods. M restricted to elevations of 17 degrees and over scores -2.47% (-3.57% to -1.44%), so the result does not depend on those rows. G4: the members' median clear-sky-index spread is 0.122 raw and 0.112 after calibration in clear conditions, 0.177 and 0.165 when partly cloudy, 0.136 and 0.124 when overcast: calibration shrinks the spread by about 8%, so a null could not be blamed on it.
  • Audit (fresh Opus, one). Findings and triage: (F1, accepted) the supported verdict broke the pre-registered cap, so it is inconclusive; a re-registered G3 in a follow-up (monotone in the member's unit PV shape, not in irradiance) could lift it. (F2, accepted) MP shuffles across lead and cloud band, so it is a weak placebo; the audit's stricter shuffle keeping lead day and cloud band scores -0.78% in the scored year and -0.33% in the replicate months, and M beats it by -1.47% (-1.83% to -1.10%) and -1.43% (-2.04% to -0.82%). About two thirds of the gain needs the day's own members. (F3, accepted) the audit's Gaussian with each row's own mean and spread of the member responses scores -2.13%, so arm S failed through its inputs and form. (F4, accepted) the widths are means, and three BG2-gap figures were corrected. The gap to BG2 moved by 0.018 MW against a predicted under 0.01, so that part of the prediction failed too. MR and MP were added to the plan after it was committed. No leakage was found, the month-block bootstrap is correct (re-blocking replicate months by origin gives -2.52% to -1.05%), and C1 stays negative leaving out any substation (-1.89% to -2.50%) or any month (-2.00% to -2.44%). The report is private (data/ml-experiments/briefs/e184_audit_report.md).
  • Prediction check. The pre-registered expectation (probability about 0.7) was that no arm would reach -1%, that arm M would change the score by -0.5% to +1.0%, and that any gain would sit under 72 hours and that the gap to BG2 would change by under 0.01 MW. Arm M's -2.2% and its larger gain beyond 72 hours contradict all three, and the result also contradicts experiment 169's null on ensemble spread. The placebos MR, MP, and SP test the explanation that widening alone produces the gain, and none reproduces it. Audit triggers fired: the failed monotonic check of G3, and a result that contradicts its prediction and an earlier experiment.
  • Caveats. Arms M and F add a 51-member pass of the solar term to the weather layer and four fitted factors. The result depends on the weather layer's shape function, which falls with irradiance at low sun. The factors below 1 show that the offsets of arm A and the member spread overlap, as experiment 125 expected. The pass shifts daylight medians below the mean by 0.05 to 0.14 points. No term of the best-guess stack beyond arm A was tested on top. The replicate months hold only 6 months, so their intervals are wide.
  • What to try next. (1) Test the member pass inside the full best-guess stack and score the curtailment-cost proxy for the lower tail. (2) Check the production cost of the 51-member solar response. (3) A learned scale on the member responses (a small neural network) is a candidate extra arm; its prediction that could fail is that it beats M's -2.2% on partly cloudy rows without widening night.

docs.title: Do national system prices, Demand Flexibility Service events, or other national signals help the model understand past demand?
docs.text:
Take-home message: the national system price, Demand Flexibility Service (DFS) events, and the other national signals do not explain the bad days of the day-ahead demand forecast. We asked whether any of them explains which days the forecast gets most wrong, and whether giving the forecast's Kalman filter each day's signal value after the event would help it read the past. The answer to both questions is no. Each signal explains under 1% of the variance in the forecast's daily error score (out of fold, beyond temperature and day type), and the hindsight test made the score slightly worse. The national system price stands out a little on the 37 days with the largest unexplained error, but the excess fell just short of the pre-registered bar. No national signal explains the bad days, so local causes remain untested.

Arm D is the forecast being tested. It is arm D of experiment 155, a convex demand model with a Kalman filter (the method of de Vilmarest et al. (2024)) on ensemble weather, for six Primary substations. A Primary substation steps transmission voltage down to distribution voltage. The "37 worst unlabelled days" are the 37 substation-days with the largest forecast error that no known cause explains (a switching event, a holiday, a cold snap, a flagged reading, or an Economy 7 step), taken from experiments 172 and 175.

The test has three parts. Experiment 177 found a high national system price on 18 of those 37 days and a DFS event on 9. Part 1 tests those two signals on all 1,683 substation-days of the scored year (2025-07-03 to 2026-06-30). Part 2 tests five other national signals: national demand, embedded wind, transmission wind, embedded solar, and net interconnector flow. Part 3 replays arm D with a signal as an extra input to the filter. The loss of a day is the mean quantile score (twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles, in points of effective capacity, where lower is better) of its day-ahead forecasts (lead 15 to 39 hours, the "D+1 band"). Verdict: refuted. The pre-registered prediction (a price or DFS signal explaining at least 10% of the variance beyond temperature and day type) failed.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Part 1, all days. The price (three summaries, with temperature products) gains +0.001 out-of-fold R-squared (95% interval -0.025 to +0.022). Price plus the DFS flag, on the 1,231 days with a DFS record, gains -0.010 (-0.045 to +0.013). The DFS flag alone gains 0.000 (-0.008 to +0.003). The prediction needed +0.10 with an interval above +0.05. Temperature, day type, and substation alone have a negative out-of-fold R-squared (-0.030), because the excess loss is dominated by a few days.
  • Effect sizes. Per standard deviation of the signal, price changes arm D's daily excess loss by -0.001 (daily mean, -0.050 to +0.060), +0.059 (daily maximum, -0.051 to +0.211), and +0.003 (evening peak, -0.118 to +0.188) points, and a DFS day changes it by +0.026 (-0.043 to +0.073). The signed daily residual (actual minus mean forecast) rises by +0.407 points (+0.180 to +0.859) per standard deviation of the daily mean price, so the forecast runs a little low on dear days. The other price summaries and the DFS flag show no effect (all intervals include zero), and models of the signed residual do worse out of fold than the baseline (price + DFS -0.100, -0.190 to -0.001).
  • Matched ordinary days. A high price (top 5% of settlement periods) covers 18 of the 37 days, against 12.7 on matched ordinary days (95% range 9 to 16, p = 0.006). The excess is 5.3 days (14.4 points), just under the 5.6-day (15-point) bar, so the 18-of-37 excess does not pass the pre-registered rule. A DFS event covers 9 of the 23 days that have a DFS record, against 6.4 on matched ordinary days with a record (3 to 9, p = 0.09). Experiment 177's month-matched draws gave 14.9 and 8.5.
  • Part 2, other national signals. Out-of-fold gains over the baseline for all days: national demand +0.001 (-0.024 to +0.031), embedded wind 0.000 (-0.016 to +0.010), transmission wind -0.002 (-0.013 to +0.009), embedded solar -0.002 (-0.046 to +0.039), net interconnector flow -0.010 (-0.038 to 0.000), against price (mean and evening peak) +0.002. No signal beats price: every paired difference interval includes zero.
  • Hindsight covariate. National demand was chosen on the tuning months (gain +0.011, interval -0.012 to +0.033, the largest of the seven signals). With it, arm D's day-ahead quantile score at the five decision substations is 2.437 against 2.427 for the stored arm D, a contrast of +0.010 points (95% interval +0.004 to +0.018, worse). The system price (added after the pre-registration, as the signal this question is about) scores 2.442, a contrast of +0.015 (+0.005 to +0.028). Over leads 0.5 to 168 hours the contrasts are +0.003 (-0.004 to +0.011) and +0.017 (+0.004 to +0.030). In the day-ahead band, leaving out any one substation never flips a sign, and only the two contrasts without D14 include zero. Over all leads the national-demand contrast is within +0.006 and -0.001 and includes zero however substations are left out.
  • Tail calibration (day-ahead band, five substations): arm D covers 2.4%, 7.0%, 94.5%, and 98.2% at the 0.01, 0.05, 0.95, and 0.99 levels, and neither hindsight arm moves any of them by more than 0.15 points of coverage or 0.005 points of pinball loss. The curtailment-cost metric was not run, because the hindsight arms score worse and cannot be forecast.

docs.title: Post hoc checks
docs.text:
• Heavy tails. The excess loss is dominated by a few days, so the out-of-fold R-squared is negative for the baseline. With the day's log loss as the outcome and the price ranked, the baseline explains 11% and price adds +0.028 (+0.007 to +0.051), which is real but a quarter of the bar. With the DFS flag on its covered days, the gain is +0.009 (-0.008 to +0.028). Ranking the price against the raw excess gives +0.019 (-0.017 to +0.053).
  • Worst-5% rate. A day with a top-5% price is a worst-5% day 6.3% of the time, against 4.5% without; for a DFS day, 6.2% against 3.3%. The raw rates are small differences between small counts.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, per substation: 0.000 at each of the five decision substations, for arm D and both hindsight arms.
  • Error of the mean forecast beside the score contrast: the mean absolute error changes by +0.023 (national demand, +0.012 to +0.037) and +0.034 (price, +0.013 to +0.059) points, the same direction as the quantile score.
  • Audit triggers of the ml-experiment skill: none fired. The control (coefficients at zero) reproduced the stored arm D to 0.0 over 484,113 rows, the prediction held in direction (no signal helps), and in the day-ahead band no leave-one-out flips a sign.

docs.title: Departures from the plan
docs.text:
• The full price + DFS model uses the 1,231 days with a DFS record (the archive ends on 2026-03-27), compared with a baseline on the same days. The matched-day test for DFS uses the 23 target days inside the archive and ordinary days inside it. The p-values add one to the count of draws, so the smallest is 0.001.
  • Coverage of the national data. Transmission wind comes from Elexon's half-hourly generation by fuel, since the NESO file holds only embedded wind. The evening peak is settlement periods 33 to 38 (16:00 to 19:00 on a 48-period day).
  • Covariates are clipped to plus or minus 4 standard deviations (fixed before the replay), since one settlement period reached 2,900 pounds per megawatt-hour.
  • The two national-demand covariates (daily mean and evening peak) are strongly correlated, so the fitted band coefficients are large and of opposite sign. The replay used the pre-registered pair regardless.
  • Departures from forecast-time conditions. The covariate of the target day is read in hindsight (not forecastable), and ERA5 day-mean temperature (about 5 days late) is in the Part 1 baseline.

  • Schedule. Monthly refits of arm A2 as in experiment 136, and the standardisation and coefficients use the tuning months only. The contrast could depend on refit cadence.

  • Choices that could favour or hurt the tests. The spline knots and the signal standardisation in Part 1 use all days, including the held-out month (no outcome information). The tuning-month site median and spread are in-sample, so the tuning increments that chose the Part 3 signal are optimistic. The Part 3 replay runs national demand and system price whatever the tuning choice.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Local causes (planned and unplanned outage notices, school terms, and local events) are the sources not tested in experiments 177 or 185.
  • A small learned model of the daily loss on price, temperature, and calendar might find an interaction the linear fit cannot, such as a price effect only on cold weekday evenings. The prediction that could fail: it adds under 2% out-of-fold R-squared over the baseline, as the linear models do.

docs.title: Pre-registration (written before any result was read)
docs.text:
• Data (public, under 100 MB). Elexon settlement system prices (the cached 2025-07-02 to 2026-07-01 of experiment 177, plus 2024-07-01 to 2025-07-01 for the tuning months); the NESO DFS service-requirement archive; the NESO historic demand data for 2024 to 2026 (national demand, transmission system demand, embedded wind and solar generation, wind generation, and the interconnector flows).
  • Day definition. A local (Europe/London) calendar day. Price and national signals are aggregated over the local day's settlement periods.
  • Weather at lag times. The temperature in the Part 1 baseline is the ERA5 day-mean temperature of experiment 172. ERA5 arrives about 5 days late, so Part 1 is a diagnosis of past days and not a forecast-time model.
  • Part 3 design. The filter's residual stream is reduced by the coefficient times the standardised covariate of the day, per hour band, and each forecast adds back the coefficient times the covariate of the target day. The covariate is known for the target day only in hindsight. Coefficients are fitted on the tuning months and fixed for the scored year.
  • Chosen before results. The signal for Part 3 is chosen on the tuning months only.
  • Anonymisation. Demand series only; the sites keep their D labels.

docs.title: Experiment 186: are D8's multi-day drops a gas engine following the spark spread?
docs.text:
Take-home message: the evidence fits a gas engine below D8 that runs when electricity is dear relative to gas, but does not prove it. D8 is a substation (Marsh Lane) of National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED). Experiment 159 found 28 multi-day stretches since July 2023 in which D8's metered demand sits below the forecast, which it called drops, with a median shortfall of 2.8 MW. We asked whether a gas-fired generator below D8 explains the drops. NGED suggested an embedded gas peaker that runs when the spark spread is positive, meaning the electricity system price exceeds the cost of the gas burned to make it. We built the spread from public data (the system price from Elexon, the electricity settlement operator, and the daily gas price from National Gas, the gas transmission operator) and compared the days inside drops with ordinary days matched on weekday, season, and temperature. We also tested whether the drops are flat on/off blocks, whether they coincide with Triad half-hours (the three half-hours each winter of highest national demand, which set transmission charges), and whether the Capacity Market register lists a gas plant next to D8. The plan predicted two things: drop days have a positive spread at least 20 points more often than matched days, and at least 20 of the drops are flat blocks. The first holds and the second does not, so the verdict is partly supported. The Triad test does not support the hypothesis either.

The drops start when the spread rises and end when it falls. At 40% electrical efficiency, 82% of drop days have a positive daily spread, against 54% of ordinary days matched on weekday, season, and temperature. The 95% interval of the difference (+28.4 points) runs from +16.0 to +42.5. Most of the +28.4-point difference comes from the system price: holding the gas price at its mean still gives +24.4 points. Experiment 185 found a high system price on the worst days of the best-guess forecast, so the spread test cannot separate a gas engine from any other load that follows the system price.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Method. Public data only (about 23 MB in total; the National Gas data portal item "SAP, hourly actual" (SAP is the system average price) for the gas price, and the Elexon system price). Spark spread = system price − (gas price in pounds per MWh thermal ÷ electrical efficiency) − 5 pounds per MWh operating cost, at 35%, 40% (central), and 45% efficiency. A drop day has at least 75% of its half-hours inside a drop. Window: 2023-07-01 to 2026-06-30, 28 drops, 126 drop days, 839 ordinary days. Matching: same weekday, season within ±30 days, day-mean temperature within 2 degrees (widened to 4 or 6 if fewer than 3 days match), 1,000 draws, intervals from resampling drops.
  • Spread share. Drop days minus matched ordinary days, in percentage points: +25.8 (+10.3 to +42.1) at 35%, +28.4 (+16.0 to +42.5) at 40%, +20.1 (+9.5 to +31.7) at 45%. The same test on the evening spread (16:00 to 19:00): +6.0 (−8.8 to +21.2), +10.7 (−0.8 to +22.7), +12.4 (+1.2 to +23.5). Price alone (gas held at its mean, 40%): +24.4 (+11.0 to +38.7). The system price in the top third of days: +12.0 (−2.2 to +28.3).
  • Prices. Mean system price on drop days is 91.3 pounds/MWh against 77.9 on matched days (+13.8; +6.7 to +21.2). The gas price does not differ (−0.3 pounds/MWh thermal; −2.4 to +1.6).
  • Start and end. The mean daily spread (40%) rises by +9.8 pounds/MWh (+2.3 to +16.9) between the 5 days before and the 5 days from a drop's first day, in the predicted direction for 20 of 28 drops. It falls by 8.0 (+2.0 to +14.3, in the predicted direction) between the 5 days up to the last drop day and the 5 days after it, for 18 of 28 drops.
  • Half-hours inside drops. After removing each drop's hour-of-day mean, depth is +0.43 MW (+0.32 to +0.53) deeper in half-hours with a positive spread at 40%, higher in 27 of 28 drops. The removal matters because positive-spread half-hours cluster in the evening, when D8's shortfall is larger.
  • Shape. None of the 28 drops is a flat block under the pre-registered cutoff (relative interquartile range of the 3-hour median depth under 0.25; median 1.06). The control, a constant 2.8 MW block injected into 494 ordinary windows of the drops' lengths, has median 0.70 and passes the cutoff in 9%. The shape evidence is therefore only that the drops are less flat than injected blocks: 3 of 28 drops are below the control median. The median share of variance in a drop explained by hour of day is 0.51, and the median ramp at the start is 0.55 of the depth (end: 0.81).
  • D3, D14, and D5. None has a drop under D8's definition (24-hour median under −1.5 MW for 2 days). Runs under each series' own 5th percentile (9, 5, and 4 runs; median depths 0.4 to 0.8 MW) have median relative range 0.58 to 0.77 and none passes the cutoff, so these series do not contrast with D8 on flatness.
  • Triads. The nine Triad half-hours of 2023/24 to 2025/26 (list from Modo Energy and Drax, which report the lists that the National Energy System Operator publishes) are published after the winter ends, so a peaker can only run on a forecast of the peak. One of the nine falls inside a D8 drop (the start day of one drop), against 10% of winter weekdays in a drop (probability of at least 1 by chance: 0.62). With nine Triads the test has little power: about 0.9 are expected inside a drop by chance. Depth at the Triad half-hour exceeds the same day's median depth for 7 of the 9, but depth at the same period on other winter weekdays outside drops is equally high: the Triad excess is +0.2 MW (−1.4 to +1.7). Winter weekday depth at 16:00 to 19:00 minus other hours inside drops is −0.2 MW (−1.1 to +0.8) over 9 drops, against +1.2 MW on winter weekdays outside drops, a feature of the evening shape of the frozen convex weather-to-demand model that produces the residual (experiment 159).
  • Registers. The Renewable Energy Planning Database (published by the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, Q2 2026) lists a landfill-gas plant of 1.3 MW within 5 km of D8, and gas-fuelled plants (landfill gas, anaerobic digestion) totalling 8.6 MW within 20 km; none is a natural-gas peaker. The Capacity Market register (National Energy System Operator, 21 October 2026) lists a gas plant of 6 MW (reciprocating engines, distribution-connected) at a grid reference 0.5 km from D8's coordinates. The unit won a capacity agreement in the 2023-24 four-year-ahead auction, valid for the delivery years 2023-24 to 2037-38, and the register does not mark the agreement terminated. A second unit of 20 MW (reciprocating engines) lies at a grid reference 0.5 km from D8 on the other side. The two grid references are 1.0 km apart. The second unit was conditionally prequalified in 2022-23 and won no agreement. A reciprocating-engine unit of 20 MW also lies 21.6 km away. The register does not show whether the 6 MW plant was built, and nothing in it rules out combined heat and power. Plant names are withheld here.
  • Daily regression. The baseline out-of-fold R-squared, from temperature and season terms with one month left out, is −0.07. Adding the spark spread raises it by +0.035. Adding the gas price alone raises it by +0.038, the system price alone by −0.001, and the system price and gas price together by +0.063. Drop days and matched days do not differ in gas price, so the gain from the gas price may reflect a time trend (gas prices fell while drops became more frequent in 2025). This experiment did not test that explanation.
  • Matching on year (post hoc). 84 of the 126 drop days fall in 2025. Matching on calendar year as well, for the 101 drop days that have a same-year match, gives +31.6 points (+14.4 to +48.9), so comparing different years does not explain the difference.

docs.title: Whether the spread could become a D8 regressor
docs.text:
• Candidate hindsight regressor. A D8 on/off indicator driven by the daily spread (spread above zero at 40% efficiency) could enter D8's training as a regressor known only after the day. The indicator explains little: the regression gain is +0.034 in out-of-fold R-squared, and 51% of all days in the window also have a positive spread.
  • Forecast time. The indicator cannot be known exactly at forecast time. A spread forecast from day-ahead prices (the Elexon day-ahead market index and National Gas's forward price) might serve, but the signal is mostly the system price, which a day-ahead forecast does not reproduce.
  • Better data. The plant's own half-hourly output would settle the hypothesis and give a direct regressor.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, per site. Not applicable: the experiment scores no forecast.
  • Error of the mean forecast beside each contrast. Not applicable, for the same reason.
  • Triggers. Trigger 1 fired: the flat-block control failed, because injected constant blocks pass the pre-registered 0.25 cutoff in 9% of windows. The cutoff was too strict for the residual's noise, so the 0 of 28 count says only that the drops are less flat than injected blocks. The calibrated comparison (3 of 28 drops below the control median) is post hoc. Triggers 2 to 7 of the skill's audit list did not fire: no contradiction with experiment 185 (the price signal here is a difference between drop days and matched days, not a share of the forecast's daily loss), no nested arms, no sister experiment, no leave-one-out flip, and no later design depends on this result.
  • Audit. A fresh Opus audit ran after the code and prose reviews, with its own code (not committed; its report is kept privately). It reproduced the +28.4 points (+28.3 in its code) and found that the verdict follows the pre-registered rule. It changed or added the following.
    • Register. The register paragraph now follows the agreement terms. The first draft read the prequalification years and wrongly said the 6 MW obligation ended in September 2024.
    • Interval. Drop days shifted by whole weeks (a placebo, with real drops excluded) give a spread-share difference with mean 0 and standard deviation 9.5 to 12.5 points. That is 1.5 to 2 times the spread the cluster bootstrap implies, so the interval above is too narrow. The observed +28.4 points still has p of 0.008 or less.
    • Leave-out checks. Leaving out any one drop gives +27.3 to +30.6. Leaving out 2025 gives +41.3, and 2025 alone gives +21.8.
    • Wind. Drop days are 1.26 m/s less windy than matched days, and wind correlates with the system price at −0.37. Matching on wind speed as well gives +21.4 to +23.2.
    • Flat-block control. Injected blocks that go through the same drop detector are detected 90% of the time and pass the 0.25 cutoff 8% of the time. The claim that the drops are less flat than injected blocks holds, and only 1 of 28 drops is flatter than the median of the injected blocks (the earlier count of 3 of 28 used a control that skipped the detector).
    • Load dependence. After removing the hour-of-day profile, drops vary more than injected blocks (median 1.15 against 0.82 MW). Depth rises with expected demand: +0.61 MW per MW, positive in 25 of 28 drops, against +0.16 for the control.
    • Ordinary days. Depth is +0.60 MW higher on positive-spread days, so the association is continuous and does not need drops.
    • Other price-following units. The register lists a 10 MW battery 0.09 km from D8 and a 2.9 MW demand-side-response unit with an industrial-site component 0.15 km away. A battery cannot sustain a multi-day drop, and demand-side response can.
    • Verdict. The verdict and the 6 MW engine as a candidate stand.
  • Bad gas values. The daily gas price has four values far outside the others: 72.8 (2024-07-25), 63.9 (2026-06-12), 0.51 (2025-11-29), and 0.47 (2026-06-17) pence per kWh, against 1.9 to 5.2 for the rest. All four are excluded, and 5 of the 1,090 days in the window have no spread (a missing price or an excluded gas value).
  • Hour of day. The half-hourly contrast is computed after removing each drop's hour-of-day mean.
  • Efficiency. The spread result holds at all three efficiencies (+25.8, +28.4, +20.1 points).
  • Lab shortcuts. The residual comes from the frozen convex weather-to-demand model, driven by ERA5 (the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts reanalysis) temperature, which is not available at forecast time. Drops are defined on that residual, so they inherit its errors.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: Ask NGED whether the 6 MW gas engine registered next to D8 was built, who operates it, and what its half-hourly output is. Ask separately whether D8's other nearby price-following units (demand-side response and battery) can explain the multi-day drops. With the plant's half-hourly output, test whether D8's drops equal the plant's generation. Then test whether the plant's dispatch follows the spread. Among the public data we checked, we found no test that could separate a gas engine from other loads that follow the system price.

docs.title: Experiment 187: ensemble members through the solar term, inside the best-guess stack
docs.text:
Running each of the 51 ensemble members through the solar part of the demand model still lowers the daylight forecast score by about 2% in the full best-guess stack. About two thirds of that gain needs the day's own members. The demand forecast's bands are quantiles of its error. Experiment 184 found that the disagreement between the 51 members of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) ensemble about cloud improves those bands in daylight (the sun 5 degrees or more above the horizon). A known-answer check on a synthetic ensemble with a known response failed, so its verdict was capped at inconclusive. The check required each member's solar response to fall as irradiance rises. At low sun the unit photovoltaic (PV) shape, the output of a unit panel for a given irradiance, falls as irradiance rises, so the check was too strict. Experiment 187 uses a check that the response follows the member's own unit PV shape, which the synthetic ensemble passes on every row. We then re-scored the same arms. The re-scoring reproduces experiment 184's numbers exactly, because the reference forecast (arm A) already is the full best-guess stack: the convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors, a winter night offset, and a 14-day error profile (recipe R), with the band widths of experiments 160 and 164. The score is the quantile score, twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles, in points of effective capacity (percentage points of each substation's rated demand); lower is better. D5, D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16 are anonymised substations. The replicate months are the six even months of 2024-07 to 2025-06, and the scored year is 2025-07 to 2026-06. BG2 is the blend of five models with a solar offset from experiment 87, the production-style reference.

  • Arms and row set. A: reference (experiment 184's arm A, 2.7521 points over all rows in the scored year). M: arm A's mean plus each member's solar response, with arm A's 11 quantile offsets times one factor per lead band (0.95, 0.90, 0.90, 0.85) around each member, pooled over the 51 members. Row set fold_a_daily_gap_v1, D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16 (D9 in no contrast), leads 0.5 to 168 hours, outside the hand-filtered switching events; scored year 2025-07-02 to 2026-06-29. Mean forecasts are experiment 155's monthly refits, so no contrast depends on the retraining schedule. Ensemble weather is the stored 51-member forecast of experiment 111, available at forecast time.
  • Re-registered gate G3'. The response is the fitted solar coefficient times the difference between the member's unit PV shape and the ensemble mean's, so it must be non-increasing in the member's unit PV shape. It holds on 1,058 of 1,058 daylight rows of the fake ensemble (the CAMS irradiance of 6 scored runs at D10 times 51 multipliers from 0.6 to 1.4; the 1,058 rows are the daylight half-hours of those runs). The multiplier-1 member's response is 2e-14 points and night responses are zero. The old irradiance-monotone check holds on 1,036 rows; all 22 failures are at elevations under 17 degrees, and all 1,002 rows at 17 degrees or more pass.
  • Headline C1 (daylight, change from arm A, 95% interval). Scored year -2.23% (-2.97% to -1.48%), replicate months -1.76% (-2.57% to -1.02%). Night 0.00% in both periods, because the arm changes only daylight rows. The daylight q05-to-q95 coverage (nominal 0.90) is 0.894 for M against 0.854 for A in the scored year, and 0.901 against 0.871 in the replicate months. The rule is met in both periods.
  • Absolute scores (quantile score). Scored year, daylight A 3.632, M 3.551; night 1.981; all rows A 2.752, M 2.715. Replicate months, daylight A 3.453, M 3.392; night 2.027.
  • By lead band (daylight, A to M, scored year). Under 24 hours 3.095 to 3.047 (-1.55%); 24 to 72 hours 3.343 to 3.278 (-1.96%); 72 to 168 hours 3.906 to 3.809 (-2.48%); 12 to 36 hours 3.227 to 3.169 (-1.82%).
  • By clear-sky band of the ensemble-mean irradiance (scored year). Overcast (under 0.4) 3.127 to 3.094 (-1.04%); partly cloudy (0.4 to 0.7) 3.861 to 3.756 (-2.71%); clear (0.7 and over) 3.483 to 3.417 (-1.87%).
  • By substation (daylight, A to M, scored year). D5 5.294 to 5.127 (-3.15%); D10 3.983 to 3.931 (-1.30%); D11 2.794 to 2.763 (-1.09%); D14 2.855 to 2.805 (-1.73%); D16 3.354 to 3.240 (-3.42%). Without D5, -1.89%. In the replicate months D11 is -0.65% with an interval that includes zero (-1.92% to +0.91%).
  • Placebo shares (the percentage of M's daylight gain that each placebo recovers; scored year, replicate months). Members from another day of the same substation, month, and hour band (MP): 3%, -14%. Members from another day of the same lead day and cloud band as well (the stricter shuffle): 35% (-0.78%), 19% (-0.33%). A Gaussian with each row's own mean and spread of the responses: 95% (-2.13%), 91% (-1.60%). The responses reflected about their mean, which reverses the skew: 81% (-1.82%), 71% (-1.25%). So 65% (81%) of the gain needs the day's own members, and the size of the spread across the members carries nearly all of the gain, with the skew worth about 0.3 percentage points of the score change.
  • Gap to BG2 on the sunniest third of daylight half-hours (mean absolute error of the median, five substations, 74,728 half-hours). Arm A +0.044 MW (95% interval +0.007 to +0.072); M +0.026 MW (-0.020 to +0.059). Without D5: A +0.007, M -0.007 MW. At D5: A +0.202, M +0.170 MW, so D5 still holds most of what remains.
  • Tails (daylight, scored year; coverage / pinball loss). A: q01 0.027 / 0.265, q05 0.078 / 0.907, q95 0.933 / 0.924, q99 0.979 / 0.262. M: 0.013 / 0.230, 0.053 / 0.837, 0.947 / 0.880, 0.986 / 0.243. The gain is largest in the lower tail.
  • Checks. The median forecast minus the mean forecast at 12 to 36 hours is exactly 0.000 for arm A, and -0.14 (D5), -0.05 (D10), -0.05 (D11), -0.05 (D14), and -0.05 (D16) points for M, because the members' skewed responses pull the mixture median below the mean. The mean forecast's own daylight error changes by -0.13% (-0.45% to +0.27%) for M, the same direction as the score. No trigger from the audit rules fired in this experiment: no control failed, the quantile-score and mean-error contrasts agree in direction, the earlier null of experiment 169 was explained in experiment 184, and the control that should change nothing (the rescaling without members, MR) moves the score by -0.23% against a half-width of 0.26. The re-scoring reproduces experiment 184's numbers, so experiment 184's Opus audit (no leakage found, month-block bootstrap checked, C1 negative leaving out any substation or month) covers the same stored arrays.
  • Caveats. Experiment 187 is a re-derivation: experiment 184's scores for M were known before the rule was registered, so only the gate and the placebo shares are new. The member pass adds a 51-member solar response and four fitted factors to the weather layer. The replicate months hold 6 months, so their intervals are wide. D5 and D16 give the largest gains; D11's replicate interval includes zero.
  • Prediction check. Every part held except one. G3' passed on every row. Both intervals lie wholly below zero with point estimates under -1%. Night moved by 0.00%. Coverage lies within 0.02 of 0.90. The stricter-shuffle share fell in the predicted 25% to 45% range in the scored year (35%) but below it in the replicate months (19%).
  • Optional neural arm. Not run. A Gaussian with the row's own mean and spread already recovers 95% of the gain, so a learned scale on the spread has about 0.1 points of headroom in daylight.
  • What to try next. (1) Replace the 51-member pass by a per-half-hour mean and standard deviation of the member responses, computed from the ensemble mean and the member irradiance spread, and test whether it keeps the gain (prediction that could fail: it keeps at least 80% of -2.2%). (2) Check the production cost of the member pass. (3) Test the member pass on the curtailment-cost metric of studies.node_curtailment, because the gain is largest in the lower tail.

docs.title: Are D10's extra errors from unlogged load shifts, and does locating the onset inside the look-back help the mask?
docs.text:
Masking back to the detector's own step stamp removes almost all the extra error of masking only from the alarm time, and a search of the readings since the last forecast for a more precise onset adds nothing. Part 2 meets its pre-registered rule (supported), but its comparison arm, masking from the alarm time, is an arm that experiment 171 never used. Part 1 misses its rule (inconclusive): the interval of the gated mask's difference from no mask is not inside +/-0.03. The overall verdict, partly supported, is a judgement, because the plan registered a verdict for each part only.

Background: what a mask is. Our forecast corrects itself using recent power. A "mask" sets recent power aside while a switching alarm is active. A pair alarm is a step in power at one substation matched by an opposite step at a neighbouring metered substation. A gated alarm is a pair alarm whose balance score is 0.7 or more, meaning the two steps are close in size. RO-NC is the detector of experiment 147, which fires on a step in a refitted residual with support from neighbouring series. A step stamp is the half-hourly timestamp at which a detector says the step happened. The alarm time is the later timestamp at which the alarm became known: about 6 hours after the step for the pair alarm (a median of 12 half-hours), and 48 hours for RO-NC (96 half-hours). The look-back is the readings between the step and the forecast origin, the moment a forecast run is issued (every 6 hours in production).

Background: what experiment 171 found and what we asked. Experiment 171 found that the gated mask scores 0.030 points of effective capacity worse than no mask on 27 months of rows outside logged transfers (95% interval -0.011 to +0.074), and that leaving out one substation, D10, removes the difference. Scores are twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles, in points of effective capacity (the score in megawatts over the substation's AC capacity, times 100). A logged transfer is a movement of load between two substations recorded in the switching log of National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED). The six substations scored, anonymised as D5, D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16, are Primary substations. Part 1 asked whether D10's gated alarms follow switching that NGED did not log. Part 2 asked whether the onset of a transfer can be located more precisely in the look-back than the alarm time gives, and whether masking from the located onset beats masking from the alarm time.

Part 1 method. Of the 49 gated alarms since 2024-04-10, 40 touch a scored substation, and 31 of those match no logged transfer. We confirmed an alarm when a persistent step (the median residual over the 12 hours after the alarm's step stamp minus the median over the 12 hours before) at its substation had an opposite step of similar size (0.5 to 2 times) at its partner substations, using thresholds fixed in the plan. We removed the rows from the step to 72 hours after each confirmed event and re-scored experiment 171's rows with the same quantile score and the same month-resampled interval. A row is one forecast for one half-hour from one forecast origin. The forecast is a frozen generalised additive model with a Kalman filter, as in experiment 171.

Part 2 method. Experiment 141's 44 worlds hold 210 injected transfers, and the two alarms find them 247 times in total (a transfer found by both alarms counts twice). We score those 247 matches and 15 logged transfers found by an alarm. At the first 6-hourly origin that can see an alarm, we searched the stamps within 24 hours of the detector's step stamp for the largest step with the same sign as the alarm's step, using only readings up to that origin. The stamp found is the "located" onset. Four masks differ only in the first masked stamp: the alarm time, the detector's step stamp, the located onset, and the true onset. The extra error of a mask is its score minus the score of the mask from the true onset, in points of effective capacity, on all leads of the daily forecast issued in the first 24 hours after the alarm. C2 is the share of the alarm-time mask's extra error that another mask removes: 1 minus the extra error of that mask over the extra error of the alarm-time mask.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Part 2, decisive contrast C2 (injected, both alarms, 247 transfers). Extra error over the true-onset mask: alarm time +0.330 (+0.133 to +0.529), step stamp +0.018 (0.000 to +0.038), located onset +0.031 (+0.005 to +0.059). Reduction from the alarm time to the located onset: 0.907 (0.735 to 0.984), against the pre-registered 1/3. Verdict for part 2: supported.
  • What C2 does not show. The step stamp gives a reduction of 0.946 (0.832 to 1.001), and the located onset minus the step stamp is +0.013 (-0.008 to +0.037) points. The located onset is no better, so the gain comes from masking back to the detector's step stamp, which experiment 171 already does.
  • By alarm. Pair alarm (87 transfers): reduction 0.779 (0.519 to 0.961); extra error alarm time +0.175, step stamp +0.042, located +0.039. RO-NC (160 transfers): reduction 0.936 (0.725 to 1.021); extra error alarm time +0.415, step stamp +0.005, located +0.027.
  • Absolute scores, injected, both alarms. No mask 3.328, mask from the alarm time 3.127, step stamp 2.815, located onset 2.828, true onset 2.797, and the stream without the injected megawatts 2.483. Masking from the alarm time barely beats no mask because the readings since the step, which carry the transfer, stay in the filter.
  • Location error, injected (half-hours; median |error| / 90th percentile). Alarm time: pair 12.0 / 25.8, RO-NC 96.0 / 97.0. Step stamp: pair 0.0 / 29.6, RO-NC 0.0 / 5.1. Located onset: pair 0.0 / 33.6, RO-NC 0.0 / 16.0. The median located error is 0 half-hours, well below the 12-half-hour (6-hour) spacing of forecast origins. The located onset is closer than the step stamp for 10% (pair) and 14% (RO-NC) of transfers and farther for 14% and 26%.
  • Sensitivity (post hoc). Resampling the 39 worlds with scored transfers (of 44) gives 0.907 (0.747 to 0.974). Leaving out any one substation leaves the reduction between 0.88 and 0.97. D10 alone, 14 transfers: 0.780 (-0.351 to 0.965).
  • Real logged transfers (secondary, decide nothing). 9 transfers found by the pair alarm and 6 by RO-NC. Pair alarm: extra error over the true-onset mask alarm time -0.027 (-0.713 to +0.677), step stamp +0.151, located +0.095.
