One of five operating points (RO-NC at 4 hours) reaches 20% or more on both injections, so the prediction of under 20% holds for four of five.
  • Regimes. Share flagged against share below -2.5 MW: 2023-09 to 2025-12, 40% against 26%; 2026-02 to 2026-03, 41% against 12%; 2026-04 to 2026-06, 43% against 2%. D8's residual noise (median absolute step-to-step error) is 0.17 to 0.27 MW in clean months and 0.35 to 0.75 MW from 2024-05, rising most after 2025-03, when 8.91 MW of solar was connected. A local noise multiplier (post hoc) leaves the flagged share at 39% in 2026-04 to 2026-06. The audit found the cause is the observation model, not re-centring and not an engine: from 2025-03 steps of 1.5 to 2.5 MW occur about 69 times per 1,000 half-hours against 0.5 in clean history, in both directions, and upward excursions of more than 1 MW (26% of half-hours) outnumber downward ones (18%), which an engine cannot produce. With error correlation 0.906 the level carries little weight in the emission, so the detector reads steps.
  • Positive spells at D8 (4 or more half-hours more than 1.5 MW above a 30-day rolling median): 2.5 per 100 days in clean history, 35 in 2023-09 to 2025-02, 67 in 2025-03 to 2025-12, and 89 in 2026-04 to 2026-06. The rolling median is pulled down by the engine, so this measure cannot tell battery charging from a biased offset.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast per site: not applicable; the experiment makes no forecast.
  • Mean-forecast error beside a quantile-score contrast: not applicable.
  • Triggers that fired: trigger 1 (a control failed: the false-alarm control at D5 and D11) and trigger 2 (the step detector at 4 hours reached 24%, against a prediction of under 20%, and the unit size sits at the edge of its predicted range). An Opus audit ran, and its findings are below.
  • The gate is easy where it was run. Every injection sits in 2022-23 or July to August 2023, when D8's noise is low, so passing says nothing about 2025-26. In the audit, adding noise of 0.40 MW lowered K1 precision to 0.51 and K2 precision to 0.61, and shifting G2's record into 2026-04 gave precision 0.29. D8's innovation scale is 0.21 MW in the injected history against 0.37 to 0.53 MW in the periods the labels are needed for.
  • Lab shortcuts. ERA5-driven expected power (from the stored panel), smoothed rather than filtered posteriors for the scores (the filtered recall of any running is 0.91 to 0.94), and the unit size quantised to 0.25 MW.

  • Leakage. G2's record sets only the injections, the scoring truth, the 0-to-3 state space and the design prior; the wide prior gives the same fit. The noise fit saw July 2023 and the odd months the K2 windows overlap, but never the injected output.

  • Review caveats. The unit size is on a grid of 0.25 MW, so 1.75 MW means between about 1.6 and 1.9 MW. The plan's stop rule (a unit size outside 1.2 to 3.0 MW) never triggered. Each Primary's noise was fitted on its whole history, including any real engine, which makes its false alarms easier to pass. A K2 window that spans a clock change is up to an hour out of local-time alignment for part of its length.

  • Audit findings accepted. (1) The false-alarm bar fails at D5, D10, and D11, so the verdict is not supported. (2) The gate needs a noise-matched arm and per-window precision; K2's window in summer 2022 has precision 0.78. (3) The flags after 2025-03 are an observation-model failure. (4) Re-centring from half-hours with P(k=0) above 0.9 biases the offset up by 0.5 to 1.3 MW, which deepens apparent drops. (5) The injection and the detector use the same fixed reactive floor, so they agree by construction; at power factor 0.95 K1 precision is 0.80, and at 0.90 the energy error is -15% (K1) and -22% (K2), so those two thresholds are not robust to a load-proportional reactive power. (6) On running half-hours alone the energy error is -8.5% (K1) and -10% (K2), and false positives cancel part of it. (7) K1's truth is wrong on two days in August 2023, when the analogue was failing; those days hold 46 of K1's 61 false positives, and precision is about 0.95 without them. (8) The noise fit saw July 2023 and the odd months that K2's windows overlap.

  • Audit finding not accepted. The code reviewer's claim of a gap-handling bug: a missing previous reading already makes the previous error non-finite, which selects the stationary scale.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Re-fit the noise per regime (before and after 2025-03), then repeat the false-alarm and known-answer tests on 2025-26, with injections into months where D8 has no engine.
  • PS3 can use these labels for 2023-09 to 2025-02 only. Whether the 2026 flags are an engine that is back, solar misfit, or noise cannot be told from the residual alone; NGED's answer to question 1 would settle it.
  • Allow unit sizes of 1.5 and 2 MW together (the profile has two close peaks) and test whether D5's 1 MW engine and D11's battery are what the detector flags there.

docs.title: Retest of the faster Kalman level state with a fair known-answer gate
docs.text:
Take-home: making the level state faster does not fix offsets that last for hours. A faster filter recovers a long offset only late, and only by scoring worse on quiet days. A level shared across the four hour bands recovered under a fifth of the offset. The 15 smooth-offset days of experiment 175, on which the forecast error kept one sign for hours, are therefore not helped by the settings tried: no setting on the grid (m 3 to 50, k 2 to 6, z 0.5) recovered an injected offset of that kind without harming quiet days. Level adaptation is dropped.

We asked again whether a Kalman filter that speeds up its level state helps when the forecast error keeps one sign for hours. The level state is the slowly moving offset that the filter adds to the forecast, in the convex demand model (a generalised additive model, GAM) with a Kalman filter (GAM-K). The filter keeps one level state for each of four hour bands of the day. Experiment 190 could not tell, because its test counted many pairs (an origin and a target half-hour) that no filter with one state per hour band can learn about. This time we added a known one-signed offset to the observed power of ordinary days, as in experiment 190, and scored only the pairs the filter could know about. We measured the share of the offset's extra quantile-score loss that each filter removed (its recovery), and checked the filters on quiet days, which have no injected offset. A0 is the unchanged filter, A1 a faster per-band level, and A3 a level shared across bands (there is no A2 here; experiment 190's A2, the always-on boost, appears only in the next paragraph).

Verdict: not supported. Neither pre-registered recovery of 50% was reached within the +0.005-point bound on harm on quiet days. Experiment 190's finding stands: the always-on boost scored 0.023 points worse on the scored year, so a faster filter alone is not the answer.

docs.title: Arms and method
docs.text:
• A0: arm D of experiment 155, with the filter's level noise unchanged.
  • A1: the level's process noise is multiplied by m while the last k one-step innovations (pooled over the four hour bands) share one sign and their mean exceeds 0.5 times the day-before innovation spread. Grid: m in 3, 5, 10, 20, 50 and k in 2, 4, 6.
  • A3: as A1, and while the counter is on, one innovation moves the level of every band. Same grid. A3 was run under experiment 190's frozen setting (m 5, k 8, z 0.5), where it failed; experiment 190's stored scored-year forecasts give A3's real-row result, so no forecaster or filter was rerun on real rows.
  • Gate: offsets of 0.05, 0.10, and 0.20 of the day's median load, lasting 8, 16, and 36 hours, 8 days per substation per cell (40 days per cell), the same days and offsets as experiment 190. Every pair is labelled band_read (the target's band has a reading since the onset), other_read (it has none, another band has), or unread (no band has). Recovery is one minus the arm's excess loss over the clean A0, divided by A0's excess over the clean A0. Intervals resample whole days (4,000 resamples).
  • Selection: each setting of A1 and A3 was chosen by its recovery on the sizes 0.05 and 0.20 (A1 on band_read pairs, A3 on other_read pairs, all durations) and tested at 0.10. The chosen settings are A1 m 50, k 2 and A3 m 10, k 2.
  • Lab shortcuts: the forecast of a half-hour is the proxy-weather prediction plus the filter's correction, so weather error is absent. Origins come every 6 hours. Retraining schedule: the monthly T-all fits stored by experiment 136, shared by every arm.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Pre-registered predictions (the 0.10 size; recovery with its 95% interval):

  • P1 fails. A1 at m 50, k 2 recovered -0.95 (-7.7 to +0.2) of a 16-hour offset on band_read pairs, and 0.42 (-0.5 to +1.3) of a 36-hour offset. Four settings (m 10 k 2, m 20 k 2, m 20 k 4, m 50 k 4) reached 0.53 to 0.59, at 36 hours only. The 16-hour test holds just 141 band_read pairs (26 days).
  • P2 fails. A3 at m 10, k 2 recovered 0.11 (-1.1 to +0.8) and 0.17 (-0.3 to +0.5) of 16-hour and 36-hour offsets on other_read pairs. At experiment 190's setting A3 recovered -0.01 and -0.02.
  • P3 fails. On 40 days with no offset, A1 at m 50, k 2 scored +0.286 points against A0 (+0.145 to +0.434), and A3 at m 10, k 2 scored +0.709 (+0.482 to +0.938). The smallest-harm settings (m 3, k 6) recovered about 0.1 of a 36-hour offset.
  • P4 fails. On the scored year, A3 minus A0 is +0.0775 (95% interval +0.042 to +0.118; 0 of 5 substations better), from experiment 190's stored forecasts at m 5, k 8, z 0.5. A1 at that setting minus A0 is +0.0002 (-0.0046 to +0.0062).
  • P5 holds. In the first 6 hours after the onset, no band has been read in any pair, so no filter can learn about the offset. The share of pairs with the target band read rises from 0 to 0.05 (6 to 12 hours), 0.19 (12 to 24 hours), and 0.65 (24 to 36 hours) for the 36-hour offsets.

Where the boost helps (A1, m 50, k 2, 36-hour offset, band_read pairs): recovery is 0.64 at 24 to 36 hours after the onset and -4.4 at 12 to 24 hours. The -4.4 is not overshoot: A1 carries 0.72 of the offset there, and the ratio is large because A0 has already removed most of the excess loss (about 80%) and A1's own noise on quiet stretches is divided by the small remainder. Figure 3 clips values at -1.5.

  • At k 2 and z 0.5 the counter is on for 33% to 43% of quiet readings, so the selected settings act almost as always-on boosts. Selection ignored harm, and z stayed at 0.5.

  • With 40 quiet days the harm interval has a half-width of about 0.014 points, so the +0.005 bound of P3 could not be met even by an arm close to A0.

  • Post hoc: A3 on pairs whose target band was already read recovers -2.1 (-15.6 to -0.5) at 36 hours; the shared level adds noise to a band that was already right.

  • Experiment 190's setting for A1 (m 5, k 8) recovers 0.09 (0.00 to 0.48) at 36 hours on band_read pairs, close to arm D by construction.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median forecast minus mean forecast per site: not computed here, because no forecast was built; experiment 190 found 0.00 at every site and arm for the stored arms used.
  • Mean-forecast error beside the quantile score: not recomputed; experiment 190 reported C4 (A3 minus A1) as worse on both.
  • Triggers: trigger 1 fired (a known-answer test was failed by A3 and by A1 at 16 hours), and trigger 2 may apply, because P2 contradicts the prediction. An Opus audit ran (briefs/e197_audit_report.md, private). It reproduced the headline numbers, found no bug in the shared level, and cleared selection leakage. Its three corrections (the explanation of A3's failure, the "overshoot" reading, and the counter's on-share) are applied above. The verdict is unchanged.
  • Tails and curtailment cost were not scored: no new forecast exists.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Gate days are the even months of 2024-07 to 2025-06, on proxy weather, at 5 substations.
  • Origins are aligned to the offset's start (every 6 hours from 6 hours before it), so the first 6 hours are unread by construction, and the shares of read classes in later bins lean towards unread.
  • The 16-hour band-read test has 141 pairs from 26 days, so its interval is wide (-7.7 to +0.2).
  • Real-row evidence for A3 and A1 comes only from experiment 190's setting (m 5, k 8, z 0.5). The selected settings of this experiment were not run on real rows, because they already fail the gate's harm test.
  • The counter counts readings, so after a gap in the data it can span more than the stated hours.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• One option is to look at the mean forecast model for the 15 smooth-offset days: an input the GAM lacks, such as heating or behaviour, is the remaining candidate.
  • Another option is a small learned head that reads whether neighbouring Primaries show the same-sign residual, with the convex GAM-K as the comparison arm. The prediction that could fail: it recovers at least 20% of the excess loss on the 15 smooth-offset days, which no filter here did.

docs.title: Are the summer spikes in D8's power air-conditioning load, and does adding a cooling term lower the best-guess forecast's summer error at D8 and at the other Primaries?
docs.text:
We asked whether the upward jumps a colleague saw in the summer power of one substation, D8 (Marsh Lane, the label this project gives one of its Primary substations), are air-conditioning load, and whether the best-guess forecast needs a cooling term. The best-guess forecast is experiment 155's arm D. A cooling term is an extra forecast input that adds power when the temperature is above a threshold, called tau below. We looked at D8's June-to-September power against temperature, and at the size and timing of its departures from expected power (the output of a fitted demand model). We then added a cooling term to arm D at the five decision Primaries (D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16), the substations that have stored arm D forecasts (D8 has none), and rescored the June-to-September rows.

D8's spikes are not cooling load, and the cooling term did not help, but the experiment could not rule a cooling term out. Before 2023-08-15, D8's afternoon residual (metered minus expected power) has a partial Spearman correlation of +0.004 with the temperature above 20 degrees Celsius, controlling for day of year. Its large departures from expected power are mostly downward (the figures of D8's departures below), which matches experiments 186 and 194: a 6 MW gas engine, whose output is added back to D8's reading, causes downward shortfalls that follow the electricity price. The cooling term changed the five Primaries' summer score by -0.0002 points of quantile score (the pinball loss averaged over 11 quantiles, in points of effective capacity). The check that a threshold chosen on 4 fit months (July to September 2024 and June 2025) also helps in each held-out month failed, so the rule we fixed before seeing any result gives the verdict inconclusive. ERA5 below is the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts' reanalysis of past weather.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
D8 (experiment 159's stored table of D8's power, expected power, and ERA5 temperature; ERA5 is observed after the fact, which a live forecast would not have).

  • Departures of 1.5 MW or more from expected power in June to September: downward in 18.3%, 18.8%, 35.9%, and 52.1% of half-hours in 2022 to 2025, upward in 5.0%, 7.7%, 10.5%, and 6.5%. June 2026 reverses: 11.3% downward and 21.3% upward.
  • Each year's largest upward departure is 2.7 to 6.0 MW, and its largest downward departure is 4.6 to 9.3 MW. The median hour of both kinds is about 14:00 UTC (13:30 upward, 14:00 downward). Readings flagged as zero are 0.2% or fewer of summer half-hours in every year, so zero-reading artefacts do not explain the spikes (we did not test for stuck values).
  • Mean temperature is 19.0 degrees at upward departures, 17.6 at downward ones, and 17.0 across all summer half-hours. The daily maximum power has a correlation of 0.13 with the day's maximum temperature (a look at the data before the plan was written, not a test).
  • Prediction (1), that the correlation is below +0.15: the partial Spearman correlation of the afternoon residual with the hinge max(0, T - 20), on days of 22 degrees Celsius or more and before 2023-08-15, when the engine's readings stop carrying output, is +0.004 on 912 half-hours, below the +0.15 bar. After 2023-08-15 it is +0.051 on 1,308 half-hours.
  • We fitted the cooling hinge with tau 20 by median regression on summers 2022 and 2023 before 2023-08-15. On 15,407 later summer half-hours it changes the mean absolute residual by -0.001 MW (99% interval -0.004 to +0.001), against 1.97 MW before the term. With noise added to the temperature the change is -0.0001 MW (-0.002 to +0.001). The noise standard deviation of 1.2 degrees is an assumption, not a measured ensemble error.
  • The spikes are therefore not cooling load. The upward departures appear mostly when the downward shortfall fades in 2026. That pattern fits expected power having been learned from a window that contains the engine's shortfalls. We did not test that account here.

The five decision Primaries (arm D of experiment 155, ensemble temperature at forecast time).

  • Eligibility: at the median Primary the 4 fit months hold 111, 91, 70, 41, and 18 days above 16, 18, 20, 22, and 24 degrees Celsius, so all five thresholds were eligible. The leave-one-month-out comparison gave the best held-out score at 24 degrees, with a held-out gain in only 2 of 4 months, so the sign check failed.
  • C1 (the cooling arm's score minus arm D's, quantile score over leads 0.5 to 168 hours, June to September): -0.0002 points (99% interval -0.0103 to +0.0147; 14-day blocks, 11 blocks). Leads 0.5 to 48 hours: +0.0067 (-0.0061 to +0.0344). Leads 48 to 168 hours: -0.0030 (-0.0127 to +0.0067). Without the hottest spell (7 days): -0.0009 (-0.0035 to +0.0019). Hot days (12 days in which some Primary reaches 25 degrees, in 5 spells, a spell being a run of consecutive days): -0.0014 (-0.1241 to +0.1327) on 12,174 rows.
  • Absolute summer scores, arm D then cooling arm, in points: D5 3.182 and 3.178; D10 2.969 and 2.972; D11 2.300 and 2.307; D14 1.978 and 1.979; D16 2.314 and 2.306.
  • Placebo (200 draws of other weeks and years' temperatures, tau held at 24): gains from -0.0014 (5th percentile) to +0.0079 (95th), median +0.0019. C1 lies above the 5th percentile, so the term did not beat the placebo.
  • Known answer (0.1 MW per degree above 20 degrees injected at D10, shaped by an afternoon bell curve, driven by ERA5): the fitted effect is 49% of the injected sum, and C1 on the injected data is -0.068 (-0.155 to +0.004), so the check failed. Post hoc: forcing tau 20 gives 59%, and replacing the ensemble temperature by ERA5 gives 78% (tau chosen) or 83% (tau 20), with C1 -0.150 (-0.352 to -0.023) in the last case.
  • Prediction (2), that the correlation is below +0.15 at 5 or 6 of 6 Primaries: the partial correlation of the afternoon residual with the hinge is +0.26 at D10 and +0.21 at D9, and +0.04, +0.07, +0.01, and +0.07 at D5, D11, D14, and D16. It is below +0.15 at 4.
  • Post hoc, we selected afternoons with an ensemble-mean temperature of 25 degrees Celsius or more (leads up to 24 hours, June to September, all periods). On those afternoons, actual power minus arm D (in points of effective capacity) averages +0.90 (D5, 232 rows on 26 days), +4.68 (D10, 85 rows on 8 days), +2.48 (D11, 109 rows on 12 days), +0.60 (D14, 174 rows on 22 days), +1.17 (D16, 251 rows on 29 days), and +5.09 points (D9, 45 rows on 5 days). At 19 to 25 degrees the same difference averages -0.97, -1.08, -0.27, -1.36, -0.92, and +0.42 points.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast is 0.00 points at every Primary: arm D's median equals its mean.
  • The mean forecast's mean absolute error beside each score change, arm D then cooling arm, in points: D5 5.548 and 5.538; D10 4.997 and 4.999; D11 4.121 and 4.131; D14 3.458 and 3.454; D16 4.081 and 4.062. Neither the score nor the error moves in a consistent direction.
  • Leaving one Primary out moves C1 between -0.0020 and +0.0019. Every 99% interval includes zero.
  • Two conditions for a fresh audit were met. The known-answer check and the sign check failed, and the correlation prediction failed at 2 of 6 Primaries (the post hoc hot-end table is the explanation we tested). No audit has been run. Whether to run one is the maintainer's call, because the headline is a null. This page claims no more than inconclusive.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Arm D's spread was fitted on its tuning months (the months used to set the quantile width). Its mean includes recipe R, the step that corrects the last 14 days' error, and R may absorb part of a cooling load.
  • Only 4 summer months fit the hinge and 4 score it, from 2024 to 2026, so the scored rows are one summer (2025) plus June 2026 and hot days are few. The blocked intervals rest on 11 blocks.
  • D8 has no stored forecast from arm D, so its test uses the residual of the convex demand model, refitted on the 1st and 16th of each month (the table stored by experiments 130 and 159), with ERA5 temperature. D8's cooling term is not comparable with the Primaries'.
  • The pre-registered fit rule deviates in two small ways from the plan text: the eligibility count uses the median Primary, and the placebo draws temperatures a year (plus or minus 0 to 28 days) away for each 14-day block.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Fit a cooling hinge on the long weather history, pooled across Primaries, so that the fit holds dozens of days above 25 degrees instead of 4 to 18. Keep the known-answer injection as the gate.
  • Ask NGED whether the engine's output is still added back to D8's reading, which decides whether D8's upward departures are real demand.

docs.title: Plan
docs.text:
• Look first. Plot D8's June to September power against the day's maximum temperature and the hour of day, for each year from 2022 to 2026. Say whether the spikes are upward or downward, their size in MW, and when they occur.
  • Separate the candidates. Cooling load rises smoothly with temperature and peaks in the mid-afternoon of the hottest days. The engine shortfalls of experiments 186, 194, and 196 are downward and follow the price. Switching transfers are steps that repeat at both ends. Metering artefacts are readings of zero or a stuck value. The look sorts each large departure into one of the four by its shape, hour, and temperature.
  • Cheap test, then fit. Correlate the summer afternoon residual with temperature at every Primary, then fit the cooling hinge of the decision rule above and score it against arm D on the same rows.
  • Weather source. The hinge uses the ensemble-mean temperature at the valid time, which exists at forecast time. D8's panel uses ERA5, which arrives about 5 days late; that is a lab shortcut and is labelled.
  • Prior advice followed. Experiment 155's scoring (quantile score, rows outside the hand- filtered switching events) and its Primaries; the placebo is built from permuted days, not shifted indicators, as experiment 155's audit advised.

docs.title: Does reading D8's engine by its edge shape, by night-only evidence, and by price cut the false alarms of the quantised engine detector, and are the "false alarms" at D5, D10, and D11 real engines?
docs.text:
At one anonymised substation (D8), the engine detector from experiment 196 still flags 32.5% to 36.3% of night half-hours from March 2025, so solar panels are not the cause. None of three added tests (edge shape, night-only evidence, and a price gate) removes the flags. (D8 is one of 16 anonymised Primary substations; an engine is a gas-engine generator; a detector flags the half-hours in which its hidden Markov model gives the engine-running state the higher probability; the spark spread is the electricity price minus the gas fuel cost.) The detector from experiment 196 still flags 29% to 36% of D8's night half-hours from March 2025, when no solar panel produces power. The edge test, whose thresholds were fixed before any score was read, also discards about half of the engine signal that we added to D8's readings as a known answer. At D5 and D10, the false alarms of experiment 196 turn out to be mostly daytime flags: scored on night rows alone, experiment 196's detector passes the false-alarm bar (at most 3% of clean night half-hours flagged) at five of the six other Primaries, and the flagged days at D5, D10, and D11 do not follow the spark spread. The verdict is not supported.

We asked whether three facts about a gas engine, which experiment 196's detector ignored, would cut its false alarms. The facts are that an engine's edges are single-half-hour jumps, that it can run at night when solar panels cannot, and that it runs more when the system price is high. We tested each feature alone and together on the same known answer as experiment 196: the recorded output of a metered gas-engine generator (G2; K1 replays it at its true times in D8's reading and K2 replays it at nine shifted places in D8's engine-free history), subtracted from D8's reading. We then counted false alarms at six other Primaries and three periods of D8, and checked whether the flagged periods at D5, D10, and D11 look like engines. The method builds on Hart (1992) and Kolter and Jaakkola (2012) through experiment 196's hidden Markov model of the number of engine units running. The edge test, the night mask, and the price gate were written for this experiment.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Arms. v1 is experiment 196's detector unchanged. N sets every daytime reading to missing so that only night evidence counts. S drops a flagged spell unless both edges are one sharp jump. P drops a spell whose mean spark spread is in the lowest fifth. v2 is N plus S plus P. Post hoc: N plus P, and N plus S with either edge sharp plus P. All arms are scored on night rows, with all rows as secondary (printed_known_answers.txt, printed_false_alarms.txt).
  • Look first (printed_shape.txt). An engine's edges are sharp: 74% of G2's edges (61 edges) and 71% of the edges after injection into D8's residual (571 edges) are one clean half-hour jump, and the others have one partial half-hour. Real switching transfers are gradual: 8% of 12 starts and 25% of 12 ends are one clean jump. Unlabelled steps in D8's engine-free history are sharp as often as an engine's edges (65%, 49 steps), so sharpness cannot separate an engine from them. Only 24 of the 70 edges of the 35 labelled transfers are 1 MW or more.
  • Known answers, K1 and K2 pooled, night rows (9,542 half-hours). v1: recall at 1 unit 0.95 (0.90 to 0.98), at 2 or 3 units 1.00, precision 0.95 (0.92 to 0.97), energy error -8%. N: 0.92, 1.00, 0.88, -2%. v2: 0.53 (0.41 to 0.64), 0.66, 0.98, -40%, so every recall threshold fails. K1 and K2 alone give 0.50 (K1 is too small to read) and 0.53 at 1 unit for v2. Edge-test levels 0.5 and 0.7 give 0.58 and 0.44. Post hoc N plus P: 0.90, 0.99, 0.88, -3%. Post hoc lenient edge test: 0.88 (0.82 to 0.94), 0.99, 0.89, -4%.
  • Why the edge test fails (post hoc, printed_diag_edges.txt). At the true start of G2's runs only 69% of edges pass the test, and at the true end 81%. The likely causes, inferred and not tested, are short runs whose edges lie within 3 half-hours of each other and steps under half a unit in D8's noise.
  • K3 (G2 injected into D8's night rows from 2025-03, recall only, descriptive). v1 recall at 1 unit 0.92 (0.79 to 0.99); v2 0.36 (0.19 to 0.55). Precision is not meaningful for K3.
  • False alarms at night (flagged share; false active days a month). Bar: 3% and 1 day. v1 passes at D3 (0.4%, 0.22), D5 (0.3%, 0.07), D10 (0.1%, 0.04), D14, D16, and D8's engine-free history, and fails at D11 (4.6%, 1.08). N fails at D8's engine-free history (2.6%, 1.45). v2 is 0.0% with 0.00 days at every one of these, and v2 on all rows is also 0.0% at D3, D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16.
  • D8 from 2025-03 (relaxed bar capped at 10%). v1 flags 36.3% of night half-hours (22.9 days a month) in 2025-03 to 2025-12 and 32.5% (18.8) in 2026-01 to 2026-06. N: 33.1% and 30.3%. v2: 16.7% (10.6) and 16.5% (9.7). Post hoc lenient: 31.6% and 28.7%. The left tail below -2.5 MW holds 18.8% and 11.6% of night half-hours. Both periods fail the bar for every arm.
  • Price gate. The gate changes little: at night it removes under 1.5% of D8's flagged half-hours from 2025-03 and none at D3, D10, or D14. On all rows it cuts D5's false active days from 2.02 to 1.72 a month and D10's from 1.05 to 0.90. The gate is only scored from 2023-06 (D8's engine-free history has 576 even-month rows with a price), and K2's price is G2's own at the time it recorded the output, a choice that favours the gate.
  • Flagged periods at D5, D10, and D11 (supporting evidence only, printed_step5.txt).
    • D8 while the engine is visible (2023-09 to 2025-02, positive control): flagged days have a positive spark spread +11.1 points more often than matched unflagged days (95% 3.5 to 18.1) and a spread £19.8 per MWh higher (15.4 to 24.6); the flagged half-hours peak in the evening.
    • D5: -1.0 points (-14.4 to +12.4); 27% of flagged half-hours at night against 46% of all rows; flags peak at 10:00 to 16:00 UTC. The 13 days with 4 or more flagged night half-hours show +30.8 points (0 to 61.5), too few to read.
    • D10: -14.8 points (-31.1 to +1.6); 3% of flagged half-hours at night; flags peak at midday.
    • D11: -45.0 points (-70.0 to -15.0) from 20 flagged days; 65% at night, with a flat hour profile, which suggests a few long spells that are not an engine's evening pattern.
    • D8 from 2025-03: +6.8 points (-4.5 to +18.2), but 482 of 485 days are flagged, so only 3 unflagged days exist, reused to match 44 flagged days, and the test cannot be read.
  • ECR (printed_ecr.txt; supporting evidence, NGED has not been asked). D5 has a 1.0 MW oil engine 3.25 km away, connected 2021-03-11, before every flagged period. D10 has no gas, oil, CHP, or battery site within 5 km. D11 has a 0.2 MW battery connected 2026-04-13 and a 0.499 MW biomass steam turbine connected 2014, neither of which is a price-following engine in the flagged period. D5's flags do not follow the spark spread, so the ECR engine and the flagged periods do not match.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast per site: not applicable; no forecast is made.
  • Mean-forecast error beside a quantile-score contrast: not applicable.
  • Triggers fired (no audit was run; the experiment is short of credits for an Opus audit, and the maintainer can call one). Trigger 2: the prediction that night evidence cuts D8's night flags to under 10% failed (33%), and the prediction that flagged days at D5 follow the spark spread failed. The session tested an explanation for each: D8's night rows are flagged at about half the rate of its day rows but still at 29% to 36%, so solar is not the whole cause, and the spark-spread test shows that the positive control works. Trigger 5: v1 on night rows beats N (which holds less input) at D8's engine-free history (0.0% against 2.6%).
  • Edge-test thresholds (an edge is sharp when one half-hour carries 0.6 of the step, and the step is at least 0.5 of an engine unit, 0.875 MW) came from the look at G2's edges, so K1 and K2 could not test them independently; the test fails even there.
  • Lab shortcuts. We used the expected power in the stored panel, which is driven by ERA5 weather, smoothed posterior probabilities, the frozen 1.75 MW unit from experiment 196, noise for the other Primaries fitted on their whole history. The noise fit saw D8's odd months, so D8's engine-free history is scored on even months.
  • Edge cases. D3's coordinates are approximate (the night mask moves by minutes). Night is defined by solar elevation below -3 degrees, and an active day is a UTC date, so a night spanning midnight counts on two dates.
  • Plan review. A Sonnet reviewer raised 10 objections to the plan before any score was read; the plan was revised for 9 of them (the price in the K2 injections was kept at G2's own recording time, flagged as favourable to the gate).

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Find what causes the step changes in D8's night load after 2025-03: look at the hour of day and the size of D8's night steps, and compare them with the connection date of its 8.91 MW of 11 kV solar and of any new battery.
  • Do not run PS3 or later stages on the engine detector. Experiment 196's labels remain usable for 2023-09 to 2025-02 only.
  • If a detector of price-following assets is still wanted, use the evening pattern of D8's visible engine (Figure 5) as the signature, not the edge shape.

docs.title: Differentiable physics: a pooled learned correction head on arm D's forecast and recent errors
docs.text:
Take-home: the network's gain over arm D comes mainly from correcting how arm D's error depends on its own forecast level and the calendar, and reading recent errors adds little that we can detect. Arm D is the best forecast of experiment 155: a convex demand model, a Kalman filter (a method that updates a forecast from its recent errors), a winter night offset, and recipe R (subtract 0.75 times the mean error of the last 14 days). We asked whether a small neural network, trained on many substations at once, can correct arm D better than the filter and recipe R do. This extends experiment 142, whose network failed its test for lack of rows. We trained one network on 6 substations, scored it on 5 of them (D5, D10, D11, D14, D16) in the year from 2025-07-02, and compared it with a copy that was given no past errors and no Kalman state (the "blind head"). The result is partly supported. The network beats arm D, the blind head gets most of that gain, and a table without a network comes within 0.01 to 0.02 points of the blind head when both train on one year.

The numbers. Scores are quantile scores (twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles) in points of effective capacity, at 15.5 to 39 hours ahead, and a lower score is better. Trained on 2020 onward, the network scores 0.125 points lower than arm D (99% interval 0.060 to 0.209 points lower) and the blind head 0.100 lower, so reading errors adds 0.025 (head minus blind head -0.025, interval -0.106 to +0.029, which includes zero). Trained on the ensemble-weather year only, the network is 0.071 lower, the blind head 0.054 lower, and a table fitted with the pinball loss 0.038 lower. An Opus audit found no leakage. The extra gain from 2020-onward training needs arm D's forecast level and an ensemble-era flag together. The known-answer gate marginally failed (29% against 30%), and under the pre-registered rule that removes the neural corrector from the queue. We keep the verdict partly supported because the gate failure is within the seed range (22% to 34%) and the audit explains it. This is a weaker test than the brief planned: 6 substations, not 16 Primary substations, and no weather input.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• The head is compared with arm D, which already contains recipe R. Its contrast stands in for the pre-registered contrast with recipe R.
  • Method. One network (two hidden layers of 128 units, a 4-dimensional substation embedding, a linear skip) trained with the pinball loss at the 11 quantiles (Koenker and Bassett (1978)) on arm D's rows at leads 12 to 48 hours, following the pooled-network design of experiment 142. Quantiles are median + correction + exp(scale) x (arm D quantile - arm D median), so they cannot cross. Inputs: the last 12 half-hours of errors known at the origin (3.5 hours old), the mean error of the last 14 days at the row's half-hour, the mean error at the same weekday and half-hour in the last 4 weeks, the lead, half-hour, day of week, and arm D's mean. Stage 3 adds the Kalman level and anomaly and a flag for ensemble weather.
  • Two training sets. Stage 2: the 6 substations' stored ensemble year (2024-07 to 2025-06), 125,000 rows. Stage 3: the shared file of the sibling experiment, which adds forecasts on past weather from 2020 onward, 592,000 rows (4.7 times as many). Both score only the ensemble-weather scored year (2025-07-02 to 2026-06-29).
  • Rows against experiment 142. The gate fit has 287,000 rows from 3,900 site-runs, against about 3,200 samples in experiment 142: about 90 times the rows, but only 1.2 times the independent history.
  • Gate (6 substations, 3 seeds, 8-week injection on held-out blocks). Level step of +3 points: head 29% (22% to 34%, gate 30%), recipe R 67%. Saturday-evening shift of +3 points: head 21% (20% to 23%, gate 15%), recipe R 11%. A first version without the same-weekday input recovered -1.5% of the shift. The input was added before any scored read.
  • Scored year, five decision substations, leads 15.5 to 39 hours, outside switching events. Arm D scores 2.432 points. Stage 2: head 2.361, blind head 2.377 (C1 head minus arm D -0.071, interval -0.154 to -0.014; C2 blind minus arm D -0.054, -0.089 to -0.026; C3 head minus blind -0.017, -0.109 to +0.039). Stage 3: head 2.307, blind head 2.332 (C1 -0.125, -0.209 to -0.060; C2 -0.100, -0.140 to -0.064; C3 -0.025, -0.106 to +0.029). Experiment 169's calibrated-spread arm D scores 2.430 on the same rows, so spread calibration is not the source.
  • Plain recalibration arm (no network, stage 3 rows). A ridge regression on one-hot site by half-hour, site by day of week, site by lead band, site by forecast-level bin, and half-hour by day of week, plus an ensemble-era flag, shifts arm D's median; a per-cell factor, chosen by pinball loss, scales the quantile offsets. Fitted to all training rows it scores 0.049 points worse than arm D (interval -0.001 to +0.096). Fitted to the ensemble year only it scores -0.030 (interval -0.053 to -0.007). The audit refitted the table with the pinball loss on the same ensemble year and got -0.038, against -0.047 to -0.057 for the blind network, so the ridge's smaller gain probably came from its squared-error fit. The comparison of that ridge with the 2020-onward network is therefore not like for like.
  • Per substation, stage 3 head minus arm D: D5 -0.179, D10 -0.075, D11 -0.008, D14 -0.133, D16 -0.243, D9 -0.104. Stage 2: D5 -0.081, D10 -0.066, D11 +0.040, D14 -0.112, D16 -0.142, D9 +0.014.
  • Tails (decision substations, stage 3 head against arm D). Pinball at q99: 0.391 against 0.411. At q01: 0.347 against 0.386. Coverage at q95: 93.1% against 94.5%; at q99: 97.6% against 98.1%. The head lowers tail pinball loss but lowers coverage in the upper tail.
  • Curtailment cost and the manual heuristic. Not scored: the stored rows are single-substation demand, not node and generator forecasts.
  • Audit (Opus, fresh agent, report in the private briefs folder). No leakage: the error inputs never use a reading newer than 3.5 hours before the origin (tested by overwriting the error grid from 25 random positions), the Kalman level and anomaly are the filter state at the cut-off, and training ends before the scored year. Retrained arms match the stored contrasts within 0.01 points. In the ensemble era the level and anomaly come from experiment 136's arm A2 filter, not arm D's own filter, so they are causal but inconsistent between eras. The 2020-onward gain needs the forecast level and the era flag together: zeroing either cuts the blind arm from -0.099 to about -0.05. The spread head is worth 0.014 (one year) and 0.030 (2020 onward). The 29% step recovery reflects the data: arm D already contains the filter and recipe R, so its training errors rarely keep a level shift, and a median regression on the three error features recovers at best 30% of the step. Recipe R's 67% is not comparable, because it assumes arm D would not react to the injected errors.
  • Caveats. No ensemble weather input. Stage 3 trains on 4 years of forecasts built on past weather, whose errors are smaller than live ensemble errors, and it flags the era. The gate is one 8-week block per injection. The prediction that the stage 2 gain would be -0.04 to +0.02 was too pessimistic about the sign; the prediction that error-reading adds little held.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast per site (stage 3 head): D10 -0.69, D11 -0.01, D14 -0.79, D16 -0.33, D5 -0.13, D9 -0.11 points. These are arm D's own offsets plus the head's correction.
  • Error of the median forecast beside the score: mean absolute error arm D 4.191, stage 3 head 4.006, blind head 4.063; the contrasts point the same way.
  • Triggers that fired: (1) the known-answer gate marginally failed, 29% against 30%; (5) the blind head, nested in the head, scores almost as well; (7) the sibling experiment's design may depend on this result. The audit confirmed the contrasts and found no leakage (see Results). Leaving one substation out never changes the sign of C1 (range -0.096 to -0.156 in stage 3). The audit found nothing that changes a contrast.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Fit a pinball-loss table with a forecast-level by era term to all years. If it matches the blind network, no network is needed for this gain.
  • Add the ensemble-mean temperature and shortwave inputs, which the stored forecasts lack.

docs.title: Experiment 201: a small neural network that corrects the convex demand model's forecast
docs.text:
A small neural network that reads the convex demand model's forecast lowers that forecast's quantile score by about 0.09 points of effective capacity (3%), and adding weather, calendar, or lagged power did not help further. A negative contrast means a lower (better) score. Arm D is the best-guess forecast from experiment 155: a convex demand model whose recent errors feed a Kalman filter, with a winter night offset and a 14-day error profile (recipe R) subtracted. We trained a neural network with two hidden layers of 64 units to shift arm D's median and rescale the width of its uncertainty bands. Each arm gives the neural network more inputs: arm 1 the demand model's own inputs, arm 2 adds calendar and holiday flags, arm 3 adds ensemble-mean weather, and arm 4 adds power lagged by whole days. The neural network never saw the scored year, 2025-07 to 2026-06, which covers six substations. Experiment 142 gave a network the residual history only.

Most of the gain is a recalibration of arm D's own output, the useful lead is a lift of up to 3 points in the median below -3 °C and above 24 °C, and holidays get worse. Arms 1 to 4 each score about 0.09 to 0.11 points below arm D. A neural network given calendar, lead, and site but no forecast or weather (arm 0) scored +0.017 against arm D, which is no gain. A neural network given only arm D's forecast, lead, and time of day (arm 6) scored -0.086. The gain therefore comes from re-reading arm D's own output. The neural network mostly raises the median on hot days and very cold days, which suggests the convex demand model lacks a temperature term.

The pre-registered prediction failed on both conditions. The interval of arm 3 or arm 4 was not wholly below -0.02 points, and bank holidays and Christmas worsened by more than 0.05 points. The Christmas group is one month (2025-12, plus 2 days of 2026-01), so its interval is not informative.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Arms and inputs. Arm 1 has 19 input columns, arm 2 28, arm 3 32, and arm 4 41, so the arms differ in their number of input columns. Arm 0 (blind: lead, calendar, site; 25 columns), arm 5 (arm 1 without the filter's level and anomaly), and arm 6 (arm 1 without the temperature, solar, and darkness terms) are post hoc. Network: two hidden layers of 64, zero-initialised output, weight decay 1e-3, early stopping on every fourth month of the pool, pinball loss over 11 quantiles, 3 seeds.
  • Row set. Training uses every row before 2025-07: past-weather rows from 2020-01 to 2024-06, plus ensemble-era rows of experiment 155's tuning and replicate months. Scoring uses the 561,363 scored-year rows (one per substation, forecast issue time, and valid time) at the six substations D5, D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16, outside the hand-filtered switching events. Arm D rows are experiment 155's stored forecasts, and its five-substation score reproduces experiment 155's 2.756 exactly.
  • Scores over leads 0.5 to 168 h (points; arm D 2.691). Arm 0 2.709; arm 1 2.599; arm 2 2.587; arm 3 2.597; arm 4 2.584; arm 5 2.621; arm 6 2.606.
  • Contrast against arm D (97.5% month-blocked interval). Arm 1 -0.092 (-0.197 to -0.001); arm 2 -0.104 (-0.196 to -0.020); arm 3 -0.094 (-0.195 to -0.002); arm 4 -0.107 (-0.219 to +0.032); arm 0 +0.017 (-0.019 to +0.065); arm 5 -0.070 (-0.162 to +0.005); arm 6 -0.086 (-0.173 to -0.031). At day D+1: arm 1 -0.064, arm 3 -0.055, arm 4 -0.071.
  • Special groups, arm 3 minus arm D. Cold nights -0.189; sunny daylight -0.096; Economy 7 nights -0.120; bank holidays +0.437 (+0.290 to +0.570); Christmas +0.352 (-0.374 to +0.360, from one month). The bank-holiday and Christmas groups hold 19 days from one year (9 at Christmas).
  • Tail calibration, arm D then arm 3. Coverage of q01 2.3% then 2.1%; q05 7.1% then 7.3%; q95 94.7% then 93.7%; q99 98.2% then 97.8%. Pinball at q95 1.452 then 1.391; at q99 0.445 then 0.441. Arm 4's q95 coverage fell to 90.3%.
  • Known-answer gate (passed). On the scored year the network recovered 71% of an injected interaction (cold-evening effect up to 3 points plus a 1-point Saturday-evening shift): 24% of the cold-evening part and 76% of the Saturday part. On rows with no injection the network scored 0.005 points worse than the same network trained on the real power. Post hoc: the pre-registered wording measured change against arm D, which cannot work because the network also improves arm D (-0.09), so the recovery and the harm are measured against a control network trained on the real power.
  • What the network learned. The median shift is 0 to 0.5 points between 0 and 21 °C and rises to +1.7 (arm 1) or +3.3 (arm 3) points at 24 to 27 °C and to +1.3 or +2.9 at -6 °C (figure 3); it is near zero at every lead except the last day (figure 4).

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Difference from experiment 200's blind arm. The pooled correction head of experiment 200 reports that a head with its error and Kalman-state inputs zeroed keeps most of its gain (-0.100 of -0.125). Our arm 0 is blinder: it has no input from arm D at all, so it gains nothing (+0.017). The two agree where they overlap: arm 6, which keeps arm D's mean, bands, lead, and time of day but not the weather, scores -0.086, and arm 5, which drops the filter state, scores -0.070. The gain therefore comes from a function of arm D's own mean and the calendar, not from reading its recent errors.

  • Median minus mean, per site. Arm D's q50 equals its mean exactly at all six substations (0.000), so rescaling the bands cannot move the median.

  • Error of the median beside the quantile score. The mean absolute error of the median is 4.623 for arm D and 4.581 (arm 1), 4.535 (arm 2), 4.554 (arm 3), 4.476 (arm 4), the same direction as the quantile score.
  • Leave one substation out. Every leave-one-out contrast for arms 1 to 4 stays between -0.047 and -0.147; D16 carries the most (-0.32 alone).
  • Audit triggers. The ml-experiment skill lists seven conditions that call for an audit. Trigger 2 (a result contradicts its own prediction) fired (arms 1 and 2 were predicted to gain 0.00 to 0.01 and gained about 0.09 to 0.10); arms 0, 5, and 6 test the explanation and support it (see above), so no audit was run. Triggers 1, 3, 4, and 5 did not fire. Trigger 6 was not checked against a sister experiment.

docs.title: Caveats and what to try next
docs.text:
• Early-era rows have smaller weather error than live rows. The 2020-01 to 2024-06 training rows use ERA5 (the ECMWF reanalysis) and CAMS (the Copernicus atmosphere service) as the weather, so a neural network trained on them may under-correct. The scored year uses ensemble-mean weather only.
  • One scored year and six substations. The gain rests on 12 months, and D16 gives the largest share of it. Sixteen Primaries were planned; the other ten lack a pinned solar capacity and ensemble frames, so they were not built.
  • The gain is concentrated in three substations. Arm 1 scores -0.162 at D5, -0.091 at D14, and -0.320 at D16, but +0.024 at D10 and +0.028 at D9; arm 3 is +0.038 at D9. Arm 4's q99 coverage is 96.0% and its q99 pinball is 0.511 against arm D's 0.445.
  • The gate's weather part was weak. The cold-evening effect was injected from the observed temperature while the network sees the ensemble-mean temperature, and only 24% of that part was recovered; the pass rests on the Saturday part (76%). The statement that weather adds nothing is therefore weaker than the calendar and lag statements.
  • Two small leaks and a clip. 4,320 training rows from the last replicate run have valid times inside the scored year (targets only, 0.8% of valid times). The spread tables are refitted on the odd months of the training period, so training bands are slightly better calibrated than the scored year's. Network inputs are clipped at 5 standard deviations because a lagged-power spike of 140 points sent arm 4 far outside the data in a first run.
  • No refit through the scored year, and one seed pool. The network is trained once on rows before 2025-07. A weekly refit, as production would use, was not tested.
  • Wind, humidity, and school holidays were not available in the stored arrays, so arm 3 has temperature and shortwave only, and the calendar has no school-holiday flag.
  • A candidate follow-up is extra heating and cooling terms in the convex demand model. The prediction that could fail: adding a cooling hinge above 21 °C and a steeper heating hinge below 0 °C to arm D lowers its score by at least 0.05 points without a network.

docs.title: Experiment 202: the two-number solar summary in a rolling replay of the live weather layer
docs.text:
Storing two numbers per half-hour for each weather forecast keeps the whole 2.3% improvement in the daylight quantile score when the numbers are produced the way the live service would produce them. The quantile score measures the forecast's uncertainty bands. The two numbers are the mean and the standard deviation of how much solar generation each of the 51 ensemble members implies (the ensemble is 51 runs of one weather model from perturbed starting conditions), stored as 4-byte floating-point (float32) columns in the weather layer, the part of the service that holds weather data. Two fitted factors per lead band rescale the numbers, and we refitted those factors each month on history that had completed before the month began.

Experiment 193 found that the two numbers keep 98% of the 2.2% daylight gain that running all 51 members gives (experiment 187). Experiment 193 fitted its factors on interleaved months, some later than the months they were applied to, and held the numbers in 8-byte (float64) precision. Here we replayed the scored year of experiment 193: for each month, the factors came from the trailing 365 days of runs whose last valid time (origin plus 168 hours) was before the month's first origin, the two columns were rounded to float32, and each run used only its own 00 UTC ensemble run (published 9 hours before the origin). The score is the quantile score (twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles, in points of effective capacity; lower is better). Arm A is experiment 187's full best-guess forecast; arm M passes all 51 members through the solar term; Q2 is experiment 193's two-number arm with fixed factors; R2 is the replay. D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16 are anonymised substations. Each interval is a 95% interval from resampling whole months.

The rule registered before the run was met: R2's daylight change from arm A is -2.30% (interval -2.96% to -1.61%), under the -1.5% threshold, with all five substations negative. The verdict is supported.

  • Arms and row set. A and M are experiment 187's, read from experiment 184's stored arrays; Q2 is experiment 193's stored arm. R2: Gaussian points from the two float32 columns, factors per lead band (offset 0.75 to 0.9, spread 1.0 to 1.4, refitted monthly), the fit rows being every stored run (all substations) of the trailing 365 days that had completed. R2o: factors fitted on the scored month itself, an in-sample ceiling outside the verdict. RR: placebo with every response zero. Row set fold_a_daily_gap_v1, five substations, leads 0.5 to 168 hours, outside switching events; 211,576 daylight rows in 291 complete runs and 12 month blocks (a 13th, 2026-07, holds no daylight row). Monthly refits of the mean forecast (experiment 155) are unchanged.
  • Headline C1 (daylight, change from arm A). R2 -2.30% (-2.96% to -1.61%); Q2 -2.20% (-2.88% to -1.49%); M -2.23% (-2.97% to -1.48%); R2o -2.75% (-3.46% to -2.07%); RR -0.17% (-0.33% to +0.02%). R2 minus Q2: -0.11% (-0.24% to +0.06%). R2's share of M's gain: 103% (93% to 116%).
  • Absolute scores (quantile score, daylight). A 3.632; M 3.551; Q2 3.553; R2 3.549; R2o 3.533; RR 3.626. All rows: A 2.752, R2 2.714. Night 1.981 and twilight 2.299 for every arm, because only daylight rows change.
  • Substations (daylight, R2; Q2 in brackets). D5 -3.25% (-3.27%); D10 -1.87% (-1.18%); D11 -0.89% (-0.99%), interval -1.67% to -0.01%; D14 -1.61% (-1.65%); D16 -3.20% (-3.35%). Leaving one substation out keeps the change between -1.9% and -2.6% with every interval under zero.
  • Lead bands (daylight, R2). Under 24 hours -1.80%; 24 to 72 hours -1.91%; 72 to 168 hours -2.57%. A separate 12 to 36 hour band gives -1.89%. By cloud cover: overcast -0.81% (interval -1.74% to +0.11%), partly cloudy -2.80%, clear -1.96%; the sunniest third -4.75% (-6.92% to -3.18%).
  • Months and halves. First six months -2.13%, last six -2.44%, so the early months with less history do not fall short. Monthly changes run from +0.94% (2025-12) to -4.23% (2026-03).
  • By valid hour of the day (stand-in for the slot cut). The brief's four 6-hourly forecast slots cannot be scored: the stored forecasts have one origin per run (09:00 UTC after the 00 UTC run), so a 15:00, 21:00, or 03:00 origin would need the forecast stack refitted and re-run, and this experiment does not do that. By valid hour (UTC): 06 to 09 -1.88%; 09 to 12 -2.50%; 12 to 15 -2.08%; 15 to 18 -2.93%; 18 to 21 -0.62% (interval -1.16% to +0.12%).
  • Tails (daylight; coverage / pinball loss). R2: q01 0.016 / 0.236, q05 0.058 / 0.838, q95 0.941 / 0.877, q99 0.983 / 0.245. Q2: 0.013 / 0.233, 0.051 / 0.839, 0.947 / 0.879, 0.986 / 0.242. A: 0.027 / 0.265, 0.078 / 0.907, 0.933 / 0.924, 0.979 / 0.262. Daylight q05-to-q95 coverage: A 0.854, Q2 0.896, R2 0.883 (nominal 0.90). The curtailment-cost saving against manual_heuristic was not scored, because the experiment changes daylight band widths on stored rows and writes no node-level forecast frame.
  • Gates. G1: the copied code with experiment 193's fixed factors reproduces its stored Q2 to 7.6e-06 (largest quantile difference). G2: float32 against float64 columns changes the daylight quantile score by 1.2e-10. G3: every run's initialisation plus 9 hours is at or before its origin (derived from the run index, so the gate checks the date arithmetic only). G4: RR recovers 7% of R2's gain, under 20%. G5: the fit code run on experiment 193's tuning rows with float64 columns returns experiment 193's four stored factor pairs exactly, so the monthly fit is a test of the same code path. G1 tests the apply path only. All pass.
  • Checks. The median forecast minus the mean forecast at 12 to 36 hours for R2 is -0.14 (D5), -0.03 (D10), -0.05 (D11), -0.04 (D14), and -0.05 (D16) points, the same pattern as Q2; arm A is 0.000. R2 shares its mean forecast with Q2 (arm A's mean plus the mean response), whose daylight mean absolute error changed by -0.13% (-0.45% to +0.27%) in experiment 193, the same direction as the score. No audit trigger fired: no control failed (RR moved the score by -0.17% against a half-width of 0.18); R2 matches its prediction (-2.30% against an expected -1.9% to -2.2%) and experiment 193's; the leave-one-out check keeps the sign; no nested arm beat its container (R2o, the in-sample ceiling, beats R2 by design); the interval width (1.35 points) matches Q2's 1.39; no later design depends on this headline.
  • Caveats. The replay reuses experiment 187's rows and arm A, whose offsets, Kalman state, and 14-day profile were calibrated on the 2024-07 to 2025-06 months, so the fit rows are in-sample for arm A and the scored rows are not (shared with experiments 187 and 193). The switching mask and usable-row filter use hindsight and filter the fit rows as well as the scored rows. The 00 UTC run is the only run used, so the replay does not test a missing or late run. Fit rows pool all seven substations (the scored contrast uses five). The first month (2025-07) has 12 months of history, all of it from one summer. Two cuts (overcast daylight, and valid hours 18 to 21 UTC) have intervals that include zero.
  • What to try next. (1) Build the two columns into the weather layer and the serving path, and measure the runtime saving (prediction that could fail: the stored columns reproduce R2's score to 0.001 points). (2) Score R2 on the node curtailment metric of studies.node_curtailment, because the gain is largest at q01 (pinball loss -11%). (3) Re-run the replay at 15:00, 21:00, and 03:00 origins once the forecast stack can be re-run at those origins, to test the slot cut.

docs.title: Do the extra real transfers that experiment 195's learned score finds lower the masked forecast's error, without harm on ordinary days?
docs.text:
Masking the forecast with the alarms of experiment 195's learned score did not lower the error after real switching transfers by a reliable margin, and it did not meet the no-harm limit on ordinary days. A switching transfer moves load between Primary substations for hours or days. A "mask" sets the forecast's recent power readings aside while an alarm says a transfer is under way. The pair alarm (a step at one substation matched by an opposite step at a neighbour) fed the mask of experiment 163, and experiment 195's learned score, a statistical score trained to flag transfers, was meant to find more transfers. On the 7 logged transfers that best guess 2 (the best-guess forecast of experiment 87) also scores, the learned-score mask scored 0.99 points of effective capacity worse than the pair-alarm mask (7.31 against 6.32). On the wider set of 11 transfers it scored 0.46 points better (5.62 against 6.08), but the 95% interval for that difference runs from -3.5 to +3.7. The 11-transfer sign flips when the substation labelled D16 is left out. The pattern in the transfers is consistent with this explanation: the learned alarms often fire late in a transfer or near its end, while the pair alarm fires at the start of the long ones.

Switching transfers contaminate the forecast's recent-power correction. The forecast is a generalised additive model with a Kalman filter (Kalman, 1960) on its recent errors (GAM-K, as in experiment 163). Experiment 163 found that masking while the pair alarm is active brings the error after real transfers down to that of a forecast with no recent power. Experiment 195 found that a learned score on the detectors' features matches 22 to 24 of 35 real transfers lasting over 1 day against 19 for the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC). This experiment replays those alarms through the mask of experiments 163 and 171 and scores the forecast.

The replay masks the unchanged GAM-K forecast with experiment 195's alarms. Nothing is refitted. An alarm sets readings missing from its step stamp, once the alarm is known, until its end is known. Three alarm sources were replayed: the "R re-ranker" (a small neural network, known 4 days after the step because it reads 4 days after the step), a logistic regression on the same features (known 2 days after the step), and experiment 195's re-run of RO-NC (2 days). The pair alarm and the unmasked forecast were recomputed on the same rows as controls. A score is twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles, in points of effective capacity (percent of a substation's effective capacity; lower is better), on the six Primary substations of experiments 163 and 171.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Verdict: partly supported under the pre-registered rule, and a weak result. G1' (gain on the 11-transfer set) holds on its point estimate (-0.46, bar -0.3). G1 (the brief's bar on the 7 transfers that best guess 2 also scores) fails (+0.99). G2 (no harm on ordinary days) fails because its upper bound, +0.086, is above the +0.05 limit. The G1' interval, -3.5 to +3.7, includes zero, and leaving D16 out gives +0.64.
  • Units. A transfer is one logged event. The 7, 11, and 13 transfers are distinct events, and a bootstrap resamples whole transfers. Two of the 11 touch two of the six substations, so the 11 transfers hold 13 scoring windows (one substation and one transfer each).
  • Arms. Alarm sources LEARNED_R (re-ranker, known 192 half-hours after the step), LEARNED_F (logistic regression, 96), RONC_195 (96), and, post hoc, LEARNED_R96 (the re-ranker as if known at 96). Controls: K0 (no mask), PAIR_NEW (every pair alarm), and PAIR_GATED (balance score of at least 0.7). Nothing is refitted: the cached daily GAM-K runs of 2024-04 to 2026-06 are reused. Two shortcuts apply. The end of an alarm that experiment 147 also raised is known at the later of experiment 147's stamp and the estimated end plus 60 half-hours, where the plan said 96 (a re-run with 96 leaves every transfer score unchanged and moves the ordinary-day contrast by +0.0005). The cached runs are daily (09:00 UTC) and not 6-hourly, because the cached member forecasts exist only for those runs.
  • The controls reproduce. On the 7 transfers, K0, PAIR_NEW, and best guess 2 score 13.686, 6.321, and 10.091, as experiment 163 printed. The pooled gated pair-alarm contrast is +0.030 (-0.012 to +0.074), against +0.030 (-0.011 to +0.074) in experiment 171; the bootstrap draws differ in the third decimal.
  • Mean score of the 72 hours after a transfer ends (points). The 7 transfers that best guess 2 also scores: K0 13.686, PAIR_NEW 6.321, PAIR_GATED 6.336, LEARNED_R 7.310, LEARNED_F 7.370, RONC_195 7.361, best guess 2 10.091. The 11 transfers of experiment 163's scored and replicate months: K0 10.129, PAIR_NEW 6.083, PAIR_GATED 5.752, LEARNED_R 5.623, LEARNED_F 5.660, RONC_195 5.707. All 13 transfers in every cached run (post hoc): K0 8.313, PAIR_NEW 5.351, PAIR_GATED 5.119, LEARNED_R 4.829, LEARNED_F 4.795, RONC_195 4.782.
  • Gain contrasts (arm minus PAIR_NEW, 95% interval from resampling whole transfers). LEARNED_R: 7 transfers +0.989 (-2.229 to +6.963); 11 transfers -0.460 (-3.505 to +3.718); 13 transfers -0.522 (-3.086 to +2.704). LEARNED_F and RONC_195 differ from LEARNED_R by under 0.1 points on each set. Each learned mask beats no mask by 3.5 to 6.4 points, and so does the pair alarm (-7.365 on the 7 transfers).
  • One transfer decides the 7-transfer result, and its scoring window overlaps the next transfer. A 580-hour transfer at D5 (card ce4b82, where a card is the identifier of a logged transfer) scores 22.45 with no mask, 12.81 with the pair alarm, and 22.45 with the re-ranker. No learned alarm lies near its onset. The only learned alarm there is the onset of the next transfer on the same series (card b2f7c0), known after the 72-hour scoring window closes. The 72 hours after ce4b ends lie wholly inside b2f7c0, so those 849 rows measure the forecast during b2f7c0. The overlap comes from experiment 163's row set, and no other of the 13 scoring windows of the 11 transfers overlaps another transfer. Leaving ce4b out would move G1 to -1.608 and G1' to -2.126 (post hoc, and not used to claim a pass).
  • The learned masks gain where the pair alarm does harm. At D16 in the replicate months (card 500860) the pair-alarm mask scores 11.07 against 7.71 with no mask, because its fragmented weak alarms keep the mask open until 166 half-hours after the end. The re-ranker scores 2.32. Three transfers carry the sign of the 11-transfer gain: ce4b adds +1.36 to the contrast, card 500860 adds -0.90, and b2f7c0 at D5 adds -0.77. Leaving card 500860 out gives +0.488.
  • At these substations, the learned alarms do not come earlier. Of the 45 logged transfers at the six substations, an alarm matching the transfer is known before the transfer ends for 16 with the pair alarm, 8 with the re-ranker, 11 with the logistic regression, and 10 with RO-NC (printed_found.txt). An alarm matches at all for 20 (pair alarm), 19 (re-ranker), 27 (logistic regression), and 20 (RO-NC) of the 45. The re-ranker's 19 include ce4b, which is really the onset of b2f7c0. Experiment 195 counted 35 transfers over 1 day and a stricter rule, so its counts of 24 and 19 are not comparable.
  • Ordinary days (G2): mask minus no mask on 1,579,711 rows over 27 months, where no mask scores 2.718. LEARNED_R +0.031 (-0.020 to +0.086), and +0.031 (-0.097 to +0.175) from November to March. LEARNED_F +0.109 (+0.022 to +0.226), and +0.286 in winter. RONC_195 +0.144 (+0.054 to +0.258), and +0.291 in winter. The gated pair alarm +0.030 (-0.012 to +0.074). Per fold, LEARNED_R gives +0.039, +0.017, and +0.036. None of the learned masks meets the +/-0.05 limit.
  • The learned scores are partly in-sample on ordinary days. Experiment 195 trained them with the real record's even-month candidates as negatives. The re-ranker's contrast is +0.048 (-0.052 to +0.156) on odd months, which it was not trained on, and +0.014 (-0.006 to +0.036) on even months. The odd-month figure is the fairer estimate of the harm a deployed score would do.
  • The learned masks cover fewer half-hours than the gated pair alarm. From the half-hour an alarm is known to the half-hour its end is known, the re-ranker's alarms span about 18,800 half-hours per fold (three folds), against 33,557 for the gated pair alarm over the same rows.
  • Leaving one substation out (ordinary days, pooled). D10 carries the pair alarm's harm: +0.002 without D10. The re-ranker's estimate without D10 is +0.012, the logistic regression's -0.000, and RO-NC's +0.028.
  • Tail calibration on the 11-transfer rows (coverage at the 0.01, 0.05, 0.95, and 0.99 quantiles, then pinball loss in points). No mask: coverage 0.297, 0.353, 0.841, 0.893; loss 3.55, 4.98, 2.69, 1.47. Pair-alarm mask: 0.172, 0.247, 0.898, 0.937; 1.47, 2.53, 1.42, 0.57. Re-ranker mask: 0.130, 0.178, 0.935, 0.980; 2.14, 3.01, 0.93, 0.25. The re-ranker mask has better upper-tail coverage and loss than the pair-alarm mask and worse lower-tail loss. Every mask leaves the lower quantiles too high: the measured power falls below the 0.01 quantile in 13% to 30% of rows, because these rows follow a transfer and the spread is that of the unmasked forecast.
  • Checks: median and mean forecast. The median forecast minus the mean forecast per site (ordinary rows, points) is the same for K0 and LEARNED_R to three decimals (D10 -0.058, D11 -0.030, D14 +0.037, D16 +0.017, D5 -0.146, D9 -0.019), because the mask changes the correction only through the mean.
  • Checks: mean-forecast error and audit. The error of the mean forecast points the same way as every quantile-score contrast: LEARNED_R minus PAIR_NEW +0.525 (7 transfers) and -1.221 (11 transfers), and LEARNED_R minus K0 on ordinary days +0.042 (-0.031 to +0.123). Leaving D16 out flips the 11-transfer gain from -0.46 to +0.64, which triggers an audit.
  • Checks: audit findings. An independent audit re-derived G1, G1', and G2 from the stored per-row scores with its own code and reproduced them (+0.989, -0.460, and +0.031 with -0.020 to +0.088). It matched the controls to experiment 163's and 171's stored rows within 2e-6, and found the onset stamps causal and the fold mapping equal to experiment 195's. All of its findings are in this page (the ce4b overlap, the in-sample caveat, the end-rule deviation, and the timing counts); none was rejected.
  • Caveats. The learned alarms come from three folds that hold out whole Primary pairs. Each transfer uses the fold that held out its pair, and ordinary rows average the three folds' scores. The 7, 11, and 13 transfers are few, so every gain interval is wide. Experiment 195 found the extra transfers small (0.4 to 0.9 MW each). The pair alarm raised 242 alarms and the learned alarms 104 to 150 per fold.
  • What this narrows. Finding more transfers is not the bottleneck: the re-ranker matches no more transfers than RO-NC at these substations and masks no better. The missing piece is an early alarm on the long transfers, which among the alarms tested here only the pair alarm gives. A candidate next experiment is the union of the pair alarm and the learned alarms (pair alarm when its balance score passes, learned alarm otherwise), judged on the 13-transfer set and the ordinary rows. Experiment 195's look-ahead features cannot give an early alarm, so another candidate is a small neural network that reads only data up to the alarm, such as the first 24 hours after a step.

docs.title: Experiment 204: a bulk supply point is forecast no better from all its children than on its own
docs.text:
Take-home: putting every child Primary substation into the sum did not improve the forecast of either bulk supply point (BSP). A BSP is the substation above a group of Primaries. D13 (Skegness) and D17 (Boston) are the two BSPs studied. The top-down forecast treats the BSP's own half-hourly reading as a stand-alone series. The bottom-up forecast adds forecasts of the children (the Primaries beneath the BSP) to a forecast of the remainder, the BSP's reading minus the weighted children's readings. Scores are quantile scores in points: percentages of the BSP's effective capacity (its reference power), and lower is better.

The bottom-up forecast, with the children that report apparent power (MVA) converted to signed flow, scored 4.375 points at D13 against 4.370 for the top-down forecast (C1, bottom-up minus top-down: +0.005, 97.5% interval -0.037 to +0.040) and 7.532 against 7.542 at D17 (-0.011, -0.057 to +0.038). Each interval comes from resampling whole calendar months of the scored year. The intervals do not exclude a difference of up to about 0.06 points either way, so experiment 161's null result gave no sign of being caused by the sum covering too little of the BSP. The verdict is inconclusive, because both intervals include zero, and the plan's rule reads that as no detectable gain from coverage.

We asked whether the bottom-up forecast of a BSP beats the top-down forecast once the sum includes every child Primary that has a long history, as experiment 161 could not test. Experiment 161 summed only the 3 children per BSP that report real power (MW). This experiment adds the 4 children at D13 and the 3 at D17 (D3, D12, D22) that report apparent power. Apparent power hides the sign of the flow, so a child whose solar panels push power back up the network at midday (reverse flow) reads positive when its flow is negative. This experiment builds each such child's signed flow with the fold-aware generalised additive model of experiment 152, which fits a hidden (latent) signed flow and the reading that follows from it. We found that the children's forecasts give no detectable gain over the BSP's own forecast chain: the bottom-up error equals the top-down error, and the children's forecast errors correlate positively with the remainder's. With each child's reading known exactly (the oracle), the score gains 24% at D13 and 12% at D17, so better child forecasts would help, but the current child forecasts do not. Scored rows are the 291 daily runs of 2025-07-02 to 2026-06-29, leads 0.5 to 168 hours, outside switching events.

Scope. D13 is Skegness (7 children) and D17 is Boston (9 children). The sum covers 7 children at D13 and 6 at D17. D8 (Marsh Lane) stays in D17's remainder, because its series changes meaning in April 2025 and no consistent history exists. The two Wrangle transformers (D15 and D18) stay there too, because they have under 8 months of readings, so arm (e) of the plan was not run. The metered generators under each BSP also stay in the remainder.

Arms. All arms use the top-down forecast's spread of quantiles around the mean, so they differ in the mean only.

  • (a) top-down: the best-guess forecasting chain of experiment 155 (arm D) applied to the BSP alone.
  • (b) partial bottom-up: experiment 161's sum over the 3 children per BSP that report real power (MW).
  • (c) full, apparent power read as signed: the sum over every child with a long history, each apparent-power child's reading and forecast taken as signed.
  • (d) full, fold-aware: the same sum with each apparent-power child's signed flow forecast by experiment 152's fold-aware model, and the sign of its past readings set from that model.
  • (d, sign at probability 0.5): arm (d) with the sign set wherever the fitted flow is more likely than not to be reverse (arm (d) requires a probability of 0.9).
  • Oracle: arm (d) with the children's observed readings in place of their forecasts, a control with no verdict.

The contrasts are C1 (bottom-up (d) minus top-down), C2 ((d) minus (c)), C4 (C1 by lead band), C6 (C1 at the 0.01, 0.05, 0.95, and 0.99 quantiles), and C7 (oracle minus top-down). The scored year is the 291 daily runs from 2025-07-02. The replicate year is the even months of 2024-07 to 2025-06.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Every bottom-up arm scored the same as top-down, within the noise. Experiment 161's partial bottom-up arm (b) is reproduced exactly on 161's own rows (4.345 and 7.674 with the top-down spread table, 4.387 and 7.706 with its own; top-down 4.361 and 7.672). The table below uses the smaller set of rows on which every arm has a forecast. Adding 4 children at D13 and 3 at D17 to arm (b) moves the score by +0.021 (-0.011 to +0.050) at D13 and by -0.012 (-0.049 to +0.026) at D17. In the replicate year (even months of 2024-07 to 2025-06), C1 is -0.038 (-0.102 to +0.026) at D13 and 0.000 (-0.041 to +0.043) at D17.

Arm (scored year) D13 score D17 score (a) Top-down 4.370 7.542 (b) Partial bottom-up, MW children only, top-down spread table 4.354 7.543 (c) Full, apparent power read as signed 4.375 7.551 (d) Full, fold-aware signed flow 4.375 7.532 (d, sign at probability 0.5) Full, signed flow 4.375 7.523 Oracle: observed children 3.324 6.617 Manual heuristic 5.485 8.305 Climatology 5.908 8.833

Rows are the shared rows, 95,547 at D13 and 79,839 at D17. The sum of the children's effective capacities is 117% of D13's and 99% of D17's (against 42% and 56% for arm (b)); the children peak at different times, so this is not a share of the load.

The sign of the converted flow mattered at D17 only, and not detectably. (d) minus (c) is -0.000 (-0.001 to +0.000) at D13, where no child has reverse flow, and -0.019 (-0.051 to +0.011) at D17, where D12 has it. Setting the sign at probability 0.5 instead of 0.9 gives -0.028 (-0.058 to -0.003) at D17, the one sign contrast whose interval excludes zero. This contrast was not pre-registered and is not adjusted for the number of contrasts, so it is a lead for later work, not a finding.

The fitted flow of D12 is reverse on 18.5% of its usable half-hours at probability 0.9 and 26.9% at 0.5. D22 has none at 0.9 and 39 half-hours at 0.5. The other five apparent-power children in the sum have none.

No lead band favoured full bottom-up with confidence. C1 by band at D13 is -0.011, -0.006, and +0.015 (0.5 to 24, 24 to 72, 72 to 168 hours), and at D17 -0.034, -0.031, and +0.005. Every interval includes zero. The estimates are lowest below 72 hours at both BSPs.

Most of each BSP's error is in the remainder, and the children's errors share its cause. At D13 the remainder's error has a standard deviation of 7.9 points and the weighted children's summed error 4.7 points; at D17 the figures are 15.4 and 5.4. The two parts' errors correlate positively (0.48 and 0.32). The bottom-up error (10.95 and 17.91) is therefore about the same as the top-down error (10.94 and 17.94). The remainder is the load that no Primary in the sum meters: the generators beneath the BSP, losses, and D8 and the Wrangle transformers at D17.

The fold-aware flow recovers the signed sum where reverse flow is large. At the larger injection (power factor 0.97 folding) the summed flow's mean absolute error is 3.65 MW against 6.62 MW for reading the magnitude as signed, 45% lower; with no injection the two are 1.46 and 1.47 MW. Both pre-registered pass conditions hold: at least 20% lower at level 2.0, and at most 5% worse at level 0. Level 0 uses the idealised q0 folding, the only level-0 folding experiment 152 stored. At level 1.0 the figures are 2.58 against 3.04 MW.

BSP, arm Coverage at 0.01 0.05 0.95 0.99 D13 top-down 0.018 0.067 0.920 0.969 D13 (d) 0.017 0.068 0.919 0.969 D17 top-down 0.018 0.071 0.906 0.963 D17 (d) 0.016 0.069 0.902 0.962

Both arms are too narrow in the tails by the same amount, because they share the top-down spread table. C6, the pinball loss at the four tail quantiles, differs from top-down by 0.02 or less at both BSPs, and the 0.99 quantile at D17 (+0.020, +0.004 to +0.040) is the one interval that excludes zero.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, per BSP and arm: 0.000 for every arm, because the residual table is centred.
  • Mean forecast's error beside each contrast (mean absolute error): C1 +0.023 at D13 and -0.027 at D17, the same sign as the quantile score; C2 -0.001 and -0.048; C7 (oracle) -1.95 and -1.55.
  • Controls: the reproduction of experiment 161 passed (4.361 and 7.672 for top-down, 4.387 and 7.706 for (b) on its rows). The known-answer check passed. The oracle gained 24% at D13 (predicted 20% to 40%) and 12% at D17 (below the predicted 20%), which matches the error decomposition (figure 3) and is no data-handling fault: the oracle's error equals the remainder's.
  • Audit triggers: the ml-experiment skill lists seven. Trigger 2 (a result contradicts its prediction) fired: C1 was predicted at -3% to -10% at D13 and came out at +0.1%. The explanation was tested and is recorded here: the oracle and the decomposition show the bottom-up error equals the top-down error. Trigger 1 (a control fails) did not fire. Trigger 3 (the quantile score and the mean's error disagree in sign) did not fire. Trigger 4 (leaving one site out flips a verdict) does not apply to two BSPs. Trigger 5 (a nested arm beats its container) did not fire. Trigger 6 (an interval more than twice or less than half as wide as a sister experiment's) did not fire: the C1 intervals are 0.6 to 0.9 times the width of experiment 161's. Trigger 7 (a later design depends on the headline) did not fire. No Opus audit was run, because only the explained trigger 2 fired and the verdict is inconclusive either way.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Two BSPs, one scored year, and the weights come from one winter (2023-10 to 2024-03). Five of the six D17 weights and five of the seven D13 weights sit on the bounds (0.8 or 1.2); the unbounded fit gives weights from 0 to 5.9 and explains 82% (D13) and 45% (D17) of the BSP's variance, against 76% and 38% for the bounded fit.
