  • Fill a missing 0.01 or 0.99 quantile from the 0.05 or 0.95 quantile before capping, instead of padding with nulls, in any scorer that reads the three non-farm generators' forecasts.

docs.title: How long can an arrangement last before a no-lag forecast learns it as normal?
docs.text:
A forecast that uses no recent power still learns a load transfer as normal. A load transfer is a spell in which an operator moves part of one substation's demand onto a neighbouring substation by changing how the electricity network is connected. The way the network is normally connected is the normal running arrangement (NRA). We took 10 Primary substations (substations that step 33 kV down to 11 kV) and added a transfer of 25% of each substation's own power to its recorded power, for 7 to 90 days or for good. We refitted the forecast at the start of every month. The forecast, called GAM_ONLY, is a generalised additive model fitted by convex least squares, with no lagged power among its inputs. We compared each forecast with the forecast trained on the unaltered series, which stands for the NRA. The difference between the two forecasts is the bias: a positive bias means the transfer was learned as normal.

The prediction was that a 30-day transfer of 25% of load would bias the forecast by under 0.1 points of effective capacity (1 point is 1% of the substation's capacity). The prediction did not hold, so the verdict is not supported: in the 48 hours after the end the bias is 2.49 points (95% interval 2.04 to 3.05), which is 19% of the transfer. Even a 7-day transfer, the shortest we tested, is learned as 8.5% of its size, so any limit on how long an arrangement can last before it counts as normal is shorter than 7 days and is not located. The next experiment should test durations of 1 to 6 days and a training mask. Two conditions limit the result: the weather inputs are the ERA5 and CAMS estimates of past weather (the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts' reanalysis and the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service's irradiance), not ensemble forecasts, and the forecast has no lagged power. The share-of-load injection is the one of experiment 141, and the forecast settings are the GAM-K settings of experiment 252.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Every figure is in points of effective capacity unless it is a percentage, a mean over 10 substations and 4 onset dates, with a 95% interval from resampling substations and onset dates independently. The mean transfer for the 25% size was 13.3 points. e00274_report.py prints every number in printed_report.txt. A receiver is a substation that gains load and a donor is one that loses load. A BEFORE row is a forecast row dated before the transfer began.

  • Controls passed. The bias in the 3,720 groups of BEFORE rows and in the 1,920 groups of rows with a transfer of size 0 is exactly 0.
  • Headline (24-month window, 25% of load, receiver). The bias in the 48 hours after the end is 1.21 points (0.72 to 1.76) at 7 days, 2.67 (1.14 to 5.56) at 14 days, 2.49 (2.04 to 3.05) at 30 days, 3.94 (3.29 to 4.69) at 60 days, and 4.20 (3.32 to 5.28) at 90 days. As shares of the transfer these are 8.5%, 18.0%, 19.1%, 30.4%, and 31.9%. The bias grows less than in proportion to the duration, so the prediction of proportional growth to 90 days did not hold. The bias is also not monotone: 2.67 at 14 days has a wide interval.
  • The bias scales with the size of the transfer. The share learned at 30 days is 19% at 10%, 25%, and 40% of load, and a transfer of 10% of load gives 1.00 points (0.82 to 1.22).
  • Training window (30 days, 25% of load). The share learned is 32% (25% to 38%) with a 12-month window, 19% (16% to 22%) with a 24-month window, and 15% (11% to 20%) with the whole history.
  • Decay after the end (30 days, 25% of load). The share learned is 2.8% in months 1 to 3 after the end (bias 0.37 points, 0.31 to 0.44) and 5.0% in months 4 to 12 (0.66 points, 0.48 to 0.87). For 90 days the shares are 5.3% and 15.2%. The share in months 4 to 12 is larger than in months 1 to 3, and no season-by-season breakdown was run to say why.
  • Rows inside the transfer. The learned share is 0% at 7, 14, and 30 days, 6.2% at 60 days, and 11.4% at 90 days. A fit at a cut has seen only the earlier part of the transfer, so these rows lag by up to a month. A transfer of 30 days or shorter has its inside rows forecast by the fit cut at the onset, which has seen none of the transfer, so the bias there is 0 by design.
  • Permanent step (25% of load). The share learned is about 20% from month 2 to month 10 after the step begins. With a 24-month window it is 48% at month 12, 61% at month 13, and 100% from month 24. With a 12-month window it is 55% at month 11 and 97% at month 12. With the whole history it is 54% at month 24 and 70% at month 36. The prediction of half learned within 12 months (24-month window) failed, because half was reached at month 13. The prediction of half learned within 6 months (12-month window) failed, because half was reached at month 11.
  • Sign and shape (30 days, 25% of load, 24-month window). When the transfer removes load from a donor substation, the bias is 2.47 points (2.05 to 2.97) and the share learned is 19.0%. When the transfer is a fixed block of MW with a flat shape, the bias is 2.72 points (2.19 to 3.24) and the share is 20.3%. The share for a share-of-load transfer is 19.1%, so the three are similar.
  • Season and substation. A transfer beginning in winter gives a bias of 2.65 points (1.89 to 3.47) and one beginning in summer gives 2.33 (1.95 to 2.69). Across substations the bias ranges from 1.47 points (D12) to 3.04 (D2), and the share learned from 17% to 21%.
  • The limit for NGED. No tested duration, including 7 days, has an interval upper bound below 0.1 points or below 5% of the transfer, for any size or window. The limit, if it exists, is below 7 days and is not located.
  • Signed error against the NRA series (30 days, 25% of load). In the 48 hours after the end, the clean-trained forecast is 2.8 points too high and the injected-trained forecast is 5.3 points too high. The error NGED would see is therefore larger than the learned bias alone. The 48-hour group is small.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• The 48-hour figure depends on where the fit is cut. For D3 with a transfer ending on 1 July, the mean forecast difference over one fixed week was 2.13 points for a fit cut at the end of the transfer, 0.88 for a fit cut 12 hours later, 0.76 for a fit cut a day later, and about 1.0 for fits cut 3 and 10 days later (diagnose_report.txt). We did not find why 12 hours of extra clean data lowers the bias by 60%. The solar-capacity season year runs from September to August, so the cause is not that year boundary. The 48-hour figure is therefore an upper bound that holds at the cut, and the months 1 to 3 figure (2.8% at 30 days) is the steadier measure.
  • Where the bias sits. For D3 and D11 after a 30-day winter transfer, the forecast difference is similar in every temperature band below 15 C (D3: 1.1 to 1.3 points; D11: 0.7 to 1.5), so the transfer is not learned mainly as a temperature response. The difference varies by time of day (D3: 0.8 to 1.7 points over four 6-hour blocks). For D3 it is 0.5 points in the first week after the end and 1.3 to 1.5 points in weeks 2 to 5.
  • Median minus mean. GAM_ONLY is a least-squares forecast of the mean, so it has no median-minus-mean gap to report. The signed error against the NRA series is in the Results.
  • Audit triggers. Two of the seven audit triggers of the ml-experiment skill fired. The result contradicted its own prediction in size: the prediction expected 0.5 to 1 points and the experiment measured 2.5. The explanation we tested is the cut sensitivity above, and it does not remove the result, because the bias is still 0.9 points 12 hours later and 0.4 points in months 1 to 3, both above 0.1. The second trigger is that the statement to NGED rests on this result and no other experiment has replicated it. No Opus audit was run, because this session was limited to Sonnet models.

docs.title: Caveats and what to try next
docs.text:
• The forecast has no drift term and no lagged power (the GAM-K settings), so the production GAM stack with the Kalman filter correction would behave differently.
  • The weather inputs are the ERA5 and CAMS estimates of past weather, not ensemble forecasts.
  • The transfer is injected as a share of the receiver's own power or as a flat block, so it follows the receiver's daily shape or has none. Real transfers have shapes of their own.
  • The existing masks (the lockdown window and the hand-filtered events) remove some rows from both the clean and the injected training sets. Real arrangements in the unmasked history sit in both.
  • Only monthly refits were tested. Weekly refits are expected to learn a transfer sooner, but this experiment did not test them.
  • The next experiment should test transfers of 1 to 6 days and a training mask that removes known transfers, and should look for the cause of the cut sensitivity.

docs.title: Does training the metered-farm neural head on years of past weather lower the day-ahead score?
docs.text:
Training the neural network that corrects a solar farm's power forecast on years of rows built from past weather barely improves its forecast, and improves XGBoost's forecast more. National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED) meters the output of six solar farms, labelled A to F here. Experiment 243 fitted H5 on only 17 months of European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) ensemble weather forecasts (many runs of one weather model). H5 is a physical model of a farm's output (the "plant") plus a neural network that adds offsets for 11 quantile levels, which give a probability band around the plant's forecast. We added nearly six years of rows (2019-09 to 2025-07) built from past weather (Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service irradiance and ERA5 temperature), with an "era flag" that marks them, and measured the quantile score on the 12 months 2025-09 to 2026-08, which no arm trained on. The quantile score is twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantile levels (the loss that penalises a quantile forecast on the side it errs), in percent of the farm's capacity; lower is better. It is scored on daylight half-hours at 12 to 36 hours ahead. The idea follows experiment 200 and experiment 211, where past-weather rows helped a neural network that corrects a substation's forecast.

The prediction fails. Version L2 (H5 on past-weather plus ensemble rows with the flag) beats version L0 (H5 on ensemble rows only) by 0.47% (95% interval -1.1% to +0.1%), against at least 2% predicted. XGBoost, a gradient-boosted tree model, gains 1.7% (1.2% to 2.2%) from the same rows (version X2 against X0), so L2's gain is 1.2 percentage points smaller than XGBoost's (interval 0.6 to 1.7), the opposite of the predicted sign. The stop rule (stop if L2 gains under 1% at 4 or more of the 6 farms) fires: L2 gains under 1% at five farms (farm E gains 1.3%), so the versions fitted on the other five farms' rows were not run. The shuffled-power control scores 3.9% worse than L2 (2.5% to 5.0%), so the gain that exists comes from the weather-to-power relation and not from a prior on the power level.

docs.title: Arms, rows, and weather
docs.text:
• Arms (five random seeds for the neural networks; one fit on rows before 2025-09, the screening schedule, with no retraining in the scored year). L0: H5 on ensemble rows only. L1: past-weather plus ensemble rows, no flag. L2: L1 plus the era flag. L3: L2 pretrained on past-weather rows, then fine-tuned on ensemble rows. X0, X2: XGBoost on ensemble rows, and on both with the flag. Control: L2 with the past-weather rows' power shuffled across days of the same farm, month, and half-hour.
  • Rows. Experiment 243's 41,654 daylight half-hours in the scored year, equal weight per farm, intervals from resampling the 12 scored months 20,000 times. L0 reproduces experiment 243's stored H5 exactly (5.475 against 5.475, identical to the last digit).
  • Weather at each time. Past-weather rows use Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) irradiance (about 2 days late) and ERA5 temperature (about 5 days late): neither exists at forecast time, and both appear only in training rows before 2025-07. Scored rows use the ECMWF ensemble (00 UTC run), which exists at forecast time. Lagged power (own power one day earlier, or two days earlier when the lead is over 24 hours) exists at forecast time.
  • Spread stand-in. Each past-weather row takes the median ensemble spread of the same farm, month, half-hour, and cloud-cover tercile, from ensemble rows before 2025-09.
  • Row counts (farm A). 9,709 ensemble training rows, 41,028 past-weather rows (4.2 times as many), and 1,660 validation rows (2025-07 to 2025-08, ensemble only). Farm E has 4,685 past-weather rows because its history starts in 2024-10.
  • Quantile order. H5 sorts its outputs before scoring. Before sorting, the 11 offsets give quantiles out of order in 31% of scored rows for L0, 33% for L2, and 31% for L3. Experiment 273 found 0 crossing rows in the stored files of experiment 243, because the fit scripts sort the 11 quantiles before writing them; the files here are written the same way, so the scores are sorted-quantile scores and the crossing rate above is a property of the unsorted network output.

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text:
• Quantile score (95% interval): X2 5.40 (4.86 to 5.86); L3 5.44 (4.89 to 5.92); L2 5.45 (4.90 to 5.92); L0 5.47 (4.95 to 5.93); X0 5.49 (4.95 to 5.96); L1 5.52 (4.95 to 6.02); control 5.67 (5.12 to 6.11).
  • Contrasts in quantile score: C1 L2 against L0 -0.47% (-1.11 to +0.07; 98.3% interval -1.28 to +0.19). C2 (L2 gain minus X2 gain) +1.19 points (0.64 to 1.73). C3 L2 against control -3.88% (-5.03 to -2.46). L3 against L0 -0.55% (-1.20 to -0.00). L2 against L1 -1.24% (-2.09 to -0.18). X2 against X0 -1.66% (-2.21 to -1.22).
  • Per farm, L2's gain over L0 (negative is worse): A -0.7%, B +0.4%, C +0.5%, D +0.4%, E +1.3%, F +0.7%.
  • Tail calibration (pinball loss in points of capacity, coverage as a share of scored rows):
Arm Pinball 0.01 Pinball 0.05 Pinball 0.95 Pinball 0.99 Coverage 0.01 Coverage 0.99 L0 0.334 1.393 1.265 0.344 3.3% 98.5% L2 0.334 1.385 1.229 0.328 3.3% 98.5% L3 0.341 1.386 1.238 0.330 3.3% 98.4% X0 0.370 1.393 1.228 0.485 3.8% 99.3% X2 0.370 1.373 1.193 0.483 3.7% 99.5%
  • Upper tail: L2's 0.99 pinball loss is 4.6% lower than L0's (2.1% to 7.8%); L3's is 4.1% lower. The 0.01 quantile is unchanged for L2 and 2.0% worse for L3 (0.3% to 3.9%). The curtailment-cost metric was not scored, because it scores a substation node together with its generators, not one farm.
  • Post hoc explanation tests (labelled post hoc, verdict unchanged). L2 with the offsets table taken from ensemble rows only scores 5.455 (-0.36% against L0, interval -0.86 to +0.06). L2 with only the past-weather rows before the ensemble era (no overlap with ensemble months) scores 5.439 (-0.65%, interval -1.14 to -0.26). Neither test lifts the gain above 0.7%, so the small gain does not come from the offsets table or from overlapping months.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, per arm (points of capacity, mean over farms): L0 +0.52, L2 +0.55, L3 +0.61, X0 -0.52, X2 -0.15, control +0.01. H5's median sits above its mean by a similar amount (+0.52 to +0.61) in every H5 arm, so the extra rows do not shift the forecast.
  • Error of the mean forecast beside the quantile score. The mean forecast's absolute error (points of capacity) is 9.93 for L0, 9.95 for L2, 9.94 for L3, 10.17 for X0, and 10.12 for X2. L2 against L0 is +0.16% (-0.31 to +0.55) in mean-forecast error, against -0.47% in quantile score; both intervals include zero. The median forecast's error is 9.85 for L0 and 9.84 for L2.
  • Audit triggers that fired. The result contradicts its prediction and the finding of experiment 200 for a substation, and the two post hoc tests above do not explain the contradiction.
  • Audit triggers that fired nominally. The quantile score and the mean-forecast error point in different directions for C1, and both intervals include zero.
  • Audit triggers that did not fire. The shuffled-power control scores worse than L0, as designed, because it adds rows whose power is random. Leaving out any one farm keeps the sign of the L2 gain (five of six farms agree). No arm that contains another beats it by more than noise, and no later design depends on this result. No Opus audit was run.

docs.title: Caveats and what to try next
docs.text:
• One fit on rows before 2025-09, with no retraining in the scored year; a weekly refit could change every arm's absolute score, and the contrast between arms may depend on it.
  • The spread stand-in is a single rule. A neural network trained with a better spread might use the extra rows better.
  • The past-weather rows hold no forecast error, because CAMS and ERA5 are close to the truth, so a head that learns the forecast's error can learn it only from the 17 ensemble months. Rows of an older ensemble forecast (for example the ensemble history before 2024-04 that other experiments fetched) would hold that error and are the next test.
  • Experiment 257 found a linear fit recovers 90% of the neural head's gain, so the next test is the linear fit that experiment 257 called P2, with the extra rows and the era flag.
  • The XGBoost versions train on the two validation months as well (about 17% more ensemble rows at farm A), because XGBoost has no epoch to select, while the neural networks use those months only to choose the epoch. C2 compares each version's own gain, so the difference should matter little.

docs.title: Why does an XGBoost model forecast the three metered wind farms better than a physics model of the wind turbines, and is the metering noise the reason?
docs.text:
Take-home: XGBoost beats the physics model because it corrects the wind speed, not because it learns the metering noise. The physics model scored 0.31 points of capacity worse than XGBoost on the rows that experiment 210's mask keeps, and 0.27 worse on all rows, so XGBoost's lead does not shrink when the noisy rows are removed. Wind direction, the 10 m wind speed, and the hour of day carry the lead, and no change to the physics model's power curve, spread, or scale closed more than about a sixth of the lead. These inputs explain only about 6% of the physics model's remaining error, so most of that error is still unexplained.

We asked why an XGBoost model forecasts the three metered wind farms (W1, W2, and W3) better than a physics model of the wind turbines, which we call the core. The core turns the 10 m and 100 m wind speeds and the air temperature into power through a fitted power curve, an air-density correction, and an apparent-power layer. The maintainer's first guess was that XGBoost learns the metering noise: the reactive-power floor of the apparent-power readings, the deadband, and the dip near cut-in (the wind speed at which a turbine starts). We scored both models with ERA5 (a past-weather estimate) as the weather, which separates the wind-farm model's error from the weather forecast's error, and with the 51 ensemble members of the ECMWF ensemble forecast, the production setting. We then removed noisy rows from the scoring and from the training, and changed the core and XGBoost one piece at a time. The guess is refuted. XGBoost's lead sits at 9 to 14 m/s wind, where the core's fitted power curve is steep, and comes from reading the wind direction and the 10 m wind speed. The experiment did not find which interaction between those inputs and the wind speed does the work.

Scores are quantile scores in points of capacity, and every contrast is the first model minus the second. The quantile score estimates the continuous ranked probability score, and smaller is better, so a positive contrast means the second model is better. Kept rows are the half-hours that experiment 210's mask keeps, and idle-band rows are the half-hours it drops: near-zero readings, plus runs of at least 12 hours at high wind. The method builds on experiment 230, whose core, ERA5 training rows, and scoring code this experiment copies. Both models were trained on all rows before 17 June 2025 and scored on experiment 33's 53 Tuesday runs of July 2025 to June 2026 (107,121 rows, of which 96,479 are kept rows and 10,642 are idle-band rows). Intervals resample whole months and the three seeds; farms are not resampled. XGBoost uses 500 rounds with column subsampling off, and each model was fitted once on all history.

The diagnostics are named D1 to D10. D1 and D2 vary the rows scored and the rows trained on, D3 locates the gap, D4 and D5 look for the inputs XGBoost uses, D6 to D8 and D10 change the core's power curve, spread, scale, or wind speeds, and D9 varies the length of training.

docs.title: Is metering noise the cause? (D1 and D2)
docs.text:
• The pre-registered prediction failed. The gap on the kept rows (+0.310, interval 0.215 to 0.416) is larger than on all rows (+0.270, 0.190 to 0.371), against a predicted gap of half or less. When both models trained without the idle rows the gap was +0.302 on the kept rows (0.206 to 0.413), no smaller in any meaningful way. The noise hypothesis (H-noise) is refuted.
  • On the idle-band rows XGBoost is not better. The gap there is -0.089 (-0.450 to 0.050) with ERA5 as the weather, and -0.156 (-0.325 to -0.075) with the ensemble, where the core is better.
  • The gap concentrates above the core's fitted rated speed: +0.605 (0.401 to 0.784) with ERA5 and +0.384 (0.262 to 0.538) with the ensemble, against +0.284 above cut-in.
  • Training without the idle rows helps with the ensemble and not with ERA5. With the ensemble, the core improved by 0.075 (0.053 to 0.094) and XGBoost by 0.062 (0.040 to 0.079) on the kept rows. With ERA5 the score worsened by 0.006 and 0.014, both with intervals that include zero.
  • In the production setting the gap is smaller: +0.129 (0.073 to 0.189) on the kept rows, in line with experiment 230's +0.126. A binned power curve on the 100 m speed alone ties XGBoost there (-0.008, -0.109 to 0.093), and the core is worse than the binned curve by 0.137 (0.033 to 0.237).
Setting Model All rows Kept rows Wind above rated ERA5 as the weather Physics core 5.834 6.174 9.857 ERA5 as the weather XGBoost 5.564 5.864 9.253 ERA5 as the weather Binned curve 6.100 6.469 10.138 51 ensemble members Physics core 11.136 11.792 28.944 51 ensemble members XGBoost 11.035 11.663 28.559 51 ensemble members Binned curve 11.033 11.655 27.581

docs.title: Where the gap sits (D3)
docs.text:
• Wind speeds from 9 to 14 m/s carry 65% of the total gap, and the mean gap per half-hour there is 0.22 to 0.42 points. Above 16 m/s the core is better (rows are few: 7,141 of 289,237 scored half-hours at 16 m/s and over).
  • Every direction sector has a positive mean gap (0.06 to 0.26), and the south-west sector carries the most (21%), because it holds the most half-hours.
  • The gap is positive at every farm (held-out-year fits: 0.13, 0.19, and 0.13 at W1, W2, and W3; scored cases: 0.28, 0.19, and 0.34), in every season (0.09 in June to August, 0.17 to 0.19 in December to February and September to November), and at every hour of day (0.10 at 08:00 to 12:00 UTC, 0.19 at 00:00 to 04:00 UTC).
  • The gap is largest in the middle years. The held-out-year fits give 0.02 in the first (partial) year, 0.14 to 0.20 in the next four, and 0.13 in the last; the scored cases of the final year give 0.27.
  • With the ensemble, the gap peaks at lead day 1 (0.34) and falls to near zero at lead days 6, 10, and 11.

docs.title: What XGBoost uses (D4)
docs.text:
• The 100 m wind speed alone scores no better than the binned curve (6.476 against 6.469 on the kept rows), and 0.302 worse than the core.
  • Adding direction takes XGBoost level with the core (0.023 worse than the core, interval -0.156 to 0.195, a tie), and temperature then adds 0.100 (0.004 to 0.215).
  • Adding the 10 m wind speed and direction passes the core: this step gives 0.269 (0.176 to 0.372), and XGBoost then leads the core by 0.345 (0.243 to 0.454).
  • Hour of day and day of year add another 0.124 (0.036 to 0.211), and the year then makes the score worse by 0.442 (0.235 to 0.697).
  • ERA5 surface pressure, dew point, and gusts are not on disk for these farms, so air density rests on temperature alone and the extra wind level is the 10 m speed and direction only.
  • With the ensemble the order is the same: XGBoost with direction, temperature, and the 10 m wind (X4) leads the core by 0.213 (0.121 to 0.306), and the hour and day of year add 0.100 (0.027 to 0.176).

docs.title: What the core's error depends on (D5)
docs.text:
• A small XGBoost model of the core's median residual explains only 6.2%, 7.5%, and -0.7% of its variance at W1, W2, and W3 on the held-out year. Most of the core's error is not a function of these inputs.
  • Permutation importance is largest for the 100 m wind direction at W2 and W3 (25 and 23 points squared) and for the 100 m wind speed at W1 (18), followed by the hour of day (12 to 15), the 10 m wind speed (9 to 14), and, at W2 only, the day of year (17). Air temperature adds 1 to 6, and the year adds none.
  • The partial-dependence curves for direction are uneven rather than smooth (a swing of about 12 points at W2), so no simple sinusoidal direction term is likely to capture them.

docs.title: Is the core's power curve, spread, or scale the cause? (D6 to D8 and D10)
docs.text:
• D6, the power-curve form, is not the cause. A monotone neural curve gained 0.008 (0.002 to 0.014), a free density exponent lost 0.009, and the direction-dependent term gained 0.052 (-0.027 to 0.141, a tie). The binned curve scored worse than the core by 0.295, because it lacks the 10 m speed.
  • D7, the loss and the spread, is not the cause. Fitting the core on pinball loss with a speed-dependent spread gained 0.011 (0.004 to 0.018) and binning the residual quantiles on hub speed worsened it by 0.001.
  • D8, slow change, is not the cause. A per-year scale on the core worsened the score by 0.011 (-0.127 to 0.138, a tie) and a per-month scale made it worse by 0.088 (0.032 to 0.142). XGBoost with the year as an input was worse than XGBoost with only the hour and day of year by 0.442 (0.235 to 0.697), and worse than XGBoost with no date column by 0.318 (0.106 to 0.561), on the kept rows with ERA5 as the weather.
  • D10, a farm-specific wind-speed scale, is not the cause. The core gained 0.011 (0.005 to 0.017) and XGBoost gained 0.001, because a tree model does not respond to a monotone rescaling of one input. The scale fitted a fixed generic power curve and is a weak stand-in for the weather grid cell's mismatch.

docs.title: Learning curve (D9)
docs.text:
• XGBoost trails the core with 3 months of training (-0.573, -0.773 to -0.376), probably trails it at 6 months (-0.161, -0.372 to 0.055), ties it at 12 (+0.057), and leads by 0.223 at 24, 0.276 at 48, and 0.310 with all of the training history (about 69 months).
  • The core stops improving after 48 months (0.033 from 24 to 48 months, then none: the 48-month core is 0.003 better than the 69-month core), and XGBoost is still improving at 48 months (0.032 from 48 to 69). A gap that grows with the data while the core stays flat points to a structural error in the core, not to variance in XGBoost.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Both models forecast a median below the mean, most strongly with the ensemble (kept rows, points of capacity): -0.22 for the core and -0.19 for XGBoost with ERA5, and -5.27 and -5.22 with the ensemble. The low median is the bias experiments 259 and 261 traced to the ensemble's wind, and both models share this bias.
  • The error of the median and the mean forecast agrees with the quantile score. On the kept rows the contrast of absolute error of the median is +0.470 (0.337 to 0.620) and of the mean +0.488 (0.367 to 0.620) with ERA5, and +0.213 and +0.131 with the ensemble.
  • Leaving one farm out keeps the sign. The gap on the kept rows with ERA5 is +0.315, +0.344, and +0.272 without W1, W2, and W3, and with the ensemble +0.143, +0.124, and +0.120.
  • The tail quantiles agree between the two models, apart from the 0.01 level with ERA5 (pinball loss on the kept rows, core against XGBoost): 0.272 against 0.251 at the 0.01 level and 0.364 against 0.377 at the 0.99 level with ERA5, and 0.288 against 0.285 and 0.658 against 0.659 with the ensemble. The curtailment-cost metric was not run, because no arm here is a proposed forecast.
  • Audit trigger 5 fired: XGBoost with the year (X6) scored worse than the same inputs without it (X5), by 0.44 points. We suspected the year only fails when it extrapolates beyond the training range. A follow-up fit holding out each July-to-June year in turn, inside the training range, found the year helps in 4 of 6 held-out years by 0.03 to 0.50 and hurts in 2 by 0.12 to 0.43, with an overall change of -0.014 points. The suspicion is not confirmed, and the year input is unreliable in both settings. No other trigger fired. No independent audit was run, and no headline in this write-up depends on the year arm.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: Which interaction between the wind direction, the 10 m wind speed, and the 100 m wind speed does XGBoost use? A small neural correction of the core's effective wind speed, fed the direction and the ratio of the 10 m to the 100 m speed, would test it directly and would keep the physics core's smooth power curve. The core also loses to a binned curve in the production setting, so the same experiment should be scored with the ensemble.

docs.title: Departures from the plan
docs.text:
• Seeds: the core variants are deterministic, so their three seeds repeat one fit. The monotone neural curve (P_net) used one seed.
  • The rows above cut-in and above rated speed use the core's fitted cut-in and rated speeds against ERA5 100 m wind speed, as experiment 230 did. The fitted hub heights are 32 to 37 m, so the rated speeds are lower than the physical ones.
  • The by-year table of D3 uses every half-hour of November 2019 to June 2025 under fits that hold out each July-to-June year in turn, which is a different row set from the scored cases.
  • The last two input sets of D4: the "all inputs" set adds the year. ERA5 surface pressure, dew point, other wind levels, and gusts were not on disk for these farms.
  • The ensemble setting was run for D1, D2, the D4 input sets X4 to X6, and the core variants of D7 and D8, and not for D6's neural curve, D9, and D10.

docs.title: What the curtailment metric says about climatology, the manual heuristic, XGBoost BG2, and the GAM stack
docs.text:
On ordinary days the curtailment metric ranks the four existing forecasts as the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) does and can tell the GAM stack from BG2, but inside the windows around the 7 logged load transfers it cannot separate the stack from BG2. The curtailment metric is the cost of the generation that would have to be cut because a forecast let a substation's flow exceed a limit; experiment 268 defined it. We applied it to the forecasts that already exist, using the demand at each substation only (no generators attached), and measured how small a difference the scored rows can resolve. A load transfer is a logged switching of demand from one substation to another.

The four forecasts are climatology (average power for the same time of year and day), the manual heuristic (the rule National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED) uses today), BG2 (best guess 2, an XGBoost forecast configured like the production service), and the GAM stack of experiments 220 and 251. The GAM stack combines a generalised additive model (GAM) with a Kalman filter on its recent errors, a small neural-network head, and a summary of how the ensemble weather forecast's solar output varies. The scored rows are one year (2025-07-02 to 2026-06-30) at six Primary substations (D5, D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16), which step 33 kV down to 11 kV. This is step 3 of the load-shift decision program; the steps that follow are described under "How small a difference one year of rows can resolve".

Verdict: supported on the pre-registered rows, with one prediction failed and the BG2 separation narrow. At the 0.5 limit the avoidable cost (cost above a perfect forecast) orders the forecasts climatology, manual heuristic, BG2, GAM stack, from worst to best, and climatology minus the stack is GBP 35.5 million (95% 21.4 to 54.5 million). The failed prediction is that BG2 minus the stack would include zero: it is GBP 7.35 million (1.6 to 14.9 million). Primaries have no published limit, so every money figure on this page ranks forecasts and states no money saved.

After a logged transfer ends, the order reverses on CRPS. The unmasked stack is then the worst forecast on CRPS, but 7 transfers cannot separate the stack from the other forecasts. On cost at the 0.5 limit the worst forecast after a transfer is BG2, and the order is not reversed.

docs.title: Row groups: ordinary days and the windows around load transfers
docs.text:
Rows are the six Primaries' half-hours with a 12 to 36 hour lead for cost, and all leads for CRPS and MAE. G0 uses experiment 251's rows (the stack is its arm 1). G1 to G5 use experiment 163's rows, where the stack is the unmasked GAM-K stack K0 (a different build, with five stored quantiles), so the first column of the table is K0 for G1 to G5. The logged transfers are the 7 of experiment 163; the group sizes are rows, and the unit of resampling is a transfer, or a calendar month for G0 and G1.

Group Rows (transfers) CRPS: stack (K0 from G1), BG2, manual heuristic, climatology Avoidable cost at 0.5, GBP million G0 all 251 rows 561,207 2.58, 2.72, 3.40, 3.67 44.82, 52.17, 75.36, 80.30 G1 ordinary 556,809 2.73, 2.70, 3.39, 3.66 44.86, 50.73, 74.42, 79.12 G2 before the alarm 11 (1) 19.21, 16.15, 14.13, 24.00 no half-hour at a 12 to 36 hour lead G3 during 12,168 (3) 5.94, 7.38, 10.24, 10.16 3.46, 8.46, 15.42, 18.08 G4 after the end 3,675 (7) 13.69, 10.09, 7.65, 7.49 2.49, 2.65, 1.69, 1.72 G5 near (G2 + G3 + G4) 15,854 (7) 7.75, 8.01, 9.64, 9.55 5.95, 11.11, 17.11, 19.80
  • What the groups show. During a transfer the stack is best (CRPS 5.94). After the transfer ends, the stack is worst (13.69, against 7.49 for climatology), because the stack carries the transfer's lagged power into its forecast. G4 minus the stack: BG2 -3.59 CRPS points (95% -5.71 to +0.12), climatology -6.19 (-8.62 to +1.71).
  • Cost during and after a transfer. During a transfer (G3, 3 transfers), BG2, the manual heuristic, and climatology cost more than the stack at the 0.5 limit (BG2 minus stack GBP 5.0 million, 0.001 to 13.6 million). After the end, the only cost interval that excludes zero is BG2 minus the stack at the 0.75 limit (GBP -0.05 million, -0.12 to -0.002).
  • The intervals are not reliable. With 3 transfers there are only 10 distinct resamples, so the G3 figures are point estimates by transfer and not 95% intervals. The 7-transfer intervals of G4 and G5 understate the uncertainty for the same reason. The transfers are also not independent: 3 of them appear in both G3 and G4, and one involves two Primaries. Several G3 and G5 CRPS and cost intervals for climatology and the manual heuristic against the stack exclude zero, and they carry the same warning.
  • Row-group sizes. G2 has 11 rows from one transfer and no scored half-hour, so it is unreadable. The cost columns use only half-hours at a 12 to 36 hour lead: 80,143 in G1, 1,997 in G3, 926 in G4, and 2,923 in G5, while the CRPS columns use all leads. 243 rows sit in both G3 and G4, so G5 counts them twice (1.5% of its rows).
  • Splits (G6). Season, G1: BG2 minus the stack is +0.22 CRPS points (95% +0.16 to +0.26) from November to March and -0.20 (-0.36 to -0.03) from April to October, so the stack's gain is a winter gain, as in experiment 251. Duration, G5: none of the 7 transfers lasted under 6 hours, 5 lasted 6 to 24 hours (1,138 rows), and 2 lasted over a day (14,716 rows). Substation, G5: transfers appear at D5 (10,725 rows, 3 transfers), D16 (4,335, 2), D14 (692, 3), and D10 (102, 1), and none at D9 or D11. The stored transfers carry no size, so the split by size of shift is not available, and the margins of 7 days either side are not stored, so G5 is the union of the three phases only.

docs.title: How small a difference one year of rows can resolve
docs.text:
One year of scored rows resolves a difference of about 7% of the CRPS and 19% of the avoidable cost between BG2 and the GAM stack, and the near-transfer rows resolve far less. The smallest resolvable difference is 2.8 standard errors of the paired difference (80% power at the 5% level), from resampling whole calendar months, or whole transfers in the near groups.

  • Ordinary year, BG2 minus the stack. Cost: observed GBP 7.35 million, smallest resolvable 9.75 million (18.7%). CRPS: observed 0.137, smallest resolvable 0.196 points. Tail-weighted CRPS at the 95th percentile (twCRPS): observed 0.028, smallest resolvable 0.044. The difference is real by the 95% interval and below the 80%-power size, so it was found with little to spare.
  • Climatology and the manual heuristic. Climatology minus the stack is resolved (cost observed 35.5 against 23.9 million; CRPS observed 1.09 against 0.46). Climatology minus the manual heuristic is not (cost 4.9 against 10.4 million).
  • Load-shift effects against the resolvable size. Experiment 208's effect on the pooled year is 0.005 points, about 40 times below the smallest resolvable CRPS difference of 0.196 points. Its effect of 1.50 points after a transfer is below the smallest resolvable difference in G4 (4.02 points for BG2 against K0, 7 transfers) and just above G5's (1.43 points, 7 transfers, G3 2.36 with 3). The resolvable differences above use a multiplier of 2.8 standard errors. That multiplier makes them about 10% to 15% too small at 12 months (a small-sample multiplier near 3.1 fits), and more at 3 to 7 transfers. In G4 the smallest resolvable cost difference is GBP 0.69 million at the 0.5 limit, in G5 12.2 million.
  • Consequence for steps 4 to 6. The curtailment part of the three questions cannot be answered from the real record of 7 transfers. It needs injected worlds with many shifts, and CRPS and twCRPS from the same worlds as the fallback measure.
  • Events. At the 0.5 limit 35,670 of 80,794 scored half-hours (44%) are above the limit, at 0.75 3,996, at 0.9 164. At 0.5 the metric is therefore close to an accuracy ranking of the 0.95 quantile, and at 0.9 it cannot rank forecasts.

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text:
• Scores on the 561,207 shared rows (95% interval from resampling 12 months), CRPS; MAE of the median; twCRPS at the 95th percentile of earlier power. Stack 2.579 (2.436 to 2.725); 4.510; 0.152. BG2 2.715 (2.534 to 2.917); 4.767; 0.180. Manual heuristic 3.397 (3.097 to 3.714); 6.034; 0.211. Climatology 3.665 (3.304 to 4.037); 6.558; 0.224. Weak XGBoost (experiment 251's reference arm) 5.697; 6.206; 0.301.
  • Contrasts (first minus second, CRPS). BG2 minus stack +0.136 (+0.005 to +0.278); manual heuristic minus stack +0.818 (+0.573 to +1.088); climatology minus stack +1.086 (+0.778 to +1.419); climatology minus manual heuristic +0.268 (+0.125 to +0.427). These contrasts match experiment 251.
  • Avoidable cost at 0.5, GBP million (six Primaries, 12 to 36 hour leads, GBP 2,000 per MWh). Stack 44.82 (35.52 to 54.20); BG2 52.17 (38.41 to 67.82); manual heuristic 75.36 (54.69 to 99.48); climatology 80.30 (58.54 to 106.24); weak XGBoost 234.22 (156.30 to 324.33); a perfect forecast still costs 46.35 million in total, because some flow exceeds the limit however well it is forecast.
  • Cost contrasts at 0.5, GBP million. BG2 minus stack 7.35 (1.55 to 14.91); manual heuristic minus BG2 23.19 (14.72 to 33.33); climatology minus BG2 28.13 (17.80 to 40.75); climatology minus manual heuristic 4.94 (-1.80 to 12.65), so climatology and the manual heuristic are not separated.
  • Sweep. At 0.75, BG2 minus stack 1.97 (0.01 to 5.25), manual heuristic minus BG2 5.34 (1.96 to 9.36), climatology minus manual heuristic 0.56 (-0.29 to 1.52). At 0.9 the contrasts rest on 164 half-hours: BG2 minus stack 0.08 (0.01 to 0.17), and the climatology contrasts include zero.
  • Cuts of the 0.5 cost (BG2 minus stack, GBP million). November to March 6.66 (2.09 to 12.74), April to October 0.68 (-1.57 to 2.89); leads 0 to 12 hours 5.96 (1.56 to 11.33), 36 hours to 7 days 32.84 (2.61 to 69.87). By Primary the estimate is positive at all six and the interval excludes zero at D10 and D14 only.
  • Bulk supply points D13 and D17 (demand only, 12 to 36 hour leads). Climatology and the manual heuristic exist at both (experiment 87's stored references), and so do the top-down GAM forecast (experiment 161) and the bottom-up forecast (experiment 204); no BG2 and no experiment 220 stack exist there. CRPS: top-down 6.05, bottom-up 6.06, manual heuristic 6.92, climatology 7.22. Avoidable cost at 0.5, GBP million: top-down 140.34 (86.46 to 197.17), bottom-up 140.57 (85.43 to 198.46), manual heuristic 169.79 (98.01 to 248.65), climatology 174.85 (104.69 to 249.44). Climatology minus top-down is 34.51 (-3.85 to 78.82), so two bulk supply points cannot separate climatology from the top-down forecast at 0.5, and at 0.75 it is 6.95 (1.09 to 15.16). Top-down minus bottom-up is -0.23 (-3.31 to 2.85).
  • Child Primaries. D13 has children D2, D4, D9, D10, D11, D19, and D21. D17 has children D3, D5, D8, D12, D14, D15, D16, D18, and D22. Only D5, D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16 have stored forecasts of the four arms.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, per Primary, for the stack (points of capacity). D10 +0.72, D11 -0.50, D14 -0.20, D16 -0.84, D5 +0.01, D9 -0.75. Only the stack stores a mean (arm D's, before the head's correction), so the other arms have no mean to compare.
  • Mean-forecast error beside the contrasts. The stack's MAE of the mean is 4.62 against 4.51 for its median. BG2 stores no mean, so the BG2 contrast has no mean-forecast partner. The median MAE moves with CRPS in every contrast (BG2 minus stack +0.257, +0.008 to +0.497).
  • Triggers. The skill lists seven audit triggers. Trigger 2 (a prediction failed) fired once, for the BG2 interval that was predicted to include zero. We tested an explanation: the cost gain is the winter gain of experiment 251 (November to March 6.66 million, April to October 0.68 million with an interval including zero), and the interval excludes zero at 0.5 because 44% of half-hours are above the limit.
  • Triggers that did not fire. Trigger 4 (a result that depends on one series): leaving out each Primary in turn keeps BG2 minus the stack positive with an interval above zero at 0.5, and at 0.75 the interval touches zero when D10, D14, or D16 is left out. Trigger 6 (an implausibly narrow interval): the BG2 interval is 13.4 million wide on a cost of 98.5 million, and experiment 251's is 0.27 wide on 2.58. Triggers 1, 3, and 5 did not fire, because a perfect forecast has zero breach, no mean exists for BG2, and there are no nested arms.
  • Trigger 7 fired. Steps 4 to 6 build on this result, so a fresh agent audited it. The findings are under "Audit".

docs.title: Audit
docs.text:
A fresh agent re-derived the headline numbers with its own code from the stored arrays.

  • Reproduced. CRPS of all four forecasts, the BG2 minus stack CRPS contrast (0.1365, 0.004 to 0.275), the avoidable costs at 0.5 (44.82, 52.17, 75.36, and 80.30 million), BG2 minus stack GBP 7.35 million (1.61 to 14.88), and the after-transfer CRPS of K0, BG2, the manual heuristic, and climatology. Accepted: the page's numbers stand.
  • Robust. The order climatology, manual heuristic, BG2, stack holds for cut quantiles q90, q95, and q99, breach ratios 10, 20, and 50, any lead window, and leaving out any one Primary except D14 (the auditor's "D16" is time series 16, which is D14 in these labels), where climatology and the manual heuristic tie (58.49 against 58.65 million). Climatology minus the stack survives every change.
  • Fragile. In the auditor's resample, BG2 minus the stack includes zero at breach ratio 50, at the 0.75 limit, and on 12 to 24 hour leads alone. Without D14 it halves to 3.39 million (0.13 to 7.20), and the 24 to 36 hour half carries 6.27 of the 7.35 million. The page therefore calls the separation narrow. Accepted: the verdict wording and caveats say so. The page's own resample at the 0.75 limit gives 1.97 million (0.01 to 5.25), which only just excludes zero. At the 0.9 limit climatology costs less than the manual heuristic, which the page already attributes to 164 events.
  • Code review (fresh Sonnet). Leakage, units, row alignment, and the metric call checked and fine. Accepted and applied to the page: the 3-transfer and 7-transfer intervals are not reliable (stated under the row-group table and in the figure subtitle); the first table column is K0 for G1 to G5; the cost and CRPS columns use different leads; 243 rows are in both G3 and G4; the small-sample multiplier makes the smallest resolvable differences about 10% to 15% too small; the headline quotes the range 1.4 to 4.0 points, not G4's value alone; the capacity-file note and the 156 dropped rows are stated. Not applied: deduplicating G5 (stated instead, 1.5% of its rows), and a t-based multiplier (stated instead).

docs.title: Caveats and what to try next
docs.text:
• Node-only demand proxy. The six Primaries and the two bulk supply points are scored as nodes with no generators attached, a positive demand reading is assumed to be the flow that can breach, and planned cuts are assumed delivered. Generator-aware scoring at D13 and D17 needs a farm table for those two points that no file we found provides, and the forecasts of the six solar farms that experiments 224 and 243 stored are not mapped to them. The stored forecasts here are complete (11 quantiles for the Primaries, no padded quantile), so the generator padding problem found in experiment 255's farm frames does not touch this scoring.
  • Not a saving. The scaled limit is a fraction of the largest earlier demand. The page ranks forecasts and does not estimate money saved. The manual heuristic's implied risk level is not used, because the heuristic enters only as a forecast.
  • Capacity file. Point-to-MW conversion uses experiment 1156's effective capacities, which include the scored year (series 18: 9.115 MW against 8.834 before it; others under 1%). The limits come from raw MW flows before the scored year, so no limit leaks.
  • Dropped rows. Joining experiment 87's references onto experiment 163's rows drops 156 of 572,819 rows (26 per Primary, all ordinary).
  • Stack builds differ. G0 uses the stack with the neural-network head (arm 1). G1 to G5 use K0, the unmasked GAM-K stack, whose five stored quantiles give CRPS and pinball losses at q95 and q99 but not twCRPS. On ordinary rows K0's CRPS is 2.73 against arm 1's 2.58.
  • Seeds and schedule. One seed, no refits; the stack's monthly refits and BG2's weekly refits are those of experiments 220 and 87. Weather at lag times is the ensemble weather available at forecast time. No downloads.
  • What to try next. Steps 4 to 6 should use injected worlds with many shifts and a node whose limit is crossed on enough half-hours, with CRPS and twCRPS as the fallback. A scoring of the six solar farms at D13 and D17 needs the farm-to-node map first.

docs.title: How much forecast skill does the best-guess demand stack lose when its convex model, its neural network head, and its solar factors are retrained less often?
docs.text:
Retraining the small neural network that corrects the median (the head) more often did not help, and the convex demand model's monthly refit is worth keeping. We asked how much forecast skill the best-guess demand stack loses when its three retrained parts are retrained less often. The stack is the combined demand forecast of experiment 251, built from three parts. The first is the convex model, a generalised additive model (GAM) whose coefficients a Kalman filter updates (called arm D in experiment 155). The second is the head (experiment 201). The third is the solar factors (experiment 202): two numbers per half-hour, the mean and the standard deviation of the 51 weather-ensemble members' solar responses, each rescaled by a fitted factor. We refitted each part on a different schedule. We scored the 561,363 half-hourly rows of 2025-07 to 2026-06 in total across six anonymised substations. The quantile score is twice the mean pinball loss (the standard error of a quantile forecast) over 11 quantiles, in percentage points of the substation's effective capacity (its rated demand); lower is better. BG2 is the XGBoost best-guess demand model of experiment 87.

Verdict not supported. The plan predicted two things. P1: the convex model tolerates quarterly instead of monthly refits, losing under 0.02 points. P2: the head trained once scores at least 0.03 points worse than the quarterly head. P2 failed, because the head trained once scored 0.008 points better than the quarterly head. P1's point estimate held (+0.010), but its 99% interval reaches +0.032, so the decision rule calls P1 inconclusive. P3 held (the monthly head minus the quarterly head +0.001), and P4 held (quarterly minus monthly solar factors -0.0001). The stop rule (stop before the head arms if monthly and quarterly refits differ by under 0.01 at 5 of 6 substations) did not fire: they differ by under 0.01 at 2 of 6. We measured the convex model's cadence on its own forecasts. We then added the head and the solar factors to the monthly-refit forecasts only, and did not rebuild the whole stack on quarterly refits. The contrasts C1 to C5 below are the five planned comparisons: C1 and C2 for the convex model, C3 and C4 for the head, C5 for the solar factors.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Schedule and what was refitted. Convex model: experiment 136's stored fits on all substations' history with a 24-month window, weekly, monthly (the stack's own schedule), and quarterly (the monthly fits cut in January, April, July, and October); the Kalman filter runs throughout. Head: the experiment 201 variant that sees calendar flags, three random seeds, retrained at each month start from 2025-07 (12 retrains, 36 fits) with every training target dated before the retrain date. Solar factors: experiment 202's replay, refitted at the month or the quarter start. Retraining the head took 2.7 s per fit on the GPU, and refitting the convex model took 0.4 s per substation, so no schedule saves meaningful compute. BG2's weekly and monthly refits are experiment 87's.
  • Absolute scores, six substations: the table gives the quantile score, the mean absolute error of the median, and the tail-weighted CRPS at the 95th percentile of earlier power.
Forecast Quantile score Median error Tail CRPS BG2 refitted weekly 2.715 4.766 0.202 BG2 refitted monthly 2.752 4.805 0.204 Convex model, monthly refits 2.691 4.623 0.191 Convex model, weekly refits 2.692 4.613 0.193 Convex model, quarterly refits 2.702 4.636 0.192 Stack, head trained once 2.578 4.510 0.171 Stack, head retrained quarterly 2.587 4.526 0.170 Stack, head retrained monthly 2.588 4.528 0.170

The stack scores about 0.13 below BG2 refitted weekly at every head schedule. - C1, convex model quarterly minus monthly: +0.010 (99% interval -0.014 to +0.032). Post hoc, at the 95% level and excluding October: winter (November to March) +0.022 (+0.014 to +0.027), summer (April to September) +0.002 (-0.028 to +0.033). By substation: D10 +0.044, D5 +0.016, D16 +0.013, D11 +0.006, D14 -0.000, D9 -0.016. - C2, weekly minus monthly: +0.001 (99% -0.018 to +0.019); post hoc, 95% level, October excluded: winter +0.020 (+0.007 to +0.034), summer -0.014 (-0.031 to +0.006). - C3, head trained once minus quarterly retrained (stack): -0.008 over all rows (99% -0.017 to 0.000); April to June -0.011 (week-block 99% -0.027 to +0.005, because three months are too few to resample). Once minus monthly retrained is -0.009. - C4, monthly minus quarterly head: +0.001 (99% -0.006 to +0.008). - C5, solar factors quarterly minus monthly, daylight rows: -0.0001 (99% -0.0008 to +0.0003) for the solar summary alone, and -0.0001 (99% -0.0008 to +0.0004) with the head added. - Tails (coverage and pinball loss; stack with head trained once against BG2 refitted weekly): q01 coverage 0.013 and loss 0.172 against 0.010 and 0.211; q99 coverage 0.984 and loss 0.211 against 0.983 and 0.253. Tails move by under 0.002 across head cadences. - Post hoc: the head fitted at 2025-07 with this experiment's pipeline and never retrained ("own once") scores 2.582, 0.004 below the quarterly head (95% -0.013 to +0.003) and 0.004 above experiment 201's stored head (-0.004 to +0.012). - What to try next: a retest of the head's cadence once a second year of ensemble weather exists, because one year cannot show slow drift; and a stack rebuilt end to end on quarterly convex-model refits, which would test the interaction with the head.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, per substation: exactly 0.000 at all six substations at every convex-model cadence, because arm D's median is its mean forecast by construction.
  • Mean-forecast error beside each contrast: the median's absolute error moves with the quantile score in C1 (+0.013 against +0.010), C2 (-0.009 against +0.001, within noise), and C3 (once 4.510 against quarterly 4.526), so trigger 3 did not fire.
  • Triggers (the seven audit triggers of the experiment guide): trigger 1, a failed control, did not fire (the gates reproduced experiment 155's arm D and experiment 202's solar arm exactly). Trigger 2, a result contradicting its prediction, fired for P2 and was resolved here: the head trained once scored 0.004 better than the same pipeline's head trained at 2025-07 and never retrained, a gap whose 95% interval (-0.004 to +0.012) includes zero, so retraining adds nothing measurable. Trigger 4, a sign flip when one site is left out, did not fire: leaving one substation out leaves C1 between +0.003 and +0.016 and C3 between -0.007 and -0.010. Triggers 5 and 6 (a nested arm beating its parent, and interval widths) did not fire. Trigger 7, later work depending on an unreplicated result, is open: later work may rely on the one-year result.
  • Departures from the plan: the last-quarter C3 interval uses week blocks as well as month blocks, because three months are too few to resample. The cadence contrast is read at the arm D level, as planned; the stack approximation was not run separately.

docs.title: Does a smooth monotone heating curve, with thermal lag and wind, lower the demand forecast's error on cold nights and winter days?
Take-home message
docs.text: A straight-line heating response is close to what one winter of data can distinguish from a curve. Three changes to the heating term (a smooth monotone curve, lagged temperatures, and wind) each moved the day-ahead score by less than 0.02 points outside cold nights, and none beat the current model on cold nights. A small neural network learned a plausible curve, flat above about 12 C and 1.4 to 3 times steeper per degree below 3 C than from 6 to 12 C. Trained longer, it lowered the cold-night score by 0.13 points, but the interval includes zero, the gain reversed in the previous year, and the network failed a test on synthetic data. The audit traced the gain to one cold spell in January 2026. The card keeps the straight line. A retest would need a second winter of scored cold nights.

docs.title: What was asked
docs.text:
We asked whether the demand model's straight-line heating response is too rigid. The model (experiment 114's T-all, with the recent-error Kalman filter, "T-all-K" here) adds heating power in proportion to how far four trailing-mean temperatures fall below 15.5 C. We replaced or extended that response in four ways and scored each against T-all-K on the five decision Primaries over 2025-07 to 2026-06, using ERA5 past weather, so every score is a ceiling for a forecast made from a weather forecast. The ideas build on experiment 126, whose screens of monotone ramps, exponentially weighted temperatures, and wind chill all tied on winter rows, and on experiment 121, where five heating hinges gained only 0.016 points. The network follows the monotone-network design of experiment 250.

The first fit of the network under-fitted. The training fit and the known-answer test pointed to the network, not the hypothesis, so a second network (A3b) was trained longer and given more inputs. A3b is labelled post hoc throughout, and the pre-registered contrasts are reported as measured.

docs.title: Arms and rows
docs.text:
• A0, T-all-K: hinge at 15.5 C on the 6, 24, 72, and 168 hour mean temperatures, split by day type and half of the hour band (experiment 114's T-all, penalty weight 1.0); Kalman filter with T-all's per-site hyperparameters from experiment 126, used for every arm. Reproduced exactly: the forecast equals experiment 126's stored scored-year forecast on all 104,897 rows.
  • A1: A0 plus a smooth monotone curve (decreasing cubic smoothsteps between knots at 0, 4, 8, 12, 16, and 20 C, non-negative coefficients) on the four trailing means, per hour band.
  • A2: A1 plus the same curve on exponentially weighted temperatures (time constants 1 and 3 days) and on the previous two days' mean temperatures.
  • A2w: A2 plus the 24-hour and 72-hour mean wind speed times the cold hinge of the 24-hour and 72-hour mean temperature.
  • A3 (pre-registered): T-all's heating columns replaced by a monotone network (2 hidden layers of 16 units, non-negative weights on temperature and wind) on three daily mean temperatures and the 24-hour wind; 3 seeds; 90 epochs. A3 without wind is the same without the wind input.
  • A3b (post hoc): the same network on A0's four trailing means plus the two previous-day means and the wind, trained for 200 epochs at a higher learning rate. A3b without wind drops the wind input.
  • Rows: dp_mw_v1 on past weather, five decision Primaries (D5, D10, D11, D14, D16), D9 scored beside them in the verdict year only, outside the hand-filtered events, day ahead. Cold nights are 22:00 to 08:00 local time on days with a mean temperature of at most 3 C (1,220 rows in the scored year). Yearly refits, not weekly; a contrast of 0.02 points or more does not depend on the cadence. The conditional retest on ensemble weather (fold_a_daily_gap_v1) was not run, because no arm passed.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Absolute scores, scored year (quantile score, points):

    Arm Cold nights November to March All rows A0, T-all-K 2.144 2.306 2.216 A1 2.206 2.303 2.208 A2 2.190 2.299 2.206 A2w 2.185 2.283 2.198 A3 (pre-registered) 2.759 2.607 2.364 A3b (post hoc) 2.012 2.265 2.198 A3b without wind (post hoc) 1.981 2.285 2.212 A3c (post hoc) 2.065 2.303 2.210

  • C1, A1 minus A0: cold nights +0.062 (99% interval -0.040 to +0.127), replicate year -0.001, better at 3 of 5 Primaries. All rows -0.008 (-0.024 to +0.009). Label: tie.
