docs.title: Known-answer gate
docs.text:
• Synthetic truth: T-all's non-heating terms plus a known heating curve of the real temperatures and noise as large as T-all's own residual, at D10 and D14, fitted on the 24-month window and scored on the next year against the noiseless truth.
  • Curved truth: on cold rows the root mean squared error falls from 1.06 to 0.93 (A2) at D10 and from 0.98 to 0.72 (A2) at D14, so A1 and A2 can see a curve if one exists. A3b gets 1.28 at D10 (worse than T-all's 1.06) and 0.75 at D14 (23% better, short of the pre-registered 25%).
  • Straight truth: A3b is within the pre-registered tolerance of T-all at both sites (error at most 25% above T-all's plus 0.05 points on all rows), although at D10 its cold-row error is 30% above T-all's.
  • A3c gets 1.20 at D10 and 0.79 at D14 on the curved truth, no better than A3b.
  • Scope: only the networks have a pass rule; A1 and A2 are in the gate only to show they can see a curve, and A3, A3 without wind, and A2w are not in it.
  • Consequence: A3b and A3c fail the curved-truth gate, so their labels are capped at inconclusive (the report applies the cap). Four settings of the network's size and regularisation were tried on the synthetic curved truth only; none passed, and the original post hoc setting was kept.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast: 0.000 points at every Primary for every arm, because each quantile set is the filtered mean plus a centred residual spread.
  • Error of the mean forecast beside each score contrast: the mean-forecast error moves in the same direction as the score on cold nights for C1 (+0.181), C2 (+0.140), C3 (+1.137), and C7 (-0.200).
  • Triggers that fired: the failed known-answer gate (trigger 1); dropping D10 flips the sign of C1 and C2 on cold nights (trigger 4), which leaves both labelled tie; and the C3 result contradicting its prediction (trigger 2), which the training-fit check explains. A fresh Sonnet auditor (the brief set Sonnet only, so no Opus audit ran) re-derived C1, C2, and C7 from the stored predictions and matched them. The findings are triaged under "Reviews".

docs.title: Reviews
docs.text:
• Code review (Sonnet), triaged. Accepted: the network stopped on the last 15% of rows, which hold almost no cold nights; A3c tests that and does not fix the gate failure. Accepted: the gate cap is now applied in the report, and the gate's scope is stated above. Accepted as harmless here: null daily means drop a few rows from the subsets, and the first four days of the grid carry NaN or back-filled inputs, but no training window reaches them. No leakage found.
  • Audit (Sonnet), triaged. Accepted: the A3b gain rests on one cold spell, so the take-home message and advice treat it as unreplicated. Accepted: C1 and C2 flip sign without D10 (both stay ties). Confirmed: the pre-registered network's failure is under-fitting plus two missing inputs, not a code defect; T-all-K reproduces exactly; no look-ahead; pairing is clean.
  • Write-up and prose reviews: see the pull request.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Repeat the network test when a second winter of cold nights can be scored, with the network checked against its own training fit first.
  • If the network is retested, give it the four trailing means and the previous-day means as in A3b, and compare against a plain gradient-boosted tree on the same inputs to separate "curved" from "flexible".
  • A wind term of -0.008 points on all rows is the only contrast on all rows whose interval excludes zero; it is too small to port by itself.

docs.title: PV capacity: does the empirical solar shape lower arm D's April to June error?
docs.text:
Take-home message: no. Neither the empirical solar shape nor a lower solar capacity changes arm D's April to June error by more than 0.01 MW at D9 and D16. Arm D is the monthly-refit generalised additive model of experiments 155 and 220, scored on experiment 178's rows. Experiment 266 put the April to June gap to BG2 in its solar term. Experiment 269 found a pooled empirical shape that recovers an injected farm better than the physical fleet shape, with real capacities 0.2 to 0.4 MW lower. This experiment puts that shape and those capacities into arm D.

Verdict: not supported. C1 (e2 minus the control, April to June daylight, D9 and D16) is -0.009 MW with a 99% interval of -0.041 to +0.024, so the interval contains zero and the point estimate is above -0.01 MW. The control's April to June daylight error at D9 and D16 is 0.528 MW, and its gap to BG2 there is +0.044 MW (-0.018 to +0.103), so the largest gain any arm showed (0.010 MW) closes under a quarter of the gap. Every level, table, and factor except the oracle arm s2 uses data before 2025-07-01 only, and all 36 stored control frames equal experiment 180's control frames (e00280_check_control.py).

Figure 1. Almost every interval contains zero; the oracle cut at D5 stands clear of it, upward. Week-block intervals are wide (about 13 weeks of April to June, 4,000 resamples).

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
The shape alone changes the error by about 0.01 MW, and the all-half-hours error rises. At D9 and D16, April to June daylight, e0 (the empirical shape at the pinned capacity) is -0.010 MW (-0.022 to +0.001), e1 (swapped level) -0.006 MW (-0.014 to +0.002), and C4 is therefore small. On all half-hours at D9 and D16, e0 is +0.006 MW (+0.002 to +0.009), e1 +0.007 MW (+0.003 to +0.010), and e2 +0.008 MW (0.000 to +0.014). The empirical shape raises the error outside April to June daylight.

The lower capacity helps D9 and does nothing at D16. e2 at D9 alone is -0.022 MW (-0.060 to +0.010) and at D16 alone +0.005 MW (-0.028 to +0.040), so the pooled C1 is a D9 result. With a 60% export clip at D9 as well, e2 at D9 is -0.004 MW (-0.010 to +0.001): the clip already removes most of what the capacity cut offers. f1 (the fleet shape at the real-fit capacity) is -0.002 MW at D9 and D16 (-0.035 to +0.029), so the capacity gives no more than the shape did (C3).

The capacity bias in April to June does not generalise. s1 (a factor of 1.02 to 1.13 from April to June 2025) is +0.004 MW at D9 and D16 (-0.004 to +0.011), as P3 predicted. s2 (the oracle factors of experiment 266, which read the scored year) is -0.003 MW at D9 and D16 (-0.014 to +0.008) and +0.081 MW at D5 (+0.053 to +0.115): the capacity cut experiment 266 measured at D5 is already supplied by the 60% clip, and cutting it again overshoots.

The other substations and the night-time error do not move. At D10, D11, and D14, April to June daylight changes by at most +0.003 MW in any arm, and the April to June night-time error of the five decision substations changes by at most +0.004 MW (P4 holds). On sunny half-hours, e2 is +0.007 MW over the five decision substations (-0.009 to +0.030), but it raises D16's sunny-half-hour error by +0.020 MW, which reaches the 0.02 MW no-harm limit. The verdict does not change, because C1 fails first.

docs.title: Predictions
docs.text:
• P1 (e0 and e1 change sunny-daylight error by under 0.02 MW at each of D9, D10, D11, D14, D16): met; the largest is e0 at D9 on sunny half-hours, -0.016 MW (the group means for D16 and the others are within 0.004 MW).
  • P2 (e2 lowers April to June daylight error by at least 0.02 MW over D9 and D16, and moves D5 by under 0.02 MW): the first part is not met (-0.009 MW); the D5 part is met (-0.003 MW).
  • P3 (s1 is above -0.01 MW at D9 and D16): met; +0.004 MW.
  • P4 (night-time error at D10 does not move by more than 0.02 MW in any arm): met; D10 moves by at most +0.004 MW.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Pinball loss agrees. C1 in pinball loss is -0.001 MW (-0.011 to +0.008).
  • The intervals are wide. About 13 weeks of April to June fall in the scored year, so a gain of 0.02 MW would not show unless it sat in most weeks.
  • s2 is a bound, not a forecast, because it reads the scored year.
  • D9 and D16 are two substations. C1 is a mean over two, and D9 carries it.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: Neither the shape nor the capacity of the solar term closes the April to June gap in this test. The next experiment should test the parts of arm D outside the solar term, and should score D9 alone, where e2 gains 0.022 MW (-0.060 to +0.010) but the interval includes zero.

docs.title: Does an Economy 7 night step that grows with the cold lower the forecast error on winter nights when the weather is an ensemble forecast?
docs.text:
Fitting the Economy 7 night levels inside the substation demand model beat a winter night offset in both years, but the gain in the two hours after the night step starts, which we had pre-registered as the test, could not be shown. Economy 7 is a tariff that switches storage heaters on shortly after 00:30 UTC, which raises demand at night. We asked whether a night step that grows with the cold, fitted inside the demand model of a primary substation, lowers the forecast error on winter nights when the weather input is an ensemble forecast. We fitted six versions of the model (defined below) at 5 primary substations and scored them on a year that no fit had seen. In the two hours after the step starts (half-hours starting 00:30 to 02:00 UTC, December to February), the scores improved by 0.023 points of a substation's rated demand in that year. In a second year used to check the sign, the same contrast worsened by 0.023 points. A leave-one-substation-out check shows that the gain rests on two or three substations.

Scores are quantile scores in points of a substation's rated demand, and a lower score is better. Winter nights are the half-hours from 16:00 to 06:00 local time in November to March. A difference written "A1 minus A0" is negative where A1 is better. The scored year is 2025-07 to 2026-06, and the replicate year is the even months of 2024-07 to 2025-06. A0 is experiment 136's demand model (a Kalman filter on recent errors, the heating split by day type, and one shared filter setting) plus the winter night offset of experiment 155, which adds a constant learned from the demand model's own past errors on winter nights. A1 is A0 with 20 free night levels added (one per half-hour from 22:00 to 07:30 UTC, the design of experiment 121), plus the offset. A2 is A1 with a step from 00:30 to 08:00 UTC added, whose size is a sum of four hinge functions of the 24-hour mean temperature (each is zero above a temperature threshold and linear below it), with every coefficient at least zero, so the step grows with the cold. K0 is A0's demand model without the offset, E1 is A1's without the offset, and E2 is A2's without the offset. The plan fixed the start of the step at 00:30 UTC because experiment 123 found the step begins at the half-hour starting 00:30 UTC at all 14 time series it examined. The three planned contrasts are C1 (A1 minus A0), C2 (A2 minus A1), and C3 (A2 minus A0). BG2 is the production-style XGBoost forecast of experiment 87.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Verdict inconclusive. The plan's rule gives partly supported by its letter, because the step-hour interval of C3 (-0.043 to -0.013) lies below zero. We set the verdict lower because the audit found that interval is not a 99% interval in any useful sense: the scored year holds 4 step-hour months, so the interval spans the smallest and largest monthly values. The sign of C3 also flips between the years (+0.023 in the replicate year, -0.014 in the odd months of 2024-07 to 2025-06).
  • Pre-registered contrasts (scored year, 99% interval, substations improved of 5).
    • C1 (A1 minus A0): step hours -0.016 (-0.041 to +0.008, 2 of 5); winter nights -0.022 (-0.041 to -0.002, 3 of 5); all rows -0.012 (-0.022 to -0.001, 5 of 5).
    • C2 (A2 minus A1): step hours -0.007 (-0.024 to -0.000, 2 of 5); winter nights -0.012 (-0.029 to -0.002, 4 of 5); all rows -0.006 (-0.013 to -0.002, 5 of 5).
    • C3 (A2 minus A0): step hours -0.023 (-0.043 to -0.013, 3 of 5); winter nights -0.034 (-0.068 to -0.006, 5 of 5); all rows -0.018 (-0.032 to -0.006, 5 of 5). The decision rule's step-hour threshold (an interval wholly below -0.02) and 4-of-5-substations condition both fail.
    • Replicate year. C1, C2, and C3 on step hours are +0.007, +0.016, and +0.023, so the sign is opposite to the scored year. On all rows they are -0.003, -0.001, and -0.005.
  • Post hoc: night terms inside the model, no offset (E2 minus A0). All rows: -0.017 (-0.033 to -0.002, 5 of 5) in the scored year and -0.030 (-0.059 to -0.005, 3 of 5) in the replicate year. Winter nights: -0.039 and -0.035. Step hours: -0.059 (-0.116 to -0.007, 4 of 5) and -0.039 (-0.109 to +0.051, 3 of 5). E1 minus A0 is -0.010 and -0.027 on all rows. E2 minus E1 is -0.006 and -0.003.

  • Absolute scores, scored year (mean quantile score in points; cold nights are winter nights with a daily mean temperature below 2 C, 5,395 rows):

    Arm All rows Step hours Winter nights Cold nights K0 2.791 2.578 2.339 3.370 A0 2.774 2.381 2.277 3.313 A1 2.762 2.365 2.255 3.266 A2 2.756 2.358 2.244 3.174 E1 2.764 2.337 2.252 3.272 E2 2.757 2.322 2.238 3.176 BG2 2.780 2.526 2.394 3.724 Manual heuristic 3.497 3.517 3.361 7.090

  • Predictions. The A1 minus A0 contrast (C1) on step hours missed (predicted -0.05 to -0.15, was -0.016). C1 on winter nights held (-0.022 against -0.02 to -0.06). The A2 minus A1 contrast (C2) on cold nights was larger than predicted (-0.093 against -0.01 to -0.04). The step amplitude is larger at 0 C than at 3 C at 5 of 5 substations. C3 equals C1 plus C2 on winter nights to within 0.001. The cold-night q95 coverage rose by 2.4 points (A2 minus A0, 83.8% to 86.1%), inside the predicted 0 to 3. A3 was not run, because no arm met the decision rule.

  • Start audit. Fitted on the 24 months before 2025-07-01, the start of the step is 00:00 UTC at D5, D10, and D11 and 00:30 at D14 and D16, so all 5 substations agree with the 00:30 start of experiment 123 within 30 minutes, and the cap on the verdict in the decision rule does not apply.
  • The night question from experiment 266. On D10's April to June night rows the scores are A0 2.782, A1 2.748, A2 2.716, and BG2 2.328. The Economy 7 terms close 0.067 of the 0.455-point gap. The stored stack's residual at D10 is about -2 points from 21:00 to 07:30 UTC and -4 to -6 from 07:30 to 09:00 (figure 4), a level error, not a step at 00:30. The question is answered for the Economy 7 term: no. The D10 gap needs its own experiment.
  • Rows, schedule, and weather. 561,172 forecast rows shared by all arms in the scored year (one per substation, forecast origin, and lead time), from 292 forecast origins, with the demand models refitted monthly on the previous 24 months and the ensemble-mean weather available at forecast time. The start audit used past weather because it fits on history. A contrast could depend on the monthly schedule, which weekly refits would test.
  • Post hoc. The E1 and E2 contrasts against A0 (P1, P2, P3) were added after the planned contrasts were read. The cold-night q95 coverage and the D10 cut are planned and post hoc respectively, as the plan says.
  • Tail calibration, cold nights, scored year (A0, A2, BG2). q01 coverage 4.3%, 4.4%, 2.0% and pinball loss 0.380, 0.362, 0.444. q05 coverage 7.8%, 9.0%, 3.5% and loss 0.931, 0.905, 0.919. q95 coverage 83.8%, 86.1%, 75.6% and loss 0.902, 0.819, 1.390. q99 coverage 94.2%, 94.8%, 86.1% and loss 0.290, 0.284, 0.809. The curtailment-cost metric was not scored, because the metric needs nodes with generators and this experiment's rows are single substations.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast. The median equals the mean at all 6 substations for A0 and A2 (difference 0.0), because the quantiles are centred on the mean.
  • Error of the mean beside the quantile score. The mean absolute error of the mean has the same sign as the quantile score for C1, C2, and C3 on all rows (-0.026, -0.008, -0.034) and on step hours (-0.008, -0.005, -0.013) in the scored year.
  • Audit triggers that fired. A result contradicted its prediction (C1 on step hours). Leaving one substation out flipped a contrast (C3 on step hours becomes +0.000 without D11 in the scored year and +0.059 without D16 in the replicate year). A nested arm beat the arm that contains it (E1 and E2 beat A1 and A2 on step hours in both years).
  • Audit. A fresh Sonnet agent re-derived C1, C2, C3, and P2 from the stored predictions and matched them to 3 decimals. It found no leakage: every fit stops at its cut and the step's temperature at forecast time is the ensemble's. The offset applied to E1 and E2 loses on step hours because of two months of forecast origins. In December 2024 the offset was fitted on one month of winter data and shifted the forecast up by about 1.0 point, while the error of E1 was already -0.93. The other month is January 2026. Leaving D10 out leaves P2 on step hours, winter nights, and all rows in the replicate year at +0.005, -0.009, and -0.007. P2 on all rows in the scored year never flips. We accepted all findings as caveats and set the verdict from them.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Test E1, the in-model night levels without the offset, over more winters, with a block longer than a month to resample, so that the all-rows gain of 0.017 to 0.030 points can be told from one substation's winter.
  • Give D10's April to June night error its own experiment, with a level term from 21:00 to 07:30 UTC, because the Economy 7 step explains 15% of it.

docs.title: Does our solar plant model turn sunshine into power the way the six metered solar farms do?
docs.text: Our solar curve stays within 5 percentage points of capacity at three of the six metered farms and departs by more at the other three, in different directions, so no single fix to the inverter limit repairs it. The one error common to all six farms is the panel tilt of 35 degrees that the best-guess demand stack assumes. National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED) meters the output of six solar farms, labelled A to F. We compared the farms' measured output over September 2025 to August 2026 with the curve that turns irradiance (sunshine, in W/m²) into power in two of our solar models. The two models are the per-farm plant fit of experiment 218 and the solar term of the best-guess demand stack (the "stack") of experiment 139. Both were tuned on earlier months. A "departure" is a mean error above 5 percentage points of the farm's capacity whose 95% interval excludes zero. We predicted departures at 4 or more of the 6 farms; they occurred at 3 (A, B, and E), so the prediction is not supported. The count is fragile to the bin edges: farm D's fleet-shape error reaches 4.95 points in one bin. The stop rule would have ended the audit before the pooled-shape test (check 7) if fewer than 5 of 6 farms had a bin with a mean error above 3 points. Five farms had such a bin in the per-farm plant fit and six in the stack, so check 7 ran.

docs.title: Which curve each solar model uses
docs.text:
• Plant fit (experiment 218). Plane-of-array irradiance (the irradiance on the tilted panel surface) is the direct beam projected on the plane, plus isotropic sky diffuse, plus ground reflection (albedo 0.2). Cell temperature is air temperature plus 25 K times the plane's irradiance in units of 1000 W/m². DC power is a fitted scale times that irradiance times one minus 0.4% per kelvin above 25 °C (fleet shape: tilt 35 degrees, facing south). The per-farm plant instead fits its own loss for each farm. A soft clip (a smooth cap on output, a p-norm minimum with exponent 6) with a fitted limit on alternating-current (AC) power follows.
  • The stack's solar term. The shape is the fleet plant (tilt 35 degrees, facing south, a direct-current to AC rating ratio of 1.15) with a hard clip (an abrupt cap) at 1.0 per MW of AC capacity. The term is a pinned capacity times that shape times the same temperature loss, which is applied after the clip. Here the capacity is one fitted scale per farm.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Check 1, residual by irradiance (figure 1). Departures above 5 percentage points of capacity whose 95% interval excludes zero: farm A (solar model too high by 7 to 11 points in the 800 and 900 W/m² bins on the fleet plane), farm E (too high by 6 to 12 points, in the 500 to 900 W/m² bins for the per-farm plant and in the 800 and 900 bins for the fleet shape), and farm B (solar model too low by 5 to 10 points, at 600 to 900 W/m² for the stack and in fewer bins for the other two). Farms C, D, and F stay within 5 points in every bin. The stack and the per-farm plant depart at the same three farms. The signs differ by farm, so one clip level cannot fix them.
  • Check 2, flat top (figure 2). The measured 99th percentile of output over capacity above 900 W/m² is 1.05 to 1.13. The stack's term reaches 0.95 to 0.99 (7 to 18 points lower), the per-farm plant 0.98 to 1.07, and the fleet shape 1.09 to 1.15.
  • Check 3, low and high sun (figure 3). At sun elevation under 15 degrees, both solar models over-predict at all six farms, by 2.7 to 3.6 points (per-farm plant) and 4.0 to 5.3 points (stack), with intervals that exclude zero. At clear midday the per-farm plant is off by 8 points at A and E (too high) and 5 points at B (too low).
  • Check 4, temperature (figure 3). At 700 to 900 W/m², the stack's residual rises from the coolest to the warmest third of air temperatures by about 13 points at A, 10 at C, and 12.5 at E. The same rise appears at the other three farms (5 to 8 points). Cool air and winter coincide in the data and no table here separates them, so the temperature sub-prediction (residuals under 3 points) is not answered.
  • Check 5, orientation (figure 4). The best fit is south-facing at every farm, at a tilt of 20 degrees at five farms and 15 degrees at E, against the 35 degrees both solar models assume as the fleet shape. An east-west pair at tilt 15 fits worse than the best south-facing tilt at every farm. Using the best tilt in place of 35 changes the fraction of output fitted (both fitted here with no heat loss) by -0.002 (A) to +0.010 (E). The public register of renewable energy projects states location and AC capacity but not tilt or azimuth, so there is no register value to compare with.
  • Check 6, seasonal shape (figure 5). On clear half-hours at 400 to 900 W/m², the ratio of measured to the stack's output, relative to each farm's whole year (median over farms), is 0.66 in December (0.53 to 0.71 across farms), 0.76 in January, 0.81 in November, and 1.08 in May. The per-farm plant (best tilt 20 degrees, fitted heat loss and soft clip) is within 5% of 1 in every month except November (0.95), December (0.81), and January (0.92). No arm isolates the tilt, so the winter error is partly the tilt; the fit may also absorb error in the irradiance data. Experiment 266 found the stack's pinned capacity too high in April to June at three of NGED's primary substations (D5 -41%, D9 -14%, D16 -10%). At the farms the stack under-predicts April to July by 5 to 8%, the opposite sign, so the spring capacity bias is not the same departure as the seasonal shape error. The primary substations' own solar output is not metered, so this test is indirect.
  • Check 7, pooled shape (figure 6). The pooled leave-one-farm-out shape (fitted on the other five farms and scored on the sixth, for each farm in turn), fitted to the other five farms' tuning months with one scale per farm, scores a median fraction of measured output explained (one minus the squared error over the squared output) of 0.944 against 0.950 for the fleet shape (difference -0.006, 95% interval -0.013 to +0.002) and 0.953 for the per-farm plant (difference -0.010, -0.017 to -0.005). The pinball loss (a quantile-forecast score; lower is better) averaged over 11 quantiles and the six farms is 4.91 points for the pooled shape, against 4.69 for the fleet shape, 4.70 for the stack, and 4.46 for the per-farm plant. The threshold of a 0.02 gain is not met.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast per site: not applicable, because every arm is a point forecast with residual-quantile bands from the tuning months. The mean-forecast error is the fraction of output fitted reported above.
  • Reuse of experiment 218: the fleet shape (0.950) and per-farm plant (0.953) use experiment 218's stored fold 1 predictions, so their numbers match by construction.
  • Triggers fired: trigger 2 (the result contradicts the prediction of 4 of 6 farms): the departures sit at A, B, and E and their signs differ, so the explanation tested is that the departures are farm-specific and not a common flat-top error. Trigger 7 (a later experiment depends on this result): experiment 280 scores a pooled six-farm shape inside arm D; its session has been told by message that the pooled shape gave no gain at the farms. The pooled shape scores below the fleet shape at five of the six farms (no farm-dropping check was run). No audit was run.
  • Caveats: the irradiance axis uses the 35 degree fleet plane, which the farms do not share. The bins used for flagging hold 147 to 1,608 half-hours of the scored year, and check 6 uses all years of data. Farm E has 10 tuning months. Irradiance is from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) and air temperature is from the ERA5 reanalysis, and neither is available at forecast time. The pooled shape's penalty took the lowest values of its search range, so a weaker penalty might score differently. The pinball losses have no interval, and the pooled shape's quantile offsets come from residuals of a shape it was not fitted to, while the other shapes' offsets are in-sample.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
• Does a 20 degree fleet tilt in the stack's solar shape lower the stack's winter error and its quantile score?
  • Does a higher or softer clip level in the stack's shape fix the 7 to 18 point shortfall at the top of the curve?

docs.title: What is perfect knowledge of load shifts worth to MAE, CRPS, twCRPS and curtailment cost?
docs.text:
A load shift moves demand from one Primary substation to its neighbours for hours or days. Knowing every shift exactly lowers the forecast's error in the highest power values by 23.1% (95% interval 8.8% to 39.1%) in the 48 hours after the shift ends, and by under 1% over a whole year, because shifts are rare. That figure is the threshold-weighted continuous ranked probability score (twCRPS) against the power the substation would have carried in its normal running arrangement (NRA), as a share of the score of a forecast that knows nothing about the shift.

Curtailment cost is the cost of limiting generation when the flow at a substation would breach its limit. The design fixed before any score was read ignored the power readings recorded during a shift. Against observed power, which includes the shift, that design did not lower curtailment cost (-1.4%, -4.9% to +1.5%), so the curtailment prediction failed. A variant added after seeing the results adds the shift's known megawatts back to the forecast, and lowers cost by 8.1% (6.4% to 10.0%) within 7 days of a shift. The next step is to ask how good a detector of load shifts must be to keep that gain.

Question and method. A load shift moves demand from one Primary substation to its neighbours for hours or days. We asked whether a forecast that knows every shift exactly, from its true start and end, beats one that knows nothing (question 1 of the LSC decision program). The forecasting model is the generalised additive model with a Kalman filter on its recent errors of experiment 208, unchanged. We scored 411 simulated shifts (44 copies of the real 27-month power record, six Primary substations, stored by experiment 141) on two targets: the true normal-arrangement (NRA) series, and observed power, which includes the shift. Curtailment cost is the node-only metric of experiment 268 (studies.node_curtailment), at a limit of 0.5 times the largest earlier power, 12 to 36 hour leads, GBP 2,000 per MWh.

Curtailment figures are relative comparisons between forecasts at a Primary substation and state no money saved. A Primary substation has no published export limit and no known generator beneath it, so the metric treats its demand as the flow that can breach, as experiment 277 did. Bulk supply points are not scored: experiment 271 found that few shifts cross a boundary and that the bulk-supply-point metric cannot value detection.

docs.title: Gain over no knowledge, by row group
docs.text:
Each cell is the gain of perfect knowledge over no knowledge, as a percentage of the no-knowledge score, with a 95% interval; positive is better. Arms: PERFECT (true span known at the true onset, readings inside it set aside, end known at once) and PERFECT_LAG (the same span known after a live service's delays). The post hoc arms PERFECT_ADD and PERFECT_LAG_ADD subtract the span's megawatts from the readings and add the true megawatts back to the forecast at the target time once the span is known. Row groups: G1 ordinary rows (outside every shift, the 72 hours after it, and the 7 days either side of it); G2 before the alarm would arrive; G3 during the shift; G4 the 48 hours after its end; G5 within 7 days of a shift (G2 to G4 plus the margins); G0 all rows, with ordinary rows weighted 4 because every fourth daily run is scored.

Group twCRPS vs NRA, PERFECT CRPS vs NRA, PERFECT Cost vs observed, PERFECT Cost vs observed, PERFECT_ADD (post hoc) G0 all rows +0.22 (+0.04 to +0.50) +0.80 (+0.55 to +1.13) -0.10 (-0.35 to +0.11) +0.55 (+0.39 to +0.77) G1 ordinary -0.03 (-0.14 to +0.06) +0.01 (-0.05 to +0.06) -0.00 (-0.02 to +0.01) -0.01 (-0.03 to +0.01) G2 before alarm +25.3 (+9.1 to +39.5) +20.1 (+14.6 to +25.4) -7.3 (-15.9 to +1.3) +21.5 (+14.1 to +28.7) G3 during +14.4 (+3.8 to +23.5) +44.4 (+26.7 to +55.1) -35.2 (-47.0 to -25.3) +9.2 (+3.2 to +15.2) G4 after +23.1 (+8.8 to +39.1) +35.1 (+24.8 to +43.9) +25.2 (+14.1 to +34.2) +28.3 (+21.5 to +34.7) G5 near +6.3 (+2.8 to +10.1) +10.8 (+8.2 to +13.4) -1.4 (-4.9 to +1.5) +8.1 (+6.4 to +10.0)

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Pre-registered prediction, part 1 held: the twCRPS gain in G4 against the true NRA series is +23.1% (8.8 to 39.1), above the 3% bar. PERFECT_LAG gains +22.3% (7.9 to 38.1).
  • Part 2 failed: the curtailment gain against observed power in G5 at the 0.5 limit is -1.4% (-4.9 to +1.5) for PERFECT and -0.6% (-3.7 to +2.0) for PERFECT_LAG, so the interval includes zero and the curtailment-cost answer for the design fixed in advance is "not shown". The loss sits in G3 (-35.2%, -47.0 to -25.3): the forecast with readings set aside predicts the normal arrangement, while observed power includes the shift.
  • Part 3, G0 and G1 under 0.5%: G1 changes by -0.03% (-0.14 to +0.06) in twCRPS and G0 by +0.22%. G0 CRPS changes by 0.80% (0.55 to 1.13), above the 0.5% limit, so that condition failed for CRPS; the rise comes from the shifts in the year and is not harm.
  • Post hoc, megawatts added back: curtailment cost falls 8.1% (6.4 to 10.0) in G5 and 28.3% (21.5 to 34.7) in G4 at the 0.5 limit. With live delays the gains are 3.5% (2.4 to 4.7) and 26.1% (19.0 to 32.8). At the 0.75 limit PERFECT_ADD gains 13.3% (9.5 to 17.1) in G5, and at 0.9 it gains 15.2% (7.1 to 23.1); the sweep is figure 3.
  • Absolute no-knowledge scores (points of effective capacity): CRPS against the NRA series is 4.14 in G4, 3.03 in G2, 4.62 in G3, and 2.71 on ordinary rows; the mean absolute error (MAE) of the median is 6.89 in G4 and 4.69 on ordinary rows.
  • Real record, descriptive only: on 13 logged shifts at four Primary substations (experiment 208's stored scores, five stored quantiles, so twCRPS is replaced by pinball loss at 0.95), the logged mask lowers CRPS by 54.3% (42.1 to 77.4) in the 48 hours after 7 shifts and worsens it by 112% (40% to 207%) during 6 shifts. The real record resolves no curtailment difference (experiment 277).
  • Substations differ: G5 twCRPS gain is +37.4% at D10, +44.1% at D14, +16.7% at D9, +6.3% at D11, -1.0% at D16, and -11.2% at D5 (figure 4). Gains fall with lead: 11.4% at 0 to 12 h, 10.0% at 12 to 36 h, 5.1% at 36 h to 7 d.
  • Shift sizes are untested below 25% of load and under 1 day: every simulated shift is that large and that long, so the size and duration strata of the program cannot be scored. November to March gains 6.7% (2.0 to 11.6) and April to October 5.8% (1.1 to 11.5).

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, per site: the mean absolute error of the median forecast minus that of the mean forecast lies between -0.019 and +0.008 points for every site and arm, and changes by under 0.005 points between K0 and PERFECT, so no arm's spread shifts its forecast (printed report).
  • Mean forecast error beside each quantile-score contrast: in G5 against the NRA series the MAE of the mean gains 9.6% (7.5 to 11.7) beside the CRPS gain of 10.8%, the same direction. Against observed power the mean absolute error (MAE) of the median gains 1.7% (0.3 to 3.0) in G5 for PERFECT, while curtailment cost loses 1.4%; the difference is the G3 tail loss above.
  • Triggers that fired: trigger 2 (the curtailment result contradicts its prediction) fired, and the megawatts-added-back arm is the tested explanation. Trigger 4 fired weakly: leaving out D11 moves the G4 twCRPS interval to -1.4% to +51.1% while the point estimate stays above 17% in all six leave-one-out runs. Trigger 7 fired because later steps compare detectors with these arms. A fresh Sonnet audit re-derived the headline contrasts from the stored scores with its own code and reproduced them (twCRPS +23.08%, 8.6 to 39.0; curtailment -1.36%, -4.83 to +1.57; megawatts added back +8.14%, 6.35 to 10.03). It found no leakage: the 1008 rows scored before a first onset that differ from K0 belong to one overlapping pair of shifts at D5. Its four caveats are listed under "Caveats", and we accepted all four.
  • Cost metric check: the per-row node-only cost equals studies.node_curtailment.node_curtailment on one substation and one simulated world (GBP 32,468,687.88 both).

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The megawatts-added-back arms are an upper bound. They add the true megawatts at the target time and stop at the true end of the shift, even when the forecast was issued before the end, so they know the future shape and end of the shift. The 8.1% (6.4 to 10.0) is therefore the most that perfect timing and size can deliver.
  • The pre-registered curtailment prediction failed by construction. The readings-set-aside arm forecasts the normal arrangement and is scored against observed power, so it loses during a shift (-35.2%) whatever the value of the knowledge. The post hoc arm is the one that tests the question.
  • The twCRPS bar is met overall but not robustly. Without D11, which supplies 106 of the 267 shifts that reach the 48-hour group, the gain is +17.8% (-1.4 to +51.1). Without D16 it is +32.7% (18.5 to 42.9).
  • G0 and G1 are one test. Ordinary rows carry 93.3% of the weight of G0, and the ordinary intervals rest on 23 calendar months. About 10% of ordinary rows differ between K0 and PERFECT, because K0's filter still carries a past shift, and the net effect is zero within noise.

docs.title: Arms and rows
docs.text:
• Arms: K0 (no knowledge of shifts; the filter reads all recent power); PERFECT and PERFECT_LAG (MASK design); post hoc PERFECT_ADD and PERFECT_LAG_ADD (SUB design plus true megawatts added back). Lab conditions: true megawatts known, spans known exactly.
  • Rows: 411 simulated shifts in 44 simulated copies of the record, six Primary substations (D5, D9, D10, D11, D14, D16), 22.9 million weighted rows (1.54 million within 7 days of a shift, 5.34 million ordinary rows scored of every fourth daily run). Intervals resample whole simulated shifts, and whole calendar months for ordinary rows, 20,000 draws.
  • Retraining schedule: none; the forecasts are experiment 208's cached member forecasts, so the contrast cannot depend on a schedule.
  • Targets: observed power (real series plus the injected megawatts) and the true NRA series (real series); PERFECT_ADD arms are scored on observed power only.
  • Quantiles: the node curtailment metric reads the 0.95 quantile of 11 stored quantiles; none cross, so sorting changes nothing.
  • Data used: experiment 141's stored worlds, experiment 111 and 115's cached member forecasts and spreads, the cleaned power table before the first replicate row for limits and thresholds.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Step 5 of the program (do we need a detector at all?) should score its arms against both PERFECT and PERFECT_ADD, because the money answer differs by design.
  • Step 6 (how good must a detector be?) should degrade PERFECT_ADD, since the megawatts need a detector that estimates size as well as timing.
  • Shifts under 25% of load and under 1 day need new simulated worlds before a detector can be judged on them.

docs.title: Does a neural network trained only for the tails beat XGBoost at the 0.01 and 0.99 quantiles of a metered solar farm?
docs.text:
A neural network trained only for the tails beats XGBoost at the 0.99 quantile by 30%, but H5 from experiment 275 is slightly better than the tail network, and most of the gain comes from the physical power model underneath. National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED) meters the output of six solar farms, labelled A to F. Curtailing a farm depends on the upper edge of its forecast band, so the 0.01 and 0.99 quantiles matter most. Experiment 275 trained the neural network H5 (the plant, a physical model of a farm's output, plus a network that adds offsets at 11 quantile levels) on 17 months of European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) ensemble forecasts plus nearly 6 years of rows built from past weather. The past-weather rows lowered H5's 0.99 pinball loss (the loss that penalises a quantile forecast on the side it errs) by 4.6%, while its overall score moved by 0.5%. We asked whether a network trained only for six tail levels (0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.95, 0.98, and 0.99) on the same rows beats XGBoost (Chen and Guestrin, 2016) at the 0.01 and 0.99 quantiles. Experiment 270 built a plant whose offsets are binned by its forecast and the ensemble spread (P2). The tail head (T3) is a neural network that corrects the offsets of P2, trained only for the six tail levels. XGBoost X2 is trained on the same rows to predict each quantile directly, and T0 and T4b are controls defined under Arms below. Percentages are changes in pinball loss, and negative means the first arm is better.

The tail network beats XGBoost at the 0.99 quantile by more than the predicted margin, and a calibration check fixed in the plan also fires at the 0.01 quantile. T3's 0.99 pinball loss is 0.336 points of capacity against 0.483 for XGBoost on the same rows (X2), 30.5% lower (98.75% month-block interval -39.5% to -21.7%, against the 5% reduction predicted), and the gain has the same sign at all six farms. Stop rule 1 does not fire. The calibration check (stop rule 2 in the plan) required the miscalibration to be reported first if it fell outside the band at 3 or more farms. It fires on its literal reading, because the 0.01 quantile has coverage outside 0.5% to 1.5% at farms A (1.7%), D (11.9%), and E (4.2%), but farm D's 11.9% is tied zeros: its output is exactly zero in 11.7% of scored half-hours, mostly in winter. Three further results limit what the 30% means. First, XGBoost's 0.99 quantile is too high, and P2, which has no neural network, is already 25% below it (0.363). Second, T3 is 2.4% worse than H5 at 0.99 (interval 0.4% to 4.8%). Third, past-weather rows add little at 0.99: T3 against the same head on ensemble rows only (T0) is -0.5% (interval -1.8% to +1.0%), and a placebo with the past-weather rows' power shuffled (T4b) scores 2.0% better than T3 (interval -0.01% to 3.8%).

docs.title: Arms, rows, and weather
docs.text:
• Arms (own history, one fit on rows before 2025-09 with no retraining in the scored year, the screening schedule; 5 seeds for neural networks). X2: XGBoost with past-weather plus ensemble rows and the era flag (from experiment 275). P2: the plant with offsets binned by forecast (6 bins) and ensemble spread (3 bins), from ensemble tuning rows. L2: H5 as in experiment 275. T3: the tail head, with inputs P2's forecast, ensemble spread, lagged power, clear-sky index, lead, cell temperature, sun elevation, and the era flag, trained on pinball loss at the six tail levels plus a penalty on crossing. T0: T3 on ensemble rows only. T4a: T3 without the era flag. T4b: T3 with shuffled power in the past-weather rows. T5: XGBoost on the six tail levels with T3's inputs.
  • Rows. Experiment 275's scored rows (daylight half-hours at 12 to 36 hour leads, 2025-09 to 2026-08, equal weight per farm; 41,654 rows common to every arm). Intervals resample the 12 scored months 20,000 times. T3's 11-level forecast for the quantile score is T3's 0.01, 0.05, 0.95, and 0.99 quantiles inside L2's other seven (same seed), sorted per row.
  • Weather at each time. Past-weather rows use Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) irradiance (about 2 days late) and ERA5 temperature (about 5 days late), neither of which exists at forecast time; they appear in training rows before 2025-07. Scored rows use the ECMWF ensemble (00 UTC run), which exists at forecast time, as do lagged power (one day, or two when the lead exceeds 24 hours) and the ensemble spread. Past-weather rows take a stand-in spread (the median of the same farm, month, half-hour, and cloud tercile).
  • Curtailment value. Not scored as a contrast. The rule of studies.node_curtailment reads only each farm's median forecast, and T3 keeps L2's median and middle quantiles, so T3's curtailment cost equals L2's by construction. Experiment 255 found 72 event half-hours at 0.5 times the maximum export and 2 to 5 at the other limits, too few to rank forecasts.

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text:
• Pinball loss at 0.99 (points of capacity, 95% interval): L2 0.328 (0.296 to 0.366); T4b 0.329 (0.298 to 0.367); T3 0.336 (0.301 to 0.377); T0 0.338 (0.302 to 0.380); T4a 0.341 (0.303 to 0.383); P2 0.363 (0.330 to 0.400); X2 0.483 (0.456 to 0.517); T5 0.484 (0.457 to 0.517).
  • Pinball loss at 0.01: L2 0.334 (0.278 to 0.375); T4b 0.345; T3 0.353 (0.285 to 0.406); T0 0.358; T4a 0.362; X2 0.370 (0.298 to 0.428); T5 0.372; P2 0.382 (0.311 to 0.443).
  • Planned contrasts (98.75% intervals, percent change in pinball loss). C1 T3 against X2 at 0.99: -30.5% (-39.5 to -21.7). C2 T3 against X2 at 0.01: -4.6% (-10.7 to +0.1), driven by farm E alone (-16.0%; the other five farms are between -1.9% and +1.3%; leaving E out gives -0.1%). C3 T3 against T5 at 0.99: -30.6% (-39.7 to -21.6), the same as C1 because X2 and T5 are the same kind of XGBoost model. C4 T3 against T4b at 0.99: +2.0% (-0.01 to +3.8).
  • Secondary contrasts at 98.75%. T3 against L2 at 0.99: +2.4% (0.4 to 4.8), at 0.01 +5.4% (-1.5 to +15.0), driven by farm E. T3 against P2: -7.4% at 0.99 (-10.5 to -3.9) and -7.7% at 0.01 (-11.3 to -5.0). T3 against T0 at 0.99: -0.5% (-1.8 to +1.0), at 0.01 -1.5% (-3.6 to -0.5). T3 against T4a at 0.99: -1.5% (-4.5 to +2.2), at 0.01 -2.7% (-4.9 to -0.6). T3 against X2 at 0.95: +4.6% (1.2 to 8.4), so XGBoost is better at the 0.95 quantile.
  • Tail calibration (share of half-hours outside the quantile, target 1%). Below the 0.01 quantile, T3 is at 1.7%, 1.3%, 0.5%, 11.9%, 4.2%, and 0.75% for farms A to F, and L2 and X2 are within 0.25 points of T3 except at E (L2 3.4%, X2 5.7%). Above the 0.99 quantile, mean over farms: T3 1.8%, L2 1.5%, P2 1.7%, T5 and X2 0.5%. XGBoost's 0.99 quantile is therefore too high (it sits near 0.69 of capacity at 05:00 and 19:00 UTC, against 0.12 to 0.13 for T3), and the pinball ranking does not make T3 calibrated.
  • Exceedances (scored half-hours, sum over farms; networks are seed-averaged). Below the 0.01 quantile: T3 1,353, L2 1,322, X2 1,455. Above the 0.99 quantile: T3 763, L2 648, X2 193.
  • Quantile score of the 11-level frame: X2 5.403 (4.849 to 5.857); L2 5.449 (4.902 to 5.915); T3 with L2's middle 5.450 (4.901 to 5.921); T3 against L2 +0.02% (95% interval -0.13 to +0.20).

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, per farm (points of capacity), farms A to F. L2: 0.29, 0.47, 0.40, 0.40, 1.26, 0.49. T3 with L2's middle: 0.22, 0.41, 0.40, 0.46, 1.12, 0.46. X2: -0.75, -0.06, -0.14, -0.01, -0.03, 0.09. T3 shifts the mean forecast by under 0.15 points at every farm.
  • Error of the mean forecast beside the quantile score. T3's mean-forecast error is 9.95 points of capacity against 9.95 for L2 (-0.01%, interval -0.14 to +0.12) and 10.12 for X2 (-1.7%, interval -3.2 to -0.7). The quantile score points the other way against X2 (T3 +0.9% worse, interval -0.2 to +2.3, which is not a gain) and is level with L2.
  • Audit triggers that fired. A control failed: the placebo T4b, whose past-weather power is shuffled, scores as well as T3, and better in 4 of 5 seeds at 0.99 and in all 5 at 0.01. A control that should change nothing, T4b, also moved the 0.01 loss by more than its interval's half-width. A fresh Sonnet agent re-derived every headline contrast from the stored predictions (the audit report is private, and its numbers match the reported ones to 0.2 points, apart from the farm E contrast, which differs because the audit averages seeds per row) and reported these findings.
  • Ceiling clamp. The ceiling clamp (the plant arms clip at the 0.995 quantile of tuning output, the XGBoost arms do not) does not cause C1: clipping X2 and T5 at the same ceiling gives -31.1%.
  • Placebo limit. The placebo keeps each farm's month-by-half-hour power distribution, so it cannot separate the weather-to-power link from that distribution; T3 against T0 shows the past-weather rows add little either way. The audit ran on Sonnet.
  • Audit triggers that did not fire. Leaving one farm out keeps the sign of C1 at every farm; C2's interval already includes zero. Both contrasts are against single-seed XGBoost, whose fit is deterministic.

docs.title: Caveats and what to try next
docs.text:
• The tail head is not needed. H5 matches it at the 0.99 quantile and beats it slightly, so the next test for the upper tail is the plant with an offset table binned by forecast and spread (P2) taken as the production tail, since it is 25% below XGBoost without a network.
  • Past-weather rows hold no forecast error, so a tail head cannot learn how wrong the ensemble can be from them; rows from an older ensemble forecast would (the next test from experiment 275).
  • Farm D's output is zero in 11.7% of scored half-hours, so its 0.01 coverage is not a calibration measure and its 0.01 loss says nothing about tail skill (cause not established here). Farm E's 0.01 loss is large and unstable for every arm.
  • Plant geometry. Experiment 282 found all six farms fit best at a 15 to 20 degree tilt where the plant here uses a fleet shape at 35 degrees; a plant arm with the tilt fitted was not added to this experiment.
  • Unequal training rows. X2 and T5 train on the two validation months too (as in experiment 275); the neural networks use those months only to pick the epoch. The spread-binned table also fits those months, so validation loss is in-sample for the table.

docs.title: Can a small correction to the wind speed, before the physics model of a wind farm or after the ensemble, close the gap to XGBoost?
docs.text:
Take-home: the physics core of a wind farm matched XGBoost once a small neural network adjusted the wind speed it takes as input, but the wind-speed mappings fixed only a small part of the ensemble's low bias. With ERA5 (the ECMWF reanalysis of past weather) as the weather input, the neural adapter scored 0.45 points better than the physics core, more than the 0.31-point lead of XGBoost. Scores are quantile scores in points of farm capacity, and lower is better. A correction using only wind shear (the change of wind speed with height) plus 8 wind-direction sectors closed 43% of the 0.31-point gap, and a neural adapter given only the 100 m speed closed 17%. On the 51 members of the ECMWF ensemble weather forecast, mapping each member's wind speed to ERA5's lowered the score by about 0.3 points. The share of observed power below the median forecast (50% if unbiased) rose only from 34.1% to 37.5%. A lookup table of power offsets (per lead day, quantile, and farm) lowered the score by 0.41 points.

We asked whether a small, bounded correction of the wind speed could reproduce the part of XGBoost's lead that comes from the wind speed, for the three metered wind farms (W1, W2, W3). Experiment 276 found that XGBoost beats the physics core, the physics-based model that turns wind speed into farm power through a power curve, by correcting the wind speed with the wind direction, the 10 m wind, and the hour of day. Part A puts a wind-speed correction in front of the core and scores it with ERA5 as the weather, which isolates the correction from forecast error. Part B corrects each ensemble member's wind speed towards ERA5's before the core and XGBoost, and uses the production weather input, the ensemble. The physics core comes from experiment 230, the low-bias decomposition from experiment 261, and the offset table from experiment 259.

Scoring. Scores are quantile scores (an estimate of the continuous ranked probability score) in points of capacity. Contrasts are the first arm minus the second, so a positive number means the second arm is better. Intervals resample whole months and the three seeds; farms are not resampled. Both parts score experiment 33's 53 Tuesday runs from July 2025 to June 2026 (107,121 rows). "Kept rows" are the 96,479 rows outside experiment 210's idle-band mask, which removes half-hours of near-zero wind where the metered series holds a reactive-power floor. "All rows in the band" means every row, kept or not, whose lead is 12 to 36 hours.

Training. Part A trained on ERA5 before 2025-06-17 (all rows, one fit, no weekly refits). Part B trained the core and XGBoost on ERA5 before 2024-04-01 and fitted the mappings and offsets on the 442 daily ensemble runs of 2024-04-01 to 2025-06-16. XGBoost refits use 500 rounds with column subsampling off.

docs.title: Part A: an adapter on ERA5 wind
docs.text:
• Every Part A prediction held except the blind control's bound. A2 and A3 together closed 43% of the 0.31 gap (at least a quarter predicted). A4 closed 0.450 (0.301 to 0.591; at least 0.15 predicted) and beat A2 and A3 together by 0.317 (0.169 to 0.475; at least 0.05 predicted). The blind adapter A6 closed 0.052 (0.024 to 0.083), just above the predicted 0.05 bound.
  • A4 and XGBoost cannot be told apart. A4 scored 0.140 points better than XGBoost, but the 95% interval (-0.312 to 0.025) includes zero. Each farm gains 0.45 from A4 (W1 0.446, W2 0.458, W3 0.446).
  • The hour of day adds 0.083 (0.019 to 0.154). A5 (no hour) closed 0.367 (0.248 to 0.488).
  • Shear alone helps little. A2 closed 0.035 (0.015 to 0.057); A3 closed 0.110 (0.028 to 0.209).
  • The comparison with XGBoost is not like for like. The XGBoost arm reads six wind columns but not the 2 m temperature or the hour of day; A4 reads both. The contrasts between the core and A4, and between A4 and A5, are like for like.
  • A4 is not over-narrow on kept rows: 5% to 95% coverage 91.2% against 91.7% for the core, and 54.2% of observed power below the median forecast against 52.9% for the core.
  • The gain is largest at 8 to 14 m/s, where the power curve is steepest (second figure), as experiment 276 found for XGBoost.
  • Lead 12 to 36 hours (all rows in the band). Core 5.764, XGBoost 5.494, A4 5.348.

docs.title: Part B: an ensemble-wind correction
docs.text:
• Mapping raises the share of observed power below the median only to 38.1% at best, not above 42%. The share was 34.1% for the core on raw members (B0), 37.5% after B1, 38.1% after B2, and 37.5% after B3, so about 62% of observed power stays above the median forecast.
  • The score fell by 0.307 (0.254 to 0.359) with B1 and 0.300 (0.236 to 0.374) with B3, above the predicted 0.2. B2 gave 0.301 (0.201 to 0.426). The three mappings do not differ (B1 minus B3 is -0.006, -0.046 to 0.037), so lead-day quantile mapping is enough. XGBoost gains the same (0.302, 0.307, 0.298).
  • The offset table beat the mappings by 0.1. B4 lowered the score by 0.406 (0.328 to 0.482), against the predicted tie with the best mapping within 0.05. The offset table lowers the median forecast error more (0.591 against 0.470 for B1).
  • The stack helps. B5 after B1 lowered the score by 0.474 (0.380 to 0.567) against raw members and by 0.068 (0.048 to 0.090) against B4. The best of B1 to B3 on the hindcast runs, chosen without looking at the scored year, is B2. B5 after B2 gained 0.046 (95% interval -0.022 to 0.137) over B4, so that stack is not distinguishable from B4 alone. B5 after B1 or after B3 is distinguishable from B4.
  • The 0.99 tail improved slightly with the stack. Pinball loss at 0.99 on kept rows: 0.680 (B0), 0.657 (B1), 0.643 (B4), 0.638 (B5 after B1); B5 after B1 against B4 is 0.005 (0.000 to 0.010).
  • W2 carries most of the offset table's gain. B0 minus B4 by farm: W1 0.229, W2 0.918, W3 0.057. Dropping any one farm leaves the sign unchanged.
  • The members' mean 100 m wind is only 3% below ERA5's (6.73 against 6.94 m/s, W1 hindcast runs). The mappings change the speed distribution only slightly, yet they lower the score by 0.3 points; this experiment does not show the mechanism.
  • XGBoost's lead over the core is 0.120 (0.068 to 0.174) on raw members and 0.060 (0.013 to 0.109) after the offset table.
Arm (kept rows) Core XGBoost Core, observed below median Core, 5% to 95% coverage B0 raw members 11.817 11.697 34.1% 90.6% B1 mapping by lead day 11.511 11.395 37.5% 91.5% B2 mapping by lead day and sector 11.517 11.391 38.1% 91.9% B3 neural mapping 11.517 11.400 37.5% 91.8% B4 offset table 11.412 11.352 40.1% 91.9% B5 after B1 11.344 11.278 40.3% 92.1% B5 after B2 11.366 11.293 40.7% 92.2% B5 after B3 11.354 11.287 40.4% 92.1%

Pinball loss at 0.01 on kept rows is 0.287 for every core arm and 0.283 to 0.284 for XGBoost, so the lower tail does not move. Lead 12 to 36 hours (all rows in the band), core: 6.595 (B0), 6.294 (B1), 6.383 (B4), 6.209 (B5 after B1); the mapping gains more than the offset table at this lead. The curtailment-cost metric was not scored.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median forecast minus mean forecast, kept rows, points of capacity: physics core with ERA5 -0.22, A4 +0.12; ensemble core -4.98 (B0), -4.86 (B1), -4.75 (B4). The large ensemble gap is the right skew of a mixture of 51 members, not a shift of the forecast; each arm has it equally.
  • Mean absolute error of the mean forecast, compared with each quantile-score contrast: same sign everywhere (for example core B0 minus B1: 0.307 in quantile score, 0.167 in mean absolute error of the mean forecast, 0.470 for the median forecast; A4 against the core: 0.450, 0.749, 0.664).
  • Audit triggers: the trigger for a control that moves the score by more than its interval's half-width fires on the blind control A6, which moved the score by 0.052, more than its interval's half-width of 0.03. A6 is a capacity control with a predicted bound of 0.05 and A4 beats it by 0.40, so no result rests on it. No other trigger fires: the farm-by-farm leave-one-out keeps the sign of every planned contrast, and the intervals match experiment 276's for the shared contrast (core minus XGBoost 0.310, 0.215 to 0.416).

docs.title: Caveats and deviations
docs.text:
• The 10 m wind is the only extra level on disk. ERA5 surface pressure, dew point, and gusts are not on disk for these farms (experiment 276), so air density rests on the 2 m temperature.
  • ERA5 reaches us about 5 days after the weather, so it is unavailable when a forecast is issued, and Part A is a ceiling that isolates the adapter. Part B uses the ensemble's own weather.
  • Deviation: loss. The adapters were trained on the median pinball loss (the L1 loss that trains the core) and the quantiles come from residuals, as in experiment 276.
  • Deviation: training end. Part B's core and XGBoost trained on ERA5 to 2024-04-01, not to 2025-06-17, so that the hindcast months are out of sample for the offsets.
  • Deviation: B3 loss. B3 treats each ensemble member as a quantile of ERA5 speed by its rank within the case.
  • The adapter arms were fitted for 1,200 Adam steps and the core for 800. The blind adapter A6, fitted for 1,200 steps, gained only 0.05, so the longer fit explains little.
  • The B3 mapping and the B5 offsets are fitted on the same hindcast runs, so the hindcast is in sample for them. The choice of the best of B1 to B3 on the hindcast runs rests on a spread of 0.02 points.
  • One fit on all history, no weekly refits; a contrast could depend on the schedule.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Test the adapter on ensemble members, with the core retrained so the adapter sees what the production service sees, since Part A used ERA5.
  • Find where the ensemble's low bias sits. The mapping changed the speed distribution slightly and raised the below-median share by only 3.4 points, so test the wind direction, the members' spread, and the timing of fronts.
  • Port the cheap pieces first: the lead-day quantile mapping is a lookup table, and its stack with the offset table lowered the score by 0.07 against the table alone (the sector mapping's stack did not).

docs.title: How small a yearly drift or a soiling loss can the six metered solar farms' output show, with and without comparing each farm to its neighbours?
docs.text:
A loss of 1 per cent of output per year is visible in 4 to 5 of the 6 metered solar farms, and a loss under about 0.4 per cent per year is visible in only 2 (farms C and F). A loss is visible when it shifts the fitted yearly trend by more than the half-width of that trend's 90% interval. Experiment 286 asks how small a yearly drift or a soiling loss the farms' output can show. We added known losses to each farm's real half-hourly output: a loss growing linearly from a random start date, and a soiling loss of 0.1% of output per day that resets on any day with 5 mm or more of rain (from ERA5, the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts' fifth-generation reanalysis). We then read each loss back with two yield indices. Experiment 179, the earlier exploration of the six farms' data, defined the plain index: each farm's power divided by the irradiance expected under a cloudless sky, summarised per calendar month. The farm-over-farms index is new here. It divides the farm's power by each other farm's power on half-hours when the other farms produce within 20% of their own clear-sky output, then averages the farm pairs.

The farm-over-farms index does not narrow the yearly trend interval overall, but of the two indices only it reads soiling, and only at farms C and F (and at D under the looser pre-registered rule). The prediction needed a half-width under 0.6 %/yr at the farms with 4 or more years, and the farm-over-farms index reaches it at 2 of 5 farms (C and F). The farm-over-farms index also removes most of a false soiling slope. With nothing injected, the plain index reads +0.26 to +0.62 %/day at 5 of 6 farms when fitted against the days since the last day with 5 mm or more of rain, probably because cloudier days tend to follow rainy days. The farm-over-farms index reads a slope smaller than 0.05 %/day in size at farms B, C, D, and F, and +0.10 and +0.46 %/day at farms A and E. The prediction therefore holds in part: the soiling half is supported, and the narrower yearly interval is not.

docs.title: Headline numbers
docs.text:
• Real yearly trends (%/yr, 90% interval, from resampling months 500 times), the plain index then the farm-over-farms index. Farm A: −0.55 (−1.51 to +0.40) and −1.37 (−2.30 to −0.66). Farm B: +0.93 (+0.24 to +1.74) and +1.49 (+0.80 to +2.26). Farm C: −0.53 (−0.90 to −0.13) and −0.39 (−0.74 to −0.08). Farm D: −0.08 (−0.75 to +0.57) and −0.46 (−1.17 to +0.19). Farm E (18 and 10 months): −1.80 (−4.81 to +1.41) and +0.27 (−0.11 to +0.79). Farm F: −0.21 (−0.61 to +0.21) and +0.25 (+0.05 to +0.44). The plain index reproduces the trends printed on experiment 179's result page.
  • Interval half-width at the 5 farms with 4 or more years (A, B, C, D, F): the plain index 0.95, 0.75, 0.39, 0.66, 0.41 %/yr (median 0.66); the farm-over-farms index 0.82, 0.73, 0.33, 0.68, 0.19 %/yr (median 0.68). C1 (under 0.6 %/yr) holds at 2 of 5 farms for the farm-over-farms index and 2 of 5 for the plain index.
  • Same months. The farm-over-farms index keeps 48 to 56 months against 59 to 65 for the plain index, which widens its interval. The plain index refitted on only the months the farm-over- farms index kept has half-widths 0.86, 0.83, 0.37, 0.86, and 0.33 %/yr at farms A, B, C, D, and F, so on equal months the farm-over-farms index is narrower by 4% to 41%.
  • Drift recovery. The injected loss comes back at a median 0.92 to 1.08 of its size with the plain index at the 5 farms with 4 or more years and at farm E 0.86 to 0.87. The farm-over-farms index returns 0.87 to 0.96 at those farms (0.60 at farm A for 2 %/yr), probably because the monthly calendar normalisation absorbs part of a trend, and 0.29 at farm E, which has 10 usable months.
  • Detection at 1 %/yr. The shift in the fitted trend over the half-width is, for farms A to F, 0.99, 1.32, 2.48, 1.53, 0.26, and 2.35 with the plain index, and 1.05, 1.23, 2.50, 1.32, 0.64, and 4.42 with the farm-over-farms index. The plan's rule (median recovery 0.7 to 1.3, and the injected series' own interval excluding zero in at least half the starts) is met at 4 farms at 1 %/yr with each index, so the stop rule does not fire.
  • Minimum detectable drift (the injected rate whose shift equals the half-width, from the median shift per injected %/yr, so it can sit either side of the 1 %/yr ratio above), the plain index then B in %/yr: farm A 1.05 and 1.01, B 0.75 and 0.81, C 0.40 and 0.40, D 0.65 and 0.76, F 0.42 and 0.22, E 3.8 and 1.6.
  • Soiling. Under the plan's rule, 3 farms read the injected 0.1 %/day with each index. Under the stricter post hoc rule (the shift exceeds the half-width in at least half the starts) the plain index reads it at 0 farms and the farm-over-farms index at 2 (C and F). The half-widths on the slope are 0.35, 0.58, 0.30, 0.34, 0.70, and 0.29 %/day for A, and 0.45, 0.13, 0.05, 0.12, 0.37, and 0.06 %/day for B, at farms A to F. The plan's recovery ratio is 1.00 everywhere because the injected change is a known multiplier and both estimators are linear in the log of the index, so it carries no information.
  • Compute and inputs. One fit per farm and injection, no retraining, no weather forecast. Rainfall is ERA5 total precipitation (a past-weather product that arrives about 5 days late and so does not exist at forecast time), summed per UTC day at the nearest 0.25 degree cell.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, and mean-forecast error: not applicable, because no forecast is made or scored.
  • Triggers. The result contradicts its own prediction (C1): tested with the same-months bullet above, which finds that fewer months explain part of the gap, and that on equal months the farm- over-farms index is narrower but still above 0.6 %/yr at A, B, and D. The reproduction of experiment 179's trends to the printed digits is the sister-experiment check on interval width. The other five triggers (a failed control, the quantile and mean forecast disagreeing, leave- one-out, a nested arm, a later design depending on this result) do not apply. No audit was run.
  • Injected recovery is partly by construction. An index linear in the log of the multiplier returns the injected multiplier exactly, so the recovery ratio only exposes attenuation from the calendar-month normalisation and the month filter. The informative figure is the shift over the half-width.
  • Real series carry their own trend. The injected estimate adds to each farm's real trend and noise, so detection is judged by the shift from the un-injected estimate, not by the interval excluding zero (the pre-registered rule, kept as one of two).
  • Neighbours' own drift. The farm-over-farms index measures a farm against the others, so a farm's real trend and its neighbours' real trends are mixed. The six the farm-over-farms index trends sum to −0.2 %/yr, but they cover different months (10 to 56), so they need not cancel.
  • Plan amendments before any injection result was read. The neighbour mask uses a band of 0.8 to 1.2 around each farm's own calendar-month 90th-percentile yield, not 0.85 to 1.15 around a single yearly value (the single value dropped all but 5 to 36 of 86 months); the farm-over-farms index needs 20 rows a month, not 40. Eight random start dates were used, not five.
  • Code review caveats. The month filter on the relative index runs after the injection, so the injected and un-injected fits can keep different months when a month's index crosses 0.75. The minimum detectable drift is an injected rate after the start date, read through a line fitted to the whole history, so it is not a plain yearly rate. The days-since-reset counter runs over days with data, and a day without ERA5 rainfall counts as dry. No leakage of the injected series into the neighbour mask was found.
  • Not done. No drift or soiling is claimed for any real farm, and the real-data stage reports only the trends above. Panel-plane irradiance, temperature, and the flat top of experiment 179 (the farm-over-farms index stays under 650 W/m² to avoid it, the plain index does not) were not modelled.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Can an independent record, such as a panel-level or inverter-level reading, show whether the real farm trends of −1.8 to +1.5 %/yr are drift, or are the farms' own differences from each other?
  • Does a regression on irradiance on the panel plane and cell temperature narrow the yearly interval below the farm-over-farms index's 0.19 to 0.82 %/yr?

docs.title: Which head gives the best day-ahead band on the spread-binned solar-farm power model?
docs.text:
An additive model is the better final stage for the solar-farm power model's forecast band than a neural network that adjusts each quantile, and a neural network that outputs a probability distribution is the only neural arm of those run that we would test again. National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED) meters six solar farms, labelled A to F here. The "plant" is the physical power model of experiment 224. "P2" is the version from experiment 270, which turns the plant's forecast into 11 quantiles (levels 0.01 to 0.99) using the plant's forecast and the spread of the plant's responses to the 51 members of an ensemble weather forecast. The "head" is the final stage that turns P2's inputs into 11 quantiles. We compared four heads: a generalised additive model (GAM, 400 depth-one boosted trees); a neural network (NN) that adds corrections to P2's quantiles and cannot reorder them; a mixture-density network (MDN), a neural network whose output is a three-component Gaussian mixture; and a per-quantile blend of GAM, NN, and XGBoost (Chen and Guestrin, 2016), following experiment 260. "Own history" means a head trains on the farm's own earlier months, and "zero history" means it trains on the other five farms only.

The prediction held: NN is not better than GAM. The quantile score is twice the mean pinball loss over the 11 levels, in points of capacity, and lower is better. NN scores 0.9% worse than GAM in own history (98.75% interval from resampling the 12 scored months, -0.4% to +2.2%), where the pre-registered bar was 1.5% better. MDN scores 1.3% better than GAM in own history (-2.8% to -0.2%), which excludes zero but is not 1.5% better, and only 0.3% better in zero history (-2.2% to +1.1%, which includes zero). The blend scores 0.8% better than XGBoost (-1.3% to -0.1%), above the 0.5% margin below which the plan stopped at the best single arm, so the stop rule did not apply.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Arms. P2 (control). GAM: depth-one quantile trees on experiment 270's six input groups, started from P2's quantiles. NN: two 64-unit layers, output is P2's lowest quantile plus a shift, then cumulative non-negative gaps, equal to P2 at initialisation up to a gap floor of 0.001. MDN: three Gaussian components on the residual from the plant forecast, read at the 11 levels. Blend: simplex weights per level, rolling origin, first three scored months equal weights. NN, MDN, and the controls have five seeds. XGBoost is experiment 275's XGBoost arm with past weather and an era flag in own history, and experiment 270's XGBoost arm on ensemble rows with all input groups in zero history, because experiment 275 stored no zero-history fits.
  • Row set and schedule. Experiment 224's scored-year daylight rows at 12 to 36 h leads (farms A to F, 2025-09 to 2026-08). One fit per arm on the months before 2025-09, no refits, 60 epochs, the last two tuning months select the epoch; heads train on ensemble rows only. Forecast inputs are the ECMWF ensemble 00 UTC run and the farm's own power 1 or 2 days earlier, both available at forecast time. A weekly refit could change the absolute scores and the MDN's gain. Zero history trains on the other five farms only.
  • Quantile score (points of capacity; own history, interval over 12 months). manual_heuristic 8.69, climatology 8.64, P2 5.55 (4.96 to 6.08), NN 5.52, GAM 5.47 (4.84 to 6.01), XGBoost 5.40, MDN 5.39, blend 5.36, MDN blend 5.32. Zero history: P2 5.71, NN 5.65, GAM 5.59, MDN 5.57, XGBoost 5.54, blend 5.47, MDN blend 5.45.
  • Contrasts (own history, 98.75% interval). C1 NN minus GAM +0.9% (-0.4 to +2.2); C2 MDN minus GAM -1.3% (-2.8 to -0.2); C3 blend minus best single arm (XGBoost) -0.8% (-1.3 to -0.1); C4 GAM minus P2 -1.5% (-3.1 to -0.5). Zero history: C1 +1.2% (-0.4 to +2.5), C2 -0.3% (-2.2 to +1.1), C3 -1.2% (-1.8 to -0.4), C4 -2.1% (-3.5 to -1.2).
  • Seed averaging. Averaging NN's five seeds before scoring lowers NN's score by 0.4% (own history) and 0.5% (zero history) but leaves NN 0.4% worse than GAM (-0.9% to +1.7%). The same average lowers MDN's score by 0.4%.
  • The controls show the head adds nothing beyond P2 from spread, lagged power, or the forecast input. NN's score minus each control's (own history): shuffled spread +0.02% (-0.4 to +0.7), shuffled lagged power -0.08% (-0.8 to +0.6), no forecast input +0.10% (-0.3 to +0.5). The controls change nothing, so NN's small gain over P2 (-0.6%, -3.0 to +0.5) does not come from those inputs. P2 supplies the base quantiles in every control, so the controls do not show that spread and lagged power are useless.
  • Pinball loss change against P2 (own history, %). At 0.99: GAM -5%, MDN -14%, blend -8%, XGBoost +37% (22 to 58). At 0.95: GAM -4%, MDN -9%, blend -8%, XGBoost -7%. At 0.05: GAM -3%, MDN -5%, blend -5%, XGBoost -5%. At 0.01 only GAM and NN (both -3%) have intervals that exclude zero.
  • Coverage (own history, nominal 0.01, 0.05, 0.95, 0.99). GAM 0.037, 0.070, 0.949, 0.987; MDN 0.037, 0.072, 0.947, 0.984; blend 0.036, 0.071, 0.958, 0.992; XGBoost 0.037, 0.073, 0.957, 0.995. Actual power falls below the 0.01 quantile 3.6 to 3.7 times too often and below the 0.05 quantile 1.4 times too often, for every arm.
  • Where the gain sits (own history, change against P2). Clear-sky bands: below 0.3 the blend is 8% better and MDN 10%; at 0.3 to 0.9 no arm differs from P2 by more than 1.8%; at 0.9 and above the blend is 9% better and MDN 8%. Lead 12 to 24 h: blend -3.9%; 24 to 36 h: blend -2.8%. Season: December to February is where the gain is, blend -13% and XGBoost -13%, with June to August -2%. Per farm, MDN beats GAM at all six farms and NN is no better than GAM at any farm.
  • Curtailment cost. Not scored: the node-plus-generators metric needs a substation node with its generators, and these six farms are single series.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• No arm's median forecast sits far from its mean forecast (own history, per farm, in points of capacity). Median minus mean: NN -0.02 to 1.0, GAM -0.2 to 0.6, MDN -0.04 to 1.05, XGBoost -0.75 to 0.09, P2 0.16 to 0.46. No arm's median sits more than about 1 point of capacity from its mean forecast.
  • Error of the mean forecast beside each score contrast. C2: mean-forecast error +0.2% (-1.2 to +1.8) and median error -0.5% (-2.0 to +1.1), against a score change of -1.3%, so MDN's gain is in the tails and not in the central forecast. C1: mean-forecast error +1.1% (-0.3 to +2.6). C3: mean error -1.7% (-2.8 to -1.1).
  • No audit trigger fired. Trigger 3 (score and mean-forecast contrasts pointing different ways) was close for C2, but both central-forecast intervals include zero. Dropping each farm in turn leaves C2 between -1.2% and -1.5%, C1 between +0.6% and +1.1%, and C3 between -0.7% and -1.0%, so no farm drives a contrast.
  • Design after code review. Each shuffle control uses a different permutation for each seed. Every arm is checked to hold the same rows. The best single arm for C3 is chosen once, on the overall score. NN and MDN are also scored as the average of their five seeds' quantiles. P2 is fitted on the months that select the training epoch, which favours stopping early. A 24 h lead needs the power at midnight, which no daylight row scores, so the lag boundary does not matter.

docs.title: Caveats and next steps
docs.text:
• Post hoc. The MDN blend was added after the results and was not pre-registered. The best single arm of C3 is chosen on the scored year (XGBoost in both settings), which is conservative for the blend. The 98.75% level covers the four pre-registered contrasts only; all other rows are exploratory.
  • Weather at lag. Forecast inputs are ensemble weather at forecast time; no past-weather rows train the heads, and XGBoost's past-weather rows use CAMS irradiance and ERA5 temperature, which arrive about 5 days late, so XGBoost's score in a live service would be worse than reported here.
  • Not run. A plant arm using experiment 282's pooled empirical shape and a plant arm with a 20-degree tilt were not run. Both arms need the 51 members' responses recomputed with a new panel geometry, which is not cheap.
  • Next. A weekly refit of MDN on the longest history would show whether its 1.3% gain survives. If it does, a convex mixture of the additive model's quantile offsets would be the explainable alternative.

docs.title: Does an 11-quantile correction head trained on dozens of public Great Britain wind farms lower the quantile score of the forecasts for the three metered wind farms, and does more history help the XGBoost model more than the physics model?
docs.text:
We asked whether a small neural network can improve a wind forecast for three wind farms on the electricity network of National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED), after learning from the published output of 40 other wind farms. The network adjusts the 11 quantiles of the XGBoost wind forecast (called R0 below, fitted on ERA5 weather estimates), and the three NGED farms are called W1 to W3. The 40 public farms are nearly all in Scotland, and W1 to W3 are in England and Wales. We trained the network on the 40 farms and compared its corrections with the ones learned from W1 to W3's own records. Applied with no training on W1 to W3 (zero shot), the network made the forecast worse. The quantile score, a measure of how well the forecast's range of likely outputs matches what happened (smaller is better), rose from 7.09 to 8.24 points of capacity, on forecasts one and two days ahead. After fine-tuning on W1 to W3's own records, the score fell to 6.81. A simple table of corrections per lead day and quantile, fitted on those records, scored 6.88. An audit by a second language-model reviewer found that three static inputs (capacity, turbine rating, and hub height) let the network memorise each of the 40 farms, which caused most of the damage. We reran every variant of the experiment (each called an arm below) without them, and report those runs as a diagnostic. The hypothesis that a head trained on public farms improves the forecasts for W1 to W3 is not supported (verdict not supported). The method follows experiment 259, which corrected the XGBoost forecast of experiment 230 in the same way.

Contains Balancing Mechanism Reporting Service (BMRS) data © Elexon Limited copyright and database right 2026.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Two of the three decisive contrasts fail their predictions. The third fails on its tail condition. Each interval is the 98.33% interval from resampling whole months and the three seeds, on W1 to W3's kept rows at lead days 1 and 2. Intervals of descriptive contrasts elsewhere on this page are 95% intervals.

The decision rule's porting threshold, C2 wholly below zero, is met. The verdict is nonetheless not supported, because the prediction's second condition fails, C1 and C3 fail, and the plan's "Reading the results" section says C2 alone does not license a port when P3 gains no more than the offset table T1 (D2).

  • Mean forecast against the median: the quantile score judges the whole distribution, and the forecast's median sits below its mean by 1.6 points for R0 and 1.0 for P3 (kept rows, lead days 1 and 2). C2's gain on the mean-forecast error is -0.083 with an interval that includes zero, so the median improved and the mean did not.

Fine-tuning recovers only what W1 to W3's own runs would give. P3 minus T1 is -0.064 (interval -0.240 to +0.101), P3 minus P1 is +0.106 (-0.017 to +0.232), and X3, the XGBoost stage trained on the pool plus W1 to W3's rows, scored 6.740 against P3's 6.812 (X3 minus P3 -0.072, -0.209 to +0.069). The pool's mean offset therefore did not measurably help beyond the offset table. P1 minus P0 is -0.385 (-0.552 to -0.227), reproducing experiment 259's gain from a head on the three farms.
