  • Headline pair, 99.58% intervals (family level of 5%, k = 12 contrasts). Mixture w = 0.5 minus B2 on event-lag rows: -0.151 (-0.487 to +0.042) at the six, +0.050 (-0.013 to +0.122) at the eight. Outside events: +0.010 (-0.002 to +0.024) at the six, +0.017 (+0.008 to +0.027) at the eight. Mixture w = 0.5 minus the forecast with lags outside events: -0.019 (-0.071 to +0.032) at the six, +0.004 (-0.034 to +0.040) at the eight.
  • The pre-registered decision rule is met at the six and not at the eight. The rule asks for an upper interval end of at most +0.1 on event-lag rows and at most +0.05 outside events. At the six the upper ends are +0.042 (mixture w = 0.5 minus B2, event-lag rows), +0.024 (the same arm outside events), and +0.032 (minus the forecast with lags outside events). At the eight the event-lag upper end is +0.122, over the +0.1 margin, although the interval includes zero. The claim is interim until the maintainer reads the audit findings (see Checks).
  • One event, at D16, drives the six's gain over the forecast with lags. With each Primary left out in turn, mixture w = 0.5 minus the forecast with lags on event-lag rows stays between -0.90 and -1.73 except without D16, where it is -0.179 (-0.517 to +0.032). The contrast against B2 survives without D16 (-0.014, -0.076 to +0.033). D9 has no event-lag rows, so the six has five Primaries with event-lag rows.
  • The per-lead weight on the forecast with lags falls from 0.90 at day 1 to 0.62 at day 10 (mean over months). The per-lead arm therefore gives no gain on event-lag rows (-0.62 against -0.90 for w = 0.5), and gains 0.001 (six) and 0.007 (eight) points over the best fixed weight on all rows (prediction P5).
  • Mixing distributions beats averaging quantiles only slightly. Mixture minus quantile average at w = 0.5 is -0.079 (-0.160 to +0.006) at the six and -0.032 (-0.071 to +0.004) at the eight on event-lag rows.
  • Widening by 1.15 changes no sign on event-lag rows. The widened arm is the raw arm with each quantile moved from the median by 1.15 times its distance. Differences against the widened forecast with lags are within 0.1 of the raw differences (for example w = 0.5 mixture: -0.82 at the six, event-lag rows). B2 is raw only. Outside events at the eight, the widened mixture is worse than the widened forecast with lags by +0.028 (+0.006 to +0.052), against +0.004 raw (audit re-derivation).
  • One Primary, D16, drives the six's gain. Mixture w = 0.5 minus the forecast with lags on event-lag rows per Primary, at the six: D16 -3.35 (4,644 rows), D5 -0.12 (10,460), D10 -0.45, D14 -0.28, D11 +0.03. D18 (neither group) is +4.18 (198 rows) and D12 (an eight Primary) is +0.61.
  • The mixture scores worse at D15 and D18, which are in neither group. Outside events the w = 0.5 mixture is +2.33 CRPS against the forecast with lags at D15 and 0.94 worse than B2. The cause is probably a poor forecast without lags there; the printed report does not show it.
  • The mixture moves the median less sharply at event onsets than the forecast with lags. The largest half-hour change of the median across an event onset, 95th percentile (points of capacity): forecast with lags 15.8, lagless 16.0, w = 0.5 mixture 12.9, B2 13.3 (384 onsets).
  • On cold nights the mixture gains more at the six. Event-lag rows, 538 rows in 10 events: mixture w = 0.5 minus lags -1.71 (-3.08 to -0.06); eight: +0.24 (-0.09 to +0.49).
  • The mixtures do not lower avoidable curtailment cost during events. The totals are GBP over the six signed-MW Primaries, at a limit of 0.9 times the maximum. During events the w = 0.5 mixture costs 89,000 GBP more than the forecast with lags (6.65 million against 6.56 million GBP) and B2 costs 61,000 GBP more. The GAM stack costs 3.74 million GBP less.
  • Curtailment cost in the 7 days after events and across all rows. After events the w = 0.5 mixture is 3,800 GBP and B2 is 3,000 GBP below the forecast with lags, and the stack is 112,000 GBP above. Across all rows the w = 0.5 mixture is 102,000 GBP and B2 is 40,000 GBP above the forecast with lags, and the stack is 4.87 million GBP below.
  • Widening by 1.15 lowers cost on all three arms alike. The widened forecast with lags is 81,700 GBP lower during events and 207,100 GBP lower across all rows. The widened w = 0.5 mixture is 61,200 GBP lower during events, and the widened per-lead mixture is 243,300 GBP lower across all rows, each against the raw forecast with lags. The reduction comes from the widening, not from the mixing, and the widened arms cost 2,000 to 3,600 GBP more in the 7 days after events.
  • Tail calibration (six, event-lag rows). The q95 coverage is 0.884 (forecast with lags), 0.894 (w = 0.5 mixture), and 0.895 (B2), all below the nominal 0.95. The q99 coverage is 0.967, 0.968, and 0.969, against a nominal 0.99. The q05 coverage is 0.115, 0.009, and 0.009, against a nominal 0.05, so the mixture's lower tail is too wide. The 90% band is 26.6 points wide for the mixture and 23.0 for the forecast with lags.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median forecast minus mean forecast. Not available: the stored arms hold the median and quantiles, not the mean. The error of the median forecast stands beside each contrast instead.
  • Median error beside the CRPS contrast (event-lag rows). Six: w = 0.5 minus lags CRPS -0.90 and median absolute error -1.37; B2 minus lags -0.75 and -0.49; w = 0.5 minus B2 -0.15 and -0.88. Eight: w = 0.5 minus lags +0.14 and +0.23. The two measures agree in sign everywhere.
  • Triggers fired. Trigger 2 (the 0.94 share contradicts the reading in experiment 395; tables B1 to B5 test an explanation). Trigger 4 (D16 drives the six's gain; the leave-one-out lines in the printed report show it). Trigger 7 (a learned blender trained on synthetic steps would depend on the Job 1 result).
  • Audit (Sonnet, fresh; report briefs/e401_audit_report.md in the private folder). One error found and fixed: the 99.58% intervals used the wrong percentiles (they were about 92% intervals), which changed the eight's verdict from within margin to over it. Job 1's numbers reproduce on the same 75,704 rows, with no leak found; 11 of the 16 events with 3 lags last over 7 days, which explains why the forecast without lags has already absorbed them. The audit's own exact-CRPS integrator agrees in sign with the 11-quantile CRPS (mixture w = 0.5 minus B2: -0.163 against -0.151 at the six, +0.065 against +0.050 at the eight), and the 11-quantile CRPS runs about 25% below the exact CRPS in level. The monthly b0 boosters match experiment 381's monthly control (median q50 difference 0.28% of capacity). The signed response on rows with lags in an event and the target outside is +0.048 at 1 or 2 lags and +0.022 at 3 lags, against 0.09 and 0.34 in the synthetic arm, but the gap between the two forecasts is at the noise floor of two different fitted models (unsigned gap 0.138 against a floor of 0.122), so "about 0.03" is an upper bound on what the lags do, not a measured size. The synthetic steps are large (median 0.19 of capacity). The mixture's small gap to B2 is partly by construction, because B2's mean weight on the forecast with lags is 0.59.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Weekly bundle boosters are not stored, so Job 1's synthetic arm uses b0 and its real arm the monthly control; the response comparison (table B5) uses the weekly forecasts for both.
  • The weekly forecast with lags and the weekly forecast without lags are different fitted XGBoost models (experiments 381 and 383), so their difference includes more than the lags. The difference at 0 lags is -0.007, which sets the size of that background.
  • Experiment 395 is unmerged (PR 49): experiment 395's Part F rows, tags, and corrected label table are read from the stored work folder and from a copy of the CSV in experiment 400's folder.
  • Lead range is days 1 to 10 (lead under 240 hours), the whole NGED range of 1 to 10 days.
  • The intervals at the eight are wide: they rest on 19 events, and the per-Primary numbers from as few as 77 rows (D19, D4).
  • Departures from the plan. The synthetic rows use all clean rows of 5 runs (the 15th of October, December, February, April, and June, issued at 09:00), not 5,000 rows per event, and are not matched to the real rows' lead distribution. The synthetic rows do not drop flagged half-hours, which the real arm drops. The exact CRPS of the mixtures was not computed (CRPS comes from the 11 quantiles, as the protocol defines it).
  • The per-lead weight uses actuals up to the start of the scored month, so a forecast issued up to 10 days before the month, with a valid time inside it, gets a weight fitted on actuals that did not yet exist at its issue time. Experiment 400's learned blend probably has the same convention.
  • The curtailment totals use experiment 400's row convention: valid times from 2025-10-01 over all stored lead days (not only days 1 to 10), flagged half-hours included, and a scoring start of 2025-07-01. They are comparable with experiment 400's totals, not with the CRPS tables above.
  • Not tested: whether the lags matter at all in real events, because the real events in the scored months are few (52, 27, and 16 events by lag status).

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: The next experiment should test whether the forecast with lags and the forecast without lags differ in real events only through the lags, by refitting both with identical settings. It should also test whether the response of 0.03 of the step is the whole story or a training effect.

docs.title: Plan
docs.text: Two stored-forecast jobs from the load-shift Discuss session (maintainer-approved 2026-10-30). Both re-score or re-predict stored forecasts; no booster is refitted. Sonnet only. Protocol demand-v1. All numbers are interim until the Sonnet audit.

docs.title: Job 1: why do the real-event and synthetic-step medians disagree?
docs.text:
• The two numbers. Experiment 395 Part E predicts experiment 391's plain monthly control b0 with a synthetic step added to the first k lagged-power inputs: the median moves by 1.3%, 17.3%, and 36.8% of the step at k = 1, 2, 3. Part F scores real labelled events with the corrected signs and finds the median at 0.52, 0.83, and 0.94 of the event reading with 0, 1 or 2, and 3 lags in the event.
  • The two quantities differ in definition, and the plan reports both on both arms. Part E's response share is (q50 with the step - q50 without) / step. Part F's share is 1 - (actual - q50) / step. The second share equals 1 when the median matches the observed reading, whatever the cause, and it equals 1 - measured step / labelled step when the forecast ignores the event.
  • (a) Same events. The real arm is experiment 381's monthly control (rows of Part F; it scores 0.60, 0.83, 0.94). The synthetic arm uses b0's stored boosters: for each corrected event with a measurable depth and at least 10 rows in a lag-status group, take every clean scored row of the same Primary (no target in a padded event, no lag in an event, not flagged) in the months where boosters exist, add the corrected signed depth (as a fraction of the Primary's capacity) to the k newest lagged inputs and to the actual reading, where k = 0, 1, 2 (reported separately and as "1 or 2"), and 3. The row sample keeps the lead distribution of the event's real rows (up to 5,000 rows per event and k, fixed seed). The comparison is the per-event median share, then the median over events, for the real and the synthetic arm on the same event list, using both share definitions on the synthetic arm.
  • The weekly bundle's boosters are not stored (only experiment 391's n1, b0, and later boosters exist), so the comparison runs on the monthly control for both arms, as the brief allows. The first step checks that b0's predictions on the clean rows match experiment 381's monthly control to within a stated tolerance; if they do not, the page says so and uses b0 alone for both arms.
  • (b) Why 0.52 at 0 lags. Four small calculations on the real rows with 0 lags in the event:
    1. Labelled against measured depth. Recompute the share with the event's measured step (measured_depth_first_mw in the corrected table) in place of the labelled depth. The Part F tables report a measured step of 0.63 times the labelled depth.
    2. A blind forecast. Compute the share of experiment 383's raw lagless forecast (no power lags at all) on the same rows. A forecast blind to the event shows 1 - measured / labelled rather than 0, so the lagless share is the zero-information reference.
    3. Forecast noise. Take clean rows of the same Primaries with a zero-size step and compute the same share: its median and its spread show how much forecast error moves the per-event median.
    4. The 48-hour dilution. Recompute the real share on the first 48 hours, the first 6 hours, and the rest of each event separately, and on events by length class, to separate the dilution of a deepening step from the events' own shape.
  • Reported: a table of real and matched-synthetic shares by lag status with intervals, the four calculations in one table, and two figures (real against synthetic share by lag status; the zero-information reference against the 0-lag share).

docs.title: Job 2: fixed mixture of the forecast with lags and the forecast without lags
docs.text:
• Inputs. The forecast with lags is experiment 381's weekly bundle; the forecast without lags is experiment 383's raw lagless arm (work/arms/lagless.parquet, not arm c2). The scored rows, the label table, and the flagged-zero handling are experiment 400's (Part F slice table; flagged half-hours tagged and dropped; the count per scored set is stated on the page).
  • Arms. (1) Fixed weight w on the forecast with lags in {0.3, 0.5, 0.7}. (2) A per-lead weight: for each scored month, for each lead day 1 to 10, the w in {0.1, 0.2, ..., 0.9} that minimises the exact CRPS of the mixture on the earlier months' rows (flagged half-hours dropped, pooled over Primaries); the page reports whether the chosen weight rises or falls with lead. (3) Each weight function as a mixture of distributions (CDF mixing, experiment 400's e00400_mixture) and as an average of quantiles. Each arm is written raw and widened by 1.15, where "widened by 1.15" means each quantile moves from the arm's median by 1.15 times its distance (the convention of experiment 383's widen). The 1.15 arms are the widened versions of the raw arms, not new fits. B2 and the w = 0.5 mixture come from experiment 400's tables, and 400's B2 is raw only; the page says so wherever B2 is compared with a widened arm.
  • Reported, per group (signed-MW six, MVA-only eight) and per Primary: the Part F harm table (CRPS minus the forecast with lags by lag count inside an event), the cost outside events, smoothness (largest half-hour change in the median across an event onset), avoidable curtailment cost during events, in the 7 days after, and on all rows, as differences against the forecast with lags and the GAM stack, and cold-night rows (the coldest 5% of valid times at each Primary). Tail calibration (0.01, 0.05, 0.95, 0.99 pinball loss and coverage) sits beside CRPS.
  • Audit. The claim "a fixed mixture does as well as B2" goes to the Sonnet audit before any adoption sentence is written.

docs.title: Process and sizing
docs.text:
• Stored. Small tables under the private work/ folder; nothing new in git beyond scripts and the page.
  • Production serving path / degradation rule. Not touched.
  • More than one design. Yes (synthetic placement; weight function): the plan fixes both.
  • Callers. The scripts import experiments 391, 395, and 400.
  • Cadence and compute. Prediction-only with b0's monthly boosters; stored forecasts only for Job 2; no GPU; at most 2 cores; MemoryMax=6G; systemd-run --user --scope -p OOMPolicy=continue.
  • Advice followed. Train on injected events, not real rows alone (experiment 400): Job 2 only re-weights stored forecasts and does not fit a surprise response.
  • Cut for D15 and D18 (maintainer, 2026-10-30). No row before 2025-03-01 enters: every stored forecast is scored from 2025-10-01 and no training is done here.
  • Caveats stated in advance. Weekly-bundle boosters are not stored. Experiment 395 is unmerged (PR 49); the corrected label table is copied from its head. Experiment 400's learned blend is raw only.

docs.title: Experiment 402: a learned gate between a forecast with power lags and a forecast without them
Results
docs.text:
The gate removes most of the harm from corrupted lags on injected load shifts and gains little on real ones. Definitions used below. A load shift is demand moved from one substation to its neighbours. A harm row is a forecast row whose target is outside every event but whose lagged readings (the readings 1 day, 2 days, and 7 days before the forecast origin, at the same time of day) touch one. The six are the 6 Primary substations with signed-MW readings and the eight are the 8 with MVA-only readings; two further Primaries (D15 and D18) are report-only. A gate is a small XGBoost model that sets the weight w of a mixture w times the forecast with lags plus (1 minus w) times the forecast without lags. Every score is a mean exact continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) of the mixture, in points of effective capacity (percentage points of a substation's effective capacity); smaller is better. "Forecast R1" is experiment 392's forecast with lags trained with the labelled events removed. "The R0 pair" is the forecast with lags refitted here on plain targets, beside experiment 392's forecast without lags. The scores come from two evaluations. Step 4 scores forecast R1 leave-one-month-out over four months (2025-10, 2026-01, 2026-03, 2026-06). Step 5 scores the R0 pair forward-only (2026-01, 2026-03, 2026-06).

Caveat that applies to every table below: NGED's logs miss some load-shift events. The score on clean rows is therefore optimistic, and the real-event slices undercount events.

A perfect event flag would add little at the six and nothing at the eight (step 1, analytic ceilings). The flag oracle is a gate that is told which rows have a lag inside an event. Held out by event, it beats the fitted constant mixture per group by about 0.14 points on harm rows at the six (95% interval -0.47 to +0.10). Prediction P1 asked for at least 0.3 points, so P1 is not met. One event (event 55 at D16) supplies 110% of the gain: with that event left out the gain is +0.016 points, so the sign flips. At the eight, the forecast with lags beats every mixture on harm rows. A constant weight chosen by the decile of the gap between the two forecasts' medians needs no labels and captures most of the flag oracle's gain at the six. The per-row oracle weight would lower the score by 0.7 points on harm rows at the six, and separately by 0.41 points on clean rows at the six, where there is no event to detect, so most of its gain comes from knowing the outcome.

Injected shifts pass on a share of the step close to real events (step 2, real-event counterfactual). Replacing the lags inside a labelled event by the stage-1 median, the median share of the step that the forecast with lags passes on is 0.15 with one lag inside the event (186 rows, 17 events), 0.17 with two (62 rows, 14 events), and 0.32 with three (17 rows, 6 events). The synthetic step of the same size gives 1.09, 1.11, and 1.20 times those shares. The shares differ by less than a factor of 2 (prediction P2), so the injection stays as designed. The three-lag estimate rests on 6 events. These shares agree with experiment 395 Part E, which found a median share of 0.368 with all three lags affected, and not with Part F, which found 0.94.

The gate gains 0.6% to 2.3% on injected rows and under 0.5% on real rows (steps 4 and 5). Mean exact CRPS over all rows of the injected test world (seed 2) and over all real-event rows. "Gate, full" is the gate fitted separately for each metering group, fed all features; "Gate, flag" also sees the true event flag and bounds it. The constant mixture is fitted per group on injected events for the injected rows and on real labels for the real rows.

Rows Forecast with lags Forecast without lags 50/50 mixture Constant mixture per group Gate, full Gate, flag Injected, six, forecast R1 4.576 4.439 4.307 4.306 4.247 4.232 Injected, eight, forecast R1 5.449 5.522 5.297 5.312 5.278 5.246 Real, six, forecast R1 4.291 4.439 4.220 4.210 4.207 not defined Real, eight, forecast R1 5.196 5.522 5.220 5.172 5.226 not defined Injected, six, R0 pair 4.822 4.778 4.605 4.637 4.531 4.524 Injected, eight, R0 pair 5.475 5.414 5.288 5.286 5.263 5.244 Real, six, R0 pair 4.533 4.778 4.515 4.516 4.492 not defined Real, eight, R0 pair 5.191 5.414 5.202 5.169 5.198 not defined
  • Prediction P3 holds at the six, and holds narrowly at the eight for one of three gate variants. On forecast R1 the full gate captures 79% of the flag gate's gain over the constant mixture per group at the six and 52% at the eight when one gate is fitted per metering group. The pooled gate (one gate for both groups) captures 73% and 46%, and the gate with the metering group as an input captures 75% and 48%. At the eight the stop rule (under half) therefore fires for two of the three variants, and the series is not stopped only because the maintainer's lenient rule applies. On the R0 pair the per-group full gate captures 94% and 56% (pooled 87% and 73%). The gate that sees only the lagged readings' surprise and the lead time captures 69% to 76% at the six and 69% to 81% at the eight, so the window means, the median gap, and the neighbour features add little at the six and nothing at the eight.
  • Prediction P4 is only partly met, and its intervals include zero. On real harm rows at the six the full gate beats the 50/50 mixture by 0.10 points on forecast R1 (95% interval -0.26 to +0.02, event 146 at D5 supplying 64% of it) and by 0.08 for the R0 pair (-0.25 to +0.07, event 146 supplying 96%). Against the constant mixture fitted on injected events the gain is 0.04 points on forecast R1 (-0.17 to +0.04) and -0.02 on the R0 pair (-0.26 to +0.20), where one event (149 at D5) decides the sign; against the constant mixture fitted on real labels it is 0.11 on forecast R1. A gain under 0.1 points counts as small gain, so the gain is small or borderline. Over all real rows at the six the gate and the constant mixture fitted on real labels differ by 0.003 points, which is zero within noise. At the six the gate scores no worse on clean rows than the 50/50 mixture. At the eight the clean-row score is 0.003 worse.
  • The gate does what it was built for on injected load shifts, though the simpler options come close. On injected harm rows at the six its mean weight on the forecast with lags is 0.42, against 0.51 on clean rows, and it scores 4.11 against 4.34 for the 50/50 mixture, 4.23 for the constant mixture per group, 4.14 for the forecast without lags, and 5.29 for the forecast with lags. At the eight it scores 5.55, against 5.51 for the forecast without lags.
  • At the six the gate scores worse than the 50/50 mixture when the target is inside a real event. On real rows at the six whose target is inside a labelled event (7,960 rows, 11 events) the gate scores 10.75 against 10.50, and its mean weight on the forecast with lags is 0.38. Dropping any single Primary leaves the sign unchanged. A gate trained on real labels (not usable for substations without labels) scores 10.41 there. At the eight (4,278 rows) the gate scores better than the 50/50 mixture, 11.92 against 12.08.
  • Real harm rows are few, and the eight are unstable. There are 11,194 harm rows at the six and 6,609 at the eight, drawn from the 11 labelled events in the test months. These gains are estimates and not tests. At the eight, dropping D3 or D8 flips the sign of the gate's contrast against the forecast with lags.

Upper-tail coverage is 0.65 to 0.68 inside real events at the six, for every arm (forecast R1, real rows). Coverage is the share of actual readings at or below the forecast's quantile, so the target is 0.95 for q95 and 0.99 for q99. The gate leaves tail coverage where the 50/50 mixture has it: at the six on harm rows its q95 coverage is 0.883 against 0.880 for the 50/50 mixture and 0.857 for the forecast with lags, and inside events all arms miss the target by about 0.28 at q95 and 0.22 at q99. The 50/50 mixture, the constant mixture, and the gate raise q95 coverage over the forecast with lags on clean rows by about 0.015.

Rows Forecast with lags Forecast without lags 50/50 mixture Gate, full Six, harm rows (11,194): q95 / q99 coverage 0.857 / 0.957 0.813 / 0.964 0.880 / 0.966 0.883 / 0.968 Six, target inside an event (7,960): q95 / q99 0.652 / 0.776 0.651 / 0.768 0.675 / 0.780 0.674 / 0.774 Six, clean rows (148,539): q95 / q99 0.903 / 0.979 0.877 / 0.978 0.919 / 0.981 0.919 / 0.980 Eight, harm rows (6,609): q95 / q99 0.905 / 0.982 0.921 / 0.983 0.933 / 0.983 0.932 / 0.984 Eight, target inside an event (4,278): q95 / q99 0.920 / 0.979 0.953 / 0.984 0.954 / 0.983 0.955 / 0.984 Eight, clean rows (217,827): q95 / q99 0.917 / 0.983 0.911 / 0.982 0.930 / 0.983 0.930 / 0.983

Event plots. Figure 1 and Figure 2 show three labelled events at the six Primaries with signed readings (D5, D16, D5) and three at the eight with MVA-only readings (all D8), as forecast R1 saw them. In these six events the weight on the forecast with lags is low (about 0.3) through the first two events at the six and stays low for days after the second ends. It rises above 0.5 inside the third event at the six. At the eight it falls from about 0.6 to about 0.4 inside the first two events and does not move in the third. The plots show one forecast per day (issued at 09:00, shortest lead).

docs.title: Not run
docs.text:
• The first look is complete but narrow. The per-Primary contrast intervals, the smoothness and promptness measurements, the lag-encroachment sweep, the avoidable-curtailment table, and the cold-night table in the plan were not produced. Tail coverage (q95 and q99) is reported for forecast R1 on real rows only, from e00402_tails.py, and not for the R0 pair. The slice report (e00402_report.py) gives the per-group harm, event, and clean tables only.
  • Four monthly forecast refits were scored, not twelve.
  • Neighbour graph at scale. A data-derived neighbour graph would need a connection list for each of about 1,300 substations. The gate here used NGED's list for 16 Primaries (the 14 scored and the 2 report-only).

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• The planned comparison of the median forecast with the mean forecast per Primary was not computed, so a bias between the two is untested. Every score here is the exact CRPS; the protocol's 11-quantile CRPS was not tabulated.
  • No audit trigger applies to the production code, because the experiment changes nothing under src/ or packages/. Two triggers are met on the results: P1 is not met, and one event (event 55 at D16) supplies more than the whole step 1 gain. The page records each, and the manager decides whether an audit follows.

docs.title: Plan
docs.text:
• Question. Experiment 400 fitted a mixture weight from the lag surprise scores on real rows and found that the weight hardly moved around load shifts, because event-lag rows are 2.6% of the fit. Can a gate trained on injected events, whose truth is known, learn when to trust the lags? The gate must need no NGED load-shift labels, because about 1,300 substations will have none. The real label table (sw_block_detector_label_table_corrected.csv, 133 rows, 112 usable) is used only to choose the injected depth and duration distributions and to evaluate.
  • Design source. The proposal, its two debate rounds (round 1 Sonnet, round 2 critic), and the maintainer's instructions of 2026-10-30 are in briefs/load_shift_lag_gate_brief.md. The critic's corrections govern. Credit: the mixture-of-two-forecasts blend is experiment 400's; the surprise scores are experiment 391's stage 1; the R1 boosters and the injection harness are experiments 392 and 395 (Part E).
  • Gate model. One weight per row, depending on lead time. The CDF of the mixture is F2 + w (F1 - F2), so its exact CRPS is A w² + B w + C with A = ∫(F1-F2)², B = 2∫(F1-F2)(F2-H), C = CRPS(F2), where F1 has lags, F2 has none, and H is the step at the actual. The label is w* = -B / (2A), the sample weight is A, and the gate is a shallow XGBoost squared-error booster with identity link, prediction clipped to [0, 1]. A logistic baseline is the first arm. A small neural network is tried only if the XGBoost gate plateaus. The CDFs are linear between the 11 quantiles with the outer segments extended to levels 0 and 1, as in experiment 400.
  • No over-smoothing (maintainer). Load-shift events are sudden. The only smoother allowed is causal and short, along valid time within one run. Report each smoother's half-life and the delay of the blend's response at an onset against the unsmoothed weight. A delay of more than a few half-hours is a failure of that smoother.
  • Injection. Clean periods only (no labelled event, flagged zeros dropped). A donor Primary loses a fraction f of its own series and one or more connected recipient neighbours gain it (load conserved, both polarities). f is the table's depth divided by the donor's trailing 30-day mean; the depth quantiles in MW at 0, 10, 25, 50, 75, 90, 100% are about 0.17, 0.52, 0.70, 1.10, 2.2, 3.0, 5.4, and the duration quantiles in hours about 2.4, 4.8, 8.1, 47.9, 84, 168, 747 (the proposer's tally, re-counted in step 1). A parametric rule needs no table: log-uniform interpolation of f between these quantiles. 30% of events have no observed recipient (31 of 112 rows name one Primary; swept at 0%, 30%, 60%). Transient spikes and outliers that are not load shifts are injected too: single half-hours and runs of up to 6 half-hours at 0.5 to 3 times the donor's trailing 30-day standard deviation, both signs. Injected events never enter evaluation.
  • Gate features. For each of the three lags: the single-step surprise and the signed MW residual, with window statistics at half-widths 1.5, 3, 6, 12 h (24 h; 84 h for the week lag only): mean, median, min, max, standard deviation, signed sum, count above the band, and a triangular tent mean. All windows of all three lags truncate at the telemetry cut-off, as e00391_fit.py does with NEWEST_AGE. Neighbour features from the neighbours' own surprise at the same lag time: max, min, sum, and the counts above +1 and below -1. The sign logic is learned. The gap between the two forecasts' medians is a named feature, ablated.
  • Surprise source and alignment. Every surprise comes from experiment 391's stage-1 ens table (work/stage1/ens/<site>.parquet), which refits monthly from 2024-10-01 and predicts only the half-hours from its refit to the next, so u is out of sample for every lag time from 2024-10. For an injected series the injected value is passed through the stored stage-1 quantiles of that half-hour (no new prediction). The four forecast refits (2025-10-01, 2026-01-01, 2026-03-01, 2026-06-01) each use lag times at or before the origin, whose stage-1 refit is the one at the start of that lag time's month. Stage 1 reads the ENS control member and keeps one row per valid time (150 rounds, eta 0.15); the forecasts with and without lags pool 51 members at 500 rounds. The gate therefore sees a surprise from a different recipe than the forecasts. Step 4 checks that the surprise separates injected events from clean periods at the lag times, and reports the gap as a caveat.
  • Cleaned data. Every training row, lag, and scoring actual uses cleaned data with flagged substation_zero half-hours dropped. The count dropped per fold is reported.
  • Steps (stop rules above).
    1. Analytic ceilings (no fit; at most 4 cores, MemoryMax=10G in total with step 2). A, B, and C per row from experiment 381's weekly bundle (forecast with lags) and experiment 383's work/arms/lagless.parquet (forecast without lags), over Part F's rows. Evaluate the per-row oracle weight, the flag oracle (best constant w on event-lag rows, the fitted constant elsewhere), and the fitted constant mixture with lead time. One stated widening: both forecasts are used raw, as in experiment 400. Also on the R1 pair's four months.
    2. Real-event counterfactual and synthetic sweep (at most 4 cores, shared with step 1). Re-predict experiment 392's R1 lagged boosters (00392-.../work/boosters/r1_lagged/<site>_s0_<refit>.ubj) with the lags inside each corrected labelled event replaced by the stage-1 median, and compare the share of the step passed on with that of synthetic steps of the same depth and lag count. This settles the disagreement between experiment 395 Part E (median moves 36.8% of a step with all three lags affected) and Part F (median share 0.94).
    3. Refit the lagged forecast on plain targets (arm R0 lagged) at the four refit dates. 500 rounds, monthly recipe, experiment 392's e00392_fit.py --arms r0 --forms lagged, boosters saved under this experiment's folder. Starts when the manager grants the GPU slot, in parallel with step 2. About 2 hours of GPU; cores and GPU processes reported to the manager before it starts.
    4. Gate screen on the R1 pair. Leave-one-month-out across the four refit months (training rows with valid time on or after the first of the scored month are cut). Arms: (a) fitted constant mixture; (b) gate given the injected truth flags; (c) single-step surprise only; (d) all window statistics; (e) own-Primary-only; plus nested feature sets. Core estimate given to the manager before it starts.
    5. Forward-only confirmation on the R0 pair. Train on injected events only; evaluate on real events that end at least 14 days before the scored month, logged transfers (66) and scanned events separately, with and without D8 and D5. Optional real-label arm, separate: it could not be repeated at scale, and 46 of the 112 labels were found by scanning the series the gate reads.
  • Per-group splits (maintainer, relayed 2026-10-30). Before steps 4 and 5, every gate arm in step 4 is run three ways: one pooled gate, one gate with the metering unit (signed MW or MVA-only) as an input, and a separate gate per group. The fitted constant mixture and the flag oracle get the same split (one weight per group against one pooled weight), so that the upper bound is stated per group. Every table reports per Primary as well as per group; D15 and D18 are report-only.
  • Why the MVA-only eight differ. Step 1 reports, per Primary, whether the lags help the forecast with lags outside events, how many events each Primary has, and how deep and long they are relative to capacity.
  • Event time-series plots (maintainer, relayed 2026-10-30). The result page shows at least 6 time-series plots of real events from the corrected label table, covering both metering groups (signed MW and MVA-only). Each plot marks when the event starts and ends and shows the actual reading, the median, and the 90% band of the forecast with lags, the forecast without lags, and each gate's blend. Plots follow the dataviz skill. Generators are not involved (demand series only), so no anonymisation is needed.
  • Caveat: unlabelled events (relayed 2026-10-30). NGED says load-shift events may be missing from their logs (one on 2022-01-12 is not in the label table). Clean-lag rows and clean training periods can therefore contain events that no label covers. The harm table's baseline (clean-lag rows) is optimistic, and the real-event slices undercount events. Every write-up repeats this caveat. Injected events stay the main training signal because they need no logs.
  • Changes after the Opus plan review.
    • Comparators. Every stop rule and contrast uses the fitted constant mixture per group (one weight per lead day and metering group) as its comparator, and also reports the forecast without lags. The pooled constant is descriptive only. Step 1 also reports leave-one-Primary-out and leave-one-event-out contrasts, and clusters the bootstrap by load-shift event (all Primaries the event touched).
    • Non-inferiority margin. The contrast over harm rows, clean rows, and the 7 days after each event is pooled per group. Clean rows are 96% of rows at the six, so the clean-row margin at the six is 0.005 points. At the eight the target is non-inferiority against the forecast with lags (margin 0.01 points). The gate with the metering unit as an input and the gate per group are the headline arms; the pooled gate is descriptive.
    • Arms. Arm (b) gets the injected flags plus every feature of arm (d) and bounds it; the flag-only version is a separate arm. A new arm (f) is the same gate trained on real, unmodified rows (label w* needs only actual readings), so a gain is credited to the injection only if (d) beats (f). Step 1 adds feature oracles (a constant per group, lead day, and decile of the absolute gap between the two medians).
    • Folds. Step 4 is true leave-one-month-out, cutting training rows whose valid time or lag time is in the scored month and origins within 14 days before it. Step 5 is forward-only and evaluates harm rows whose target is in the scored month; the 14-day rule applies to the training events of the real-label arm. Constants are cross-fitted on the same folds.
    • Injection. Step 2 adds a variant that scales the series by a fraction (the injection the plan uses) beside the constant step, and repeats on the R0 lagged boosters. At the eight, only windows whose reading stays above 20% of capacity receive an injection. Spike size is 4 to 20 times the stage-1 residual's median absolute deviation. A sensitivity arm chooses clean base periods without labels.
    • Power. Step 5 is an estimate with a leave-one-event-out table, not a test. Step 1 is repeated on the R1 pair (using experiment 392's stored forecasts) and on the R0 pair.
  • Pre-registered contrasts (step 5). Each of arms (c), (d), (e), and the logistic baseline minus the forecast with lags, minus the fitted constant mixture, and minus the forecast without lags, on (i) rows whose target is outside every event and whose lags touch one, by number of lags, at the six and at the MVA-only eight; (ii) all other rows outside the 7 days after. The Bonferroni k is fixed in the commit that precedes step 5. Intervals: months resampled for pooled rows, events for event slices.
  • Reports (as in the brief): the harm table; cost outside events per Primary; weight by lag status, injected kind, and lead; smoothness and promptness; the lag-encroachment sweep on the blend; avoidable curtailment during events and in the following 7 days; cold nights separately; tail coverage at 0.01, 0.05, 0.95, 0.99. What a data-derived neighbour graph would need at scale is stated in the write-up.
  • Compute. Steps 1 and 2: at most 4 cores and MemoryMax=10G in total, run with systemd-run --user --scope -p MemoryMax=10G -p OOMPolicy=continue, one BLAS thread per process, spawn start method. Later steps wait for the manager.
  • Earlier advice followed. Experiment 400's two advice items: train on injected events, and include a fitted constant-weight mixture beside the fixed 50/50 mixture.
  • Cadence. Monthly refits only (maintainer, 2026-10-30).

docs.title: Does one pooled mixture density network beat one network per Primary for Primary demand, and where does the gain fall?
docs.text: Take-home message: one pooled neural network beats one network per Primary at both substation groups. Pooled A0 (the pooled network with uniform input-group weights) lowers the CRPS at days 1 to 10 by 0.185 points of capacity at the six signed-MW Primaries (95% interval -0.300 to -0.061) and by 0.161 points at the eight MVA-only Primaries (-0.272 to -0.089), and 11 of the 14 countable Primaries gain. The gain does not grow where the history is shorter (correlation -0.02), so the mechanism the prediction named is not what carries it. At D15 and D18 the result is mixed: D18 gains 0.98 points and D15 loses 1.66 under A0, while the pooled plain network gains at both. The verdict is supported (interim), because the pre-registered rule held on five test months.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
CRPS at days 1 to 10, mean over Primaries with equal weight, in points of capacity.

Group Per-Primary plain Pooled plain Pooled A0 A0 minus per-Primary (95% interval) Signed-MW six 3.536 3.295 3.351 -0.185 (-0.300 to -0.061) MVA-only eight 3.952 3.881 3.791 -0.161 (-0.272 to -0.089) MVA-only seven (no D8) 3.336 3.294 3.227 -0.109 (-0.124 to -0.090) D15 and D18 (report-only) 10.494 9.278 10.835 +0.336 (-1.815 to +2.709)
  • Per Primary, the largest gains under A0 are D10 (-0.647, interval -0.798 to -0.478), D8 (-0.528), and D18 (-0.980). D2 (-0.073) and D21 (-0.131) gain with intervals that exclude zero.
  • D11 (+0.017), D5 (+0.030), D3 (+0.103), and D15 (+1.663) do not gain, and none of their intervals excludes zero.
  • The pooled plain network gains more than A0 at the signed-MW six (-0.241 against -0.185) and less at the MVA-only eight (-0.071 against -0.161).

docs.title: Predictions and decision rule
docs.text:
• P1 held. Both groups have negative differences with intervals below zero.
  • P2 failed. The correlation of the gain with months of history is -0.02, not below -0.3.
  • P3 failed. D15 loses under A0, so D15 and D18 do not both gain more than the median Primary.
  • P4 failed narrowly. The best three Primaries carry 60% of the summed gain, and the prediction required under 60%.
  • The decision rule is met: both group intervals lie below zero and 11 of 14 Primaries gain.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Five test months (2025-10, 2025-12, 2026-01, 2026-03, and 2026-06) give few resamples for the month-block bootstrap, so every interval is interim.
  • A0 differs from the per-Primary network in two ways: pooling, and the five-token input encoder. The pooled plain network separates them: it gains 0.241 and 0.071 points at the two groups.
  • The forecasts and scores are those of experiment 397; nothing was refitted.

docs.title: Problems caused by the move
docs.text: None.

docs.title: A learned trust weight for each lagged power reading does not beat a fixed 50/50 mixture around load-shift events
docs.text:
No variant we trained beats a fixed 50/50 mixture of the plain network and the lagless forecast (B-mix) on real harm rows at the signed-MW six, so the learned trust weights add complexity without a measured gain. The numbers are interim and unaudited: five scored months, one to three seeds per month, and no correction for multiple comparisons. Weighted by events, B3 (attention over the lags) is +0.13 and B6 (learned windows) is +0.15 points of capacity behind B-mix on real harm rows, and the ranges when any one month is left out include zero. Before weighting, B3 and B6 looked 0.14 and 0.02 points ahead, because two months that each hold a single real harm event pulled the average.

  • The design is too small to see a difference below about 0.3 to 1.0 points of capacity. The smallest difference detectable with 80% power, from the spread of the five monthly values, exceeds most of the contrasts reported here. With a t multiplier instead of a normal one, the range is about 0.4 to 1.3.
  • Inside real events, a single month decides the sign. Scored against NRA-corrected actuals, B0, B1, and B6 beat B-mix at the signed-MW six by 0.5 to 0.6 points. Dropping, in each month, the event that contributes most to the difference turns each of those into a loss of 0.2 to 0.3.
  • The trust weights are almost inert. B1's mean trust is 0.91 outside real events and 0.94 inside them. B1o, which receives the true event flags, shows no consistent drop inside events.

Terms. NRA is the normal running arrangement, the electricity network as it is when no load transfer is active. An NRA-corrected actual is the metered actual with the load that experiment 435 estimates a real event moved between Primaries removed. A Primary is a primary substation. A load-shift event is a period when load was transferred between Primaries. Points of capacity are the score (CRPS, the continuous ranked probability score, computed from 11 quantiles) as a percentage of the Primary's capacity. The signed-MW six are the Primaries (D5, D9, D10, D11, D14, D16) that report signed power; the MVA-only eight report apparent power only.

What was tested. A trust head is a small neural network that outputs one weight per lagged power reading, saying how far to trust it. The experiment trained a mixture density network with a lagless module (a forecast that never sees recent power), a calibration module, and a trust head, on real power plus events injected by experiment 428. It compared the variants below with B-mix.

Arm What it is B-mix Fixed 50/50 mixture of the A0-inj forecast and the lagless forecast; the reference A0-inj Plain network on the injected data B0 Constant weight per lag (per group, lead band, and lag) B1 Learned trust weight per lag B1o B1 plus the true per-lag event flags (positive control) B3 Attention over the lags B4c B1 plus 5 weekly lags B6 B1 plus learned windows over the surprise series B7 B1 plus a 7-day history S1 Plain network plus the lag surprise at 3 lags

A harm row is a forecast target outside every real event whose day window lies inside one, so a trust head should discount the lag. A clean row has no real event near it. The inert rule says a trust head is inert when its mean trust outside events minus inside events is under 0.1. Every contrast is the arm's score minus B-mix's, in points of capacity, so negative is better than B-mix. The arms B1g, B1m, B2, B4a, B4b, B5, and B1-rw are defined in the plan below.

docs.title: Event-weighted pooling and the size of the design
docs.text:
Weighting each month by its number of real events removes B3's and B6's lead on harm rows. The rows below are the signed-MW six on forecasts with leads from 0 to 240 hours (NGED's horizon is 1 to 10 days, and table P of experiment 435 uses the same range), raw quantiles. "Mean of months" averages the five monthly contrasts equally, "event-weighted" weights each month by the number of real-event clusters its rows touch (18 on harm rows, 25 inside events, 37 on clean rows), and "multi-event months" averages the three months with more than one harm-row event.

Arm Harm: mean of months Harm: event-weighted Harm: multi-event months Inside events: event-weighted Clean: event-weighted A0-inj +0.12 +0.17 +0.19 +0.14 +0.29 B0 +0.14 +0.49 +0.63 +0.36 +0.38 B1 +0.14 +0.31 +0.37 +0.58 +0.28 B3 -0.14 +0.13 +0.21 -0.16 +0.09 B4c -0.04 +0.25 +0.34 +0.26 +0.22 B6 -0.02 +0.15 +0.20 +0.25 +0.10 S1 +0.10 +0.15 +0.16 +0.18 +0.22

B3's and B6's lead comes from 2025-12 and 2026-03, which each hold one harm event. On harm rows B3 scores -0.92 and -0.42 there, and B6 -0.31 and -0.39. Averaged over the three multi-event months, every arm trails B-mix. Rescoring with the 1.15 widening of experiment 428, or with table P factors refitted on each arm's own earlier months (clean real rows, per group and lead band), moves every entry of the table by 0.03 or less, so the miscalibration of the tails does not explain the difference between the arms.

The design can detect a difference of only about 0.3 to 1.0 points of capacity. The minimum detectable effect, taken as 2.8 times the standard error of the five monthly differences (a normal approximation for a two-sided 5% test at 80% power), is 0.4 to 1.0 on harm rows, 0.3 to 0.9 inside events, and 0.3 to 0.8 on clean rows, depending on the arm. With four degrees of freedom the multiplier is about 3.6, which makes each figure about 30% larger. The range is rough, because five values give a poor estimate of their own spread.

The event counts differ by definition, not by error. In the five scored months 46 corrected events overlap the scored period (21 at the signed-MW six, 16 at the MVA-only eight, 9 at D15 and D18) and 42 padded event runs do (a run merges events that fall within the padding). Experiment 445's 49 and experiment 435's 41 count the same events with different windows. The label table's 112 is a row count, and 184 corrected events (170 padded runs) is the whole history. The bootstrap clusters used here are the events a row's lag windows touch, so they can exceed the padded runs.

The lagless table's 90% band is too narrow. It covers 79 to 82% of actuals on clean and harm rows in every lead band, and 48 to 52% inside events.

docs.title: Scoring inside events against NRA-corrected actuals
docs.text:
A single month decides the sign of the result inside events. Experiment 435 estimates the load that each event removed from or added to the Primary (a measured deviation for 34 of 184 events, the labelled depth for the other 150). Subtracting that from the metered actual gives a corrected actual. The rows below score the real-event rows against it at three depth factors, at the signed-MW six, arm minus B-mix, mean over months.

Arm Depth 0.75 Depth 1.0 Depth 1.25 Depth 1.0, largest event of each month dropped Metered actual A0-inj +0.34 +0.35 +0.36 +0.20 +0.12 B0 -0.55 -0.49 -0.44 +0.21 +0.18 B1 -0.69 -0.63 -0.60 +0.29 +0.53 B3 +0.01 +0.08 +0.08 +0.34 -0.20 B4c -0.22 -0.09 -0.01 +0.58 +0.10 B6 -0.65 -0.58 -0.54 +0.23 +0.11 S1 +0.37 +0.42 +0.47 +0.26 +0.13

At the MVA-only eight every arm trails B-mix against the corrected actuals (+0.5 to +1.0 at depth 1.0, and +0.27 to +0.91 with the largest event of each month dropped).

docs.title: Pooled over months, all leads
docs.text:
The tables and figures 1 to 4 below come from e00404_pool.py, on forecasts of every stored lead (up to 14.6 days), so they differ from the audit tables above, which keep leads of 0 to 240 hours. Each contrast is the mean over the arm's cells of the arm's score minus the reference arm's score on the same rows, in points of capacity (negative is better than the reference), with a 95% interval from resampling whole months (seeds within a month are averaged first, so the mean is a mean of month means). A cell is one scored month and one seed. B-mix, A0-inj, B0, B1, B1o, B3, and S1 have all 7 cells (2026-06 seeds 0 to 2; 2026-03, 2026-01, 2025-12, and 2025-10, seed 0). B4c and B6 have 5 cells (the five months, seed 0). B7 has 1 cell (2026-06, seed 0). Every interval is wide because it rests on at most five months, the arms have different cells, only four cells hold a real-event row at the MVA-only eight, a bootstrap over five blocks under-covers, and no correction for multiple comparisons is applied.

No arm separates from B-mix at the signed-MW six, except that four arms have 95% intervals that exclude zero on the wrong side (A0-inj on clean rows and inside events, S1 on clean rows, B1 inside events), with the caveats above. B-mix is a fixed mixture of the saved A0-inj network's forecast and the cross-fitted lagless table's forecast, each with weight one half.

Arm Real harm rows Real clean rows Rows inside real events A0-inj +0.19 [-0.05, +0.39] +0.35 [+0.17, +0.60] +0.20 [+0.03, +0.33] B0 +0.06 [-0.57, +0.68] +0.43 [-0.01, +1.05] +0.27 [-0.18, +0.72] B1 +0.09 [-0.26, +0.39] +0.34 [-0.11, +0.90] +0.49 [+0.21, +0.79] B1o 0.00 [-0.49, +0.49] +0.22 [-0.17, +0.73] +0.24 [-0.17, +0.57] B3 -0.16 [-0.63, +0.25] +0.21 [-0.06, +0.68] -0.06 [-0.47, +0.24] S1 +0.19 [-0.13, +0.45] +0.31 [+0.05, +0.61] +0.16 [-0.26, +0.50] B4c (5 cells) -0.12 [-0.69, +0.40] +0.23 [-0.04, +0.49] +0.17 [-0.20, +0.61] B6 (5 cells) -0.12 [-0.50, +0.26] +0.17 [-0.06, +0.46] +0.16 [-0.18, +0.51] B7 (1 cell) -0.03 +0.04 +0.98

Score minus B-mix at the signed-MW six, in points of capacity. B-mix's own scores are 3.79 on real harm rows, 3.37 on real clean rows, and 5.03 inside real events (the values for the arms with 5 cells are measured against B-mix on those 5 cells).

B-mix is ahead on clean rows at the MVA-only eight. Every arm is worse than B-mix on real clean rows there (B3 +0.14 [-0.05, +0.34], the best; B0 +0.48 [+0.30, +0.65]). On real harm rows only A0-inj and S1 have intervals that exclude zero (B3 +0.29 [-0.17, +0.85]; B4c +0.33 [-0.49, +0.96]). Three of the seven cells hold a single real harm event at the MVA-only eight.

The pooled differences hide a large spread between cells. B3's difference from B-mix on real harm rows runs from -1.09 to +0.53 across the 7 cells, and the most negative values come from cells with a single real harm event (diamonds); the largest positive value does not.

B3 is ahead of B1 inside real events, and B6 is ahead of B1 on both row classes. The contrast against B1 at the signed-MW six: B3 minus B1 is -0.24 [-0.52, +0.03] on harm rows and -0.56 [-0.75, -0.36] inside events (7 cells); B6 minus B1 is -0.16 [-0.26, -0.03] and -0.31 [-0.58, -0.02] (5 cells). B0 minus B1 is -0.03 [-0.35, +0.29] on harm rows, so B1's learned weights do no better than B0's constant weights.

The trust weights are almost inert, even given the true event flags. The mean over the 7 cells of the geometric mean of B1's three trust weights is 0.91 on real rows whose lags lie outside real events (padded) and 0.94 inside them, so the inert rule (outside minus inside under 0.1) fires on the padded flag. B1o gives 0.91 outside and 0.90 inside. B0's constant weight is 0.98 everywhere.

Reading of the oracle control. B1o, with the true per-lag event flag as three extra trust-head inputs, scores 0.00 [-0.49, +0.49] against B-mix on real harm rows and +0.24 [-0.17, +0.57] inside real events, against B1's +0.09 and +0.49. The exact flags point to a gain of 0.09 on harm rows (-0.09 [-0.29, +0.10], an interval that includes zero) and of 0.26 inside events (-0.26 [-0.48, -0.05]), yet B1o stays behind B-mix inside events, so the limit may lie in the calibration module, the lagless forecast, or the mixture rule as well as in detecting events. Only the B1 version of the oracle exists.

The encroachment sweep shows B1 and B0 follow a shifted lag more than A0-inj does. A step of 5% of capacity added to the newest 3 lags moves the median of A0-inj by 0.12 of the step, of B1 by 0.22, and of B0 by 0.25 (lead band 0, 2026-06 seed 0). Band widths stay within 0.99 and 1.03 of their unshifted width for all arms, and the masked-lag control moves by 0.0 (about 1e-8) for B0 and B1. This is one month and one seed, covers all 16 Primaries, and the 3-lag step spans 7 days. The sweep was not run for B3, B6, or S1.

Which pre-registered predictions held (signed-MW six, real harm rows unless stated).
