B-mix, S1, B1g (B1 plus the gap between the lagged and lagless means), B1o, and the encroachment sweep were added after the plan was written. B1g is indistinguishable from B1 (harm rows -0.17 and -0.16 against B-mix on 2026-06 seed 0). Training and scoring worlds come from experiment 428's injected worlds, and the lagless tables were cross-fitted with K=6 contiguous blocks.

docs.title: Question
docs.text:
We test whether one neural network can learn how much to trust each lagged power reading, with no event labels. A load-shift event moves demand between neighbouring Primaries for hours or weeks. The power the network sees at the same time yesterday or last week can then be abnormal, and a forecast that copies that power inherits the abnormality. NGED cannot supply event labels for about 1,300 substations, and every binary event detector tried so far has scored poorly. The maintainer's design replaces the detector with a continuous trust weight per lagged input, learned end to end.

  • Lagless module. A mixture density network (3 Gaussians) that sees weather, solar geometry, calendar, holidays, and a Primary embedding, and no power lag.
  • Calibration module. A second network that outputs a lagged mixture (3 Gaussians) from the lagless forecast, the three lags, the Primary embedding, and an indicator of signed-MW or MVA-only metering. It does not see the trust inputs.
  • Trust head. A separate small network that reads only the trust inputs below, the lead time, the Primary embedding, and the metering indicator, and outputs one weight in [0, 1] per lag. Feeding the trust inputs only to this head stops the calibration module from falling back on the lagless forecast inside the lagged head, which would leave the trust weight unidentified and let it collapse to a constant, as the logistic gate of experiment 400 did (about 0.6).
  • The three lags. lag_origin (the newest reading before the forecast origin), lag_same_time_latest_day (the reading at the target's time of day on the latest day before the origin), and lag_same_time_latest_week (the same on the latest week before the origin), as in the weekly XGBoost member. Each carries its age in hours and an is-missing flag.
  • Output. A mixture of the lagless and lagged distributions (6 Gaussians), never an average of quantiles. The weight on the lagged mixture is the product of the 3 per-lag trust weights, so one untrusted lag lowers it, and the lagless distribution takes the weight 1 minus that product. Arm B1m replaces the product by the mean of the 3 weights.
  • Training scheme (a departure from fully end to end). Cross-fitting makes the lagless forecast a precomputed table. The lagless module trains on its own mixture negative log-likelihood, and the rest of the network trains on the final mixture negative log-likelihood of the clean series, on injected events, with the lagless forecast held fixed. No separate stage on event labels is used. The fully joint version, in which the lagless module trains jointly with a stop-gradient and no cross-fit, is arm B9, run last and labelled in-sample.
  • Series. Each Primary series is one series per substation.

docs.title: Review against the latest evidence
docs.text:
The plan was reviewed against the pages merged since the brief was written (experiments 387, 398, 399, 401, and 403, and the standing practices of the ml-experiment skill, read from main on 2026-10-30). Four changes follow; none alters the scope.

  • Fixed-mixture control. Experiment 401's advice is to use a fixed mixture with a weight of 0.3 to 0.5 on the forecast with lags as the control for any learned blend at the signed-MW Primaries. The plan adds a free arm F0: a fixed mixture, with weight 0.4 on the lagged forecast of A0-inj and 0.6 on L0, computed from stored forecasts. F0 is reported at the signed-MW six only, and not at the MVA-only eight or at D15 and D18.
  • How the lag response is measured. The lag response is the forecast with lags minus the forecast without lags on the same rows, and never 1 minus the residual over the labelled step.
  • Standing practices followed. Monthly refits; cleaned data, with the number of dropped substation_zero half-hours reported per fold; the D15 and D18 cut at 2025-03-01; every fitted network saved in the experiment's data folder; stored predictions reused as references; tails and the avoidable-curtailment cost reported beside CRPS; example forecast plots and event plots; draft pull request. The plan departs from the practice of four screen folds: it uses the five screen folds of experiment 397, so that its scores sit on the same rows as experiments 397 and 403, and labels every number interim.
  • Evidence that tempers the expected gain. Experiment 401 found real events move the forecast by 0.03 of the step or less, and that one event at D16 carries most of a fixed mixture's gain at the six. Experiment 402's ceilings3.txt found the flag oracle's gain has an interval that includes zero. The batch 0 and batch 1 stop rules already encode this.

docs.title: Design choices fixed by this plan
docs.text:
The smoother and the surprise source are fixed here because the brief leaves them open. Each is a stated choice; a different choice is a later experiment.

  • Light causal smoother. After the trust head, a causal moving average of 3 half-hours is applied over the lag's valid times, so that weights do not jump between adjacent half-hours. Events start suddenly, so the smoother is short. The write-up reports how many half-hours the smoothed trust weight takes to cross 0.5 after an injected onset, beside the unsmoothed weight.
  • Trust weights start at 0.5 with no regulariser. The write-up reports whether they stay near 0.5.
  • Stop-gradient. The surprises and the gap between the lagged and lagless medians pass through a stop-gradient, so the lagless module cannot shape its own surprises through the trust head.
  • Cross-fitted lagless forecast (leakage rule). For each monthly refit, the months before the scored month in the training window are split into K = 6 contiguous blocks. For each block, a lagless module is fitted on the other 5 blocks and forecasts the held-out block. The 6 cross-fitted forecasts form the table of out-of-sample lagless forecasts for the training rows. One further lagless module is fitted on all months before the scored month, for the scored month and for test-time inference. A lag whose valid time falls before the scored month takes its surprise from the cross-fit table and not from the further module, because the further module was fitted on those months. The table is shared across all arms and seeds, and is fitted once per refit and seed. The calibration module and the trust head both take the table's lagless mixture as input in training, and the further module's mixture at test time. A stop-gradient on the lagless forecast stops the lagless module shaping its own surprises. Cross-fitting never uses the scored month or later. The other blocks include later months than the held-out block, which a live forecast would not have, so the training surprises are somewhat larger than a fully fitted lagless forecast would give; the write-up lists this mismatch as a caveat. If the timed fits show K = 6 is too expensive, the plan settles on a smaller K and tells the manager.
  • Forecast origin and lead of the lagless forecast. At a lag's valid time, the lagless forecast uses the ECMWF ENS (European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts ensemble) mean and spread of the freshest run available at the forecast origin (the latest run published by the valid time, leads 9 to 33 hours). That run exists at forecast time. ERA5 is not used. The training table applies the same freshest-run rule at every origin.
  • One pass on the ensemble summary. The network sees the ENS mean and spread of each weather variable once. The 51-member scheme runs only as a check on the best arm.

docs.title: Trust inputs
docs.text:
• Per lag. The single-step surprise (the lag minus the lagless median at the lag's valid time) in capacity-normalised MW, kept signed, and the same value in units of the lagless band width. Both are given, because a clipped score loses magnitude.
  • Per lag, window statistics of the surprise over windows centred on the lag (half-widths 1.5, 3, 6, 12, and 24 hours, and 84 hours for the week lag only): mean, median, minimum, maximum, standard deviation, signed sum, count above the band, and a 12-hour triangular tent mean. Every window is truncated at the forecast origin and at the telemetry cut-off, and a truncated tent is renormalised to sum to 1.
  • Neighbours. The same quantities for neighbouring Primaries from neighbours_nged.json (in the folder of experiment 383), with the signed logic learned and never hand-coded. Bulk supply points are added if their stored series exist; if not, the write-up says they were left out. At scale the graph must come from the data (for example the correlation of forecast residuals); the write-up states what that needs.
  • Lag age and is-missing flag for each lag, and the gap between the lagged and lagless medians.
  • Recomputation after injection. Every one of these inputs is recomputed from the injected series, including the neighbour, bulk-supply-point, B6, and B7 windows.

docs.title: Arms
docs.text:
All arms use the pooled plain mixture density network of experiment 397 (arm plain_pooled) as their base: one network for all 16 Primaries, a learned Primary embedding, a 3-component Gaussian mixture head. The maintainer's update of 2026-10-30 moved the base from the uniform-token arm of experiment 397, called U0 here, to the plain network. The interim scores of experiment 397 (unaudited) were 3.264 at the signed-MW six and 3.860 at the MVA-only eight for the plain network, against 3.320 and 3.775 for U0, and the plain network's lead rests mainly on one fold, so this plan infers no ranking between them. Both modules get the Primary embedding. The group gate over input groups stays closed in every arm. Every arm trains on the injected data below, except A0.

Batch 0 (a cheap check before batch 1). Re-score the stored forecasts of experiment 402 on harm rows with the lags inside each real event replaced by clean counterfactual values, using experiment 401's harness. This gives the most that any lag-trust method can gain, because experiment 401 found real events move the forecast by only 0.02 to 0.03 of the step, yet the forecast with lags scores 5.119 against 4.292 without lags on harm rows, so most of that gap is the two forecasts differing as whole forecasts. If the counterfactual gain is under 0.1 CRPS points at the signed-MW six, the plan skips batches 1 and 2.

Deviation from the batch 0 rule. Experiment 411 ran batch 0 and was inconclusive. The gain at the signed-MW six was -0.836 CRPS points (95% interval -2.578 to +1.226) on 9 events. One D5 event flips the sign: without it the gain is +0.460 (95% interval -0.102 to +1.631). At the eight MVA-only Primaries the gain was +0.024 (95% interval -0.574 to +1.529). The harness scored only 15 of the 184 corrected events. Experiments 411 and 414 reached only 9 signed-MW-six events. The 4 test months and the sign, step, and bias filters capped that count, not gaps: 129 of the 184 events lie outside the test months. The ceiling is therefore a thin figure from XGBoost models alone. Batch 1 runs regardless, with no 12-refit extension and no looser event filters on this experiment's account. The point estimate is under 0.1, so the rule as written would skip batches 1 and 2, but the interval spans zero. The neural Discuss session therefore ruled that batches 1 and 2 run. The batch 1 stop rule stays as written.

Batch 1:

  • L0 (free). The lagless module's own forecast, scored on all rows and on harm rows. Experiment 402's weights suggest the lags help the signed-MW six only at days 1 to 2, and L0 shows that directly.
  • A0. The pooled plain network with the three lags, trained on the plain clean data (the reference for the architecture alone).
  • A0-inj. A0 trained on the same injected data as B1. B1 minus A0-inj isolates the architecture, and A0-inj minus A0 isolates the training data.
  • B0. Constant trust: B1's architecture with one learned constant trust weight per metering group, lead band, and lag that does not depend on the trust inputs (the control experiment 400 recommended). B1 minus B0 isolates the trust inputs.
  • B1. The architecture above, with the three lags.
  • B2. A0-inj with token-level lag dropout during training (each lag token zeroed with probability 0.2 and flagged missing) and no lagless module.
  • B5. B1 without lag_origin.
  • B-mix (reference, free). A fixed 50/50 mixture of A0-inj's lagged forecast and the lagless module's forecast (the neural Discuss session's request, 2026-10-31). It is scored on the same harm rows and event slices as every arm. Experiment 402 step 4 (interim, unaudited) found that a simple mixture captured most of a lag-surprise gate's gain on injected shifts at the six signed-MW Primaries (mean CRPS 4.307 for the mixture, 4.250 for the gate, 4.576 with lags, 4.439 without). Any trust head or attention over lags in this experiment must beat B-mix to count.

Design iterations after batch 1 (maintainer, 2026-10-31). The maintainer expects several design iterations (tokens and attention) and is optimistic about the idea, so a null at batch 1 does not end this experiment. The plan allows at least two design iterations after batch 1 before concluding. The batch 1 stop rule still decides whether the full batch 2 grid runs. If it fires, each iteration changes the trust head or the attention over tokens, is scored on the same rows against B-mix, and is reported as one more named arm. The manager is asked before the total passes 12 hours.

Batch 2 (runs straight away if the batch 1 stop rule does not fire):

  • Carry-forward rule (maintainer, 2026-10-30). B3 attends across the lag set that wins among B4a, B4b, B4c, and B1's three lags, together with the XGBoost lag experiment 388 when its page is available. The order of work therefore runs B4a, B4b, and B4c before B3. If B3 has already run with the 3 lags, it is rerun with the winning set. The adopted set is named in the arm label (for example B3-lags5), and the write-up says which earlier components were adopted and which were not, with the reason.
  • B3. B1's lagless module and cross-fitted table, with an attention gate in place of the trust head and the product rule. The gate attends over 4 tokens: the 3 lag tokens (each the lag value with its age, missing flag, and trust inputs) and a lagless-forecast token. Its query is built from the lead time, the Primary embedding, and the metering indicator. The output is the gated sum of tokens fed to a 3-component mixture head. B3 minus B2 tests attention over lags, and B1 minus B3 compares the trust head with attention.
  • B6. B1 with a 1D convolutional neural network over the surprise series in a window of 24 hours either side of each lag (97 half-hourly steps), in place of the hand-built window statistics. Each window is zero-padded and truncated at the forecast origin. The network has two convolution layers (kernel 5, 16 channels) with global pooling.
  • B4a, B4b, and B4c. B1 with more lags: the same weekday and time from each of the last N = 1, 3, and 5 weeks, plus the median across the N weeks and the median minus the latest week. The three values of N are three separate arms.
  • B8a and B8b (low priority; run after B1 reads clean). B1 plus an auxiliary probe head that reads the trust head's hidden layer and predicts, for each lagged timestep, whether the injected generator put it inside an event or a spike. The loss is binary cross-entropy at a weight of 0.1 of the mixture loss in B8a and 0.3 in B8b. The probe trains only on the injected labels, which are known truth and need no NGED label, and it is never used at forecast time. Real-event labels come from the 112-row corrected table, so the write-up reports the event count per metering group beside every area figure, and says plainly if the probe works on injected events and fails on real ones, which would mean the injection is unrealistic.
  • B1m. B1 with the mean of the 3 trust weights as the mixture weight.
  • B1-rw and B1-nn (neighbour controls). B1-rw replaces each Primary's neighbour inputs with those of a degree-matched randomly chosen set of other Primaries (the graph rewired, with the same number of neighbours). B1-nn removes the neighbour inputs. B1 minus B1-rw tests whether neighbour identity matters in the trust head, and B1 minus B1-nn tests whether the neighbour inputs matter at all. The cross-fitted tables are reused.
  • B9 (last). The fully joint version of B1: the lagless module trains jointly with a stop-gradient and no cross-fit. It is labelled in-sample.
  • B7 (lowest priority; runs last). B1 plus a 1D convolutional neural network over the latest 7 days of actual demand up to the forecast origin, with the same trust inputs.

The maintainer's expectation (not a result): B1 beats B2.

docs.title: Training data and events
docs.text:
Training uses injected, load-conserving events with clean targets. A drop at a donor Primary reappears at the connected recipients, with the depth as a share of the donor's trailing 30-day mean (truncated at the forecast origin). Durations and depths follow the corrected label table sw_block_detector_label_table_corrected.csv in the folder of experiment 395 (use the corrected signs). In 30% of events no recipient is observed (a guess, varied as a sensitivity). Transient spikes that are not load shifts are injected too. The targets stay clean, so a target is never inside an injected event. The loss is the mixture negative log-likelihood, which is a proper scoring rule like CRPS and is what experiment 397 used.

Injection rate. 20% of training rows have at least one lag inside an injected event or spike, against about 2.6% in real data. The rate is a stated default, and the worker states and justifies any change. The injection is fixed per refit and seed, saved to disk, and not resampled each epoch. The generator tunes its coverage on the real arrays until the realised share of rows reaches 20%.

Which experiment the injection follows. Experiment 395 Parts E and F disagree on the share of a step that reaches the forecast (36.8% with all three lags affected in the synthetic sweep of Part E, against a median share of 0.94 for real events in Part F; experiment 401 shows the 0.94 is not a lag effect). The injection writes the full event depth into the lag values, as a real event does, and does not set a share of the forecast. The share that reaches the forecast is then an output, measured by the lag-encroachment sweep.

Realism check before training: match surprise statistics, not a lag response. In experiment 401's counterfactual (replace the lags inside each real event and re-predict), the real lag response of the forecast is about 0.02 to 0.03 of the event step, against 0.32 to 0.34 for synthetic events of the same kind (interim and unaudited). That response belongs to the fitted forecaster and not to the injection, so the plan does not tune the injection to a response. It matches the injected surprise statistics (the window statistics of the surprise series, the event depth as a share of the series, and the duration) to those of real events, and redesigns the injection if they differ by more than a factor of 2, as the lag-gate brief requires. For each fold, the injected depths and durations are drawn, and all tuning is done, only from real events outside that fold's scored month, so that the events that score an arm never tune its training data. The write-up reports the fitted network's counterfactual lag response on injected and on real events as a diagnostic. Every arm is judged on real events as well as injected ones. The plan follows experiment 395 Part F (the full depth in the lag values) and not Part E.

Evidence on constant-step injection. Experiment 402's redone step 2 (interim, unaudited) gave the median share of a step passed on by the R1 boosters as 0.133, 0.150, and 0.305 for real events with 1, 2, and 3 lags inside, against 0.146, 0.158, and 0.328 for a synthetic constant step (ratios 1.05 to 1.10; 17, 14, and 6 events). The factor-of-2 rule does not fire, so a constant-step injection is realistic for those boosters, and experiment 402 repeats the check on its R0 lagged boosters. The two experiments measure different quantities: experiment 401 takes the forecast with lags minus the forecast without lags, and experiment 402 takes the share of the step passed on. The plan uses both as diagnostics on the fitted networks and does not tune the injection to either.

Harm-row results are a lower bound. Because some events are unlogged, harm-row results are reported as a lower bound on harm. Our series are one per substation, not per transformer, so a transformer-level event that conserves load across a substation's transformers does not appear.

Shared injected worlds and B-mix (agreed with experiment 428, 2026-10-31). Both experiments read experiment 428's world files seed{N}.npz (power over capacity, shape [16, grid], and the event code, shape [16, grid]; the data folder of experiment 428, work/worlds/), built by experiment 402's inject on experiment 422's cleaned power with 10% coverage over 2024-05-01 to 2026-07-01. Training uses seeds 100 to 102 and scoring uses the held-out seeds 200 to 202, so the scored months contain injected events and harm rows. Row classes come from experiment 428's e00428_predict.Flags. B-mix halves the weights of the lagged forecast's components and of the frozen lagless table's components and pools them on the capacity scale. Experiment 404 therefore does not run its own injection.

Frozen lagless table. The cross-fitted lagless tables are frozen as built on 2026-10-31 by commit 63d3799f of this branch: K = 6 contiguous blocks, a pooled module with a Primary embedding, 6 epochs, seeds 0 to 2, and scored months 2025-10, 2025-12, 2026-01, 2026-03, and 2026-06. Experiment 428's surprise-channel arm and recent-history encoders read the same files, so no rebuild happens unless the experiment 428 worker and the manager agree first. In the 2026-06 table the 90% band covers 0.81 of observed power for the cross-fitted rows, so the bands are somewhat narrow, and the write-up states this.

Generator. This experiment imports experiment 402's generator (e00402_inject.py), merged to main in PR 56 under ml-experiments/00402-lag-gate-learned-weight-injected-load-shifts-part-1/. The merged file differs from the draft copy first used here: the donor change is computed from the donor's mean over its whole series and keeps the donor's shape. It differs from the generator first written here in four ways: spikes are 4 to 20 times the stage-1 residual median absolute deviation, MVA-only Primaries receive events only where the reading stays above 20% of capacity, and base periods can exclude windows with a large stage-1 surprise. The signature takes the MVA-only set and each Primary's residual deviation in MW. The write-up says which commit of the generator each fit used. The depths and durations come from the table's real events, so the test distribution informs the generator's distributions even though the real events never enter training; the write-up states this.

Caveat on unlabelled events (carried into every write-up). NGED says load-shift events may be missing from its logs. The clean-lag rows and the clean training periods can therefore contain events that no label covers. The harm table's clean-lag baseline is then optimistic, and the real-event slices undercount the rows whose lags lie inside an event. Injected events stay the main training signal because they need no logs.

Real events are a held-out test only. The label table's events never enter training. The write-up reports the real-event count per fold and excludes folds without label coverage from the harm rows.

docs.title: Leakage rules
docs.text:
• Cut every training row whose valid time is on or after the first day of the scored month.
  • Truncate every window of every lag at the telemetry cut-off and at the forecast origin.
  • Take surprises only from the cross-fitted lagless forecast described above, recomputed against the injected lag values after injection (surprises from the clean series would carry no event signal), never from the scored month or later.
  • Inject the donor and its recipients together, so that the neighbour inputs never leak the clean value.
  • Drop flagged exact-zero half-hours (substation_zero) from training, lags, inference, and scoring actuals.
  • For D15 and D18, drop every row before 2025-03-01 from training rows, lag inputs, inference inputs, and scoring actuals (maintainer rule, 2026-10-30). This experiment does not test the cut. Experiment 399 may later supply better per-Primary dates, and the plan then follows them.

docs.title: Scoring
docs.text:
• Harm rows (defined once). A harm row is a half-hour of the real held-out data whose target is outside every real corrected event (unpadded, with the 7 days after each event excluded, as experiment 400 did) and at least one of whose 3 origin lags lies inside a real corrected event. The B4 arms' extra lags do not redefine the harm rows. A contrast on harm rows is the difference of the two arms' mean CRPS on those same rows, and scoring uses real data only.
  • Three row sets, scored separately beside the headline (the neural Discuss session's request, 2026-10-31): harm rows, clean rows (no lag and not the target inside an event), and rows whose target is inside a labelled real event. Experiment 402's slice tables (interim, unaudited) found that an injected-trained gate protects harm rows without losing on clean rows, but is worse than the fixed 50/50 mixture where the target is inside a real labelled event (signed-MW six: 10.75 and 11.42 against 10.50 and 11.25, in points of effective capacity), because it cuts the lag weight to about 0.4. All experiment 402 figures are interim until its page merges. Every arm, B-mix included, is scored on all three sets, with whole-event bootstrap intervals.
  • Dominant events and coverage (neural Discuss session, 2026-10-31). Real-event gains rest on very few events: in experiment 402 (interim, unaudited), one D16 event carried 110% of the step 1 flag-oracle gain and one D5 event carried 64% of the real-harm gain. The write-up lists the events that dominate each real-event slice and reports each slice with and without its largest event. It also reports the 95% quantile's coverage inside real events beside CRPS, because every arm of experiment 402 covered only 0.65 to 0.68 of the targets there (target 0.95). The signed-MW six and the MVA-only eight are scored separately everywhere, because at the eight the gate beat the 50/50 mixture inside a real event and at the six it did not.
  • The harm table of the lag-gate brief: rows whose target is outside every event but whose lags lie inside one, minus the rows with clean lags, by number of lags inside the event. Each arm minus A0 on the harm rows, with whole-event bootstrap intervals.
  • The lag-encroachment sweep (experiment 392's protocol, required of every load-shift experiment by the maintainer, 2026-10-31): add a step of 5% of capacity to the lags of clean rows for k = 1, 2, and 3 lags, and report the median's shift as a share of the step, the band width ratio, and where the probability mass sits, for every arm. The code path and protocol come from the merged experiment 392 scripts on main (e00392_sweep.py: shifted_matrix, clean_rows, sweep_site, widen, with_ratios). The protocol adds D (5% of capacity, and 2.5% for neural networks, both signs) to the 1, 2, then 3 most recent lag columns of clean rows, over the lead bands from 24 to 72 hours and the others, on the four screen folds, with an origin stride of 3 and the 1.15 widening. It reports the median shift as a share of D, the band-width ratio, and the coverage of clean and event-level readings. Experiment 404's network needs a predict-on-modified-lags interface for it. The sweep also includes a lag-masked control, whose shift must be exactly 0, the trust weight of each lag at each k, and 3 seeds.
  • Probe (B8). The precision-recall area of the probe on held-out real events from the corrected label table, per metering group.
  • Loss outside events and the overall five-fold CRPS, per Primary.
  • Tails. Coverage and pinball loss at q01, q05, q95, and q99, raw and at the 1.15 widening, beside every headline score.
  • Example forecast plots (maintainer rule, 2026-10-30). Example time series charts of probabilistic forecasts against the actuals: one day-ahead forecast, and one full 14-day horizon of a single forecast, with bands that widen with the horizon. Both are shown for one signed-MW Primary and one MVA-only Primary (4 charts), and one further chart shows a real load-shift event. Each shows the actuals, the median, and the 90% band for B1 and the reference arms. Substations are not covered by the anonymisation rule, and no metered generator's series appears here.
  • Event time-series plots (maintainer rule, 2026-10-30). At least 6 plots, covering both metering groups (at least 3 from the signed-MW six and 3 from the MVA-only eight), each marking when the event starts and ends and showing the actual power, the median forecast, the 90% band (q05 to q95), and the trust weight of each of the 3 lags (for B3, the per-lag attention weights). Each plot compares the reference arms (A0, A0-inj, B0) with B1 on the same event. The set includes real events from the corrected label table, injected events, and at least one transient spike, and each plot is labelled real or injected. The set also includes the failure cases: the plots with the largest harm-row loss, not only favourable examples. Both groups of events use anonymised labels only where a metered generator's series appears, and none does here.
  • Checks. The median minus the mean forecast per Primary, the error of the mean beside every quantile-score contrast, and which of the seven audit triggers of the ml-experiment skill fired.
  • Saved outputs, per arm, fold, and seed: per-row per-lag trust weights, the combined trust, the event class of each row (inside, touching, or clean, unpadded), per-row CRPS, B3's attention weights, the B8 probe scores, and the forecast quantiles q01 to q99.
  • Folds, seeds, cadence. The five screen folds of experiment 397, monthly refits, 3 seeds. More seeds only for a contrast within the seed noise.

docs.title: Code reviews
docs.text:
A fresh Sonnet review of the lagless builder ran before its first build. It found no leakage of the scored month. It found that the cross-fit scaler used the held-out block's statistics, which the builder now avoids by fitting a scaler per fold, and an off-by-one in the first valid index.

A fresh Sonnet review of the training, scoring, and trust-input code ran before the first fit. It found six defects, all fixed or recorded. The forecast rebuilt its scalers from all origin days instead of the saved training scalers (fixed). The padding between Primaries was too short for lag centres before the table start (fixed). The score weighted unevenly spaced quantile levels equally (fixed with the project's level weights). A clamp on the lagged weight zeroed its gradient (fixed). The product rule identifies only the product of the three trust weights, so the per-lag columns cannot be read as per-lag trust, and the write-up does not interpret them. The B3 gate takes the lead, the Primary embedding, and the metering indicator, not the trust inputs, as the plan says. B0 now learns one weight per metering group, lead band, and lag.

docs.title: Interfaces for the later evaluation experiment
docs.text:
A separate lag-trust evaluation experiment will run on this experiment's saved networks once the maintainer releases it (manager, 2026-10-31; design in briefs/lag_trust_evaluation_design_answer.md, section 4). The maintainer holds it until experiments 404 and 428 have each had several design iterations and a design is picked, so batch 1 does not trigger it. This experiment therefore builds in five interfaces, and saves every fitted network:

  • A predict function that accepts modified lag values and recomputes every trust input from them with the e00404_trust.py functions.
  • Per-row outputs: the trust weight of each lag, the combined trust, and the q01 to q99 quantiles of the final, lagged, and lagless mixtures.
  • Inference overrides for the neighbour inputs: off, rewired, shuffled, and time-shifted.
  • A deterministic evaluation mode with dropout off, so the lag-masked control returns exactly 0.
  • Saved per-row tables keyed by Primary, origin, valid time, seed, and event class.

The write-up says which event count each figure uses: experiment 402's label rows (133 rows, 112 usable) or experiment 411's 184 corrected events. Experiment 392's one-lag figure is 0% to 2%.

docs.title: Compute
docs.text:
The concurrency limit is 1 GPU process under 8 GB of GPU memory, 1 feeder core, and MemoryMax=8G, a stricter slot than the brief's 16 GB, because of the machine's load. The manager asked for a request for more resources if a batch would take over 12 hours.

Fit counts. Each fit is one arm on one refit with one seed. The brief reports 50 to 200 seconds per fit and about 600 fits in all; the plan's own count follows, and the first task after the slot is granted is to time one fit of each kind and report K and the timed duration to the manager.

  • Cross-fitted lagless networks. 6 block fits plus 1 final fit, so 7 per refit and seed, and 105 over the 5 refits and 3 seeds. They are precomputed once per refit and seed and shared by every arm.
  • Injected windows. The injected series and every window statistic, neighbour input, and B6 or B7 window are precomputed once per refit, with a fixed injection seed, and shared by every arm and seed.
  • Batch 1. 6 arms times 5 refits times 3 seeds is 90 fits (A0 is read from experiment 397 if its rows match, which would remove 15).
  • Batch 2. B3, B6, B4a, B4b, B4c, B8a, B8b, B1-rw, B1-nn, B1m, B7, and B9 are 12 arms, 180 fits.
  • Memory per fit. A pooled refit has about 7 million rows. With the trust inputs (about 150 columns in float32) the host matrix is about 4 GB, which fits the 8 GB cap with the batch streamed to the GPU in blocks of 16,384 rows. B6 and B7 add window tensors that are built in blocks from the precomputed series, not stored in full. These figures are estimates; the first task after the slot is granted is to time and measure one fit of each kind.

Order of work once granted: batch 0 (the counterfactual re-score of the stored forecasts, which takes no fit); the cross-fitted lagless networks; the realism check; A0 (reused if experiment 397's rows match); A0-inj; B0; B1; B2; B5; the stop-rule check; then batch 2 if the stop rule passes, in the order B4a, B4b, B4c, B3, B6, B8a, B8b, B1-rw, B1-nn, B1m, then B7 and B9. Every arm is in scope over the weekend, gated only by the pre-registered stop rules.

docs.title: Problems caused by the move
docs.text: (The move of the research code from the production repository to this one.) None so far. Experiment 397's modules live on an unmerged branch, so this experiment copies the files it needs into its own folder.

docs.title: Does an explicit solar-power term inside the mixture density network, with its capacity learned end to end, improve the net-demand forecast at the six signed-direction Primaries?
docs.text: Status: done. The known-answer test failed its placebo gate, so no score arm ran. The sections below are the plan, written before any fit; "Results" at the end reports what happened. The plan follows the Discuss session's weekend brief, its Opus-reviewed revision, and the Sonnet review's eight must-fix items.

docs.title: What is asked
docs.text: The question is whether a physical solar term, learned jointly with the demand forecast, lowers the net-demand error where the GAM stack did not gain. The GAM stack gained 0.047 points (interval -0.029 to +0.135) from a better capacity estimate on the sunniest third (experiment 349). The score moves about 0.02 points per 10% of capacity (the capacity-response page), so five folds may not resolve a capacity contrast. The main question is therefore whether a small neural adapter improves a physical solar forecast (C3 minus C2), which does not depend on resolving capacity.

docs.title: Terms
docs.text:
• Net demand. The power the Primary's meter reads. Embedded solar lowers it, so net demand is the demand without solar minus the solar output.
  • Signed-MW six. The Primaries D5, D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16, which the meter reports in signed megawatts, so reverse flow shows as negative values. D15 and D18 are also signed, but they are report-only after the short-history cut (below). MVA-only eight. The eight Primaries whose meters fold reverse flow into positive values.
  • Solar term. The embedded solar output at one Primary: a capacity (AC megawatts at the 99th percentile of daylight output, the unit of docs/studies/embedded-pv-capacity.md) times a physical response to the forecast irradiance and temperature.
  • Capacity. One value per Primary and season-year (September to August, named by its September), as on the studies page.

docs.title: Data and rows
docs.text:
The rows are experiment 397's. The pooled plain network of experiment 397 stage 2 (16 Primaries, learned 8-wide Primary embedding, 3-component Gaussian head, 2 hidden layers of 64) is the base. It is fed the ECMWF ENS mean and spread of each weather column once per run (the summary scheme, the maintainer's default of 2026-10-30). Folds are the five screen months (2025-10, 2025-12, 2026-01, 2026-03, 2026-06) with monthly refits on a 730-day window, and 3 seeds per arm. Rows come from the raw matrices of experiment 397 (work/raw/summary), and substation_zero half-hours are dropped from training, lags, inference, and scoring actuals as experiment 397 does.

The short-history cut is applied. For D15 and D18, all rows before 2025-03-01 are dropped from training, lags, inference, and scoring (common.md, 2026-10-30). D15 and D18 stay report-only.

Weather at lag times. The lags are the Primary's own power at the lag times, so they carry embedded solar already. The network uses no weather at lag times, so the ERA5 delay does not apply here. The forecast-time irradiance is the ENS shortwave mean and standard deviation, both available at forecast time.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Net-demand mixture. The demand module is the pooled plain network and outputs a mixture over standardised demand z (power divided by effective capacity, then standardised per Primary, as in experiment 397). The solar module outputs a mean m and a standard deviation s of the solar output in the same units. The net-demand mixture keeps the weights of the demand mixture. Component k has mean mu_k - m and variance sigma_k^2 + s^2, on the assumption that demand and solar errors are independent. This is one pass of the network per run, and the spread of the solar output comes from the ENS spread input.

Solar module. The unit shape is computed offline, outside the network, and is fixed. It is the AC output per MW of AC capacity of a plant with tilt 35 degrees, azimuth 180 (south), a DC to AC ratio of 1.15, and the existing 0.4% per degree derating, using the studies.pv_physics chain (the Erbs split, isotropic sky, inverter clip) from the ENS mean shortwave and 2 m temperature, at the Primary's latitude and longitude. These values are the population values of briefs/dp_pv_design_note.md (experiment 73 found that orientation is not identified at a Primary). The unit shape is evaluated at the ENS mean shortwave and at the mean plus and minus one ENS standard deviation (a 3-point quadrature), giving a mean u and a spread u_sd of the unit shape. The unit shape is scaled so that its 99th percentile over daylight half-hours is 1, so that capacity has the unit of the studies page.

Capacity and the prior. The solar mean is C[p, y] * u * g, where C[p, y] is the capacity of Primary p in season-year y, and g is the adapter multiplier (1 in C1 and C2). The solar output is clipped at C[p, y]. The studies page table (docs/studies/assets/embedded_pv_capacity_table.csv) gives a centre and a 95% interval for each Primary and season-year. The prior for C[p, y] is a Gaussian centred on the centre of that table with a standard deviation of one quarter of the 95% interval's width. The prior and the pinned capacity of C1 use only season-years that ended before the refit: a cell whose season-year has not ended takes the latest completed season-year's value (no hindsight). For D5, whose season-years are flagged, the centre is the midpoint of the library range and the standard deviation is the range's width over four. The prior is a Gaussian log-prior in nats, added to the summed loss, so that in the mean loss it is divided by the effective row count. It is weak by design: the data dominate wherever they are informative, and the C4 minus C3 contrast measures how much the prior matters at all. At test time the capacity is the as-of value of the last season-year in the training window, held flat across the scored month (experiment 129's advice: no hindsight capacity).

Adapter (C3, C4, C5). A two-layer network of width 16 reads the ENS mean and spread of 2 m temperature, longwave radiation, the clearness index (shortwave over 1000 W/m2 times the cosine of the zenith), the unit shape's spread, the sine and cosine of the day of year, and the cosine of the zenith. It outputs g = exp(0.5 * tanh(a)), so g lies between 0.61 and 1.65, and the solar output is clipped to lie between 0 and C[p, y]. The output layer starts at zero weights, so training starts from g = 1. The adapter shares its weights across Primaries.

Demand module in the C arms. Irradiance and the solar summary are removed from the demand module's inputs. That means the mean and spread of shortwave radiation and the three solar-geometry columns (cosine of zenith, sine and cosine of azimuth), which together let a network rebuild the clear-sky solar bell. The matching control A0-noirr has the same removal and no solar module. Removing the geometry also removes the network's only season signal besides temperature, and A0-noirr pays that cost too, so the contrast of a C arm against A0-noirr is like for like. This choice is the plan's reading of "irradiance and the solar summary", and a reviewer may overrule it.

The eight MVA-only Primaries. The solar module does not run there, and they predict the observed magnitude directly, as in experiment 397. They are reported separately, and no C-arm contrast includes them, because A0-noirr removes irradiance there without a solar module to replace it. A neural signed model for them waits for the signed-label gate of briefs/xgboost_mva_signed_label_cams_brief.md.

docs.title: Arms
docs.text:
Arm Demand inputs Solar module Capacity A0 experiment 397 inputs none none A0-noirr A0 without shortwave mean and spread and without solar geometry none none C1 as A0-noirr yes, no adapter pinned to the experiment 269 estimate (real_capacities.parquet, estimate_mw, per site and season-year), not trained C2 as A0-noirr yes, no adapter learned per Primary and season-year, with the Gaussian prior C3 as A0-noirr yes, with the adapter as C2 C4 as A0-noirr as C3 as C3 with no prior, every capacity starting at a neutral 3 MW C5a as A0-noirr as C3 monthly path (free in time), symmetric smoothness penalty on month-to-month changes; changes only the time variation C5b as A0-noirr as C3 per season-year, with the persistence penalty (below); changes only the penalty

C3's penalty and C5's. C3 has one capacity per season-year with no penalty on year-to-year change beyond the Gaussian prior. C5b adds the persistence penalty a Gaussian penalty on the relative step r = (C[y] - C[y-1]) / C[y-1], with standard deviation 0.25 for a rise and 0.25 / sqrt(10) for a fall (a fall costs 10 times a rise of the same size), so a rise is cheap and a fall is dear. C5a replaces the season-year capacity with a monthly path and penalises the relative month-to-month change with standard deviation 0.05, symmetrically. A full C5 (monthly path and persistence penalty together) is run only if both C5a and C5b move the score by more than their minimum detectable effects. Every sudden fall of a learned capacity (more than 10% in one step) is reported as a candidate meter failure, together with the date, because NGED subtracts metered solar from the Primary's demand and a failed meter changes the Primary's series.

docs.title: Known-answer test (runs first, gates the score arms)
docs.text:
The test adds a known extra capacity of one metered farm to the six Primaries and asks whether the learned capacity rises by that increment. It runs on one refit, the 2026-06 fold (the most data), because the trained capacities are read from the fitted network and no scoring is needed.

  • Injection. The held-out farm's recorded output, normalised by its own 99th percentile (the farm_norm of experiment 129), is scaled to an increment X equal to 50% of the studies page's 2025/26 capacity at each Primary, and subtracted from the Primary's power (the sign convention of experiment 129's inject). The same subtraction applies to the three lags, which are rebuilt from the lag times, so a lag does not reveal the injected series. Injected tables are computed once per refit and saved in the experiment's private work/ folder. A half-hour with a farm dropout is NaN and drops out of training, as in experiment 129.
  • Held-out farm. The solar module's shape is physical (fixed population values), so no farm defines it. The studies-page prior was calibrated on the six farms, so a prior centred on that page could pull the recovery towards the page's value. C4 has no prior and so removes that circularity. The one farm with a short history is not used. The held-out farm is a fixed one of the others, and the three farms left are are the divisor farms: each is injected on its own into every Primary, in separate fits, and the divisor at a Primary is the median recovery of the three. A farm's label may appear in code and logs inside the private folder, and no published page carries a farm's series or name.
  • Recovery is the learned capacity increment (injected minus not injected, at the last season-year in the window) divided by X, then divided by the divisor.
  • Gates, copied from experiment 129's page (its "Gates" table): recovery after the divisor within 0.75 to 1.25 at 5 of the 6 Primaries (experiment 129 used 4 of 5); the placebo difference of fits at most 0.20 of the real-sky recovery, median and maximum over Primaries (the placebo injects the held-out farm's output with its days shuffled within the month, so the cloud pattern is wrong and only the daylight shape is right; a learned increment should be small); and a drift gate.
  • The drift gate cannot run as written. Experiment 129's drift gate is under 0.05 per 5 years of constant-farm recovery, and the networks here train on a 730-day window with ensemble weather only from 2024-04, so there are 2 season-years, not 5 years, to measure drift on. The gate is restated as: the recovery of the held-out farm differs between its two season-years by under 0.10 of X. This restatement is a post-hoc scaling, so it is reported and does not gate.
  • Arms in the test. C2 and C4, 3 seeds each, for these conditions: no injection, held-out farm, three divisor farms, and placebo (6 conditions per arm and seed), and C2 with experiment 129's increment penalty (0.1) on the held-out farm. That is (6 + 6 + 2) x 3 seeds = 42 fits (each of C2 and C4 has 6 conditions; C2 with the increment penalty has a control and the held-out farm).
  • Decision. The score arms (C1, C3, C4, C5a, C5b, A0, A0-noirr) run only if C2 passes the recovery gate and the placebo gate. If C2 fails, the page writes up the failure, with C4 beside it, and the score arms stop. C1 and C2 can be scored if only the drift restatement fails.

docs.title: Pre-registered contrasts and rules
docs.text:
All contrasts are at the signed-MW six, CRPS at days 1 to 10 (the headline band), in points of effective capacity, with the month-block bootstrap of studies.eval_protocol at 95% (20,000 resamples) and a Bonferroni correction across the eight contrasts below. The MVA-only eight are reported, not contrasted.

  1. C3 minus C2 (the adapter; the main question).
  2. C2 minus A0-noirr (the physical term against no irradiance).
  3. C2 minus A0 (the physical term against the free irradiance input).
  4. C3 minus A0.
  5. C2 minus C1 (learned against pinned capacity).
  6. C4 minus C3 (the prior).
  7. C5a minus C3 (time variation).
  8. C5b minus C3 (the persistence penalty).

Minimum detectable effect. For each contrast, the standard deviation over the 5 folds of the seed-to-seed difference (the difference between two seeds of the contrast's two arms, for each pair of seeds), times 2. A contrast is a gain only if its interval excludes zero and its point estimate exceeds that minimum detectable effect. The adapter question (contrast 1) is decided by this rule alone.

Scoring slices. Net-demand CRPS on all half-hours, the sunniest third of daylight half-hours, sunny April to June, and the sunny-flag bias at D12. Tails: coverage and pinball loss at q01, q05, q95, and q99, raw and at the 1.15 widening, against the widened reference. The cost at the scaled export limit uses studies.node_curtailment at f = 0.9. Learned capacity per Primary against the studies page, with intervals from seeds, and the capacity path with each sudden fall flagged.

docs.title: Net-demand mixture variance, and extra reports (fourth review)
docs.text:
The solar variance is learned and bounded. In the score arms the solar standard deviation is the ENS-spread response times a learned positive scalar (shared across Primaries), clipped at half the Primary's capacity so that no row can have a solar variance larger than its plausible output. The net-demand variance is sigma_k^2 + s^2 - 2 rho sigma_k s, where rho is a learned correlation between the solar error and the demand error, one value per arm, bounded to -0.5 to 0.5 and starting at 0. The known-answer fits (which do not score) use independence and the unscaled spread; the score arms add the scalar, the clip, and rho. A PIT histogram of the net-demand mixture at the signed-MW six checks the calibration, in daylight and at night.

Two more reports. C3 minus A0 is reported beside the main contrast, as the practical question (does the explicit solar term beat the same network given irradiance?). The share of the daylight variance that A0-noirr's demand module takes up from solar geometry, calendar, and the Primary embedding alone is reported too. Removing irradiance does not fully remove the identifiability problem, because cloud cover and temperature remain proxies for it, so capacity is identified only from the irradiance anomaly within each geometry-and-season cell.

docs.title: Example charts
docs.text: The write-up shows probabilistic forecasts against actuals. For one signed-MW Primary and one MVA-only Primary, it shows a day-ahead forecast and one full 14-day forecast from a single run, with the quantile bands (they should widen with the horizon) and the actual power. Charts of metered generators are anonymised.

docs.title: Review of the code
docs.text: The code was reviewed by a fresh Sonnet agent before any fit. It found two high-severity problems (a prior and a pinned capacity that used the whole season-year, including months after the refit, and a placebo shuffle that differed between the target and the lags) and five medium ones (the prior's weight differing from the plan, relative rather than absolute penalty steps, an adapter input that duplicated the unit shape, the no-prior arm starting at the studies value, and weight initialisation not seeded). All seven are fixed, and the plan text above now matches the code.

docs.title: Compute and fit counts
docs.text:
• Score arms. 8 arms x 5 refits x 3 seeds = 120 fits. At 50 to 200 seconds per fit that is 2 to 7 hours.
  • Known-answer test. 42 fits. Total 162 fits.
  • Resources. One GPU process under 8 GB, one feeder core, MemoryMax=8G (the manager's limit until it is raised), OMP_NUM_THREADS=1. The injected tables are written once per refit and read by every fit that needs them.

docs.title: Stored forecasts, to be listed in the write-up
docs.text: Monthly XGBoost (experiment 389), the weekly bundle (experiment 381), BG2, and the GAM stack. Their paths are listed in the write-up after the scoring script reads them, and nothing is refitted.

docs.title: Earlier advice followed and departed from
docs.text:
• Followed. Use an as-of capacity, never a hindsight capacity (experiment 129). Test a penalty on jumps on a step-up injection before adopting it (experiment 129; the increment-penalty arm). Report absolute skill beside contrasts.
  • Departed from. Experiment 129's five-year drift gate is restated for a two-season-year window (above).

docs.title: Checks the write-up will report
docs.text: Median minus mean forecast per site; the mean-forecast error beside each quantile-score contrast; which of the audit triggers fired.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Take-home message: the known-answer test could not be passed, so the score arms did not run, and the test as built cannot separate a read of the sky from a read of the daylight profile. All statements below are for the 2026-06 fold, 3 seeds, 6 Primaries, one held-out farm, and one shuffle. The test added one real farm's output, scaled to 50% of each Primary's studies-page capacity, to the six signed-MW Primaries (D5, D9, D10, D11, D14, D16), and fitted C2 and C4.

  • Recovery gate: passed, and uninformative. After experiment 129's divisor, C2 recovers 0.87 to 0.95 of the injected capacity at all 6 Primaries (needed: 0.75 to 1.25 at 5). C4 recovers 0.88 to 0.96. The raw recovery is lower, 0.35 to 0.85 for C2. The divisor (0.38 to 0.93) is the median recovery of three other farms, which carry the same kind of signal, so the ratio sits near 1 whatever the network reads (audit, finding 4).
  • Placebo gate: failed. With the farm's days shuffled within each month, C2 recovers 0.60 to 0.91 of the real-sky amount (median 0.73, maximum 0.91, limit 0.20). C4 recovers -1.88 to 1.23 (median absolute 0.43), and its ratio is unstable where the held-out recovery is small: D5's -1.88 divides by a raw recovery of 0.14.
  • The gap between real and shuffled sky is within seed noise at most Primaries. In C2 at the as-of cell, the held-out minus placebo recovery is 0.35, 0.04, 0.12, 0.13, 0.09, and 0.17 of the injected capacity at D5, D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16, against seed standard deviations of 0.07 to 0.28 for the held-out farm (audit, finding 3).
  • Drift: reported, not gating. C2's raw recovery falls from the 2024/25 to the 2025/26 season-year by 0.07, 0.11, 0.05, 0.04, 0.07, and 0.10 of the injected capacity at D5, D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16 (restated limit 0.10: D9 exceeds it and D16 sits on it). The 2025/26 cell holds only September to May of rows.
  • Increment penalty: no effect. C2 with experiment 129's increment penalty (0.1) recovers the same amounts as C2 (within 0.02 at every Primary).

docs.title: Audit
docs.text:
The placebo control failed, which triggers an audit. A fresh Sonnet agent ran it. It found no bug in the injection, the rows, or the placebo map, and found that the 0.20 gate is out of reach here.

  • The shuffled series keeps most of the real series. The half-hourly correlation of the shuffled with the real injected series is 0.79. A month-by-half-hour mean profile explains 78.5% of the real series' variance, and the day-to-day sky explains the other 21.5%. A least-squares read-out of the ensemble unit shape gives a shuffled-over-real ratio of 0.97, and even a forecast that matched the real day-to-day sky perfectly would give 0.84. The observed C2 ratios (0.60 to 0.91) sit at or below that benchmark.
  • The network has no other home for the profile. The C arms remove irradiance and solar geometry from the demand module, and the module keeps no day-of-year term, so the seasonal daylight amplitude goes into the solar term. Experiment 129's placebo of 0.12 came from a target whose demand terms could represent the profile.
  • The ensemble forecast does carry some sky. The correlation of the ensemble unit shape's day-to-day anomaly with the real farm's is 0.37 (0.01 with the shuffled series). Weak forecast skill is therefore neither necessary nor sufficient for the failure.
  • C4's smaller placebo response is a hint only. At four Primaries C4's placebo-over-held ratio (0.32 to 0.47) is below C2's. The prior or the 10-to-1 persistence penalty may inflate C2's ratio. This was not tested.
  • Verdict. inconclusive stands, because the CRPS hypothesis was never tested.

Predictions. K1's first half held (C2 recovers within the tolerance at 6 of 6 Primaries). Its second half did not: C4's divided recovery (0.88 to 0.96) is as tight as C2's (0.87 to 0.95). Predictions P1 to P5 are untested because the score arms did not run.

What the next experiment should answer. Can a solar capacity be read once the placebo is calibrated to the network? The test would give the demand module a day-of-year by hour term, or inject only the farm's day-to-day anomaly with its monthly profile removed, and set the placebo limit from the profile-only benchmark.

docs.title: Problems caused by the move
docs.text: None beyond a draft pull request for experiment 397 that is not merged: its code was imported from a separate checkout.

docs.title: Reviews
docs.text:
• Code review (before the first fit). A fresh Sonnet agent found two high-severity and five medium-severity problems; all are fixed (see "Review of the code" above).
  • Write-up review. A second fresh Sonnet agent found nine points (the drift range, the take-home scope, a C4 placebo caveat, unclosed predictions, the verdict wording, two untested readings stated as findings, a cross-experiment claim, line wrapping, and the farm letters). All are applied.
  • Audit. The findings above are applied: the take-home, lessons, advice, and the "9 to 40%" wording changed. The audit's persistence-penalty hint is recorded and not acted on.

docs.title: Does the pooling gain of the mixture density network come from sharing parameters or from the Primary embedding, and does it grow when each Primary's training history is short?
docs.text: Take-home message: the Primary embedding is what makes pooling work, and a pooled network helps most where one Primary has little history. One pooled network with no Primary input scores 0.574 points of capacity worse than one network per Primary at the six signed-MW Primaries (95% interval +0.428 to +0.738), so sharing parameters alone gives no gain. Adding the 8-wide Primary embedding turns that into a gain of 0.216 points (−0.296 to −0.129). The pooling gain grows as one Primary's history shortens: with that Primary cut to 3 months (and 3 other Primaries cut with it), the pooled network beats the per-Primary network by 1.151 points at the signed-MW six (−1.932 to −0.461) and by 0.660 points at the MVA-only eight (−1.067 to −0.253). The verdict is not supported: the hypothesis that the gain comes from shared parameters and does not grow with short history failed on both counts. Every number comes from five test months, so all are interim.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) at days 1 to 10, mean over Primaries with equal weight, in points of capacity (smaller is better). All arms except the last two columns use the D15 and D18 start cut.

docs.title: Predictions
docs.text:
• P1 failed. The no-embedding network is 0.574 points worse than the per-Primary network, not 0.161 points better.
  • P2 failed. At the MVA-only eight the no-embedding network is 0.693 points worse than the per-Primary network, not 0.047 better.
  • P3 failed. At 3 months the pooled gain is 0.935 points larger than at the full window at the signed-MW six, and 0.544 larger at the MVA-only eight, against a limit of 0.10.
  • P4 held. The per-Primary network at 3 months is 1.765 points above its full-window value at the signed-MW six.
  • P5 partly held. The start cut lowers the CRPS at D15 and D18 for both networks. The start cut moves the signed-MW six and the MVA-only eight by under 0.03 points for the per-Primary network, but moves the pooled network's MVA-only eight by −0.046.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• No Primary input means no scale. The target is each Primary's power over capacity, standardised by that Primary's training mean and standard deviation, so the no-embedding network predicts a standardised value without any Primary-specific level or spread. The missing level and spread probably explain most of the no-embedding network's loss. The arm therefore tests "no learned Primary identity" and does not test a network given static covariates in its place (the follow-on experiment 1c).
  • Each pooled fit cuts the history of 4 of the 16 Primaries. The other 12 keep full history, so "one Primary's history" in this page means one of those 4 cut Primaries, scored only on its own half-hours, and the plan's "other 15 at full history" became 12.
  • Interim. Five test months give wide intervals, most of all at D15 and D18.
  • Unlogged load-shift events. NGED says load-shift events may be missing from its logs, so the training rows and the scoring rows can hold events no label covers.
  • Training rows keep flagged exact zeros; the scoring actuals drop them (1,179 half-hours).

docs.title: Plan as committed before any fit
Question and design
docs.text:
We split the pooling gain into two parts and test whether it depends on history length. Campagne et al. (2026) separate the gain from sharing parameters across sites from the gain from graph edges. Experiment 403 found that one pooled network scores lower than 16 per-Primary networks. This experiment asks how much of that gain survives when the pooled network has no Primary input at all, and whether the gain grows where history is short.

  • The networks. Experiment 397's plain mixture density network (setting g09, summary scheme, 3 Gaussian components), on its five screen folds (test months 2025-10, 2025-12, 2026-01, 2026-03, and 2026-06), with three seeds averaged in quantile space, and the same folds, refits, row weights, and scoring rows. No XGBoost model is used.
  • Arms at the full 24-month window (with the D15 and D18 start cut). per_primary (one network per Primary), pooled_emb (one network with an 8-wide Primary embedding), and pooled_noemb (one network with no Primary input).
  • Arms at 3, 6, and 12 months (the history test). This mimics a new substation joining a pooled network. per_primary_h<H> cuts every Primary to its last H months of rows before the refit; each Primary's network sees only its own rows, so this equals cutting that Primary alone. pooled_emb_h<H> is fitted four times per fold and seed, each time with a different quarter of the Primaries (every fourth, by index) cut to H months and the other 12 at full history; each fit is scored only on its cut quarter, and the four quarters are joined. Cutting four Primaries at once instead of one is a deviation from a strict one-at-a-time test, made so that the test needs 4 pooled fits per fold, seed, and length instead of 16.
  • The start cut. D15 and D18 lose every training row before 2025-03-01, and every row whose weekly lag reaches back before that date (maintainer's rule of 2026-10-30, from experiment 399). The scoring rows start in 2025-10, so no scoring actual or inference input is affected.
  • Controls without the cut. Experiment 397's plain_own and plain_pooled forecasts, read and never written, give contrast C5. They are the same networks without the start cut.

docs.title: Components adopted from earlier results
docs.text:
• Adopted. One pooled network with a Primary embedding (experiment 403: it scored lower than per-Primary networks); the ensemble mean and spread passed through the network once (experiment 397: within 0.05 points of 51 passes; experiment 394 found the mean carries most of the gain); the half-life of 0.5 years and monthly refits of the XGBoost member; the 1.15 widening of experiments 389 and 397; and the D15 and D18 start cut of experiment 399. Every arm of this experiment is therefore one-pass and cut, and the arm names say what changed.
  • Not adopted. Attention over input groups (experiment 397: the gate stayed within 0.01 of uniform), which survives only as the a0 arm that redoes experiment 403's contrast; and dropping the spread columns, which experiment 394 suggests is harmless but which no arm here tests.

docs.title: Standing practices followed, and the deviation
docs.text:
• Followed. Monthly refits; the D15 and D18 start cut; every fitted network saved in the private data folder; stored forecasts reused as references and never refitted; a few-fold screen with every number labelled interim; example forecast charts; a fresh Sonnet code review before the first fit. The scorer drops the half-hours that the cleaned power table flags as exact zeros (substation_zero) from the actuals of every arm, and prints how many.
  • Departure: the training rows are not cleaned of flagged zeros. The fits started before the cleaning rule was issued, and these arms must share their rows with experiment 397's networks to isolate the embedding and the history length. Experiment 398 found that dropping the flagged half-hours moved the CRPS by at most 0.008 points in four earlier experiments.

docs.title: Fit counts, time, and memory
docs.text:
• Fits. pooled_noemb, pooled_emb, and per_primary at the full window: 3 arms by 5 folds by 3 seeds, so 15 pooled fits for each of the two pooled arms and 15 sets of 16 per-Primary networks. Three history lengths add 180 pooled fits (4 quarters by 3 lengths by 5 folds by 3 seeds) and 45 sets of 16 per-Primary networks.
  • Time. Experiment 397 fitted one pooled plain network in about 50 s and one set of 16 per-Primary networks in about 50 s on the GPU. Shorter histories train on fewer rows, so the whole experiment is expected to take about 5 hours.
  • Memory. One GPU process with at most 8 GB of host memory (the 397 screen peaked at 7.9 GB for a 4.2-million-row fold), and one feeder core. A fold's raw rows are the per-Primary files that experiment 397 wrote once, so no table is rebuilt per arm.

docs.title: Not in this experiment
docs.text: Experiment 1c (leave-one-Primary-out with static covariates in place of the embedding) is a separate, optional experiment that runs after this one if a slot is free.

docs.title: Checks the write-up reports
docs.text:
• Absolute CRPS of every arm beside experiment 397's uncut networks, per group and per Primary.
  • Example forecasts. For D10 (signed-MW) and D4 (MVA-only), the pooled network's median, 50% band, and 90% band against what happened: one day-ahead forecast and one full 14-day forecast from a single run, in winter (made on 2026-01-12) and summer (made on 2026-06-15).
  • C4 per Primary against months of history, with the correlation at each history length.
  • Unlogged load-shift events. NGED says load-shift events may be missing from its logs. Training rows in every arm can therefore hold events no label covers, so a gain measured here is measured on rows that may include them.

docs.title: Counting towards the demand-v2 stop rule
docs.text: This experiment does not count. It tests where the pooling gain comes from, not a new demand model, so no idea's count rises whatever the verdict.

docs.text: None.

docs.title: Which change to the pooled mixture density network's output, or to its row weights, improves the tails of the Primary demand forecast beyond a global widening factor?
docs.text: Take-home message: widening the shared neural network's quantiles by 1.15 is the best of the fixes tested for its narrow outer bands, and none of the four tail changes beat it. At the six signed-MW Primaries (those whose power flows both ways, measured in signed megawatts) the widened pooled plain neural network (ctrl_w115) covers 0.891 of outcomes with its 95% quantile and 0.959 with its 99% quantile. Five mixture components, split-normal components, a widening fitted per lead band, and a neural network trained directly on quantiles each failed their registered test. No arm reaches the 0.92 to 0.98 band registered for the per-lead-band widening's q95 coverage. Five components was best on CRPS (continuous ranked probability score) among the four tail arms, and came closest to passing T1, but cut the q99 pinball loss by only 1.9% (0.354 against 0.361) against a 3% bar. The quantile-head neural network, widened, cut the q99 pinball loss by 15.8% (0.304) but raised the CRPS by 0.066 points of capacity (+0.052 to +0.078), so it fails T4. Two changes are worth testing next: the quantile-head neural network as a separate tail model, and a widening fitted on weeks closer to the test period. The verdict is not supported. Every number comes from five test months, so all are interim.

docs.title: Predictions
docs.text:
• T1 failed. With 5 components and the 1.15 widening, the q99 pinball loss at the signed-MW six is 0.354 against 0.361, 1.9% lower and short of the 3% bar. The CRPS is +0.008, inside the 0.02 limit.

Its pinball loss on sunny low-demand half-hours is below the reference's at q01 (0.168 against 0.174) and above it at q05 (0.651 against 0.641). The widened head is above the reference at both (0.178 and 0.662).
  • H1 held. A half-life of 1 year is not better than the control by more than 0.02 at either group: +0.009 at the signed-MW six and +0.026 at the MVA-only eight.
