Arm Change Score Change vs skeleton (99% interval) 0.01 / 0.99 pinball vs skeleton g0_onepass skeleton 6.842 w32 width 32 6.824 -0.27% (-0.84% to +0.38%) -0.0032 / +0.0006 w128 width 128 6.834 -0.12% (-0.88% to +0.39%) -0.0019 / +0.0046 w256 width 256 6.853 +0.15% (-0.49% to +0.84%) -0.0027 / +0.0087 d1 1 hidden layer 6.847 +0.07% (-0.64% to +0.55%) -0.0019 / -0.0046 d3 3 hidden layers 6.842 +0.00% (-0.53% to +0.48%) -0.0030 / +0.0049 d4 4 hidden layers 6.838 -0.06% (-1.12% to +1.16%) -0.0032 / +0.0085 e4 farm embedding 4 6.869 +0.38% (-1.03% to +1.75%) -0.0028 / -0.0071 e8 farm embedding 8 6.842 -0.01% (-1.32% to +1.27%) -0.0041 / -0.0064 e16 farm embedding 16 6.841 -0.03% (-1.58% to +1.44%) -0.0034 / -0.0045 perfarm one network per farm 6.830 -0.18% (-1.95% to +1.18%) -0.0138 / -0.0028 lr0005 learning rate 5e-4 6.823 -0.29% (-1.01% to +0.40%) -0.0023 / +0.0065 lr001 learning rate 1e-3 6.823 -0.29% (-0.99% to +0.30%) -0.0021 / +0.0071 lr004 learning rate 4e-3 6.810 -0.47% (-1.41% to +0.08%) -0.0017 / +0.0061 wd0 weight decay 0 6.842 +0.00% (+0.00% to +0.00%) +0.0000 / +0.0000 wd001 weight decay 1e-3 6.842 -0.00% (-0.01% to -0.00%) -0.0000 / -0.0000 wd01 weight decay 1e-2 6.840 -0.03% (-0.06% to -0.01%) -0.0000 / -0.0000 ep10 10 epochs 6.842 +0.00% (-0.00% to +0.00%) +0.0000 / +0.0000 ep40 40 epochs 6.842 -0.00% (-0.00% to +0.00%) +0.0000 / +0.0000 k1 1 mixture component 7.058 +3.15% (+1.43% to +5.52%) +0.0007 / +0.0773 k2 2 components 6.837 -0.08% (-0.84% to +0.68%) -0.0013 / +0.0084 k5 5 components 6.826 -0.23% (-0.59% to +0.06%) +0.0008 / -0.0020 do01 dropout 0.1 6.832 -0.15% (-0.89% to +0.41%) -0.0024 / +0.0027 do02 dropout 0.2 6.863 +0.30% (-0.89% to +1.30%) -0.0029 / +0.0063 hl05 recency half-life 0.5 year 6.843 +0.00% (-0.62% to +0.54%) -0.0027 / +0.0025 hl1 recency half-life 1 year 6.835 -0.11% (-0.77% to +0.44%) -0.0017 / -0.0002
  • No level passed the rule. The rule needs a gain of at least 0.5%, a 99% interval that excludes zero on the favourable side, and no tail harm above 0.02 points. The lowest point estimate is −0.47% (learning rate 4e-3), and its interval reaches +0.08%.
  • Two weight-decay arms have intervals that exclude zero, on a gain of 0.003% to 0.03%. The weight-decay intervals are narrow because the arms barely differ from the skeleton, and the gain is far under the margin.
  • Training length changes nothing because the best epoch is early. The 10-epoch and 40-epoch arms score the same as the 20-epoch skeleton to 13 decimal places. A rerun of the seed-0 skeleton for 40 epochs with a logged validation curve picked epoch 3 at three refits and epoch 2 at the fourth. The validation loss (the mean negative log-likelihood on the last 61 days of training rows; lower is better) then rises steadily: for the first refit it is −0.72 at the best epoch and −0.48 at epoch 40. Weight decay at 1e-4 to 1e-2 and a learning rate under 4e-3 change little because training stops improving after 2 or 3 epochs.
  • The embedding arms are no better, and the per-farm arm is no better than the pooled one. The per-farm networks score 0.18% better (−1.95% to +1.18%) with the widest interval of all arms.
  • The lower tail is under-covered in every arm, and only one mixture component changes the tails. Coverage of the 0.01 quantile is 5.2% to 5.5% in every arm (target 1%), and coverage of the 0.99 quantile is 98.1% to 99.2% (target 99%). Dropout 0.2 moves the 0.99 coverage to 99.2%.
  • Example forecasts of the skeleton are in Figures 2 and 3.

Figure 2. The skeleton's forecast of farm A for the 12 to 36 hours after a summer run and a winter run (three-seed average). Bands show the 25% to 75% and 5% to 95% quantiles; dots are the observed output.

Figure 3. The same two runs over days 1 to 10.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, per farm (points of capacity, seeds 0 to 2): the skeleton's median sits 0.45 to 0.83 above its mean at the six farms. The learning rate 4e-3 arm gives 0.13 to 0.74, width 32 gives 0.39 to 0.73, and one mixture component gives −0.06 to +0.07. One component forces a symmetric distribution, so its median and mean agree, and its score is the worst.
  • Error of the mean forecast beside the score: for learning rate 4e-3, the mean absolute error of the mean forecast is lower than the skeleton's at all six farms, as is the quantile score, so the two agree. For one mixture component, the mean absolute error is higher at five farms and the score is higher at all six.
  • Audit triggers. Trigger 5 (a control that should change nothing moves the score by more than its own interval's half-width) fires weakly. The two weight-decay arms move by 0.003% and 0.03%, more than their narrow half-widths of 0.003% and 0.02%, and the best-epoch curve above explains why they differ at all. Width 32 and two mixture components score slightly better than the reference network that contains them (−0.27% and −0.08%), with intervals that include zero. Trigger 6 (interval width against a sister experiment) is borderline: the embedding, per-farm, 4-layer, and 1-component arms have half-widths of 1.1% to 2.1%, against about 0.5% to 0.65% for the others, because their forecasts differ more from the reference network. The other triggers did not fire. No control or placebo exists. The result agrees with its prediction. A leave-one-farm-out check was not run, because no contrast is a candidate for adoption. The numbers review (a fresh Sonnet agent that re-derived the contrasts with its own code) matched every table row.
  • Minimum detectable effect. The plan took 0.40% at three seeds by scaling the spread of six skeleton seeds. The spread of seeds 0 to 2 alone gives 0.52%. The best arm's gain of 0.47% is below the margin under either value, so no verdict changes.
  • Best-epoch script: e00443_best_epoch.py produced the curve above, and its log is in the experiment's private data folder.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Each level is a single point in a coarse grid. A change of two settings together (for example a wider network with a lower learning rate) was not tested, because the plan runs a random search only after a single setting moves.
  • The screen is not corrected for 25 contrasts. Each interval is a 99% interval on its own, so 25 screens are expected to produce about 0.25 false passes. None did.
  • The scored year is the same year as in experiment 430, so a choice that suits another year would not show here.
  • Lead range: the scored lead range is days 1 to 10 (12 to 252 hours) for the six metered solar farms; day-ahead (12 to 36 hours) is band d1.
  • Weather at lag times: the farm network has no power lags, and its weather inputs are the ensemble run available at forecast time.
  • Stored networks: the fitted networks are not saved (see Design); the quantile tables are in the experiment's private data folder.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text: Look for solar gains in the inputs next. In this experiment the network stopped improving after 2 or 3 epochs and no single setting moved the score, although combinations of settings were not tested. Experiment 430 found a clear-sky column worth 0.4%. A better irradiance product is one input change that has not been tried.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
The skeleton is experiment 430's g0_onepass. It is a mixture-density network: it reads the standardised inputs (calendar, sun position, ensemble mean and spread of shortwave radiation, and the other columns of experiment 345's list), has two hidden layers of 64, and outputs a mixture of three Gaussians for the farm's output as a fraction of its ceiling. It is trained with AdamW at learning rate 2e-3, weight decay 1e-4, batch 2048, for 20 epochs with the best epoch chosen on the last 61 days of the training rows. One network is pooled over the six farms and the six day bands and refitted quarterly, four refits from 2025-09. A job is one (arm, seed, refit); the stored skeleton supplies seeds 0 to 5.

Stage 1 changes one factor at a time (25 arms, 3 seeds, 4 refits: 300 jobs).

Factor Skeleton level Other levels Hidden width 64 32, 128, 256 Depth (hidden layers) 2 1, 3, 4 Farm embedding width none 4, 8, 16, and per-farm networks (six networks, each trained on one farm only) Learning rate 2e-3 5e-4, 1e-3, 4e-3 Weight decay 1e-4 0, 1e-3, 1e-2 Epochs 20 10, 40 Mixture components 3 1, 2, 5 Dropout (after each hidden layer) 0 0.1, 0.2 Row-recency weight (half-life of the loss weight, by the row's age at the refit) none 0.5 year, 1 year

The loss-weight factor is the row-recency half-life, the one loss weight the design note lists for demand networks; no tail or pinball weight is tested.

Stage 2 (run only if a factor moved) is a random search; it was not run. 45 configurations are drawn at random from the levels of the moved factors (each other factor stays at its skeleton level), two seeds each (360 jobs). The best three by mean score are refitted on seeds 3 to 5 and judged against the skeleton's seeds 3 to 5.

Compute. Stage 1 was 300 jobs at 11 to 17 s each on the GPU, in one process under 8 GB with MemoryMax=8G, OMP_NUM_THREADS=1, and one feeder core: about 1.2 hours.

Standing practices. The farm network follows experiment 345's quarterly refits so that the rows match. The farm rows are experiment 310's, with its idle-band handling. The fitted networks are not saved: a job's output is its quantile table, and the sweep's 700 networks are small enough to refit in minutes. Stored predictions reused: experiment 430's g0_onepass seeds 0 to 5, so the skeleton is not refitted; the gate (G0) refits one job to prove the new code reproduces it.

Scoring details. The 0.01 and 0.99 pinball differences are row-pooled means in 100 times the raw pinball loss, as in experiment 430. The per-farm arm fits one network per farm, but its input standardiser is still computed over all six farms' rows before the refit cutoff. The "embedding" factor includes the per-farm arm, so it counts as moved if the per-farm arm passes.

Gate G0. The new code with every factor at its skeleton level must reproduce the stored g0_onepass forecasts for seed 0 and all four refits to within 1e-4 points of capacity. If it misses, the run stops and reports.

docs.title: Which label-free detectors find idle half-hours at the three metered wind farms, at any wind speed, without flagging genuine low output?
docs.text:
The texture rules tested here do not clearly improve on the experiment 210 mask. The texture detector D1 is a logistic regression on the shape of a wind farm's power readings (how much consecutive half-hours differ and how often they repeat), ignoring the level. D4 smooths D1's flags across neighbouring half-hours. Recall is the share of injected idle half-hours a detector flags. False drop is the share of genuine or synthetic low-output half-hours it flags wrongly. D1 finds injected idle blocks of 12 hours or more (recall 0.74 to 0.90 across the three farms) but misses 3-hour blocks (0.08 to 0.33), with false-drop rates of 0.06 to 0.12. The experiment 210 mask (an ERA5 wind threshold plus a rule for unbroken 12-hour runs of low readings) recalls every injected block of 12 hours or more. Neither D1 nor D4 passes the pre-registered gate (recall at least 0.80 and false drop at most 0.05) at any farm, so the verdict is not supported.

The question and what it narrows. The design for a wind idle-noise detector (Stage 1) asks for a detector that finds idle half-hours at any wind speed, which the ERA5 wind threshold of experiment 210 cannot do. ERA5 is the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts fifth-generation reanalysis, an estimate of past weather. This experiment runs every part of Stage 1 that needs no human label, on three kinds of pseudo-label (none of them ground truth): idle blocks pasted into generating periods, low output that is genuine (real) or synthetic (rescaled), and a few real events (storm shutdown, negative readings). The tests run here did not settle whether the detectors work on real idle stretches, so the next step is hand labels or outage records from the network operator (National Grid Electricity Distribution, NGED).

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
All numbers are interim scored output of this experiment. The gate: recall at least 0.80, false drop at most 0.05, and recall at least 0.10 above the experiment 210 mask's at matched false drop. Recall is the equal-weight mean over block-length by wind-bin cells; false drop is the equal-weight mean over the real sets and the synthetic set. Test years only, with every fitted value tuned on the other parity of years. Intervals resample calendar-year blocks.

Farm Candidate Recall (95% interval) False drop Passes A D1 0.72 (0.70 to 0.75) 0.061 no A D4 0.72 (0.70 to 0.75) 0.058 no A Experiment 210 mask 0.75 0.066 not gated B D1 0.58 (0.53 to 0.63) 0.076 no B D4 0.59 (0.54 to 0.63) 0.061 no B Experiment 210 mask 0.75 0.200 not gated C D1 0.66 (0.59 to 0.73) 0.115 no C D4 0.66 (0.57 to 0.75) 0.115 no C Experiment 210 mask 0.71 0.441 not gated
  • Which parts of the gate fail. Recall is below 0.80 at all three farms for D1 and D4, and the false drop is above 0.05 at all three. At the mask's own false-drop rate, D1 does not exceed the mask's recall by 0.10 at any farm. At Farm A the two rates match (0.72 against 0.75). At Farm C D1 reaches recall 0.84 at false drop 0.38, against the mask's 0.71 at 0.44. At Farm B D1 was not measured at the mask's rate of 0.20, because its false-drop sweep stops at 0.13 (recall 0.61).
  • Short blocks account for the recall shortfall. D1's recall for blocks of 12 hours or more is 0.90 at Farm A, about 0.74 at Farm B, and 0.79 at Farm C, against 0.19, 0.08, and 0.33 for 3-hour blocks. D4 changes recall by 0.00 to 0.01 (its minimum detectable effect over D1 is 0.005 to 0.023), so smoothing adds nothing here.
  • The experiment 210 mask recalls long blocks automatically. It recalls every injected block of 12 hours or more and none of 3 hours, because the pasted blocks are exactly the kind of unbroken low-reading run its rule drops (prediction P5). Its false-drop rate is high at Farm B and Farm C (0.20 and 0.44), because the synthetic low output is also an unbroken run of low readings at high wind. The mask therefore cannot tell a rescaled run from an outage. A real outage may differ from a rescaled run in ways these pseudo-labels do not show.
  • The residual rule D3 cannot separate idle from low output at high wind. D3 compares the reading with the power the ERA5 wind implies. It flags 69% to 81% of the synthetic low output (false drop 0.23 to 0.38 in total) and recalls 0.56 to 0.64 of the injected blocks. Requiring both D1 and D3 gives false drops of 0.1% to 1.5% and recall of 0.44 to 0.59. That combination does not enter the verdict.
  • Level-matched area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of D1's score (sure-idle against sure-generating rows, test years): 0.92 (0.88 to 1.00) at Farm A, 0.71 (0.66 to 0.77) at Farm B, and 0.74 (0.69 to 0.79) at Farm C.
  • Real data at high wind. D1 flags 3.8%, 7.3%, and 20.3% of half-hours with ERA5 wind above 1.5 times the used cut-in at Farm A, B, and C (the mask flags 0.5%, 0.7%, and 7.4%). At Farm C the flags form 86 runs of 24 hours or more and 40 of 48 hours or more, the longest 263 hours. D1 also flags 2.8%, 4.6%, and 10.1% of half-hours with power of at least 10% of capacity at high wind, so a share of the flags at Farm C are false. Of the 7,270 high-wind half-hours that D1 flags at Farm B, 3,069 are also flagged at Farm C.
  • Farm B negative readings (evidence of non-generation). At high wind D1 flags 41% of the 713 negative readings (D4 35%, the mask 10%). Prediction P6 required 70%, so P6 fails. Over all winds D1 flags 57% and the mask 75%.
  • Storm shutdown. Only 3, 0, and 4 half-hours have ERA5 wind of 22 m/s or more with power in the idle band at Farm A, B, and C, which is too few for any rate.
  • Predictions. P1 fails (neither D1 nor D4 passes at Farm B or Farm C). P2 fails in its mechanism: Farm A fails the gate on recall and on the real sure-generating rows (false drop 0.089), not on the synthetic low output (0.032). P3 fails (D4 raises recall by at most 0.01). P4 holds in part: D3 flags 69% to 81% of the synthetic low output, short of 90%, and fails alone, while D1 and D3 together pass the false-drop gate but fail recall. P5 holds. P6 fails.

docs.title: What a hand-labelled sample would add
docs.text:
• The question the pseudo-labels did not settle is whether a flagged half-hour at moderate or high wind is a whole-farm outage, a partly available farm, or an ERA5 error at a 25 km cell. The pseudo-labels here come from the same readings and ERA5 wind that the detectors read.
  • Precision of a recall estimate. D4 flags at least 6 half-hours at high wind on 8%, 16%, and 28% of farm-days at Farm A, B, and C. These shares are upper bounds on idle prevalence, because D4 also flags some generating rows. A random sample of 100 farm-days per farm would then hold at most about 8, 16, and 28 idle days, giving half-widths on a recall of 0.8 of at least about 0.28, 0.20, and 0.15. A sample of 100 days drawn from days that a detector flags would give about 0.08.
  • Minimum detectable effects. Paired recall differences smaller than 0.04 to 0.11 (D1 against the mask, 2.8 times the standard error over seven year blocks) cannot be told from zero. The intervals of D1 minus the mask include zero at Farm A (-0.05 to 0.00) and Farm C (-0.13 to 0.02), and exclude it in the mask's favour at Farm B.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Injection flatters recall. The pasted floor is an exact copy of calm-night readings from the opposite parity of years, with hard joins every 12 half-hours. Recall excluding the half-hours next to a join differs by at most 0.012. The 3-hour and 24-hour windows reach past a join, so that exclusion understates the join's effect.
  • The false-drop sets are not independent of the detectors. The synthetic low output shrinks the differences between half-hours along with the level, which should make it look more idle. D1 is also trained on part of that set. The real sets (power 3% to 8% of capacity at ERA5 wind of 6 m/s or more, or of 1.5 times cut-in to 6 m/s) contain any idle rows at high wind that the study seeks. The set from 1.5 times cut-in to 6 m/s is empty at Farm A, whose cut-in used is 4.5 m/s.
  • Tune-year thresholds transfer imperfectly. D1's threshold gives a 5% false drop on the tune years and 6% to 12% on the test years. A sweep of D1 at false-drop targets of 1%, 2%, and 10% shows that tightening does not recover the gate at Farm B or Farm C.
  • Cut-in and ERA5 are not refitted per fold. The used cut-in comes from experiment 210's report (fitted on all years) and defines the high-wind rows and the mask's outage rule. The idle band, wind threshold, power curve, logistic fit, and thresholds are fitted on the tune years only.
  • Seven cells had fewer than 10 blocks per fold and were dropped from the recall average: the 48-hour and 96-hour moderate-wind cells at Farm A and Farm B, and the 24-hour, 48-hour, and 96-hour moderate-wind cells at Farm C. Ten replicates re-pick the same locations, so intervals resample calendar years, of which there are about seven.
  • One texture rule was tested. D1 is one logistic regression on one set of statistics, and D1a (the single best statistic of experiment 431) is in the stored tables only. Other texture rules may do better.
  • Checks. No forecast is scored, so the median-minus-mean, tail, and curtailment checks do not apply, and none of the audit triggers applies. The three customer-generator series are never flagged by the production cleaning rule, so no substation_zero rows were dropped.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Offer hand labels or ask NGED for outage dates and a reactive-power channel; the tests run here did not settle the question.
  • Keep the experiment 210 mask for the training and evaluation row sets for now.
  • Stage 5 of the design (capacity change points) was not run here and is the next label-free item.

docs.title: Experiment details
docs.text:
• Code: ml-experiments/00444-wind-idle-detectors-label-free-bake-off/ (e00444_bakeoff.py, e00444_summarise.py, e00444_charts.py), importing experiment 431's feature code (ml-experiments/00431-wind-idle-data-look/) and experiment 210's wind-threshold fit (ml-experiments/00210-wind-idle-noise-mva-artefact/). Data: the experiment's folder under data/ml-experiments/ (private).
  • Cadence, weather, and cleaning: no forecast and no refit. ERA5 100 m wind (research-only, about 5 days late) is used by the pseudo-labels, D3, and the mask; D1 and D4 read the power series only and are usable as-of.
  • Reviews: one Sonnet plan review (nine findings, all accepted and written into the plan before any code), one Sonnet code review before scoring (ten findings; eight fixed, one documented, one rejected as harmless), one Sonnet numbers review (sixteen findings, applied), and one Sonnet prose review (applied).

docs.title: If a detector knew exactly which recent power readings lie inside a load-shift event, how much would a lagged and lagless forecast mixture gain?
docs.text:
Take-home message: telling a mixture of two forecasts exactly which recent power readings lie inside a load-shift event did not make the mixture better than simply averaging the two forecasts 50/50, so in these data the limit lies in the two forecasts or the event labels, not in the event detector. The hypothesis that exact event flags would improve the mixture is refuted.

We forecast the power drawn at NGED's Primary substations (the substations that step down from the high-voltage electricity network), up to 14 days ahead. A load-shift event is a period in which the network operator moved load between substations, so recent power readings do not show normal demand. The lagged forecast uses the recent readings (lags) of the substation's own power, and the lagless forecast does not. B-mix averages the two with equal weight. We replaced the equal weight with rules that use an exact record of which of the three lags lie inside an event. The hard rule uses the lagless forecast whenever any lag is flagged (marked as inside an event), and the soft rule weights the lagless forecast by the share of flagged lags. Both rules scored worse than B-mix, in real events and in events we added to otherwise normal data. We re-scored forecasts that experiment 404 had stored, so no neural network was fitted.

Figure 2 shows how the scores change with the number of flagged lags. With all three lags flagged, the lagless forecast is barely better than the lagged forecast on the added events, and worse inside real events, while the average of the two is better than either in most row sets. An equal average of two lagged forecasts from different fit seeds (the control at the end of this page) recovers 0.29 of B-mix's gain over a single lagged forecast on real clean rows, so about two thirds of B-mix's gain in 2026-06 at the six is not explained by averaging forecasts of one kind. The scores in Figure 2 and the control give no support to a better detector as the way to improve this pair of forecasts, given the labels available. One candidate next experiment is O-mask, which hides the flagged readings from the lagged forecast.

How to read the numbers. Every number is interim and unaudited. The score is the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) in points of capacity, from 11 quantiles (smaller is better), pooled over five test months (2025-10, 2025-12, 2026-01, 2026-03, 2026-06) at fit seed 0. A contrast is the arm minus B-mix on the same rows, so a positive number favours B-mix. Intervals resample whole events (95%). "Inside real events" are rows whose valid time lies inside a padded real event or in the 96 half-hours after it. "Real harm" rows lie outside every event but have a day window of recent power that touches an event. The lagged head is the A0-inj network of experiment 404 and the lagless head is its frozen cross-fitted forecast (each month's lagless forecast comes from a fit that did not see that month), so B-mix is exactly experiment 404's arm. The signed-MW six are the Primaries metered in signed megawatts, and the MVA-only eight are the remaining Primaries.

docs.title: Headline numbers
docs.text:
• Arms. O-hard, O-soft, O-lagless (the lagless head alone), and O-floor (post hoc). O-floor puts weight 0.5 + (flagged lags) / 6 on the lagless head, so it equals B-mix when no lag is flagged. The stored experiment 404 arms A0-inj, B1, and B3 are reference rows. B6 and S1 are not stored for all five months, so they are not scored.
  • Inside real events, signed-MW six, minus B-mix (20 events): O-hard +0.465 (+0.198 to +0.644), and +0.374 (+0.154 to +0.592) without the largest event; O-soft +0.429 (+0.180 to +0.607); O-lagless +0.414 (+0.065 to +0.630); O-floor +0.326 (-0.004 to +0.540); A0-inj +0.155 (-0.025 to +0.448). B-mix scores 7.855, O-hard 8.320.
  • Inside real events, MVA-only eight (18 events): O-hard +0.677 (+0.291 to +1.333), O-soft +0.423 (+0.133 to +0.815), O-floor +0.323 (+0.048 to +0.779).
  • Real harm rows, six: O-hard +0.255 (+0.151 to +0.371), O-soft +0.197 (+0.093 to +0.320), O-floor +0.073 (+0.015 to +0.159). B-mix scores 3.351.
  • Injected harm rows, six: O-hard +0.292 (+0.261 to +0.325), O-soft +0.238 (+0.215 to +0.263), O-floor +0.029 (+0.010 to +0.050). B-mix scores 3.987.
  • Clean rows: O-hard equals A0-inj, which is 0.390 worse than B-mix on real clean rows at the six (3.959 against 3.569). O-floor equals B-mix exactly on clean rows (control passed).
  • Number of flagged lags (six, pooled): on injected harm rows with three flagged lags the lagged head scores 4.10, the lagless head 4.03, and B-mix 3.49. Inside real events with three flagged lags the lagged head scores 9.48, the lagless head 10.19, and B-mix 9.51.
  • Every month and seed. O-hard minus B-mix inside real events is positive in all seven month-and-seed combinations (2026-06 seeds 0 to 2 and the four other months): +0.21 to +0.70 at the six.
  • Tails, six, inside real events (pinball loss; share of actuals below the quantile): B-mix q01 0.600 (7.9%), q99 2.307 (71.8% below); O-hard q01 0.806 (9.0%), q99 2.794 (69.1%); O-floor q01 0.807, q99 2.694. Of the two tails reported, the upper tail shows the larger loss: O-hard's q99 loss is 0.487 above B-mix's.
  • Event counts. events_corrected.parquet holds 184 corrected events: 78 at the six, 88 at the eight, and 18 at the report-only D15 and D18. Neighbouring events on one Primary merge into 170 padded runs. The five scored months overlap 49 corrected events (2026-06 has 2, 2026-03 has 4, 2026-01 has 15, 2025-12 has 10, and 2025-10 has 18; an event straddling a month boundary counts in both). A padded run is an event with 48 half-hours of padding on each side, merged with any neighbouring event that the padding touches.
  • Compute and code. No fit: forward passes of experiment 404's saved A0-inj networks (monthly refits, cross-fitted lagless tables) on one CPU core. Cleaned power with the D15 and D18 cut as in experiment 404. Copies of experiment 404's modules at PR 58 commit 1ddeab7e (e00445_*.py, code-identical after renaming).
  • Stored forecasts. data/ml-experiments/00445-flag-oracle-o-rule-ceiling-for-lag-event-detectors/work/predictions/<arm>/.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast (points of capacity, per Primary, clean world). For O-hard it ranges from -2.33 (D15) to -0.03 (D22), mostly small and negative, as for the lagless head alone (-1.75 at D12 to +0.29 at D18). No Primary has a gap of more than 2.6 points (O-soft at D15).
  • Error of the median beside each contrast. The mean absolute error of q50 inside real events at the six is 9.81 for B-mix, 10.06 for A0-inj, 10.06 for O-lagless, 10.19 for O-hard, 10.17 for O-soft, and 9.99 for O-floor, so the median agrees in direction with every quantile-score contrast (trigger 3, a disagreement in direction, did not fire).
  • Ensembling-control reviews (run late, after the control was written). A fresh Sonnet agent reviewed the ensemble code (it found a stray break that stopped the build after the first world; fixed, and the B-mix check now runs every world). A second fresh Sonnet agent re-derived the ensembling-control numbers and found no difference over 0.01. A second prose review of the whole page was triaged; its valid findings were applied.
  • Numbers review. A fresh Sonnet agent re-derived the pooled means, by-count mean, point contrast, and identity check from the stored forecasts with its own code and found no wrong number. The reviewer's own clustering gave O-floor's inside-event interval a lower endpoint of +0.02 to +0.03 against -0.004 here, so O-floor's gap to B-mix inside real events is marginal. The reviewer's point estimates agreed.
  • Triggers. Trigger 2 (a result contradicts its own prediction) fired: the result contradicts predictions P1 (O-rules beat B-mix on injected harm rows: they lose by 0.29 and 0.24) and P2 (hard minus B-mix between -0.4 and +0.2 inside real events: it is +0.465). A likely explanation, supported by Figure 2 but not isolated, is that the 50/50 average gains from averaging two forecasts that score alike (Figure 2). O-floor keeps the average and removes most of the loss on injected rows (+0.029). Trigger 4 (leaving out one site or event flips a verdict) did not fire: removing the largest event leaves the O-hard inside-event contrast positive. Triggers 1, 5, 6, and 7 (a failed control, a nested arm beating its container, an interval twice or half as wide as a sister experiment's, and an unreplicated headline that a later experiment depends on) did not fire; the control O-floor equals B-mix on clean rows. P3 held: O-hard equals A0-inj on clean rows.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Interim. One fit seed per month, five months, 20 events at the six. In 2026-06, seeds 1 and 2 give the same sign (+0.34 and +0.28 for O-hard inside real events), scored separately.
  • Unlogged events. NGED (the electricity distribution network operator that supplies the data) says load-shift events may be missing from their logs. Clean rows can therefore hold unlogged events, a harm table measured on clean rows is optimistic, and real-event slices undercount.
  • Flags are exact only on the simulated worlds. On real data the flag is the padded hand-labelled event, so labels that miss an event, or rows inside an event whose actuals are not the normal running arrangement, would make the real-event result worse than the oracle name suggests.
  • Avoidable-curtailment cost not computed. The measure needs forecasts for each grid supply node and its generators, which experiment 404 does not store.
  • O-floor is post hoc. Its weights were chosen after the first scores. O-floor's rows, rule, and intervals were not tuned on the scored rows.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Run O-mask. Train a lagged neural network and score it with each flagged lag replaced by "missing". If the lagged head improves inside events once it cannot see the flagged lags, the gain comes from the head and not from a switch.
  • Make the lagless head better inside events. Inside real events with three flagged lags the lagless head is 0.71 points worse than the lagged head, so the lagless forecast also misses the events.

docs.title: Addendum: ensembling control (pre-registered 2026-10-31, before any ensemble score was read)
docs.text:
Question: is B-mix's edge over a single head an ensembling gain (averaging two forecasts) or a gain from combining a lagged and a lagless forecast? No new fits; forward passes of experiment 404's saved A0-inj networks and its stored lagless tables, and stored S1 forecasts.

  • Arms. Equal-weight density mixtures of two lagged heads (A0-inj seeds i and j, the 404 equivalent of R-inj); of two lagless heads (tables of seeds i and j); a 3-way mixture of lagged heads (seeds 0 to 2), a 3-way and a 5-way mixture of lagless heads (seeds 0 to 2 and 0 to 4); and the stored S1 seeds i and j mixed from their stored quantiles (approximate, validated against the exact mixture of A0-inj and the lagless head before use). Reference rows: B-mix (A0-inj seed i with the lagless table of seed i), each single head, and the post hoc O-floor rule.
  • Cells. Lagged-head ensembles and S1 ensembles exist only for 2026-06, where 3 seeds are stored. Lagless-head ensembles exist for all 5 months (lagless tables of seeds 0 to 4). Other months have one lagged seed, so only B-mix and the lagless ensembles are scored there.
  • Rows. The tables of this page: clean, injected harm, real harm, inside real events, signed-MW six and MVA-only eight, with and without the largest event.
  • Reading rule. Let G_B be the single lagged head's score minus B-mix's, and G_E the single lagged head's score minus the lagged-plus-lagged mixture's, both averaged over the 3 seeds (pairs for G_E), on real clean rows at the six in 2026-06. If G_E / G_B is at least 0.5, B-mix beats single heads mostly through ensembling, and the next step is to compare every trust arm with a seed-matched ensemble of its base. If it is at most 0.25, the lagged and lagless diversity does the work. Between those values the result is mixed and reported as such. Inside real events the same ratio is reported as a second reading.

docs.title: Results of the ensembling control
docs.text:
• Question and reading. Does averaging forecasts of one kind recover B-mix's gain over a single forecast? The pre-registered ratio is G_E / G_B, the gain of an average of two lagged forecasts over a single lagged forecast, divided by the gain of B-mix over a single lagged forecast (Figure 6). At least 0.5 means ensembling, at most 0.25 means diversity, and in between is mixed.
  • Reading: mixed, leaning towards diversity. At the six Primaries in 2026-06 the ratio is 0.29 on real clean rows (the primary reading), 0.23 inside real events, 0.25 on injected clean rows, and 0.25 on injected harm rows. With a three-way average of lagged forecasts the ratios are 0.39, 0.31, 0.33, and 0.34.
  • Scores on real clean rows, six, 2026-06. The single lagged forecast scores 3.239. Relative to it, B-mix is -0.267 (-0.361 to -0.183), the average of two lagged forecasts -0.078 (-0.090 to -0.069), and the three-way average -0.104 (-0.119 to -0.092). B-mix minus the three-way average is -0.164 (-0.246 to -0.086), so B-mix is better than three lagged forecasts averaged.
  • S1. S1 is the network with the surprise at each lag as an extra input. Its stored forecasts were averaged from their quantiles, which is approximate (it differed from the exact mixture by 0.0001 points on 60,000 validation rows). The average of two S1 seeds is -0.069 (-0.084 to -0.057) against a single S1, and B-mix minus that average is -0.119 (-0.261 to +0.010).
  • Averaging lagless forecasts. Averaging lagless tables from different seeds gains less than B-mix does over a single lagless table, but a five-way average is about as good as B-mix. Pooled over five months at fit seed 0 at the six, inside real events the five-way average scores 7.795 against 7.855 for B-mix (B-mix minus the five-way average +0.060, -0.259 to +0.322), and on real clean rows B-mix minus the five-way average is -0.127 (-0.472 to +0.116). At the MVA-only eight inside real events the five-way average scores 8.418 against 8.664. B-mix is still better on injected harm rows (-0.101, -0.147 to -0.057).
  • O-floor beside the five-way lagless average (post hoc). In 2026-06, O-floor minus B-mix is -0.021 (-0.062 to +0.049) on real clean rows and +0.098 (+0.035 to +0.162) inside real events.
  • Cells. Lagged and S1 averages exist for 2026-06 only (three fit seeds). Averages of lagless tables exist for all five months (tables of seeds 0 to 4).
  • Caveat. Inside real events at 2026-06 the intervals rest on two events at the six, so the second reading is weak.

docs.title: Reuse and credit
docs.text: The lagged head, lagless table, row classes, scoring, and event-cluster bootstrap come from experiment 404 (copied as e00445_*.py). The row classes and flag construction follow experiment 428, and the flag oracle idea follows experiment 402.

docs.title: Do scale-only bands trained on ambiguous jumps, and tail-calibrating changes, beat a recalibration table on the S1 network?
docs.text:
Take-home message: training the forecast neural network on examples of genuine level changes makes its upper bands wide where a jump in recent power is ambiguous, but the same training makes the bands too wide on clean rows and raises the clean-row error by more than the limit we set, so no arm passes. The extra scale-only path learned no widening by itself, and none of the five tail changes brought clean-row upper-tail coverage into the target range. Verdict: not supported. Every number is interim, from four test months.

Two questions drove the experiment: whether training on genuine level changes widens the bands where a jump is ambiguous, and whether a change to the tails fixes the clean-row coverage. The demand forecast is a neural network that returns 11 quantiles. First, can the neural network be taught to widen its upper bands when a recent power reading may be corrupted by a load-shift event, or may instead be a genuine level change (a new connection, or a generator curtailed for days)? We trained it on simulated worlds in which some jumps are genuine level changes added to both the recent readings and the target, and we added a separate path that can only widen the bands. Second, can a change to the tails of the output distribution bring the clean-row upper tails into their target range? We scored every arm against the forecasts of experiments 428 and 439. Training on genuine level changes widened the bands where intended, and the widening spilled over onto clean rows. The separate widening path and the tail changes did not help. The "after table P" rules (table P is the stratified recalibration table of experiment 435) cannot be settled yet (see "What is still interim").

docs.title: How to read the numbers
docs.text:
Unless a column says otherwise, every number is a score at days 1 to 10, after the 1.15 widening of the bands, at the six Primary substations metered in signed megawatts (the "signed-MW six"). CRPS is the continuous ranked probability score in percentage points of effective capacity (smaller is better). Coverage at q95 is the share of readings at or below the 95th-percentile forecast, so the target is near 0.95. The MVA-only eight are the Primaries metered in unsigned megavolt-amperes (MVA). The four test months are 2025-10, 2026-01, 2026-03, and 2026-06, with seeds 0 to 2. The arms are listed in the plan below. In short: S1 is the neural network given three lagged power readings plus the surprise at each; R-inj is the same neural network without the surprise; U1n-2 and U1n-5 are S1 trained on worlds with genuine level changes in 2% and 5% of training rows; U2, U2i, U2c, and U2-clean add the scale-only path (U2i adds an interval-score term, U2c adds a coverage-matching penalty, and U2-clean trains on worlds with no genuine level changes); U3 masks lags at prediction time; and T1 to T5 are the Brief C tail changes on the S1 base.

Row sets. A clean row has recent power outside every logged load-shift event. An injected harm row holds a simulated load-shift event added to clean power. An injected genuine-level-change row (gen_jump) has a genuine level change in force at one of the three lags. A real event row has its target inside a logged event, and a real harm row has a target outside every event but recent power inside one. The injected genuine level changes come from the same generator as the training worlds of U1n and the scale-only arms, with different random draws, so those rows are in-distribution for the U arms only. The comparison on them between S1 or R-inj and a U arm is therefore not like for like.

docs.title: Brief B: genuine level changes in the training worlds
docs.text:
Training on worlds with genuine level changes widens the upper bands on the rows where a jump is ambiguous. Table 1 gives the signed-MW six. On injected genuine-level-change rows, q99 coverage rises from 0.909 (S1) and 0.916 (R-inj) to 0.983 (U1n-2) and 0.993 (U1n-5). On real event rows, which the training worlds did not simulate, q99 coverage rises from 0.852 (S1) to 0.947 (U1n-2) and 0.995 (U1n-5).

The same training also widens the bands on clean rows, where they were already close to target. Clean-row q95 coverage rises from 0.915 (S1) to 0.938 (U1n-2), inside the target range of 0.93 to 0.97. Clean-row q99 coverage rises from 0.981 to 0.996, above the target range of 0.98 to 0.995. The clean-row CRPS rises by 0.076 points (95% interval 0.063 to 0.090, minimum detectable effect 0.077) for U1n-2 and by 0.132 (0.117 to 0.147) for U1n-5. Both are above the pre-registered limit of 0.03.

Arm Clean CRPS Clean q95 Clean q99 Genuine-change CRPS Genuine-change q99 Real event q99 Real harm q99 pinball R-inj 2.947 0.914 0.980 5.815 0.916 0.845 0.254 S1 2.865 0.915 0.981 5.860 0.909 0.852 0.276 U1n-2 2.941 0.938 0.996 5.543 0.983 0.947 0.284 U1n-5 2.997 0.950 0.999 5.257 0.993 0.995 0.316 U2 2.936 0.938 0.997 5.531 0.982 0.945 0.268 U2i 2.934 0.937 0.997 5.483 0.983 0.944 0.265 U2c 2.936 0.938 0.997 5.531 0.982 0.945 0.268 U2-clean 2.919 0.914 0.979 5.847 0.911 0.855 0.279 U3 2.975 0.936 0.995 5.790 0.970 0.916 0.278

Table 1: signed-MW six, seeds 0 to 2, four test months. The row counts are 254,725 clean rows, 43,009 genuine-change rows, 31,898 real event rows, and 40,643 real harm rows. The last column is the q99 pinball loss on real harm rows (points).

The scale-only path (U2) learned no widening, and U2 scores like U1n-2. The mean scale factor of U2 is 1.000 on every row set, including injected harm and genuine-change rows. The path is connected: U2i has the same code and reaches factors up to 3.3, which rise with the surprise. U2 learned no widening because the last-layer bias of the factor fell from -5.0 to about -5.17, and the factor stays 1.0 even at a surprise of 5 or 20. U2 and U2c have the same scores to three decimals on every row set, so the coverage-matching penalty did nothing. U2i's interval-score term does produce widening: on genuine-change rows its CRPS is 5.483 against 5.531 for U2, and its q99 pinball loss is 0.371 against 0.431. Its mean scale factor is 1.001 on clean rows, 1.011 on injected harm rows, 1.037 on genuine-change rows, and 1.015 on real event rows. Within 0.007 CRPS points on clean rows, U2, U2i, and U2c match U1n-2 (2.941), so the widening on clean rows also came from the training worlds.

The band-width ratios show where the widening lands. The ratio is the mean width of the 5% to 95% band on the named rows over the same arm's width on matching unaffected rows. U1n-2 and U2 widen the band by a ratio of about 1.07 on genuine-change rows in the first day after the change began (U2-clean: 1.006), and by about 1.13 at 1 to 3 days. After 3 days the ratio falls to 0.97, so the band is no wider than on unaffected rows. U1n-5 stays wide after 3 days (1.39). U2-clean keeps a ratio of 0.994 on injected harm rows, inside 0.02 of 1.00. Because U2 matches U1n-2 here, the first-day widening comes from the location neural network trained on the new worlds, not from the scale path.

Contrasts against S1 show a clear rise in CRPS on clean and injected harm rows and a clear fall on genuine-change rows. Table 2 gives CRPS differences with 95% intervals from resampling origin days within test months, and the minimum detectable effect (MDE) from the seed spread of R-inj. On real event and real harm rows every interval includes zero, except U1n-5 on real harm rows (+0.107, 0.030 to 0.174).
