  • By lead band (RC28-bias): q95 coverage is 0.954 (0 to 12 hours), 0.949 (12 to 36 hours), 0.945 (36 to 72 hours), 0.942 (days 4 to 5), and 0.925 (days 6 to 10); q99 is 0.994, 0.991, 0.990, 0.989, and 0.985. In the 12 to 36 hour band q01 is 0.0041 and q05 0.0311, so q01 sits just under its 0.005 floor there.
  • Cold winter nights (clean rows): RC28-bias q95 is 0.917 and q99 0.985 (raw 0.835 and 0.944; table P 0.904 and 0.970). The four pre-registered arms stay under target (q95 0.772 to 0.864).
  • Real events against NRA-corrected actuals: every rolling arm scores worse than raw (CRPS 22.4 raw; 24.5 RC28; 25.5 RC28-bias; 26.3 RC7), because the buffers hold event residuals. Table P gives 22.6 and the widening 22.3. A rolling correction does not repair event rows, and RC28-bias makes them worse.
  • Christmas week (22 to 31 December, clean rows): RC28-bias q95 is 0.972 and q99 0.997, above the 0.97 and 0.995 ceilings; RC28 gives 0.942 and 0.979.
  • The eight (report only): RC28-bias gives q01 0.0095, q05 0.0469, q95 0.9312, q99 0.9851, q99 pinball loss 0.231, and CRPS 4.248, against raw 0.0053, 0.0364, 0.9216, 0.9813, 0.238, and 4.245, so it passes the four coverage targets at the eight too and changes CRPS by +0.003 (95% interval -0.039 to +0.045). The pre-registered arms are worse than raw at the eight: RC28 CRPS 4.271 and q99 pinball loss 0.298, RC14 CRPS 4.428.
  • Curtailment cost at the six (£ million over the scored rows, 95% interval, lower is better; avoidable-curtailment cost on rows with no labelled event that BG2 also holds): at f = 0.9, raw 2.18 (0.19 to 5.78), table P 1.79, RC28 1.08, RC28-bias 1.01, BG2 1.37, manual_heuristic 2.02. At f = 0.75: raw 8.63 (2.88 to 17.71), table P 6.81, RC28-bias 4.93, BG2 8.24, manual_heuristic 12.88. At f = 0.5: raw 24.10 (15.43 to 36.18), table P 21.75, RC28-bias 18.47, BG2 25.92, manual_heuristic 37.79. RC28-bias minus raw is -5.63 (-14.58 to -0.12) at f = 0.5. The intervals are wide and overlap at f = 0.9.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median forecast beside the quantile contrasts: the mean absolute error of the median at the six falls from 4.95 points (raw) to 4.67 (RC14), 4.69 (RC28), and 4.69 (RC28-bias), the same direction as CRPS. At the eight the median error rises to 6.31 for RC14 and stays at 6.09 for RC28 and RC28-bias (raw 6.10). The mean forecast is not stored (only quantiles), so the median minus mean forecast was not computed.
  • Audit triggers: (2) the result contradicts the pre-registered prediction P1, and the explanation tested is the median-only arm above; (5) the bias-only arm, which holds less of the correction, beats RC28 that contains it on q95, q99, and q99 pinball loss; (4) one Primary (index 9) carries most of the CRPS gain: the CRPS change of RC28-bias against raw is -0.96 at that Primary and -0.32, -0.21, -0.07, -0.02, and +0.27 at the other five. That Primary supplies 79% of the row-weighted summed gain with 17% of the rows, the other five average -0.07 per Primary (-0.052 weighted by rows), and the January 2026 fold dominates (-0.64, against -0.16 over the five folds). Without that Primary, RC28-bias still clears all four coverage clauses (q01 0.0074, q05 0.0398, q95 0.9358, q99 0.9878). A fresh Sonnet audit re-derived the headline numbers from the stored seed predictions with its own code and confirmed them (CRPS, the four coverages, q99 pinball loss). It found three further points, all accepted: a static median offset per Primary and lead band, fitted leave-one-fold-out, already gives CRPS 3.289 and q95 0.9365, so most of the gain of RC28-bias is a persistent under-forecast and not adaptivity (on the four folds with earlier-only fits the static offset gives CRPS 3.451 and q95 0.924, against 3.358 and 0.934 for RC28-bias, so rolling does add value there); table P and the two constants rescale spread only, so a fairer benchmark is a static offset, possibly followed by the two constants; and a live buffer would see raw delivered readings, including stuck meters, while these buffers use cleaned actuals.
  • Code review: a fresh Sonnet review ran before the first scored run and found no blocking problem. Triaged: the shifts command now asserts that no buffer row is later than the delivery cutoff or initiated at or after the origin; the check command now also compares q01 and q99; the sensitivity run with blocks of 14 origin days was added. The delivery delay counts 12 half-hour steps from the target's label; if the label is the start of the half-hour the true lag is 12.5 steps, a one-step effect that this experiment does not test. The curtailment cost was added as a separate script, as experiment 483 does.

docs.title: Serving cost
docs.text:
Table P Two constants Rolling conformal (RC28) Median-only (RC28-bias) Stored at training 20 factors per metering group 2 factors per metering group nothing nothing Computed at each origin nothing nothing 11 quantiles per Primary and lead band from the last 28 days' errors the median of those errors State kept by serving none none the last 28 days of forecasts and delivered actuals per Primary and lead band the same state Updates per year 12, with each monthly refit 12, with each monthly refit 365 (every daily origin) 365 Missing actuals table unaffected unaffected buffer shrinks; fall back to the 1.15 widening below 100 residuals the same

A rolling correction adds a data dependency on the delivered power readings, which the forecast already reads for its lags, and it needs the previous forecasts to be stored. Serving keeps the buffer across a monthly model refit, but the buffer's residuals then come from the previous XGBoost model; the stored data cannot show how a buffer behaves for the week after a refit.

docs.title: Caveats and next steps
docs.text:
• Caveats: five non-contiguous folds are few, and January 2026 dominates the worst cases for every arm. The buffers hold forecasts from the previous month's model at each month's start. The post hoc arm was chosen after the scores of the pre-registered arms were seen, and 79% of its row-weighted CRPS gain across the six Primaries comes through one Primary. RC28-bias makes real-event rows worse. NGED's event labels are incomplete. The stored lead range is 0 to 240 hours.
  • Next steps (for the maintainer to decide): repeat the median-only arm on fresh months (July 2026 stays unused) and at the eight; test a static per-Primary offset as the benchmark, and whether a per-Primary offset, which the median shift approximates, belongs in the forecaster's training instead of in a serving buffer.

docs.title: Does an explicit solar-output column, built from a capacity fitted on earlier months, improve the demand forecast at the six primary substations metered in signed megawatts?
docs.text: Giving the demand neural network a column of "the solar output a fixed capacity would give" did not improve the forecast at the six primary substations metered in signed megawatts. Primary substations are called Primaries below. At the six Primaries named "signed-MW six" the meter reports import and export with opposite signs; the other ten Primaries are metered differently, and eight of them only in megavolt-amperes. We tested one extra input for experiment 425's best neural network (arm A, pretrained on past-weather rows and fine-tuned on ensemble forecasts). The input is the solar output that a fixed capacity would give under the forecast weather. The capacity comes from experiment 474's method, a convex fit of solar capacity to the Primary's metered power, using only months before each test month. We fine-tuned arm A with the column on five test months and three seeds, and compared the new forecasts with the forecasts already stored for arm A. On sunny middays (CAMS clear-sky index of 0.7 or more, 10:00 to 15:00 UK time) the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS, a score for a whole forecast distribution, here in megawatts; lower is better) moved by -0.014. The 98.33% interval is -0.027 to +0.000, and the smallest change the experiment could detect (the minimum detectable effect) is 0.225. The verdict is refuted: the largest gain the interval allows, 0.027, is about a tenth of the 0.225 we could detect. In the text below a difference of 1 MW of CRPS is "1 point".

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Arms. The two arms are arm A (experiment 425, seeds 0 to 2, stored forecasts) and the column arm (arm A fine-tuned from the same pretrained weights with the column, three seeds, five folds: 2025-10, 2025-12, 2026-01, 2026-03, 2026-06). Retraining is monthly, the fine-tuning learning rate is 2e-4, and the forecast uncertainty is widened by a factor of 1.15. Each of the 15 fine-tunes took 27 to 60 seconds on the GPU.
  • Column. The column is the fold's capacity for each Primary multiplied by experiment 405's solar shape of one megawatt of capacity (from the ensemble-mean weather), divided by 3 MW so that the values sit near 1. The capacities are 2.0 to 4.1 MW of alternating current at the six Primaries (computed by e00501_capacity.py). The full-history fit reproduces experiment 474's stored values exactly. The column is zero at the other 10 Primaries.
  • Tested contrasts. Each contrast is the column arm's CRPS minus arm A's, on forecast days 1 to 10 at the signed-MW six, with the same rows in both arms. A Bonferroni correction for three contrasts sets the interval level to 98.33%, and the intervals come from resampling whole test months. A count is the number of Primary-half-hour forecasts.
Slice Difference Interval Minimum detectable effect C1 sunny-midday half-hours (34,432) -0.014 -0.0265 to +0.0001 0.225 C2 all daylight half-hours (158,999) +0.0004 -0.0009 to +0.0013 0.134 C3 all half-hours (429,350) -0.0009 -0.0025 to +0.0001 0.104
  • Report-only groups (not in the Bonferroni count, same interval level). Eight Primaries metered only in megavolt-amperes: C1 +0.0078 (+0.0014 to +0.0161), C2 -0.0001 (-0.0010 to +0.0008), C3 +0.0001 (-0.0004 to +0.0008). D15 and D18, the two Primaries with a short history that is cut at 2025-03-01: C1 -0.0154 (-0.0382 to +0.0020), C2 -0.0128 (-0.0330 to -0.0011), C3 -0.0047 (-0.0109 to -0.0004). The column is zero at the eight, so the shifts there presumably come from the shared neural-network weights.
  • By fold (C1, points). 2025-10 -0.030, 2025-12 -0.008, 2026-01 +0.012, 2026-03 -0.025, 2026-06 -0.011. Leaving out each Primary in turn leaves C1 between -0.008 and -0.018.
  • Absolute scores (signed-MW six, days 1 to 10, rows shared with the references): arm A 3.220, column arm 3.219, BG2 3.428 (the weekly XGBoost best guess of experiment 87), S0M 3.569 (the monthly XGBoost recipe of experiment 389, widened), manual heuristic 4.134, climatology 4.392. Arm A's sunny-midday CRPS by fold: 2025-10 4.41, 2025-12 3.73, 2026-01 5.59, 2026-03 4.08, 2026-06 3.07.
  • Lead bands (signed-MW six): at 12 to 36 hours the CRPS is 2.822 for arm A and 2.820 for the column arm. At 36 hours to 10 days it is 3.268 for both.
  • Tails (signed-MW six, days 1 to 10; nominal coverage 0.01, 0.05, 0.95, 0.99): coverage at q01, q05, q95, and q99 is 0.007, 0.022, 0.895, and 0.962 for the column arm, and 0.007, 0.022, 0.895, and 0.963 for arm A. The q99 pinball loss is 0.326 and 0.325. The CRPS on cold winter nights (the scoring machinery's cold-night slice) is 5.049 for both arms.
  • Curtailment. The avoidable curtailment cost over the six Primaries, in pounds, summed over the scored months, at limit fraction f (the limit is f times the node's largest export before the scored year): at f = 0.9 the column arm costs 6.857 million and arm A 6.865 million; at f = 0.75, 16.94 million and 16.97 million; at f = 0.5, 38.16 million and 38.21 million. The manual heuristic costs 61.66 million at f = 0.5. Whether the manual heuristic matches NGED's practice is the maintainer's unconfirmed understanding.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast. The median minus the mean forecast per Primary (the mean of the 11 quantiles, in MW) differs between the arms by under 0.001 MW at every Primary. The mean-forecast absolute error differs between the arms by about as little as the median-forecast absolute error.
  • Triggers. The plan's audit lists seven conditions that would call for a further check. None occurred. No control failed, because the capacity fit reproduces experiment 474. The result does not contradict experiments 349, 352, and 416, which found a flat response. The quantile score and the mean-forecast error agree. Leaving out one Primary does not flip the sign of C1. The column arm can ignore its extra column, and it did not beat arm A by more than the width of the interval. We found no other experiment on the same rows to compare interval widths against.
  • Unattributable. Experiment 474's capacities fail its placebo test at every step of its ladder. A gain would therefore not have shown that the capacities are right. The absence of a gain does not show that the capacities are wrong. Experiment 474's caveats for D5 (an export limit the solar term cannot represent), D9, and D16 (a pinned capacity that is too high) apply.
  • Rows. In each fold, fine-tuning dropped 68,680 rows for the D15 and D18 start cut and 2,155 to 2,925 rows for flagged exact-zero half-hours. Across the 12 months for which arm A's forecasts are stored, scoring dropped 1,179 actual values because they were flagged exact zeros. Clean rows may hold events that NGED's logs do not label.
  • Leaks left. Three constant scale factors use data after the fold: the recovery divisor (the known-answer recovery of experiment 474, 0.956 to 0.994), the farm-output normalisation (the 99th percentile of each metered solar farm's output over all history), and u99 (the 99th percentile of the unit solar shape, over D10's ensemble forecasts at all dates). The 2025-10 fold identifies its capacity increment from three months of data. The weather inputs at lag times are the same as arm A's, so arm A's caveat about past weather applies unchanged.

docs.title: What serving would need
docs.text:
• Stored: one capacity for each of the six Primaries, refitted with each monthly refit of the neural network or once a year if the capacity is held. One capacity fit for one Primary took about 13 seconds.
  • Computed at serving: experiment 405's solar shape of the ensemble-mean shortwave radiation and temperature for each half-hour, times the capacity.
  • Added complexity: serving would need a capacity table for the six Primaries and a monthly or annual capacity refit, in return for no gain at the detectable size.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text: This experiment's demand forecast score neither validated nor rejected the capacities, so the 10th and 90th percentile capacity arms were not run. Experiment 479's anomaly estimator is the one candidate we know of for a capacity that could pass a known-answer test.

docs.title: Does dropping only the week lag, only the day lag, or only the origin lag cut the leak of a step in the power lags into the XGBoost demand median at a smaller score loss than dropping all three?
docs.text: Dropping one power lag does not remove the leak at every event length, and every single-lag drop costs about 0.05 points of capacity (CRPS) on rows with no labelled event. The day lag carries the leak of events up to 3 days and the sensitivity to a stuck meter or a dropout. The week lag carries part of the leak of events of 5 to 7 days. Dropping the week lag makes short events and bad data worse. The three lags are power readings 1 day, 2 days, and 7 days (the origin, day, and week lags) before the forecast time. NGED's event labels are incomplete, so "rows with no labelled event" may hold unlogged events, the harm rows are optimistic, and the real-event slices undercount. Every number is interim and unaudited.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Arms. All fitted like experiment 402's arm (a): monthly refits (2025-10-01, 2026-01-01, 2026-03-01, 2026-06-01), 500 rounds, eta 0.05, 11 quantiles, CUDA, six Primaries metered in signed megawatts (D5, D9, D10, D11, D14, D16). "No week lag" and "no day lag" are 24 fits each. "a-rep" is a second CUDA fit of the three original lags (24 fits). "No origin lag" is experiment 388's arm E, re-scored on the same rows with no fits; experiment 388 fitted it separately, so its device and code path may differ from arm (a)'s.
  • Cadence. Monthly refits, as the standing rule says for research. The contrasts could depend on the schedule; no weekly check was run.
  • Reused. Arm (a) from experiment 402 (r0_lagged), arm (b) (no lags) from experiment 392 (r0_lagless), the 50/50 mixture of (a) and (b) (f), and experiment 465's sweep.parquet for arms (a) and (b). Code reused: experiments 87, 383, 392, 402, and 465.
  • Rows. The intersection of finite actuals and every arm's forecast, valid time before 2026-07-01, leads to 240 hours, no flagged zeros dropped at these six Primaries (0 in every fold). Rows with no labelled event: 326,964; harm rows (a lag lies in an event and the target does not): 5,449; rows inside events: 8,740; rows within 7 days after an event: 14,441. The 12 to 36 hour band has 34,214 rows with no labelled event.
  • Noise floor. Arm (a) minus a-rep is -0.0002 CRPS [-0.0012, +0.0006], so the device and seed noise is below 0.02 and the equivalence limit stays 0.11 (experiment 465's range).

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
CRPS in points of effective capacity, six Primaries, leads to 240 hours, no widening, intervals are month-block bootstraps at the 95% Bonferroni level (k = 12). With 4 months (harm rows 3), each interval is the range of the monthly differences, so the equivalence statements are screen-level. Smaller is better.

  • Absolute scores, rows with no labelled event: all three lags 3.096; no lags 3.247; 50/50 mixture 3.064; no week lag 3.145; no day lag 3.145; no origin lag 3.077.
  • Contrast against all three lags, rows with no labelled event: no week lag +0.049 [-0.034, +0.102] (inside the 0.11 limit, so equivalent); no day lag +0.049 [+0.015, +0.113] (the upper end is just outside the limit); no origin lag -0.019 [-0.034, -0.011]. The sign count over the four months: no week lag is worse in 3 of 4 months and no day lag in 4 of 4.
  • Contrast against no lags, rows with no labelled event: no week lag -0.102 [-0.268, +0.038]; no day lag -0.102 [-0.257, +0.115]; no origin lag -0.170 [-0.404, +0.060].
  • 12 to 36 hour band, rows with no labelled event: no week lag +0.038 [-0.034, +0.110]; no day lag +0.110 [+0.069, +0.175]; no origin lag -0.016 [-0.061, +0.001].
  • Within 7 days after an event (absolute): all three lags 4.950; no lags 4.184; mixture 4.293; no week lag 4.415; no day lag 5.146; no origin lag 4.944. Dropping the week lag recovers about two thirds of the gain from dropping all lags here.
  • Harm rows (descriptive; the intervals span about 0.5 to 1 point and cannot show equivalence): all three lags 3.897; no lags 3.686; mixture 3.570; no week lag 3.718 (-0.179 against all three lags, interval -0.271 to +0.383); no day lag 4.085 (+0.188 [-0.055, +0.249]); no origin lag 3.949.
  • Tails, rows with no labelled event (no widening; with the 1.15 widening no interval changes sign): q99 pinball loss 0.341 (all three lags), 0.345 (no week lag), 0.343 (no day lag), 0.338 (no origin lag), all within the +0.02 limit. q95 coverage 0.902, 0.895, 0.898, and 0.905.
  • Leak of a step of 5% of capacity (readings-level sweep, 24 to 72 hour leads, pooled over two Primaries (D5, D16) and two refit dates (2026-01-01, 2026-06-01); median shift as a share of the step):
Step length All three lags No week lag No day lag No lags 24 hours 0.06 0.20 -0.01 0 3 days 0.06 0.22 -0.01 0 5 days 0.19 0.22 0.13 0 7 days 0.33 0.22 0.29 0
  • Bad data (median shift in points of capacity, 24 to 72 hour leads; the injection is experiment 465's): a stuck meter for 24 hours: -0.82 (all three lags), -2.20 (no week lag), -0.02 (no day lag). A dropout to zero for 6 hours: -0.19, -1.35, -0.09. A spike of 20 times the week-on-week median change: +3.79, +5.32, +5.50. The band width ratio stays between 0.98 and 1.19.
  • Predictions. P1 partly: no week lag costs +0.049 (inside the limit), but the readings-level leak is 0.20 to 0.22, not at most 0.20, and the column-level sweep was not run. P2 not tested (the sweep of the origin lag was not run). P3 not supported for short events: the day lag arm leaks -0.01 up to 3 days and 0.13 at 5 days, and 0.29 at 7 days is inside 0.20 to 0.30. P4 holds: the 50/50 mixture (3.064) beats every new arm on rows with no labelled event.
  • Stop rule. Not triggered, because the week lag arm cuts the 7-day leak below 0.25 at a loss under +0.30. The MVA-only eight were not fitted, because no arm cuts the leak at every length without raising it at another.

docs.title: Checks and caveats
docs.text:
• Not run. Avoidable curtailment, cold nights, the whole-event intervals for event slices, the column-level sweep of every lag subset, example forecast time series, and load-shift event plots. The leak figures use two Primaries and two refit dates because of the brief's cost limit, so they are a screen.
  • Audit triggers. Two fired: every interval rests on 4 months (3 for harm rows), and the leak figures rest on 4 site-refit cells whose spread is wide (for example 0.16 to 0.37 for the no week lag arm), so both are screens. The mean-forecast check could not be run because the stored forecasts hold quantiles only.
  • Unlogged events. NGED says load-shift events may be missing from its logs, so clean rows can hold events and the harm-row table is optimistic.
  • Device. The arms of experiment 502 and arm (a) are CUDA fits. Arm E of experiment 388 may be a CPU fit; its contrast against arm (a) can carry up to 0.06 to 0.11 of device difference (experiment 465).

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
• Does a day-lag-free forecast mixed 50/50 with the no-lag forecast match the mixture of all three lags (3.064) on rows with no labelled event and after events?
  • Does the readings-level sweep of the origin lag arm show a leak above 0.06?

Scripts: e00502_fit.py, e00502_score.py, e00502_sweep.py, e00502_figures.py. Predictions: work/arm_preds/{a_rep,nowk,noday} (private data folder); boosters in work/boosters/.

docs.title: Does training the XGBoost demand forecast with 10% of its power lags randomly missing, plus a rule that treats an exactly-zero, stuck, or implausibly distant lag as missing, shield the median forecast from a dropout, a stuck reading, and a spike in the lags, without losing accuracy on rows with no labelled event?
docs.text:
Training the XGBoost demand forecast with 10% of its power lags randomly missing loses no accuracy, and it lets a serving rule shield the median forecast from a dropout and a stuck reading. Gap training means that, in each training row, each of the three power lags (the readings one origin lag, one day, and one week before the forecast target) is independently replaced by a missing value with probability 0.10. The rule for an exactly-zero lag and the rule for a run of 12 identical readings never fire on the real rows of the four scored months, so on real data arm G-A is identical to arm G. The rule for a lag more than 6 times the residual median absolute deviation (MAD) from the stage-1 median shields spikes of 8 times the MAD or more, but it fires on 2.8% of rows with no labelled event and adds +0.0175 to the CRPS there. The three rules together, applied to a forecast trained without gaps, are worse than no rule. NGED's event labels are incomplete, so "rows with no labelled event" may hold unlogged events, and every real-event slice undercounts. Every number is interim and unaudited, except that a separate Claude session re-derived the headline scores (see Checks).

Figures 4 and 5 show a day-ahead and a 14-day forecast with no labelled event, figures 6 to 8 show the forecasts under an injected dropout, spike, and stuck reading, and figure 9 shows a labelled event at D14 (D14 is an anonymised Primary label).

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Scores are the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), the mean pinball loss over the 11 quantiles, in points of effective capacity (percent of the series' capacity). The stage-1 median is the median forecast of experiment 391's lagless first-stage XGBoost model for the lag's time, and the MAD is the median absolute deviation of that model's errors at the Primary. The injections add a dropout to zero, a stuck reading, or a spike to the readings behind the lags; the shift of the median is the change in the median forecast, as a share of the size of the injection. Harm rows are rows whose target lies outside a labelled event but whose lag lies inside one. A contrast is the first arm minus the second, so negative favours the first. Arms: (a) the original lags (experiment 402); (b) the lagless forecast (experiment 392); (f) their fixed 50/50 mixture; G, the gap-trained forecast with no rule; G-A, G with the rules for a zero and for a run of 12 identical readings; G-B, G with those two rules and the distance rule; (a-rule-2), (a) with the zero and stuck-run rules (identical to (a) on real rows); (a-rule-3), (a) with all three rules; (a-rep), experiment 502's CUDA repeat of (a). The signed-MW six are the 6 Primaries metered in signed megawatts (D5, D9, D10, D11, D14, D16). Months are the resampling unit (4 scored months, 3 with labelled events). Every interval is a month-block interval at the Bonferroni level of 99.58% for the 12 pre-registered contrasts, and all are in contrasts.csv. Leads are 0 to 240 h unless stated.

  • Fits. 24 XGBoost models of G were fitted on the GPU, one for each of the 6 Primaries and each of the 4 monthly refit dates. A rule-applied forecast was written for each of G and (a).
  • Absolute scores, rows with no labelled event (326,964 half-hours). (a) 3.0959, (a-rep) 3.0958, (b) 3.2471, (f) 3.0637, G 3.0722, G-A 3.0722, G-B 3.0898, (a-rule-3) 3.1912. On harm rows (18,693 half-hours): (a) 4.047, (b) 3.645, (f) 3.630, G 3.934, G-B 4.229, (a-rule-3) 5.774.
  • Noise floor. (a-rep) minus (a) is -0.00016 [-0.0012, +0.0006] on rows with no labelled event. The repeat uses the same seed, so it bounds GPU nondeterminism only. The seed and the mask draw are not repeated.
  • Clean rows (rows with no labelled event). G minus (a) is -0.024 [-0.047, +0.008]; G-B minus (a) is -0.006 [-0.051, +0.039]. Both intervals lie inside ±0.11, so P2 holds. G minus (b) is -0.175 [-0.417, +0.033] and G-B minus (b) is -0.157 [-0.331, +0.020]. At 12 to 36 h, G minus (a) is -0.014 [-0.048, +0.013], and G-B minus (a) is -0.013 [-0.040, +0.013]. G-B minus G is +0.0175 [-0.013, +0.085] (by month -0.013, +0.085, +0.003, and +0.000) across all leads.
  • Harm rows (a lag inside a labelled event, target outside it). G minus (a) is -0.113 [-0.207, -0.007] over 18 events. G-B minus (a) is +0.182 [-0.602, +0.913]. Leaving out one Primary moves the G-B contrast from -0.165 to +0.405, and dropping the single largest event (D16, 4,130 of the 18,693 rows) moves it from +0.182 to -0.158. The sign of that contrast is decided by one event, so the contrast is descriptive only.
  • During and after events. During a labelled event, G minus (a) is +0.049 [+0.047, +0.401] and G-B minus (a) is +1.097 [+0.065, +1.130], both worse than (a). For the 7 days after an event, G minus (a) is -0.162 [-0.200, -0.091] and G-B minus (a) is +0.200 [-0.623, +0.466].
  • Shift of the median under the corruption, lead 24 to 72 h, as a share of the corruption (figure 2). A dropout to zero for 6 h: (a) 0.035, G 0.034, G-A 0.008, G-B 0.008, (a-rule-2) 0.059. A stuck reading for 24 h: (a) 0.181, G 0.131, G-A 0.081, G-B 0.081, (a-rule-2) 0.353. A spike of 8 times the MAD: (a) 0.098, G 0.102, G-A 0.102, G-B 0.013. A spike of 15 times the MAD: (a) 0.059, G-B 0.006. A spike of 5 times the MAD: (a) 0.120, G-B 0.098. Over 0 to 240 h the dropout shares are 0.037 for G, 0.039 for (a), and 0.009 for G-A; the stuck share is 0.328 for (a-rule-2) against 0.181 at 24 to 72 h for (a). (a-rule-2) is better than (a) at D11 and D9 for a dropout and at D9 for a stuck reading.
  • Rule firing on the injections (G-B). The distance rule newly fires in 99% of the cases with a spike of 8 times the MAD, 100% with 15 times, 24% with 5 times, and 13% with a stuck reading. The rule for a zero fires in 100% of the dropouts and the rule for a run in 100% of the stuck readings.
  • Genuine step of 5% of capacity (lead 24 to 72 h). The share of the step that reaches the median is 0.09 to 0.45 depending on its length, the same for G, G-A, and G-B to within 0.01, and G-B's band width is within 0.7% of the band width without the step. The distance rule sets 0.4% to 1.4% of the lag values to missing, so it is not a detector of load-shift events (P3 holds, though the 5% step is far below the 19% to 33% threshold, so the test is weak).
  • Rule firing on real rows. The rule for a zero and the rule for a run fire on none of 518,076 forecast keys. The distance rule sets at least one lag to missing on 2.8% of rows with no labelled event, 27.7% of harm rows, 51.9% of rows during an event, and 30.3% of the 7 days after. Of the rows with no labelled event, 12,042 have a lag inside an event and the distance rule fires on 36% of them. The remaining 314,922 rows have no event in the target or in any lag, and the rule fires on 1.6% of them (0.58% of lag values; the clean sweep rows give 0.46%). The false alarms sit at D5 (4.5%), D14 (3.0%), and D9 (2.0%), and are about 0% at D10, D11, and D16. Part of the false alarms may be unlabelled events. P1's false-alarm limit of 1% holds per lag value on the 314,922 rows (0.58%) and fails per row. Over all 326,964 rows with no labelled event the rate is 1.23% per lag value. A fourth flag, for a lag with no stage-1 value, is set on 167 forecast keys.
  • Loss where the distance rule fires. CRPS on the 9,229 rows with no labelled event where the rule fires: (a) 5.834, G 5.716, G-B 6.338. G-B scores about 0.62 worse on those rows (a selected-row figure), which gives the +0.0175 on all rows.
  • Cold nights (zenith above 95 degrees, 2 m temperature at or below 3 degrees Celsius; 17,254 half-hours). CRPS: (a) 4.670, G 4.656, G-B 4.877, (b) 5.756, (f) 4.903. Coverage of q95 is 0.741 for (a), 0.736 for G, and 0.732 for G-B (0.769, 0.763, and 0.761 at a widening of 1.15).
  • Tails. On rows with no labelled event, coverage of q01, q05, q95, and q99 is 0.0033, 0.0357, 0.900, and 0.978 for G, against 0.0033, 0.0355, 0.902, and 0.978 for (a). G-B has q95 coverage 0.8996 and q99 0.9784. The pinball loss at q95 is 0.888 for G, 0.885 for G-B, and 0.895 for (a).
  • Avoidable curtailment cost (all rows, six Primaries, pounds, sum of 4 months). At f = 0.9, (a) 8.90e6, G 8.86e6, G-B 9.24e6, (b) 9.20e6, (f) 8.97e6. At f = 0.75, (a) 2.14e7, G 2.16e7, G-B 2.34e7, (b) 2.58e7, (f) 2.24e7. At f = 0.5, (a) 4.82e7, G 4.82e7, G-B 5.02e7, (b) 6.04e7, (f) 4.80e7. The cost is dominated by 2026-01. G minus (a) is lower in 2 of 4 months at f = 0.9 and f = 0.5, and in 1 of 4 at f = 0.75. The cost inside events and after them is undefined, because the cost function lacks a perfect-forecast arm on those slices.
  • Work at serving. Gap training adds nothing at serving. The rules for a zero and for a run need only the last 7 days of readings. The distance rule needs the stage-1 median at each lag time (a stage-1 pass over the last 7 days per series) and the MAD of the stage-1 residual.
  • Predictions. P1 is partly met. A dropout (0.008) and a stuck reading (0.081) fall under 0.10 with G-A, and a spike of 8 times the MAD or more falls under 0.10 only with G-B (0.013 against 0.102 for G-A). The false-alarm rate is 0.58% per lag value but 1.6% per row. P2 holds for G, G-A, and G-B. P3 holds: the distance rule sets 0.4% to 1.4% of the lags to missing under a 5% step. P4 holds: no arm beats (f) on rows with no labelled event, as (f) scores 3.0637 against 3.0722 for G.
  • Decision rule. The smallest gain worth porting G-A is zero on the shifts at a clean-row loss inside ±0.11: G-A meets it, and it adds nothing at serving. G-B must cut the shift by 0.05 beyond G-A and does so only for spikes of 8 times the MAD or more (0.09 beyond), at a loss of +0.0175 on rows with no labelled event. The stop conditions do not fire. The verdict is "more robust, not more accurate" for the rules. For gap training alone the verdict is "no loss, with a favourable point estimate": the interval includes zero, and the dropout and stuck shifts fall only when the rules are added (0.034 and 0.131 for G against 0.008 and 0.081 for G-A).
  • Checks. A separate Claude session re-derived the scores of (a), G, G-A, and G-B from the stored forecasts (326,964 shared half-hours; a 3.0959, G 3.0722, G-B 3.0898) and confirmed the contrasts. It checked that the distance rule uses no reading younger than the origin minus 3.5 h, that the gap mask is applied only when training, and a hand-built dropout of 12 half-hours at D5 gave the same lags and flags as the module. The median minus the mean of the 11 quantiles is small and similar across arms at every Primary. The MAE of the median on rows with no labelled event is 5.417 for (a), 5.385 for G, 5.426 for G-B, and 5.666 for (b) (points of capacity).

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• One event decides the harm-row contrast of the distance rule. The leave-one-Primary-out range is -0.165 to +0.405 and dropping event 55 at D16 flips the sign. No harm-row claim about G-B is made.
  • The noise floor is a same-seed repeat. The seed and the gap-mask draw are not repeated, so the gain of G over (a) (-0.024) has no bound on seed variance. G beats (a) at each of the six Primaries (-0.004 to -0.036), and that consistency supports the sign of the gain.
  • G-A is not an independent arm. It equals G bitwise on real rows because the rules for a zero and a run never fire there, so the 12 pre-registered contrasts are 8 distinct comparisons. The injections for a dropout and a stuck reading are exactly what those two rules match, so G-A's 0.008 shows how G handles a missing lag, not how well the rules detect.
  • The distance rule only catches large departures. At 6 times the MAD the threshold is 19.0% to 33.5% of capacity depending on the Primary. A spike of 5 times the MAD is caught in 24% of cases.
  • The training masks differ from serving masks. Training draws each lag of each row independently, while serving sets a lag missing for every lead of an origin at once. This was not tested.
  • Labels are incomplete. Part of the 1.6% of false alarms may be unlabelled events.

docs.title: Not done
docs.text:
• No fit used a different seed or gap rate, and the 10% gap rate, the 6 times MAD distance, and the 12-step run are single settings.
  • G was fitted at the six Primaries only. The MVA-only eight were not run.
  • BG2 and manual_heuristic were not reproduced on these rows.
  • Real-event rows were not NRA-corrected, and avoidable curtailment inside and after events is undefined.

docs.title: Running the scripts
docs.text: • Running the scripts needs PYTHONPATH entries for the folders of experiments 87, 377, 381, 383, 390, 391, 392, 402, and 465.

docs.title: Do satellite irradiance values that a live service could have at forecast time lower the pooled demand neural network's error at the eight Primaries whose meters report apparent power only?
docs.text:
Satellite sunshine measurements that a live service could have at forecast time did not help the demand neural network. The same measurements read at the forecast's own half-hour would have helped a lot. We scored the forecast with the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS; lower is better), in points (1 point is 1% of a substation's capacity). At the eight Primary substations (the main distribution substations) whose meters report apparent power in megavolt-amperes (MVA) rather than signed megawatts, the demand neural network of experiment 425 (arm A) scored 4.699. With three columns built only from satellite data that exists at forecast time, it scored 4.705, a rise of 0.1%. Columns that held the satellite irradiance measured afterwards for the half-hour being forecast lowered the score by 0.318 points (6.8%). That gain measures how much error the ensemble weather forecast of sunshine (many runs of ECMWF's weather model) causes. None of the feeds we tested supplies it. The next place to look is a nowcast (a forecast of the next few hours made from the latest observations) or a better sunshine forecast at short lead, because the realised arm gained 0.134 points at day 1 and 0.407 at days 6 to 10.

The question was whether a satellite record of recent days improves the demand neural network. We asked whether the neural network that forecasts demand at 16 Primary substations forecasts better when it can see how sunny the last few days were, as measured by the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) satellite retrieval. The network already reads the ensemble weather forecast of sunshine. We built three inputs from CAMS days that were wholly over at least 36 hours before the forecast (a delay we assumed, because the CAMS table has no availability stamp), added them to experiment 425's stored network (its arm A), fine-tuned from the stored weights, and compared the result with the stored network at five scored months. The idea comes from experiment 480, where two realised satellite columns lowered the error of an XGBoost model by 0.355 points at the same eight Primaries. The score is CRPS in points of effective capacity (1 point is 1% of a Primary's capacity). "The eight" are the eight Primaries that report only apparent power in megavolt-amperes, and "the six" are the six that report signed megawatts.

Arm What it is K3 The stored arm A, quantile average of seeds 0 to 2 (no fit). A-cams K3's neural network plus the three columns built only from data available at forecast time (the "leak-free" columns), fine-tuned (three seeds, pooled the same way). A-cams-lag-only K3's neural network plus the cloudiness column only. A-cams-real K3's neural network plus the realised unit PV shape and clear-sky index of the target half-hour, as in experiment 480 (report only; a serving system cannot supply them).

Verdict: not supported. The gate needed A-cams to lower CRPS at the eight by at least the minimum detectable effect (0.077), and A-cams raised it by 0.006. The interval excludes a gain of 0.053 (15% of experiment 480's 0.355), so at this design the neural network gained no detectable improvement from the older satellite sunshine we gave it.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Design. Five monthly folds (2025-10, 2025-12, 2026-01, 2026-03, 2026-06), seeds 0 to 2, experiment 470's intersection of rows (experiment_470_intersection_v1), widening 1.15, the D15 and D18 start cut of 2025-03-01, flagged exact-zero half-hours dropped (1,179 scoring actuals, and 2,155 to 2,925 fine-tuning rows per fold), valid times from 2026-07-01 not scored. Monthly refits; each network starts from the stored pretrained arm A weights of the same month and seed, with zero weights for the new first-layer columns, then fine-tunes at a learning rate of 2e-4. Code: this folder, importing experiments 397, 425, 454, 470, and 494 (the scoring pattern). Fitted networks: the experiment's private work/models/ folder, never in git.
  • Columns. Origins are 09:00 UTC. For an origin on date D0 the cutoff is 21:00 UTC on D0-2, so the latest wholly available day is D0-3, which ends 57 hours before the origin. The three columns are: (a) the CAMS irradiance at the target half-hour's time of day on that day. (b) the mean of that irradiance over that day and the two before, and (c) the day's summed irradiance over its summed clear-sky irradiance. The lag-features study found the previous whole day available at 09:00 UTC after February 2026, so a service could be one to two days fresher than this design.
  • Minimum detectable effect (three seeds, five folds). 0.077 points at the eight and 0.124 at the six (experiment 428's definition, from the seed spread of the stored arm A). Bonferroni count 12 (3 arms x 2 groups x CRPS and q99 pinball loss); 100,000 origin-day block-bootstrap resamples.
  • CRPS, difference to K3 (points; Bonferroni interval).
Arm Eight Six (no labelled event) A-cams +0.006 [+0.001, +0.011] +0.010 [+0.004, +0.017] A-cams-lag-only +0.004 [-0.000, +0.009] +0.009 [+0.003, +0.015] A-cams-real (report only) -0.318 [-0.393, -0.246] -0.467 [-0.577, -0.359]
  • Absolute CRPS (points). At the eight: K3 4.699, A-cams 4.705, A-cams-lag-only 4.703, and A-cams-real 4.381. At the six: K3 3.463, A-cams 3.474, A-cams-lag-only 3.472, and A-cams-real 2.997.
  • Equivalence at the 0.02 limit. The q99 pinball loss difference of A-cams is +0.001 at the eight (upper bound +0.002) and -0.000 at the six (upper +0.001), so A-cams is equivalent to K3 in the q99 tail at both groups. CRPS at the six is not tested for equivalence, because the minimum detectable effect there (0.124) exceeds 0.02.
  • Tails. q99 coverage is 0.9908 (A-cams) against 0.9911 (K3) at the eight and 0.9845 against 0.9847 at the six; q95 coverage 0.949 against 0.950 and 0.922 against 0.924. q99 pinball loss 0.252 (A-cams) against 0.251 (K3) at the eight. A-cams-real has q99 pinball loss 0.238 at the eight.
  • Where the realised arm gains. By lead at the eight: -0.134 at day 1, -0.256 at days 2 to 5, -0.407 at days 6 to 10. On sunny midday rows (clear-sky index at least 0.7, 10:00 to 15:00 UTC) -1.110 at the eight and -1.222 at the six. At D12 alone -0.635 (K3's CRPS there is 8.589), and at the eight without D12 -0.273. The realised arm gains nothing at D8 (+0.005) and in the 2025-12 fold (+0.038 at the eight), and it loses on cold winter nights: +0.098 at the eight and +0.121 at the six.
  • Descriptive slices for A-cams (95% intervals, not corrected). D12 alone +0.014 [+0.002, +0.027]; the eight without D12 +0.005 [+0.001, +0.009]; cold winter nights +0.008 at the eight [-0.005, +0.022] and +0.008 at the six [-0.005, +0.021]; the 12 to 36 hour band +0.004 at the eight [-0.000, +0.009] and +0.013 at the six [+0.006, +0.020]; sunny midday -0.004 at the eight [-0.013, +0.004] and -0.015 at the six [-0.029, -0.001]. Fold by fold at the eight A-cams ranges from -0.003 to +0.018.
  • Avoidable-curtailment cost at the six, difference to K3 (experiment 470's measure). At f = 0.9: A-cams +0.016 [-0.001, +0.048], A-cams-real +0.129 [-0.012, +0.353]. At f = 0.75: +0.082 [+0.001, +0.206] and +0.809 [-0.035, +1.997]. At f = 0.5: +0.111 [-0.031, +0.327] and +0.091 [-1.704, +2.410]. The realised columns therefore do not lower the curtailment cost at the six, although they lower CRPS. All the neural networks cost far less than manual_heuristic at f = 0.75 and 0.5 (K3 -5.8 and -16.1).
  • D15 and D18 (report only). CRPS 10.83 (K3), 10.86 (A-cams), 10.50 (A-cams-real).
  • Why the leak-free columns do not help (tested). (1) The validation loss of the fine-tuned A-cams neural network is higher than the stored arm A's in 14 of 15 fits (mean +0.0008), so the fine-tune found no use for the columns. (2) The daily correlation of cloudiness between two days is 0.25 at one day, 0.16 at three days, and 0.10 at seven (figure 4), so a three-day-old value holds little information. (3) The same fine-tune does use the realised columns (validation loss 0.24 to 0.29 against 0.33 to 0.39), so the recipe can use informative columns. (4) Setting the A-cams columns to their training mean at forecast time changes CRPS by -0.006 [-0.013, +0.000] at the eight, and moving the day one day earlier changes it by +0.000 [-0.006, +0.006]. A null here may still mean that the columns were not learned in the fine-tune from zero weights; a retrained network was not tested.
  • Serving table. A-cams needs a CAMS feed that arrives about a day late (not ingested today), one stored cloudiness value per Primary per day plus three half-hourly values per target, and leaves the number of neural networks per pass unchanged. The fallback when the feed is late (set the columns to their training mean and widen the bands) changes CRPS by -0.006 points [-0.013, +0.000] at the eight (no loss) in the prediction-only check. Because A-cams gains nothing, adding the feed is not worth it. A-cams-real cannot be served at any lead, because its columns describe the target half-hour itself.
  • Fit times. 26 to 31 s for A-cams-lag-only and 29 to 60 s for A-cams-real per seed; 67 to 120 s for A-cams, which includes two extra prediction-only forecasts. 45 fine-tunes took about 1 hour of one GPU process.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean. The stored forecasts hold 11 quantiles only. The mean of the quantiles minus the median per site differs by under 0.03 points between K3 and A-cams (D12 +2.94 for both), so the new columns do not shift the forecast.
  • Median error beside CRPS. The mean absolute error of the median forecast moves with CRPS: K3 and A-cams agree to within 0.02 points at every Primary, and A-cams-real lowers it at 13 of 14 Primaries (at D8 it rises by 0.08).
  • Triggers of the audit rules. None fired. No control failed. The result contradicts the prediction (P1: a gain of 0.05 to 0.15), and the explanation tests above record why. The quantile-score and median-error contrasts agree. Leaving out D12 leaves the sign and verdict of the gate unchanged (+0.005 without D12). The nested arm A-cams-lag-only beats A-cams by 0.002, less than the half-width (0.005) of A-cams's interval. The realised arm's interval at the eight is 0.55 times as wide as experiment 480's.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Only a 36-hour-old feed was tested. A fresher feed (the previous whole day) was not fitted. The correlation in figure 4 suggests a small gain at most (0.25 at one day).
  • Selection bias. The five folds that choose the candidate also score it, and July 2026 stays unused.
  • Fine-tune only. The new columns start at zero weight and the network was fine-tuned for about 10 epochs, so the experiment cannot say whether a network trained with the columns from the start would use them.
  • The horizon is 1 to 10 days, the range NGED care about. The realised columns are an upper bound, because a service never has them.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Nowcast. Test a satellite or station nowcast of sunshine as an input at leads under 6 hours, where the ensemble's forecast is least accurate.
  • A fresher feed. A feed with the previous whole day (available at 09:00 UTC) has not been tested; testing it would take one arm and 15 fits, about 0.2 GPU-hours.
  • Sunshine forecast error. The realised arm's gain per lead band bounds what a better sunshine forecast could add (0.318 points, 6.8% of CRPS at the eight).

docs.title: Does one effective-capacity rule for wind and solar, the 99.9th percentile of the most recent 365 or 730 days of power, keep the quantile score and the upper tail at every series?
docs.text:
Take-home: setting each series' capacity (the power that stands for 1.0 in the neural network's input scale) from its last 730 days of power, instead of all earlier power, nearly gives one rule for wind and solar but still fails at three solar farms. The share of actuals above the 99% quantile forecast is 0.85% for wind and 1.45% for solar, against a limit of 1.5%, and the score of Solar A (one solar farm) worsens by 0.4% against the old capacity, down from 2.3% under experiment 461's rule. The rule written down before any fit still fails at Solar B (share 1.506%) and when Solar C or Solar D is left out of the solar total (1.537% and 1.517%). A 365-day window is worse.

Capacity is the divisor that turns a series' power into a fraction between 0 and 1 for the neural network. The margin is the largest worsening of a series' score the plan accepts (0.1% of capacity for wind, 1% of the pooled score for solar), and the Bonferroni interval widens the 95% interval to account for the 44 intervals reported. Experiment 461 set it to the 99.9th percentile of all earlier power, which suited the three wind farms and not Solar A or Solar E. Here the 99.9th percentile is taken over only the last 730 days (P-730) or 365 days (P-365) before each fit's training ends, and the same wind neural network (member_plain, 5 seeds) and solar network (a2_member, 3 seeds, 4 quarterly refits) are refitted. P-all is experiment 461's all-earlier-power rule and P-old is the 99th percentile of the whole record (experiments 429 and 430). Farms A to C are three metered wind farms and Solar A to F are six metered solar farms.

Terms. Table P, the limit (at most 1.5% of actuals above the 99% quantile forecast), and pooled (summed over all series of one technology) are as in experiment 461. A window with under 8,000 valid half-hours (solar: daylight half-hours) falls back to P-all.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• C1, wind: no rolling arm differs from P-all beyond fit-to-fit spread. Pooled score 1.1744 MW (P-all), 1.1757 (P-730), 1.1764 (P-365), 1.1765 (P-old). P-730 minus P-all is +0.0013 MW (95% interval +0.0003 to +0.0021; Bonferroni interval -0.0005 to +0.0024). Pooled share above q99: 0.882% (P-all), 0.849% (P-730), 0.883% (P-365). The minimum detectable effect is 0.0034 MW, the mean gap between two P-old single-seed fits. Margins are 0.0209 MW (Farm A), 0.0090 MW (Farm B), and 0.0027 MW (Farm C), so Farm C's margin is under the minimum detectable effect and its verdict is inconclusive. The wind decision rests on the pooled score and the tail limit, and both pass.
  • C2, solar P-730 fails the rule narrowly. Pooled score 0.6602 MW against 0.6627 (P-all) and 0.6601 (P-old). Pooled share 1.449% (passes). Series above 1.5%: Solar B 1.506% and Solar E 2.355%. Dropping one series leaves pooled shares of 1.451% (A), 1.437% (B), 1.537% (C), 1.517% (D), 1.297% (E), 1.460% (F), so dropping C or D fails the pooled rule. No series worsens by more than the margin of 1% of the pooled old score (0.0066 MW; Solar F +0.0038 MW is the largest).
  • C3, solar P-365 fails more. Pooled share 1.496%; Solar A 1.535%, Solar B 1.552%, Solar E 2.365% are above 1.5%; dropping C, D, or F gives 1.569%, 1.576%, 1.513%. Solar D and Solar E fall back to P-all at every refit, so there they equal P-all. Solar A's score is 1.68% better than P-old (95% interval -0.0192 to -0.0004 MW), not significant after the Bonferroni correction for 44 intervals.
  • Solar A follows its capacity. Score against P-old: +2.29% (P-all, ratio 1.14), +0.44% (P-730, ratio 1.105 and 1.039 at the last refit), -1.68% (P-365, ratio 1.017 and 1.002). P-730 minus P-all at Solar A is -0.0096 MW (-1.81%; Bonferroni interval -0.0177 to -0.0012). This fits the hypothesis that Solar A's high capacity under P-all is the cause. A level shift in Solar A's earlier output is a hypothesis: experiment 453 covers April to August only, and this page does not test it. The trailing p99.9 in figure 3 follows the monthly maximum only loosely.
  • Solar E is untestable. Its history (21,852 to 31,278 half-hours) is under 730 days, so P-730 equals P-all there, and P-365 falls back. Solar E stays at 2.35% to 2.37% above q99 in both arms, against 2.41% for P-all. The cause is unknown: experiment 461 remarked that Solar E's short history makes its capacity noisy, without testing whether that explains the tail. Two fits with the same capacity (P-all and P-730) differ by about 0.05 points of share, which is noise on a 1.5% limit.
  • Tails after table P, pooled (cover at nominal 1%, 5%, 95%, 99%). Wind P-all, P-730, P-365: q01 1.35%, 1.37%, 1.37%; q05 5.44%, 5.53%, 5.52%; q95 95.13%, 95.25%, 95.23%; q99 99.12%, 99.15%, 99.12%; q99 pinball 0.0641 MW in all three. Solar: q01 3.29%, 3.28%, 3.29%; q05 6.69%, 6.68%, 6.79%; q95 94.45%, 94.66%, 94.59%; q99 98.50%, 98.55%, 98.50%; q99 pinball 0.0248, 0.0247, 0.0244 MW. Solar D's q01 coverage is 12.3% in every arm, so the capacity rule does not cause it.
  • Capacities (new over old, P-730 and P-365 at the last refit): Farm A 1.027 and 1.027, B 1.041 and 1.057, C 1.067 and 1.036; Solar A 1.039 and 1.002, B 1.121 and 1.125, C 1.053 and 1.040, D 1.083 and 1.079 (fallback), E 1.057 and 1.057 (fallback), F 1.058 and 1.060. The window half-hours above each capacity number 22 to 36 for P-730 (Solar E 22 to 29) and 15 to 18 for P-365 (Solar D and Solar E fall back; full table in work/report505.txt).
  • Rows, seeds, cadence. Rows are equal across arms: wind 54,899 scored forecasts (one per forecast run and lead), solar 345,510. Seeds: 5 wind, 3 solar. Solar refits are quarterly and wind is one fit, as in experiment 461; the difference between P-730 and P-all could depend on the refit schedule. Bonferroni count: 44 intervals (two rolling arms, two references, 11 each), level 99.89%; leave-one-out intervals are extra and carry no Bonferroni correction. Production effort: one number per series per refit from power already stored.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The 1.5% limit is a point-estimate rule. Solar B at 1.506% and Solar A at 1.535% are within noise of the limit, and no interval is computed for a share, so the verdict "fails" is the pre-registered rule applied literally.
  • Capacity is fixed per fit. The arms therefore differ in the training-target scale as well as in the divisor.
  • Retraining schedule is experiment 461's (wind one fit, solar quarterly), not weekly.
  • Scored range stops at true day 10 (lead 240 hours); solar scoring is not restricted to 12 to 36 hours.
  • The avoidable-curtailment cost does not apply to wind and solar farms.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Reviews. A fresh Sonnet reviewed the plan and the code before the first fit, a second re-derived the headline numbers from the stored forecasts, and a third reviewed the prose; each is triaged in the pull request.
  • Mean of the median forecast minus the actual, pooled after table P. Wind -0.64 MW (P-old), -0.61 (P-all), -0.61 (P-730), -0.63 (P-365). Solar +0.089, +0.078, +0.089, +0.092 MW. Per series the largest moves are Solar E (+0.37, +0.43, +0.48 MW under P-all, P-730, P-365) and Solar A (+0.099, +0.061, +0.013 MW).
  • Triggers. One audit trigger is met: dropping Solar C or Solar D flips the pooled share rule under P-730. That leave-one-out condition is part of the rule written before any fit, so the flip is the reported result and the verdict was already "not supported". The check that a capacity ratio of 1 reproduces experiment 461's forecasts was not rerun, because only capacity() differs from experiment 461's fit loop, whose check passed.
  • Margin clause. The rule's "no series worsens by more than the margin" clause is applied to point estimates. The upper 95% bounds at Solar A (+0.0082 MW) and Solar F (+0.0074 MW) exceed the 0.0066 MW margin.
  • Minimum detectable effect. The 0.0034 MW is the gap between two P-old single-seed fits; the five P-all fits differ by 0.0077 MW and the P-730 fits by 0.0047 MW, so the true minimum detectable effect is probably larger.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Keep the all-history p99.9 for wind and the old capacity for Solar A and Solar E.
  • If one rule is still wanted, judge the 1.5% limit by an interval on the share, and test a 730-day window at Solar A and Solar E with a weekly refit.

docs.title: What can the data not yet used say about the sign of real power at the eight Primaries whose meters report apparent power only?
docs.text:
Take-home. A dip of the apparent power towards zero at sunny middays is a useful screen but not a signed label. Eight primary substations (D2, D3, D4, D8, D12, D19, D21, D22) have meters that report apparent power in MVA, which includes reactive power and is never negative, so NGED has no signed history of real power (MW) there. We asked whether four kinds of evidence not used before can say whether real power ever changes sign at those eight. We measured how low the meter reading falls on sunny middays, and we calibrated that dip against the six primary substations that report signed MW, after adding the recorded output of a real solar farm to their demand. We tried a rule that compares expected solar output with expected demand, and we read the upstream meters and the metered generator behind D8. When the reading carries no reactive power, the dip finds almost every sign change. At power factor 0.97 (the realistic case, where reactive power is about a quarter of the demand) the threshold that finds 89% of the added sign changes also flags 34% of days that have none, in a test that leaves one primary substation out at a time.

Verdict: partly supported. No forecasting model was fitted, so there is no forecast score. The Bonferroni count (the number of intervals reported) is 70. This page is interim. Counts are lower bounds, because NGED's event labels are incomplete.

Terms. The dip is the lowest reading of the day between 10:00 and 15:00 UK time, on days with a clear-sky index of 0.7 or more. The reactive floor is a reactive-power term added to the real power to mimic an MVA meter. An injection level of 2.0 means the added solar farm is twice the median sunny-midday reading. The area under the curve is the chance that a randomly chosen sign-change day has a lower dip than a randomly chosen ordinary day (1.0 is perfect, 0.5 is chance). Gated means the rule applies only when the sun is high enough.

docs.title: Part 1: dip depth (one table of the eight)
docs.text:
• Statistic. For each UK day with at least 6 sunny half-hours (clear-sky index 0.7 or more, UK clock 10:00 to 15:00), the minimum reading. A crossing is a day on which the signed power is both below and above zero in the window. Cleaned power, July 2026 untouched, D15 and D18 cut before 2025-03-01.
  • Calibration at the six (pooled, 5,155 to 5,392 days). Injected solar farms are labelled Solar A to C and sized as in experiment 408 (level 1.0 and 2.0 times the median sunny-midday reading). Crossing counts at level 0 (real): 63 days: 58 at D10 and 5 at D5; at level 1.0, 1,300; at level 2.0, 1,568.
  • Area under the curve (reactive floor 0, 2, and 4 points are identical because a constant floor does not change the ranking). Level 0: 0.995 (0.990 to 0.999). Level 1.0: 0.954 (0.941 to 0.967). Level 2.0: 0.916 (0.899 to 0.931). Power factor 0.97: level 0: 0.995 (0.990 to 0.998); level 1.0: 0.879 (0.847 to 0.910); level 2.0: 0.838 (0.808 to 0.867). The difference between floor 0 and power factor 0.97 is 0.075 (0.055 to 0.096) at level 1.0 and 0.078 (0.061 to 0.095) at level 2.0 (minimum detectable effect 0.029 and 0.024, 2.8 standard errors, shared month-block resamples).
  • Threshold, frozen on the six at level 2.0 before the eight were read. Floor 0: 6.9 points of capacity, true-positive rate 0.87 and false-positive rate 0.20 leaving one Primary out. Power factor 0.97: 19.1 points, true-positive 0.89 and false-positive 0.34 leaving one Primary out.
  • Applied to the eight (raw MVA reading, floor-0 threshold 6.9 points). Share of sunny days below the threshold: D8 6.7% (minimum reading 0.26 points), D22 1.2% (minimum 0.16), D12 1.2% (minimum 5.0), D2, D3, D21 0%, D4 and D19 0%. For comparison, D5 (5 sign-change days at level 0) has 2.7% of days below it and D10 (real reverse flow) 11.8%. The power factor 0.97 threshold (19.1 points) flags 17.8% to 23.9% of days at D8, D12, and D22 and 46.1% at D5, which has almost none, so it does not discriminate.
  • Pre-registered statements. The area under the curve is at least 0.8 at floor 0: met (lower end 0.899). The prediction that only D12 dips and D8 does not is not met: D8 and D22 dip, and D12 does not (experiment 370 found reverse flow at D12). NGED's own labels: D8 "Yes", D12 and D22 "Maybe", the other five "No"; the dip share agrees with the label at D8 and D22 and disagrees at D12. The prediction of 0.6 to 0.7 at power factor 0.97 was too low (0.84 to 0.88); the pre-registered rule (area under the curve below 0.7) does not bar a detection claim, but a delivered signed label may not claim to detect a crossing, because the false-positive rate is 34% leaving one Primary out; this is stricter than the pre-registered rule.

docs.title: Part 4: gated rule (circular, diagnostic only)
docs.text:
• Rule. Reverse flow if the unit PV shape is at least 0.3 and capacity times shape exceeds the night-time demand level of the same month and day type. Capacity: experiment 474's 2025 AC capacity (p10, p50, p90) in points of capacity. That table was fitted on the signed power of the Primary it labels and failed its placebo gate at every rung (95th-percentile placebo recovery 0.25 to 0.51), so every Part 4 figure at the six is circular. Experiments 477 and 479 recover 0.62 to 0.72 of a known capacity. At level 2.0 the injected farm's size is added to the capacity.
  • Result at the six (p50 capacity). Pooled false-reverse rate on reverse-free sunny half-hours: 18.6% at level 0 and 53.4% at level 2.0, against experiment 408's 3.6%; recall 98.1% and 99.1%. Per Primary (level 0) D5 37.9% and D10 58.1%. The rule calls reverse flow far too often because night-time demand is below daytime demand and no temperature adjustment was made.
  • Decision. Not an improvement on experiment 408's rule: the line is closed as implemented. Comparison with experiment 412 was not made at D5 and D10, because the rule's false-reverse rate is already far above the 6.7% to 16.9% that experiment 412 reached.
  • The eight. No stored capacity table covers them. At the six's capacities (29.6 to 55.0 points) the rule calls reverse flow on 56% to 75% of gated sunny half-hours at D12 and 0% to 61% elsewhere: D12 stands apart because its night-time demand level is 21 points against 39 to 60 elsewhere.

docs.title: Part 2: short check
docs.text:
• Units and negatives (cleaned readings). All four nodes report signed MW. Negative share: D1 69.4%, D6 33.3%, D17 8.8%, D13 1.1%. D1 is mostly generation (69.4% negative) and D6 partly so (33.3%).
  • Children and metered share. D1: 13 children in the hierarchy file, 8 in our series (4 of the eight: D2, D4, D19, D21); D13: 12 and 7 (the same four); D6: 17 and 12 (D3, D8, D12, D22); D17: 16 and 11 (the same four). Share metered 58% to 71%, so the unmetered remainder is too large for a closure to resolve a sign; experiment 152 found a D12 closure coefficient of 1.02, a variance cut of 0.7%, and an interval that includes zero.
  • Generator behind D8 (a metered gas engine; experiment 182). On 392 sunny-midday half-hours with generator data its output stays below D8's night-time demand level at every half-hour, so it gives no evidence of export (the generator's MW and D8's MVA are compared directly; units unchecked). The hierarchy files do not link generators to Primaries, so the other seven cannot be checked.

docs.title: Part 3: what a delivered label could claim
docs.text:
• Wording. "Inferred; reverse flow is possible at D8, D22, and D12 (NGED marks D8 'Yes' and D12 and D22 'Maybe'); the signed forecast equals the apparent-power forecast elsewhere." At power factor 0.97, the realistic case, a dip is not a detection.
  • Evidence. D8 and D22 dip to 0.26 and 0.16 points on at least one sunny day, mostly since 2024 at D8; D12 does not in the 10:00 to 15:00 window (minimum 5.0 points), which the audit traced to the window rather than to an absence of crossings, and experiment 370's fit found reverse flow there. Nothing here is proof.
  • False-reverse. Dip threshold at power factor 0.97: 34% leaving one Primary out. Experiment 412: 6.7% to 16.9%. Experiment 408: 3.6% at level 2.0. Gated rule here: 19% to 53%.
  • What an estimate adds at a Primary with no reverse flow. The estimate adds nothing, and five of the eight never dip in the window.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median forecast minus mean forecast per site and the error of the mean forecast: not applicable, no forecast was made.
  • Triggers fired. The trigger "a result contradicts its own prediction" fired: the prediction that only D12 dips was contradicted. A fresh Sonnet audit re-derived the numbers from raw data (all matched, no code bug) and tested the explanations; its report is in the private briefs/506_audit.md.

docs.title: Audit findings (why D8 and D22 dip and D12 does not)
docs.text:
• The fixed 10:00 to 15:00 window is the main reason D12 is missed (supported). D12 exports strongly at midday: on clear May to July days its median midday apparent power is 81.6 points against 15.6 in dark hours, so the midday reading never nears zero (0% of days below 6.9 points). The crossing, if there is one, happens in the shoulders: 7.2% of April to August days have a daily minimum below 6.9 points between 05:00 and 08:00 and 5.9% between 17:00 and 20:00. Over the whole day the share is 24% at D12, 19% at D8, 2.3% at D22, and 0% at D2 and D4. The window dip statistic therefore cannot confirm or deny reverse flow at a strongly exporting Primary, and the same blindness carries into the six-Primary calibration.
  • D12's 13 in-window dips are not solar (supported). All fall from October to February at low sun and low demand.
  • D8 and D22 dips are not outages, flagged readings, or holiday effects (supported). Dark-hour readings are normal (a dark-hour daily minimum below 6.9 points on 1.0% of D8 days and 0.0% of D22 days), the dips are short runs of 3 to 4 half-hours inside 08:00 to 17:00, and the dip rate rises with clear-sky index at D8 from 1.1% on cloudy days to 7.8% on clear days.
  • The D8 dips are recent (supported). Share of sunny days below 6.9 points at D8: 0% in 2019 to 2022, 0.7% in 2023, 3.9% in 2024, 23% in 2025, and 32% in 2026. At D22: 0% to 2022, then 0.7%, 2.4%, 4.2%, and 2.5%. This fits new embedded generation or a changed load arrangement, and fits experiment 370's finding that D8's fit moved between its two cuts.
  • Untested. Whether the D8 and D22 dips are solar output or load switched away in the daytime (D8's median midday power is 54 points against 55 at night), and whether a reactive floor of about 5 points explains D12's shoulder minima.
  • Deviations: the window and months use the UK clock, while experiment 412's use UTC; the power factor arm's demand proxy is the night-time level, which understates daytime demand; month blocks pool the six Primaries.

docs.title: Code review findings accepted as caveats (Parts 2 and 4)
docs.text:
• The unit of the capacity is unverified: 474's AC capacity in points is multiplied by a shape scaled by experiment 412's pooled 99th percentile, so every Part 4 call could be off by a constant factor.
  • The gross demand is the night-time level over all years (the tested period included), not the plan's stored demand forecast adjusted for temperature; it is biased low, which explains the high false-reverse rate. The plan's margin was not applied.
  • The capacity is the 2025 season-year row, fitted on the tested rows (circular), and at level 2.0 the capacity adds the injected size (an oracle). Rows where the farm has a gap are dropped.
  • Intervals are plain 95% month-block intervals; the Bonferroni count is stated but no interval is widened by it; undefined bootstrap draws were dropped silently. The false-reverse rate is on gated rows, a different population from experiment 408's 3.6%, so the comparison is indicative only.
  • For the eight, the shares called are shares of half-hours, not false-reverse rates, and the demand level is built from MVA, which includes reactive power.
  • The metered share counts only children with a series in our set, so it is a lower bound. The generator behind D8 was identified from experiment 182, not from the hierarchy files.

docs.title: Reuse and cost
docs.text: CPU only, a few minutes per script. Scripts import experiment 87's grid_times and read experiment 412's stored CAMS arrays, experiment 39's farm frame, and experiment 474's table.

docs.title: Is there enough to gain from repairing shifted power readings, rather than down-weighting them, to justify a learned 14-day history encoder?
docs.text:
This page is interim and unaudited: it reports a perfect repair of shifted lag readings (an oracle) and one non-learned repair, and no learned encoder. We asked whether the power readings of the last 14 days need repairing, or whether down-weighting them (as experiments 402 to 482 did) is enough. We injected shifts into the readings of 14 Primary substations: temporary load transfers (family A), and genuine level changes that move the true power (family B). We retrained the lag correction of experiment 472, a small neural network that adjusts the forecast using the last three lag readings, and scored it with the lags repaired in three ways: not repaired ("plain"), repaired by an oracle that knows the injected shift, and repaired by total-variation denoising of the 14-day residual (the reading minus the forecast of a model that has no power input).

The learned encoder (rung T1) was not run because the line is paused, not because a kill rule fired. The oracle improved the score, so the stop rule (a) did not fire. The non-learned repair did not keep half of the oracle's gain, so rule (b), which would have promoted it in place of the encoder, did not fire either. The next step would have been the noise curve and one encoder fit.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Scores are CRPS in points of capacity (lower is better), on the four screen folds (2026-06, 2026-01, 2025-10, 2026-03), three fit seeds each, on held-out injected worlds 200 to 202. "The six" are the six Primaries that report signed MW, and "the eight" are the eight that report MVA only. The minimum detectable effect (MDE) is experiment 454's formula: 2.8 times the mean standard deviation of paired seed differences, over the square root of 4 folds. Intervals are the exact 95% month-block resamples of the four fold means, a coarse resample. The weather is ERA5 reanalysis and CAMS in both history and forecast, with one seed.

Rows and worlds Group Oracle minus plain Total-variation minus plain Old worlds (experiment 428): harm and target rows with an injected shift six -0.214 (-0.314 to -0.132), MDE 0.014 not run Old worlds: same rows eight -0.466 (-0.581 to -0.309), MDE 0.223 not run New generator worlds: rows where a shift touches a lag six -0.589 (-0.674 to -0.505), MDE 0.089 +0.045 (-0.006 to +0.139) New generator worlds: same rows eight -0.727 (-0.793 to -0.661), MDE 0.088 -0.012 (-0.018 to -0.005)
  • Rule (a) did not fire: repairing the lags helps. At the six, the old-world oracle gain was 15.6 times the MDE, with an interval excluding zero. At the eight it was 2.1 times the MDE. The zero-lag control (experiment 472's correction with all lag inputs set to zero) was worse than plain by 0.49 (six) and 0.91 (eight) points on the old worlds, and by 2.43 and 2.65 on the new worlds, so the lag readings carry information.
  • The oracle gain sits on temporary shifts. On new-world rows where a temporary (family A) shift touches a lag, the oracle gain was 1.25 (six) and 1.58 (eight) points. Where only a genuine (family B) shift touches a lag, it was 0.24 and 0.24. The oracle that removes a constant level per temporary shift (oracle-constant) gained 0.57 (six) and 0.68 (eight) over plain, close to the exact oracle, so most of the gain needs only the right level.
  • The oracle's gain depends on how it is applied. Training on shifted lags and scoring on exact lags (oracle re-prediction) gained 0.18 (six) and 0.21 (eight) on the old worlds, against 0.21 and 0.47 for the retrained oracle. The old-world gain at the eight roughly halves.
  • Prediction P1 (an oracle gain of at least 0.3 points) was met on the new worlds and at the eight on the old worlds, and was missed at the six on the old worlds (0.21).
  • Total-variation repair did not keep half of the oracle gain, on the new generator worlds. The paired difference between the repair's loss and the halfway point to the oracle was +0.34 (0.25 to 0.45) at the six and +0.35 (0.31 to 0.39) at the eight; a negative value would have meant the repair keeps more than half. At the six the repair was worse than plain by 0.045 points. At the eight it kept 1.6% of the oracle gain (0.012 of 0.727). With 60% of the steps genuine, instead of the generator's 79%, the paired difference was +0.37 and +0.38, so the result did not change at that share. The repair was not run on the old worlds.
  • Rows with no shift touching a lag. The repair's change in CRPS against plain was +0.028 (-0.000 to +0.084) at the six and 0.000 at the eight, and in q99 pinball loss +0.011 (-0.000 to +0.031) at the six and +0.000 at the eight. The rule's bound applies to rows with no labelled event on the old worlds, which were not scored for this repair, so the bound was not tested. The oracle, retrained on exact lags, was 0.09 points worse than plain on these rows at the six (0.016 to 0.185) and 0.05 worse at the eight (0.03 to 0.09). We have not tested why.

docs.title: Tuning, and why the repair result is weak
docs.text: The tuning picked the weakest repair, so this test cannot show whether any non-learned repair works. On a separate tuning world (origins in 2024, no scored month), all 30 settings (6 weights times 5 values of tau) gave a larger mean lag error than no repair (0.124 spreads, where a spread is the Primary's residual standard deviation). The best setting, weight 16 and tau 5, the largest of each, gave 0.127. The criterion averages over all tuning windows, most of which have no shift touching a lag, and any repair adds noise to those windows. A setting tuned only on windows with a temporary shift in force was not tried, because the plan fixed the criterion before any score was read. The take-home message therefore does not claim that total-variation denoising cannot tell a temporary shift from a genuine level change; this test never examined that.

docs.title: Outcome against the plan
docs.text: Item Outcome Rule (a): stop if the oracle does not beat plain by more than the MDE Did not fire (old worlds, both groups) Rule (b): promote total-variation repair if it keeps at least half the oracle gain Did not fire (new worlds); not run on old worlds Rule (c): stop the encoder if its errors fall where the noise curve keeps under half the gain Not evaluated: no encoder, no noise curve P1: oracle gain of at least 0.3 points Partly met (above) P2: total-variation repair keeps under half Met on the new worlds; weak evidence (tuning) P3: encoder errors fall in the useful part of the noise curve Not tested

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The lab setting flatters detection. ERA5 knows the weather that happened, so the reading minus the forecast is smaller than at serving. A single-seed null is informative only when far from the MDE, and the six-Primary total-variation result (+0.045, MDE 0.089) is not far from it.
  • The NGED event labels are incomplete, so counts of events are lower bounds.
  • Generator. The generator makes 79% of the steps in force at the origin genuine, not the planned 60%. The 79% follows from the shares and durations chosen (derived 78%).
  • Code review. A code review found 12 problems before any number was read. Seven were fixed: the oracle now uses the cleaned readings, events are a function of seed, Primary, and day, the size cap applies to the final step, circuit events draw a fraction of 0.3 to 1, the self-test tolerance is relative, an N0 slice no longer wraps, and the injection spread comes from the earliest table. Not fixed: the oracle and plain fit seeds are not paired by world, which makes the seed spread in the MDE approximate; the row count was not asserted against experiment 404's scoring rows. The review's other findings were fixed or do not change a number.
  • N0. Of the 34 events with a measured deviation, the median coefficient of variation of the deviation is 0.44, and 29 have a correlation above 0.5 with the Primary's own daily demand, so a flat step describes most real events poorly. The generator draws shapes in the planned thirds regardless (tables in the private work/n0/ folder).

docs.title: Do dips of apparent power in the sun-position shoulders show reverse flow at D12, and are the D8 and D22 midday dips solar output, load transfers, or a gas engine running?
Results
docs.text:
Take-home. A dip of the apparent power at the sun's edges is much better than a midday dip at telling when a substation's power changes sign, but only up to export about three times the night import, and D12 (about five times) lies beyond what we could calibrate. At D12 the shoulder dips are as common on cloudy days and in the dark as on sunny days, so they show low demand and not solar export. At D8, 55 of the 71 midday dip days have an engine running at most dip half-hours, which is consistent with the gas engine, although the engine flag also tracks any low D8 reading and so is weak evidence. The data cannot say which cause explains the other 16 D8 dip days or the 13 D22 dip days, and the sunny-versus-cloudy test does not support a solar cause at D22. Verdict: partly supported. The audit is recorded below. Counts are lower bounds, because NGED's event labels are incomplete.

What we asked. Experiment 506 looked for a dip of the apparent power (MVA, never negative) only between 10:00 and 15:00. We asked two questions. First, does a dip at the edges of the sun's path find the days when power changes sign better than a midday dip, once the export is several times the night-time import, as at D12? Second, are the short midday dips at D8 and D22 solar export, a load transfer, or the gas engine behind D8? We added recorded solar-farm output (Solar A to C) to the six primary substations that report signed power, at 1, 2, 4, and 8 times their median sunny midday reading, and measured how well each window's lowest reading finds the days on which the signed power changes sign. No forecasting model was fitted.

Terms. D2 to D22 are NGED's primary substations (a Primary is a substation that steps 33 kV down to 11 kV). The six are the Primaries that report signed real power in megawatts (MW). The eight (D2, D3, D4, D8, D12, D19, D21, D22) report apparent power in megavolt-amperes (MVA), which includes reactive power and is never negative. A reading is in points of the substation's capacity. The export-to-import ratio is the midday reading divided by the night-time reading on clear days from May to July. The area under the curve is the chance that a day on which the power changes sign has a lower window minimum than a day on which it does not (1.0 is perfect, 0.5 is chance); a window is usable when the area is at least 0.8 and its interval's lower end is above 0.6. Floor 0 and power factor 0.97 are two ways of making the six's readings look like apparent power. A placebo is the same statistic on days or hours where no export is expected. NGED is National Grid Electricity Distribution, and CAMS is the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service, the source of the clear-sky index.

docs.title: Figures
docs.text:
Figure 1: how well each window finds sign-change days, by export-to-import ratio.

Figure 2: share of days with a midday dip at D8 and D22, by year.

Figure 3: share of D8's dip half-hours flagged as engine running.

Figure 4: how often the shape test calls a drop solar-shaped, on known answers and on the dip days.

docs.title: Part A: the shoulders
docs.text:
• Windows. Shoulders are the half-hours with the sun between 5.6 and 19.0 degrees above the horizon (where the clear-sky fleet shape is 0.05 to 0.3), rising for the morning and setting for the evening. April to September only. Day-worlds (a day counted once per injected level): 3,329 (ratio below 1.5), 1,529 (1.5 to 3), 829 (3 to 6), and 429 (above 6). The farm shape was extended below 15 degrees of elevation on about 11% of half-hours.
