  • Differentiable physics: literature scan

docs.title: Differentiable physics: literature scan
docs.text:
This page holds bare-bones notes from a small literature scan, made on 2026-10-20 to inform the design of the differentiable-physics experiments. A Sonnet agent read the papers listed in the last section in full. Every number below comes from the full text of the paper named, and all the papers are held in the project's private library folder literature/papers/. The notes are a working record, not a reviewed survey. The project's main review is The current state of the art in energy forecasting. The papers report a normalised root mean square error (nRMSE) and a normalised ranked probability score (nRPS), each in its own normalisation.

Scope caveat for all GAM results: they are regional or national load (GB GSP Groups, France, US cities), day-ahead, not Primary substations.

docs.title: 1. Tricks we're missing (ranked)
docs.text:
1. Put the Kalman state on the coefficients of the frozen GAM effects, with learned diagonal noise, not only on a level plus anomaly.
    • Paper: de Vilmarest et al. (2024), Sec. II-B, Table I. Freeze the fitted effects, standardise them, and let the weight vector theta_t of (effects, intercept) follow a random walk. Q is diagonal, found by greedy likelihood (R package viking).
    • Gain (14 GB GSP Groups, 2021, nRMSE): Kalman-dynamic 0.332 vs offline GAM 0.635, GAM refitted yearly 0.387, GAM refitted daily 0.377, Kalman with Q=0 (static) 0.380. So: Q=0 only matches daily refits; the learned Q is what wins (about 12% better than daily refitting).
    • Second source: de Vilmarest and Goude (2022), Table III (MAE in MW, competition month): linear model offline 22.8, dynamic 14.9, dynamic with Q set big and proportional to I 11.2, VIKING 11.5. Q proportional to I was best there but not in the pre-competition data, so the Q choice depends on how much the data drifts.
    • Slot-in: after the convex fit, freeze the fitted columns (daily profile, heating, solar, holiday). Run a Kalman filter whose state is one multiplier per block of hours on each column. Experiment 106 filtered only level and anomaly; this lets heating sensitivity and PV scale adapt.
    • Cost: CPU seconds per site per year for the filter; minutes to fit Q on a training year.
  2. Let the Kalman state learn capacities, so the explicit capacity input matters less.
    • Paper: de Vilmarest et al. (2024), Sec. IV-D. Remove the embedded solar and wind capacity inputs: offline nRMSE rises by more than 10%; Kalman-adapted nRMSE falls by 0.4%. Scope: 2019, GB GSP Groups.
    • Slot-in: our convex PV capacity is already non-decreasing; a PV-scale multiplier in trick 1 gives a cheap second estimate, and the gap between the two flags capacity steps.
    • Cost: free once trick 1 exists.
  3. Fit the quantile regression on the Kalman residuals (not the offline residuals), with the GAM prediction, its square, and hour-of-day as covariates; optionally adapt it online.
    • Paper: de Vilmarest et al. (2024), Table II (nRPS, 2019 / 2020 / 2021): offline GAM + offline quantile regression 0.231 / 0.338 / 0.454; Kalman Gaussian quantiles 0.212 / 0.217 / 0.222; Kalman + offline quantile regression 0.206 / 0.214 / 0.217; Kalman + online gradient descent with step size chosen by Bernstein online aggregation (BOA) 0.202 / 0.201 / 0.209.
    • Reading: nearly all the gain comes from filtering the mean (0.231 to 0.206 in 2019). The extra from the online quantile step is 2 to 6%.
    • Slot-in: replace our residual-quantile spread by the covariate quantile regression. Online gradient descent on the pinball loss is five lines. Cost: CPU seconds.
  4. Covariate-dependent Generalised Pareto tails for the extreme quantiles.
    • Paper: Browell and Fasiolo (2021), Sec. V-B and Table IV. Quantile regression on GAM residuals for the body; GPD beyond the 1st and 99th percentile with a scale that depends on covariates. Plain quantile regression is not calibrated beyond 1% and 99%. The conditional GPD cut upward reserve by up to 24.6% and downward by up to 10.8% against a static GPD (probability levels 0.01% to 0.25%).
    • Fit in mgcv (R); in Python it needs a small custom maximum-likelihood fit. Fits our curtailment-tail goal. Cost: CPU minutes per site.
  5. Learn the observation variance online (VIKING) rather than a fixed sigma.
    • Paper: de Vilmarest (2022); used in de Vilmarest and Goude (2022) Table III (VIKING 11.5 vs dynamic 14.9 on the linear model; no better than hand-set big Q). Gain is modest and mainly saves tuning. Cost: CPU seconds.
  6. Exponentially smoothed temperatures with two time constants, plus smoothed daily min and max.
    • Obst et al. (2021), Sec. 3: GAM terms f(Temp95), f(Temp99), f(TempMin99, TempMax99), f(t, Temp), factors per step on half-hourly data. Also the GEFCom2014 winner's smoothed temperature, alpha = 0.95 (Fasiolo et al. (2021), Sec. 7). No paper isolates the gain.
    • Slot-in: add two decayed columns (our 6 h to 1 week means are the same idea) plus smoothed daily extremes. Cost: minutes.
  7. Detrend the target before the tree model.
    • Rubattu et al. (2023), Sec. 3: fit a linear trend in the training fold, subtract it, fit LightGBM, add it back. Shown in Fig. 3 as zero-mean residuals; no number. Same paper: temporal-hierarchy combination improved CRPS about 5% and interval score about 10% (BigDEAL 2022 data, not public). For the XGBoost side of the blend only.
  8. Intraday autoregressive correction of the residuals, one model per horizon.
    • de Vilmarest and Goude (2022), Sec. III-B and Table II: offline GAM MAE 20.7 to 19.3 MW in a stable period; MLP 57% lower in the unstable year. Likely already covered by our anomaly state; check before building.

docs.title: 2. Our current choices against the literature
docs.text:
• Fixed 15.5 C hinge: no paper found uses a hinge. All the GAM papers above fit a free smooth of temperature (cubic spline) and let the data find the threshold (Fasiolo et al. (2021) f(T) with rank 15; Obst et al. (2021)). So the literature neither supports nor contradicts a fixed threshold; a spline would be the check, and a learned threshold is the nearer middle road.
  • Smoothed temperatures (6 h, 1 d, 3 d, 1 week): supported. Every EDF-line paper uses exponential smoothing at two time constants (0.95 and 0.99 per step); see trick 6. With half-hourly steps those are roughly 10 h and 50 h (the scan's own conversion, not stated in the paper).
  • Monthly drift knots: weakly supported. The literature's answer to level shifts is the Kalman coefficient state, which beat yearly and daily refits (trick 1). The finding of experiment 106 (drift adds nothing once the filter runs) agrees. No paper tested monthly spline knots.
  • Kalman level and anomaly states: supported, but narrower than the literature's state (trick 1). Adapting only the level discards the slow-changing heating and PV sensitivities that de Vilmarest et al. found drifted.
  • Residual-quantile spread (per block of hours and quarter): supported as a first step (Table II: offline quantile regression on filtered residuals already gives most of the gain), but poorly calibrated in the tails (Browell and Fasiolo: beyond 1% and 99%).
  • Convex, non-negative, non-decreasing PV capacity: no paper found tests monotonic capacity. de Vilmarest et al. let the capacity coefficient move freely and it learned embedded capacity (trick 2). Tang et al. (2024) estimate capacity with a neural network from 24 h net-load curves, so a convex physical fit is a different route.

docs.title: 3. Hierarchy
docs.text:
• Reconciliation barely helps the bottom level. Nespoli et al. (Swiss low-voltage grid, 24 bottom series): minT with graphical-lasso covariance cut aggregate RMSE by up to 10% but bottom-level RMSE by under 1%; minT with Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage made the bottom level worse. Nespoli et al.'s suggested fix: reconcile conditionally on the previous steps' forecast errors.
  • Projection helps little when every node uses the same model. Brégère and Huard (2022) (GB household populations, 3-month test, errors summed over all nodes): projection alone cut error about 1% for GAM, 5% for random forest; adding an online expert-aggregation step cut it a further 10 to 15%. Read: the gain came from mixing in other nodes' forecasts as experts, not from the constraint.
  • Probabilistic reconciliation: Jeon et al. (2019), temporal hierarchy, two Crete wind farms: reconciling ranked (not stacked) samples improved CRPS; best method cut 24 h CRPS by 26.6% and 21.1% at the two farms. Temporal, not across sites, so only indirect support for our sums.
  • No paper found that tested ensemble copula coupling, the Schaake shuffle, or the variogram score on substation demand; none found for soft hierarchical losses or hierarchical Bayesian load models with measured bottom-level gains. Searches: arXiv API titles and our library. Not exhaustive.
  • Practical reading: for Primaries (bottom), expect under 1 to 5% from reconciliation. The finding of experiment 36 (child forecast error is the limit) agrees. The larger payoff the literature shows is for BSP and GSP aggregates, and from online expert mixing.

docs.title: 4. Solar disaggregation
docs.text:
• Identification by regression on an irradiance proxy plus a load proxy. Kara et al. (2018): net active power regressed on measured reactive power (load proxy) and a nearby irradiance reading, daytime only, with a correction for capacitor-bank switches (threshold 90 kvar per phase). Recovered a 7.5 MWp site with RMSE about 450 kW (about 6%); validated against the site's own meter. Our analogue: MVAr, where NGED telemetry has it.
  • Unsupervised, validated on metered PV. Sossan et al. (2019): PV modelled as capacity-weighted sum over 21 tilt/azimuth planes from transposed GHI; four estimators; best (frequency-band method) nRMSE 4.6 to 5.6% for 4 Swiss houses (35.3 kWp) with ground-truth PV meters. Also tested at 50% and 25% of capacity.
  • Neighbour controls: Cheung et al. (2023) use neighbouring customers without PV as the load model; MAE 28.37% below a prior disaggregation model (Ausgrid, 300 customers). Needs known no-PV customers; at Primary level the equivalent is nearby Primaries with little PV.
  • Capacity from net-load shape. Tang et al. (2024): a model trained on summer data only had 18.1% lower RMSE than an all-year model with a third of the training data; Monday to Thursday only gave 26.9% lower RMSE; error about 10% once more than 20% of households have PV. Supports fitting PV capacity on the summer or shoulder windows only, and averaging curves (doubling averaged curves cut RMSE 25.1%, 17.5 to 13.1 kW).
  • Validation pattern across the papers: a metered subset gives ground truth; sensitivity to sampling time and penetration; none validates at Primary scale against known capacity. A synthetic known-answer injection (as in the gate of experiment 109) is stricter than what they did.
  • Not read in full (so no claims): Kanchana et al. (2026) GAN data curation (paywalled page only).

docs.title: 5. Papers saved (all in literature/papers/)
docs.text:
Newly downloaded:

  • fasiolo-2021-fast-calibrated-additive-quantile-regression.pdf: smoothed pinball loss and calibrated learning rate; beats boosting and the GEFCom2014 winner on EDF data.
  • de-vilmarest-2022-viking-variational-bayesian-variance-tracking.pdf: online noise-variance learning for the Kalman filter.
  • bregere-2022-online-hierarchical-forecasting-power-consumption.pdf: aggregation plus projection on a hierarchy of GB households.
  • jeon-2019-reconciliation-probabilistic-forecasts-wind-power-arxiv.pdf: probabilistic temporal reconciliation.

Already held and read in full for this scan:

  • de-vilmarest-2024-adaptive-probabilistic-net-load.pdf: the main source (tricks 1 to 3).
  • de-vilmarest-2021-state-space-models-win-dataport-competition.pdf: Q choices and intraday correction.
  • obst-2020-adaptive-methods-covid-lockdown-france.pdf: GAM temperature terms; Kalman variants.
  • browell-fasiolo-2021-regional-net-load.pdf: GAM against linear benchmark (pinball skill over 10% better for GAM-Point than a Vanilla linear benchmark, all 14 GSP Groups); conditional GPD tails.
  • nespoli-2022-hierarchical-demand-forecasting-benchmark.pdf, rubattu-2023-probabilistic-lightgbm-temporal-hierarchies.pdf: reconciliation and temporal hierarchies.
  • kara-2018-disaggregating-solar-feeder-level.pdf, sossan-2018-unsupervised-pv-disaggregation-composite-power-flow.pdf, cheung-2023-btm-solar-disaggregation-varying-aggregation-levels.pdf, sensitivity-2024-distributed-pv-capacity-estimation-ann.pdf: solar disaggregation.
  • hertel-2026-load-forecasting-across-grid-levels-v2.pdf: monthly retraining helps; no hierarchy content.

Not found open (searched arXiv titles only): Wickramasuriya et al. minT paper, Ben Taieb et al. smart meter hierarchy, Rangapuram et al. coherent probabilistic forecasts.

docs.title: Calibration and uncertainty
docs.text:
On the 16 Primary substations, 6 solar farms, and 3 wind farms tested, correcting the spread of the forecast has gained little, and combining forecasts has gained more. A spread factor brought the solar 5% to 95% range from over-covering to about 90% coverage with no detectable change in accuracy, and no recalibration of the stored Primary substation quantiles passed its pre-registered tests. The gains that cleared their thresholds came from pooling ENS members for solar and wind farms, starting wind farms from the turbine power curve, and blending three stored forecasts for Primary substations. Every result rests on one validation year.

Figure 1: the uncorrected 5% to 95% range over-covers for solar in every lead band (a group of forecast lead times) and for wind in the first two days, and a spread factor corrects solar. Source: experiment 16.

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
Pooling the ERA5-trained quantiles over the ENS members beat an XGBoost model trained on ENS weather for solar and wind farms, and a stage 2 calibrator did not help. In experiment 2, the pooled mixture scored lower in CRPS by 0.62 points of capacity for wind (95% interval -0.99 to -0.26) and 0.24 for solar (-0.36 to -0.06), with the gain in the first six days. The stage 2 calibrator scored 0.40 worse than the mixture for solar (+0.26 to +0.61).

One spread factor brought solar's range to about 90% coverage with no detectable CRPS change. In experiment 16, solar coverage was 94.3% to 95.3% in every lead band before the factor and 89.5% to 91.8% after it (CRPS +0.006, 99.4% interval -0.004 to +0.024). Wind over-covered in the first two days only (95.3% and 94.4%), and no planned correction fixed that. A factor on two lead groups, chosen after seeing the results, reached 90.7% to 92.5% and changed the CRPS by -0.021 (-0.042 to -0.002), a small gain.

For wind, the base margin carries the CRPS gain, and the spread factor is a coverage fix. In experiment 20, the margin lowered the wind CRPS by 0.055 (99.58% interval -0.110 to -0.007), the spread factor alone by 0.021 (-0.043 to -0.002), and both by 0.071 (-0.133 to -0.014). The factor's extra -0.016 over the margin (-0.036 to +0.004) is not detectable. No change helped solar detectably, and the full combination for solar was 0.035 higher (-0.075 to +0.116), an interval that includes zero.

No recalibration of the stored Primary substation quantiles passed the pre-registered tests. In experiment 97, the weekly-refitted forecast of BG2 covered its q05 (the quantile at level 0.05) at 0.035 and its q95 at 0.938 at 12 to 36 hours lead, where 0.05 and 0.95 are nominal, and covered the median at 0.45. The tail test needed q01, q05, q95, and q99 within 0.01 of nominal at both the 16 Primary substations and 4 bulk and grid supply points. For example, the arm that scaled per level, lead band, and class gave Primary q95 coverage of 0.9397 and supply-point q95 coverage of 0.9248. The verdict is refuted, but 9 scored months are too few to separate a real improvement from noise. An arm that replaced the stored tails with fitted Pareto tails lowered the quantile score for Primary substations at 12 to 36 hours by 0.00009 (95% interval -0.00015 to -0.00001, against a stored 0.01882 on the scale that experiment prints) and failed the tail test.

Averaging the quantiles of three stored forecasts lowered the Primary substation quantile score by about 0.1 points, and the solar and wind gains were unresolved. In experiment 35, the lead-band blend of the monthly-refitted N1, a7_cs (an XGBoost model with seven weekly-analogue columns), and the stack scored 5.025 against 5.122 for the best of the three (quantile score -0.097, 98.33% interval -0.187 to -0.026). One fixed weight vector, the simpler arm, scored 5.020, and the two differ by +0.005 (-0.008 to +0.023). The blend was not scored against BG2. The solar (-0.039) and wind (-0.074) intervals include zero.

Figure 2: blending lowers the Primary substation quantile score, and the solar and wind gains are unresolved. Negative values are better. Source: experiment 35.

A loss based on the CRPS of the pooled members recovered about half of the harm that extra members do to the pinball loss at 16 Primary substations. In Experiment 99, 6 members per run cost the pinball loss 0.075 points (5.622 against 5.547 for the control member alone), and the CRPS loss beat the pinball loss on the same rows by 0.039 (95% interval -0.057 to -0.018), a small gain. Against the control-member recipe the CRPS arm was +0.036 (-0.022 to +0.111), so the pilot cannot say which is better.

A zero starting value gave no detectable gain for Primary substations or solar farms. In experiment 80, the differences were -0.017 (98.75% interval -0.072 to +0.054) for Primary substations and -0.010 (-0.036 to +0.028) for solar farms, and the verdict is inconclusive. The wind models that serve already receive a base margin, so a zero start changes nothing there. Wind models without a margin were worse by +0.049 (95% interval +0.032 to +0.065).

Training with lags hidden at random did not widen the 5% to 95% band where a lag is missing. In experiment 100, on 37,394 real half-hours with a missing lag (an earlier power reading) at 16 Primary substations, the band covered 0.799 for the plain XGBoost model and 0.802 for the model trained with lags hidden in 10% of rows, against a nominal 0.90. The verdict is inconclusive.

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text: These are the best of the recipes tested in this theme, and the experiments did not score them against each other. For Primary substations, the best tested is the one-fixed-weight blend of the monthly-refitted N1, a7_cs, and the stack, which experiment 35 scored against its own members and not against BG2. For solar and wind farms, the best tested is the pooled mixture with a spread factor for solar and a base margin for wind. Experiments 16 and 20 found no detectable solar CRPS gain over the pooled mixture.

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text:
Four experiments have production_status: candidate, none is adopted, and a model release plan decides whether any is ported.

  • experiment 2, pooled mixture: pool the ERA5-trained quantiles over the ENS members for solar and wind.
  • experiment 16, solar spread factor: scale the solar mixture's quantiles by one fitted factor.
  • experiment 20, wind base margin: add the power-curve base margin to the wind stage 1a model, which lowered the CRPS by 0.055.
  • experiment 35, Primary substation blend: serve a fixed-weight average of the quantiles of three forecasts, one of them refitted monthly. It was -0.102 against the best member (interval -0.201 to -0.025) and was not scored against BG2.

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
Report the pooled mixture beside any calibrator. Without it, a calibrator that is worse than pooling can look like a gain over an ENS-trained model (experiment 2). Re-check if the calibrator gets new inputs, such as lagged power, which experiment 5 found helpful for 16 Primary substations.

Fit each correction only on data from valid times (the times a forecast is for) before the first run it corrects, and expect early months to stay uncorrected. A fit that sees later outcomes flatters the correction. Experiments 16 and 97 fitted each correction only on valid times before the first run it corrected, and the arm of experiment 16 with a spread factor per lead band needed 5,000 earlier non-trivial cases (cases whose uncorrected 95% quantile exceeds 1% of capacity), so the wind 0 to 24 hour band was fitted in only 3 months and the 1 to 2 day band in 8. Re-check if the validation period or series count grows.

Compute solar coverage on non-trivial cases only. Night-time zeros sit inside every range and inflate coverage, so experiment 16 left them out. Re-check for a series that is not zero at night.

Refit each arm's own spread factor on that arm's own earlier cases. A factor fitted for other quantiles does not fit (experiment 20). Re-check if the quantiles come from an XGBoost model that experiment did not stack.

Score tail coverage and pinball loss at q01, q05, q95, and q99, count exceedances (measured values beyond a tail quantile), and keep the stored quantiles at all 11 levels. Nine scored months gave intervals of plus or minus 0.02 on q95 coverage, wider than the 0.01 bar, and cells with fewer than 30 days holding an exceedance were untestable (experiment 97). Re-check once 2 years of scored runs exist.

Test a starting value only on XGBoost models without a base margin. A base margin makes XGBoost ignore its base score, so a zero start changed nothing on the wind model with the margin (experiment 80). Re-check if the XGBoost version or objective changes.

Run a repeat fit to measure the noise floor of GPU XGBoost. Fits are not bit-reproducible: repeat fits of one 500-round model scored +0.004 apart at Primary substations and -0.007 at grid supply points, above the 0.001 tolerance and well below the intervals (experiment 80). Re-check on a different GPU or XGBoost version.

Hold the refit schedule fixed within a contrast. The CRPS-loss arms refit monthly with 150 rounds and scored 0.19 to 0.23 points above BG2's weekly stage, which probably reflects the schedule, so their absolute scores cannot be set beside it (experiment 99). Re-check if either schedule changes.

Pool pinball-trained quantiles with equal weights, not the CRPS atom masses. The CRPS gives each of the 11 quantiles a probability mass (0.02 at q01 and q99, 0.26 at q25 and q75), and pooling with those masses scored 0.025 points worse (experiment 99). Re-check if the pinball arm is replaced by a CRPS-trained one.

Apply the 14-day correction to each member before blending, and leave the monthly-refitted N1 uncorrected. Correcting the blend afterwards scored 0.048 points worse (95% interval +0.008 to +0.101), but that contrast favours the corrected-first arm, whose weights were chosen on its own scores, and correcting N1 too scored 0.135 worse than the headline blend (experiment 35). Re-check if the members change.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text: Whether a calibrator that sees recent power helps solar and wind farms is untested, although experiment 5 found it helped Primary substations. The wind two-group spread factor has not been tested on another year. experiment 99 suggests a tail-specific spread factor, or pooled-member spread statistics as input columns, for the Primary tails. Experiment 100 names an input column that flags a missing lag as an untested way to widen the band where a lag is missing. The blend gains for solar and wind may exist on more than 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms. Tracking the month-to-month swing in Primary tail coverage needs at least 2 years of scored runs. The Research plan lists what is planned next, and the Experiments page lists every experiment tried.

docs.title: Delivering uncertainty to NGED's power-flow studies
docs.text:
National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED) needs three deliverables for its power-flow studies: 11 stored quantiles per series and half-hour with a dependence table, a direct forecast of the meter of each bulk supply point (BSP), and a small set of unlabelled scenarios. The quantiles let NGED's own Python code rebuild marginal forecasts and coherent paths. A BSP is the substation that feeds a group of primary substations (Primaries). The direct forecast supplies the tail of the flow through a BSP, which a sum of node scenarios did not reproduce in any experiment we ran. This page collects the findings of experiments 434, 436, and 625 to 631 in one place. The page states the recommendation, five questions for NGED, and the corrections that later pages should carry. The results on scenario coupling rest on 10 calendar months of Tuesday runs for 16 Primaries, 3 wind farms, and 6 solar farms. The BSP results and the demand-tail results of experiments 629 to 631 rest on 5 development months, and the BSP results on 2 BSPs. NGED has not yet confirmed that any part of this design suits its workflow.

Terms: K is the number of paths in a scenario set. A quantile such as q05, q95, or q99 is the forecast at the 5%, 95%, or 99% level. CRPS (continuous ranked probability score) scores one series' marginal forecast. The variogram score scores how well a scenario set's dependence between series and leads matches reality.

docs.title: The recommendation
docs.text:
Store 11 quantiles per series and half-hour, and let the client rebuild paths from them. In experiment 628, 1,000 client draws from the 11 stored quantiles (0.01, 0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.40, 0.50, 0.60, 0.75, 0.90, 0.95, 0.99) scored within 0.3% of the pipeline's 51 values on CRPS. The client extends the quantile function past q01 and q99 with a Gaussian tail and clamps wind to 0 to 100% of capacity. Solar is not clipped at 100%, because 2.3% of solar actuals exceed it. The client code is about 70 lines, and one run's 11 quantiles for 25 series take 772 kB.

A Schaake shuffle helps the wind and solar farms and does nothing for the Primaries, so the dependence table is chosen by family. For the wind and solar farms, the table is 51 past observed paths, which a Schaake shuffle uses to rank-order independent draws. For the Primaries, the table is empty.

  • For the 3 wind farms and 6 solar farms, the Schaake shuffle scored 34.4% below independent draws on the variogram score (98.33% interval -42.5% to -26.1%, experiment 625).
  • For the 16 Primaries, no coupling we tried scored measurably better than independent draws. The fitted copula scored 0.7% lower (-1.5% to +0.2%) and a shuffle of anomaly paths 0.3% lower (-1.6% to +1.2%), and both intervals include zero. Coupling by the weather ensemble's member ranks scored 6.8% higher, which is worse. We therefore recommend no coupling for the Primaries.
  • A fitted Gaussian copula on its own scored 6.6% worse than the pipeline's version on the solar farms' variogram score. The likely reason is that the pipeline's version also uses the weather ensemble's member ranks, which the quantiles do not carry. We did not test this reason by ablation.

About 20 paths score 2% to 3% worse than 51 paths on the farms' variogram score, and 20 paths passed the registered test only for the Primaries. In experiment 625, 20 paths scored 2.0% (wind farms) to 3.1% (solar farms) worse than 51 paths on the variogram score and 1.0% worse for the Primaries, and 10 paths scored 5.2% to 11.1% worse on the farms. The CRPS of 20 paths was within 0.5% of the 51-value CRPS in all three families. By the registered tests, the farms needed K = 51 and the Primaries K = 20, so "about 20" is a rounding of mixed results.

Deliver a direct forecast of each BSP's own meter beside any node scenarios. Summing the Primaries beneath each of 2 BSPs (9 at Boston, 7 at Skegness) put 33.9% to 79.0% of actual export flows below the sum's q05 (nominal 5%) for the K1 demand network, in every coupling (experiment 629). Adding the 9 metered wind and solar farms and a time-of-day remainder reduced the export-side miss to 10.6% at Boston and 3.0% at Skegness for the Schaake shuffle, but the import side then had 14.3% and 32.6% of actual flows above the q95 (experiment 631). The direct forecast of each meter gave 4.9% and 7.2% below the q05 and 6.7% and 9.9% above the q95. Coupled sums did beat independent draws on CRPS by 2.6% to 7.7% once the farms were in. Coupling therefore still matters for the node scenarios.

If NGED runs scenarios by hand, offer a choice of at least 10 paths, chosen without labels; a hand-picked 5 did not cover the tails. Experiment 627 found that ranking the 51 paths on one summary (for example the peak Primary demand), cutting them into K groups, and drawing one path per group beat a random draw on tail coverage in all 10 months. At K = 5 no rule kept the 5th and 95th percentiles of the chosen paths within 10% of the range of the 51 paths. For a BSP's export limit, an observed daily peak export exceeded the largest of 5 chosen paths on 12% of days (1.6% for all 51 paths) and the largest of 10 chosen paths on 6.3% of days. A label such as "the low-wind scenario" does not carry from day to day or lead to lead: under the Schaake shuffle a path's wind rank between days 1 to 3 and days 4 to 10 has a rank correlation of 0.19.

The stored forecasts hold 11 quantile levels, but the production docs' delivery tables list 13. The 13 delivery levels (0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.35, 0.50, 0.65, 0.80, 0.90, 0.95, 0.98, 0.99) share 7 levels with the 11 stored levels. Delivering all 13 means re-predicting the stored forecasts at the extra levels. Experiment 628 did not measure the effect of that re-prediction.

docs.title: Five questions for NGED
docs.text:
The five items below are questions, not commitments. The answers decide which parts of the design are worth building.

  1. How many scenarios does NGED run by hand? In the advisor's illustration (an assumption, not NGED's statement), a hand-run study in a graphical tool allows about 3 to 10 runs per element per forecast, which sets how few paths the delivery must offer.
  2. How many power-flow runs can NGED afford, and are they scripted? A scripted study could allow thousands of runs, in which case NGED can draw its own scenarios from the stored quantiles. Related questions: which decision the study feeds (outage planning, flexibility procurement, or a curtailment notice), at what lead time, and what scalar each node takes (MW or MVA, which power factor, and power available or power after an active-network-management cap).
  3. Which BSPs, grid supply points (GSPs), or circuits matter? Can NGED give the weight each node carries in the flow through each constrained element, or link its electricity-network model to our series identifiers? Which nodes in the study do we not forecast, and what does NGED assume for them?
  4. Does a direct forecast of the flow through a BSP, GSP, or circuit already exist on NGED's side? We scored direct forecasts of the meters of 2 BSPs. The 2 GSPs have direct forecasts too, which we did not use in a sum.
  5. Should the delivery tables hold 11 or 13 quantile levels? The stored forecasts hold 11, and a move to 13 needs the forecasts re-predicted.

docs.title: What we tried
docs.text:
• Experiment 434 (not supported). Re-ordering the stored demand forecast's 51 values by member temperature or by past observed paths did not beat independent draws across the 16 Primaries. Temperature ranks scored 6.7% worse than independent draws on the variogram score across the Primaries. The Schaake shuffle scored 3.5% lower (better) than independent draws on the variogram score across leads at days 1 to 10.
  • Experiment 436 (partly supported; joint block void, see the erratum on its page). Across the farms, a Schaake shuffle scored 28% (wind) and 40% (solar) below independent draws, and the copula-corrected ensemble ranks 29% and 43% below. Across the Primaries nothing beat independent draws by more than 0.7%. Tying scenario k to ensemble member k scored the same as a Schaake shuffle across Primaries and wind farms and no better across solar farms.
  • Experiment 625 (partly supported). Experiment 625 ran the K sweep and the anomaly-path shuffle described above. It also re-scored experiment 436's joint block and found no difference between couplings (within +0.8%).
  • Experiment 626 (partly supported). A separate upper and lower factor brought demand's q05 and q95 exceedance to 4% to 6% in every lead band, and did not fix wind or solar. Demand's q90 was still exceeded for 11% to 16% of actuals (nominal 10%), which points to a median that sits too low rather than tails that are too narrow.
  • Experiment 627 (partly supported). Experiment 627 gave the subset results described above.
  • Experiment 628 (partly supported). Experiment 628 tested the client-side rebuild described above. The tail rule (clamp, linear, or Gaussian) changed CRPS by under 0.02%, and the stored upper tails were too narrow for any of the three rules to repair.
  • Experiment 629 (not supported). Sums of the Primaries missed the BSP export tail. The threshold-weighted CRPS test could not rank the coupling methods, because neither BSP's meter reached the scaled export limit in the development months.
  • Experiment 630 (partly supported). The stored neural-network forecasts exceeded their q90 on 13% to 17% of event-free readings (5 development months). A correction fitted on the first three months removed about a quarter to a half of the excess on the last two, because the bias changes with the season.
  • Experiment 631 (not supported). Experiment 631 scored the farm-inclusive sums described above. The cause of the import-side miss (the Primary forecasts' bias, the farms, or the remainder) was not separated.

docs.title: Corrections to carry into other pages
docs.text:
• Do not repeat that the 51 member tails are "7.6% to 8.8% too narrow" at q95. Experiment 436 took the q95 with numpy's default quantile definition. With the Weibull definition (the k-th smallest of 51 values sits at level k/52), the q95 exceedance is 5.2% for demand, 6.5% for wind, and 5.7% for solar (experiment 626). The stored upper quantiles of the demand forecasts are still too low, as experiments 626, 628, and 630 show.
  • Do not repeat experiment 436's joint-block verdict. Its scoring code mixed nodes and members, and experiment 625 replaced the joint-block scores. The within-family results of experiment 436 are unaffected.
  • Do not write that demand has no mixture. The bake-off's demand neural networks are mixture-density neural networks with 3 components, but the export stores only the mean of 5 seeds' quantiles, which is not any single mixture. The wind and solar mixture parameters were also never stored. Experiment 628 concluded that mixture parameters were not needed to rebuild marginal forecasts or a Schaake-shuffle coupling from the 11 quantiles. Recovering the parameters would need a rebuild of the inference of experiments 612 and 613, which has not been done.
  • Do not describe BSP sums as validated. Experiments 629 and 631 each rest on 2 BSPs and on a scaled export limit that was never reached, so the threshold-weighted CRPS could not rank the sums.

docs.title: Advisor review of the delivery design (2026-11-07)
docs.text:
This section summarises an advisor review that read the background docs and experiments 430, 434, and 436 and proposed the delivery design above. The review is the fullest account we have of the reasoning for the design (the answer file is private to the research team). Statements about NGED's workflow that the review flagged as unsupported are marked (guess), and every statement about NGED's workflow needs NGED's confirmation.

The binding quantity is the flow through one constrained element, and that flow is a weighted sum over many nodes. According to the background docs, for about half of NGED's generators the limit sits at a BSP or a GSP. For most of the rest it sits on a circuit and binds only after the next fault, found by power flow plus N-1 contingency analysis (one outage simulated at a time). In an almost radial part of the electricity network every weight is 1 for the nodes below the element. In a meshed 33 kV part the weights are power transfer distribution factors (the share of an injection at a node that flows through the element). The flow F through the element is then close to linear in the node injections: it is about the sum, over nodes i, of the weight w_i times the node's injection P_i.

The review corrected four parts of the working understanding.

  • Reverse flow is a breach only where it exceeds the reverse-direction rating of a transformer or circuit, or pushes voltage or protection out of limits (guess about which binds most often in the trial area).
  • According to the background docs, real-time curtailment is done by active network management (ANM), not by a study days ahead. A study 1 to 10 days ahead is more plausibly for outage planning, flexibility procurement, or warning generators of likely curtailment (guess).
  • "A power-flow model takes only scalars" is true of one run and is not the constraint. A time-series power flow takes one scalar per node per half-hour. The real limit is how many runs the analyst can afford, which depends on whether the runs are scripted.
  • The power flow needs nodes we do not forecast: unmetered generators, other Primaries, and the sites metered in MVA (megavolt-amperes, which carry no flow direction; 8 of the 16 Primaries in experiment 629). Our scenarios cover only part of the sum.

For curtailment, the tail of the sum decides the outcome, so dependence between nodes matters more than any single site's tail. The review's worked example is two neighbouring solar farms under one circuit with a 15 MW export limit, each forecast roughly Normal(6 MW, sd 2 MW) at noon (a simplification, because solar output is bounded by clear sky and capacity):

Assumed correlation sd of the sum P(sum > 15 MW) q95 of the sum 0 (independent draws) 2.83 MW 14.5% 16.7 MW 0.62 (realised in experiment 436) 3.60 MW 20.3% 17.9 MW 0.95 (ensemble copula coupling) 3.95 MW 22.4% 18.5 MW
  • Independent draws understate the chance of a breach by about a quarter and put the q95 1.2 MW too low. An overstated correlation puts the q95 0.6 MW too high, so generators are curtailed more than needed. The curtailment metric prices a breach at 20 times the curtailed energy, so overstating dependence is the safer error, but not a free one.
  • Experiment 436's finding that nothing beat independent draws across the Primaries does not mean the Primaries are independent. Their realised correlation was 0.29, so the sd of a sum of 16 equal Primaries is 2.3 times the independent value. Experiment 436's tail table showed 13.9% of actual group net flows above the q95 of independent-draw sums, against 6.6% for the Schaake shuffle and 2.6% for ensemble copula coupling. The variogram score barely moved. Experiment 436 also found the 51-value marginals too narrow in the upper tail, so these exceedances partly reflect the marginals. The review's conclusion is that the group-sum exceedance rate is the right instrument for this decision, and the variogram score is the wrong one.
  • Demand and solar errors are negatively correlated (-0.36 realised), so in the export direction a sunnier-than-forecast day also lowers demand through embedded solar and the two errors add. No experiment has tested cross-family dependence.
  • A Gaussian copula has no tail dependence. A Schaake shuffle copies real past days and keeps tail dependence empirically, limited by the size of its date pool, which favours the shuffle for the tail.

No single delivery option wins. The review's comparison:

Option Analyst's work Gets the tail right? Can we validate it? Many draws (marginals plus copula), analyst picks Moderate: sampling code, then choosing what "extreme" means Only as far as the marginal tails and the copula's tail dependence allow; 1,000 draws carry about +/-0.3 points of Monte Carlo error at q99 Indirectly, through group sums (a) Pre-chosen stress scenarios per element Least: feed K vectors straight into the power flow Yes at the chosen level, if the element flow's quantile is right The element quantile, yes; the split across nodes, no (b) Distribution of the element flow itself Low, but the result cannot be fed into a power flow Best, where the element is metered Yes, against the element's own meter (c) Importance sampling or conditional simulation High: weighted samples confuse non-statisticians Yes, efficiently Same as option (a) (d) Quantiles of group sums as extra series Low Yes for the named groups Yes
  • Option (b) has an advantage: the Boston and Skegness BSPs are metered and already among the series, so a direct forecast is trained and scored on the true flow with no copula. The review argued that a sum of node scenarios cannot match it, because unmetered load, losses, and the direction-blind MVA Primaries sit inside the BSP meter but outside any sum of our nodes. Experiments 629 and 631 found that sums of the Primaries missed the export tail of both BSPs, that adding the metered wind and solar farms removed most of the export-side miss at Skegness but widened the import-side miss, and that the direct forecast of each BSP meter came closest to nominal (within two binomial errors on three of four tails in experiment 631). Neither experiment tested the unmetered load, the losses, or the MVA Primaries separately.
  • Options (a) and (c) reduce to one recipe. For element E, day d, and level tau (for example 0.5, 0.9, 0.95, and 0.99 of that day's peak export), deliver the coherent vector of node values most likely given that the flow equals its tau quantile. Under a Gaussian copula and a linear flow this vector has a closed form, mu + Sigma w (q - mu_F) / sigma_F squared. With Schaake paths, the vector is the drawn path whose element flow lies nearest the quantile. The label "Skegness export, day 3, 95th percentile" names the target quantity and level, is recomputed in every run, and never refers to a member's identity, so nothing carries over from day to day.
  • A deterministic bounding case is worth adding beside the statistics: maximum generation with minimum demand. For solar, maximum generation is clear-sky output capped at capacity and needs no tail statistics. The added value is the probability that a day approaches that ceiling (guess that NGED's analyst already runs this case).

The review recommended validating the element flow against its own meter on four quantities.

  • The exceedance rate at q90, q95, and q99 (and the 1%, 5%, and 10% levels on the export side), by lead band, with summer middays separately.
  • Threshold-weighted CRPS at the scaled limit (0.9 times the maximum export observed before the scored period). The score is proper and fits curtailment, because it scores every half-hour and weights only the region above the line.
  • The Brier score of the flow exceeding the scaled limit, with a reliability diagram.
  • The tier 1 curtailment energy proxy of studies.node_curtailment, with the realised unmet fraction.

The independent sample is the weather day, not the half-hour, so q99 cannot be validated. Export-side tails live on roughly 150 to 180 summer half days a year per BSP (estimate). A q95 test then rests on about 8 to 9 exceedance days per BSP per year (binomial error about +/-1.6 points on a 5% rate), and a q99 test on about 2. The review said the firm limit had been reached once in the pilot, a statement we could not trace to experiments 629 or 631, which found the scaled limit never reached in the development months. The review listed what cannot be validated with our data:

  • q99 and beyond.
  • Tail dependence in the far tail.
  • Any element that is not metered, including every post-fault circuit.
  • Combined rare events, such as an outage on a clear-sky, low-demand day.
  • The split of a stress scenario across nodes, as distinct from the sum.

The review advised stating these limits to NGED's analyst rather than covering them with a score.

The review's recommended design. For each element NGED names, starting with the export side of the Boston and Skegness BSPs:

  • Deliver the element flow's quantiles from a direct forecast of the metered flow.
  • Deliver 3 to 5 conditional stress vectors per element per day, at tau in {0.5, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99} of the daily peak export, generated from Schaake paths and rescaled to hit the element quantile.
  • Keep per-node marginals (the review said 13 quantiles; the stored forecasts hold 11, see question 5) with widened tails, and the Schaake template dates, in Amazon S3 object storage, so a scripted analyst can draw more scenarios.

The fallback is marginals plus a Schaake or copula table with client-side sampling, a 20-line client recipe, and published group-sum quantiles for the two BSPs so the analyst can check their own sums. The review's cheapest next experiment was a CPU-only re-score of experiment 436's stored scenario tables as BSP-group sums against the BSP meters. That proposal led to experiments 629 and 631, which used the daily-run forecasts rather than experiment 436's stored tables. The design with conditional stress vectors (the second bullet) has not been built or tested, and is the open question below.

docs.title: Open question
docs.text: No experiment yet tests how to make coherent node scenarios agree with the direct forecast of the flow through a BSP or GSP. NGED's power-flow study needs node injections, and the direct forecast supplies the flow through the element. Experiment 631 shows that the two disagree in the tails when the node scenarios are summed. One candidate design conditions the node scenarios on a quantile of the direct forecast. No experiment tests it yet, and we do not know whether NGED wants it. Questions 3 and 4 above bear on it.

docs.title: Recommended changes to the production docs
docs.text: These are recommendations for a later pull request to the production repository, not commitments. Each quotes the passage as it stands on origin/main of the production repository on 2026-11-10. Where a passage depends on the state of the production code, which this research repository cannot see, the entry says to check the code before editing.

docs.title: docs/roadmap/delivery-tables.md
docs.text:
• Table 1's three-representation framing leaves out the dependence table, the direct BSP forecast, and the scenario subsets. The page says: "The Milestone 1 report describes three ways of expressing uncertainty. We may deliver one or several of these: ... 3. Ensemble of percentile forecasts — per-member and per-percentile." Add a short section after Representation 3, headed "Coherent scenarios, direct flow forecasts, and scenario subsets", with this text: "A power-flow study needs one value per node and half-hour in each scenario, and the scenarios must move together as the nodes do in reality. We propose, pending NGED's answers: (1) the 11 stored quantiles per series and half-hour together with a dependence table: for the wind and solar farms, 51 past observed paths to drive a Schaake shuffle; for the 16 Primaries, none; (2) a direct forecast of the meter of each bulk supply point, because summing node scenarios did not reproduce the tail of the flow through a bulk supply point in any experiment we ran; (3) on request, 10 or more scenarios chosen without labels by stratifying the 51 paths on one summary." Link claim (1) to experiment 625, claim (2) to experiments 629 and 631, and claim (3) to experiment 627.
  • Representation 1 describes scenarios as the NWP members. The page says: "ensemble_member | int8 | ID of the NWP ensemble member driving this forecast. ECMWF ENS has 51 members." and the Representation 3 table repeats the member identifier. Experiment 436 found that tying scenario k to ensemble member k scored the same as a Schaake shuffle across Primaries and wind farms and no better across solar farms, and that ensemble copula coupling overstated the correlation between Primaries (0.93 against 0.29 realised). Add a note: "A delivered scenario need not be one weather member's forecast. The scenarios built from the stored quantiles are numbered 1 to 51 with no link to any weather member, and no scenario carries a label that holds from one lead to the next." Check the code before editing the field description, because the code may still deliver one forecast per member.
  • Representation 2 lists 13 percentile levels, and the stored forecasts hold 11. The page says: "p1, p2, p5, p10, p20, p35, p50, p65, p80, p90, p95, p98, p99". The stored forecasts hold 0.01, 0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.40, 0.50, 0.60, 0.75, 0.90, 0.95, and 0.99, which share 7 of the 13 levels. Add under the table: "The research forecasts store 11 levels, not these 13. The two sets share p1, p5, p10, p50, p90, p95, and p99. Delivering all 13 needs the forecasts re-predicted at the extra levels, and we do not yet know whether NGED needs them." Keep the 13-level table, and state the open question as a bullet, not as a decision.
  • Representation 2's note does not say how far to trust the tails. The page says: "NGED is far more interested in the tails than the shoulders." Add: "On 44 Tuesday runs of 2025-09 to 2026-06, the stored q99 of the Primaries was exceeded by 1.0% to 1.6% of event-free actuals for the XGBoost forecasts and 1.9% to 3.1% for the neural networks (experiment 628). On 5 development months, the neural networks' stored q90 was exceeded by 13% to 17% of event-free actuals (experiment 630). The upper tail of demand is therefore too low. Extending the quantile function past q01 and q99 with a tail rule does not repair this (experiments 628 and 630)."

docs.title: docs/techniques/probabilistic-forecasting.md
docs.text:
• The page's closing section says the full pipeline is planned, not what we found about coherence. The section "How this maps onto the project" ends: "The full pipeline ... a quantile-objective XGBoost emits Representation 3; the pooling recipe above derives Representation 2 for delivery." Add a section before it, headed "Making scenarios coherent across sites and leads", with this content: "A quantile forecast describes each site and half-hour separately. A power-flow study needs scenarios whose sites and leads move together. In the experiments we ran, a Schaake shuffle of 51 past observed paths scored 34% below independent draws on the variogram score across 3 wind farms and 6 solar farms. No coupling scored measurably better than independent draws across 16 Primaries, and ranking the draws by the weather ensemble's members scored 6.8% worse there. About 20 paths lose 2% to 3% of the 51-path score on the farms. Summing node scenarios to a bulk supply point did not reproduce the tail of the flow through that point, and a direct forecast of the meter came closer to the nominal rate (4.9% to 9.9% of actuals beyond each tail, against 5%)." Link experiments 436, 625, 629, and 631.
  • The tail caveat quotes a literature finding but not our own. The page says: "The mixture's own p1 and p99 may therefore need the same parametric-tail treatment before they can be trusted." Add after it: "In our own data, a Gaussian tail beyond q01 and q99 gave the best lower-tail coverage of the three tail rules we tested (0.20% to 0.45% of actuals below the 0.2% quantile, against 0.53% to 1.05% for clamping), but on the upper side 0.66% to 1.19% of actuals lay above the 99.8% quantile, against 0.2% nominal, and the tail rule changed CRPS by under 0.02% (experiment 628). None of the three tail rules repaired stored quantiles whose upper tail was already too low."
  • The page does not say that the research forecasts are quantile forecasts stored per site and half-hour. Its section "Turning 51 quantile sets into one: the pooling recipe" describes pooling 51 members times K quantile levels. Check the code and experiments 425, 429, and 430 before editing: if the research default stores one set of 11 quantiles per site and half-hour (as experiment 628 reports), add a sentence "The research forecasts store one set of 11 quantiles per site and half-hour, from which the 51 scenario values are interpolated" and say which pipeline each recipe applies to.
  • The claim about Vincentization is untested here. The page states as settled that level-by-level averaging discards the between-member spread. None of the experiments on this page tested it, so leave the passage as it stands and do not cite our results for it.

docs.title: Calibration and uncertainty: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00689 fixed-lookback-width-scale-versus-seed-averaging-at-refit-boundaries The steps in band width at the model refits (Primaries 11 and 13, and six widenings in February) come from the new model's raw band width differing from the old one's, so a scale fitted on the previous 90 days of the old model's forecasts cannot remove them; the seed average of the quantiles is not the cause. not supported not-for-production A single width scale fitted on the previous 90, 45, or 180 days does not remove the steps in band width at the refits of Primary 11 and the six February widenings, and moves the ratio farther from 1 in 67% of affected cells (the median step of an affected cell goes from 15% stored to 24%). Fitting the scale per seed and averaging gives nearly the same ratios, so seed averaging is not what drives the steps. A scale fitted on the new model's own forecasts could follow a refit, but those forecasts do not exist until after it; this experiment did not test one. primary 00688 winter-normal-running-coverage-median-error-and-events-part-1 The winter shortfall of the normal-running Primaries' 90% bands (q05-to-q95 coverage 80% in 2025-12 and 2026-01 after experiment 683's walk-forward scale) comes from a month-long error in the median forecast and from half-hours inside load transfers, not from bands that are too narrow for the errors the median makes. supported not-for-production The 90% bands of the 16 Primary substations' normal-running forecasts miss in winter mostly because the median forecast is off by a different amount each month, and partly because of load transfers, not because the bands are too narrow. Shifting each band by its month's observed median error and dropping the transfers lifts coverage from 80% in both months to 90% in December 2025 and 89% in January 2026, with the band width almost right. A candidate next step is a way to correct the median level during the month, not a model of the band width. primary 00684 backtest-positive-demand-output-distributions-and-physical-solar-night-zero A positive output family at the four Primaries that cannot go below zero, and a hard zero at every solar half-hour whose sun is at or below the horizon at the middle of the half-hour, remove the negative lower quantiles and the non-zero night quantiles of the backtest files without reducing accuracy. partly supported candidate A Gaussian mixture conditioned on power at or above zero fixes the negative lower quantiles at the four demand series. CRPS improves clearly at two series, is indistinguishable at one, and worsens by 0.03 points of capacity at one, so the model is a candidate to replace the post hoc clamp. A gamma mixture inside the same shared network made two series much worse and is dropped. A hard zero at night at each half-hour's own sun position removes every non-zero solar night quantile, changes no daylight score, and lowers night CRPS, while the share of night observations above q99 rises because the gate sets those quantiles to zero. also relevant 00683 walk-forward-calibration-of-the-quantile-bands-in-the-one-year-backtest-files The quantile bands stored in the one-year backtest files are too narrow for the Primaries, the bulk supply points (BSPs), and the grid supply points (GSPs) (q05-to-q95 coverage 81% to 88% against 90%), and the shortfall is a width error that a per-series, per-lead-band scale on the half-width of the band removes, when the scale is fitted only on forecasts whose actual power was already known at the start of the month. partly supported candidate Widening the stored bands by a factor fitted only on earlier months brings the bulk supply points, grid supply points, solar, and the prevailing Primaries output to within 2 points of the nominal 90% coverage, with a CRPS rise of at most 0.047 points of capacity. Widening does not rescue the normal-running Primaries: coverage stays at 87% on average and at 80% in two winter months, which is consistent with bands that are wrong by more than their width. A learned width head or a winter correction to the median are candidates for the next experiment, and a median-level shift fitted per series made every file worse. primary 00664 pv-sum-of-distributions-spread-and-recalibration The job of the explicit solar term is as much to calibrate the spread of the net-demand forecast as to shift its centre. In experiments 644 and 655 the explicit term subtracted one number (the member-average solar curve) from every forecast quantile, so the solar uncertainty (capacity times cloud uncertainty) never reached the output. Building the net-demand distribution as the gross-demand distribution minus the solar curve of a randomly drawn ensemble member beats the free network on sunny middays, and the gain is more than a recalibration of the free network's quantile widths would give. refuted not-for-production The free network's spread is not what is wrong on sunny middays. The realised power falls below its 5% quantile in about 9% of half-hours at lead days 1 to 2, where 5% is nominal, and its upper band is too wide, which is a one-sided bias that a width recalibration cannot fix. Building the net-demand distribution from the gross-demand distribution minus a randomly drawn ensemble member's solar curve is worse than the free network at all three lead bands (0.29 to 0.38 points), and recalibrating the free network or the sum did not beat the free network either. also relevant 00663 end-detector-for-the-prevailing-forecast-followup-to-654 A detector that reads the freshest half-hours of (observed power minus the NRA forecast) at a Primary and at its electrical neighbours, and outputs the probability that a load shift has ended, lets the prevailing forecast of E0 (frozen K1 plus the survival-hazard head R-haz) and of J2 (the end-to-end network of experiment 654) drop a shift sooner after it ends, and cuts the share of event-free rows on which the prevailing forecast wrongly departs from the NRA forecast. not supported not-for-production A learned end detector made the prevailing forecast better in the 24 hours after an injected shift ends (-0.9 to -1.1 scaled points of capacity) and worse while the shift is in force (+0.2 to +0.3 for E0d), and the neighbour graph added no consistent gain, because three random rewirings of it scored within 0.08 points of the real graph. On the final-test window the detector made E0 worse (4.81 against 4.26) and J2 slightly better (4.85 against 5.02), and the plain E0 was the best prevailing forecast of all (4.26). The veto on event-free rows is not met for E0d, and J2d passes it by its interval but not in every month. The detector is not worth the neighbour feed. also relevant 00652 two-output-forecast-with-explicit-rules-and-survival-hazard A prevailing-conditions head that outputs a signed depth and a survival probability per lead day, and is trained on a stated mixture of shift durations, scores a lower CRPS than K1 shifted by its own decayed recent error (R0 at 168 h) and than a no-fit hazard baseline (K1 shifted by its recent error and decayed by the best single survival curve), at every origin state in which a shift is in force, once every forecast is scored under its own rules. not supported not-for-production A prevailing forecast that continues a load shift cuts the error where a shift is in force from 9.9 to 5.8 points of capacity (unscaled), but a survival curve fitted to shift durations, with no neural network, scores 5.85 and so does as well as a neural network that learns the survival, when the shifts follow the training mixture. On held-out durations the learned survival output is better by 0.74 points, so the tie is not general. In the last day before a shift ends, the learned forecast scores 3.5 points worse than K1 and the fitted curve 4.6 points worse, which is the price of not knowing the end. also relevant 00650 extended-shift-departure-head-against-decayed-recent-error A departure head trained on an extended shift generator (shifts that end at random times, constant and proportional shapes, step and ramp onsets, depths from 3 to 50 points of capacity, donor and receiver conserved across real neighbours) forecasts the arrangement now in force better than K1 shifted by its own decayed recent error (R0 at tau 168 h), on a shift family that no arm trains on, after the band-widening share of the gain is removed. partly supported not-for-production Training the departure head on shifts that end at random times, with varied shapes and depths, makes it beat the no-fit shift by 2.3 points of capacity inside shifts outside its training range, and beat the head trained on the old bank by 1.5 points. The head still carries a shift past its end and scores 3.6 points worse than K1 there, so it is not ready for production. The next step is a head that ends a shift as soon as the gap signals say so. also relevant 00648 demand-encoder-size-and-hyperparameter-search-on-k1-and-the-class-2-candidate Experiment 447 found the S1 demand network insensitive to its settings. K1 and the class 2 candidate differ from S1: the lag encoder reads two lags with a learnt lag ID, and the candidate adds neighbour summaries. Their parts may no longer sit at a flat optimum, so changing the width or depth of the lag encoder, the width of the neighbour-summary encoder, the number of mixture components, the hidden width, the dropout, the learning rate, or the maximum number of epochs lowers days 1 to 10 event-free CRPS by more than the margin without making the network follow an injected load-shift more. not supported not-for-production Making the lag encoder wider or deeper, or the hidden layers bigger, does not improve the K1 or class 2 candidate demand neural networks by the margin we required (0.11 CRPS points); the best gain is 0.04 points and comes from one short-history Primary (D15), while the six MW Primaries get slightly worse. Dropout 0.0 hurts; a doubled learning rate lowered the score by 0.04 points in both neural networks, but no interval was computed. The neighbour-summary bottleneck gains 0.05 points but makes the forecast follow an injected load-shift more, so it fails its guard. No change helped detectably, so keep the sizes as they are and look for gains in the inputs, as experiment 447 advised. also relevant 00647 two-output-forecast-departure-head-on-frozen-k1 The arrangement now in force (the prevailing forecast) can be forecast better by a separate departure head added to the normal-running-arrangement forecast of K1 than by shifting K1's quantiles by its own recent error with a decaying weight (R0). The head may read K1's outputs, K1's frozen encoder embeddings, or an encoder retrained on the departure loss, and the normal-running-arrangement output stays K1 or, in the joint neural network, no worse than K1. partly supported not-for-production On injected load shifts the departure head scores 10.0 points of capacity below K1, but shifting K1 by its own recent error with no fit (tau 168 h) already closes most of that gap, so the head is only 0.9 points better, and the no-fit shift matches the head after a shift ends. Widening K1's band with no signal gets 60% to 68% of the head's gain, and about 3.3 points come from reading the gap signals. On real flagged days the gain rests on the verified pair in 2026-01. The next step is an experiment that separates the signal from the widening and from the no-fit shift, using shifts that end on varied days, before any head is considered for production. also relevant 00646 per-ens-member-neural-demand-networks-pooled-quantiles Running K1 and K3 once per ensemble member, and pooling the 51 member outputs into one mixture, improves the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), the upper-tail coverage, and the event-free scores over the networks that read the ensemble mean and spread, without raising the share of an injected load-shift that the forecast follows. not supported not-for-production For K1 and K3 on the five development months, giving the demand networks the mean and spread of the 51 ensemble members matched running them once per member and pooling the 51 answers, once the bands had equal width. The mean-and-spread input needs one pass through the neural network per forecast instead of 51. Pooling mainly widens the forecast band. Retraining the networks on one member at a time raised the CRPS by 0.02 to 0.07 points of capacity (the K1 interval includes 0). In this test the member inputs gave no gain beyond the mean and spread, so any gain from the ensemble would have to come from another input or from the training method. primary 00642 roster-upper-tail-correction-out-of-sample-leave-one-month-out A correction to the upper quantiles that is fitted without looking at the month it is scored on can bring the Candidate's and K1's event-free q90 and q95 exceedance within 1.5 percentage points of nominal (10% and 5%) on held-out months, because experiment 630 found the excess on ordinary days at most Primaries and a constant shift fitted on three months removed only part of it. The arms that let the correction vary with the Primary, lead band, hour of day, or the last 8 weeks of errors can follow the season that one constant could not. partly supported not-for-production Shifting each stored demand forecast to the level of the previous 28 days, and then widening its upper range, brings the share of readings above the forecast 90th percentile (q90) to between 9% and 12.5% in every test month at 14 of the 16 primary substations, against 10% to 16% before, but it makes the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS, the score of the whole forecast distribution) about 2% worse. The other two substations, D15 and D18, hide that increase in a pooled score, because their level changed in March 2026 and 45% of their readings were above q90 that month before any correction. A next experiment could treat D15 and D18 separately and test a shift applied to the upper quantiles only. primary 00631 bsp-group-sum-with-metered-generators-against-direct-bsp-forecast Experiment 629 found that sums of the 16 Primaries beneath two bulk supply points (BSPs) put 31% to 79% of actual flows below their q05 (nominal 5%), and that the metered wind and solar series beneath the BSP explained much of the gap (R squared 0.94 at Skegness). The claim here is that, once those metered farms are added to the sum together with a fitted remainder, a coupled scenario set (J3, the Schaake shuffle, or J5, the fitted copula) puts the q05 and q95 exceedance of the BSP flow within the binomial error of nominal at both BSPs, and beats independent draws (J0) on CRPS. not supported not-for-production Adding the nine metered wind and solar farms to the sum of Primaries fixes most of the export-side tail miss of Primaries-only sums (Skegness 41.7% to 3.0% of actual flows below the q05, on this experiment's rows), but the import side swings from too wide or about right (Boston 0.1%, Skegness 4.4% above the q95) to too narrow (14.3% and 32.6%), and no sum has both tails near 5% at both bulk supply points (BSPs). Coupling the scenarios (Schaake shuffle or fitted copula) improves the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) by 2.6% to 7.7%, so coupling matters once the farms are in. The direct forecast of each BSP meter is still the safer tail forecast, which means the deliverable should be a direct BSP forecast beside any node scenarios. primary 00630 roster-upper-demand-tail-calibration-event-days-and-bias-correction The three stored neural-network forecasts (K1, the class-2 Candidate, and K3) exceed their q90 and q95 for more actuals than nominal (an earlier quick check on all rows: 14% to 17% above q90, 8% to 10% above q95) on ordinary days as well as on load-shift event days, at most Primaries, so the excess is a bias of the median that a shift fitted on the first three development months removes on the last two. partly supported not-for-production The stored demand forecasts put too little weight on high demand on ordinary days, not only during load-shifts: the share of readings above the forecast q90 was 13% to 17% against a nominal 10%, and highest on cold nights and at long leads. A correction fitted on the first three development months removed only part of the excess on the last two, because the bias changes with the season.
