The correction also scores worse on bank holidays and, in point estimate, on Christmas. also relevant 00200 dp-pooled-correction-head-on-kalman-state Experiment 142's small network failed its known-answer gate with about 1,100 samples from one year at five substations. The same kind of network, trained on rows pooled across many Primary substations and years, learns to correct arm D's forecast from the recent errors, the calendar, the lead, and the ensemble-mean weather, and so beats recipe R (subtract 0.75 times the mean error of the last 14 days) at day D+1. partly supported not-for-production A small neural network trained on arm D's own past errors lowers the day-ahead score by 0.07 to 0.12 points at five substations, but a copy that sees no recent error gets most of that gain. The gain comes from correcting how arm D's error depends on its forecast level and the calendar, and a pinball-loss table comes within 0.01 to 0.02 points of the network on one year of data. also relevant 00193 dp-ens-two-number-solar-summary Experiment 187 found that passing each of the 51 ensemble members through the solar term lowers the daylight quantile score of the full best-guess stack by 2.23%, and that a Gaussian with each row's own mean and spread of the 51 responses recovers 95% of that gain. Two numbers per half-hour (the mean and the standard deviation of the members' solar responses) therefore carry nearly all of the gain, so a serving path can store two columns instead of running 51 passes. supported candidate Summarising the 51 ensemble weather members' solar estimates by their mean and standard deviation lowers the daylight quantile score by about 2% (98% of the gain from running all 51 members, 93% in the replicate months), at the five substations scored over one year. The weather layer could store two columns per half-hour instead of 51, and the 10th and 90th percentiles add nothing measurable. A follow-up experiment could test the two numbers in the live weather layer. also relevant 00192 dp-ens-members-temperature-cold-nights Experiment 187 found that passing the 51 ECMWF ensemble members through the solar term of the demand model lowers the daylight quantile score by 2.2%. The demand response to heating is also nonlinear (a hinge at 15.5 degrees C), and the ensemble mean smooths away the cold tail. Passing each member's temperature through the temperature terms therefore lowers the quantile score on cold winter nights. not supported not-for-production Running each ensemble member's temperature through the demand model gave no detectable improvement in the forecast bands on cold winter nights, because the 51 members' temperatures differ too little to signal the day's error. The cold-night bands are already too narrow. The cause of the cold-night error is still unknown; widening the bands directly, and testing wind, night cloud cover, and switching as inputs, are the candidates. also relevant 00187 dp-ens-members-in-stack Experiment 184 found that running each of the 51 ensemble members through the solar term of the convex demand model lowers the daylight quantile score by 2.2%, but its verdict was capped at inconclusive because a monotone gate failed on rows where the unit PV shape itself falls as irradiance rises. With a gate that matches that shape, the same arm passes, and its gain lies where the best-guess stack leaves the largest sunny-daylight error, at the substation D5. supported candidate Running each of the 51 ensemble weather members through the solar part of the demand model still improves the daylight forecast bands by about 2% on top of the full best-guess stack, and night is untouched. About two thirds of the gain needs that day's own members, and two numbers per half-hour (the mean and spread of the members' solar responses) carry nearly all of it, so a cheaper two-number version is the next thing to test. also relevant 00184 dp-ens-daylight-calibration Experiment 169 found that passing the ensemble's spread to the width of the forecast's bands adds nothing when scored over all half-hours. The benefit may be confined to daylight half-hours, especially sunny and partly cloudy ones, where the clouds that the 51 ensemble members disagree about change the output of embedded solar generation, and so the demand. Passing each member's irradiance through the convex model's solar term (arm M), or using the spread of the members' irradiance as a fraction of clear-sky to set the band width in daylight (arm S), calibrates the daylight bands better than the existing bands (arm A). inconclusive not-for-production Running each of the 51 ensemble weather members through the solar part of the demand model improves the daylight forecast bands by about 2%, mostly in the lower tail and on partly cloudy half-hours, while night is untouched. Placebos that widen the bands the same way but without the real members gain little, so most of the benefit is information about cloud. The next step is a production-cost check of the member pass and a test of its gain on top of the best-guess forecast. also relevant 00176 calibration-band-shape-smooth-in-lead The q05 to q95 band of the combined forecast (experiment 169's arm A) is not smooth along the lead because each cell of the spread table (hour band, calendar quarter, one of four lead bands) is a quantile of a few hundred correlated residuals, and neighbouring cells are fitted independently. Replacing the table with offsets that are a non-decreasing piecewise-linear function of lead (fix P), shrinking each cell towards the table pooled across substations (fix S), or both (fix PS), gives a band whose median width never falls from one lead day to the next, without worsening the quantile score or the cold-night coverage. inconclusive not-for-production D5's forecast band already widens steadily with lead time on the rows we score, and the dips appear only when switching-event rows are added, so these results give no reason to smooth the stored table. A smooth widening curve does not reduce accuracy but does not remove the dips either. Pulling noisy table cells towards a pooled table helps D10 and D14, hurts D5, and leaves cold-night coverage slightly low, so shrinkage needs testing on more substations before anyone adds shrinkage to the production forecast. primary 00173 dp-christmas-more-years-and-sites The convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors and recipe R (the mean error of the last 14 days by half-hour, held to 0.75 of its size), which scored 1.13 times an ordinary weekday over 24 December to 2 January at five substations in two Christmases (experiment 170), keeps a Christmas-to-weekday error ratio under 1.3 in every Christmas back to 2019-20 and at 14 or more of 16 Primary substations, and does not over- or under-forecast 25 and 26 December by more than 5% of that day's demand. inconclusive not-for-production Where the demand model had a winter of training data, the error over 24 December to 2 January was 0.97 to 1.22 times an ordinary weekday in all four Christmases from 2022-23 to 2025-26, so no special-day term is justified. The pre-registered run failed because the training rows of Christmas 2020-21 and 2021-22 (and of one substation in 2023-24) held little or no winter, since the lockdown window is left out of training. A forecast for a substation with under 180 days of usable history should be flagged, not trusted. also relevant 00172 dp-error-budget-worst-days The error of the stage 2 assembly (experiment 155's arm D) is concentrated on a small number of days that the project already knows how to label. The worst 5% of days, ranked by their pinball loss above the site's median day, carry at least 30% of the total excess loss, and at least half of those days carry one of six labels: a switching event, a metering error or flagged reading, a cold snap, an Economy 7 step, a holiday, or a combination. inconclusive not-for-production A small number of bad days carries a large share of the forecast's error: the worst 5% of days carry about 42% of the excess loss, and about half of those days coincide with a switching event, a holiday, or a cold snap. Switching events are the largest group, on days that carry 29% of the excess loss, so a forecast that improves only ordinary days leaves most of the loss in place. Cold snaps carry 5% of the excess in this mild scored winter, so this year cannot show whether a cold-night term pays. The formal verdict is inconclusive because one control narrowly failed. also relevant 00170 dp-bg-stage3-drift-and-holiday-scoring The convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors, ensemble-mean weather, the heating split by day type, one shared filter noise setting, and the pinned solar capacity (experiment 136's arm A2) improves further when it gets a drift term (experiment 167's D1) on top of the two post-forecast corrections of experiment 155's arm D (a winter night offset and recipe R's 14-day mean error profile). The mechanism is that the drift term removes a slow demand-level error that the monthly refit on 24 months of history leaves in, and neither the offset (winter nights only) nor recipe R (a 14-day profile held to 0.75 of its size) removes that error. Training on every year of history adds a further gain, because the drift term and the pinned capacity let the old years teach the heating and calendar terms. refuted not-for-production A slowly varying demand level (a drift term) improved the forecast by 0.40 points in experiment 167 but worsened it by 0.03 points once the forecast has the Kalman filter on recent errors (lower scores are better), and training on all years of history did not change that. The filter already appears to remove the slow level error that the drift term fixes, because without the filter the drift term improves the score by about 0.2 points. The drift term should not be added to experiment 155's arm D. Christmas (24 December to 2 January) scored 1.13 times an ordinary weekday at the same half-hours, below the 1.5 times predicted, and recipe R improved the Christmas score by 0.04 points. also relevant 00169 calibration-combined-fixes-and-ensemble-spread The spread across the 51 ensemble members of the temperature and of the downward shortwave radiation at a substation predicts how wide the forecast's residuals are, beyond the hour band, calendar quarter, lead, and the cold-day widening of experiment 164. A convex quantile model that scales the quantile offsets by a non-decreasing function of those two spreads lifts the cold-night q95 coverage of the combined forecast to 0.90 or more. partly supported not-for-production Combining the smooth spread table with the cold-day widening reproduces its 0.896 coverage of the 95% quantile on cold nights, and adding the spread of the ensemble weather forecast (how much its 51 members disagree) lifts that to 0.907. The lift comes from widening the 95% and 99% quantiles by 4% and 10%, which the same model gives with its spread terms removed, so the ensemble spread is not what lifts cold-night coverage. A later experiment could test a bias correction of the mean forecast on the coldest days, and judge cold nights over more than one winter. primary 00164 calibration-cold-night-tail-under-coverage The q95 coverage of experiment 160's smooth-table forecast on cold nights (day mean temperature below 2 °C) stays near 85% because the spread table is too narrow when it is cold, not because the mean forecast is biased. Widening the quantiles on days the ensemble forecasts as cold, by a factor fitted on the tuning months, lifts cold-night q95 coverage to 90% or more without worsening the all-row score. refuted not-for-production On cold nights the 95% quantile of the best forecast is exceeded on about 15% of readings, and mostly because its prediction interval is too narrow, not because its mean forecast is biased. Widening only the upper quantiles on days the weather forecast calls cold reduces that share to about 10% without changing the all-hours score, but no fix reached the pre-registered 90% coverage in the scored year, and only 10 cold days back that year's figure. The coldest forecasts (0 °C or below) are also biased low, so correcting the mean forecast on those days is the next experiment to run. primary 00161 dp-bsp-top-down-against-bottom-up A bulk supply point (BSP) is forecast better bottom-up than top-down. The top-down forecast is the best-guess GAM-K chain (experiment 155's arm D) applied to the BSP's reading as a stand-alone series. The bottom-up forecast adds the arm D forecasts of the BSP's child Primary substations that report real power, each times a weight learned from earlier readings, to arm D's forecast of the remainder (the BSP's reading minus those children's weighted readings). The mechanism is that the child Primaries' own forecasts are better than the BSP's chain can infer from the BSP's sum, because each child has its own heating, solar, and calendar response and its own recent errors, and the sum is not exact (losses, unmetered load, children that report apparent power), so the remainder and the weights absorb the difference. inconclusive not-for-production Forecasting a BSP from its children's forecasts plus a remainder did not beat forecasting the BSP as a stand-alone series at either BSP: the bottom-up score was 0.6% worse at D13 and 0.5% worse at D17. The likely reason is that the children this test could use (three real-power Primaries per BSP) cover 42% and 56% of the BSP's capacity, and the BSP's error lives in the rest. The oracle control also missed its pre-registered threshold, which was set too high. The verdict is inconclusive because both intervals include zero. also relevant 00160 calibration-band-width-fix-on-stage-2-winner The q05 to q95 band of the stage 2 winning arm (experiment 155's arm D with arm A's spread table) widens in steps along the lead, because the spread table has only four lead bands (up to 24 hours, 48, 144, and 168), fitted separately per hour band and calendar quarter. Interpolating each hour band by quarter cell between the lead-band centres, forcing the width to be non-decreasing in lead, or both, removes the steps without worsening the quantile score. supported candidate The 90% prediction interval (from the 5% to the 95% quantile) of experiment 155's best forecast was equally wide on lead days 2 to 5, because its stored spread table has only four lead bands. Interpolating the table between the band centres removes the equal days and raises the quantile score by 0.002 points, below the pre-registered ceiling of 0.01, but it narrows the interval at 24 to 72 hours and widens it from 72 hours on, so one substation loses 0.009. It does not fix the cold-night upper tail: the forecast exceeds the 95% quantile on about 15% of cold-night rows, against 5% for a calibrated forecast. primary 00155 dp-bg-stage2-assembly-night-offset-and-error-correction A GAM-K forecast (the convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors, experiment 111) that already has the heating split by day type, one shared filter noise setting, the pinned solar capacity, and the ensemble mean as its weather input (experiment 136's arm A2) improves further when two post-forecast corrections are added: a winter night offset (experiment 137) and the 14-day mean error profile of recipe R (experiment 115). The mechanism is that the two corrections remove different errors, a level error that repeats on winter nights and a half-hour-of-day shape error that repeats day to day, so their gains add. The assembled arm then scores below experiment 111's GAM-K and BG2 (experiment 87) over leads 0.5 to 168 hours, and its tails on cold nights and on holidays are no worse than the uncorrected arm's. inconclusive candidate Adding recipe R, which subtracts 0.75 times the mean error of the last 14 days by half-hour, lowers the stage 1 assembly's score by about 0.04 points (1.3%), and the winter night offset adds nothing once R is in. The assembly with R scores 2.754 against BG2's 2.780, which is better by 0.026 points with an interval too wide to rank the two. The pre-registered placebo control failed, so the formal verdict is inconclusive, but the choice of winning arm (R alone) does not depend on it. also relevant 00142 differentiable-physics-sequence-model-on-gam-k-residuals A small neural network that reads GAM-K's last 14 days of residuals, the calendar, and the target day's forecast weather predicts the day-ahead residual better than the hand-built Kalman filter with the 14-day error profile (recipe R of experiment 115), and gives better tails when it is trained with the pinball loss at the 11 quantiles. inconclusive not-for-production A small neural network that reads the last 14 days of GAM-K's errors did not learn to adapt to changes in them: when we added a known step or a Saturday-evening shift to real errors, it recovered none of it, so we did not score it on the scored year. Nothing was scored, so this result does not compare it with the hand-built Kalman filter and recipe R. also relevant 00136 dp-bg-stage1-assembly-on-the-ensemble-mean A convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors (GAM-K, experiment 111), given experiment 114's heating split by day type (T-all) and experiment 133's single shared filter noise setting (POOL), and driven by the ensemble mean of the ECMWF ensemble (ENS) instead of its 51 members, forecasts Primary demand 0.5 to 168 hours ahead at least as well as BG2 (experiment 87) and better than experiment 111's GAM-K. The mechanism is that the three gains came from different parts of the model (the hinge, the filter noise, the weather input) and so add, and that experiment 125 found that the members' own spread adds no tail skill, so one forecast on the mean loses nothing. inconclusive not-for-production Putting everything that has helped so far into the convex demand model and driving it from the ensemble mean gives a forecast that scores the same as the production recipe (BG2) and as experiment 111's GAM-K, and the experiment cannot tell any of the three apart. Using the ensemble mean makes the score about 0.04 points worse than using all 51 members, and the heating split and the shared filter noise improve it by about 0.05, so the assembly did not add up to the hoped-for gain. also relevant 00133 differentiable-physics-vk-learned-noise-and-observation-variance-in-gam-k On GAM-K's filter (a level and a transient per hour band, per substation), noise settings chosen per substation by day-ahead score lower the day-ahead quantile score below the fixed settings of experiment 111, which were chosen by marginal likelihood on 184 non-contiguous days. An online observation variance in the manner of VIKING (de Vilmarest and Wintenberger, 2022), used to scale the spread, then improves the coverage of the 0.95 quantile on cold nights, which experiment 125 found at 73% to 78%, because recent large errors widen the spread. The mechanism under test is that the size of recent proxy-driven residuals predicts the size of the next day's error on cold nights. inconclusive not-for-production Choosing the filter's noise settings for each substation by how well they forecast the next day did not improve the forecast on later months: the gain of 0.044 points on the months used to choose shrank to 0.009 on the scored year, inside the noise. A single setting shared by every substation did at least as well as the per-substation settings, so tuning the filter's noise per substation looks unnecessary, although the grid did not find a minimum. Letting the observation variance follow recent errors did not widen the forecast where it matters, on cold nights, where the 0.95 quantile still covered only 86% to 88% of readings. also relevant 00125 differentiable-physics-n8-ens-members-through-gam-k-and-the-spread-around-them Placing GAM-K's residual quantiles, fitted on a forecast driven by the analysis proxy (so they hold model and filter error and almost no weather error), around each of the 51 ENS members gives tails closer to nominal than today's table, which is fitted on ensemble-mean residuals, and the gain is largest at long leads and on cold winter nights, where the hinge turns a temperature error into a large demand error. The comparison is against GAM-K re-tuned on the same factor grid, so a plain scale error cannot pass for a better design. inconclusive not-for-production Putting the forecast-error table around each of the 51 weather members, and fitting it on analysis-driven forecasts so that it holds no weather error, did not improve the tails of GAM-K's demand forecast. The weather members' spread is small against the model's own error, so the weather error was counted twice in the code but is too small to matter. The next step is the cold winter nights, where demand exceeds the 95% quantile about a quarter of the time in every arm. The verdict is inconclusive, because no arm reached 14 of 16 calibration cells. also relevant 00119 differentiable-physics-enc-weather-patch-encoder-on-ens A small neural network that reads the ENS grid boxes around a Primary, and not only the one box GAM-K reads, lowers GAM-K's quantile score a little on average and more on the cold, showery, and badly forecast days NGED cares about, either as a correction to GAM-K's quantiles or as a replacement for its single-box temperature and irradiance. inconclusive not-for-production A small neural network that reads the ensemble weather around a Primary lowers GAM-K's quantile score by 0.062 points of effective capacity in one scored year and 0.035 in the other (both statistically significant, 5 of 5 substations better), and the gain is smaller in winter (0.041 and 0.027 points) but never a loss. About two-thirds of the gain survives when the network reads the wrong date's weather (0.043 and 0.022), so it is probably a recalibration of GAM-K's quantiles with the lead, the hour, and GAM-K's own forecast, and the surrounding boxes add nothing to the centre box (patch minus centre box: -0.002 and +0.003 points). The known-answer gate failed, so the verdict is inconclusive, and the next step is a plain recalibration of GAM-K's quantiles with the centre box's extra fields (dew point, pressure, precipitation, and member spread), not a patch encoder. also relevant 00117 differentiable-physics-h2-graph-prior-on-pooled-convex-parameters A penalty on the differences between interconnected Primaries' parameters (heating slopes, PV capacity as a share of effective capacity, the profile's scale, and the holiday coefficients) narrows those parameters' month-block bootstrap intervals without breaking their coverage when neighbouring Primaries are alike, and worsens the full-history quantile score by at most 0.03 points. refuted not-for-production At the weight tested, tying the parameters of interconnected substations together did not improve the forecast: in the scored year it worsened the quantile score by 0.020 points on all days (the interval spans zero) and by 0.173 points in winter evening peaks (the replicate year gave -0.021). On synthetic substations with a known truth it narrowed only heating-slope intervals, and the 80% intervals of PV capacity held the truth 17% of the time against 78% without the tie. A tie on heating slopes alone worsened the real score by 0.006 and 0.001 points, an exploratory lead and not a result. also relevant 00107 differentiable-physics-rolling-origin-history-and-tails Refitted quarterly from 2023-07 to 2026-04 and scored on the next 3 months, the convex model's two history contrasts (all years against 12 months, drift against none) keep one sign at almost every origin. A second claim, labelled separately as C5 and not part of the verdict: a level-dependent spread brings its 95% and 99% quantiles within 1 point of nominal coverage without worsening the quantile score. partly supported not-for-production Giving the convex demand model a drift term lowered its score at 10 of 12 quarterly refits, by 0.45 points when trained on all years (interval 0.23 to 0.68). In a post hoc split, about three-fifths of that size is one substation (D10) at the 2023-24 refits, and the 2025-26 refits give 0.30, as in experiment 104. All years without drift scored worse than 12 months at 8 of 12 refits, and all years with drift against 12 months has no stable answer: winter-quarter refits favour more years, summer ones are level. The spread that depends on the forecast level made the 95% and 99% quantiles worse, so the tail coverage still needs a different method. The verdict is partly supported, because only the drift contrast is stable; a second spread (the conformal spread) is not interpreted, because it was built with a flaw. also relevant 00100 drop1-random-lag-dropout-widens-intervals An XGBoost quantile model for Primary substation demand that is trained with labelled switching half-hours removed from its targets and with its lagged power inputs set to missing at random intervals, and that has those lags set to missing when they lie inside a labelled switching event, widens its 5% to 95% band on the half-hours whose lags are missing, so that the band's coverage moves from 0.784 towards the nominal 0.90, without widening the band elsewhere. inconclusive not-for-production Training the demand forecast with lags hidden at random did not make its band wider on half-hours where a lag is missing: on real rows the band covered 0.80 (hidden in 10% of training rows) to 0.84 (30%) of actuals, against a nominal 0.90. Hiding lags in 30% of rows did remove the accuracy loss that masking alone causes on injected transfers (-0.02 points, 95% interval -0.35 to +0.38 against the plain model). Hiding lags in 10% of rows left +0.26 (98.75% interval -0.15 to +0.85), not separable from zero or from the loss. An input that tells the XGBoost model a lag is missing, or a separate XGBoost model of the quantile spread, are untested routes to a wider band. primary 00099 crps1-crps-type-loss-over-ens-members-primary-demand-pilot Training the Primary-substation quantile model on the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) of the pooled ensemble forecast, with several ensemble members as separate rows, scores lower on the quantile score and covers the tails closer to nominal than training the same rows with the pinball loss, because the pinball loss makes every member's row learn the whole predictive spread and pooling the 51 members then counts the weather uncertainty twice. small gain not-for-production The CRPS loss beat the pinball loss on the same 6 members per run by 0.039 points (-0.057 to -0.018). primary 00097 cal1-post-hoc-recalibration-of-bg2-quantiles-tails A post-hoc recalibration of the stored quantiles of the best-guess forecast (BG2, experiment 87), fitted on earlier months only, brings the coverage of the 0.01, 0.05, 0.95, and 0.99 quantiles to within 0.01 of nominal in the 12 to 36 hour lead band of each class, without making the centre of the distribution worse. refuted not-for-production The stored best-guess quantiles cover the lower tail too widely (q05 covers 0.035) and the upper tail slightly too narrowly (q95 covers 0.938), at 12 to 36 hours for Primary substations, and no post-hoc recalibration fitted on earlier months moved coverage by more than its own interval. primary 00080 bm0-zero-base-margin-xgboost-quantile-models XGBoost starts a quantile model from a base score that it estimates from the training labels, one value for each of the nine quantile levels (experiment 78 found 0.403 at the 5% level to 0.899 at the 95% level for one series, with 500 boosting rounds and no early stopping). Replacing that start with zero (a base margin of zero in every row, which is the same as a base score of zero) lowers the quantile score of the production-style models for Primary substation demand (retrained weekly), bulk supply point and grid supply point demand (retrained weekly), solar farms, and wind farms. The gap is not a symptom of too few boosting rounds, so four times as many rounds, or early stopping, does not remove it. inconclusive not-for-production Starting XGBoost from zero did not lower the quantile score of any production-style XGBoost model: Primary substations -0.017 points of capacity (98.75% interval -0.072 to +0.054), bulk and grid supply points +0.006 (-0.091 to +0.092), the frozen Primary stack -0.033 (-0.084 to +0.031), solar farms -0.010 (-0.036 to +0.028). primary 00035 lead-weighted-quantile-blend-of-stored-models For Primary substation demand, solar farms, and wind farms, averaging the quantiles of two or three forecast models that experiments 19, 20, 30, and 33 already scored (N1 is the ENS-trained single-stage XGBoost model, and the stack is N1 with the 14-day correction and a spread factor of 1.15), with one weight per lead band chosen only on earlier months, lowers the quantile score below the best single member by more than the threshold set for each technology (0.05 points of capacity for Primary demand and solar, 0.10 for wind). supported candidate Averaging the quantiles of three stored demand models lowered the Primary demand error by 0.10 points of capacity against the best single model (98.33% interval -0.19 to -0.03), so the estimate clears the 0.05 threshold for moving it into production. For solar and wind the gains were too small to resolve on 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms. primary 00020 solar-wind-stack-cams-stage0-spread-margin For the 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms, stacking the candidate changes of experiments 00012, 00014, and 00016 (a CAMS-trained stage 1a and a stage 0 quantile mapping for solar, a power-curve base margin for wind, and a fitted spread factor for both) gives a lower continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) than the pooled ERA5-trained mixture of experiment 00002. partly supported candidate For wind, a starting guess from the turbine power curve lowered the error by 0.055 points of capacity (99.58% interval -0.110 to -0.007), and adding a spread factor made the total 0.071 (-0.133 to -0.014); the spread factor's extra -0.016 (-0.036 to +0.004) is not detectable. For solar, no change helped detectably, and the full stack was 0.035 points higher with an interval that includes zero (-0.075 to +0.116). primary 00016 pooled-mixture-calibration-solar-wind For the 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms, a correction fitted on earlier validation months (a scalar spread factor, a spread factor per lead band, a location-and-scale calibrator, or a free quantile calibrator) brings the 5% to 95% band of the pooled ERA5-trained mixture closer to 90% coverage in every lead band, without raising the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) by more than 0.05 points of capacity. partly supported candidate For solar, one spread factor brought the 5% to 95% band from covering 94.3% to 95.3% of cases down to 89.5% to 91.8%, with no detectable change in accuracy. For wind, no planned correction fixed the first two days, and a spread factor on two lead groups, added after seeing the results, brought every lead band to 90.7% to 92.5% coverage and has not been tested on another year. primary 00002 stage2-calibrator-and-mixture-vs-ens-quantile A shared per-technology calibrator and a learned blend, fed by ERA5-trained stage 1a quantiles applied to ENS weather, give a lower continuous ranked probability score than the pooled stage 1a mixture and than a quantile model trained on ENS weather. partly supported candidate Pooling the ERA5-trained solar and wind quantiles over the 51 weather-forecast members beat a model trained on archived weather forecasts: wind by 0.62 points of capacity (95% interval -0.99 to -0.26) and solar by 0.24 (-0.36 to -0.06), with the gain in the first six days. A second calibration model on top did not improve on the pooling and made solar worse by 0.40 points (+0.26 to +0.61). The result rests on 6 solar farms, 3 wind farms, and one validation year. primary
