docs.title: Priority
docs.text: Id Question Priority Waits for State 483 Does a widening or table P make the tails of the first-release demand candidates honest? 1 Experiment 470 Finished (partly supported): The first-release demand candidates are too wide on the lower tail and too narrow on the upper tail, so a widening of both tails makes the lower tail worse while it repairs the upper one. See experiment 483. 492 Can two constants per metering group replace table P for the first-release demand candidates? 2 Experiment 483 Finished (partly supported): At the eight MVA-only Primaries, one lower constant and one upper constant per metering group, fitted on earlier months, recalibrate the demand forecast as well as table P (20 factors per metering group) does, so table P can be dropped there. See experiment 492. 630 Is the roster networks' upper demand tail too low on ordinary days, and does a bias correction fitted on earlier months remove the excess? 1 Nothing Finished (partly supported) 625 How few member paths do NGED's power-flow studies need, and does a Schaake shuffle of anomaly paths help the Primaries? 3 Experiments 434 and 436 (finished) Finished (partly supported) 629 Do coherent Primary scenarios, summed to a bulk supply point, give a trustworthy tail for the flow through that point? 4 Experiments 625 and 626 (finished) Finished (not supported) 631 Once the metered farms beneath a bulk supply point are in the sum, does a coherent scenario sum give a usable tail for the flow through that point? 5 Experiment 629 (finished) Finished (not supported) 689 Does a width scale fitted on a fixed lookback remove the steps in band width at the model refits, or does seed averaging matter? 2 Experiment 683 (finished) Finished P14 Which coupling step, ECC-Q or the Schaake shuffle, gives better coherence scores at short and long leads? 6 The scoring harness and experiment 00016 Answered for the farms and the Primaries by experiments 434, 436, and 625; open for coherence with the direct forecast of the bulk supply point's meter (see the delivery recommendation) 627 Which 3, 5, or 10 of the 51 coherent member paths should NGED's power-flow studies use, with no label attached to any path? Done Nothing Finished (partly supported): Picking 5 of the 51 forecast paths by cutting them into 5 equal groups on one summary and taking one path from each covers their spread better than picking 5 at random, in every month, but still misses the tails: the stratified rules leave a gap of 11% to 12% of the range at the 5th percentile and 13% to 14% at the 95th. 628 Can NGED rebuild coherent scenarios from stored quantiles alone, and which tail rule should the client use? Done Nothing Finished (partly supported): NGED can rebuild the marginal forecasts and a Schaake-shuffle coupling from 11 stored quantiles per site and half-hour plus a small dependence table. 1,000 client-drawn scenarios score within 0.3% of the 51 scenarios the pipeline builds on CRPS, and a Schaake shuffle of 51 stored past paths matches the pipeline's shuffle on the variogram score. 642 Can a correction fitted on other months bring the upper demand tail of K1 and the Candidate within 1.5 percentage points of nominal without raising CRPS by more than 1%? Done Nothing Finished (partly supported): Shifting each stored demand forecast to the level of the previous 28 days, and then widening its upper range, brings the share of readings above the forecast 90th percentile (q90) to between 9% and 12.5% in every test month at 14 of the 16 primary substations, against 10% to 16% before, but it makes the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS, the score of the whole forecast distribution) about 2% worse. 646 Does running the demand networks once per ensemble member and pooling the 51 outputs beat giving them the ensemble mean and spread? Done Nothing Finished (not supported): For K1 and K3 on the 5 development months, giving the demand networks the mean and spread of the 51 ensemble members matched running them once per member and pooling the 51 answers, once the bands had equal width. 688 Do the 90% bands of the normal-running Primaries miss in winter because of median error and load transfers, or because the bands are too narrow? Done Nothing Finished (supported): The 90% bands of the 16 Primary substations' normal-running forecasts miss in winter mostly because the median forecast is off by a different amount each month, and partly because of load transfers, not because the bands are too narrow.

docs.title: Planned experiments
docs.text: Experiment Hypothesis Relevance 00654 two-output-network-end-to-end-with-end-detector One network, trained end to end (K1's body plus a prevailing head that reads the lag-encoder outputs, with no hand-built gate), gives a prevailing forecast at least as good as the frozen K1 plus the survival-hazard head R-haz of experiment 652, with no loss to the normal-running- arrangement (NRA) output; and a learned end detector that reads the freshest half-hours lets the prevailing forecast drop a shift faster after it ends. also relevant

docs.title: P14: coupling
docs.text: The coupling step turns calibrated quantiles back into 51 coherent members. The arms are ECC-Q with the interpolation, tail, and tie rules of the staged forecast roadmap page, and the Schaake shuffle, scored by the variogram score and the CRPS of summed solar farms in a weather cell, by lead band. Experiments 434, 436, and 625 have since compared the couplings: a Schaake shuffle of past observed paths scored 34% below independent draws across the wind and solar farms, and no coupling beat independent draws across the 16 Primaries. Experiments 629 and 631 found that summed node scenarios did not give a usable tail for the flow through a bulk supply point. The delivery recommendation states the current position.

docs.title: Curtailment cost
docs.text:
The current understanding and the options for next work are on the state and next steps page.

We can now score a demand forecast by the curtailment cost of its errors at a bulk supply point, but the two supply points of the pilot hold too few events to rank forecasts at the headline limit of 0.9 times their earlier maximum export, so no forecast has yet been shown to curtail less there.

Curtailment is the capping of generators beneath a substation when its export would pass a limit. The scoring code plans the caps from a forecast of the substation's export, then charges the energy lost to the caps plus a penalty for export that stays over the limit. Both experiments of the theme are worked examples of that code, and neither had a registered prediction. Experiment 84 ran the scoring code on 2 bulk supply points, Boston and Skegness, and experiment 83 scored the tails of the forecasts of 20 demand series (16 Primary substations, 4 supply points).

Boston and Skegness together have 19 half-hours beyond 0.9 times their earlier maximum export in the scored year, and more than 100 per node only at half that maximum. The scored year runs from 2025-07-02 to 2026-06-30. The figure counts export and import in separate panels, and also plots Bicker Fen, which is not scored. Source: experiment 84.

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
The code runs and reproduces a hand-worked answer exactly. All eight quantities of a made-up half-hour (a 45.0 MW limit and two generators) agree with the hand calculation (experiment 84). The verdict of both experiments is inconclusive, because neither registered a contrast.

The pilot cannot rank forecasts at the headline limit. Each arm is a pair of forecasts, one of the substation's export and one of its generators' output. The scaled limit is a fraction of a node's maximum export before 2025-07-02. At 0.9 times, the cost rests on 19 half-hours (all 19 scored), and no difference between arms is significant at the 5% level. At 0.75 times, with 46 half-hours (41 scored), the stack costs GBP 2,440,720 more than the best guess (95% interval 96,371 to 6,686,043). At 0.5 times, with 323 half-hours (268 scored), the best guess costs GBP 10,802,520 less than climatology (-20,880,964 to -3,342,553), and its gap to the NGED baseline includes zero. We have no evidence that NGED operates at 0.5 times, so that limit is a rehearsal (experiment 84). The costs are retrospective, from an energy proxy (generator energy cut plus 20 times the energy left over the limit, at GBP 2,000 per MWh), and are a calibration to history, not a saving.

The two arms are experiment 84's, and match the glossary entries only in part. The stack is the substation forecast fitted once and corrected from its own recent errors, with a generator forecast fitted once. The best guess (weekly retrained) is the substation forecast retrained every week with each generator forecast retrained monthly. Experiment 84 does not state whether either arm applies a half-life or the glossary's spread factor of 1.15.

The best guess (weekly retrained) has the lowest avoidable cost of the arms at all three scaled limits, but only some of its gaps are significant. Avoidable cost is an arm's cost minus the perfect forecast's cost, where the perfect forecast has every quantile equal to the metered value. The figure has one panel per scaled limit at GBP 2,000 per MWh, and shorter bars are better. Source: experiment 84.

Most of the best guess's avoidable cost at 0.9 times is breach, not unneeded cuts. Breach is export that stayed over the limit because the forecast did not order enough cuts. Of the GBP 571,823 avoidable cost, 81% is breach: the forecast ordered 13.6 MWh of cuts on event half-hours against 35.1 MWh needed. Another 20% is output cut when metered export was within the limit (experiment 84).

A forecast that fits a whole distribution can plan far more curtailment. In experiment 97, on 17 half-hours at one node (it scores the stored BG2 forecasts of node-only mode, so its count differs from experiment 84's 19), Student-t and skew-normal fits planned 911 and 1,364 MWh of curtailment against 57.5 MWh for the stored forecast, which gave avoidable costs of GBP 2.36 million and 3.12 million against 618,171. The other recalibrations were not separable from the stored forecast (experiment 97).

In an exploratory run, the stored demand forecasts of experiment 48 were too narrow in both tails. The run pooled 20 demand series, every lead, runs from 2025-07-02, and the arms best guess stack, manual_heuristic, and climatology. Coverage of the 0.05 quantile was 0.066 to 0.085 and of the 0.95 quantile 0.891 to 0.927, and weekly retraining had the lowest pinball loss at both levels. The experiment gives no interval, and the 0.01 and 0.99 levels were not stored (experiment 83, on forecasts stored by experiment 48). For the later BG2 forecast, q05 coverage reads 0.035 at the point estimate, which is too wide a lower tail (16 Primary substations, 12 to 36 hours, about 9 months, no interval given; experiment 97).

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text: The only metric design implemented plans caps from the 0.95 quantile of the substation's export forecast and scores at a limit scaled from the node's earlier maximum. The generators beneath the node cut the excess in proportion to their capacity, and the cost is the energy proxy with a breach ratio of 20 (experiment 84). Experiment 84 compared the price and the DCUSA form only, and tried no other quantile, sharing rule, or breach ratio. This is a metric design, not a forecast design: no forecast design curtailed less with significance at the headline limit.

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text: Nothing is ready. Both experiments are not-for-production. The cost-savings roadmap describes the metric and the larger delivery that would allow a ranking (cost-savings metrics).

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
• Score curtailment at the substation, not at a single meter. Experiment 83 first built a single-series metric and withdrew it, because the limit binds at a substation (experiment 83). Otherwise the metric scores each meter against its own history, which does not measure curtailment. Re-check if a per-meter limit becomes known.
  • Count the events before ranking. At 0.9 times the maximum only 19 half-hours qualify, and no difference is significant (experiment 84). Otherwise a ranking rests on a few half-hours. Re-check when the delivery of about 2,500 series is scored.
  • Score at a scaled limit, and show the published thermal limit as a reference. Boston's export reached its published limit once, and the maintainer's unconfirmed understanding is that NGED curtails early to keep headroom (experiment 84). Re-check if NGED confirms its operating practice (issue #1318).
  • Label every cost "calibration to history, not a saving". The perfect forecast still costs GBP 87,460 at 0.9 times, because the cap also removes output above a generator's estimated capacity (experiment 84). Otherwise a cost reads as money NGED would have saved. Re-check if the metric is validated against a real curtailment event.
  • The NGED baseline is an assumption. It is the manual heuristic's substation forecast with every generator at full capacity, from the maintainer's unconfirmed understanding of NGED's practice (experiment 84). Re-check once NGED describes its practice.
  • Rank under the energy proxy and under the DCUSA form separately. Changing the price does not reorder the arms, but the DCUSA form charges every instructed generator its whole headroom, and climatology's avoidable cost becomes negative under it (experiment 84). Otherwise the choice of cost form decides the ranking unnoticed. Re-check if a different price or cost form is added.
  • Report how many generator-half-hours had no forecast. Across the six arms, 13% had none, so those generators were not capped and added to breach (experiment 84). Otherwise a forecast set with more gaps looks worse for that reason alone. Re-check with other forecast sets.
  • Report the unscored half-hours. Scoring needs a stored forecast at 12 to 36 hours lead, which drops 5 of 46 events at 0.75 times, and the dropped half-hours hold 14% of the excess energy at 0.5 times (experiment 84). Re-check if the forecast lead window or the stored forecast sets change.
  • Check the sign of each node. Boston and Skegness are inferred as import-positive, Bicker Fen's sign is unconfirmed, and Walpole's is unknown, so the metric excludes them (experiment 84). A wrong sign swaps export and import. Re-check when NGED supplies the signs.
  • Store the 0.01 and 0.99 quantiles, and score tails with studies.tail_calibration. The stored sets of experiment 48 stop at 0.95, so the tail table could not be read at 0.99 (experiment 83). Later sets store 11 levels (experiment 97). Re-check if a forecast set again stores fewer levels.
  • Publish generator figures only as sums over at least 4 generators. Experiment 84 reports no generator singly, and the table joining generators to substations stays in the private data folder (experiment 84). Re-check if a node has fewer than 4 generators.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text:
• Whether any forecast curtails less than another with significance, once about 2,500 series are scored (the January 2027 delivery).
  • How NGED chooses its operating limit, and how it allocates caps among generators.
  • Whether the tails of the forecasts are too narrow in general: experiments 83 and 97 disagree on the lower tail, on different forecasts and periods.

The Research plan lists what is planned next, and the Experiments page lists every experiment.

docs.title: Curtailment cost: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00601 nra-curtailment-cost-and-tail-calibration-of-assembled-candidates The G4 gated band does not raise the curtailment cost of C1 or A1 on event-free rows, and it lowers that cost in the 7 days after an injected load-shift ends. partly supported candidate On injected load-shifts the G4 band brings the q95 exceedance close to the nominal 0.05 in the 7 days after the end (0.048 to 0.049) and lowers the curtailment cost of both forecasts at limits 0.75 and 0.5 of the past maximum. At the headline limit of 0.9 the reduction is small and rests on one Primary. On the real December 2025 pair the band does not help D16, the Primary whose load rose, so the cost of that event is almost unchanged. primary 00484 hard-row-weighting-in-demand-network-fine-tuning Experiments 435 and 470 left cold nights worse than the tail target, and avoidable curtailment cost ranks the candidates differently from CRPS. Fine-tuning the pretrained network with larger weights on the rows that decide NGED's costs lowers the error on those rows without raising it elsewhere. not supported not-for-production Giving larger fine-tuning weights to cold nights, to high-flow half-hours at the six signed-MW Primaries, or to winter did not improve the forecasts that matter to NGED. Cold-night error at the eight fell by 0.068 points under W-cold, which is inside the noise floor of 0.17, and avoidable-curtailment cost did not change. Weighting winter (W-season) raised CRPS at the eight. One weight value (3) and one pretrained neural network were tested, so the result suggests the hard rows are limited by the inputs rather than the weighting. The next step to try is a different input or neural-network architecture. also relevant 00471 manual-heuristic-calibration-and-analogue-upgrades If the 13 (and later 12) equally weighted historical analogues of the manual heuristic are recalibrated with a correction fitted on a trailing window of past errors, the quantile score falls against the faithful heuristic, because the heuristic's empirical 95th percentile of 13 members is exceeded about 11.4% of the time even when the analogues are perfect. The heuristic also carries a level bias. not supported not-for-production A simple recalibration of the 13 historical analogues behind NGED's manual heuristic did not improve its forecasts over the five months we scored. Fitting a calibration on the last 28 or 56 days of errors, or shifting the analogues by their recent error, left the average error score unchanged or worse at the eight MVA-only substations and the six signed-MW substations. The Gaussian fit lowered the score on cold winter nights (0.90 points at the eight) but raised it at the six in Christmas week, so the faithful heuristic stays the benchmark that the neural-network and XGBoost models are compared against. also relevant 00402 lag-gate-learned-weight-injected-load-shifts-part-1 A gate that sets the weight of a mixture of two XGBoost demand forecasts (one with the three power lags, one without) from the surprise of the lagged readings, trained only on injected load-shift events with known truth, beats the fitted constant mixture around real load shifts and costs no more than it outside them. partly supported not-for-production A gate trained only on injected load shifts, with no labels from National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED), learns to lower the weight on the forecast with power lags from 0.51 to 0.42 when a lagged reading falls inside a load shift, and so removes most of the harm that the lags do in that case. The gain on real load shifts is small (0.10 points at most against the 50/50 mixture, and 0.04 or less against the constant mixture fitted on injected events), and the gate scores worse than the 50/50 mixture when the target itself is inside a real labelled event at the six Primaries. The fitted constant mixture per group is a simpler forecast than the gate and comes within about 1.4% of its exact CRPS on injected rows. Training the gate on real and injected events together is untested. also relevant 00401 real-and-synthetic-load-shift-median-share-and-fixed-forecast-mixture Job 1. When a synthetic step of the corrected labelled depth is injected into clean periods at the same Primary and the same lag status as each real labelled event, the plain monthly control's median still follows the step by much less than it follows the real event, so the gap between 36.8% (experiment 395 Part E) and 0.94 (Part F) is not an artefact of the depth or the rows. Job 2. A fixed-weight mixture of the weekly forecast with power lags and the forecast without them scores within 0.1 points of effective capacity of experiment 400's learned blend B2 on rows with lags in an event, at the six Primaries with signed readings. partly supported not-for-production The median share of a load-shift step that experiment 395 called "followed" (0.94 with 3 lags in the event) is mostly not a response to the lags: a forecast with no power lags at all reaches 0.95, and the forecast with lags moves its median by at most about 0.03 more than the forecast without lags on the same rows, which is at the noise floor of two different fitted forecasts. Real events are far less visible to the lags than synthetic steps are, so the synthetic lag-encroachment sweep overstates what a real event does to the forecast. A fixed 50/50 mixture of the two forecasts does about as well as the learned blend at the six Primaries with signed readings, and not at the eight, where the interval allows it to score 0.12 points worse. At the six, one event at D16 carries most of the gain over the forecast with lags. also relevant 00400 lagged-lagless-forecast-blend-around-load-shifts-stored A mixture of the weekly XGBoost forecast with power lags and the XGBoost forecast without power lags, weighted by a smooth function of the lags' surprise scores and of lead time, scores better than the forecast with lags on the rows whose lags touch a load-shift event, and costs no more than 0.02 points of effective capacity on rows outside events. not supported not-for-production The lag surprise scores from experiment 391 did not tell a blend when to trust the power lags: the fitted weight hardly moved around events, so every learned blend behaved like a mix of about 60% forecast with lags and 40% forecast without lags. A fixed 50/50 mix helps on event-lag rows at the six Primaries with signed readings and costs a little elsewhere, so a smooth blend driven by these scores is not worth porting. The next step is a learned blender trained on injected events, which supplies the event examples that the real rows are too few to give. also relevant 00392 xgboost-nra-load-shift-masked-targets Removing load-shift events from the training targets of the monthly XGBoost demand model gives a forecast that stays near the normal running arrangement (NRA) level while a transfer is under way, and a mask built by the "deep and long" detector does so almost as well as a mask built from NGED's 66 hand-labelled transfers. Giving the unmasked model the surprise of its lags and of its neighbours (arm R5) gives the same NRA behaviour with no detector. not supported not-for-production Removing the labelled load-shift events from the XGBoost model's training targets does not make its forecast ignore a load shift in its lagged power inputs (the readings from the forecast origin, one day earlier, and one week earlier). When all three lagged inputs sit inside a synthetic load shift, the median forecast of the XGBoost model still moves by about 40% of the load shift's size, with or without the mask, and the band does not widen. Only dropping the lagged power inputs removes the effect, at a cost of about 0.7 percentage points of capacity in the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS). A mask built by an automatic load-shift detector (arm R2) was dropped and not tested. also relevant 00383 load-shift-xgboost-oracle-first-part-1 On the rows whose power lags lie inside a hand-labelled load-shift event, the weekly XGBoost demand model's 5% to 95% band covers about 0.80 of the readings against 0.90 nominal. Nulling those lags (with 30% random lag dropout in training) or serving a lagless model on those rows, plus widening the band, brings the coverage within 0.03 of 0.90 and lowers the q95 and q99 pinball loss by 10% or more, without harming rows outside events. not supported not-for-production Telling the weekly XGBoost model which of its recent-power inputs lie inside a load-shift event does not fix its upper tail: nulling the inputs makes no measurable difference, and a lagless model helps at the six Primaries whose meters record the sign of the flow but hurts at the eight that do not. Fixed widening raises coverage on these rows but leaves it under the 0.90 target, and a factor fitted on earlier months reaches it only by doubling the band. The detector was not built, because even with perfect event labels no gain is established; the next experiment should try to widen the band by a learned amount on the flagged rows, or to forecast the transfers instead. also relevant 00344 wind-research-default-1-speed-dependent-offsets Experiment 340 found that a constant upward shift of the wind quantiles gains 0.09 to 0.12 points on the kept rows but worsens the rows below cut-in by 0.51 to 0.78, and that the default's median is too low at 8 to 15 m/s and too high below 5 m/s. An offset that depends on the ensemble-mean 100 m wind speed at forecast time lifts the quantiles where the power curve is steep and leaves them alone where the forecast is near zero, so it keeps the gain without the low-wind harm. The starting point is Wind farms research default 1, the three metered wind farms W1 to W3 are scored, and the lead range is 1 to 10 days. not supported not-for-production Letting the wind forecast's quantile offsets depend on the forecast wind speed gains only about 0.02 points of capacity when fitted on the same retrospective forecasts (hindcast runs) that fit the quantile offset table, and the gain cannot be told from zero. Fitted on the six months just before the scored year (July 2025 to June 2026), the same speed-dependent correction gains 0.146 points and does not worsen the half-hours where the forecast wind speed is below the turbines' cut-in speed. The speed-dependent bias is therefore real, and it changes from year to year. Refitting the correction on recent months is the untested option that could capture it. also relevant 00342 wind-research-default-1-upper-tail-offsets-and-head The upper quantiles of Wind farms research default 1 are too low: in experiment 324 the observed power exceeded q99 in 1.8% of half-hours (1% nominal) and q95 in 6.7% (5% nominal). Three corrections fitted on the hindcast can fix that without harming the headline score. x1 is a table of offsets for q90 to q99 that also depends on the ensemble-mean wind speed. x2 is a small boosted-tree head, fed the default's quantiles and summaries of the ensemble members' wind speed, that adds offsets to q90, q95, and q99. x3 lets the share of ensemble members above the farm's saturation speed set a probability mass at the farm's scale. not supported not-for-production The wind forecast's upper quantiles miss too often (observed power exceeds q99 in 1.8% of half-hours against 1% intended), and corrections fitted on past forecasts do not fix that: the offsets keyed by wind speed, the tail head, and the mass at the farm's cap all leave the share at 1.8% to 1.9% and change the upper-tail loss by about 1% or less. A head that sees the ensemble members does no better than one that sees only the default's quantiles, so in these 3 farms the members add no information about the upper tail. The remaining miss is consistent with the scored year differing from the hindcast years, which the next experiment could attack by refitting more often or by training on the most recent months. also relevant 00340 wind-research-default-1-constant-shift-then-low-wind-drop Experiment 336 found that dropping the ERA5 training rows below the turbines' cut-in speed (x2) gains 0.117 points on the kept rows, and its audit traced about 85% of the gain to a constant upward shift of the quantiles. If that is right, a constant shift fitted on the 442-run hindcast (arm S) reproduces most of the gain without changing the training rows. Arm S+X2, which also drops the low-wind rows, then adds little beyond the shift. Wind farms research default 1 is the starting point, the three metered wind farms W1 to W3 are scored, and the lead range is 1 to 10 days. not supported not-for-production A single upward shift of the wind quantiles, fitted on past forecasts, does nothing, because the forecast's offset table already fits those runs. Moving the quantiles up by 0.8 to 1.2 points of capacity does reproduce most of the gain of dropping low-wind training rows, but it also worsens the forecast at low winds by 0.5 to 0.8 points, the same harm that stops X2 being adopted. An untested option that could lift the forecast at 8 to 15 m/s and leave it alone below 5 m/s is a correction that depends on wind speed. also relevant 00339 wind-research-default-1-adapter-plus-mixture-head A three-component Gaussian mixture head on the hindcast, fed the quantiles of the physics core plus adapter and the ensemble members' summaries of speed, direction, and temperature (experiment 324's W4), lowers the quantile score of Wind farms research default 1 on the kept rows of the three metered wind farms W1 to W3 at 1 to 10 day leads. The head loses on the idle half-hours because it is trained on kept rows only, and the maintainer's view is that a forecast-time rule (predict the idle floor where the ensemble-mean wind speed is below cut-in) needs no idle detector. Three arms are tested: x1 the head as in experiment 324, x2 x1 plus the rule, x3 the head trained on all hindcast half-hours. partly supported candidate A small neural-network head that re-draws the physics-plus-adapter wind forecast's quantiles gains 0.27 points of capacity (2.4%) on the farms' normal half-hours and keeps that gain on the replicate months, but the same head given no weather summaries does as well, so the gain is a recalibration that a simpler correction partly reproduces. A simple rule that predicts the idle floor at low wind recovers none of the head's loss on the idle-band readings, and training the head on those readings removes the gain. also relevant 00336 wind-research-default-1-below-cut-in-zeroing The maintainer proposes that, for wind, rows where the wind speed is below the turbines' cut-in speed carry only noise, so zeroing them lowers the quantile score of Wind farms research default 1 on the kept rows of the three metered wind farms W1 to W3 at 1 to 10 day leads. Three readings are tested, each added alone: x1 sets the forecast to zero power whenever the ensemble-mean 100 m speed is below the farm's cut-in speed, x2 drops the ERA5 training rows below cut-in from the XGBoost model and the offset table, and x3 sets the training target to zero on those rows. At most one is adopted, in the order x1, x2, x3. partly supported candidate Setting the wind forecast, or the training target, to zero below the turbines' cut-in speed does not improve the forecast, because the farms still produce small real output there. Leaving the low-wind rows out of training gains 0.12 points of capacity (about 1% of the default's score) on the kept rows, but mostly by lifting the quantiles upward, which a constant upward shift may reproduce (not yet tested). also relevant 00335 primary-demand-default-3-tail-calibration-at-0-5-to-240-hours The 0.01, 0.05, 0.95, and 0.99 quantiles of Primary demand research default 3 miss their nominal rates past 96 hours (experiments 317 and 320 found 2.1% to 2.9% of observations below q01 and a 1.8% upper tail at 7 to 10 days). A calibration fitted per 24-hour lead band and per group (season, day or night, cold winter night) on the forecast errors of earlier origins brings the tails to nominal at every lead from 0.5 to 240 hours without worsening the quantile score. not supported not-for-production Primary demand research default 3 is already close to calibrated at 1 to 10 days: its 5% to 95% band covers 89.3% to 90.9% and 1.1% to 1.95% of observations fall below q01. Calibrations fitted on earlier months move the tail shares only part of the way, and none is worth adopting. A table fitted in-sample on the same year would fix the tails and slightly improve the score, which shows the table can describe that year but not that the miss repeats across years, so testing the miss on a second year is the next step. also relevant 00332 lsc-curtailment-cost-of-label-free-mask Treating as missing the readings that a label-free load shift detector flags (arm A of experiment 327) lowers curtailment cost during and after load shifts, against no mask (arm C), without raising it on ordinary half-hours. not supported not-for-production Masking the load shifts that a label-free detector finds lowers curtailment cost by about a third when the forecast is judged against the normal running arrangement. Judged against the power the electricity network actually carried, which is what a curtailment instruction responds to, the mask changes cost by -3.0% with an interval from -24% to +30%, and it costs 1.3% more on ordinary half-hours. Adding the true moved megawatts to the true spans lowered cost during a shift, but adding them to the label-free mask did not, so this result cannot say what a live service needs. also relevant 00327 lsc-label-free-detect-mask-train-pipeline A forecast of the normal running arrangement (NRA) can be trained and corrected on power with the load shifts set to missing, where a label-free detector finds the load shifts. The detector reads only how unusual the observed power is inside the predictive bands of a demand model that uses no lagged power, and no NGED switching label enters any threshold, mask, or training row. partly supported candidate A forecast of the normal running arrangement recovers faster after a load shift when the readings that a label-free detector flags are treated as missing: during and after injected shifts the 95% pinball loss falls from 1.79 to 1.04 points of capacity. On ordinary days the masked forecast is no worse, and slightly better. Without one site (D11) the gain shrinks to 0.30 points, and retraining the demand model on masked power adds nothing beyond masking the filter. also relevant 00326 wind-research-default-1-change-arms Each of four changes, added alone to Wind farms research default 1, lowers the quantile score on the kept rows of the three metered wind farms W1 to W3 at 1 to 10 day leads: (a) 2 m temperature and an air-density column as XGBoost inputs, (b) hour of day and day of year as XGBoost inputs, (c) the ERA5-trained neural adapter's effective wind speed as an extra XGBoost column, and (d) one wind-speed scale factor, fitted on the hindcast to the implied wind, applied to every member's 100 m speed before the XGBoost model. At most one is adopted, in the order c, b, a, d. supported candidate Feeding XGBoost the neural adapter's corrected wind speed lowers the wind forecast's score by 0.10 points of capacity, about 0.9% of the default's score, at 1 to 10 day leads (99.75% interval -0.19 to -0.01). The change is negative at every farm and at short and long leads. The three other changes were not separable from zero. Only a port that puts the adapter in the production service can use the gain, so the maintainer decides. also relevant 00321 metered-farm-lower-tail-recalibration-and-tail-head Metered solar farms research default 1 (the blend assembled by experiment 300, scored to 10 days by experiment 310) lets the actual output fall below its 0.01 quantile 3.3% to 3.7% of the time, and no mixture-density head tried in experiment 318 changes that. Default plus a recalibration table, a zero-inflated lower tail, or a tail-targeted head brings the share of actual values strictly below the 0.01 quantile close to 1% at leads of 1 to 10 days, without raising the quantile score and without losing experiment 318's 0.99 gain. partly supported candidate The solar-farm forecast's lowest quantile was already close to correct: only 1.2% to 1.4% of actual values fall strictly below the 0.01 quantile, because the earlier 3.3% counted the 3.0% of half-hours that read exactly zero. A recalibration table, a zero-inflated head, and a tail head each lower the own-history score by 0.04 points or less (the unshrunk table raises it by 0.03 to 0.05 points), so none is adopted. A shrunk recalibration table does lower the score by about 0.05 points for a farm with no history, and two heads lower the 0.99 pinball loss by 3.7% to 8.5% while covering the 0.99 quantile only 98.3% to 98.9% of the time. also relevant 00312 lsc-how-good-must-a-detector-be-against-the-band-head A load shift detector that is far from perfect can still beat the best forecast that uses no detector, so a detector need not be near-perfect to be worth building. The one detector-based arm in experiment 297 that beat that forecast was the one that subtracts the true megawatts from the readings during a shift and adds them back to the forecast. This experiment degrades that arm one axis at a time to find where it stops beating the no-detector forecast. It also asks whether the surprise of recent readings against GAM_ONLY's residual bands (band position), or perfect knowledge of a shift, added as inputs to the no-detector quantile head, improves the head. This is question 3 of the LSC decision program, redefined by the Discuss ruling of 2026-10-23. not supported not-for-production A load shift detector does not need to be near-perfect to improve on the best forecast that uses no detector: with the true megawatts added back, finding half the shifts, learning of each up to 3 days late, or misjudging the megawatts by half still lowers curtailment cost against that forecast. The detector tested earlier (RO-NC) finds only a third of the shifts, below the break-even of one half (measured with every other property perfect). The surprise of recent readings against the forecast's bands (band position) found more, 37% of shifts on even months, but still under one half and with about 90% of its alarms false, so the next step is a detector that finds more shifts. also relevant 00309 lsc-two-forecast-gap-choosing-without-truth NGED sees two forecasts and not the true switching state. A forecast with no lagged power (GAM_ONLY) forecasts the normal running arrangement, and a forecast with lags (K0) forecasts what will flow while an abnormal arrangement lasts. A rule that reads only the gap between the two forecasts, how long it has lasted, and a neighbour check can choose between them nearly as well as knowing the truth. This experiment is part 2 of the brief briefs/sw_lsc_two_forecasts_divergence_and_selection_brief.md, and it builds on experiment 308. not supported not-for-production NGED cannot pick between the two forecasts from the gap alone. A rule on the gap, or on the 24-hour mean of measured power minus the no-lag forecast, did no better than always using the no- lag forecast in the injected worlds, and worse than always using the forecast with lags in the real record. An oracle that knows the true switching state gained little, except in the 72 hours after a real shift ended, so the most promising signal to test next is a flag for the end of a shift. The gap is a filtered copy of the measured-power residual, so it adds no information that the measured power lacks. also relevant 00304 metered-farm-node-sum-tail For the solar farms that share a bulk supply point, adding each farm's quantiles overstates the upper tail of the farms' summed output, adding independent bands understates it, and summing the 51 ensemble members' farm forecasts member by member gives calibrated 0.95 and 0.99 quantiles, because the ensemble carries the farms' shared dependence on cloud. not supported not-for-production The band for the combined output of the three farms beneath one substation comes out too wide if the weather forecast's 51 members are summed member by member, because the members' forecasts for the three farms move together almost perfectly while the farms' actual forecast errors are less closely linked. That band is almost the same as the band from adding each farm's quantiles. A band that assumes the farms' errors are unrelated is too narrow. A band from a Gaussian copula with a correlation fitted on the errors of the other 11 months comes closest to the stated probability. Only 5 half-hours in the scored year exceed 0.75 times a substation's maximum export, so this experiment cannot say what the band widths mean for curtailment cost. also relevant 00297 lsc-need-a-detector-no-detector-arms-against-the-mask A forecast that never learns which readings are load shifts can match a forecast that uses a detector, because its bands and its recent-power correction can be made to tell a load shift from ordinary variation by themselves. This is question 2 of the LSC decision program. not supported not-for-production A forecast with no detector that recalibrates its bands and reads how far the recent-power correction has moved scores better than the RO-NC detector near load shifts, so with RO-NC a detector is not shown to be needed. Perfect knowledge with the true megawatts added back still lowers curtailment cost by 6.5% (3.9 to 9.2) against that forecast, so the next step is to run the better LSC detector (LR_b20) on the same simulated shifts and judge it against a forecast that has the recalibrated bands. also relevant 00296 lsc-benefit-by-event-class-long-deep-versus-small-shifts Load shifts of at least 2 days and at least 10% of a Primary substation's load carry most of the benefit of knowing every load shift exactly, and shifts that are shorter than 12 hours or under 10% of load carry little. This is the question behind the "long-and-deep" detector of the LSC decision program. supported not-for-production A detector that finds only load shifts of at least 2 days and at least 10% of a substation's load would deliver about 96% of the upper-tail forecast benefit and about 90% of the curtailment-cost benefit of knowing every shift, if it were perfect. Detecting shifts from 6 hours to 2 days would add 3% to 8% more, and detecting shifts down to 5% of load would add 1% to 2%. The next step is to weight these shares by how often a real long-and-deep detector finds each class, which waits for Part 1 of the long-deep detector experiment. also relevant 00288 pooled-head-on-public-wind-farms A neural head that adds 11 quantile offsets to the XGBoost wind forecast (R0) and was trained on dozens of public onshore wind farms (metered output from Elexon's Balancing Mechanism Reporting Service) lowers the quantile score of the three metered wind farms (W1 to W3) against R0 alone, and a head trained on the pool beats the same head trained on W1 to W3 only, because experiment 259's head had too few farm-years to learn a correction that transfers. A second hypothesis: XGBoost keeps improving as the training history grows from 12 to 48 months while the physics core is flat after 24 months, and a pool of public farms replaces the missing history. not supported not-for-production Training the correction on 40 public wind farms did not help the forecasts for the three NGED wind farms. Applied directly, it made them worse, because the public farms' capacity, turbine rating, and hub height let the head memorise each farm. Without those inputs it did no harm, and after a short fine-tune on the three farms' own data it gained about as much as a simple offset table fitted on those farms, so the public farms added nothing measurable. also relevant 00284 metered-farm-tail-head-past-weather Experiment 275 found that adding years of past-weather rows lowered the 0.99 pinball loss of the neural head H5 by 4.6% while its overall score moved by 0.47%. A small neural network trained with a loss restricted to the tail quantiles (0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.95, 0.98, 0.99), on the same past-weather plus ensemble rows with an era flag, lowers the 0.01 and 0.99 pinball loss of a metered solar farm's forecast below that of XGBoost trained on the same rows. partly supported not-for-production A neural network trained only to forecast the extreme edges of a solar farm's output band does beat XGBoost at the 0.99 quantile (the upper edge that matters for curtailment) by 30%, but the existing H5 network does slightly better still, and most of the gain comes from building the band around the physical power model and not from tail-only training. The years of past-weather rows add under 1% at the 0.99 quantile, and at the 0.01 quantile the share of half-hours below it is outside 0.5% to 1.5% at three farms (marginally at A, because of exact zeros at D, and clearly only at E). also relevant 00283 lsc-perfect-knowledge-value-to-forecast-and-curtailment Knowing every load shift exactly (its true start and end) lowers the error of the forecast of the normal running arrangement (NRA) in the 48 hours after a shift, and lowers the curtailment cost of the forecast of observed power in the days around a shift, while leaving ordinary rows unchanged. This is question 1 of the LSC decision program. partly supported not-for-production Perfect knowledge of load shifts lowers the forecast's error most in the 48 hours after a shift ends (23% lower upper-tail score, 95% interval 9% to 39%) and by under 1% over a whole year, because shifts are rare. Curtailment cost against observed power falls by 8% (6% to 10%) near a shift only when the known shift's megawatts are added back to the forecast, and does not fall when recent readings are merely set aside. The next step is to ask how good a detector must be to keep that gain, using the megawatts-added-back arm as the target. also relevant 00277 lsc-curtailment-metric-on-existing-forecasts The curtailment-cost metric of experiment 268 (studies.node_curtailment, sorted quantiles) ranks the four existing forecasts as the other metrics do, and can resolve the differences between them well enough to judge the load-shift questions of the decision program. supported not-for-production Over a year of ordinary days, the curtailment metric ranks the four existing forecasts the way the other scores do, and it can tell the GAM stack from BG2 (BG2 costs GBP 7.35 million more on the six Primaries at the 0.5 limit, a figure that ranks forecasts and is not money saved). Inside the windows around the 7 logged load transfers, the GAM stack cannot be separated from BG2, because those windows hold only 926 to 2,923 scored half-hours. Questions about load shifts need injected worlds with many more shifts, not the real record. primary 00271 lsc-load-shifts-net-out-at-bulk-supply-points A load shift between two Primary substations under the same bulk supply point (BSP) leaves the power flow at the BSP unchanged, so it barely changes the curtailment cost at the BSP, and only a load shift that crosses from one BSP to the other changes the cost noticeably. The step 7 program brief for the load-shift (LSC) decision program asks this in order to know whether the money question can be asked at BSP level. partly supported not-for-production A load shift between two Primary substations under the same bulk supply point changes the curtailment cost at that bulk supply point by 0.2% at a random time and 0.7% just before days that would be curtailed (interval up to 1.08%), because the two Primaries' forecast errors partly cancel. A load shift across the boundary between the two bulk supply points changes it by 1.4% at a random time and 5.5% just before curtailed days. Only 4 of the 54 hand-filtered real events that involve two Primaries cross the boundary, so the curtailment metric at bulk supply points cannot say whether detecting load shifts is worth money, and that question has to be asked at Primary substations. also relevant 00268 lsc-curtailment-metric-v2-member-wise-ens A member-wise input path added to studies.node_curtailment (ensemble members of the node's demand and of each farm's output, paired by member, reduced to the quantiles the rule reads) gives the same avoidable cost as the quantile path when the members are drawn from the same quantile function, and scores nodes that experiment 255 could not (Primaries that connect a farm, and the bulk supply points D13 and D17 with member-wise inputs). partly supported not-for-production The curtailment metric can now take ensemble members for a substation's demand and for each solar farm, and on experiment 255's rows it reproduces the earlier answer. A third of the stored solar-farm forecasts list their quantiles out of order. Sorting them moves the cost of some forecasts by up to 3.7% and leaves every comparison between forecasts with the same sign, but it swaps which of two near-equal forecasts is cheapest. Forecasts that are already quantile sets can be scored now. Forecasts driven by ensemble members need member frames that we did not find in the experiment folders we searched. primary 00265 dp-gas-engine-bands-prior-and-visibility-switch Widening a Primary's forecast bands from its own past residuals (experiment 264, arm 2b) has coverage far from nominal in the first quarter, when there is no history, and after a change in the site's behaviour. A prior taken from the other Primaries' residuals, shrunk towards the site's own trailing residuals as they accrue, fixes the first quarter. A causal switch on the share of large drops in the trailing 30 days returns the widening to normal when D8's engine becomes visible in the readings (around April 2026). Together they hold D8's q05-to-q95 coverage within 5 points of 0.90 in every quarter, without raising the cost in quantile score, and without harming Primaries that have no engine. not supported not-for-production In this year of forecasts, the other five Primaries' residuals did not predict D8's errors, so a starting estimate from them left D8's bands too narrow in the first quarter, and returning to normal widening after the engine's drops faded made them too narrow again. Widening from D8's own history (experiment 264) remained the best of the arms tried. We tested no other fix for the first quarter, and none of the other five Primaries had a heavy lower tail. also relevant 00264 dp-gas-engine-asymmetric-bands-at-d8 D8's forecast bands are too narrow in both directions, and part of the lower-tail miss is a 6 MW gas engine (probably three units of about 2 MW) that runs in spells and cannot be detected. A spread that widens as-of, using only residuals already resolved at the forecast origin, and that widens most in the direction the engine pushes (net demand falls), gives honest q05 to q95 bands at D8 without raising the quantile score at the Primaries that have no engine. not supported not-for-production A forecast band that learns from the residuals it has already seen narrows most of the gap at D8: the quantile score falls by 9% to 19% and the share of readings inside the 90% band rises from 42% to between 80% and 87%. The extra gain of the engine mixture over simple widening is not evidence of an engine, because the mixture fits a running engine at two substations that have none. Plain two-sided widening with an earlier residual history is the option these results support, and NGED's own output for the engine would be the data to test an engine model. also relevant 00259 wind-plant-plus-quantile-offset-head For the three metered wind farms (W1 to W3), a small neural network that reads the 51-member mixture of a wind model and the ensemble's wind summaries, and adds an offset to each of 11 quantiles, lowers the quantile score against the wind model alone (R1, the physics core), matches the XGBoost best guess (R0), and lowers the pinball loss at the 0.99 quantile, once it can learn from daily runs of the ensemble forecast over 15 months (about 440 runs) instead of the 13 to 40 Tuesday runs that experiment 221's head saw. partly supported candidate A correction learned from 15 months of daily ensemble forecasts lowered the wind forecast's quantile score by 4.5% to 5.5% on the three metered wind farms, but the neural network and the ensemble's wind summaries were not what earned it. The 51 ensemble members' median sits too low: the observed power was below the physics core's median on 34% of rows, not 50%. A lookup table with one offset per lead day, quantile, and farm recovers 92% of the gain. The open question is where that low bias comes from. also relevant 00255 metered-farm-node-curtailment-value When six metered solar farms beneath two bulk supply points are curtailed by the node-plus-generators rule of studies.node_curtailment, a forecast of each farm's output (the plant, XGBoost, or the plant with a neural head) avoids more curtailment cost than the NGED baseline, which assumes every generator runs at full capacity, and the neural head's lower 0.99 pinball loss does not show in the metric, because the rule uses only a farm's median. inconclusive not-for-production Forecasting each solar farm's output instead of assuming every farm runs at full capacity cut the cost of curtailing at one of two substations (Boston, 40% lower) and raised it at the other (Skegness, 24% higher), so across both the saving is about a quarter, smaller than the uncertainty in the estimate. The neural network's better upper tail does not show in this cost, because the rule reads only each farm's median, and it lowers the cost by 3% against XGBoost, far under the 10% that would justify serving a neural network. Ranking farm forecasts by curtailment cost needs many more substations. also relevant 00251 dp-final-best-guess-assembly-clip-and-coast-against-bg2 The full best-guess stack of experiment 220 (arm D, the neural-network head, and the two-number solar summary) beats BG2, the manual heuristic, climatology, and a weak production-style XGBoost model over the scored year of 2025-07 to 2026-06. Adding the hand-set 60% clip at D5 lowers the D5 error on sunny half-hours when the neural-network head is absent, and adds nothing measurable when the head is present, because experiment 232 found the head cancels most of the clip's gain. supported candidate Over the one year we can score, the full best-guess demand forecast (arm D, a small neural network that corrects its median, and a two-number summary of the ensemble's solar response) beats BG2 by 0.136 points of quantile score (5%; lower is better) and the manual heuristic by 0.818 points, and it beats the manual heuristic on every headline metric we scored, including curtailment cost. The gain over BG2 is a winter gain: the stack is level with BG2 in summer and worse in April to June, and at D5 on sunny hours it is clearly worse than BG2. Adding the 60% solar clip at D5 helps only when the neural-network head is left out at D5, so the next work is the solar term at D5, not another stacked part. also relevant 00213 calibration-online-band-adaptation-from-coverage-misses Moving a scale on each quantile offset of experiment 169's arm A up after a reading falls outside that quantile, and down after a reading falls inside it, in the style of adaptive conformal inference (Gibbs and Candes, 2021), lifts the cold-night q95 coverage to 0.90 or more without a second fitted spread model, because a run of misses on a cold spell widens the band before the spell ends. inconclusive not-for-production Letting the forecast widen or narrow its bands after each recent miss does not fix the under-coverage on cold nights: it lifts the 95% quantile's coverage from 0.896 to 0.906 in the scored year and lowers it in the other months, and it worsens the all-row, bank-holiday, and Christmas scores. A fixed widening of the upper quantiles does as well, so the cold-night gap is a shortfall that a signal arriving after the misses cannot learn in time, and the next step is to correct the mean forecast on the coldest days before any further work on the bands. also relevant 00169 calibration-combined-fixes-and-ensemble-spread The spread across the 51 ensemble members of the temperature and of the downward shortwave radiation at a substation predicts how wide the forecast's residuals are, beyond the hour band, calendar quarter, lead, and the cold-day widening of experiment 164. A convex quantile model that scales the quantile offsets by a non-decreasing function of those two spreads lifts the cold-night q95 coverage of the combined forecast to 0.90 or more. partly supported not-for-production Combining the smooth spread table with the cold-day widening reproduces its 0.896 coverage of the 95% quantile on cold nights, and adding the spread of the ensemble weather forecast (how much its 51 members disagree) lifts that to 0.907. The lift comes from widening the 95% and 99% quantiles by 4% and 10%, which the same model gives with its spread terms removed, so the ensemble spread is not what lifts cold-night coverage. A later experiment could test a bias correction of the mean forecast on the coldest days, and judge cold nights over more than one winter. also relevant 00164 calibration-cold-night-tail-under-coverage The q95 coverage of experiment 160's smooth-table forecast on cold nights (day mean temperature below 2 °C) stays near 85% because the spread table is too narrow when it is cold, not because the mean forecast is biased. Widening the quantiles on days the ensemble forecasts as cold, by a factor fitted on the tuning months, lifts cold-night q95 coverage to 90% or more without worsening the all-row score. refuted not-for-production On cold nights the 95% quantile of the best forecast is exceeded on about 15% of readings, and mostly because its prediction interval is too narrow, not because its mean forecast is biased. Widening only the upper quantiles on days the weather forecast calls cold reduces that share to about 10% without changing the all-hours score, but no fix reached the pre-registered 90% coverage in the scored year, and only 10 cold days back that year's figure. The coldest forecasts (0 °C or below) are also biased low, so correcting the mean forecast on those days is the next experiment to run. also relevant 00160 calibration-band-width-fix-on-stage-2-winner The q05 to q95 band of the stage 2 winning arm (experiment 155's arm D with arm A's spread table) widens in steps along the lead, because the spread table has only four lead bands (up to 24 hours, 48, 144, and 168), fitted separately per hour band and calendar quarter. Interpolating each hour band by quarter cell between the lead-band centres, forcing the width to be non-decreasing in lead, or both, removes the steps without worsening the quantile score. supported candidate The 90% prediction interval (from the 5% to the 95% quantile) of experiment 155's best forecast was equally wide on lead days 2 to 5, because its stored spread table has only four lead bands. Interpolating the table between the band centres removes the equal days and raises the quantile score by 0.002 points, below the pre-registered ceiling of 0.01, but it narrows the interval at 24 to 72 hours and widens it from 72 hours on, so one substation loses 0.009. It does not fix the cold-night upper tail: the forecast exceeds the 95% quantile on about 15% of cold-night rows, against 5% for a calibrated forecast. also relevant 00125 differentiable-physics-n8-ens-members-through-gam-k-and-the-spread-around-them Placing GAM-K's residual quantiles, fitted on a forecast driven by the analysis proxy (so they hold model and filter error and almost no weather error), around each of the 51 ENS members gives tails closer to nominal than today's table, which is fitted on ensemble-mean residuals, and the gain is largest at long leads and on cold winter nights, where the hinge turns a temperature error into a large demand error. The comparison is against GAM-K re-tuned on the same factor grid, so a plain scale error cannot pass for a better design. inconclusive not-for-production Putting the forecast-error table around each of the 51 weather members, and fitting it on analysis-driven forecasts so that it holds no weather error, did not improve the tails of GAM-K's demand forecast. The weather members' spread is small against the model's own error, so the weather error was counted twice in the code but is too small to matter. The next step is the cold winter nights, where demand exceeds the 95% quantile about a quarter of the time in every arm. The verdict is inconclusive, because no arm reached 14 of 16 calibration cells. also relevant 00084 substation-limit-curtailment-cost-worked-example The substation-limit curtailment metric (studies.node_curtailment) can run end to end on the pilot's two bulk supply points, Boston and Skegness, and the pilot holds enough half-hours beyond a scaled limit to rank forecasts. This is a worked example of new code, not a test of a forecasting idea. inconclusive not-for-production Two bulk supply points have 19 half-hours beyond a limit of 0.9 times their earlier maximum export in the scored year, so the pilot proves the arithmetic and cannot rank forecasts at the headline limit. primary 00083 curtailment-cost-and-tail-calibration-worked-example A tail-calibration table, built in packages/studies, can rank the stored quantile forecasts of experiment 48 by how well they cover the tails of the forecast distribution. This is a worked example of new code, not a test of a forecasting idea. inconclusive not-for-production Every forecast is too narrow in both tails: coverage of the 0.05 quantile is 0.066 to 0.085 and of the 0.95 quantile is 0.891 to 0.927. primary
