docs.title: Curtailment cost: state and next steps
docs.text:
No forecast has been shown to curtail less at the bulk supply points, and on the six MW Primaries the experiments read for this page rank the stack ahead of BG2 and the weekly XGBoost model. Curtailment is the capping of generators beneath a substation when its export would pass a limit. The scoring code plans the caps from a forecast of the substation's export, then charges the energy lost to the caps plus a penalty for export that stays over the limit. The code runs, reproduces a hand-worked answer, and has scored several forecasts, but the pilot holds too few events to rank forecasts at the headline limit. An option for the next step is to score the January 2027 delivery of about 2,500 time series with the same code.

Terms. NGED is National Grid Electricity Distribution. A bulk supply point (BSP) is a substation that steps 132 kV down to 33 kV or 66 kV, and a Primary is a primary substation. MW is real power, and MVA is apparent power. GBP is pounds sterling. The stack, BG2 (the second best-guess recipe), climatology, and the manual heuristic are defined in the glossary. A node is a substation scored together with the generators beneath it. The NGED baseline is the manual heuristic's substation forecast with every generator at full capacity. A scaled limit is a fraction (0.9, 0.75, or 0.5) of a substation's maximum export before 2025-07-02. An arm is one pair of forecasts, one of the substation's export and one of its generators' output. Avoidable cost is an arm's cost minus the cost of a perfect forecast. All costs are calibration to history, not savings.

docs.title: What works
docs.text:
The metric code runs and reproduces a hand-worked answer exactly. All eight quantities of a made-up half-hour (a 45.0 MW limit and two generators) agree with the hand calculation (Experiment 84). The code plans caps from the 0.95 quantile of the export forecast and shares the cut among generators in proportion to their capacity. The cost is an energy proxy: the generator energy cut, plus 20 times the energy left over the limit, at GBP 2,000 per MWh. Experiment 84 varied the price and the cost form only, and Experiment 268 changed how the planned cut is built.

The metric accepts ensemble members. Member-wise inputs reproduce Experiment 255 to within 2.0% per arm (Experiment 268). Of the stored farm-forecast rows, 34% have crossing quantiles, which a set of members cannot reproduce.

On the six MW Primaries, the stack costs less than BG2 and the weekly XGBoost model. At 0.5 times the maximum, BG2 costs GBP 7.35 million more than the stack (95% interval 1.6 to 14.9 million). That figure ranks the two forecasts and is not money saved (Experiment 277). The stack is cheaper than the weekly XGBoost model at 4 of 6 MW Primaries at 0.9 times and at all 6 at 0.5 times (Experiment 381). The cost is undefined at the eight MVA-only Primaries.

The three final demand networks breach the 0.9 limit at one Primary only. On July to October 2026 at the six MW Primaries (0.9 limit, 0.95 planning quantile), only D9 breaches the limit, at about GBP 520 a day for the networks against GBP 484 for the manual heuristic. At the 0.75 limit, D9 costs GBP 4,400 to 6,400 a day against GBP 5,600 for the heuristic, and the Candidate is lowest (Experiment 620).

The G4 band does not raise cost on event-free rows. On injected load shifts, the combination of A1 and the G4 band lowers the cost in the 7 days after the shift by GBP 124 per Primary-day (Bonferroni interval -268 to -19). The 0.9-limit saving rests on one Primary, D16, and on the real December 2025 pair D16's cost is almost unchanged (Experiment 601).

docs.title: What does not work
docs.text:
The pilot cannot rank forecasts at the 0.9 limit. Boston and Skegness, the two BSPs of the pilot, together have 19 half-hours beyond 0.9 times their maximum in the scored year (2025-07-02 to 2026-06-30), and no difference between arms is significant at the 5% level at that limit. At 0.75 times, with 46 half-hours, the stack costs GBP 2,440,720 more than the best guess (95% interval 96,371 to 6,686,043). At 0.5 times, with 323 half-hours, the best guess is GBP 10,802,520 cheaper than climatology (-20,880,964 to -3,342,553), and its gap to the NGED baseline includes zero. We have no evidence that NGED operates at 0.5 times, so that limit is a rehearsal (Experiment 84).

At 0.9 times, the best guess has the lowest avoidable cost of the six arms, and most of that cost is breach. Its avoidable cost is GBP 571,823, and 81% of that is breach: the forecast ordered 13.6 MWh of cuts on event half-hours against 35.1 MWh needed (Experiment 84).

Fitting a whole distribution to a forecast plans far more curtailment than the stored forecast does. On 17 half-hours at one node, Student-t and skew-normal fits planned 911 and 1,364 MWh of curtailment against 57.5 MWh for the stored BG2 forecast, with 33.7 MWh needed. Their avoidable costs were GBP 2.36 million and 3.12 million against 618,171. The other recalibrations were not separable from the stored forecast (Experiment 97).

Load-shift events do not separate forecasts by curtailment cost. Across 33 events at the six MW Primaries, no difference in avoidable cost during events is established, because 2 to 11 events per Primary account for the cost, and one Primary accounts for most of it (Experiment 478). Across all rows, that experiment found the stack far cheaper than the weekly XGBoost forecasts at two Primaries, but the arms carry different widening (1.15 on the arms of Experiment 383), so the gap mixes widening with skill.

No curtailment cost exists for the BSPs and GSPs of the final models. No manual heuristic baseline exists for them (Experiment 669).

docs.title: Where the pages disagree
docs.text: Experiments 83 and 97 disagree on the lower tail because they score different forecasts and periods. In Experiment 83, on the older forecasts of Experiment 48 pooled over 20 demand series, coverage of the 0.05 quantile was 0.066 to 0.085, so the lower tail was too narrow. In Experiment 97, on BG2 for 16 Primaries at 12 to 36 hours, coverage was 0.035, so the lower tail was too wide (Experiment 83; Experiment 97). Experiment 97 scores the later forecast.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Which forecast curtails least, once about 2,500 series are scored? Experiment 84 names this as its next question, and the same function scores any number of nodes.
  • How does NGED choose its operating limit, and how does it allocate caps among generators? The idea that NGED curtails early to keep headroom is the maintainer's unconfirmed understanding, and the questions for NGED are collected in issue #1318.
  • Are the NGED baseline and the signs of the nodes right? The baseline comes from the same unconfirmed understanding. Boston and Skegness are inferred as import-positive, Bicker Fen's sign is unconfirmed, and Walpole's is unknown, so the metric excludes both.

docs.title: Next experiments
docs.text:
The theme's research plan has no proposal waiting, so the options below come from the "next step" sections of merged pages.

  1. An option is to score the January 2027 delivery of about 2,500 series with the unchanged code. This option comes from Experiment 84. It depends on the delivery, and it is the only option that could rank forecasts at the headline limit.
  2. An option is to store the 0.01 and 0.99 quantiles in every forecast set. This option comes from Experiment 83. The stored sets of Experiment 48 stop at the 0.95 quantile, and later sets store 11 levels.
  3. An option is to judge any tail recalibration over at least 2 years of scored runs. This option comes from Experiment 97, whose 9 scored months gave intervals of plus or minus 0.02 on the coverage of the 0.95 quantile.

A gap, not a plan option: curtailment cost has not been scored for the BSPs and GSPs, the eight MVA Primaries, wind and solar farms, or the year-backtest files of the final models.

docs.title: What is parked, and why
docs.text:
Load-shift event detection and unmetered photovoltaic capacity are paused until January, so no curtailment work that depends on them is under way. A ranking of forecasts waits on the delivery of the larger series set, and the questions about NGED's practice wait on NGED's answers.

Before using any cost from this theme, check these reporting rules (Experiment 84):

  • Label every cost "calibration to history, not a saving", because the perfect forecast still costs GBP 87,460 at 0.9 times.
  • Report the 13% of generator-half-hours that had no forecast, because those generators were not capped.
  • Report the unscored half-hours, which hold 14% of the excess energy at 0.5 times.
  • Publish generator figures only as sums over at least 4 generators, to keep NGED's metered generators anonymous.

docs.title: Demand inputs
docs.text:
The current understanding and the options for next work are on the state and next steps page.

At Primary substations, a calendar-and-solar set of inputs lowered the demand forecast error by 0.1 points of capacity or more with an interval clear of zero: the hour and weekday, the COVID indicator, a Christmas column limited to the 14 days either side of 25 December, and an explicit forecast of the unmetered solar output. A heating term gave 0.14 points in cold hours up to 48 hours ahead on one winter, which is under its 0.3 target. The electricity price, school terms, statistics of installed solar capacity, substation fingerprints, and the PV_Live estimate of solar generation gave no gain of 0.1 points that held up.

The experiments added one kind of information at a time to an XGBoost demand forecast and scored the change against the same XGBoost model without it. They scored 13 to 16 Primary substations (experiment 74: 5), over one or two validation years, and experiments 27 and 28 scored two grid supply points. Errors are in points of capacity, a negative change is an improvement, and each number names its metric: the error of the median (the mean absolute error of the middle forecast) or the quantile score. Several gains in the selection year (the year used to choose inputs) vanished in the confirmation year (the later year used to check them) or against a control.

For Primary substations on the confirmation year (July 2025 to June 2026), adding the hour and weekday to the weather lowered the error of the median by 0.46 points (99.4% interval -0.61 to -0.30), the largest single input. The panels show the same contrasts for the 2 bulk and 2 grid supply points, which have too few series to settle. Source: experiment 6, an ERA5-trained stage 1a XGBoost model on 14 Primaries.

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
The hour and weekday, the COVID indicator, and a windowed Christmas column help; school terms do not. In experiment 6 the hour and weekday lowered the error of the median by 0.55 points on the selection year, a third of the 1.5 predicted, and the pre-registered COVID indicator by 0.26 (-0.40 to -0.10). The Christmas column is weaker evidence. The 15 December to 7 January window was chosen after the run, and the column lowered the Primary error there by 1.78 points (95% interval -2.30 to -1.26) and changed it by 0.00 elsewhere. The gain is concentrated: the median-error series barely moved (3.96 to 3.95 in the confirmation year) and a series picked after the fact fell from 22.23 to 4.13. Dropping the column from the chosen set changed the selection-year Primary error by +0.14 (-0.06 to +0.35), and the whole-year effect was -0.10. Experiment 11 found no gain from return-to-work or school-term columns on Lincolnshire Primaries: +0.20 at Easter (99.2% interval -0.19 to +0.59) and -0.29 in half-terms (-0.68 to +0.07). The experiment's own rule gives refuted, and its write-up reads Easter and half-terms as inconclusive.

The Christmas columns cut the Christmas error and leave other days unchanged. Source: experiment 6, post hoc windows (chosen after seeing the results), three folds.

An explicit forecast of the unmetered solar output lowers the daylight error; same-time analogues may too, and the data could not rank the two. In experiment 74, five Primaries refitted monthly and scored on daylight April-to-September rows, the explicit offset lowered the quantile score by 0.149 (99.17% interval -0.201 to -0.104) and 3 analogues by 0.095 (-0.185 to -0.007), against a monthly refit with neither. An offset built from another date's sunshine scored 0.246 worse than the real offset. Statistics of installed capacity did not help 16 Primaries (+0.006, -0.022 to +0.033; experiment 31).

Both ways of telling the XGBoost model about sunshine lowered the daylight error, and the intervals overlap. Source: experiment 74, 5 Primaries, one validation year.

Satellite sunshine as a training input gave no resolved gain, and a correction of the forecast sunshine a further small one. Training on CAMS irradiance changed the Primary quantile score by -0.035 (97.5% interval -0.070 to +0.001), refuted against 0.2 planned (experiment 9). Mapping the ENS shortwave onto CAMS lowered it by a further 0.067 (-0.094 to -0.039), which makes the pair 0.102 better than the ERA5-trained arm, but the monthly ratio to CAMS still ran from 0.81 to 1.13, so the verdict is inconclusive (experiment 14). PV_Live, Sheffield Solar's estimate of solar generation, gave no resolved gain at the two grid supply points Walpole and Bicker Fen (experiment 27, -0.03; experiment 28, -0.14 with interval -0.34 to +0.04).

The electricity price gave no gain that held against a control. The price at the target half-hour lowered the pooled error of the median by 0.52 in the selection year (97.5% interval -0.88 to -0.11) and 0.18 in the confirmation year (-0.50 to +0.08), and a price from another week matched about 0.45 of the 0.52 (experiment 15). Price changes (experiment 25) and lagged prices (experiment 10) did no better.

Substation fingerprints and a heating term gave little. Fingerprints changed the quantile score by +0.02 (-0.05 to +0.10; experiment 32). A heating term lowered it by 0.143 in cold hours up to 48 hours ahead (98.75% interval -0.203 to -0.034) and by 0.022 over all rows (-0.042 to +0.000), on 16 Primaries over one winter in which three ISO weeks hold 66% of the cold rows. The q95 forecast was still exceeded in 16.2% of those hours (experiment 94). Experiments 24 and 30 are in the candidates below.

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text: Among the experiments of this theme, no single one assembled the parts; the parts that beat their controls are below. Experiment 87 (the production-reference theme) assembled several of them in BG2. Give the weather-to-power XGBoost model the hour and weekday and the days to Christmas inside a 14-day window (experiment 6). Where a clean solar capacity estimate exists, add the forecast unmetered solar output as a base margin (experiment 74, using the offset of experiment 64; experiment 74 is not-for-production). In BG2 the offset lowered the score by 0.114 on its daylight April-to-September rows at the 5 Primaries that carry one, and by 0.010 over the whole year at all 16 Primaries (experiment 87). The stage 0 mapping (experiment 14) and the heating term (experiment 94) are candidates, not yet part of the design.

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text:
Five experiments here are marked candidate, and each rests on one validation year or an unconfirmed input.

  • Stage 1a inputs (experiment 6): the clock, the COVID indicator (-0.26), recency weights (-0.32, half-life 2 years), and the windowed Christmas column for the ERA5-trained stage 1a XGBoost model. A training start of 2023-09 stays unconfirmed (0.86 better on the confirmation year, 0.05 on the selection year).
  • Stage 0 (experiment 14): a quantile mapping of ENS shortwave onto CAMS for a CAMS-trained stage 1a, 0.067 points better.
  • Pooling (experiment 24): one XGBoost model per substation type or size band (3 or 4 models instead of 20), 0.15 points worse (99.44% interval +0.03 to +0.26), with the series identifier.
  • Weekly mean and median (experiment 30): two extra columns in N1 with the 14-day correction, 0.05 points better than N1 with it (-0.08 to -0.02). The arm is post hoc, and against the experiment 19 stack the 0.03 gain touches zero (-0.06 to +0.00).
  • Heating term (experiment 94): a per-series base margin. The experiment advises a second winter before porting.

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
• Add a placebo twin of every added input, a copy with the same level but the wrong timing. A price from another week matched 0.45 of the 0.52-point price gain (experiment 15), the shuffled price matched most of the gain at the battery site (experiment 10), an offset from another date scored 0.246 worse (experiment 74), and a shuffled capacity control matched the register products (experiment 31). Without the twin, a column that only carries a level is credited. Re-check with a different data source.
  • Check a calendar column against a half-year flag and score it inside the special days. The unwindowed days-to-Christmas column flips sign every late June, so it acts as a half-year flag, and a time-of-year harmonic matched the Christmas gain but worsened summer (experiment 6). A column can also help a few days a year and barely move the yearly mean. Add a placebo calendar shifted by a fixed number of days (experiment 11). Re-check with more years than 3.
  • Fix colsample_bytree at 1.0 in every arm of a column ablation. Experiments 6, 30, 31, and 32 did so because column subsampling hands the wider arm a free win. None measured the size of that effect. Re-check if the arms are ever given equal column counts.
  • Give every arm the same starting level. A start at zero lowered the error by 0.071 (-0.099 to -0.047) against XGBoost's estimated base score in experiment 78, and experiment 74 quotes 0.07 to 0.10 points, so it started every arm at the median of the training labels (experiment 74). Experiment 76 did not test the effect. Re-check with a different pipeline.
  • Judge a lag set against N1 with the 14-day correction. The weekly lags gained 0.30 without the correction and lost 0.09 with it (experiment 30). Re-check if the correction changes.
  • Read a selection-year gain only after a confirmation year. The price gain at the battery site fell from -0.92 to -0.06 (experiment 10), and a 2023-09 training start gained 0.05 and then 0.86 (experiment 6). Re-check with a third year.
  • Test an input on the weather it will be served with. A CAMS-trained XGBoost model lowered the daylight error by 0.88 reading CAMS and by 0.04 reading ENS (experiment 9), and an ERA5-trained solar forecast ran 1.8 to 3.0 points too high on ENS members (experiment 28). Re-check with a different weather product.
  • Report a pooled share with and without the largest-residual substation. One substation set the pooled share in experiment 7. Re-check on new series.
  • Give every pooled XGBoost model the series identifier, and no fixed-window statistics for a held-out series. Dropping the identifier raised the score by 0.82 for by-type pools (experiment 24), and training-window statistics worsened a held-out substation by 1.39, probably because 7 series learn them as identifiers (experiment 32). Re-check with a pool of hundreds of series.
  • Score cold-hour and special-day contrasts on more than one winter. Three ISO weeks held 66% of the cold rows at leads up to 48 hours (experiment 94), and the Christmas windows rest on three Christmases (experiment 6). Re-check when a second winter exists.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text:
• A second validation year. The analogues on top of the offset (-0.066, -0.149 to +0.015) and the heating term need one.
  • Battery response to price. Only the largest battery site was testable, and national demand and wind scored at least as well as the price, so the price may be a proxy for them.
  • Stage 0 on more than 14 months of ENS and all members, and half-term effects with more than 9 half-terms.

The theme's research plan lists the proposals still waiting.

docs.title: Demand inputs: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00632 gru-attention-sequence-network-for-primary-demand A sequence neural network (Seq: an encoder gated recurrent unit over the last 7 days, a decoder gated recurrent unit over the next 7 days that starts from the encoder's state, and three self-attention layers over all tokens), pre-trained on ERA5 and CAMS weather with one Primary embedding for all 16 Primaries, forecasts the next 7 days of demand better than the existing pre-trained networks, because it reads the last 6 days of power and not only a day lag and a week lag. refuted not-for-production The sequence neural network is not worth porting. Seq is not shown better than the per-row lag neural network P2-pre (CRPS 2.90 against 2.86 at the eight MVA Primaries, 2.12 against 2.15 at the six MW Primaries) and loses to P2-hist6, a per-row neural network that reads six daily lags (2.80 and 2.13). No ablation (no attention, no recurrence, neighbour inputs) and not the 3-week history beat Seq by more than seed noise. Seq follows an injected load-shift more than P2-pre does (a share of 0.40 against 0.27 of the shift at the eight MVA Primaries from day 4 of the event), and training it on synthetic shifts cuts that to 0.15 but raises CRPS by about 0.12 points. Stage 3 (ensemble weather) does not run. also relevant 00585 lag-count-and-year-ago-lags-through-the-lag-encoder The lag encoder of the modular network (experiment 572's v3+D5, the control N2) reads one day-old and one week-old reading of a Primary's power. A reading from 364 days earlier (the same weekday and half-hour) carries information that the two recent lags cannot at long leads, where the week lag is 2 to 3 weeks old, and on holidays that repeat each year. The manual heuristic already uses last year's values. partly supported not-for-production Reading the power from a year ago did not make the forecast better on average and did not make it safer around load-shift events; it narrowed the 90% interval and lowered the share of readings on the safe side. It did lower the error at Christmas and New Year at the six MW Primaries (0.53 at 120-240 h for the weekday-aligned lag), but that is one December. Dropping the day lag reduced following most (0.116 against 0.196), at the cost of 0.137 CRPS. also relevant 00579 encoder-capacity-and-architecture-arms-on-the-modular-network The weather encoder and the datetime encoder of the modular network are small (about 2,500 weights each). The datetime encoder has the most to learn for demand forecasting, so capacity may limit it, and the inputs it is given (hour harmonics 1 and 2, a day-of-week one-hot, solar geometry, holiday columns) may limit it too. The weather encoder has only 7 inputs, so capacity should not limit it. not supported not-for-production Making the weather and datetime encoders of the modular demand network larger, or giving the datetime encoder richer inputs such as an Economy 7 proxy, did not lower the forecast error beyond what a different random seed changes at the eight MVA Primaries, so capacity is not what limits the forecast there. At the six MW Primaries a larger datetime encoder lowered the error by 0.135 points of capacity, but a copy with the same depth and no extra width achieved more than half of that, so the gain may come from depth or from training noise rather than capacity. The next step is more seeds for DL and DT at the six MW Primaries, and no further architecture arms. primary 00570 price-encoder-part-1-known-answer-test-and-pretrained-stack Price-following assets such as batteries and gas engines put price-driven variation into a series' power that weather and calendar cannot explain. A price encoder that sees the true price while the modular lag-free network is pre-trained can absorb that variation, so the weather encoder and the datetime encoder learn cleaner patterns from the same targets. The price encoder is discarded before fine-tuning, so serving needs no price feed. not supported not-for-production Training a price encoder (a neural network part fed electricity prices) beside the weather and datetime encoders did not make those encoders cleaner: after fine-tuning, the forecast was no better, and at the six MW Primaries it was worse by 0.29 points of CRPS (the probabilistic forecast error, as a percentage of each Primary's capacity) than a forecast trained without price. Most of that harm also appears when the encoder sees only noise, so the extra encoder itself lowers accuracy, and at the eight MVA Primaries the price content adds nothing the data can resolve. The same encoder could not recover an injected price-driven generator in a controlled test (it recovered 45% of the injected battery rule's output and none of the threshold and rank rules'), so the next step is a controlled test with a larger injected generator before any further real-data price work. primary 00569 modular-network-inputs-through-matching-encoders-in-pretraining-and-fine-tuning-run-1 Experiment 562 added five input groups to the modular lag-free network at fine-tuning only. Each group may help once it is also pre-trained on ERA5 and CAMS rows and enters through the encoder that matches its content: thermal-lag and solar-gain windows (B1) and look-ahead windows (B2) through the weather encoder, school terms and holidays (B3a) through the datetime encoder, national signals of the previous day (B3b) and the whole-day price shape (B4) through a small parallel encoder. A sixth group (B3c) adds, to B3a, the number of schools within 2 km of each Primary as a gate on the school columns. not supported not-for-production Letting the demand network read thermal-lag, solar-gain, look-ahead, school-term, national-signal, and price-shape columns during pre-training as well as fine-tuning, through the encoder that matches each group, did not help: none of them beat a shuffled-day placebo of the same width on all rows, cold nights, Christmas week, or high-spread days, and a school-proximity input made the eight MVA Primaries worse. This test cannot see small gains (one seed), and the network pre-trained from scratch with extra columns scored worse than plain M0's stored weights, which is the larger effect to understand first. The next step is a second seed and a plain M0 re-pre-trained under the same recipe, so that the control and the arms differ only in the columns. primary 00562 modular-lag-free-network-null-input-retry-with-placebos The modular lag-free network of experiment 545 (arm M0) has a weather encoder and a datetime encoder, so it may extract signal from four groups of inputs that earlier networks found null or harmful: thermal-lag and solar-gain windows (B1), look-ahead weather windows (B2), school-term and national-signal columns (B3, one arm for each), and a whole-day price shape that is present only while training (B4). Each real arm is compared with a shuffled-day placebo of the same number of columns, so a gain counts only if it exceeds what extra columns give regardless of content. not supported not-for-production Giving the modular lag-free demand network extra inputs that earlier networks found useless did not help over a whole year: no group beat a shuffled-day control of the same width by the threshold. The exception is the thermal-lag and solar-gain group (B1), which lowered the error on cold winter nights at the six signed-MW substations by about 0.2 points of capacity (3 months only, an effect the data can barely resolve). On all rows at the eight it made no difference against plain M0. The next step is a larger cold-night test of that group on the best lagged network. primary 00561 wind-components-era5-and-ens-summary-data-prep The wind components (east and north, at 10 m and 100 m) can be added to the ERA5 pretraining table and to the ensemble summaries from data already on disk, and total cloud cover can be added to both from ERA5 on disk and from the Dynamical.org ensemble store. partly supported not-for-production The wind direction inputs and ERA5 cloud cover are ready for every run and every hour. Ensemble cloud cover is ready only for the 222 most recent runs (2025-11-21 to 2026-06-30), so an experiment that uses it cannot train on the earlier ensemble history. The production table does not store cloud cover yet. primary 00552 icon-eu-four-runs-a-day-lag-free-demand NGED wants the forecast updated every 6 hours. The ECMWF ensemble runs once a day, so a lag-free forecast issued at 06, 12, or 18 UTC repeats the same weather inputs. ICON-EU runs four times a day, so a small adaptor that maps the latest ICON-EU run to the seven mean-weather inputs of experiment 524's frozen stage-1 network could improve the forecast at the issue times that the ECMWF run does not refresh. not supported not-for-production A fresher weather run did not improve the forecast: with 4 months of ICON-EU history, the ICON-EU-based forecast was worse than the ECMWF-based one in March and April and level with it in May and June. This is spring only and gives no evidence about winter. The next step is to wait for more ICON-EU history, or to test the same question on a source with years of runs. also relevant 00550 lag-light-network-trailing-temperature-windows-with-placebo The three trailing temperature windows (means of the ensemble-mean 2 m temperature over the 6, 24, and 72 hours ending at the valid time) still lower the error on cold winter nights when the network also reads the day-ago and week-ago power lags (R-DW of experiment 539), because the windows describe the weather of the last three days and a lag of one day or one week carries only one reading of it. supported candidate The three trailing temperature windows still help the lag-light demand network on cold winter nights by about 0.10 points of capacity, the same size as without the lags, so the day-ago and week-ago lags do not already carry that information. Over all rows the windows do nothing we can show. The next step is to judge the windows on cold nights, with more winter folds. also relevant 00549 k2-s1-blend-and-climatology-stored-check Part 1. Averaging the 11 stored quantiles of R-DW (experiment 539) and the retrained K2-S1 (experiment 541, a different kind of network: monthly lag-free heads plus lagged heads) with a fixed weight per lead band forecasts better than either, because the two networks have different inputs and architectures and so make less correlated errors than L-1d and R-DW did in experiment 547. Part 2. A blend with a calendar-only or climatology forecast helps the demand forecast only at 120 to 240 h. partly supported not-for-production Averaging R-DW with the rebuilt K2-S1 improves the 1 to 5 day forecast by about 0.02 points of capacity, less than half the 0.05 we asked for, so serving a second neural network for it is not justified. No stored blend of climatology or a calendar-only forecast into a demand network helped by 0.05 at 5 to 10 days; the one climatology gain, for wind farms in experiment 262, vanished once the offset table was applied. The proposed climatology head and weather-input dropout therefore have no stored evidence behind them. also relevant 00548 lag-free-release-candidate-assembly-with-trailing-temperature-windows The lag-free recipe assembled from parts that already have evidence (ERA5 and CAMS pretraining, daily refit with a 90-day half-life, trailing temperature windows, flat 1.15 widening) reaches the score of the lag-enabled network A-pool at 120 to 240 h of lead but not at 24 to 48 h, where the gap is mostly the recent-power inputs. partly supported candidate A demand forecast that sees no recent power but does see the recent temperature scored slightly better than the same forecast without the temperature, although no interval excluded zero. At 5 to 10 days ahead its gap to the forecast that does see recent power was inside what the seeds can resolve. At 0 to 5 days ahead, for the eight Primary substations metered in MVA only, it stayed 0.13 to 0.34 points of capacity worse. The temperature columns did not close that gap. Of the approaches tested in experiments 539 and 541, only adding the power from a day and a week ago closed most of it, and that approach also made the forecast follow an injected load shift more closely (5.68 against 4.49 points of capacity). also relevant 00547 lag-light-and-lag-free-blend-by-lead-band-stored-forecasts Averaging the 11 stored quantiles of L-1d (a daily-refit lag-free network, experiment 511) and R-DW (the same network plus day-ago and week-ago power, experiment 539) with a fixed weight per lead band forecasts better than either parent, because the two networks make partly different errors and the best weight on the lag-light network differs by lead. not supported not-for-production Averaging the lag-free network with the lag-light network gives no better forecast than the lag-light network alone: at 1 to 5 days ahead the two scores differ by under 0.01 points of capacity, far below the 0.05 we asked for. In this test the lag-free network added nothing the lag-light network lacks. A blend with a network of a different kind, such as K2-S1 rebuilt on origin-time weather, is untested. also relevant 00546 teacher-student-distillation-into-lag-free-demand-network A lag-free network (the student) fine-tuned against the forecast of a teacher that sees the day-ago and week-ago lags (experiment 539's R-DW), in addition to the real target, scores closer to A-pool than the lag-free network L-1d does, because the teacher's forecast carries information about the weekly pattern that the weather and calendar inputs can recover but the real target alone teaches slowly. The student reads no lag at any time, so it adds no load-shift leak route. refuted not-for-production A demand network that cannot see recent power learned nothing useful from a teacher that can: it scored slightly worse than the same network trained on the real target alone, and stayed 0.26 to 0.38 points of capacity behind A-pool at 1 to 5 days ahead. The day-ago and week-ago power must therefore be an input at forecast time, or the gap stays. The next step is to choose between accepting the injected load-shift leak that those lags bring and a robust same-slot summary of the recent weeks. also relevant 00544 lag-light-demand-network-robust-same-slot-median-and-lag-dropout Experiment 539's lag-light network (the lag-free network plus the day-ago and week-ago power readings, each with a missing flag and an age) closes 76% to 83% of the lag-free network's gap to the lag-enabled network A-pool, but it follows an injected load shift more than the lag-free network does. Two changes could keep the gain and cut the weakness. (1) R-MED: replace each single reading by the median of the same half-hour over many days, which one shifted day cannot move. (2) R-DROP: train with the readings removed in 30% of rows, so the network also works when they are late or absent. not supported not-for-production Averaging the same half-hour over several past days did not make the lag-light demand network safer against load-shift events: it forecast worse and followed an injected shift more. Randomly removing the readings during training made the network lean less on them, so it kept under half of the gain. It does work with no readings at all, at the level of the lag-free network. The next step is a different guard against shifted readings, such as the detector's probability, or accepting experiment 539's leak. also relevant 00540 lag-gap-what-closes-the-gap-to-lag-enabled-models The lag-enabled demand models beat the lag-free network L-1d at 24 to 120 h because of their recent-power (lag) inputs, and the gap is not shown to come from head count, recency weighting, restart, or network family. Refit cadence is not separated from the lags. supported not-for-production The demand network that sees no recent power scores 0.2 to 0.3 points of capacity worse (CRPS) than the network that does, at 1 to 5 days ahead for the eight Primary substations metered in MVA only. Adding the power from the same time a day ago and a week ago closes about four fifths of that gap (a point estimate with wide intervals). In one seed, those inputs also made the forecast follow an injected load shift more. An earlier apparent advantage at 5 to 10 days came from weather that was issued after the forecast was made. also relevant 00526 lagless-demand-network-trailing-weather-window-placebo-repeat Experiment 515 found that trailing temperature windows (W-T) lower cold-night CRPS at the eight MVA-only Primaries by 0.150 points, but a shuffled-day placebo over nine columns (W-null) lowered it by 0.071, and W-T minus W-null was -0.079 [-0.290, +0.089]. That comparison mixes real against shuffled windows with three columns against nine. The claim here is that W-T beats a shuffled-day placebo built from exactly W-T's three columns (W-Tnull) on cold nights at the eight, so the gain comes from the content of the windows and not from extra input columns or from the fold in which W0 scores badly. partly supported candidate Trailing temperature windows lowered cold-night error at the eight MVA-only Primaries by 0.093 points of capacity more than a shuffled-day placebo of the same three columns did (11 seeds, 9 of 10 folds), which is a small gain only just above what the seeds can resolve. Nothing resolved at the six signed-MW Primaries or in summer, and the check that persistence-filled windows match the default build failed, so this is a candidate and not a settled result. primary 00525 metering-type-flag-lagless-demand-network The 8-wide Primary embedding of the lag-free network is mostly its random start, so it may not carry the one fact that separates the eight MVA-only Primaries from the six signed-MW Primaries: apparent power cannot be negative, and signed power can. One extra 0/1 input column (1 for apparent power in MVA) tells the network that fact directly. If the embedding already carries it, the column adds nothing; if the column improves the forecast or removes the mixture's probability mass below zero at the eight, the embedding is too thin. not supported not-for-production Telling the lag-free demand network which Primaries report apparent power (MVA) and which report signed MW did not make its forecast better. At the eight MVA-only Primaries the flag made the score slightly worse, as a randomly permuted flag did, and it did not remove the forecast probability below zero. At the six signed-MW Primaries it helped by about 0.03 points, a gain the permuted flag did not reproduce but that is too small to port. also relevant 00522 primary-embedding-data-look-lagless-demand-network The Primary embedding of the lag-free neural network does more than label the 16 Primaries. The embedding is the 16 x 8 table of vectors that tells the network which Primary (primary substation) a row belongs to. The network is the L0PT network of experiment 448: it reads no lagged power and is pretrained on ERA5 and CAMS estimates of past weather. Each vector starts as a random N(0, 1) draw. The hypothesis is that the movement from that start is small, is not arranged by a Primary's physical behaviour, and is not needed by the network, because a random fixed label is enough to separate 16 Primaries. partly supported not-for-production The lag-free demand network's Primary embedding is not just a random label: pretraining moves each vector about half its length, and scoring a Primary with its own random start vector instead of its trained vector raises the error by 0.8 to 1.3 points of capacity, so the movement is used. The movement is only weakly arranged by physical behaviour (winter daily shape, through the size of the movement and not its direction) and does not tell signed-MW from MVA-only Primaries, so giving the network per-Primary descriptors, and not only a learned label, is worth testing next. also relevant 00517 lagless-demand-network-lockdown-flag-removal The flag is 0 in every scored month and in every fine-tune row, so it can only matter through the pretraining rows from 2019-09, which hold the 2020-03-23 to 2021-07-19 lockdown. A lag-free network pretrained on those rows without the flag may fit them worse, or may be pulled off its normal behaviour by them. Dropping the lockdown rows may then help the network more than keeping the flag. inconclusive candidate No arm is a clear replacement for the lockdown flag, and the experiment cannot rank the arms. Removing the flag while keeping the lockdown rows scored 0.029 points worse at the six signed-MW Primaries, and dropping the lockdown rows as well scored 0.033 points better than keeping the flag at the eight MVA-only Primaries, but leaving out one Primary at a time removes the first difference and weakens the second. Every difference is below the minimum detectable effect of 0.12 to 0.13 points. primary 00516 lagless-demand-network-learned-weather-window-cnn A lag-free demand network sees weather at the valid time only, yet buildings warm up and cool down slowly and sunshine through windows offsets heating on a cold day. A small convolutional encoder over the 24 hours of ensemble-mean weather around the valid time can learn which part of that history matters, so it improves the lag-free network, and it improves it by more than the hand-built trailing windows of experiment 515 (the second PR of the maintainer's 2026-11-02 weather-window brief; the hand-built arms are experiment 515's). not supported not-for-production A small convolutional encoder over 24 hours of ensemble-mean weather did not improve the lag-free demand network: on all rows both encoders scored 0.07 to 0.13 CRPS points worse than the base, with every interval including zero. The same encoder reading shuffled-day windows scored numerically better than the one reading real windows, but that difference is also unresolved. primary 00515 lagless-demand-network-trailing-weather-window-features A demand network that reads no lagged power sees only the weather at the valid time, but a building warms and cools slowly, heating is switched on late, and sunshine through windows offsets heating on a cold day. Trailing means of temperature and shortwave over the previous 6 to 72 hours, or the 24-hour product of the two, therefore let the lag-free network forecast cold winter nights and cold sunny days better. Earlier neural tests of trailing weather (experiments 419, 437, 441, 442) all fed the network three origin lags of power, which may have carried the same information, so their nulls may not transfer. inconclusive not-for-production Trailing temperature windows lowered cold-night CRPS at the eight MVA-only Primaries by 0.150 points in 10 of 10 folds, but a shuffled-day placebo lowered it by 0.071, and nothing resolved at the six signed-MW Primaries or on all rows, so the effect is not resolved. primary 00513 lagless-demand-network-whole-day-price-shape-at-training-time The Market Index price of a whole local day, known exactly at training time, carries information about price-following embedded batteries and gas engines behind a Primary, so a lag-free demand network that sees it in training forecasts those Primaries better. At serving time no price exists, so this experiment first asks the upper-bound question: does the true shape, given at both training and scoring time, help at all? not supported not-for-production Even a perfect, hindsight price shape for the whole day does not lower the lag-free demand network's error at NGED's Primaries by a measurable amount, and the oracle gains no more at the Primaries with a known battery or gas engine. The oracle gain is the bound for a training-time-only price arm (price dropout, an auxiliary price head, or a teacher network), and that bound is not resolvable from zero, so those arms were not run. An option for batteries and price-following generators is to model their output as a separate target or a subtracted term; whether to test it belongs to the roadmap. primary 00504 neural-demand-leak-free-recent-cams-irradiance-inputs Giving the pooled demand neural network (experiment 425's arm A, which already reads the ensemble forecast of shortwave radiation) three extra inputs built only from Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) satellite irradiance that a live service would have at the forecast origin lowers its continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) at days 1 to 10 at the eight Primaries that report only apparent power in megavolt-amperes (MVA): D2, D3, D4, D8, D12, D19, D21, and D22. The reason is that recent observed sunshine says how much embedded solar generation hides in those readings, which the ensemble forecast does not. not supported not-for-production Satellite sunshine measurements that a live service could have at forecast time (whole days at least 36 hours old) did not help the demand neural network in this fine-tuning design: its error rose by 0.1% at the eight Primaries that report only apparent power. The same satellite columns read at the forecast's own half-hour would cut the error by 6.8%, so the improvement comes from knowing the sunshine of the target half-hour, not from older sunshine, and better sunshine forecasts or a nowcast are the next place to look. The experiment did not test a fresher feed (the previous day). primary 00496 simplify-demand-network-input-and-output-pruning Four inputs or outputs of the demand neural network can be removed one at a time, each within the equivalence limit: (a) the seven ensemble-spread inputs (the mean forecast stays), (c) the four holiday columns that describe the Christmas period and bank holidays, merged into one day-type column, (d) the three inputs that describe the weekly lag (its value, its missing flag, and its age), and (b) the second and third Gaussian of the three-Gaussian output. Serving then needs fewer inputs and a smaller output layer. partly supported candidate The demand neural network can drop its 7 ensemble-spread inputs (46 inputs down to 39) with no loss on the scored whole sample: the CRPS change was +0.012 points at the 8 MVA-only Primaries and -0.043 at the 6 signed-MW Primaries, both inside the limit, although it scored 0.187 points worse at the six on cold winter nights (3 folds, almost all from December) and 0.408 worse at the six on rows with a labelled event. The other three simplifications were not shown equivalent: merging the holiday columns (at both groups), dropping the weekly lag (at the eight), and using one Gaussian instead of three (at the eight). also relevant 00480 xgboost-cams-columns-at-mva-only-primaries-lab-conditions Giving the monthly XGBoost demand model two extra input columns per half-hour, the unit photovoltaic (PV) output shape and the clear-sky index, both computed from realised Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) irradiance, lowers the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) at days 1 to 10 at the eight MVA-only Primaries (D2, D3, D4, D8, D12, D19, D21, D22), because embedded solar generation hides inside their apparent-power readings and the model has no input that says how much of it a half-hour had. supported candidate Giving the XGBoost demand model the satellite-measured sunshine of each half-hour lowered its error at all 16 primary substations in the point estimates, by 0.36 points of capacity over the eight that report apparent power and by 0.48 over the six that report real power. A live service cannot have this input for the first day ahead, because the satellite data arrives about a day late, so the gain is an upper bound. The next step is to measure how much of the gain remains when the columns come from the ensemble weather forecast. primary 00442 thermal-lag-cold-night-test-on-six-winter-folds The maintainer expects thermal lags to help mostly on difficult winter rows, with no harm elsewhere. Experiment 441 (rescoring experiment 437) found that bundle T gains at least 0.05 CRPS points on cold winter nights at both metering groups, but its intervals include zero, not every fold was negative, and the slice's minimum detectable effect (0.12 to 0.26) is above 0.05. Adding winter months to the folds lets the cold-night slice resolve a gain of that size. not supported not-for-production Thermal-lag columns are not supported as a help on cold winter nights on these six monthly folds, which is not the same as no effect. The average change was a gain of 0.086 points at the six signed-MW Primary substations, but that gain depends mainly on one Primary substation (D16). It was a gain of 0.014 at the eight MVA-only Primary substations, where the gain seen in experiment 441 did not replicate in the two new winter months. The folds cannot rule out a gain of 0.05, because the smallest gain they could reliably detect is 0.15 to 0.19. primary 00441 difficult-row-rescore-of-the-neural-demand-input-bundles The annual mean score of experiment 437 hides a gain that is concentrated on difficult rows. The maintainer expects thermal-lag columns (bundle T) to help mostly on cold winter nights, solar-gain columns (bundle S) to help on cold sunny days, look-ahead columns (bundle F) to help on cold winter nights and heat waves, and calendar and tariff columns (bundle C) to help at Christmas and on bank holidays. NGED needs good forecasts on exactly those rows, with no harm on the others. inconclusive not-for-production The input bundles did not help on the difficult rows either, but the four test months are too few to say they do nothing: on cold winter nights the smallest gain these data could reliably show is 0.12 to 0.23 points of capacity, several times the 0.05 bar. Thermal lag (bundle T) was the only arm that looked better on cold winter nights at both groups of Primaries, and its signed-MW gain came from two Primaries. The larger finding is that the signed-MW Primaries' 95% and 99% upper quantiles cover only 76% and 83% of cold winter night half-hours, which is a larger shortfall than any bundle's gain. primary 00437 neural-demand-thermal-lag-solar-gain-and-tariff-feature-bundles The pooled plain mixture density network of experiment 425 sees one valid time per row, so it cannot see the hours before or after that time. Adding columns that summarise those hours (bundle T, thermal lag; bundle S, solar gain; bundle F, look-ahead) or that carry the calendar, tariff, and national signals (bundle C) lowers its continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) at days 1 to 10, because the network trains across all 16 Primaries (and, in the pretrained form, across 6 years of ERA5 and CAMS history) and may find signal that the per-Primary XGBoost model and the GAM stack missed. not supported not-for-production Adding thermal-lag, solar-gain, look-ahead, calendar, tariff, or national-signal columns to the pooled plain mixture density network did not lower its continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) by the registered 0.03 points of capacity, in either the ensemble-only or the pretrained form. Seven of the eight arms were worse than their control at the six signed-MW Primaries, by 0.016 to 0.059 points. The thermal-lag bundle lowered the CRPS at the eight MVA-only Primaries (by 0.022 and 0.029) in only 2 of 4 folds, which is too weak a result to act on. The screen could not detect effects below 0.045 to 0.064 points, so the bundles are left out, not ruled out. primary 00423 pooled-mdn-shared-date-time-encoder A small encoder that turns the half-hour of day, day of week, day of month, day of year, and the bank-holiday name into one learned vector, shared across the 16 Primaries, lets the pooled plain mixture density network share what it learns about holidays across Primaries and across holidays of one kind, so it forecasts bank-holiday weeks better than the hand-made calendar columns and is no worse elsewhere. not supported not-for-production A small calendar encoder shared by the 16 Primary substations did not forecast demand better than the 18 hand-made calendar columns. With holiday names and dates it scored 0.27 points of capacity worse (8% worse, in a range of 0.10 to 0.43) on the continuous ranked probability score at the six substations that report signed power, and with dates only it scored 0.37 worse. One possible reason, not tested, is that each day of the year appears only once or twice in the 24-month training window. The planned test on bank-holiday weeks could not detect any difference smaller than 0.34 points, and all five test months are interim. primary 00408 xgboost-signed-label-and-cams-columns-at-mva-only-primaries At the eight MVA-only Primaries, the monthly XGBoost demand model gives a signed real-power forecast, without losing skill on the MVA reading, when (a) two CAMS columns (the unit solar shape and the clear-sky index of the half-hour itself) are added to its inputs and (b) reverse flow is labelled before training: a reading is flipped to negative only on very sunny half-hours, where a physics rule says the substation exports power in the shape of solar output. partly supported not-for-production Satellite solar columns lower the forecast error at almost every Primary, but only when the model knows the realised sunshine, which production does not until about a day later. The attempt to read a signed MW forecast from an unsigned MVA meter failed its known-answer test again, so there is still no trusted signed forecast at the eight MVA-only Primaries. also relevant 00399 xgboost-short-history-start-cut-d15-d18 Dropping the first months of the two short-history Primaries, D15 and D18, from the monthly XGBoost demand model's training rows lowers its error at those Primaries, because the readings taken while the meters were being commissioned teach the model a wrong level. partly supported candidate Dropping the noisy first weeks of D15 and D18 from the training rows helps the monthly XGBoost forecast only a little: about 1% lower error at both, mostly in the first scored months, when the history was shortest. Cutting 6 months is not safe, because it made D18 worse. The larger problem at D15 is a level error that no start cut fixes: the median forecast is about 21 points of capacity too low, against 3 for the generalised additive model (GAM) stack, so the next experiment should look at D15's level, not its start. also relevant 00396 xgboost-recipe-screen-demand-calendar-winter-hyperparameters-ensemble-summary At least one change in each of five families (calendar columns, winter weather columns, hyperparameters, ensemble-summary inputs, a split of the model by lead band) lowers the days 1 to 10 CRPS of the weekly member of experiment 87, refitted monthly, by more than the refit noise floor at the signed-MW six or the MVA-only eight Primaries, and the families that act on a specific slice (holiday days, winter and the top demand quartile, high ensemble spread) gain more on that slice than on all rows. partly supported candidate Giving the weekly XGBoost demand model the ensemble's view of the weather, either its mean and spread or a model trained on the ensemble mean, lowered the error by 0.4% to 2.7% in both test months, and no other change we tried did so as clearly. Holiday columns help on Easter bank holidays but raised the error on all days in January and at the signed-MW six at Easter, and winter weather columns do not help, so a full-year test should start with the ensemble-input arms. also relevant 00394 xgboost-ensemble-mean-and-std-columns-separately Experiment 389's gain from four ensemble columns (the mean and standard deviation across the 51 members of temperature and of shortwave) comes mostly from the two mean columns, because the gain was largest at 0 to 24 hours and at the middle quantiles and absent at q01 and q99. supported not-for-production Giving the XGBoost demand forecast, as an extra input, the mean across 51 ensemble weather members of the temperature and of the shortwave radiation lowers its error (CRPS) by 0.052 points of capacity at the 6 substations that record the direction of flow, and by 0.029 points at the other 8. That is the whole improvement of four extra columns at the 6 and 82% of it at the 8 (0.035 points). The members' spread adds almost nothing, and it does not help more on days when the members disagree most. The tails do not materially improve with either input: on cold nights the forecast's 95% quantile lies above only 0.77 to 0.78 of outcomes at the 6. primary 00387 xgboost-folded-latent-loss-at-mva-only-primaries A single XGBoost model per Primary, refitted weekly with experiment 87's recipe but with a loss that scores the absolute value of a signed latent power against the metered apparent power (a folded loss), recovers the reverse-flow V-shape at the MVA-only Primaries that the plain model misses, and recovers a signed power forecast that agrees with known signed truth. not supported not-for-production Training the XGBoost model on a folded signed power did not improve the forecast at the eight Primaries whose meters report unsigned apparent power, and it did not fix the under-forecast of sunny half-hours at D12. The signed power it reports follows the start we gave it, not the readings, so it cannot yet be shown to NGED as a forecast. A signed forecast needs a structural way to fix the sign, such as demand minus a non-negative generation term. also relevant 00103 differentiable-physics-1-data-look The trial area's power records hold enough clean, demand-only history for the series to go ahead as designed: 6 MW Primaries with at least 12 months before July 2025, and 8 MVA Primaries with over 3 site-years each of rows with no sunlight. supported not-for-production The data lets the series go ahead, with three changes: start 13 of the 16 Primaries later than their first record (19.4 months later at D4), fix the lockdown window in advance because the data does not isolate it from drift, and count eligible long-history MW sites at each tuning year's first day (5 at 2024-07-01, so 4 of 5 must improve in Part 2's tuning contrast). The power timestamps show no 30-minute error on either side of the 2026-03-26 fix: at the 6 metered photovoltaic series the median offsets are +0.9 minutes before it and +4.7 after, and the correction is right to within 3 minutes, but offsets at the Primaries are not resolved beyond 0 to +8 minutes. also relevant 00094 explicit-heating-offset-primary-demand For the 16 Primary substation demand series, adding a per-series heating term to the XGBoost model's base margin lowers the forecast error in cold hours (ENS 2 m temperature below 3 C), because the term extrapolates linearly beyond the coldest training hour and cannot be damped at long leads, whereas trees predict a flat response there. The term is the heating degree-hours (15.5 C minus the temperature, floored at zero) times a per-series, per-hour-of-day coefficient fitted by least squares on the training window only. small gain candidate The heating term lowered the quantile score by 0.143 points of capacity in cold hours at leads up to 48 hours (98.75% interval -0.203 to -0.034), under the 0.3 threshold, and by 0.022 over all rows (-0.042 to +0.000). primary 00074 an1-same-time-analogues-vs-explicit-solar-forecast-demand At the 5 Primary substations (substations that feed 11 kV circuits from the 33 kV network) with a clean solar-capacity estimate, when the XGBoost model is refitted every month on the latest 12 months of data (P-roll), an explicit forecast of the unmetered solar output, given to the model as a starting offset (experiment 64's arm am), lowers the daylight April-to-September quantile score by more than same-time-of-day analogues do. An analogue is a recent day, at the same half-hour of the day and of the same day type (working day, weekend, or bank holiday), whose satellite-based sunshine was closest to the sunshine forecast for the target. The model receives the observed power on the K nearest such days (K is 1, 3, or 5) as input columns. Once the explicit offset is in the model, the analogue columns add less than 0.05 points of capacity. inconclusive not-for-production Both ways of telling the monthly-refitted model about sunshine lowered the daylight error: the explicit forecast of the panels' output by 0.149 points of capacity (99.17% interval -0.201 to -0.104) and the 3 analogues by 0.095 (-0.185 to -0.007) against the reference. primary 00032 substation-fingerprints-pooled-demand For demand series of Primary substations, adding a numeric fingerprint of each substation (its location, its mean level and daily and weekly shape over the training window, and its level over the 14 days before the forecast origin) to a by-type pooled XGBoost quantile model closes part of the 0.15-point gap between the pooled model with the series identifier and per-series models, and lets a substation held out of the pool be forecast better than a pooled model with no fingerprint. inconclusive not-for-production Adding numeric substation fingerprints to the pooled model changed the Primary score by at most 0.02 points of capacity, and training-window statistics made a held-out substation worse by 1.39 (inconclusive overall; recent power statistics alone helped it by 0.23, post hoc). also relevant 00031 embedded-pv-features-primary-demand For the 16 Primary substation demand series, giving the single-stage ENS-trained quantile model N1 trailing estimates of each substation's embedded (unmetered) solar capacity, built from the Embedded Capacity Register (ECR) as a prior for Primaries and a floor for BSP and GSP series, plus an amount learned from recent power and irradiance, lowers the quantile score on sunny days, and a linear PV offset or a sunshine-shaped correction does so more reliably than extra tree columns. inconclusive not-for-production C3, A3 (PV products with the register) minus B0, quantile score over all leads: +0.006 points of capacity (99.17% interval -0.022 to +0.033). primary 00030 lagged-power-feature-sets-primary-demand For the 16 Primary substation demand series, giving the single-stage ENS-trained quantile model N1 the 13 power lags that manual_heuristic uses (the same weekday and time of day 1 to 6 weeks back, and 49 to 55 weeks back), as separate columns beside N1's three lags measured from the forecast origin, lowers the quantile score. inconclusive candidate C3, all 13 lags minus N1 (seed 0 only): -0.01 points of capacity on the quantile score (99.375% interval -0.45 to +0.43). primary 00028 pvlive-forecast-in-stage2-gsp-demand For the two grid supply points (GSPs) Walpole and Bicker Fen, giving the stage 2 calibrator a forecast of the GSP's solar generation at the target time, from a simple XGBoost model of Sheffield Solar's PV_Live estimate applied to ECMWF ensemble (ENS) weather, lowers the quantile score below that of the same calibrator without a solar forecast. inconclusive not-for-production C1, solar forecast minus no solar forecast, over all leads: -0.14 points of capacity (95% interval -0.34 to +0.04). primary 00027 pvlive-lags-in-stage2-gsp-demand For the two grid supply points (GSPs) Walpole and Bicker Fen, giving the stage 2 calibrator Sheffield Solar's PV_Live estimate of the GSP's solar generation at the lag times, next to the lagged delta (metered demand minus the stage 1a expectation), lowers the quantile score below that of the same calibrator without PV_Live. refuted not-for-production C3, delta plus PV_Live minus no PV_Live, over all leads: -0.03 points of capacity (98.33% interval -0.13 to +0.09). primary 00025 price-change-features-stage1-demand Giving the ERA5-trained stage 1 demand model the change in the intra-day price over the last half-hour, 1 hour, 2 hours, and 6 hours, in addition to the price at the target half-hour, lowers its error at observed power for Primary substations, and by more than the same columns built from a price taken from another week. Batteries and other dispatchable generation respond to how the price moves, not only to its level. small gain not-for-production On Primary substations, adding price changes to the price level lowered the error by 0.037 points of capacity in the selection year (97.5% interval -0.056 to -0.018) and 0.050 in the confirmation year (-0.083 to -0.018). primary 00024 pooling-groupings-demand-xgboost For demand series of Primary substations, one XGBoost quantile model trained across a group of series (all series, one model per substation type, or one model per size band), given the series identifier as a categorical column, scores no more than 0.3 points of capacity worse than one model per series, so that the number of models can fall from one per series to one per group. supported candidate Pooling the 16 Primary substations into 3 or 4 XGBoost models (with the series identifier) scored 0.15 points of capacity worse than 20 per-series models (99.44% interval +0.03 to +0.26), inside the 0.30 margin; one model for all 20 series was 0.29 worse, and dropping the identifier cost 0.8 to 1.0. also relevant 00015 same-time-price-stage1-demand Adding the intra-day price at the same half-hour as the target (Elexon Market Index Data, observed at time t, not forecast and not lagged) to the ERA5-trained stage 1 demand model, which already sees the weather at time t, lowers its error at observed power across all fitted series pooled, and by more than a price taken from another week does. inconclusive not-for-production C1, price against no price, pooled: -0.52 points (97.5% interval -0.88 to -0.11) in the selection year and -0.18 (-0.50 to +0.08) in the confirmation year. primary 00014 cams-trained-stage1-with-stage0-ens-correction-demand A stage 0 that maps the ECMWF ensemble (ENS) member's shortwave irradiance onto the irradiance of the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) lowers the Primary substation quantile score of the CAMS-trained stage 1a XGBoost demand model, relative to feeding that model the raw ENS shortwave, because the ENS shortwave is about 7% above CAMS and stage 1a never saw that offset in training. inconclusive candidate C2, stage 0 minus raw ENS for the CAMS-trained arm, Primary quantile score over all leads: -0.067 points of capacity (97.5% interval -0.094 to -0.039), better than the planned -0.03. also relevant 00011 school-term-and-return-to-work-columns-stage1a-demand For the ERA5-trained stage 1a XGBoost demand model at Primary substations in Lincolnshire, columns for the return to work after New Year and for Lincolnshire's school terms lower the mean absolute error of the median in the weeks after Christmas, at Easter, and in the half-term holidays, against the same XGBoost model with a Christmas column that is set only within 14 days of 25 December. refuted not-for-production Return and term columns against the base arm, Primary substations: +0.06 points from 2 to 20 January (99.2% interval -0.17 to +0.30), +0.20 over the Easter window (-0.19 to +0.59), and -0.29 over the half-term holidays (-0.68 to +0.07). primary 00010 elexon-price-lags-stage1a-demand Adding the Elexon Market Index Data price from exactly 7 days earlier to the ERA5-trained stage 1a demand model lowers its error at the substations that host price-responsive batteries, and does so by more than adding the same-lag national demand and wind output, which price follows. inconclusive not-for-production C1 at B2, price against base: -0.92 points (98.3% interval -2.10 to +0.07) in the selection year and -0.06 (-0.38 to +0.23) in the confirmation year. primary 00009 cams-trained-stage1a-vs-era5-trained-demand A stage 1a XGBoost demand model trained with irradiance from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) in place of ERA5 shortwave, and applied to the shortwave of ECMWF ensemble (ENS) members, has a lower quantile score at Primary substations than the same model trained on ERA5 shortwave, because the satellite-derived irradiance is closer to the irradiance that the substations' embedded solar generation responded to. refuted not-for-production C1, CAMS-trained minus ERA5-trained, Primary quantile score over all leads: -0.035 points of capacity (97.5% interval -0.070 to +0.001), a sixth of the planned 0.2-point gain. also relevant 00007 cams-static-correction-stage1a-residual Most of the daytime residual of the stage 1a demand model at Primary substations is a fixed error in the ERA5 irradiance input and not a growing embedded-solar capacity, so a correction with fixed coefficients on irradiance from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS), fitted on one year of out-of-fold residuals, removes most of the residual in the next year. inconclusive not-for-production The static correction removes 46.6% of the next year's daylight squared residual, just below the planned 50%, and a fixed bias alone removes 39.1%. also relevant 00006 stage1a-demand-input-feature-sweep For a weather-to-power XGBoost model trained on ERA5 for substation demand, the local clock (hour of day and day of week) is the input that lowers the held-out error most, and the other non-lag inputs tested here (holiday encodings, time of year, trailing temperature means, sun position beyond zenith and azimuth, UTC offset, windchill, and a COVID indicator) each lower it by less. partly supported candidate P1, hour and weekday against the weather block alone, Primary substations: -0.55 (99.4% interval -0.71 to -0.41) on the selection year and -0.46 (-0.61 to -0.30) on the confirmation year, the largest single input but about a third of the predicted size. primary

High (maintainer request, 2026-10-31) Nothing Done: no bundle met the bar; thermal lag (bundle T) is the only candidate for a retest on more folds 442 Does thermal lag (bundle T) lower the pooled neural network's error on cold winter nights, on six winter-weighted folds?
