docs.title: Done experiments
docs.text: Experiment Hypothesis Relevance

docs.title: Demand inputs: state and next steps
docs.text:
Extra weather, calendar, price, and satellite inputs have given the demand forecast little beyond the inputs already in the final model. The overview page holds the XGBoost results. This page covers the neural-network results, which came later, and ranks the options for further tests. Final models describes what the production port builds. In this page, "the Candidate" is the demand neural network that the final models use for the 16 Primary substations.

Terms. CRPS is the continuous ranked probability score, an error measure for probabilistic forecasts, in points of capacity. A negative contrast means the first arm is better. The six MW Primaries are the six Primary substations whose meters report signed megawatts (MW). The eight MVA Primaries report apparent power only, in megavolt-amperes (MVA). A cold night is a half-hour below 5 degrees C between 18:00 and 08:00 local time. A placebo is the same columns with the values taken from a shuffled other day, so the level is right and the timing is wrong. The minimum detectable effect is the smallest difference that seed spread alone would resolve. ENS is the ECMWF ensemble weather forecast, ERA5 is the fifth-generation ECMWF reanalysis, and CAMS is the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service satellite estimate of sunlight (glossary). M0 is the plain modular neural network that the add-on experiments use as their control.

docs.title: What we know
docs.text:
No input group tested on a neural network beat its control by the registered bar over a whole year. Eight bundles of thermal-lag, solar-gain, look-ahead, calendar, tariff, and national-signal columns did not lower the CRPS of the pooled neural network by 0.03 points in 3 of 4 folds, and seven of the eight were worse at the six MW Primaries (Experiment 437).

When the same columns entered pre-training through a matching encoder, no group beat its placebo by the minimum detectable effect. The closest was the thermal-lag and solar-gain group (B1) at the six MW Primaries: -0.135 (interval -0.31 to +0.04), against a minimum detectable effect of 0.30 (Experiment 569).

Adding the 14 thermal-lag and solar-gain columns to the modular neural network changed error little and lowered the leak of injected shifts. Against the control without them, the columns moved the CRPS by +0.010 at the eight MVA Primaries and -0.046 at the six MW Primaries in the 0 to 24 hour band. The leak of an injected shift into the forecast fell from 7.7 to 5.4 points against the placebo (Experiment 574). Experiment 677, which builds up the Candidate one component at a time, is pending, and Final models will state its result.

The one candidate input group is the thermal-lag and trailing-temperature group, and only on cold nights. The gain is small and shifts between experiments:

  • Experiment 437 found a gain of 0.022 at the eight MVA Primaries in 2 of 4 folds.
  • Experiment 442 found the cold-night contrast at the eight fell from the 0.05 or more of Experiment 441 to -0.014 (-0.102 to +0.138), and at the six it was -0.086 (-0.241 to +0.141).
  • Experiment 515 found trailing temperature windows lowered cold-night CRPS at the eight by 0.150 (10 of 10 folds) while a placebo lowered it by 0.071, so the experiment called the effect not resolved.
  • Experiment 562 found a thermal-lag and solar-gain group 0.231 better than its control on cold nights at the six, from 3 monthly blocks, at a minimum detectable effect of 0.227.

Experiment 526 supersedes Experiment 515 because it used 11 seeds. The two experiments share folds. Experiment 526 found the real windows beat the placebo by 0.093 (-0.133 to -0.053, 9 of 10 folds) at the eight, only just above the minimum detectable effect of 0.083. Nothing resolved at the six or in summer. The seam check failed: that check compares the windows built from lagged weather with windows that fill the hours before the forecast origin with the run's first value.

Satellite sunshine helps only when it is read at the target half-hour. Two columns of realised CAMS irradiance lowered the XGBoost CRPS at all 16 Primaries in the point estimates, with the interval wholly below zero at 15 (Experiment 480: -0.355 at the eight, -0.476 at the six). A live service lacks that input for the first day ahead, because the satellite data arrives about a day late. Satellite values a live service could hold, from whole days at least 36 hours old, raised the neural network's CRPS by 0.006 at the eight and 0.010 at the six (Experiment 504).

The ensemble mean of temperature and shortwave carries the XGBoost gain from the ensemble. Two mean columns lowered the CRPS by 0.052 at the six and 0.029 at the eight, and the spread columns added almost nothing (Experiment 394).

docs.title: What does not work
docs.text:
Learned or larger components did not beat the hand-made inputs.

  • A convolutional encoder over a 24-hour weather window scored 0.07 to 0.13 worse than the 37-column base on all rows, with every interval including zero (Experiment 516).
  • A shared calendar encoder scored 0.27 worse than the hand-made calendar columns at the six (Experiment 423).
  • Larger encoders did not help beyond seed noise at the eight (Experiment 579).

Price did not help, even as a training-time-only input. A hindsight price shape for the whole day gave -0.048 at the six and +0.037 at the eight, against a minimum detectable effect of about 0.17. The arms that would have trained a teacher neural network on the price (price dropout and a teacher network) were therefore not run (Experiment 513). A price encoder trained beside the weather encoders made the fine-tuned forecast 0.29 worse at the six (Experiment 570). The XGBoost price tests are on the overview page.

The lockdown flag is neither shown to be needed nor shown to be removable. In Experiment 517, arm C0 keeps the flag, C1 removes the flag and keeps the 2020 to 2021 lockdown rows, and C2 removes the flag and drops those rows. C1 scored 0.029 worse than C0 at the six. C2 scored 0.044 better than C1 at the eight, and 0.033 better than C0 at the eight. The experiment judges that it cannot rank the arms, because leaving out one Primary at a time weakens both results and every difference is below the minimum detectable effect of 0.12 to 0.13.

The 95% and 99% upper quantiles of the six MW Primaries cover only 76% and 83% of cold winter-night half-hours (Experiment 441). That shortfall is larger than any input's gain, so calibration is a likelier lever on cold nights than another input.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Does the trailing-temperature gain at the eight survive on a held-out winter? Experiments 515 and 526 share folds, so a new winter is the first independent test.
  • How much of Experiment 480's satellite gain survives when the columns come from the ensemble forecast? The experiment named this as its next step.

docs.title: Next-experiment options
docs.text:
The options are ranked by how much a production port depends on the answer.

  1. An option is to wait for Experiment 677 and then test removing the 14 thermal-lag and solar-gain columns from the Candidate. Experiments 574 and 569 found the columns neutral on error, so the question is whether the port can drop them and the pipeline step that builds them. Experiment 677's build-up is pending (see Final models), and it may answer the question first. The plan page lists no separate experiment for this option.
  2. An option is to retest trailing temperature on more winter folds with the placebo and seam check of Experiment 526. The question is whether the 0.093 gain at the eight is real. It depends on option 1, because a column the final model drops needs no retest. Experiment 562 asked for a larger cold-night test on the best lagged neural network.
  3. An option is to re-run Experiments 569 and 562 with a second seed and a re-pretrained plain control. Experiment 569 named this step, because its pre-trained control scored worse than the stored weights of plain M0. It matters mainly if option 1 shows the columns help.
  4. An option is to score Experiment 480's satellite columns with ensemble-forecast values. The question is what remains of the 0.355 to 0.476 gain in a live service. Its result applies to the XGBoost path more than to the final neural network.
  5. An option is to add more seeds for the larger datetime encoder at the six. Experiment 579 suggested it, and its own conclusion is that no further architecture arms are needed, so the production value is small.

docs.title: What is parked
docs.text:
The convolutional window encoder is parked. Experiment 516 recommended spending no more fits on learned windows until Experiment 515's placebo question was resolved, and Experiment 526 resolved it only partly.

Price inputs are parked. The oracle bound of Experiment 513 is not resolvable from zero, and Experiment 570 failed its known-answer test, so the next step named there is a controlled test with a larger injected generator before any real-data price work. Modelling batteries and price-following generators as a separate target is a roadmap question, not an experiment of this theme.

The lockdown flag stays as the default. Experiment 517 cannot rank the arms, and the flag is zero in every scored month, so the production port can follow the default of the final model.

Load-shift event detection is paused until January. It is the subject of the lsc-detectors theme, and the options above do not depend on it.

docs.title: Differentiable physics (demand, calendar, and weather)
docs.text:
The current understanding and the options for next work are on the state and next steps page.

This theme covers the demand model of a six-part series on forecasting with physical terms.

Background: Differentiable physics: background explains the models in plain terms.

The series builds models of Primary substation demand from a daily profile, holiday and heating terms, and a solar term, fitted by gradient-based optimisation. This theme holds the part that builds the model and asks whether more years of history help it. The series' finding so far is in experiment 104: the convex model trained on 12 months beat lagless XGBoost with its default start by 0.25 points (post hoc), and all years with drift are level with 12 months, so more years are not yet shown to help. Experiment 63 is an earlier, smaller linear test of the same decomposition into a weather baseline, a solar term, and transfer terms. The Experiments page lists every experiment, and the Research plan lists what is planned next.

docs.title: Differentiable physics (demand, calendar, and weather): experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00413 differentiable-physics-demand-network-part-1 A pooled network that forecasts Primary demand as a Primary-specific mix of shared learned daily shapes plus a Primary-specific mix of shared learned temperature and solar responses, with a plain mixture density head on the residual, scores within 0.03 points of the pooled plain mixture density network on the 2026-01 fold, and its learned curves can be read. not supported not-for-production A neural network built from shared, readable parts (learned daily shapes and temperature responses) forecast substation demand less accurately than the plain neural network on five test months: by 0.17 points of capacity at the 6 substations that record the direction of flow, and by 0.23 points at the other 8. Its error in the middle of the distribution was larger at both groups. At the six it covered the highest outcomes better, but at the eight it was worse in both tails. Under the default rule the design does not advance, and whether to pursue it is the maintainer's call. primary 00281 economy7-night-step-smooth-in-temperature A forecast of primary substation demand whose night level is a set of free levels for each UTC night half-hour (experiment 121's NS-U), and then a step whose size is a monotone function of the cold, scores better in the Economy 7 step hours and on cold winter nights than the same forecast with only the winter night offset (experiment 155), when the weather input is the ensemble-mean forecast and not past weather. Economy 7 is the tariff that switches storage heaters on shortly after 00:30 UTC. Experiment 121 found a gain of 0.233 points on winter nights on past weather and asked for a test on weather forecasts. inconclusive not-for-production Fitting the Economy 7 night levels inside the demand model, and not adding a winter night offset afterwards, lowered the day-ahead error by about 0.02 to 0.03 points of rated demand over all rows in both years and by about 0.04 points on winter nights, but the gain in the two hours after the step starts could not be shown: it changes sign between the two years and depends on two or three substations. Letting the step grow with the cold added almost nothing over free night levels. The Economy 7 term does not explain the night-time gap at D10 in April to June. primary 00279 dp-heating-curve-monotone-lagged-temperature-and-wind The heating response of the convex demand model T-all-K (a hinge at 15.5 C on four trailing-mean temperatures, split by day type) is too rigid. A smooth, monotone, non-negative curve on the same temperatures (A1), the same curve also on exponentially weighted and previous-day mean temperatures that carry the building's thermal lag (A2), or a small monotone neural network on three daily mean temperatures and the wind speed (A3), lowers the day-ahead quantile score on cold nights and winter days at the five decision Primaries, and the fitted curve is not a straight line. not supported not-for-production A smooth heating curve, a thermal lag, and wind each leave the day-ahead forecast within about 0.02 points of the straight-line heating response, so the evidence does not justify adding any of them. A small neural network learns a plausible curved heating response and lowers the error on cold nights by 0.13 points, but that gain comes from one cold spell in January 2026, did not appear in the previous year, and the network failed a test on synthetic data, so the substation card keeps the straight line for now. primary 00198 d8-summer-spikes-cooling-load-and-residual-test The summer spikes a colleague saw in D8's power (time series 26, Marsh Lane) are air-conditioning load: they rise smoothly with temperature, peak in the afternoon of the hottest days, and repeat every year. The best-guess forecast has a heating hinge but no cooling term, so its summer residual (metered minus forecast) rises with temperature, and a cooling hinge on the ensemble mean temperature fitted on past residuals lowers its summer score. inconclusive not-for-production D8's afternoon power does not rise with temperature, and its large summer departures from expected power are mostly downward shortfalls of 1.5 MW or more, which grow from 18% of summer half-hours in 2022 to 52% in 2025, so the spikes are not air-conditioning load. A cooling term added to the best-guess forecast changed the summer score at the five decision Primaries by 0.0002 points (interval -0.010 to +0.015), but the 4 fit months held too few hot days and the known-answer control failed, so the experiment cannot rule a cooling term out. On afternoons of 25 degrees Celsius or more, metered power exceeds the forecast by 0.6 to 5.1 points on average at each of six Primaries, so a term fitted on the full multi-year history of past weather, pooled across Primaries, is the next test. primary 00173 dp-christmas-more-years-and-sites The convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors and recipe R (the mean error of the last 14 days by half-hour, held to 0.75 of its size), which scored 1.13 times an ordinary weekday over 24 December to 2 January at five substations in two Christmases (experiment 170), keeps a Christmas-to-weekday error ratio under 1.3 in every Christmas back to 2019-20 and at 14 or more of 16 Primary substations, and does not over- or under-forecast 25 and 26 December by more than 5% of that day's demand. inconclusive not-for-production Where the demand model had a winter of training data, the error over 24 December to 2 January was 0.97 to 1.22 times an ordinary weekday in all four Christmases from 2022-23 to 2025-26, so no special-day term is justified. The pre-registered run failed because the training rows of Christmas 2020-21 and 2021-22 (and of one substation in 2023-24) held little or no winter, since the lockdown window is left out of training. A forecast for a substation with under 180 days of usable history should be flagged, not trusted. also relevant 00145 differentiable-physics-analog-day-error-correction-on-gam-k Averaging GAM-K's past day-ahead errors over the days most similar to the target day (same day type, with holiday identity for holidays, similar forecast daily mean temperature, and a season window of a few weeks either side of the date) gives a better correction than averaging the last 14 days alike (recipe R of experiment 115) or the same-day-type days of the last few weeks (experiment 134). The reasoning is that demand errors repeat on days that resemble each other. The errors that repeat most, on holidays and on cold days, are the ones that a 14-day average dilutes. small gain candidate Averaging the errors of the 20 most similar past days (same day type, within 13 weeks of the same date, last year's days included) beat recipe R (the 0.75-weighted mean error of the last 14 days) by 0.041 points at day D+1, the calendar day after the forecast origin (about 1.7% of R's score of 2.436). That gain is larger than the 0.011 points that the weekday term of experiment 134 gained. Matching on forecast temperature helped by only 0.005 points, and copying the error of the same holiday last year made holidays worse, so the next step is a day-type profile with a season window and no correction copied from an earlier holiday. also relevant 00143 differentiable-physics-holiday-aware-updating-of-the-gam-k-filter The Kalman filter of GAM-K lets a holiday's reading error teach it a wrong level, which carries into the days after the holiday; leaving holiday readings out of the filter's update (and nothing else) lowers the day-ahead score on those following days, and does not hurt the holiday targets or the rest of the year. not supported not-for-production Leaving holiday readings out of the day-ahead filter's update does not reliably help the days after a holiday: the effect had the opposite sign after Christmas 2024 and Christmas 2025, and its 99% interval in the scored year (-0.309 to +0.036 points) includes zero. In 10 of 12 holidays, the holiday readings' error had the same sign as the error on the following days, so these readings are not usually contamination. Setting the correction to zero on holiday days, as experiment 118 did, is the action that hurts (+0.62 points on holiday days). Two Christmases give no basis for changing the filter this Christmas. also relevant 00137 differentiable-physics-e7-economy-7-night-step-term-in-the-forecast An additive night term, fitted on the base forecast's own past errors as a function of the ENS-mean daily temperature and the UTC clock time, lowers the day-ahead quantile score on the half-hours from 01:00 to 03:00 UTC on cold winter nights, without raising the score elsewhere. The mechanism is that the base GAM-K forecast (experiment 133's shared-noise arm) runs below actual demand from about 01:00 on cold nights (experiment 123), so a correction learned from earlier winters removes a bias the forecast repeats. inconclusive not-for-production The day-ahead forecast runs about 2.5 points too low on cold winter nights from 01:00 UTC, and a correction learned from its own past errors removes that bias and lifts the 0.95 quantile's coverage there from 80% to 93%. An audit showed that a plain winter night offset does as well, so the experiment found a winter night bias, not a step that grows with cold. The verdict is inconclusive: one winter, 365 headline rows, and a failed placebo. primary 00126 differentiable-physics-s1-cheap-screens-added-to-gam-k Each of six families of cheap additions to the day-ahead convex model GAM-K lowers its score after the Kalman filter, winter first: a free or monotone temperature curve (A-free, A-mono), exponentially smoothed temperatures (S-ewma) or smoothed daily extremes (S-mm), wind chill (C-wind) or apparent temperature (C-hw) inside the heating hinge, a school-term term (D-sch), lighting from solar elevation (E-sol), and a filter whose noise differs by regime (F-mix). A second family of four exploratory screens: a switching Kalman filter with three hidden regimes (G-skf), a learned periodic basis for the year cycle (W-basis), a soft cold/mild mixture of heating slopes (W-mix), and a cross-substation anomaly from weather-station residuals (W-stn). One hypothesis per arm, in "Arms" and "Four exploratory screens". inconclusive not-for-production None of the thirteen cheap additions to the day-ahead GAM-K lowered the winter score by a margin we can trust. E-sol (lighting from solar elevation) came closest, at -0.036 points on dark winter evenings, but its interval (-0.122 to +0.024) is too wide to call, because six of the thirteen screens had a half-width above their 0.03 to 0.05-point margin. Only W-basis (learned year cycle) was clearly worse, in every month, site, and year. F-mix and W-stn looked worse too, but each rests on 2 to 3 calendar months. G-skf found injected load transfers 4 to 7 times as often at 25% and 40% transfers as the plain filter, but failed its own power gate and recovered no faster. primary 00123 differentiable-physics-e7-storage-heating-night-step-estimation At Primary substations, demand steps up in the half-hours from 00:30 to 02:30 on winter nights, the step grows with cold, and the pooled step over the six decision series is positive at a daily mean of 3 C. At D5, D10, and D16, which were chosen because winter 2025-26 showed the step, it is 5 to 10 points (1% of each series' 99th percentile of demand); at the other decision series it is smaller. inconclusive not-for-production The night step at Primary substations is about 10 points on a 3 C day, where one point is 1% of a substation's near-peak demand, and it starts around 01:00 and looks fixed to UTC rather than the local clock (a check chosen after seeing the data). The rise on cold winter nights is the feature an operator would see: the day-ahead forecast runs 6 to 10 points below actual demand from about 01:00 at D5 and D16 on the two pre-registered winters, and at D10 in winter 2024-25 alone (7.6 points at 01:00); at D10 in winter 2023-24 the baseline is instead 9 to 17 points too high all night. The step appears at 13 of the 14 substations, and its full size rests on summer nights having no step, which the gate cannot test. The verdict is inconclusive because the gate is weaker than it looks: it holds one real test of the interval, and that test under-covers. primary 00122 differentiable-physics-three-winter-backtest-gam-k On past weather, the convex model with the Kalman filter (GAM-K) forecasts Primary demand one day ahead better than both the plain convex model (GAM) and lagless XGBoost, in each of the three winters 2023-24, 2024-25, and 2025-26, by at least 1 point of mean absolute error. supported not-for-production In all three winters, the convex demand model with the recent-error filter (GAM-K) forecast Primary demand one day ahead 1.8 to 3.1 points of capacity better than the same convex model without the filter, and 2.0 to 3.1 points better than lagless XGBoost. The gain is consistent with the filter removing a level error that a fit frozen for a year carries, and lagless XGBoost has no recent power to correct the same error. GAM-K's filter settings were fitted on the 2023-24 winter, and the convex model's ridge penalty was tuned on a year that contains the 2024-25 winter, so those two gains are partly in-sample. 2025-26 has the least tuning leakage, but it was read in an earlier analysis before this plan, and no winter is clean on both counts. A post hoc check at the audit subtracted each plain model's own winter-mean error at each substation, which no forecaster could know in advance: GAM-K stayed ahead of the plain GAM by 0.63, 0.71, and 0.35 points and ahead of lagless XGBoost by 0.95 to 1.05 points, so 5 of the 6 contrasts would miss the 1-point bar. Most of the gain is therefore level tracking, and this result does not show that GAM-K beats a model that sees recent power. The scoring uses past weather, so the gain under live weather forecasts is unknown. primary 00121 differentiable-physics-mh-multi-hinge-heating-curve-and-night-step In the convex model of Primary demand in the form Part 6 made the DP's candidate (GAM-K), on past weather, replacing the single fixed 15.5 C heating hinge by five hinges (10, 12, 14, 16, and 18 C) with non-negative slopes, so the heating curve never falls as it gets colder and stays convex, lowers the day-ahead quantile score after the recent-error filter. Second question (NS): GAM-K leaves a 4 to 7 point step at 01:00 on winter nights at three substations (a pattern like storage heating switching on), and a night-step term lowers the score on winter nights without worsening the other rows by more than 0.02 points. Indexed in UTC against local time, the winning indexing is reported. inconclusive candidate Adding night-time levels indexed on the UTC clock lowers the day-ahead error on winter nights by about 0.23 points after the recent-error filter, at all 5 substations in both winters, and the forecast then shows the 01:00 jump in demand that the current forecast misses on cold winter nights. Five heating bends instead of one gain only 0.016 points, within noise. The synthetic tests could not show that a step this small can be detected, so the night result needs a test on weather forecasts and an audit before it enters the model. primary 00120 differentiable-physics-sh-convex-daily-shape-library A convex model in which each Primary's daily profile is a non-negative mix of K = 3 or 4 shared daily shapes per day type, plus a penalised deviation, forecasts Primary demand with 2 years of history at least 0.05 points better than experiment 109's shrinkage towards one fleet-mean profile. That needs the library to beat the per-site profile by about 0.02 points, because the fleet-mean model is 0.031 worse than it; the plan predicts a tie or a small gain, so supported is a long shot. The stability of the shapes and the shape mix of each substation are descriptive. inconclusive not-for-production In a test with synthetic substations, 5 Primaries were too few for a library of 3 shared daily shapes to recover the shapes we planted, so the check failed on 7 of 10 lines and the verdict is inconclusive. In the scored year the library scored the same as the fleet-mean model and 0.030 points worse than a profile per substation (0.068 worse in winter), and its forecast reproduced a tenth to a half of the Economy 7 night step on cold winter nights. also relevant 00119 differentiable-physics-enc-weather-patch-encoder-on-ens A small neural network that reads the ENS grid boxes around a Primary, and not only the one box GAM-K reads, lowers GAM-K's quantile score a little on average and more on the cold, showery, and badly forecast days NGED cares about, either as a correction to GAM-K's quantiles or as a replacement for its single-box temperature and irradiance. inconclusive not-for-production A small neural network that reads the ensemble weather around a Primary lowers GAM-K's quantile score by 0.062 points of effective capacity in one scored year and 0.035 in the other (both statistically significant, 5 of 5 substations better), and the gain is smaller in winter (0.041 and 0.027 points) but never a loss. About two-thirds of the gain survives when the network reads the wrong date's weather (0.043 and 0.022), so it is probably a recalibration of GAM-K's quantiles with the lead, the hour, and GAM-K's own forecast, and the surrounding boxes add nothing to the centre box (patch minus centre box: -0.002 and +0.003 points). The known-answer gate failed, so the verdict is inconclusive, and the next step is a plain recalibration of GAM-K's quantiles with the centre box's extra fields (dew point, pressure, precipitation, and member spread), not a patch encoder. also relevant 00117 differentiable-physics-h2-graph-prior-on-pooled-convex-parameters A penalty on the differences between interconnected Primaries' parameters (heating slopes, PV capacity as a share of effective capacity, the profile's scale, and the holiday coefficients) narrows those parameters' month-block bootstrap intervals without breaking their coverage when neighbouring Primaries are alike, and worsens the full-history quantile score by at most 0.03 points. refuted not-for-production At the weight tested, tying the parameters of interconnected substations together did not improve the forecast: in the scored year it worsened the quantile score by 0.020 points on all days (the interval spans zero) and by 0.173 points in winter evening peaks (the replicate year gave -0.021). On synthetic substations with a known truth it narrowed only heating-slope intervals, and the 80% intervals of PV capacity held the truth 17% of the time against 78% without the tie. A tie on heating slopes alone worsened the real score by 0.006 and 0.001 points, an exploratory lead and not a result. also relevant 00114 differentiable-physics-n3-n4-interactions-and-heating-threshold Two labelled claims about the convex model of Primary demand in the form Part 6 made the DP's candidate (GAM-K: 24 months, no drift, pinned capacity, Kalman filter), on past weather. N3: interaction terms (heating by day-type group, heating on eight sub-band blocks, lighting by day-type group), each shrunk towards the base by a difference penalty, lower the day-ahead quantile score after the filter. N4: a per-site heating threshold, chosen by profiling the training loss, is recoverable on synthetic substations at real noise, is identified away from 15.5 C at one or more real substations under the per-site printing rule, and lowers the score after the filter. partly supported not-for-production Splitting the convex model's heating terms between the first and second half of each part of the day lowered its day-ahead error after the recent-error filter by about 0.04 points (97.5% interval 0.014 to 0.070), at all 5 substations in both years, but the gain label rests on one substation (D5), and the gain is a temperature-dependent shape of the day more than a heating effect. Letting heating or lighting differ between weekdays and weekends adds nothing, and choosing a heating threshold separately for each substation did not clearly help (0.01 points, within noise). Every number uses past temperature, not forecasts, so the gain needs a test on weather forecasts before GAM-K's convex model changes; the PV panel-orientation mix (N13) was dropped because earlier experiments found it unidentified. primary 00113 differentiable-physics-n5-convex-identification-at-realistic-noise On synthetic substations built from the real calendar and weather, with noise as large and as autocorrelated as the convex model's real residuals, the convex model's 80% month-block bootstrap intervals cover the truth 70 to 90% of the time, separately for each hour band's heating slope and for the latest season-year's PV capacity. Labelled separately, not in the verdict: the day-of-year harmonics and the drift term make those intervals wide, by absorbing the seasonal cycles of temperature and clear-sky PV. refuted not-for-production At real noise levels, the convex model's 80% month-block bootstrap intervals contain the true heating slope and the true rooftop PV capacity 84% of the time each, but a heating slope is weak (the interval is about 38% of the slope wide). The pre-registered verdict is refuted, because with independent noise the capacity interval covers the truth only 52% of the time, and the cause is mainly a bias of about 0.24 points from the drift penalty at its tuned step of 3,000 (at Part 4's step of 30 the bias is 0.02 points and coverage 78%, a post hoc check). The truth here has the model's own form, so the test cannot show the bias that a wrong PV shape causes. also relevant 00112 differentiable-physics-vp-variable-projection-fit-of-pooled-model Part 3's pooled DP lost to the per-site DP because gradient descent did not reach the optimum, not because pooling hurts: solving every linear coefficient exactly at each step, with gradient steps only on the non-linear parameters, makes the pooled DP at least as good as the per-site DP on substations with 2 years of history. inconclusive not-for-production Solving the pooled model's linear coefficients exactly did not make its forecasts better. With the interaction neural network on, the exact fit drove the network's last layer and the seasonal and holiday terms to very large, weakly penalised values: it forecast up to 280 points too high on four days of spring 2026 (the weekend of the clock change, Good Friday, and Easter Monday), and it was 0.7 points worse on the other days. With the network off, the exact fit is stable and within 0.03 points of the gradient fit, so the optimiser was not what held the pooled model back; the known-answer test failed, and with the network on the model cannot recover heating even from noise-free data. also relevant 00110 differentiable-physics-5-embedded-generation-and-capacity The convex differentiable-physics model can represent the generation side of a Primary substation without making its demand forecast worse: an MVA meter through an observation layer, a flat unmetered generator found where one exists and not invented where none does, and an export-limited PV clip; and its PV capacity stays the same when the routes by which demand terms can imitate solar are closed. inconclusive not-for-production The demand forecast could not yet account for generators connected behind a substation. Rooftop solar capacity fitted from the data was not precise or consistent enough to trust, so the capacity from outside estimates stays in use. A generator-finding component reported a generator at every substation tested, so it stays switched off. A limit on exported solar helped only at the one substation known to export-limit. Treating the meter as apparent power improved the forecast at the 8 substations that report only apparent power by 0.13 points of capacity, but the test of the meter's flow direction failed, so that gain is provisional. also relevant 00109 differentiable-physics-n0-partially-pooled-convex-model A convex model whose per-substation coefficients are a fleet mean plus a ridge-penalised per-substation deviation forecasts Primary demand as well as the per-substation convex model when both have 2 years of history, and clearly better when the substation has 4 weeks or 3 months. inconclusive not-for-production The known-answer test of this method failed under its pre-registered definition, and only one of five runs (each on a new seed, runs 2 to 5 being post hoc redefinitions) passes every line, so the verdict is inconclusive. Taking the numbers alone, for the five MW Primaries tested, one convex model shared across substations forecast a new substation with only 4 weeks of history 3.3 points better than a convex model fitted to that substation alone (and 0.8 points better with 3 months), far more than the 0.5 to 2.0 predicted, and scored 0.03 points worse on substations with 2 years of history. On the six held-out Primaries it came within 0.2 points of experiment 105's neural pooled model with 4 weeks (the neural model 0.13 better) and 0.12 better with 3 months, without that model's loss on long histories, which suggests that the loss in experiment 105 came largely from the neural fit. Complete pooling scored 0.07 points worse than partial pooling at 4 weeks in the scored year (interval touching zero) and no differently in the replicate year. The gains should be relied on only after a rerun of the gate. also relevant 00107 differentiable-physics-rolling-origin-history-and-tails Refitted quarterly from 2023-07 to 2026-04 and scored on the next 3 months, the convex model's two history contrasts (all years against 12 months, drift against none) keep one sign at almost every origin. A second claim, labelled separately as C5 and not part of the verdict: a level-dependent spread brings its 95% and 99% quantiles within 1 point of nominal coverage without worsening the quantile score. partly supported not-for-production Giving the convex demand model a drift term lowered its score at 10 of 12 quarterly refits, by 0.45 points when trained on all years (interval 0.23 to 0.68). In a post hoc split, about three-fifths of that size is one substation (D10) at the 2023-24 refits, and the 2025-26 refits give 0.30, as in experiment 104. All years without drift scored worse than 12 months at 8 of 12 refits, and all years with drift against 12 months has no stable answer: winter-quarter refits favour more years, summer ones are level. The spread that depends on the forecast level made the 95% and 99% quantiles worse, so the tail coverage still needs a different method. The verdict is partly supported, because only the drift contrast is stable; a second spread (the conformal spread) is not interpreted, because it was built with a flaw. also relevant 00105 differentiable-physics-3-pooled-and-per-site-demand-model One differentiable-physics model fitted across all the Primary substations forecasts a substation as well as the same model fitted to that substation alone when both have two years of history, and forecasts clearly better when the substation is new (4 weeks of history) or short of history (3 months). inconclusive not-for-production One neural-network demand model fitted across 15 Primary substations forecasts a substation with only 4 weeks of history far better than a per-site copy of the same model (score 4.04 against 14.38 on the six scored substations), but forecasts a substation with 2 full years of history worse than a per-site copy (3.42 against 3.04 on the five decision substations, worse at all 5). By the pre-registered rule pooling is not yet a success, because that full-history result (C1) is refuted, and a failed known-answer check (gate test 2, injected-farm recovery) caps the verdict at inconclusive. Post hoc, for a new substation the pooled model also beat a per-site convex model fitted to the same 4 weeks (mean absolute error 6.88 against 12.79). also relevant 00104 differentiable-physics-2-simple-structural-model A convex demand-minus-solar model, trained on every usable year with a slowly drifting level per hour band, forecasts Primary demand better than the same model trained on the last 12 months. inconclusive not-for-production A simple model of demand minus solar, trained on 12 months, scored 0.25 points better than lagless XGBoost with its default start (post hoc; a lower score is better). Most of that lead is in the forecast spread, because the error of the mean forecast differs by only 0.08 points, and four of the five pre-registered positive controls failed, so the verdict is inconclusive. More years of history did not clearly help: the scored year and the tuning year gave opposite signs for two history-window contrasts, and a first version of this page had the wrong sign for both because its spread carried the previous year's mean bias. primary 00063 sw2-10-linear-joint-fit-v2-in-miniature On the 8 Primary substations metered in MW, one linear fit per Primary that holds a weather baseline without radiation inputs, the embedded-solar capacity of experiment 00045 times the CAMS unit PV shape, and one share-of-the-donor's-net-power term per labelled transfer, (C1) lowers the error of the median forecast outside switching on held-out months, in hindsight, below that of the same baseline with radiation inputs by at least 0.35 points of capacity, (S1) recovers an injected solar capacity to within 0.15 of its size, and (S2) recovers an injected transfer share to within 0.05. inconclusive not-for-production C1 is -0.322 points of capacity (-0.437 to -0.207), close to the 0.35-point threshold, but the S1 and S2 gates failed for reasons of test design, so the verdict is inconclusive. primary

docs.title: Differentiable physics (demand, calendar, and weather): research plan
docs.text:
The cheap screens of inputs to the convex model are bundled into one experiment. Experiment 104 found that all years of history without drift scored worse than 12 months, and that a drift held constant recovered that. The recent-level drift and the day-type filter are covered by the KFE experiment, so this page lists the input screens only.

Experiment Question Priority Waits for State N3 and N4, interaction terms and heating threshold Do interaction terms in the convex model, and a heating threshold chosen per substation, lower its error? Done, partly supported None Interaction terms (N3) gained, mostly at one substation, and the per-site heating threshold (N4) tied (experiment 114) S1, cheap screens added to GAM-K (experiment 126) Do cheap additions to the day-ahead GAM-K lower the score, winter first? Done, inconclusive None None of 13 screens showed a trusted gain; E-sol (-0.036 on dark winter evenings) is the lead for a retest on ENS weather; W-basis worse in every month, site and year; F-mix, W-stn undecided on 2 to 3 months E7F, Economy 7 night-step term in the forecast (experiment 137) Does an additive night term, fitted on the base forecast's own past errors, lower the day-ahead score on cold winter nights from 01:00 UTC? Done None Finished (inconclusive): The day-ahead forecast runs about 2.5 points too low on cold winter nights from 01:00 UTC, and a correction learned from its own past errors removes that bias and lifts the 0.95 quantile's coverage there from 80% to 93%. An audit showed that a plain winter night offset does as well, so the experiment found a winter night bias, not a step that grows with cold. See experiment 137. Weather encoder retest Does a small learned encoder over a patch of weather cells lower the error on hard cases (convective and frontal days, wind and solar sites) once the base forecast is recalibrated? 3 A plain recalibration of GAM-K's quantiles, which experiment 119 found accounts for most of the encoder's gain Queued, after the recalibration

Later parts are listed in their own themes.

docs.title: Bundled cheap screens
docs.text:
The six screens share one experiment and run on 6 CPU cores in about 2 hours. Each has one hypothesis:

  • Free temperature spline. A free spline of temperature fits better than the fixed 15.5 °C hinge.
  • Smoothed temperatures. Temperature smoothed at two decay rates, plus smoothed daily minimum and maximum, adds skill to the convex model's means of 6 hours to 1 week. The GAM papers on regional load use these terms: Obst et al. (2021) for French load, and Fasiolo et al. (2021) for the winning GEFCom2014 entry. No paper isolates the gain from the smoothing alone.
  • Humidity and wind chill. Feeding humidity and wind chill into the heating hinge lowers the winter error.
  • School-term calendar. A school-term term lowers the error in term-time weeks, once data availability is checked.
  • Lighting from solar elevation. Lighting modelled from solar elevation beats a fixed clock curve on dark winter evenings.
  • Filter-noise mixture. A filter noise that depends on the regime (cold snap, mild, holiday) beats one fixed noise.

docs.title: Weather encoder retest
docs.text: The retest repeats the weather-encoder comparison on the hard cases, with a recalibrated base forecast. The encoder replaces single-cell inputs with a learned view of a patch of cells, and the aim is a lower error on convective and frontal days, when a single cell misses the neighbouring weather. Experiment 119, the first encoder experiment, ended inconclusive, and about two-thirds of its gain survived when the network read the wrong date's weather. The retest therefore waits for a plain recalibration of GAM-K's quantiles, and runs on the GPU. The encoders technique page is the first thing to read.

docs.title: Differentiable physics (demand, calendar, and weather): state and next steps
docs.text:
The convex model of Primary demand is a readable alternative to lagless XGBoost, but none of the terms added to it has a confirmed gain. The convex model fits a daily profile, holiday terms, a heating term, a lighting term, and a solar term by convex optimisation, a method that has a single best answer. "Lagless" means the XGBoost model receives no recent readings of the substation's own power. This page is a selection of the theme's experiments.

GAM-K is the version of the convex model that the series chose as its candidate. GAM is short for generalised additive model, a model that adds one smooth curve per effect. GAM-K is a GAM fitted on 24 months of history, with no drift term, with the solar capacity pinned (fixed to a value estimated beforehand), and with a Kalman filter. The Kalman filter corrects each forecast with its recent errors.

None of this theme's terms appears in the final models. The Primary demand forecast in the final models is a neural network, and whether it already captures the winter night bias is untested.

Scores are quantile scores unless stated, in points of effective capacity. One point is 1% of a substation's capacity, and a lower score is better, so a negative contrast favours the added term. Experiment 63 and Experiment 122 score mean absolute error of the median instead. The experiments use past weather unless stated, so each gain is a ceiling for the weather forecasts used in production. Verdict words (supported, partly supported, small gain, not supported, inconclusive) are defined in the glossary. Experiment 126 adds three labels. undecidable means the interval is too wide to read, tie means the arms differ by 0.02 points or less, and not powered means the known-answer test could not show that the effect is detectable.

docs.title: What works
docs.text:
The Kalman filter makes GAM-K better than both plain models in each of three winters. Experiment 122 (verdict supported) scored mean absolute error. GAM-K beat the plain GAM by 1.83 to 3.06 points and lagless XGBoost by 2.00 to 3.10 points in all three winters, and every contrast met the 1-point bar. Two of the winters were partly in the data the models were fitted on. After subtracting each model's winter-mean error, 5 of 6 contrasts miss the 1-point bar, so most of the gain is level tracking.

Splitting each heating slope between the two halves of its hour band lowered the filtered score by 0.039 points. Experiment 114 gives an interval of -0.070 to -0.014 and a gain at 5 of 5 substations in both years, with the score falling from 2.255 to 2.216. About 38% of the gain appears on warm rows where every heating term is zero, and without substation D5 the estimate is -0.030, which is small gain. The verdict is partly supported.

docs.title: What is inconclusive, does not work, or is unproven
docs.text:
A winter night offset raised the 0.95 quantile's coverage on cold winter nights from 80% to 93%, but the result is inconclusive. In Experiment 137, a term fitted on the day-ahead forecast's own past errors cut the mean error on those rows from 2.5 to 0.2 points and lowered the score by 0.484 points (99% interval -0.777 to -0.169) on 365 headline rows. Over all rows the gain is only -0.032 points, and the term worsened the 22:00 to 23:00 half-hours. A plain winter night offset with no temperature does as well, so the experiment found a winter night bias and not a step that grows with cold. The shuffled-night placebo gained as much as the term, so the test could not separate the term from chance, and the data covered one winter.

Fitting night levels inside the model beat the winter night offset by 0.02 to 0.04 points, which is inconclusive. Experiment 281 found the gain on all rows and on winter nights in both years. The gain in the two hours after the step starts changes sign between the two years. A step that grows with the cold added almost nothing over free night levels.

Day-type interactions, a per-site heating threshold, and a learned year cycle add nothing. In Experiment 114, letting heating or lighting differ between weekdays and weekends moved the score by +0.002 and -0.0001 points, and a per-site heating threshold moved it by -0.012 points with an interval spanning zero. In Experiment 126, the learned year cycle (W-basis, a periodic curve fitted in place of the fixed seasonal terms) made the score 0.091 points worse (interval 0.025 to 0.149) and was worse in every month, site, and year.

None of 13 low-compute screens showed a trusted gain. Experiment 126 labelled seven screens undecidable, two tie, two not powered, one worse, and one inconclusive. Lighting from solar elevation (E-sol) came closest, at -0.036 points on dark winter evenings with an interval of -0.122 to +0.024. G-skf, a Kalman filter fitted to the residuals, found injected load transfers 4 to 7 times as often as the plain filter at 25% and 40% transfers, but failed its power gate, so it is a detector only.

A smooth heating curve, a thermal lag, and wind each left the score within 0.02 points of the straight-line heating response. Experiment 279 (not supported) tested these on cold nights. A small neural network lowered the cold-night error by 0.13 points, but the gain came from one cold spell and failed a known-answer test. Experiment 413 (not supported) built a neural network from readable shared parts, and it scored 0.17 and 0.23 points worse than the plain neural network at six MW and eight MVA Primaries.

A neural network that reads the weather around a substation gained 0.062 and 0.035 points, and about two-thirds of the gain survived another date's weather, which suggests quantile recalibration. Experiment 119 scored one year in each direction. The known-answer gate failed, so the verdict is inconclusive.

More history is not shown to help, even with a drift term. In Experiment 104, all years of history without drift scored 0.25 points worse than 12 months. With a drift term, the contrast between all years and 12 months was -0.04 (interval -0.30 to +0.21), and the all-years model scored 2.78 against 2.82 for 12 months. Four of five positive controls (synthetic tests of an effect known to exist) failed, so the verdict is inconclusive. The same experiment's 12-month convex model beat lagless XGBoost by 0.25 points (post hoc, chosen after seeing results). Drift is covered by the theme Differentiable physics: long history and drift.

A hindsight solar term lowered the error by 0.322 points, short of the 0.35-point threshold. Experiment 63 compared a linear fit of baseline, solar, and load-transfer terms with the frozen Flexpectation v1 XGBoost baseline, in mean absolute error. The interval is -0.437 to -0.207, with sunshine and capacity taken from the past. The injection checks failed for reasons of test design, so the verdict is inconclusive. The load-transfer terms were barely exercised (2 event-substation pairs).

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Whether a seasonal night offset removes the night bias is unknown. Experiment 137 cannot separate it from a cold-driven step with one winter of data, and Experiment 281 answers only part of the question.
  • Whether the half-band heating split survives weather forecasts and monthly refits is unknown. Experiment 114 used past temperature only.
  • Whether the weather encoder's gain is a recalibration of the quantiles is untested directly. Experiment 119 suggests so through the wrong-date copy.

docs.title: Next-experiment options
docs.text:
An option is to test lighting from solar elevation again on forecast weather. The source is Experiment 126's "What to try next". The test would use the ECMWF ensemble (ENS) weather forecast, the earlier winters, and a row set that narrows the interval below 0.03 points.

An option is to test a seasonal night offset on a second winter (2026-27). The source is Experiment 137's advice. It needs at least 50 cold-night rows per substation and a placebo that shuffles temperature within each calendar month.

An option is to confirm the half-band heating split on ENS weather with monthly refits. The source is Experiment 114's advice, before any port into GAM-K.

An option is to run a plain recalibration of GAM-K's quantiles first. The source is Experiment 119's "What to try next" and the research plan. The recalibration would use the centre box's extra fields (dew point, pressure, precipitation, and member spread). The plan queues a weather encoder retest on convective and frontal days after it, because Experiment 119 found the surrounding boxes add nothing.

docs.title: Parked
docs.text:
The per-site heating threshold, the learned year cycle, and the weather-patch encoder are parked. Experiments 114, 126, and 119 found no trusted gain from them.

Load-shift event detection is paused until January. The state at the pause is in the load-shift detector pause page. The unmetered PV (photovoltaic) capacity work is paused until January as well.

The background to the models is in Differentiable physics: background.

docs.title: Differentiable physics: embedded generation
docs.text:
The current understanding and the options for next work are on the state and next steps page.

The summary of this theme is in progress. The differentiable-physics series builds models from physical terms (demand, heating, solar) whose parameters are fitted to the power a Primary substation draws. This theme covers the generation side of a Primary substation: whether the convex model can read an MVA meter, find a flat unmetered generator where one exists and not invent one where none does, represent an export-limited solar clip, and identify how much rooftop solar sits behind each substation. The Experiments page lists every experiment tried, with its verdict and a take-home message, and the Research plan lists what is planned next.

docs.title: Differentiable physics: embedded generation: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00698 gas-engine-state-tracker-part-5-does-pv-harm-the-disaggregation The weather-driven variation of the solar generation behind D8's meter makes the tracker's daylight labels of the gas engine worse, beyond the harm that the lower level of the reading and the fold of the reading at zero cause. inconclusive not-for-production The test could not decide, under its own rule, whether solar panels behind D8's meter make the tracker's labels of the gas engine worse through their weather variation. The numbers it did produce point to harm. In the 10:00 to 15:00 window, injecting the output of a real solar farm lowers the tracker's F1 score by 0.14 and raises its false-flag share by 0.14 compared with a smooth solar curve of the same size (8.9 MW at D8). Most of the F1 harm comes from the lower level of the reading and its fold at zero, whereas the rise in the false-flag share comes from the farm's weather contrast. The labels' weekday and price patterns from experiment 697 may be best kept to the net era as a precaution, but this experiment computed nothing for that experiment's window of 16:00 to 19:00. also relevant 00697 gas-engine-state-tracker-part-4-running-patterns D8's gas engine runs to a schedule that follows the working week: it runs more on weekday evenings than on weekend evenings, by more than the tracker's errors alone would show. supported not-for-production The recorded demand at D8 behaves as if its gas engine runs more on weekday evenings (16:00 to 19:00) than on weekends, and more in half-hours with a high system price, and a test engine with no weekday pattern does not produce that. The evidence comes from the tracker's estimates and not from a meter on the engine, the labels understate any pattern, and the price, the red band, and D8's own evening demand all peak together. The pattern is a lead for a possible next experiment and not a result that a forecast can use, and the one metered engine record agrees in direction on only 7 weeks. also relevant 00696 gas-engine-state-tracker-part-3-engine-state-in-the-pre-training-mixer At D8, giving the pre-training mixer of experiment 677's step 9a neural network the tracked gas-engine state at the valid time (the expected engine output as a share of capacity and the probability that one or more units run), so that the weather encoder and the date-time encoder need not explain the engine's steps, and then training the stage 2 and stage 3 networks with a fresh mixer that has no engine input, lowers the CRPS of the forecast of D8's metered apparent power against the same neural network pre-trained without the state. not supported not-for-production Letting the neural network see the gas engine's state while it learns from weather and the calendar, and then dropping that knowledge before the forecast, did not improve the forecast of D8, and we cannot distinguish the change from zero. At another substation with an engine added, where the true state is known, a post hoc split of the results shows a gain of about 0.06 points when the engine is off and a loss of about 0.23 points when it runs. Weighted by the 19% of half-hours when the engine runs, the two cancel. One explanation that fits, not measured directly, is that the weather and calendar parts of the neural network lose the engine's daily pattern and the fresh final stage cannot recover it. The result does not support a gain from extra signal in pre-training only, at D8. A next experiment could combine the pre-training state with a way of putting the engine back after pre-training, and test the combination at the host first. also relevant 00695 gas-engine-state-tracker-part-2-cleaned-target-and-climatology-add-back At D8, removing the inferred gas-engine output from the training target and from the lagged-power inputs of the demand neural network, and adding the engine back at forecast time as a climatological distribution over the number of running units (passed through the apparent-power fold), lowers the error of the forecast of D8's metered apparent power, against the same neural network trained on the raw reading. not supported not-for-production Taking the gas engine out of D8's recorded demand before training, and adding the engine's average running pattern back when forecasting, did not improve the forecast. The cleaned arm was no better than the raw arm, and a post hoc reading of the same data suggests it was probably about 0.1 points of capacity worse over all rows. At another substation with an engine injected, cleaning gained about 0.1 points, within noise. Knowing whether the engine runs at the forecast's valid time would lower the error by 1.4 to 2.4 points against the raw arm, but no forecast has that knowledge. No gain was found, and cleaning plus a calendar add-back is not worth porting; one open question is whether the engine's state can be forecast from information available at the origin. also relevant 00694 gas-engine-state-tracker-part-1 The engine at D8 (3 identical units of about 2 MW) can be tracked by walking forwards through the raw half-hourly reading with a hidden-state model of the number of units running, with no demand forecast, no price, and no weather. D8's reading is apparent power (MVA, never negative), so a model that lets the reading fold, y = sqrt((L - k u)^2 + q^2) for demand level L, k units running, and unit size u, tracks the engine better than a model of signed steps. partly supported not-for-production A filter that tracks how many of D8's three gas-engine units are running, using only the substation's half-hourly reading, scores F1 0.68 on the one real engine record we hold (it finds most running half-hours but also flags others), and higher on easier synthetic schedules. It raised no false alarms at 8 substations, but it almost never finds a 1 MW unit, and the unit size it infers depends on the grid of sizes tried. The next experiment should test it on a harder, record-like schedule and on registered engines it has not seen. also relevant 00674 mva-sign-labels-soft-and-hard-pv-prior-day-labeller A per-Primary day labeller that combines the lowest reading at the edges of the sun's path (experiment 508) with the W-shape score of experiment 417 finds the days on which an apparent-power Primary exported, up to an export of about three times the night import. A soft PV prior (the evidence needed to call a day reverse flow rises as the day gets less sunny) keeps the recall of a labeller with no prior and lowers its false reverse flow on cloudy days. A hard PV-high mask repeats experiment 417's trade: far fewer false calls and far lower recall. Neither prior removes the false calls on low-demand days. inconclusive not-for-production A day labeller that reads the lowest reading at the edges of the sun's path and a W-shape score finds injected solar export (64% of days at 1.5 to 3 times the night import, 31% below 3 times) but misses 54 of 59 real reverse-flow days, which are shallow and short. It is therefore not a usable sign label for the eight apparent-power substations. A hard sunny-days mask removes 68% of false calls at 1.5 to 3 times but loses 39% of recall pooled below 3 times, and the soft prior is no better than no prior. A simple midday rule (day ratio below 0.3), chosen after seeing the real days and found mostly at one substation, caught 52 of the 59, so the next labeller should start from the midday dip. P4 held only in the pooled bin and P5 failed. primary 00508 mva-shoulder-hours-and-d8-d22-dips-solar-or-load-shift (A) A strongly exporting Primary such as D12 crosses zero in the shoulders of the sun's path, so the minimum apparent power in the shoulder windows, calibrated on the six signed-MW Primaries with injected solar farms, separates sign-change days once export is several times the night import, and the midday window stops working at that export-to-import ratio. (B) The short midday dips at D8 and D22 are a mix of causes, and the gas engine behind D8 explains a large share of the D8 dips. partly supported not-for-production On injected solar output, the lowest reading at the edges of the sun's path finds the days when a substation's power changes sign better than the midday dip does, for export 1.5 to 3 times the night import; above that the method cannot be calibrated. D12 exports about five times its night import, and its dips at the edges are as common on cloudy days as on sunny days, so they do not show solar export. A detector flags the gas engine as running in most half-hours of 55 of D8's 71 dip days, which is consistent with the engine but weak evidence, and the data cannot say what causes D22's 13 dips or D8's other 16. primary 00506 mva-sign-evidence-dip-depth-and-gated-solar-rule Real power at a Primary can change sign only if its apparent power dips close to its reactive floor at sunny middays, so the depth of that dip, and a rule that calls reverse flow only when expected solar output exceeds expected gross demand, carry usable evidence of the sign at the eight Primaries that no fitted treatment has recovered. partly supported not-for-production The apparent power at a sunny midday dips close to zero on some days at D8 and D22, but a dip is weak evidence of a sign change once the meter carries realistic reactive power: at power factor 0.97 the dip threshold that finds 89% of injected sign changes also flags 34% of days with none. A simple rule that calls reverse flow when expected solar output exceeds the night-time demand level called 19% of half-hours reverse where there was none, so it is not a way to label the sign. NGED's marked Primaries (D8 "Yes", D12 and D22 "Maybe") are the primary substations to ask NGED about, and D12 never falls below 5.0 points of capacity in these readings. primary 00501 explicit-pv-column-from-the-474-capacity-table Experiment 425's pooled neural network (arm A) already reads irradiance, so it can learn solar output from weather alone. Adding one input column, the solar output that a fixed capacity would give (the capacity fitted by experiment 474's method on months before the fold, times experiment 405's physics shape of the ensemble-mean weather), lowers the CRPS of the sunny-midday half-hours at the signed-MW six. refuted not-for-production Giving the demand neural network an explicit solar-output column, built from a capacity fitted on earlier months (apart from three constant scale factors), did not improve the forecast at the six primary substations metered in signed megawatts. More cloud in summer half-hours could lower the 90th percentile, because the clear-sky filter is modelled and not observed; the 99th percentile falls by less (1% to 6%). also relevant 00180 dp-sunny-daylight-fix-d5-solar-shape At D5, the one substation where the best GAM loses clearly to BG2 on sunny daylight half-hours, the loss comes from the fixed south-facing fleet solar shape. A different panel tilt or azimuth does nothing measurable. D5 is the only one of the six substations whose site table marks an export clip, so the next question is whether the 60% ceiling is stable from year to year. primary 00179 metered-solar-farm-exploration At least 4 of the 6 metered solar farms show AC clipping, meaning output that flattens below the level that clear-sky irradiance alone would give, so that the AC limit can be separated from the DC capacity. not supported not-for-production Four of the six metered solar farms have output that flattens at about 1.05 times their effective capacity once clear-sky irradiance passes about 650 W/m² (read off Figure 1), but the pre-registered test was too strict to say so, and the flat top could be an export cap (a limit on grid export set by the network operator), a panel-angle effect, or a summer-heat effect rather than a limit in the inverters. Before any DC-versus-AC follow-up, check each farm's export-cap record and get an independent DC capacity. also relevant 00178 dp-sunny-daylight-gap-diagnosis On sunny daylight half-hours the best GAM scores worse than the BG2 XGBoost model, and the gap is concentrated in one level of one cut (hour of day, clear-sky band of the ensemble irradiance, lead band, or substation), which names the cause as a fixed-shape mismatch or an irradiance-input problem. partly supported not-for-production On the sunniest third of each substation's daylight half-hours, the best generalised additive model (GAM) has a mean absolute error 0.05 MW higher than BG2 across six substations, not the 0.13 MW of an earlier plot of errors by weather condition. Most of the gap is at one substation, D5, where the GAM is worse than BG2 at every hour, lead, and clear-sky band. D9 is a smaller second loss, and the other four substations show no clear gap, so how the model represents solar generation at D5 and D9 is a better place to look than the irradiance forecast for all substations. primary 00167 dp-full-history-gam-24-months-or-all-years-with-drift With the PV capacity pinned to the as-of table (explicit PV) and the heating split by day type (T-all), the convex demand model (the GAM) trained on every year of history back to late 2019 with a drift term scores better than the same model trained on the last 24 months, when both are refitted at 12 quarterly origins on past weather (ERA5 and CAMS). The mechanism is that explicit PV removes the changing solar capacity from the target, so the old years teach the heating and calendar terms without the capacity growth that made the all-years fits of experiments 104 and 107 unstable, and the drift term absorbs the remaining slow change in the demand level. supported candidate Adding a drift term (a slow adjustment to the demand level) improved the forecast at 11 of 12 quarterly refits. The quantile score, where lower is better, fell by 0.40 points when training on the last 24 months and by 0.55 points when training on all years back to late 2019. Training on all years instead of 24 months adds only 0.10 points on top of a drift term, and gives no gain without one, so extra years of history help little. also relevant 00157 differentiable-physics-joint-pv-capacity-known-answer Letting the convex demand model (studies.dp_gam) fit the solar capacity as a smooth non-negative path across months, with a penalty on growth, finds more of a known solar farm's injected output than the two-stage capacity of experiment 129, which steps once per season-year and was recovered at 0.78 to 0.88. not supported not-for-production In this test, letting the solar capacity change month by month did not find more of an injected solar farm than a capacity that changes once a year. For the five farms tested, one scale of the fixed fleet solar shape fits a median of 93% of a farm's output, so the target of 0.95 to 1.05 was out of reach for most farms before the fit ran. No forecast was run, and the monthly capacity is not worth taking to the forecast stage. primary 00152 dp-mva-fold-aware-gam-k-at-mva-only-primaries At the MVA-only Primaries, the GAM-K forecast driven by the ensemble mean (experiment 136's arm A2) forecasts the MVA reading better when it models the fold: it fits the demand model through the meter (experiment 110's L0), corrects the forecast with a Kalman filter whose state is the signed flow, and builds its quantiles by folding a signed predictive distribution. The gain is concentrated at Stickney (D12), the one trial Primary where reverse flow is the usual state on sunny middays, and the change is harmless at the Primaries without reverse flow. inconclusive not-for-production At Stickney (D12), the one Primary with clear reverse flow, drawing the quantiles around a signed flow and folding them at zero lowered the score by about 0.4 points on sunny middays against the same fit with symmetric quantiles, and it did no harm at the other seven Primaries. The whole-year gain against reading the apparent power as signed power is of similar size, but its interval in the scored year includes zero. The known-answer test on five Primaries with hidden farms passed on the sign at the larger injection and failed at the smaller injection and on the upper tail's coverage, so the experiment does not support a port yet. primary 00149 differentiable-physics-full-history-gam-era5-cams When the convex model's solar term is explicit (a pinned capacity times a unit solar shape in both arms), training on every year of a substation's history back to 2019 gives a lower quantile score than training on the last 24 months, once a drift term lets the model follow the slow level change. The mechanism is that more years pin down the temperature, calendar, and weekday terms better, and the drift term absorbs the level change that made all-years training unstable in experiments 104, 106, and 107. inconclusive not-for-production Training the demand model on every year back to 2019, instead of the last 24 months, lowered its forecast error by only about 3% (0.08 points of substation capacity), and the difference could be chance. The drift term helped much more, lowering the error by 0.38 points on 24 months and 0.50 points on all history, but a post hoc audit found that a plain correction by the mean error of the last 28 training days recovers 86% to 94% of that gain, so the gain is a recent-level correction and the drift form is not shown to beat the simpler fix. We did not test whether explicit heating, switching, or pooled terms would make the longer history help. also relevant 00139 differentiable-physics-pv-as-of-capacity-in-gam-k Feeding the convex model with the Kalman filter (GAM-K, experiment 111) the as-of solar capacity of experiment 129 in place of experiment 45's pinned capacity lowers the quantile score on the sunniest third of half-hours, and does not raise it on the darkest third. The mechanism is that the pinned capacity is a hindsight growth prior, and the as-of capacity is read from each Primary's own power before the forecast origin. refuted not-for-production Replacing the pinned solar capacity with a capacity read from each substation's own power did not improve the forecast, and made sunny half-hours worse by 0.11 points of capacity. A more accurate capacity (the hindsight arm) only matched the pin, so the accuracy of the capacity number is not what limits the solar part of the forecast. This experiment does not locate the remaining sunny-day error; it did not test the ensemble's cloud forecast, the solar shape, the Kalman filter, or the non-solar load. primary 00129 differentiable-physics-pv-capacity-known-answer-test The AC capacity of the unmetered solar behind each of the five decision Primaries can be inferred offline, one value per September-to-August season-year, from CAMS irradiance, ERA5 temperature, and the Primary's net power, with an 80% range that holds its coverage when the real panels differ from the assumed south-facing shape and when a day-long cloud-driven demand is present. partly supported not-for-production The capacity of the small solar panels behind five Primary substations can be read from the substations' power. For 2025/26 the arm 2 estimate is 3.3 to 4.5 MW of AC capacity per Primary, and it grew by 0.4 to 2.8 MW since 2021/22. The range around each estimate is 1.2 to 1.6 MW wide, but it is a spread over test scenarios and not a calibrated 80% interval. The method has not been shown to work on real panels that face other ways or on overcast-day demand, so a card should show the range with those caveats. primary 00128 differentiable-physics-kfd-shared-day-anomaly-and-sparse-q-in-gam-k Adding to experiment 111's level-and-anomaly filter (GAM-K) one day-level error state shared by all four hour bands, and estimating the level noise sparsely from zero, makes the filter's midday correction track an injected solar-panel-shaped change in real residuals better than GAM-K, and lowers the day-ahead score on ENS. Real residuals carry a day-level error shared across the four hour bands: the daily means of GAM-K's one-step innovations in different hour bands correlate at 0.18 to 0.23 (control P-premise). An earlier diagnosis of experiment 118's residuals gave 0.58 on a different quantity, the daily means of the residuals, which cannot separate a day-level error from a slow drift shared by all bands. inconclusive not-for-production The day-ahead forecast was not scored, because the filter with one shared day-level error state failed its test on injected changes in real recorded errors, and the experiment stopped there. The errors at different times of day do move together (a correlation of about 0.2 between their daily innovations), but a single shared state probably also soaks up errors that belong to one time of day, so it cannot follow a slow, solar-panel-shaped change. Options for a next experiment are a day-level state for each time of day with a shared part, an explicit solar-panel term, and a test with an injected change large enough to detect; the verdict is inconclusive. also relevant 00118 differentiable-physics-kfe-kalman-filter-on-the-gam-effects-on-ens Freezing the convex model's fitted effects and letting a weight on each follow a random walk, with a diagonal noise matrix fitted by likelihood on the tuning months, forecasts day-ahead demand on ENS better than experiment 111's filter of one level and one anomaly per hour band (GAM-K), because heating slopes, PV capacity, profile scale, and holiday effects drift faster than a 24-month fit follows. The fitted noise matrix beats one step variance shared by every weight, so the gain comes from how each effect drifts and not from the weights' freedom alone. inconclusive not-for-production Letting the convex model's PV, heating, profile, and holiday weights drift did not improve the day-ahead forecast over experiment 111's level-and-anomaly filter (0.015 points worse at D+1, interval -0.013 to +0.048), and did no better in winter or on cold days. Switching the correction off on holidays is much worse (+1.24 points) and halving it is not better, so the filter still helps on holidays. The weights cannot be read as measurements, because the known-answer gate failed on real residuals, although two of its bars were mis-set. Keep experiment 111's filter, and the next step is a filter that fixes the PV weight and moves the others; the verdict is inconclusive. also relevant 00113 differentiable-physics-n5-convex-identification-at-realistic-noise On synthetic substations built from the real calendar and weather, with noise as large and as autocorrelated as the convex model's real residuals, the convex model's 80% month-block bootstrap intervals cover the truth 70 to 90% of the time, separately for each hour band's heating slope and for the latest season-year's PV capacity. Labelled separately, not in the verdict: the day-of-year harmonics and the drift term make those intervals wide, by absorbing the seasonal cycles of temperature and clear-sky PV. refuted not-for-production At real noise levels, the convex model's 80% month-block bootstrap intervals contain the true heating slope and the true rooftop PV capacity 84% of the time each, but a heating slope is weak (the interval is about 38% of the slope wide). The pre-registered verdict is refuted, because with independent noise the capacity interval covers the truth only 52% of the time, and the cause is mainly a bias of about 0.24 points from the drift penalty at its tuned step of 3,000 (at Part 4's step of 30 the bias is 0.02 points and coverage 78%, a post hoc check). The truth here has the model's own form, so the test cannot show the bias that a wrong PV shape causes. primary 00110 differentiable-physics-5-embedded-generation-and-capacity The convex differentiable-physics model can represent the generation side of a Primary substation without making its demand forecast worse: an MVA meter through an observation layer, a flat unmetered generator found where one exists and not invented where none does, and an export-limited PV clip; and its PV capacity stays the same when the routes by which demand terms can imitate solar are closed. inconclusive not-for-production The demand forecast could not yet account for generators connected behind a substation. Rooftop solar capacity fitted from the data was not precise or consistent enough to trust, so the capacity from outside estimates stays in use. A generator-finding component reported a generator at every substation tested, so it stays switched off. A limit on exported solar helped only at the one substation known to export-limit. Treating the meter as apparent power improved the forecast at the 8 substations that report only apparent power by 0.13 points of capacity, but the test of the meter's flow direction failed, so that gain is provisional. primary
