docs.title: N13: PV orientation mix
docs.text:
Experiment 114 dropped N13, so the design below is not queued. It stays as the design for any later experiment on solar orientation.

The proposal gives the convex model three non-negative solar capacities, one each for south, east, and west, in place of one south-facing unit shape. The model stays convex, and an east-west array should get a larger east and west share. The shares count as identified only if they pass the coverage rule of experiment 113, which asks that 80% intervals cover the injected truth 70 to 90% of the time. The experiment passes if the shares are identified and the score does not get worse. The run takes minutes on the CPU. It was first considered for the same bundle as the interaction-term and heating-threshold experiment, which ran without it as experiment 114.

The later parts of the differentiable-physics series are planned one at a time, from the result of the part before.

docs.title: Planned experiments
docs.text: Experiment Hypothesis Relevance 00474 pv-capacity-placebo-gated-ladder-and-per-primary-intervals Experiment 269's pooled empirical plant table (raw recovery 0.892 of an injected farm) can be gated against a placebo that keeps the season and the time of day but breaks the day-to-day weather link, and a physics-shaped constraint ladder on top of it raises or holds recovery while the placebo stays under the gate. Month-block intervals on the capacity then cover an injected capacity in at least 70% of injections at the nominal 80% level, including a load that follows the clouds. also relevant

docs.title: Differentiable physics, embedded generation: state and next steps
docs.text:
Only a clamp at zero on the quantiles of the eight MVA Primaries reached the final models, and the evidence does not call for adding more. Embedded generation is generation connected behind a Primary substation. A Primary substation steps voltage down from 33 kV to 11 kV (glossary). This series tested four kinds of embedded generation: unmetered rooftop solar, a solar export limit, a gas engine, and the loss of the sign of power at meters that report apparent power (MVA, which has no sign). The tests found one clear gain, a ceiling on the solar output at one substation. They also found that the solar capacity read from the data cannot be validated. The final models have no explicit term for unmetered solar, no export clip, and no gas-engine term.

D5 to D22 are anonymised labels for Primaries. BG2 is the best-guess forecast (glossary). The metric is the quantile score (glossary), in points of capacity (percent of a Primary's reference power) unless a unit is given, and a negative change is an improvement. Verdict words such as inconclusive, partly supported, and not supported are defined in the glossary. PV means photovoltaic (solar) generation. GAM means generalised additive model. The stack is the demand forecast built from a convex GAM, a Kalman filter, and correction stages. This page is a selection; the experiments page lists every experiment.

docs.title: What works
docs.text:
Capping the solar output that the forecast subtracts at 60% of the held capacity helps at D5 and nowhere else. The held capacity is the fixed solar capacity (the pin) that the demand model subtracts, and the cap (the clip) mimics an export limit. Experiment 180 cut D5's loss to BG2 on sunny half-hours from +0.202 MW to +0.069 MW. Experiment 214 showed that 97% of the gain remains when the cap is chosen from earlier data only (0.129 MW of 0.133 MW). Among the other five Primaries tested, none shows a clear gain, and D9 cannot be told apart from no gain (0.03 MW better, interval -0.076 to +0.007 MW).

A ceiling learned from the substation's own recent data closes most of the clip's gain. Experiment 247 found that the learned ceiling closes 96% (interval 62% to 104%) of the hand-set clip's gain at D5. One year of data cannot show that it reaches the pre-registered 80%, and at D9 the share is 93% with an interval of 70% to 189%.

docs.title: What did not work
docs.text:
Correction layers on top of the clip add nothing reliable. Experiment 232 found that the stored correction heads (small neural networks that shift the demand forecast) cancel most of the clip's gain.

Fitting through the apparent-power meter at Stickney (D12) scored better on one substation, and the result is inconclusive. Experiment 152 folded the forecast quantiles at zero, because reverse flow (power flowing from the substation back into the grid) is hidden when the meter reports apparent power. The fold scored 0.40 points better on D12's sunny middays and did no harm at the other seven apparent-power Primaries. The verdict is inconclusive because the whole-year interval includes zero and the known-answer test (injecting a known signal and checking that the fit recovers it) failed at two injection settings. Experiment 372 was not supported: its D12 gain of 0.57 points on sunny half-hours cannot be told from zero.

Solar capacity read from each Primary's own power cannot yet be shown to be a calibrated measurement. Experiment 129 gave 3.3 to 4.5 MW of AC capacity per Primary at five Primaries, with a spread over test scenarios and not a calibrated 80% interval. Experiment 241 got within 10% of injected capacity at 5 of 5 Primaries, but its intervals cover only 59% to 79% of injected farms, and 0% to 2% when demand follows cloud. Experiment 477 found that a neural-network PV module reads a placebo (the farm's daylight profile with a shuffled sky) as strongly as the real farm, so its placebo gate failed.

Reading the capacity from the data did not improve the forecast. Experiment 139 was refuted: a capacity read from the Primary's own power made sunny half-hours 0.11 points worse. Experiment 351 was not supported: a capacity from the clear-sky output curve made them 0.065 points worse (interval +0.017 to +0.126). Experiment 349 scored 0.047 points worse with the estimate of Experiment 269 (interval -0.029 to +0.135).

A capacity above the pin hurt, and a capacity below it did not. Experiment 352 found that a capacity 20% too low moved the sunny-half-hour score by 0.010 points, while 20% too high made it 0.124 points worse. The curve is flat from 0.8 to 1.0 times the pin. The experiment advises against refining the capacity inside that range.

An explicit solar term did not beat letting the neural network read the sunshine forecast. Experiment 409 found a change of about -0.06 points of capacity, with an interval including zero. Experiment 416 found the two within 0.03 points of continuous ranked probability score (CRPS, glossary) over 12 months. The explicit term was nominally 0.23 points worse on sunny middays.

None of the gas-engine terms tried beat plain band widening at one Primary. Experiment 264 found that widening the bands from past residuals lowers the quantile score by 9% to 19%. An engine mixture did no better than plain widening, because the mixture also fits a running engine at two Primaries that have none. Experiment 294 found that an engine term using the last settled day's state made the score 10.3% worse. The engine has not been modelled from the readings, and NGED's own record of the engine's output would be the data to test an engine model.

docs.title: What is known about the apparent-power meters
docs.text:
The rule plus the stage-2 corrections trails BG2 by 0.53 points at the eight MVA Primaries. Experiment 374 found that the rule with the stage-2 corrections (the stack's last correction stage) scores no worse than the stack's arm A1 at those eight Primaries.

A dip towards zero at midday is a screen and not a sign label. Experiment 506 found that at power factor 0.97, the threshold that finds 89% of injected sign changes also flags 34% of days with none.

A day labeller finds only 5 of 59 real reverse-flow days at the six MW Primaries. Experiment 674 was inconclusive.

Reverse flow at D12 is possible, and no experiment has proved it. Experiment 152 fitted reverse flow on 100% of D12's sunny middays. Experiment 506 audited that: D12's midday median is 81.6 points against 15.6 in dark hours, so its midday reading never nears zero. A crossing, if any, would be in the shoulders of the day. Experiment 370 found reverse flow at D12 and at none of the other seven. Experiment 679 found that if the meters follow NGED's power factor of 1 plus a small reactive floor, the conversion loss is about 0.5 points (80% interval -1 to 8), so the 0.97 loss was probably an overestimate.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
Whether D8, D12, and D22 ever export is unknown. NGED's signed power at D12 and D8 would settle the question without a fit, as Experiment 674 notes.

Whether the gas engine at one Primary can be known before the half-hour it affects is unknown. Experiment 294 names a forecast of the engine's state and NGED's own record of running hours.

Whether any capacity estimate beats the pin is unknown. The experiments above tested the convex stage out to 7 days only, and 7 to 10 days is untested.

docs.title: Next-experiment options
docs.text:
An option is to stop here for production. This is the page's own judgement. The final models need none of these parts, and the series has found no gain that a final model could use.

An option is to run the sign test on real signed days. The source is Experiment 674's "What to try next": calibrate the midday dip on real days where they exist, and ask NGED for a few weeks of signed power at D12 and D8. The dependency is data from NGED.

An option is to test the capacity estimate with a cap. The source is Experiments 349 and 352's "What to try next": cap any estimate at the pin, and test a per-Primary export clip at D5 and D9.

An option is to build typed generator nodes once a flat node stays off where no generator exists. The source is the research plan. A flat node is one generator term shared by all substations. Experiment 110 found that the flat node read 12 to 35 points at all five decision Primaries (the five Primaries on which the pre-registered tests are scored).

docs.title: Parked
docs.text:
Orientation mix for rooftop solar is dropped. The research plan records that Experiments 73 and 77 found the mix unidentified or immaterial, and that Experiment 114 dropped it.

Unmetered solar capacity and load-shift event detection are paused until January. The load-shift detector state page describes the pause.

docs.title: Differentiable physics: the forecast engine
docs.text:
The current understanding and the options for next work are on the state and next steps page.

The summary of this theme is in progress. The differentiable-physics series builds models from physical terms (demand, heating, solar) whose parameters are fitted by gradient descent. This theme covers whether such a model, driven by ECMWF ensemble weather forecasts, forecasts Primary substation demand up to 7 days ahead as well as the production recipe does, on its own or as the starting point of the production recipe's XGBoost model. The Experiments page lists every experiment tried, with its verdict and a take-home message, and the Research plan lists what is planned next.

docs.title: Differentiable physics: the forecast engine: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00306 summer-gap-solar-interactions-with-temperature-and-day-type The April-to-June daylight excess of arm D (the convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors) over BG2 (the production-style XGBoost forecast) at the substations D5 and D9 is an additive-structure problem. On cold clear spring days heating demand and rooftop solar output are both large, and an additive model must give the solar term one weight on every day. Experiment 299 found the D5 excess largest on clear midday half-hours (+1.67 points). Letting the solar shape interact with temperature (shape times the heating hinge) and with day type (shape times a weekend indicator) lets the model give those days a different solar weight. refuted not-for-production Letting the rooftop-solar term vary with temperature and with weekdays versus weekends does not close the April-to-June gap to BG2: at the two substations with the gap, the extra columns close about 0% of it. Two linear interaction columns therefore do not explain the gap. The next test is what BG2 uses that the convex demand model does not (item 5 of the summer-gap brief). also relevant 00305 summer-gap-what-bg2-knows-that-arm-d-does-not BG2 (experiment 87's production-style XGBoost forecast) beats the convex best-guess model (arm D) at the Primary substations D5 and D9 in April to June mainly through interactions of the sunshine inputs with temperature or with recent power, and not through the main effect of sunshine. refuted not-for-production The production-style forecast does not beat the convex best-guess model in April to June at two Primary substations through interactions of sunshine with temperature or with recent power: forbidding them removes under 3% of its advantage on the half-hours where the convex model trails most, and 16% on all daylight half-hours. A refit allowed no interactions at all keeps 92% of the advantage on the worst half-hours but only 45% on all daylight half-hours, so the worst half-hours come from the shape of single inputs and typical ones partly from other interactions. also relevant 00299 summer-gap-timing-night-level-and-error-correction The April-to-June excess of arm D (the convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors) over BG2 (the production-style XGBoost forecast) at the substations D5 and D9 is a step that starts at the March clock change and sits at short leads, which would point at a local-time mismatch or at BG2's use of recent power. D10's night-time level offset of about -2 points (21:00 to 07:30 UTC) is a step on one date, not a smooth drift with temperature. The Kalman filter and the correction head are net harmful at D5 and D9 in April to June. not supported not-for-production The spring excess of the best-guess demand forecast over BG2 grows with sunshine, appearing on clear midday half-hours at D5 and across the whole day at D9. It is not concentrated in the 4 weeks after the clock change or at short leads, so the next test is the solar term's response on clear half-hours at D5. The Kalman filter and the correction heads are not the cause: removing the filter changes little, and at D5 the heads reduce the excess. D10's night-time offset varies partly with month and has no single date on which it changes. also relevant 00266 summer-gap-diagnostics-solar-term The best-guess demand stack (experiment 251's arm 1) trails BG2, the production-style XGBoost forecast, in April to June 2026 mainly because of its explicit solar term (the subtracted estimate of unmetered rooftop solar output), and not because of the neural-network head, the two-number summary of the ensemble's solar response, the Kalman filter, or the heating and lighting terms. The gain was largest in winter and on Christmas rows. For a substation with 24 months of history, pooling changed the score by less than 0.02 points, which is too small to justify making each forecast depend on five other substations' data. The test cannot say whether pooling the heating curve alone would help a 3-month substation. also relevant 00155 dp-bg-stage2-assembly-night-offset-and-error-correction A GAM-K forecast (the convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors, experiment 111) that already has the heating split by day type, one shared filter noise setting, the pinned solar capacity, and the ensemble mean as its weather input (experiment 136's arm A2) improves further when two post-forecast corrections are added: a winter night offset (experiment 137) and the 14-day mean error profile of recipe R (experiment 115). The mechanism is that the two corrections remove different errors, a level error that repeats on winter nights and a half-hour-of-day shape error that repeats day to day, so their gains add. The assembled arm then scores below experiment 111's GAM-K and BG2 (experiment 87) over leads 0.5 to 168 hours, and its tails on cold nights and on holidays are no worse than the uncorrected arm's. inconclusive candidate Adding recipe R, which subtracts 0.75 times the mean error of the last 14 days by half-hour, lowers the stage 1 assembly's score by about 0.04 points (1.3%), and the winter night offset adds nothing once R is in. The assembly with R scores 2.754 against BG2's 2.780, which is better by 0.026 points with an interval too wide to rank the two. The pre-registered placebo control failed, so the formal verdict is inconclusive, but the choice of winning arm (R alone) does not depend on it. primary 00152 dp-mva-fold-aware-gam-k-at-mva-only-primaries At the MVA-only Primaries, the GAM-K forecast driven by the ensemble mean (experiment 136's arm A2) forecasts the MVA reading better when it models the fold: it fits the demand model through the meter (experiment 110's L0), corrects the forecast with a Kalman filter whose state is the signed flow, and builds its quantiles by folding a signed predictive distribution. The gain is concentrated at Stickney (D12), the one trial Primary where reverse flow is the usual state on sunny middays, and the change is harmless at the Primaries without reverse flow. inconclusive not-for-production At Stickney (D12), the one Primary with clear reverse flow, drawing the quantiles around a signed flow and folding them at zero lowered the score by about 0.4 points on sunny middays against the same fit with symmetric quantiles, and it did no harm at the other seven Primaries. The whole-year gain against reading the apparent power as signed power is of similar size, but its interval in the scored year includes zero. The known-answer test on five Primaries with hidden farms passed on the sign at the larger injection and failed at the smaller injection and on the upper tail's coverage, so the experiment does not support a port yet. also relevant 00145 differentiable-physics-analog-day-error-correction-on-gam-k Averaging GAM-K's past day-ahead errors over the days most similar to the target day (same day type, with holiday identity for holidays, similar forecast daily mean temperature, and a season window of a few weeks either side of the date) gives a better correction than averaging the last 14 days alike (recipe R of experiment 115) or the same-day-type days of the last few weeks (experiment 134). The reasoning is that demand errors repeat on days that resemble each other. The errors that repeat most, on holidays and on cold days, are the ones that a 14-day average dilutes. small gain candidate Averaging the errors of the 20 most similar past days (same day type, within 13 weeks of the same date, last year's days included) beat recipe R (the 0.75-weighted mean error of the last 14 days) by 0.041 points at day D+1, the calendar day after the forecast origin (about 1.7% of R's score of 2.436). That gain is larger than the 0.011 points that the weekday term of experiment 134 gained. Matching on forecast temperature helped by only 0.005 points, and copying the error of the same holiday last year made holidays worse, so the next step is a day-type profile with a season window and no correction copied from an earlier holiday. primary 00144 differentiable-physics-weather-forecast-bias-persistence-on-gam-k The day-ahead error of the ensemble weather forecast (temperature and irradiance) repeats from one day to the next, so the trailing mean of recent weather errors can correct GAM-K's demand forecast beyond what the Kalman filter already does. refuted not-for-production In this test, the day-ahead temperature and irradiance forecasts did not repeat their errors from one day to the next: the correlation between one day's error and the next day's was at most +0.11, against a stop threshold of 0.2. A correction that feeds recent weather errors into the demand forecast therefore has little signal to use, so no demand forecast was fitted. Two caveats apply: wind was not tested, because experiment 111's ensemble store does not hold it, and the reference was a later forecast (the analysis proxy), not observed weather, so a bias against observations is not ruled out. primary 00143 differentiable-physics-holiday-aware-updating-of-the-gam-k-filter The Kalman filter of GAM-K lets a holiday's reading error teach it a wrong level, which carries into the days after the holiday; leaving holiday readings out of the filter's update (and nothing else) lowers the day-ahead score on those following days, and does not hurt the holiday targets or the rest of the year. not supported not-for-production Leaving holiday readings out of the day-ahead filter's update does not reliably help the days after a holiday: the effect had the opposite sign after Christmas 2024 and Christmas 2025, and its 99% interval in the scored year (-0.309 to +0.036 points) includes zero. In 10 of 12 holidays, the holiday readings' error had the same sign as the error on the following days, so these readings are not usually contamination. Setting the correction to zero on holiday days, as experiment 118 did, is the action that hurts (+0.62 points on holiday days). Two Christmases give no basis for changing the filter this Christmas. primary 00142 differentiable-physics-sequence-model-on-gam-k-residuals A small neural network that reads GAM-K's last 14 days of residuals, the calendar, and the target day's forecast weather predicts the day-ahead residual better than the hand-built Kalman filter with the 14-day error profile (recipe R of experiment 115), and gives better tails when it is trained with the pinball loss at the 11 quantiles. inconclusive not-for-production A small neural network that reads the last 14 days of GAM-K's errors did not learn to adapt to changes in them: when we added a known step or a Saturday-evening shift to real errors, it recovered none of it, so we did not score it on the scored year. Nothing was scored, so this result does not compare it with the hand-built Kalman filter and recipe R. primary 00141 switching-detector-fed-into-gam-k Telling GAM-K's Kalman filter when the RO-NC detector has seen a load transfer lowers the forecast's quantile score on days after a transfer begins, because the filter's level then adapts within hours instead of over days. The same signal given as plain features (event age and signed step size) does the same, more weakly. not supported not-for-production Telling the forecast's filter when a load transfer started and ended helped inside the transfer and hurt in the 72 hours after it, because the filter holds the transfer's step over the whole 7-day forecast. The switching detector's alarm arrives 48 hours after the step and did no better than a random placebo. The next test is a correction that decays over the typical transfer duration. also relevant 00139 differentiable-physics-pv-as-of-capacity-in-gam-k Feeding the convex model with the Kalman filter (GAM-K, experiment 111) the as-of solar capacity of experiment 129 in place of experiment 45's pinned capacity lowers the quantile score on the sunniest third of half-hours, and does not raise it on the darkest third. The mechanism is that the pinned capacity is a hindsight growth prior, and the as-of capacity is read from each Primary's own power before the forecast origin. refuted not-for-production Replacing the pinned solar capacity with a capacity read from each substation's own power did not improve the forecast, and made sunny half-hours worse by 0.11 points of capacity. A more accurate capacity (the hindsight arm) only matched the pin, so the accuracy of the capacity number is not what limits the solar part of the forecast. This experiment does not locate the remaining sunny-day error; it did not test the ensemble's cloud forecast, the solar shape, the Kalman filter, or the non-solar load. also relevant 00137 differentiable-physics-e7-economy-7-night-step-term-in-the-forecast An additive night term, fitted on the base forecast's own past errors as a function of the ENS-mean daily temperature and the UTC clock time, lowers the day-ahead quantile score on the half-hours from 01:00 to 03:00 UTC on cold winter nights, without raising the score elsewhere. The mechanism is that the base GAM-K forecast (experiment 133's shared-noise arm) runs below actual demand from about 01:00 on cold nights (experiment 123), so a correction learned from earlier winters removes a bias the forecast repeats. inconclusive not-for-production The day-ahead forecast runs about 2.5 points too low on cold winter nights from 01:00 UTC, and a correction learned from its own past errors removes that bias and lifts the 0.95 quantile's coverage there from 80% to 93%. An audit showed that a plain winter night offset does as well, so the experiment found a winter night bias, not a step that grows with cold. The verdict is inconclusive: one winter, 365 headline rows, and a failed placebo. also relevant 00136 dp-bg-stage1-assembly-on-the-ensemble-mean A convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors (GAM-K, experiment 111), given experiment 114's heating split by day type (T-all) and experiment 133's single shared filter noise setting (POOL), and driven by the ensemble mean of the ECMWF ensemble (ENS) instead of its 51 members, forecasts Primary demand 0.5 to 168 hours ahead at least as well as BG2 (experiment 87) and better than experiment 111's GAM-K. The mechanism is that the three gains came from different parts of the model (the hinge, the filter noise, the weather input) and so add, and that experiment 125 found that the members' own spread adds no tail skill, so one forecast on the mean loses nothing. inconclusive not-for-production Putting everything that has helped so far into the convex demand model and driving it from the ensemble mean gives a forecast that scores the same as the production recipe (BG2) and as experiment 111's GAM-K, and the experiment cannot tell any of the three apart. Using the ensemble mean makes the score about 0.04 points worse than using all 51 members, and the heating split and the shared filter noise improve it by about 0.05, so the assembly did not add up to the hoped-for gain. primary 00135 differentiable-physics-n10-joint-kalman-and-demand-fit Fitting the convex demand model (GAM-K) so that its coefficients minimise the day-ahead error after the Kalman correction, instead of the plain error before it, lowers the day-ahead quantile score at 12 to 36 hours below the two-stage fit (fit the demand model, then filter its residuals), without moving the fitted shapes to explain recent-level structure that the filter already tracks. not supported not-for-production We fitted the demand model so that its coefficients minimise the error left after a Kalman filter (a running correction of recent errors) has adjusted the forecast. That made the day-ahead forecast much worse, because the filter can absorb a shift in the slow parts of the demand model, so the fit barely constrains those parts. Tying the fit to the two-stage coefficients removed the damage and also removed any gain: the quantile score was within 0.013 points of the two-stage score, in either direction. The two-stage design (fit the demand model, then filter its residuals) stays. also relevant 00134 differentiable-physics-same-weekday-error-profile-on-gam-k Adding a same-weekday component to the 14-day all-days error profile (recipe R of experiment 115) lowers GAM-K's day-ahead quantile score, because demand errors repeat from week to week (Saturdays differ from Tuesdays) and the all-days profile averages that structure away. not supported not-for-production The gain is too small to count: using the same weekday's recent errors, instead of the last 14 days' errors alike, lowers the day-ahead error by about 0.011 points (0.5%) at five Primary substations, and the scored-year interval includes zero. The gain is on Mondays and Fridays and is absent midweek. Grouping days into five day types did better than seven separate weekdays, so day types are the version to test next, with the profile limited to day D+1. primary 00133 differentiable-physics-vk-learned-noise-and-observation-variance-in-gam-k On GAM-K's filter (a level and a transient per hour band, per substation), noise settings chosen per substation by day-ahead score lower the day-ahead quantile score below the fixed settings of experiment 111, which were chosen by marginal likelihood on 184 non-contiguous days. An online observation variance in the manner of VIKING (de Vilmarest and Wintenberger, 2022), used to scale the spread, then improves the coverage of the 0.95 quantile on cold nights, which experiment 125 found at 73% to 78%, because recent large errors widen the spread. The mechanism under test is that the size of recent proxy-driven residuals predicts the size of the next day's error on cold nights. inconclusive not-for-production Choosing the filter's noise settings for each substation by how well they forecast the next day did not improve the forecast on later months: the gain of 0.044 points on the months used to choose shrank to 0.009 on the scored year, inside the noise. A single setting shared by every substation did at least as well as the per-substation settings, so tuning the filter's noise per substation looks unnecessary, although the grid did not find a minimum. Letting the observation variance follow recent errors did not widen the forecast where it matters, on cold nights, where the 0.95 quantile still covered only 86% to 88% of readings. primary 00130 ro-nc-detector-on-the-gam-k-residual The refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC) finds more of the moved megawatts (MW) of injected load transfers when its residual is the one-step innovation of the convex demand model with the Kalman filter (GAM-K), than when it is the residual of the lagless XGBoost model of experiment 82. A lower residual noise should lift more of the donor steps of 2 to 4 noise units over the 4.0 threshold. In experiment 82, 401 of the transfers that RO-NC missed had no metered receiver and a donor step of 2 to 4 noise units. inconclusive not-for-production A detector of load transfers found about 2 more of every 100 megawatts moved when it was built on a demand forecast from the convex model without recent power than when it was built on the lagless XGBoost forecast (a difference of +0.023 in the share found, interval -0.001 to +0.046, under the +0.03 bar). It found 18 of the 35 real transfers lasting over 1 day against 12, but the convex model was trained with those real transfers masked, so that count flatters it. Built on the Kalman filter's one-step errors the detector found far less (0.488 of the moved power against 0.772), most likely because the filter follows a transfer's step within hours and so absorbs it, which we did not test. Most of the detector's remaining misses are small steps with no metered receiving substation, so a stronger signal for those transfers is the next idea to try. The maintainer has chosen to treat the gain as an improvement and to build later detector work on the frozen convex residual; that decision lies outside the pre-registered rule, so the verdict stays inconclusive. also relevant 00128 differentiable-physics-kfd-shared-day-anomaly-and-sparse-q-in-gam-k Adding to experiment 111's level-and-anomaly filter (GAM-K) one day-level error state shared by all four hour bands, and estimating the level noise sparsely from zero, makes the filter's midday correction track an injected solar-panel-shaped change in real residuals better than GAM-K, and lowers the day-ahead score on ENS. Real residuals carry a day-level error shared across the four hour bands: the daily means of GAM-K's one-step innovations in different hour bands correlate at 0.18 to 0.23 (control P-premise). An earlier diagnosis of experiment 118's residuals gave 0.58 on a different quantity, the daily means of the residuals, which cannot separate a day-level error from a slow drift shared by all bands. inconclusive not-for-production The day-ahead forecast was not scored, because the filter with one shared day-level error state failed its test on injected changes in real recorded errors, and the experiment stopped there. The errors at different times of day do move together (a correlation of about 0.2 between their daily innovations), but a single shared state probably also soaks up errors that belong to one time of day, so it cannot follow a slow, solar-panel-shaped change. Options for a next experiment are a day-level state for each time of day with a shared part, an explicit solar-panel term, and a test with an injected change large enough to detect; the verdict is inconclusive. primary 00126 differentiable-physics-s1-cheap-screens-added-to-gam-k Each of six families of cheap additions to the day-ahead convex model GAM-K lowers its score after the Kalman filter, winter first: a free or monotone temperature curve (A-free, A-mono), exponentially smoothed temperatures (S-ewma) or smoothed daily extremes (S-mm), wind chill (C-wind) or apparent temperature (C-hw) inside the heating hinge, a school-term term (D-sch), lighting from solar elevation (E-sol), and a filter whose noise differs by regime (F-mix). A second family of four exploratory screens: a switching Kalman filter with three hidden regimes (G-skf), a learned periodic basis for the year cycle (W-basis), a soft cold/mild mixture of heating slopes (W-mix), and a cross-substation anomaly from weather-station residuals (W-stn). One hypothesis per arm, in "Arms" and "Four exploratory screens". inconclusive not-for-production None of the thirteen cheap additions to the day-ahead GAM-K lowered the winter score by a margin we can trust. E-sol (lighting from solar elevation) came closest, at -0.036 points on dark winter evenings, but its interval (-0.122 to +0.024) is too wide to call, because six of the thirteen screens had a half-width above their 0.03 to 0.05-point margin. Only W-basis (learned year cycle) was clearly worse, in every month, site, and year. F-mix and W-stn looked worse too, but each rests on 2 to 3 calendar months. G-skf found injected load transfers 4 to 7 times as often at 25% and 40% transfers as the plain filter, but failed its own power gate and recovered no faster. also relevant 00125 differentiable-physics-n8-ens-members-through-gam-k-and-the-spread-around-them Placing GAM-K's residual quantiles, fitted on a forecast driven by the analysis proxy (so they hold model and filter error and almost no weather error), around each of the 51 ENS members gives tails closer to nominal than today's table, which is fitted on ensemble-mean residuals, and the gain is largest at long leads and on cold winter nights, where the hinge turns a temperature error into a large demand error. The comparison is against GAM-K re-tuned on the same factor grid, so a plain scale error cannot pass for a better design. inconclusive not-for-production Putting the forecast-error table around each of the 51 weather members, and fitting it on analysis-driven forecasts so that it holds no weather error, did not improve the tails of GAM-K's demand forecast. The weather members' spread is small against the model's own error, so the weather error was counted twice in the code but is too small to matter. The next step is the cold winter nights, where demand exceeds the 95% quantile about a quarter of the time in every arm. The verdict is inconclusive, because no arm reached 14 of 16 calibration cells. primary 00123 differentiable-physics-e7-storage-heating-night-step-estimation At Primary substations, demand steps up in the half-hours from 00:30 to 02:30 on winter nights, the step grows with cold, and the pooled step over the six decision series is positive at a daily mean of 3 C. At D5, D10, and D16, which were chosen because winter 2025-26 showed the step, it is 5 to 10 points (1% of each series' 99th percentile of demand); at the other decision series it is smaller. inconclusive not-for-production The night step at Primary substations is about 10 points on a 3 C day, where one point is 1% of a substation's near-peak demand, and it starts around 01:00 and looks fixed to UTC rather than the local clock (a check chosen after seeing the data). The rise on cold winter nights is the feature an operator would see: the day-ahead forecast runs 6 to 10 points below actual demand from about 01:00 at D5 and D16 on the two pre-registered winters, and at D10 in winter 2024-25 alone (7.6 points at 01:00); at D10 in winter 2023-24 the baseline is instead 9 to 17 points too high all night. The step appears at 13 of the 14 substations, and its full size rests on summer nights having no step, which the gate cannot test. The verdict is inconclusive because the gate is weaker than it looks: it holds one real test of the interval, and that test under-covers. also relevant 00122 differentiable-physics-three-winter-backtest-gam-k On past weather, the convex model with the Kalman filter (GAM-K) forecasts Primary demand one day ahead better than both the plain convex model (GAM) and lagless XGBoost, in each of the three winters 2023-24, 2024-25, and 2025-26, by at least 1 point of mean absolute error. supported not-for-production In all three winters, the convex demand model with the recent-error filter (GAM-K) forecast Primary demand one day ahead 1.8 to 3.1 points of capacity better than the same convex model without the filter, and 2.0 to 3.1 points better than lagless XGBoost. The gain is consistent with the filter removing a level error that a fit frozen for a year carries, and lagless XGBoost has no recent power to correct the same error. GAM-K's filter settings were fitted on the 2023-24 winter, and the convex model's ridge penalty was tuned on a year that contains the 2024-25 winter, so those two gains are partly in-sample. 2025-26 has the least tuning leakage, but it was read in an earlier analysis before this plan, and no winter is clean on both counts. A post hoc check at the audit subtracted each plain model's own winter-mean error at each substation, which no forecaster could know in advance: GAM-K stayed ahead of the plain GAM by 0.63, 0.71, and 0.35 points and ahead of lagless XGBoost by 0.95 to 1.05 points, so 5 of the 6 contrasts would miss the 1-point bar. Most of the gain is therefore level tracking, and this result does not show that GAM-K beats a model that sees recent power. The scoring uses past weather, so the gain under live weather forecasts is unknown. also relevant 00121 differentiable-physics-mh-multi-hinge-heating-curve-and-night-step In the convex model of Primary demand in the form Part 6 made the DP's candidate (GAM-K), on past weather, replacing the single fixed 15.5 C heating hinge by five hinges (10, 12, 14, 16, and 18 C) with non-negative slopes, so the heating curve never falls as it gets colder and stays convex, lowers the day-ahead quantile score after the recent-error filter. Second question (NS): GAM-K leaves a 4 to 7 point step at 01:00 on winter nights at three substations (a pattern like storage heating switching on), and a night-step term lowers the score on winter nights without worsening the other rows by more than 0.02 points. Indexed in UTC against local time, the winning indexing is reported. inconclusive candidate Adding night-time levels indexed on the UTC clock lowers the day-ahead error on winter nights by about 0.23 points after the recent-error filter, at all 5 substations in both winters, and the forecast then shows the 01:00 jump in demand that the current forecast misses on cold winter nights. Five heating bends instead of one gain only 0.016 points, within noise. The synthetic tests could not show that a step this small can be detected, so the night result needs a test on weather forecasts and an audit before it enters the model. also relevant 00119 differentiable-physics-enc-weather-patch-encoder-on-ens A small neural network that reads the ENS grid boxes around a Primary, and not only the one box GAM-K reads, lowers GAM-K's quantile score a little on average and more on the cold, showery, and badly forecast days NGED cares about, either as a correction to GAM-K's quantiles or as a replacement for its single-box temperature and irradiance. inconclusive not-for-production A small neural network that reads the ensemble weather around a Primary lowers GAM-K's quantile score by 0.062 points of effective capacity in one scored year and 0.035 in the other (both statistically significant, 5 of 5 substations better), and the gain is smaller in winter (0.041 and 0.027 points) but never a loss. About two-thirds of the gain survives when the network reads the wrong date's weather (0.043 and 0.022), so it is probably a recalibration of GAM-K's quantiles with the lead, the hour, and GAM-K's own forecast, and the surrounding boxes add nothing to the centre box (patch minus centre box: -0.002 and +0.003 points). The known-answer gate failed, so the verdict is inconclusive, and the next step is a plain recalibration of GAM-K's quantiles with the centre box's extra fields (dew point, pressure, precipitation, and member spread), not a patch encoder. primary 00118 differentiable-physics-kfe-kalman-filter-on-the-gam-effects-on-ens Freezing the convex model's fitted effects and letting a weight on each follow a random walk, with a diagonal noise matrix fitted by likelihood on the tuning months, forecasts day-ahead demand on ENS better than experiment 111's filter of one level and one anomaly per hour band (GAM-K), because heating slopes, PV capacity, profile scale, and holiday effects drift faster than a 24-month fit follows. The fitted noise matrix beats one step variance shared by every weight, so the gain comes from how each effect drifts and not from the weights' freedom alone. inconclusive not-for-production Letting the convex model's PV, heating, profile, and holiday weights drift did not improve the day-ahead forecast over experiment 111's level-and-anomaly filter (0.015 points worse at D+1, interval -0.013 to +0.048), and did no better in winter or on cold days. Switching the correction off on holidays is much worse (+1.24 points) and halving it is not better, so the filter still helps on holidays. The weights cannot be read as measurements, because the known-answer gate failed on real residuals, although two of its bars were mis-set. Keep experiment 111's filter, and the next step is a filter that fixes the PV weight and moves the others; the verdict is inconclusive. primary 00116 differentiable-physics-nra-edge-flows-between-primaries Flows on the electricity network's interconnection edges, fitted to a frozen convex model's residuals with a sparse-step penalty, recover injected conserved transfers between MW-metered Primaries; removing them gives a normal running arrangement (NRA) model trained without hand labels that forecasts no worse outside events; and fed causally into the Kalman filter as a known input, they improve the metered forecast during and after a transfer. inconclusive not-for-production The method that looks for load moved between neighbouring substations did not work: with the settings we fixed in advance it found under a quarter of the load we added artificially, and it changed no forecast. Looser settings found more, but they also found load moving between substations that are not connected, probably the slow drifts of demand that our model does not describe. The gate failed for a structural reason: at the settings we fixed in advance, the fit cannot find any transfer shorter than 7 to 9 days, and the longest test transfer lasts under 5 days, so the failure is a limit of the method as specified, not a bug in the solver. The zero flow we first saw on the unconnected pairs was also an artefact of the order the fit visits its paths, so those pairs were never clean. Adding a drift term to the model, or accepting a flow only where the two substations are connected, is the next thing to test. also relevant 00115 differentiable-physics-w1-diurnal-shape-state-on-ens GAM-K's remaining day-ahead error on ENS is mostly in the shape of the day inside each hour band, and that shape drifts faster than the convex model's monthly knots follow. A 48-half-hour shape state with zero mean in each hour band, added to the Kalman filter and updated from every reading the telemetry delay allows, lowers GAM-K's day-ahead quantile score at most decision substations, in months that played no part in choosing the idea's form and in the scored year. inconclusive not-for-production Teaching the physics-based forecast the shape of the day from recent readings lowers its day-ahead error by 0.075 points at five Primary substations (about 3%), in two separate periods and more in winter (0.11, a post hoc breakdown), but averaging the last 14 days' errors by half-hour gains as much, so the learned shape state is not needed on this evidence. The shape state's own check failed: it learns an injected change too slowly (0.35 against a floor of 0.4), so the verdict is capped at inconclusive. A faster shape state, tried afterwards and labelled post hoc, passed that check and beat both K0 and the recipe, which a rerun with the check fixed in advance would need to confirm. primary 00114 differentiable-physics-n3-n4-interactions-and-heating-threshold Two labelled claims about the convex model of Primary demand in the form Part 6 made the DP's candidate (GAM-K: 24 months, no drift, pinned capacity, Kalman filter), on past weather. N3: interaction terms (heating by day-type group, heating on eight sub-band blocks, lighting by day-type group), each shrunk towards the base by a difference penalty, lower the day-ahead quantile score after the filter. N4: a per-site heating threshold, chosen by profiling the training loss, is recoverable on synthetic substations at real noise, is identified away from 15.5 C at one or more real substations under the per-site printing rule, and lowers the score after the filter. partly supported not-for-production Splitting the convex model's heating terms between the first and second half of each part of the day lowered its day-ahead error after the recent-error filter by about 0.04 points (97.5% interval 0.014 to 0.070), at all 5 substations in both years, but the gain label rests on one substation (D5), and the gain is a temperature-dependent shape of the day more than a heating effect. Letting heating or lighting differ between weekdays and weekends adds nothing, and choosing a heating threshold separately for each substation did not clearly help (0.01 points, within noise). Every number uses past temperature, not forecasts, so the gain needs a test on weather forecasts before GAM-K's convex model changes; the PV panel-orientation mix (N13) was dropped because earlier experiments found it unidentified. also relevant 00111 differentiable-physics-6-ens-forecast-engine-against-bg2 Driven by ECMWF ENS forecasts, the convex DP demand model forecasts Primary demand up to 7 days ahead better than lagless XGBoost given the same recent-level correction, and, used as the base margin of the BG2 recipe's lagged XGBoost, makes the production recipe better like for like. partly supported candidate Driven by real ensemble weather forecasts, the physics-based demand model with a filter on its recent errors (GAM-K) scored 2.80 points against 2.78 for the production recipe (BG2) at five Primary substations. The 0.02 difference cannot be told from zero (-0.109 to +0.157), and the comparison is not like for like. GAM-K scored 0.13 points better than lagless XGBoost with the same filter (-0.305 to +0.014, 4 of 5 substations better), so the verdict is partly supported. The filter's gain is the firmly supported part: 0.15 points, 0.39 in the first day, with the sign held in the replicate months. Giving lagged XGBoost the physics model's forecast as a starting point changed nothing measurable. The known-answer gate passed 22 of 22 readings on its second run, after a sign error in the gate's own test data (both runs are kept). The departures were that the XGBoost compute estimate was 20 times too low, so the margin arms refitted monthly; lagless XGBoost for the scored year reused SIMP1's refits and had no spread factor; and the confirmation comparison was not run. GAM-K is a candidate for Flexpectation v2's roughly 1,300 substations on the measured filter gain, with four caveats: five substations over one year, a short XGBoost history, the undecided XGBoost comparison, and a margin that gave no gain. primary

docs.title: Differentiable physics: the forecast engine: research plan
docs.text:
Part 6 of the series was the first experiment of this theme, and its follow-ups wait on the maintainer. The rows below are proposals, not agreed work, and the priorities are a suggested order for the maintainer to change.

docs.title: CAL: tail calibration and a coherence pass
docs.text:
The maintainer postponed CAL on 2026-10-20. The question is whether the tails of the convex model with the Kalman filter (GAM-K) on ECMWF ensemble weather are calibrated in every lead band, and which re-spreading of the same mean forecast fixes the bands that are not. Experiments 107 and 111 found the pooled tails close to the nominal 95% and 99%, so the work is in particular cells: some substations in winter, the night hours, and one or two lead bands. Curtailment depends on the upper tail, so those cells matter more than the pooled figure.

The mean forecast stays fixed, and only the spread changes. Four methods are candidates, each reusing the stored fits of experiment 111 so that no new model is fitted:

  • a rolling conformal offset per substation, lead band, and quantile;
  • the Kalman filter's own predictive variance, scaled by a table of standardised residuals;
  • the same variance widened by the spread across the ensemble members;
  • separate lower and upper widening factors per lead band.

A cell counts as calibrated when its coverage lies within a binomial band set by the number of distinct substation-days in the cell. A substation-day is the unit because the errors of one substation's half-hours within a day move together. Before any method is scored, a blocking known-answer test checks that the band does not flag a forecast that is calibrated by construction, and that the band and the methods detect and remove a miscalibration of the size that matters. The decision rule asks for a method that passes in the replicate months and in the scored year without raising the quantile score by more than 0.02 points of effective capacity.

The coherence pass tests whether the ensemble sums across substations are calibrated against the observed sum. Calibrated marginals for each substation do not make the sum of several substations calibrated, because the sum depends on how the errors of different substations move together. The test turns each substation's calibrated quantiles back into ensemble members with ensemble copula coupling (ECC), or with the Schaake shuffle, which orders the members by a template taken from history. It then sums the members across substations and scores the summed ensemble against the observed sum, and scores the joint distribution with the variogram score. The staged probabilistic forecast already specifies ECC and the coherence scores for the production forecast. The pass asks whether the convex model's spread, once calibrated, keeps the cross-substation dependence that those scores reward. It runs after the per-substation calibration, on the same rows.

docs.title: N7: paired residuals at switching events
docs.text: Where both sides of a hand-filtered switching event are metered, the donor's and the receiver's residuals should be anti-correlated and sum to roughly the moved power. The experiment reports the share of events where the two residuals sum to within 20% of the moved power. A high share would show that a later model can treat a transfer as a conserved flow between two nodes. Only a minority of the events have both sides metered, so the result describes those events and does not generalise to the rest. The run takes minutes on the CPU.

docs.title: Schaake shuffle against ECC
docs.text: The comparison tests which way of restoring dependence across substations gives the better summed ensemble. Ensemble copula coupling (ECC) orders each substation's calibrated quantiles by the ranks of the ensemble members. The Schaake shuffle orders them by a template taken from history. Both then give members whose sums across substations are scored against the observed sum, with the variogram score. It reuses the members of N8 (experiment 125) and takes about 1 CPU hour. It is the comparison that CAL's coherence pass needs, so CAL can reuse its result.

docs.title: Tail quantile regression on filtered residuals
docs.text: The proposal fits a quantile regression on the Kalman filter's residuals, with the model's prediction, its square, and the hour of day as covariates. de Vilmarest et al. (2024) did this for net load in the 14 GB grid supply point groups, and the regression gave a small gain over Gaussian quantiles on the same residuals. They also adapted the regression online by gradient descent on the pinball loss. In their results nearly all of the improvement came from filtering the mean, and the quantile step added 2 to 6%. Their data are regional and national load, so the gain at Primary substations is untested. The method replaces the residual-quantile spread of the convex model, and runs in CPU seconds.

docs.title: Conditional Pareto tails
docs.text: The proposal models the quantiles beyond 1% and 99% with a generalised Pareto distribution whose scale depends on covariates. Browell and Fasiolo (2021) found that plain quantile regression is not calibrated beyond those probabilities. A conditional Pareto tail cut the upward reserve requirement by up to 24.6% and the downward reserve by up to 10.8%, against a static Pareto tail. Their fit uses the R package mgcv, so a Python version needs a small custom maximum-likelihood fit, which takes CPU minutes per substation. The proposal serves the curtailment goal, which depends on the extreme upper quantiles.

docs.title: ERA5-only winter-by-winter backtest, earlier winters
docs.text: The backtest replaces the forecast weather with ERA5, so that the release candidate and XGBoost can be judged over the winters that the ensemble-weather experiments do not cover. Experiment 122 covers the winters of 2023-24 to 2025-26, so this backtest covers 2019-20 to 2022-23 and has low priority. The release candidate is the convex model with the Kalman filter (GAM-K), plus whichever of the night steps and the multi-hinge heating terms win their experiments. XGBoost is the production recipe (BG2) and its lagless version. ERA5 removes forecast-weather error, so the result ranks model structure on past weather and does not give production skill. The report gives winter-by-winter paired contrasts next to the ensemble-weather result, and says whether the two rankings agree. The run is cheap and uses the CPU only.
