docs.title: Differentiable physics, forecast engine: state and next steps
docs.text:
A demand forecast built from physical terms beat the production-style XGBoost forecast (BG2) by 0.136 points over one year at six MW Primary substations, but only from November to March. From April to June the same forecast is worse than BG2. The year is July 2025 to June 2026, the only year with BG2 forecasts, and the gain's 95% interval (-0.277 to -0.005) just excludes zero.

A Primary is a primary substation. A point is 1% of a substation's effective capacity, and the quantile score is twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles, in points. Negative differences between scores are better. Verdict words such as inconclusive, partly supported, small gain, undecidable, tie, and not powered are defined in the glossary. BG2 is the recipe of Experiment 87. The final-models page uses none of this theme's models for Primary demand.

The convex demand model sums physical terms: daily profile, holidays, heating, lighting, and unmetered rooftop solar PV (photovoltaic generation). GAM-K is a generalised additive model (GAM), meaning the convex demand model, plus a Kalman filter on its recent errors. Recipe R subtracts 0.75 times the mean error of the last 14 days. Arm D is GAM-K with a winter night offset and recipe R (Experiment 155). The stack is arm D, a small neural-network correction of the median (H), and a two-number summary of the ensemble's solar response (S: mean and spread per half-hour). ENS is the ECMWF 51-member ensemble forecast and ERA5 is the ECMWF estimate of past weather.

docs.title: What works
docs.text:
On ENS weather, the Kalman filter lowers the convex model's score by 0.151 points. The gain is 0.392 points at leads under 24 hours (Experiment 111). The same filter lowers lagless XGBoost by about the same amount (-0.154, nearly all at day 14).

On ERA5 weather, much of the filter's gain is a level correction. In mean absolute error of the median, the filter's gain was 1.8 to 3.1 points. After debiasing, GAM-K stays ahead by only 0.35 to 1.05 points, and 5 of 6 contrasts would miss the 1-point bar (Experiment 122).

GAM-K cannot be told apart from BG2 at five substations. It scored 2.80 against 2.78 (-0.109 to +0.157).

The correction network and the solar summary add to each other. Together they lower the quantile score by 0.136 points (5%), 99% of the sum of their separate gains (Experiment 220).

Over the one scored year, the stack beats BG2 and the manual heuristic. The stack beats BG2 by 0.136 points (9 of 12 months, a negative estimate at all six substations, two intervals excluding zero) and the manual heuristic by 0.818 points (12 of 12 months) (Experiment 251, Experiment 228).

Coasting the filter through a reading gap beats the uncorrected model. Coasting (running the filter without new readings, with widened bands) scored 0.25 to 0.44 points better at every gap length (3, 6, 24, and 72 hours). Against dropping only the filter the result is undecidable: all four intervals include zero (3 hours -0.147, -0.321 to +0.030; 72 hours +0.013, -0.152 to +0.203) (Experiment 205).

docs.title: What does not work
docs.text:
Most additions to the filter and the fit gave no usable gain. Of 13 low-compute additions, 7 were undecidable, 2 a tie, 2 not powered, and 1 (a learned year cycle on the W-basis, a set of smooth weather functions) clearly worse (Experiment 126).

Fitting the demand model through the filter made the forecast worse. Tying the fit back to the two-stage fit removed the damage and the gain (Experiment 135).

A drift term gains about 0.19 points without the filter, and almost nothing with it. With the filter it worsens the score by 0.031 points on 24 months (99% interval +0.008 to +0.059) and by 0.011 on all years. The earlier 0.40-point gain was on a weaker base without ensemble weather, offset, or recipe R (Experiment 170).

Recipe R carries the arm D gain, not the winter night offset. Recipe R changes the score by -0.037 (99% interval -0.062 to -0.016). The offset adds +0.002 (-0.004 to +0.009) on top of it, and a placebo offset gained as much (inconclusive).

Running the error table around each of the 51 members did not improve the tails (Experiment 125).

The cold-night bands of arm D are too narrow, and the stack's correction overshoots. Arm D's 95% quantile covered 0.73 to 0.78 of cold nights (Experiment 192). The stack's coverage was 0.965 and BG2's 0.781 (Experiment 251).

The disagreement between 20 independently trained correction networks did not predict the error (correlation 0.00), but the result is not conclusive. The experiment's own check failed: the spread fell 8% under a shifted input (Experiment 244).

docs.title: Where the stack is weaker than BG2
docs.text:
From April to June 2026 the stack is worse than BG2, and the gap is localised but not explained. The gap is a solar-term gap at D5 and D9 on daylight half-hours, plus a night-time gap at D10 (Experiment 266). The correction network, the solar summary, the filter, and the ensemble sunshine forecast do not cause it. At D5 the excess sits on clear midday half-hours (+1.67 points), and at D9 it spreads across the day (Experiment 299).

Two tests of what BG2 knows about sunshine were refuted. Banning sunshine interactions in XGBoost removed 2.7% of BG2's advantage (Experiment 305). Adding solar-by-heating and solar-by-weekend columns closed 0.4% (Experiment 306).

Past weather explains about a third of the excess loss on the unlabelled worst days. The worst 5% of days carry about 42% of the excess loss, and load-shift events are the largest labelled group (Experiment 172, inconclusive). Of the 72 worst days, 37 carry no label. Past weather removes 31.5% of their excess loss (Experiment 174, partly supported). The loss could come from events at one substation. None of six other data sources explains the days (Experiment 177).

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• The cause of the stack's April to June gap at D5, D9, and D10 is unknown.
  • The cause of the unlabelled worst days is unknown.
  • Whether the ranking against BG2 holds in other years and at all 16 Primaries is unknown. Only July 2025 to June 2026 holds BG2 forecasts, at six substations.
  • Whether a special-day term is needed at Christmas is unknown. Christmas error was 0.97 to 1.22 times a weekday on fits with at least 180 training days (a post hoc subset), but the pre-registered ratios reached 1.91 and the test failed its positive control (Experiment 173, Experiment 228).
  • Which demand line the production port should follow is unresolved. The research default log names the stack as the first Primary demand research default. The final-models page documents the neural-network Candidate (the Primary demand forecast on that page), with no Kalman filter or convex model. No experiment of this theme compares the two.

docs.title: Options for next experiments
docs.text:
Each option comes from the research plan or from the "What to try next" section of the named experiment.

  1. An option is to test the D9 solar shape: an export clip, a morning-and-afternoon solar shape, and a month-varying night term at D10 (Experiments 266 and 299). Question: does a change to the solar term close the spring gap to BG2? A D5 clip adds nothing once the correction network is in (Experiment 251).
  2. An option is to run the margin arms at weekly cadence (plan page). Question: does the convex forecast help lagged XGBoost when XGBoost refits weekly, as production does? Starting XGBoost from the convex forecast changed nothing in Experiment 111 (-0.023, -0.217 to +0.183). Dependency: GPU budget.
  3. An option is to fetch the 2021 to 2024 ensemble history from Source Cooperative (plan page). Question: do three more years give XGBoost a fair training history? Dependency: the maintainer's approval and an AWS virtual machine.
  4. An option is to mask load-shift readings from the filter (Experiment 205). Question: does masking avoid the 14-point loss that unmasked readings caused on one date?
  5. An option is to ablate the correction network's inputs one at a time, or to fit a gradient-boosted model with pinball loss (Experiment 209's next steps, not supported: era splits changed the score by under 0.003). Dependency: none.

docs.title: Parked
docs.text:
Only tail calibration and the coherence pass (CAL) are postponed. Four further methods in the plan page's queue have their own dependencies:

  • N7 (paired residuals at load-shift events) waits for nothing and needs minutes of CPU.
  • Schaake shuffle against ensemble copula coupling (two ways to restore dependence between quantile forecasts) is a coherence test and waits for the Experiment 125 member forecasts.
  • Tail quantile regression on filtered residuals is independent of CAL and needs stored residuals.
  • Conditional Pareto tails (a heavy-tailed fit to residual extremes) wait for tail quantile regression.

Load-shift event detection and unmetered PV capacity work are paused until January and are not options on this page.

The experiments page lists every experiment of the theme.

docs.title: Differentiable physics: long history and drift
docs.text:
A Kalman filter on recent residuals lowered the quantile score by 0.61 points, using estimates of past weather, but whether old years of history help is still not settled.

The first experiment of this theme shows that the data lets the series go ahead, with three changes: start most Primary substation series later than their first record, fix the lockdown window in advance, and count eligible long-history sites at each tuning year's first day. The second shows that a simple model of demand minus solar does not clearly gain from every usable year: without a drift term it scored worse than on the last 12 months, and with a drift term the model was level with 12 months. The third shows that the filter lowers the score, and that the benefit of old years changed sign between two scored years. This theme covers whether a differentiable-physics model of Primary substation demand can use old years of history and cope with drift in the demand level over the years. The Experiments page lists every experiment tried, with its verdict and a take-home message, and the Research plan lists what is planned next.

docs.title: What the experiments found
docs.text:
• 00103 - Differentiable physics, part 1: The first months of 13 of the 16 Primary substations are cut (19.4 months at D4), the data does not isolate the 2020 lockdown from drift, and the power timestamps show no 30-minute error on either side of NGED's fix of 2026-03-26.
  • 00104 - Differentiable physics, part 2: A simple model of demand minus solar, fitted as one convex optimisation per substation, scored 0.25 points higher (worse) when trained on every usable year without a drift term than on the last 12 months. Adding a drift term lowered the score by 0.29, so all years with drift was level with 12 months (0.04 points better, 98.33% interval from 0.30 better to 0.21 worse, 2 of 5 substations better), and the planned comparison is inconclusive. A first version of the page had the opposite sign for two contrasts, because its forecast spread carried the previous year's mean bias; the page now carries a Correction section. The experiment belongs mainly to the demand: calendar and weather theme.
  • 00106 - Differentiable physics, part 4: A Kalman filter that corrects each day-ahead forecast with the errors observed up to 3.5 hours earlier lowered the quantile score by 0.61 points in the scored year and 1.02 in the year before, at all five long-history substations. More years of history gave -0.22 points in the scored year and +0.32 in the year before, so the verdict is partly supported. With the filter running, a drift term added nothing measurable and refitting made the score slightly worse. Against lagged XGBoost at the same lead, the filtered model was 0.138 points better, which is not significant. The filter's residuals use estimates of past weather.
  • 00107 - Differentiable physics, rolling-origin history and tails: Refitting the convex model every quarter, 12 times from 2023 to 2026, adding a drift term to the model trained on all years lowered the score at 10 of 12 refits (0.45 points, 99% interval 0.23 to 0.68 better). In a post hoc split, about three-fifths of that size is one substation (D10) at the 2023-24 refits, and the 2025-26 refits give 0.30, as in experiment 104. All years without drift scored worse than 12 months at 8 of 12 refits, and all years with drift against 12 months has no stable answer, with winter-quarter refits favouring more years. A spread that depends on the forecast level made the 95% and 99% quantile coverage worse. The verdict is partly supported.

docs.title: Differentiable physics: long history and drift: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00575 stepwise-offset-large-step-and-mirrored-pair-recovery Experiment 573 injected steps of 2% to 6% of capacity, which may drown in the weather-error noise of the forecast's daily residuals. Steps as large as the labelled load-shifts (a median of 19% of capacity) are found by the daily-knot offset (S1) or the gated-jump offset (S2) when they last a week or more. not supported not-for-production A free per-day offset on top of the frozen demand network cannot find load-shift-sized steps. Even a step of 20% of capacity that lasts a month is only partly followed (median 49% of its size at the better penalty, 9% at the heavier one), and the labelled load-shifts mostly last under 4 days. Do not build a detector on this offset; a detector needs the step to be an explicit part of the model, such as a labelled-event input or a state estimate, rather than a by-product of an offset. also relevant 00574 part-d-primaries-only-modular-recipe-lag-encoder-offset-and-add-one-arms Four add-ons to the modular lag-encoder neural network with the D5 offset (P0) each lower CRPS: the multi-variable ensemble spread columns in the mixer (P1), thermal-lag and solar-gain columns through the weather encoder (P2), an expected signal for the lag encoder taken from encoders trained on ERA5 and CAMS only (P3), and a three-step schedule with a 3-day embargo (P4). The factors that meet the keep rule, plus P2 by the maintainer's policy, form a final candidate (P5) that stays within 0.04 of A-pool-24 at 24-120 h at the eight MVA Primaries. partly supported candidate The best demand recipe we have fitted (P5) combines experiment 572's lag-encoder neural network and offset with a fresh mixer fitted on the whole ensemble history up to the cutoff, a 3-day embargo, and the thermal-lag and solar-gain columns. At the six MW Primaries it improves on P0, the best earlier recipe, by 0.22 points of capacity at 1 to 5 days (interval excludes zero), and at the eight MVA Primaries by a smaller 0.09 (interval includes zero). P5 beats the daily-refit references at every lead band, and follows an injected 7-day shift of the history less than half as much (2.9 against 7.3 points). The multi-variable ensemble spread columns do not help the network and should stay out. also relevant 00573 stepwise-output-offset-known-answer-step-recovery D5 adds one offset per Primary and month, with a slope penalty, so a step in a Primary's level (a new estate, a persistent transfer, a metering change) is smeared over months and a short step cannot be seen. An offset that is constant between days and changes abruptly (daily knots held constant between knots, with an L1 total-variation penalty, or a sparse set of jumps chosen by hard-concrete gates) recovers the date and size of an injected step. not supported not-for-production At the penalties we tried, an offset that is allowed to jump did not find steps of 2% to 6% of capacity in the demand forecast's residuals. The weights that stop apparent false steps also stop the real ones. The next step is to test whether a second signal, such as a neighbour series or a label, separates a step from slow drift, before relying on a free offset to date level changes. also relevant 00572 two-offset-part-1-lags-versus-the-slow-output-offset A slow per-Primary output offset (D5) carries the Primary's current level into the forecast, as lagged power does. If so, a lag-free modular network with an offset learnt in pre-training (E2) scores about as well as the best lag network (v3) at 24 to 240 hours, and adding the offset to the lag network (v3+D5) gains little. Lags should still matter in the first 24 hours. partly supported candidate A slow output offset does not make lags unnecessary: at the eight MVA Primaries the best forecast uses both, and the lag network with the offset beat the offset alone by 0.224 points of capacity at 1 to 5 days. At the six MW Primaries the offset alone and the lag network are not distinguishable. The stop rule of the brief (the gain at both groups) is not met, so continuing on the lag network with the offset rests on the eight MVA Primaries alone. also relevant 00571 drift-offset-and-embedding-hybrid-known-answer-worlds A slow per-Primary output offset (D5 of experiment 565) absorbs level shifts, and a drift embedding that modulates the encoders (A10) absorbs changes in behaviour, such as a growing temperature sensitivity or a changed daily shape. Experiment 565's joint fit of both (the hybrid) was worse than the offset alone, but a joint fit lets the two components compete for the same slow variance, so that failure does not refute the hypothesis. Building the hybrid so the components cannot compete (staged, multiplicative-only, or orthogonal) should recover both kinds of injected change in worlds where the answer is known. not supported not-for-production When we inject level steps (and a growing temperature sensitivity, which the steps dominate) into real substation histories, the monthly drift embedding recovers nearly all of the oracle's gain and the output offset alone recovers under a third, so the embedding is not limited to changes in behaviour and the offset is not the better carrier of levels. The joint hybrid that did badly on the real data did not do badly in this world, so competition is not shown to be the cause. The growing-sensitivity part of the question stays open until a readable sensitivity-only world is built. also relevant 00565 drift-embedding-variants-six-designs Substations change slowly over years, and the Primary embedding is static, so the modular lag-free demand network follows slow change only through its daily fine-tune. A designed slow signal can carry that change. Stage 1 asks the cheapest version: an exponentially weighted mean of the network's own past residuals, older than 24 hours, added to the forecast quantiles. partly supported candidate A slow, per-Primary offset added to the demand forecast improves it at the eight MVA Primaries, and in the injected-shift fits we ran it leaked no more of a recent load shift than the plain network. The other four ways of carrying slow change showed no gain, so the next step is the offset alone, on more random seeds and at the six MW Primaries, where the direction holds but the interval still includes zero. also relevant 00170 dp-bg-stage3-drift-and-holiday-scoring The convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors, ensemble-mean weather, the heating split by day type, one shared filter noise setting, and the pinned solar capacity (experiment 136's arm A2) improves further when it gets a drift term (experiment 167's D1) on top of the two post-forecast corrections of experiment 155's arm D (a winter night offset and recipe R's 14-day mean error profile). The mechanism is that the drift term removes a slow demand-level error that the monthly refit on 24 months of history leaves in, and neither the offset (winter nights only) nor recipe R (a 14-day profile held to 0.75 of its size) removes that error. Training on every year of history adds a further gain, because the drift term and the pinned capacity let the old years teach the heating and calendar terms. refuted not-for-production A slowly varying demand level (a drift term) improved the forecast by 0.40 points in experiment 167 but worsened it by 0.03 points once the forecast has the Kalman filter on recent errors (lower scores are better), and training on all years of history did not change that. The filter already appears to remove the slow level error that the drift term fixes, because without the filter the drift term improves the score by about 0.2 points. The drift term should not be added to experiment 155's arm D. Christmas (24 December to 2 January) scored 1.13 times an ordinary weekday at the same half-hours, below the 1.5 times predicted, and recipe R improved the Christmas score by 0.04 points. also relevant 00167 dp-full-history-gam-24-months-or-all-years-with-drift With the PV capacity pinned to the as-of table (explicit PV) and the heating split by day type (T-all), the convex demand model (the GAM) trained on every year of history back to late 2019 with a drift term scores better than the same model trained on the last 24 months, when both are refitted at 12 quarterly origins on past weather (ERA5 and CAMS). The mechanism is that explicit PV removes the changing solar capacity from the target, so the old years teach the heating and calendar terms without the capacity growth that made the all-years fits of experiments 104 and 107 unstable, and the drift term absorbs the remaining slow change in the demand level. supported candidate Adding a drift term (a slow adjustment to the demand level) improved the forecast at 11 of 12 quarterly refits. The quantile score, where lower is better, fell by 0.40 points when training on the last 24 months and by 0.55 points when training on all years back to late 2019. Training on all years instead of 24 months adds only 0.10 points on top of a drift term, and gives no gain without one, so extra years of history help little. primary 00149 differentiable-physics-full-history-gam-era5-cams When the convex model's solar term is explicit (a pinned capacity times a unit solar shape in both arms), training on every year of a substation's history back to 2019 gives a lower quantile score than training on the last 24 months, once a drift term lets the model follow the slow level change. The mechanism is that more years pin down the temperature, calendar, and weekday terms better, and the drift term absorbs the level change that made all-years training unstable in experiments 104, 106, and 107. inconclusive not-for-production Training the demand model on every year back to 2019, instead of the last 24 months, lowered its forecast error by only about 3% (0.08 points of substation capacity), and the difference could be chance. The drift term helped much more, lowering the error by 0.38 points on 24 months and 0.50 points on all history, but a post hoc audit found that a plain correction by the mean error of the last 28 training days recovers 86% to 94% of that gain, so the gain is a recent-level correction and the drift form is not shown to beat the simpler fix. We did not test whether explicit heating, switching, or pooled terms would make the longer history help. primary 00135 differentiable-physics-n10-joint-kalman-and-demand-fit Fitting the convex demand model (GAM-K) so that its coefficients minimise the day-ahead error after the Kalman correction, instead of the plain error before it, lowers the day-ahead quantile score at 12 to 36 hours below the two-stage fit (fit the demand model, then filter its residuals), without moving the fitted shapes to explain recent-level structure that the filter already tracks. not supported not-for-production We fitted the demand model so that its coefficients minimise the error left after a Kalman filter (a running correction of recent errors) has adjusted the forecast. That made the day-ahead forecast much worse, because the filter can absorb a shift in the slow parts of the demand model, so the fit barely constrains those parts. Tying the fit to the two-stage coefficients removed the damage and also removed any gain: the quantile score was within 0.013 points of the two-stage score, in either direction. The two-stage design (fit the demand model, then filter its residuals) stays. primary 00128 differentiable-physics-kfd-shared-day-anomaly-and-sparse-q-in-gam-k Adding to experiment 111's level-and-anomaly filter (GAM-K) one day-level error state shared by all four hour bands, and estimating the level noise sparsely from zero, makes the filter's midday correction track an injected solar-panel-shaped change in real residuals better than GAM-K, and lowers the day-ahead score on ENS. Real residuals carry a day-level error shared across the four hour bands: the daily means of GAM-K's one-step innovations in different hour bands correlate at 0.18 to 0.23 (control P-premise). An earlier diagnosis of experiment 118's residuals gave 0.58 on a different quantity, the daily means of the residuals, which cannot separate a day-level error from a slow drift shared by all bands. inconclusive not-for-production The day-ahead forecast was not scored, because the filter with one shared day-level error state failed its test on injected changes in real recorded errors, and the experiment stopped there. The errors at different times of day do move together (a correlation of about 0.2 between their daily innovations), but a single shared state probably also soaks up errors that belong to one time of day, so it cannot follow a slow, solar-panel-shaped change. Options for a next experiment are a day-level state for each time of day with a shared part, an explicit solar-panel term, and a test with an injected change large enough to detect; the verdict is inconclusive. also relevant 00122 differentiable-physics-three-winter-backtest-gam-k On past weather, the convex model with the Kalman filter (GAM-K) forecasts Primary demand one day ahead better than both the plain convex model (GAM) and lagless XGBoost, in each of the three winters 2023-24, 2024-25, and 2025-26, by at least 1 point of mean absolute error. supported not-for-production In all three winters, the convex demand model with the recent-error filter (GAM-K) forecast Primary demand one day ahead 1.8 to 3.1 points of capacity better than the same convex model without the filter, and 2.0 to 3.1 points better than lagless XGBoost. The gain is consistent with the filter removing a level error that a fit frozen for a year carries, and lagless XGBoost has no recent power to correct the same error. GAM-K's filter settings were fitted on the 2023-24 winter, and the convex model's ridge penalty was tuned on a year that contains the 2024-25 winter, so those two gains are partly in-sample. 2025-26 has the least tuning leakage, but it was read in an earlier analysis before this plan, and no winter is clean on both counts. A post hoc check at the audit subtracted each plain model's own winter-mean error at each substation, which no forecaster could know in advance: GAM-K stayed ahead of the plain GAM by 0.63, 0.71, and 0.35 points and ahead of lagless XGBoost by 0.95 to 1.05 points, so 5 of the 6 contrasts would miss the 1-point bar. Most of the gain is therefore level tracking, and this result does not show that GAM-K beats a model that sees recent power. The scoring uses past weather, so the gain under live weather forecasts is unknown. also relevant 00118 differentiable-physics-kfe-kalman-filter-on-the-gam-effects-on-ens Freezing the convex model's fitted effects and letting a weight on each follow a random walk, with a diagonal noise matrix fitted by likelihood on the tuning months, forecasts day-ahead demand on ENS better than experiment 111's filter of one level and one anomaly per hour band (GAM-K), because heating slopes, PV capacity, profile scale, and holiday effects drift faster than a 24-month fit follows. The fitted noise matrix beats one step variance shared by every weight, so the gain comes from how each effect drifts and not from the weights' freedom alone. inconclusive not-for-production Letting the convex model's PV, heating, profile, and holiday weights drift did not improve the day-ahead forecast over experiment 111's level-and-anomaly filter (0.015 points worse at D+1, interval -0.013 to +0.048), and did no better in winter or on cold days. Switching the correction off on holidays is much worse (+1.24 points) and halving it is not better, so the filter still helps on holidays. The weights cannot be read as measurements, because the known-answer gate failed on real residuals, although two of its bars were mis-set. Keep experiment 111's filter, and the next step is a filter that fixes the PV weight and moves the others; the verdict is inconclusive. also relevant 00115 differentiable-physics-w1-diurnal-shape-state-on-ens GAM-K's remaining day-ahead error on ENS is mostly in the shape of the day inside each hour band, and that shape drifts faster than the convex model's monthly knots follow. A 48-half-hour shape state with zero mean in each hour band, added to the Kalman filter and updated from every reading the telemetry delay allows, lowers GAM-K's day-ahead quantile score at most decision substations, in months that played no part in choosing the idea's form and in the scored year. inconclusive not-for-production Teaching the physics-based forecast the shape of the day from recent readings lowers its day-ahead error by 0.075 points at five Primary substations (about 3%), in two separate periods and more in winter (0.11, a post hoc breakdown), but averaging the last 14 days' errors by half-hour gains as much, so the learned shape state is not needed on this evidence. The shape state's own check failed: it learns an injected change too slowly (0.35 against a floor of 0.4), so the verdict is capped at inconclusive. A faster shape state, tried afterwards and labelled post hoc, passed that check and beat both K0 and the recipe, which a rerun with the check fixed in advance would need to confirm. also relevant 00112 differentiable-physics-vp-variable-projection-fit-of-pooled-model Part 3's pooled DP lost to the per-site DP because gradient descent did not reach the optimum, not because pooling hurts: solving every linear coefficient exactly at each step, with gradient steps only on the non-linear parameters, makes the pooled DP at least as good as the per-site DP on substations with 2 years of history. inconclusive not-for-production Solving the pooled model's linear coefficients exactly did not make its forecasts better. With the interaction neural network on, the exact fit drove the network's last layer and the seasonal and holiday terms to very large, weakly penalised values: it forecast up to 280 points too high on four days of spring 2026 (the weekend of the clock change, Good Friday, and Easter Monday), and it was 0.7 points worse on the other days. With the network off, the exact fit is stable and within 0.03 points of the gradient fit, so the optimiser was not what held the pooled model back; the known-answer test failed, and with the network on the model cannot recover heating even from noise-free data. also relevant 00108 differentiable-physics-shared-anomaly-factor-across-substations The residuals of the frozen convex demand model carry a component shared across Primaries, and a shared state estimated from the other substations' residuals, available at the forecast origin, lowers the day-ahead quantile score by more than the per-site Kalman filter of Part 4 already does. inconclusive not-for-production The experiment stopped at its known-answer gate, where three of seven tests failed, so it cannot say whether a shared factor improves the forecast. On injected anomalies the shared filter, tuned on 2023-24, carried under 5% of the injected points (the plan asked for 40% or more), and it corrected no better than the per-site filter (2.402 against 2.397 points of mean absolute error over days 2 and 3 of the episodes). Part of the test was mis-specified, so a corrected test would be needed before any real score. also relevant 00107 differentiable-physics-rolling-origin-history-and-tails Refitted quarterly from 2023-07 to 2026-04 and scored on the next 3 months, the convex model's two history contrasts (all years against 12 months, drift against none) keep one sign at almost every origin. A second claim, labelled separately as C5 and not part of the verdict: a level-dependent spread brings its 95% and 99% quantiles within 1 point of nominal coverage without worsening the quantile score. partly supported not-for-production Giving the convex demand model a drift term lowered its score at 10 of 12 quarterly refits, by 0.45 points when trained on all years (interval 0.23 to 0.68). In a post hoc split, about three-fifths of that size is one substation (D10) at the 2023-24 refits, and the 2025-26 refits give 0.30, as in experiment 104. All years without drift scored worse than 12 months at 8 of 12 refits, and all years with drift against 12 months has no stable answer: winter-quarter refits favour more years, summer ones are level. The spread that depends on the forecast level made the 95% and 99% quantiles worse, so the tail coverage still needs a different method. The verdict is partly supported, because only the drift contrast is stable; a second spread (the conformal spread) is not interpreted, because it was built with a flaw. primary 00106 differentiable-physics-4-all-years-drift-and-recent-level The differentiable-physics model trained on every usable year from 2019-09 with a drift term forecasts Primary demand better than the same model on its best window, and assimilating recent residuals through a Kalman filter makes it better again, by more than a simple moving-average correction does. partly supported not-for-production Correcting each day-ahead demand forecast with the errors the model made up to 3.5 hours earlier lowered the quantile score by 0.61 points (from 2.90 to 2.29) in the scored year and by 1.02 points in the year before, at all five long-history substations. The gain relies on estimates of past weather that a live service would not have, and against lagged XGBoost at the same lead the filtered model scored 2.349 against 2.487, a difference that is not significant. Whether old years of history help is not settled, because the contrast changed sign between the two years, so the verdict is partly supported. primary 00104 differentiable-physics-2-simple-structural-model A convex demand-minus-solar model, trained on every usable year with a slowly drifting level per hour band, forecasts Primary demand better than the same model trained on the last 12 months. inconclusive not-for-production A simple model of demand minus solar, trained on 12 months, scored 0.25 points better than lagless XGBoost with its default start (post hoc; a lower score is better). Most of that lead is in the forecast spread, because the error of the mean forecast differs by only 0.08 points, and four of the five pre-registered positive controls failed, so the verdict is inconclusive. More years of history did not clearly help: the scored year and the tuning year gave opposite signs for two history-window contrasts, and a first version of this page had the wrong sign for both because its spread carried the previous year's mean bias. also relevant 00103 differentiable-physics-1-data-look The trial area's power records hold enough clean, demand-only history for the series to go ahead as designed: 6 MW Primaries with at least 12 months before July 2025, and 8 MVA Primaries with over 3 site-years each of rows with no sunlight. supported not-for-production The data lets the series go ahead, with three changes: start 13 of the 16 Primaries later than their first record (19.4 months later at D4), fix the lockdown window in advance because the data does not isolate it from drift, and count eligible long-history MW sites at each tuning year's first day (5 at 2024-07-01, so 4 of 5 must improve in Part 2's tuning contrast). The power timestamps show no 30-minute error on either side of the 2026-03-26 fix: at the 6 metered photovoltaic series the median offsets are +0.9 minutes before it and +4.7 after, and the correction is right to within 3 minutes, but offsets at the Primaries are not resolved beyond 0 to +8 minutes. primary

docs.title: Differentiable physics: the network
docs.text: The summary of this theme is in progress. The differentiable-physics series models Primary substation demand from physical terms. This theme covers what the connections between Primary substations add: power flowing along the interconnections between neighbouring Primary substations when the network operator switches load from one to another, and a forecast of demand under the normal running arrangement (NRA), with those transfers removed. The Experiments page lists every experiment tried, with its verdict and a take-home message, and the Research plan lists what is planned next.

docs.title: Differentiable physics: the network: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00685 event-table-on-the-final-test-window-all-primaries None. This is a data product: the event table of experiment 680, run unchanged on the residual panel extended to 2026-10-31, so that the one-year-backtest flags at four Primaries can be set beside the events the table can see. inconclusive not-for-production From 2026-07-01 to 2026-10-31 the event table finds 13 candidate events (14 rows) at the 15 Primaries and no transfer between time_series_id 13 and 16 in July or August, nothing at id 11 in September, and one open fall at id 18 from 2026-10-04. The one-year-backtest flags at ids 13, 16, 11, and 18 are therefore not explained by events the table can see. A level offset in the lag-free forecast remains a candidate explanation that this table does not test. One transfer from id 13 to id 16 opens on 2026-10-26 and is still open at the end of the window. Every row is a candidate, never a label. also relevant 00682 event-table-reconstruction-from-edge-flows-part-2-change-cost-model Experiment 680 found that searching from either end of a transfer raises the paired share by +0.09 (long and deep) but adds 442 decoded transfers for 63 correct ends. A model that decides every pair jointly, by the saving in change cost against the misfit of one common flow, with the recipient share bounded by a prior, accepts only pairs whose two steps are explained better by one flow than by two steps that stand alone. It therefore pairs at least 0.10 more of the injected transfer megawatts than E1-J in both the long and deep and the medium and deep cells, with a share of decoded transfers that match no injected end no higher than E1-J's. not supported not-for-production Explaining pairs of steps by one flow on an edge, chosen by a fixed cost per change, does not find the donor and recipient of an injected load transfer better than the simple searches: it pairs 0.33 of the long and deep megawatts against 0.29 for the one-way search and 0.38 for the two-way search. It accepts almost every pair that roughly conserves megawatts, 2990 transfers for 329 correct ends, and a graph that connects any two Primaries pairs nearly as much as the real neighbours. Within the 15 Primaries tested, this cost objective gains almost nothing from knowing the real edges, and the edge-flow line closes here. also relevant 00680 event-table-reconstruction-from-edge-flows-part-1-symmetric-search Experiment 675 found that the donor is the bottleneck of experiment 670's search: E1-J finds 0.73 of the recipient megawatts in the long and deep cell but only 0.44 of the donor megawatts, and 0.87 of the recipient megawatts it found but left unpaired belong to transfers whose donor it had not found. A donor search that starts from each unpaired rise of 4 noise units or more, and looks at each connected Primary for a fall of 2 noise units or more that starts up to 36 half-hours before the rise, can recover those donors, and so pairs at least 0.10 more of the injected transfer megawatts than E1-J in both the long and deep cell and the medium and deep cell. partly supported not-for-production Searching from each unpaired rise for the matching fall at a neighbouring Primary pairs 0.38 of the injected transfer megawatts in the long and deep cell, against 0.29 for the one-way search, a gain of 0.09. The gain of 0.09 disappears on a rewired graph (0.057 paired), but its interval includes zero in one of three other generator configurations. It falls just short of the 0.10 needed to adopt the search, and the search adds 442 decoded transfers, most of which match no injected end. The donor is still found for only 0.48 of its megawatts, so the joint reconstruction model of part 2 has room to add something, and the share of decoded transfers that match no injected end is the number to watch. also relevant 00678 donor-posterior-hybrid-for-load-transfer-pairing Experiment 675 found that the donor was not found for 0.87 (long and deep) and 0.84 (medium and deep) of the recipient megawatts that E1-J found and left unpaired, and that a logistic regression on the node inputs (F) finds 0.63 of the long and deep donor megawatts against E1-J's 0.44 at the same false-donor rate. A donor alarm from such a probe, refined to a start time and an end time and handed to the recipient search of experiment 670 as an extra donor step, pairs more transfer megawatts than E1-J does. It reopens the graph line only at the level of a donor posterior feeding the existing search; the edge-state network of the original plan is not built here. not supported not-for-production A donor probe feeding E1-J's recipient search pairs a little more than E1-J (0.36 against 0.29 of long and deep megawatts), not the +0.10 that was predicted, and far below the 0.60 that would have made it the event table. The stop rule closes the graph line at 15 Primaries. The donor alarm helps a little, and a neural encoder adds nothing over a logistic regression within the seed spread. The rewired graph pairs almost nothing, which shows only that the recipient search needs the real neighbours. also relevant 00676 pretrained-graph-model-for-load-transfers-part-2-edge-state-network Experiments 672 and 678 each closed the graph line at 15 Primaries under their stop rules, and the maintainer asked to continue it. Experiment 678 bolted a donor posterior onto E1-J's recipient search; the explicit per-link state with a recipient lag, decoded jointly with the Primaries' states, is a core of the design that experiments 672 and 678 did not test. A network that learns the state of every link (off, first Primary donates, second Primary donates) hour by hour, and the lag at which the recipient follows, pairs more injected transfer megawatts in the long and deep and the medium and deep cells than the hybrids of experiment 678 do. A post hoc variant of experiment 678, whose added donors may end in under 2 days, pairs more short-event megawatts than experiment 678 did, at a false-transfer rate that stays within 1.5 times E1-J's. not supported not-for-production A neural network that learns the state of every link between two Primaries, and the delay before the recipient follows, pairs no more transfer megawatts than the donor-probe hybrids or the search of experiment 670 (paired share of long, deep transfer megawatts: 0.32 for the new network, 0.29 for the search, 0.35 and 0.36 for the hybrids). A copy with its link features removed does as well, because the decoder already restricts recipients to the real neighbours. At 15 Primaries the learnt-graph line is closed, and a next step needs more Primaries or the whole fleet's adjacency, a more realistic injector, and more verified events. also relevant 00675 pretrained-graph-model-for-load-transfers-part-1-diagnostics-and-frozen-probe Experiment 672 trained a graph neural network on 120 injected worlds and 6-hour blocks. The network found donors about as often as E1-J (0.47 of the long and deep donor megawatts against 0.44) and then paired few of them (0.09). Three changes have not been tested: a network that first learns each Primary's ordinary variability by reconstructing masked windows of real history, an input set that includes the same step statistics E1-J uses, and a residual that is not distorted by the convex demand model's error. This experiment first asks where E1-J loses the recipient megawatts it finds (0.73 found, 0.22 paired), then asks whether a pretrained encoder, frozen and read by a logistic probe, finds donors and recipients better than a random encoder of the same shape and better than the event table's features alone. It reopens the graph line that experiment 672's stop rule closed at 15 Primaries, at the maintainer's request. not supported not-for-production The donor of a transfer, not the link to its recipient, is what the event table of experiment 670 misses. An encoder pretrained to reconstruct masked windows of real residuals made the probe worse, not better, so the stop rule drops masked pretraining. The stop rule's first clause points experiment 676 to a randomly initialised encoder and its second clause to the causal arm's weights, so the choice is open. also relevant 00672 graph-model-that-finds-the-donor-of-a-load-transfer Experiment 670 found that the event table with a recipient search (E1-J) pairs 0.29 (0.20 to 0.40) of the injected megawatts in the long and deep cell, and that two losses limit it: the event table finds only 0.44 of the donor megawatts, and the search pairs only 0.22 of the recipient megawatts although it finds 0.73. A graph neural network that reads every Primary's residual and the electricity network's links together, and is trained on experiment 660's injected worlds with an objective for the donor itself, finds the donor of a transfer by the matching recipient step at a linked Primary, which a per-Primary detector cannot see when the donor step is small. It therefore finds more donor megawatts and pairs at least 0.10 more than the search in the long and deep and in the medium and deep cells. not supported not-for-production A graph neural network trained on injected transfers pairs the two ends of a transfer far less often than the search of experiment 670 (0.08 against 0.29 of megawatts in the longest and deepest transfers), and it finds the donor about as often as the search does. This result closes the graph line at 15 Primaries under the pre-registered stop rule, and the graph network's own placebo and no-link arms show that the links add a little pairing and no reliable donor finding. also relevant 00670 event-table-recipient-search-on-six-cell-grid Experiment 653's event table pairs few injected load transfers (0.18 of the megawatts at the two ends) because each end must clear the full detection penalty on its own. A search at each connected Primary for a recipient step of opposite sign, started within 36 half-hours of a deep donor step, needs only the small recipient step to be present, and so pairs at least 0.6 of the injected megawatts in transfers that are both long (over 7 days) and deep (8 noise units or more), the bar that experiment 653 set for any model of edges. not supported not-for-production A search at the neighbouring Primaries for the recipient of each large downward step lets the event table pair 0.29 of the injected transfer megawatts in the longest and deepest transfers, against 0.09 without the search, but not the 0.60 that was needed to adopt it. The shortfall is two losses: the event table finds only 0.44 of those donor megawatts, and the search pairs only 0.22 of the recipient megawatts although it finds 0.73. The result sits on the 0.30 line (leave-one-out range 0.26 to 0.31), so it does not show that pairing is unidentifiable at 15 Primaries. A graph model would have to improve both donors and recipients, and its margin over this search is the next question. also relevant 00579 encoder-capacity-and-architecture-arms-on-the-modular-network The weather encoder and the datetime encoder of the modular network are small (about 2,500 weights each). The datetime encoder has the most to learn for demand forecasting, so capacity may limit it, and the inputs it is given (hour harmonics 1 and 2, a day-of-week one-hot, solar geometry, holiday columns) may limit it too. The weather encoder has only 7 inputs, so capacity should not limit it. not supported not-for-production Making the weather and datetime encoders of the modular demand network larger, or giving the datetime encoder richer inputs such as an Economy 7 proxy, did not lower the forecast error beyond what a different random seed changes at the eight MVA Primaries, so capacity is not what limits the forecast there. At the six MW Primaries a larger datetime encoder lowered the error by 0.135 points of capacity, but a copy with the same depth and no extra width achieved more than half of that, so the gain may come from depth or from training noise rather than capacity. The next step is more seeds for DL and DT at the six MW Primaries, and no further architecture arms. also relevant 00223 dp-bsp-generators-as-children-and-double-count-test The metered generators that NGED lists under a bulk supply point (BSP) are children of that BSP as much as the Primaries are: the BSP's reading is the Primaries' demand plus the unmetered load minus the generators' output. If the Primaries' readings already include a generator's output, adding that generator to the sum double-counts it. This experiment first tests, from the readings alone, which generators the BSP's remainder carries and which a Primary already carries, and then asks how much the BSP's forecast improves when the generators the BSP carries are summed as children. inconclusive not-for-production The two bulk supply points' readings move with the metered generators that NGED lists under them, and the Primaries' readings show only small coefficients on the same generators. The size of the movement is not the clean one-for-one that adding the generator to the sum needs, so the experiment did not test whether adding the generators improves the bulk supply point forecast. A better test is to separate the unmetered solar and the battery's price-driven dispatch first. also relevant 00204 dp-bsp-full-bottom-up-with-signed-mva-children A bulk supply point (BSP) is forecast better bottom-up than top-down when the sum covers every child Primary. Experiment 161 summed only the three children per BSP that report real power (MW) and have a long history, which reached 42% of D13's effective capacity and 56% of D17's, and the bottom-up forecast scored 0.5% to 0.6% worse than the top-down forecast. This experiment adds the children that report apparent power (MVA). A child's apparent-power reading is the magnitude of its flow, so a child with reverse flow at midday needs a signed flow before it can enter a sum. The fold-aware model of experiment 152 supplies that signed flow as a latent variable. inconclusive not-for-production Adding every child Primary to the sum did not improve the forecast of either bulk supply point: the bottom-up score matched the top-down score (+0.1% at D13, -0.15% at D17), and the intervals include zero. Converting the children that report apparent power to signed flow changed the score by at most 0.03 points, at the one bulk supply point where a child has reverse flow. Even with every child's reading known exactly the BSP's score gains only 12% to 24%, and the children's forecasts gave no detectable gain over the BSP's own chain, so the next gain may lie in forecasting the generators and the unmetered load beneath each BSP. also relevant 00161 dp-bsp-top-down-against-bottom-up A bulk supply point (BSP) is forecast better bottom-up than top-down. The top-down forecast is the best-guess GAM-K chain (experiment 155's arm D) applied to the BSP's reading as a stand-alone series. The bottom-up forecast adds the arm D forecasts of the BSP's child Primary substations that report real power, each times a weight learned from earlier readings, to arm D's forecast of the remainder (the BSP's reading minus those children's weighted readings). The mechanism is that the child Primaries' own forecasts are better than the BSP's chain can infer from the BSP's sum, because each child has its own heating, solar, and calendar response and its own recent errors, and the sum is not exact (losses, unmetered load, children that report apparent power), so the remainder and the weights absorb the difference. inconclusive not-for-production Forecasting a BSP from its children's forecasts plus a remainder did not beat forecasting the BSP as a stand-alone series at either BSP: the bottom-up score was 0.6% worse at D13 and 0.5% worse at D17. The likely reason is that the children this test could use (three real-power Primaries per BSP) cover 42% and 56% of the BSP's capacity, and the BSP's error lives in the rest. The oracle control also missed its pre-registered threshold, which was set too high. The verdict is inconclusive because both intervals include zero. primary 00131 differentiable-physics-nra-edge-flows-drift-term Adding a slowly varying offset to each substation, fitted jointly with the flows on the interconnection edges, lets the flow fit find injected transfers that last hours to days without putting flow on pairs of substations that are not connected, which experiment 116's fit could not do. inconclusive not-for-production Letting each substation drift slowly did reduce the load that the fit wrongly moves between substations that are not connected, by half to three quarters at an equal or higher detection rate. It did not remove that false load, and the settings that keep it near zero find only about half of the transfers we added artificially and report them too small. In the replicate year part of the false load sits in two jumps in one substation's data that nobody had labelled. We therefore cannot yet read these flows as switching events. primary 00116 differentiable-physics-nra-edge-flows-between-primaries Flows on the electricity network's interconnection edges, fitted to a frozen convex model's residuals with a sparse-step penalty, recover injected conserved transfers between MW-metered Primaries; removing them gives a normal running arrangement (NRA) model trained without hand labels that forecasts no worse outside events; and fed causally into the Kalman filter as a known input, they improve the metered forecast during and after a transfer. inconclusive not-for-production The method that looks for load moved between neighbouring substations did not work: with the settings we fixed in advance it found under a quarter of the load we added artificially, and it changed no forecast. Looser settings found more, but they also found load moving between substations that are not connected, probably the slow drifts of demand that our model does not describe. The gate failed for a structural reason: at the settings we fixed in advance, the fit cannot find any transfer shorter than 7 to 9 days, and the longest test transfer lasts under 5 days, so the failure is a limit of the method as specified, not a bug in the solver. The zero flow we first saw on the unconnected pairs was also an artefact of the order the fit visits its paths, so those pairs were never clean. Adding a drift term to the model, or accepting a flow only where the two substations are connected, is the next thing to test. primary

docs.title: Differentiable physics: the network: research plan
docs.text: The proposed next steps are a topology check on candidate flows, or a smaller level penalty combined with a check for unlabelled jumps; neither option is planned. Experiment 116 ended inconclusive because the known-answer gate failed: every setting that found injected transfers also found flow between substations with no interconnection. Experiment 131 added a per-substation drift term. At equal or higher recall the drift term cuts the flow on unconnected pairs by half to three quarters, but no setting meets the recall targets and the placebo limit together, and the level penalty shrinks the flows the fit finds.

docs.title: Differentiable physics: pooling across substations
docs.text:
The current understanding and the options for next work are on the state and next steps page.

The summary of this theme is in progress. The differentiable-physics series builds models from physical terms (demand, heating, solar) whose parameters are fitted by gradient descent. This theme covers whether one such model fitted across many Primary substations can match a model per substation, and beat it for a new substation or one with a short history. The Experiments page lists every experiment tried, with its verdict and a take-home message, and the Research plan lists what is planned next. Experiment 112 found that fitting the pooled model exactly did not remove its gap to per-substation models: with the interaction network on, the exact fit forecast far too high on four days.

docs.title: Differentiable physics: pooling across substations: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00200 dp-pooled-correction-head-on-kalman-state Experiment 142's small network failed its known-answer gate with about 1,100 samples from one year at five substations. The same kind of network, trained on rows pooled across many Primary substations and years, learns to correct arm D's forecast from the recent errors, the calendar, the lead, and the ensemble-mean weather, and so beats recipe R (subtract 0.75 times the mean error of the last 14 days) at day D+1. partly supported not-for-production A small neural network trained on arm D's own past errors lowers the day-ahead score by 0.07 to 0.12 points at five substations, but a copy that sees no recent error gets most of that gain. The gain comes from correcting how arm D's error depends on its forecast level and the calendar, and a pinball-loss table comes within 0.01 to 0.02 points of the network on one year of data. also relevant 00158 dp-partly-pooled-gam-shapes-heating-and-calendar-curves A GAM-K forecast (the convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors, experiment 111) fitted jointly across six Primary substations, so that each substation's heating curve, lighting curve, daily profile, holiday effects, and Christmas shape are a fleet mean plus a penalised deviation of its own, forecasts better than the same model fitted to each substation alone, now that the solar capacity is pinned and the filter handles recent switching. The mechanism is that a substation sees only two winters and two Christmases in a 24-month window, so its own curves are noisy, and five other substations carry information about the shapes that physically are shared. Capacity, level, and the band means stay per substation. The gain is largest for a substation with 3 months of history and on Christmas rows, and no pooled arm is worse than the per-site fit by more than 0.02 points on ordinary rows. partly supported candidate In this test on six Primary substations, fitting the demand model's shared curves (heating, lighting, daily profile, holidays) across all six let a substation with only 3 months of history score 3.01 points instead of 3.64 (lower is better), within 0.17 points of the same substation with 24 months of its own history. The gain was largest in winter and on Christmas rows. For a substation with 24 months of history, pooling changed the score by less than 0.02 points, which is too small to justify making each forecast depend on five other substations' data. The test cannot say whether pooling the heating curve alone would help a 3-month substation. primary 00154 differentiable-physics-n0-gate-2-heating-error-against-truth When the partly pooled convex regression model of experiment 109 is fitted to only 4 winter weeks of one substation, its fitted heating curve is closer to the injected truth than the curves of the no-pooling and complete-pooling fits. The curve is as close to the truth as a fair oracle's curve (within 10%). The model recovers the sign of the substation's own heating offset relative to the fleet's curve. The fleet's shared curve is recovered as well as an average of per-site fits recovers it. partly supported not-for-production On synthetic substations with a known answer, a partly pooled demand model fitted to 4 winter weeks of one substation estimated that substation's heating response with a smaller error than fitting the substation alone (2.8 to 3.6 against 4.1 to 11.5 points of capacity) and than copying the fleet's curve (3.4 to 4.6), on every seed. It recovered the fleet's shared curve about as well as separate fits did. Neither the pooled fit nor the fair oracle recovered the sign of the substation's own heating offset reliably (the pooled fit got the sign right at 6 or more of 8 substations on only 2 of 5 seeds), so on these synthetic fleets and one January, a partly pooled model can share the heating curve but cannot learn a substation's own offset from 4 weeks. primary 00150 differentiable-physics-n0-gate-rerun-fair-oracle-five-seeds When the reference estimator estimates every coefficient from the same 4 weeks of rows (so that no coefficient is fixed at its true value), the partially pooled convex model of experiment 109 recovers the injected truth about as well as that reference on most of 5 random seeds, and its tuning rule picks a deviation penalty within one grid step of the best one on most of the 5 seeds. inconclusive not-for-production The rerun of the synthetic known-answer test could not say whether the pooled model shrinks substation deviations correctly, because a control that keeps no deviation at all passed the shrinkage line on 2 of 5 seeds when 4 June weeks were held. Capacity from 4 weeks was within 25% of the truth at 8 of 8 synthetic substations on every seed, the tuning rule picked a penalty within one grid step of the best on 5 of 5 seeds, and the pooled fit's heating error was below a fair reference estimator's on 5 of 5 seeds. The full-history line passed on only 2 of 5 seeds. A post hoc rerun on 4 January weeks separated the controls, so a test that scores heating error against the injected truth in winter should settle the question. primary 00124 differentiable-physics-h-bsp-closure-audit-and-bsp-hint A bulk supply point (BSP) reading, fitted jointly with the Primaries beneath it as the sum of their demand terms plus the metered generators plus a penalised remainder, with a tuned weight, limits the damage that a metering error at one Primary does to that Primary's forecast, without raising the Primaries' forecast error when no error is present. not supported not-for-production The bulk supply point reading halved the damage from injected scale errors, but it made forecasts on clean data worse at every weight above zero: by at least 0.385 points of capacity in the corrected re-run, about 17 times the 0.023-point limit (2.355 points or more in the first run). A synthetic system that closes exactly loses clean accuracy the same way, so the loss does not come mainly from a wrong multiplier. The cause is untested. As a detector of metering errors the reading is weak: a 25% scale error lasting 30 days is found in 0% of cases by a fit that includes it and in 50% by a fit trained only on earlier rows, which then false-alarms on 61% of later windows. primary 00120 differentiable-physics-sh-convex-daily-shape-library A convex model in which each Primary's daily profile is a non-negative mix of K = 3 or 4 shared daily shapes per day type, plus a penalised deviation, forecasts Primary demand with 2 years of history at least 0.05 points better than experiment 109's shrinkage towards one fleet-mean profile. That needs the library to beat the per-site profile by about 0.02 points, because the fleet-mean model is 0.031 worse than it; the plan predicts a tie or a small gain, so supported is a long shot. The stability of the shapes and the shape mix of each substation are descriptive. inconclusive not-for-production In a test with synthetic substations, 5 Primaries were too few for a library of 3 shared daily shapes to recover the shapes we planted, so the check failed on 7 of 10 lines and the verdict is inconclusive. In the scored year the library scored the same as the fleet-mean model and 0.030 points worse than a profile per substation (0.068 worse in winter), and its forecast reproduced a tenth to a half of the Economy 7 night step on cold winter nights. primary 00117 differentiable-physics-h2-graph-prior-on-pooled-convex-parameters A penalty on the differences between interconnected Primaries' parameters (heating slopes, PV capacity as a share of effective capacity, the profile's scale, and the holiday coefficients) narrows those parameters' month-block bootstrap intervals without breaking their coverage when neighbouring Primaries are alike, and worsens the full-history quantile score by at most 0.03 points. refuted not-for-production At the weight tested, tying the parameters of interconnected substations together did not improve the forecast: in the scored year it worsened the quantile score by 0.020 points on all days (the interval spans zero) and by 0.173 points in winter evening peaks (the replicate year gave -0.021). On synthetic substations with a known truth it narrowed only heating-slope intervals, and the 80% intervals of PV capacity held the truth 17% of the time against 78% without the tie. A tie on heating slopes alone worsened the real score by 0.006 and 0.001 points, an exploratory lead and not a result. primary 00113 differentiable-physics-n5-convex-identification-at-realistic-noise On synthetic substations built from the real calendar and weather, with noise as large and as autocorrelated as the convex model's real residuals, the convex model's 80% month-block bootstrap intervals cover the truth 70 to 90% of the time, separately for each hour band's heating slope and for the latest season-year's PV capacity. Labelled separately, not in the verdict: the day-of-year harmonics and the drift term make those intervals wide, by absorbing the seasonal cycles of temperature and clear-sky PV. refuted not-for-production At real noise levels, the convex model's 80% month-block bootstrap intervals contain the true heating slope and the true rooftop PV capacity 84% of the time each, but a heating slope is weak (the interval is about 38% of the slope wide). The pre-registered verdict is refuted, because with independent noise the capacity interval covers the truth only 52% of the time, and the cause is mainly a bias of about 0.24 points from the drift penalty at its tuned step of 3,000 (at Part 4's step of 30 the bias is 0.02 points and coverage 78%, a post hoc check). The truth here has the model's own form, so the test cannot show the bias that a wrong PV shape causes. also relevant 00112 differentiable-physics-vp-variable-projection-fit-of-pooled-model Part 3's pooled DP lost to the per-site DP because gradient descent did not reach the optimum, not because pooling hurts: solving every linear coefficient exactly at each step, with gradient steps only on the non-linear parameters, makes the pooled DP at least as good as the per-site DP on substations with 2 years of history. inconclusive not-for-production Solving the pooled model's linear coefficients exactly did not make its forecasts better. With the interaction neural network on, the exact fit drove the network's last layer and the seasonal and holiday terms to very large, weakly penalised values: it forecast up to 280 points too high on four days of spring 2026 (the weekend of the clock change, Good Friday, and Easter Monday), and it was 0.7 points worse on the other days. With the network off, the exact fit is stable and within 0.03 points of the gradient fit, so the optimiser was not what held the pooled model back; the known-answer test failed, and with the network on the model cannot recover heating even from noise-free data. primary 00110 differentiable-physics-5-embedded-generation-and-capacity The convex differentiable-physics model can represent the generation side of a Primary substation without making its demand forecast worse: an MVA meter through an observation layer, a flat unmetered generator found where one exists and not invented where none does, and an export-limited PV clip; and its PV capacity stays the same when the routes by which demand terms can imitate solar are closed. inconclusive not-for-production The demand forecast could not yet account for generators connected behind a substation. Rooftop solar capacity fitted from the data was not precise or consistent enough to trust, so the capacity from outside estimates stays in use. A generator-finding component reported a generator at every substation tested, so it stays switched off. A limit on exported solar helped only at the one substation known to export-limit. Treating the meter as apparent power improved the forecast at the 8 substations that report only apparent power by 0.13 points of capacity, but the test of the meter's flow direction failed, so that gain is provisional. also relevant 00109 differentiable-physics-n0-partially-pooled-convex-model A convex model whose per-substation coefficients are a fleet mean plus a ridge-penalised per-substation deviation forecasts Primary demand as well as the per-substation convex model when both have 2 years of history, and clearly better when the substation has 4 weeks or 3 months. inconclusive not-for-production The known-answer test of this method failed under its pre-registered definition, and only one of five runs (each on a new seed, runs 2 to 5 being post hoc redefinitions) passes every line, so the verdict is inconclusive. Taking the numbers alone, for the five MW Primaries tested, one convex model shared across substations forecast a new substation with only 4 weeks of history 3.3 points better than a convex model fitted to that substation alone (and 0.8 points better with 3 months), far more than the 0.5 to 2.0 predicted, and scored 0.03 points worse on substations with 2 years of history. On the six held-out Primaries it came within 0.2 points of experiment 105's neural pooled model with 4 weeks (the neural model 0.13 better) and 0.12 better with 3 months, without that model's loss on long histories, which suggests that the loss in experiment 105 came largely from the neural fit. Complete pooling scored 0.07 points worse than partial pooling at 4 weeks in the scored year (interval touching zero) and no differently in the replicate year. The gains should be relied on only after a rerun of the gate. primary 00105 differentiable-physics-3-pooled-and-per-site-demand-model One differentiable-physics model fitted across all the Primary substations forecasts a substation as well as the same model fitted to that substation alone when both have two years of history, and forecasts clearly better when the substation is new (4 weeks of history) or short of history (3 months). inconclusive not-for-production One neural-network demand model fitted across 15 Primary substations forecasts a substation with only 4 weeks of history far better than a per-site copy of the same model (score 4.04 against 14.38 on the six scored substations), but forecasts a substation with 2 full years of history worse than a per-site copy (3.42 against 3.04 on the five decision substations, worse at all 5). By the pre-registered rule pooling is not yet a success, because that full-history result (C1) is refuted, and a failed known-answer check (gate test 2, injected-farm recovery) caps the verdict at inconclusive. Post hoc, for a new substation the pooled model also beat a per-site convex model fitted to the same 4 weeks (mean absolute error 6.88 against 12.79). primary

docs.title: Differentiable physics: pooling across substations: research plan
docs.text:
The rows below are the planned and proposed experiments of this theme, in priority order (1 is first). Experiment 105, the first of the theme, is finished: pooling helped a new or short-history substation and was worse at full history.

Experiment Question Priority Waits for State Onboarding design (proposed) Does a pooled model for onboarding and a per-site model for mature substations beat either alone? 2 Experiment 105: pooled onboarding scored 4.04 against 14.38 for a per-site model on 4 weeks, and was worse at full history Proposed Part 4 (proposed) Does a drift term (a slowly changing demand level), trained from 2019-09, beat the same model on its best window? 3 Experiment 112 (finished: an exact variable-projection fit did not improve the pooled model, and its known-answer test failed at realistic noise) Proposed Part 5 (proposed) Does the MVA observation layer (a model of how a meter that reads apparent power relates to real power) help the MW sites and recover MW at MVA sites? 4 Experiment 105 and a better capacity fit Proposed N9, scale-up Does the pooled model on every v1 series it can take, including MVA substations, improve full-history skill and capacity identification? 5 Nothing; 3 to 5 GPU hours Queued BSP as a Kalman observation Does treating the BSP reading as an extra observation in the Kalman filter improve the Primaries' forecasts? 6 Experiment 124 (finished: a BSP term in the joint fit raised clean-forecast error) Proposed Top-down against bottom-up Does a direct forecast at a BSP or grid supply point (GSP) beat the sum of the Primary forecasts, and does reconciling the levels help either? 7 The closure audit Proposed Metered generators in the graph Do metered generators, entered as export-positive nodes at the BSP, make the BSP relation close better? 8 The closure audit Proposed Unmetered wind at higher levels Can unmetered wind at the BSP and GSP be estimated as the part of the residual that follows the wind forecast? 9 The closure audit Proposed

Experiment 109 gives the pooled convex model N for the next experiments to start from, and experiment 150 reran its known-answer gate. The rerun was inconclusive: capacity from 4 weeks was within 25% at 8 of 8 substations on 5 of 5 seeds, the tuning rule was within one grid step of the best penalty on 5 of 5 seeds, and the pooled fit's heating error beat a fair oracle's, but the shrinkage line could not tell a good fit from a bad one on 4 June weeks. Experiment 154 then scored the heating error against the injected truth on 4 winter weeks: the pooled fit beat no pooling and complete pooling on 5 of 5 seeds and recovered the fleet's shared curve as well as separate fits, but the sign of a substation's own offset was found on only 2 of 5 seeds, by the fair oracle no more reliably.

Experiment 158 fitted GAM-K's shared curves jointly across six substations. A substation with 3 months of history scored 3.01 points instead of 3.64 (-0.629, 99% interval -1.639 to -0.091), and a substation with 24 months scored the same as without pooling (+0.004, -0.006 to +0.014).
