docs.title: N9: scale-up
docs.text: The proposal fits the pooled model on every v1 series it can take, including MVA substations through the Part 5 meter layer. More substations, and the sunlit rows of MVA substations teaching the solar term, should improve full-history skill and make capacity better identified. The experiment runs no onboarding arms. It starts from experiment 109's convex pooling if the gate rerun supports it, and otherwise from per-site fits with the shared meter layer. It needs 3 to 5 GPU hours.

docs.title: Hierarchy: Primaries, BSPs, and GSPs
docs.text:
Experiment 124 found that adding the BSP reading to the Primaries' fit raised clean-forecast error at every weight tried. The raise was 0.4 to 4.6 points of capacity, although the reading cut the damage from injected metering errors by about 41%. The closure audit found that the Primaries and generators close one of the two BSPs up to factors of 0.85 to 1.16, and an exactly specified synthetic system lost clean accuracy the same way, so the cause is untested. Experiment 36 had found that the sum of Primary forecasts added nothing at the two BSPs.

Three facts shape the design:

  • The remainder is large. In the data checked, the BSP residual has a daily-mean standard deviation larger than the typical switched load, so the audit has to say what the remainder contains before any constraint uses it.
  • The GSP relation cannot be closed. Most of the power at each GSP is unmetered.
  • Reconciliation helps the aggregates most. Nespoli et al. (2022) found that reconciling cut the aggregate error by up to 10% and the bottom-level error by under 1%, and Brégère and Huard (2022) found that most of the gain came from mixing in other nodes' forecasts, not from the constraint. The expected gain at the Primaries is therefore small, and the proposals below aim at the BSP and GSP levels.

The BSP as a Kalman observation tests whether the closure relation, with its unmetered remainder as state noise, helps the Primaries' filters. It runs on the CPU in about 2 hours.

Top-down against bottom-up at the BSP and GSP levels asks which direction gives the better forecast at each level. The arms are a direct forecast of the BSP, the sum of the Primary forecasts plus the generators, and a minimum-trace reconciliation of the two, each scored at both levels. The topology is soft, not a hard sum: the hierarchy enters as a hint that the levels should roughly agree, because the unmetered remainder makes an exact balance wrong.

Metered generators enter the graph as export-positive nodes at the BSP. The Primary series are the disaggregated demand, which already has the metered generators taken out, and the generators connect at the BSP busbar. Adding them as nodes should make the BSP relation close better. Their series are generator data, so any published figure shows them only as an anonymised, capacity-normalised series, never beside a name.

Unmetered wind at the BSP and GSP levels is invisible at the Primaries and may show up higher. The audit's residual, regressed on the weather forecast's wind speed at the BSP, would give a first estimate of how much unmetered wind sits there. The estimate only counts if the wind-driven part of the residual is separate from the solar part, so it waits for the audit.

docs.title: Differentiable physics, pooling across substations: state and next steps
docs.text:
Fitting one differentiable-physics demand model across several Primary substations helped a substation with 4 weeks to 3 months of history. At full history (2 years) pooling lost a little, and no gain in this theme passed a known-answer test. The differentiable-physics pooling work is not in the final models: the Primaries' Candidate there is a neural network pooled across all 16 Primaries (Experiment 403). The glossary defines Primary (primary substation), BSP (bulk supply point), GSP (grid supply point), and MVA (megavolt-ampere, apparent power). The theme is unfinished.

Scores are quantile scores, in points of capacity (1% of a substation's capacity), and a lower score is better. A contrast is the score of one arm minus the score of another, so a negative contrast favours the first arm. The verdict words (supported, partly supported, inconclusive, and the rest) are defined in the glossary. The decision substations are the five Primaries D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16, on which the pre-registered tests were scored. A partly pooled fit shares curves across substations but lets each substation depart from them (shrinkage). Onboarding means forecasting a substation that has just joined. A known-answer test fits a model to synthetic data with a known truth.

docs.title: What works
docs.text:
A pooled neural-network demand model gives a new substation a usable forecast from 4 weeks of readings. The model was fitted across 15 Primaries. On the five decision substations it scored 4.18 after onboarding on 4 weeks, against 15.13 for the same model fitted to those 4 weeks alone (-10.95, 98.33% interval -15.12 to -7.28). With 3 months it scored 4.38 against 5.47 (-1.09, -2.01 to -0.34). On six held-out Primaries including D9 (21 months of history), the 4-week scores were 4.04 and 14.38. The verdict is inconclusive because a known-answer check failed. The per-site neural comparator was weak: pooled 4-week onboarding only ties a climatology fitted on the full history (+0.12, -0.33 to +0.57) and is worse than the manual heuristic (+0.70, +0.23 to +1.19). (Experiment 105).

The pooled convex model N keeps the onboarding gain and loses 0.03 points at full history. On the five MW Primaries, N scored 4.35 against 7.60 for a per-site convex model on 4 weeks (-3.25, 99% interval -5.20 to -1.59, better at 5 of 5). With 2 years of history N was 0.03 points worse (+0.012 to +0.056, inside the 0.10 margin). Experiment 105's neural model lost 0.385 points there, which suggests the neural fit caused most of that loss. The verdict is inconclusive, because the known-answer test failed its pre-registered definition (Experiment 109).

On synthetic substations with a known answer, sharing the heating curve beat fitting each substation alone. On 4 winter weeks, the pooled fit's heating error was below no pooling and complete pooling on 5 of 5 seeds, and close to a fair oracle (a reference estimator given the true form of the curve). The sign of a substation's own heating offset was right at 6 or more of 8 substations on only 2 of 5 seeds,. The verdict is partly supported (Experiment 154). A June-weeks rerun was inconclusive (Experiment 150).

Pooling the shared curves in the generalised additive model (GAM) forecast engine helped a substation with 3 months of history. The forecast is GAM-K, a GAM with a Kalman filter on recent errors. On six Primaries, a substation with 3 months of history scored 3.01 instead of 3.64 (-0.629, 99% interval -1.639 to -0.091), against 2.84 for the same substation with 24 months of its own history. The gain held at all five decision substations and in all 12 months of the scored year. The verdict is partly supported (Experiment 158).

docs.title: What does not work
docs.text:
Pooling loses a little at 2 years of history, and no gain here passed a known-answer test. At five Primaries with 2 years of history, the pooled neural network scored 3.42 against 3.04 for per-site fits (+0.385, 98.33% interval +0.178 to +0.689, worse at 5 of 5). The pooled convex model N lost 0.03 points. At 24 months, complete pooling of the GAM lost 0.29, and partly pooling it changed the score by +0.004 (-0.006 to +0.014) (Experiment 158).

Fitting the pooled neural network exactly made the forecast worse. The exact fit (a variable projection, which solves the linear weights in closed form) reached a training objective 16,000 to 27,000 nats (units of log-likelihood) lower, yet scored 5.49 against 3.27 for the gradient fit. It forecast 20 to 280 points too high on four days of spring 2026, because the exact solve made the last layer of the interaction neural network (which lets heating and calendar effects interact) very large. With that network off, the exact fit matched the gradient fit within 0.03 points (Experiment 112).

Adding the BSP reading to the Primaries' fit made the clean forecast worse. At every weight above zero it worsened clean-forecast error by 0.385 to 4.6 points, against a limit of 0.023. An exactly specified synthetic system lost accuracy in the same way, so the cause is untested.

The BSP reading was a weak monitor of metering errors. The closure audit checks whether a BSP's reading equals the sum of its Primaries' readings plus an unmetered remainder (the closure relation). A fit trained on earlier rows found a 25% scale error lasting 30 days in 50% of injections and false-alarmed on 61% of later windows. The verdict is not supported (Experiment 124).

Pooling only the heating curve did not help a substation with 3 months of history. It scored 0.507 points worse than no pooling, with an interval that includes zero (-0.073 to +1.024). The arms also differed in ridge (a penalty on large coefficients), so the test cannot say which shared curves carry the gain of Experiment 158.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text: Whether the convex pooled model N passes a known-answer test is unknown. The gate of Experiment 109 failed as pre-registered, and Experiment 150 was inconclusive. Every onboarding gain above is a screening result.

docs.title: Next-experiment options
docs.text:
No option in this theme is a prerequisite for the production port. The options are in the research plan's priority order, not the hierarchy and pooling page's, which lists options 5 to 7 in its own order.

  1. An option is a drift term, a slowly changing demand level, trained from 2019-09 (plan Part 4). The question is whether it beats the same model on its best shorter window. The forecast-engine page cites Experiment 170 finding drift worsened the score by 0.03 once the Kalman filter was in. Experiment 105's arm that used all years of history plus a drift term scored 2.784 against 3.072 on five substations.
  2. An option is the MVA observation layer (plan Part 5). The question is whether a model of how a meter that reads apparent power relates to real power helps MW sites and recovers MW at MVA sites. It waits for a better capacity fit.
  3. An option is a scale-up of the pooled model to every v1 series it can take (plan N9). It waits for nothing and needs 3 to 5 GPU hours.
  4. An option is to treat the BSP reading as an extra observation in the Kalman filter of each Primary (plan). The question is whether the closure relation, with its unmetered remainder as state noise, helps the Primaries' forecasts. Experiment 124 also proposes using the residual as a separate monitor outside the fit.
  5. An option is to compare a direct forecast at a BSP or GSP with the sum of the Primary forecasts, and to reconcile the two (plan). It depends on the closure audit. The hierarchy page holds the evidence so far (Experiment 204, Experiment 386, and Experiment 426).
  6. An option is to enter metered generators as export-positive nodes at the BSP (plan). The hierarchy page cites Experiment 223, which puts separate unmetered solar and battery dispatch first.
  7. An option is to estimate unmetered wind at the BSP and GSP from the residual (plan). It waits for the closure audit.
  8. An option is to give the heating curve and the calendar families separate penalties in the partly pooled GAM (Experiment 158's next step).
  9. An option is to rerun the pooled exact fit with stronger penalties, or to compare the pooled model without its interaction neural network (Experiment 112's closing section).

docs.title: Parked
docs.text:
Onboarding a substation with little history is parked. The hierarchy and pooling page parks it, and the maintainer's priority is the production port. Parked with it are the pooled-for-new, per-site-for-mature design, and pooling the heating columns of Experiment 114's model split four ways by day type, and the real-substation test of the 3-month gain.

Pooling for a substation with 2 years of history, adding the BSP reading to the Primaries' loss, and learning a substation's own heating offset from 4 weeks are parked. "What does not work" gives the results.

Load-shift event detection and unmetered PV capacity are paused until January. Any pooled experiment that needs either waits with them.

docs.title: Generator forecasting
docs.text:
The current understanding and the options for next work are on the state and next steps page.

For 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms over one validation year, the largest gain was from the Met Office's UKV weather forecast at wind farms, about 0.2 points of capacity at 24 to 54 hours ahead (a small gain: its interval excludes zero but not the pre-registered 0.15), measured on a research archive and not the live feed, so it is an upper limit. No input met its pre-registered gain threshold. Seven of the eight experiments scored forecasts for Tuesday runs from July 2025 to June 2026. The eighth tested a monitor for a lost inverter at the solar farms, and it reliably found only large, long losses. No experiment in this theme is a candidate for production.

UKV is the Met Office's 2 km weather forecast for the UK. Most experiments start from the ENS weather forecast and ask what one added input does. A negative difference in a score means a better forecast, and a point of capacity is 1% of a farm's effective capacity.

At 24 to 54 hours ahead, adding UKV lowers the wind farms' quantile score by 0.198 points (95% interval -0.316 to -0.069), whereas a shuffled copy of UKV changes it by +0.013 (-0.012 to +0.040). Source: experiment 54. The bars for lead day 0 are exploratory.

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
A second weather forecast helps wind farms a little and solar farms by an amount the data cannot resolve. For wind farms, experiment 54 gave UKV's wind to an XGBoost model trained on ENS. The quantile score fell by 0.198 points, a small gain because the interval's near end (-0.069) did not reach the pre-registered 0.15. The gain was -0.413 at one farm and +0.018 at another (exploratory). For solar farms, experiment 57 found -0.035 (95% interval -0.119 to +0.037). That interval excludes gains above 0.12 points and includes the 0.10 that would justify a new weather feed, so the verdict is inconclusive. Both experiments read UKV from the CEDA research archive, whose licence is non-commercial and which differs statistically from the live feed, so each result is a ceiling on what a service could get.

Averaging in two more weather forecasts did not resolve a wind gain. In experiment 52, averaging the quantiles of the best guess with those of the same model fed ICON-EU and the ECMWF high-resolution forecast scored -0.055 (95% interval -0.200 to +0.072) at lead days 1 and 2. The experiment fed runs about half a day older than the ENS run, with uncorrected winds, so it tested a handicapped version of the idea. At days 3 to 6 the blend scored +0.122 (+0.028 to +0.221, worse), because of the spread factor.

Recent power added nothing detectable. In experiment 23, giving the second-stage calibrator (see stages 0, 1a, and 2) the farm's lagged power changed the CRPS by -0.012 for solar (99.58% interval -0.122 to +0.088) and +0.012 for wind (-0.090 to +0.146). The 14-day correction raised the CRPS of the pooled mixture by +0.437 for solar (+0.215 to +0.664) and +0.413 for wind (-0.003 to +0.924), and cut the 5% to 95% band's coverage to 53% to 77%.

A recent-capacity feature and fitted physics gave no gain, and new training inputs gave small ones. These experiments score the CRPS, except experiment 12, which scores the mean absolute error of the 51-member average.

  • Recent-capacity feature (experiment 26): solar -0.018 (98.75% interval -0.162 to +0.096), wind +0.013 (-0.054 to +0.101). One solar farm gained 0.235 points and another lost 0.085.
  • Fitted physics model in place of the XGBoost stage 1 (experiment 29, 6 solar farms): +0.079 (98.75% interval +0.029 to +0.135), worse. Adding the physics output to the XGBoost columns changed nothing (-0.000, -0.015 to +0.018).
  • Satellite sunlight (CAMS) as the training input (experiment 12): -0.140 (99.5% interval -0.277 to -0.044) for solar (6 farms), just short of the pre-registered -0.15. A power-curve base margin for wind gave -0.030 (-0.061 to -0.007), and a training start in 2023 or 2024 moved the error by under 0.3 points.

On 5 solar farms with artificial losses added, only a 25% loss was found reliably (0.84 to 0.86 for the best monitor at 90 days, and 0.86 for the hysteresis rule at 30 days), and a 10% loss mostly was not. Source: experiment 72. The change-point monitor found 0.84 of 25% losses lasting 90 days and 0.45 of those lasting 30 days, which breached the pre-registered stop rule of 0.80, so the verdict is refuted. A hysteresis rule (alarm after 7 valid days at least 10% below normal) found 0.86 of the 25% losses lasting 30 days but 0.13 or less of 10% losses. The monitor beat neither baseline by an interval that excludes zero: against the rolling median its difference in detection rate was +0.045 (97.5% interval -0.015 to +0.090). A farm gives about 3 usable days a week from April to September, and the only real losses held were one farm's three low months.

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text:
No recipe tested here beat the best guess by a pre-registered, resolved margin, so the best guess remains the reference for solar and wind farms. The best guess for farms is a pooled mixture over the 51 ENS members of XGBoost quantile models trained on ERA5, with a spread factor and, for wind, a power-curve base margin. Experiments 23, 26, and 29 used the same mixture without the spread factor as their benchmark.

  • Wind, 24 to 54 hours: an XGBoost model trained on ENS and given UKV's wind scored 5.921, against 6.119 for the same model without UKV and 6.337 for the best guess (experiment 54). The contrast with the best guess is exploratory, -0.416 (-0.693 to -0.136), and UKV comes from the research archive.
  • Solar, 24 to 54 hours: the ENS-trained model scored 3.140 and the best guess 3.247, a difference of -0.107 (-0.327 to +0.053) that cannot be resolved (experiment 57). Adding UKV scored 3.105.

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text: None of the eight experiments is a candidate: all are marked not-for-production. The wind result of experiment 54 would need a matched history of the live UKV feed, and the Open-Meteo history the experiment found reaches lead day 0 only.

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
• Add a shuffled-input arm beside every arm that adds input columns. The shuffled UKV changed the wind score by +0.013 and the solar score by +0.002, so the gain was not extra columns (experiment 54, experiment 57). In experiment 26 the shuffled solar feature scored 0.023 worse than no feature, so a contrast against the shuffle and one against no feature differ (experiment 26). Re-check: a different model or a larger set of columns.
  • Call a UKV result from the CEDA archive a ceiling. The archive is not the live product, so the gain may not reach a service (experiment 54, experiment 57). Re-check: a matched live UKV history.
  • Say whether night rows are in a solar score. Experiment 57's pooled score includes night rows, which score near zero, and its daylight-only contrast was -0.074 (-0.259 to +0.079), so check the size on daylight rows as well (experiment 57). Re-check: a pre-registered daylight-only threshold.
  • Do not add the mean-error 14-day correction to a farm forecast. Observed power minus the median is positive on average for a right-skewed target even when the quantiles are calibrated, so the correction adds a bias, and coverage fell to 53% to 77%. The post hoc median version scored +0.010 (solar) and -0.064 (wind), with intervals that include zero (experiment 23). Re-check: a daily history, which experiment 23 lacked, because its weekly runs left at most two runs in a window.
  • Test recent power in a calibrator trained on pooled members. The calibrator trained on the ENS control member alone scored 0.27 (solar) and 0.31 (wind) points worse than the pooled mixture in the absolute scores (the contrast interval for wind includes zero), so the lag test used a weaker baseline (experiment 23). Re-check: a calibrator trained on pooled members.
  • Fit a spread factor under the weights the blend will use. A factor fitted on earlier months blended under other weights made the blend +0.122 worse at days 3 to 6, against +0.005 without it (experiment 52). Re-check: a factor refitted after each weight change.
  • Feed other weather products the runs the service would read. Experiment 52 used runs about half a day older than ENS and uncorrected winds, so its null result may understate the products (experiment 52). Re-check: 00 UTC runs of the ENS run's date, with bias-corrected winds.
  • Read per-farm contrasts, and treat intervals as covering these farms only. The intervals resample months and not farms. The UKV gain was -0.413 at one wind farm and +0.018 at another, and one solar farm drove the point estimate of experiment 26 (experiment 54, experiment 26). Re-check: more than 6 solar and 3 wind farms.
  • Test fitted orientation against a different irradiance-transposition model. A test with the fitted model's own physics showed a tilt bias of +0.11 degrees, and a different sky model showed +6.2 (experiment 29). Re-check: a different fitted physics model.
  • Score a monitor on the unmodified record as well as on a placebo. The change-point monitor's false-alarm rate was 0.29 per farm-year on the week-shuffled placebo and 0.54 on the real record, where one farm's winter dip raised 6 of 18 alarms (experiment 72). Re-check: another year of record.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text:
• Whether the live UKV feed gives wind farms the gain the research archive did, which needs a matched live history at lead days 1 and 2.
  • Whether solar farms gain from a source of a different kind, such as a satellite-based nowcast, since UKV here added little, and a second global ensemble added under 1% to the sunshine forecast at five Primary substations (experiment 50, as experiment 57 reports it).
  • Whether a wind feature of 75th-percentile power over wind speed cubed helps. It scored -0.061 (-0.107 to -0.025) in experiment 26's contrast C5, one of its 12 contrasts and outside the 4 that decide the verdict.
  • Whether CAMS-trained solar models hold their -0.140 on more than 6 farms or a second year.
  • Whether a loss of 10% or less at a solar farm can be found from outage notices or trip logs, which need labelled events.
  • Whether ENS-trained wind models beat the ERA5-trained best guess at 24 to 54 hours: -0.218 (-0.472 to +0.069) in experiment 54.

The Experiments page lists every experiment in this theme, and the Research plan lists what is planned next.

docs.title: Generator forecasting: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00684 backtest-positive-demand-output-distributions-and-physical-solar-night-zero A positive output family at the four Primaries that cannot go below zero, and a hard zero at every solar half-hour whose sun is at or below the horizon at the middle of the half-hour, remove the negative lower quantiles and the non-zero night quantiles of the backtest files without reducing accuracy. partly supported candidate A Gaussian mixture conditioned on power at or above zero fixes the negative lower quantiles at the four demand series. CRPS improves clearly at two series, is indistinguishable at one, and worsens by 0.03 points of capacity at one, so the model is a candidate to replace the post hoc clamp. A gamma mixture inside the same shared network made two series much worse and is dropped. A hard zero at night at each half-hour's own sun position removes every non-zero solar night quantile, changes no daylight score, and lowers night CRPS, while the share of night observations above q99 rises because the gate sets those quantiles to zero. also relevant 00668 documentation-of-the-one-year-backtest-files-models-training-and-performance Not a hypothesis test. The page documents the five one-year backtest files so that an engineer can re-implement each model and a colleague at NGED can read the files. inconclusive not-for-production The five backtest files forecast better than climatology at every lead band for the Primaries, BSPs, GSPs, and solar, and for wind out to day 10; the wind network is 1.8% worse at days 10 to 14. The gain falls with lead time, for Primaries from 35.3% at days 0 to 1 to 26.9% at days 10 to 14. The files describe one year that overlaps the development months, so the scores are not a ranking. also relevant 00666 one-year-backtest-of-simple-wind-and-solar-networks Descriptive. Over daily forecast origins from 2025-11-01 to 2026-10-31, the networks of experiment 659 (wind S, solar PLP), retrained monthly (wind) or quarterly (solar) on data available before each refit, produce calibrated 11-quantile forecasts out to 14 days, and solar PLP trained on leads out to 336 h scores no worse at days 10 to 14 than climatology. inconclusive not-for-production The two simple networks produce complete, sorted 11-quantile forecasts to 14 days for 3 wind farms and 6 solar farms, and wind S matches experiment 659 on the rows both cover. Solar PLP at days 10 to 14 beats climatology from April to September but not from November to March. Its median is high in spring and low in autumn (seasonal or caused by refit age; this experiment cannot separate them), its lower tail is about three times too frequent, and its upper tail on very sunny days is still too low, so use the 10 to 14 day solar band with care. primary 00659 simple-shared-network-with-fixed-physics-lite-power-wind-and-solar A pooled network with two hidden layers of 64 units and a three-component Gaussian mixture, given only the ensemble mean and spread of raw weather, scores within the minimum detectable effect of the current default of its technology (wind default 2, solar a2_member). Adding the mean and spread of a fixed physics-lite power across the 51 members lowers the score further. partly supported candidate A small shared neural network that sees only the average and spread of the ensemble weather forecasts is no worse than the current, more elaborate defaults for the 3 wind farms and the 6 solar farms over the 5 development months. Its wind lead over wind default 2 is mostly the default scoring badly on idle readings set to zero, so read it as "no worse", not "better". A hand-written power curve as an extra input made no difference for wind and a small one for solar. The upper tail on very sunny days is still too low in every arm. primary 00631 bsp-group-sum-with-metered-generators-against-direct-bsp-forecast Experiment 629 found that sums of the 16 Primaries beneath two bulk supply points (BSPs) put 31% to 79% of actual flows below their q05 (nominal 5%), and that the metered wind and solar series beneath the BSP explained much of the gap (R squared 0.94 at Skegness). The claim here is that, once those metered farms are added to the sum together with a fitted remainder, a coupled scenario set (J3, the Schaake shuffle, or J5, the fitted copula) puts the q05 and q95 exceedance of the BSP flow within the binomial error of nominal at both BSPs, and beats independent draws (J0) on CRPS. not supported not-for-production Adding the nine metered wind and solar farms to the sum of Primaries fixes most of the export-side tail miss of Primaries-only sums (Skegness 41.7% to 3.0% of actual flows below the q05, on this experiment's rows), but the import side swings from too wide or about right (Boston 0.1%, Skegness 4.4% above the q95) to too narrow (14.3% and 32.6%), and no sum has both tails near 5% at both bulk supply points (BSPs). Coupling the scenarios (Schaake shuffle or fitted copula) improves the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) by 2.6% to 7.7%, so coupling matters once the farms are in. The direct forecast of each BSP meter is still the safer tail forecast, which means the deliverable should be a direct BSP forecast beside any node scenarios. also relevant 00628 quantile-form-client-side-scenario-rehydration NGED reads stored forecasts from S3 and builds scenarios in Python. The stored forecasts of experiments 425, 429, and 430 hold 11 quantiles (0.01, 0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.40, 0.50, 0.60, 0.75, 0.90, 0.95, 0.99) per site and half-hour. The claim is that a client holding only these 11 quantiles, plus a small dependence table, draws 1,000 coherent scenarios per run that score within 1% of the 51 scenarios the pipeline builds (experiment 436's J5 and J3) on CRPS, and within 1 percentage point on exceedance at the 0.01, 0.05, 0.95, and 0.99 levels, provided the client extends the quantile function past the outer levels with a good tail rule. partly supported not-for-production NGED can rebuild the marginal forecasts and a Schaake-shuffle coupling from 11 stored quantiles per site and half-hour plus a small dependence table. 1,000 client-drawn scenarios score within 0.3% of the 51 scenarios the pipeline builds on CRPS, and a Schaake shuffle of 51 stored past paths matches the pipeline's shuffle on the variogram score. The only loss we measured is for the fitted copula on solar farms (6.6% worse on the variogram score). The pipeline's version also uses the weather ensemble's member ranks, which the quantiles do not carry, and that is the likely cause. Mixture parameters were not needed for any of this. The tails of the stored quantiles are too narrow for any of the three tail rules to fix. also relevant 00627 scenario-subset-selection-from-51-coherent-paths NGED will run a handful of power-flow studies by hand, so they need K of the 51 coherent member paths (K = 3, 5, 10) that cover the distribution of the 51, without labelling any path. A path that is low wind on day 1 need not be low wind on day 2, so a label such as "the low-wind scenario" does not carry over. We test whether picking K paths by stratifying on one summary of the run (S) or by clustering the 51 joint paths (C) covers the 51-path distribution better than a simple random sample (R). partly supported not-for-production Picking 5 of the 51 forecast paths by cutting them into 5 equal groups on one summary and taking one path from each covers their spread better than picking 5 at random, in every month, but still misses the tails: the stratified rules leave a gap of 11% to 12% of the range at the 5th percentile and 13% to 14% at the 95th. For a bulk supply point's limit, an observed daily peak export beat the largest of 5 chosen paths on 12% of days (1.6% for all 51); 10 paths chosen by that substation's own peak export came closest (6.3%, against 7.3% for a random 10). NGED should treat 10 paths as a minimum when the tail matters. also relevant 00625 coherent-members-from-quantiles-k-sweep-and-path-checks Experiments 434 and 436 already scored independent draws (IND), ensemble copula coupling (ECC), a Schaake shuffle (SS), and member-wise quantiles (MW) at 51 paths. A Schaake shuffle gave the wind farms and solar farms variogram scores 28% to 43% below IND but gave the 16 Primaries nothing. This experiment tests three new claims. (1) SS paths cut to K = 10 lose under 2% of the variogram score of K = 51. (2) A Schaake shuffle that orders by anomaly paths (observed power minus the mean of the same clock time on the four preceding same-weekdays) gives the Primaries a variogram score at least 5% below IND, because observed-power paths mix the seasonal level with the weather anomaly. (3) SS paths put neighbouring solar farms in opposite sky states less often than IND does and about as often as the observations do. partly supported not-for-production NGED can get coherent wind-farm and solar-farm paths from a Schaake shuffle of past observed paths, which scores 34% below independent draws across the farms, and 20 paths lose 2% to 3% of the 51-path score across the farms (10 paths lose 5% to 11%). The 16 Primaries gain nothing from any coupling we tried, including a shuffle of anomaly paths, because their errors are only weakly correlated, so independent draws are close to right there. Experiment 436's joint-block scores were wrong (a reshape mixed members and nodes) and are replaced by the values here, which show no difference between couplings on the joint block. also relevant 00618 solar-effective-capacity-sunny-rows-and-known-answer-test A farm's capacity moves rarely, so a piecewise-constant level fitted to one daily number taken from its very sunny half-hours (clear-sky index at least 0.9, clear-sky irradiance at least 700 W/m2, six half-hours in a row) recovers injected capacity steps, raises few false steps, and shows whether Solar A, Solar B, and Solar D produced more in 2021 to 2023 than now. partly supported not-for-production Very sunny half-hours are enough to find a sudden change of 8% or more in a solar farm's capacity at Solar A, B, C, and F, with at most 0.7 false changes a year; Solar D has too few of them and needs a change of 12%. Applied to the real histories, the method finds a fall of 12.6% at Solar A (its output in 2021 to 2023 was 14% higher than in 2025 to 2026, as experiment 453 saw), but at Solar B the output in 2021 to 2023 was 11% lower, not higher, and Solar C and Solar F show no change. The estimate lags a slow fall, so a smooth drift of 10% in three years leaves the final level 2% to 5% too high. also relevant 00617 wind-turbine-step-capacity-known-answer-and-fit The effective capacity of a metered wind farm moves in whole-turbine steps. A hidden Markov model on the daily upper envelope of power in the saturation range of the power curve recovers injected turbine outages of 2 or more turbines lasting 14 days or longer. refuted not-for-production A hidden Markov model that looks for whole-turbine drops in the daily top of wind-farm power cannot reliably find outages shorter than about two months, and it raises 2 to 4 false alarms a year on data that hold no outage. The cause is too few days with wind strong enough to show full output, not the model, so the effective capacity of the metered wind farms cannot be tracked this way. primary 00615 bakeoff-wind-and-solar-development-month-backtests On the 5 development months, one candidate per technology (wind default 2 for the wind farms, a2_member for the solar farms) scores better than the other candidates of its technology in the headline band, and the stored and rebuilt forecasts can be scored by the one set of rules that experiment 609 fixed for the final test. partly supported not-for-production For the 3 wind farms, the physics-plus-neural-network forecast scores clearly better than a seasonal average and a little better than the older XGBoost forecast. For the 6 solar farms, the neural network scores better than the simpler references, but its lead over the additive-curve (GAM) reference is within the noise. Refitting it every quarter instead of every year made no detectable difference, and its upper band is too low on very sunny days (17% of observations above the 99% line, against a target of 1%). also relevant 00609 bakeoff-wind-and-solar-design The wind and solar part of the final bake-off can be run from stored fitted artefacts and a small number of refits for under 8 GPU-h in total, and every scoring choice can be fixed before any candidate is scored on the final test. inconclusive not-for-production Fitting is cheap for wind and solar: one wind head refit takes about 25 seconds per seed and one solar refit about 1 minute per seed. The expensive part is the data. The ensemble inputs of both technologies must be extended to 2026-10-31 by experiment 607 first, and the nine generators have had no exact-zero reading since 2026-03-26. We therefore score the generators in two ways, on the rows present and on a version that fills night half-hours of the solar farms with zero, and we do not compare final-test scores with development scores unless the same filter was applied to both. also relevant 00513 lagless-demand-network-whole-day-price-shape-at-training-time The Market Index price of a whole local day, known exactly at training time, carries information about price-following embedded batteries and gas engines behind a Primary, so a lag-free demand network that sees it in training forecasts those Primaries better. At serving time no price exists, so this experiment first asks the upper-bound question: does the true shape, given at both training and scoring time, help at all? not supported not-for-production Even a perfect, hindsight price shape for the whole day does not lower the lag-free demand network's error at NGED's Primaries by a measurable amount, and the oracle gains no more at the Primaries with a known battery or gas engine. The oracle gain is the bound for a training-time-only price arm (price dropout, an auxiliary price head, or a teacher network), and that bound is not resolvable from zero, so those arms were not run. An option for batteries and price-following generators is to model their output as a separate target or a subtracted term; whether to test it belongs to the roadmap. also relevant 00505 rolling-p99-9-effective-capacity-for-wind-and-solar If effective capacity is the 99.9th percentile of the power in the most recent 730 (or 365) days instead of all earlier power, then one rule serves wind and solar: the pooled share of actuals above the table-P q99 stays at most 1.5% for both technologies, no series is worse than 1.5% (except a series with under 8,000 valid half-hours), and no series loses score beyond its margin, because a trailing window follows a level shift in a series' output (Solar A, B, and D produced more in 2021 to 2023 according to experiment 453, a hypothesis that covers April to August only). not supported not-for-production Setting each series' capacity from only the last 730 days of power keeps wind unchanged and brings the pooled share of actuals above the 99% quantile to 0.85% for wind and 1.45% for solar, and Solar A's score worsening against the old capacity falls from 2.3% to 0.4%. It still misses the rule written down before any fit at Solar B (1.506%) and when Solar C or Solar D is dropped, so wind keeps its all-history rule and solar keeps the old capacity at Solar A and Solar E. primary 00499 two-constant-tail-widening-in-place-of-table-p-for-wind-and-solar Table P (a factor per farm, lead band, and tail quantile, plus experiment 451's clip) can be replaced for wind and for solar by two constants (one scaling q01 and q05, one scaling q95 and q99), fitted on earlier months only, with no loss of tail calibration. inconclusive candidate Two numbers per farm tune the wind and solar tails about as well as table P's 16 factors per farm did on the stored forecasts: pooled coverage differs by under 0.005 and tail pinball loss by under 1% (intervals reach 2%). The stored year is too short to certify that formally, so table P stays for now. For solar, table P leaves 1.98% of actuals above q99 against the 1.5% limit; one pair for all six solar sites meets that limit (1.50%) but misses table P's q05 coverage by 0.0145. also relevant 00498 solar-e-annual-refit-schedule-only-read At Solar E the 1.28% loss that experiment 493 reported (its contrast C3) comes mostly from the network design (one pass against the 51-member encoder), and the schedule-only loss (annual against quarterly refits of the encoder, contrast C2) is smaller than 1%. supported not-for-production Refitting the Solar E neural network once a year instead of every quarter raises its quantile score by about 0.3% (lower is better), which is less than the 1% limit, so Solar E does not block annual refits. The 1.3% loss that experiment 493 reported at Solar E comes mostly (about four-fifths) from using the simpler one-pass network instead of the 51-member encoder, and about one-fifth from the refit schedule. also relevant 00493 solar-annual-against-quarterly-refits Refitting the pooled solar network once a year, on data to the end of August 2025, scores within 1% of refitting it every quarter, for the one-pass network and for the 51-member encoder, so a production solar forecast needs one refit a year instead of four. supported candidate The solar neural network can be refitted once a year instead of every quarter: for both networks we tested, the quantile score changes by less than 0.6%, inside the 1% limit, with little margin for the encoder and from one refit date and one scored year. One further comparison fails: at Solar E the one-pass network with annual refits is 1.3% worse than the 51-member encoder with quarterly refits, and most of that gap comes from the network design and not from the schedule. also relevant 00482 best-models-performance-analysis-injected-shifts-and-wind-references A forecast that reads lagged power follows an injected load shift that no neighbour mirrors more than a forecast that reads no lagged power does, the forecast that mixes lagged and lagless heads (K2-S1) limits the harm of an unmirrored shift, and the pooled plain network (A-pool), which never saw an injected shift in training, follows the shift most. partly supported not-for-production A forecast that mixes lagged and lagless heads (K2-S1) was in none of the eight scenarios meaningfully worse than the lagless forecast when we injected load shifts into its lags, and it was a little better in three. The pooled neural network that was never trained on shifted lags (A-pool) is the one that suffers: it is up to 2.45 points of capacity worse, and its 95% quantile covers only 72% of actuals in the worst scenario. At the wind farms, member_plain is level with research default 2 and 0.4 points better than research default 1. also relevant 00476 generator-x-first-forecast-dispatch-lags-weather-price H1: Generator X's output has autocorrelation (short spells, a two-peak daily cycle) that a mixture density network fed the origin lags and calendar inputs can use, so it scores better than same-hour climatology and than last-output persistence over days 1 to 10. H2: ensemble weather at the site and lagged market price add nothing, because experiment 473 found no usable relationship with weather proxies and only a weak one with price. not supported not-for-production Generator X's output cannot be forecast better than a plain climatology (the usual output at the same half-hour, weekday type, and season) with the inputs we hold: the best arm gains 0.015 points of quantile score, below the 0.019-point noise floor. The network does sharpen the tails (a lower loss at the 1% and 99% quantiles than climatology) but loses in the middle of the distribution, and it cannot predict whether Generator X imports or exports. The next step is a different kind of input, such as the operator's dispatch schedule, and not a better network. primary 00473 three-generators-data-look H0: each of Generators X, Y, and Z is a series whose half-hours the data-validation checklist finds usable and whose regime (running hours, idle level, sign) a weather-and-calendar forecast could describe, so none needs a dispatch or price input. refuted not-for-production Generator X is the only one of the three with a current, long record, and its output shows a weak relationship with price, so it is the one candidate for a first forecast. Generator Y has been inactive (output at or below 3.9% of its maximum) since mid-2024 and Generator Z has only 400 active half-hours, so neither can be scored on current behaviour. Stage 2 should cover Generator X, and Generator Y only if the maintainer accepts folds that end in mid-2024. primary 00468 best-models-performance-analysis-with-time-series-graphs The best forecasters' failures are concentrated in a few identifiable situations (a stormy week for wind, a cloudy week for solar, and the first days of a load shift that the lagged power does not reflect), and a set of time-series graphs makes those situations visible. partly supported not-for-production The wind and solar forecasts keep their tails close to nominal over a year, but single months miss by a factor of two or three, so a service that relies on one month's tails should widen its bands. In seven real demand events, the forecast that reads lagged power (S1) was less accurate than the forecast that does not in three, and the mixture K2-S1 was more accurate in six, so lagged power helps in some events and hurts in others. The injected-shift scenarios and the wind reference contrasts are not done yet. also relevant 00466 wind-and-solar-recency-weighting If each training row's loss is weighted by 0.5 to the power of its age at the refit divided by a half-life, then the quantile score of the wind neural network member_plain and the solar neural networks g0_onepass and a2_member improves, because farms change efficiency slowly and each upgrade of the ECMWF ensemble shifts the statistics of the inputs. not supported not-for-production Weighting recent training rows more does not improve the wind or solar forecasts. The wind network scores 0.22% to 0.25% worse with half-lives of 9 and 4.5 months, and the best solar arm gains 0.14%, which is less than the difference between two fits of the same network. The wind and solar neural networks are insensitive to recency within the range that the short history allows, so this line closes. primary 00464 solar-efficiency-history-stage-0-post-hoc-scaling Part of the solar forecast error is a slow change in each farm's efficiency (soiling, degradation, a level shift). The ratio of actual power to the power the observed weather should have produced, taken as a trailing median over weeks to months, estimates that efficiency, so multiplying the stored forecast quantiles by it lowers the quantile score at the farms whose output level changed (Solar A, Solar B, and Solar D, from experiment 453) and leaves the other farms unchanged. not supported not-for-production Scaling the stored solar forecasts by each farm's recent efficiency (actual power over the power the observed weather should have produced) did not lower the quantile score at any of the six farms, including the three whose output level changed between years. The best of 18 methods moved one farm by -0.46% and made the others worse, so slow efficiency change is not the error that limits the solar forecast. This was tested on the stored a2_member forecasts only. The median is slightly better calibrated when the factor is fitted to the wind that the farms' power implies than when it is fitted to ERA5 on the same rows (1.7 percentage points), but the quantile score is not better. primary 00303 wind-adapter-in-production-setting Experiment 285 found that, with ERA5 as the weather, a small neural adapter in front of the physics core of a wind farm scored better than XGBoost. On the 51 ensemble members in the scored year, an adapter fine-tuned on the ensemble hindcast beats XGBoost plus experiment 259's offset table (the benchmark that matters), because the adapter corrects the wind speed itself and the table corrects only the power. partly supported not-for-production A small neural correction of the wind speed, fitted to ERA5 and run on the 51 ensemble members, does about as well as XGBoost with a lookup table of offsets (0.09 points better, too little to justify porting). Fitting the correction on the one year of ensemble hindcasts made the forecast worse, probably because that year differs from the scored year; we did not test the cause. primary 00288 pooled-head-on-public-wind-farms A neural head that adds 11 quantile offsets to the XGBoost wind forecast (R0) and was trained on dozens of public onshore wind farms (metered output from Elexon's Balancing Mechanism Reporting Service) lowers the quantile score of the three metered wind farms (W1 to W3) against R0 alone, and a head trained on the pool beats the same head trained on W1 to W3 only, because experiment 259's head had too few farm-years to learn a correction that transfers. A second hypothesis: XGBoost keeps improving as the training history grows from 12 to 48 months while the physics core is flat after 24 months, and a pool of public farms replaces the missing history. not supported not-for-production Training the correction on 40 public wind farms did not help the forecasts for the three NGED wind farms. Applied directly, it made them worse, because the public farms' capacity, turbine rating, and hub height let the head memorise each farm. Without those inputs it did no harm, and after a short fine-tune on the three farms' own data it gained about as much as a simple offset table fitted on those farms, so the public farms added nothing measurable. primary 00285 wind-effective-wind-adapters A small bounded correction of the wind speed that the physics core of a wind farm reads, learned from the wind direction, the 10 m to 100 m speed ratio, the 2 m temperature, and the hour of day, closes at least half of XGBoost's lead over the core on the three metered wind farms (W1, W2, W3) when ERA5 is the weather. A correction of each ensemble member's wind speed towards ERA5's removes the ensemble's low bias. partly supported candidate The physics model of a wind farm matched XGBoost once a small neural network adjusted the wind speed it takes as input, so XGBoost's lead can be reproduced by a smooth correction of wind speed. On the ensemble weather, mapping each member's wind speed to ERA5's helped by 0.31 points but fixed only a small part of the ensemble's low bias, and a lookup table of power offsets by lead day helped more. primary 00276 wind-xgboost-vs-physics-gap-diagnostics The XGBoost model beats the physics core on the three metered wind farms (W1, W2, W3) because it learns the metering noise (the reactive-power floor of the apparent-power series, the deadband, and the dip near cut-in) that the physics core ignores. refuted not-for-production XGBoost beats the physics model of the wind farms because it corrects the wind speed using the wind direction, the 10 m wind, and the hour of day. It does not learn the metering noise: the lead is as large on rows without idle readings as on all rows. No change to the physics model's power curve, spread, or scale closed more than about a sixth of the gap, so the next step is a flexible correction to the physics model's wind speed. primary 00262 wind-aifs-members-and-climatology-by-lead For the three metered wind farms (W1 to W3), a lead-dependent mixture of the ECMWF ensemble's member forecasts, the AIFS ensemble's member forecasts (both run through experiment 230's ERA5-trained XGBoost wind model A0r), and climatology lowers the quantile score and the 0.99 pinball loss against the ECMWF members alone, after both are corrected by a table of offsets per lead day, quantile, and farm; and a small neural gate that reads the two ensembles' spread and disagreement chooses better weights than weights by lead alone. partly supported candidate Adding the AIFS ensemble's wind forecasts to the ECMWF ensemble's improves the wind forecast at 3 to 6 days ahead, by about 5% of the quantile score, but does not improve the high-power tail that matters for curtailment. Climatology and a small neural network that picks the mixing weights add nothing once the table of offsets has corrected the common low bias. The AIFS arms also need testing on a second year, because one year of Tuesday runs sets the weights. primary 00261 wind-low-bias-decomposition The low bias in the three metered wind farms' forecast (observed power below the physics core's median on 34% of rows, not 50%) comes mostly from the ensemble's weather input, not from the core, the farms, or the mixing of the 51 members. partly supported not-for-production The wind forecast's low median comes mostly from the ensemble's weather: its 10 m and 100 m wind speeds are slower than ERA5's, and the same physics core fed ERA5 wind has 52.8% of rows below its median. Mixing the 51 members adds about a tenth of the shift, and training the physics core and the XGBoost model on 9 months of ensemble forecasts removes between a fifth and a third of the gap. The fix to test next is a correction of the ensemble's wind speeds before the model reads them. primary 00259 wind-plant-plus-quantile-offset-head For the three metered wind farms (W1 to W3), a small neural network that reads the 51-member mixture of a wind model and the ensemble's wind summaries, and adds an offset to each of 11 quantiles, lowers the quantile score against the wind model alone (R1, the physics core), matches the XGBoost best guess (R0), and lowers the pinball loss at the 0.99 quantile, once it can learn from daily runs of the ensemble forecast over 15 months (about 440 runs) instead of the 13 to 40 Tuesday runs that experiment 221's head saw. partly supported candidate A correction learned from 15 months of daily ensemble forecasts lowered the wind forecast's quantile score by 4.5% to 5.5% on the three metered wind farms, but the neural network and the ensemble's wind summaries were not what earned it. The 51 ensemble members' median sits too low: the observed power was below the physics core's median on 34% of rows, not 50%. A lookup table with one offset per lead day, quantile, and farm recovers 92% of the gain. The open question is where that low bias comes from. primary 00256 wind-temperature-density-shear-columns Adding 2 m air temperature (arm T1) to the six wind columns of the XGBoost wind model lowers the quantile score on the three metered wind farms (W1 to W3), because air density and stability change the power a turbine produces at a given forecast wind speed. A density column (T2) carries the same information as temperature, and a shear and solar-elevation column set (T3) adds a further gain at night. partly supported candidate Giving the XGBoost wind forecast the air temperature helps a little, about 0.7% of the score, and the evidence just misses the bar we set beforehand. Columns that carry the time of day and the season help more, and their gain sits in daytime and summer rows. That pattern is not explained by the air density we could test (a function of temperature alone) or by shear, and it is consistent with a correction for biases in the ensemble wind at certain hours and seasons. A repeat on other months would show whether the time-of-day and season columns still help. primary 00242 wind-physics-core-part-3-member-tails For the three metered wind farms (W1, W2, W3), running each of the 51 ensemble members through an ERA5-trained wind model and mixing the 51 forecasts gives better 0.01 and 0.99 quantiles than running the model once on the ensemble mean of the weather inputs and applying the same spread factor, because the model is non-linear near cut-in and rated wind, so a model of the mean weather is not the mean of the model. supported not-for-production Keep running all 51 ensemble members through the wind model. Running the ensemble mean once raises the error at the 99% quantile by a factor of 2.1 for the physics model and 3.3 for XGBoost, probably because averaging the members removes the high winds that produce full output, and the single spread factor tried here does not repair that. The physics model and XGBoost differ by under 0.01 points on the tails, so the choice between them does not matter here. primary 00240 no-xgboost-forecast-sprinkle-part-2 A small XGBoost residual model on the plant forecast's median error, an XGBoost spread model for the quantile offsets around it, or both, close at least half of the gap in quantile score between the XGBoost-free metered solar forecast (the plant fed the mean and spread of 51 ensemble members, experiment 224's arm 3) and the full XGBoost forecast (experiment 224's arm 5) at 12 to 36 hour leads. partly supported candidate For solar farms, the best way to add XGBoost to the physical plant forecast is to let XGBoost predict the spread around the plant's mean, not to correct the mean: that forecast scores 4.3% better than the plant alone and 1.6% better than full XGBoost, and wins at the upper tail that matters for curtailment. Correcting the mean with XGBoost made the quantile score 0.18 points worse, about as much as a model trained on shuffled residuals. For wind, experiment 230's XGBoost stage on the physics core closes 71% of the gap to full XGBoost at 12 to 36 hours, and 44% over all leads. also relevant 00234 no-xgboost-forecast-audit-part-1 For Primary substation demand, a metered solar farm, and a metered wind farm, the best forecast that uses no XGBoost anywhere scores within 2% of the quantile score of the best forecast that uses XGBoost, at 12 to 36 hour leads. partly supported candidate An XGBoost-free forecast of Primary substation demand scores 7.5% better than BG2, the XGBoost best guess, at 12 to 36 hours ahead, on one year and six substations. The XGBoost-free solar and wind forecasts score 2.8% and 5.0% worse, and lose at the 0.01, 0.05, and 0.95 quantiles. Only the solar plant model's 0.99 quantile beats XGBoost, and that is the tail that matters for curtailment. The next experiment tests small XGBoost components inside the XGBoost-free solar and wind forecasts. also relevant 00233 wind-physics-core-part-2-capacity-availability For the three metered wind farms (W1, W2, W3), the ratio of observed power to the power that the fitted physics core of experiment 230 expects, taken over the half-hours when the core expects rated power and averaged over a trailing 60 days, shows an injected capacity loss of 25% within 60 days of the loss starting, at every farm, and raises no alarm on a slow drift of the observed power of the size seen in the flat top of metered solar farms (experiment 183). not supported not-for-production A monitor that compares observed power with the wind-turbine model only in strong wind, where the power curve is flat, cannot show a 25% loss of capacity in time at any of the three wind farms, because strong-wind half-hours are rare: a trailing 60-day window holds enough of them to give a reading on only 21% of days at W1, 45% at W2, and 5% at W3. A variant added after the results were seen, which uses every half-hour at 20% of maximum output or more, finds a 25% loss with a median delay of 27 days at W1, 52 at W2, and 34 at W3, but a smooth 9% seasonal swing then raises false alarms, and a 10% loss is found at only 27% to 73% of start dates. The next step to test is a monitor on the whole power curve with a seasonal baseline; the real series also shows single months with low output (W2 in winter 2025 to 2026, W3 in 2024 to 2025) that nothing here explains. primary 00230 wind-physics-core-part-1 For the three metered wind farms (W1, W2, W3), a physics core fitted by gradient descent (hub-height wind from the ERA5 100 m and 10 m speeds, an air-density correction, a smooth monotone power curve with a cut-out, and an idle layer for the reactive-power floor of the MVA series) run through the 51 ENS members scores within 0.1 points of capacity of the XGBoost best guess (experiment 33) on the quantile score, and the measured gap between the ERA5-input ceiling and a simple power curve is under 0.02 points, which would mean the 25 km weather cell, and not the turbine physics, limits the forecast. not supported not-for-production A physics model of a wind farm, fitted to the three metered farms, forecasts them slightly worse than the XGBoost best guess, so it should not replace it. Most of the forecast error comes from the error in the ensemble wind forecast, not from the power curve: with ERA5 wind as the forecast, the same physics core cuts the score by 43%. The idle layer and the small neural adapter add nothing, and training the physics core on ERA5 instead of the ensemble control member improves it by 0.4 points. primary 00223 dp-bsp-generators-as-children-and-double-count-test The metered generators that NGED lists under a bulk supply point (BSP) are children of that BSP as much as the Primaries are: the BSP's reading is the Primaries' demand plus the unmetered load minus the generators' output. If the Primaries' readings already include a generator's output, adding that generator to the sum double-counts it. This experiment first tests, from the readings alone, which generators the BSP's remainder carries and which a Primary already carries, and then asks how much the BSP's forecast improves when the generators the BSP carries are summed as children. inconclusive not-for-production The two bulk supply points' readings move with the metered generators that NGED lists under them, and the Primaries' readings show only small coefficients on the same generators. The size of the movement is not the clean one-for-one that adding the generator to the sum needs, so the experiment did not test whether adding the generators improves the bulk supply point forecast. A better test is to separate the unmetered solar and the battery's price-driven dispatch first. also relevant 00221 wind-correction-head-on-stored-predictions A small neural-network head, fed the nine quantiles of the wind best guess (experiment 33's ERA5-trained mixture over the 51 ENS members, with the power-curve base margin and the spread factor) plus the ensemble mean and spread of the 100 m wind speed and the direction sector, lowers the quantile score at lead days 1 and 2 against the best guess by at least 0.1 points of capacity. The head is pooled over the three farms and trained on earlier months only. inconclusive not-for-production Training a small neural network to correct our wind-farm forecast did not help at 1 to 2 days ahead: the best version scored 0.05 points better and the version that also sees the weather forecast scored 0.18 points worse, with intervals that include zero. With only three farms and 9 scored months, the network may learn the months it trains on and narrow the forecast band too far on the next month. The stored forecast's band was already near the best width. A different kind of correction, or many more farms, is the next thing to try. primary 00210 wind-idle-noise-mva-artefact H0: the noise in the three metered wind series (W1 and W3 in MVA, W2 in MW) occurs only at low wind speed, because the meters have a deadband, the reactive power drifts, and reactive power control runs only while the turbines turn. If H0 holds, a rule on ERA5 100 m wind speed alone, with no observed power, finds the rows to drop from training and evaluation. not supported not-for-production The noisy near-zero rows in the three metered wind series do not occur only at low wind. A rule on ERA5 wind speed alone drops about 9% to 15% of half-hours but still misses about 60% of the idle-band half-hours, probably because ERA5's 25 km cell is a poor guide to the wind at each farm (untested). The rows this experiment flags are stored for the main wind experiment to use, and W3's first 2 years are a candidate to drop. primary 00102 simp1-simplifying-the-bg2-best-guess-before-production A single weekly-refitted XGBoost model without the three power lags, the solar offset, the 14-day correction, or the blend scores within 0.15 points of capacity of BG2 at the 16 Primary substations, within 0.30 at the 4 bulk and grid supply points, within 0.10 at the 6 solar farms, and within 0.30 at the 3 wind farms. We expect the Primary claim to fail and the other three to be close calls (see the prediction). Separately, the solar offset helps most where it should, at midday in summer at the 5 Primary substations that have one. partly supported candidate Removing the three recent-power inputs from the best-guess XGBoost forecast makes it worse at Primary substations (by 0.36 points of capacity once one substation's commissioning months are cut, and most of that comes from one substation whose demand level fell in March 2026) and at supply points (by 0.28). The wind farm forecasts lost nothing measurable and the solar farm forecasts little. The blend of 5 models can shrink to 3, and the solar offset lowers the score by 0.18 points at midday in summer at the 5 substations that use it. also relevant 00072 p35-step-loss-monitor-for-solar-farms For the 5 metered solar farms with a long record (labelled A, B, C, D, and F), a monitor can find a loss of generating capacity, such as a lost inverter, from the farm's own power telemetry. The monitor divides each day's power by the power a physics model expects on clear, unclipped hours, divides that ratio again by the same day's ratio at the other farms, and fits a piecewise-constant level to the result with an L0 penalty (an optimal-partitioning change-point fit). It finds a 25% loss that lasts 30 days, starting from April to September, within 28 days of its onset in at least 80% of injections, at no more than 0.5 false alarms per farm-year. It finds more injected losses of 10% than two simpler monitors that are tuned to the same false-alarm rate: a rolling median of the same signal, and the hysteresis rule of the capacity studies (called HYST here) run on the same signal. refuted not-for-production A change-point monitor of a solar farm's daily output found 0.84 of 25% losses lasting 90 days and 0.45 of those lasting 30 days, below the 0.80 the plan needed, so the verdict is refuted. On 10% losses it did not beat a rolling median by an interval that excludes zero (+0.045, 97.5% interval -0.015 to +0.090). primary 00057 product-trained-xgboost-solar-farms For the six metered solar farms, an XGBoost quantile model trained on ENS and given UKV's shortwave radiation, total cloud, and temperature as extra input columns scores lower on the quantile score at lead hours 24 to 54 than the same model trained on ENS alone, with every arm trained on the same window, rows, and seeds. UKV is read from the CEDA archive, which is not the live product, so the contrast is a ceiling read. inconclusive not-for-production Giving UKV forecasts to an ENS-trained solar-farm model changed the quantile score by -0.035 points of capacity at 1 to 2 days ahead (95% interval -0.119 to +0.037), which is too small to resolve. The data cannot show a gain and cannot rule out the 0.10-point gain that would justify a new weather feed. UKV helped the six solar farms far less than it helped the three wind farms. primary 00054 product-trained-xgboost-wind-farms For the three metered wind farms, an XGBoost quantile model trained on ENS and given UKV's wind as extra input columns scores lower on the quantile score at lead days 1 and 2 than the same model trained on ENS alone, with every arm trained on the same window, rows, and seeds. UKV is read from the CEDA archive, which is not the live product, so the contrast is a ceiling read. small gain not-for-production Giving the Met Office's UKV wind forecast to an ENS-trained wind-farm model lowered the quantile score by about 0.2 points of capacity at 1 to 2 days ahead (95% interval 0.07 to 0.32), and a shuffled-UKV placebo shows the gain is information and not extra columns. The UKV data come from a research archive and not the live feed, so the gain is an upper limit on what a service could get. primary 00052 more-nwp-products-for-wind-farms For the three metered wind farms, averaging the quantiles of the experiment 33 wind best guess (the ERA5-trained mixture over the 51 ENS members, with the power-curve margin and the spread factor) with the quantiles of the same ERA5-trained model fed ICON-EU's and IFS 0.25 degree's forecast wind lowers the quantile score at 1 to 2 days ahead, with weights chosen only on earlier months. inconclusive not-for-production Averaging the wind best guess with two extra weather forecasts, ICON-EU and the ECMWF high-resolution forecast, scored 0.055 points of capacity better at lead days 1 and 2, but the 95% interval (-0.200 to +0.072) includes zero. Three wind farms cannot show whether the extra forecasts help, and the blend scored 0.122 worse at days 3 to 6. primary 00029 physics-stage1-solar-pytorch For the 6 metered solar farms, replacing the XGBoost stage 1 with a differentiable PyTorch physics model (priors on tilt, azimuth, DC capacity, and the AC-to-DC ratio, fitted to metered power with CAMS irradiance and ERA5 temperature), applied to each ENS member and followed by a per-farm quantile XGBoost stage 2, gives a lower continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) than the pooled XGBoost mixture of experiment 00020. refuted not-for-production C1, PyTorch physics stage 1 minus the XGBoost stage 1: +0.079 (98.75% interval +0.029 to +0.135), worse. primary 00026 capacity-features-solar-wind For the 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms, giving each farm's stage 1a quantile model a feature that states the farm's recent effective capacity (the 99th percentile of its power at the steps with the most irradiance for solar, or the most wind for wind, over the trailing 28 days) lowers the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) of the pooled mixture below that of the same model without the feature. inconclusive not-for-production C1, the single 28-day feature minus no feature: solar -0.018 (98.75% interval -0.162 to +0.096), wind +0.013 (-0.054 to +0.101). primary 00023 lagged-power-and-error-correction-solar-wind For the 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms, giving the stage 2 calibrator the farm's recent observed power (lagged power, or summaries of the latest day), or shifting the forecast by its own recent error (the 14-day correction of experiments 00017 and 00019), lowers the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) below that of the same calibrator without recent power. inconclusive not-for-production C1, lagged power added to the calibrator: solar -0.012 (99.58% interval -0.122 to +0.088), wind +0.012 (-0.090 to +0.146). primary 00012 solar-wind-stage1a-inputs-cams-and-training-start For the ERA5-trained stage 1a XGBoost model of the 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms, applied to the 51 ENS members and averaged, at least one change to the inputs (CAMS irradiance in place of ERA5 shortwave as the training input, a stage 0 model that calibrates ENS irradiance to CAMS, a clear-sky-ratio target for solar, or a power-curve base margin for wind) lowers the mean absolute error of the member average. inconclusive not-for-production C1, CAMS-trained minus ERA5-trained, solar: -0.140 (99.5% interval -0.277 to -0.044), short of the -0.15 that counts as a gain. primary
