docs.title: Planned experiments
docs.text: Experiment Hypothesis Relevance

docs.title: Generator forecasting: state and next steps
docs.text:
A small neural network that reads only the ensemble weather forecast is the final model for both the 3 metered wind farms and the 6 metered solar farms. The wind neural network (called S) reads 10 weather columns, 3 lead-time columns, and 3 farm columns (which farm it is). The inputs are summaries of the ECMWF ENS ensemble forecast (see ENS, ERA5, and CAMS). The solar neural network (called PLP) reads weather means and spreads, the sun's elevation and azimuth, the lead time, and a fixed hand-written power formula. Final models describes both. Neither is adopted for production.

Scores are only comparable within one experiment. Experiments 659 and 666 report mean pinball loss. Experiment 668 and the final models report CRPS (continuous ranked probability score), which is twice the mean pinball loss. Both are in points of capacity (see the glossary), and smaller is better, so a negative contrast favours the first arm named. A q99 is the 99% quantile of a forecast, and about 1% of observations should exceed it. Experiments 666 and 668 give the only final-model scores, and both come from one backtest year that overlaps the development months. Experiment 659 uses 5 development months (October, December, January, March, and June origins). Experiments 429, 461, and 466 use 53 Tuesday runs, and Experiments 54 and 57 use 52.

docs.title: What works
docs.text:
A simple pooled neural network is no worse than the elaborate defaults it replaces. In Experiment 659, wind S scored 3.684 against 3.766 for wind default 2 (the earlier wind recipe) on rows with idle readings zeroed. The difference is -0.082 (99% interval -0.151 to -0.008), and the interval is sensitive to the resampling seed.

The wind lead over wind default 2 comes from idle readings, so the two are tied. On all rows the difference is -0.036 (-0.087 to +0.020), and on kept rows it is +0.019 (-0.018 to +0.066). Experiment 429 found the same tie between a plain pooled network and wind default 2 (10.533 against 10.518, where 10.533 is the arm that passes members through an encoder and a one-pass version scores 10.541). Wind S is justified by being simpler.

Solar PLP scored 3.279 against 3.308 for the earlier solar default. The difference is -0.028 (-0.089 to +0.012), a tie. The fixed power formula improved solar by 0.021 and changed wind by +0.001, so wind S reads no formula.

Calendar columns hurt wind. Adding hour-of-day and day-of-year columns made wind S 0.094 worse (0.012 to 0.180) in Experiment 659.

Capacity at the 99.9th percentile of earlier power is safe for wind. In Experiment 461, retraining the wind network with this capacity kept the score (-0.17%, inside fit-to-fit spread) and left all 3 farms under the 1.5% limit on observations above q99.

A year-long backtest exists. Experiment 666 produced quantile forecasts to 14 days for 365 daily origins, and wind S matched Experiment 659 on the rows both cover (4.174 against 4.179). Experiment 668 resamples origin days (a 95% day-block bootstrap), where earlier experiments resampled months.

docs.title: What does not work
docs.text:
Weighting recent training rows more does not help. No half-life from 4.5 months to 3 years improved the wind or solar score by the margin, and wind scored 0.22% to 0.25% worse with short half-lives (Experiment 466). Recency weighting stays closed until the ECMWF ensemble history is longer than 2 years.

The 14-day error correction made the wind interval include zero and solar worse. The correction changed the CRPS by +0.437 (+0.215 to +0.664) for solar and +0.413 (-0.003 to +0.924) for wind (Experiment 23). A recent-capacity feature changed it within noise (Experiment 26). The final wind and solar networks read no power lag.

A hidden Markov model could not track wind-farm capacity steps. It found 31%, 32%, and 14% of outages of 2 or more turbines lasting 14 days or more, and raised 3.5 false steps a year at two farms, because only 11% to 21% of days have wind strong enough to show full output (Experiment 617).

Texture-based idle detectors did not beat the existing idle mask. They missed 3-hour idle blocks (recall 0.08 to 0.33), and no detector passed the gate at any wind farm (Experiment 444).

A second weather product added little for solar and a small amount for wind. The UKV forecast (the Met Office's 2 km weather forecast) lowered the wind quantile score by 0.198 at 24 to 54 hours ahead, measured on a research archive that differs from the live feed (Experiment 54). For solar the gain was -0.035, which the data cannot resolve (Experiment 57).

One metered generator that is neither wind nor solar is not forecastable from the inputs held. In Experiment 476, no network version beat same-hour climatology: the best gain was 0.015 against a minimum detectable effect of 0.019. Lagged market price was the one input worth a dispatch-data experiment, and no live price feed exists. The next step is a different kind of input, such as the operator's dispatch schedule.

A rolling capacity does not give one rule for wind and solar. In Experiment 505, a 730-day window (the window the final models use) gave a pooled share above q99 of 0.849% for wind and 1.449% for solar. It fails the 1.5% limit at Solar B (1.506%). The advice is the all-history p99.9 capacity for wind and the old capacity for Solar A and Solar E.

The ensemble's 100 m wind is about 1.1 m/s slower than the farms' power implies. A speed factor closed 70% to 79% of the gap to the ERA5 oracle (Experiment 307). Wind S does not use that design.

docs.title: Open weaknesses
docs.text:
The upper tail on very sunny days is too low in every solar arm. On 27 sunny farm-days, 10.6% to 12.7% of observations exceeded q99 (Experiment 659). Experiment 666's own sunny-day definition gives 2.8%, so the two figures are not comparable and the problem is unresolved.

The wind upper tail is too low in plain neural networks. Before recalibration, 2.17% to 2.78% of observations exceeded q99 in every arm of Experiment 429 (wind default 2: 2.15%), against a limit of 1.5%. A table of quantile rescalings clipped at the farm's largest earlier output brought every farm under the limit (Experiment 450, Experiment 451).

The final wind file has no such table, and its share above q99 is over the limit. The share is 0.016 at days 0 to 1 and 0.023 at days 10 to 14 (Experiment 666), against 0.015.

Wind coverage is below nominal on high-wind days and in some months. On kept rows in the 5 development months, q05-to-q95 coverage in January and March was 0.88 to 0.89 for S and 0.855 and 0.867 for wind default 2 (Experiment 659). On the 44 high-wind days, coverage is 0.82 for S and 0.83 for wind default 2, with 4.4% to 5.2% above q99.

Wind S is no better than climatology beyond day 10. It scores 9.86 at days 10 to 14, against 9.68 for climatology (Experiment 666).

Solar PLP is worse than climatology from November to March at days 10 to 14. Experiment 666 shows the gap at 0.03 to 0.42 points, although the mean absolute error gain is 5.7%. PLP is better than climatology at days 10 to 14 from April to September.

The solar median is high in spring and low in autumn. One year with quarterly refits cannot separate a seasonal effect from refit age.

The dawn and dusk bands are badly calibrated. A night gate at each half-hour's own sun position gave coverage of 0.69 and 0.75 at dawn and dusk at two farms. Experiment 684 covered only 3 months of origins (Experiment 684).

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Options 1 and 2 come from the open questions of the final models page. Options 3, 4, and 5 come from Experiments 505, 54, and 57.

  1. An option is to test a calendar input or more frequent refits for solar, to see whether they remove the seasonal bias in the median.
  2. An option is to test the open question "Whether wind needs a power lag or a different long-lead rule", given wind's score against climatology at days 10 to 14.
  3. An option is to test a 730-day capacity window with a share limit judged by an interval rather than a point estimate, plus a weekly refit at Solar A and Solar E (Experiment 505).
  4. An option is to build a matched history of the live UKV feed and test it for wind at lead days 1 and 2. This needs a source that holds live UKV at those leads, which Open-Meteo's history does not (it reaches lead day 0 only; Experiment 54).
  5. An option is to test a satellite-based nowcast at lead day 0 for solar farms, because UKV and a second global ensemble each added little. Experiment 57 lists it as an untested candidate.

docs.title: Parked
docs.text:
The wind refit-schedule test is parked. In the development months, a single fit, a quarterly refit, and a twice-monthly refit scored within 0.013 of each other for wind S (Experiment 659).

Load-shift event detection and unmetered PV capacity are paused until January and belong to the demand themes.

docs.title: Gross-demand simulation
docs.text:
It is worth running one small known-answer test of a simulator that fits, to each Primary substation's metered power, a list of the assets behind the meter and a few parameters per asset. The simulator's value would be an asset list per Primary and scenarios mostly at long horizons, not a better short-range forecast. NGED cannot confirm the asset list beyond the register, so the list is shown as inferred. Gross demand is the demand before the embedded generation behind a substation is netted off; a Primary's meter records only the net. No experiment in this theme has run yet.

The asset list has to come from NGED's Embedded Capacity Register. In the four experiments read for this theme that let a fit decide on its own whether a generator exists, the fit reported generators that are absent or unconfirmed. At the 16 Primaries in the study area the register lists 98 connected generation or storage entries (one technology at one site each), most of them small solar. The register omits assets below 50 kW, and in the one case checked, the register names a different Primary from the one whose meter records a 6 MW gas engine.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text:
• An asset-inventory simulator: what fitting an asset list with a few parameters per asset, instead of the state of each asset at every half-hour, can and cannot identify; what the register and the repository already supply; the maintainer's answers; what a forward model with real operating logic means and which parts exist; the candidate uses ranked; the smallest test; the risks; and the open question for the maintainer.
  • The simulator discussion of 2026-11-09: the take-home of the discussion session that started this theme, with the discussion's numbers checked against merged pages.
  • Options for proposing the simulator to NGED: an AI advisor's analysis of 2026-11-10, recorded as options: whether to propose the simulator as a complement to the forecast, what NGED's planning chain already has, a phased outline, the risks, and open questions.
  • Experiments and Research plan: empty until an experiment is agreed.

docs.title: An asset-inventory simulator
docs.text:
An asset-inventory simulator is worth one small test on data whose answer is known, as a source of an asset list per substation and of scenarios, mostly at long horizons, and not as a better short-range forecast. The simulator would fit, for each Primary substation (a substation that steps 33 kV down to 11 kV), a list of the assets behind its meter and a few parameters per asset. Examples are a solar capacity, the size of each unit of a gas engine and how long the engine usually runs, and a battery's power. The simulator would then run in the forward direction, from assets to power, to give scenarios. The forward direction needs a model with real operating logic for each asset type, described under What the forward direction means. Fitting a fixed list, rather than explaining every half-hour, drops the step that failed in the gas-engine experiments read for this page: deciding when each asset is on.

The maintainer's answers make the asset list a deliverable and long-horizon scenarios the main use. NGED hold nothing beyond the Embedded Capacity Register about what sits under each substation, so no ground truth exists to check the list against, and the list is shown as inferred. See Maintainer's answers (2026-11-10).

Two conditions, drawn from the merged experiments, decide whether the idea can work. The asset list has to start from NGED's Embedded Capacity Register, because in the four experiments read for this page that let a fit decide on its own whether a generator exists, the fit reported generators that are absent or unconfirmed. And the output has to be judged on known-answer tests, because the half-hourly power the meter records (demand minus the generation below it) cannot separate several assets of one type.

The smallest test would add real metered generator output to the readings of the six Primaries metered in megawatts (MW), and give the fit an asset list that includes one asset known to be absent. The other Primaries are metered in apparent power (MVA). The test is described under The smallest test and is an option for the maintainer, who has not yet chosen it; nothing has been started. The test would show cheaply whether the fit recovers the capacities and running-time parameters of assets it is told about, and whether it gives near-zero capacity to a listed asset that is absent.

This page answers from merged pages and stored files, using data before 2026-07-01 only. The discussion that led to it is recorded on The simulator discussion of 2026-11-09. The register counts below come from scripts/register_coverage.py, beside this page, run on one core.

docs.title: Terms used on this page
docs.text:
• Primary: a primary substation. The 16 Primaries in the study area are D2 to D5, D8 to D12, D14 to D16, D18, D19, D21, and D22, the anonymised labels of the glossary.
  • Net series: the half-hourly power a Primary's meter records, which is demand minus the output of the generators connected below it.
  • Strict disaggregation: splitting every half-hour of the net series into the contribution of each asset, for example dating each start and stop of a gas engine.
  • Asset inventory: a list of the assets behind one Primary, with a few fitted parameters per asset and no half-hour-by-half-hour state.
  • Register: NGED's Embedded Capacity Register (ECR), August 2026 release, which lists connected and accepted generation and storage of 50 kW and above. It is read by studies.ecr_reader.
  • Register name: the text in the register's Primary column. The 15 register names that match the study area cover the 16 Primaries, because Wrangle T1 (D15) and Wrangle T2 (D18) share one.
  • Slot: one technology at one registered site; a site can hold up to three.
  • Known-answer test: a test that adds a known asset's output to a real reading, so a fit can be scored against the truth.
  • Noise unit: a Primary's usual difference between successive 6-hour means, as defined in experiment 653.
  • Recovery: the share of a known, injected asset's capacity that a fit finds again; 1 is all of it.
  • NGED's metered generators are anonymised as Wind A to C, Solar A to F, Battery A, and Gas A.

docs.title: Maintainer's answers (2026-11-10)
docs.text:
• The asset list is itself a deliverable. NGED do not know exactly what sits under each substation, and they have nothing beyond the register, so no ground truth exists. A confirmed asset list per substation is one of the main benefits, together with a forward simulator of demand.
  • NGED cannot confirm the lists beyond the register. The known-answer test is therefore the main validation, and each list is shown as inferred.
  • Scenarios matter much more at long horizons. They are also interesting at days 1 to 10 for what-if questions. One example: a generator known to exist that has been off for months turns on during the 10-day horizon, and the question is what happens to the substation's demand.
  • A forward model means real operating logic. A battery model implements what a battery scheduler would do given the available price signals and the state of charge, with several scheduling profiles, because there are several ways to optimise. The same holds for other price-driven generators. A gas generator is a physical model written as equations that capture its ramping time, its minimum on-duration, and similar limits.
  • Training the forecaster on simulated series is conceivable if the simulator becomes good enough. The maintainer calls training on simulated series "a bit sketchy".
  • Not yet answered: whether the decoy rule should apply to solar too (see Open question).

docs.title: What the forward direction means
docs.text:
The forward direction needs, for each asset type, a model that decides what the asset does from the signals it would see. A fitted profile of the asset's past output is not enough. The table says which parts of the research repository (nged-ml-research) already hold such a model.

Asset type Forward model wanted In the repository today Battery A scheduler with the price signals available and the state of charge, in several profiles Partly. studies.battery_dispatch holds a daily linear-programme schedule for a price taker, with a state of charge, an energy limit, a cycle cap, and a rank-rule schedule; studies.battery_templates holds tariff-window, charge-only, merchant, Agile-tariff, and home-battery schedules; studies.battery_state_space holds the differentiable estimator that mixes them. The estimator fits the schedules to substation data. We found no module that runs the schedules forward for a registered battery Other price-driven generator An optimiser that follows the price signal within the plant's limits No. We found none in src/studies or in the experiments read for this page Gas engine Plant equations with ramping time, minimum on-duration, and similar limits No. The engine detector is a hidden Markov model of whole-number units and spell lengths, fitted to the residual (experiments 196 and 291), and has no ramping or minimum-on-duration equation Solar Output from sunshine and panel geometry Yes: the physics solar plant curve (experiment 282), with the assumed tilt fitting worse than the farms' best Wind Output from each ensemble member Yes: the physics wind plant run on each ensemble member, followed by a mixture-density head (experiment 347) Demand under the assets Calendar, temperature, heating, holidays, and the night step Yes: the demand GAM (studies.dp_gam)

The demand GAM, the solar and wind plants, and the battery schedules exist. The gas-engine equations and the other price-driven generators do not. The only recorded gas-engine output we read for this page is Gas A's, which covers 44 days.

docs.title: Strict and relaxed disaggregation identify different quantities
docs.text:
Strict disaggregation asks the net series for the state of every asset at every half-hour, and the gas-engine experiments did not get that state reliably. The relaxed formulation asks for a per-asset capacity and a distribution of running times. Both quantities are averages over many events, so each event only has to be found often enough to estimate the average.

The D8 gas-engine line is the closest precedent for the relaxed formulation, and it shows both what works and what does not. The best-supported account of D8 is that a 6 MW gas engine below it stopped being added back into D8's reading on 2023-08-15. After that date D8's power falls well below what a fitted model expects whenever the engine runs (experiment 194). NGED has not confirmed this account. A hidden Markov model of up to three units of about 1.75 MW detects when the engine is running, when the engine's recorded output is added to D8's reading, but raises too many false alarms at three of six other Primaries (experiment 196). The detector reports the engine as running during 27 of the 28 multi-day drops at D8 after 2023-08-15 (experiment 291), but the drops and the detector are both computed from the same residual.

Knowing the engine's state helped the forecast only when the state was read at the half-hour being forecast. With the state of the last settled day, the engine term made the forecast 10% worse (experiment 294). Experiment 294 did not try to forecast the state, so whether the state can be forecast is open. The relaxed formulation sidesteps the question by modelling how often and how long the engine runs. The unit size is not yet estimated well: experiment 294's fitted unit is 1.4 to 1.5 MW against a recorded 1.97 MW.

docs.title: What the net series can identify
docs.text:
The net series identifies large, long, or slowly changing quantities.

  • The total solar capacity behind a Primary, at season-year resolution. The capacity fit finds a median 0.78 to 0.86 of a real solar farm's output added to a Primary (experiment 129). The neural-network probe reads 2.4 to 3.9 MW of unmetered solar at each of the six MW Primaries, after dividing by the share of an injected real farm that the probe finds (experiment 649).
  • A step in solar capacity, when the step is large and the capacity is free to change each month. A known step was found to within 2% of its size and within one month of its date (experiment 207).
  • A recorded engine's running half-hours, when the engine's output is injected and its units are large against the noise (experiment 196). The same detector does not give the engine's state or unit size reliably in the real series (experiments 196, 199, and 294).
  • Long, deep steps of any cause. For injected load shifts that last more than 7 days and step 8 noise units or more, the event table finds 0.67 of the injected megawatts (experiment 665).

docs.title: What the net series cannot identify
docs.text:
The net series does not identify small, short, or numerous assets, or the cause of a step.

  • Several assets of one type behind one meter. The net series carries their sum, and the solar-capacity methods above estimate one total. The register lists 77 connected solar slots across the 15 register names, with two or more at 12 of them, and solar below 50 kW is not listed at all. A per-site split would have to come from the register, not from the data.
  • Assets that never make a visible step. Real batteries whose output was added to NGED's metered power were mostly not detected or sized, a provisional finding, and the estimator reports about 2.6% of peak flow where no battery exists (the unmetered battery capacity study). Solar growth makes no clean step either; the event table reads solar growth as false events, half of which last 3 days or less (experiment 686).
  • Short events. For load shifts of a day or less, the event table finds 0.16 to 0.26 of the injected megawatts (experiment 665). Gas A ran in 0.170 of half-hours, about 4 hours a day, in spells with a median of 2 hours, over its 44 recorded days (experiment 194). Spells that short sit in that class unless the units are large against the noise.
  • The cause of a step. A load transfer, a generator starting, and a change in demand all look like a step in the net series. At D8 the drops and the engine detector are both computed from the same residual, so experiment 291 could not call the engine proved. D8's night load also stepped after March 2025 for a reason no tested explanation covers (experiment 199).

docs.title: Fits left free to add generators report generators that are absent or unconfirmed
docs.text: In the four experiments read for this page that let a fit decide whether a generator exists, the fit reported generators that are absent or that could not be confirmed. A generator-finding component reported a generator at every substation tested, and was switched off (experiment 110). The engine mixture of experiment 264 fitted a running engine at two substations that have none. In a year with no solar steps, a monthly solar capacity invented steps above 0.5 MW at 2 of 5 Primaries (experiment 207). A scan of the real series found about as many solar steps as the same scan invents where none exists, so none of the steps could be called real (experiment 215). The relaxed formulation is likely to avoid this failure only if the list of asset types per Primary comes from outside the net series.

docs.title: What the register can supply
docs.text:
The register gives, for each connected asset of 50 kW and above, its technology, its registered MW, its connection date, its connection voltage, and its register name. The register also carries storage MWh and duration, a combined heat and power flag, a flexible-connection flag, export and import limits, and, for assets accepted but not yet connected, a target energisation date. The register does not carry running hours, a dispatch rule, or an output profile, so the running-time parameters of a relaxed fit must come from the data.

At the 16 Primaries the register lists 98 connected slots, most of them small solar. Of the 98 slots, 93 (57.0 MW) connect at 11 kV or below, behind the Primary's meter, and 5 (0.43 MW) give no voltage. Of the 98 slots, 97 carry a connection date.

Asset class Slots Registered MW Register names with one or more Solar 77 33.2 15 (all) Bioenergy (biomass, biogas, landfill gas) 8 11.1 6 Gas or oil engine 2 7.0 2 (D14 6.0 MW, D5 1.0 MW) Type not given 7 4.3 6 Wind 1 1.2 1 (D9) Storage 3 0.65 3

The register also lists 16 slots (3.7 MW) accepted to connect at these Primaries: 13 solar (3.0 MW), 2 storage (0.4 MW), and 1 wind (0.28 MW). Those slots are the new connections a planning scenario could add before they appear in the net series.

Three limits make the register a starting estimate that the fit may overrule, and not the truth.

  • The register omits assets below 50 kW, and the other registers do not fill the gap. At 8 of the 12 Primaries with a probe interval, the probe's interval lies above the solar capacity that three registers list together, the Feed-in Tariff report and the Renewable Energy Planning Database included (experiment 673). The registers together therefore miss part of the solar capacity. The Feed-in Tariff report, which does list small sites, ends in March 2025.
  • The register name and the meter that records an asset can differ. The 6 MW gas engine that appears in D8's readings is registered under D14, and experiment 194 warns against reading the register's Primary column as the substation whose meter records the asset. In that case, an asset list read from the Primary column alone would put the engine at the wrong Primary.
  • Some rows cannot be placed. Across the whole register, 655 connected rows carry no coordinate and 203 carry a coordinate inflated by a power of ten (experiment 673), and 7 slots at the study Primaries give no technology.

NGED's metered generators are the cases where the true output is known. The three wind farms and the six solar farms are metered directly (Final models for the production port), and so are a battery and a biofuel generator (D codes). Gas A's own readings give a known answer for only 44 days, from 2023-07-03 to 2023-08-15 (experiment 194).

docs.title: What the repository already has
docs.text:
The ten parts below exist in the repository, and each has a known weakness.

Part What it gives Status and weakness Source Demand generalised additive model (GAM) with explicit terms (studies.dp_gam) A convex baseline of demand from calendar, temperature, heating, holidays, clock changes, and the night step of storage heating Used in the best-guess stack; on data with realistic noise the heating slope is poorly determined (interval about 38% of the slope wide) Experiment 113, experiment 123 Solar capacity fit and probe Unmetered solar MW per Primary, season-year resolution Recovery 0.78 to 0.86 of an injected farm; reads a cloud-following load as solar Experiments 129, 649, 673; Unmetered PV capacity: what we know Physics solar plant curve Solar output from sunshine and panel geometry Within 5 points of capacity at 3 of 6 metered farms; the assumed 35 degree tilt fits worse than the farms' best 15 to 20 degrees Experiment 282 Physics wind plant Wind farm output from each ensemble member, with a small neural-network correction The current research-default wind forecast; its upper quantiles are too narrow Experiment 347 Engine detector Running state of a gas engine with whole-number units Finds a recorded engine when injected; too many false alarms elsewhere Experiments 196, 291 Battery estimator Battery power and energy from a price-driven schedule Simulated batteries above 10% to 20% of peak flow are found; real ones mostly not (provisional) Unmetered battery capacity study Injected-event generator Load transfers added to real power history A classifier cannot tell its events from 49 real windows (area under the curve 0.55) Experiment 660 Event table Steps per Primary, with start, end, and size Finds 0.67 of long, deep injected megawatts and 0.16 to 0.26 of events of a day or less Experiments 653, 665 Substation cards Fitted per-Primary properties: solar capacity, daily profile, heating response, holiday effects Point estimates without intervals; provisional Experiment 104 Injection harness A real metered farm's output added to a Primary's reading, with the recovery measured The known-answer route of experiments 129, 231, 269, and 474 Experiment 231

The missing part is a joint fit that holds a register-constrained list of assets and estimates their parameters together. Each part above was fitted alone, with the other assets left as unexplained variation or ignored. An asset-inventory fit would put the solar term, the engine term, and the battery term into one fit, with the register deciding which terms exist at each Primary.

docs.title: Candidate uses, ranked
docs.text:
The two uses that rank highest are an asset list per Primary, shown as inferred, and scenarios at long horizons for curtailment and planning. The ranking is a judgement of the value to NGED against the effort of building and testing, and the ranking puts the asset list and the long-horizon scenarios first because the maintainer gave them most weight. The values are our estimates. Each use carries a prediction that could fail and the measurement that would show it.

Rank Use Value to NGED Effort to build and test Prediction that could fail How it would be measured 1 An asset list per Primary, with parameters, beside the register High: a stated main benefit; shows where the register name and the meter disagree, as for the D8 engine registered under D14 Low: reuses the parts above On injected known answers, capacity within 20% for every listed asset that steps 8 noise units or more, and under 0.5 MW for a listed asset that is absent The smallest test below; the list is then shown as inferred 2 Scenarios at long horizons (months ahead), for curtailment and planning High: a stated aim of the forecast, and the horizon the maintainer says matters most Medium to high: needs a running-time model per asset, forward models with real operating logic, and a demand scenario model Issued a month ahead, between 0.5% and 2% of held-out half-hours fall above the scenarios' 0.99 quantile, and likewise below the 0.01 quantile, with a narrower 0.01-to-0.99 band than a block bootstrap of the Primary's own residual history Coverage and pinball loss at the 0.01, 0.05, 0.95, and 0.99 quantiles on held-out months of 2026-01 to 2026-06 3 A what-if at days 1 to 10, such as a dormant generator that turns on Medium to high: a question the maintainer named Medium: needs a gas-engine plant model, which does not exist Replaying a known start or stop, such as the D8 engine's change on 2023-08-15, the simulated change in the net series is within 30% of the observed change (a proposed threshold) Error of the simulated step against the observed step on the known events 4 A new connection added from the register before it appears in the data Medium to high for planning; needs NGED to say which connections matter Medium For assets connected in 2024 to 2026, a scenario that adds the registered asset at its connection date moves the post-connection error of the solar or step term by at least half the asset's registered MW Retrospective: hold out the data after each connection date and compare with and without the registered asset 5 A fallback when telemetry is missing or wrong Medium: the service must degrade, not fail Low The forward simulator scores better than climatology at days 1 to 10 when no recent power is available CRPS and tail pinball loss against climatology and the lag-free forecast on the same rows 6 Simulated series for a known-answer test bed, and conceivably for training the forecaster Medium: helps the evaluation problem behind the discussion; the maintainer calls training on simulated series "a bit sketchy" Low once use 1 exists Existing forecasting methods keep their ranking on the simulated series (Kendall rank correlation of at least 0.8 with their real scores, where 1 means the same ranking) Rank transfer, as proposed in the discussion 7 Counterfactuals ("the load without the engine") Low until NGED asks Low None measurable: no truth exists Not measurable

Use 5 is unlikely to matter, because a lag-free forecast already covers missing telemetry. The fallback would have to beat that forecast, not climatology, to change the service. Onboarding a Primary with a short history would be another use. The maintainer has paused onboarding work, so onboarding is not ranked here.

docs.title: The smallest test
docs.text:
A known-answer test of the inventory fit on the six MW Primaries, with real metered output added and an asset list that is partly wrong, is the cheapest test that could stop the idea. The test is an option for the maintainer, not a planned experiment.

  • Rows: the cleaned half-hourly readings of the six MW Primaries from 2024-07-01 to 2026-06-30.
  • Injected assets, one set per Primary: a metered solar farm's output at 50% of the Primary's solar capacity, as in experiment 231; Battery A's recorded output; and an engine of two 2 MW units whose running spells are drawn from a fixed distribution with Gas A's recorded median of 2 hours.
  • The list given to the fit: the injected solar farm, the battery, and the engine, plus one decoy engine (an engine that is listed but not injected). At one Primary in three, the injected battery is left off the list.
  • The fit: the demand GAM, one solar capacity term, an engine term with a unit size, a unit count, and a log-normal spell-length distribution, and a battery term from the battery estimator. No half-hourly state is reported.
  • Predictions that could fail:
    • the fit recovers each listed, injected asset's capacity within 20%, and the engine's median spell length within 30%;
    • the decoy engine gets under 0.5 MW at 5 or more of the 6 Primaries;
    • the residual of the fit shows the unlisted battery as a daily cycle.
  • Stop rule: stop if the decoy gets 1 MW or more at 3 or more of the 6 Primaries. A fit that finds a listed engine wherever it is told to look would give an asset list that cannot be trusted.
  • Effort: CPU only, about a day of one-core fits. The figure is a guess, scaled from the size of the solar-capacity fits.
  • Option for later: a language-model loop that matches the registers to the signals and edits the simulator, to be compared with this fit; see option 6 of the plan.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Circularity. A simulator fitted to the metered record and tested against the same record passes any test that shares its assumptions. The test above uses real metered output as the truth, so the injected asset's shape is not the simulator's own. The demand beneath the injected asset is still the fitted GAM's own output, so scenario calibration must be scored on months the fit has not seen.
  • Diversity against calibration. A scenario generator can be made so wide that it covers every month and is no longer informative. Each scenario test must report the band width beside the coverage, and compare with a block bootstrap of the Primary's own history, which needs no asset inventory at all.
  • What NGED could still say. NGED's records may cover the running hours of the larger engines, which Primaries have export limits or flexible connections, and whether any metered generator's output is still added back into a Primary's reading. We have not asked.
  • Validation of the asset list. NGED cannot confirm which assets sit behind which meter beyond the register, so only known-answer tests validate the list. The D8 engine registered under D14 shows that agreement with the register is not proof.
  • Bands may do the work. At D8, widening the bands from past residuals cut the quantile score by 9% to 19% and lifted the share of readings inside the 90% band from 42% to between 80% and 87% (experiment 264). A scenario use must beat that simpler widening before an engine term is worth adding.

docs.title: Open question for the maintainer
docs.text: • Should the decoy rule apply to solar too? Every register name lists solar, so a decoy can only be tested for engines, batteries, and wind. If solar matters most, the existing solar-capacity work already covers the inventory's solar term, and the test can drop the solar term.

docs.title: Gross-demand simulation: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00698 gas-engine-state-tracker-part-5-does-pv-harm-the-disaggregation The weather-driven variation of the solar generation behind D8's meter makes the tracker's daylight labels of the gas engine worse, beyond the harm that the lower level of the reading and the fold of the reading at zero cause. inconclusive not-for-production The test could not decide, under its own rule, whether solar panels behind D8's meter make the tracker's labels of the gas engine worse through their weather variation. The numbers it did produce point to harm. In the 10:00 to 15:00 window, injecting the output of a real solar farm lowers the tracker's F1 score by 0.14 and raises its false-flag share by 0.14 compared with a smooth solar curve of the same size (8.9 MW at D8). Most of the F1 harm comes from the lower level of the reading and its fold at zero, whereas the rise in the false-flag share comes from the farm's weather contrast. The labels' weekday and price patterns from experiment 697 may be best kept to the net era as a precaution, but this experiment computed nothing for that experiment's window of 16:00 to 19:00. primary 00697 gas-engine-state-tracker-part-4-running-patterns D8's gas engine runs to a schedule that follows the working week: it runs more on weekday evenings than on weekend evenings, by more than the tracker's errors alone would show. supported not-for-production The recorded demand at D8 behaves as if its gas engine runs more on weekday evenings (16:00 to 19:00) than on weekends, and more in half-hours with a high system price, and a test engine with no weekday pattern does not produce that. The evidence comes from the tracker's estimates and not from a meter on the engine, the labels understate any pattern, and the price, the red band, and D8's own evening demand all peak together. The pattern is a lead for a possible next experiment and not a result that a forecast can use, and the one metered engine record agrees in direction on only 7 weeks. primary 00696 gas-engine-state-tracker-part-3-engine-state-in-the-pre-training-mixer At D8, giving the pre-training mixer of experiment 677's step 9a neural network the tracked gas-engine state at the valid time (the expected engine output as a share of capacity and the probability that one or more units run), so that the weather encoder and the date-time encoder need not explain the engine's steps, and then training the stage 2 and stage 3 networks with a fresh mixer that has no engine input, lowers the CRPS of the forecast of D8's metered apparent power against the same neural network pre-trained without the state. not supported not-for-production Letting the neural network see the gas engine's state while it learns from weather and the calendar, and then dropping that knowledge before the forecast, did not improve the forecast of D8, and we cannot distinguish the change from zero. At another substation with an engine added, where the true state is known, a post hoc split of the results shows a gain of about 0.06 points when the engine is off and a loss of about 0.23 points when it runs. Weighted by the 19% of half-hours when the engine runs, the two cancel. One explanation that fits, not measured directly, is that the weather and calendar parts of the neural network lose the engine's daily pattern and the fresh final stage cannot recover it. The result does not support a gain from extra signal in pre-training only, at D8. A next experiment could combine the pre-training state with a way of putting the engine back after pre-training, and test the combination at the host first. primary 00695 gas-engine-state-tracker-part-2-cleaned-target-and-climatology-add-back At D8, removing the inferred gas-engine output from the training target and from the lagged-power inputs of the demand neural network, and adding the engine back at forecast time as a climatological distribution over the number of running units (passed through the apparent-power fold), lowers the error of the forecast of D8's metered apparent power, against the same neural network trained on the raw reading. not supported not-for-production Taking the gas engine out of D8's recorded demand before training, and adding the engine's average running pattern back when forecasting, did not improve the forecast. The cleaned arm was no better than the raw arm, and a post hoc reading of the same data suggests it was probably about 0.1 points of capacity worse over all rows. At another substation with an engine injected, cleaning gained about 0.1 points, within noise. Knowing whether the engine runs at the forecast's valid time would lower the error by 1.4 to 2.4 points against the raw arm, but no forecast has that knowledge. No gain was found, and cleaning plus a calendar add-back is not worth porting; one open question is whether the engine's state can be forecast from information available at the origin. primary 00694 gas-engine-state-tracker-part-1 The engine at D8 (3 identical units of about 2 MW) can be tracked by walking forwards through the raw half-hourly reading with a hidden-state model of the number of units running, with no demand forecast, no price, and no weather. D8's reading is apparent power (MVA, never negative), so a model that lets the reading fold, y = sqrt((L - k u)^2 + q^2) for demand level L, k units running, and unit size u, tracks the engine better than a model of signed steps. partly supported not-for-production A filter that tracks how many of D8's three gas-engine units are running, using only the substation's half-hourly reading, scores F1 0.68 on the one real engine record we hold (it finds most running half-hours but also flags others), and higher on easier synthetic schedules. It raised no false alarms at 8 substations, but it almost never finds a 1 MW unit, and the unit size it infers depends on the grid of sizes tried. The next experiment should test it on a harder, record-like schedule and on registered engines it has not seen. primary

docs.title: Gross-demand simulation: research plan
docs.text: No experiment in this theme is planned, and the options below are queued for the maintainer to choose. The project is not starting further experiments unprompted. The reasoning is on the asset-inventory simulator page. An advisor's analysis of how to propose the simulator to NGED, with phases as options, is on Options for proposing the simulator to NGED. The latest finished experiment, experiment 697 (running patterns of the D8 gas engine), found that the tracker's labels of D8's gas engine show a higher running share on weekday evenings than on weekends (+0.392 in the net era and +0.256 in the solar era). Six null controls, each a real reading with a patternless engine injected, produce a smaller difference. The running share also rises with the half-hourly system price. The evidence comes from the tracker and not from a meter on the engine, so option 3 below could test both findings against the one metered engine record. Experiment 696 (engine state in the pre-training mixer), found that telling the neural network about D8's gas-engine state during pre-training only did not change the forecast error (+0.009 means no change, in points of capacity; positive is worse). A post hoc split at a host substation with a recorded engine added showed a gain when the engine was off and a loss when it ran, which cancel when weighted by how often the engine runs. One option from the split is to combine a pre-training state with a way of putting the engine back after pre-training, tested at the host first.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Question Cost Depends on 1. Known-answer test of the inventory fit (first) Does the fit recover the capacities and running-time parameters of listed, injected assets, and give near-zero capacity to a listed asset that is absent? CPU only; one-core fits Nothing; the test is described under The smallest test 2. Battery scheduler as a forward model Do several scheduling profiles (price taker, tariff window, charge only), run forward with a state of charge, reproduce the recorded output of Battery A? Low to medium: reuses studies.battery_dispatch and studies.battery_templates Option 1 for the joint fit; Battery A's record for the check 3. Gas-engine plant equations Can equations with ramping time and minimum on-duration reproduce the known spells of Gas A and the D8 engine's change? Medium: no such model exists, and the running data is 44 days for Gas A Nothing for the equations; option 1 for use in the fit 4. Long-horizon scenario calibration Issued a month ahead, are the scenarios' tail quantiles calibrated, and narrower than a block bootstrap of the Primary's own history? Medium to high Options 1 to 3 5. Days-1-to-10 what-if for a dormant generator Does a simulated turn-on reproduce a known start or stop within 30% (a proposed threshold)? Medium Option 3 6. Language-model loop on the register match and the simulator (an idea) Does a large language model (LLM) that matches Primary signals to the registers and edits the simulator's assets, parameters, and operating profiles recover the known answers better than the plain register-constrained fit? Unknown; the loop would add LLM calls to the CPU-only fits of option 1 Option 1 first: the plain fit and its known-answer test must exist before the loop has anything to be compared against

docs.title: Option 6 in detail: a language-model loop
docs.text:
Option 6 is an idea, not agreed work, and no experiment has been started. The maintainer's thought is that an LLM could help with the fuzzy matching between the signals in a Primary's time series and the very incomplete registers (the Embedded Capacity Register and the other registers on the asset-inventory page). The LLM could also make adjustments to the simulator's assets, parameters, and operating profiles, so that the simulator's statistical properties match the observed Primary data as closely as possible.

The nearest evidence is one reviewer on one task, and it does not settle whether the loop would work. In experiment 692, a Claude Sonnet reviewer judged a figure of each candidate load transfer from the event table. It missed the pre-registered precision gate: 0.45 against 0.80. The reviewer's precision was 0.75, still under 0.80, after the 22 recurring candidates were removed from the calibration set, a post-hoc reading. Those candidates are events in the real record that the injected truth leaves out. The experiment did not test an LLM editing a simulator.

The asset-inventory page's own risks apply to the loop. The risks are circularity and bands doing the work (see Risks), and fits left free that invent generators (see that section). A loop that edits assets freely could also invent generators to match the statistics. The controls the loop would need, as options:

  • Register-constrained asset types: the LLM may only choose among asset types that the register lists for the Primary.
  • Held-out months: the match is scored on months the loop has not seen.
  • A fixed budget of edits: each run has a set number of changes.
  • Every move logged: each edit and the reason given for it are stored.
  • The same known-answer test as option 1: real metered output added to the readings, with an absent decoy asset and an unlisted asset.

The loop passes only if it matches option 1's plain fit on the known-answer test, and a proposed stop rule ends it otherwise. The prediction that could fail: the loop recovers each listed, injected asset's capacity within 20% and the engine's median spell length within 30%, as in the smallest test, and gives the absent decoy asset under 0.5 MW at 5 or more of the 6 Primaries. Stop if the decoy gets 1 MW or more at 3 or more of the 6 Primaries, the stop rule of the smallest test.
