docs.title: 15. Message from a peer session (Discuss: Graph approach to switching events), 2026-11-09 14:56 UTC
docs.text:
Answer from Discuss edd07c, from the merged pages of experiments 651, 653 and 658 (no new fits). Numbers are the pages' own.

  1. Experiment 651 (graph layer): it was a forecast experiment, not a labeller. It reports follow of injected shifts and CRPS, not detection by size bin. The graph layers barely used neighbours (moving from a mirrored to an unmirrored shift changed the median by under 1% of the shift), and a degree-preserving rewired graph scored the same as the real graph. FLOW-E's correction was never scored as a detector. So no evidence that a graph layer improves detection.
  2. Event tables:
    • Experiment 653 (penalised segmentation, 15 Primaries, CPU): 0.64 of injected MW found (0.58 to 0.70) for events of 4 noise units or more lasting a day or more; paired correctly only 0.18 of injected transfer ends. By duration, MW-weighted recall: 3 h to 1 d 0.24; 1 to 7 d 0.63; 7 to 21 d 0.70; 21 to 60 d 0.78; over 60 d 0.60; permanent 0.40. Pulses under 6 h never found. Real record 2024-01 to 2026-06: 246 events (6.6 per Primary-year; 211 solo shifts, 4 edge transfers = 2 pairs) and it matched 8 of 77 logged shifts under the strict rule, where LR_b20's 78 alarms matched 19. So it does worse than earlier detectors on real labels and raises about 3 times the alarms. Verdict not supported.
    • Experiment 658 (bidirectional recurrent neural network on the same panel and injector, 1.5 years of training): worse again, 0.48 to 0.52 of injected MW found, 0.16 to 0.17 paired, 0.4 to 0.8 real events per Primary-year. A classifier separated injected from verified real events with an area under the curve of 0.91, so the injector is unlike real events and may be limiting the result. Neural line closed on this panel; a larger history or a more realistic injector is untested.
  3. Recipients outside the 16 Primaries: an unseen partner shows as a "shift without a partner", a separate class. Of 231 injected edge transfers in 653, 148 decoded as nothing, 51 as a solo shift, 31 as an edge event (all 31 with the right partner, so pairing is precise but recall is low). Conservation is loose by design: recipient share window 0.3 to 1.5 of the donor's step, following experiment 459's half-sized leak. Widening the window to 0.1 to 3 recovers at most 7 points of pairing (0.22), so the leak is not what limits pairing; half of the ends are simply not found.
  4. Label incompleteness: it limits validation heavily. The recall by size above is on injected events, not on real ones; the only real-recall figure is 8 of 77 logged shifts, and experiment 580 found that of 27 mirrored sustained pairs in the telemetry only 1 matches a label, so unlabelled real events make precision unmeasurable and real recall a loose lower bound. The labeller can report its own recall by duration band and size (653 does, on injected events), so a score can carry a coverage caveat, but only as good as the injector's realism (AUC 0.91 says it is not yet realistic). A shared generator with realness checks is being built now (a worker on the shared injected-event module).
  5. My view (judgement, not a result): not yet. At 15 Primaries the labeller finds about two thirds of injected MW for events of a day or longer, almost none of the short ones, and pairs under a fifth of transfers, so its labels would miss most short events and most partners, and would be biased towards large, long, solo events. That is enough for descriptive tables per Primary (start, end, amount), not for scoring forecasts under both the NRA and prevailing rules. A simulator with exact truth is still needed for that evaluation. The labeller could still supply real durations and a stratum of event-free rows (more than 14 days from any detected event).

docs.title: 16. Session reply, 2026-11-09 14:56 UTC
docs.text:
Short answer: the graph session found no evidence that a graph approach labels transfers well, so heavy labelling of real data cannot yet replace a simulator for evaluation. The numbers below are its own, from the merged pages of experiments 651, 653 and 658.

What it found:

  • No evidence for the graph layer.
    • Experiment 651 was a forecast experiment, not a labeller, and it never scored detection.
    • Its graph layers barely used neighbours: a mirrored versus an unmirrored shift moved the median by under 1% of the shift.
    • A degree-preserving rewired graph scored the same as the real graph.
  • Penalised segmentation (experiment 653, not supported).
    • It found 0.64 of injected MW for events of 4 noise units or more lasting a day or more.
    • MW-weighted recall by duration was 0.24 for 3 hours to 1 day, 0.63 for 1 to 7 days, 0.70 for 7 to 21 days, 0.78 for 21 to 60 days, and 0.60 above 60 days. Pulses under 6 hours were never found.
    • It paired only 0.18 of injected transfer ends.
    • On the real record it matched 8 of 77 logged shifts and raised about three times the alarms of the earlier detector, which matched 19.
  • Recurrent neural network (experiment 658).
    • It was worse again: 0.48 to 0.52 of injected MW found, and 0.16 to 0.17 paired.
    • A classifier told injected events from verified real events with area under the curve 0.91, so the injector is unlike real events and may be limiting the result.
    • That neural line is closed on this panel.
  • Recipients outside the 16 Primaries.
    • An unseen partner shows as a shift without a partner.
    • Of 231 injected transfers, 148 decoded as nothing, 51 as a solo shift, and 31 as a paired event, all with the right partner.
    • The half-sized leak is not what limits pairing: widening the share window recovers at most 7 points.
  • Label incompleteness.
    • The only real-recall figure is 8 of 77 logged shifts.
    • Experiment 580 found that of 27 mirrored sustained pairs in the telemetry, only 1 matches a label. Precision is therefore unmeasurable and real recall is a loose lower bound.

What this means for your question:

  • Labelling is biased towards large, long, solo events. It misses most short events and most partners, so it cannot score forecasts under both the normal-running-arrangement and prevailing rules.
  • It still gives useful descriptive output. That means per-Primary event tables (start, end, amount), real event durations, and a stratum of rows more than 14 days from any detected event.
  • The injector's realism is now the shared weak point.
    • A simulator would need an event generator that passes a realness test, and the AUC of 0.91 says the current one does not.
    • A worker is building a shared injected-event module with realness checks.
    • Any simulator would reuse that module, so waiting for it costs nothing.

Revised view:

  • Do the labelling and the realistic injector first. Both feed a simulator later.
  • Exact truth for evaluation still needs a simulator or a realistic injector. Labels alone will not do it at present.
  • My earlier estimates stand: the first experiments I proposed are unchanged, and none has started.

docs.title: 20. Message sent to a peer session (Discuss: Graph approach to switching events), 2026-11-09 18:04 UTC
docs.text:
Reply from the gross-demand-simulator Discuss session on labelling MVA reverse flow, PV capacity and large generators. No new fits. "Evidence" means a merged page I read; "view" is my judgement. I have NOT read experiments 618, 624 or 649 (no merged page found), so they are not used.

Order I would want (view): (1) MVA reverse flow, (2) large-generator steps, (3) PV capacity. Reason: (1) has a measurable label and a known-answer route; (3) has the weakest evidence.

  1. MVA reverse flow at the eight MVA Primaries

    • Evidence, experiment 508: a dip of apparent power at the sun's edges (shoulder hours) tells the sign change much better than a midday dip, but only up to export about 3 times the night import. D12 (about 5 times) is beyond what was calibrated. At D12 the shoulder dips are as common on cloudy days and in the dark as on sunny days, so there they show low demand, not export. Verdict partly supported.
    • Known-answer test (view): inject a metered solar farm's output into a signed MW Primary, take the magnitude, and check the label recovers the sign. The six MW Primaries give exact truth, and experiment 508's calibration limit sets the size range to test.
    • Edge-state fit (view): a per-Primary, per-day state "exporting at midday", with a prior tied to clear-sky hours. Emit a "sign unknown" class beyond roughly 3 times night import instead of forcing a call.

  2. Large generators (gas engines, farms) as solo steps

    • Evidence, experiment 264 (gas-engine bands, promising), and experiments 206 and 207: in 206 a metered farm's meter outage did NOT reappear in its Primary's power at D10 (not supported), so farm outages are not a usable label. In 207 a known step in solar capacity was found in size and within a month, but at the pre-registered penalty the fit invented steps at 2 of 5 Primaries (D10 and D11), so the gate failed.
    • Known-answer test (view): inject metered wind, solar and battery series as solo steps of known start, end and size, anonymised (Wind A to C, Solar A to F, Battery A, Gas A). Report recall by size and duration as experiment 653 does.
    • Edge-state fit (view): a solo-step state with a longer minimum duration than transfers, plus a "generator" class for steps that repeat with the generator's schedule. Expect false steps at D10 and D11 first, per experiment 207.

  3. PV capacity (slow steps)

    • Evidence, experiments 129, 157, 231, 269, 474: recovery of an injected farm is 0.75 to 0.88 for the season-year fit and 0.67 to 0.78 for the monthly fit; the monthly fit did not beat the yearly one (157, not supported). Experiment 231 traced about 0.17 of the loss to demand terms absorbing solar and to the fixed shape; 269 found the plant shape, not the sunshine, explains the nearest-farm gain (0.892 raw recovery with the pooled empirical shape). Experiment 474 found no candidate shape passes its placebo test, and intervals were honest only with a cloud-load term; experiment 129's coverage was close to circular.
    • Known-answer test (view): reuse the injection harness of 129 to 474 (a real metered solar farm added to a Primary) and judge a graph labeller's capacity steps against the same placebo gate, with step size, timing and invented-step rate reported.
    • Edge-state fit (view): a slow, monotone capacity-step state, penalised hard, since experiment 207 shows the penalty trades missed steps against invented ones.

Caveats for all three (evidence):

  • NGED's event labels are incomplete, so recall on real data is a lower bound and precision cannot be measured. Report coverage beside every result.
  • Injected-event realism is already a limit (your AUC 0.91 in experiment 658).

My view on sequencing: build the MVA sign label first and prove it on injected metered farms at the six MW Primaries before running it at the eight MVA Primaries, where there is no truth.

docs.title: Hierarchy and pooling
docs.text:
The current understanding and the options for next work are on the state and next steps page.

One XGBoost model shared by a group of Primary substations forecasts almost as well as one model per substation (0.15 points of capacity worse, 99.44% interval +0.03 to +0.26), but the one test of a substation outside the pool (8 Primaries, one seed) found fingerprints made it worse, and forecasts of the series beneath 2 bulk supply points added nothing.

Pooling means training one XGBoost model on the rows of several series, with the series identifier as a column, so that 20 models become 3 or 4. The pooling results are from one validation year (July 2025 to June 2026) on 16 Primary substations and 4 supply points, with ENS weather. The hierarchy results cover 2 bulk supply points and 2 grid supply points, and 4 series cannot separate the designs.

Every pooled arm scores worse than one model per series (positive is worse), by 0.15 to 0.29 points with the series identifier and 0.8 to 1.0 without it. Source: experiment 24; C1 to C3 and C5 to C7 use 16 Primary series, and C4, C8, and C9 use all 20 series.

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
Three or four pooled models score 0.15 points of capacity worse than 20 per-series models on the 16 Primaries, inside the pre-registered margin of 0.30. The scores are the quantile score over all leads after the 14-day correction and a spread factor of 1.15 (the stack of experiment 19, with a half-life of 0.5 years). Per-series models score 5.32, one model per substation type 5.47 (C1, +0.15, 99.44% interval +0.03 to +0.26), and one model per capacity band 5.47 (C3, +0.15, +0.05 to +0.26). The type pools beat manual_heuristic (5.89) by 0.42 (exploratory, -0.68 to -0.19). The verdict is supported (experiment 24).

One model for all 20 series falls outside the margin. It scores 5.61 on the 16 Primaries (C2, +0.29, +0.19 to +0.42). On the 2 bulk supply points alone it loses 0.80 (0.64 to 1.00, exploratory, 95%), and the 4 supply points are too few to separate the type pools from per-series models (+0.03, -0.15 to +0.15, exploratory, 95%; experiment 24).

For Primaries, the number of models matters more than which series share one. Random groups of 5 score 5.47 on the 16 Primaries, the same as the type pools. On all 20 series the type pools beat random groups by 0.06 (C9, -0.13 to -0.01), and on the 4 supply points by 0.29 (exploratory, interval not given; experiment 24).

The series identifier is essential. Dropping it raises the score of the type pools by 0.82 (C7, +0.46 to +1.23) and of the all-series pool by 0.85 (C8, +0.72 to +1.00) (experiment 24).

Describing each substation with numbers added nothing to the identifier for series seen in training. Adding a substation's location, its mean level and shape over the training window, or its level over the previous 14 days to the identifier moved the score by at most 0.02 points (C1 to C4; C4, +0.02, 99.375% interval -0.05 to +0.10). The verdict is inconclusive by the pre-registered rule, though the data exclude a gain above 0.05. Training-window statistics alone, without the identifier, scored 0.01 points worse than the identifier (C5, 99.375% interval +0.00 to +0.02, inside the 0.15 margin; experiment 32).

A substation held out of the pool was forecast worse with training-window statistics than with no fingerprint (C7, +1.39, +0.99 to +1.91), and better with recent power statistics alone (post hoc, -0.23, -0.29 to -0.16, 95%). The test used 8 held-out Primaries, one seed, and a pool of 7 other series. The write-up suggests, without testing it, that 7 distinct fingerprints act as 7 identifiers (experiment 32).

Forecasts of the series beneath a bulk supply point did not lower its score. Adding the summed median forecasts of the Primaries and generators beneath a bulk supply point changed its score by +0.04 (99.17% interval -0.18 to +0.25) at Boston and +0.19 (-0.10 to +0.73) at Skegness. At the 2 grid supply points, generic wind and solar columns changed it by -0.02 (-0.06 to +0.03) and -0.04 (-0.13 to +0.07). The pre-registered rule marks the bulk-supply-point family and the wind-and-solar family refuted and the ERA5-trained family inconclusive, so the experiment is inconclusive (experiment 36).

The six planned contrasts all include zero; the two exploratory rows are the ERA5-trained N1 at the bulk supply points, and Boston's excludes it.

An N1 trained on ERA5 and applied to ENS members lowered the grid supply point scores by 0.36 and 0.40, but its intervals span -1.8 to +1.0. N1 is the single-stage XGBoost quantile model. Only Boston, a bulk supply point, resolved a gain, of 0.41 (0.15 to 0.66, exploratory, 95%) (experiment 36).

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text:
Of the pooled designs tested, one model per capacity band or per substation type scored best, and with the 14-day correction none beat one model per series on the 16 Primaries.

  1. Train an XGBoost quantile model (experiment 24's recipe, N1 fitted per group instead of per series: 9 quantile levels, ENS control member, lead hour, calendar columns, three power lags, power scaled by each series' effective capacity) on 3 capacity bands (the series split into thirds by effective capacity) or 4 substation types. Each pool holds all 20 series, including the 4 supply points.
  2. Give every XGBoost model the series identifier as a categorical column.
  3. Apply the 14-day correction and a spread factor of 1.15 to each series' quantiles.

The capacity-band and type pools score the same to two decimals (experiment 24). The pre-registered rule chose capacity bands because they have fewer models.

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text:
Experiment 24 is candidate; experiments 32 and 36 are not-for-production.

  • Pooled XGBoost models for Primary demand (experiment 24). The XGBoost forecaster would train 3 or 4 models instead of 20 and store them at 73 to 94 MB instead of 435 MB, for a loss of 0.15 points of quantile score on the 16 Primaries, with the 14-day correction. Each model would need the series identifier, and a new series would need a retrain. The test covered 20 series, so it says nothing about 2,500 substations.
  • Nothing from experiments 32 or 36 is ready. No fingerprint helped a series seen in training, and no forecast column lowered a bulk or grid supply point's score.

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
• Keep the series identifier in every pooled model. Without it, the type pools lost 0.82 and the all-series pool 0.85 (experiment 24). Re-check with a different model type or a different pool of substations.
  • Score pooled arms with and without the 14-day correction. The correction lowers per-series models by 1.0 and type pools by 0.6, so type pools beat per-series models by 0.30 uncorrected (exploratory, 95%, -0.56 to -0.03) and lose 0.15 corrected (experiment 24). A ranking measured on one stack may not carry to another. Re-check if the correction changes.
  • Scale boosting rounds (the number of trees) with the pool size, or say they were not scaled. Experiment 24 fixed 500 rounds and depth 6, so the all-series loss may be partly lower capacity per series. Re-check with rounds scaled to rows.
  • Do not compare fit seconds across arms. Other sessions loaded the machine during the capacity-band and random-group fits of experiment 24, so only model counts and saved sizes are reliable. Re-check with timings on an idle machine.
  • Match a held-out substation's fingerprint window to the pool's. The held-out substation's 28-day statistics differed from the pool's 15-month ones, and using the whole window removed about two thirds of the C7 damage (post hoc; experiment 32). Re-check with a pool of hundreds of series.
  • Do not read the oracle's gain as headroom for forecasts. The oracle is the same XGBoost model given the observed values of the series beneath a bulk supply point. It lowered the score by 5.6 and 3.4, while forecasts of those series lowered it by none (experiment 36). Re-check if the child forecasts come from a different weather source.
  • Note how the columns of forecasts of the series beneath a supply point were built. Experiment 36 fitted them by time block, so a block's forecasting model saw months on both sides, and training used the ENS control member while validation used each member. Look for a gain that changes when the columns are fitted strictly out of time, or when training uses every member.
  • Do not compare supply-point scores across experiments 24 and 36. Experiment 24 applies the 14-day correction to all 20 series, including the 4 supply points. Experiment 36 left it off at supply points because experiment 21 found it unproven there, so its scores are uncorrected. Re-check when a supply-point experiment states which stack it used.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text:
• Whether pooling holds at hundreds of series, and for substations the pool never saw.
  • Whether supply points pool at all; 4 series cannot say.
  • Whether an N1 trained on ERA5 helps at supply points beyond Boston.
  • Whether one model shared across substations, with drift and long history, beats separate models. That is the subject of the differentiable-physics background and the sub-themes long history and drift and demand calendar and weather.

The Research plan lists what is planned next, and Experiments lists every experiment. Experiment 103 appears there as also relevant: its data look fixes the rows and dates the pooled differentiable-physics model uses, and it has no pooling result.

docs.title: Hierarchy and pooling: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00669 one-year-backtest-of-the-lag-network-at-bulk-and-grid-supply-points Descriptive, not a hypothesis test. The lag-enabled network of experiment 633 (experiment 622's arm lagged_b1) forecasts the 2 bulk supply points (BSPs: D13 Skegness and D17 Boston) and the 2 grid supply points (GSPs: D6 Walpole and D1 Bicker Fen) every day for a year from 2025-11-01, at leads of 0 to 14 days, with no neighbour inputs and no model of load-shift events. supported not-for-production The lag-enabled network forecasts the 2 bulk and 2 grid supply points with a CRPS of 7.4 points of capacity on day 0, rising to about 10.5 from day 7 to day 14 (bulk supply points 4.3 to 6.3, grid supply points 10.5 to 14.6), and its 90% band covers 0.87 of readings. Against experiment 633's 24-hour-lag network on July to October 2026 origins it scores 0.30 points lower at hours 0 to 72 (7.24 against 7.54), but only 0.16 of that in July, the one month in which both networks were trained to the same date, so most of the gain is the monthly refits. The network follows no load shift, and the largest miss in the year looks like one. also relevant 00651 graph-layer-over-electrical-neighbours-in-the-demand-network-part-1 A graph layer between the existing encoders (weather, date-time, lag) and the mixer of the class 2 candidate, on the electrical neighbour graph (29 edges among 16 Primaries), learns when to use a neighbour. It keeps the candidate's follow of an injected load shift and removes the candidate's extra event-free error at the six MW Primaries, and the electrical graph does this better than a degree-preserving rewired graph. not supported not-for-production A graph layer over the electrical neighbours did not remove the class 2 candidate's extra error at the six MW Primaries, and did not help it resist a false load shift. The graph layers made little use of the neighbours, and an arm whose graph was wired at random did as well as the arm with the real graph. The extra error is the same with no neighbour information at all, so the first place to look for the cause is the class 2 training choices (E3 rows, the D5 offset, and signal dropout), not the electricity network's topology. also relevant 00633 bakeoff-final-test-bg2-and-lag-enabled-bsp-gsp-network Part 1. BG2 rebuilt as one fit at 2026-07-01 ("BG2-single-fit": experiment 87's weekly XGBoost member, fitted once on data before 2026-07-01, a mixture over the 51 ensemble members with spread factor 1.15) scores within 0.10 CRPS points of K1, the ungated class 2 candidate, and K3 of experiment 620 at the 16 Primaries, and the ranking of BG2 against the three networks on the held-out months equals its ranking on the five development months. Part 2. The lag-enabled network of experiment 622 (arm lagged_b1) beats BG2 and the climatology at days 1 to 3 at the bulk and grid supply points that have readings in the window. partly supported not-for-production BG2-single-fit scores lower CRPS than all three demand networks at the 16 Primaries, but part of that lead is a lag advantage (3.5-hour against 24-hour power lags) and part is following load-shifts, which an NGED normal-running-arrangement forecast should not do. Removing the flagged days halves the lead over K1, and at Primary D18 BG2's median follows 0.56 of the transfer against 0.33 for the lag-free K3. At the 2 bulk and 2 grid supply points the lag-enabled network ties BG2 and beats the manual heuristic. also relevant 00631 bsp-group-sum-with-metered-generators-against-direct-bsp-forecast Experiment 629 found that sums of the 16 Primaries beneath two bulk supply points (BSPs) put 31% to 79% of actual flows below their q05 (nominal 5%), and that the metered wind and solar series beneath the BSP explained much of the gap (R squared 0.94 at Skegness). The claim here is that, once those metered farms are added to the sum together with a fitted remainder, a coupled scenario set (J3, the Schaake shuffle, or J5, the fitted copula) puts the q05 and q95 exceedance of the BSP flow within the binomial error of nominal at both BSPs, and beats independent draws (J0) on CRPS. not supported not-for-production Adding the nine metered wind and solar farms to the sum of Primaries fixes most of the export-side tail miss of Primaries-only sums (Skegness 41.7% to 3.0% of actual flows below the q05, on this experiment's rows), but the import side swings from too wide or about right (Boston 0.1%, Skegness 4.4% above the q95) to too narrow (14.3% and 32.6%), and no sum has both tails near 5% at both bulk supply points (BSPs). Coupling the scenarios (Schaake shuffle or fitted copula) improves the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) by 2.6% to 7.7%, so coupling matters once the farms are in. The direct forecast of each BSP meter is still the safer tail forecast, which means the deliverable should be a direct BSP forecast beside any node scenarios. also relevant 00629 bsp-group-sum-of-nodes-against-direct-bsp-forecast Experiment 436 found 13.9% of actual group net flows above the q95 of independent-draw sums (J0), against 6.6% for the Schaake shuffle (J3). The claim here is that, summed to a bulk supply point (BSP) and scored against the BSP's own meter, a coupled scenario set (J3 or the fitted copula J5) puts the export-side q95 exceedance within the binomial error of 5% and has a lower threshold-weighted CRPS at the scaled limit than J0, and that the direct forecast of the BSP meter does not beat every summed set by 5%. not supported not-for-production Summing coherent scenarios of the 16 Primaries did not give a usable export tail for either BSP: 31% to 79% of actual flows fell below the sum's q05 where 5% should, in every coupling and every demand network, while the direct forecast of each BSP's own meter was close to nominal (4.6% and 6.9%). The missing metered generators explain much of the gap (R squared 0.94 at Skegness), so the next step is a sum that includes them, or to deliver the direct BSP forecast alongside the node scenarios. also relevant 00628 quantile-form-client-side-scenario-rehydration NGED reads stored forecasts from S3 and builds scenarios in Python. The stored forecasts of experiments 425, 429, and 430 hold 11 quantiles (0.01, 0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.40, 0.50, 0.60, 0.75, 0.90, 0.95, 0.99) per site and half-hour. The claim is that a client holding only these 11 quantiles, plus a small dependence table, draws 1,000 coherent scenarios per run that score within 1% of the 51 scenarios the pipeline builds (experiment 436's J5 and J3) on CRPS, and within 1 percentage point on exceedance at the 0.01, 0.05, 0.95, and 0.99 levels, provided the client extends the quantile function past the outer levels with a good tail rule. partly supported not-for-production NGED can rebuild the marginal forecasts and a Schaake-shuffle coupling from 11 stored quantiles per site and half-hour plus a small dependence table. 1,000 client-drawn scenarios score within 0.3% of the 51 scenarios the pipeline builds on CRPS, and a Schaake shuffle of 51 stored past paths matches the pipeline's shuffle on the variogram score. The only loss we measured is for the fitted copula on solar farms (6.6% worse on the variogram score). The pipeline's version also uses the weather ensemble's member ranks, which the quantiles do not carry, and that is the likely cause. Mixture parameters were not needed for any of this. The tails of the stored quantiles are too narrow for any of the three tail rules to fix. also relevant 00627 scenario-subset-selection-from-51-coherent-paths NGED will run a handful of power-flow studies by hand, so they need K of the 51 coherent member paths (K = 3, 5, 10) that cover the distribution of the 51, without labelling any path. A path that is low wind on day 1 need not be low wind on day 2, so a label such as "the low-wind scenario" does not carry over. We test whether picking K paths by stratifying on one summary of the run (S) or by clustering the 51 joint paths (C) covers the 51-path distribution better than a simple random sample (R). partly supported not-for-production Picking 5 of the 51 forecast paths by cutting them into 5 equal groups on one summary and taking one path from each covers their spread better than picking 5 at random, in every month, but still misses the tails: the stratified rules leave a gap of 11% to 12% of the range at the 5th percentile and 13% to 14% at the 95th. For a bulk supply point's limit, an observed daily peak export beat the largest of 5 chosen paths on 12% of days (1.6% for all 51); 10 paths chosen by that substation's own peak export came closest (6.3%, against 7.3% for a random 10). NGED should treat 10 paths as a minimum when the tail matters. also relevant 00626 widen-the-tails-of-the-51-scenario-member-values In experiments 434 and 436 the 51 values per node and half-hour were too narrow in the tails: the q95 of the 51 values was exceeded by 7.6% to 8.8% of actuals (target 5%). A factor per family and lead band, fitted on earlier months only, that rescales the 51 values about their median (arm B), or re-draws them from a wider quantile function (arm C), brings the q05 and q95 exceedance rates to within 1 point of 5% in every family and lead band on later months, while the variogram and energy scores of the Schaake-shuffled paths move by less than 2% and the CRPS of the 51 values moves by less than 1%. partly supported not-for-production Rescaling the 51 scenario values with a separate upper and lower factor (arm D) brought demand's q05 and q95 exceedance to 4% to 6% in every lead band, but did not fix wind or solar. Demand's q90 is still exceeded for 11% to 16% of half-hours (target 10%), which points to a forecast that sits too low rather than too narrow. In experiment 436, most of the apparent q95 excess came from its quantile definition, not from the forecast. The next step is a bias correction for demand, then a re-check of the tails. also relevant 00625 coherent-members-from-quantiles-k-sweep-and-path-checks Experiments 434 and 436 already scored independent draws (IND), ensemble copula coupling (ECC), a Schaake shuffle (SS), and member-wise quantiles (MW) at 51 paths. A Schaake shuffle gave the wind farms and solar farms variogram scores 28% to 43% below IND but gave the 16 Primaries nothing. This experiment tests three new claims. (1) SS paths cut to K = 10 lose under 2% of the variogram score of K = 51. The top-down forecast is the best-guess GAM-K chain (experiment 155's arm D) applied to the BSP's reading as a stand-alone series. The bottom-up forecast adds the arm D forecasts of the BSP's child Primary substations that report real power, each times a weight learned from earlier readings, to arm D's forecast of the remainder (the BSP's reading minus those children's weighted readings). The mechanism is that the child Primaries' own forecasts are better than the BSP's chain can infer from the BSP's sum, because each child has its own heating, solar, and calendar response and its own recent errors, and the sum is not exact (losses, unmetered load, children that report apparent power), so the remainder and the weights absorb the difference. inconclusive not-for-production Forecasting a BSP from its children's forecasts plus a remainder did not beat forecasting the BSP as a stand-alone series at either BSP: the bottom-up score was 0.6% worse at D13 and 0.5% worse at D17. The likely reason is that the children this test could use (three real-power Primaries per BSP) cover 42% and 56% of the BSP's capacity, and the BSP's error lives in the rest. The oracle control also missed its pre-registered threshold, which was set too high. The verdict is inconclusive because both intervals include zero. also relevant 00158 dp-partly-pooled-gam-shapes-heating-and-calendar-curves A GAM-K forecast (the convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors, experiment 111) fitted jointly across six Primary substations, so that each substation's heating curve, lighting curve, daily profile, holiday effects, and Christmas shape are a fleet mean plus a penalised deviation of its own, forecasts better than the same model fitted to each substation alone, now that the solar capacity is pinned and the filter handles recent switching. The mechanism is that a substation sees only two winters and two Christmases in a 24-month window, so its own curves are noisy, and five other substations carry information about the shapes that physically are shared. Capacity, level, and the band means stay per substation. The gain is largest for a substation with 3 months of history and on Christmas rows, and no pooled arm is worse than the per-site fit by more than 0.02 points on ordinary rows. partly supported candidate In this test on six Primary substations, fitting the demand model's shared curves (heating, lighting, daily profile, holidays) across all six let a substation with only 3 months of history score 3.01 points instead of 3.64 (lower is better), within 0.17 points of the same substation with 24 months of its own history. The gain was largest in winter and on Christmas rows. For a substation with 24 months of history, pooling changed the score by less than 0.02 points, which is too small to justify making each forecast depend on five other substations' data. The test cannot say whether pooling the heating curve alone would help a 3-month substation. also relevant 00154 differentiable-physics-n0-gate-2-heating-error-against-truth When the partly pooled convex regression model of experiment 109 is fitted to only 4 winter weeks of one substation, its fitted heating curve is closer to the injected truth than the curves of the no-pooling and complete-pooling fits. The curve is as close to the truth as a fair oracle's curve (within 10%). The model recovers the sign of the substation's own heating offset relative to the fleet's curve. The fleet's shared curve is recovered as well as an average of per-site fits recovers it. partly supported not-for-production On synthetic substations with a known answer, a partly pooled demand model fitted to 4 winter weeks of one substation estimated that substation's heating response with a smaller error than fitting the substation alone (2.8 to 3.6 against 4.1 to 11.5 points of capacity) and than copying the fleet's curve (3.4 to 4.6), on every seed. It recovered the fleet's shared curve about as well as separate fits did. Neither the pooled fit nor the fair oracle recovered the sign of the substation's own heating offset reliably (the pooled fit got the sign right at 6 or more of 8 substations on only 2 of 5 seeds), so on these synthetic fleets and one January, a partly pooled model can share the heating curve but cannot learn a substation's own offset from 4 weeks. also relevant 00150 differentiable-physics-n0-gate-rerun-fair-oracle-five-seeds When the reference estimator estimates every coefficient from the same 4 weeks of rows (so that no coefficient is fixed at its true value), the partially pooled convex model of experiment 109 recovers the injected truth about as well as that reference on most of 5 random seeds, and its tuning rule picks a deviation penalty within one grid step of the best one on most of the 5 seeds. inconclusive not-for-production The rerun of the synthetic known-answer test could not say whether the pooled model shrinks substation deviations correctly, because a control that keeps no deviation at all passed the shrinkage line on 2 of 5 seeds when 4 June weeks were held. Capacity from 4 weeks was within 25% of the truth at 8 of 8 synthetic substations on every seed, the tuning rule picked a penalty within one grid step of the best on 5 of 5 seeds, and the pooled fit's heating error was below a fair reference estimator's on 5 of 5 seeds. The full-history line passed on only 2 of 5 seeds. A post hoc rerun on 4 January weeks separated the controls, so a test that scores heating error against the injected truth in winter should settle the question. also relevant 00124 differentiable-physics-h-bsp-closure-audit-and-bsp-hint A bulk supply point (BSP) reading, fitted jointly with the Primaries beneath it as the sum of their demand terms plus the metered generators plus a penalised remainder, with a tuned weight, limits the damage that a metering error at one Primary does to that Primary's forecast, without raising the Primaries' forecast error when no error is present. not supported not-for-production The bulk supply point reading halved the damage from injected scale errors, but it made forecasts on clean data worse at every weight above zero: by at least 0.385 points of capacity in the corrected re-run, about 17 times the 0.023-point limit (2.355 points or more in the first run). A synthetic system that closes exactly loses clean accuracy the same way, so the loss does not come mainly from a wrong multiplier. The cause is untested. As a detector of metering errors the reading is weak: a 25% scale error lasting 30 days is found in 0% of cases by a fit that includes it and in 50% by a fit trained only on earlier rows, which then false-alarms on 61% of later windows. also relevant 00120 differentiable-physics-sh-convex-daily-shape-library A convex model in which each Primary's daily profile is a non-negative mix of K = 3 or 4 shared daily shapes per day type, plus a penalised deviation, forecasts Primary demand with 2 years of history at least 0.05 points better than experiment 109's shrinkage towards one fleet-mean profile. That needs the library to beat the per-site profile by about 0.02 points, because the fleet-mean model is 0.031 worse than it; the plan predicts a tie or a small gain, so supported is a long shot. The stability of the shapes and the shape mix of each substation are descriptive. inconclusive not-for-production In a test with synthetic substations, 5 Primaries were too few for a library of 3 shared daily shapes to recover the shapes we planted, so the check failed on 7 of 10 lines and the verdict is inconclusive. In the scored year the library scored the same as the fleet-mean model and 0.030 points worse than a profile per substation (0.068 worse in winter), and its forecast reproduced a tenth to a half of the Economy 7 night step on cold winter nights. also relevant 00117 differentiable-physics-h2-graph-prior-on-pooled-convex-parameters A penalty on the differences between interconnected Primaries' parameters (heating slopes, PV capacity as a share of effective capacity, the profile's scale, and the holiday coefficients) narrows those parameters' month-block bootstrap intervals without breaking their coverage when neighbouring Primaries are alike, and worsens the full-history quantile score by at most 0.03 points. refuted not-for-production At the weight tested, tying the parameters of interconnected substations together did not improve the forecast: in the scored year it worsened the quantile score by 0.020 points on all days (the interval spans zero) and by 0.173 points in winter evening peaks (the replicate year gave -0.021). On synthetic substations with a known truth it narrowed only heating-slope intervals, and the 80% intervals of PV capacity held the truth 17% of the time against 78% without the tie. A tie on heating slopes alone worsened the real score by 0.006 and 0.001 points, an exploratory lead and not a result. also relevant 00109 differentiable-physics-n0-partially-pooled-convex-model A convex model whose per-substation coefficients are a fleet mean plus a ridge-penalised per-substation deviation forecasts Primary demand as well as the per-substation convex model when both have 2 years of history, and clearly better when the substation has 4 weeks or 3 months. inconclusive not-for-production The known-answer test of this method failed under its pre-registered definition, and only one of five runs (each on a new seed, runs 2 to 5 being post hoc redefinitions) passes every line, so the verdict is inconclusive. Taking the numbers alone, for the five MW Primaries tested, one convex model shared across substations forecast a new substation with only 4 weeks of history 3.3 points better than a convex model fitted to that substation alone (and 0.8 points better with 3 months), far more than the 0.5 to 2.0 predicted, and scored 0.03 points worse on substations with 2 years of history. On the six held-out Primaries it came within 0.2 points of experiment 105's neural pooled model with 4 weeks (the neural model 0.13 better) and 0.12 better with 3 months, without that model's loss on long histories, which suggests that the loss in experiment 105 came largely from the neural fit. Complete pooling scored 0.07 points worse than partial pooling at 4 weeks in the scored year (interval touching zero) and no differently in the replicate year. The gains should be relied on only after a rerun of the gate. also relevant 00105 differentiable-physics-3-pooled-and-per-site-demand-model One differentiable-physics model fitted across all the Primary substations forecasts a substation as well as the same model fitted to that substation alone when both have two years of history, and forecasts clearly better when the substation is new (4 weeks of history) or short of history (3 months). inconclusive not-for-production One neural-network demand model fitted across 15 Primary substations forecasts a substation with only 4 weeks of history far better than a per-site copy of the same model (score 4.04 against 14.38 on the six scored substations), but forecasts a substation with 2 full years of history worse than a per-site copy (3.42 against 3.04 on the five decision substations, worse at all 5). By the pre-registered rule pooling is not yet a success, because that full-history result (C1) is refuted, and a failed known-answer check (gate test 2, injected-farm recovery) caps the verdict at inconclusive. Post hoc, for a new substation the pooled model also beat a per-site convex model fitted to the same 4 weeks (mean absolute error 6.88 against 12.79). also relevant 00103 differentiable-physics-1-data-look The trial area's power records hold enough clean, demand-only history for the series to go ahead as designed: 6 MW Primaries with at least 12 months before July 2025, and 8 MVA Primaries with over 3 site-years each of rows with no sunlight. supported not-for-production The data lets the series go ahead, with three changes: start 13 of the 16 Primaries later than their first record (19.4 months later at D4), fix the lockdown window in advance because the data does not isolate it from drift, and count eligible long-history MW sites at each tuning year's first day (5 at 2024-07-01, so 4 of 5 must improve in Part 2's tuning contrast). The power timestamps show no 30-minute error on either side of the 2026-03-26 fix: at the 6 metered photovoltaic series the median offsets are +0.9 minutes before it and +4.7 after, and the correction is right to within 3 minutes, but offsets at the Primaries are not resolved beyond 0 to +8 minutes. also relevant 00036 hierarchy-aware-bsp-gsp-forecasts For the two bulk supply points (BSPs) Boston and Skegness and the two grid supply points (GSPs) Walpole and Bicker Fen, forecasts of the series beneath each point, and an N1 model trained on ERA5 and applied to ENS members, lower the quantile score below that of N1 trained on ENS. inconclusive not-for-production Forecasts of the series beneath two bulk supply points added nothing (+0.04 and +0.19 points of capacity), nor did wind and solar columns at two grid supply points; an N1 trained on ERA5 lowered the grid supply point scores by 0.36 and 0.40 with intervals spanning -1.8 to +1.0. primary 00032 substation-fingerprints-pooled-demand For demand series of Primary substations, adding a numeric fingerprint of each substation (its location, its mean level and daily and weekly shape over the training window, and its level over the 14 days before the forecast origin) to a by-type pooled XGBoost quantile model closes part of the 0.15-point gap between the pooled model with the series identifier and per-series models, and lets a substation held out of the pool be forecast better than a pooled model with no fingerprint. inconclusive not-for-production Adding numeric substation fingerprints to the pooled model changed the Primary score by at most 0.02 points of capacity, and training-window statistics made a held-out substation worse by 1.39 (inconclusive overall; recent power statistics alone helped it by 0.23, post hoc). primary 00024 pooling-groupings-demand-xgboost For demand series of Primary substations, one XGBoost quantile model trained across a group of series (all series, one model per substation type, or one model per size band), given the series identifier as a categorical column, scores no more than 0.3 points of capacity worse than one model per series, so that the number of models can fall from one per series to one per group. supported candidate Pooling the 16 Primary substations into 3 or 4 XGBoost models (with the series identifier) scored 0.15 points of capacity worse than 20 per-series models (99.44% interval +0.03 to +0.26), inside the 0.30 margin; one model for all 20 series was 0.29 worse, and dropping the identifier cost 0.8 to 1.0. primary
