docs.text: Experiment Hypothesis Relevance

docs.title: Hierarchy and pooling: state and next steps
docs.text: Pooling many series in one neural network lowered the error at the Primaries, but pooling in an XGBoost model did not, and neighbour or hierarchy information has not yet improved any forecast. Terms such as CRPS (continuous ranked probability score), BSP (bulk supply point), GSP (grid supply point), and Primary (primary substation) are defined in the glossary. One neural network across all 16 Primaries beat 16 separate neural networks by 0.185 points of capacity at the six MW Primaries and 0.161 points at the eight MVA Primaries (Experiment 403). The embedding of the Primary identifier carries that gain, and the gain is larger for a Primary with little history (Experiment 406). Pooling the 4 supply points with the Primaries beat a neural network fitted at the Primaries alone by 4.1 and 15.2 points (Experiment 415). For the production port, one lag-enabled neural network per group forecasts the 2 bulk supply points and the 2 grid supply points, as Final models documents.

docs.title: What works
docs.text:
One XGBoost model per substation type or per capacity band scores within the pre-registered margin of one XGBoost model per series. On the 16 Primaries, three or four pooled XGBoost models score 0.15 points of capacity worse than 20 per-series XGBoost models (5.47 against 5.32, 99.44% interval +0.03 to +0.26, margin 0.30). The saved models shrink from 435 MB to 73 to 94 MB. The result comes from one validation year and 20 series, so it says nothing about 2,500 substations (Experiment 24).

One pooled neural network across the 16 Primaries scores lower CRPS than 16 separate neural networks. The gain is 0.185 points at the six MW Primaries (95% interval -0.300 to -0.061) and 0.161 points at the eight MVA Primaries (-0.272 to -0.089), and 11 of the 14 Primaries with long history gain (Experiment 403).

The Primary embedding makes the pooling work, and pooling helps most where one Primary has little history. A pooled neural network without the embedding scores 0.57 points worse than separate neural networks at the six MW Primaries, and the embedding turns that into a gain of 0.22. With one Primary's history cut to 3 months, the pooled neural network is 1.15 points better at the six MW Primaries (Experiment 406).

One neural network per group forecasts the bulk and grid supply points better than a climatology and than the weekly XGBoost forecast at the bulk supply points. The pooled neural network scored 0.47 points of capacity lower than the weekly XGBoost forecast at the bulk supply points in all 4 test months, and tied it at the grid supply points with very wide bands (Experiment 415). The lag-enabled neural network of the production port scores a CRPS of 4.27 at the bulk supply points and 10.52 at the grid supply points at days 0 to 1, against 7.23 and 18.69 for climatology (Final models).

Giving the demand neural network the previous day's and week's power helps a little at the bulk supply points. When the lag-enabled and lag-free neural networks differ only in the lags, the lags lower the error at days 1 to 3 by 0.11 points of capacity at the 2 bulk supply points, a gain that passes the pre-registered bar. The gain fades to zero by about day 6. At the 2 grid supply points the gain is 0.73 points but is below the minimum detectable effect, so it is not shown (Experiment 622). Experiment 622 supersedes Experiment 619, whose offsets were unmatched and whose gain was smaller than 5 development months could resolve (Experiment 619).

docs.title: What does not work
docs.text:
The series identifier cannot be dropped from a pooled XGBoost model, and numeric fingerprints of a substation add nothing to it. Dropping the identifier raised the score of the type pools by 0.82 and of the all-series pool by 0.85 points (Experiment 24). Adding location or training-window statistics changed the score by +0.00 (C1 and C2, both within plus or minus 0.05), and adding recent-window statistics changed it by +0.02 (C4, 99.375% interval -0.05 to +0.10).

A fingerprint did not carry a substation held out of the pool, except for recent-window statistics. A substation held out of the pool was forecast worse with training-window statistics than with no fingerprint (+1.39, +0.99 to +1.91), from one seed and 8 held-out Primaries. Recent-window statistics alone lowered the held-out score by 0.23 (-0.29 to -0.16) in a post hoc arm added after the first run (Experiment 32).

One XGBoost model for all 20 series falls outside the margin. The model scores 0.29 points worse than per-series XGBoost models on the 16 Primaries (+0.19 to +0.42), and 0.80 points worse on the 2 bulk supply points alone (Experiment 24).

Adding the 4 supply points to the neural network's training rows did not improve the 16 Primaries. The change was smaller than the experiment could detect, and its sign differed between the 8 MVA Primaries (+0.026) and the 6 MW Primaries (-0.054). A fair test of whether pooling helps needs many more extra series than NGED's data holds (Experiment 564).

Forecasts of the series beneath a bulk supply point did not lower its score. Summing the Primary and generator forecasts beneath Boston and Skegness changed the score by +0.04 and +0.19 points, and the intervals include zero (Experiment 36). Putting every child Primary into the sum changed the score by +0.005 points at Skegness and -0.011 at Boston, with intervals that include zero (Experiment 204).

A scaled sum of the Primary forecasts scored worse than a neural network that sees the node's own readings. The sum scored 34% to 60% higher error than the neural network (Experiment 426).

The recent errors of interconnected neighbours predicted under 2% of a Primary's own day-ahead error. Adding true neighbours' lag residuals lowered the held-out squared error by 0.01% against own lags only (Experiment 426).

Adding the bulk supply point reading to the differentiable-physics fit of the Primaries made the forecast worse. The clean-forecast error rose by 0.4 to 4.6 points at every weight tried (Experiment 124).

The first-release recipe did not clearly beat the plain pooled neural network at the supply points. At the bulk supply points the difference was inside the noise (-0.14 and +0.09). At the grid supply points the recipe was about 0.5 points better, close to the refit noise of about 0.4 (Experiment 475).

A 0/1 metering-type input did not help. At the 8 MVA Primaries it made the score worse by 0.038 points, as a randomly permuted flag did. At the 6 MW Primaries it helped by 0.030 points, a gain too small to port (Experiment 525).

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
Pooling is unsettled at hundreds of series. All pooled results use at most 20 series (Experiments 24 and 564).

A substation never seen by the pool is tested only for XGBoost models. Experiment 32 used one seed and 8 Primaries. The write-up suggests, without testing it, that 7 distinct fingerprints act as 7 identifiers.

The largest observed miss at a grid supply point looks like a load shift. The demand at Walpole stepped up on 2026-10-19 while the median fell, and the neural network has no neighbour inputs and no load-shift component (Final models). Whether neighbours help inside load-shift events is untested. Experiment 426 did not measure it, and Experiment 404 has no neighbour inputs.

The 90% band at the supply points is too narrow. The band covers 0.867 of readings at the bulk supply points and 0.877 at the grid supply points, against 0.90 (Final models).

docs.title: Next experiments, as options
docs.text:
For the production port, no experiment in this theme is a prerequisite. The bulk-and-grid neural network and its retraining recipe are specified in Final models. The options below are ordered by how directly they bear on the port. None is started. Options 2 to 6 come from the differentiable-physics pooling plan. The closure audit is Experiment 124's fit of how much of each bulk supply point's reading its metered children and generators explain, with the rest as an unmetered remainder.

  1. An option is to compare the 3.5-hour lag cap with a longer cap on matched refit schedules. The question is which cap scores better at the supply points. A fit costs about 2 GPU-hours for the one-year run (Final models). Nothing blocks it, and Final models lists it as open.

  2. An option is to compare a top-down with a bottom-up forecast at the bulk and grid supply points. The question is whether a direct forecast beats the sum of the Primary forecasts plus generators, and whether reconciling the two helps. Experiment 204 found the bottom-up forecast with every child Primary matched the top-down forecast (+0.1% and -0.15%, intervals include zero). Experiment 386 found the generalised additive model stack 1.0 points (bulk supply points) and 2.0 points (grid supply points) worse than the weekly XGBoost forecast (Experiment 386). The topology would enter as a soft hint, because the unmetered remainder makes an exact sum wrong.

  3. An option is to use the bulk supply point reading as an observation in the Kalman filters of the Primaries. The question is whether the closure relation, with its unmetered remainder as state noise, helps the Primaries' filters. The experiment runs on the CPU in about 2 hours and depends on the closure audit of Experiment 124.
  4. An option is to treat metered generators as export-positive nodes at the bulk supply point. The question is whether the closure relation then holds better at the 2 bulk supply points. Experiment 223 found that the remainders move with the generators but not one-for-one, and it recommends separating unmetered solar and battery dispatch first (Experiment 223). Any figure would show the generators anonymised.
  5. An option is to test unmetered wind at the bulk and grid supply points. The question is whether the closure residual follows the weather forecast's wind speed. The test depends on the closure audit and on separating the wind part of the residual from the solar part.
  6. An option is a pooled differentiable-physics model on every v1 series, including MVA substations. The question is whether full-history skill and capacity identification improve. The experiment needs 3 to 5 GPU hours. The design differs from the pooled neural network.

docs.title: Parked
docs.text:
Neighbour graph neural networks are parked, because the signal they would pass along is near zero. Experiment 426 found no neighbour-error signal, so no graph neural network was fitted.

Pooling for onboarding substations with little history is parked. The pooled model forecast a substation with 4 weeks of history far better than a per-site copy (4.04 against 14.38), and worse at 2 full years (3.42 against 3.04) (Experiment 105).

Load-shift event detection is paused until January. The pause is described on the load-shift detectors state page. Any neighbour test inside load-shift events waits with it.

Wider fingerprint designs are parked. Experiment 32 found no gain for series seen in training, and recent-window statistics alone helped a held-out substation by 0.23 in a post hoc test.

docs.title: Lagged power and error correction
docs.text:
The current understanding and the options for next work are on the state and next steps page.

On 16 Primary substations over one validation year, both recent power fed to a second-stage calibrator and a correction by the mean error of the last 14 days lower the forecast error, by similar amounts against different reference forecasts; on solar farms, wind farms, and supply points neither has been shown to help.

A summary of what the experiments found about load-shift events collects the answers to ten questions on one page.

Recent measured power can enter the forecast as input, or shift the forecast by its recent errors. The experiments put lagged power into stage 1b (a second model that corrects the weather-only forecast) or into the stage 2 calibrator, and tested variants of the 14-day correction. All scores are the quantile score in points of capacity, and lower is better. The five experiments of this theme scored 73 forecast runs, one every 5 days from July 2025 to June 2026. Other experiments cited use other run sets, stated where cited. Stage 1a is the weather-only forecast, trained on ERA5 and CAMS estimates of past weather.

Lagged power in the calibrator scored better than lagged power in stage 1b in every lead band (C1, stage 1b with a lag-free calibrator minus the calibrator with lags, where positive means stage 1b is worse; 99% intervals; 16 Primary substations). Source: experiment 5.

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
Recent power lowers the error, and it lowers it more in the calibrator than in stage 1b. For 16 Primary substations up to 48 hours ahead, the calibrator with lagged power scored 5.31, stage 1b with a calibrator that sees no lags scored 6.14, and a calibrator with no lags scored 7.11. The contrast is +0.84 (+0.28 to +1.50 at 99%), so the pre-registered idea that stage 1b is the better place was refuted. Using both placements lowered the score by at most 0.12 more. Stage 1b scored better at 8 of the 16 series, so the average hides a mixed result (experiment 5).

Summaries of recent power added no resolvable gain to the raw lags. Adding the minimum, mean, and maximum of the last 24 hours and of the same weekday changed the score by -0.02 (-0.14 to +0.13 at 98.75%; inconclusive). Replacing the raw lags with the summaries worsened it by 0.29 (+0.11 to +0.51). Summaries alone still beat no recent power (-1.18, -1.83 to -0.58) (experiment 8). Experiment 30 tested more lag columns in N1 and is on the demand inputs page.

With only the data a live service has, the two-stage chain is not distinguishable from N1. The lagged inputs of experiments 5 and 8 use estimates of past weather that a live service lacks, so they are ceilings. Experiment 18 rebuilt them from weather available at the forecast origin and from NGED's real telemetry delay (the wait before a power reading arrives; 7 hours). Over all leads the chain minus N1 was +0.08 (-0.11 to +0.25 at 99.17%; inconclusive). Up to 48 hours it was -0.27 (-0.62 to +0.03), and beyond 3 days +0.15 (-0.07 to +0.36). The chain scored 0.52 above the manual_heuristic baseline (-0.25 to +1.25; interval includes zero). Lag anomalies lowered the score by only 0.04 against raw lagged power (-0.12 to +0.07).

The chain is level with N1, and above manual_heuristic beyond 3 days (point estimate; the interval includes zero). Source: experiment 18.

The 14-day correction lowered the Primary score by about 1 point, a gain of similar size to lagged power in the calibrator against a different reference. Experiments 19 and 21 scored the correction on the same 73 runs and 16 Primary substations as experiments 5 and 18. N1 plus the correction scored 5.34 over all leads, against 6.33 for N1. The chain of experiment 18 scored 6.41, and lagged power in that chain gained -1.05 (-1.64 to -0.58) against a calibrator without lags (experiment 18, C2). The references differ and no paired interval compares them. Experiment 19 (power 3.5 hours old) gave -0.99 (-1.84 to -0.15 at 99.44%). Experiment 21 gave -0.99 (-1.82 to -0.18 at 99.375%) with power 2 days old. Experiment 19 is on the production reference and best guess page.

The correction lowered the Primary score, no variant beat the plain 14-day additive form, and the correction did not lower the score of the 4 bulk and grid supply point series. Source: experiment 21.

No variant of the correction beat the plain 14-day additive form on Primary substations. A 7-day window was worse (+0.19, +0.11 to +0.28), a 28-day window was level or slightly better (-0.07, -0.15 to +0.01), a multiplicative form was far worse (+2.28, +0.50 to +5.46), and a per-half-hour shift (+0.02) and recency weights (+0.04) changed nothing (experiment 21).

The correction is unproven for supply points, solar farms, and wind farms. On 4 bulk and grid supply point series it raised the score by 0.36 (-0.19 to +0.98 at 99.375%; inconclusive; experiment 21) and by 0.305 (95% interval 0.060 to 0.594) in the BG2 ablation on 292 daily runs (experiment 87). On 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms (53 Tuesday runs), lagged power left the calibrator's CRPS unchanged to about 0.1 points, and the correction raised it for solar (+0.437, +0.215 to +0.664) and did not clearly change it for wind (+0.413, -0.003 to +0.924) (experiment 23).

Lags near switching were tested in two other themes. Training with lags hidden at random did not widen the 5% to 95% band where a lag is missing. On 292 daily runs, the band covered 0.799 of real masked half-hours (37,394) for the plain model and 0.802 with lags hidden in 10% of rows, against 0.90 nominal (+0.003, -0.093 to +0.101 at 98.75%; inconclusive; experiment 100). Telling a monthly-refitted XGBoost model how unusual each lag is raised the score outside switching by 0.355 (+0.209 to +0.513 at 97.5%; refuted; experiment 90).

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text:
Of the designs tested in this theme, the stage 2 calibrator with raw lagged power is the best use of lagged power, and the additive 14-day correction is the best correction.

  1. Give the stage 2 calibrator (arm L3, the calibrator with lagged power, of experiment 5) the power 24, 48, 168, and 336 hours before the target, the four stage 1a residuals at those times, and five residuals at the newest observation. Keep the raw lags (experiment 8).
  2. For a live service, build the lag residuals from weather available at the origin (experiment 18), and apply a spread factor of 1.15 (-0.04, -0.08 to -0.00). This design did not beat N1.
  3. For Primary substations, add the mean error of the last 14 days of the forecast median to every quantile, using a window of 14 days or longer and an additive shift (experiment 21). No experiment combined the chain with the correction.

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text: No experiment in this theme is marked candidate; all five are not-for-production. The correction for Primary demand is a candidate in experiments 19, 33, and 87, described on the production reference and best guess page, and experiment 30 is a candidate on the demand inputs page. Experiment 21 supports the correction with power 2 days old, which gave the same all-lead gain as power 3.5 hours old, so the service need not wait for fresher telemetry. It supports no use at supply points.

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
• Compare a lagged arm with a calibrated arm that has no lags. A calibrator without lags lowered the stage 1a score by 1.02 up to 48 hours (exploratory contrast E4, whose interval includes zero at some leads), and stage 1a alone scored 8.12 against 8.14 for day-type climatology. Against stage 1a alone, lags look about 1 point better than they are (experiment 5). Look for a lagged arm whose comparison has no calibrator.
  • Label an arm a ceiling when its lag residuals use estimates of past weather. The arms of experiments 5 and 8 used ERA5 at lag times, and rebuilding them from serving sources worsened the score by 0.13 (+0.02 to +0.25; experiment 18). Re-check with a different weather source for the lag times.
  • State the telemetry delay of every lagged arm. Experiment 5 used 0.5 hours (the newest half-hour before the origin), experiment 13 3.5 hours, and experiment 18 7 hours. Three and a half hours more delay worsened the chain by 0.13 over all leads and 0.16 up to 48 hours, so scores with different delays do not compare (experiment 18). Re-check on a different delay.
  • Report how many series agree with the mean. C1 of experiment 5 (above) was +0.84 on average while stage 1b was better at 8 of the 16 Primary substations (experiment 5). Look for a mean over series with mixed signs.
  • Do not correct a skewed target by the mean of observed minus median. That shift raised the solar CRPS by 0.437 and the wind CRPS by 0.413 (interval includes zero) and cut the 5% to 95% coverage to 53% to 77%. A median shift was tried once, post hoc, and moved the CRPS by +0.010 for solar and -0.064 for wind, with intervals that include zero (experiment 23). Re-check with a pre-registered median shift.
  • Check the base forecast's bias before applying the correction. N1's two bulk supply point series had a bias of +0.01, so the correction only added noise (experiment 21), and in experiment 87 a frozen model with the correction scored 13.559 against 13.369 without it (experiment 87). Look for a base forecast with little bias.
  • Build the correction's error history from the runs a live service would have. Experiments 19 and 21 measured each past half-hour's error from a run 0 to 5 days earlier, with runs 5 days apart, and applied it up to 15 days ahead. A daily service sees smaller errors at shorter leads, and experiment 87 scored the correction on 292 daily runs (experiment 19, experiment 21). Look for a run schedule other than every 5 days.
  • Keep a control that keeps the event rows when testing masked lags. Dropping event and closure rows from training (the mask arm, which also sets lags inside labelled events to missing) narrowed the band on unmasked rows by 4% and lowered its coverage from 0.906 to 0.894, so the masked arms differ from the plain model in more than the dropout (experiment 100). The masked rows came from an estimated 15 to 20 events, mostly at three substations. Look for a masked arm without a control that keeps the rows.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text:
• Whether lagged power helps once the correction is in place: no experiment here combined them.
  • Whether the staged chain beats N1 at leads up to 2 days. Its point estimate was lower there, but the interval includes zero.
  • Whether the correction helps supply points when more than 4 series are scored, or helps solar and wind farms when it uses a median shift.
  • Whether an input that flags a missing lag, or a separate model of the band width, widens the band where a lag is missing. Experiment 100 tested only random dropout.

The Research plan lists what is planned next, and the Experiments page lists every experiment.

docs.title: Lagged power and error correction: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00695 gas-engine-state-tracker-part-2-cleaned-target-and-climatology-add-back At D8, removing the inferred gas-engine output from the training target and from the lagged-power inputs of the demand neural network, and adding the engine back at forecast time as a climatological distribution over the number of running units (passed through the apparent-power fold), lowers the error of the forecast of D8's metered apparent power, against the same neural network trained on the raw reading. not supported not-for-production Taking the gas engine out of D8's recorded demand before training, and adding the engine's average running pattern back when forecasting, did not improve the forecast. The cleaned arm was no better than the raw arm, and a post hoc reading of the same data suggests it was probably about 0.1 points of capacity worse over all rows. At another substation with an engine injected, cleaning gained about 0.1 points, within noise. Knowing whether the engine runs at the forecast's valid time would lower the error by 1.4 to 2.4 points against the raw arm, but no forecast has that knowledge. No gain was found, and cleaning plus a calendar add-back is not worth porting; one open question is whether the engine's state can be forecast from information available at the origin. also relevant 00693 oracle-transfer-flag-in-the-candidate-part-1 A perfect telemetry detector, which knows that a reading lay inside a load transfer (and when the transfer began, once a reading after the onset exists), lowers the CRPS of the Candidate demand network on transfer-affected rows by at least 0.3 points of capacity against a placebo flag, without raising CRPS on event-free rows by more than 0.05. inconclusive not-for-production Telling the demand forecast exactly when a load transfer is happening did not make it clearly better on simulated transfers. The forecast that reads yesterday's power loses only 0.1 points of capacity to a transfer, and the forecast that adapts to a transfer scores about the same with a perfect flag or a random one on the deciding simulation. The test could not rule out a gain or a loss of half a point or more, because three refits of the same forecast already differ by about 0.4 points, so no conclusion about a real switching detector is safe. A repeat needs at least 10 refits per arm. also relevant 00691 causal-detector-features-plus-extra-lags-in-the-prevailing-head The detector features of experiment 687 (F1) and the extra lagged power block of experiment 681 (L1) carry partly different information, so a head that reads both (FL1) reacts to the start of a load shift sooner than the better of the two single-input heads. not supported not-for-production Reading both the detector features and the extra lagged power makes the prevailing output follow a new load shift 1.75 days sooner than experiment 652's head, but only 0.16 days sooner than the features alone (interval -0.45 to +0.14), so the lags add under 0.5 days to the features and no new feature is proposed. The in-force score improves by 0.20 points of capacity, below the 0.30 bar, and false alarms on event-free rows rise by 5 points. primary 00687 causal-detector-features-for-the-prevailing-forecast-heads Per-lag causal step statistics in noise units, the gap with the all-Primaries median removed, the opposite-sign neighbour gap, the routine-step rate, and a return-to-level statistic carry information about whether a lag lies inside a load shift that the gap summaries of experiments 606 and 610 do not, and a small prevailing head that reads them reacts sooner to the start and the end of a shift than the same head reading extra lagged power inputs (the arm of experiment 681). partly supported not-for-production Giving the prevailing head a step detector's statistics makes it follow a new load shift about 1.6 days sooner than experiment 652's head, and releases a shift about 0.6 days sooner on average (median 0, so the 1-day bar is not met at the end). Simply adding recent lagged power gets 1.25 days at the start, so the detector features are not shown to be better than extra lags. The in-force score improves by 0.12 points of capacity [-0.33, +0.06], an interval that includes zero and is below the 0.30 bar. primary 00681 extra-lagged-power-inputs-for-the-prevailing-forecast Giving the prevailing head of experiment 667's Candidate more lagged power inputs, newer than the 24-hour and 7-day lags it reads today, shortens the time the prevailing output takes to cover half of a new load level after a confirmed load shift starts. small gain candidate Giving the prevailing forecast 8 to 14 extra lagged power inputs makes it follow a new load level about 20 hours sooner on 1152 simulated load shifts, and 120 hours sooner at D5 in one verified real transfer (D16 did not change), without making the normal-running (NRA) output or the event-free forecast worse. The gain is under the 24 hours set in advance as worth the extra inputs. On injected events 8 inputs give 19.1 of the 20.4 hours, but at D5 only 72 of the 120 hours, and the 8-input set scores worst inside the real events, so which set to port is open. primary 00677 building-up-the-candidate-demand-network-one-component-at-a-time Descriptive, not a hypothesis test. A reverse ablation measures the order-dependent contribution of each Candidate component. Predictions that could fail are listed in the front matter field prediction and repeated under "Predictions that could fail" below. partly supported not-for-production Pre-training the date-time and weather encoders on ERA5 and CAMS (step 3b, 8.30) is the first step to beat the manual heuristic (8.73), and the lags bring step 5 to 7.88. Steps 6 to 8 add no annual skill: the Candidate (step 8) scores 7.99, which is 0.105 worse than step 5. Steps 6 to 8 cut the share of an injected shift that the median copies from 5.9% to 2.8%, and they raise MAE by 0.05 to 0.12 off the logged events. Monthly refits improve step 5 and step 8 by about 0.47. The year overlaps the Candidate's development months, so the scores are not a ranking. also relevant 00668 documentation-of-the-one-year-backtest-files-models-training-and-performance Not a hypothesis test. The page documents the five one-year backtest files so that an engineer can re-implement each model and a colleague at NGED can read the files. inconclusive not-for-production The five backtest files forecast better than climatology at every lead band for the Primaries, BSPs, GSPs, and solar, and for wind out to day 10; the wind network is 1.8% worse at days 10 to 14. The gain falls with lead time, for Primaries from 35.3% at days 0 to 1 to 26.9% at days 10 to 14. The files describe one year that overlaps the development months, so the scores are not a ranking. also relevant 00667 one-year-backtest-of-the-two-output-demand-network-at-primaries Descriptive, not a hypothesis test. The one-year backtest is the first real-rows test of the Candidate plus the R-haz head. Prediction that could fail: extending the Candidate from 10 to 14 days leaves its score at days 0 to 10 within 0.10 points of capacity of experiment 620's. inconclusive candidate The Candidate with a 14-day survival head forecasts a year of daily origins at 16 Primaries with a CRPS between 3.5 and 4.4 points of capacity, rising 28% (prevailing) or 18% (NRA) from days 0 to 1 to days 7 to 14. Both outputs are too narrow: the q05 to q95 band covers 0.81 (NRA) and 0.85 (prevailing) of half-hours, and as little as 0.72 for the NRA output in August. The prevailing output has the lower CRPS on average and in 9 of 12 months (a comparison that is not like for like, because the NRA output deliberately excludes load shifts that the metered power contains), but the November and December folds use a fallback survival curve with no trained head, and the prevailing output loses to the NRA output at two Primaries. The year overlaps the development months and the final test, so none of this is a ranking. advice: - >- Do not read the q05 to q95 columns as a 90% interval. Widen or recalibrate them before use; the width is a follow-up, not something this backtest tuned (coverage by lead band table). - >- Treat the prevailing rows of 2025-11 and 2025-12 as the fallback method: they equal the NRA rows on 74% and 65% of origins (Method). - >- Read the survival output beyond day 10 as the bank generator's duration prior, not as an estimate from observed events (Caveats). also relevant 00663 end-detector-for-the-prevailing-forecast-followup-to-654 A detector that reads the freshest half-hours of (observed power minus the NRA forecast) at a Primary and at its electrical neighbours, and outputs the probability that a load shift has ended, lets the prevailing forecast of E0 (frozen K1 plus the survival-hazard head R-haz) and of J2 (the end-to-end network of experiment 654) drop a shift sooner after it ends, and cuts the share of event-free rows on which the prevailing forecast wrongly departs from the NRA forecast. not supported not-for-production A learned end detector made the prevailing forecast better in the 24 hours after an injected shift ends (-0.9 to -1.1 scaled points of capacity) and worse while the shift is in force (+0.2 to +0.3 for E0d), and the neighbour graph added no consistent gain, because three random rewirings of it scored within 0.08 points of the real graph. On the final-test window the detector made E0 worse (4.81 against 4.26) and J2 slightly better (4.85 against 5.02), and the plain E0 was the best prevailing forecast of all (4.26). The veto on event-free rows is not met for E0d, and J2d passes it by its interval but not in every month. The detector is not worth the neighbour feed. primary 00652 two-output-forecast-with-explicit-rules-and-survival-hazard A prevailing-conditions head that outputs a signed depth and a survival probability per lead day, and is trained on a stated mixture of shift durations, scores a lower CRPS than K1 shifted by its own decayed recent error (R0 at 168 h) and than a no-fit hazard baseline (K1 shifted by its recent error and decayed by the best single survival curve), at every origin state in which a shift is in force, once every forecast is scored under its own rules. not supported not-for-production A prevailing forecast that continues a load shift cuts the error where a shift is in force from 9.9 to 5.8 points of capacity (unscaled), but a survival curve fitted to shift durations, with no neural network, scores 5.85 and so does as well as a neural network that learns the survival, when the shifts follow the training mixture. On held-out durations the learned survival output is better by 0.74 points, so the tie is not general. In the last day before a shift ends, the learned forecast scores 3.5 points worse than K1 and the fitted curve 4.6 points worse, which is the price of not knowing the end. primary 00651 graph-layer-over-electrical-neighbours-in-the-demand-network-part-1 A graph layer between the existing encoders (weather, date-time, lag) and the mixer of the class 2 candidate, on the electrical neighbour graph (29 edges among 16 Primaries), learns when to use a neighbour. It keeps the candidate's follow of an injected load shift and removes the candidate's extra event-free error at the six MW Primaries, and the electrical graph does this better than a degree-preserving rewired graph. not supported not-for-production A graph layer over the electrical neighbours did not remove the class 2 candidate's extra error at the six MW Primaries, and did not help it resist a false load shift. The graph layers made little use of the neighbours, and an arm whose graph was wired at random did as well as the arm with the real graph. The extra error is the same with no neighbour information at all, so the first place to look for the cause is the class 2 training choices (E3 rows, the D5 offset, and signal dropout), not the electricity network's topology. primary 00650 extended-shift-departure-head-against-decayed-recent-error A departure head trained on an extended shift generator (shifts that end at random times, constant and proportional shapes, step and ramp onsets, depths from 3 to 50 points of capacity, donor and receiver conserved across real neighbours) forecasts the arrangement now in force better than K1 shifted by its own decayed recent error (R0 at tau 168 h), on a shift family that no arm trains on, after the band-widening share of the gain is removed. partly supported not-for-production Training the departure head on shifts that end at random times, with varied shapes and depths, makes it beat the no-fit shift by 2.3 points of capacity inside shifts outside its training range, and beat the head trained on the old bank by 1.5 points. The head still carries a shift past its end and scores 3.6 points worse than K1 there, so it is not ready for production. The next step is a head that ends a shift as soon as the gap signals say so. primary 00648 demand-encoder-size-and-hyperparameter-search-on-k1-and-the-class-2-candidate Experiment 447 found the S1 demand network insensitive to its settings. K1 and the class 2 candidate differ from S1: the lag encoder reads two lags with a learnt lag ID, and the candidate adds neighbour summaries. Their parts may no longer sit at a flat optimum, so changing the width or depth of the lag encoder, the width of the neighbour-summary encoder, the number of mixture components, the hidden width, the dropout, the learning rate, or the maximum number of epochs lowers days 1 to 10 event-free CRPS by more than the margin without making the network follow an injected load-shift more. not supported not-for-production Making the lag encoder wider or deeper, or the hidden layers bigger, does not improve the K1 or class 2 candidate demand neural networks by the margin we required (0.11 CRPS points); the best gain is 0.04 points and comes from one short-history Primary (D15), while the six MW Primaries get slightly worse. Dropout 0.0 hurts; a doubled learning rate lowered the score by 0.04 points in both neural networks, but no interval was computed. The neighbour-summary bottleneck gains 0.05 points but makes the forecast follow an injected load-shift more, so it fails its guard. No change helped detectably, so keep the sizes as they are and look for gains in the inputs, as experiment 447 advised. primary 00647 two-output-forecast-departure-head-on-frozen-k1 The arrangement now in force (the prevailing forecast) can be forecast better by a separate departure head added to the normal-running-arrangement forecast of K1 than by shifting K1's quantiles by its own recent error with a decaying weight (R0). The head may read K1's outputs, K1's frozen encoder embeddings, or an encoder retrained on the departure loss, and the normal-running-arrangement output stays K1 or, in the joint neural network, no worse than K1. partly supported not-for-production On injected load shifts the departure head scores 10.0 points of capacity below K1, but shifting K1 by its own recent error with no fit (tau 168 h) already closes most of that gap, so the head is only 0.9 points better, and the no-fit shift matches the head after a shift ends. Widening K1's band with no signal gets 60% to 68% of the head's gain, and about 3.3 points come from reading the gap signals. On real flagged days the gain rests on the verified pair in 2026-01. The next step is an experiment that separates the signal from the widening and from the no-fit shift, using shifts that end on varied days, before any head is considered for production. primary 00646 per-ens-member-neural-demand-networks-pooled-quantiles Running K1 and K3 once per ensemble member, and pooling the 51 member outputs into one mixture, improves the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), the upper-tail coverage, and the event-free scores over the networks that read the ensemble mean and spread, without raising the share of an injected load-shift that the forecast follows. not supported not-for-production For K1 and K3 on the five development months, giving the demand networks the mean and spread of the 51 ensemble members matched running them once per member and pooling the 51 answers, once the bands had equal width. The mean-and-spread input needs one pass through the neural network per forecast instead of 51. Pooling mainly widens the forecast band. Retraining the networks on one member at a time raised the CRPS by 0.02 to 0.07 points of capacity (the K1 interval includes 0). In this test the member inputs gave no gain beyond the mean and spread, so any gain from the ensemble would have to come from another input or from the training method. also relevant 00641 d15-d12-error-diagnosis-and-cheapest-fixes Most of K1's excess error at D15 and D12 sits in a small number of multi-day level shifts (unlabelled transfers) at D15 and in a midday peak at D12, so a per-Primary level correction at D15 and a midday-aware correction at D12 lower their CRPS, rather than the error being spread evenly as noise no forecast could remove. not supported not-for-production D15's forecast error is a one-sided bias that lasts for days but not weeks: in March 2026 K1's median forecast was about 1.3 MW below the median reading. Correcting the forecast with the previous 14 days of errors recovered about a quarter of the possible gain at D15, with an interval that includes zero, and made the other 14 Primaries worse. The cause of the offset has to be found before it can be fixed. D12's error is largest at midday, twice its night error, and the same correction did not lower it. also relevant 00632 gru-attention-sequence-network-for-primary-demand A sequence neural network (Seq: an encoder gated recurrent unit over the last 7 days, a decoder gated recurrent unit over the next 7 days that starts from the encoder's state, and three self-attention layers over all tokens), pre-trained on ERA5 and CAMS weather with one Primary embedding for all 16 Primaries, forecasts the next 7 days of demand better than the existing pre-trained networks, because it reads the last 6 days of power and not only a day lag and a week lag. refuted not-for-production The sequence neural network is not worth porting. Seq is not shown better than the per-row lag neural network P2-pre (CRPS 2.90 against 2.86 at the eight MVA Primaries, 2.12 against 2.15 at the six MW Primaries) and loses to P2-hist6, a per-row neural network that reads six daily lags (2.80 and 2.13). No ablation (no attention, no recurrence, neighbour inputs) and not the 3-week history beat Seq by more than seed noise. Seq follows an injected load-shift more than P2-pre does (a share of 0.40 against 0.27 of the shift at the eight MVA Primaries from day 4 of the event), and training it on synthetic shifts cuts that to 0.15 but raises CRPS by about 0.12 points. Stage 3 (ensemble weather) does not run. primary 00620 bakeoff-final-test-demand-networks-at-primaries Each of the three frozen candidate demand networks (K1 with the gate, the ungated class 2 candidate, and the lag-free K3), trained only on data before 2026-07-01, is better than the climatology and manual-heuristic comparators on the held-out forecast origins 2026-07-01 to 2026-10-31, and the ranking of the three candidates on those months agrees with their ranking on the five development months. partly supported candidate A network trained once on data before July 2026 and never refitted scored no better than the manual heuristic over the next four months, and no worse for K1 and the candidate. K1 and the candidate beat the heuristic at 12 of 16 Primaries on CRPS. They lose at four Primaries, D14, D15, D16, and D18, and the losses at these four are what the wins at the other 12 offset. All three bands are too narrow, so the neural networks are over-confident. The pooled result rests on one unlabelled load transfer between D14 and D18: on event-free rows K1 and the candidate beat the heuristic by 0.26 and 0.25 points, and without D15 and D18 by 0.24 and 0.20 points. Both are descriptive second readings, not used to rank. Refitting during the window, which weekly production retraining would do, is untested. also relevant 00614 bakeoff-roster-backtest-export-and-final-test-runner The stored forecasts of experiments 612 and 613 can be repackaged for the three candidate neural networks (class 1 K1, class 2 candidate, class 3 K3) over the five development months so that event-free q05-q95 coverage recomputed from the exported files matches the coverage those experiments printed, and a runner can check the timing rules row by row, score each frozen candidate exactly once, and refuse to run a second time. supported not-for-production The stored forecasts of the three candidate neural networks are now in one folder that a colleague can score without refitting anything, and the numbers recomputed from it match experiment 613 exactly, and experiment 612 when rebuilt from its two seeds. The runner for the one final test is written and tested on a development month with two dummy candidates. It has not been run on the final test, and the three real neural networks still need wiring into it once the maintainer freezes the three candidate neural networks. also relevant 00613 nra-roster-contrasts-with-intervals-five-seeds Experiment 612 left three claims resting on point estimates inside the tolerance. With seeds 0 to 4 on the five development months, the interval of each contrast lies inside the tolerance (0.01 coverage, 0.03 absorption, the printed minimum detectable effect in continuous ranked probability score, CRPS) for (1) the class 2 candidate against K1, (2) O2 against D5 in K1, K2, and K3, and (3) E3 against the 3-day embargo on coverage. partly supported candidate The class 2 candidate matches the gate on injected load-shifts: its coverage and safe-side share are within 0.01 of K1's. It still fails the rule fixed in advance, because its event-free CRPS is not shown equivalent in 3 of 4 cells. The candidate follows less of an injected shift than K1 does (lower is better), and it covers more event-free rows only because its band is wider. Five seeds did not tighten the event-free comparisons enough to prove that O2 equals D5, so that swap rests on the point estimates and on explainability. primary 00612 nra-combined-networks-three-class-roster-completion Once the two-constant tail widening is fitted on each network's own forecasts, the steadier offset O2 is equivalent to D5 in K1, K2, and K3, and a class 2 network that reads neighbour summaries with signal dropout (K2 plus experiment 610's P7 with D50) matches K1's day-4-to-end coverage at the gate's band width without the gate. partly supported candidate With tail constants fitted on each neural network's own forecasts, the steadier offset O2 does not measurably change coverage in K1, K2, or K3. The test is too coarse to prove O2 equal to D5, and three small differences go against O2. The class 2 candidate, with a band 12 to 18% wider than its unscaled band, covers like K1 on injected load-shifts. The candidate follows and absorbs far less than K1 does. The claim that the candidate replaces the gate rests on point estimates inside the tolerance, not on intervals inside it. Removing the offset raises the follow of an injected shift by 0.036. primary 00610 nra-neighbour-summary-lag-encoder-inputs-iteration In experiment 606, summaries over all electrical neighbours (arm P7) cut the median forecast's follow of a load-shift from 0.119 (A1) to 0.035, but raised the event-free CRPS by 0.021 at the eight MVA Primaries and by 0.068 at the six MW Primaries. The cost is caused partly by a mismatch between training and test signals (the signals of the training rows come from a network that saw those rows), and partly by a network that has learnt to depend on signals that are sometimes uninformative. Building the signals out of fold, dropping them on part of the training rows, or passing them through one scalar lowers the cost without lowering the benefit. not supported not-for-production The neighbour-summary inputs (P7, from experiment 606) make the A1 demand network follow a load- shift much less, but none of the 27 variants and the placebo that we tried keeps ordinary-day accuracy at the six MW Primaries without losing that benefit. The closest variant (P7+D50, with signals hidden on half of the training rows) is within the minimum detectable effect at the eight MVA Primaries and 0.015 percentage points of capacity short at the six MW Primaries. A possible next step is blending the P7 forecast with the A1 forecast at the six MW Primaries, rather than trying more input permutations. The audit found that seed noise and the two-month interval make the extra-error differences between arms unreliable. primary 00608 nra-combined-networks-per-class-and-leave-one-out Each part of the three combined networks (K1, lag and gate; K2, lag without an explicit gate; K3, lag-free) earns its place: removing any one lowers a measure it was added for by more than that measure's tolerance. partly supported candidate On injected load-shifts, the lag-and-gate network (K1) keeps the normal running arrangement inside its band on 0.927 of rows from day 4 of a shift to its end, and the gated band is the largest single part of that (0.041). In the tested arm, the steadier offset narrows the band, so the lag neural network keeps the current offset D5 in this test. The event-free band is too narrow (0.88 against 0.90), and the two-constant widening repairs it only at the eight MVA Primaries. primary 00606 nra-lag-encoder-signal-permutations-gap-averages-and-neighbours The A1 demand network follows a load-shift (reads shifted lags as if they were normal) partly because its lag encoder has no input that says how far a lag is from what the lag-free forecast expected. Giving the lag encoder the gap between each lag and the lag-free forecast at the lag's own time, with exponentially weighted averages of that gap over the last days, lowers follow, and summaries of the gaps at all electrical neighbours lower it further. partly supported candidate Giving the demand network's lag encoder a weighted history of how far each recent lag sits from the lag-free forecast, and the same history at its electrical neighbours, cut the share of an injected load-shift that the forecast follows from 0.119 to 0.035. Stretched to the hand-built gate's width, the network then covers the normal running arrangement as often as the gate does (0.932 against 0.928, within noise). Two fold months, injected events that mirror each shift at one neighbour, and a cost in event-free CRPS (up to 0.068 points of capacity at the six MW Primaries) mean this is a candidate to test further, not a replacement for the gate yet. primary 00603 nra-lag-perturbation-in-pretraining-and-split-mixer Showing the network synthetic lag-only load-shifts during pre-training and step 2, and not only in the step-3 fine-tune, and keeping the first half of the mixer (stage 1, which reads the weather, datetime and lag embeddings) frozen from pre-training onwards, makes the network trust unusual lagged power less.
