docs.title: Planned experiments
docs.text: Experiment Hypothesis Relevance 00654 two-output-network-end-to-end-with-end-detector One network, trained end to end (K1's body plus a prevailing head that reads the lag-encoder outputs, with no hand-built gate), gives a prevailing forecast at least as good as the frozen K1 plus the survival-hazard head R-haz of experiment 652, with no loss to the normal-running- arrangement (NRA) output; and a learned end detector that reads the freshest half-hours lets the prevailing forecast drop a shift faster after it ends. primary

docs.title: Lagged power and error correction: state and next steps
docs.text:
Recent power readings (lags) improve the demand forecast at short and medium leads, and the final demand networks read them. The Primary substation demand network (the Candidate, a neural network described in final models) reads the day-ago and week-ago readings, each at least 24 hours old, plus neighbour and gap signals. Its prevailing head, which forecasts the arrangement now in force, reads 14 extra lagged inputs at least 6 hours old (Experiment 681). The bulk and grid supply point network reads lags at least 3.5 hours old. The wind and solar networks read no power lag (wind and solar page).

Scores are CRPS in points of capacity unless stated, and lower is better. CRPS is the continuous ranked probability score, and one point of capacity is 1% of a series' capacity; the glossary defines both, and also MVA, MW, N1, BG2, and the frozen XGBoost model. A contrast is written as the first forecast minus the second, so a negative contrast favours the first. "Worse by 0.36" always means the score rose by 0.36. The early experiments used 16 Primaries, as stated for each result. The experiments on load-shift events (transfers of demand between neighbouring Primaries) are in the load-shift summary. Load-shift detection is paused until January, so the options below concern the lagged inputs themselves.

docs.title: What works
docs.text:
Day-ago and week-ago power closes most of the gap between a forecast that sees recent power and one that does not. At 1 to 5 days ahead for the eight MVA Primaries, the network without recent power scored 0.2 to 0.3 worse than the network with it. Adding only the day-ago and week-ago readings closed about four fifths of that gap, a point estimate with wide intervals (Experiment 540). A lag encoder (the part of the neural network that reads lagged power) using readings at least 24 hours old then beat the network without lags by 0.07 to 0.15 at 1 to 5 days, as point estimates against the lag-free reference M0 (Experiment 560).

The slow output offset does not replace lags at the eight MVA Primaries. The offset is a slowly changing level shift added to the network's output. The lag network with the offset beat the offset alone by 0.224 (interval +0.006 to +0.394) at the eight, and by 0.049 at the six MW Primaries against the lag-free network with the offset (Experiment 572). That experiment also tested 3.5-hour lags at the Primaries. They beat the lag-free network by 0.257 at the eight and 0.159 at the six at 0 to 24 hours, but beat 24-hour lags by only 0.070 and 0.055. These are descriptive contrasts.

One lag-light network for all 14 Primaries is a defensible choice. A lag-light network reads only the day-ago and week-ago lags. It scored 0.081 better than the lag-free recipe at the six MW Primaries over 1 to 5 days, so choosing a recipe per group gave up accuracy (Experiment 557).

No lag input is newer than the forecast origin. A timestamp audit of 104 million lag checks found 0 violations (Experiment 551).

Extra lagged inputs make the prevailing output react to a load shift sooner. Fourteen extra lagged inputs made the prevailing output cover half of a new load level about 20 hours sooner (95% interval 16.3 to 24.8) over 1,152 simulated shifts, and 120 hours sooner at Primary D5 in one verified event (Experiment 681). The final models include them.

In the early two-stage XGBoost design, recent power in the second stage beat recent power in the first. For 16 Primaries up to 48 hours ahead, the stage 2 calibrator with lags scored 5.31, stage 1b with a lag-free calibrator 6.14, and a calibrator without lags 7.11 (Experiment 5).

Removing the three recent-power inputs from BG2 made Primary scores worse by 0.36. The figure holds once one substation's commissioning months were cut (Experiment 102).

docs.title: What does not work
docs.text:
The 14-day correction lowered the Primary score by about 1 point in the early design, and no variant beat the plain additive form. The correction adds the mean error of the last 14 days (see the glossary). It scored -0.99 (interval -1.82 to -0.18) with power 2 days old (Experiment 21).

The 14-day correction made the score worse at the supply points and for solar. At 4 bulk and grid supply point series it made the score 0.36 worse (interval includes zero) (Experiment 21) and 0.305 worse in BG2 (interval 0.060 to 0.594), so BG2 serves the supply points without it (Experiment 87). On 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms it made the CRPS worse by 0.437 for solar (interval +0.215 to +0.664) and by 0.413 for wind (interval -0.003 to +0.924, which includes zero) (Experiment 23).

Extra lag columns, summaries, and year-ago lags added no resolvable gain. None of five added lag column sets lowered the XGBoost CRPS for days 1 to 10 (Experiment 388). A year-ago lag changed CRPS by +0.019 at the eight MVA Primaries over 24 to 120 hours (interval includes zero), although it lowered the Christmas and New Year error at the six MW Primaries by 0.53 at 120 to 240 hours, in one December (Experiment 585).

Random lag dropout did not widen the band where a lag is missing. The q05-to-q95 band covered 0.799 of masked half-hours for the plain model and 0.802 with dropout at 10% of training rows (0.836 at 30%), against 0.90 nominal. On synthetic transfers, masking lags without dropout made the score 1.36 points worse than the plain model, and 30% dropout brought that to -0.02 (-0.35 to +0.38). Dropout also made the score worse by up to 0.046 on unmasked rows, above the 0.02 limit. The verdict was inconclusive (Experiment 100).

Detector features added to extra lags did not make the prevailing output react sooner. The head with both reacted 1.75 days sooner than the head of experiment 652, but only 0.16 days sooner than extra lags alone (interval -0.45 to +0.14) (Experiment 691; the features alone are in Experiment 687). Both were not supported.

docs.title: Where the pages disagree
docs.text: The long-lead advantage that Experiment 521 reported for K2-S1 came from a look-ahead in its weather. K2-S1 is a mixture of two lagged heads and two lag-free heads, and 521 placed it ahead of the daily lag-free network at 5 to 10 days. Once the lag-free heads read only weather known at the forecast origin, K2-S1 scored 0.43 (eight) and 0.41 (six) worse than its own earlier score at 120 to 240 hours. Against the daily lag-free network, K2-S1 is worse by point estimate in every lead band, but the intervals include zero except for the eight at 12 to 24 hours (Experiment 541). The lag gain is therefore a short-lead and medium-lead gain, 0.2 to 0.3 at 24 to 120 hours in 540.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
Three Primaries (D4, D12, and D19) carry 85% of the lag gain at the eight MVA Primaries, and the reason is unknown. The gain is as large at night as in sunny half-hours (Experiment 576).

Lags may be unsafe in a cold, holiday, or event week. The lag-light network without dropout scored 0.171 worse than the lag-free network in Christmas week at the eight MVA Primaries, past the 0.10 limit set in advance, on 9 target days in one winter. The variant with dropout stayed within 0.15 when its readings were removed (Experiment 551).

A longer embargo lowers the load-shift leak of lagged networks, and the proposed limit is not yet met. The share of a shift that the median forecast carries fell from 0.160 to 0.114 (interval 0.073 to 0.154, which includes the proposed limit of 0.10) with a 7-day embargo plus half weight on the next 7 days (Experiment 599). The load-shift summary holds the rest.

docs.title: Ranked next experiments (options)
docs.text:
1. An option is to find what D4, D12, and D19 share. Experiment 576 names it as the next step. The answer would show which Primaries need lags.
  2. An option is to run a lag-free head that also sees the lead time. Experiment 541 names it as the untested next step for the long-lead gap.
  3. An option is to judge the trailing temperature windows on cold winter nights with more winter folds. Experiment 550 found a gain of about 0.10 there, and names the extra folds as the next step.
  4. An option is to test 3.5-hour lags in the Candidate. Final models lists the question as open.

docs.title: Parked
docs.text:
Load-shift event detection and lag-trust methods are paused until January. The 38 load-shift experiments are in the summary. The planned end-to-end two-output network with an end detector (experiment 654 in the research plan) is load-shift work and is paused with them.

The 14-day correction for supply points, solar, and wind is parked. Of the experiments read for this page, none shows a gain there, and the final networks use no such correction.

docs.title: LSC detectors
docs.text:
A short report on whether a better detector is worth building is on the decision report page. A plain-words summary of the event-table and graph-model line (experiments 653 to 676) is on the event-table summary page.

The best switching detector, RO-NC, finds most of the moved power (the megawatts a transfer moves) of injected load transfers of 25% or more of the receiving load, but only about a third of that of the 35 real transfers lasting over 1 day, and no experiment yet shows that using a detector improves a forecast.

A load transfer is a switching operation that moves part of one Primary substation's demand onto neighbouring substations for hours or days. Detectors find these transfers from power readings alone. We score them on injected transfers, whose start, end, and size are known, and on 35 real transfers lasting over 1 day that a language model and a hand filter judged visible. The real transfers include 21 under 25% of the receiving load, so the two scores are not like for like. All results are from the lab, on 16 Primary series, and use hindsight to place the end of each transfer.

RO-NC and the refit-offset detector (X) find the most moved power on the 35 real transfers lasting over 1 day (RO-NC 0.357), and the 35 are too few to rank them. Source: experiment 101.

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
On injected transfers, RO-NC finds 0.770 of the moved power, against 0.656 for the benchmark PF14. The difference is +0.114 (+0.074 to +0.182; experiment 82). Neither part helps transfers lasting 15.6 to 60 days. Recall here is MW-weighted.

  • Not ignoring alarms near the monthly refit of the demand model removes PF14's blind spot: a second model refitted half a month later gave +0.050 (+0.012 to +0.107), and lifting the suppression alone gave +0.056 (+0.016 to +0.113), so the second model adds nothing on injected transfers (experiment 71).
  • Counting the neighbours that step the same way as the alarming substation: +0.048 (+0.021 to +0.096; experiment 70).

On real transfers, RO-NC finds fewer than injected transfers of the same step size and metering predict: 12 of the 35 lasting over 1 day (0.357 of their moved power; 0.169 to 0.553), against 18.8 expected, and none of the 31 shorter ones. On the 14 real transfers of 25% or more of the receiving load, it finds 0.559 (0.203 to 0.816), an interval that includes 0.770, so that band alone shows no gap, but it finds 6 of those 14 where 10.5 are expected. Of the 35, 6 sit where the detector's residual panel holds no readings and 12 have a step under 4 noise units, and even the 17 with readings and a larger step are found less often than injected ones; the verdict is partly supported (experiment 101).

RO-NC finds none of the real transfers shorter than 1 day, and more of those moving 25% or more of the receiving load than of those without a metered receiver (all 66 real transfers).

RO-NC misses small steps, mostly where the receiver is unmetered. Of the 35 real transfers over 1 day, it finds 6 of 14 of 25% or more of the receiving load and 2 of 10 with no metered receiver. Among injected transfers that step by 4 noise units or more, the single-series detector D0 found 0.56 with a metered receiver and 0.35 without (experiment 58). Before the PF14 end rule, a wrong interval end was most of D0's misses among large transfers with a metered receiver, and about a third of its misses among transfers with a donor step of 6 noise units or more (experiment 59, experiment 60).

The early detectors D0 and D1 each found under a fifth of 600 injected transfers (experiment 43). Moving D0's interval end to the strongest opposite step found +0.191 more (+0.148 to +0.237; experiment 61), and the post hoc rule PF14 did better (0.688 against 0.646, no paired interval; experiment 66).

The changes listed here found no clear gain. Each was tested against a detector without it, at the same number of unexplained alarms. Refuted: several averaging windows (experiment 59), profile-weighted steps (experiment 60), whitening the residual (experiment 62), scoring onset and return steps as a pair (experiment 61), and one joint fit across substations (experiment 67). Inconclusive or partly supported: a bank-holiday column (experiment 47), a neighbour veto (experiments 55 and 58), refitting without detected transfers (experiment 68), solar and heating corrections (experiment 98), a joint linear fit of solar and transfer terms (experiment 63, of the differentiable-physics demand sub-theme), and accepting weaker onset alarms (experiment 69), and adding neighbours' opposite-sign steps to a substation's own step (+0.019, -0.011 to +0.062; experiment 65).

Using a detector has not yet improved a forecast, in one validation year (experiments 44 and 86) or four (experiment 38) on 16 Primary series. In each result below, a positive change means a worse forecast.

  • Masking: leaving the half-hours that D1 flags out of the 7-day error correction of the stack (experiment 17's H0.5 proxy, with a half-life of 0.5 years) raised the tail error outside logged switching by 57% (0.4% to 134%), because one interval ran for 60 days. A mask from NGED's logs lowered it on the 14-day correction by 8.9% (-21.8% to 0.0%), 95% of that in one closure (experiment 38).
  • Ceiling: in the band of events the labeller finds most reliably (3 of the 16 Primaries), a perfect detector would lower the best guess's quantile score by 0.42% (-0.47% to 1.96%) (experiment 44).
  • Corrected lags: lags corrected with RO-NC's labels raised the score by 0.056 points of capacity outside switching (0.016 to 0.126) and did not lower it inside logged events (experiment 86, of the switching-labels-in-the-forecast theme).

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text:
RO-NC is PF14 with two changes (experiment 82).

  1. Subtract an XGBoost demand model's forecast, which uses no past power, from each Primary's power, and refit the model monthly.
  2. Take the 24-hour step of that residual from whichever of two such models, refitted half a month apart, did not refit within 24 hours of the stamp. Lifting the suppression alone does as well on injected transfers (experiment 71), but RO-NC was tested only with two models.
  3. Score each candidate alarm with a logistic regression on its own step, the largest opposite neighbour step, the number of neighbours, and the number that step the same way.
  4. Set the threshold to allow 80 unexplained alarms over all 16 Primary series on odd months, and end each interval at the first opposite step of at least half the onset step.

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text:
Nothing is ready for the serving path. Experiments 70, 71, and 82 are marked candidate, but each is training-time only: the residual uses ERA5 weather, which arrives about 5 days after the event, and the end rule uses hindsight.

  • Experiment 71: +0.050 on injected transfers. Experiment 70: +0.048, unconfirmed on real transfers (7 found against 8 for PF14). Experiment 82: +0.114, and 12 against 8 on the 35 real transfers, a weak signal.
  • An untested option is to run RO-NC retrospectively to build a table of switching events for NGED. Experiment 44 found that a perfect detector would improve the best guess's quantile score by little, so the table would serve NGED's own use of the events (roadmap page: switching events).

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
• Count events, not half-hours, and show every event. In experiment 37, 99.9% of the stack's confirmed tail score lay on two series, almost all in one 370-hour closure, and in experiment 38 one closure in January 2026 held 95% to 105% of every masking gain (experiment 37, experiment 38). A pooled half-hour total then reads as many closures when it is one. Re-check on a longer period or other series.
  • Match the unexplained-alarm count on every month a rule reads. A threshold matched on odd months left even months 15% under the first round's alarm count (experiment 68), and a shared threshold grid left D0 at 0.14 alarms per series-month and D1 at 0.38 (experiment 37). Otherwise a detector looks better by raising more alarms. Re-check if the demand model or period changes.
  • Spread injected transfers across series and time before training on them. Experiment 58's 620 even-month transfers shrank to 103 once no two on one series lay within 1 day (experiment 68). Otherwise a few overlapping events count many times. Re-check if the injection sampler changes.
  • Compare like with like when quoting injected and real recall. 0.770 is MW-weighted recall on large injected transfers, and 0.34 is a count over all 35 real transfers, 21 of them under 25% of the receiving load (experiment 101). Otherwise a gap the sample cannot show is reported as a finding. Re-check if the labelled real set grows.
  • Score on several injection shapes and by donor step. Recall depends on the donor step in noise units (experiment 58), and experiment 60 tested one step statistic on five shapes. Otherwise a mix of small and large steps hides which transfers are missed. Re-check if the injection builds transfers a new way.
  • Interval ends need hindsight. The strongest-opposite-step end rule needs up to 14 days of later data (experiment 65), and an interval that started at a return step ran for 60 days (experiment 38). Otherwise a detector scored with hindsight is mistaken for one that could run live. Re-check when a detector is run on live data, or an end rule without hindsight is tried.
  • Recompute moved_share_of_receiver before scoring against the experiment 41 labels. 62 of 81 stored values are NaN, partly because series ids were written as strings (experiment 44). Otherwise a filter on that column silently drops most events. Re-check if the labelled set is rebuilt.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text:
• Whether any detector finds real transfers with a step under 4 noise units, or shorter than 1 day.
  • How RO-NC does on real transfers once the readings missing for two Primary substations are restored.
  • Whether the detector's labels improve a forecast of the normal running arrangement; the logged events in experiment 86 are too few to show it.

The Research plan lists what is planned next, and the Experiments page lists every experiment.

docs.title: Is a better load shift detector worth building?
docs.text:
The evidence does not show that a better detector would change the decision, because the case for a detector in the forecast is not yet made on curtailment cost. The current label-free detector (it uses no NGED switching log) finds 25 of the 35 real load shifts lasting over 1 day. Masking the readings it flags (treating them as missing in the Kalman filter) lowers the forecast error during and after injected shifts from 1.79 to 1.04, in points of effective capacity on the 95% pinball loss, where lower is better. Against the power the electricity network actually carries, the mask shows no clear change in curtailment cost.

A load shift is a switching operation that moves part of one substation's demand onto neighbouring substations for hours or days. The normal running arrangement (NRA) is the network as normally configured. Injected load shifts are shifts we add to real power series, so their size and timing are known; the real record has 35 logged shifts over 1 day. Gains during a shift come mostly from injected shifts, and one Primary substation (anonymised as D11) carries part of the main result. Each question below has one answer, one figure, and the experiments behind them.

docs.title: 1. Does perfect knowledge of load shifts help?
docs.text:
For the NRA forecast, perfect knowledge lowers the error during and after a shift, but by far less than predicted and by almost nothing over a year. The error falls by 1.50 points (95% interval 1.08 to 1.96) in the 48 hours after a transfer ends and by 1.46 points (0.69 to 2.29) during it, against a predicted 3 points or more. Averaged over a year it falls by about 0.005 points, because shifts are rare (experiment 208, verdict not supported).

For curtailment cost, the answer depends on the series the forecast is judged against. Against the true NRA series, masking the shifts a label-free detector finds lowers cost by 32.8% (95% interval 17% to 53%). Against observed power, which a curtailment instruction responds to, the change is -3.0% (-24% to +30%) and ordinary half-hours cost 1.3% more (experiment 332). Perfect knowledge beats the best forecast with no detector on observed power only when the true moved megawatts are also added back, by 6.5% (3.9 to 9.2; experiment 297). The real record at the D13 bulk supply point is too small to resolve a cost difference (experiment 332).

docs.title: 2. Do we need an explicit detector?
docs.text:
This is not settled. The label-free pipeline has not been run against the best forecast with no detector, and the existing evidence points both ways.

A forecast that recalibrates its bands with no detector matches or beats masks on the upper-tail score near a shift. Within 7 days of a shift, a quantile head (a small model that predicts forecast quantiles from the Kalman filter's recent correction) beats the RO-NC mask on the upper-tail score. RO-NC is the earlier switching detector built on neighbouring-substation counts. The head also beats the perfect mask, but that margin disappears when one Primary (D16) is left out (experiment 297).

A label-free detector plus a mask beats a Kalman filter with no mask. During and after injected shifts the 95% pinball loss falls from 1.79 to 1.04, against 0.81 when the true spans are masked. Without D11 the loss falls by 0.30 points instead of 0.75. The change on ordinary real days is -0.016 points (98.75% interval -0.060 to +0.010), so the harm-side end is within the ±0.05 bar (experiment 327, verdict partly supported, scored on past weather and not on ensemble weather).

The disagreement between the two forecasts cannot choose which forecast to use. One forecast uses recent power and the other does not. A rule on their disagreement recovered none of the gain from choosing with the true answer, and the disagreement adds no information beyond the residual of measured power (experiment 309). As a detector, the 24-hour mean residual is the better signal: it matches 20 of the 35 real shifts, against 11 for the disagreement (experiment 308).

docs.title: 3. How good must a detector be, and is ours good enough?
docs.text:
On curtailment cost against the no-detector head, a mask needs to find about half the shifts. With the true megawatts added back, the mask still beats the head when it finds half the shifts or when it raises false alarms at 1 in 2. It also wins with a 3-day delay (gain 1.4%, 0.3 to 2.5), and with the megawatts wrong by 50%. It loses at 25% found. On the upper-tail score, a 2-day delay or a 50% megawatt error removes the margin (experiment 312).

The label-free detector finds more than half of the real shifts, but the bar was measured on injected worlds with the true megawatts. The label-free detector finds 25 of the 35 real shifts at 8.8 alarms per found shift (experiment 327), and 15 of the 19 long-and-deep ones. The label-free mask adds no megawatts, and adding them did not help in experiment 332. On the injected worlds RO-NC found 33% of the shifts, and a signal based on how far power sits in the forecast's bands found 37%, with about 90% of its alarms false (experiment 312).

Checking neighbouring substations removes a third of the false alarms. The check removes 30% to 37% of the 24-hour residual detector's false alarms and loses none of the real shifts it found (experiment 315).

Detectors based on the daily mean residual do no better on long, deep shifts. They match 8 to 12 of the 19 long-and-deep real shifts and are clearly worse on the other 16 (experiment 298, verdict not supported). A forecast refitted monthly absorbs long shifts: for a 30-day transfer of 25% of demand it absorbs 19% of the shift. It absorbs 10% to 13% if the flagged days are left out of the refit, and 2.8% if the true shift days are left out.

docs.title: What is still open
docs.text:
• The pipeline against the no-detector head. This comparison decides question 2, and no experiment has run it.
  • A curtailment-cost saving against observed power. None is shown for the label-free mask. Whether NGED's cost is judged against the NRA or against observed power decides whether masking pays.
  • Injected shifts carry most of the evidence. Injected shifts may be easier to detect than real ones, and the real record cannot score the gain during a shift.
  • Message for NGED. A forecast refitted monthly partly learns shifts of 14 days or more as normal.

docs.title: The event-table line in plain words
docs.text: Reading only the power data, we find about two thirds of the megawatts of long, deep load shifts, but we name both substations of a transfer for only about a third of its megawatts. Nothing we tried reached the 0.60 share set for adopting a method, so the results describe single substations well and do not yet say where a transfer went. The line ran from experiment 653 to experiment 682, which tested a reconstruction by edge flows after the graph models of experiments 672 and 676. NGED's event labels are incomplete, so every count of real events on this page is a lower bound.

docs.title: What the line was trying to do
docs.text:
A load transfer moves part of one Primary substation's demand onto neighbouring Primaries for hours or days. The line asked whether power readings alone can build a table of such events, with the donor Primary, the recipient Primaries, the start, and the end. The tests inject fake transfers, made by one shared generator (experiment 660), into the real power history of 15 Primaries, because the real record holds almost no verified long transfers.

Five terms recur. E1 is the event table of experiment 653, which cuts each Primary's residual (the demand forecast error) into steps. E1-J is E1 plus the recipient search of experiment 670, which looks at each connected Primary for a step of the opposite sign shortly after a large downward step. Found means an injected event has a decoded event at the right Primary, with the right sign and start. Paired means the decoded donor and recipient are the right two Primaries. Every share is weighted by megawatts. A noise unit is a Primary's usual difference between successive 6-hour means. A deep shift is 8 noise units or more and a shallow one is 2 to 8. A long shift lasts over 7 days (or has no end), a medium one 1 to 7 days, and a short one 1 day or less.

docs.title: What works
docs.text:
• Long and deep shifts are found. E1 finds 0.67 of the injected megawatts of shifts longer than 7 days and 8 noise units or more deep (experiment 665).
  • The search for the recipient triples the pairing. E1-J pairs 0.29 of the long and deep transfer megawatts and 0.25 of the medium and deep ones, against 0.09 for E1 (experiment 670). Rearranging the connections at random removes the gain, so the gain comes from the real neighbours.
  • Searching from the rise as well as the fall helps a little more. E1-J-sym, which also looks for the donor of each unpaired rise, pairs 0.38 of the long and deep megawatts against 0.29, and 0.32 of the medium and deep megawatts against 0.25, but adds 442 decoded transfers for 63 more correct ends (experiment 680).
  • Choosing edge flows by a fixed cost per change does not help. E1-F, which accepts a pair of steps when one flow explains both better than two separate steps, pairs 0.33 of the long and deep megawatts, below the symmetric search, and decodes 2990 transfers for 329 correct ends. A graph that connects any two Primaries pairs nearly as much as the real neighbours, so the edge-flow line closes at 15 Primaries (experiment 682).
  • The real record supports the method only thinly. The one verified transfer, between Primaries D5 and D16 in December 2025, is paired in the right direction, but the decoded starts are late.

docs.title: What does not work
docs.text:
• Pairing stays below 0.40, whatever was added. The graph neural network of experiment 672 paired 0.08. The donor-probe hybrids of experiment 678 paired 0.36 at best, and the edge-state neural network of experiment 676 paired no more than the hybrids.
  • The donor is the bottleneck. Experiment 675 found that, of the recipient megawatts that E1-J located but left unpaired, 0.87 belonged to transfers whose donor E1-J had not found. A pretrained encoder made the donor probe worse, and a logistic regression on the node inputs did as well as any neural encoder.
  • Short events are not paired. Transfers of a day or less are paired for 0.08 (deep) and 0.03 (shallow) of their megawatts, and ending the added donors after 6 hours instead of 2 days did not change that (experiment 676, post hoc).
  • False transfers are common. Of the transfers E1-J decodes, 69% match no injected end (experiment 670).
  • Long and deep events cannot be checked on the real record. None of the 77 shifts that NGED's logs record as lasting more than 1 day falls in the long and deep type.

docs.title: What the table is good for
docs.text:
• Descriptive tables per Primary. The table gives each Primary's steps, their sizes, and their durations, including the event-free stratum (time more than 14 days from any logged or verified event).
  • Training and testing data for other detectors. The injected worlds have known starts, ends, and partners.
  • A first screen of candidate transfers for NGED to check. The table's long and deep calls can go to NGED for confirmation, because the real record cannot confirm them.

docs.title: What a next step would need
docs.text:
• More Primaries, or the adjacency of the whole fleet. At 15 Primaries the recipient is often unmetered or below its noise, and 8 of the 15 Primaries report apparent power (MVA), which has no sign and so cannot show which way power flows (experiment 674 found the sign label from a day labeller unusable at those Primaries).
  • A more realistic injector. The generator is checked against 49 real windows of power history and 2 verified transfers.
  • More verified events. The 77 logged shifts longer than 1 day include none in the type where the methods work best.

docs.title: LSC detectors: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00697 gas-engine-state-tracker-part-4-running-patterns D8's gas engine runs to a schedule that follows the working week: it runs more on weekday evenings than on weekend evenings, by more than the tracker's errors alone would show. supported not-for-production The recorded demand at D8 behaves as if its gas engine runs more on weekday evenings (16:00 to 19:00) than on weekends, and more in half-hours with a high system price, and a test engine with no weekday pattern does not produce that. The evidence comes from the tracker's estimates and not from a meter on the engine, the labels understate any pattern, and the price, the red band, and D8's own evening demand all peak together. The pattern is a lead for a possible next experiment and not a result that a forecast can use, and the one metered engine record agrees in direction on only 7 weeks. also relevant 00694 gas-engine-state-tracker-part-1 The engine at D8 (3 identical units of about 2 MW) can be tracked by walking forwards through the raw half-hourly reading with a hidden-state model of the number of units running, with no demand forecast, no price, and no weather. D8's reading is apparent power (MVA, never negative), so a model that lets the reading fold, y = sqrt((L - k u)^2 + q^2) for demand level L, k units running, and unit size u, tracks the engine better than a model of signed steps. partly supported not-for-production A filter that tracks how many of D8's three gas-engine units are running, using only the substation's half-hourly reading, scores F1 0.68 on the one real engine record we hold (it finds most running half-hours but also flags others), and higher on easier synthetic schedules. It raised no false alarms at 8 substations, but it almost never finds a 1 MW unit, and the unit size it infers depends on the grid of sizes tried. The next experiment should test it on a harder, record-like schedule and on registered engines it has not seen. also relevant 00693 oracle-transfer-flag-in-the-candidate-part-1 A perfect telemetry detector, which knows that a reading lay inside a load transfer (and when the transfer began, once a reading after the onset exists), lowers the CRPS of the Candidate demand network on transfer-affected rows by at least 0.3 points of capacity against a placebo flag, without raising CRPS on event-free rows by more than 0.05. inconclusive not-for-production Telling the demand forecast exactly when a load transfer is happening did not make it clearly better on simulated transfers. The forecast that reads yesterday's power loses only 0.1 points of capacity to a transfer, and the forecast that adapts to a transfer scores about the same with a perfect flag or a random one on the deciding simulation. The test could not rule out a gain or a loss of half a point or more, because three refits of the same forecast already differ by about 0.4 points, so no conclusion about a real switching detector is safe. A repeat needs at least 10 refits per arm. also relevant 00692 event-table-reviewer-calibration-gate A Sonnet reviewer shown one figure per candidate transfer of the event table (E1-J-sym) agrees with the injected truth well enough to remove most false transfers. not supported not-for-production A Claude Sonnet reviewer looking at one picture per candidate load transfer recognised clean transfers: it called 24 of 32 true transfers a transfer, including both verified real transfers, and got the direction right in 23 of those 24. It called a transfer on only 6 of 28 other false candidates and 2 of 20 injected look-alikes (candidates built to resemble transfers). It failed the precision gate set beforehand (0.45 against 0.80), because 21 of its 29 false calls were on five candidates that recur in the real record under many injected worlds and that the injected truth does not list. On this evidence the reviewer can neither be adopted nor dropped. A calibration set whose negatives hold no real-record events is needed first. primary 00691 causal-detector-features-plus-extra-lags-in-the-prevailing-head The detector features of experiment 687 (F1) and the extra lagged power block of experiment 681 (L1) carry partly different information, so a head that reads both (FL1) reacts to the start of a load shift sooner than the better of the two single-input heads. not supported not-for-production Reading both the detector features and the extra lagged power makes the prevailing output follow a new load shift 1.75 days sooner than experiment 652's head, but only 0.16 days sooner than the features alone (interval -0.45 to +0.14), so the lags add under 0.5 days to the features and no new feature is proposed. The in-force score improves by 0.20 points of capacity, below the 0.30 bar, and false alarms on event-free rows rise by 5 points. also relevant 00690 slow-level-state-on-primaries-13-and-16-july-august The slow level of the edge-state addendum (a smooth seasonal level fitted with candidate windows masked, then frozen) follows the July to August 2026 change in level that the stored normal-running forecasts miss at Primaries 13 and 16. partly supported not-for-production The level miss at Primaries 13 and 16 in July and August is tracked by a smooth slow level: adding it to q50 halves the median absolute error at both Primaries, in hindsight and not as a forecast. The same level moves the two control Primaries by 5.5% and 7.5%, above the 5% limit set in advance, so the verdict is partly supported. primary 00687 causal-detector-features-for-the-prevailing-forecast-heads Per-lag causal step statistics in noise units, the gap with the all-Primaries median removed, the opposite-sign neighbour gap, the routine-step rate, and a return-to-level statistic carry information about whether a lag lies inside a load shift that the gap summaries of experiments 606 and 610 do not, and a small prevailing head that reads them reacts sooner to the start and the end of a shift than the same head reading extra lagged power inputs (the arm of experiment 681). partly supported not-for-production Giving the prevailing head a step detector's statistics makes it follow a new load shift about 1.6 days sooner than experiment 652's head, and releases a shift about 0.6 days sooner on average (median 0, so the 1-day bar is not met at the end). Simply adding recent lagged power gets 1.25 days at the start, so the detector features are not shown to be better than extra lags. The in-force score improves by 0.12 points of capacity [-0.33, +0.06], an interval that includes zero and is below the 0.30 bar. also relevant 00686 event-table-transfer-timing-and-false-solar-growth-events (1) At the two verified transfers the recipient's step begins hours after the donor's, so a detector that requires both onsets to coincide would reject real transfers. (2) Most of the false events that experiment 653's masked arm decodes under injected solar growth are slow ramps or misfits of the slow level, which a better slow level would remove, and fewer than a third are steps inside a run of sunny days. partly supported not-for-production The two verified transfers give no sign of a lag between the substation that lost demand and the one that gained it: the D3/D22 steps coincide within noise, and the D5/D16 steps are 2.5 hours apart at the end and too noisy at the onset to say. The 14.5 and 15 hours reported earlier is the gap between the labelled times. Of the false events that solar growth causes, few are abrupt steps in a sunny run, but half last 3 days or less, so a better solar-capacity curve would remove only part of them. primary 00685 event-table-on-the-final-test-window-all-primaries None. This is a data product: the event table of experiment 680, run unchanged on the residual panel extended to 2026-10-31, so that the one-year-backtest flags at four Primaries can be set beside the events the table can see. inconclusive not-for-production From 2026-07-01 to 2026-10-31 the event table finds 13 candidate events (14 rows) at the 15 Primaries and no transfer between time_series_id 13 and 16 in July or August, nothing at id 11 in September, and one open fall at id 18 from 2026-10-04. The one-year-backtest flags at ids 13, 16, 11, and 18 are therefore not explained by events the table can see. A level offset in the lag-free forecast remains a candidate explanation that this table does not test. One transfer from id 13 to id 16 opens on 2026-10-26 and is still open at the end of the window. Every row is a candidate, never a label. primary 00682 event-table-reconstruction-from-edge-flows-part-2-change-cost-model Experiment 680 found that searching from either end of a transfer raises the paired share by +0.09 (long and deep) but adds 442 decoded transfers for 63 correct ends. A model that decides every pair jointly, by the saving in change cost against the misfit of one common flow, with the recipient share bounded by a prior, accepts only pairs whose two steps are explained better by one flow than by two steps that stand alone. It therefore pairs at least 0.10 more of the injected transfer megawatts than E1-J in both the long and deep and the medium and deep cells, with a share of decoded transfers that match no injected end no higher than E1-J's. not supported not-for-production Explaining pairs of steps by one flow on an edge, chosen by a fixed cost per change, does not find the donor and recipient of an injected load transfer better than the simple searches: it pairs 0.33 of the long and deep megawatts against 0.29 for the one-way search and 0.38 for the two-way search. It accepts almost every pair that roughly conserves megawatts, 2990 transfers for 329 correct ends, and a graph that connects any two Primaries pairs nearly as much as the real neighbours. Within the 15 Primaries tested, this cost objective gains almost nothing from knowing the real edges, and the edge-flow line closes here. primary 00680 event-table-reconstruction-from-edge-flows-part-1-symmetric-search Experiment 675 found that the donor is the bottleneck of experiment 670's search: E1-J finds 0.73 of the recipient megawatts in the long and deep cell but only 0.44 of the donor megawatts, and 0.87 of the recipient megawatts it found but left unpaired belong to transfers whose donor it had not found. A donor search that starts from each unpaired rise of 4 noise units or more, and looks at each connected Primary for a fall of 2 noise units or more that starts up to 36 half-hours before the rise, can recover those donors, and so pairs at least 0.10 more of the injected transfer megawatts than E1-J in both the long and deep cell and the medium and deep cell. partly supported not-for-production Searching from each unpaired rise for the matching fall at a neighbouring Primary pairs 0.38 of the injected transfer megawatts in the long and deep cell, against 0.29 for the one-way search, a gain of 0.09. The gain of 0.09 disappears on a rewired graph (0.057 paired), but its interval includes zero in one of three other generator configurations. It falls just short of the 0.10 needed to adopt the search, and the search adds 442 decoded transfers, most of which match no injected end. The donor is still found for only 0.48 of its megawatts, so the joint reconstruction model of part 2 has room to add something, and the share of decoded transfers that match no injected end is the number to watch. primary 00678 donor-posterior-hybrid-for-load-transfer-pairing Experiment 675 found that the donor was not found for 0.87 (long and deep) and 0.84 (medium and deep) of the recipient megawatts that E1-J found and left unpaired, and that a logistic regression on the node inputs (F) finds 0.63 of the long and deep donor megawatts against E1-J's 0.44 at the same false-donor rate. A donor alarm from such a probe, refined to a start time and an end time and handed to the recipient search of experiment 670 as an extra donor step, pairs more transfer megawatts than E1-J does. It reopens the graph line only at the level of a donor posterior feeding the existing search; the edge-state network of the original plan is not built here. not supported not-for-production A donor probe feeding E1-J's recipient search pairs a little more than E1-J (0.36 against 0.29 of long and deep megawatts), not the +0.10 that was predicted, and far below the 0.60 that would have made it the event table. The stop rule closes the graph line at 15 Primaries. The donor alarm helps a little, and a neural encoder adds nothing over a logistic regression within the seed spread. The rewired graph pairs almost nothing, which shows only that the recipient search needs the real neighbours. primary 00676 pretrained-graph-model-for-load-transfers-part-2-edge-state-network Experiments 672 and 678 each closed the graph line at 15 Primaries under their stop rules, and the maintainer asked to continue it. Experiment 678 bolted a donor posterior onto E1-J's recipient search; the explicit per-link state with a recipient lag, decoded jointly with the Primaries' states, is a core of the design that experiments 672 and 678 did not test. A network that learns the state of every link (off, first Primary donates, second Primary donates) hour by hour, and the lag at which the recipient follows, pairs more injected transfer megawatts in the long and deep and the medium and deep cells than the hybrids of experiment 678 do. A post hoc variant of experiment 678, whose added donors may end in under 2 days, pairs more short-event megawatts than experiment 678 did, at a false-transfer rate that stays within 1.5 times E1-J's. not supported not-for-production A neural network that learns the state of every link between two Primaries, and the delay before the recipient follows, pairs no more transfer megawatts than the donor-probe hybrids or the search of experiment 670 (paired share of long, deep transfer megawatts: 0.32 for the new network, 0.29 for the search, 0.35 and 0.36 for the hybrids). A copy with its link features removed does as well, because the decoder already restricts recipients to the real neighbours. At 15 Primaries the learnt-graph line is closed, and a next step needs more Primaries or the whole fleet's adjacency, a more realistic injector, and more verified events. primary 00675 pretrained-graph-model-for-load-transfers-part-1-diagnostics-and-frozen-probe Experiment 672 trained a graph neural network on 120 injected worlds and 6-hour blocks. The network found donors about as often as E1-J (0.47 of the long and deep donor megawatts against 0.44) and then paired few of them (0.09). Three changes have not been tested: a network that first learns each Primary's ordinary variability by reconstructing masked windows of real history, an input set that includes the same step statistics E1-J uses, and a residual that is not distorted by the convex demand model's error. This experiment first asks where E1-J loses the recipient megawatts it finds (0.73 found, 0.22 paired), then asks whether a pretrained encoder, frozen and read by a logistic probe, finds donors and recipients better than a random encoder of the same shape and better than the event table's features alone. It reopens the graph line that experiment 672's stop rule closed at 15 Primaries, at the maintainer's request. not supported not-for-production The donor of a transfer, not the link to its recipient, is what the event table of experiment 670 misses. An encoder pretrained to reconstruct masked windows of real residuals made the probe worse, not better, so the stop rule drops masked pretraining. The stop rule's first clause points experiment 676 to a randomly initialised encoder and its second clause to the causal arm's weights, so the choice is open. primary 00672 graph-model-that-finds-the-donor-of-a-load-transfer Experiment 670 found that the event table with a recipient search (E1-J) pairs 0.29 (0.20 to 0.40) of the injected megawatts in the long and deep cell, and that two losses limit it: the event table finds only 0.44 of the donor megawatts, and the search pairs only 0.22 of the recipient megawatts although it finds 0.73. A graph neural network that reads every Primary's residual and the electricity network's links together, and is trained on experiment 660's injected worlds with an objective for the donor itself, finds the donor of a transfer by the matching recipient step at a linked Primary, which a per-Primary detector cannot see when the donor step is small. It therefore finds more donor megawatts and pairs at least 0.10 more than the search in the long and deep and in the medium and deep cells. not supported not-for-production A graph neural network trained on injected transfers pairs the two ends of a transfer far less often than the search of experiment 670 (0.08 against 0.29 of megawatts in the longest and deepest transfers), and it finds the donor about as often as the search does. This result closes the graph line at 15 Primaries under the pre-registered stop rule, and the graph network's own placebo and no-link arms show that the links add a little pairing and no reliable donor finding. primary 00670 event-table-recipient-search-on-six-cell-grid Experiment 653's event table pairs few injected load transfers (0.18 of the megawatts at the two ends) because each end must clear the full detection penalty on its own. A search at each connected Primary for a recipient step of opposite sign, started within 36 half-hours of a deep donor step, needs only the small recipient step to be present, and so pairs at least 0.6 of the injected megawatts in transfers that are both long (over 7 days) and deep (8 noise units or more), the bar that experiment 653 set for any model of edges. not supported not-for-production A search at the neighbouring Primaries for the recipient of each large downward step lets the event table pair 0.29 of the injected transfer megawatts in the longest and deepest transfers, against 0.09 without the search, but not the 0.60 that was needed to adopt it. The shortfall is two losses: the event table finds only 0.44 of those donor megawatts, and the search pairs only 0.22 of the recipient megawatts although it finds 0.73. The result sits on the 0.30 line (leave-one-out range 0.26 to 0.31), so it does not show that pairing is unidentifiable at 15 Primaries. A graph model would have to improve both donors and recipients, and its margin over this search is the next question. primary 00665 event-table-recall-by-length-and-depth The penalised segmentation of experiment 653 and the neural network of experiment 658 find most of the injected megawatts of events that are both long and deep, the kind a human operator would see at once, and the 0.64 and 0.52 headline recalls are low because they average in short and shallow events of which neither method finds more than a quarter of the megawatts. partly supported not-for-production Where an injected load shift lasts more than 7 days and steps 8 noise units or more, the event table of experiment 653 finds 0.67 of the injected megawatts and the neural network of experiment 658 finds 0.65. Shallower and shorter shifts are found less often: for shifts of a day or less the event table finds 0.16 to 0.26 and the neural network 0.01 to 0.06. No type of shift has its two ends linked well (0.42 at best, from 14 injected transfers). On the real record, none of the 77 shifts that NGED's logs record as lasting more than 1 day falls in the long and deep type, so the type where the methods work best is almost empty. primary 00663 end-detector-for-the-prevailing-forecast-followup-to-654 A detector that reads the freshest half-hours of (observed power minus the NRA forecast) at a Primary and at its electrical neighbours, and outputs the probability that a load shift has ended, lets the prevailing forecast of E0 (frozen K1 plus the survival-hazard head R-haz) and of J2 (the end-to-end network of experiment 654) drop a shift sooner after it ends, and cuts the share of event-free rows on which the prevailing forecast wrongly departs from the NRA forecast. not supported not-for-production A learned end detector made the prevailing forecast better in the 24 hours after an injected shift ends (-0.9 to -1.1 scaled points of capacity) and worse while the shift is in force (+0.2 to +0.3 for E0d), and the neighbour graph added no consistent gain, because three random rewirings of it scored within 0.08 points of the real graph. On the final-test window the detector made E0 worse (4.81 against 4.26) and J2 slightly better (4.85 against 5.02), and the plain E0 was the best prevailing forecast of all (4.26). The veto on event-free rows is not met for E0d, and J2d passes it by its interval but not in every month. In a post hoc variant, adding the count of neighbours that stepped the same way raised the share found. primary 00063 sw2-10-linear-joint-fit-v2-in-miniature On the 8 Primary substations metered in MW, one linear fit per Primary that holds a weather baseline without radiation inputs, the embedded-solar capacity of experiment 00045 times the CAMS unit PV shape, and one share-of-the-donor's-net-power term per labelled transfer, (C1) lowers the error of the median forecast outside switching on held-out months, in hindsight, below that of the same baseline with radiation inputs by at least 0.35 points of capacity, (S1) recovers an injected solar capacity to within 0.15 of its size, and (S2) recovers an injected transfer share to within 0.05. inconclusive not-for-production C1 is -0.322 points of capacity (-0.437 to -0.207), close to the 0.35-point threshold, but the S1 and S2 gates failed for reasons of test design, so the verdict is inconclusive. also relevant 00062 sw2-9-whitened-residual-step-detector Removing the half-hour-to-half-hour memory of the residual before the step statistic is taken (a first-order autoregressive filter, fitted per series and half-hour of day on odd months) makes the switching detector find a larger share of the MW moved by injected load transfers than the same detector on the unfiltered residual (D0M), at the same rate of unexplained alarms. The gain holds on transfers whose shape the detector does not assume. refuted not-for-production Removing the residual's half-hour-to-half-hour memory made the switching detector find fewer load transfers: 0.34 to 0.37 of the moved power against 0.44 to 0.47 without the filter. The filter shrinks a day-long step faster than it shrinks the noise, and a first-order filter cannot fix that. primary 00061 sw2-6-paired-step-intervals A detector that looks for an onset step and its opposite return step together, scoring the pair and choosing the return stamp with a prior on the duration of real transfers, finds more of the MW moved by injected load transfers than the best single-window detector (D0M, the 24-hour step with a tracked end), at the same rate of unexplained alarms. The gain comes from interval ends: about a third of D0M's transfers with a donor step of 6 noise units or more have the right start and a wrong end (experiment 60). refuted not-for-production Taking the end of each alarm interval from the strongest opposite step in the next 14 days found 0.19 more of the moved power than the single-step detector. Scoring the onset step and the return step as one pair found 0.13 to 0.21 less, so the end of the interval is the main limit on the single-step detector's recall. primary 00060 sw2-7-profile-weighted-step-detector A step statistic that weights each half-hour by the series' expected power (the daily profile of the fitted weather model), D3, finds more of the MW moved by injected load transfers than the constant-step statistic, D0M, at the same rate of unexplained alarms. The gain holds on transfers whose shape D3 does not assume (a constant MW, a share of the receivers' own profiles, and a mix of the two fitted to real transfers), not only on a share of the donor's profile, which is how the injection built every transfer in experiments 43, 55 and 58. refuted not-for-production A switching detector that weights each half-hour by the substation's predicted power found the same share of the moved power as one that expects a constant step, within 0.005 on five shapes of transfer (0.44 to 0.47). The shape of the moved load is therefore not why transfers are missed: among transfers with a large step, about a third have an alarm at the right start but the wrong end. primary 00059 sw2-13-several-windows-in-one-detector One detector that combines the step statistic of experiment 43's detector D0 at windows of 4, 12, 24, and 48 hours, after calibrating each window to the same false-alarm rate on odd months, finds more of the injected load transfers, weighted by the MW each moves, than the best single window at the same false-alarm rate on even months. refuted not-for-production Neither the maximum nor the sum of four window lengths found more of the moved power than the 24-hour window alone (0.423 and 0.451 against 0.473). Among large transfers with a metered receiver, most misses are an interval end placed outside tolerance and not a missed alarm. primary 00058 sw2-8b-donor-step-recut-and-stronger-veto (1) The gap in recall between injected load transfers with a metered receiver (0.50) and without one (0.17), seen in experiment 55, comes mostly from the injection giving the second group a smaller donor step, so the gap shrinks to under half its size when the two groups are compared at the same donor step in noise units. (2) A neighbour veto stronger than experiment 55's strongest (1.5 noise units), at 1.25 or 1.0, lets the 24-hour threshold fall further and finds more injected transfers than no veto. partly supported not-for-production Much of the gap in recall between injected transfers with a metered receiver (0.50) and without one (0.17) comes from the injected step being too small to see: 211 of 274 transfers without a metered receiver step by less than the alarm threshold, and the gap falls from 0.33 to -0.002 at equal step size (interval -0.166 to +0.119). A stronger neighbour veto raised the share found by 0.013, which cannot be told from no gain (98.33% interval 0.000 to +0.029). primary 00055 sw2-8-neighbour-veto-single-series-detector Keeping every alarm of the single-series detector D0 at the 24-hour window, except those vetoed because at least two neighbouring Primary substations stepped the same way and none stepped the opposite way, lets the alarm threshold fall at the same rate of unexplained alarms, and the detector then finds more injected load transfers than D0 alone. inconclusive not-for-production A neighbour veto removed the alarms that look like a weather or calendar miss and let the detector's threshold fall from 4.00 to 3.70, but the share of 620 injected transfers found rose only from 0.355 to 0.363 (98.75% interval -0.003 to +0.022). The result is inconclusive, and a stronger veto was not tried. primary 00047 sw2-4-better-residual-switching-detector Adding one column, the signed days to the nearest bank holiday in England, to experiment 17's lagless ERA5-trained XGBoost demand model H0.5 (refitted monthly, with H0.5's absolute-error loss unchanged) gives a residual in which the single-series detector D0 at the 24-hour window finds more injected load transfers at the same rate of unexplained alarms. inconclusive not-for-production Adding a bank-holiday column to the demand model raised the share of 89 simulated transfers that the detector found by 0.011 (98.75% interval -0.010 to +0.044), which the experiment is too small to tell from zero. The column lowered the demand error on bank holidays by about 1.15 points of capacity, but the detector's matched threshold rose instead of falling. primary 00044 sw2-2-switching-share-of-best-guess-score Half-hours in labelled switching events, and half-hours whose lagged power falls inside one, carry a larger share of the best guess's quantile score and tail score than their share of half-hours, and a perfect switching detector could lower the Primary quantile score or tail score by 3% or more. refuted not-for-production In the band of events the labeller finds most reliably, a perfect switching detector would lower the best guess's quantile score by 0.42% (95% interval -0.47% to 1.96%) and its tail score by nothing, against a threshold of 3%. Switching in that band touches 3 of the 16 Primary series and few half-hours, in one validation year. also relevant 00043 sw2-1-detector-scoreboard Experiment 37's neighbour-balance detector D1 finds injected load transfers between Primary substations more often than its single-series detector D0, when a transfer counts as found only if both its start and its end are placed correctly. refuted not-for-production Two simple switching detectors each found under a fifth of 600 simulated transfers, and no more than 0.29 in any size group. Over a 24-hour window the neighbour check found fewer large transfers than the single-series detector (0.21 against 0.29), and it helped only over the 4-hour window. primary 00041 sw2-0a-labeller-gate A labeller that reads features computed from raw power and the switching logs, and that uses no forecasting model as its deciding evidence, can find injected load transfers and reject placebo windows well enough to label the real logged closures of the 16 Primary substation demand series. partly supported not-for-production The AI model Sonnet called none of 120 placebo windows a switching event and timed starts and ends well, but it found 0.74 of the large, long fake transfers, under the 0.80 bar. It found 0.89 of them where the receiving substation has its own power readings and 0.60 where it does not. primary 00038 switching-mask-value For the 16 Primary substation demand series, excluding the half-hours of detected switching events from the history of the stack's error correction lowers the stack's threshold-weighted error at each series' historical 99th percentile on half-hours outside logged switching, by enough to justify adding a detector to the serving path. refuted not-for-production Leaving the half-hours that an early switching detector (D1) flags out of the 7-day error correction made the forecast worse on half-hours outside logged switching: the error rose 57% (95% interval 0.4% to 134%), where a 5% fall was needed. The rise came from an interval builder that ran one interval for 60 days, so masking with this detector is refuted as built. primary 00037 switching-first-look For the 16 Primary substation demand series, logged network switching (normal open points closed for hours or days) moves load that appears in the telemetry as a pair of opposite steps whose sum is conserved across the donor and its receiving neighbours, and a detector that tests that balance against the static interconnection list finds those transfers at a lower false-alarm rate than a detector that looks at each series alone. inconclusive not-for-production A detector that compares each substation with its neighbours found 0.33 of the switched power in the 18 visible validation transfers, and beat a single-series detector by about 0.14 in a rough post hoc comparison at equal alarm rates, which has no interval. The 18 transfers are too few to show whether the detector meets the 0.35 bar, so the result is inconclusive. primary

Done Nothing Finished (not supported): Subtracting an estimate of the unmetered solar output from the demand forecast's errors changed nothing, because the forecast already allows for the sunshine at these six substations. 658 Does a neural network that reads all 15 Primaries' demand residuals at once find and pair load-shift events better than the penalised segmentation of experiment 653? Done Nothing Finished (supported): We built one shared tool that adds fake load transfers between neighbouring Primary substations to real power history. 665 How much of an injected load-shift event does each event-table method find, split by how long the event lasts and how deep the step is?
