docs.title: Planned experiments
docs.text: Experiment Hypothesis Relevance

docs.title: Better irradiance for the metered farms
docs.text: Experiment 218 found that the plant's shape is not what limits the fit: giving each farm its own plant parameters raised the fraction of output explained by only 0.003 over one shape shared by all farms. The next question is whether a solar-irradiance product other than the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS), or a blend of products, raises the fraction of the six farms' output explained by the plant model. The experiment fails if the best blend raises that fraction by less than 0.02 over CAMS alone.

docs.title: XGBoost with the plant's mean and the members' spread
docs.text: Experiment 224 found that an XGBoost model scores lower pinball loss at the 0.01 to 0.95 quantiles and the plant at the 0.99 quantile. The proposal is to give an XGBoost model two extra input columns, the plant's mean response and the standard deviation of the 51 plant responses, and to refit it weekly. The experiment fails if the quantile score improves by less than 2% over plain XGBoost, or if the 0.99 pinball loss stays above the plant's.

docs.title: Metered solar farms: state and next steps
docs.text: This page summarises what the experiments on the six metered solar farms (Solar A to F) have found, and which experiments an option could run next. Every figure comes from a merged result page, linked at its first use. The scores are the quantile score and the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), both defined in the glossary, which also defines ENS (the ensemble weather forecast), ERA5, and CAMS (the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service). "Points of capacity" are quantile-score units as a fraction of the farm's capacity, and in a signed contrast a negative value is better. The Solar A to F labels follow the earlier experiment pages, and the labels in experiment 668 differ. Final models describes the final solar network.

docs.title: Take-home message
docs.text:
A small neural network that reads only the ensemble weather forecast forecasts the six farms about as well as any more elaborate design we tried. In the one-year backtest of the final solar network, the CRPS on daylight half-hours is 37.1% better than climatology at days 0 to 1 (95% day-block interval 34.6% to 39.6%) and 7.6% better at days 10 to 14 (6.0% to 9.0%). Climatology is the farm's own power for the same month and half-hour of day in earlier history. The backtest is one year that overlaps the development months (experiment 668).

The weather input and the upper tail may be what limits the forecast. The network settings, the plant model, pretraining, and extra weather sources each moved the score by 2% or less. No experiment has yet isolated the weather input as the cause of the shortfall on very sunny days.

Two options bear on this. One is to test another irradiance product or a blend of products, and the other is to add XGBoost plant-response columns (options 1 and 2 below).

docs.title: What works
docs.text:
The final network beats climatology on average at days 10 to 14, but not in every season. The network PLP (a shared mixture-density neural network over the six farms, with 3 Gaussian components) reads the ensemble mean and spread of the weather, the sun's elevation and azimuth, the lead, and a fixed physics-lite power, with no calendar or farm column (experiment 659, experiment 666). At days 10 to 14 it is worse than climatology from November to March (by 0.03 to 0.42 points of capacity) and better from April to September.

The assembled forecast keeps its skill from 1 to 10 days ahead. The blend of experiment 310 has a quantile score 38.7% better than climatology at day 1 (interval -44.2% to -33.3%, 98.75%) and 10.1% better at days 8 to 10. The mixture-density network alone is 37.9% better at day 1. These results use the physical plant, which the final network lacks. A plant-fed XGBoost model has no skill over climatology at days 8 to 10.

One pass over the ensemble mean and spread is enough. Experiment 430 tested four richer designs: passing the 51 ensemble members through an encoder, a plant model inside the network, pretraining on ERA5 and CAMS, and point masses at zero and at capacity. None beat the one-pass network by the 1% margin.

A pooled network matches separate networks. One network over the six farms scores within 0.8% of a separate network for each farm (experiment 345). The interval is about 4 points wide. Adding wind farms makes solar 0.7% to 2.3% worse, so the two fuels are trained separately.

A physical plant model adds little once the neural network sees the weather. A weather-only forecast scores within 0% to 3.4% of the plant-based forecast up to 10 days ahead, and the intervals include zero except for XGBoost, which is 2.8% better (experiment 313).

The neural network can be refitted once a year. Moving from quarterly to annual refits changes the quantile score by less than 0.6% for both one-pass networks tested (experiment 493). Experiment 493 did not test the network PLP.

Hard zeros at night are safe. A zero set at each half-hour's own sun position removes every non-zero night quantile and changes no daylight score, tested at two farms (experiment 684). Solar B has small negative readings on 8% of night half-hours (experiment 433), so the zero is a forecast rule, not a property of the data.

docs.title: What does not work
docs.text:
The upper tail on very sunny days is too low in every design. On very sunny days 10.6% to 12.7% of observations exceed the 0.99 quantile in every simple arm (experiment 659). A band-widening rule fitted on earlier months did not improve the score. Experiment 318 found that clock and cloud-spread inputs lower the 0.99 pinball loss by about 5% at days 3 to 7, which leaves the overall score unchanged and does not cure the sunny-day exceedance share.

Dawn and dusk are badly calibrated. At the two farms tested, the coverage of the 5% to 95% band is 0.69 and 0.75, and 0.30 and 0.24 of observations fall at or below the 0.01 quantile (experiment 684). The 0.01-quantile shares on this page are not comparable, because each is measured on different rows.

The median is biased by season. It is high in spring and low in autumn, and the network has no calendar input (experiment 666). One year with quarterly refits cannot separate a seasonal effect from refit age.

Network settings, more history, and other weather sources add little.

  • None of 25 one-at-a-time changes to the neural network improves the score by 0.5% (experiment 443).
  • Adding the Met Office UKV forecast to the ensemble lowers the day-ahead error by 1.8% and 1.3% (experiment 229), and adding the German ICON-D2 forecast as well gains about 1.0% (experiment 246).
  • The ensemble's irradiance on the cells around a farm improves the quantile score by 0.36% (experiment 292).
  • Nearly 6 years of past-weather rows added to the training lower the quantile score by 1.7% (experiment 275).

Per-farm plant parameters do not help. Giving each farm its own panel tilt, azimuth, heat loss, and inverter limit raises the fraction of output explained by 0.003 (0.953 against 0.950); the same plants fit only 0.91 with the ensemble weather (experiment 218).

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
Exact zeros may not explain the lower-tail shortfall. Experiment 321 shows that exact zeros (3.0% of daylight half-hours) account for the earlier 3.3% to 3.7% at or below the 0.01 quantile. Strictly below it, the share is 1.2% to 1.4% with the farm's own history, 1.4% to 2.1% with none, and 4.6% at Solar E. Experiment 430 reports 5.1% to 5.3% at or below the quantile on its own rows, which zeros alone may not explain. The final network has 0.028 to 0.032 below the 0.01 quantile, about 3 times too frequent (experiment 666).

The cause of the sunny-day shortfall is not isolated. Experiment 293 found that a higher or softer cap on the plant's power does nothing, so the shape of the plant is not the cause. Experiment 218 points at the irradiance forecast, and no experiment has tested that directly.

Two farms (Solar D and Solar E) have idle runs of 17 to 24 days on clear days. Outages are too rare in the scored year to test an availability state: five farms have at most 34 outage half-hours and the sixth has 165 (experiment 301).

The value of the forecast for curtailment is unresolved. Forecasting each farm's output cut the curtailment cost by 40% at one substation and raised it by 24% at another, which is smaller than the uncertainty (experiment 255).

docs.title: Options for the next experiments
docs.text:
Each option comes from the research plan or from a merged page's "What to try next".

  1. An option is to test another irradiance product or a blend of products (research plan, from experiment 218). The question is whether it raises the fraction of output explained by the plant model by at least 0.02 over CAMS alone. Experiments 443 and 292 name the input as the next place to look, and experiment 618 names ERA5 surface radiation for Solar D.
  2. An option is to give an XGBoost model the plant's mean response and the spread of the 51 plant responses as two extra columns, refitted weekly (research plan, from experiment 224). The plan's failure rule is a quantile-score gain under 2%, or a 0.99 pinball loss above the plant's.
  3. An option is to remove or measure the seasonal bias in the median with a calendar input or monthly refits (experiment 666 and Final models).
  4. An option is to ask NGED (National Grid Electricity Distribution) what happened at Solar B, where the output in an earlier period was 11% lower, not higher (experiment 618).
  5. An option is to score the final network with the node metric once each farm is paired with its substation (experiment 300), which needs more substations than experiment 255 had.

docs.title: What is parked, and why
docs.text: Capacity tracking from the farms' output is paused until January. It belongs to the unmetered-PV-capacity work that the maintainer paused. Experiment 618 finds a sudden change of 8% or more at Solar A, B, C, and F, with at most 0.7 false changes a year. Experiment 636 stopped its line under its stop rule.

docs.title: Production reference and best guess
docs.text:
The current understanding and the options for next work are on the state and next steps page.

On one validation year, the best recipe tested so far beats the stored production-style forecast at Primary substations, supply points, 6 solar farms, and 3 wind farms. Most of the gain at Primary substations comes from correcting each forecast by its mean error over the previous 14 days, and refitting weekly adds a little more. The experiments scored one validation year (July 2025 to June 2026), and several settings were chosen on that year, so the gains are probably optimistic. Nothing from this theme is adopted in production, and the best training source for solar and wind farms is unsettled.

Over all lead times, BG2 has a lower mean absolute error of the median than manual_heuristic for all four target classes, for example 7.43 against 8.70 at Primary substations (experiment 87).

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
The stored production-style forecast loses to a simple rule. In experiment 13, the xgboost_baseline forecast had an error of the median 1.69 points of capacity above manual_heuristic's (99% interval +0.98 to +2.59; 16 Primaries). N1 was level with manual_heuristic (+0.22, -0.54 to +0.97), so that verdict was inconclusive.

The 14-day correction supplies nearly all of the early gain. In experiment 19, the correction lowered N1's quantile score by 0.99 points, and the stack of experiment 19 (N1 with the correction, a half-life, and a spread factor) beat manual_heuristic by 0.56 (99.44% interval -0.93 to -0.26). The half-life added nothing to a frozen model. In experiment 87, the correction on a frozen XGBoost model lowers the Primary score by 1.38 of the 1.67 points that BG2 gains, and weekly refitting lowers it by a further 0.12 (95% interval 0.05 to 0.20).

The best guess of experiment 33 beats the production-style forecast by 3.8 to 6.3 points. The experiment 33 contrasts are 4.89 for Primary demand (98.33% interval -5.66 to -4.06), 3.81 for solar farms (-5.07 to -2.64), and 6.27 for wind farms (-7.65 to -5.28), all at the 98.33% level. The farm contrasts use 53 Tuesday runs and the Primary contrast 73 runs. The correction applied to production explains 1.38 of the 4.89 Primary points. No arm widened production's band, so the share due to calibration is untested. The production-style 0.95 quantile was exceeded in 49% of Primary cases, against 7% for the best guess.

BG2 beats the previous best forecast at Primaries and supply points. BG2 lowered the score by 0.283 at the 16 Primaries (98.75% interval -0.425 to -0.146) and by 0.634 at the 4 supply points (-1.111 to -0.279). Adding the five-model blend lowered the Primary score by 0.086 (0.038 to 0.135). The solar offset lowered it by 0.114 (0.075 to 0.164) on the rows it can touch, which are the daylight rows from April to September at the 5 of 16 Primaries that carry an offset. Over all scored rows the gain dilutes to 0.010.

The correction is the largest step, and weekly refitting, the blend, and the solar offset add small steps (experiment 87).

The solar and wind farm models cannot yet be ranked. The ensemble-trained model scored 0.050 points worse than the ERA5-trained mixture at 6 solar farms (98.75% interval -0.125 to +0.168) and 0.228 worse at 3 wind farms (-0.178 to +0.653). Neither interval rules out a loss above the margin we would accept (0.10 and 0.30), which is why the verdict of experiment 87 is partly supported.

Better weather would add little for Primary demand. In experiment 22, ERA5 weather in place of ENS weather lowered the score by 0.10 points (99.38% interval -0.16 to -0.04), and not at all within 2 days. A demand model retrained on ERA5 lowered the score by 0.27 against an ENS-trained N1 with the correction (experiment 33). Both are ceilings, because ERA5 arrives about 5 days late.

Whether the metering unit causes the MVA-only skill gap is unsettled. In experiment 56, skill was 10.5 percentage points lower at the 8 MVA series than at the 8 MW series over all hours (95% interval 2.1 to 17.5, resampling months), and the gap was smaller at sunny middays (April to September, 10:00 to 13:30 UTC: 5.6, -5.0 to 14.6). Resampling series instead of months gives -2.0 to 20.2 over all hours, so the data cannot separate the metering from which series were chosen. The experiment found no evidence of a need for special handling and cannot rule out a loss of about 15 points at sunny middays.

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text:
BG2 is the best of the recipes tested here for Primaries and supply points, and no recipe is ranked for farms.

  • Primaries: a five-member quantile blend with a solar offset at 5 of 16 Primaries, scoring 5.260 against 5.543 for the frozen stack (experiment 87).
  • Supply points: the weekly-refitted XGBoost model with no correction, scoring 12.925 against 13.559 for the frozen stack (experiment 87).
  • Solar and wind farms: the ERA5-trained mixture of experiment 33 and the ensemble-trained model of experiment 87 are within each other's intervals.

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text:
Experiments 19, 33, and 87 are marked candidate; none is adopted.

  • Primary demand: add the 14-day correction and the spread factor of 1.15 to N1 (experiment 19, experiment 33). Applied to the production forecast, the correction raised the threshold-weighted CRPS above the 99th percentile of history from 0.067 to 0.107 (higher is worse), and on N1 from 0.058 to 0.064, so check the tail when porting it.
  • Primaries and supply points: refit weekly, and blend five models at Primaries (experiment 87). Serve supply points without the correction.
  • Solar and wind farms: either the ERA5-trained mixture or the ensemble-trained model beats the production-style forecast, and which to serve is unresolved. Adding the power-curve base margin lowered the wind score by 0.057 (95% interval 0.024 to 0.098), and the solar bands need recalibration (experiment 87).

Experiments 13, 22, and 56 are not-for-production.

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
• Score every arm on the same cases. Without it, arms with missing forecasts are compared on different rows. The stored production forecast lacked 124 of 282,916 solar and wind cases and manual_heuristic lacked 195 (experiment 33). Look for arms with different run sets or ensemble members.
  • Compare with manual_heuristic as well as production. The quantile score at the 16 Primaries over 73 runs was 9.52 for production and 5.89 for manual_heuristic, so a gain over production alone overstates a new XGBoost model (experiment 13, experiment 33). Look for a changed production recipe.
  • Do not add the correction to supply points without a new test. It raised the supply-point score by 0.305 (0.060 to 0.594) in experiment 87, and experiment 33 found no gain there (+0.38, -0.12 to +0.92). The farms were not tested. Look for a second validation year or more than 4 supply points.
  • Build the correction history from daily forecasts. Experiment 19 used runs 5 days apart, so past errors were probably larger than a daily service would see, whereas experiment 87 scored 292 daily runs and its assembly script builds each correction from earlier runs. Look for a forecast service that runs less often than daily, which would make the history sparser.
  • Treat settings tuned on the scored year as optimistic. The spread factor, the blend scheme, the choice of which Primaries get the solar offset, and the half-life were chosen on the validation year (experiment 87). Look for results on a later year.
  • Read a staircase and a drop-one ablation separately. Adding the blend lowers the staircase score by 0.086, whereas removing it from BG2 raises the score by 0.091, because each starts from a different forecast (experiment 87). Look for a new member of the blend.
  • Report tail coverage and pinball loss as well as the quantile score. The quantile score hid that BG2's solar bands are too wide (experiment 87) and that production covers only 10% to 20% of cases (experiment 33). Look for a new weather source or target class.
  • Do not rely on the production-style row until its origin is confirmed. It was read from a stored table of unconfirmed origin, so its 10.54 may not match the deployed forecast (experiment 87). Look for a comparison with the current production forecasts.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text:
• Whether the correction and the weekly refit hold their gains on a second validation year.
  • Which training source suits solar and wind farms, which needs more than 6 solar and 3 wind farms.
  • Whether the solar offset helps on daylight rows from April to September.
  • Whether the 10.5-point all-hours skill gap of MVA-only Primaries (2.1 to 17.5 over months, -2.0 to 20.2 over series) is caused by the metering, which needs more than 8 MVA series.
  • Whether monthly retraining without the correction beats the best guess of experiment 33: it scored 5.12 on one seed against 5.32, and needs a test on three seeds and more than one validation year.

The Research plan lists what is planned next.

docs.title: Production reference and best guess: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00696 gas-engine-state-tracker-part-3-engine-state-in-the-pre-training-mixer At D8, giving the pre-training mixer of experiment 677's step 9a neural network the tracked gas-engine state at the valid time (the expected engine output as a share of capacity and the probability that one or more units run), so that the weather encoder and the date-time encoder need not explain the engine's steps, and then training the stage 2 and stage 3 networks with a fresh mixer that has no engine input, lowers the CRPS of the forecast of D8's metered apparent power against the same neural network pre-trained without the state. not supported not-for-production Letting the neural network see the gas engine's state while it learns from weather and the calendar, and then dropping that knowledge before the forecast, did not improve the forecast of D8, and we cannot distinguish the change from zero. At another substation with an engine added, where the true state is known, a post hoc split of the results shows a gain of about 0.06 points when the engine is off and a loss of about 0.23 points when it runs. Weighted by the 19% of half-hours when the engine runs, the two cancel. One explanation that fits, not measured directly, is that the weather and calendar parts of the neural network lose the engine's daily pattern and the fresh final stage cannot recover it. The result does not support a gain from extra signal in pre-training only, at D8. A next experiment could combine the pre-training state with a way of putting the engine back after pre-training, and test the combination at the host first. also relevant 00695 gas-engine-state-tracker-part-2-cleaned-target-and-climatology-add-back At D8, removing the inferred gas-engine output from the training target and from the lagged-power inputs of the demand neural network, and adding the engine back at forecast time as a climatological distribution over the number of running units (passed through the apparent-power fold), lowers the error of the forecast of D8's metered apparent power, against the same neural network trained on the raw reading. not supported not-for-production Taking the gas engine out of D8's recorded demand before training, and adding the engine's average running pattern back when forecasting, did not improve the forecast. The cleaned arm was no better than the raw arm, and a post hoc reading of the same data suggests it was probably about 0.1 points of capacity worse over all rows. At another substation with an engine injected, cleaning gained about 0.1 points, within noise. Knowing whether the engine runs at the forecast's valid time would lower the error by 1.4 to 2.4 points against the raw arm, but no forecast has that knowledge. No gain was found, and cleaning plus a calendar add-back is not worth porting; one open question is whether the engine's state can be forecast from information available at the origin. also relevant 00689 fixed-lookback-width-scale-versus-seed-averaging-at-refit-boundaries The steps in band width at the model refits (Primaries 11 and 13, and six widenings in February) come from the new model's raw band width differing from the old one's, so a scale fitted on the previous 90 days of the old model's forecasts cannot remove them; the seed average of the quantiles is not the cause. not supported not-for-production A single width scale fitted on the previous 90, 45, or 180 days does not remove the steps in band width at the refits of Primary 11 and the six February widenings, and moves the ratio farther from 1 in 67% of affected cells (the median step of an affected cell goes from 15% stored to 24%). Fitting the scale per seed and averaging gives nearly the same ratios, so seed averaging is not what drives the steps. A scale fitted on the new model's own forecasts could follow a refit, but those forecasts do not exist until after it; this experiment did not test one. also relevant 00688 winter-normal-running-coverage-median-error-and-events-part-1 The winter shortfall of the normal-running Primaries' 90% bands (q05-to-q95 coverage 80% in 2025-12 and 2026-01 after experiment 683's walk-forward scale) comes from a month-long error in the median forecast and from half-hours inside load transfers, not from bands that are too narrow for the errors the median makes. supported not-for-production The 90% bands of the 16 Primary substations' normal-running forecasts miss in winter mostly because the median forecast is off by a different amount each month, and partly because of load transfers, not because the bands are too narrow. Shifting each band by its month's observed median error and dropping the transfers lifts coverage from 80% in both months to 90% in December 2025 and 89% in January 2026, with the band width almost right. A candidate next step is a way to correct the median level during the month, not a model of the band width. also relevant 00684 backtest-positive-demand-output-distributions-and-physical-solar-night-zero A positive output family at the four Primaries that cannot go below zero, and a hard zero at every solar half-hour whose sun is at or below the horizon at the middle of the half-hour, remove the negative lower quantiles and the non-zero night quantiles of the backtest files without reducing accuracy. partly supported candidate A Gaussian mixture conditioned on power at or above zero fixes the negative lower quantiles at the four demand series. CRPS improves clearly at two series, is indistinguishable at one, and worsens by 0.03 points of capacity at one, so the model is a candidate to replace the post hoc clamp. A gamma mixture inside the same shared network made two series much worse and is dropped. A hard zero at night at each half-hour's own sun position removes every non-zero solar night quantile, changes no daylight score, and lowers night CRPS, while the share of night observations above q99 rises because the gate sets those quantiles to zero. primary 00683 walk-forward-calibration-of-the-quantile-bands-in-the-one-year-backtest-files The quantile bands stored in the one-year backtest files are too narrow for the Primaries, the bulk supply points (BSPs), and the grid supply points (GSPs) (q05-to-q95 coverage 81% to 88% against 90%), and the shortfall is a width error that a per-series, per-lead-band scale on the half-width of the band removes, when the scale is fitted only on forecasts whose actual power was already known at the start of the month. partly supported candidate Widening the stored bands by a factor fitted only on earlier months brings the bulk supply points, grid supply points, solar, and the prevailing Primaries output to within 2 points of the nominal 90% coverage, with a CRPS rise of at most 0.047 points of capacity. Widening does not rescue the normal-running Primaries: coverage stays at 87% on average and at 80% in two winter months, which is consistent with bands that are wrong by more than their width. A learned width head or a winter correction to the median are candidates for the next experiment, and a median-level shift fitted per series made every file worse. also relevant 00681 extra-lagged-power-inputs-for-the-prevailing-forecast Giving the prevailing head of experiment 667's Candidate more lagged power inputs, newer than the 24-hour and 7-day lags it reads today, shortens the time the prevailing output takes to cover half of a new load level after a confirmed load shift starts. small gain candidate Giving the prevailing forecast 8 to 14 extra lagged power inputs makes it follow a new load level about 20 hours sooner on 1152 simulated load shifts, and 120 hours sooner at D5 in one verified real transfer (D16 did not change), without making the normal-running (NRA) output or the event-free forecast worse. The gain is under the 24 hours set in advance as worth the extra inputs. On injected events 8 inputs give 19.1 of the 20.4 hours, but at D5 only 72 of the 120 hours, and the 8-input set scores worst inside the real events, so which set to port is open. also relevant 00677 building-up-the-candidate-demand-network-one-component-at-a-time Descriptive, not a hypothesis test. A reverse ablation measures the order-dependent contribution of each Candidate component. For the 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms it is the weekly-refitted XGBoost model trained on the ensemble forecast's own history. partly supported candidate BG2 beat the previous best forecast at the 16 Primary substations by 0.283 points (98.75% interval -0.425 to -0.146) and at the 4 bulk and grid supply points by 0.634 (-1.111 to -0.279). primary 00056 mva-only-primaries-skill-against-mw-primaries The best guess (experiment 33's N1 with the 14-day correction and the spread factor) forecasts the 8 trial Primary substations metered in MVA clearly worse, relative to manual_heuristic, than the 8 metered in MW, and the gap is largest at sunny middays, when embedded solar can push net flow through zero and an MVA meter reads the magnitude of that flow with no direction. inconclusive not-for-production At sunny middays the best guess has 5.6 percentage points less skill at the 8 Primary substations metered only in MVA than at the 8 metered in MW, but the 95% interval (-5.0 to 14.6) includes zero. docs.title: Simplifying the neural demand, wind, and solar forecasters: series result
docs.text:
Of the four demand input and output prunings tested, only dropping the 7 ensemble-spread inputs was equivalent to the baseline network at both metering groups, and that pruning loses on the rows where the forecast tails matter, so the final assembly step was not run. The pruning is experiment 496. Scores are CRPS (continuous ranked probability score, in points of effective capacity; lower is better). On rows with no labelled event, the change was +0.012 at the eight and -0.043 at the six, both inside the equivalence limit. On cold winter nights at the six, the network without spread inputs scored 0.187 points worse, and on the six's rows with a labelled event it scored 0.408 points worse. The whole-sample equivalence claim does not show those losses.

Terms. A Primary is a primary substation. "The eight" are the 8 Primaries whose telemetry is in megavolt-amperes only, and "the six" are the 6 Primaries whose telemetry is in signed megawatts (MW). NGED's event labels are incomplete, so "rows with no labelled event" may still hold unlabelled events. A seed is one random initialisation of a neural network, a refit is a fresh training run on newer data, and fine-tuning continues training a pretrained network on archived ensemble weather forecasts. q95 and q99 are the 95% and 99% points of the forecast distribution, and coverage is the share of actuals at or below a quantile. Table P is the recalibration table of widening factors per metering group, lead band, and tail quantile from experiment 483. Solar A to F are the six anonymised metered solar farms.

Scope. Most numbers come from the five demand months of experiment 449 (2025-10, 2025-12, 2026-01, 2026-03, 2026-06). Experiment 492 used four of those folds, and the solar experiments 493 and 498 used 12 scored months. Every score is selection-biased, and the demand results are interim.

docs.title: Serving table
docs.text:
The candidate serving settings below need fewer networks and refits than the baselines. They keep the inputs and the recalibration table that the experiments did not show to be removable. No page records these settings as adopted in a production release.

Family Candidate setting Evidence Demand: networks per serving pass 2 seeds Experiment 481: a second seed scores 0.035 points better than one; later seeds gain at most 0.011 each (5 months). Demand: refits Pretrain once, fine-tune monthly Experiment 494: equivalent to a fresh refit at the eight and the six over 5 months; saves about 42 of the 80 GPU seconds per seed-refit. Demand: inputs Keep the 7 ensemble-spread inputs Experiment 496: dropping them scores +0.187 on cold winter nights at the six. Demand: recalibration Keep table P Experiment 492: two constants match table P at the eight only. Experiment 500: none of the three pre-registered rolling conformal rules passes the q95 floor at the six. Wind: networks per serving pass 1 seed Experiment 481: one seed meets the pre-registered rule; a second seed gains 0.041 points. Solar: refits Annual, not quarterly Experiment 498: for the encoder at Solar E, annual refits score +0.26% (10 seeds), inside the 1% limit. Experiment 493: both networks tested pass at the 1% limit. Solar: network design Keep the 51-member encoder (a2_member) Experiment 493: the one-pass network with annual refits scores 1.28% worse than the encoder with quarterly refits at Solar E, mostly from the network design.

docs.title: Tried and not adopted
docs.text:
Each of these was a candidate simplification, and none was shown to lose nothing.

  • Distilling the five-network pool into one student network (experiment 489): not supported. At the eight the students score within 0.006 of a single seed (4.762 to 4.770, against 4.764 for the single seed and 4.680 for the pool).
  • Distilling the lagged-plus-lagless mixture into one lag-robust network (experiment 490): not supported. On rows with no labelled event at the six, the student scores 3.79 points against 3.51 for the mixture of one lagged network and the lagless forecast (B-mix), a gap of 0.28.
  • Averaging weights during fine-tuning (experiment 491): gains almost nothing. At the eight, an exponential moving average scores 4.760 and a stochastic weight average 4.757, against 4.762 for one ordinary network and 4.680 for the pool.
  • Two constants per metering group (experiment 492): matches table P at the eight; at the six, q95 coverage is 0.011 to 0.013 lower.
  • Two constants per farm for wind and solar (experiment 499): inconclusive. The pre-registered rule needs the minimum detectable effect to lie below each limit, and it does not, except for wind q99 coverage. Wind coverage stays within 0.004 of table P at every tail, and solar per-farm constants within 0.005, but the stored year is too short to show equivalence.
  • Rolling conformal recalibration (experiment 500): not supported. With buffers of 7, 14, and 28 days, q95 coverage at the six stays between 0.874 and 0.913, below the 0.93 floor. A rule added after the scores were seen, which shifts all 11 quantiles by the median error of the last 28 days, brings q95 to 0.935 and q99 to 0.988, but most of its CRPS gain comes from one Primary.
  • Three other demand prunings (experiment 496): none equivalent at both the eight and the six. The CRPS change at the eight and the six is +0.095 and +0.229 for merging the four holiday columns into one day-type column, +0.152 and +0.082 for one Gaussian instead of three, and +0.079 and +0.050 for dropping the weekly lag. Dropping the weekly lag also scored 0.167 worse on cold winter nights at the six.

docs.text: Experiment Hypothesis Relevance

docs.title: Production reference and best guess: state and next steps
docs.text:
The BG2 best guess beats the stored production-style forecast, and a simple weekly-refitted XGBoost model comes within 0.05 points of BG2 at the six MW Primaries. Scores are the quantile score, an estimate of the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), in points of capacity. In a contrast, a negative value means the first forecast is better. A Primary is a primary substation. The six MW Primaries report signed megawatts, and the eight MVA Primaries report apparent power in megavolt-amperes only (glossary). Where a result uses another set of Primaries, the paragraph says so.

The final models supersede the BG2 recipe as the design for the Primaries. The final models page documents the neural Candidate (P7+D50 with a prevailing head), which is the Primaries design, together with the wind and solar networks. BG2 is the XGBoost reference of Experiment 87: a five-member blend with a 14-day correction and an explicit solar offset at five Primaries. BG2 is part of the final test. The neural simplification series records which simplifications the networks can take.

docs.title: What works
docs.text:
The stored production-style forecast loses to the manual_heuristic at Primaries. The manual_heuristic forecasts each half-hour from the power at the same weekday and time in earlier weeks. In Experiment 13, the xgboost_baseline forecast (the production recipe, read from a stored table of unconfirmed origin) had a mean absolute error of the median 1.69 points above the manual_heuristic (99% interval +0.98 to +2.59; 16 Primaries). A gain over production alone therefore overstates a new forecast, so every comparison needs the manual_heuristic beside it.

The best guess beats the production-style forecast by 3.8 to 6.3 points. Experiment 33 found 4.89 points for Primary demand (98.33% interval -5.66 to -4.06), 3.81 for solar farms, and 6.27 for wind farms.

BG2 beats the manual_heuristic for all four target classes. In Experiment 87, the mean absolute error of the median at Primaries is 7.43 for BG2 against 8.70, and the quantile score is 5.260 against 6.182.

Most of the Primary gain comes from the 14-day correction. In Experiment 87, the correction on a frozen XGBoost model lowers the Primary score by 1.38 of the 1.67 points that BG2 gains. At the four supply points the correction made the score 0.305 worse (0.060 to 0.594), so BG2 serves them without it.

The three recent-power inputs are the part of BG2 that cannot be removed. Experiment 102 found that removing them made the Primary score 0.36 points worse once one substation's commissioning months were cut, and the supply-point score 0.28 worse. The wind farm forecasts lost nothing measurable. The experiment did not test a lag-free model with a level term.

A plain weekly XGBoost model is nearly as good as the five-member blend. Experiment 379 found it within 0.05 points of BG2 at the six MW Primaries and within 0.02 at the eight MVA Primaries. Two of BG2's five members (the monthly XGBoost and the pooled-by-type model) added nothing measurable.

The weekly XGBoost model matches the GAM stack at most Primaries. Experiment 381 compares it with the stack of generalised additive models. It was level with the stack at 9 of 14 Primaries and better at 4 (D8, D12, D22, and D5). At the six MW Primaries it is 0.08 worse (-0.12 to +0.27), and worse at D11 (+0.15) and D14 (+0.30), so one demand recipe does not suit both groups. Removing the Kalman filter makes the stack 0.12 worse at the six MW Primaries (Experiment 380).

On the five development months, K1 beat BG2 by 0.32 points at 13 Primaries. K1 is the neural network of Experiment 620 with a band that widens while a load shift is detected. The contrast is on rows with no labelled event (Experiment 645; interval -0.42 to -0.22).

Default 3 matches BG2 at the six MW Primaries. Experiment 378 scored research default 3 (the GAM-stack demand forecast) at -0.12 against BG2 at the six, and 0.16 worse at the eight MVA Primaries without D8 and 0.63 worse with it.

docs.title: What does not work
docs.text:
On July to October 2026, BG2 beat K1 by 0.71 points, and the lead is smaller than it looks. In Experiment 633, BG2 scored 4.23 and K1 scored 4.94 (Experiment 620). The 4.23 is BG2 fitted once. The lead halves on event-free rows to 0.38 (3.91 against 4.29). BG2 also reads power 3.5 hours old, against at least 24 hours for K1. The current reading is Experiment 645: on the development months, away from the transfers, K1 was the better of the two, so BG2's lead in the window is not a standing advantage.

A network fitted once did no better than the manual_heuristic on that window. In Experiment 620, K1 scored 4.94 against 4.85 for the manual_heuristic (not separable), and K1 lost at four Primaries (D14, D15, D16, and D18). Experiment 620 names load transfers at D14 to D18 and a single fit as candidate causes. The weekly-refit arm was skipped because its estimated 3.7 hours or more exceeded the 3-hour cap.

Removing days with load shifts reverses the K1 result. Experiment 637 removed the days a frozen detector flags (6.1% of rows, 119 Primary-days, 102 of them at D18). K1 minus the manual_heuristic moved from +0.10 (-0.03 to +0.22) to -0.15 (-0.26 to -0.05), with CRPS 4.29 against 4.44. The Candidate moved from +0.15 to -0.13, and K3 stayed worse (+0.20). D14 still loses, because the detector flags only 5 of its 112 days.

The GAM stack does not transfer unchanged to the eight MVA Primaries. In Experiment 252, a solar term at each monthly refit gave point estimates at or below BG2 at five of the eight, while D8, D12, and D22 stayed worse. Experiment 360 found that BG2's lead at D8 is more likely to come from what its members learn than from blending (one substation, one year).

The q05 to q95 band covers too few readings in the final-test networks. It covered 0.73 to 0.77 of readings in Experiment 620. BG2's 95% quantile covers 93.2% at the six MW Primaries against a nominal 95% (Experiment 379).

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• It is unknown whether the 14-day correction and the weekly refit hold on a second year. The recipe was chosen on one validation year (July 2025 to June 2026), so its gains are probably optimistic.
  • It is unknown why K1 lost ground after July 2026. Experiment 633 names the lags (3.5 hours against 24 hours) and BG2 following load shifts: BG2's median follows 0.56 of the D18 transfer and K3's follows 0.33.
  • The best training source for solar and wind farms is unresolved. Experiment 87 could not rank the ensemble-trained model against the ERA5-trained mixture at 6 solar and 3 wind farms. ENS is the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts ensemble, and ERA5 is its reanalysis (glossary).
  • The cause of the MVA-only skill gap is unresolved. Experiment 56 found 10.5 percentage points of skill against the manual_heuristic (15.0% for the MW group, 4.5% for the MVA group; 95% interval 2.1 to 17.5). Experiment 384 tested 16 Primaries and showed no hypothesis; the only difference was a weaker price correlation (0.08 against 0.17).

docs.title: Next experiments
docs.text:
Each option below comes from the research plan or from a merged result's "What to try next".

  1. An option is to score the lag-enabled network against BG2 with equal 3.5-hour lags. It comes from Experiment 633's advice and removes the lag asymmetry.
  2. An option is to refit K1 and the Candidate every 14 days through July to October 2026. It comes from Experiment 620's advice, to test whether ageing weights explain the narrow bands. Experiment 667, with monthly refits over a year, is partial evidence.
  3. An option is to run the weekly-refit BG2 arm that Experiment 633 skipped. The arm was skipped because of its estimated cost.
  4. An option is a boosted-tree sunshine term in the stack against research default 3. The plan lists it as proposed with medium priority, beside a hard switch on the member share of cold ensemble members (D3b).

docs.title: Parked
docs.text: Wind and solar refit schedules wait, and so does load-shift event work. Load-shift detection and unmetered PV capacity are paused until January. The neural simplification series holds the wind and solar serving settings.

docs.title: Retraining and training history
docs.text:
The current understanding and the options for next work are on the state and next steps page.

On 16 Primary substations, refitting the XGBoost demand model every week with no error correction scored 0.20 to 0.24 points of capacity below a model fitted once with the correction, on two separate sets of forecast runs (292 runs at 16 Primaries, and 274 control-member-only runs at 13). The gain is fragile: three substations carry much of it, and refitting weekly instead of monthly adds only 0.04 to 0.13 points. Models trained on one old year scored worse than ones trained on a recent year, but one substation drives most of that gap.

This theme asks how often to refit the demand forecast of Primary substations, and how much history to train on. The comparison throughout is the stack: an N1 model fitted once, with the 14-day correction and a spread factor of 1.15. Scores are quantile scores in points of capacity, and a negative contrast is an improvement. Refitting solar and wind models gained little, and the cause of the penalty on older training years is not yet found.

Monthly and weekly refitting scored below the stack, though monthly minus the stack has a 99.375% interval of -0.44 to +0.08, and the 14-day correction did not help a refitted model (16 Primaries, 73 runs; experiment 34).

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
A 12-month window, a half-life of 1 year or less, or the 14-day correction beat training on all history, and a model never retrained lost most (experiment 17). Against an all-history model retrained monthly, the mean absolute error of the median changed by -0.84 for a 12-month window (99.44% interval -1.19 to -0.53), -0.92 for a half-life of 0.5 years (-1.22 to -0.64), +0.52 for yearly retraining (+0.30 to +0.81), and +3.80 for never retraining (+3.12 to +4.47). The test used ERA5 weather, which arrives about 5 days late, so these are ceilings.

Refitting monthly scored 0.20 below the stack in experiment 34, and the pre-registered interval included zero. The contrast was -0.20 (95% interval -0.38 to -0.01; 99.375% interval -0.44 to +0.08), so the verdict is inconclusive. Weekly minus monthly was -0.07 (99.375% interval -0.18 to -0.00).

Weekly refitting beat the stack again on two further sets of runs. In experiment 48, on the 292 daily runs that experiment 34 left out, the contrast was -0.20 (99.44% interval -0.40 to -0.035) and weekly minus monthly was -0.13 (-0.24 to -0.03). In experiment 81, on 274 runs from July 2023 to March 2024 at 13 Primaries, scored with the control member only, the contrast was -0.240 (99.17% interval -0.360 to -0.145) and weekly minus monthly was -0.039 (-0.064 to -0.012). On an earlier set, July 2022 to March 2023, it was -0.080 (99.17% interval -0.187 to +0.051 in the text; the figure draws 95% intervals, -0.165 to +0.017): the same sign, with an interval that includes zero.

Weekly refitting beat the stack in July 2023 to March 2024 and had the same sign, with intervals that include zero, in July 2022 to March 2023 (13 Primaries, experiment 81).

Three substations carry much of the gain, so it is not established across all 16. In experiment 48 the contrast without D8 was -0.14 (99.44% interval -0.34 to +0.04), and without D8, D12, and D5 -0.08 (-0.24 to +0.10). A t-interval over the 12 months gave -0.43 to +0.04. In experiment 81, D8 alone gained 2.05 (95% interval -2.60 to -1.44), and without D8, D12, and D5 the contrast was -0.093 (95% interval -0.189 to -0.014). Experiment 81 found no sign that the weekly gain grows as 9 km weather data accumulates: it fell from -0.552 in December to -0.137 in March.

The 14-day correction helps a model fitted once in experiments 17, 19, and 48, and stops helping a refitted one. It lowered the frozen model's score by 1.45 (95% interval -1.87 to -0.98; experiment 48), though it did not help the frozen model on experiment 81's runs (+0.091, -0.005 to +0.187). On a weekly model it raised the score by 0.23 (99.375% interval +0.03 to +0.44; experiment 34) and by 0.08 to 0.16 with intervals that include zero (experiment 48). It supplied nearly all of the stack's gain over N1: -0.99 of -1.00, and the stack scored 0.56 below manual_heuristic (99.44% interval -0.93 to -0.26; experiment 19).

Averaging the quantiles of several models gained 0.04 to 0.10 points. Three models gave -0.097 against the best member (98.33% interval -0.187 to -0.026; experiment 35). Five models gave -0.076 against weekly refitting (99.17% interval -0.135 to -0.023; experiment 49), and four gave -0.038 (99.17% interval -0.070 to -0.007), short of the 0.05 threshold (experiment 81). The three-model and five-model averages include the frozen stack as a member.

Refitting solar and wind models gained little. Monthly refitting minus a frozen model was -0.044 at 6 solar farms (99.44% interval -0.158 to -0.003) and +0.007 at 3 wind farms (-0.001 to +0.014), for ERA5-trained models (experiment 48). Six and three farms cannot say more.

Older training years hurt in models trained once on a single year, mostly through one substation, and neither the average level nor the weather product explains it. A model trained on 2021-07 to 2022-06 scored 1.57 worse than one trained on 2024-07 to 2025-06 on 13 Primaries with control-member weather (98.3% interval 1.14 to 2.00), but 0.61 (95% interval 0.41 to 0.81) without one substation, and removing each substation's trailing 365-day level took off 42% of that, under the half predicted (experiment 93). The gap was 1.71 with ERA5 weather in both years (99% interval 1.15 to 2.29), as large as with forecast weather, so the 18 km to 9 km change of weather product is not the main cause (experiment 95). The long-history sub-theme tests a physics-based model that may use old years. Experiment 95 also gave 0.61 without D8 on the control member and 0.78 on ERA5. Half-life contrasts under refitting were unresolved (experiments 34, 49, and 81).

The old-year penalty was as large on ERA5 as on forecast weather, so the weather product is not the main cause (13 Primaries, experiment 95).

These changes did not help a refitted model. Re-tuning the spread factor moved the score by -0.0001 (99.17% interval -0.012 to +0.018), and substation fingerprints in a pooled model by +0.009 (-0.037 to +0.050; experiment 49). A zero starting value moved it by -0.017 (98.75% interval -0.072 to +0.054; experiment 80). Dropping the Christmas column and changing the half-life from 0.5 to 2 years were unresolved (experiments 49 and 81).

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text: The best of the recipes tested here for Primary demand is an N1 per substation, refitted weekly with no correction, with an average of quantiles over other models that includes the frozen stack. Weekly refitting scored 5.44 against 5.64 for the stack on 292 daily runs (experiment 48), and the five-model average scored 4.968 against 5.044 for weekly refitting on 73 runs (experiment 49). The half-life, the Christmas column, and the correction were not shown to help a refitted model (experiments 34, 49, and 81). BG2 builds on this recipe.

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text:
Experiments 17, 19, 34, 35, 48, 49, and 81 are marked candidate; none is adopted. The other experiments of the theme are not-for-production.

  • Refit the Primary demand model weekly and drop the 14-day correction (experiments 34, 48, and 81). This adds a scheduled job that refits 16 series at about 10 seconds each on a graphics card (experiment 34). Monthly refitting gets most of the gain over the stack (-0.20 in experiments 34 and 81; -0.08 with an interval that includes zero in experiment 48), so the case for weekly over monthly is 0.04 to 0.13 points.
  • Refit the bulk and grid supply point models weekly (experiment 48: -0.66 against the stack, 99.44% interval -1.23 to -0.27, on 4 series).
  • Serve an average of quantiles at Primaries (experiments 35 and 49). It needs several models, and experiment 81 found a four-model version short of its threshold.
  • The 14-day correction helps a model fitted once (experiments 17 and 19). A 12-month window or a 0.5-year half-life beat all history under monthly refitting in experiment 17, on ERA5 weather; their value under weekly refitting is unresolved (experiments 34, 49, and 81).

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
• Use a monthly 12-month-window refit for contrasts of 0.05 or more, and quote absolute and tail scores from weekly refits. The window (150 rounds, learning rate 0.15) reproduced the monthly-minus-weekly gap to within 0.01 at 0.03 to 0.10 of the fit time, but scored 0.16 above full weekly refitting (experiment 85, experiment 34). For contrasts about cadence, retraining rules, or the correction, window, or half-life, use the weekly refit on all history with 150 rounds instead, because conclusions about them change with the schedule (experiment 85). Re-check for another model family or a contrast under 0.05.
  • Do not use quarterly refits to compare arms. Quarterly minus weekly was +0.381 (95% interval +0.207 to +0.565) on the 12-month window, three times the monthly gap (experiment 85). Re-check on other row sets.
  • Compare a refit arm only with a same-code repeat of its control. In experiment 75 only 9% of per-case scores matched the stored weekly run to 0.001, with a largest gap of 4.39 points, although the mean matched to 0.0001. Repeats moved the mean by 0.004 to 0.007 in experiment 80 and by 0.001 in experiment 85. Otherwise a per-case or per-event contrast reads fit noise. Re-check on CPU fits.
  • Retest the 14-day correction after any change of refit cadence or target class. It helps a frozen model, hurts a weekly one in experiment 34 (+0.23, 99.375% interval +0.03 to +0.44), and stopped helping in experiment 48 (intervals include zero). Experiment 81's frozen model gained nothing from it. At supply points adding it raised the score by 0.305 (95% interval 0.060 to 0.594; experiment 87). For farms, a correction by the mean error raised the continuous ranked probability score by 0.437 (solar, 99.58% interval +0.215 to +0.664) and 0.413 (wind, -0.003 to +0.924), and a median of the window's errors moved it by +0.010 and -0.064, post hoc with intervals that include zero (experiment 23). A 7-day window and a multiplicative form were worse than the 14-day additive form, and the correction did not help 4 supply-point series (experiment 21). Re-check with another correction window or model.
  • Report every contrast with and without the series that carries it. D8 alone gained 2.05 (experiment 81) and has a 13.1-point old-year gap while the other 12 substations range from 0.0 to 2.6 (experiment 95). Otherwise a pooled interval reads as a gain across all series. Re-check on other substations.
  • Do not screen features on a frozen model. The weekly-analogue columns gained 0.05 on a frozen model and 0.01 under monthly refitting (experiment 34). Re-check with other recent-demand features.
  • Do not stand in warm-start boosting for refitting. Warm starts got worse with more updates (7.76 against 6.21 for the weekly chain over the daily months; +1.55, +0.33 to +3.21), and a proxy that sees later data is a screening device, not a forecast score (experiment 34).
  • Quote absolute scores only within one experiment's runs. The stack scored 5.32 on experiment 34's 73 runs and 5.64 on experiment 48's 292, and experiment 81's control-only scores match neither. The stack of experiment 19 has a half-life of 0.5 years, and the stacks of experiments 33, 34, 48, and 87 use the 2-year weighting. Re-check which stack a new experiment uses.
  • Check that a 12-month window can test an input. The COVID indicator is constant inside the window, so it cannot be tested (experiment 49). Look for the input's variation within the window.
  • A single month cannot show a weather-product change. The frozen model's lead over manual_heuristic swings from 11.6% in April to 1.2% in June to 8.8% in August (experiment 81). Re-check with a model trained on one product.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text:
• Whether weekly refitting beats the stack at all 16 Primaries on a year the project has not scored, and with the full ensemble; the Research plan lists the longer ENS history.
  • Whether any of the gain is adaptation to the 9 km weather product (experiment 81 could not separate them).
  • What makes older training years worse. Drift differs by series (experiment 92, inconclusive), and experiment 95 suggests changes in solar, heating, or the electricity network without testing any.
  • Whether the Christmas column and the half-life matter under weekly refitting.

The Experiments page lists every experiment of the theme.

docs.title: Retraining and training history: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00640 demand-fit-age-refit-k1-k3 A demand network fitted on data that ends A weeks before the forecast month scores worse the larger A is, and the loss is under 1% of the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) for every 4 weeks of fit age, for K1 (the lag-using network with the gate) and for K3 (the lag-free network, the control). refuted candidate A demand network fitted 4 weeks before the forecast month scores about 3% worse (K1) than one fitted at the month's start. The loss reaches about 10% at 16 weeks and falls back to about 6% at 26 weeks, with wide intervals. K3 loses less in the first 4 weeks. The loss at D15 and D18 is several times larger, but this experiment cannot say whether fit age, their short training history, or level shifts in their power cause it. A refit every 4 to 8 weeks is worth running for K1, and weekly refits are not shown to be worth more. primary 00577 static-between-steps-offsets-and-probabilistic-offset-widening The learnt offsets of D5 (experiment 565) wander from month to month, although a substation's true offset should stay constant for months and then step. A penalty that allows only sparse steps (a total-variation penalty on the first differences, or gated jumps) therefore gives a steadier offset without costing accuracy. Separately, the offset is the least certain part of the forecast, so adding its uncertainty to each mixture component's variance, and a small heavy-tailed component for a step that happened since the refit, improves the tails and the calibration beyond what a constant widening does. refuted not-for-production The slow offset (D5) is already as good as these refinements can make it on this data. Making the offset steadier or wider does not help the forecast, so keep D5 as it is; the penalty and widening ideas are not worth carrying into the next model release. primary 00575 stepwise-offset-large-step-and-mirrored-pair-recovery Experiment 573 injected steps of 2% to 6% of capacity, which may drown in the weather-error noise of the forecast's daily residuals. Steps as large as the labelled load-shifts (a median of 19% of capacity) are found by the daily-knot offset (S1) or the gated-jump offset (S2) when they last a week or more. not supported not-for-production A free per-day offset on top of the frozen demand network cannot find load-shift-sized steps. Even a step of 20% of capacity that lasts a month is only partly followed (median 49% of its size at the better penalty, 9% at the heavier one), and the labelled load-shifts mostly last under 4 days. Do not build a detector on this offset; a detector needs the step to be an explicit part of the model, such as a labelled-event input or a state estimate, rather than a by-product of an offset. primary 00574 part-d-primaries-only-modular-recipe-lag-encoder-offset-and-add-one-arms Four add-ons to the modular lag-encoder neural network with the D5 offset (P0) each lower CRPS: the multi-variable ensemble spread columns in the mixer (P1), thermal-lag and solar-gain columns through the weather encoder (P2), an expected signal for the lag encoder taken from encoders trained on ERA5 and CAMS only (P3), and a three-step schedule with a 3-day embargo (P4). The factors that meet the keep rule, plus P2 by the maintainer's policy, form a final candidate (P5) that stays within 0.04 of A-pool-24 at 24-120 h at the eight MVA Primaries. partly supported candidate The best demand recipe we have fitted (P5) combines experiment 572's lag-encoder neural network and offset with a fresh mixer fitted on the whole ensemble history up to the cutoff, a 3-day embargo, and the thermal-lag and solar-gain columns. At the six MW Primaries it improves on P0, the best earlier recipe, by 0.22 points of capacity at 1 to 5 days (interval excludes zero), and at the eight MVA Primaries by a smaller 0.09 (interval includes zero). P5 beats the daily-refit references at every lead band, and follows an injected 7-day shift of the history less than half as much (2.9 against 7.3 points). The multi-variable ensemble spread columns do not help the network and should stay out. also relevant 00573 stepwise-output-offset-known-answer-step-recovery D5 adds one offset per Primary and month, with a slope penalty, so a step in a Primary's level (a new estate, a persistent transfer, a metering change) is smeared over months and a short step cannot be seen. An offset that is constant between days and changes abruptly (daily knots held constant between knots, with an L1 total-variation penalty, or a sparse set of jumps chosen by hard-concrete gates) recovers the date and size of an injected step. not supported not-for-production At the penalties we tried, an offset that is allowed to jump did not find steps of 2% to 6% of capacity in the demand forecast's residuals. The weights that stop apparent false steps also stop the real ones. The next step is to test whether a second signal, such as a neighbour series or a label, separates a step from slow drift, before relying on a free offset to date level changes. primary 00572 two-offset-part-1-lags-versus-the-slow-output-offset A slow per-Primary output offset (D5) carries the Primary's current level into the forecast, as lagged power does. If so, a lag-free modular network with an offset learnt in pre-training (E2) scores about as well as the best lag network (v3) at 24 to 240 hours, and adding the offset to the lag network (v3+D5) gains little. Lags should still matter in the first 24 hours. partly supported candidate A slow output offset does not make lags unnecessary: at the eight MVA Primaries the best forecast uses both, and the lag network with the offset beat the offset alone by 0.224 points of capacity at 1 to 5 days. At the six MW Primaries the offset alone and the lag network are not distinguishable. The stop rule of the brief (the gain at both groups) is not met, so continuing on the lag network with the offset rests on the eight MVA Primaries alone. also relevant 00571 drift-offset-and-embedding-hybrid-known-answer-worlds A slow per-Primary output offset (D5 of experiment 565) absorbs level shifts, and a drift embedding that modulates the encoders (A10) absorbs changes in behaviour, such as a growing temperature sensitivity or a changed daily shape. Experiment 565's joint fit of both (the hybrid) was worse than the offset alone, but a joint fit lets the two components compete for the same slow variance, so that failure does not refute the hypothesis. Building the hybrid so the components cannot compete (staged, multiplicative-only, or orthogonal) should recover both kinds of injected change in worlds where the answer is known. not supported not-for-production When we inject level steps (and a growing temperature sensitivity, which the steps dominate) into real substation histories, the monthly drift embedding recovers nearly all of the oracle's gain and the output offset alone recovers under a third, so the embedding is not limited to changes in behaviour and the offset is not the better carrier of levels. The joint hybrid that did badly on the real data did not do badly in this world, so competition is not shown to be the cause. The growing-sensitivity part of the question stays open until a readable sensitivity-only world is built. primary 00569 modular-network-inputs-through-matching-encoders-in-pretraining-and-fine-tuning-run-1 Experiment 562 added five input groups to the modular lag-free network at fine-tuning only. Each group may help once it is also pre-trained on ERA5 and CAMS rows and enters through the encoder that matches its content: thermal-lag and solar-gain windows (B1) and look-ahead windows (B2) through the weather encoder, school terms and holidays (B3a) through the datetime encoder, national signals of the previous day (B3b) and the whole-day price shape (B4) through a small parallel encoder. A sixth group (B3c) adds, to B3a, the number of schools within 2 km of each Primary as a gate on the school columns. not supported not-for-production Letting the demand network read thermal-lag, solar-gain, look-ahead, school-term, national-signal, and price-shape columns during pre-training as well as fine-tuning, through the encoder that matches each group, did not help: none of them beat a shuffled-day placebo of the same width on all rows, cold nights, Christmas week, or high-spread days, and a school-proximity input made the eight MVA Primaries worse. This test cannot see small gains (one seed), and the network pre-trained from scratch with extra columns scored worse than plain M0's stored weights, which is the larger effect to understand first. The next step is a second seed and a plain M0 re-pre-trained under the same recipe, so that the control and the arms differ only in the columns. also relevant 00568 attention-mixer-modular-network-with-lead-and-spread-token The modular network M0 of experiment 545 concatenates its encoders' outputs and feeds them to a multi-layer-perceptron (MLP) mixer. A self-attention mixer that reads each encoder's output as a separate token, plus a token built from the lead time and the ensemble spread of several weather variables, extracts more from the same encoders, and does so without raising the injected-shift or real-event leak. not supported not-for-production A self-attention mixer over the encoder outputs does not forecast Primary demand better than the simpler MLP mixer, and at the eight MVA Primaries it is worse. The attention mixer's small gain at the six MW Primaries also appears when the ensemble spread is shuffled between days, so it does not come from the spread. A next experiment could look for what the relative-spread block lets the networks do with the recent shift, not for a better mixer. primary 00567 neighbour-lag-encoders-synthetic-load-shifts-in-pretraining-and-fine-tuning A load transfer lowers the donor Primary's lags and raises a neighbour's lags by the same amount, while a genuine level change shows at one Primary only. A network that reads its neighbours' lags as well as its own can check whether the sum is conserved, so it can discount a transferred lag and still follow a genuine level change. Training it on synthetic load transfers, in both pretraining and fine-tuning, lowers its CRPS inside real labelled load-shift events whose recipient is another Primary, at no cost outside events. not supported not-for-production Adding the neighbours' lags to the lag-encoder demand neural network raised CRPS across all rows, and synthetic load-shift training did not give a shown gain at the real events that name a recipient. The neural network does not use the neighbours' lag values, so the next attempt needs a way to force their use, or a different signal. also relevant 00566 combination-block-lag-encoder-with-three-step-schedule-and-embargo-real-event-leak The lag encoder of experiment 560 (variant 3, capped 24-hour lags, block dropout) lowers 24-120 h CRPS at the eight but leaks an injected load shift more than L-1d does. Training the mixer once on the whole history (the three-step schedule, experiment 559's A1), leaving the newest 3 days out of each fine-tune (the embargo, experiment 556), or both, lowers the leak measured on real labelled events and keeps most of the lag encoder's accuracy gain. partly supported not-for-production A larger refit leak for the lag encoder than for the lag-free network is not shown on real labelled load-shift events, and the three-step schedule and the 3-day embargo cut the leak by a third to a half with no accuracy cost shown. That is the part of the leak that comes from refitting. The larger part, 0.12 to 0.13 of an event's depth, comes from the network reading corrupted lags at forecast time, and neither protection touches it. also relevant 00565 drift-embedding-variants-six-designs Substations change slowly over years, and the Primary embedding is static, so the modular lag-free demand network follows slow change only through its daily fine-tune. A designed slow signal can carry that change. Stage 1 asks the cheapest version: an exponentially weighted mean of the network's own past residuals, older than 24 hours, added to the forecast quantiles. partly supported candidate A slow, per-Primary offset added to the demand forecast improves it at the eight MVA Primaries, and in the injected-shift fits we ran it leaked no more of a recent load shift than the plain network. The other four ways of carrying slow change showed no gain, so the next step is the offset alone, on more random seeds and at the six MW Primaries, where the direction holds but the interval still includes zero. primary 00564 pooled-primary-bsp-gsp-m2-reduced Adding the 2 bulk supply points (BSPs) and 2 grid supply points (GSPs) to the training rows of the modular lag-free network M0 (experiment 545, replicated in 554), with a one-hot input saying whether a series is a Primary, a BSP, or a GSP, lowers the Primaries' CRPS at leads of 24 to 120 h, because the weather and calendar encoders see more examples of how weather and calendar drive load. not supported not-for-production Adding two bulk and two grid supply points to the training rows of the demand network did not make its forecasts at the 16 Primaries better: the change is smaller than the experiment could resolve, and its sign differs between the two groups of Primaries. The same network forecasts the four extra series better than a climatology, so pooling is a way to cover them with one network, not a way to improve the Primaries. A test of whether pooling helps needs many more extra series than NGED's data holds. also relevant 00562 modular-lag-free-network-null-input-retry-with-placebos The modular lag-free network of experiment 545 (arm M0) has a weather encoder and a datetime encoder, so it may extract signal from four groups of inputs that earlier networks found null or harmful: thermal-lag and solar-gain windows (B1), look-ahead weather windows (B2), school-term and national-signal columns (B3, one arm for each), and a whole-day price shape that is present only while training (B4). Each real arm is compared with a shuffled-day placebo of the same number of columns, so a gain counts only if it exceeds what extra columns give regardless of content. not supported not-for-production Giving the modular lag-free demand network extra inputs that earlier networks found useless did not help over a whole year: no group beat a shuffled-day control of the same width by the threshold. The exception is the thermal-lag and solar-gain group (B1), which lowered the error on cold winter nights at the six signed-MW substations by about 0.2 points of capacity (3 months only, an effect the data can barely resolve). On all rows at the eight it made no difference against plain M0. The next step is a larger cold-night test of that group on the best lagged network. also relevant 00560 modular-lag-encoder-capped-lags-and-block-dropout A lag encoder trained in ERA5/CAMS pretraining, next to the weather and datetime encoders of experiment 545's M0, lets the modular network use power lags that are at least 24 hours old. Feeding the encoder what the weather and datetime encoders say about each lag's own time ("expected") lets it read the lag as a deviation from normal, which a lag alone does not give. partly supported not-for-production Adding a lag encoder to the modular demand network let it use power readings at least 24 hours old, and it then forecast the 1 to 5 day horizon at the eight MVA-only Primaries better than the network with no lags (0.07 to 0.15 points of capacity), and better than the 24-hour-capped reference networks of experiment 558. The best version also reads the weather and calendar at the time of each lag, and its gain over lags alone is not shown at the eight and absent at the six. Every version that reads lagged power leaks an injected load shift more than L-1d does (6.1 to 8.1 against 4.49 points of capacity), so whether to adopt a lag version depends on cutting that leak. also relevant 00559 m0-leak-ladder-three-step-schedule-frozen-encoders-and-penalty M0's injected-shift leak (7.3 to 7.7 points of capacity, against 4.49 for the single network L-1d) comes from the fresh mixer that is trained only on the recent days at every daily refit. Training that mixer once on the whole ensemble history (step 2) and then fine-tuning gently (step 3) lowers the leak while keeping most of M0's gain at 24 to 120 h. partly supported not-for-production The changes that make the lag-free network react less to a recent shift in demand also make its forecasts worse at the eight MVA-only Primaries, so none of them is ready for production. The simplest, a one-off training of the mixer on the whole history followed by daily fine-tuning, loses about a fifth as much gain as the strongest penalty. Adding trailing temperature or a per-Primary drift term did not lower the leak, and wind lowered it no more than its placebo did. primary 00556 lag-free-finetune-absorption-of-load-shift-events-and-unlearn-time When a load-shift event lies in the rows the lag-free demand neural network is fine-tuned on, the network absorbs part of the event into its median forecast, and the absorbed share grows with the event length. A rule inside the scheduled fine-tune (an embargo on the newest 3 days of targets, or weights clipped by a label-free residual rule) cuts the absorbed share without slowing adaptation to a genuine lasting level change or worsening the score. partly supported not-for-production A short load-shift event in the data the lag-free neural network is refitted on moves the next week's forecast by a small share of the event (about one in ten for a 3-day step of 10% of capacity at all Primaries together, and 1.5% of the depth on average for real labelled events, though one of 74 absorbed 27.6%), and the effect fades over about 2 weeks. Leaving the newest 3 days out of each refit removes the effect for short events but costs 0.057 points of CRPS and delays adaptation to a genuine change by about 3 days, so the maintainer decides whether the protection is worth the cost. Down-weighting rows that look like outliers cut the leak by only 14%. primary 00554 m0-replication-five-seeds-leak-mitigations-and-leave-d8-out The modular network M0 (a weather encoder, a datetime encoder, and a fresh mixer at fine-tuning) keeps most of its gain over the single network L-1d when both are averaged over 5 seeds instead of 2, and the gain does not depend on D8 alone. One of M0's two changes (the separate encoders, or the fresh mixer) raises its injected-shift leak, and a longer recency half-life or a 3-day refit cadence brings the leak down to the production limit. partly supported not-for-production The modular demand network that reads weather and calendar through separate encoders still beats the single network at 1 to 5 days ahead at the eight MVA-only Primaries when both are averaged over 5 seeds (0.18 points of capacity), and most of that remains with the slower learning rate. About half of the gain comes from one Primary, D8, and the other seven gain by about 0.09 with an interval that includes zero, so the gain is real but narrower than the headline. The experiments that would find which part of the network raises the injected-shift leak were not run. primary 00545 modular-lag-free-demand-network-weather-and-datetime-encoders A lag-free demand network built from a weather encoder, a datetime encoder, and a mixer, where the mixer is replaced at fine-tuning by one that also reads ensemble spread and lead time, forecasts as well as the single multilayer network L-1d does (M0 is the modular network). Adding an auxiliary forecast head after each encoder (M1) forces each encoder to carry information about the power distribution on its own, and so improves the forecast at 24 to 120 hours. partly supported not-for-production Giving the lag-free demand network separate weather and datetime encoders improved the 1 to 5 day forecast at the eight MVA-only Primaries by about 0.14 to 0.21 points of capacity, and most of the gain remained when the new mixer learned no faster than the old network. The network also has a higher point estimate of the leak of an injected load shift (7.6 against 4.49 points of capacity, with overlapping fold ranges), and more than half of the gain at the eight comes from one Primary, so the next step is to find out which of the two changes makes the network follow recent data harder and whether the gain holds without D8. The auxiliary heads did not help. primary 00543 lag-free-network-auxiliary-recent-level-and-reverse-flow-heads The lag-free network trails the lagged network (A-pool) because it never sees recent power. A second output that predicts the recent power level (the newest observed value and the day-ago and week-ago values, used as training targets only and never as inputs) makes the shared hidden layers carry level information, so the lag-free network closes part of the gap without any lag input at forecast time. refuted not-for-production Training the lag-free network to also predict the recent power level did not give it the benefit of lag inputs: its forecast got slightly worse (0.05 points of CRPS at the eight), and the gap to the lagged network stayed at 0.27 points. The recent level has to enter as an input, so the next step is to choose which lagged inputs to feed (the day-ago and week-ago lags closed 76% to 80% of the gap in experiment 539), not to try to learn them as a side task. also relevant 00524 two-stage-lagless-forecaster-stage-1-and-ensemble-calibrator A lag-free demand network can be split in two.
