The cause of the spread is not located. also relevant 00278 stack-retraining-cadence The best-guess stack (arm D, the neural network head, and the two-number solar summary) needs its neural network head retrained at least quarterly, but its convex model (a generalised additive model with a Kalman filter on its coefficients) tolerates quarterly instead of monthly refits, because the filter absorbs the drift between refits. not supported not-for-production Retraining the small neural network that corrects the demand forecast's median, every quarter or every month, scored no better than training it once before the scored year, so it needs no retraining schedule over a year. The convex demand model should keep its monthly refits, which take 0.4 s per substation: refitting quarterly instead scored 0.010 points worse overall (not shown to be acceptable) and weekly refits gained nothing. Refitting the two solar factors quarterly instead of monthly changed nothing. also relevant 00275 metered-farm-long-history-neural-head Experiment 243 fitted H5 (the solar-farm power model plus a neural network that outputs all 11 quantile offsets) on about 17 months of ensemble forecasts. Adding each farm's rows built from past weather (Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service irradiance and ERA5 temperature, back to 2019-09) as extra training rows, with a flag that marks them, lowers H5's quantile score on the ensemble-driven scored year, and the neural head gains more from the extra rows than XGBoost does. not supported not-for-production Training the neural network that corrects a metered solar farm's power forecast on nearly six years of past-weather rows, as well as on 17 months of ensemble forecasts, lowers the quantile score by only 0.5%, far under the 2% we predicted. The same rows improve XGBoost by 1.7%, so the neural network is not the better way to use extra history. The extra rows do lower the loss at the 99% quantile (the upper edge of the forecast band, which matters for curtailment) by 4.6%. also relevant 00274 lsc-long-arrangement-audit-gam-refit A forecast with no lagged power learns a long-lasting change of running arrangement as the normal pattern, because the monthly refit trains on whatever the meter recorded. The learned share grows with the duration of the arrangement, and the duration beyond which the forecast of the normal running arrangement (NRA) is wrong by more than a stated tolerance sets the limit that can be told to NGED. not supported not-for-production A forecast that uses no recent power still learns a load transfer as normal, and the forecast learns the transfer quickly: a transfer lasting only 7 days leaves the forecast 1.2 points of effective capacity too high for the next 2 days, and a transfer lasting 30 days leaves it 2.5 points too high (about a fifth of the transfer). No tested duration, down to 7 days, was short enough to avoid this. Masking known transfers out of training is the obvious remedy, but this experiment did not test it, and the next experiment should test it together with transfers of 1 to 6 days. also relevant 00167 dp-full-history-gam-24-months-or-all-years-with-drift With the PV capacity pinned to the as-of table (explicit PV) and the heating split by day type (T-all), the convex demand model (the GAM) trained on every year of history back to late 2019 with a drift term scores better than the same model trained on the last 24 months, when both are refitted at 12 quarterly origins on past weather (ERA5 and CAMS). The mechanism is that explicit PV removes the changing solar capacity from the target, so the old years teach the heating and calendar terms without the capacity growth that made the all-years fits of experiments 104 and 107 unstable, and the drift term absorbs the remaining slow change in the demand level. supported candidate Adding a drift term (a slow adjustment to the demand level) improved the forecast at 11 of 12 quarterly refits. The quantile score, where lower is better, fell by 0.40 points when training on the last 24 months and by 0.55 points when training on all years back to late 2019. Training on all years instead of 24 months adds only 0.10 points on top of a drift term, and gives no gain without one, so extra years of history help little. also relevant 00149 differentiable-physics-full-history-gam-era5-cams When the convex model's solar term is explicit (a pinned capacity times a unit solar shape in both arms), training on every year of a substation's history back to 2019 gives a lower quantile score than training on the last 24 months, once a drift term lets the model follow the slow level change. The mechanism is that more years pin down the temperature, calendar, and weekday terms better, and the drift term absorbs the level change that made all-years training unstable in experiments 104, 106, and 107. inconclusive not-for-production Training the demand model on every year back to 2019, instead of the last 24 months, lowered its forecast error by only about 3% (0.08 points of substation capacity), and the difference could be chance. The drift term helped much more, lowering the error by 0.38 points on 24 months and 0.50 points on all history, but a post hoc audit found that a plain correction by the mean error of the last 28 training days recovers 86% to 94% of that gain, so the gain is a recent-level correction and the drift form is not shown to beat the simpler fix. We did not test whether explicit heating, switching, or pooled terms would make the longer history help. also relevant 00107 differentiable-physics-rolling-origin-history-and-tails Refitted quarterly from 2023-07 to 2026-04 and scored on the next 3 months, the convex model's two history contrasts (all years against 12 months, drift against none) keep one sign at almost every origin. A second claim, labelled separately as C5 and not part of the verdict: a level-dependent spread brings its 95% and 99% quantiles within 1 point of nominal coverage without worsening the quantile score. partly supported not-for-production Giving the convex demand model a drift term lowered its score at 10 of 12 quarterly refits, by 0.45 points when trained on all years (interval 0.23 to 0.68). In a post hoc split, about three-fifths of that size is one substation (D10) at the 2023-24 refits, and the 2025-26 refits give 0.30, as in experiment 104. All years without drift scored worse than 12 months at 8 of 12 refits, and all years with drift against 12 months has no stable answer: winter-quarter refits favour more years, summer ones are level. The spread that depends on the forecast level made the 95% and 99% quantiles worse, so the tail coverage still needs a different method. The verdict is partly supported, because only the drift contrast is stable; a second spread (the conformal spread) is not interpreted, because it was built with a flaw. also relevant 00106 differentiable-physics-4-all-years-drift-and-recent-level The differentiable-physics model trained on every usable year from 2019-09 with a drift term forecasts Primary demand better than the same model on its best window, and assimilating recent residuals through a Kalman filter makes it better again, by more than a simple moving-average correction does. partly supported not-for-production Correcting each day-ahead demand forecast with the errors the model made up to 3.5 hours earlier lowered the quantile score by 0.61 points (from 2.90 to 2.29) in the scored year and by 1.02 points in the year before, at all five long-history substations. The gain relies on estimates of past weather that a live service would not have, and against lagged XGBoost at the same lead the filtered model scored 2.349 against 2.487, a difference that is not significant. Whether old years of history help is not settled, because the contrast changed sign between the two years, so the verdict is partly supported. also relevant 00104 differentiable-physics-2-simple-structural-model A convex demand-minus-solar model, trained on every usable year with a slowly drifting level per hour band, forecasts Primary demand better than the same model trained on the last 12 months. inconclusive not-for-production A simple model of demand minus solar, trained on 12 months, scored 0.25 points better than lagless XGBoost with its default start (post hoc; a lower score is better). Most of that lead is in the forecast spread, because the error of the mean forecast differs by only 0.08 points, and four of the five pre-registered positive controls failed, so the verdict is inconclusive. More years of history did not clearly help: the scored year and the tuning year gave opposite signs for two history-window contrasts, and a first version of this page had the wrong sign for both because its spread carried the previous year's mean bias. also relevant 00095 age2-old-year-penalty-with-the-same-weather-product-demand The extra forecast error of an old training year (experiment 93) comes mostly from the change of weather product between the old years (18 km grid spacing) and the recent year (9 km), not from the age of the training data, so an old year and a recent year that use the same weather product score about the same. refuted not-for-production The old-year penalty does not shrink when both years use ERA5: the 2021-07 year is 1.71 points worse than the 2024-07 year on ERA5 (99% interval 1.15 to 2.29) and 1.57 worse on the control member (1.12 to 2.03), so the weather product is not the main explanation and the penalty goes with how old the training year is. primary 00093 age1-old-training-year-after-level-normalisation-demand A year of training data hurts a Primary substation demand forecast with its age only because the substation's average demand level differed in that year, so subtracting a trailing 365-day level from the targets and the power lags removes most of the penalty for an old training year. refuted not-for-production Subtracting a trailing 365-day level removes 42% of the old year's penalty (C1 1.57, C2 0.91 points), under the half the prediction required, and without the one series that carries most of the penalty it removes none (0.61 to 0.68). primary 00092 lv0-drift-diagnostics-on-stored-predictions-demand Most of the drift in Primary substation demand since 2022 is a per-series level or smooth trend, not a change of daily shape, so a slow per-series level term, not a new weather response, is what a long-history or pooled XGBoost model is missing. inconclusive not-for-production Drift is large and differs by series, but a level shift alone does not explain the loss from extra history or the pooling gap. primary 00085 cheaper-retraining-schedules-rank-arms-like-weekly-demand For the 16 Primary substation demand series, a cheaper retraining schedule ranks two pairs of arms the way full weekly retraining ranks them: the cadence pair (monthly minus weekly retraining) and the starting-value pair (a zero starting value minus XGBoost's estimated starting value, the contrast of experiment 80). The cheaper schedules are (a) a monthly refit on a rolling 12-month window with 150 rounds and eta 0.15 (P-roll), (b) the same refit every quarter, (c) a monthly refit at the full setting (whole history, 500 rounds, eta 0.05), and (d) a weekly refit on the whole history with 150 rounds and eta 0.15. A schedule that passes can replace weekly retraining in research experiments. partly supported not-for-production Monthly minus weekly retraining is +0.125 (95% interval +0.036 to +0.229) at the full setting, +0.118 (+0.033 to +0.216) with a 12-month window, and +0.125 (+0.038 to +0.227) with 150 rounds. primary 00081 r11-control-member-second-validation-year-demand The Primary substation demand findings of experiments 48 and 49 keep their sign on forecast runs the project has not scored: the daily 00:00 UTC ECMWF ensemble (ENS) control-member runs of 2023-07-01 to 2024-03-31 (July to March, with no April to June). For the 13 Primary substations that have power data throughout, weekly refitting of the XGBoost demand model N1 without error correction scores below the stack (frozen N1 with the 14-day correction and the spread factor 1.15), and weekly refitting scores below monthly refitting. supported candidate C1, weekly minus the stack: -0.240 points (99.17% interval -0.360 to -0.145). primary 00080 bm0-zero-base-margin-xgboost-quantile-models XGBoost starts a quantile model from a base score that it estimates from the training labels, one value for each of the nine quantile levels (experiment 78 found 0.403 at the 5% level to 0.899 at the 95% level for one series, with 500 boosting rounds and no early stopping). Replacing that start with zero (a base margin of zero in every row, which is the same as a base score of zero) lowers the quantile score of the production-style models for Primary substation demand (retrained weekly), bulk supply point and grid supply point demand (retrained weekly), solar farms, and wind farms. The gap is not a symptom of too few boosting rounds, so four times as many rounds, or early stopping, does not remove it. inconclusive not-for-production Starting XGBoost from zero did not lower the quantile score of any production-style XGBoost model: Primary substations -0.017 points of capacity (98.75% interval -0.072 to +0.054), bulk and grid supply points +0.006 (-0.091 to +0.092), the frozen Primary stack -0.033 (-0.084 to +0.031), solar farms -0.010 (-0.036 to +0.028). also relevant 00049 vp1-screening-reference-under-p-roll-demand For the 16 Primary substation demand series, once the XGBoost quantile model N1 is refitted every month without the 14-day error correction, (a) a spread factor chosen on earlier months only lowers the quantile score below the fixed factor 1.15, (b) an average of the quantiles of retrained and stored XGBoost models, with one weight vector chosen per month on earlier months, still lowers it below the best single member, and (c) each adopted input (the Christmas column, the COVID indicator, a half-life of 0.5 years) changes the score when dropped, and the substation fingerprints of experiment 32 change it when added to a pooled XGBoost model, all under the cheap rolling-window refit P-roll. supported candidate B1, the blend minus its best member: -0.076 points (99.17% interval -0.135 to -0.023). primary 00048 weekly-retraining-confirmation-and-extension-demand-generators On the 292 daily ENS forecast runs of the validation year that experiment 34's 73 runs leave out, weekly retraining of the Primary substation demand model N1, with no error correction, lowers the quantile score below the best-guess stack (frozen N1 with the 14-day correction and spread factor 1.15) by more than zero points of capacity; monthly retraining of the ERA5-trained solar and wind stage 1a models changes the score by less than 0.05 points; and, once the model retrains weekly, neither a 7-day nor a 14-day error correction helps. supported candidate C1, weekly retraining minus the stack: -0.20 points (99.44% interval -0.40 to -0.035). primary 00035 lead-weighted-quantile-blend-of-stored-models For Primary substation demand, solar farms, and wind farms, averaging the quantiles of two or three forecast models that experiments 19, 20, 30, and 33 already scored (N1 is the ENS-trained single-stage XGBoost model, and the stack is N1 with the 14-day correction and a spread factor of 1.15), with one weight per lead band chosen only on earlier months, lowers the quantile score below the best single member by more than the threshold set for each technology (0.05 points of capacity for Primary demand and solar, 0.10 for wind). supported candidate Averaging the quantiles of three stored demand models lowered the Primary demand error by 0.10 points of capacity against the best single model (98.33% interval -0.19 to -0.03), so the estimate clears the 0.05 threshold for moving it into production. For solar and wind the gains were too small to resolve on 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms. also relevant 00034 retraining-cadence-and-cheap-proxies-demand For the 16 Primary substation demand series, retraining the single-stage ENS-trained quantile model N1 monthly (half-life 0.5 years, no 14-day error correction) lowers the quantile score below the best-guess stack (frozen N1 with the 14-day correction and spread factor 1.15) by more than 0.10 points of capacity; the gain from retraining more often flattens between monthly and weekly retraining; and the 14-day correction stops helping once the model is retrained. A second, separately reported claim is that at least one cheap proxy for monthly retraining ranks arms the way full monthly retraining ranks them. inconclusive candidate C1, monthly retraining minus the stack: -0.20 points (99.375% interval -0.44 to +0.08, 95% interval -0.38 to -0.01). primary 00023 lagged-power-and-error-correction-solar-wind For the 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms, giving the stage 2 calibrator the farm's recent observed power (lagged power, or summaries of the latest day), or shifting the forecast by its own recent error (the 14-day correction of experiments 00017 and 00019), lowers the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) below that of the same calibrator without recent power. inconclusive not-for-production C1, lagged power added to the calibrator: solar -0.012 (99.58% interval -0.122 to +0.088), wind +0.012 (-0.090 to +0.146). also relevant 00021 error-correction-variants-bsp-gsp-demand A recent-error correction of N1's quantiles, measured with power that is 2 days old, lowers the quantile score of the 4 bulk supply point (BSP) and grid supply point (GSP) demand series as it does for the 16 Primary substations, and some variant of the correction (a 7-day or 28-day window, multiplicative, per-half-hour-of-day, or weighting recent days more) beats the plain 14-day additive correction. inconclusive not-for-production The 14-day additive correction lowered the Primary quantile score by 0.99 points of capacity (99.375% interval -1.82 to -0.18) when the newest power was 2 days old, as it did with 3.5-hour-old power in experiment 19. On the 4 bulk and grid supply point series it raised the score by 0.36 (-0.19 to +0.98), so it is unproven there. No variant beat the plain additive 14-day form: a 7-day window was worse (+0.19) and a multiplicative form far worse (+2.28). also relevant 00019 primary-demand-stack-vs-manual-heuristic For the 16 Primary substation demand series, stacking three changes on the single-stage ENS-trained quantile model N1 (a 14-day correction from the model's own recent errors, a recency half-life of 0.5 years, and a spread factor of 1.15) beats manual_heuristic on ENS weather, which N1 alone does not. supported candidate C1, the full stack minus manual_heuristic, quantile score over all leads: -0.56 points of capacity (99.44% interval -0.93 to -0.26). also relevant 00017 training-window-and-retraining-rule-drift-demand For the stage 1a XGBoost demand model trained on ERA5 weather, Primary substation demand drifts (experiment 13 saw every arm under-forecast its validation year by 1.3 to 3.1 points of capacity), so a model trained on a recent window, weighted towards recent rows, retrained monthly, or corrected by the error of the last 14 days, has a lower error than the same model trained on the whole history and never retrained. supported candidate C9, the 14-day correction against A: -1.52 points (99.44% interval -1.95 to -1.13). primary

docs.text: Experiment Hypothesis Relevance

docs.title: P16: a longer ENS history
docs.text: The ENS backfill from Source Cooperative (2021-03 to 2024-03) could give an earlier validation fold, and the full fetch cannot run autonomously. Issue #959 (Extend ECMWF ENS training history) describes the fetch. The archive is in us-west-2. Fetching the control member alone is about 530 GB and 4 to 5 hours, and fetching all 51 members is about 30 TB, which needs a cloud machine in that region and the maintainer's approval of the cost. The issue also ties autonomous use of the fetch to the scorer-protection work in issue 958. Every experiment since 00003 scores the same year on the same 16 series, so choices tuned there overfit it, and an earlier fold is the remedy. For demand, a longer training history has hurt so far, so the backfill is valuable first as validation data.

docs.title: Retraining and training history: state and next steps
docs.text:
For the Primary demand forecast, refitting more often than monthly gains a small, real amount, and the numbers say daily for the lag-free neural network and weekly for the XGBoost model. Neither gain is large. Daily refitting of the lag-free neural network scored 0.065 points of CRPS better than weekly refitting, about 1.3%. Weekly refitting of the XGBoost model scored 0.20 to 0.24 points of capacity below the stack on two sets of runs, but three substations carry much of that gain. Final models describes what the first release does, which is a monthly refit followed by a fine-tune. The daily and weekly advice on this page is a different cadence.

Terms. Refit, stack, N1, the 14-day correction, D codes, quantile score, CRPS (continuous ranked probability score), and points of capacity are defined in the glossary. The eight MVA Primaries are the eight Primary substations measured in MVA only, and the six MW Primaries are the six Primary substations measured in signed MW. K1 and K2-S1 are lagged demand neural networks, which take recent power as inputs. A negative contrast is an improvement.

docs.title: What works
docs.text:
Refit the lag-free demand neural network every day rather than every week. The daily refit scored 4.854 CRPS points at the eight and 3.493 at the six, against 4.920 and 3.555 for the weekly refit. The gains were 0.065 and 0.061 points, with Bonferroni intervals that exclude zero, and twice-weekly refitting gained 0.036 and 0.041 (experiment 511). The neural network gets about 0.02 points worse for each day since its refit, so most of the gain is freshness. A daily fine-tune takes about 3 seconds. Weekly refitting had already beaten monthly refitting by 0.17 to 0.19 points (experiment 510).

Refitting the XGBoost model for Primaries weekly, and dropping the 14-day correction from it, scored better than the stack. Weekly refitting scored 0.20 below the stack in experiment 48 (99.44% interval -0.40 to -0.035, 292 daily runs at 16 Primaries) and 0.240 below it in experiment 81 (99.17% interval -0.360 to -0.145, 274 control-member runs at 13 Primaries). Monthly refitting already scored 0.20 below the stack in experiment 34, and the case for weekly over monthly is only 0.04 to 0.13 points. Experiment 48 (292 runs) covers N1 frozen at its fit date, and experiment 81 covers its own 274 runs, so both results stand.

Pretraining the neural network on ERA5 and CAMS weather, then fine-tuning on ensemble weather, lowered the error. ERA5 is the ECMWF reanalysis, CAMS is the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service, and ENS is the ECMWF ensemble forecast. The gain was about 0.06 points (2.1%) at the six MW Primaries and 0.16 points (4.2%) at the eight MVA Primaries (experiment 418). Pretraining once and fine-tuning each month scored within 0.03 points of pretraining at every refit and halves the graphics processing unit (GPU) time (experiment 494).

The 14-day correction helps an XGBoost model fitted once. It lowered a frozen model's score by 1.45 points in experiment 48 and supplied most of the stack's gain over N1 (experiment 19).

docs.title: What does not work
docs.text:
The 14-day correction stops helping a refitted XGBoost model. It raised a weekly model's score by 0.23 (99.375% interval +0.03 to +0.44) in experiment 34. In experiment 48 the 7-day correction raised it by 0.16 and the 14-day correction by 0.08, both with intervals that include zero.

Shorter recency windows, mixed pretraining, and ENS rows in pretraining did not help the neural network. Half-lives of 30 and 60 days did not reach the -0.05 bar against 90 days and raised the leak of an injected load shift from 6.1 to 9.5 points of capacity, and pretraining on ERA5, CAMS, and ENS rows together scored 0.062 (eight MVA Primaries) and 0.045 (six MW Primaries) behind (experiment 511). Any ENS share in pretraining made the eight MVA Primaries 0.06 to 0.22 points worse, steeply from 50%: 10% scored +0.076, 25% +0.059, 50% +0.105, 75% +0.183, and ENS only +0.220 (experiment 519). A daily warm start scored worse than a daily restart (experiment 511).

Replaying ERA5 and CAMS rows during fine-tuning did not fix cold winter nights. Cold-night CRPS at the eight MVA Primaries moved by -0.012, +0.026, and +0.047 points for the three replay arms, against a minimum detectable effect of 0.169 points (experiment 487). The small gain at the six MW Primaries came mostly from one month.

Smooth recency weights on the generalised additive model added nothing over a 24-month training window (experiment 331). Averaging the quantiles of several XGBoost models gained 0.04 to 0.10 points, and a four-model version fell short of its threshold in experiment 81.

docs.title: What is uncertain
docs.text:
The XGBoost weekly gain is fragile. In experiment 48 the contrast without D8, D12, and D5 was -0.08 (99.44% interval -0.24 to +0.10). In experiment 81, D8 alone gained 2.05 points against the stack. In experiment 355, weekly refitting lowered D8's score by only 0.045 against monthly refitting (99% interval -0.118 to +0.001), so the 2.05 compares weekly refitting with the stack, and the 0.045 compares weekly with monthly refitting.

The monthly-refit gain was not distinguishable from zero in its pre-registered test. Experiment 34's pre-registered interval for monthly refitting included zero (-0.44 to +0.08). Experiment 81's weekly gain in fold C (the 2022-23 winters) was -0.080 with an interval from -0.187 to +0.051.

Experiments 48 and 81 disagree on the 14-day correction's value to a frozen model. Experiment 48 found a gain of 1.45 points, and experiment 81 found +0.091 (-0.005 to +0.187) on its own runs.

Older training years score worse, and the cause is not found. One substation drives most of the gap, and the gap was 1.71 points with ERA5 weather in both years, so the weather product is not the main cause (experiment 95). Removing each substation's trailing 365-day level removed 42% of the gap with all 13 series, and none of it without the largest substation (experiment 93).

A network fitted long before the forecast month loses accuracy, and the size of the loss is uncertain. A network fitted 4 weeks earlier scored about 3% worse, about 10% at 16 weeks, and about 6% at 26 weeks, with wide intervals, and D15 and D18 (two of the D codes) lost several times more (experiment 640). The two Christmas weeks confirm the weekly gain at the six MW Primaries but not at the eight MVA Primaries (experiment 512).

The lag-free neural network stays behind the lagged neural network. After a daily refit it was still 0.091 (eight MVA Primaries) and 0.071 (six MW Primaries) behind K2-S1 (experiment 511).

docs.title: Options for what to do next
docs.text:
1. An option is to port the daily fine-tune of the lag-free neural network, taken from experiment 511's next step. The question is whether the fine-tune, at about 3 seconds a day, fits the serving path. Final models refits monthly with a fine-tune and applies experiment 599's rule, which drops the newest 7 days of rows and halves the weight of the next 7 days. A daily cadence would have to keep that rule. The option needs engineering time and no new experiment.
  2. An option is to test refitting every 4 to 8 weeks for K1, taken from experiment 640's next step. Experiment 640 judged this worth running, and found weekly refitting not shown to be worth more for K1. The option needs a set of refits, and the D15 and D18 histories need separate treatment.
  3. An option is to test an ENS-share variant aimed at the tails, taken from experiment 519's next step. Experiment 519 found the 99th-percentile loss fell by up to 0.03 points, but only with the source flag set at fine-tuning. The option needs a few GPU fits, and the seed noise of 0.06 to 0.08 points limits what it can show.
  4. An option is to test a longer ENS history. The question is whether the backfill (2021-03 to 2024-03) gives an extra validation fold or improves the single-stage or stage 2 models. It is option P16 in the Research plan, and it needs a cloud machine in us-west-2, which the maintainer must approve (issue #959 (Extend ECMWF ENS training history)).
  5. An option is to find the cause of the old-year penalty, taken from experiment 95's next step. The question is whether solar growth, heating, or changes in the electricity network drive it. Experiment 95 suggests them without testing any. The option needs a diagnostic experiment.

docs.title: What is parked
docs.text: The research plan's other planned work is on hold. Option 4 above waits for an approved cloud fetch. Load-shift event detection, and absorbing load-shifts in a refit, are paused until January (see Load-shift event detection: state at the January pause).

docs.title: Solar disaggregation
docs.text:
At the 5 Primary substations with a clean solar-capacity estimate, giving the XGBoost demand forecast a forecast of the output of the solar panels behind the substation lowered its daylight April-to-September error by 0.15 points of capacity in one validation year; against a reference that also starts from zero the gain is 0.08 (post hoc, 95% interval -0.11 to -0.05).

A Primary substation's meter reads demand minus the output of the solar panels connected below it, and NGED does not meter those panels. A least-squares fit of calendar-and-temperature demand minus a solar capacity times a satellite-based sunshine shape recovers most of the solar capacity of solar-farm output that we added to real series. The forecast gain depends on the sunshine forecast: a term built from the true sunshine lowers the error by about a fifth, and a term built from the ECMWF ensemble forecast gains little beyond 2 days ahead.

Arm am (the forecast solar output, given to XGBoost as a base margin) scores 4.467 against 4.620 for d0, the best guess of experiment 33, and every arm scores better than its own placebo twin (the same arm given the sunshine of another date). Source: experiment 64. Scores are quantile scores in points of capacity; lower is better. The rows are daylight half-hours of April to September at the 5 Primaries (D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16), from July to September 2025 and April to June 2026.

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
A simple fit finds most of the solar capacity that we inject, and the capacity is close to unbiased on pure solar output. On the 8 Primaries metered in both directions, the daily fit recovers 0.854 (95% interval 0.815 to 0.866) of the capacity of real solar-farm output added to the demand, and the half-hourly fit 0.773 (0.740 to 0.818). Six of the 8 pass four checks on their real series: placebo sky, season, cloud term, and day type (experiment 39). A misfit test gives a median capacity of 0.992 of the truth on pure solar output (0.951 to 1.032), but detects a load that follows the day's mean cloud in only 0.35 of trials (experiment 40).

An explicit solar term lowers the error of the XGBoost forecast, and the sunshine forecast limits the gain. Built from the true sunshine, the term lowers the score of d1l (d0 without its radiation inputs) by 0.966 (97.5% interval -1.431 to -0.595). Built from ENS sunshine with a coefficient fixed at 1, it lowers it by 0.056 (-0.191 to +0.064), short of the 0.35-point gain the plan required (experiment 46, refuted). With a weight fitted per series, forecast-horizon band, and season, and the term given as a base margin, the score of d0 falls by 0.152 (98.75% interval -0.199 to -0.111), and by 0.272 (-0.420 to -0.145) under 48 hours. With monthly refits the explicit term gains 0.149 (99.17% interval -0.201 to -0.104) and three same-time sunshine analogues gain 0.095 (-0.185 to -0.007); the two are not separated, and the verdict is inconclusive (experiment 74).

Beyond 10 days all of the gain, and over all leads about half of it, is XGBoost starting from zero. Beyond 10 days the fitted weight is zero, yet a refit with a base margin of zero and no solar term scores 0.102 below d1l and am 0.098 below d1l (both uncorrected, 95% intervals; experiment 76). Over all leads am is 0.152 below d0 and 0.082 below a d0 that starts from zero (-0.113 to -0.052; post hoc, 95%; experiment 78). Whether a zero start matters in production-style forecasts is not settled: see the gotcha below.

The starting-point read in this figure is for am_sy (am with a capacity re-estimated each season-year), which is 0.100 below d0 started from zero, not the 0.082 of am. Source: experiment 78.

Neither the panel shape nor a fresher capacity is where the next gain lies. A fitted blend of east-, south-, and west-facing shapes changed the score of am by -0.001 (98.33% interval -0.018 to +0.014) (experiment 77, refuted). A capacity re-estimated before every forecast run lowered it by 0.018 (98.75% interval -0.036 to -0.004), under the 0.05 threshold (experiment 78, small gain).

A weekly capacity series, the panel mix, and a loss monitor were not shown to work. A weekly capacity fit that penalises falls more than rises recovered none of a 30% fall and gave 0.66 false steps per Primary-year, against a limit of 0.5 (experiment 45, refuted). The east-south-west shares were not identified: the median share error with noise was 0.200 against a limit of 0.15, although the blend predicted held-out blocks 1.3% better than all-south panels (98.75% interval -2.4% to -0.5%; experiment 73, partly supported). A change-point monitor of a solar farm's daily output found 0.84 of 25% losses lasting 90 days and 0.45 of those lasting 30 days (experiment 72, refuted).

At the 8 Primaries metered only in MVA, the real readings showed almost no reverse flow, so the fit could not be tested on them. In the injection test at the 8 MW-metered Primaries, with the sign of the readings hidden, the unfolding fit's median capacity error was 0.092 against 0.290 for a naive fit, and its balanced accuracy for the direction of flow 0.78 to 0.81, below the 0.80 the rule needed. On the real MVA-only Primaries the fit found no reverse flow at 7 of 8; at the eighth the flow is negative on 75% to 87% of daylight half-hours from 2021, and signed power is needed to check it (experiment 79, partly supported).

The data could not tell us whether the gain holds in a second year, at Primaries without a clean capacity estimate, or on rows outside April to September. The weights of experiment 64 rest on one July-to-September period.

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text:
The best of the recipes tested in this theme gives XGBoost a solar offset built from a solar capacity per season-year and a calibrated ENS sunshine anomaly. The steps are:

  1. Fit one solar capacity per Primary per season-year, by least squares, and refresh it once per season-year (experiment 39, experiment 45, experiment 78).
  2. Multiply the capacity by the calibrated ENS sunshine anomaly: how much sunnier or cloudier the day is than average for that month and half-hour, rescaled by a slope fitted on the training window. The weight is fitted per series, forecast-horizon band, and season, and is zero from 10 days (experiment 64).
  3. Give the product to XGBoost as a base margin, not as an input column or a shift after the fit: am beats the input-column arm by 0.093 (95% interval 0.057 to 0.129, exploratory; experiment 64).
  4. Use an all-south panel shape (experiment 77).

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text:
Experiments 64 and 78 are candidate.

  • The solar offset (experiment 64). Production would need a capacity table, a table of weights, the ENS calibration slopes at predict time, and a base margin set on each prediction matrix; the write-up says the live service cannot supply these as built.
  • Refresh the capacity table once per season-year (experiment 78). A weekly vintage differs from the season-year vintage by -0.005 (95% interval -0.013 to +0.003, exploratory).
  • A zero start is untested in production-style forecasts, so it is not yet a candidate. Experiment 78 advised testing it; experiment 80 could not tell the two starts apart.
  • The offset's gain inside the full forecast is 0.114 on the rows it can touch. In BG2 (a blend of XGBoost forecasts, with the offset at 5 of 16 Primaries) the offset lowers the score by 0.114 (0.075 to 0.164) on April-to-September daylight rows of the 5 offset Primaries, and by 0.010 (0.000 to 0.019) over all rows of the 16 Primaries, because only 8.5% of those rows can carry an offset. The gate was chosen on the same validation year (experiment 87).

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
Score a zero-start twin before crediting an input. XGBoost's estimated starting prediction (its base score) raised the score of d0 by 0.071 over all leads (zero start minus estimated start -0.071, -0.099 to -0.047), and the gain of am where its weight is zero is reproduced by a refit with a zero margin and no solar term (experiment 76, experiment 78). Experiment 80 (inconclusive) could not tell a zero start from the default at the 16 Primaries refitted weekly (-0.017, 98.75% interval -0.072 to +0.054, which does not exclude -0.07). Re-check: the zero-start twin of whichever recipe, correction, and number of boosting rounds you use (experiment 80).

Give every solar-term arm a placebo twin. The twin of am scores 0.300 worse (0.198 to 0.407), so the gain comes from the timing of the sunshine. Shift the twin cyclically and do not permute it at random: a random permutation paired runs that forecast the same valid time, so the permuted anomaly stayed correlated with the real one (experiment 64, experiment 77). Re-check: a different sunshine source. These experiments ran no shuffled-capacity control.

Report each contrast with and without the 14-day correction. The correction carried the base margin's effect from shorter leads into leads beyond 10 days: am minus am0 was -0.035 corrected (98.33% interval -0.074 to +0.003) and +0.004 uncorrected (95% interval -0.012 to +0.021) (experiment 76). Re-check: a forecast with a different correction window.

Score a solar term on daylight April-to-September rows that have both a CAMS shape and an observed power, and name the row set. Experiments 46, 64, 74, 77, and 78 share 68,903 rows per seed. Experiment 87's headline scored all rows of all 16 Primaries, so its 0.010 cannot be compared with 0.15; on the matching gated rows it found 0.114 (experiment 46, experiment 87). Re-check: a study that scores winter or night rows. CAMS is the Copernicus satellite sunshine estimate (glossary).

Check a contrast's sign in each valid month before reading the pooled interval. The ENS solar term lowered the score of d1l in April, May, and September (-0.204, -0.232, -0.262) and raised it in June, July, and August (+0.117, +0.183, +0.024) under a pooled interval of -0.191 to +0.064 (experiment 46). Re-check: a validation period longer than 6 valid months.

Use one capacity per season-year, which runs from September to August in these experiments. The differentiable-physics code runs it from July to June. The latest week of a real-time weekly estimate had 3.63 times the path error of the same week in the final fit, and no penalty pair met the limits (experiment 45). Re-check: a penalty set per Primary, which experiment 45 did not test.

Do not treat a fitted capacity as a measurement. The fit can absorb cloud-driven demand, and the misfit test misses a load that follows the day's mean cloud. Run the placebo-sky, season, cloud-term, and day-type checks on the real series, and inject more than one farm: the ratios of Solar farm E left the capacity at 0.825 of the truth (experiment 39, experiment 40). Re-check: an independent register of installed solar.

Do not publish the fitted orientation shares. They changed by a median 0.24 between consecutive season-years, and the 1.3% fit gain did not reach the forecast (-0.001; experiment 73, experiment 77). Re-check: shares fitted on a longer record, or a known answer with the real noise that they recover to within 0.15.

Do not fit a signed model to an MVA-only series. The magnitude folds reverse flow into positive power, and in the injection test at the 8 MW Primaries the naive fit's capacity error was 0.29 to 1.00 (experiment 79). Re-check: a few weeks of signed power at the Primary in question.

Read coverage as well as the score. The ENS solar term moved the share of sunny-row actuals below the 0.05 quantile from 0.151 to 0.045, though the score barely changed (experiment 46). Re-check: coverage on sunny and cloudy rows for any new solar term.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text:
• Whether the gain holds in a second validation year and beyond the 5 Primaries with a clean capacity estimate.
  • Whether a better sunshine forecast closes the gap to the true-sunshine oracle. The NOAA GEFS ensemble was refuted as a replacement for ENS. The Met Office UKV blended with ENS gave a small gain in squared error of the sunshine-anomaly forecast (not of demand), and the UKV archive used has a non-commercial licence (experiment 50, experiment 53).
  • Why the true-sunshine term loses at sunny summer middays: the coefficient of 1 is too large, and the cause is not identified (experiment 51).
  • Whether a solar term helps a joint demand fit (experiment 63, experiment 104).

The Research plan lists the proposed next experiments.

docs.title: Solar disaggregation: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00698 gas-engine-state-tracker-part-5-does-pv-harm-the-disaggregation The weather-driven variation of the solar generation behind D8's meter makes the tracker's daylight labels of the gas engine worse, beyond the harm that the lower level of the reading and the fold of the reading at zero cause. inconclusive not-for-production The test could not decide, under its own rule, whether solar panels behind D8's meter make the tracker's labels of the gas engine worse through their weather variation. The numbers it did produce point to harm. In the 10:00 to 15:00 window, injecting the output of a real solar farm lowers the tracker's F1 score by 0.14 and raises its false-flag share by 0.14 compared with a smooth solar curve of the same size (8.9 MW at D8). Most of the F1 harm comes from the lower level of the reading and its fold at zero, whereas the rise in the false-flag share comes from the farm's weather contrast. The labels' weekday and price patterns from experiment 697 may be best kept to the net era as a precaution, but this experiment computed nothing for that experiment's window of 16:00 to 19:00. also relevant 00679 pv-mva-conversion-loss-reactive-floor-at-half-level NGED say to assume power factor 1 with a small always-present reactive floor. At the injection level that matches the five MVA Primaries that never fold (0.5 times the midday reading), the conversion loss of the linear probe (signed-world recovery minus apparent-power-world recovery) is smaller under a reactive-floor world than under the power-factor 0.97 world that experiments 656, 662, and 671 used. supported not-for-production If the substation meters follow NGED's statement (power factor 1 plus a small constant reactive floor), the linear probe loses almost nothing (about 0.5 points of recovery) when the farm is half the midday reading, so the 10-point loss seen with a power factor of 0.97 was probably an overestimate for those five MVA Primaries. Their calibration can use the signed-world factor alone, though the 80% interval (-1 to 8 points) does not rule out a loss of up to about 8 points, which would fall in the 5-to-12-point band. primary 00674 mva-sign-labels-soft-and-hard-pv-prior-day-labeller A per-Primary day labeller that combines the lowest reading at the edges of the sun's path (experiment 508) with the W-shape score of experiment 417 finds the days on which an apparent-power Primary exported, up to an export of about three times the night import. A soft PV prior (the evidence needed to call a day reverse flow rises as the day gets less sunny) keeps the recall of a labeller with no prior and lowers its false reverse flow on cloudy days. A hard PV-high mask repeats experiment 417's trade: far fewer false calls and far lower recall. Neither prior removes the false calls on low-demand days. inconclusive not-for-production A day labeller that reads the lowest reading at the edges of the sun's path and a W-shape score finds injected solar export (64% of days at 1.5 to 3 times the night import, 31% below 3 times) but misses 54 of 59 real reverse-flow days, which are shallow and short. It is therefore not a usable sign label for the eight apparent-power substations. A hard sunny-days mask removes 68% of false calls at 1.5 to 3 times but loses 39% of recall pooled below 3 times, and the soft prior is no better than no prior. A simple midday rule (day ratio below 0.3), chosen after seeing the real days and found mostly at one substation, caught 52 of the 59, so the next labeller should start from the midday dip. P4 held only in the pooled bin and P5 failed. also relevant 00673 pv-capacity-for-nged-per-primary-with-register-cross-check The calibrated probe capacities of experiments 649 and 671 are consistent with the registered solar capacity that lies inside each Primary's service-area polygon: at every Primary that has a probe interval, the 90th percentile of the probe is at or above the register floor, once the capacity that NGED already meters is removed from the floor. supported not-for-production For National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED): a neural-network probe reads 2.4 to 3.9 MW of unmetered solar at each of the six MW Primaries and 1.25 to 6.62 MW at the five main MVA Primaries. At 8 of the 12 Primaries that have a probe interval, the interval lies above the solar capacity that three registers list inside the service area. The MVA figures assume that NGED's meters read power factor 1 with a small reactive floor, where experiment 679 finds a conversion loss of 0.5 points (80% interval -1.0 to 7.7). The upper end of that interval does not rule out a loss of 7.7 points, and every figure is a whole-summer value. primary 00671 pv-mva-fold-probe-fair-denominator-and-d3-d4-disagreement Experiment 662's bar A1 failed because its denominator was the fold model's recovery on a signed target that never folds, where the fold model collapses. With the linear probe's signed-world recovery as the denominator, the apparent-power conversion costs no recovery at Primaries where the floor does not apply. The linear and fold probes disagree at D3 and D4 on the real twins because the fold model reads extra capacity from its reactive term, not because the curve is folded. partly supported not-for-production Turning a substation's flow into apparent power does cost the linear solar probe some recovery even where the flow never nears zero, and the cost grows with the size of the solar farm. The fold model avoids most of that loss, but its extra capacity at D2, D3, D4, and D19 comes almost entirely from two free reactive-power terms. For those five Primaries the linear probe, scaled by the recovery measured on injected farms, is the better-supported reading, with the fold model's reading as an upper bound. primary 00664 pv-sum-of-distributions-spread-and-recalibration The job of the explicit solar term is as much to calibrate the spread of the net-demand forecast as to shift its centre. In experiments 644 and 655 the explicit term subtracted one number (the member-average solar curve) from every forecast quantile, so the solar uncertainty (capacity times cloud uncertainty) never reached the output. Building the net-demand distribution as the gross-demand distribution minus the solar curve of a randomly drawn ensemble member beats the free network on sunny middays, and the gain is more than a recalibration of the free network's quantile widths would give. refuted not-for-production The free network's spread is not what is wrong on sunny middays. The realised power falls below its 5% quantile in about 9% of half-hours at lead days 1 to 2, where 5% is nominal, and its upper band is too wide, which is a one-sided bias that a width recalibration cannot fix. Building the net-demand distribution from the gross-demand distribution minus a randomly drawn ensemble member's solar curve is worse than the free network at all three lead bands (0.29 to 0.38 points), and recalibrating the free network or the sum did not beat the free network either. primary 00662 pv-probe-through-the-mva-fold-matched-level-redesign The donor-day probe of experiment 621, with its linear regression replaced by a fold model, reads the capacity of unmetered solar at the eight Primaries metered in megavolt-amperes. Experiment 656 could not settle whether the probe reads capacity through the fold, because its bar A1 compared two injection levels, its fold fit started too low to reach a 6-times farm, and its intervals ignored the variation between trained networks. This experiment repeats the test with those three faults removed. partly supported not-for-production We added a known solar farm to the data of six substations and turned their flow into apparent power, which never goes negative. A probe that models the fold finds 0.7 to 0.9 of the farm at every size we tried, where a simple linear probe fails once the farm can push flow through zero. The test still failed several of its own pre-registered checks, mostly because two small-demand substations (D5 and D10) behave differently, so the capacity table for the eight apparent-power substations stays provisional. primary 00661 pv-ens-time-resolution-shortwave-interpolation-audit-and-bias-adapter The explicit solar term gains about 0.75 CRPS points with CAMS and ERA5 weather (experiment 639) and loses 0.25 to 0.37 with ECMWF ensemble weather (experiments 644 and 655). One cause is the ensemble's coarse time step, which is 3 hours to lead 144 hours and 6 hours after. A second cause would be a faulty interpolation of the ensemble's shortwave flux to half-hours. A third is forecast cloud error. This experiment tests the first two directly and tests a bias adapter as a remedy for the third. refuted not-for-production The ensemble forecast's coarse time step (3 hours, then 6 hours) is not why telling the demand network each substation's solar capacity makes the forecast worse: the same capacity term still helps by about 0.8 points of capacity when real weather is averaged into 3-hour or 6-hour windows first. The most likely remaining cause is the ensemble's cloud forecast error, which was not tested here, and a small neural correction of the sunshine input did not fix it. primary 00657 event-table-with-explicit-solar-term-against-plain-arm Subtracting an explicit solar term (the capacity of unmetered solar behind a Primary from experiment 649, times a physics curve built from recorded ERA5 irradiance, times one gain pooled over the six Primaries and fitted on the tuning years) from the six megawatt Primaries' residuals lowers the rate of false events on sunny middays, and loses no more than 0.03 of the injected megawatts that the plain arm of experiment 653 finds. not supported not-for-production Subtracting an estimate of the unmetered solar output from the demand forecast's errors changed nothing, because the forecast already allows for the sunshine at these six substations. The false events that the previous experiment found are not concentrated at sunny midday either, so the next step is to look at them one by one. also relevant 00656 pv-probe-through-the-mva-fold-at-eight-primaries The donor-day probe of experiment 621, with its linear regression replaced by a fold model that knows apparent power is the length of a real-power part and a reactive-power part, reads the capacity of unmetered solar at the Primaries metered in megavolt-amperes. It reads it at the five Primaries whose midday flow never nears zero (Tier A), and through the fold where the midday flow crosses zero (Tier B). inconclusive not-for-production We tested, on six substations metered in signed megawatts, whether a probe of a trained neural network can find a solar farm that we added to the data. To mimic the eight substations metered in megavolt-amperes, we first converted the flow to apparent power, which never goes negative. A simple linear probe finds two thirds of a small farm and fails once the farm's output can exceed the substation's demand. A probe that models the fold finds 0.7 to 0.8 of farms up to twice the midday demand, and 0.88 of a six-times farm after we widened its starting capacities. A capacity table looks possible for the five MVA Primaries that never fold. The three that do fold need a second try with a second cutoff. primary 00655 pv-member-level-cell-temperature-term-and-forecast-sunniness-tracker Experiment 644's explicit solar term lost to the free network, and its physics curve used the ensemble-mean shortwave irradiance (no spread), a 35-degree tilt, and a cell temperature equal to the air temperature plus 25 K times the output per unit capacity, with no wind term. A curve computed for each of the 51 ensemble members and then averaged, with a cell temperature in place of the air temperature, beats the free network on sunny middays. Separately, the 14-day error correction of experiment 644 keeps at least half of its gain when it is applied by the ensemble forecast's sunniness instead of the observed sunniness. refuted not-for-production Giving the demand network a solar-output curve computed for each of the 51 ensemble members, with the panel temperature and not only the air temperature, still makes the sunny-midday forecast worse than the free network (the network with no solar curve) by 0.2 to 0.35 points of capacity, so this result gives no support for continuing the explicit-solar line. The 14-day error correction that looked 0.3 to 0.6 points better in experiment 644 gains almost nothing once it can only use the ensemble forecast's own sunniness, so the correction's earlier gain probably depended on knowing what actually happened. primary 00649 pv-capacity-table-season-year-from-stored-probes The stored donor-day probes of the lag-free neural networks (experiments 621 and 634), divided by the leave-one-farm-out recovery of an injected real farm and widened by the spread of recoveries across farms, give an 80% capacity interval per Primary and summer half-year that overlaps experiment 474's R4 interval at 4 or more of the 6 MW Primaries. supported not-for-production A neural-network probe, scaled by how much of an added real solar farm it finds again, estimates 2.4 to 3.9 MW of unmetered solar behind each of the six MW Primaries. Its intervals overlap the separately fitted regression table of experiment 474 at all six, with medians 6% below to 14% above. The estimates describe a whole summer and cannot show how capacity changed from one year to the next. primary 00644 pv-explicit-term-with-ens-forecast-weather The sunny-midday gain of experiment 639's explicit solar term over the free network survives when the weather inputs are ECMWF ensemble forecasts at lead 1 to 10 days instead of CAMS and ERA5, and it is more than the gain of a bias correction that uses recent errors. refuted not-for-production Telling the demand network each Primary substation's solar capacity does not help once the weather is an ensemble forecast: it scores worse than the plain network at every lead from 1 to 10 days. A simple correction from the previous 14 days' errors beat the plain network by 0.3 to 0.6 points of capacity on sunny middays and the explicit network by 0.7 to 0.8, so the explicit-capacity line stops and the tracker is the candidate to test next, with its own placebo and a version that needs only forecast sunniness. primary 00643 pv-explicit-term-against-bias-shifted-free-network-and-more-placebo-permutations The sunny-midday gain of experiment 639's explicit solar term over the free network is more than a bias in the free network. If the gain were only a bias, a free network whose sunny middays are shifted by a constant fitted on training months alone, or given a trainable sunny-midday offset with as many parameters as the explicit term's offset, would match the explicit network. partly supported not-for-production The explicit solar term beat both bias corrections that the plan fixed in advance, so the rule set in the plan says to build an ensemble-weather version. Neither correction could see the forecast's bias, which appears only after training, and a simple correction from the previous 14 days' errors, added after the results, scored better than the explicit term in the real months. The gain over the free network is therefore largely a bias, and one Primary carries most of it. Compare the explicit term with that correction, using ensemble weather forecasts, before any production work. primary 00639 pv-explicit-hindcast-probe-set-capacity-step-world A demand network that is given a solar capacity from outside, and subtracts a physics solar curve of that capacity from its target, forecasts sunny middays better than a network that learns the solar response from free irradiance inputs, after a capacity step that the probe has measured. The gain, if any, comes from tracking capacity and not from a better mean score. partly supported not-for-production Giving a demand neural network a physics solar curve, with a capacity set by the probe, forecasts sunny middays clearly better than letting the network learn solar from irradiance, when the weather inputs are recorded values and not forecasts. Much of the gain is that the free network's median forecast runs too high. Swapping capacities between Primaries lowered the step-world score by too little to detect, so this test does not show that the probed capacity tracks a capacity change. The next checks are a version with weather forecasts, and a free network whose forecast is shifted by its bias. primary 00638 pv-probe-step-placebo-climatological-and-ordinary-year-followup Experiment 634's failure to follow a capacity step (a calibrated read of 0.32 to 0.38 of a 4 MW spring-2025 step, and 1.2 to 2.1 MW read from a shuffled-shape placebo) was caused by the unusually sunny spring of 2025 (clearness 0.76 against 0.61 to 0.69 in other years), and not by a limit of the probe that holds in any year. The shuffled-shape placebo kept a month-level sky link, so a placebo whose shape is the farm's multi-year day-of-year mean, with no link to the sky of any one date, reads close to zero. partly supported not-for-production The probe can follow a rise in solar capacity when the rise starts in an ordinary spring: it found 0.82 to 0.88 of a 4 MW step, where it found 0.32 to 0.49 of the same step in the very sunny spring of 2025. A placebo with no link to the sky read about a third of the sunny-spring step, so most of the earlier failure came from the weather of that spring. The probe still reads a little more than a learner that cannot tell the date would, and we do not yet know why. primary 00636 metered-solar-monthly-slope-capacity-known-answer-test A least-squares regression of a farm's output on a fitted irradiance expectation over all daylight half-hours of a month, weighted by the clear-sky index squared, finds a known capacity step of 10% within 3 months at 4 of the 5 testable farms (Solar A, B, C, D, and F). It finds the step whether the loss is in alternating-current output or in direct-current capacity under inverter clipping, and it raises few false steps in cloudy months and under random curtailment. refuted not-for-production A monthly fit of a solar farm's output against irradiance can spot a 10% loss of capacity within 3 months at Solar C and Solar F, and a loss of 6.3% or more at Solar C, but not at Solar A, B, or D, whose own history is too noisy. A loss of direct-current capacity hidden under the inverter limit is found as often as a plain loss of output, because very few half-hours are clipped. The line stops here under its stop rule. also relevant 00635 pv-probe-metered-neighbour-pv-as-sky-input Giving a lag-free neural network the normalised output of a metered solar farm near the Primary, as a second sky input beside the CAMS (Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service) shortwave pixel, raises the share of an injected real farm that the donor-day probe reads back (median 0.68 per injected AC MW in experiment 621), because a measured local sky closes the part of the gap that comes from a satellite pixel sitting several kilometres from the farm. not supported not-for-production A measured output from a solar farm 5 to 25 km from the substation does not help the probe find an injected solar farm: it reads back 0.69 of the injected megawatts, against 0.68 with the satellite sky alone. The neural network does use the neighbour's output: its probabilistic score on the six MW Primaries improves by 2.1%. The missing third of the farm is therefore not a sky-pixel error, and a possible next test is the farm's own shape: clipping, orientation, and energy per unit of peak. primary 00634 pv-probe-capacity-step-world-and-energy-recovery (1) Measured in injected energy instead of injected AC megawatts, the donor-day probe of a lag-free neural network recovers a real injected farm at a factor closer to 1 and tighter across Primaries and farms than the 0.65 to 0.71 it reads in megawatts. It finds a 25% loss that lasts 30 days, starting from April to September, within 28 days of its onset in at least 80% of injections, at no more than 0.5 false alarms per farm-year. It finds more injected losses of 10% than two simpler monitors that are tuned to the same false-alarm rate: a rolling median of the same signal, and the hysteresis rule of the capacity studies (called HYST here) run on the same signal. refuted not-for-production A change-point monitor of a solar farm's daily output found 0.84 of 25% losses lasting 90 days and 0.45 of those lasting 30 days, below the 0.80 the plan needed, so the verdict is refuted. On 10% losses it did not beat a rolling median by an interval that excludes zero (+0.045, 97.5% interval -0.015 to +0.090). also relevant 00064 pvdis-5-net-demand-as-demand-minus-forecast-solar At the 5 Primary substations (substations that feed 11 kV circuits from the 33 kV network) with a clean solar-capacity estimate, a demand forecast that carries an explicit solar term (the substation's embedded solar capacity times a calibrated forecast of the solar output) scores no worse than experiment 00033's best-guess recipe d0 by more than 0.10 points of capacity on daylight April-to-September rows, and the solar term carries real solar information, because the same arm with the forecast sunshine taken from another date scores worse. The solar term is built in four ways: added to the forecast after the fit with a coefficient fitted on the training window (sf), given to the XGBoost model as an input column (a), given to it as a starting offset so that the trees fit only the remainder (am), or removed from the training target and added back after the fit (b, "demand minus solar"). supported candidate Giving the XGBoost model the forecast solar output as a starting offset, with a weight fitted on the training window, beat the best guess d0 by 0.152 points of capacity (98.75% interval -0.199 to -0.111; leads under 48 hours -0.272, -0.420 to -0.145), and each of the four arms beat its own placebo twin. primary 00063 sw2-10-linear-joint-fit-v2-in-miniature On the 8 Primary substations metered in MW, one linear fit per Primary that holds a weather baseline without radiation inputs, the embedded-solar capacity of experiment 00045 times the CAMS unit PV shape, and one share-of-the-donor's-net-power term per labelled transfer, (C1) lowers the error of the median forecast outside switching on held-out months, in hindsight, below that of the same baseline with radiation inputs by at least 0.35 points of capacity, (S1) recovers an injected solar capacity to within 0.15 of its size, and (S2) recovers an injected transfer share to within 0.05. inconclusive not-for-production C1 is -0.322 points of capacity (-0.437 to -0.207), close to the 0.35-point threshold, but the S1 and S2 gates failed for reasons of test design, so the verdict is inconclusive. also relevant 00051 pvdis-3b-midday-loss-of-the-solar-term At June-to-August midday on day+2 and day+3, the solar term of experiment 00046 scores worse than the best guess d0 (C6 +0.477 and +0.172 points of capacity) mainly because the fixed coefficient of 1 is too large for the sunniest rows, which a PV inverter clips, and not because the ENS members add noise. partly supported not-for-production At June-to-August midday the oracle shift's coefficient of 1 is too large in effect: the residual of the d1l median has a slope of -0.42 to -0.69 on it in every month and hour bin, and a fitted coefficient lowers the median's error by 0.991 points (-1.473 to -0.495). primary 00046 embedded-solar-share-of-primary-forecast-error At the five Primary substations metered in MW that have a clean 2023/24 capacity estimate, an explicit solar term lowers the error of the demand forecast that experiment 00033's best-guess recipe produces without its shortwave and longwave radiation inputs (arm d1l) by at least 0.35 points of capacity on daylight April-to-September rows. The solar term shifts every forecast by minus the capacity of experiment 00040 times the calibrated ENS forecast of the solar anomaly (a fitted slope on the ensemble mean, plus each member's own deviation from the mean), with the coefficient fixed at 1. The contrast is against d1l and not against the best guess. refuted not-for-production The ENS solar term lowers the quantile score of d1l by 0.056 points (97.5% interval -0.191 to +0.064), against a threshold of 0.35, so the verdict is refuted. primary 00045 pvdis-4-weekly-capacity-asymmetric-l1 On the 8 Primary substations (substations that feed 11 kV circuits from the 33 kV network) metered in MW, a least-squares fit of the daylight power to a calendar-and-temperature demand term minus a weekly capacity times one PV shape from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS), with weekly capacity increments under an asymmetric L1 penalty (a penalty on the sum of absolute increments, light on rises and heavy on falls), meets six conditions. It recovers a known injected capacity path (ramps, steps, and temporary falls, injected into a semi-synthetic baseline) with a median error of at most 0.15 of the path's mean capacity. It beats a capacity that is constant within each season-year by at least 20% on ramps and steps. It produces at most 0.5 false steps of 10% of capacity per Primary-year at the median Primary, and at most 1.0 at the worst Primary, on the placebo sky and on a constant injected path. Its path drifts upward on noise by at most 0.05 of capacity over 5 years. It recovers a 30% fall lasting 26 weeks at 0.5 or more of its depth, and an 8-week fall at under 0.5. Its 90% bootstrap interval covers 0.85 to 0.95 of non-step weeks and at least 0.60 of step weeks. Capacity is the 99th percentile of the half-hourly AC output, in MW, of the embedded solar (solar connected inside the distribution network, mostly unmetered by NGED) behind a Primary. refuted not-for-production No weekly capacity fit met the limits fixed in advance for tuning: the best penalty pair recovered none of a 26-week fall of 30% and gave 0.66 false steps per Primary-year at the median Primary, against a limit of 0.5. Weekly changes in embedded solar capacity cannot yet be read from Primary-substation data at the accuracy a weekly series needs, so the next experiment should use one capacity per season-year and read it as a range. primary 00040 pv-capacity-error-bars On the 8 directional (MW) Primary substations, comparing the PV capacity that six least-squares arms fit to the same series (they differ in how much cloud-driven demand each allows) detects a cloud-driven demand load that pushes the half-hourly fit's capacity at least 25% off, with at least 80% power and a false-positive rate of at most 10% on pure injected PV, so that a bounded error bar can be attached to the capacity at every Primary where no such load is detected. partly supported not-for-production The misfit test is calibrated (median capacity over truth 0.992, 95% interval 0.951 to 1.032; false-positive rate 0.055) and detects four of the five confound shapes that no fit contains at 25% of capacity, but it detects a day-long cloud load in only 0.35 of draws, so the pre-registered power rule fails and the verdict is underpowered. primary 00039 pv-disaggregation-cams-injection On the 8 directional (MW) Primary substations, a calendar-plus-temperature demand term minus one PV shape driven by Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) irradiance recovers the P99 capacity of real solar-farm output injected into the real demand series to within 25%, and the same fits on the un-injected series pass four checks that a weather-correlated demand confound would fail. partly supported not-for-production A fit of calendar-plus-temperature demand minus one satellite-driven solar shape recovers 0.854 (daily fit, 95% interval 0.815 to 0.866) of the capacity of real solar-farm output added to the demand of the 8 directional Primaries. On the real series 6 of the 8 pass four checks that a demand confound would fail, and one fails the placebo-sky check, so the verdict is partly supported. primary
