Month-block intervals on the capacity then cover an injected capacity in at least 70% of injections at the nominal 80% level, including a load that follows the clouds. primary

docs.title: P2: embedded-solar capacity from lagged residuals
docs.text:
The embedded-solar proposal rests on one follow-up check of experiment 00006's residuals, which motivated two different questions. Experiment 00007 then ran a first test and was inconclusive. The check was run by the 00006 session on CAMS irradiance at each demand series' own location, and its figures and script are in the write-up of PR #1202 (Experiment 6: which input features work best for the ERA5-trained demand model). It was not pre-registered. At Primary substation 12, the median-error Primary substation, the residual of the chosen-feature stage 1a XGBoost model averaged -5.3 points of capacity from 08:00 to 16:59 in the June, July, and August of the confirmation year (July 2025 to June 2026), against -1.0 at night. In July 2025, a linear fit on 431 daylight hours explained 25.5% of the hourly residual's variance with irradiance from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS), 3.8% with ERA5 shortwave, and 43.3% with both. Across the 14 Primary series that have CAMS values, CAMS alone explained more than ERA5 alone in all 14: a median of 23.7% against 2.9%, and 39.8% with both. In one series the error is a level shift that irradiance does not explain, and in another the residual correlates positively with CAMS irradiance.

The check cannot yet say whether the cause is embedded solar capacity or an error in ERA5's irradiance. At Primary substation 12 the joint fit gives coefficients of opposite sign and similar size for ERA5 and CAMS, and CAMS minus ERA5 alone explains 33.9%, so much of the residual tracks the difference between the two irradiance products. Stage 1a has already learned an irradiance response from ERA5, so a fixed error in ERA5's cloud field would produce the same pattern without any change in solar capacity. Daytime lighting load and behaviour on sunny days could also contribute. At Primary substation 12, CAMS explains 25% of the variance on weekdays and 10% on weekends, so the weekday mix matters too. The check has no time dimension, because it covers one month, one seed, and one fold, and with hourly autocorrelation the effective sample is far below 431 hours. Because stage 1a already uses ERA5 shortwave, the comparison of 25.5% with 3.8% is not like for like, and the partial R² of CAMS given ERA5 would be a fairer figure.

Experiment 00007 was the cheap first test of an irradiance error against a capacity change. It added CAMS irradiance to ERA5 shortwave and fitted a static correction on one year of residuals. The correction removed 46.6% of the next year's daylight squared residual against the 50% planned, and one substation sets the pooled figure, so the verdict is inconclusive. A further test could compute the three candidate statistics on residuals from walk-forward (out-of-fold) stage 1a fits, because residuals from a model fitted on the same period are shrunk and would look different in operation.

The three candidate statistics each compare what stage 1a predicted with what the substation metered. Each uses the residual, the metered power over capacity minus stage 1a's prediction at the observed weather.

  • The solar slope: regress the residual on irradiance over the trailing 14 to 28 days, in daylight hours only. A more negative slope means more embedded solar than stage 1a learned. The slope mixes capacity change, irradiance error, and other demand that varies with irradiance, so the regression could use the clear-sky index with day-of-week and temperature controls. Noise in the estimation irradiance biases the slope towards zero.
  • The sunny-minus-cloudy daytime residual: the mean residual on sunny days minus the mean on cloudy days at matched hours, with a named clear-sky-index threshold. A day-minus-night residual is not a substitute. Commercial load is daytime-heavy, electric-vehicle charging and storage are night-heavy, and heat pumps are daytime and seasonal, so their trends would appear as false solar change.
  • The change from the same calendar window a year earlier: this year's 28-day slope minus the slope in the same 28 days of the previous year. A ratio of the 28-day to the 365-day slope is unstable, because the slope is seasonal and the denominator can be near zero or change sign.

The correction could be given to stage 2 as a linear offset, not as a tree feature. Gradient-boosted trees cannot extrapolate beyond their training range, and embedded solar capacity grows steadily, so a product of the slope and the forecast shortwave would still be held flat by a tree. A linear term, in stage 1b or in stage 2, would extrapolate correctly, and the tree feature would be the comparison arm. The slope is estimated against observed irradiance and applied to forecast irradiance, which differ in bias and scale, so the conversion has to be stated. The past-weather source used at lag times has to be available at forecast time, because ERA5 arrives about 5 days late, and training has to use that same source. CAMS is observed after the fact and has no forecast, so the CAMS satellite-derived irradiance can feed the statistics only at lag times. The CAMS irradiance at each demand series' own location comes from PR #1201 (Download and validate CAMS irradiance at the demand series' locations), which covers the 22 series of experiment 00003 (16 Primary demand series, 4 bulk-supply and grid-supply point flows, and 2 non-demand series, a battery and a biofuel generator). The experiment could compute each statistic from ERA5 alone and from CAMS and ERA5 together.

A decision rule could be fixed before any fit. One candidate: the trend in the monthly change from a year earlier is negative at 70% or more of the substations in the top quartile of registered embedded solar capacity per unit of substation capacity, with a block-bootstrap 95% interval that excludes zero, and it is absent in the night-time residuals. A second candidate: the linear-offset arm lowers the confirmation-year daylight quantile score at Primary substations by at least 0.2 points of capacity, with a month-block bootstrap interval that excludes zero. Otherwise the hypothesis is refuted. The thresholds are proposals for the planning step to confirm.

Resolution limit. The top quartile of 16 Primary substations by embedded solar capacity is 4 substations, so a rule of "70% of them" means 3 of 4, which no interval can support. The slope statistics need more substations or a continuous measure of capacity.

docs.title: PVDIS: separating embedded solar from Primary demand
docs.text:
The PVDIS line estimates how much unmetered solar capacity sits behind each Primary substation, how that capacity changes over time, and whether an explicit solar term improves or explains the net demand forecast. The line serves three purposes, and the second matters about as much as the first:

  • Skill: a lower error in the net demand forecast at each substation.
  • Explanation: a forecast that NGED can read as demand minus solar. A solar term that leaves the error level but splits the forecast into parts an engineer recognises is still worth keeping, so experiment 64 (PVDIS-5) tested non-inferiority as well as gain.
  • Capacity: a time series of unmetered solar capacity per Primary. NGED holds almost no information on unmetered solar today, so an estimate with honest error bars is useful even when the estimate is far from perfect.

The capacity estimate runs offline, weekly or monthly, and the production forecast only reads the latest capacity table. Nothing in this line adds a fitting step to the serving path. Experiment 73 (PVDIS-6) found that the mix of panel orientations behind each Primary, the quantity the UniversalSolarFleetNode sketched in differentiable physics would fit, is not stable across season-years, so the explicit solar forecast keeps one south-facing shape.

Experiments 00039 and 00040 are parts 1 and 2 of the series, and the parts below follow the exploratory protocol in the ml-experiment skill. Opus plans each part after reading the result of the part before, so the designs below are proposals that each part's plan may change. Experiment 00039 fitted one capacity per Primary per season-year, from a calendar and temperature demand term minus one CAMS-driven solar shape. On real solar-farm output injected into the real demand, the half-hourly fit recovered a median 0.773 (0.740 to 0.818) of the injected capacity, and a fit on daily sums recovered 0.854 (0.815 to 0.866). Experiment 00040 compared six fits, which differ in how much cloud-driven demand each allows, and took the six-arm capacity C as its estimate. C recovered a median 0.992 (0.951 to 1.032) of the injected capacity. Experiment 00040 also attached a bound on the error that an undetected demand load would cause, of 0.18 to 0.23 at five Primaries. A demand load that rises with sunshine cannot be told apart from solar.

The Opus review of experiment 00040 recommended stopping the series, publishing a season-year capacity table, and not using capacity as a forecast feature; the parts below continue because the goals changed. That review judged the series against the questions it had then: whether a further experiment could narrow the capacity bound, and whether capacity improves the forecast score. Four experiments (00007, 00009, 00022, and 00031) found small or no gains from solar inputs. The maintainer has since added two goals: a forecast that explains itself, and a capacity series that changes week by week for NGED. Experiment 64 (PVDIS-5) rested on the explanation goal and on what differs from those four experiments, not on a claim that the review missed the forecast question. The same review found that the daily fit is about 2.6 times more exposed than C to an undetected day-long load, so every part reports C as the capacity and keeps the daily fit as a cross-check.

Rules shared by every part:

  • Substations. Only the 8 Primaries metered in MW, each carrying its status from the earlier review into every result: Kirton is reported only as a range (1.2 to 4.4 MW), because its daylight cloud load was flagged in 6 of 7 season-years; Wrangle T1 is excluded from any claim that a Primary is free of a confound; Trusthorpe is marked low-power. The 8 Primaries metered only in MVA fold solar into the magnitude of the flow, and experiment 00039 fitted a negative capacity at Stickney in every year. Experiment 00079 (PVDIS-7) treats them separately.
  • Service areas. TimeSeriesMetadata.area_wkt holds one polygon per Primary. Wrangle T1 and Wrangle T2 are two transformers at one substation, feeding different circuits, and share one polygon. Each transformer keeps its own capacity fit, and any comparison against an outside count of solar uses the sum of the two against the shared polygon. Before any outside comparison, a check reports overlaps and gaps between neighbouring polygons, whether each Primary's location falls inside its own polygon, and how the union of the polygons compares with the two BSPs' area.
  • Irradiance. CAMS for past weather, because the past-weather solar study found the CAMS solar estimate the most accurate of the products it compared. ENS for forecasts. Where a capacity fitted on CAMS is applied to ENS, the ENS irradiance is first calibrated against CAMS, by lead, on data from the fold's training window only.
  • Capacity used in a forecast is a real-time vintage. A forecast experiment reads the capacity that a fit truncated at the fold's training end would give, never a path smoothed over the whole record. A path fitted once over all data passes information from later weeks back to earlier weeks through the penalty and the constraint.
  • Switching is masked. The logged closures, padded by 24 hours, are removed from every capacity fit until SW2-0b's labels exist. A transfer moves a share of the donor's net load, including the donor's solar, so an unmasked transfer looks like a step in capacity. The logs miss some real switching, so unlogged transfers remain a source of false steps.
  • Known answers first. Every capacity method is scored on experiment 00039's injection harness before its result on the real series is trusted.
  • Loads that track sunshine are a named confound. Seaside visitor load at the coastal Primaries (Skegness, Ingoldmells, Chapel St Leonards, and Trusthorpe), irrigation pumping, cooling of crop stores, and air conditioning all rise on sunny days and bias the fitted capacity low. Daytime domestic load falls on sunny days, as people go outside, and biases the fitted capacity high. Each write-up reports the coastal Primaries separately and compares school-holiday weeks with term-time weeks.

docs.title: PVDIS-T: the capacity table, a study
docs.text: Publish a season-year capacity table now, built from experiment 00040's outputs with no refit, and replace it with PVDIS-4's weekly series once that part has run. NGED's need is to improve on almost no information, so the season-year table is useful before the weekly series exists. The study reports C as the capacity, keeps sampling uncertainty separate from the named systematic scenarios, and carries each Primary's status from the earlier review. The joint fit of experiment 00063 read the same capacities.

docs.title: Unmetered PV capacity: what we know
docs.text:
A probe of a trained neural network reads the whole-summer capacity of photovoltaic (PV) solar panels behind each Primary substation, with a calibration measured on injected real solar farms. The probe followed a step in capacity only when the step began in an ordinary spring. An explicit solar term built from the probed capacity improved the forecast with estimates of past weather and worsened it with ensemble forecast weather. The maintainer paused the work after 10 November 2026. This page is meant to let a reader restart it in January.

Sources. Every figure comes from a merged result page of the theme, linked at its first use. Items marked "(brief)" come from briefs in data/ml-experiments/briefs/ of the production repository (pv_probe_design_review_answer.md, pv_probe_brief_changes_after_621_623.md, pv_next_c_multi_pixel_cams_brief.md, pv_session_reply_solar_drift.md, and pv_session_reply_for_graph_labeller.md), which are not on the docs site.

docs.title: Take-home message
docs.text:
What works. The probe, divided by the recovery of injected real solar farms, estimates 2.4 to 3.9 MW of unmetered solar behind each of the six Primaries metered in MW. Its intervals overlap the regression table of experiment 474 at all six, with medians 0.94 to 1.14 times that table (experiment 649). At the five Primaries metered in MVA that never fold, a linear probe divided by a recovery factor of 0.79 reads 1.25 to 6.62 MW (experiment 673).

What does not work. The probe followed a step in capacity only when the step began in an ordinary spring, and it reads a cloud-following load as solar. Its values have season-year resolution at best. An explicit solar term does not improve a forecast made with ensemble weather. The loss is largest at day 1 to 2, at 0.37 points, and does not grow with lead.

Tested explanations for that loss are ruled out one at a time. They are the ensemble time step, the interpolation and time stamps, ensemble members and cell temperature, a bias adapter, and missing spread. Forecast cloud error is the inferred cause, with no direct test.

What to try next. The ranked options are in Options for January. The cheapest are a per-Primary yearly capacity trajectory from register curves anchored to the probe, and a direct test of the cloud-error explanation on stored quantiles.

docs.title: Terms used on this page
docs.text:
• Primaries. The 6 MW Primaries are D5, D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16, whose meters read signed real power in megawatts (MW). The five non-folding MVA Primaries are D2, D3, D4, D19, and D21, whose meters read apparent power in megavolt-amperes (MVA). The three folding MVA Primaries are D8, D12, and D22. A "fold" occurs when solar output exceeds demand: the real flow turns negative, and apparent power, which is never negative, folds it back to a positive reading.
  • Probe. The probe takes a neural network with no inputs from recent power readings (a "lag-free" network), fixes its calendar inputs, supplies the weather of other ("donor") days, and reads the change in forecast demand as solar megawatts.
  • Recovery. The probe's reading divided by the megawatts injected into the target. Recovery is measured by adding the output of real metered solar farms to a substation's demand and probing it (a known-answer test).
  • Placebo. A test that injects nothing, or a shape unrelated to the sky, so that a reading above zero is false signal.
  • Free network. The demand neural network without a solar term. The explicit solar term is a physics solar-output curve scaled by the probed capacity and given to the demand neural network.
  • Verdicts. "Supported", "partly supported", "not supported", and "refuted" refer to the pre-registered decision rule of the experiment cited.
  • Sunny midday. A half-hour between 10:00 and 15:00 UTC with an observed clear-sky index of at least 0.7 (experiment 639).
  • Points. Quantile-score or CRPS points of capacity; lower is better, and a positive gain means the explicit term scored better.
  • Past weather. Estimates of past weather (ERA5 reanalysis and CAMS satellite irradiance, see the glossary), as against ECMWF ensemble forecasts.

docs.title: What we know and what does not work
Reading capacity from a trained neural network
docs.text:
The probe reads about 0.68 of a real solar farm's megawatts, and calibration removes part of that shortfall. Experiment 621 injected the output of real metered solar farms and read 0.68 of the injected megawatts (0.66 to 0.70 at each of six Primaries). Placebos read about 0.1 (95th percentile 0.08 to 0.16, bar 0.20). The verdict was "not supported", because recovery missed the 0.85 to 1.15 bar, the raw intervals covered the truth in 0 of 144 injections, and a cloud-following load could not be told from solar.

Part of the shortfall is the shape of a real farm; the sky is not the cause. A real farm of a given peak produces about 20% less energy than the idealised curve of the same peak, and a probe that recovered energy exactly would read about 0.77 (experiment 624). In energy the probe recovers 0.78 to 0.88 (experiment 634). Clipping and sky displacement overlap with this explanation. A metered neighbouring farm 5 to 25 km away as a second sky input lifted recovery from 0.68 to 0.69 (experiment 635). A monotone network lifted it to 0.71 (experiment 623). A contrastive training loss gave a recovery of 0.00 in every world (experiment 624).

A whole-summer capacity can be read, with caveats. A constant injected capacity calibrates to 0.95 to 1.04, and the leave-one-farm-out recovery factor is 0.68 (0.67 to 0.69). Experiment 649 divides stored probe outputs by that factor, and its 80% interval covers the injected truth in 0.81 of 96 leave-one-farm-out injections (experiment 634 read 0.66 with a different widening, so the two are not comparable). The calibration rests on four injected farms that resemble each other, so it may not transfer to a fleet of rooftop panels.

docs.title: Capacity steps and the sunny spring of 2025
docs.text:
A step that began in the very sunny spring of 2025 was read at 0.32 to 0.51, and part of what the probe reads is the weather of the step's months. Experiment 634 injected a step of 2 or 4 MW from April or July 2025. The calibrated read of the spring step was 0.32 to 0.51 and that of the summer step was 0.0 to 0.1, against a bar of 0.70. The clearness index was 0.76 in April to June 2025, against 0.61 in 2024 and 0.65 to 0.69 in 2020 to 2023.

A step that begins in an ordinary spring is followed. Experiment 638 read 0.82 to 0.88 of a 4 MW step that began in spring 2023, with a placebo at 0.07 to 0.12. It read 0.32 to 0.49 for the same step in spring 2025, where a placebo built from the multi-year day-of-year mean read 0.08 to 0.28. The verdict was "partly supported". No July-to-September in the record has a clearness index above 0.63, so a step in summer 2024 stands in for a sunny summer, and it read 0.45 to 0.55.

A step in a sunnier-than-usual season should be scored beside a climatological placebo before it is read as capacity. This is a rule drawn from experiments 634 and 638, and experiment 638 recommends reporting per training window until the excess in the facts below is explained.

docs.title: Adding a physics solar term to the demand neural network
docs.text:
With estimates of past weather the explicit solar term gains, and with ensemble weather it loses. Experiment 639 gave a demand network a physics solar curve with the probed capacity. On sunny middays at the six MW Primaries with past weather, the free network scored 0.75 points worse (98.75% day-block interval 0.51 to 1.01). Experiment 644 repeated the test with ECMWF ensemble weather. The free network then scored better by 0.37, 0.25, and 0.27 points at day 1 to 2, day 3 to 5, and day 6 to 10 (99.7% intervals, raised for 19 comparisons: -0.54 to -0.20, -0.45 to -0.08, and -0.40 to -0.14). The explicit term lost at five of the six Primaries, at all 10 lead days, and at every level of forecast sunniness. The verdict of experiment 644 was "refuted".

Much of the past-weather gain was the free network's bias. In experiment 643 the free network's median ran 4.1 points too high on sunny middays. A 14-day error correction, added after the results, scored 0.48 points better than the explicit term in the real months (interval -0.66 to -0.30). One Primary carried most of the gain in experiment 639, and two Primaries scored slightly better with the free network.

Five explanations for the ensemble-weather loss were not supported by one test each, and a sixth is inferred.

  • The ensemble's 3-hour and 6-hour time steps: averaging past weather into 3-hour and 6-hour windows still leaves a gain of 0.84 and 0.77 points (experiment 661). Experiment 661 calls its separate test across lead bands weak.
  • The shortwave interpolation and time stamps: the audit found zero time-stamp shift and a pipeline identical to production to 0.0 W/m2 (experiment 661).
  • Ensemble members and cell temperature: a curve per member with a Faiman cell temperature still lost by 0.35, 0.23, and 0.21 points (experiment 655).
  • A learned bias adapter stayed 0.13 to 0.29 points behind the free network (experiment 661).
  • Missing spread: building the distribution as gross demand minus a random member's solar curve lost by 0.29 to 0.38 points (experiment 664).
  • Forecast cloud error is the inferred cause and has no direct test. The loss at every level of forecast sunniness (experiment 644) means it is not confined to days the ensemble calls cloudy. The 14-day error correction keeps almost none of its gain when it uses only forecast sunniness (experiment 655). That is what forecast cloud error would produce. It is also what would happen if scoring rows selected on observed sunniness favoured the arm that knew it.

docs.title: Converting real power to apparent power at the MVA Primaries
docs.text:
Under NGED's stated power factor 1 with a small reactive floor, the linear probe loses about 0.5 points at half the midday reading. Half the midday reading is the level of the five non-folding MVA Primaries. The 80% interval is -1.0 to 7.7 points, so a loss of 7.7 points is not excluded (experiment 679). Experiment 679 measured 10.7 points (7.8 to 17.1) under the power factor 0.97 world that experiment 656 and experiment 662 assumed, and experiment 671 measured 5 to 12 points there at four MW Primaries. The reactive floor of experiment 679 is an assumption of 0.10 times the median sunny-midday reading, and the real meters' reactive power is unknown.

The three recovery factors for the MVA linear probe give figures that differ by about 16%. Experiment 673 divides by 0.79, the signed-world recovery of experiment 662's first rotation, and lists 0.68 as a sensitivity. Experiment 679 measures a signed recovery of 0.746 and recommends the signed-world factor alone.

The three folding Primaries (D8, D12, and D22) are report-only. D5 and D10 are report-only for the MVA conversion only, because their midday readings of 0.88 and 1.2 MW put a 2 MW test farm past the fold. Their 6 MW capacities stand. At D2, D3, D4, and D19 the extra capacity of the fold model comes almost entirely from two free reactive-power terms, so experiment 671 treats the linear probe as the better-supported reading and the fold model as an upper bound.

docs.title: Earlier attempts
docs.text:
Of 14 earlier experiments, experiment 129 passed all its gates, against a weaker placebo. The table is from a design review written on 7 November 2026 (brief). The review judged the probe a neural version of experiments 235 and 479, with a likely recovery of 0.75 to 0.90.

Experiment Method What it found 129 Convex generalised additive model, one capacity per season-year Passed all four gates (recovery at 5 of 5 Primaries, placebo 0.12); the range 1.2 to 1.6 MW is a scenario spread 235 Matched sunny-minus-cloudy day pairs Recovery 0.758; a cloud-following load added 0.295; December-to-January placebo 0.33 241 Divide by the median recovery of other farms Within 10% at 5 of 5; the 80% interval covers 59 to 79%, and 0 to 2% with a cloud load 269 Pooled empirical plant table driven by CAMS 0.892 (99th-percentile ratio) and 0.966 (capacity ratio); satellite sunshine is not the limit 349, 352 Better capacity inside the generalised additive model stack Sunny score flat in capacity (0.047 worse; flat surface), per the review 405 Mixture-density network with learned-capacity solar term A day-shuffled placebo kept 0.60 to 0.91 of real recovery (limit 0.20) 409 Same, with a day-of-year term and anomaly-only injection Anomaly read-out 0.03 to 0.05 MW against seed noise of 0.18 to 0.59 MW; the test could not decide 416 Explicit solar term, 5 seeds, 12 months Sunny-midday +0.227 points, interval -0.135 to +0.560; capacities 0.4 to 0.7 of the reference, 1.5 at D5 474 Placebo-gated ladder on the generalised additive model No rung passed: profile placebo 0.25 to 0.40, and 0.49 to 0.51 with cloud terms 477 Neural PV module on stored fits, lag-masked Placebo read 0.90 to 0.95 of the injected MW against 0.86 to 0.92 for the real farm 479 Within-month anomaly regression Placebos pass, mostly by construction; recovery 0.62 to 0.83; a cloud load fakes 0.2 to 0.3 of a 2 MW farm 501 Explicit PV column from the experiment 474 table Sunny-midday -0.014 points against 0.225 detectable (the fifth null) 504 Recent CAMS columns in the neural network Leak-free columns null; target-time CAMS -0.318 at the eight MVA Primaries and -0.467 at the six MW Primaries

Two figures from the same review bound what a method can detect (brief). Experiment 129 found capacity growing 0.4 to 2.8 MW over about 4 years, which is about 0.1 to 0.7 MW per year. The within-month minimum detectable capacity of experiment 479 is 0.05 to 0.35 MW.

docs.title: Findings that are not on one merged page
docs.text:
The polygons are small relative to the weather grid (brief). Only the 16 Primaries have an area_wkt service-area polygon. The areas run from 14.7 to 215.7 km2, with a median of 102 km2, against about 25 km2 for one CAMS pixel, so a median polygon spans about 4 pixels. A multi-pixel CAMS download was written and never run (brief). Displacement of the sky by 5 to 17 km lowered recovery by under 0.05 in experiment 624 (the brief says 0.02 to 0.04), and a metered neighbour's output moved recovery by 0.008 in the unpaired medians of experiment 635 (paired difference -0.004, 90% interval -0.010 to +0.026).

NGED states that its meters read power factor 1 with a small reactive floor. The maintainer relayed the statement, and experiments 673 and 679 use it. The size of the floor is an assumption.

The probe reads above a regression that cannot see the date. In experiment 638 a regression of the injected capacity on the unit curve and temperature reads 0.39 to 0.42 raw for a real step in spring 2023, against 0.57 to 0.59 for the probe. The remaining excess is 0.1 to 0.2 raw (a fraction of the injected megawatts) for a real step and 0.05 to 0.1 for a placebo. The cause was not found. Weekday, holiday, and pandemic columns are an untested candidate.

The free network is biased one way on sunny middays. In experiment 664, realised power falls below the free network's 5% quantile in 9.3% of half-hours at day 1 to 2, and above its 95% quantile in 1.9%. The lower band is too narrow and the upper band too wide, so a recalibration of the width cannot fix the bias.

The probe interval lies below the registered floor at D2, D3, D5, and D21. The "floor" is the sum of registered solar capacity inside the service area, with metered sites removed (experiment 673). The D2 flag depends on the recovery factor: with 0.68 the interval overlaps the floor. At D5 one site of 2.70 MW accounts for most of the 4.55 MW floor. A sensitivity in experiment 673 that adds the Feed-in Tariff band of 50 kW to 1 MW moves D10 below the floor and D11 and D16 to "overlaps". Experiment 267 found a 2021 shortfall at D10 and D11 that remains unexplained.

No register gives a dated capacity curve for domestic PV installed after March 2025 (brief). The Feed-in Tariff report covers 2010-04-01 to 2025-03-31 by postcode district, the Embedded Capacity Register lists sites of 50 kW and above, and the Renewable Energy Planning Database lists mostly sites of 150 kW and above. A cumulative registered curve could be built from commissioning dates for earlier years.

Wind capacity estimation is parked. Experiment 617 failed its known-answer test.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• What causes the loss with ensemble weather? Forecast cloud error is inferred and untested.
  • How did capacity change from year to year? The probe has season-year resolution at best, and the estimated drift of 0.1 to 0.7 MW per year overlaps the within-month minimum detectable capacity of 0.05 to 0.35 MW.
  • Why does the probe read above a regression that cannot see the date? The cause is unknown.
  • Do the MVA figures hold? They depend on the unknown reactive power of the meters. D2, D3, D5, and D21 sit below their register floors and need NGED's own list of connected solar.

docs.title: Options for January
docs.text:
These options are listed in order of the information each gives per hour of work, and none is agreed work.

  1. A per-Primary yearly capacity trajectory, 2019 to 2026. It asks whether a composite curve tracks the capacity drift. The curve combines the season-year capacities of experiments 129, 474, and 479 from 2021, the probe of experiment 649, a cumulative register curve by service-area polygon, and a term for the unregistered share. It takes about a day on CPU and depends on nothing.
  2. A direct test of the cloud-error explanation. It regresses the explicit-minus-free gain on forecast cloud error, using the stored quantiles of experiments 644 and 655. It takes about half a day and depends on nothing.
  3. An asymmetric sunny-midday quantile bias correction for the free network. It asks whether the one-sided bias of experiment 664 can be removed. It takes about 1 to 2 GPU-hours and has a serving-path implication, so the maintainer decides first.
  4. Injected-farm tests at the five non-folding MVA Primaries with the reactive floor built in. They ask whether the 0.5-point loss of experiment 679 holds at D2, D3, D4, D19, and D21. They take about 0.5 GPU-hours and need the code of experiment 662 extended.
  5. Explicit PV as a graph-detector arm. It depends on option 1.
  6. NGED connection records. They would settle D2, D3, D5, and D21, and are an option only if the maintainer later allows requesting them.

docs.title: Load-shift labels in the forecast
docs.text:
The current understanding and the options for next work are on the state and next steps page.

Giving the Primary demand forecast switching labels has not yet improved it on real data. On injected transfers it recovers the lost accuracy only when the megawatts (MW) moved are known: it closes 83% of the extra error with the true MW, against 16% (interval -17% to +67%, so not distinguishable from zero) with the MW from the RO-NC detector.

A load transfer moves part of one Primary substation's demand onto its neighbours for hours or days. The question is whether telling the XGBoost forecast about transfers lets it forecast the demand the normal running arrangement would have carried. The labels come from NGED's logs or from the RO-NC detector, whose own results are on the switching detectors page. All results are from the lab: 16 Primary series, one validation year (292 daily forecast runs, July 2025 to June 2026), and labels that use hindsight.

The share of the extra error recovered depends on where the MW comes from: 50% to 83% with the true MW, 16% to 36% with RO-NC's MW as built (intervals include zero), and 43% with the largest overlapping step (chosen after seeing the results). The extra error (the "gap") is the error of the plain forecast minus the error of the same forecast on unmodified lags (the "ceiling"). Source: experiment 88.

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
On real data, no label-based change lowered the score by an amount the data can show. A label source is "oracle" when it is NGED's logs and "detector" when it is RO-NC. The score is the quantile score in points of capacity; a positive change is a worse forecast.

  • Dropping labelled switching from the training targets, or adding the moved MW, changed the score outside switching by under 0.06. Masked minus plain was +0.004 (98.33% interval -0.026 to +0.025); only 22 of the 82 labelled events fall in the scored year (experiment 75).
  • On the 37,394 half-hours whose lag (an earlier power reading used as an input) lies inside a logged event, no correction was shown to help. Oracle labels changed the score by -0.29 (98.33% interval -2.06 to +0.68) and detector labels by +0.48 (-0.06 to +1.72). Outside switching, the detector labels raised the score by 0.056 (+0.016 to +0.126). The detector marks 8.1 times as many half-hours as the logs, and 15% of the logged ones (experiment 86).
  • A perfect detector would lower the best guess's quantile score by 0.42% (95% interval -0.47% to 1.96%) on events moving 25% or more of the receiver's load for over a day, against a 3% threshold. Those events touch 3 of the 16 series, and if events on badly metered substations are dropped, 2 remain and every bound's point estimate lies between -0.3% and -0.1%. For all 22 visible events the bound is 2.35% (-0.22% to 5.73%), resting on a few short events (experiment 44).

A perfect detector would lower the quantile score by little in the band of events the labeller finds most reliably. Source: experiment 44.

Two ways of marking suspect lags without a hand label did not help. A probability that a lag lies inside a transfer, built from the causal RO-NC detector, lowered the Brier score (the mean squared error of a probability) by 3.3% against the yes-or-no flag (97.5% interval -7.6% to +1.6%) where the plan needed 20%, and its area under the curve against NGED's logs was 0.53 (experiment 91; the 11.2% gain reported there is a post hoc subset). Giving the forecast the unusualness of each lag against a climatology raised the score by 0.355 (97.5% interval +0.209 to +0.513) and narrowed the band on rows with a lag in a logged event (experiment 90; verdict refuted).

On injected transfers, the true MW recovers most of the error and the detector's MW does not. The cases are forecast origins inside a transfer (2,452 cases from four onset months), scored against the unmodified power. The XGBoost model trained on NGED's logged transfers and given the true MW scored -0.790 points against plain (98.75% interval -1.397 to -0.412), closing 83% (70% to 91%) of the gap. With RO-NC's MW, the model trained on RO-NC's transfers scored -0.149 (-1.174 to +0.148, negative in 2 of 4 months). Counting overlapping detector intervals once, chosen after seeing the results, gave -0.406 (-1.223 to -0.083). After a transfer ended, the as-built MW raised the error by 0.35 to 0.46 for up to 7 days (experiment 88).

Adding about three times as many synthetic transfers to the training data did not help. The synthetic-trained model scored +0.079 (98.75% interval -0.031 to +0.153) against the real-trained model with the true MW, and +0.032 (-0.019 to +0.067) with RO-NC's MW. The MW source set the share of the gap closed (83% with the true MW, 32% to 53% with the detector's). Source: experiment 96.

Hiding lags that lie inside a transfer made the forecast worse. Setting them to missing raised the score by 0.409 (98.33% interval +0.281 to +0.517) on rows with such a lag, and training on all history since March 2021 instead of 12 months changed it by +0.009 (-0.052 to +0.069) (experiment 89). Hiding lags at random during training did not widen the 5% to 95% band on rows with a missing lag: its coverage was 0.799 for the plain forecast and 0.802 with 10% of training rows hidden, against 0.90 nominal (experiment 100; inconclusive).

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text:
The best of the recipes tested here, on injected transfers only, corrects each lag by the MW moved, using the largest overlapping detector step as the MW. In experiment 88 this (post hoc) closed 43% (17% to 71%) of the gap with the RO-NC-trained model, and correcting the lags alone closed 48% (18% to 71%). The recipe:

  1. Subtract the signed MW at each lag from the lag, and give the three MW values as columns (experiments 75, 88).
  2. Take one MW per half-hour from the largest overlapping step, not the sum (experiment 88).
  3. Do not also drop the transfer's half-hours from the training targets: it added +0.070 (-0.015 to +0.171) over lag correction alone (experiment 88).

No recipe has beaten the plain forecast on real logged events.

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text: Nothing is ready for the serving path. All 9 experiments of this theme are not-for-production: each uses hindsight labels, and the detector's residual uses ERA5 weather, which arrives about 5 days late. The evidence does not support a detector or a label table in the forecast.

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
• Do not set lags inside a labelled switching event to missing. The forecast got worse on rows with such a lag and on rows outside switching (experiment 89, +0.054 outside switching; the mask arm of experiment 100 lost 1.36 points on injected transfers). Random dropout in 30% of training rows removed that loss. Re-check with a model trained to read missing lags.
  • Count the half-hours a label source marks before using it to mask or correct. The union of RO-NC and the logs marks 9% to 16% of half-hours per year from 2022, RO-NC alone marks 8.1 times the logged half-hours, and masking on the union raised the error (experiment 89, experiment 86). Re-check with a detector that marks about as many half-hours as the logs.
  • Take one MW per half-hour from the largest overlapping detector step, not the sum. The as-built MW, which adds overlapping intervals, did not beat the plain forecast (-0.149, -1.174 to +0.148), and the largest step did (-0.406, -1.223 to -0.083), though that choice was post hoc. A lingering return step kept the correction on after a transfer ended (experiment 88; the loss comes from the 21% of marked cases with overlapping intervals, not from a scale error in the MW). The 16% result rests on February 2026, and the oracle contrast C2 keeps its sign and stays between -0.62 and -0.92 when any of the four months is left out.
  • A detected transfer is known late. At the newest usable lag the detector had marked 32% of the moved MW in the first 24 hours after onset, against 73% in days 1 to 3 (experiment 88), and its probability separated poorly in that first day (area under the curve 0.61 for the calibrated probability and 0.60 for the flag; experiment 91). A gain scored with hindsight ends is therefore an upper bound (experiment 75). Re-check on live data or with an end rule that needs no hindsight.
  • Score a forecast of the normal running arrangement against real data only outside events. Real rows inside an event have no valid normal-arrangement truth, so experiments 75, 86, and 100 score real rows outside events and use injected transfers for the rest (experiment 100). Re-check if a source of the true normal-arrangement power appears.
  • Count events, not half-hours, and expect wide intervals. The 37,394 rows with a lag in a logged event come from an estimated 15 to 20 events, 81% of them from 3 substations (experiment 100). Six trustworthy events fall in the scored year, and without those where a donor or receiver has over half its readings missing, 2 remain and every bound lies between -0.3% and -0.1% (experiment 44). Injected scores rest on 4 onset months (experiments 88 and 96), so read the sign in each month. Re-check on a longer period.
  • Run a same-code repeat of the control arm before reading a change under about 0.05. Only 9% of per-case scores from a graphics-card refit matched experiment 48's to 0.001, the largest gap was 4.39 points, and the +0.004 of masked minus plain is at the level of that noise (experiment 75). Re-check if the fit is made deterministic.
  • Give any "drop the event rows" arm a control that keeps them. The mask arm, which also dropped 9% of training rows, narrowed the band on unmasked rows by 4% and lowered its coverage from 0.906 to 0.894 (experiment 100). Without the control, the effect of dropping rows is credited to masking lags. Re-check with the control run.
  • Report the pre-registered rows first, and name a post hoc subset. Experiment 91's 11.2% gain is on rows chosen after seeing the results; the planned rows gave 3.3% with an interval including zero (experiment 91). Re-check against the plan's decision rule.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text:
• Whether the detector's MW, with each transfer counted once and ended promptly, recovers more than the 43% of the gap that the post hoc rule did in experiment 88.
  • Whether any label improves the forecast on real transfers: the logged events in a year are too few (experiment 86).
  • Whether a missing-lag indicator column, or a separate XGBoost model of the quantile spread, widens the band where a lag is missing (experiment 100).
  • Whether synthetic transfers trained with the detector's errors, not the exact MW, help (experiment 96).

The Research plan lists what is planned next, and the Experiments page lists every experiment.

docs.title: Load-shift labels in the forecast: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00693 oracle-transfer-flag-in-the-candidate-part-1 A perfect telemetry detector, which knows that a reading lay inside a load transfer (and when the transfer began, once a reading after the onset exists), lowers the CRPS of the Candidate demand network on transfer-affected rows by at least 0.3 points of capacity against a placebo flag, without raising CRPS on event-free rows by more than 0.05. inconclusive not-for-production Telling the demand forecast exactly when a load transfer is happening did not make it clearly better on simulated transfers. The forecast that reads yesterday's power loses only 0.1 points of capacity to a transfer, and the forecast that adapts to a transfer scores about the same with a perfect flag or a random one on the deciding simulation. The test could not rule out a gain or a loss of half a point or more, because three refits of the same forecast already differ by about 0.4 points, so no conclusion about a real switching detector is safe. A repeat needs at least 10 refits per arm. primary 00660 shared-generator-of-injected-load-transfer-events A generator that adds load-transfer events to real power history, with every assumption set from a measured number or marked unmeasured, produces windows that a classifier cannot tell from real events (area under the curve under 0.65), and a detector tuned on one configuration of the generator loses at most 0.05 of its recall on another. supported not-for-production We built one shared tool that adds fake load transfers between neighbouring Primary substations to real power history. On the features a detector reads, a classifier cannot tell the fake events from real ones (area under the curve 0.55, where 0.5 is chance), and a detector tuned on one kind of fake event finds as many events of another kind. The evidence is thin (49 real windows, 2 verified transfers), so the tool is usable for training and for first tests, within what 49 real windows can show, and any real-event result still needs checking on real events. also relevant 00658 edge-state-event-table-neural-network A bidirectional recurrent neural network that reads every Primary's residual and the electricity network's neighbour links together, and is trained on synthetic events injected into the real residual, finds more injected load-shift megawatts than the penalised segmentation of experiment 653 at the same rate of false events, and pairs the two ends of an injected transfer far more often than the 0.18 that experiment 653 reached, because the network learns from many thousand injected transfers what a donor and a recipient look like together. not supported not-for-production A neural network that reads all 15 Primaries' demand residuals together did not find or pair injected load-shift events better than the penalised segmentation of experiment 653: it found 0.48 to 0.52 of the injected megawatts against 0.64, and paired 0.16 to 0.17 of injected transfers against 0.18. The network called far fewer events on the real record (0.4 to 0.8 per Primary-year against 6.6), because the decoder setting chosen on injected worlds suppresses events, not because its events are more precise. A classifier separates the injected events from verified real ones (area under the curve 0.91; 81 injected against 56 real events). The same signal given as plain features (event age and signed step size) does the same, more weakly. not supported not-for-production Telling the forecast's filter when a load transfer started and ended helped inside the transfer and hurt in the 72 hours after it, because the filter holds the transfer's step over the whole 7-day forecast. The switching detector's alarm arrives 48 hours after the step and did no better than a random placebo. The next test is a correction that decays over the typical transfer duration. primary 00116 differentiable-physics-nra-edge-flows-between-primaries Flows on the electricity network's interconnection edges, fitted to a frozen convex model's residuals with a sparse-step penalty, recover injected conserved transfers between MW-metered Primaries; removing them gives a normal running arrangement (NRA) model trained without hand labels that forecasts no worse outside events; and fed causally into the Kalman filter as a known input, they improve the metered forecast during and after a transfer. inconclusive not-for-production The method that looks for load moved between neighbouring substations did not work: with the settings we fixed in advance it found under a quarter of the load we added artificially, and it changed no forecast. Looser settings found more, but they also found load moving between substations that are not connected, probably the slow drifts of demand that our model does not describe. The gate failed for a structural reason: at the settings we fixed in advance, the fit cannot find any transfer shorter than 7 to 9 days, and the longest test transfer lasts under 5 days, so the failure is a limit of the method as specified, not a bug in the solver. The zero flow we first saw on the unconnected pairs was also an artefact of the order the fit visits its paths, so those pairs were never clean. Adding a drift term to the model, or accepting a flow only where the two substations are connected, is the next thing to test. also relevant 00100 drop1-random-lag-dropout-widens-intervals An XGBoost quantile model for Primary substation demand that is trained with labelled switching half-hours removed from its targets and with its lagged power inputs set to missing at random intervals, and that has those lags set to missing when they lie inside a labelled switching event, widens its 5% to 95% band on the half-hours whose lags are missing, so that the band's coverage moves from 0.784 towards the nominal 0.90, without widening the band elsewhere. inconclusive not-for-production Training the demand forecast with lags hidden at random did not make its band wider on half-hours where a lag is missing: on real rows the band covered 0.80 (hidden in 10% of training rows) to 0.84 (30%) of actuals, against a nominal 0.90. Hiding lags in 30% of rows did remove the accuracy loss that masking alone causes on injected transfers (-0.02 points, 95% interval -0.35 to +0.38 against the plain model). Hiding lags in 10% of rows left +0.26 (98.75% interval -0.15 to +0.85), not separable from zero or from the loss. An input that tells the XGBoost model a lag is missing, or a separate XGBoost model of the quantile spread, are untested routes to a wider band. also relevant 00096 sw2-23-synthetic-switches-injected-into-training A forecast of the normal running arrangement (NRA, the network as it is when no switching transfer is on) recovers the power a Primary substation would have drawn had no transfer happened better when its XGBoost model was also trained on many synthetic transfers than when it was trained on the real logged transfers only. In a synthetic transfer, known MW is added to the recorded power of a donor and its receivers, the half-hours of the transfer are dropped as training targets, the lags are corrected by the transfer's MW, and the MW is given as a column. The gain holds when the MW at forecast time comes from the causal refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC) or from the largest detector step, and not only when the MW is the injected truth. inconclusive not-for-production C1, synthetic-trained minus real-trained with the injected MW: +0.079 points of capacity (98.75% interval -0.031 to +0.153). primary 00091 sw2-26-calibrated-probability-of-abnormal-arrangement The refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC), run causally (with only the data before a forecast origin), can give for each past half-hour in the lag window a probability that the half-hour lies inside an abnormal running arrangement (ARA). The probability is calibrated, and it separates better than the detector's yes-or-no flag. inconclusive not-for-production A probability built from the causal switching detector was not shown to beat the detector's yes-or-no flag: on the planned rows its Brier score was 3.3% lower (97.5% interval -7.6% to +1.6%), against the 20% the plan required. Only in a post hoc subset of injected transfers large enough to see was the gain 11.2% (-20.3% to -2.0%). Against NGED's switching logs it has almost no skill (area under the curve 0.52 to 0.53), so a rule that widened the uncertainty bands when the probability is high would cover only about 8% of the half-hours that the logs mark as switching. primary 00090 sw2-28-lag-unusualness-inputs-all-rows-and-switching For the 16 Primary substation demand series, telling the monthly-refitted (P-roll) XGBoost model how unusual each of its three lags is (the probability integral transform, PIT, of each lag against a probabilistic climatology of the series) lowers the quantile score on all half-hours outside switching, and widens the quantiles on the half-hours whose lag lies inside a logged switching event, when both arms train on normal-arrangement targets only. refuted not-for-production C1, clim_pit minus plain on all rows outside switching: +0.355 points (97.5% interval +0.209 to +0.513). primary 00089 sw2-22-longest-history-nra-forecast-with-ara-lags-masked For the 16 Primary substations, an XGBoost demand model refitted monthly and trained on the longest history of ECMWF ensemble control-member forecasts (2021-03 onward), with every half-hour inside an abnormal running arrangement (ARA) removed from the training targets, scores below the same model on the standard 12-month window, and setting to missing every lagged power input that lies inside an ARA lowers the score on the half-hours whose lags lie inside an ARA. refuted not-for-production C1, LM minus L on rows with a lag in an ARA: +0.409 points (98.33% interval +0.281 to +0.517). primary 00088 sw2-21-nra-forecast-recovers-normal-arrangement-during-and-after-injected-switches When a Primary substation (a substation that steps down to the local distribution network) is inside a load transfer, or has just left one, an XGBoost demand model that was trained without the transfer's half-hours as targets, with the lags corrected by the transfer's signed MW and the MW as a column ("full NRA", NRA being the normal running arrangement), forecasts the power the substation would have drawn had no transfer happened better than the plain model does. This holds when the MW comes from the RO-NC detector of experiment 82 (a logistic score on the 24-hour residual step) run causally on data up to the forecast origin, but by less than when the MW comes from the injected truth. inconclusive not-for-production C1, arm 4 with RO-NC MW as built minus plain: -0.149 points of capacity (98.75% interval -1.174 to +0.148), closing 16% (-17% to +67%) of the gap to the ceiling, negative in 2 of 4 months. primary 00086 sw2-12-detector-labels-for-nra-forecast On the 292 daily ENS forecast runs of experiment 48, giving the monthly-refitted (P-roll) Primary demand model the lags minus the MW that switching moved, together with that MW as three columns, lowers the quantile score on the half-hours whose lag sits inside a switching event, when the events and MW come from the RO-NC load-transfer detector of experiment 82 instead of NGED's logs, and the gain is smaller than with the oracle labels of experiment 41 by the share of events RO-NC misses. inconclusive not-for-production Lags corrected with the detector's labels did not lower the quantile score on rows with a lag inside a logged event. primary 00075 sw2-11-nra-forecast-with-labelled-switching-masks On the 292 daily ENS forecast runs of experiment 48, a weekly-refitted Primary substation demand model whose training targets leave out the labelled switching half-hours forecasts the normal running arrangement (NRA) no worse than the plain weekly model, and giving the model the signed MW that switching moved at each lagged power input, or replacing each lag by the lag minus that MW, lowers the quantile score on half-hours outside switching. inconclusive not-for-production C1, masked minus plain: +0.004 points (98.33% interval -0.026 to +0.025). primary 00044 sw2-2-switching-share-of-best-guess-score Half-hours in labelled switching events, and half-hours whose lagged power falls inside one, carry a larger share of the best guess's quantile score and tail score than their share of half-hours, and a perfect switching detector could lower the Primary quantile score or tail score by 3% or more. refuted not-for-production In the band of events the labeller finds most reliably, a perfect switching detector would lower the best guess's quantile score by 0.42% (95% interval -0.47% to 1.96%) and its tail score by nothing, against a threshold of 3%. Switching in that band touches 3 of the 16 Primary series and few half-hours, in one validation year. primary

docs.title: Load-shift labels in the forecast: research plan
docs.text:
No proposal in this theme is waiting. Experiment 693 found no gain from a perfect transfer flag, but its refits were too noisy to rule out a gain or a loss of up to about half a point of capacity. A repeat needs at least 10 refits per arm and fold, a placebo drawn from an independent world, and real training rows given a matched share of non-zero flags.

Experiment 00116 (differentiable physics, NRA) also bears on this theme. It fits flows on the interconnection edges between Primary substations and scores them on injected transfers; see the Network research plan.

docs.title: Planned experiments
docs.text: Experiment Hypothesis Relevance

docs.title: Load-shift labels in the forecast: state and next steps
docs.text:
Telling the Primary demand forecast about load shifts has not improved it on real data, and the final demand models use no label table or detector. On injected load shifts, labels recover most of the lost accuracy only when the megawatts (MW) moved are known exactly. The final models page describes how the final models cope without labels. The theme page holds the full results, and the state of the event detector records where the detector work paused.

A load shift is a transfer of demand between neighbouring Primary substations for hours or days. The normal running arrangement (NRA) is the electricity network configuration without any load shift. A lag is an earlier power reading used as an input. RO-NC is the refit-offset neighbour-count detector, which flags a load shift from a 24-hour step in a Primary's forecast error (see the detector page). The gap is the extra error of a forecast on lags that a shift has changed, against the same forecast on unchanged lags.

Scores are quantile scores, which are twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantile levels. They are in points of effective capacity (1% of a substation's capacity), and a positive change is a worse forecast. NGED's event labels are incomplete, so every count of real events is a lower bound. Unless a paragraph says otherwise, results come from 16 Primary series and 292 daily forecast runs. Verdict words in backticks, such as inconclusive, follow the glossary's definitions.

docs.title: What we know
docs.text:
On real data, no label-based change lowered the score by an amount the data can show. Dropping labelled load-shift half-hours from the training targets changed the score by +0.004 (98.33% interval -0.026 to +0.025), and only 22 of 82 labelled events fall in the scored year (Experiment 75, inconclusive).

A perfect detector could lower the quantile score by little in the year tested. In the band of events that the event labeller (a script that marks load-shift events from NGED's logs and the power series) finds most reliably, a perfect detector would lower the quantile score by 0.42% (95% interval -0.47% to 1.96%), against a 3% threshold. These events touch 3 of the 16 series. Over the 22 events visible in the power data, the bound is 2.35% (-0.22% to 5.73%), an interval that includes zero and straddles the threshold (Experiment 44, refuted).

Only the true MW recovered most of the gap on injected load shifts. With the true MW and a forecast trained on NGED's logged shifts, 83% (70% to 91%) of the gap closes. With the MW from RO-NC as built, 16% (-17% to 67%) closes, which cannot be told from zero (Experiment 88, inconclusive). These shares rest on 2,452 forecast origins inside injected transfers (4 onset months, 13% of origins).

Taking one MW per half-hour from the largest overlapping step recovered more, but the choice was made after seeing the results. The loss comes from overlapping detector intervals that add up (21% of marked cases). The lag correction alone closed 48% (18% to 71%) of the gap, and the RO-NC-trained booster that also drops those half-hours from its training targets closed 43% (17% to 71%) (Experiment 88).

A calibrated probability of a lag inside a load shift did not beat the detector's yes-or-no flag. On injected transfers, the probability lowered the Brier score (the mean squared error of a probability forecast) by 3.3% (97.5% interval -7.6% to +1.6%), against a 20% requirement. Its area under the curve against NGED's logs (where 0.5 is chance) was 0.53, so the experiment advises against a band-widening rule built on it (Experiment 91, inconclusive).

Feeding the detector's alarm into the GAM-K Kalman filter did not help. GAM-K is the generalised additive demand model whose Kalman filter corrects each forecast with its recent errors. The alarm helped inside a transfer and hurt for 72 hours after it ended. The alarm came 48 hours after the step, which was no better than a random placebo (Experiment 141, not supported).

After the alarm, subtracting the detected MW closes much of the gap, but the weather alone closes more. Subtracting closed 71% (25% to 85%) of the gap to a forecast fed the true NRA series, and the weather model alone closed 78%. Counting missed transfers, subtracting gained nothing and masking gained 21% (Experiment 151, partly supported).

A second Kalman filter state for the transfer added nothing over masking. It closed 78% of the gap and masking the readings inside the alarm closed 81% (Experiment 153, partly supported).

docs.title: What does not work
docs.text:
Hiding lags that lie inside a load shift made the forecast worse. Setting them to missing worsened the score by 0.409 (+0.281 to +0.517) on the 352,765 rows with a lag inside an abnormal running arrangement (the union of RO-NC and the logs). (Experiment 89, refuted).

Giving the forecast the unusualness of each lag worsened the score by 0.355 (+0.209 to +0.513) (Experiment 90, refuted).

Three times as many synthetic shifts in training did not help. The score changed by +0.079 (-0.031 to +0.153) (Experiment 96, inconclusive).

Random lag dropout in training did not widen the band enough. The 5% to 95% band covered 0.799 on rows with a missing lag for the plain forecast and 0.836 with 30% of training rows hidden (the best arm), against 0.90 nominal. The band width did not change (Experiment 100, inconclusive).

Every label experiment on this theme used hindsight labels (labels known only after the event), so nothing here is ready for the serving path.

docs.title: What the final models do instead
docs.text:
The final demand models for Primaries contain no label table and no detector input. They use three substitutes.

  • Injected shifts in training. The lag encoder, the part of the neural network that reads the lagged power, trains on random synthetic shifts covering 5% of each Primary's rows.
  • A refit embargo. The newest 7 days of training rows are held back and the 7 days before them are down-weighted by half. This cut the share of a shift leaked into the median forecast 7 days after it ends from 0.16 to 0.114 (Experiment 599, partly supported).
  • A prevailing output. A second output mixes the NRA quantiles with a shifted copy, and extra lagged inputs make it react to a new shift 20.4 hours sooner on injected events, below the 24 hours set in advance. Which extra-lag set to port is open, because the 8-input set scored worst inside the 2 real events that can be read (Experiment 681, small gain).

The embargo's leak of 0.114 is above the proposed 0.10 bar, and the six MW Primaries lose 1.3 points of q05 to q95 coverage (Experiment 599).

Detector features for the prevailing output were not adopted. The features reacted 1.59 days sooner than the earlier head, but extra lagged power alone reacted 1.25 days sooner (Experiment 687, partly supported). Its reaction times are not comparable with Experiment 681's, which used different events and folds.

The prevailing output is better overall, and December 2025 is the exception. It scored 0.17 points better than the NRA output for origins in 2026-01 to 2026-06 and 0.42 better in 2026-07 to 2026-10 (Experiment 668). After the one verified shift, at D5 and D16 in December 2025, it scored worse than the NRA output for 7 days after the shift ended. December 2025 is a fallback month (B-haz fallback head).

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Whether the detector's MW, with each shift counted once and ended promptly, recovers more than the 43% of the gap is unknown. Only a post hoc rule has been scored.
  • Whether any label improves the forecast on real shifts is unknown. The logged events in one year are too few (Experiment 100).

docs.title: Next-experiment options
docs.text:
Each option below comes from the "What to try next" section of the experiment named. The final models come first and load-shift event detection is paused until January, so options that need a better detector wait for it.

  1. An option is to re-run Experiment 88 with the de-duplicated MW. The rerun would keep the largest of overlapping same-sign intervals and let the MW decay after the end (from Experiment 88). It depends on the detector work.
  2. An option is to replace a masked lag with a forecast of the NRA (from Experiment 89).
  3. An option is to train synthetic shifts with the detector's errors (from Experiment 96).
  4. An option is to widen the band where a lag is missing, with an indicator column (from Experiment 100).
  5. An option is a Kalman-filter correction that decays over the typical transfer duration (from Experiment 141).
  6. An option is a detector that alarms sooner, paired with a forecast that drops recent power while a transfer is suspected (from Experiment 151).
  7. An option is a gated embargo that starts only when a gate fires (from Experiment 599).

docs.title: What is parked
docs.text:
Hindsight-label results are parked until a causal detector is better, which is January work. The detector state page records why.

Experiment 116 (differentiable physics, edge flows between Primaries) is inconclusive. Its known-answer gate failed: the fit cannot see transfers shorter than 7 to 9 days, and it found 0.22 of the injected MW over 1 day. The network research plan holds its follow-ups, a drift term and a topology check.

The experiments page lists every experiment in the theme.

docs.title: Weather products and blending
docs.text:
The current understanding and the options for next work are on the state and next steps page.

Of the weather changes tested, only training on estimates of past weather (ERA5) clearly lowered the error in a test without power lags, for 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms up to 6 days ahead, and no extra weather forecast has yet been shown to help in a way a live service could use.

A weather product is a source of weather data, such as the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) ensemble (ENS), the Met Office's UKV (a 2 km forecast of the UK), the US ensemble GEFS, or ICON-EU (the German weather service's regional forecast). The experiments trained XGBoost models on one product's history, then added a second product as extra input columns or as a blend. They scored 6 solar farms, 3 wind farms, and 16 Primary substations, each over one validation year. For Primary demand, even weather as accurate as ERA5 lowered the score by only 0.10 points.

Training on ERA5 lowered the mean absolute error of the ensemble-mean forecast at 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms up to day 6, and not beyond. Source: experiment 1. Lower is better.

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
Training on ERA5 lowered the solar and wind farm error up to day 6. Over all leads, the ERA5-trained XGBoost model scored 15.39 against 17.09 for wind (-1.70, 95% interval -2.33 to -1.08) and 7.67 against 8.25 for solar (-0.57, -0.83 to -0.32), in points of capacity, with no calendar or lag columns (experiment 1). The contrasts were revised after two reviews, so they are not pre-registered. A later test used the quantile score and power lags at 24 to 54 hours. It found the ENS-trained model 0.218 points lower than the ERA5-trained best guess for wind (-0.472 to +0.069) and 0.107 lower for solar (-0.327 to +0.053). Both differences are unresolved (experiment 54, experiment 57).

For demand series it did not carry over. On 22 series that are not wind or solar farms, 16 of them Primaries, the ERA5-trained model scored 1.37 points worse (+0.68 to +2.17) with weather columns only. Starting the ERA5 history in 2023-09 instead of 2019-09 lowered the error by 1.32 (-1.81 to -0.90), a post hoc read that does not separate drift in the series from bad early data (experiment 3).

Weather as accurate as ERA5 gave a small gain for Primary demand, measured only for a model trained on ENS. Swapping ENS for ERA5 weather in the stack of experiment 19 (a half-life of 0.5 years) lowered the quantile score by 0.10 (99.38% interval -0.16 to -0.04) at 16 Primaries over 73 runs. Shortwave radiation alone gave -0.084, and inside 2 days there was no gain (experiment 22). Training on CAMS sunshine instead of ERA5 shortwave gave -0.035 (97.5% interval -0.070 to +0.001), against a planned 0.2 (experiment 9). Mapping the ENS shortwave onto CAMS first (stage 0) gave a further -0.067 (97.5% interval -0.094 to -0.039). The CAMS-trained arm with stage 0 scored 0.102 below the ERA5-trained arm. The verdict stays inconclusive because the monthly mismatch to CAMS reached 18.6% (experiment 14).

A second global ensemble, GEFS, did not improve the sunshine anomaly. The anomaly is a forecast's sunshine minus its own monthly mean, scored against the CAMS anomaly at 5 Primaries on daylight rows from April to September. Cross-validated squared error was 1.109 times ENS's for GEFS (worse in all 9 held-out months) and 1.002 times for a fitted blend, against the 0.99 needed (refuted, experiment 50).

GEFS correlated worse with the CAMS anomaly than ENS did, and the blend matched ENS. Source: experiment 50.

A UKV and ENS blend lowered the squared error of the same anomaly by 7.6% over 0 to 54 hours in cross-validation, and the validation year cannot confirm it. The validation correlation gain was +0.011 (-0.006 to +0.027), and the blend beat ENS in 3 of the 6 months of forecast origin that the intervals resample. The test was post hoc. Six or 7 origin months understate the uncertainty (experiment 53).

UKV wind lowered the wind-farm quantile score by about 0.2 points at 24 to 54 hours, a small gain that is an upper limit. An ENS-trained XGBoost model given UKV wind as extra columns, trained on UKV's own history, scored -0.198 (-0.316 to -0.069) at 3 wind farms. The interval's end nearest zero does not reach the pre-registered 0.15, and a shuffled-UKV placebo scored +0.013 (-0.012 to +0.040). One farm gained clearly (-0.413) and one did not (+0.018), post hoc. The UKV data come from the CEDA archive, which differs statistically from the live feed (experiment 54; UKV-CEDA study).

Giving UKV wind to an ENS-trained model lowered the wind-farm score, and the shuffled-UKV placebo did not. Source: experiment 54.

The same test with UKV shortwave, cloud, and temperature at 6 solar farms was inconclusive. The score changed by -0.035 (-0.119 to +0.037), so a gain of 0.10 can be neither shown nor ruled out (experiment 57). Averaging the wind best guess with ICON-EU and the ECMWF high-resolution forecast (IFS) gave -0.055 (-0.200 to +0.072) at days 1 and 2, also inconclusive, and the products' runs were half a day older than ENS (experiment 52).

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text:
The best recipe tested here depends on the target, and none beat the reference by a resolved margin. For farms the reference is the best guess, as the generator-forecasting Summary explains.

  • Solar and wind farms, up to day 6: train the weather-to-power model on ERA5 and apply it to each of the 51 ENS members (experiment 1). This was measured without power lags, and experiments 54 and 57 found the ENS-trained model within an unresolved margin at 24 to 54 hours. For solar, CAMS sunshine as the training input scored -0.140 (99.5% interval -0.277 to -0.044), short of the planned -0.15 and inconclusive (experiment 12).
  • Wind farms, 24 to 54 hours: add UKV wind as columns to an ENS-trained model, trained on UKV's history (experiment 54). This is an upper limit, measured on the CEDA research archive.
  • Primary substations: keep the model trained on ENS. If training on estimates of past weather, start in 2023-09 (experiment 3) and map the ENS shortwave onto CAMS (experiment 14).

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text:
Two experiments are marked candidate, and neither is ready to port as it stands.

  • ERA5-trained weather-to-power model for solar and wind farms (experiment 1). Production would train on ERA5 and CAMS history and serve ENS members, which needs the staged design. The caveat under "Best design so far" about power lags applies.
  • Stage 0 mapping of ENS shortwave onto CAMS for Primaries (experiment 14). Production would fit the mapping on 14 or more months of ENS and CAMS pairs. The mapping left monthly mismatches, widened the member spread by 27%, and needs a CAMS-trained model.

No second weather product (GEFS, UKV, ICON-EU, IFS) is ready. Experiments 50, 52, 53, 54, and 57 are not-for-production.

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
• Train each product on its own history. The arms are ENS-trained, ENS plus the other product as columns, and the other product alone; an ERA5-trained model is only a reference. A model trained on ENS and fed ERA5 weather understates what ERA5 training would give (experiment 22). The ERA5-trained wind model fed uncorrected ICON-EU winds alone scored 2.5 points worse than the best guess, and IFS winds 1.3 points worse, at days 1 and 2 (experiment 52). Re-check when the model, the product, or the bias correction changes.
  • "Better weather adds little" was measured only for a model trained on ENS. Experiment 22 trained on the ENS control member, and ERA5 differs from ENS in bias (mean shortwave 132.6 against 139.1 W/m2). Experiment 9's CAMS-trained arm gained 0.88 daylight points at observed weather and 0.04 over all leads with ENS input (experiment 9). Look for a Primary demand model trained on ERA5 and scored on experiment 22's stack.
  • Pass a shuffled-product placebo through every step. In experiment 54 the placebo showed that extra columns alone do nothing. In experiment 52 it scored +0.343 because July's equal weights and the spread factor, not the shuffled forecasts, drove the score, so fit the spread factor on blends made under the same weights (experiment 54, experiment 52). Re-check if the blend weights or the spread factor are fitted a different way.
  • Use the live feed, and check its variables on a recent run. The CEDA UKV archive has no 100 m wind and lacks four hourly steps, UKV was upgraded on 2026-01-21, and Open-Meteo's UKV history stops at lead day 0 (experiment 54, experiment 57). Feeds gain fields over time, so an old date gives a wrong answer. Re-check when a live UKV history exists.
  • Feed the run the service would have. Experiment 52 fed runs half a day older than ENS, and experiment 53 assumed a 3-hour UKV delivery time without measuring it (experiment 53). Look for a measured delivery time before reading a blend's gain. Re-check once the live delivery time is known.
  • Give a guard arm the variant it guards. A guard arm is a control built to catch one artefact; in experiment 3 it was the ENS-trained arm with one row per valid time. The ENS training frame repeats each valid time about 15 times, so calendar columns let an ENS-trained model memorise the calendar position, and a one-row-per-valid-time guard arm with lags failed by construction (experiment 1, experiment 3). Re-check when the input columns or the training rows change.
  • Calibrate each source's anomaly, and cross-validate by whole months. GEFS's raw anomaly was about 15% too large, and the interval width follows the number of origin months (experiment 50, experiment 53). Re-check with a longer validation period, which gives more origin months.
  • Check the hour-of-day peak of every source. CAMS and ENS are means labelled at the period end and UKV is instantaneous, so a mislabelled UKV control peaked at 10 UTC instead of 12 UTC (experiment 53). Re-check for any new product whose shortwave is instantaneous.
  • Take the planned threshold from a contrast between like arms. Experiment 9 planned 0.2 and resolved 0.035 (experiment 9). Report a pooled share with and without the largest series: a fixed CAMS correction removed 46.6% of the daylight squared residual, one substation set the pooled figure, and a fixed bias alone removed 39.1% (experiment 7, inconclusive). Re-check whenever a pooled share is quoted.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text: Whether a live UKV history gives the wind-farm gain, whether ICON-EU and IFS help when read at the service's own time, and whether a source of a different kind helps solar farms. Experiment 50 tested GEFS against the CAMS solar anomaly at 5 Primaries only. The open proposals are in the research plan.

docs.title: Weather products and blending: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00646 per-ens-member-neural-demand-networks-pooled-quantiles Running K1 and K3 once per ensemble member, and pooling the 51 member outputs into one mixture, improves the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), the upper-tail coverage, and the event-free scores over the networks that read the ensemble mean and spread, without raising the share of an injected load-shift that the forecast follows. not supported not-for-production For K1 and K3 on the five development months, giving the demand networks the mean and spread of the 51 ensemble members matched running them once per member and pooling the 51 answers, once the bands had equal width. The mean-and-spread input needs one pass through the neural network per forecast instead of 51. Pooling mainly widens the forecast band.
