Lagged power, calendar columns, and extra weather variables add little in own history. also relevant 00262 wind-aifs-members-and-climatology-by-lead For the three metered wind farms (W1 to W3), a lead-dependent mixture of the ECMWF ensemble's member forecasts, the AIFS ensemble's member forecasts (both run through experiment 230's ERA5-trained XGBoost wind model A0r), and climatology lowers the quantile score and the 0.99 pinball loss against the ECMWF members alone, after both are corrected by a table of offsets per lead day, quantile, and farm; and a small neural gate that reads the two ensembles' spread and disagreement chooses better weights than weights by lead alone. partly supported candidate Adding the AIFS ensemble's wind forecasts to the ECMWF ensemble's improves the wind forecast at 3 to 6 days ahead, by about 5% of the quantile score, but does not improve the high-power tail that matters for curtailment. Climatology and a small neural network that picks the mixing weights add nothing once the table of offsets has corrected the common low bias. The AIFS arms also need testing on a second year, because one year of Tuesday runs sets the weights. also relevant 00246 metered-farm-ens-ukv-icond2-blend The DWD ICON-D2 regional weather forecast (2 km grid, run every 3 hours, 48 hours ahead) carries information about cloud over a metered solar farm that neither the ECMWF ensemble nor the Met Office UKV carries, so adding it to the ensemble plus UKV lowers the farm's day-ahead error. The evidence against is that at day 1 every single product lost to the ensemble mean for solar in the matched-lead study, and ICON-D2's errors are likely to be correlated with UKV's. Every gain is an upper limit for production, because the UKV archive used is the CEDA research archive. small gain not-for-production Adding the German ICON-D2 weather forecast to the ECMWF ensemble and the Met Office UKV lowers the day-ahead error of a metered solar farm by about 1%, which is under the 1.5% we set as worth a fourth weather source. ICON-D2 is available for only 12 to 29 hours of the day ahead at an 08 UTC forecast time, and the UKV archive used is a research archive, so this is an upper limit for production. also relevant 00237 dp-two-number-solar-summary-with-clip The mean and standard deviation of the 51 ensemble members' solar responses lower the daylight quantile score of the demand forecast also when each member is passed through the clipped solar term, because cloud uncertainty and the clip both act at midday only partly on the same rows. supported candidate At D5, in one year of data, summarising the ensemble weather members as a mean and a standard deviation keeps at least about 90% of its gain when the solar output is clipped at 60% of the solar capacity held for D5 (110%, interval 91% to 141%). On the sunniest third of daylight rows the point estimate of the remaining gain is about half (interval -12% to 88%). A post hoc arm using the standard deviation alone kept the gain there, which suggests testing that form. also relevant 00229 metered-farm-ens-ukv-blend The Met Office UKV weather model (2 km grid, 54 hours) carries information about cloud over a solar farm that the 51-member ECMWF ensemble lacks, so giving a metered solar farm's forecast both products lowers its day-ahead error against the ensemble alone, and closes part of the gap between the ensemble-driven fit (0.91 of output on sunny half-hours) and the fit with observed weather (0.973) of experiment 218. Every gain is an upper limit for production, because the UKV archive used here is the research archive on CEDA, which differs statistically from the live UKV. small gain not-for-production Adding the Met Office UKV forecast to the ECMWF ensemble lowers the day-ahead error of a metered solar farm by about 1% to 2%. The gain is under the 3% we set as worth a second weather source, and the farms' fit on sunny half-hours moves only about 6% of the way to the fit with observed weather. The UKV archive used here is a research archive, and the live UKV differs, so this result is an upper limit for production; a weather product of a different kind is the option we see for a larger gain. also relevant 00202 dp-ens-two-number-rolling-replay Experiment 193 found that two numbers per half-hour (the mean and the standard deviation of the 51 ensemble members' solar responses) lower the daylight quantile score by 2.20% in the scored year. Its two fitted factors per lead band were fitted on interleaved months (the odd months of 2024-07 to 2025-06), some of them later than the replicate months they were applied to, and its numbers were held in float64. A replay of the live weather layer, which stores the two numbers as float32 columns computed from the one ensemble run published before each origin and refits the factors each month on history that has completed before that month, keeps most of the gain. supported candidate A weather layer that stores two numbers per half-hour (the mean and spread of the 51 ensemble members' solar-generation estimates) and refits its two scaling factors every month, using only runs that had finished before the month began, lowers the daylight quantile score (the score for the forecast's uncertainty bands) by 2.3% at five substations over one year, which is as much as running all 51 members. This confirms experiment 193's result under production-style timing, so the next step is to build the two columns into the weather layer. also relevant 00193 dp-ens-two-number-solar-summary Experiment 187 found that passing each of the 51 ensemble members through the solar term lowers the daylight quantile score of the full best-guess stack by 2.23%, and that a Gaussian with each row's own mean and spread of the 51 responses recovers 95% of that gain. Two numbers per half-hour (the mean and the standard deviation of the members' solar responses) therefore carry nearly all of the gain, so a serving path can store two columns instead of running 51 passes. supported candidate Summarising the 51 ensemble weather members' solar estimates by their mean and standard deviation lowers the daylight quantile score by about 2% (98% of the gain from running all 51 members, 93% in the replicate months), at the five substations scored over one year. The weather layer could store two columns per half-hour instead of 51, and the 10th and 90th percentiles add nothing measurable. A follow-up experiment could test the two numbers in the live weather layer. also relevant 00192 dp-ens-members-temperature-cold-nights Experiment 187 found that passing the 51 ECMWF ensemble members through the solar term of the demand model lowers the daylight quantile score by 2.2%. The demand response to heating is also nonlinear (a hinge at 15.5 degrees C), and the ensemble mean smooths away the cold tail. Passing each member's temperature through the temperature terms therefore lowers the quantile score on cold winter nights. not supported not-for-production Running each ensemble member's temperature through the demand model gave no detectable improvement in the forecast bands on cold winter nights, because the 51 members' temperatures differ too little to signal the day's error. The cold-night bands are already too narrow. The cause of the cold-night error is still unknown; widening the bands directly, and testing wind, night cloud cover, and switching as inputs, are the candidates. also relevant 00187 dp-ens-members-in-stack Experiment 184 found that running each of the 51 ensemble members through the solar term of the convex demand model lowers the daylight quantile score by 2.2%, but its verdict was capped at inconclusive because a monotone gate failed on rows where the unit PV shape itself falls as irradiance rises. With a gate that matches that shape, the same arm passes, and its gain lies where the best-guess stack leaves the largest sunny-daylight error, at the substation D5. supported candidate Running each of the 51 ensemble weather members through the solar part of the demand model still improves the daylight forecast bands by about 2% on top of the full best-guess stack, and night is untouched. About two thirds of the gain needs that day's own members, and two numbers per half-hour (the mean and spread of the members' solar responses) carry nearly all of it, so a cheaper two-number version is the next thing to test. also relevant 00184 dp-ens-daylight-calibration Experiment 169 found that passing the ensemble's spread to the width of the forecast's bands adds nothing when scored over all half-hours. The benefit may be confined to daylight half-hours, especially sunny and partly cloudy ones, where the clouds that the 51 ensemble members disagree about change the output of embedded solar generation, and so the demand. Passing each member's irradiance through the convex model's solar term (arm M), or using the spread of the members' irradiance as a fraction of clear-sky to set the band width in daylight (arm S), calibrates the daylight bands better than the existing bands (arm A). inconclusive not-for-production Running each of the 51 ensemble weather members through the solar part of the demand model improves the daylight forecast bands by about 2%, mostly in the lower tail and on partly cloudy half-hours, while night is untouched. Placebos that widen the bands the same way but without the real members gain little, so most of the benefit is information about cloud. The next step is a production-cost check of the member pass and a test of its gain on top of the best-guess forecast. also relevant 00174 dp-unlabelled-worst-days-weather-shared-or-single-site Most of the excess loss on the unlabelled worst days of experiment 172 is weather error, and the unlabelled worst days are mostly shared with other Primaries. Replacing the ensemble-mean weather with the estimate of past weather (ERA5 temperature and CAMS irradiance) in arm D's forecast removes at least 50% of the unlabelled days' excess loss, and at least a third of the unlabelled days are also in the worst 5% of days of at least one other Primary. partly supported not-for-production Most of the forecast's error on its worst unlabelled days is not weather error: with past weather in place of the forecast weather, about 69% of the excess loss stays. Other Primaries share these days about as often as random shifting gives, so the data show at most a weak shared cause. The remaining loss could therefore come from events at one substation, such as undetected switching, a change in behaviour, or a metering fault. The next place to look is the substation's own recent readings and the switching records on those days. also relevant 00125 differentiable-physics-n8-ens-members-through-gam-k-and-the-spread-around-them Placing GAM-K's residual quantiles, fitted on a forecast driven by the analysis proxy (so they hold model and filter error and almost no weather error), around each of the 51 ENS members gives tails closer to nominal than today's table, which is fitted on ensemble-mean residuals, and the gain is largest at long leads and on cold winter nights, where the hinge turns a temperature error into a large demand error. The comparison is against GAM-K re-tuned on the same factor grid, so a plain scale error cannot pass for a better design. inconclusive not-for-production Putting the forecast-error table around each of the 51 weather members, and fitting it on analysis-driven forecasts so that it holds no weather error, did not improve the tails of GAM-K's demand forecast. The weather members' spread is small against the model's own error, so the weather error was counted twice in the code but is too small to matter. The next step is the cold winter nights, where demand exceeds the 95% quantile about a quarter of the time in every arm. The verdict is inconclusive, because no arm reached 14 of 16 calibration cells. also relevant 00119 differentiable-physics-enc-weather-patch-encoder-on-ens A small neural network that reads the ENS grid boxes around a Primary, and not only the one box GAM-K reads, lowers GAM-K's quantile score a little on average and more on the cold, showery, and badly forecast days NGED cares about, either as a correction to GAM-K's quantiles or as a replacement for its single-box temperature and irradiance. inconclusive not-for-production A small neural network that reads the ensemble weather around a Primary lowers GAM-K's quantile score by 0.062 points of effective capacity in one scored year and 0.035 in the other (both statistically significant, 5 of 5 substations better), and the gain is smaller in winter (0.041 and 0.027 points) but never a loss. About two-thirds of the gain survives when the network reads the wrong date's weather (0.043 and 0.022), so it is probably a recalibration of GAM-K's quantiles with the lead, the hour, and GAM-K's own forecast, and the surrounding boxes add nothing to the centre box (patch minus centre box: -0.002 and +0.003 points). The known-answer gate failed, so the verdict is inconclusive, and the next step is a plain recalibration of GAM-K's quantiles with the centre box's extra fields (dew point, pressure, precipitation, and member spread), not a patch encoder. also relevant 00111 differentiable-physics-6-ens-forecast-engine-against-bg2 Driven by ECMWF ENS forecasts, the convex DP demand model forecasts Primary demand up to 7 days ahead better than lagless XGBoost given the same recent-level correction, and, used as the base margin of the BG2 recipe's lagged XGBoost, makes the production recipe better like for like. partly supported candidate Driven by real ensemble weather forecasts, the physics-based demand model with a filter on its recent errors (GAM-K) scored 2.80 points against 2.78 for the production recipe (BG2) at five Primary substations. The 0.02 difference cannot be told from zero (-0.109 to +0.157), and the comparison is not like for like. GAM-K scored 0.13 points better than lagless XGBoost with the same filter (-0.305 to +0.014, 4 of 5 substations better), so the verdict is partly supported. The filter's gain is the firmly supported part: 0.15 points, 0.39 in the first day, with the sign held in the replicate months. Giving lagged XGBoost the physics model's forecast as a starting point changed nothing measurable. The known-answer gate passed 22 of 22 readings on its second run, after a sign error in the gate's own test data (both runs are kept). The departures were that the XGBoost compute estimate was 20 times too low, so the margin arms refitted monthly; lagless XGBoost for the scored year reused SIMP1's refits and had no spread factor; and the confirmation comparison was not run. GAM-K is a candidate for Flexpectation v2's roughly 1,300 substations on the measured filter gain, with four caveats: five substations over one year, a short XGBoost history, the undecided XGBoost comparison, and a margin that gave no gain. also relevant 00057 product-trained-xgboost-solar-farms For the six metered solar farms, an XGBoost quantile model trained on ENS and given UKV's shortwave radiation, total cloud, and temperature as extra input columns scores lower on the quantile score at lead hours 24 to 54 than the same model trained on ENS alone, with every arm trained on the same window, rows, and seeds. UKV is read from the CEDA archive, which is not the live product, so the contrast is a ceiling read. inconclusive not-for-production Giving UKV forecasts to an ENS-trained solar-farm model changed the quantile score by -0.035 points of capacity at 1 to 2 days ahead (95% interval -0.119 to +0.037), which is too small to resolve. The data cannot show a gain and cannot rule out the 0.10-point gain that would justify a new weather feed. UKV helped the six solar farms far less than it helped the three wind farms. also relevant 00054 product-trained-xgboost-wind-farms For the three metered wind farms, an XGBoost quantile model trained on ENS and given UKV's wind as extra input columns scores lower on the quantile score at lead days 1 and 2 than the same model trained on ENS alone, with every arm trained on the same window, rows, and seeds. UKV is read from the CEDA archive, which is not the live product, so the contrast is a ceiling read. small gain not-for-production Giving the Met Office's UKV wind forecast to an ENS-trained wind-farm model lowered the quantile score by about 0.2 points of capacity at 1 to 2 days ahead (95% interval 0.07 to 0.32), and a shuffled-UKV placebo shows the gain is information and not extra columns. The UKV data come from a research archive and not the live feed, so the gain is an upper limit on what a service could get. also relevant 00053 ukv-vs-ens-solar-anomaly At the five Primary substations metered in MW that decide experiment 00046's verdict (D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16), the Met Office UKV forecast of the solar anomaly (the output of a generic solar fleet minus its own month-by-half-hour mean), alone or blended with the ECMWF ensemble mean (ENS) using weights fitted on the training window, tracks the CAMS solar anomaly more closely than ENS alone does within the UKV's lead range of 120 hours. small gain not-for-production At 5 Primary substations, a fitted blend of the Met Office's UKV and ENS lowered the cross-validated squared error of the sunshine anomaly by 7.6% over 0 to 54 hours (3.8% to 13.8% in each band), but the validation year cannot confirm it (correlation gain +0.011, 95% interval -0.006 to +0.027). The test was post hoc and its intervals rest on 6 or 7 origin months, so they understate the uncertainty. UKV alone was worse than ENS, and the UKV data are a research archive, so any gain is an upper limit. primary 00052 more-nwp-products-for-wind-farms For the three metered wind farms, averaging the quantiles of the experiment 33 wind best guess (the ERA5-trained mixture over the 51 ENS members, with the power-curve margin and the spread factor) with the quantiles of the same ERA5-trained model fed ICON-EU's and IFS 0.25 degree's forecast wind lowers the quantile score at 1 to 2 days ahead, with weights chosen only on earlier months. inconclusive not-for-production Averaging the wind best guess with two extra weather forecasts, ICON-EU and the ECMWF high-resolution forecast, scored 0.055 points of capacity better at lead days 1 and 2, but the 95% interval (-0.200 to +0.072) includes zero. Three wind farms cannot show whether the extra forecasts help, and the blend scored 0.122 worse at days 3 to 6. also relevant 00050 second-weather-forecast-for-solar-anomaly At the five Primary substations metered in MW in experiment 00046's verdict set (anonymised series D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16), an anomaly forecast that blends the NOAA GEFS ensemble mean with the ECMWF ENS ensemble mean, with weights fitted on the training window only, tracks the CAMS solar anomaly more closely than ENS alone. Laid into experiment 00046's solar term with its fitted lead-dependent coefficient, the blended anomaly lowers the quantile score by at least 0.1 points of capacity against the same term built from ENS alone. refuted not-for-production The stage 1 gate stopped the experiment: in cross-validation on the training window GEFS's squared error against the CAMS anomaly is 1.109 times ENS's (worse in all 9 held-out months) and the fitted blend's is 1.002 times, against the 0.99 needed. primary 00022 era5-weather-ceiling-primary-demand For the 16 Primary substation demand series, giving the winning recipe of experiment 00019 (the single-stage ENS-trained quantile model N1 with a recency half-life of 0.5 years, the 14-day error correction, and the 1.15 spread factor) ERA5 weather in place of ECMWF ensemble (ENS) weather at serving time lowers the quantile score by at least 0.3 points of capacity over all leads. refuted not-for-production ERA5 weather in place of ENS weather lowered the quantile score over all leads by 0.10 points of capacity (99.38% interval -0.16 to -0.04), so the 0.3-point gain the rule asked for is ruled out. also relevant 00014 cams-trained-stage1-with-stage0-ens-correction-demand A stage 0 that maps the ECMWF ensemble (ENS) member's shortwave irradiance onto the irradiance of the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) lowers the Primary substation quantile score of the CAMS-trained stage 1a XGBoost demand model, relative to feeding that model the raw ENS shortwave, because the ENS shortwave is about 7% above CAMS and stage 1a never saw that offset in training. inconclusive candidate C2, stage 0 minus raw ENS for the CAMS-trained arm, Primary quantile score over all leads: -0.067 points of capacity (97.5% interval -0.094 to -0.039), better than the planned -0.03. primary 00009 cams-trained-stage1a-vs-era5-trained-demand A stage 1a XGBoost demand model trained with irradiance from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) in place of ERA5 shortwave, and applied to the shortwave of ECMWF ensemble (ENS) members, has a lower quantile score at Primary substations than the same model trained on ERA5 shortwave, because the satellite-derived irradiance is closer to the irradiance that the substations' embedded solar generation responded to. refuted not-for-production C1, CAMS-trained minus ERA5-trained, Primary quantile score over all leads: -0.035 points of capacity (97.5% interval -0.070 to +0.001), a sixth of the planned 0.2-point gain. primary 00007 cams-static-correction-stage1a-residual Most of the daytime residual of the stage 1a demand model at Primary substations is a fixed error in the ERA5 irradiance input and not a growing embedded-solar capacity, so a correction with fixed coefficients on irradiance from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS), fitted on one year of out-of-fold residuals, removes most of the residual in the next year. inconclusive not-for-production The static correction removes 46.6% of the next year's daylight squared residual, just below the planned 50%, and a fixed bias alone removes 39.1%. primary 00003 era5-trained-stage1a-vs-ens-trained-demand A weather-to-power XGBoost model trained on ERA5 (2019-09 onward) and applied to the 51 ENS members, with the member forecasts averaged, has a lower mean absolute error on electricity demand series than the same columns trained on ENS weather. not supported not-for-production D1, s1_memberavg minus ens_trained, weather only, all leads: +1.37 (+0.68 to +2.17), 22 series; with calendar +1.38 (D2, against the one-row-per-valid-time arm: +1.67); with calendar and lags +0.10 (-0.26 to +0.50). primary 00001 era5-trained-stage1a-vs-ens-trained A weather-to-power XGBoost model trained on ERA5 and CAMS (2019-09 onward) and applied to ENS weather has a lower point-forecast error than the same columns trained on ENS weather. supported candidate P1 (revised), s1_memberavg minus ens_trained, all leads: wind -1.70 (-2.33 to -1.08), solar -0.57 (-0.83 to -0.32); material up to day 6, not beyond. primary
